evidence: Lower part of the right circular painting, slightly left of center: between dark tree clumps and slope rocks a pale diagonal planar area is exposed, possibly a roof surface or eaves, but most of the building itself is obscured by ink. | Right circular painting, center to lower part: mountain forms and trees are layered in dense ink, the foreground waterside is left unpainted, and the suspected dwelling appears to lie within a layer half-obscured by trees and rocks. | Right circular painting, lower part: no clearly identifiable bridge, path, or porch is seen directly connecting to the suspected dwelling, so an accessible movement connection is difficult to confirm.
distinction: If the pale structure is indeed a waterside dwelling, its partially screened layering among trees and rocks is closer to C2; but the outline is unclear, and it cannot be confirmed whether it marks a particular scenic spot.

evidence: Whole painting: the picture is composed of several groups of figures; no mountains and rocks, water bodies, trees, or any identifiable buildings are seen, so there is no spatial relationship between built elements and natural scenery to assess. | Upper right to center: multiple figures overlap front to back, with the shoulders and backs of the front row partially covering the bodies of the back row; this occlusion is an overlapping among figures and does not show concealment and revelation of scenery. | Lower right: a red drum-shaped object and the surrounding figures obscure one another, but there is no terrain, shoreline, or path around them to indicate their location.
distinction: The front-to-back overlapping that recurs in the painting is closer to the layered sense of 'concealment and revelation'; but the painting has no terrain, waterside, or built elements, so assigning C2 is only the closest classification of the visible spatial organization.

evidence: Lower center to right of the painting: large numbers of horses are scattered across open gentle slopes and flat ground, lacking identifiable built elements such as houses, bridges, or paths. | Left inscription area: a long textual inscription and seals, not spatial built elements within the picture. | Distant view: the mountain outlines are low, flat, and continuous, forming no clear relationship with building sites, concealment and revelation, or passage openings.
distinction: No accessible clues such as buildings, bridges or paths, doors or windows are seen in the painting; only the distribution of horses on gentle terrain can be observed. In the absence of evidence of built elements, the terrain-responsive relationship in which the terrain supports the overall scene is taken as the closest attribution, rather than access to secluded settings.

evidence: Right bank: a large tree and slope rocks stand at the water's edge, forming the main visual focal point on the right side of the painting. | Center to left: open water spreads horizontally, with waterbirds and reeds scattered about; most of the left side is blank or inscription paper, with no houses, bridges, porches, or walkable paths seen. | Beneath the tree and along the bank: dark planar areas connect with bank rocks and tree shadows, and no roof, wall, or building base can be made out.
distinction: C3 is assigned only as the closest attribution based on the gathering effect of the tree and rocks on the right bank upon the waterscape; C1 would require visible built elements arranged according to the slope-and-bank terrain, and this painting lacks evidence of built elements.

evidence: Central mountain hollow: where the left and right mountain forms and tree clumps enclose the space there is a pale rectangle, with a dark horizontal outline visible at its top, possibly a small dwelling or pavilion. | Middle-ground center: the edges of this structure are overlapped by the surrounding trees and rocks, and only the central wall surface or opening is relatively clear, presenting a half-hidden, half-exposed state.
distinction: The painting gives greater prominence to the partial screening of the suspected dwelling by trees and rocks and to front-to-back layering; the mountain-hollow position alone is not yet sufficient to confirm terrain-responsive arrangement such as the dwelling's platform or sloping bank.

evidence: Lower edge of the right circular painting, toward the right: there is a very faint ink shoreline and dotted brushstrokes, possibly a small waterside structure or trees and rocks, but the outlines are difficult to distinguish from the ground color and the calligraphic strokes. | Right circular painting, center and upper part: a large dark space is dominated by vertical calligraphy, with no clearly identifiable paths, bridges, porches, or concealment-and-revelation relationships seen. | Left circular painting: a golden circular calligraphy leaf, with no identifiable built elements seen.
distinction: The suspected small structure lies at the lower edge of the open waterside and appears more like an accent within the painting marking a scenic spot; no clear arrangement according to slopes, concealment-and-revelation composition, or path guidance is seen, so C1, C2, and C4 are not assigned.

evidence: Left to center of the painting: an old tree with a crooked trunk and clearly detailed features extends diagonally from the left slope bank toward the water, its branch tips and two perched birds resting at a position slightly left of center, becoming the most concentrated point of sight. | Lower right and lower part: stacked rocks on the right form a bank, and below, the water surface is depicted with fine dense curves to show flow, leaving a stretch of blank water mist between it and the trees and rocks on the left; the scenery unfolds around this focal point. | Upper part and background: the upper half is largely blank with faint horizontal pale ink washes, so that the foreground where the tree, rocks, and perched birds are located forms the only clear point of anchorage; no buildings, bridges, or paths are seen.
distinction: The whole painting has no identifiable built elements such as houses, bridges, or paths, so it cannot be judged as C1 on the basis of how buildings follow the lie of the mountains; the most prominent structure in the painting is the tree, rocks, and perched birds together marking a single nearshore scenic spot, and it can only be assigned, as the closest attribution, to the compositional logic of scenic accentuation.

evidence: Lower center: on the water a narrow elongated shape resembling a small boat is visible, with two people in it, one in blue seated and one in brown standing holding a long pole, forming an activity of crossing the water or moving through the landscape. | Right side: a huge cliff face occupies the right half; below the cliff are slope rocks and miscellaneous trees, with no clear built elements such as eaves, walls, or bridges and paths seen. | Left side and middle ground: low flat islets and distant mountains meet a broad misty water surface, the waterside is open, and no identifiable building base or access path is seen.
distinction: Only the boat crossing and the figures' activity hint at movement through the landscape; there is a lack of clear evidence of buildings marking famous sites by scenic points or arranged according to the terrain, so it is closer to C4 than to C3.

evidence: Center: an arched woven handle rises from behind the flower cluster, its upper section overlapped front and back by leaves and flower heads, presenting a concealment-and-revelation layering. | Lower center: the woven basket body and the patterned ring foot are half-hidden beneath flowers and leaves, with only part of the outline exposed, overlapping front to back with the foreground flowers and leaves. | Overall background: the background is a flat-painted silk ground, with no mountain forms, slope platforms, waterside, or paths seen that could correspond to natural terrain for built elements.
distinction: What is visible in the painting is the revealing and hiding of the vessel's form by flowers and leaves and their front-to-back overlapping, not the vessel marking a landscape scenic spot; moreover, the painting lacks landscape features such as mountain edges or watersides that could be marked out.

evidence: Lower part to slightly left of center of the painting: a thick, twisted tree trunk extends upward from the lower edge, with sparse branches, surrounded mostly by blank silk ground. | Upper right and edges: inscriptions and several red seals are visible, with no built or movement elements such as eaves, walls, bridges, paths, or watersides seen.
distinction: The painting contains only the layering of occlusion formed by tree trunks and blank space, with no buildings marking a specific scenic spot, so C3 is not assigned.

evidence: Lower left corner along the painting's edge: a section of dark eaves or roof outline is exposed, mostly hidden by foliage and slope rocks in front, with only a portion visible. | Lower right slope bank to the right side: pine trees and a rock face form the foreground, a figure sits on the slope bank, creating front-to-back layering with the distant mountains on the left and the empty expanse in the center. | Left center: pale-ink distant mountains are juxtaposed with a large area of unpainted space, with a clear spatial distance between the foreground building fragment and the distant view.
distinction: The main point of interest is the roof half-screened and half-revealed by foreground natural elements and thus participating in the composition, rather than visible building bases unfolding with mountain forms and slope platforms.

evidence: Slightly right of center: a standing figure stands at the water's edge, beside whom a seated figure is located on the foreground slope bank, forming a clear focal point of sight in the painting. | Left side: a giant pine and a rock face occupy the left half, with branches extending toward the center; the foreground is a waterside slope bank, and to the right opens out into a broad water surface. | Whole painting: no clearly identifiable built components such as roofs, eaves, walls, or bridge railings are seen.
distinction: The painting uses the waterside figure together with the pine and rocks as a scenic focal point, closer to scenic accentuation; but with no actual building, it cannot be confirmed as terrain-responsive built arrangement.

evidence: Right-hand painting: on a brownish-yellow surface several fish and water plants are painted, with no identifiable built elements such as houses, bridges or paths, or platforms seen. | Right center to lower right: the school of fish and water plants are distributed around open water, forming a visual focal point, but there is no concealment-and-revelation, terrain-responsive, or access relationship between buildings and landscape. | Left-hand painting: a yellow paper surface with multiple columns of inscriptions and seals, providing no evidence of built space within the picture.
distinction: The painting takes fish and water plants as its main subject, with no built elements participating in terrain-responsiveness, concealment and revelation, scenic accentuation, or access; C3 is merely the closest focal-style spatial organization in the absence of clear built elements, and building-based scenic accentuation cannot be concluded from it.

evidence: Center-left of the painting: several white narcissus flowers and slender leaves unfurl from lower left to upper right, surrounded by a large area of empty brown silk ground, with no outlines of mountains and rocks, slopes or terraces, or waterside. | Full width: within the circular fan-shaped painted panel only flowers and leaves are visible; no built elements or movement-through-the-landscape elements such as buildings, eaves, walls, bridges, paths, doors, or ferry crossings are seen. | Right edge of the painting: a vertical title slip of paper is pasted outside the painted panel; it is an addition outside the painting and is not treated as evidence of spatial relations within the painting.
distinction: The painting places isolated flowers on the broad empty silk ground, with the main subject marking out that area of empty white space; this is closer to an arrangement in which a single scene element defines one vista, rather than siting built structures according to mountain forms and banks.

evidence: Center to lower part of the painting: a horizontal gentle slope and low ground are visible, forming the main natural site. | Right side of the painting: the trunk and foliage of a tree occupy the right side, with an earthen slope visible near its roots. | Lower left of the painting: an animal stands on the sloping ground, with no traces of built elements such as houses, bridges, or roads seen around it.
distinction: The painting forms its space with natural sloping ground and tall trees, lacking instances of identifiable built elements concealed and revealed by woodland, so it is closer to C1, organized according to terrain, than to C2.

evidence: Central circular area: several columns of calligraphic text are visible; no architectural outlines, mountains and rocks, or water surface are seen. | Lower left: a red seal is visible, but it has no discernible spatial connection to landscape or built elements. | Overall painting: the circular painted panel and the surrounding woven pattern are clearly discernible; no movement-through-the-landscape clues such as bridges, paths, doors, or corridors are seen.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built elements and landscape relations; it can only be assigned to the closest category on the basis of the central marker role of the inscription and seal; there is no visible counterpart for siting, concealment and revelation, or access to secluded settings.

evidence: Upper part to center-left of the right-hand painted panel: a large blue-green rock face overhangs from above and curves inward, forming a sheltering space resembling a rock cave. | Lower center-left of the right-hand painted panel: a figure in red sits on a pale mat beneath the overhanging rock face; a figure in grey sits kneeling to the front right of the red-clad figure. | Right-hand painted panel: no clearly identifiable built or passage elements such as roofs, walls, door openings, bridges or paths are visible.
distinction: The overhang of the rock face and the recessed space where the figures are placed form layers of screening and exposure, which is closer to visible spatial organization than to scenic accentuation; but lacking concealment and revelation of architecture, it can only be assigned with low confidence.

evidence: Overall background: a large area of blank silk ground, with no identifiable mountain peaks, water bodies, trees, or house outlines seen. | Upper right: a person sits behind a low platform or desk, the platform consisting of a flat board and legs, with no roof, pillars and beams, or walls, making it difficult to confirm as a building. | Upper center: a horizontally placed rectangular component with short legs stands isolated in the blank space, not connected to roads, bridges or paths, or landscape.
distinction: The desk on the right is merely an isolated visual focal point, lacking a base-site relationship corresponding to mountain forms and watersides; by comparison, the 'scenic accentuation' of C3 is only a barely corresponding fit.

evidence: Whole painting: only birds perched on thorny branches are seen, accompanied by bamboo leaves; no buildings, mountain forms, water surfaces, or paths are seen. | Lower right: bamboo leaves and branches interweave, forming local front-to-back occlusion, but what is occluded is the birds and branches and leaves, not identifiable built elements. | Center to upper center: several birds are distributed along the branches, and the spatial organization relies mainly on the interpenetration of branches and front-to-back layering, with no connection between buildings and scenic points or entry clues.
distinction: Although there is local concealment-and-revelation layering created by branches and leaves, the painting has no built elements as the subject of concealment and revelation, nor buildings marking scenic spots.

evidence: Center of the right-hand painted panel: an elder sits on an ornamented seat, surrounded by attendants and kneeling figures; the group of figures is concentrated in the middle of the painting. | Upper part of the right-hand painted panel: above the elder is a dark green canopy-like object; no discernible tree branches or building eaves are seen. | Background of the right-hand painted panel: the background is a large area of flatly applied color; no mountains and rocks, water surface, slopes or terraces, bridges or paths, or architectural outlines are seen.
distinction: Only a visual focus formed by the figures and the canopy is seen; there is no organization of architecture according to terrain, concealment and revelation, or paths, so it is assigned to the closest category as a point-like concentration.

evidence: Lower right: a roofed waterside pavilion-dwelling is half-open, located between the waterside and tree clumps, with railings in front. | Lower right, in front of the pavilion: outside the pavilion's railings a short bridge or boardwalk-like structure connects, extending toward the water and bank on the left and forming a passage approaching the pavilion. | Center, slightly low: in front of the pavilion the stream bank and unpainted space open out, and the bridge-path clue connects with the water surface, directing movement toward the interior of the pavilion.
distinction: Although the tree clumps provide screening, the bridge and path in front of the pavilion clearly organize the spatial process of approach to and entry into the pavilion, and concealment and revelation are not dominant.

evidence: Central, slightly right, at the foot of the slope: between tree clumps a horizontal roof ridge and roof surface are exposed, the lower part of the building itself hidden by tree trunks and slope rocks, with only the roof outline visible | Center to left: several tall pines stand upright in a group, their crowns overlapping above and enclosing the front of the dwelling, so that the dwelling is wedged between gaps in the middle-ground trees | Lower right rocky slope path: a tiny figure walks on a path on the slope surface, the path extending toward the lower left of the painting, with no clear continuous connection leading to the dwelling seen
distinction: The dwelling is indicated mainly by its roof half-screened and half-revealed among the tree clumps, marking its middle-ground layer, rather than being presented through a clearly identifiable base-site layout that follows the slope; the screening relationship is therefore closer to the main expression than placement according to terrain.

evidence: Right side, upper middle: the eaves, railings, and part of the body of a storied pavilion are exposed from among the willow crowns, the lower half of the building hidden by tree clumps. | Center to right: dense willows overlap front to back, enclosing the pavilion so that the building is half-hidden and half-visible among the woodland, forming layers. | Lower left: a wooden bridge spans the water surface, with pedestrians on the bridge; the end of the bridge connects to the willow-shaded bank, hinting that one may enter the grove, but no continuous visible path to the pavilion is formed.
distinction: The half-screened relationship between the pavilion and the willow grove is the most direct organization in the painting and covers the main composition; although the bridge hints at entry, it forms no continuous visible path leading to the pavilion.

evidence: Whole painting: no identifiable built entities such as roofs, walls, bridges, paths, or doors are seen; the main subject is an old tree, two birds, rock masses, and flowing water. | Right side to center: the old tree's trunk extends horizontally from right to left, with two birds perched on the branch, the trunk forming a foreground screening against the blank space behind. | Lower left to lower part: rock blocks are layered and form front-to-back occlusion over the water surface, with the water flow exposed between the gaps in the rocks.
distinction: The painting organizes space mainly through the front-to-back occlusion and exposure of branches and rock masses, rather than through built elements marking specific scenic spots; since there are no visible buildings, C3 is only a relatively close alternative explanation.

evidence: Center-left of the circular painted panel of the right leaf: a figure is seen riding on a dark water-borne conveyance, surrounded by dense fine water ripples, forming the main subject of crossing the water. | Upper right of the circular painted panel of the right leaf: a round object hangs above the water ripples, forming a diagonal spatial connection with the central conveyance, but no shoreline, bridge or path, or building entrance is seen. | Circular painted panel of the right leaf: no discernible built outlines such as eaves, walls, or doorways are seen; the painting consists mainly of water ripples, the figure's conveyance, and the round object.
distinction: The painting uses a water-borne conveyance to express the relation of crossing water; this is more like a movement-through-the-landscape clue than the marking of a vista by built elements in C3; but with no clear architecture or entrance, it is assigned only with low confidence.

evidence: Upper right and right side: slender branches and leaves extend in from outside the painting, covering and screening the upper part of the slope rocks and their surroundings, forming a front-to-back layering of foreground foliage and rear slope rocks. | Lower right: slope rocks, a turtle, and weeds overlap one another, with some rocks and the turtle's body screened by grass and leaves, exposure and concealment coexisting. | Lower left: low-lying flowers and grasses are scattered in front of the open slope surface, forming a foreground layer of plants.
distinction: The visible space mainly presents the front-to-back screening layering among branches and leaves, slope rocks, and the turtle, rather than a corresponding relationship in which built elements are placed according to terrain height.

evidence: Running across the lower part of the painting: a long bridge spans the water surface, with a roofed pavilion at its center and the bridge body supported by dense bridge pillars, both ends connecting to the banks. | Lower left: a multi-storied pagoda and waterside houses are arranged along the waterside, surrounded by tree clumps and connected to the left end of the bridge. | Lower right: on the slope bank are houses, willows, and rocky spits, close to the water's edge, forming with the other end of the bridge a spatial arrangement through which one can come and go.
distinction: The bridge and the houses on both banks form a continuous passable clue, so that the painting presents a spatial process of approaching the opposite bank from this bank via the bridge; this explains the main compositional role better than houses merely arranged along the bank.

evidence: Waterside slightly left of center: the pitched roof and eaves of a dwelling are partially exposed among the branches and leaves of a tree clump, and the building is not fully open. | Foreground right: the trunk and crown of a large foreground tree form a screen, creating a front-to-back screening layering with the dwelling on the left. | Lower left to center-left: the dwelling is close to the waterside and hidden in the tree clump, with a small boat visible nearby, but no clear bridge, path, or corridor connection is seen.
distinction: Although the dwelling is near the waterside, the painting mainly forms concealment-and-revelation layering by having tree branches and leaves screen and reveal the roof and eaves, rather than chiefly presenting a base site unfolding along the slope bank.

evidence: Left center, slightly low: a pavilion-dwelling with pillars, railings, and a thatched roof stands on a low platform, its front open toward the right. | Right side and center: the open face of the pavilion-dwelling directly faces the large blank area on the right side of the painting, and the building forms a clear orientation relationship with this open face. | Upper left and lower right: tree trunks and foliage cover the left section of the roof, and foreground shrubs approach the platform base, but neither obscures the main body of the pavilion-dwelling.
distinction: The tree crowns and shrubs only partially press upon the roof and platform base and have not yet formed the main relationship of organizing space through concealment and revelation; the open orientation of the pavilion-dwelling corresponds to the large blank area on the right, giving greater prominence to its role as a waterside scenic accent.

evidence: Whole painting, four segments: in each segment only cut flowering branches and leaves are seen, the background being brown silk ground, with no mountains and rocks, water bodies, slope platforms, or any buildings seen. | Center of each segment: flowering branches extend horizontally, surrounded by unpainted space, lacking identifiable spatial connection with terrain, shoreline, or paths. | Between segments: the painting is divided by pale separator strips, which are mounting or segment boundaries and do not constitute built-element-and-landscape relationships within the picture.
distinction: The painting has no built elements and no landscape-site relationships; if forced into a category, C3 can only be assigned on the basis of the isolated flowering branches presented as points against an empty background, rather than the terrain-responsive arrangement of C1.

evidence: Upper right of the right circular panel, toward the right: a building or terrace enclosed by red pillars and green railings is visible, extending horizontally along the rear of the courtyard, its lower edge partly obscured by densely packed figures. | Middle to foreground of the right circular panel: a large number of figures fill the courtyard; the terrace is mainly located at the elevated rear edge of the activity space, becoming the visual focus of the scene; no clear mountains and rocks, sloping banks, or watercourses are seen participating in the siting of its base. | Junction of the right side of the right circular panel and the terrace: near the railed terrace and step-like elements, no clearly continuous road, bridge path, or gateway leading to the foreground is seen; the access relationship is unclear.
distinction: The main category is based on the terrace serving as the visual focus of the courtyard's open face; C4 requires a clearer connection by road, bridge, or gateway, whereas here no continuous accessible path is seen between the foreground and the terrace.

evidence: Upper right: a bird perches on a slender branch curving down to the right; no traces of built elements such as roofs, eaves, or walls are seen. | Upper left: branches and leaves hang down from the upper left; most of the rest of the painting is blank silk ground; no discernible access clues such as bridges, paths, or doorways.
distinction: The painting shows a bird perched on a branch amid flowers and birds; there are no built elements; if forced to classify by compositional focus, it is closer to a single isolated object marking a spot of scenery, rather than terrain-responsive siting or creating a setting through concealment and revelation.

evidence: Left side of the painting: a figure holding a staff stands, surrounded by a large area of blank background, with no traces of architecture | Center of the painting: two figures stand facing each other, apparently conversing, with no mountains and rocks, trees, or houses in the background | Right side of the painting: a figure stands in profile; apart from the figures, the entire painting is almost entirely unpainted space or the silk ground color
distinction: The painting entirely lacks landscape scenery and built elements; there are only figures arranged against a blank background, and the figures are forced to serve as the visual focus, only barely approaching the compositional logic of scenic accentuation, but lacking the relationship between nature and built elements that its definition requires.

evidence: Left to center of the painting: multiple pavilions, covered corridors, and enclosing walls are stacked in terraces along the slope, with roof ridges rising and falling with the terrain, forming a stepped terrace layout | Lower center of the painting: zigzag steps and railings are visible connecting the upper and lower levels of buildings, indicating that passages between levels are set according to the slope | Upper part and background of the painting: pale ink outlines of peaks and blank misty areas are visible behind the building complex; the buildings spread out against the foot of the mountain and gather upward
distinction: Although the steps and corridors suggest accessible paths, the painting is mainly organized by the built layout of terraces divided along the slope and stacked according to the terrain, rather than emphasizing the process of movement from the exterior into the depths.

evidence: Left to central foreground: several bare trees grow from the undulating sandy bank, their trunks and branches occupying the foreground; around the roots only earth, rocks, and weeds are seen, with no discernible roofs, walls, or building bases. | Lower right sandbar: several waterfowl gather at the edge of the sandbar, facing the open water, forming the most definite focal point of activity in the painting. | Middle and distant ground: pale ink distant shores and low hills spread horizontally; the space is dominated by open water, and no clear access clues such as bridges, paths, or doorways are seen.
distinction: The painting forms a wintry-shore scene through the waterside, sandbar, and waterfowl, but lacks verifiable built entities; compared with terrain-responsive placement of buildings, it is closer to organizing a scene by marking a spot with scenery, and is therefore assigned to C3.

evidence: Lower left to left edge: pine trees and sloping rocks extend from the lower edge of the painting, forming a near bank and a discernible shoreline. | Right-center water surface: a small boat carrying several people lies across the water, facing the bank trees on the left across the water, becoming the only discernible clue to movement or crossing in the painting. | Upper and middle areas: a large area of empty water and a pale circular form hanging high; there are no clear built elements such as houses, bridges, or paths.
distinction: The small boat more directly suggests movement on the water and a ferry-like access relationship, rather than marking a specific spot of scenery with architecture; but because clear built elements are lacking, it is assigned only with low confidence.

evidence: Lower right water surface of the right panel: on the open water there is a small boat or boat-shaped scenic accent, a relatively isolated trace of human activity in the painting; no discernible roofs, walls, or bridge structures are seen. | Left to central foreground of the right panel: several willow trees slant from the near bank toward the water, their trunks meeting the bank rocks, branches and leaves forming darker masses in the upper part. | Upper part and right side of the right panel: low, flat distant mountains meet a large expanse of open water and mist; the painting is dominated by the water area and unpainted space.
distinction: The lone boat on the open water mainly serves to concentrate the scenery, and is therefore closer to C3; however, it lacks the bridge, path, shoreline landing, or continuous access relationship required by C4.

evidence: Center: the main subject of the painting is a canopied carriage and its occupants, with a rider on the left and two standing figures on the right. | Surroundings: a large area of blank background; no discernible built or landscape elements such as mountains and rocks, water surfaces, trees, sloping platforms, houses, bridge paths, or doorways are seen.
distinction: The carriage, horses, and figures suggest travel and a facing spatial relationship, but the painting has no architecture and no discernible paths, so it can only barely be assigned to access to secluded settings; the terrain-responsive, concealment and revelation, or scenic accentuation relationships required by the other categories are all invisible.

evidence: Left cliff slope: houses with double-tiered roofs are arranged in staggered fashion up and down the rocky slope, the higher houses close to the cliff face and the lower houses at the foot of the slope. | Around the left houses: trees grow close against the buildings, their trunks and crowns covering part of the eaves and wall surfaces, forming layers in which the buildings are embedded among woods and rocks. | Right half: a large open area spreads to the right, with a low distant ridge lying across it, forming an opening and closing contrast with the dense trees and houses on the left.
distinction: Although the tree crowns clearly screen and reveal the houses, the dominant relationship is that the houses are placed in tiers according to the rocky slope and correspond in height to the slope foot and cliff face, rather than merely forming scenery through concealment and revelation.

evidence: Whole painting: the main subjects are figures, pine trees, flying cranes, and sloping rocks; no discernible houses, pavilions, bridges, doorways, or paths are seen. | Center, slightly below: the group of figures is concentrated beneath the pine tree, layered front and back to form the visual focus, with no building bases or spatial clues to follow around them. | Upper left and right side: a flying crane is at the upper left, while pine branches extend horizontally from the upper right, enclosing the background space of the central figures.
distinction: There are no built entities; the focusing of the central figure group is closest to the sense of scenic accentuation in C3; by contrast, the terrain-responsive siting, concealment and revelation layers, or path connections required by C1, C2, and C4 respectively are all invisible.

evidence: Lower left to slightly left of center: a house with an eaved roof and an open front eave sits on a relatively flat rock platform at the foot of a slope; behind and to the left of the house, sloping rocks and bare trees extend upward | Slightly left of center: bare tree trunks and branches extend from the side of the house and pass above the roof; the trees and rocks are adjacent to the house, but the building itself and the eaves are fully visible | Right side to lower right: open water extends along the shoreline to the front of the house, with a small boat in the water; no visible bridge, path, or doorway connects the house with the water surface or mountain path
distinction: The house is placed at the foot of the slope on a rock platform by the shore, and its form is complete and discernible; the trees are merely nearby accompanying scenery and do not form an organized layering of concealment and revelation, so terrain-responsive placement is closer to the main relationship than concealment and revelation forming a setting.

evidence: Lower center of the right circular panel: a house-like structure is visible, with a horizontal roof line and vertical wall/pillar lines partly exposed, the rest blending with the surrounding dark linear patterns. | Middle and surroundings of the right circular panel: dense dark horizontal and wavy lines surround the suspected house, causing its outline to appear intermittently and forming layers of partial screening.
distinction: The main category is based on the layering of partial exposure of the building amid the surrounding dark scenery; no clear organization of terrace, sloping bank, or waterside base is seen, so C1 is less fitting than C2.

evidence: Horizontal bare branches in the center and lower right: five sparrows perch on horizontally extending branches, which stretch from left to lower right, the birds' postures echoing one another. | Branches and leaves at the upper left and lower part: bare branches and leaves interweave in front of and behind the birds, partly screening their bodies and forming a visible front-to-back layering. | Background and surroundings: the painting is a large blank silk ground; no built elements such as mountains and rocks, water surfaces, architecture, bridge paths, or doorways are seen.
distinction: The painting contains only flowers, birds, branches, and leaves, with no built elements; if judged by the visible spatial relationships, the partial screening and revealing of the birds by branches and leaves is closer to concealment and revelation forming a setting, rather than marking scenery with architecture.

evidence: Left side to lower middle: a large tree takes root in the undulating rocky slope, its roots meeting the slope rocks, and the rocky slope extends toward the center of the painting. | Lower right: two figures stand on open ground, with no roofs, walls, bridges, doorways, or clear paths seen around them. | Whole painting: the painting forms an open, sparse space with trees, rocks, and figures, and there is no discernible relationship of placement, concealment and revelation, or access between architecture and landscape.
distinction: No clear built elements are seen, so only the closest C1 classification can be made on the basis of the spatial support relationship of the trees, rocks, and sloping ground; the clues of architectural concealment and revelation, scenic accentuation, or paths on which C2, C3, and C4 depend are all invisible.

evidence: Lower right and right edge of the right circular panel: a steep rocky bank and dense trees occupy the near foreground, the rocky bank opening toward the water on the left. | Water surface slightly left of center in the right circular panel: on the open water, small boat shapes and upright mast-like lines are visible, in a state of sailing or mooring on the water. | Upper part and left half of the right circular panel: distant mountains are low and flat, and a large area of the water surface is unpainted; no clearly identifiable built entities such as roofs, walls, bridge paths, or doorways are seen.
distinction: The clue of a boat moving on the water suggests an accessible, navigable process of entry, which is closer to the organization of the painting than an interpretation that merely marks scenery with an isolated scenic accent; however, clear built entities are lacking.

evidence: Upper left and lower left: an insect with spread wings is at the upper left of the painting, and a long-antennaed insect is at the lower left; both are surrounded by blank ground color, with no architecture, sloping platforms, or waterside | Right middle to lower right: grass blades and slender branches extend diagonally from the right side, flower heads and leaves overlapping one another, and a pale butterfly rests above the flowers and leaves, with front-to-back screening formed among the branches and leaves | Whole painting: what is visible throughout is grasses and insects and flowers and plants; there are no built or landscape elements such as roofs, eaves, walls, bridges, paths, or mountains, rocks, and water surfaces
distinction: Although the flowers, plants, and insects form a discernible small scene, it is more like marking a spot of scenery; but the painting has no built elements at all, so only the closest concealment-and-revelation layering can be chosen from the screening and revealing between grass blades and insects and butterflies, rather than a terrain-responsive placement relationship

evidence: Left side to upper part of the painting: several tall pine trees slant upward from the lower left, their branches and leaves covering the upper half and forming dense shade in the foreground. | Foreground slightly right of center: two figures, one behind the other, stand on a grassy slope by the water; surrounding slope rocks, pine shade, and open water enclose the focal point of the painting. | Upper right background: blue-green distant mountains spread horizontally, separated from the near foreground pines and figures by unpainted space of water surface and bank.
distinction: The painting uses the open waterside spot where the figures are as the focal point of the scenery, and no process of entry connecting bridge paths with built elements is seen; it is therefore closer to scenic accentuation than to access to secluded settings.

evidence: Lower left to center: large sloping rocks pile up from the lower left toward the upper right, their surfaces undulating and forming the main terrain framework of the painting | Rock crevices and rock tops: stems of many flowers and plants extend from between the rocks, with blossoms and leaf clusters distributed according to the height of the rocks; no houses, bridge paths, or artificial structures are seen | Right side: tall rocks and herbaceous branches and leaves overlap front and back, the branches and leaves screening part of the rock surfaces and forming shallow front-to-back layering
distinction: The painting shows only flowers and trees growing according to the height of rock crevices and distributed with the shapes of the rocks, which is closer to a relationship of placement according to the site's topography; there is no clear layering in which built elements create scenery through concealment and revelation by means of trees, mountains, and rocks.

evidence: Middle of the right side: a group of figures surrounds a canopied carriage (or throne/imperial carriage), positioned above cloud vapor/water waves; its form is relatively prominent and has characteristics of an artificial structure | Left side and center: the handscroll unfolds, showing a large number of water-wave patterns, mountains and rocks, and trees; figures ride beasts, wade in water, or stand among them, distributed across different scenes | Whole painting: the painting is mainly in fine outline (baimiao), with landscape background (water, clouds, rocks) setting off the figures' activities; no clear fixed house architecture is seen
distinction: The figures and the suspected carriage in the painting mainly serve to identify different scenes of deities (scenic accentuation), rather than emphasizing the relationship of base layout placed according to terrain.

evidence: Center: a bird stands on the rim of a round vessel, the vessel located in the lower middle of the painting. | Entire background: the background is uniform silk ground; no mountains, water surfaces, sloping banks, trees, bridge paths, or architecture are seen.
distinction: The painting contains only an isolated bird and vessel, lacking mountains and woods, waterside, and paths; compared with the terrain-responsive placement required by C1, here only the focusing effect of a single object in an empty scene is taken as the closest assignment.

evidence: Middle, toward the right: a huge arched bridge spans the river, connecting the two banks; pedestrians on the bridge and boats beneath it form a busy traffic node, guiding the eye across the water. | Left side: a city gate tower stands, with dense streets extending into the city, crowds active along the streets, presenting the path and spatial transition into the city. | Throughout the painting: the river and riverside roads link the countryside on the right with the urban market on the left, forming a continuous thread of travel that gives the painting a spatial process of moving from one place to another.
distinction: Although the rainbow bridge and city gate tower serve to mark scenery, the painting as a whole emphasizes the organization of traversable space linking different areas through bridges, roads, and the river.

evidence: Circular painted panel of the right leaf: a bird perches on a broken branch, with a few leaves around it and a large area of blank space; no mountains and rocks, water body, architecture, or paths are seen. | Circular painted panel of the left leaf: mainly calligraphic inscription and seals, forming no discernible landscape or built space.
distinction: The painting has no clear built elements; the right leaf forms a focal effect through a single subject and unpainted space, closer to scenic accentuation than to a concealment-and-revelation relation in which architecture is screened by natural scenery.

evidence: Slightly right of center: a round ink-colored rock stands alone on pale ground, with fine moss dots scattered around it, forming the main solid entity of the painting. | Lower left: a tiny figure crouches beside a bamboo clump, facing the central rock, holding an object, near the edge of the painting. | Left and right sides: bamboo clumps grow inward from both sides of the painting, leaving pale open ground between them and the central rock and figure.
distinction: The main category is based on the local arrangement of the figure with the rock and bamboo marking the focal point of the scenery, rather than natural objects screening architecture to form layers of concealment and revelation; no discernible architecture is seen in the painting.

evidence: Upper part to right edge of the painting: branches and leaves hang down from above, and several fruits are half hidden by leaves and branches, showing only their lit surfaces; the relationship of exposure and concealment is clearly visible. | Slightly below center: a larger fruit is in the foreground, with leaves covering its edges from different directions, forming front-to-back layering. | Middle of the right edge: another fruit is only partly exposed, together with the central fruit and leaves forming a layer-by-layer progression from front to back.
distinction: The painting is mainly organized by the layering of branches and leaves screening front and back and fruits half revealed; however, there is no landscape scenery to be marked, nor any built elements, so it can only be assigned as the closest fit.

evidence: Right half of the painting: three figures sit around a writing desk, on which are books and brush and inkstone; to the right are placed a large vase and flowering branches; no architecture, roads, or bridges are seen. | Right half background: the background is flat brown, with no discernible beams and pillars, doors and windows, mountains and rocks, or water-body layers. | Left half of the painting: a continuous decorative ground pattern, with no scenery within the painting, and cannot serve as a clue to landscape or built elements.
distinction: Only the figures, writing desk, and flower vessel form the visual focus, closest to scenic-accent organization; however, the painting has no clear relationship between built elements and landscape, so scenic accentuation cannot be established.

evidence: Right half of the painted panel: several figures are seen around a long-handled staff and a round object on the ground; the background is flatly colored, with no buildings, platforms or bases, bridges, or paths. | Background of the right half of the painted panel: no discernible mountains and rocks, slopes or banks, water body, or trees are seen behind or around the figures, lacking a spatial relation between built elements and natural forms. | Left half of the painted panel: a blank mounting-pattern area, providing no evidence of the position of built elements or landscape within the painting.
distinction: The painting has no discernible built elements; C3 is assigned only as the closest category because the central group of figures forms a visual focus, with no evidence of architectural accentuation or correspondence with landscape.

evidence: Right half to middle right: a large tree with a gnarled trunk and branches and leaves extending upward occupies a prominent position, its branches reaching toward the center of the painting. | Left to center: several figures in long robes stand or walk in a loose formation, with the central figure facing the group on the left. | Whole painting: the background is a large area of blank space; no discernible built elements such as houses, bridges, paths, or doorways are seen.
distinction: The painting uses the large tree and figures to form a visual focus, which is closer to "scenic accentuation"-style concentration than to C4 entry along a bridge path, but it lacks an architectural entity.

evidence: Center of the right half of the painting: an elderly man sits on an carved seat, with several figures ranged around him, forming the sole gathering center of the whole painting. | Upper right: a tall-handled fan-like or canopy-like object stands above the figures, becoming a conspicuous vertical marker. | Background of the right half of the painting: the background is plain, with no mountains and rocks, water bodies, or trees seen, nor any clear houses, bridges, or paths.
distinction: C3 uses the seat, canopy, and gathered figures to form a visual marker point; the relationship of following the mountains and terrain, sloping platforms, or waterside required by C1 is not visible in the painting.

evidence: Center of the right leaf: a group of figures is seen—a long-bearded elder sits upright, with a staff-bearing attendant standing behind him, and a monkey holding an object approaches in front; around them there are no traces of buildings, walls, bridges, or paths. | Background of the right leaf: behind the figures is only flatly colored silk ground, with no discernible natural scenery such as mountains and rocks, slopes or banks, or water surface. | Left half of the painting: a large area of pink patterned mounting, separate from the right painted panel, belonging to the mounting or mounting border and not treated as evidence of space within the painting.
distinction: The whole painting has no landscape scenery; only the figures are concentrated in the right leaf to form a visual resting point, closer to the role of 'marking one spot'; but lacking a concealment-and-revelation relation between architecture and natural scenery, it cannot stand as concealment and revelation forming a setting.

evidence: Upper right: a long-tailed animal crouches on a diagonally extending branch, surrounded by a large area of blank silk ground. | Lower left: a bent branch, leaves, and two fruits extend horizontally, the only relatively clear objects in the lower part of the painting. | Whole painting: no discernible roofs, walls, bridges, paths, or waterside built elements are seen, nor any clear landscape structure.
distinction: There are no discernible built elements; C3 is closest only because isolated objects form a focus; there is no visible evidence for the relationships of terrain responsiveness, concealment and revelation, or path entry of C1, C2, and C4.

evidence: Lower left end: a small gatehouse with red eave pillars has an opening and steps, connecting to a paved courtyard in front, with figures active nearby. | Middle section: continuous covered galleries, open halls, and courtyards unfold horizontally, with rows of red pillars and door openings forming layered, traversable spaces. | Right section: courtyard walls, door openings, and paving among trees connect, with figures scattered along passageways and courtyards, the space extending into the interior of the painting.
distinction: The main category consists of gates, galleries, courtyards, and figure activity forming an accessible spatial sequence; C2 only explains the trees' partial screening of roofs and does not capture the passage organization of the entire scroll.

evidence: Upper right: the eaves and upper storey of a pavilion emerge between tree crowns, its lower part screened by branches and leaves, creating a layer of seeing the building through trees. | Center-right: dense trunks and foliage stand in front of the pavilion, partially screening the structure so that it appears half-concealed and half-revealed.
distinction: The pavilion is mainly screened and revealed by branches and foliage, forming a layered woodland setting; although there is a small path and travelers, the painting does not show a clearly accessible connection between the road and the pavilion.

evidence: Left side and lower left of the painting: several tall trees grow in a cluster to form a grove; the trunks stand on a sloping earthen bank, the branches and leaves are dense and layered in dark and light ink, and pale mist gaps remain among the trees | Slightly right of center: beyond the wooded bank a broad expanse of empty, misty water opens out; in the distance sandbars and reeds are laid out horizontally in pale ink and their edges are obscured by mist | Lower right and lower part: the low bank and the place where reeds grow thickly form a horizontal band, which together with the grove on the left bank encloses a layer-by-layer progression from front to back
distinction: The painting relies mainly on the foreground-background screening and revealing of trees, mist, and sandbars to form its layers; no identifiable eaves, gateways or paths, bridges or crossings, or other entry cues are seen, so it is closer to concealment and revelation forming a setting than to access to secluded settings.

evidence: Center to left: a branch bearing white flowers with green leaves spreads horizontally, the white flowers being the most prominent subject of the painting. | Entire painting: the background is a flat brown silk ground, with no identifiable spatial elements such as mountains, water, sloping banks, roads, bridges, or houses. | Right side and lower part: several green buds and overlapping leaves are visible; apart from plant branches and leaves, there are no clues to built elements or movement through the landscape.
distinction: The painting contains only plants and an empty ground, with neither landscape nor clear built elements; only because a single subject stands out somewhat against the open ground is it tentatively placed in C3, and this cannot be taken as a genuine scenic-accentuation relationship.

evidence: Upper right cliff top: a square pavilion sits on a platform projecting outward, the platform's outer edge fitted with a railing that turns with the cliff wall, part of the platform overhanging the rock face. | Upper right to center right: the pavilion backs onto the rock mass, its front facing the broad water below to the left, the base and roof heights following the contours of the cliff top. | Lower right bank path: at the foot of the cliff are rocky slopes, trees, and two pedestrians on a bank path, the pavilion platform standing high above the waterside below.
distinction: The pavilion's base and outer railing turn and cantilever with the cliff-top platform, directly embodying the placement of a platform and pavilion against the cliff; although its role as a waterside scenic marker is visible, it is less specific than siting according to terrain.

evidence: Right half, center: a long-haired, bare-chested figure sits on a green mat, the sole concentrated visual focus of the entire painting. | Around the green mat and below in the painting: three figures in total are distributed in front of and to either side of the mat, all facing the seated central figure. | Entire painting surface: the picture consists only of several figures on an ochre-yellow ground, with no houses, roofs, walls, bridges, paths, or any clear built structures.
distinction: The central group of figures forms a node drawing the gaze, closest to the scenic-accentuation role described under C3; but there are no built structures in the painting, so the C1 relationship of terrain-responsive siting cannot be confirmed, and evidence for both concealment-and-revelation and entry-path relationships is lacking.

evidence: Entire painting: the subject is a group of figures on horseback, the background plain, with no buildings, mountains, water, bridges, paths, or gate galleries visible. | Center to right: figures and horses are arranged horizontally, some appearing to move rightward or halt, but no road, entrance, or traversable path connected to a building can be discerned.
distinction: The painting has no built elements, bridges, paths, or gate galleries, only the implied movement of a riding party, so C4 is merely the closest assignment; C3 lacks identifiable landscape scenery and architectural markers.

evidence: Left middle section, between the great tree trunk and the rock wall: branches, hanging tendrils, and the rock mass overlap, with a pale horizontal member visible among them, resembling eaves or part of a building, but mostly screened, making its full form hard to confirm. | Left side to lower center: trees and rocks form front and back layers, a suspected built element sandwiched behind the rock wall and tree trunks, appearing half-concealed and half-revealed; its base and entrance boundaries are unclear.
distinction: The main visible relationship is the screening and revealing of a suspected built element by trees and rocks, rather than a clearly discernible base laid out following the slope.

evidence: Lower foreground to center: a low bridge or plank walkway with railings spans a pale open space, extending toward the central building complex. | Center-left: gatehouse, galleries, and roofs connect, the foreground bridge path roughly aligned with this entrance. | Center-right and rear: the building complex is arranged against rock walls and groves, and the entry relationship between the entrance and the buildings remains discernible.
distinction: The main factor is the movement connection formed by the bridge path and gate galleries, approaching and entering the building complex; C1 only explains that the buildings are sited against the mountains and rocks and does not cover this entry process.

evidence: Left side of the painting: dark cloud masses overlap front and back, a long-bodied dragon form partly hidden behind the clouds and partly revealed, forming a clear layering of concealment and revelation. | Lower left: water-wave lines spread from the lower edge, connecting with the cloud masses above, forming a spatial background where clouds and water meet. | Right side of the painting: a large area of pale paper with columns of writing is juxtaposed with the ink-toned scene on the left; no identifiable buildings, bridges, paths, or gate galleries are seen in the painting.
distinction: The main category takes the spatial layering formed by clouds partially screening and revealing the subject, while the architectural scenic accentuation required by C3 has no discernible evidence in the picture.

evidence: Center to top: clusters of dark green leaves and pale flowers overlap, some branches screened by leaves, forming a clear layering of screening and revealing. | Lower left: two birds perch on open ground below the flowering branches, with a gap between them and the dense blossoms and foliage above, forming an opening from screening to revelation. | Overall painting: apart from flowering branches, leaves, blossoms, and two birds, no clear buildings, mountains, water, bridges, paths, or discernible built elements are seen.
distinction: Although the flowering branches can form a visual focus, the painting more emphasizes the layering of leaves screening and revealing branches and flowers, so it is closer to C2 than to C3; both lack evidence of built elements.

evidence: Right center, lower part: a pavilion straddles a projecting rock platform, the platform's front edge overhanging open space and its rear attached to the mountain mass, the base integrated with the sloping rock. | Below and front left of the pavilion: the lower part of the pavilion is supported by the rock wall, a railing set at the platform edge, the whole structure arranged following the height and turns of the mountain mass on the right. | Upper part and right side: tall peak rocks occupy the upper part of the painting and extend to the right, the pavilion on the slope platform below them, its roof lower than the peak, forming a siting relationship that follows the mountain.
distinction: The pavilion is not merely a marker identifying the valley scenery; its base is clearly set on the projecting rock ledge on the right, and its main compositional role lies in siting according to terrain.

evidence: Lower part of the right circular painting, toward the left: a dark block-like outline with a sloped top and vertical side stands on a projecting rock platform, its details dim but still resembling a small house. | Lower part of the right circular painting: this block is sited according to the edge of the rock platform and the height of the water-pattern background, with no clear bridge path, gate gallery, or continuous entry cues visible.
distinction: The visible relationship leans more toward a house arranged with the rock platform and waterside than toward clearly using a building to identify a particular peak or water scene; but the identification of the house itself is uncertain.

evidence: Right section of the full picture, among trees at the mountain foot: the sloped roof of a low house is visible emerging from the woodland, most of its walls screened by tree crowns and sloping rocks. | Right section, low middle ground: the building lies low between the mountains and the foreground grove, tree crowns and sloping banks screening it front and back, so the house appears half-hidden and half-revealed among the trees.
distinction: The building is mainly concealed by trees and sloping rocks, with its roof partly revealed, forming a layering of concealment and revelation; the suspected entry connection between the foreground bridge path and the house is not clear enough, so access to secluded settings is not chosen.

evidence: Lower right foreground: a hat-wearing figure holding a staff stands on a projecting bank, body turned toward the cliff at center-right. | Left to center: a thick tree trunk slants in from lower left, branches crossing the painting, forming front-and-back screening and near-far layering with the misty cliff. | Center-right: a steep cliff emerges from the clouds, a broad expanse of open water or mist left between the cliff foot and the foreground bank.
distinction: The foreground figure and bank suggest a starting point for gazing or moving from the painting's edge into depth, closer to visible spatial organization than a scenic-accentuation reading focused on the cliff alone; but clear built elements connectable to a bridge path are lacking.

evidence: Right section, foreground and middle ground: sloping rocks, groves, and earthen banks overlap front and back, tree crowns screening one another, forming successive layers of pictorial depth, with no clearly discernible house outline among them. | Right section, between the grove and the mountain mass in the middle: gaps are left between trees and rocks, allowing the eye to pass through the foreground into a more distant bank, the space divided into several layers. | Right section, distant view: distant mountains washed in pale ink form front-and-back layers with the dark-ink trees and rocks of the foreground, but no clear indication of buildings connected by bridges or paths is seen.
distinction: The painting organizes space through trees and rocks screened and revealed front and back and layered to draw out the terrain, which is closer to the visible relationships than a verifiable correspondence between base and sloping platform or waterside.

evidence: Center of the painting: vertical running-script calligraphy occupies the main body, with no discernible building outlines, mountains, water, or trees between or around the characters. | Left side: two red square seals appear to the lower left of the writing; no spatial relationship of paths, crossings, or building sites is formed around the seals. | Outer edge of the fan: the painting is a round/oval fan format, its ground color, ink writing, and red seals forming a complete composition; no visible eaves, walls, sloping platforms, or waterside are present.
distinction: None of the built-elements–landscape relationships required by the four categories appear; C3 is chosen only as the closest single-centered marker composition under forced classification, not as architectural scenic accentuation.

evidence: Center, lower part: a roof and part of a wall emerge among a grove, screened on all sides by dense trees, the building body mostly hidden in the woodland. | Lower right foreground: a small bridge crosses the waterside, a figure on the bridge, but no clearly continuous path connection is seen between the bridge and the building in the grove. | Upper background: distant mountains washed in pale ink form front-and-back layers with the dense foreground grove, the building occupying the middle ground of these layers.
distinction: The building's main compositional role is to reveal its roof through the screening of trees, forming a layering of concealment and revelation in the woodland; although the bridge and figure at lower right suggest movement, they do not form a discernible entry connection with the building, so the basis for C4 is weak.

evidence: Left side to center of the painting: a cut branch enters from the left, leaves and fruit overlapping, the fruit partly screened by leaves, forming a relatively dense cluster of physical objects. | Center-right: a small bird perches on a slender branch, body facing right, surrounded by a large expanse of plain silk ground with nothing painted, making it a visually locatable focus. | Lower right: the slender branch extends and tapers toward the lower right, its tip bearing small leaves and fruit, with blank space beyond the branch tip and no elements such as paths, bridges, shorelines, or buildings indicating spatial entry.
distinction: There are no built elements in the painting: classifying the focal relationship of branches, fruit, and bird within the unpainted space as scenic accentuation fits the visible layout better than explaining it as a scene formed by trees screening and revealing.

evidence: Center-left: roof and walls lie among dense woodland, the roof surface and eaves partly revealed after being divided by trunks and tree crowns. | Lower right: another courtyard wall and roof lie behind sloping rocks and trees, the front part clearer, the rear part screened. | Lower left to center: a foreground stream, stones, and grove form front-and-back layers, placing the buildings in a screened middle ground.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited against mountains and beside water, the dominant relationship in the painting is the screening and partial revealing of roofs and walls by trees and sloping rocks, rather than a base unfolding with the terrain.

evidence: Middle to right half, various dark-ink passages: the main dark-ink passages consist chiefly of layered water patterns, wave crests, and ink tonal variation, with no discernible roofs, walls, bases, or bridge paths. | Left side and between painting passages: large amounts of vertical inscriptions and seals occupy the blank space, but these are writing and marks on the painting and cannot serve as evidence of built structures. | Entire scroll: a waterscape unfolds continuously across the horizontal format, spatial relationships organized mainly through water patterns, ink tones, and unpainted space, with no discernible connection between buildings and mountains, rocks, or waterside.
distinction: The painting contains only segmented waterscapes and inscriptions, lacking built structures; compared with C1's siting according to terrain, C3 is merely the closest assignment based on the organization of each waterscape segment as its own scene.

evidence: Lower left to left side: slender reeds and leaves slant into the painting from the left edge, forming foreground plants, with no roofs, walls, pillars, beams, or other built components appearing. | Lower right: a pair of colorful waterfowl swim on the water, with no bridges, paths, gates, or building bases around them. | Center and upper right: the middle of the painting is largely open, the upper right containing only tiny ink-mark-like objects, forming no discernible built elements or movement routes.
distinction: The painting has no clear built elements; only the consolidating effect of the isolated waterfowl on the open water at the right can be taken as tentatively approaching "scenic accentuation," rather than a composition with bridge paths or hidden houses.

evidence: Center-left to middle: within warm brown mist there are only vague horizontal dark shadows, not reliably identifiable as buildings. | Lower right to upper part: a slender curved branch extends diagonally from lower right to the upper edge of the painting, crossing and dividing the open composition. | Lower left and center right: two flying birds at different heights serve as visual markers within the open scenery.
distinction: With no clearly visible built elements, the closest assignment rests on the marking of the open scenery by birds and branches, not on the concealment-and-revelation relationship of discernible buildings.

evidence: Full width: the painting is a handscroll scene composed of figures, horses, and seating, with no discernible mountains, rocks, water, trees, or buildings. | Right side: a white-robed figure sits beside a low seat of alternating red and blue, a figure holding a feather fan standing nearby, the seat and figures forming a local visual focus. | Center and left: horses, horse handlers, and standing figures on the left are distributed across the open ground, with no entry cues such as bridges, paths, gates, or galleries.
distinction: The main category takes only the local visual emphasis formed by the low seat and figures on the right; the painting has no discernible mountain forms or sloping platforms for terrain-responsive siting, so C1 is not chosen.

evidence: Lower center foreground of the painting: a stone-paved path extends from the lower edge toward the building steps, a figure on the path, forming a clear direction of approach and entry. | Lower left building facade: the building entrance connects with the foreground stone path, the space beneath the eaves opening toward the path, with figures moving along this path. | Lower right shoreline: a low railing or plank walkway extends rightward from the platform in front of the building, still discernible after passing around the rocks, suggesting that the route continues.
distinction: The grove does partly screen the building, but the foreground stone path, figures, and railing organize the main relationship into a route that can be reached and continued into, rather than a scene formed by concealment and revelation alone.

evidence: Center to top: a tall pine occupies the main body of the painting, its trunk and branches extending upward from below, forming the main spatial framework. | Lower middle: several figures sit and stand around a lute table, the figures and table below the pine, forming the concentrated activity node of the painting. | Full picture: no clear built elements such as houses, pavilions, bridges, paths, or walls are seen; the ground is mostly blank, with only figures, the lute table, seating, and scattered objects.
distinction: The painting uses the figures beneath the pine and the lute table to form a central marker scene, but with no clear built elements there is no concealment-and-revelation to speak of; by comparison it does not constitute a scene formed by screening and revelation.

evidence: Center-right of the painting: two large pheasants stand on rocks, surrounded by branches, foliage, and rock forms overlapping one another, forming clear front-and-back screening. | Lower right: rocks and blossoms screen the birds' feet and part of their tail feathers, showing multiple layers of overlapping scenery. | Full width: no discernible built elements such as roofs, walls, bridges, paths, or gate galleries are seen.
distinction: The painting consists mainly of layered screening among flowers, birds, mountains, and rocks, not buildings identifying a particular scene; because there are no built elements, C2 is only the closest classification based on the visible layering of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower left of the painting, beneath a thick bending trunk: a low dark outline resembling a sloped roof is visible, its right edge and upper part overlapped by trunks and foliage, only partly revealed. | Center-right to lower part: an old tree trunk slants upward from the rocky slope at lower right, its branches crossing above the suspected house, together with the rock forms creating a layering of front screening and rear revealing. | Lower left rocky slope: the rocky slope meets the tree roots, the suspected house apparently sited in a hollow of the slope.
distinction: Although the house appears sited in a hollow of the rocky slope, the painting mainly establishes spatial layering through the partial screening and revealing of the roof by trees and rocks, so it is closer to C2 than to C1.

evidence: Right side of the painting surface: slender branches hang down from above, leaves scattered on the blank silk ground, with no houses, bridges, paths, mountains and rocks, or waterside seen. | Left side of the painting surface: calligraphic inscription occupies the left half, juxtaposed with the branches and leaves on the right, the painting composed mainly of writing and plants. | Full width: there are no discernible built structures, nor any landscape space that could explain relationships between buildings and terrain, concealment and revelation, scenic accentuation, or entry.
distinction: The painting presents only isolated branches and leaves against blank space, closest to C3's use of a single object to identify a scene; but lacking built structures, a genuine scenic accentuation cannot be established.

evidence: Center-right: a pale-ink peak rises from the water below, its foot meeting a large expanse of unpainted space, forming the most concentrated mountain form in the picture. | Lower part, near center: near the water surface is a very small horizontal ink dot, resembling a lone boat or a tiny man-made scenic marker, with no clear roofs, gates, bridges, or bank paths around it. | Left side and foreground: low banks, cloud and mist, and blank water surface join into an open foreground, showing no clear relationship of buildings unfolding along the slope or waterside.
distinction: The main category rests on the isolated scenic ink mark consolidating the open landscape, rather than on a discernible bridge path forming an entry or crossing route.

evidence: Circular painting at right: the painting takes loquat branches and leaves, fruit, birds and butterflies as its main subjects; branches and leaves overlap one another, forming layers of front-to-back occlusion and partial exposure. | Center and left: another circular area contains calligraphic inscription, which is not a built element or landscape element in the painting; no identifiable house, bridge, path, gate or platform base is seen in the whole work.
distinction: The screening and exposure of branches and leaves is the spatial relationship closest to that of the whole picture, but built structures are lacking, so it cannot be confirmed as borrowed-scenery screening; there is also no evidence of built structures defining a scene.

evidence: Between the mountain foot and the water surface, center-left: several pitched-roof houses are visible, arranged irregularly along a terrace at the mountain foot, backed by the mountain mass and close to a winding stream in front. | Around the building group at center-left: trees and slopes flank the buildings front and back, and the building heights roughly follow the slope on which they stand. | At the turning point of the shoreline at center-left: the water flows around the mountain foot, and the building group is on the raised side of the shoreline, its position unfolding with the terrain and shoreline.
distinction: The buildings are mainly placed according to the terrain of the mountain foot and waterside, and the terrain determines their position and unfolding; although trees screen them, concealment and revelation are not the dominant organization.

evidence: Upper-middle of the painting: a group of horizontal roofs and building bodies stands among trees on the mountainside, the lower half obscured by trees and slope rocks, with only the eaves and part of the building outlines exposed. | Center-right: foreground trees and rocks overlap the buildings front and back, and the buildings are revealed through gaps in the trees, forming visible layers of concealment and revelation. | Behind and to both sides of the buildings: towering peaks rise behind the buildings, and trees stand close to both sides, the built elements occupying a recess in the middle ground enclosed by mountains, rocks and trees.
distinction: Although the buildings are on the mountainside, the main visible relationship is the exposure of roofs and eaves beneath the screening of trees and rocks, not the terrain-responsive layout of building bases spreading with the slope.

evidence: Center to top: a huge rock mass stands vertically, occupying the main body of the painting, with heavy outlines forming an oppressive mountain-and-rock background. | Lower center: a low house-shaped structure is faintly visible among trees, its outline adjoining surrounding branches and leaves, only partly exposed. | Lower part and lower left: slope banks and trees surround the house shape; no clear bridge, path or doorway is seen running through in an identifiable way.
distinction: The primary label is based on the layers formed by the partial screening and exposure of the house shape by trees; the alternative explanation focuses on the small house defining the scene at the mountain foot, but the concealment-and-revelation relationship is more direct in the painting.

evidence: Upper right: a large moth (or butterfly) spreads its wings, occupying the upper-right space; no built structures are seen around it. | Left to lower part: leafy branches extend from bottom to top, with leaves concentrated in the left half, set apart left and right from the flying insect on the right. | Whole work: no identifiable built elements such as mountain masses, water surfaces, roads, bridges or roofs are seen in the painting.
distinction: The painting has no built elements; only the separation of the isolated flying insect at upper right from the branches and leaves at left can be loosely matched to scenic accentuation, rather than a true relationship of built structures defining a landscape.

evidence: Right scroll, center-right: a low horizontal roofed structure is visible, set on a rectangular platform whose edges are clear, the building extending horizontally with the platform. | Right scroll, center to top: a thick tree trunk stands to the left of the platform, its canopy covering above the structure; the platform meets the ground, showing the built elements placed against the tree and on the platform. | Right scroll, foreground: the rectangular platform extends downward and supports a reclining figure's couch; the building, platform and figure in front form a continuous low platform space.
distinction: Although the canopy covers above, the roof and platform base are exposed overall, with no obvious concealment-and-revelation layers created by trees and rocks; the main relationship is placement on a platform rather than concealment and revelation forming a scene.
