evidence: Right half, center: a bearded figure sits on a low platform or couch, with a standing figure beside him; no roof, walls or beams and columns are seen for the platform, making it hard to confirm as built architecture. | Right half, background: the background is nearly flatly painted, with no identifiable mountain forms, slope platforms, watersides, trees or paths; only scattered small color dots surround the figures and low platform. | Left half: the left side is a large area of pinkish textured page, separated from the painting at right, presenting no terrain or built relationships within the painting.
distinction: Only the visual anchor formed by the figures and low platform against the open background can be assigned as the closest fit; the terrain-responsive siting required for C1, the concealment-and-revelation layers required for C2, and the path-entry relationship required for C4 are all absent.

evidence: Center: a tall tree grows on an earthen slope rising above the water, the foot of the slope meeting the water ripples in the foreground, forming a waterside earthen-slope terrain. | Left and right banks and foreground: several figures are distributed near the waterside and the foot of the slope; no clear roofs, walls, bridges, gates or other artificial built elements are seen. | Background and middle: pale-ink distant mountains and unpainted space enclose the middle-ground earthen slope; the pictorial space is mainly organized by the waterside, the slope and trees.
distinction: The primary category is based on the terrain organization formed by the central waterside earthen slope and the shoreline; although traveling figures are visible, identifiable bridges or paths and entry connections are lacking, so the terrain conditions are closer to the site relationships of C1.

evidence: Right painting: an extended gentle sandbar and a large expanse of open water, with long pale-ink lines depicting layer upon layer of water flats, forming a level, distant waterscape. | Right section, near trees: several sparse-branched bare trees stand next to a low slope islet, their trunks slender and clear; no walls, roofs or other built forms are seen around them. | Middle of the water surface: several small ink marks resembling waterfowl are scattered; no identifiable artificial elements such as bridges, paths or pavilions are seen.
distinction: Because the painting has no built entities, the built relationships of terrain-responsive placement or secluded paths cannot be verified; the picture's main scene consists of natural sandbars, water surface and sparse trees, so it is closest to scene-dominant C3 rather than C1 or C4, which rely on relationships between buildings and terrain or paths.

evidence: Upper right: above the clouds stands a multi-eaved pavilion, the clearest artificial built structure in the painting. | Lower center: several figures gather, one holding a tall banner whose streamers flutter toward the pavilion above; no bridge, path, gate or identifiable entry route is seen between the figures and the pavilion. | Rest of the right painting: no clear mountains and rocks, slope banks, water surface or trees are seen; cloud patterns and a gold ground mainly set off the pavilion above.
distinction: The pavilion, isolated in the clouds, serves as a visual marker defining the scene above; although clouds surround its lower part, the pavilion is fully exposed, without front-to-back concealment by mountains, rocks and trees, so it is closer to C3 than C2.

evidence: Lower right: a square low wooden table is visible on open ground, beside trees and rocks. | Lower left: a low wooden railing runs horizontally along the lower edge of the painting, its end meeting the central open ground. | Upper right: bamboo and large garden rocks form a garden background, enclosing the central activity space.
distinction: The small table and railing mainly serve as garden scenic accents and site definition, lacking clear bridges, paths or doorways leading inward, so access to secluded settings is not adopted.

evidence: Circular painting at right: overlapping branches and leaves with flowers and fruit are painted on a flatly painted background; no roofs, walls, beams or columns or other built forms appear. | Left: running-script inscription and seals are visible, but they form no architecture in the painting or identifiable spatial built elements. | Whole work: apart from the plants within the circular painting at right, no mountains and rocks, water bodies, slope platforms, bridges or paths or other landscape elements that could relate to built structures are seen.
distinction: The primary category is assigned only as the closest fit because a single flower-and-fruit motif is highlighted within the circular painting; the concealment-and-revelation layers of buildings required for C2 have no visible evidence in the painting, so it is not adopted.

evidence: Center-left: two birds perch on a slender horizontal branch; nearby leaves and branches overlap front and back, with some leaves screening the branch in front. | Right half: another bird stands on an extending branch, with scattered leaves and fruit around it; branches and leaves form visible front-to-back layers before and behind the bird's body. | Whole work: the painting is mainly unpainted silk ground; no mountains, water surfaces, houses, paths, bridges or other built and landscape elements are seen.
distinction: The visible relationship is mainly the partial screening and front-to-back layering of branches and leaves over the birds and branch, rather than built structures defining a landscape scene, so it is closer to concealment and revelation forming a scene; however, the painting has no built elements, so this is only the closest assignment.

evidence: Right half, center: a group of figures gathers on a slope bank around a cart-like structure with an arched canopy supported by posts, the procession extending along the rocky bank. | Right half, upper part: a figure with flowing garments stands on a projecting rock terrace, below which are water and unpainted space, forming an opening and closing with the trees and rocks at right. | Right edge: tall trees and dark rock walls occupy the right edge, with a narrow bank strip between trees and rocks leading toward the group of figures.
distinction: The procession and the canopied structure form a clue of movement through the landscape along the slope bank, rather than a clear built structure defining the scene.

evidence: Right circular painting, middle ground right: the roof and eaves of a house emerge between trees and slope rocks, the building body partly screened by branches and leaves. | Right circular painting, lower right near the bank: the house's base is close to the waterside slope, with water surface and rocky bank visible in front. | Right circular painting, upper and left parts: a large area of water surface or misty unpainted space forms an opening and closing with the dense woods at right, the house standing within layers screened by trees.
distinction: The concealment-and-revelation layers of the house half-hidden among trees, with roof and eaves appearing and disappearing, are more prominent, rather than merely placement on a slope by the water.

evidence: Center-lower, where rocks and trees meet: darker horizontal block-like surfaces are wedged between rock masses, their edges screened by trees and rocks, making roofs or walls impossible to distinguish. | Bottom to middle ground: slope banks, trees and rock masses overlap front and back, forming layers from foreground into the depths of the mountain mass, but no clear bridge, path or entrance is seen. | Upper center: the main peak rises high, clouds and mist divide the mountain mass, and the spatial focus of the painting is mainly the layered landscape rather than clear built entities.
distinction: If the dark block-like surfaces belong to a house, their partial screening by rocks and trees suggests concealment-and-revelation layers, which is closer to the visible relationship than judging site placement directly from mountain forms.

evidence: Left to center-left of the painting: jagged mountains and rocks join dense tree canopies into a large mass, forming a foreground entity occupying the left half. | Center-right of the painting: three children are active on the ground, one near the edge of the trees and rocks, the figures adjacent front and back to the trees and rocks. | Whole work: no roofs, walls, doorways, bridges or identifiable roads are seen, nor any clear sign of building bases meeting mountain forms or watersides.
distinction: C2 is only a closer fit because the foreground trees and rocks and the figures form an identifiable front-to-back enclosing layer; C1 requires clear evidence of buildings placed according to terrain, but no buildings or bases are seen in the painting.

evidence: Center-left to distant view: open water spans the painting, with low, gently continuous distant mountains above the shore, forming an open, level-and-distant scene with almost no screening near the bank. | Left middle-ground waterside: a low slope bank or sandbar extends into the water, with several dark small patches on it whose outlines are blurred and cannot be reliably identified as houses or trees. | Lower right foreground: slope rocks and several tall trees form a foreground frame; no identifiable movement-connecting clues such as bridges, paths, gates or corridors are seen among them.
distinction: The overall emphasis is on the open waterside scene being defined and given visual focus, rather than on identifiable site-layout relationships of buildings placed on slopes or platforms and distributed along the bank.

evidence: Center-right, beneath the trees: by the water, a wooden platform, railing and part of a building body are visible, their upper part screened by tree canopy and branches, with only partial outlines exposed. | Right rock slope: a rock wall and slope rocks stand close to and half-enclose the wooden structure, forming front-to-back layers of rock and trees, building and water. | Lower-left water: a small boat and figures travel independently on the water; no clear bridge, path or bank connection is seen between them and the building at right.
distinction: Although the building is close to the rock slope and the water, the composition mainly uses the canopy and rock masses to screen and reveal parts of it; concealment and revelation forming layers is more dominant than mere terrain-responsive placement.

evidence: Right center: a multi-eaved pavilion and lower houses form a building group, the main pavilion rising high and the side houses extending horizontally toward the water at left. | Center to right waterside: the building group sits on a bank terrace above the water, backed by a hillside, with a large expanse of open water and mist in front; rows of trees extend along the waterside. | Right-center trees and lower part of the buildings: some trees screen the lower storeys of the houses, but the main pavilion's roof, the layers of its platform base, and the building outlines extending along the bank remain clearly visible.
distinction: The trees only partially screen the lower houses, and the relationship between the main pavilion and the bank terrace is clear; the whole more prominently shows the building group laid out according to the high waterside terrace and the mountain-foot terrain, rather than organizing the picture through concealment and revelation.

evidence: Right half: a robed figure stands in front of a white elephant in the center, with a child at lower right and an attendant holding a long pole at the right edge. | Left half: mostly mottled pinkish-brown ground, with no mountains and rocks, water surface, paths or architecture. | Right half, background: the ground around the figures and white elephant is open and empty, with no identifiable eaves, bridges, roads or tree-screening relationships.
distinction: The painting has no visible built elements; only the single visual focus formed by the figures and white elephant in the right half can be assigned to the closest "scenic accent" relationship, and it cannot be confirmed as built structures defining a scene.

evidence: Center-left: a tall, narrow rectangular frame is visible, with figures inside, its surroundings overlapping with dark outlines. | Lower center: several figures gather in front of the frame; no clear bridge, path or extending passage is seen. | Right and upper parts: outlines of varying darkness resembling branches and leaves or mountains and rocks press over the edges of the central frame, forming partial screening and front-to-back layers.
distinction: The identifiable relationship is mainly the partial screening and exposure of the central frame by tree-and-rock-like outlines, rather than a continuous enterable path or ford connection.

evidence: Right middle ground to foreground: the trunk and downward-extending branches of a thick pine screen the roof and wooden lattice of a small house behind them, with only part of the eaves and roof surface emerging between branches and leaves. | Right foreground: the small house is close to bank rocks and tree roots, its roof outline intermittently visible among branches and leaves, not becoming an independent focus in the center of the painting. | Lower center: a figure sits alone on a bank rock facing the water outlet at left; no continuous bridge deck or clear path is seen connecting him with the small house behind at right.
distinction: Although the small house is set against rocks and beside trees, the painting mainly uses the trunk and branches to screen and reveal the roof and lattice, forming layers of concealment and exposure, rather than a layout dominated by a base spreading along the slope bank.

evidence: Center: a bird stands on jagged rocks, the rock being the only solid supporting object in the painting; no roofs, walls, bridges, paths, doorways or other built signs are seen. | Surroundings: the rest of the painting is uniformly unpainted silk ground, with no mountains, watersides, paths or openings that could form spatial relationships with architecture. | Lower right: traces of seals are visible, belonging to additional content of the painting and not constituting evidence of built structures or spatial connectivity within the picture.
distinction: The primary category rests on the isolated rock and bird forming a single identifying motif that draws the picture together (scenic accent), whereas C2 requires layers of screening and exposure of built structures by mountains, rocks and trees, and here no built elements are concealed or revealed.

evidence: Right semicircular painting, lower right: a dark table and seating are visible, with figures active around them; apart from this, no building, wall, bridge or path outlines are seen. | Right semicircular painting, upper left to center: a large broad-leaved plant occupies the background, its leaves extending above the figures and table, forming partial screening and front-to-back layers. | Right semicircular painting, remaining background: a large area of the background is left unpainted; no identifiable mountains and rocks, watersides or terrain undulations are seen, making it hard to judge the relationship between built structures and natural terrain.
distinction: The sense of screening in the painting comes mainly from the broad-leaved plant, and no house is seen screened or revealed by trees; if the table arrangement is regarded as artificial, it can only count as a placement relationship, so it is assigned to C2 as the closest match for a screening composition.

evidence: Lower right: the roof, eaves and part of the walls of a house emerge from among trees and rocks, its outline identifiable. | Right middle-lower: foreground pine branches and slope rocks screen the left edge and lower part of the house, whose roof and walls are revealed from behind branches and leaves, forming concealment-and-revelation layers. | Center to left: misty mountain masses and foreground trees and rocks form an open background, making the house at lower right appear hidden among trees and rocks.
distinction: The house's main compositional role is to be screened by trees and rocks and partly revealed in layers, rather than being judged as terrain-responsive building solely from its base attached to a slope bank.

evidence: Right middle-lower, among the woods: a roof ridge and eaves partly emerge from the trees, the main body of the building screened by trees in front and behind and by slope rocks. | Foot of the slope below the central main peak: the towering mountain mass and slope foot overlap in layers, with the built structures located in the woods below, forming layered space surrounded by natural scenery. | Foreground miscellaneous trees and slope bank: foreground trees form screening, exposing only part of the roof, suggesting the hidden layer in which the built structures lie.
distinction: Although the buildings are adjacent to the mountain form and slope foot, the painting more prominently shows the layers of screening and exposure of roofs and eaves by trees, rather than a clear layout on platforms or according to the slope.

evidence: Whole scroll: the main subject is a procession of figures in outline style unfolding amid clouds, lacking identifiable mountains and rocks, water flows or architecture. | Center and both sides: figures, canopies and banners are arranged continuously across the width; no bridges, paths, corridors, gates or fords or other movement entities are seen.
distinction: The painting has no clear built structures or landscape, and only the procession of figures presents a continuous lateral movement relationship, closer than the other categories to the spatial organization of access to secluded settings.

evidence: Left to center-left: an old gnarled tree grows from among slope rocks, its trunk and branches extending upward and to the right, dense branches and leaves overlapping the rocks below, forming layers of front-to-back screening. | Right half and upper part: the right side and upper part of the painting are largely unpainted, with only a flying bird at upper right, forming an opening-and-closing contrast with the density of trees and rocks at left. | Lower-left edge: diagonally oriented slope bank or rock-surface textures are visible, but no clearly identifiable roofs, walls, bridges, gates or path facilities are seen.
distinction: The trees and rocks at left are the most striking visual focus of the painting, close to the defining-scene role of C3; but identifiable built structures as the scenic marker are lacking, so it is assigned to C2 based on the screening-and-revelation layers formed by trees and rocks.

evidence: Right painting, center-left: an old man holding a staff and a smaller figure are visible, with several monkeys and apes around them, against an ochre blank ground. | Right painting, surroundings: no identifiable built structures or landscape elements such as houses, roofs, walls, bridges, paths, mountains and rocks or water surfaces are seen in the picture. | Right painting, lower part: figures and monkeys are grouped together, with no terrain, shoreline or trees forming placement, screening or passage relationships around them.
distinction: The painting lacks relationships between built structures and landscape; C3 is assigned only as the closest category because the group of figures is the only visible focal point, not because built structures define a scene.

evidence: Upper middle of the right circular painting: the roof and eaves emerge from beneath a dense canopy; the upper part of the building is partly screened by branches and leaves. | Slightly right of center in the right circular painting: inside an open pavilion, figures in white robes sit side by side; the interior space and the exterior trees and rocks form a front-to-back layering. | Foreground of the right circular painting: foreground rocks and tree trunks block the lower part of the building and its base; the building appears behind the rocks and trees.
distinction: Although the building may be regarded as a viewing spot, the painting mainly uses the canopy and foreground rocks to screen and reveal the roof and open facade, creating front-to-back layering, rather than using the building to identify a particular peak-and-water scene.

evidence: Left and upper parts: at the left edge of the painting stands a thick-trunked willow whose hanging branches cover a large area of blank space above, forming a natural frame at the painting's left boundary | Lower right, near foreground: two barefoot men stand one behind the other on open flat ground, their bodies turned toward the space beyond the right edge of the painting; the ground beneath their feet undulates slightly | Lower left to lower middle: in the low foreground are sloping rocks and low clumps of grass extending toward a gentle slope in the middle, forming passable shallow, gentle terrain
distinction: No buildings are visible in the painting; the figures move along the foreground slope and past the tree toward the space beyond the painting, presenting a spatial relationship of traveling and passage rather than buildings identifying a scene, so C4 is taken as the closest category.

evidence: Upper part of the painting: several columns of calligraphic inscription occupy the upper area, below which is a large area of blank silk; no images of mountains and rocks, water surface, or buildings are visible. | Lower right to upper right: a branch of white plum extends diagonally upward from the lower right, its blossoms sparse, contrasting with the large blank area of silk. | Throughout: apart from the plum branch, blossoms, and inscription, no clues to built elements or movement are visible, such as roofs, eaves, walls, bridges, paths, or fords.
distinction: The main category is taken from the possible role of the plum branch as a point of scenic placement and identification within the empty painting; although C2 could discuss concealment and revelation through overlapping branches, the painting has no built entity that could be screened.

evidence: Center and left of the right circular painting: figures, a table, a screen or tall wooden board, and utensils are visible, forming an indoor activity scene; no mountains and rocks, water surface, or mountain paths are visible. | Upper and left edges of the right circular painting: the screen/furniture overlaps front and back with the figures, forming indoor screening and layering, but the screening objects are not natural mountains and rocks or trees. | Left rectangular inscription leaf: the left half is calligraphic inscription and does not participate in the spatial organization within the right circular painting.
distinction: C2 is chosen only because the partial screening by the screen, furniture, and figures creates layering; the painting lacks landscape terrain, scenic identification, or discernible paths, and the other categories have even less direct basis.

evidence: Lower left to lower middle water area: a small boat carrying several people lies crosswise among lotus leaves; the figures at the bow and stern are posed differently, and the boat's direction of travel is visible on the water. | Left and upper parts: dense willows, sloping rocks, and darker groves occupy the painting; no discernible roofs, walls, bridges, or pavilions are visible. | Middle-right water surface: lotus leaves scatter from the near bank to the distant misty water, and the boat moves among them, forming a water space that can be entered further.
distinction: The relationship of entry and travel suggested by the boat moving through the lotus pond is closer to C4 than merely using a boat to identify a scene, but the painting lacks clear buildings, so the judgment is very weak.

evidence: Lower middle, slightly right: a figure with a staff walks along a path on a sloping bank, followed by a small attendant; the path extends from the near ground toward the upper right. | Middle right: a large tree with a thick, gnarled trunk stands beside the path; sloping rocks and shrubs beneath the tree flank the path and form its boundary. | Upper right near the waterside: behind the tree a low roof-like outline is faintly visible, partly hidden by branches and trunks, its form difficult to confirm.
distinction: The clearest relationship in the painting is the approach and movement of entry formed by the path and the traveling figures, rather than trees and rocks screening and revealing a roof to create a scene; the screening and revelation is only local and the evidence is vague.

evidence: Center: two birds perch among bamboo branches; bamboo leaves and slender branches overlap from the front and around them, partly screening their bodies. | Throughout: the painting is composed of bamboo stalks, bamboo leaves, and birds in multiple layers of front-to-back relationships; the screening and revealing by branches and leaves forms local spatial layering. | Upper right: vertical bamboo stalks and dense leaves overlap each other; no architectural components, mountains and rocks, or water bodies are visible.
distinction: The painting has no built elements and no clear scenic spot; only the layered bamboo leaves create local concealment and revelation of the birds, so it is closer to the concealment-and-revelation layering of C2 than to "scenic accentuation."

evidence: Right half of the painting: two water birds are placed on a blank ground color; no discernible mountains and rocks, water surface, or buildings are visible around them. | Left half of the painting: mainly vertical columns of calligraphy; no buildings, bridges, paths, or landscape scenery are visible. | Overall: the painting consists of calligraphy juxtaposed with a flower-and-bird-type subject, lacking any verifiable relationship between built elements and landscape space.
distinction: No built elements are visible; C3 is taken only as the weakest nearby category in which the subject forms a focus; no clear competing relationship involving built elements exists.

evidence: Center, slightly right: the roof, eaves, and open eave corridor of a thatched hut emerge beneath the canopy; the building itself is partly screened by branches and leaves. | Left to center: a thick tree trunk extends diagonally upward from the left, and a dense canopy spreads across above the hut, forming screening layers front-to-back and above-and-below.
distinction: The hut mainly relies on the screening and revealing of the canopy's branches and leaves to form spatial layering, rather than being placed according to elevation conditions such as slopes, terraces, or watersides, so it is closer to C2 than to C1.

evidence: Center of the right painting: several figures and a lion-shaped auspicious beast are visible; the figures overlap each other, and the background is flat brown; no mountains and rocks, watersides, or trees are visible. | Right part of the right painting: an attendant faces the central figure in an approaching or responding posture, but no discernible passage clues such as roads, bridges, or doorways are visible. | Throughout the right painting: no clear built elements of any kind are found, such as roofs, walls, platforms, bridges, or paths.
distinction: The central group of figures can barely be regarded as the painting's visual focus, and thus is closer to scenic accentuation; but there are no buildings or landscape, nor the enterable paths required by C4, so both categories lack a basis for holding.

evidence: Center, slightly right: a black bird perches in profile on a horizontally extending dead branch, becoming the most striking single object in the painting. | Lower left to left side: branches, leaves, and slope-rock-like ink masses extend from the lower left, supporting the branch on which the bird perches and forming an identified local scene. | Throughout: no visible artificial built elements or movement clues such as houses, walls, bridges, roads, or doorways appear in the painting.
distinction: Here an isolated perched bird identifies the scene at the branch tip, rather than using buildings or roofs screened among trees to form layering; the painting actually has no built elements.

evidence: Middle-left water surface: a red multi-decked painted boat lies in an open area of water, its structure clear, becoming the visual center and marker of this stretch of waterscape. | Land on the left and right sides of the painting: red pavilions, canopies, and ceremonial processions are scattered among the mountains, rocks, and trees, strikingly marking the nodes of gathering and activity of the figures. | Overall composition: the bright red built structures contrast with the pale landscape background, identifying different scene sections and scenery within the long scroll.
distinction: Although the built structures are located by the water or on land, their main role is to identify scene nodes and draw the eye through striking form and color, rather than to emphasize a terrain-responsive correspondence with slopes and banks.

evidence: Middle-right of the right circular leaf: a group of multi-courtyard roofs and pavilions is visible, with clear eaves and roof ridges, spread out along the right edge of the painting. | Middle-left of the right circular leaf: dense groves stand in front of the buildings, their branches and leaves screening part of the eaves and walls, so that the buildings appear half hidden and half revealed. | Background and lower part of the right circular leaf: buildings and groves overlap front and back, surrounded by dense wavy lines, but no clear bridges, paths, or doorways leading to the buildings are visible.
distinction: The main reason is that the buildings are partly screened by foreground groves and revealed layer by layer, rather than merely identifying a landscape by a striking position.

evidence: Middle, slightly right of the painting: a dragonfly rests on branches and leaves; part of its body is screened by a leaf in front, with only its head and tail exposed beyond the leaf edge | Lower left to center: a plant with flower buds extends upward from the lower left, its leaves interlocking to form overlapping front-to-back layers | Lower right: a red seal is in the lower right corner of the painting, surrounded by a large area of plain ground color, with no discernible elements such as buildings, bridges, paths, or water surface
distinction: The painting shows only insects and plants with leaves; leaves partly screen the insect, forming front-to-back layering between plant and insect; but there is no landscape of peaks, waterside, or valley mouth, nor built elements identifying a scene, so it is assigned to C2 according to the visible relationship of screening and revealing, rather than to C3.

evidence: Center: the main subject of the painting is a fully opened purplish-red blossom with layered petals; below it green stems and leaves extend to both sides. | Entire background: the background is plain silk; no mountains, watersides, slopes, terraces, paths, bridges, houses, or other scenery that could be used to judge spatial relationships involving built elements is visible. | Upper right: a red square seal is in the upper right corner, a mark on the painting that does not form any discernible spatial relationship of built elements or scenery.
distinction: The painting has only a floral subject and a plain ground, with no discernible relationship between built elements and landscape; compared with the other categories, the isolated flower as a single visual focus has a slight "accentuation"-like focusing effect, but it is not a building accent.

evidence: Right half of the painting: the image is a group portrait: a long-bearded seated figure and surrounding figures in the lower middle, with another smaller cloud-riding figure above, against a basically blank background. | Lower middle of the right half of the painting: the group of figures is concentrated slightly below center, forming a single visual focus; no discernible built elements or landscape elements such as buildings, mountains and rocks, water surface, bridges, or paths are visible.
distinction: There are no clear built elements; the main category is taken only from the central convergence formed by the group of figures; no visible evidence exists for screening and revelation, paths, or terrain-responsive relationships.

evidence: Right painting: on a flat gold ground only an old man and three boys are visible; there are no mountains and rocks, water surface, trees, or architectural components around them. | Center of the right painting: the figures move around a long object; no visible roofs, walls, bridges, paths, or clear entrances appear in the painting. | Background of the right painting: the background remains largely blank, showing no terrain elevation, shoreline, or discernible screening layers.
distinction: The painting has no direct evidence of a relationship between built elements and landscape; C3 is chosen only to place the isolated figure scene on the right into the weakest sense of "scenic accentuation," while the terrain arrangement, concealment-and-revelation layers, or movement clues on which C1, C2, and C4 depend are all invisible.

evidence: Right half of the painting: an animal lies in profile on a ground with fibrous texture; no mountains and rocks, water surface, trees, or buildings are visible around it. | Left half and both side edges of the painting: multiple columns of inscription and red seals are visible, belonging to inscriptions and seals and not constituting built elements or landscape space within the painting. | Throughout: no discernible built elements such as roofs, walls, bridges, paths, doors, or platforms.
distinction: The painting lacks a relationship between built elements and landscape; C3 is closest to scenic accentuation only because of the relationship between the isolated subject and the open ground, not because buildings actually play an accenting role.

evidence: Middle ground: a carved-panel wooden railing runs across the painting, extending continuously along the lower edge of the flowers and trees behind it, separating the flat ground where the foreground figures are from the flower garden behind. | Behind the railing, slightly right: a white crane stands among the flowers and trees; flowers, leaves, and the crane's body appear above the upper edge of the railing, and front-to-back layers are visible. | Foreground: figures sit scattered on the flat ground in front of the railing; no bridges, paths, doorways, or gaps in the railing leading to the rear are visible.
distinction: The railing is a boundary laid out continuously along the edge of the flower garden, mainly serving to divide and extend with the site, rather than using an independent building to identify a particular landscape scenic spot.

evidence: Left middle ground: a low wooden railing extends horizontally from the left and is interrupted in the center by a huge rock. | Center to right: large perforated rocks and broad-leaved plants such as banana occupy the main area, forming overlapping front-to-back screening. | Foreground and lower part: many infants are scattered around the rocks; no discernible entry clues such as bridges, paths, doors, or corridors are visible.
distinction: C2 relies on the local screening of the wooden railing by rocks and banana plants to form concealment-and-revelation layers; C1 would require a visible base laid out according to terrain such as slopes, terraces, or watersides, which is not seen here.

evidence: Junction of mountain foot and waterside from the middle to the right section: below the layered blue-green peaks, at low points close to the water, small dark dotted structures are scattered, suspected to be houses, far smaller in scale than the mountains, mostly located at slope feet or where the shoreline turns. | Left-middle broad water surface: a large expanse of blue-green water and pale-ink sandbars spread horizontally; the mountains rise and fall along the bank, and no clearly discernible roads, bridges, or doorways are visible. | Between the towering peaks on the right: house-like small dots are distributed at low points at the mountain foot and among the valleys, showing no clear concealment-and-revelation layers formed by front-to-back screening by trees or rocks.
distinction: The house-like structures are mainly scattered according to terrain at slope feet and low waterside points, lacking clear layering created by screening from trees, mountains, and rocks, so they are closer to terrain-responsive placement than to concealment and revelation forming a scene.

evidence: Hall and pavilion upper middle, slightly left: the left side and upper edge of the blue-green roof, red lattice doors, and platform are covered by a dense canopy; the hall body emerges from among the branches and leaves. | Lower-left corridor pavilion: red pillars, railings, and the figures inside are only partly exposed; the roof and eave corners are partly screened by tree trunks, branches and leaves, and rocks. | Right courtyard: the right side is more open, contrasting with the half-hidden buildings in the tree shadows on the left through concealment and revelation.
distinction: The painting mainly uses the canopy to partly screen and reveal the hall, pavilion, and corridor pavilion to form layering; although the steps and railings suggest passage, they do not form an entry path running through the entire painting.

evidence: Rock platform center, slightly right: a small pavilion sits on a relatively flat rock platform, its base laid out following the turn of the rocky slope. | Upper right to middle right: cliff walls and bamboo branches enclose from above; the building is close against the rock body and joins with the slope below it as one.
distinction: The building is indeed adjacent to bamboo and rocks, but the painting mainly presents it as positioned on the rock platform and placed according to the slope; no prominent effect of organizing layers through clear screening and revealing is visible.

evidence: Left leaf: a blank pink album leaf; no painting elements such as landscape, buildings, or paths are visible. | Center of the right painting: several figures move around a long table/desk, along with small figures and a monkey, forming the visual center of the painting, but no houses, eaves, or walls are visible. | Background of the right painting: the background is basically plain silk; no mountains and rocks, water surface, sloping banks, bridges, paths, or discernible relationship between built elements and natural terrain is visible.
distinction: It can only barely be assigned to scenic accentuation based on the central focused form of the figures and the long desk on the right; the painting has no verifiable relationship between buildings and landscape, and therefore does not support explanations based on terrain, concealment and revelation, or access to secluded settings.

evidence: Lower left: a figure stands in the low-bank foreground facing the water surface to the right; no built components such as roofs, walls, or thresholds are visible around them. | Left middle to center: a large tree and rocky bank occupy the left side; no discernible building outline appears between the trees and rocks; the right side turns into open water ripples. | Right side and distant view: the water surface unfolds through ripples and unpainted space, with faint ink mountain shadows in the distance; no bridges, paths, corridors, or enterable building entities appear.
distinction: The painting forms a single viewing spot through the figure at the bank and the open water surface, closer to scenic accentuation; but without bridges, paths, or building entrances, it cannot form the entry relationship of access to secluded settings.

evidence: Central horizontal scene: figures and tables are visible scattered in groups among trees and rocks; no clear architectural components such as roofs, walls, doors, or windows are visible. | Center and slightly right: canopies, sloping rocks, figures, and tables overlap front and back, forming local screening and revealing, but those screened are mainly figures and furniture. | Middle section of the painting: no discernible entry clues such as bridges, paths, doorways, or corridors are visible; the spatial organization mainly unfolds through trees, rocks, and groups of figures.
distinction: The visible concealment-and-revelation layers are mainly between trees and rocks and the figures and tables, not buildings identifying a scene, so C2 is closer than C3.

evidence: Entire painting: mainly grape branches and leaves, clusters of fruit, and insects; no built elements or landscape elements such as buildings, mountains, water surface, or paths are visible. | Center and upper left: leaves overlap front and back and screen each other; the upper part of the fruit clusters is partly screened by leaves, forming a visible relationship of concealment and revelation. | Lower right and near the leaf surfaces: small insects rest on leaf surfaces or in blank areas, small in size and adjacent to the foliage.
distinction: The painting mainly shows the screening layers of plant branches and leaves over fruit clusters and insects, rather than buildings identifying a particular landscape, so C2 is closer than C3.

evidence: Upper left to middle of the right painting: a thick pine branch extends diagonally from the upper left and covers the upper space, forming front-to-back screening between the branches and leaves and the figures below. | Lower center of the right painting: a figure half leans beside trees and rocks, the body partly covered by pine branches and rocks; no discernible built structures such as roofs, walls, doors, windows, bridges, or paths are visible.
distinction: The discernible spatial relationship in the painting is mainly the screening layers of trees and rocks over the figure, rather than buildings identifying a specific scene; C3 lacks direct evidence of built elements serving as markers of a scenic spot.

evidence: Entire painting: the whole long scroll consists of ink-written text and red seals; no discernible built elements such as roofs, walls, beams and columns, or bridges and paths are visible. | Middle and both sides of the painting: no readable positional or screening relationships between mountains, slopes and terraces, watersides, and buildings are visible. | Whole scroll: the composition is dominated by columns of written characters and blank paper space; there are no verifiable entry paths, bridge crossings, or framed concealment-and-revelation layers.
distinction: The painting has no clear relationship between built elements and landscape space, and cannot be argued on the basis of terrain responsiveness, screening and revelation, or access to secluded settings; C3 is only a provisional classification under forced choice, and no closer alternative explanation exists.

evidence: Center of the right leaf: a figure sits cross-legged at the center of the painting, surrounded on all sides by groups of green rock-and-tree-like forms that enclose and screen. | Beside the figure on the left of the right leaf: only a small red-and-white object is in front and to the left of the figure, small in form and unclear in detail, and no built components such as roofs, walls, or doorways can be identified. | Throughout the right leaf: no discernible travel routes such as bridges, paths, corridors, doors, or fords are visible, nor any clear correspondence between building sites and mountain forms or watersides.
distinction: The painting is closest to concealment-and-revelation layering formed by the enclosure of natural objects; compared with C3, in which a subject identifies a scene, here there are no discernible built elements serving as scene markers.

evidence: Upper center: a large bird of prey spreads its wings as if diving, surrounded by dark space. | Lower half: dark, gnarled branches occupy the foreground, forming a relation of front-to-back occlusion with the main subject above. | Whole painting: no identifiable built elements such as buildings, bridges, roads, gateways, or platforms are visible.
distinction: What the painting most closely presents is a layering of revelation and occlusion between the dark branches and the main subject, rather than built elements identifying a particular scene.

evidence: Left leaf: a patterned blank paper surface, with no spatial elements such as landscape, architecture, or paths visible. | Right leaf, group of figures: the figures and banner stand on a flat gold ground, with no identifiable mountains and rocks, water surface, trees, or buildings around them. | Right leaf, full extent: no buildings, bridges, gates, roads, or terrain undulation are visible, and no specific spatial relationship between built elements and landscape can be identified.
distinction: The painting contains only a group of figures with banners and lacks clear evidence of architecture corresponding to landscape or of a path leading in; it can only be assigned by closest approximation on the basis of the focal character of the figure group, rather than true scenic accentuation.

evidence: Upper right to the top ridge: a small pavilion-like structure stands high on the ridge, between the rock face and the pines, near the upper edge of the painting. | Upper right slope and distant view: this structure clings to the raised rock peak and pine grove and becomes the visual anchor of this peak position; no clear bridge, path, or continuous traversable route is visible.
distinction: Although the structure adjoins the pines and is slightly partially screened, its main relationship is standing on the ridge and identifying the mountain scene there, rather than organizing spatial layering through concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower left: a seated figure is on a dark sloping rock at the corner of the painting. | Center-right: a broad-leaved plant spreads out on its own, with large areas of unpainted space around it. | Above and below: several insects are scattered above and below the plant, forming a viewing focus centered on the plant and the figure.
distinction: The painting forms a scenic-accent-like viewing focus through the figure, plant, and insects, but lacks an architectural entity as a basis for scenic accentuation, so it can only be assigned by closest approximation; by comparison, there is no clear relation of terrain-responsive building.

evidence: Right half, slightly below center: an open small hut or pavilion stands among dense woods, its roof and eaves partly hidden by foliage and branches above and to the sides. | Around the hut: thick trunks and dense canopy surround the building from above and both sides, forming a concealment-and-revelation relation in which foreground foliage, the building, and deep woodland shadows overlap.
distinction: The primary category rests on the screening and revealing of the building by canopy and trunks, forming woodland layers; the painting shows no clear sign of a building site unfolding according to mountain forms, slopes, terraces, or waterside, so C1 fits less closely than C2.

evidence: Right leaf, beneath the willow clump at the left of the painting: willow branches and trunks hang densely, pressing over the left bank; beneath the trees are tiny figures or livestock and dark patches, partly hidden by branches and leaves, with no confirmable roof or wall visible. | Right leaf, center to right: the water surface and shoreline unfold to the right, forming a layer of one hidden and one revealed in relation to the left-bank tree shade; no clear bridge, path, or doorway can be followed.
distinction: The concealment-and-revelation relation of tree shade to the screened subject is relatively clear, so it is closer to concealment and revelation; but it lacks a confirmable architectural entity, and scenic accentuation is only a secondary option.

evidence: Center-left: a long-tailed pheasant perches on a branch, its front body and tail feathers partly hidden by foreground leaves, forming a front-to-back occlusion layer. | Upper right and above: several butterflies flutter above branches, leaves, and flowers, while branches and leaves hang down from above and intermittently screen the background. | Lower right and lower left: hanging branches and leaves and white flowers are distributed along the edges of the painting, forming intermittent revelation and screening around the bird's body.
distinction: No built elements are visible anywhere in the painting; what is mainly visible is the organization of concealment and revelation of the bird's body by branches and leaves; it is therefore closer to the layered relation of concealment and revelation than to identifying a scene by means of architecture.

evidence: Center-right: mountains and dense woods enclose a woodland clearing where several figures gather around a table, forming the visual center of the painting. | Lower center to right: a low railing or terrace edge lies across the foreground, marking the edge of the platform where the gathering takes place. | Above and on both sides: ridges and tree canopy embrace the scene, the clearing opens toward the rear, and the gathering point corresponds to the opening and closing relation of the mountain forest.
distinction: Although the canopy encloses the gathering place, no layered concealment and revelation in which a building mass is clearly screened and then disclosed is visible; the railing or terrace edge mainly designates the woodland clearing as a gathering point.

evidence: Left half to center: a thick old tree grows from a rocky slope, its branches extending up and to the right, together framing an open space in the middle ground with the rock mass on the left. | Slightly below center: a figure holding a long staff stands on low, flat ground, surrounded by tree roots, grass, and unpainted space; no identifiable built elements such as roofs, walls, doors and windows, or bridges and paths are visible. | Right side and above: pale-ink mountain shadows and extensive unpainted space extend toward the upper right, forming an opening-and-closing relation with the trees and rocks.
distinction: The figure serves mainly as a visual anchor within the empty scene of trees and rocks, rather than as a clue to travel along an identifiable path toward built elements.

evidence: Right leaf, among the trees and rocks at the foot of the mountain at lower left: the low roof and open outline of a small pavilion or hut are visible where the mountain rock meets the waterside. | Right leaf, center to right: the towering main peak and the large expanse of unpainted water surface at the right form a strong opening and closing, and the pavilion stands at the point where the mountain rock turns toward the water.
distinction: Although the pavilion is placed against the rocky bank, its main role is to point out the scene of the open waterside face, rather than merely to show arrangement conforming to a slope or terrace.

evidence: Left side to lower left: tall trees and sloping rocks flank the bank, forming a foreground bank of woodland and rock; no clear architectural components such as roofs, walls, or column bases are visible on the bank. | Center to right: the water surface is open, and the far bank unfolds horizontally in pale ink, with the pictorial space opening into a large area of unpainted space at the right. | Right-center water: a small boat sits on the open water, and the boat itself is the only identifiable man-made scenic element in the painting; around it no dock, bridge, or path connects to the shoreline.
distinction: The lone boat forms a visual anchor on the open water, but no accessible route connecting a bridge, path, or ferry crossing to built elements on the bank is visible, so it is closer to scenic accentuation than to access to secluded settings.

evidence: Center: a solanaceous plant grows vertically, its deep purple fruits and pale purple flowers showing among the leaves, forming the single main focus of the painting. | Lower left: a clump of leafy vegetables spreads close to the ground, forming front-to-back and high-to-low relations with the tall central plant. | Full extent: on the earth-yellow ground, no architecture, mountains and rocks, water body, bridges and paths, or identifiable building site is visible.
distinction: The central plant forms a single focus, closer to scenic-accent-like emphasis; but the occlusion among leaves is only the natural layering of the plant, with no concealment-and-revelation relation involving architecture.

evidence: Right side of the painting, slightly toward the lower left, beneath the grove: the roof and eaves of a house are half revealed behind trunks and branches, with the lower part of the building screened by trees. | Around the house and in the foreground: multiple trees are staggered front and back, their branches, leaves, and trunks forming screening layers so that the house is only partially revealed. | The open area to the right of the house: the grove meets the open area at the right, constituting a spatial layer in which the house is first screened by trees and then revealed.
distinction: The main cause is the clear screening and half-revelation of the house by the grove, rather than merely the siting relation of the house clinging to a sloping bank.

evidence: Right side to above: a large tree extends diagonally from the right bank, its dense branches and leaves covering the upper part of the painting and forming a foreground frame. | Lower left to below: several small boats are moored together on the water, one of them with a rounded canopy and sail-like screening, with figures active on board. | Center-left water: outside the boat group are a large expanse of pale-ink water and mist, with the distant shoreline faintly visible, and the space appears open.
distinction: The boat group mainly identifies the nearby waterscape through its position near the waterside and through the figures' activity; no bridge, path, or continuous shoreline organizes it into a clear entry route or ferry-crossing relation.

evidence: Whole scroll: on a flat blank ground, figures, ridden beasts, and inscriptions are arranged in continuous sequence; no identifiable buildings, bridges, gates, roads, or waterside architecture are visible. | Middle portions of each section: figures and mounts are juxtaposed horizontally, with no visible path connections, architectural screening, or front-to-back layering among them. | Background and around the figures: the background is essentially devoid of natural scenery such as mountains and rocks, woodland, or water surface, and the space is mainly separated by isolated figures and inscriptions.
distinction: The visible space is a horizontal arrangement of figures and inscriptions, lacking evidence of architecture sited according to terrain, concealment and revelation forming a scene, or a path leading into seclusion; only isolated marker-like elements come close to scenic accentuation.

evidence: Center-right: a sloping rock or thick tree trunk tilts up to the right, with branches and leaves extending from its upper right end into the unpainted space, forming a front-to-back occlusion relation. | Lower left: several slender branch-like lines extend downward; no architectural components or bridges and paths are visible. | Upper right and center-left: birds skim through the unpainted space; the painting forms a small natural scene of trees, rocks, and birds, with no identifiable built traces such as roofs, wall surfaces, or doors and windows.
distinction: The painting lacks architecture to identify the scene, but the layering of concealment and revelation of the sloping rock and branches is relatively visible; therefore, absent evidence of built elements, it is closer to C2, forming a scene through concealment and revelation by natural objects, than to C3, identifying a scene by architecture.

evidence: Lower left to lower center: an open pavilion-style building with a front porch and railing stands at the foot of a rocky slope, its base resting on the rock surface, adjacent to the rock face on the left and open on the right. | Left side to above the pavilion roof: a thick pine rises diagonally from among the rocks on the left, its canopy spreading across and covering above the building, with some branches and leaves approaching the eaves. | Right side and distant view: the open face of the pavilion looks toward the open area at the right and the distant peaks; no clear bridge, path, or continuous touring route leading in is visible in the painting.
distinction: Although the pine shade partially screens the roof, the main building mass and its base are directly arranged in conformity with the rocky slope and the open side, and terrain support is more dominant than layering through concealment and revelation.

evidence: Between the grove and rock face at the foot of the mountain at center-left: a dark block-like outline is visible, partly screened by the rock mass above and trees on both sides, with no clear eaves or walls visible. | Foreground to the left of the middle ground: sloping rocks and trees are layered, forming a spatial layering of front-and-back screening and revelation of a corner; the right side leaves a relatively open landscape surface.
distinction: Although this dark outline may be placed against the rock face at the foot of the mountain, the painting more clearly presents the relation of trees and rocks half screening and half revealing it, so it is closer to concealment and revelation than to terrain-responsive layout.

evidence: Upper left to center: thick, withered branches extend diagonally across the upper half of the painting, forming the main framing and screening. | Right side, middle to lower part: a large rocky slope enters the painting from the right edge, enclosing a low space backed by a rock face. | Lower center, slightly right: a small child and two sheep are among the trees and rocks; no clear built elements such as roofs, walls, bridges and paths, or gateways are visible in the painting.
distinction: Although trees and rocks form an enclosure and partial screening, no identifiable architecture forms a scene through concealment and revelation; the child and sheep more resemble identifying a scene beneath the trees beside the rocks.

evidence: Whole painting: the painting is a round fan surface on which only vertically written ink-brush characters are visible; no pictorial elements such as mountain masses, water surface, trees, or architecture are visible. | Lower left: one seal, vermilion red, stamped below the writing, a flat imprint rather than built elements or landscape within the painting. | Surroundings and center of the painting: beyond the writing is plain blank paper; no identifiable spatial clues such as sloping terraces, shorelines, paths, bridges, or eaves are visible.
distinction: The painting contains only calligraphy and seals, with no visible landscape or built-element relations from which to judge; in the forced four-way choice, C3 is taken as the closest classification, but it equally lacks the visible scenery required for architectural scenic accentuation.

evidence: Right-hand painted panel: a saddled horse stands facing left, with a person leading it on the right; the figure and horse form the only substantive focus of the painting. | Background of the right-hand painted panel: around the horse and figure is a flatly colored brown space; no mountain forms, water body, trees, architecture, bridges or paths, or discernible terrain undulation are seen. | Left-hand painted panel: inscription text and a red seal are visible, but there are no architectural or movement-through-the-landscape spatial clues connected with the figure or horse.
distinction: The painting has no discernible paths, bridges or crossings, or relations of entry; the isolated saddled horse at most serves as a visual resting point in a blank background, closer to scenic accentuation than to access to secluded settings.

evidence: Among the trees slightly right of the middle ground: a roof, eaves, and part of a wall surface are visible emerging from behind canopy and trunks, and the building is not fully revealed. | In front of and behind the middle-ground grove: trunks, branches, and leaves lie in front of the building, and the roof outline appears intermittently through gaps in the trees, forming a layer of seeing a house within the woods. | Lower foreground: a bridge, path, and figures' activity are visible below, but there is no continuous identifiable path connection between them and the middle-ground building.
distinction: The roof and wall surface screened and revealed by the grove constitute the main spatial layer; although the foreground bridge and path suggest entry, their connection with the building is unclear, so it is less direct than concealment and revelation forming a scene.

evidence: Lower-left foreground: on a gently sloping rock terrace beneath the canopy, there is a small stopping point with a group of figures facing the waterfall to the right; no clear roof or column grid is visible. | Center-right: several streams of waterfall fall among dark rock faces, and the rocks and woodland above enclose a clear scenic opening. | Left half to center: tall woodland and sloping rocks form a dark area in the left half, separating the foreground stopping point from the waterfall on the right and constituting a facing view.
distinction: The primary category emphasizes the scenic-accentuation relation in which the stopping point on the left directly faces the waterfall and identifies the waterfall-viewing scene; C1 mainly explains the rock terrace's accommodation to terrain and does not highlight this facing-view role.

evidence: Center-left: two birds perch among slender branches, with branches and leaves overlapping in front of and behind the birds' bodies, forming a partial screening layer. | Lower right and lower left: white flowers, bamboo leaves, and slender branches are visible; no roofs, walls, bridges, paths, or any clear built elements are visible. | Background: the background of the painting is mostly plain silk ground, with no mountains, waterside, or identifiable spatial entry depicted.
distinction: There are no built elements in the whole painting; the closest approximation to C2 can only be made on the basis of the concealment-and-revelation layer shown by the overlapping of branches and leaves with the birds' bodies; there is no confirmable architectural concealment-and-revelation or scene-entry relation.

evidence: Center to lower left: the painting shows a cluster of fruit with leaves; the branches and leaves extend diagonally in from the right and gather in the middle-left of the painting. | Slightly above center: a small bird perches on a branch, its head facing left, sharing a compact visual center with the fruit and leaves. | Right side and lower part: broad leaves overlap one another, and branches run diagonally through, their forms constituting the painting's main spatial layers; no buildings, bridges or paths, or landscape scenery are seen.
distinction: The painting has no buildings and no landscape setting; if classified only with difficulty, the branches, leaves and fruit gather into a single visual focus, which comes closer to the concentrating function of "pointing out one place" rather than forming layers of concealment and revelation through screening.

evidence: Center-left: the trunk and branches and leaves of a tall tree stand in front of the main hall, screening the base, beneath the eaves, and part of the roof surface; the roof and open hall are revealed through the canopy. | Left side: another canopy screens the eaves and steps of a side hall, leaving the building partly hidden behind the woodland. | Lower right: the grove at the right screens a section of wall extending to the right, forming a front-to-back screening layer of trees, wall, and mountain mass.
distinction: The segmented screening and revealing of roofs, beneath-eaves, and walls by woodland constitutes a clear layer of partitioned scenery, and explains the main compositional method better than the adjacency of building bases and walls to the mountain foot.

evidence: Center of the round painting in the right leaf: an old tree grows diagonally from a sloping rock, its withered branches extending in all directions, forming the most concentrated visual focus of the painting. | Lower part of the right leaf, left to center: pale sloping rocks meet dark tree roots and shadowed areas; no built traces such as roofs, eaves, wall surfaces, bridges, or paths are discernible. | Upper part and right side of the right leaf: the background opens toward the rear with pale-ink void and sparse branch tips, with no visible architectural outline or clearly traversable structure.
distinction: The painting mainly forms a focused scene through the old tree and sloping rock, rather than revealing architecture through woodland and mountain rocks or leading in through bridges and paths; because no built elements are visible, it can only be assigned by closest approximation according to the scenic-focus mode.

evidence: Left side to center-left: low earth slopes and stretches of grove are layered, the slope foot meets the water, and the canopy outline and unpainted water surface form an opening and closing | Right side: a thick-trunked large tree is rooted in a raised sloping bank, its exposed roots gripping the ground, its branches and leaves extending toward the top and center of the painting | Lower center, slightly right: in the open space between the grove and the sloping bank, a person sits on the ground facing the waterside on the left, very small in scale, becoming the anchor of the scene there
distinction: The painting identifies this waterside scene through the large tree, the sloping bank, and the small scenic figure in the open space, rather than presenting the layout of a building site according to mountain forms and sloping terraces; but there is no clear architecture, so it can only be assigned by closest approximation according to the overall spatial organization.

evidence: Right side, middle to lower part: a pine with gnarled branches occupies the right side, its canopy drooping downward and screening the area where the figures below are located, forming a clear concealment-and-revelation layer. | Lower part, slightly right: two figures are visible active in the tree shade, but no clearly identifiable built components such as roofs, walls, or gateways are visible. | Left side and center: the left side is a large area of pale-ink mountain mass and rock face; the central rock mass faces the canopy on the right, enclosing a relatively empty sloping-bank ground below.
distinction: The painting organizes space mainly through the screening and revealing of canopy and mountains and rocks, rather than identifying a particular scene with clear architecture; moreover, built elements themselves are not visible, so C2 is the closest provisional classification.

evidence: Lower-left water: a small boat with a sail sits on a large expanse of open water, its dark hull and sail forming a clear visual focus against the pale background, with no shoreline, bridges and paths, or architecture directly connected to it. | Center-left water: a low, flat tree islet stretches across the mist, its grove forming a cluster, with no identifiable architectural forms such as roofs or walls. | Upper right to center: distant mountains recede into the mist in layered pale ink, forming an open and deep background with the large expanse of unpainted water surface.
distinction: The small boat is only an isolated scenic element on the open water, with no visible entry connection linking it to bridges and paths, shorelines, or reachable built elements, so it is closer to scenic accentuation than to access to secluded settings.

evidence: Upper half of the painting: a large area of unpainted silk ground; no mountain forms, water surface, trees, or buildings are visible. | Lower part of the painting: several horses are scattered across open ground with no obvious undulation; no houses, roads, bridges, or identifiable building sites are visible. | Right side: there are vertical columns of text and seals, but the painting provides no visible evidence of a relationship between built elements and landscape.
distinction: The painting contains no built elements; only a group of horses forms a visual focus in an empty ground; there is no evidence of scenery formed through concealment and revelation, of siting according to the mountains, or of a path-based entry relationship.

evidence: Right section: mainly ink-wash orchid leaves and flowers with freely extended lines; no roof, wall, beam, or column architectural components are visible. | Middle to left section: several passages of inscriptions and red seals are distributed continuously, dominated by calligraphic text; no identifiable mountain and rock forms, water bodies, or path spaces are formed. | Whole work: in this horizontal handscroll, apart from orchid plants and inscribed characters, no bridges, gateways, sloping platforms, or other built elements or movement-through-the-landscape clues are visible.
distinction: The painting has no architectural scenic accents, nor any layering of concealment and revelation of buildings by mountains, rocks, and trees; it is only tentatively assigned to C3 because the orchid plants form a concentrated visual subject, rather than to C2, which emphasizes relationships of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Left to center: the hanging branches of several willow trees cover the eaves, corridor platforms, and windows, so that the building volumes are divided by branches and leaves and partially revealed. | The hall slightly left of center: figures inside the window and the space under the eaves are visible through the willow branches, forming a front-and-back layering between the front and rear of the building. | The waterside platform at the lower right of the building: the platform, wooden railing, and the external water surface meet, while the main building body is still framed by the foreground willows in defining the viewing layers.
distinction: The half-concealment and half-revelation of the roof, corridor platforms, and window interiors by the willows forms a scenic layering that runs through the painting, and is closer to the dominant expression than the mere siting of a waterside base according to the terrain.

evidence: Upper part: a large area of inscribed characters and seals occupies the upper half of the painting; no buildings or terrain are depicted. | Lower center: a colored bird perches on a flowering branch, the branch extending from the right side toward the left. | Background of the picture surface: apart from the flowering branch, the bird, and the inscriptions, the background is essentially left empty; no mountains and rocks, water bodies, bridge paths, or houses are identifiable.
distinction: The painting has no combination of built elements and landscape, only flowers, birds, and inscriptions; C3 is the closest match only because the overall organization in which an isolated bird-and-flower subject forms a visual focus is nearest to 'scenic accentuation,' and is not architectural scenic accentuation.

evidence: Lower center and left of the painting: three figures are located on open flat ground; the two on the left wear robes, the one on the right carries a load, and the figures' orientation and steps suggest movement forward along the ground. | Right side: a cluster of trees and rocks forms a foreground screen; among the tree gaps and behind them, no houses, eaves, walls, or other identifiable built elements are visible. | Upper background: distant mountains appear faintly in light ink; a large area of open ground lies before the mountains, with no identifiable platform bases, bridges, or building outlines.
distinction: The painting comes closest to access to secluded settings through the path relationship of figures moving forward along a forest clearing; scenic accentuation requires built elements to identify a specific scene, whereas here identifiable buildings are lacking.

evidence: From the middle left to the lower left: several multi-eaved pavilions and enclosing walls are divided into several levels of terraces; the platform bases rise and fall with the mountain slope, and the building bodies unfold upward in layers along the slope. | Upper-left mountain ridge: a smaller group of red-roofed buildings is set among the ridge turn and the tree clusters, its front and rear positions rising or receding with the mountain configuration. | Woodland terrace at the middle right: a pavilion stands on a relatively flat terrace at the mountain foot, backed by the slope foot and facing the open ground below, its position conforming to the terrain.
distinction: The main pavilion group, with its platform bases unfolding in layers along the mountain slope, is the main axis of the whole painting; although bridges, paths, and boats in the foreground suggest movement through the landscape, the relationship of continuous entry into the main pavilions is less clear than the siting of terraces according to the slope.

evidence: Left mountainside: deep brown roofs and eave lines emerge from among the blue-green tree clusters and rock masses, and the main building bodies are largely obscured. | Left-center slope: lower down, roof shadows and overlapping trees and rocks are also visible, and the buildings show a layering of partial appearance and concealment. | Right water surface and distant mountains: the right half is open water and distant peaks; no clear bridge path connecting to the buildings on the left is visible.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited according to the mountains, the painting mainly forms layering through roofs concealed and revealed by trees and rocks, and thus is closer to concealment and revelation forming a scene than to mere disposition according to the terrain.

evidence: Whole painting: the handscroll unfolds horizontally with mountains and rocks, slopes, and tree clusters; groups of figures and birds and animals are scattered among them, and no clear traces of built elements such as roofs, walls, or platform bases are visible. | Center to right section: the slopes form an open surface, and several groups of figures are distributed along the terrain; no identifiable entry connections such as bridges, paths, gates, or corridors are visible. | Left and right ends: trees and rocks are dense and partially obscure the figures and animals, but the visible obscuring elements are all natural scenery, and no architectural components are exposed.
distinction: Although the screening by trees and rocks forms local concealment and revelation, only natural scenery is seen obscuring the figures, with no architectural components exposed; overall it is closer to a spatial organization unfolded by terrain than to concealment and revelation forming a built scene.

evidence: Slightly below center: an unfurled lotus leaf supports a crab, becoming the point where the painting's line of sight settles; around it, light ink expresses the openness of a water surface or muddy ground. | Left side: several leafy plants extend diagonally into the painting from the left, the direction of their stems, leaves, and flower spikes pointing toward the central lotus leaf and crab. | Lower right: in the lower right, the outlines of a muddy bank or rocks depicted in light ink meet the edge of the lotus leaf, setting off the location of the central subject.
distinction: The painting contains no identifiable buildings; it can only be assigned, as its closest match, to scenic accentuation on the basis of the layout in which the lotus leaf supports the crab and the surrounding unpainted waterside focuses the line of sight; it is not the terrain-responsive disposition of buildings according to mountain forms and watersides.

evidence: Center and lower right: flowering branches, leaves, and blossoms overlap and press upon one another, with some petals hidden by the leaves in front, forming a front-and-back layering. | Upper right and lower left: two butterflies respectively rest beside the flower clusters, surrounded by large areas of silk ground with no specific content. | Whole work: only flowers, branches and leaves, and butterflies appear in the painting; no visible buildings, mountains and rocks, watersides, bridge paths, or spatial openings.
distinction: It is assigned to C2 on the basis of the layering with which branches and leaves screen the blossoms, while the blossoms are only distributed in isolation and lack a basis for identifying a landscape scene, so C3 is not adopted; because there are no built elements or landscape, this judgment rests only on the spatial screening of flowers and plants.

evidence: Lower center of the right panel: a low, flat bridge-like structure is visible spanning between the banks, its left end near the foreground and its right end connecting toward the wooded bank. | Right side and middle ground: dead trees and sloping banks enclose a gap extending into the interior of the painting, and the bridge deck and shoreline link the foreground with the depths.
distinction: The continuous relationship between the bridge deck and the shoreline more directly suggests a movement-through-the-landscape path from one place to another, rather than merely indicating that buildings are sited according to the terrain.

evidence: Slightly left of lower center: the roofs and parts of the walls of several low thatched huts emerge among the pine forest and slope rocks, and are not fully exposed. | Foreground center to left: foreground rocks and trees obscure the lower parts of the huts, causing the huts to recede into a rear layer and forming a layering of concealment and revelation. | Upper right and center: towering cliffs and clouds and mist form a front-and-back stacking with the trees and huts below, highlighting the relationship in which the middle-ground huts are enclosed and screened by natural scenery.
distinction: Although the huts are arranged according to the slope, the painting more strongly highlights the screening and revelation of the huts by trees and rocks, rather than mainly displaying platform bases unfolding with the mountain configuration.

evidence: Middle right: two thatched huts are partially obscured by the large tree and mountain rocks on the left, with only the roofs and walls exposed, forming a clear spatial layering of concealment and revelation. | Lower left: a wooden bridge is visible spanning a stream, its body meeting the surrounding mountain rocks and trees. | Center: tall trees and mountain rocks serve as the foreground, screening the built elements behind and participating in forming the scene.
distinction: Although there are path clues at the lower left, the core of the overall composition lies in the screening and revelation of the built elements by trees and mountain rocks, and the spatial layering of concealment and revelation forming a scene is more prominent.
