evidence: Lower center: two thatched huts are visible, surrounded by trees and mountain rocks on the left and right, with only the roofs and parts of the walls exposed, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation in which they are screened by natural scenery. | Left and right sides: dense trees and mountain rocks obscure most of the built elements, forming foreground and middle-ground layers so that the built elements appear and disappear among the woodland and mountain rocks.
distinction: Although the built elements rely on the terrain, the most prominent scenic function in the painting is the formation of concealment and revelation layering through the screening of woodland and mountain rocks, rather than a layout emphasizing disposition according to the terrain.

evidence: Middle right: a winding path or plank walkway with railings extends upward along the mountain slope, forming a clear movement-through-the-landscape clue. | Middle left: houses arranged according to the mountain configuration are partially exposed among the woodland, and the extension of the path suggests an accessible relationship leading to them.
distinction: Although the houses on the left have a concealment-and-revelation relationship with the screening woodland, the clearly winding mountain path/plank walkway on the right more strongly organizes the painting's sense of spatial entry and the process of travel.

evidence: Center to lower left of the painting: a distinct diagonal long ink stroke is visible, presenting the morphological direction of a sloping bank or mountain ridge. | Entire painting: several dotted ink marks and, above them, dense ink masses are scattered, resembling moss dots, trees and rocks, or the texture of mountain bodies; no clear built outlines such as houses or bridges are visible. | Right side: vertical ink writing (inscriptions) is visible, which is not a built element within the pictorial space.
distinction: The painting mainly presents the terrain direction of sloping banks and mountain rocks; even if there were scenic accents, they are not identifiable, and it is therefore assigned to the terrain-responsive category on the basis of the visible terrain organization, rather than to the scenic-accent category.

evidence: Lower-left rocky bank and tree cluster: dense trees and slope rocks occupy the foreground, and near the water beneath the trees there is the dark outline of a low hut or pavilion, partially obscured by branches and slope rocks. | Center to right: a large area of open water and unpainted clouds and mist unfolds, and in the upper right the distant mountain ridge line and flying birds form the distant view.
distinction: If the building is established, its identifiable form is mainly revealed through screening by trees and rocks, forming a layering of concealment and revelation; this is less clear than a waterside accent that identifies an open scene.

evidence: Lower left to center: a sturdy pine tree extends from the lower left toward the upper right, its branches and leaves covering the upper middle of the painting. | Slightly below center: a figure in white sits on a protruding rock platform, facing the right side of the painting. | Middle-right distant view: light-ink mountain peaks appear in the open space, forming a clear near-and-far layering with the foreground pines and rocks.
distinction: The pine, rock, and platform together with the figure form a viewing focus facing the distant mountains, closer to scenic accentuation; although the trees and rocks frame the scene, no buildings are seen forming layering through screening.

evidence: Lower-right corner: parts of the roof and eaves are visible; the main building body is obscured by pine branches, tree clusters, and rocks at the right edge, with only part of the roof surface exposed. | Middle-lower right: the trunk and branches of a tall pine slant across and cover above the roof, forming a layering of mutual screening between the trees and the building in front and behind. | Lower-right foreground: the building is close to rocks and woodland, and its roof surface is revealed from among the natural scenery, presenting an impression of half-concealment and half-revelation.
distinction: C1 requires a clear display of the siting and layout arranged according to mountain forms and watersides; what is clearer here is the scenic relationship in which the roof is half-screened and half-revealed by pine branches and rocks.

evidence: Lower right: a boat with a mast is moored by the water, adjacent to the wooded bank on the right. | Lower left: two figures (or livestock) walk along the bank on the waterside, echoing across the water with the boat on the right. | Center and above: a large area of unpainted space expresses the open water surface; no fixed built elements such as houses, pavilions, or bridges are visible.
distinction: The painting has no fixed buildings; only boats and pedestrians indicate the open scene of the waterside, and no clear entry path or secluded-access clue is presented.

evidence: Middle left: a group of thatched huts is partially obscured by tall pines and dead trees, with only the roofs and parts of the walls exposed, forming a layering of houses hidden in the forest. | Left side: tree trunks and branches form a clear screen in front of the houses, placing the built elements in a spatial relationship of half-hidden, half-visible.
distinction: Although the built elements rely on the waterside slope, the most prominent spatial organization in the painting is the screening and revelation of the houses by trees, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship dominates the scenic composition.

evidence: Lower left: the roofs and walls of several thatched huts are partially obscured by the foreground slope rocks and trees, with only local structures exposed. | Lower center: dense tree clusters surround and obscure part of the built elements, forming a clear front-and-back spatial layering that makes the buildings appear indistinctly.
distinction: The painting more prominently highlights the layering relationship formed by the screening and revelation of buildings by trees, rather than simply emphasizing the corresponding disposition of buildings with the terrain and sloping banks.

evidence: Upper center: a pavilion stands on a sloping terrace; its building body and base are partially obscured by the foreground dead trees and mountain rocks, with only the roof and part of the eave columns exposed, forming a clear layering of concealment and revelation. | Left side: a flat bridge spans the water, with several people walking on it, forming a path clue leading to the built area on the opposite bank.
distinction: Although a bridge and pedestrians suggest a path, the concealment-and-revelation relationship between the built elements and the trees and mountain rocks is visually more prominent and dominates the spatial layering of the central scene.

evidence: Lower-middle left mountain foot: the outlines of pavilions and houses appear faintly among the dense woodland and mountain rocks, and the buildings are partially screened by natural scenery, forming a spatial layering of intermingled concealment and revelation. | Left mountainside: pavilion-style buildings are visible amid the screening of mountain rocks and trees, half-hidden and half-revealed according to the mountain configuration.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited according to the mountain configuration, the painting more strongly emphasizes the relationship of screening and revelation of the buildings by woodland and mountain rocks, forming a scene through concealment and revelation; thus C2 is more apt than C1.

evidence: Middle-lower right edge: a small building is revealed among the rocky slope and tree clusters, with its roof, eaves, and supports visible, and the dead branches and tree crowns in front partially obscuring the structure. | Dense forest at the middle-lower left: layered roofs and eaves are revealed among the trees, and most of the main building bodies are submerged in the tree clusters and mist. | Lower foreground: trees, rocks, and mist are stacked front and back, forming a layering of screening in which the buildings show only parts and must be recognized through the woodland.
distinction: Although the small building at the right edge can be regarded as a scenic accent by the rock, what the painting more prominently highlights is the layering relationship of screening and revealing by trees and rocks and the partial exposure of roofs, rather than using buildings to mark a particular landscape.

evidence: Lower left to central foreground: a light-colored winding line twists from among the tree clusters toward the middle ground, forming a spatial clue extending into the depths of the painting. | Central and lower-right slopes: several groups of trees and slope rocks screen each other front and back, but no clearly identifiable roofs, walls, bridge railings, or door openings are visible. | Upper middle: rounded mountain peaks are layered, separated front and back by unpainted clouds and mist, and the main spatial layering is formed by mountain bodies and tree clusters.
distinction: There is a winding clue in the foreground extending into the depths, closer to the path organization of access to secluded settings; but there is a lack of a confirmable building site, and terrain-responsive disposition cannot be determined on this basis.

evidence: Slightly left of the lower part of the painting: a low, flat wooden bridge or plank walkway spans shallow water; the deck and continuous posts are identifiable, with the left end meeting the sloping bank and the right end extending toward the reed-covered waterside. | Left-middle foreground: tall pines grow on slope rocks, and one end of the bridge is close to the foot of the pine forest slope, forming a spatial relationship in which the bridge path enters among the trees and rocks. | Lower-right water surface: a small boat carrying people is located on the water beyond the bridge, suggesting movement through the landscape and fishing activity along the waterside.
distinction: The wooden bridge mainly appears as an entry clue connecting the two banks and leading to the foot of the pine forest slope, rather than merely indicating that buildings are arranged according to the terrain.

evidence: Lower left to middle ground: the waterside and sloping banks form a winding shoreline extending toward the center of the painting, with figures scattered along it, some in walking postures. | Slightly right of lower center: at the base of a large tree there is a light-colored rectangular structure, with standing figures beside it, but no obvious roof, door opening, or continuous building outline. | Slightly right of center: dense tree crowns and mountain rocks join to form a screen, obscuring the upper part of the rectangular structure and the space behind it.
distinction: The figures and shoreline suggest an entry relationship approaching what appears to be a gate wall among the trees and rocks; but with the lack of a clear roof and eaves, concealment and revelation forming a scene is less apt than access to secluded settings.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: a group of riding figures is visible traveling along a path between mountain rocks and trees, forming a clear clue of travel or procession. | Whole painting: the painting consists mainly of mountain rocks, trees, and the traveling group of figures, and no clear built elements such as houses or bridges are visible.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built elements; only the path of the group of figures traveling among the mountains is visible, and it is therefore tentatively assigned to C4 on the basis of the spatial process, though there are no actual built elements to enter.

evidence: Lower right: the roof and eaves of a pavilion emerge from between the pines and slope rocks, and the lower part of the building is obscured by foreground scenery. | Lower center: a group of roofs is wedged among tree clusters and low slope rocks; most of the building bodies are hidden, with only the eave ridges showing through the branches and leaves. | Middle of the left end: multi-story pavilions meet tree clusters and cliff walls; layered eaves are partially visible, and the lower parts are obscured by trees and rocks.
distinction: The main category is the spatial layering formed by the screening of trees and rocks and the revelation of roofs; what the painting more prominently highlights is scenery formed through concealment and revelation, rather than building sites unfolding with the sloping banks.

evidence: Dense tree canopy at center-right conceals several houses, exposing only dark roofs, eaves, and parts of white walls; the buildings form a broken, intermittently revealed layering in front of and behind the trees. | Left slope down to the waterside: several houses are placed at different heights along the slope and bank, their roofs screened among the trees, with rocks and water separating them in front. | Left-center water gap: an arched bridge crosses a narrow water gap toward a clump of trees on the bank, but the connection between the far side of the bridge and the building entrance is hidden by trees, and the path is incomplete.
distinction: Although the buildings are disposed along the sloping bank, the most prominent spatial relationship in the painting is the screening and partial exposure of the houses by the trees, rather than a layout determined by terrain alone.

evidence: Lower center, at the foot of a huge rock: a low building or covered bridge lies horizontally between the foot of the rock and the water; roof, pillars, and a transverse passage are discernible. | From the left side of the building to the foreground rocky bank: traces of a low, flat bridge deck or stone path extend from the open waterside toward the building, forming a route of movement leading toward it. | To the right and above the building: the building abuts the huge rock, with trees and the rock face pressing over it from above, and the passage extending toward a dark area to the right rear.
distinction: The primary category concerns how the bridge and path lead the viewer from the open waterside toward the building at the foot of the rock and onward into depth; C1 only explains that the building is sited on a terrace at the foot of the rock and cannot encompass this relationship of entry.

evidence: Left-middle to lower part of the painting: a wooden railing is laid out in turning segments along the edge of an irregular rock terrace, changing direction with the rise and fall of the rock surface rather than being arranged in a straight line. | Lower center of the painting: two figures stand on a stone platform beside the railing, with a dark rock rising above the rock surface on one side and a rocky slope dropping away on the other. | Most of the right side of the painting: beyond the railing is a large area of misty unpainted space, with no other buildings or clear paths seen connecting to it.
distinction: The railing clearly follows the edge of the rock terrace and the terrain, chiefly embodying placement according to form; although it forms a viewing position, it does not appear to play a dominant role in marking specific distant scenery.

evidence: Lower-right waterside: a figure holding a punt pole stands at the water's edge, beside a low, flat transverse shoreline, appearing as a ferry crossing or landing point. | From lower center to lower left: a figure with a staff walks along a low, flat bank path that extends toward the pine grove and the foot of the rocks, interrupted in places by sloping rocks and trees. | Lower-left sloping bank: the pine grove and rocky slope press in on either side, and the path narrows between them; no clearly identifiable roofs or walls are seen.
distinction: The primary category is based on the visible bank path, figures, and boatman forming a spatial connection from the waterside into the pine grove, rather than on the layering produced by clearly identifiable buildings screened and revealed by trees.

evidence: Upper to central area: pale-ink mountain forms slant from the top toward the lower right, their feet extending into broad open water, creating a large-scale opening and closing of mountain and water. | Lower-right near shore: a figure holding a staff stands on the sloping bank facing the water; in the water ahead is a horizontal dark elongated form, blurred in detail, resembling a boat or a sandbar. | Whole painting: no clearly identifiable built elements such as roofs, walls, bridges, paths, or gate towers are seen.
distinction: The primary category rests on the crossing and approach relationships suggested by the figure at the water and the horizontal object on the water; C3 requires a discernible built feature to mark the scenery, but no clear building is seen in the painting.

evidence: Lower left: at the water's edge is a small pavilion/waterside kiosk with a railed platform, its roof fully visible, facing a broad expanse of open water. | Left to center: pale-ink distant mountains stretch across, the shoreline is low and flat, and the small pavilion stands at the transition between the bank and the distant mountains. | Lower right to center right: another roof appears among withered trees and rocks, partly screened by branches, while the waterside kiosk at lower left remains fully exposed.
distinction: The main pavilion marks the scenery of the open water and distant mountains through its waterside position; although a pavilion set along the bank is visible, the painting does not develop a continuous built relationship following the mountain terrain.

evidence: Lower left: several thatched houses are arranged along the gentle slope near the bank; roofs, eaves, and walls are partly hidden and partly revealed by foreground withered trees, forming front-to-back layering between houses and trees. | Center-left: tall trunks and dense fine branches stand in front of the houses, screening the right half of the dwellings and the entrance area, so that the village dwellings appear half concealed. | Lower right: a wooden bridge and zigzagging wooden railing cross a stream and extend toward the houses, but the path between them and the house doors is partly interrupted by trees.
distinction: Primary category C2 is based on the pronounced screening and revealing of the roofs and eaves of the houses by trees, forming spatial layering; compared with C4, the bridge and railing only locally suggest entry and do not run through the near-ground compositional relationship as the tree screening does.

evidence: Lower right: a wooden bridge is visible crossing the water, with travelers on the bridge, one end of which connects to a path leading toward built structures on the bank. | Center right: a thatched house stands on the sloping bank, forming a clear connection with the bridge and path below, presenting an accessible, reachable spatial relationship.
distinction: Although the built elements follow the sloping bank, the painting clearly organizes a process of movement from outside inward, approaching the built structures, through the bridge and path; the thread of access to a secluded setting is more prominent.

evidence: Center to right half: a large rock face and vines and foliage hanging from above enclose a shallow recessed cave space, where the figures' activities are concentrated; front-to-back layering is formed by the screening relationships of the rock mass and foliage. | Center-left: a figure leans back holding a long pole, from the end of which a horizontally placed object hangs beneath the foliage; around are rocks and grouped trees and stones, with no architectural components such as roofs, walls, or porches seen. | Left end and lower right: on the rocky slope at the left end are a seated figure and small items such as a gourd and a scroll stand; at lower right is a crouching figure or animal, all placed directly on the rocky ground, with no discernible building base, road, or bridge.
distinction: The painting organizes the layers around the figures chiefly through the enclosure created by the screening of rock masses and vines, rather than by clearly built structures marking a particular scene, so it is assigned to the concealment-and-revelation layering category; however, both lack clear architectural entities for support.

evidence: Center-right bamboo grove: within the bamboo grove a small roof, eaves, and part of the building itself are exposed, with bamboo stalks and leaves screening the building from the front, leaving only part visible. | Lower-right corner edge: wooden railing or platform components are visible, close to the edge of the painting, adjacent to sloping ground and figures. | Lower-right foreground: a figure in red and an attendant stand at the edge of the sloping ground facing the large misty area to the left, but no clear path leading to the bamboo-grove building can be seen.
distinction: Although the building is set within the bamboo grove on the sloping ground, the most distinct spatial relationship is the screening and revealing of the roof and eaves by the bamboo grove, rather than a building base unfolding with the mountain terrain.

evidence: Center-left mountainside: a pavilion building is erected on a projecting terrace of the mountain mass, backed by rocks and facing a more open area. | Lower-left corner at the foot of the slope: several houses are arranged at different heights along the slope, adjacent to the surrounding rocks and trees.
distinction: The primary category emphasizes that the building bases follow the mountainside terrace and the differences in height at the foot of the slope; although C3 could explain them as scenic accents, the relation of the buildings to the terrain is more concrete and more pervasive through the painting.

evidence: Lower part of the circular painted panel of the right leaf: a pavilion building is clearly visible, situated in front of mountains and rocks and trees, as one of the main views of the painting. | Upper part and rear of the circular painted panel of the right leaf: mountains and rocks and trees surround the building, and the building marks the focus of the landscape here.
distinction: The architecture is directly presented and marks the vista here, without emphasis on terrain-responsive siting or concealment and revelation, and with no obvious entry path.

evidence: Whole painting: the content consists of vertically arranged ink-written characters, with no recognizable mountains, sloping banks, water surfaces, or trees or other landscape features. | Whole painting: no built or movement elements such as roofs, walls, pillars and eaves, bridges or paths, or door openings are seen; the writing falls directly on the yellowish-brown paper surface. | Left and right columns: the columns of text form only distributions of character and line spacing, with no verifiable relationships of screening, connection, or height placement between buildings and terrain.
distinction: The painting lacks site conditions such as mountain forms and shores, and has no building base for comparison, so terrain-responsive siting cannot be established; it can only be provisionally recorded under the closest category, scenic accentuation, rather than a terrain-correspondence relationship.

evidence: Lower middle of the right panel: a house with curved eaves stands behind pine trees; the roof and eaves are partly screened by foreground pine branches, though the building's outline remains discernible. | Lower right of the right panel: another small house or pavilion eave is partly revealed among sloping rocks and trees, forming front-to-back layering with the main house. | Left to center of the right panel: cliff rocks and grouped pines form a foreground screen, with the house set among them and water spreading out to the right; the building is not fully exposed.
distinction: The main house forms layering chiefly through screening and revealing by pines and sloping rocks, rather than being organized solely by a building base following the bank slope.

evidence: Center-right of the right panel: the multiple roofs of a multi-story temple complex are staggered at different heights along stacked terraces on a steep cliff, the building bases clinging to the rocky slope in a layered arrangement following the mountain. | Lower right of the right panel: a group of low houses hugs the foot of the slope at the valley bottom, their roofs lying low among the trees, set at a different height from the temple complex above. | Lower middle of the right panel: a winding mountain path and traveling figures are visible at the valley bottom, the path appearing and disappearing among trees and rocks and not clearly extending to the central temple complex.
distinction: The main temple complex is chiefly characterized by a layered placement following the slope and spreading across rocky terraces; although the pine grove partly screens the roofs, it does not form a dominant concealment-and-revelation layering.

evidence: Right side and lower part: rocks and pines are painted on the right side of the painting, water ripples below, and a single seated figure in the lower-left corner; no traces of buildings, pavilions, or other built structures are seen.
distinction: There is no clear built structure in the painting, only natural landscape and figures; it is assigned only tentatively on the basis of the overall visible landscape organization, with no other more fitting built relationship.

evidence: Lower left and center-left: a pavilion house stands behind pine trunks, its roof and eaves partly screened by forward-reaching pine branches, forming a layered relationship with trees in front and the house behind. | Lower center to lower right: in front of the pavilion house a waterside stone platform and transverse railing extend to the right along the bank, with figures standing before the railing. | Left background: behind the pavilion house are mountain rock masses, which together with the foreground pines enclose a half-hidden, half-revealed built space.
distinction: The screening and revealing of the pavilion house by pine branches and mountain rocks constitutes the main spatial layering; although the waterside platform reflects placement according to terrain, it is less dominant than the concealment-and-revelation relationship.

evidence: Left side of the right fan: a pine extends diagonally up to the right from a rocky bank, its trunk and crown occupying the upper and left parts of the painting and forming a foreground screen. | Lower right of the right fan: a small boat is on the water near the bank, with figures visible in it, surrounded by a broad expanse of open water. | Center-right of the right fan: a transverse sandbank or sloping bank extends into the water, forming an open waterscape together with the large areas of unpainted space.
distinction: The small boat is isolated on the water and chiefly serves as a scenic accent that defines and concentrates the waterscape; no bridge, path, bank opening, or continuous route of travel forms an accessible path relationship.

evidence: Upper right: high on the cliff a building roof and part of a wall are visible, half screened and half exposed by rocks and trees, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Below: figures ride donkeys along the sloping bank, forming a path, but it does not directly connect to the building above.
distinction: Although the painting contains a route of movement, there is no clear connection of entry between the path and the building; the building presents its layering chiefly through screening by rocks and trees.

evidence: Center-right in the mist of the distant mountains: a slender, tall multi-story pagoda-shaped outline is visible, half hidden in mist, at the junction of the mountain mass and the open water. | On the stream at lower right: a small bridge with railings crosses the stream, connecting the banks and trees on either side.
distinction: The small bridge and the pagoda-shaped building in the mist chiefly serve as locating points between the foreground waterside and the distant valley, rather than as a continuous bridge and path leading a person toward some building or into depth.

evidence: Left middle ground: a group of multi-story pavilion buildings clings to terraces between steep mountain walls, their roofs staggered in height and unfolding along the layers of the mountain mass. | In front of and below the left-side buildings: trees and rock masses lie in front of and below the pavilion group, and the building bases are placed according to the mountain wall and slope rather than on flat ground. | Center to right of the painting: layered peaks and ravines occupy the main body, while the buildings are set to one side on the left mountainside, directly adjoining the mountain forms.
distinction: The pavilion group chiefly presents a relationship of layered placement at different heights along the terraces of the left mountain wall, interlocking with the mountain forms; partial screening by trees and rocks is only an accompanying phenomenon, so it is closer to terrain-responsive siting than to a dominant concealment-and-revelation composition.

evidence: In the woods at the lower right of the painting: a building roof and part of a wall are visible, covered above and to left and right by dense foliage and screened below by trunks and rocks, only partly exposed. | At the junction of the rocks and the misty opening at center-left: the outline of a small eave is visible beside the rocky slope, screened by surrounding trees and rocks and placed close to the foot of the slope.
distinction: The buildings chiefly form layering through being half screened and half revealed by tree canopy and foliage, with houses seen through the woods, rather than being organized solely by building bases following sloping terraces.

evidence: In the clump of trees in the lower-right middle ground: dark roofs and eaves are discernible among the trees, with most of the building itself screened by branches and foliage and only partly exposed. | Lower-right middle ground, sloping rocks and tree canopy: the building stands behind the canopy and among the sloping rocks, with foreground foliage and the mountain mass behind forming layers of screening front and back.
distinction: The main visible role of the building is to form concealment-and-revelation layering through screening and revealing by trees, rather than presenting a terrain-responsive layout solely by means of a building base on sloping rocks.

evidence: Lower-left foreground: a wooden bridge crosses the water, with a rider and a figure carrying a load on the bridge, its end connecting to the sloping bank and a small path. | Lower right: a courtyard on the slope has a fenced enclosure and gate, with a small path outside the gate extending toward the lower part of the painting and figures active before the gate. | Center-right mountainside: pavilions and a pagoda stand on sloping terraces, with a winding path and tiny figures on the slope leading upward.
distinction: C4 organizes the built structures into an accessible spatial process through bridges, gates, mountain paths, and traveling figures; C1 can only explain that the buildings are disposed along the sloping bank and does not emphasize movement from one place to another.

evidence: Lower left and lower center: a winding path is visible beside the building group, extending into the woods and connecting different spatial layers. | Central mountainside: a zigzagging stairway or mountain road climbs upward among the rocks toward built structures in the depth. | Right mountain wall: a plank road or path built against the mountain is visible, suggesting a spatial relationship allowing further entry into depth.
distinction: The winding paths and mountain roads run through the composition, clearly guiding the eye and the route of travel into depth, and are more dominant than placement according to terrain alone.

evidence: Right center: amid cloud and mist and screening trees, the outline of a small built structure is faintly visible, in a half-screened, half-revealed state. | Whole painting: large areas of cloud and mist and dense-ink trees divide the pictorial space, and the suspected built structure appears to be placed within the screening layers of natural scenery.
distinction: The built structure chiefly forms concealment-and-revelation layering through screening by cloud, mist, and trees, rather than serving as a clear, conspicuous marker to point out specific scenery.

evidence: Left mountainside: a group of pavilions clings to a steep ridge, their roofs staggered in height following the slope, with building bases laid out along the turns of the mountain form. | Lower center: a two-story pavilion is built on stilts at the foot of the slope by the stream bank, supported below by wooden pillars, backed by rocks and facing the low waterside. | Right center to lower right: a thatched pavilion and houses respectively cling to the sloping ground beside a waterfall and to the rocks, their roofs half screened among trees and rocks and unfolding with the slope.
distinction: The disposition of multiple buildings at different heights along the ridge, the foot of the slope, and the waterside is the dominant organizing relationship; although the foreground bridge and travelers suggest entry, the path from the bridge to the pavilions is interrupted, and its continuity is less than that of placement according to terrain.

evidence: Left-center of the painting: a group of pavilions and multi-story buildings is visible, its base directly clinging to and raised upon the rocky sloping bank on the left, presenting the form of buildings erected on a terrace. | Lower left-center of the painting: the platform in front of the buildings connects with the rocky bank below, and the overall layout unfolds in accordance with the rises and falls of the rocky terrain. | Left side of the painting: the buildings are partly screened by pines and other trees, but their main outlines are clear, forming a definite relationship of dependence on the steep rocks behind.
distinction: Although the buildings have a concealment-and-revelation relationship with the screening trees, their terrain-correspondence relationship, placed against the rocky sloping bank, is more conspicuous and dominant.

evidence: Beneath the pines at the lower right: a low wooden railing is visible, its horizontal rails and posts forming a section of railing that extends toward the tree roots on the right. | Group of figures at the lower right: the figures gather on the inner side of the railing, their positions adjoining the transverse run of the railing. | Lower center to the right bank: large foreground rocks and pines pinch off a space near the bank, and both the railing and the figures are concentrated in this recess.
distinction: The railing organizes the figures and the near-bank space beneath the pines into a locally accessible, enterable passage, emphasizing movement through the landscape more than placement according to terrain alone.

evidence: Lower right of the painting: multiple pitched-roof houses extend horizontally along the bank, their front edges partly screened by willow branches and trunks, with roofs, eaves, and open eave galleries appearing through gaps in the trees. | Lower center to lower middle of the painting: layered willow groves form front-to-back screening, and the house group is screened in sections by canopy and branches, presenting alternating concealment and revelation in the spatial layering between buildings and willows.
distinction: Although the buildings are also arranged along the bank, the painting more prominently highlights the screening and sectional revealing of the houses by the willow grove, rather than a disposition determined solely by terrain or shoreline.

evidence: Middle, slightly right: a building complex with multiple roof layers sits horizontally on a rock platform between the central main peak and the cliff mass on the right, arranged in tiers according to the height of the platform surface | Lower right to lower part: another group of houses at the foot of the mountain near the water spreads out along the sloping bank, and roofs can be seen in the zone where they meet the slope rocks | Left side: a waterfall drops down between the cliffs, closely adjacent to one side of the rock platform where the buildings are located, forming a vertical relationship between the buildings and the landscape
distinction: The buildings clearly correspond to the mountain forms by evidently relying on the rock platform and being distributed according to the slope; concealment and revelation are not dominant, so this is closer to terrain-responsive siting than to concealment and revelation.

evidence: Left side, mountainside: the built elements are screened by dense trees and projecting mountain rocks, with only part of the roofs and eaves exposed, forming a distinct layering of concealment and revelation. | Lower right, waterside: several thatched huts are partly screened among the trees and slope rocks, their roofs half hidden and half visible, integrated into the natural scenery.
distinction: Although the built elements are sited against the mountain and beside the water, the painting emphasizes more the screening and revealing of the buildings by trees and rocks; the feature of concealment and revelation forming the scene is more prominent than terrain-based placement.

evidence: Whole painting: the main subject is a giant pine tree, rocks on the right, flowing water below, and a walking scholar; no houses, bridges, or other explicit built elements are seen.
distinction: The painting lacks explicit built elements; the dynamics of the figure walking suggest a process of spatial movement, and it is only tentatively assigned to this category.

evidence: Lower part, slightly right of center: a square pavilion open on all four sides stands on relatively low, flat rocky ground in the foreground, facing a large expanse of unpainted misty open space ahead. | Lower left: several pines grow on slope rocks, located to the left rear of the pavilion; the right front of the pavilion is completely open, with no obstruction. | Middle of the painting: three green mountain peaks rise from the white clouds that span the painting, separated from the foreground pavilion by a broad area of unpainted space.
distinction: The pavilion stands at an edge overlooking water and open space and faces the peaks in the mist, serving to highlight and define this open scenery; it is not primarily a terrain-responsive placement of high-low advance and retreat according to mountain forms and slope platforms.

evidence: Lower middle toward the right, between the mountain foot and the water surface: the roof outlines of low houses are visible, backed by mountain rocks and sloping ground and fronting the waterside. | Around the houses: the building site falls at the junction of the gentle slope at the mountain foot and the shoreline, enclosed on the left and right by slope rocks and sparse trees. | Right side of the painting: the shoreline extends into the distance, and the position of the houses connects with the turning relationship between the mountain foot and the water surface.
distinction: The houses are first positioned according to the slope platform at the mountain foot and the waterside, rather than becoming a marker of that landscape by virtue of their own position.

evidence: Middle, slightly right: a building group is built on a stone-revetted platform beside the water; the platform projects toward the water surface, and the building itself extends horizontally along the shoreline | Behind and above the buildings: a huge rock cliff rises steeply behind the houses, and the houses are placed close against the cliff foot and slope platform | Foreground lower right: several tall trees rise from the lower-right rocky slope, their branches and leaves reaching in front of the houses and partially covering the lower eaves
distinction: Although the buildings are slightly screened by foreground trees, the dominant relationship is a waterside stone platform, placed against the cliff and following the bank; this is terrain-based placement rather than concealment and revelation forming the scene.

evidence: Middle ground, slightly left, among the trees: a light-colored, nearly horizontal thin line runs across the dark trees, resembling a low wall or railing in form; it is screened front and back by tree crowns and only partially exposed | Lower half to center: the foreground consists of dense ink trees and a sloping bank, transitioning upward into layered mountain peaks in mist, with the mountain masses separated into front and back layers by pale-ink unpainted space | Upper and middle parts: a large area of inscription and seals occupies the painting, below which the peaks and trees begin; the writing itself is not used as spatial evidence
distinction: The light-colored structure is almost enclosed by the trees and only partially exposed; the concealment-revelation relationship is more directly identifiable than a layout placed according to terrain, so concealment and revelation is chosen rather than terrain-responsive siting.

evidence: Lower right, sloping bank among trees: beneath the tree crowns a short horizontal dark line and vertical supports are visible, resembling a small house or shed roof in form, partially screened by branches and leaves. | In front of and along the lower edge of the lower-right trees: no clearly identifiable bridge deck, continuous path, or doorway connects with this structure.
distinction: The main visible relationship is the half-screening and half-exposure of the suspected eaves by the trees, rather than a building site unfolding according to the sloping bank; the access relationship of bridges and paths is also unclear.

evidence: Right middle: a building with a visible roof is placed among the trees on the mountain slope, its roof and walls partly screened by the trees in front | Right-side woodland: dense tree crowns are in front of the building, with the roof ridge showing through, forming a layering of front-back screening | Lower middle: slope rocks and pine woods are layered repeatedly, setting off the right-side building deep among the trees
distinction: Although the building is placed according to the slope, its dominant compositional role is that the roof is screened and revealed by the trees in front, forming a layering of concealment and display; therefore it tends toward concealment and revelation rather than purely terrain-responsive siting.

evidence: Middle right, mountain hollow: roofs, eaves, and walls are half screened behind foreground pines and mountain rocks, with a towering main peak immediately behind the house, forming a front-back layering of trees in front, house in the middle, and mountain behind | Middle left, rock platform: a small pavilion with a pyramidal roof is placed on a rounded, gentle rock platform beside the water, facing open water and distant mountains | Foreground: many pines and dry branches slant across in front of the houses, screening and framing the location of the built elements
distinction: The primary category is based on the concealment-revelation layering formed by the right-side house being half screened and half revealed by trees and rocks and receding layer by layer; if only the terrain-based placement of the pavilion on the platform were considered, it would approach C1, but concealment and revelation running through it better governs the relationship between the built elements and the landscape.

evidence: Foreground lower left: tall pines form a grove, their trunks and branch tips crossing in front of the pavilion; the pavilion roof and railings are half exposed between the trees, and seated figures are inside the pavilion | Left of center, mountain interior: layered roof-like structures are visible in a recess of the steep cliff, partially screened by folds in the rock mass, with only roof ridges and eaves exposed to indicate their layering | Below the lower-left pavilion: the pavilion sits on a rock platform beside the water, enclosed by the rock mass and tree shadows, forming a staggered front-back spatial layer
distinction: Although the pavilion, set on a rock platform beside the water, is close to terrain-responsive siting, the painting mainly organizes front-back layering through the half-screening and half-exposure of roofs by pine woods and rock masses, which is closer to concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting, slightly right: multiple roofs join at different heights, half hidden in dense trees, with eaves and roof ridges exposed among the branches and leaves | To the right of and in front of the building group: huge slope rocks and patches of mixed trees screen the lower parts and sides of the buildings, with only parts of the walls and roofs visible, forming a layering of front-back screening | Below the buildings: a white waterfall pours down along a crevice in the rock; no identifiable bridge, path, or entrance directly connects with the buildings nearby
distinction: Although the building group is arranged according to the valley and slope foot, what is clearest in the painting is the half-screening and half-exposure of roofs and walls by trees and slope rocks; the layering of concealment and revelation is more dominant than terrain-responsive placement.

evidence: Left to central foreground: many old trees with thick trunks rise from slope rocks, their branches extending horizontally and screening a large area of space behind. | Right, middle and distant ground: rounded hills recede in layers, emerging from the right side of the trees, forming a layering of front-back screening and revealing. | Lower foreground: slope rocks and tangled tree roots are visible, but no recognizable roofs, walls, bridges, paths, or doorways are seen.
distinction: The painting mainly presents the layered screening of distant mountains by trees and rocks, rather than a building site arranged according to the slope; but because explicit built elements are lacking, it is only assigned as the closest fit.

evidence: Lower left: a group of houses is located behind huge rocks and dead trees; roof surfaces, eaves, and parts of the walls are exposed among the trees and rocks, forming a distinct layering of front-back screening. | Center, slightly left: the houses are placed close against a rock platform below a large mountain mass, with trees and rocks around them partly screening the buildings; the buildings are not directly exposed as complete facades. | Lower right, water area: a small bridge and boats are visible, but there is no continuous identifiable path connecting the bridge bank with the lower-left houses.
distinction: The primary category is based on the scene formed by the obvious screening and partial exposure of the houses by trees and rocks; although the correspondence of building site, layout, and slope platform/waterside required for C1 is visible, it does not run through the painting as the concealment-revelation layering does.

evidence: Lower left to left mountain foot: many houses are arranged at different heights along the rock platform at the mountain foot, their roofs and walls turning with the slope, their front edges facing the water. | Center, slightly left, waterside: a small pavilion or waterside house is placed on a rocky promontory projecting into the water, backed by the slope foot and facing open water. | Left upper mountainside: a roof is exposed among the pines, its position receding into a recess in the mountainside, forming an upper-lower separation from the main house group below.
distinction: Although the main house group is partially screened by trees, the site relationship of its distribution along the mountain-foot rock platform and shoreline more completely organizes the painting; concealment and revelation mainly serve as an auxiliary layer.

evidence: Lower center, near the water: a group of houses sits on a waterside rock platform, with railings and eaves generally unfolding along the irregular shoreline; the building site follows the rock platform and water edge. | Left mountainside, to the right of the waterfall: small pavilions and houses are arranged at different heights according to the cliff platform, their roof positions corresponding to the slope surface and the trend of the rock strata. | Right middle, sloping bank: a small house is located between the waterside slope and the trees and rocks, its roof facing the water and positioned according to the sloping bank.
distinction: The buildings are mainly positioned in layers according to rock platforms, sloping banks, and the water edge; although trees partially screen some eaves, the concealment-revelation relationship does not govern the whole painting as terrain-responsive arrangement does.

evidence: Lower center: an elongated, upright stele-like object stands beside the roots of a pine, its outline relatively straight and different from the surrounding natural tree trunks; two figures stop in front of the stele to look. | Left to center: tall pines extend their branches horizontally, surrounding the stele-like object and the figures, making this spot a scenic point enclosed by trees and rocks and identifiable as such. | Lower right, sloping bank: figures, a horse handler, and horses are on lower sloping ground, but no clear bridge, path, or doorway is seen connecting with the stele-like object.
distinction: The stone stele, together with the figures and pines, forms a stele-reading focal marker, rather than merely a general site arrangement according to slope and trees.

evidence: Lower-left foreground: a low building with a roof is visible, close against the base of a towering cliff, situated on a flat rock platform beside the water. | Between the left cliff and the houses: the cliff rises steeply behind the houses, trees surround the sides of the buildings, and the built elements are placed according to the height difference between the cliff foot and the bank platform. | From in front of the houses to the water: the rocky bank in front of the houses opens toward the water, with figures active nearby; the shoreline becomes the boundary where the houses face the water.
distinction: The bridge and figures at lower right suggest possible movement through the landscape, but there is no clear continuous path connection between the bridge and the lower-left houses; the dominant feature of the painting remains the terrain-responsive placement of the houses against the cliff and beside the bank.

evidence: From lower left to lower middle of the painting, waterside banks and islets: waterside pavilions and houses are built on projecting banks and the edges of islets, fronting the water and backed by sloping ground and trees, arranged according to the bank. | Middle ground, slightly right, waterside and mountain foot: houses, a wooden bridge, and railings unfold along the waterside and slope foot, with the high-low positions of the buildings following the visible terrain. | Distant valley and water boundary: village houses are scattered among the mountain foot, waterside, and valley floor, forming no independent axis but coordinating with the landscape forms.
distinction: The houses are mainly distributed according to sloping banks, islets, and water forms; bridges, paths, and boat crossings are only local movement clues and do not become an entry process governing the whole painting.

evidence: Middle ground, slightly left: a group of red-roofed pavilions is set into a recess between steep cliffs on the left and right, their roofs staggered in height and layered back and upward along the slope platform. | Behind and on both sides of the pavilions: the buildings are backed by steep cliffs and flanked by rock walls, with a stream valley and trees below in front; the building site is arranged according to the recess in the rock walls and the high-low slope surface. | Left cliff of the pavilions: a winding white linear mountain path or stone steps is visible extending down along the cliff and connecting with the left side of the buildings, partially hidden among trees and rocks.
distinction: Although the stone steps on the left can lead to the pavilions, they are only a local movement clue; the terrain-responsive arrangement of the building group unfolding in multiple layers along the cliff recess and slope platform more completely organizes the middle ground of the painting.

evidence: Lower-left corner, waterside: a low shed is half screened between tall dense reeds and rocks, with only low eaves and figures under the shed visible. | Lower-left corner, from foreground to water: reeds grow upward from the foreground and partially block the shed; in front of the shed is a fishing-net frame projecting toward the water. | Middle right, far bank: distant sandbars, trees, and the opening and closing of the water surface form an open background, contrasting with the hidden shed in the lower-left corner through concealment and revelation.
distinction: The shed is indeed half screened by reeds, forming a layering of concealment and revelation; its relationship with the sloping bank is mainly just a waterside location, and no clear building-site layout responding to terrain changes is shown.

evidence: Right side and upper part: the trunk of a large tree stands on the right, its branches and leaves extending horizontally and covering the middle and upper parts of the painting, forming a dense canopy. | Lower center: a figure sits on the ground beneath the tree, the body partially enclosed by the canopy and the right-side trunk; baskets and jar-like objects are beside the tree roots. | Left side and background: only faint mountain shadows and unpainted waterside space are seen in the distance; no recognizable houses, bridges, paths, or doorways are visible.
distinction: The canopy cover and the figure hidden beneath the tree form a local layering of screening, closer to the concealment and revelation of C2 than to using architecture to define a scenic spot; but the painting has no explicit built elements.

evidence: Middle ground, lower part: the roofs and wall ridges of a horizontal courtyard emerge from between a row of tall pines; the tree crowns screen the lower part of the buildings, and the buildings and woods form a layering of front-back screening. | Lower foreground: the waterside open pavilion and the roofs of the houses on the right are covered by large tree crowns, with only parts of the eaves and spaces between columns visible; the built elements seem to emerge from the woods. | Right slope: a small pavilion or roof is half screened by rocks and trees, with only the roof and part of the structure exposed, suggesting that built elements are hidden behind the mountain scenery.
distinction: Although the buildings are arranged in layers along the waterside and slope platforms, the clearest common effect running through multiple places in the painting is the screening and revealing of roofs, eaves, and walls by trees and rocks, rather than a layout determined solely by terrain.

evidence: Left side to left of center: many halls, pavilions, and platforms are arranged in tiers along the rocky slope, with roof ridges and platform bases staggered in height, the building site rising with the slope surface. | Front edge of the buildings from center-left to lower right: the building group unfolds layer by layer from left to lower right; the lower platform rests on rock and extends toward the large open space on the right, forming an edge unfolding along the bank. | Lower foreground and left side: pines and rocks partially screen the lower corridors and roofs, but the upper pavilions remain clearly exposed, and the overall building outline is identifiable.
distinction: Although trees and rocks provide some local screening and exposure, the painting more importantly presents the siting order of the pavilion group layered along the rocky slope and unfolding along the bank, rather than mainly forming scenery through concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower-left foreground: beside a pine is a slanting wooden plank walkway or steps, and a figure with their back to the viewer is walking up along it. | Lower-right foreground: wooden railings are set along the rocky waterside, their lines extending toward the middle ground and indicating a boundary that can be walked along. | Center middle ground: two figures sit facing each other in an open area enclosed by pine shade and rocks; the foreground path and railings lead the movement route toward this gathering place.
distinction: The foreground walkway and railings mainly organize the process of movement from outside into the gathering place beneath the trees, rather than primarily a layout in which the building site follows the mountain forms.

evidence: Upper center: a figure rides a dragon amid the clouds; no roofs, eaves, walls, or other architectural components are seen around them. | Lower part and right side: pines and blue-green rock walls overlap front and back, forming screening and depth layering, but no identifiable buildings are present among the trees and rocks. | Upper part and left side: distant mountains stretch across and cloud layers open and close; no bridges, paths, doorways, or fords—any clues for entry—are seen.
distinction: No explicit built elements are seen, and C1–C4 all lack sufficient evidence; it is only tentatively assigned to C2 because the pines and rocks in the lower part form a layering of front-back screening, and this does not confirm screened buildings.

evidence: Center, slightly right, middle ground: the roof and eaves of an open pavilion emerge from behind pine branches and leaves; the wall surface and figures inside are partially visible, forming a screened image of a house. | Middle ground to foreground left: thick pine trunks and horizontally extending canopies cover the upper part of the house; trees and rocks are in front and the house behind, forming a distinct layering of concealment and revelation. | Lower foreground: a wooden gate, a small path, and pedestrians are visible, but the path leading to the house is screened by slope rocks and pine roots, and its continuity is unclear.
distinction: The layering of screening and revealing between pines and the house runs through the middle ground and more clearly organizes the painting than the foreground path clues, so it is primarily judged as concealment and revelation rather than access to secluded settings.

evidence: Lower center and foreground: a large hall occupies the lower edge of the painting, with an open platform in front; figures are active both inside the hall and in the courtyard in front. | Center to right side: tall pines, mist, and distant peaks enclose an open space, and the hall is located at the visual convergence between the foreground buildings and the distant mountains.
distinction: The main hall mainly serves as the visual focus of the foreground scenery; no obvious building-site relationship arranged according to slope and bank or following the heights of the platform is seen, so it is closer to scenic accentuation than to terrain-responsive siting.

evidence: Lower-right corner, beneath the pines: behind the pine branches is a dark roof-like component, with only part of the eave line exposed, suggesting the possible existence of small built elements. | Central foreground rock platform: figures sit together on an open rock platform, and a huge pine on the left extends a horizontal branch above the platform, together with the right-side pine branches forming a layering of front-back screening.
distinction: Although the small pavilion is also placed according to the rocky slope, its main visible relationship is that pine branches screen the roof and partially reveal it, rather than merely showing a building site conforming to the terrain.

evidence: Left middle-ground edge: the roof and eave corner of a small pavilion or house are visible; most of the building itself is screened by slope rocks, cloud mist, and the edge of the painting, appearing only partially exposed. | Lower part, foreground slightly left: the roof of a low house emerges from behind slope rocks and willow trunks, with weeping willow branches and leaves and mountain rocks screening it front and back.
distinction: The painting mainly uses the screening and partial exposure of houses by willow groves and slope rocks to form spatial layering, rather than taking a clear layout of building sites according to slope and beside the bank as the dominant expression.

evidence: Center of the painting: the main building and the side hall on the right sit on stone platforms of differing heights; the multi-eaved pavilion steps back terrace by terrace, and the building bases and railings follow the rocky slope unevenly. | Slightly below center: multiple flights of steps and terraces in front of the main building extend downward; the steps, low walls, and rock masses meet across height differences, forming upper and lower courtyards. | Between the left mountain mass and the buildings: the building complex unfolds close against the rock terrace in front of the left peak, enclosed above by pine woodland and cloud/mist, showing that the building site is confined by the mountain configuration.
distinction: The main building is placed in separate positions on multi-level platforms that respond to the height differences of the rocky slope and forms the main subject of the painting; although the bridge path at lower left suggests entry, it is screened off by trees and rocks and does not become the main spatial relationship organizing the whole picture.

evidence: Left middle: several pitched roofs are arranged laterally along the gentle shoreline between the mountain foot and the water, backed by the mountain and fronting the water. | Left-middle roof cluster: the roofs are slightly staggered in height following the shoreline, and the building complex unfolds close against the terrace at the mountain foot, with tree clusters screening only parts of the walls.
distinction: The building complex is mainly laid out laterally along the gentle terrace between the mountain foot and the waterside, reflecting terrain-responsive siting; the screening by trees is only partial and does not produce a dominant effect of organizing pictorial layers through concealment and revelation.

evidence: Center-right mountainside: multiple levels of roofs, eave galleries, and railings are arranged in layers along natural terraces between rock faces, and the building bases are set following the turns of the rock mass. | Center-right building complex, upper and lower: the upper buildings are backed by steep cliffs, the lower ones adjoin the valley floor, and the height relationship between roof surfaces and rocky platforms is clear. | Left side and around the buildings: the waterfall and deep valley on the left and the surrounding pines and rocks define the direction in which the buildings unfold, and the built elements open and close with the mountain configuration.
distinction: Although the buildings are partly screened by trees and rocks, the dominant relationship is layered placement along the cliff-face terraces; concealment and revelation do not become the main way of organizing space.

evidence: Left-middle woodland belt: two low roof ridges or pitched roofs emerge from between rows of trees, trunks and branches overlap in front of the buildings, and most of the building bodies are obscured. | Around the houses in the left middle: the houses and woodland merge into one another, only parts of the roofs are exposed, forming layers of foreground-background screening and alternating concealment and revelation. | In front of the houses and at the lower part of the painting: in front of the houses is an open sloping bank or water surface; no bridge, path, or doorway can be seen forming a recognizable entry connection with the houses.
distinction: The houses form the scene mainly through screening by trees and partial exposure, and do not clearly mark a peak edge, valley mouth, or waterside prospect.

evidence: Lower right: a pavilion is built on a protruding rock platform, with the building body, platform base, and rock face closely adjoining, showing a situation of placing the building on the platform. | Middle ground, slightly left: a square pyramidal-roofed pavilion sits on a mountainside slope, supported below by layered sloping rocks and embraced by trees on both sides. | Lower center: houses are half-hidden among trees and rocks, placed in a mountain-rock hollow and corresponding to the direction of the sloping bank and stream.
distinction: The dominant role of the buildings lies in the direct correspondence between the building sites and the mountain-rock platforms and their placement according to the terrain, rather than merely using pavilions to mark a particular prospect.

evidence: Lower middle, slightly right: the roofs and eaves of a group of pavilions emerge half-visible from tree clusters and cloud/mist, the lower parts of the buildings are obscured, forming layers of concealment and revelation. | From center to upper right: the towering main peak and the waterfall on the right occupy the upper main body, while the buildings lie low at the mountain foot below them, pressed and set off by the mountain mass and mist above. | Foreground lower left and lower right: waterside, a small boat, willows, and sloping ground are visible, but in front of the buildings cloud/mist and tree clusters intervene, and no clear bridge or path is seen directly connecting them.
distinction: The buildings form layers of concealment and revelation by being half-screened by tree clusters and cloud/mist and by having their eaves and roofs exposed in layers; compared with mere placement at the mountain foot, this better explains their dominant role in composing the scene.

evidence: Left middle-lower: a multi-roofed building complex unfolds close against the slope terrace at the mountain foot, with eaves rising and falling in layers following the slope. | Left middle-upper: a small roof appears on a protruding rock platform, below which is a steep cliff, showing that the building is placed on the platform. | Right-middle slope: a group of roofs is distributed along the ridge and slope, meeting the turns of the mountain mass.
distinction: Although the buildings are partly concealed and revealed by trees and the mountain mass, they are more importantly placed separately on cliff platforms, slope feet, and ridges, with terrain height determining their positions; therefore C2, which treats concealment and revelation as forming the scene, is not adopted.

evidence: Left middle, slightly upper: a double-eaved pavilion stands on a platform clearly higher than its surroundings; the platform edge has railings and connects in front to an open terrace, which is joined to the terrace below by steps. | Building complex from center to lower right: multiple groups of halls, galleries, and courtyards are distributed across platforms of differing heights, descending layer by layer toward the lower right along the slope, with the levels connected by steps and turning galleries. | Lower left corner: rocks and tree clusters press close to the outer edge of the platform base, and the raised part of the building complex is supported by this sloping ground and rock mass.
distinction: The main category is based on the building complex being laid out in layers along the slope, with platform bases and steps placed according to the rise and fall of the terrain; although trees obscure some roofs, the screening does not become the main concealment-and-revelation layering that organizes the whole painting.

evidence: Lower left: wooden railings, posts, and a platform base are visible at the water's edge, placed close against the rock foot and the water surface. | Left edge: the upper part of the building is cut off by the edge of the picture, exposing only the waterside platform base and railings; the roof and interior are incomplete. | Center: on the open water surface there is a canopied small boat with figures, facing the left-bank platform base across the water; no bridge, path, or gallery is seen directly connecting them.
distinction: The waterside platform base on the left is positioned following the rock foot and shoreline, mainly presenting terrain-responsive placement; although a boat moves on the water, no recognizable bridge path or doorway/gallery forms a continuous entry route, so C4 is not adopted.

evidence: From center-left to center: multiple roofs, eaves, and parts of walls emerge from between dense tree crowns, and the bases of the buildings are mostly screened by trees, forming layers of concealment and revelation. | Foreground, slightly left of center: tall trees and dense tree clusters stand across the front of the building complex, causing it to appear in sections through gaps in the trees and to be separated from the mountain mass behind. | Lower right: the water surface and a wooden bridge are clearly visible, but between the bridge and the central building complex there is no recognizable continuous path connecting them.
distinction: Although the building complex is laid out in layers along the sloping bank, the screening and exposure of roofs and eaves by tree crowns more directly organizes the middle-ground layers, so the main category is C2 rather than C1.

evidence: Lower-left foreground: a group of houses is built on a sloping platform between rocks and water, with eaves extending laterally along the waterside and supporting structures visible at the front edge near the water. | From center to right middle ground: a mountain path runs along the boundary between the slope and the water, and travelers proceed toward the upper right along the ramp, their route avoiding trees and rocks. | Right-upper mountainside: building roof outlines emerge among trees, backed by the mountain mass and situated on the mountainside slope.
distinction: The main category centers on the site relationship whereby the houses follow the rocky bank platform and their front edge fronts the water; although travelers on the mountain path are visible, the path does not directly connect to the foreground houses and does not constitute an entry route governing the whole painting.

evidence: From left to center-left: a waterfall drops between high cliffs, and below it water vapor and unpainted space form an open viewing surface. | Bottom center: two figures sit on the ground on a natural rock platform, facing the waterfall on the left, forming a clear stopping and viewing point; no roofs, beams, columns, or walls are visible. | Lower-right near foreground: a figure holding a staff stands on a rocky slope, surrounded by natural rocks and vegetation; no bridge, gallery, gate, or other clear built connecting element is visible.
distinction: The painting concentrates the prospect through the figures on the rock platform stopping to view the waterfall directly; the clear connection of entry into built structures via bridge, path, gallery, or gate required by C4 does not appear.

evidence: Lower-left rock platform: a roof and a railed platform sit directly on a protruding rock platform, and the platform edge turns with the rock ridge and faces the water. | Lower-left foreground: the roof presses against the rocky slope, bamboo branches cross in front of the eaves, and the height relationship between the built elements, the rock platform, and the bamboo grove is visible. | Lower right and distant view: beyond the platform are the open water surface and low, flat distant mountains; the building is located high at the cliff edge, forming an interface that opens from the rock platform toward the water.
distinction: The main category emphasizes terrain-responsive placement, with the roof and platform unfolding according to the height of the rock platform and cliff edge; although C3 could also explain its waterside viewing function, that is less directly visible than this placement according to the platform.

evidence: From lower left to the central water surface: a person rides a small boat floating on the water, close to the rocks on the right; the boat, as a scenic accent, concentrates the space of the water surface and marks the scene of boating. | Right side and below: rocks and water plants surround it, and the boat lies between the opening and closing of the landscape, becoming the marker that identifies the waterscape of this place.
distinction: The boat is not laid out according to variations in terrain height; rather, it floats on the water as a scenic accent, emphasizing the prospect rather than terrain-responsive placement.

evidence: From lower center of the painting to the right bank: a wooden bridge spans a rocky stream ravine; the bridge deck, posts, and railings are clearly visible, and two figures are on the bridge. | Bridgeheads and banks on both sides: the two ends of the bridge connect to rocky banks and a small path, and the path extends along the stream valley into the depth of the painting, forming an enterable spatial connection. | Behind and above the bridge: the bridge deck and figures are in the lower foreground, while behind them the stream valley and layered mountain masses unfold; tall pines slant out from the left and cover the area above, forming a movement-through-the-landscape setting from near to far.
distinction: The continuous passage relationship of the bridge, bank path, and travelers shows that its main role is to be enterable and to allow continued travel, which fits C4 better than merely building a bridge according to the terrain.

evidence: Lower left to lower middle: a hall with lattice windows and a pitched roof stands behind sloping rocks; the roof and part of the wall surface are visible, and the left front is screened by red-leaf trees and rocks. | Slightly below center of the painting: a thick pine trunk slants across in front of the building from below, obscuring part of the roof surface and facade, forming a screening layer and layers of concealment and revelation. | Lower right: a figure on horseback is visible traveling along a snow path, with stone-railing-like elements beside them, but the connection between the path and the hall entrance is not clear.
distinction: The building organizes spatial layers mainly through screening and exposure by pine trunks, rocks, and trees; although the figures' path at lower right suggests movement through the landscape, no clear continuous entry relationship leading to the building is visible.

evidence: Left half to upper part: a huge mountain mass rises from the left, its summit and ridge covered with trees; the mountain slopes down to the right and leaves a large area of blank space. | Lower left to lower middle: tall trees and protruding rocks occupy the foreground, forming a space of sloping bank and trees-and-rocks screening. | Lower right: near the shore of the open water surface is a canopied small boat with one person visible in it; no clear houses or continuous bridge path are visible, and this small boat is an isolated visual anchor in the water area.
distinction: The canopied small boat/suspected man-made object at lower right mainly serves as a visual anchor on the open water surface and shows no connection to a bridge, path, or enterable route, so it is closer to a scenic accent than to access to a secluded setting.

evidence: Slightly right of center: a group of houses is laid out according to the mountainside slope; roofs and walls are visible, surrounded by trees and rocks. | Lower left to center: the foreground has a stream, a small bridge, and a winding mountain path; two travelers proceed along the path toward the buildings. | Beside the rock face at lower left: the mountain path turns and extends along the edge of a huge rock, forming a recognizable spatial connection with the terrace where the buildings stand.
distinction: The path, small bridge, and travelers link the foreground and the mountain dwelling into an enterable spatial process, which is more dominant than mere siting according to the mountain.

evidence: Upper left: multi-level pavilions are arranged in stacked layers along the high terraces of the slope, and below them lower houses are arranged along the slope. | Lower-left foreground: the platform is close to the waterside and slope foot; railings, stairs, and retaining walls turn with the terrain, forming terraces at different heights. | Right mountainside: pavilions and terraces are distributed according to the rock faces and ridges, corresponding in position to the distant peaks and slope surfaces.
distinction: The main category is based on the visible positional relationships of terraces, slope feet, and mountainsides; although the bridge path and figures on the right suggest travel, they do not run through the whole composition to organize the built elements as terrain placement does.

evidence: Lower left: a multi-bay house and gallery sit on a rock platform protruding into the water, with the rear close against the sloping rock and the front facing the water; the roof and platform base unfold according to the heights of the rocky bank. | Slightly right of center: between pines and the sloping bank, a figure on horseback is visible traveling along a pale slope path; the path curves toward the houses on the left but is partly screened by trees and rocks. | Right mountainside: a small pavilion is half-exposed behind rocks and tree clusters, its position attached to a hollow in the mountain mass.
distinction: The main building complex is placed directly according to the heights of the rock platform, waterside, and mountain foot, with the terrain participating in its site and unfolding; although the figures' path suggests possible travel and entry, the entry connection leading to the houses is not clearly continuous.

evidence: Left-upper mountainside terrace: several halls or pavilions are visible backed against a cliff face with a platform in front; the buildings are placed on a protruding mountainside terrace. | Left-middle of the painting: a pale, winding mountain path coils upward along the slope, leading to the buildings at the upper left. | Left foreground: figures and railings are set along the sloping bank, close to the lower section of the mountain path, forming a foreground starting point for entering the mountain.
distinction: Although the buildings are clearly placed according to the mountainside terrace, the painting more prominently highlights the entry process in which the winding mountain path leads up from the foreground and approaches the terrace pavilions; therefore C4 is closer to the main spatial role than C1, which emphasizes only terrain-responsive placement.

evidence: Left middle-ground slope: a group of railed houses is arranged in layers according to the rocky slope, with bases close against the slope surface and terraces. | Lower center, slightly left: a small pavilion is built on a protruding rock platform; the roof meets the rock surface across a height difference, and its position follows the contours of the rock mass. | Right middle-ground among trees: several houses are scattered among the gentle slope and woodland, with roofs rising and falling according to the terrain.
