distinction: Although the buildings are partly screened by trees, the main relationship is that the house sites unfold according to the rocky slope and terraces; concealment and revelation are not dominant.

evidence: Slightly below center of the painting proper: two figures stand on sloping ground flanked by rock faces on the left and right; above the figures, unpainted space and cloud/mist form an opening extending into the depth of the rock gap; no roofs, walls, bridges, railings, or clear paths are visible. | Left and right sides of the painting proper: on the left are huge rocks and trees, on the right a steep rock face; the two enclose a valley-mouth-like space where the figures below the center are located.
distinction: No clear competing interpretation; compared with other categories, the painting only uses the rock-flanked sloping ground and the presence of figures to suggest a sense of space that can turn into a deep valley, but it lacks clear evidence of built elements.

evidence: Lower right: a small pavilion with a thatched roof, posts, and railings stands on a stone-built platform base, which is attached to the rock face on the right. | From lower center to lower right: a curved railed walkway with short posts extends from the lower edge of the painting toward the upper right, its direction pointing toward the rock platform where the small pavilion stands. | Middle right: the branches of a thick old tree extend from the rock face across to the center of the painting, above the small pavilion, forming local screening.
distinction: Although the small pavilion is built according to the rock platform, the curved railed walkway in the foreground clearly leads toward it, forming an approachable and enterable spatial relationship; therefore access to secluded settings is dominant, rather than mere terrain-responsive placement.

evidence: Slightly above center of the painting: multiple roofs are arranged along the mountain ridge; roof surfaces and eaves emerge from behind the rock ridge in front, and the lower parts of the buildings are obscured by rocks. | Left of the central building complex: pines and rock masses cover the front side of the buildings, with only parts of the walls and roofs visible, forming a foreground-background concealment-and-revelation relationship.
distinction: The dominant effect of the central building complex is that roof surfaces are partly obscured by rocks and pine woodland and then exposed in layers, rather than merely having their sites arranged according to the sloping terraces.

evidence: Lower foreground, slightly right of center: a wooden bridge spans between the stream banks; on the bridge deck, pedestrians and pack animals are visible crossing from left to right. | Right-middle water surface: a canopied boat floats on the river, with a person poling at the bow and a person at the stern; together with the pedestrians on the bridge, it forms a foreground passage clue. | Right end of the bridge and foreground sloping bank: the bridge connects with rocks and sloping ground on both banks, and the figures enter or leave the foreground mountain bank along the bridge deck.
distinction: The core role of the wooden bridge and the passing figures is to connect the two banks and organize a path into the foreground landscape, rather than mainly placing buildings according to mountain forms and waterside.

evidence: Center-left mountainside: multiple halls are arranged in a staggered hierarchy along the rock terraces, with roofs and walls unfolding layer by layer following the turns of the mountain mass. | Lower-left sloping bank: the building complex descends layer by layer from the slope to the water's edge, and the building bases fit the height changes of the rock strata and shoreline. | Lower-right near the water: houses are placed on a relatively gentle rock terrace at the mountain foot, backed by the mountain mass, facing the water, and adjoining the surrounding trees and rocks.
distinction: The main relationship is that the buildings are placed in layers according to the mountain terraces and sloping bank; screening by trees and rocks appears only locally and does not become the dominant concealment-and-revelation layering organizing the painting.

evidence: Left middle: a pavilion and houses are arranged in a staggered hierarchy according to the slope terraces, backed by hills, fronting sloping ground and tree clusters, with building sites rising with the terrain. | Around the buildings on the left: pine woodland surrounds the buildings, and some eaves are obscured by tree crowns, but the main pavilion and roofs remain clearly exposed. | Lower-right slope foot: figures on horseback can be seen traveling along the gentle zone at the mountain foot; the path extends toward the stream bank but does not clearly lead to the building complex on the left.
distinction: The main relationship is that the building complex is laid out according to the heights of the slope terraces and unfolds with the mountain form; although tree crowns screen it, they do not produce a dominant effect of organizing the scene through concealment and revelation.

evidence: Slightly left of center: among the trees and shrubs on the sloping platform, the pitched roof and walls of a small house emerge, with trunks and branches overlapping in front and behind. | From slightly left of center to the foreground: the woodland where the house is located is enclosed by foreground sloping rocks, trunks, and dense tree crowns, and the roof and walls are half-hidden and half-exposed. | Lower-left foreground: an arched bridge and shoreline are visible, but behind the bridge the path leading to the house is screened off by trees and rocks, and the continuous connection is not clear.
distinction: The half-concealment and half-exposure of the house's roof and walls by trees and rocks constitutes the main spatial layering, and is more directly visible than the entry process guided by bridge and path.

evidence: Lower-left mountain foot: what appears to be a wooden plank road or guardrail is visible winding along the sloping bank, and people and horses travel along it. | Lower center to right: an earthen road runs laterally across the foreground, and freight carts, riders, and herds move along the road toward the tree clusters and the depths of the sloping ground on the right. | Central tree cluster: trunks and sloping rocks pinch the road, and the path appears intermittently behind the trees, forming a clue of entry extending into the depth of the painting.
distinction: The main category expresses the spatial process of entering the depths through visible paths and the direction of travel; C1 requires clear built elements placed according to mountain forms and sloping banks, but this painting lacks identifiable buildings.

evidence: Upper right: A city gate and gate tower are built on the cliff; the arched gate opens toward the foot of the mountain, and the structure is embedded high in the rock mass. | Right to center: A mountain path winds down along the rock face; travelers are on the path, moving toward the city gate. | Center left: Among the trees on the sloping bank, figures on horseback travel along a small path, forming with the mountain path on the right a continuous route of travel.
distinction: Although the city gate is built according to the terrain of the cliff, the painting gives greater prominence to the winding mountain path, the travelers, and the accessible process of connecting with the gate opening, rather than merely showing the correspondence between the building site and the mountain forms.

evidence: Lower right foreground rock slope and grove: White walls and roofs emerge between the trees; the buildings are partly screened and partly revealed by the rocks in front and the trees on both sides. | Lower right corner by the stream bank: A small arched bridge spans a gap at the bank; it sits close to the edge of the painting and leads toward the area of trees and rocks, but the route is not fully continuous or clearly evident. | Center to upper area: A large expanse of unpainted water surface and distant mountains form an open background, against which the trees, rocks, and buildings at lower right constitute a foreground layer.
distinction: The buildings are mainly screened by trees and rocks to form a partly hidden, partly revealed foreground layer, rather than being led into by continuous bridges and paths as the dominant feature of the painting; the bridge occupies only a marginal, auxiliary position.

evidence: Slightly left of center: A four-pillared open pavilion with a pyramidal roof stands on a low platform; two figures sit facing each other inside, and the pavilion is very clear in the open foreground. | To the right of and above the pavilion: A tall tree grows close to the pavilion's right side, its branches and leaves partly covering the eaves, but the pavilion body, pillars, and beams and the figures remain largely visible. | Around the pavilion and in the distance: A low earthen bank and clusters of flowers lie in front of the pavilion, sloping ground lies to either side, and distant peaks rise and fall behind; the pavilion is the visual focus in the foreground of this open landscape.
distinction: The tree canopy only partly covers the eaves and does not produce a dominant effect of "a house seen through the woods, separated by screening"; the pavilion's role in marking and focusing the open pictorial field is more prominent.

evidence: Behind the rocks at upper middle right: A building with a pitched roof is revealed; dead branches and rocks in front screen part of its walls, creating a layered effect of concealment and revelation. | Among the willow grove at lower left: The outlines of low sheds or houses are screened by willow trunks and branches, and figures stand beside them. | Center and foreground: Water surface, sandbars, and rows of willows surround the two groups of built structures, placing the houses amid screening trees.
distinction: The principal relationship is the screening and revealing of the houses by trees and rocks, forming layers, not merely their placement against slopes and beside water.

evidence: Lower left of center, on the north bank of the stream: The pavilion is built on a platform raised on posts; the front edge of the platform is roughly level with the top line of the bank slope and is erected in response to the drop of the sloping bank toward the water. | Where the stream meets the broad water surface in the lower part of the painting: The stream flows from left to right past beneath the pavilion and then joins the large expanse of water on the right; the pavilion site lies on a narrow, flat terrace between the foot of the slope and the water. | Behind and to the right of the pavilion: A bamboo grove and rising slope lie immediately behind the pavilion, and an autumn tree stands close to its right side; the building is placed along the wooded edge at the foot of the slope, with its back to the slope and facing the water.
distinction: The correspondence between the pavilion site and the height difference of the bank slope and the stream water level is concretely visible, amounting to a building set on a platform raised according to the terrain; although it may also serve as a waterside scenic accent, its role in "marking a scenic spot" is less clear than its terrain-responsive placement.

evidence: Lower center: The ridges and eaves of several roofs emerge from among dense tree canopies, which cover the lower parts and sides of the buildings. | Lower left corner: A long roof is half screened behind foreground trees; only the ridge, eave line, and part of the roof surface are visible, and the main body of the building is blocked by trees. | Lower center: A group of houses lies low at the foot of the main peak, surrounded by dense trees, with roofs partly revealed from among the groves.
distinction: The buildings mainly form spatial layers through the screening and partial revealing of the groves, rather than having their positions determined solely by mountain slopes and terraces; therefore concealment and revelation is closer to their main role in the composition than terrain-responsive siting.

evidence: Center to right of the painting: Two sailing cargo boats lie across the water; the figures on board pole the boats and arrange basketed goods, and masts, sails, and ropes form clear boating activity on the water. | Shoreline at upper left: A row of figures tow along the bank, the towlines connecting to the mast of the boat on the left, together with the hull forming a visible link of bank towing and propulsion on the water. | Lower part and background of the whole painting: The picture consists mainly of layered water ripples and low, flat sandbars and shorelines; no stable built volumes such as houses, bridges, paths, or gate porches are seen.
distinction: The boats and towing provide a travel thread of crossing and advancing over water, closer to C4; however, there are no clear built structures in the painting, so it cannot be confirmed as in C3 that buildings serve to highlight the scenery.

evidence: Foot of the mountain at left: A pavilion is half hidden at the lower edge of the mountain mass; its roof and eave corners emerge from behind the rock face and trees, placed against the foot of the steep cliff. | Sloping bank at lower right: A group of houses spreads laterally along a gently sloping terrace, with a railed platform in front and backed by rocks and trees, the buildings rising and falling in accordance with the slope. | Foreground at bottom: Two figures walk on a small path at the foot of the mountain, the path extending toward the rocks in the center, but no continuous, clear accessible route between the path and the houses is visible.
distinction: Although the pavilion at left is screened by rocks and trees, the whole painting more prominently shows the houses placed according to the slope terraces, mountain foot, and waterside terrain; concealment and revelation do not run through it as strongly as terrain-responsive arrangement.

evidence: Pine grove and houses from lower left to center left: The canopies and trunks of several pines screen the foreground, with roofs and eaves emerging among the pine needles; the building complex shows a staggered relationship of partial concealment and partial revelation, front and back. | Waterside rock platform slightly right of center: A pavilion house stands on the rock platform, its roof and eave corners partly screened by pine branches and slope rocks, with a platform or railing exposed on the waterside, forming a layered effect of screening.
distinction: Although the buildings are likewise arranged according to slope platforms and the waterside, the painting more prominently shows the screening and revealing of roofs and eaves by pines and slope rocks, rather than having building sites determined solely by topography.

evidence: Lower left and lower center: Many pavilions and terraces are heavily screened by the branches and leaves of pines and mixed trees; only roofs, flying eaves, and parts of the upper storeys are exposed, forming a clear layering of concealment and revelation. | Lower right: A complex of buildings is hidden behind groves, tree canopies and eaves overlapping, with the main bodies of the buildings screened by trees. | Waterside and hills in the upper middle: Several smaller pavilions and houses are scattered among rocks and trees, their positions set off by the natural scenery.
distinction: The buildings do indeed serve as scenic accents, but the dominant means of spatial organization in the painting is the screening and revealing of buildings by trees, creating rich layers; C2 is therefore more apt.

evidence: Middle right of the painting: A complex of buildings is surrounded by dense pine groves and mixed trees; roofs, eaves, and parts of the walls are screened by branches and leaves, presenting a partly hidden, partly revealed state. | Inside and in front of the buildings: Through gaps in the trees, the open front gallery of the buildings and the activities of figures within can be seen; the relationship of concealment and revelation constitutes the main spatial layering of the painting.
distinction: Although the buildings are erected according to the mountain terrain, the most prominent compositional device in the painting is the use of trees to screen and reveal the buildings so as to create a deep sense of layering, rather than simply emphasizing the correspondence between buildings and topography.

evidence: Lower left corner: A complex of buildings is stacked in layers according to the mountain-slope terrain, with roofs rising and falling in a clearly stepped arrangement that follows the mountain forms. | Lower right side: A pavilion is placed by the waterside on a sandbar or islet, following the waterside terrain and corresponding to the water's edge. | Mountain foot at left: The building sites are closely integrated with the rocks and slope terraces, showing placement according to local conditions.
distinction: Although at the lower right a bridge or railing connects the pavilion and boats on the water hint at routes, the main building complex at left more strikingly shows placement following the mountain slopes and terraces; the overall built layout mainly reflects adaptation to local conditions.

evidence: Foreground rock platform at lower left: The tops of the layered green rock masses are relatively flat and bear pines; among the rocks, several small patches of level ground resembling platforms are visible, but details of building such as roofs or walls cannot be made out. | At the bottom of the rocks at lower left near the painting's edge: Below the rocks are thin traces in pale red and ochre, resembling masonry or structural members, but because the colored lines are very fine and blend with the rock feet and water ripples, it cannot be confirmed whether they are built structures. | Center to right and upper area: Most of the painting is an open water surface formed of fine ripples, with cloud vapor and distant peaks above; apart from the rocks at lower left, there are no other clear clues to buildings, bridges, paths, or gate openings.
distinction: The suspected structures on the rock platform appear rather to be placed according to the rises and falls of the rock platform than to mark the distant peaks or water scenery with clear volumes or positions; however, the built structures themselves are not clear, and both interpretations lack sufficient evidence.

evidence: Left: A tall pavilion is visible, serving as the destination or goal of the painting. | Lower left to center: Figures travel along mountain paths, plank walks, and bridges, forming a clear route of entry into the mountains. | Left: A waterfall and gaps among the rocks help convey the extension and accessibility of the space.
distinction: Although the pavilion serves as a scenic accent, the painting more strongly emphasizes the spatial process of entering the mountains through paths, bridges, and human activity.

evidence: Left: Dead trees, slope rocks, and birds are visible; no traces of buildings or man-made construction | Right and center: A large area of unpainted space, with only faint water ripples and a single flying bird; no built structures seen
distinction: No clear built structures are seen in the painting, so no valid distinction among categories can be made.

evidence: Lower left corner: On the water beside dark slope rocks is a small boat with a rounded arched canopy; a figure on board holds a pole extending toward the water, forming the only focal point on the water near the bank. | Upper middle right: In the distance is a low rocky islet with clumps of grass, very small in volume, contrasting openness with isolation against the vast, clear river surface. | Center to upper area: Most of the painting is blank water surface and sparse grass strokes; there are no discernible built structures or travel clues such as bridges, paths, gates, or building complexes.
distinction: The small boat merely marks a single waterside scene near the bank on a vast, clear water surface, rather than unfolding as terrain-responsive building distributed according to slope terraces and shorelines; C1 is therefore not adopted.

evidence: Slightly below center of the painting: Several roofs, eaves, and courtyards are screened by rows of pines; they emerge only through gaps between trunks and canopies, forming a layered relationship of concealment and revelation, front and back. | Middle ground at right: Huge rocks and groves press close to the right edge of the building complex, screening parts of the walls and courtyards so that the buildings are revealed behind rocks and tree shadows. | Mountainside at upper left: A small pavilion or house is half hidden among slope rocks and trees; its roof outline is visible but incomplete, showing the use of natural scenery to create concealment and revelation.
distinction: The buildings are organized into scenery mainly through the screening and revealing of pines, rocks, and groves, while the foreground path and figures do not form a process of entry running through the painting.

evidence: Between the red trees and the pine grove at lower left: The roof and pale walls of a small house on a slope are only partly revealed among branches and leaves, with most of the building screened by foreground trees. | On the hillside near the water at lower left: The small house is placed against a low slope and the waterside, with trees and rocks layered in front and behind, so that the building appears as a half-hidden, half-revealed mass among the woods.
distinction: The main house forms a woodland layering through being partly screened by trees and rocks; although the bridge at right suggests crossing the water, no path connecting to the dwelling or leading into deeper space is visible.

evidence: Left: Sloping banks, trees, and a crane are visible; no buildings, bridges, or other built structures are seen. | Middle and far distance: Cloud-wreathed mountains, with no obvious traces of human activity.
distinction: No built structures are seen in the painting; it is assigned according to the overall organization of the landscape, with no clear competing interpretation.

evidence: Whole painting: The painting is dominated by human activity, with gentle distant mountains and open ground in the background; no built elements such as houses, pavilions, or bridges are seen. | Lower right corner: Sloping ground and shrubs are depicted, showing natural terrain features. | Left and center: Several groups of figures walk or stand on the gentle terrain, and the spatial organization relies on the open topography.
distinction: There are no built elements in the painting; C1 concerns the topographical basis and is relatively closer to the overall gentle spatial organization, whereas C4 requires built structures connected with paths, which are absent here.

evidence: Lower center to right: A winding path extends from where the foreground figures stand toward the mountain foot on the right, connecting the foreground with the middle-ground landscape. | Lower left to center: Houses are faintly visible among the trees, forming a relationship of screening with the surrounding trees. | Top of the cliff at lower middle: A pavilion stands on the cliff top above the waterfall, marking the scenery at the height.
distinction: Although the pavilion on the cliff top serves as a scenic accent, the clear figures and winding path in the lower part of the painting form an explicit travel thread that draws the eye into the depths of the landscape; the spatial organization of access to secluded settings is more pervasive.

evidence: Lower right corner: A wooden bridge spans the water, connecting the two banks; beside the bridge is a figure carrying a load on a pole, suggesting a route of entry into the painting. | Mountain hollow at left: A complex of buildings is erected according to the mountain terrain, with steps and covered galleries connecting them and figures moving among them, showing an accessible and traversable spatial relationship. | Among the rocks in the center: Figures ride horses along a small path among rocks and trees, further reinforcing the travelable spatial thread in the painting.
distinction: Although the building complex at left reflects terrain-responsive siting, the travel thread formed by bridges, paths, and human activity in the painting is more prominent and dominates the spatial organization, leading the viewer deeper into the picture.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: Bridges and winding paths are visible connecting different building complexes, and figures walk on the paths, forming a clear thread of entry and travel. | Lower left and lower right: The building complexes are linked by small paths and bridges, guiding the eye deeper into the painting and expressing an accessible spatial process. | Center of the painting: Pavilions are placed according to the rocks, with paths or steps connected to them, suggesting accessibility from below to above.
distinction: Although the buildings also have a screened-and-revealed relationship among trees and rocks, the connecting role of bridges and paths in the painting is more prominent, clearly organizing an accessible, traversable spatial sequence.

evidence: Lower left: A small bridge spans the water, with pedestrians on it, connecting the bank with the built area on the right and providing a clear clue of entry. | Lower right and middle right: Built structures (thatched huts, pavilions) are distributed against the mountains and beside the water, linked to one another by sloping banks, trees, and implied paths, forming a traversable spatial layering. | Mountainside at right: Houses are placed in layers following the mountain terrain, suggesting a route ascending the mountain and reinforcing the spatial process from below to above and from outside to inside.
distinction: Although the built structures are set against the mountains and beside the water (C1), the connecting role of travel clues such as bridges and paths in the painting is more prominent, clearly organizing an accessible spatial process; C4 is therefore more apt.

evidence: Middle ground at right: A pavilion is built on a projecting rock platform, its site closely conforming to the forms of the rocks. | Middle ground at left and on the mountainside: Buildings are distributed in staggered fashion along mountain slopes and terraces, following the rises and falls of the mountain mass. | Lower foreground: Waterside pavilions are erected on the rocky bank by the water and unfold along the bank, corresponding to the water surface and bank rocks.
distinction: Although the built structures serve to mark the scenery, the correspondence of their sites and elevations with the mountain forms and slope terraces is more prominent and dominates the spatial organization of the painting.

evidence: Middle left: Halls and pavilions are built on a terrace at the cliff bank, surrounded and screened by trees. | Lower right to center: A long embankment or bridge crosses the water, crowded with moving figures, forming a clear touring route. | Center: The embankment path directly connects to and leads toward the built area on the terrace; figures move along the road toward the buildings, expressing an accessible spatial process.
distinction: Although trees screen the buildings, the embankment path and the moving crowds running through the painting more strongly organize the process of entering the built area, so C4 is more dominant than C2.

evidence: Slightly left of center in the painting: A thatched-roof open pavilion, inside which a figure is seen lying on a couch. | Slightly left of center of the painting: The branches and leaves of a large tree extend from the front and side, partly screening the roof and left structure of the built structure, creating a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Right and lower part of the painting: The built structure is close to the water, surrounded by reeds and lotus leaves, setting off the environmental layering in which it sits.
distinction: The marked screening of the built structure by tree branches and leaves constitutes the main spatial layering of the painting, in keeping with the definition of concealment and revelation, rather than emphasizing topographical correspondence or path guidance.

evidence: Lower left: Built structures such as thatched huts and thatched pavilions are screened among dense groves and sloping banks; parts of roofs and eaves emerge through gaps in the branches and leaves, forming a spatial layering of alternating concealment and revelation. | Lower right: Boats are moored by the bank, forming with the built structures and trees on the bank a foreground scene of riverbank activity. | Middle ground: Sailing boats move on the river, forming a contrast of near and far with the trees and buildings on the near bank, but the built structures themselves take their scenic form mainly through the screening relationships of the trees.
distinction: Although the built structures stand beside the waterside slopes, the painting more strongly emphasizes their half-screened, half-revealed relationship with the trees and branches, rather than a layout unfolding simply according to the height of the terrain.

evidence: Whole painting: The painting consists mainly of wintry woods and bare trees, flying birds, and snow-covered sandbars; no man-made structures such as houses or bridges are seen. | Lower half of the painting: Trees and sandbars extend naturally in keeping with the waterside terrain, presenting an open natural spatial relationship.
distinction: No built structures are visible in the painting; based on the overall visible organization of the natural landscape, it is assigned to the category closest to the expression of natural forms.

evidence: Lower left: An open pavilion is built against a rocky slope bank, its site closely integrated with the rocks; below, steps and railings extend toward the water, presenting a layout of a building set on a platform and unfolding along the bank. | Opposite bank at right of the painting: In the distance, pavilions are faintly visible screened behind trees, echoing the distant mountains and level slopes.
distinction: Although the pines at left screen the pavilion, the pavilion's terrain-responsive placement on the rocks by the water, with steps descending, is clearer and more dominant.

evidence: Main subject of the painting: The painting is dominated by several huge ancient trees and mountains and rocks, with several figures beneath the trees, and flowing water in the lower left; no clear houses, pavilions, or other built structures are visible. | Middle-lower part: The figures are situated among the ancient trees and mountains and rocks, showing a certain spatial layering and partly screened relationship.
distinction: There are no clear built elements in the painting, only a partly screened layering of figures and natural scenery, so it is only tentatively assigned to C2.

evidence: Right side and lower right: A large pavilion complex leans against the cliff and rock face, arranged layer upon layer upward, with terraces and corridors following the mountain's rises and falls in staggered fashion, showing the feature of buildings set on terraces. | Upper part of the painting and distant mountainside: Multiple buildings are placed according to the mountain's slopes and forms, with layout rising and falling with the mountain, corresponding to the natural terrain. | Left side and central waterside: Some buildings are arranged facing the water or along the sloping bank, with their bases meeting the water surface and land terrain.
distinction: Although the painting has clues of a bridge and figures traveling (C4), the layout of the building complex (especially the main building on the right) mainly embodies a site-related relationship of being placed according to the mountain's rises and falls, and the organizing role of terrain on building form is more dominant.

evidence: Lower left to center: Pavilion buildings are built on mountain-rock slope terraces, with long corridors and stairs connecting buildings at different heights, rising and falling in accord with the mountain. | Lower right: Buildings are arranged at the foot of the mountain, with eaves closely joined to the edges of the rocks, showing the form of buildings set against the rock.
distinction: In the painting the buildings are arranged layer upon layer on mountain-slope terraces, rising and falling in staggered fashion; the feature of site-responsive placement is most prominent, and although there are accompanying stairways and corridors, the core lies in the correspondence between building layout and the terrain's slope terraces.

evidence: Lower left: One person rides a donkey, another walks leading it, advancing along a path among the mountains and rocks toward the depth of the painting. | Middle right: A person carrying a load on a pole is crossing a simple wooden plank bridge; the bridge connects the waterside with the area where the buildings are located. | Upper left to center: A large pavilion building sits high on a terrace, and the path and bridge below point toward and lead to this building in spatial terms.
distinction: Although the buildings are built on mountain terraces, the clear path, bridge, and figures' walking steps in the painting emphasize more the process of traveling toward and approaching the buildings.

evidence: Lower left corner: An arched bridge and figures on the bridge are visible, connecting the foreground road with the waterside building complex, forming a clear clue of overland entry. | Lower right corner: A boat is visible on the water, near the waterside pavilion buildings, implying a relationship of arrival by water and movement through the landscape. | Middle-lower part of the painting: Buildings are scattered along the waterside at the mountain's foot, echoing through the shoreline and gaps in the mountains and rocks with the foreground clues of bridge and boat, presenting spatial extension.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed against the mountain and beside the water, the painting constructs clear clues of movement through the landscape and arrival through the distinct bridge, figures, and boat in the foreground, making the sense of spatial entry dominant.

evidence: Lower left: Sloping banks, mountains and rocks, and miscellaneous trees are visible, with tiny figures beneath the trees; no houses or pavilions or other built structures are visible. | Center: Large mountains and rocks rise, with woodland distributed around them, presenting the slope-and-rock organization of natural landscape. | Upper left: Sparse woods are on a distant slope, with no sign of buildings; the painting is dominated by natural terrain and trees.
distinction: No clear built elements are visible in the painting, only natural landscape and figures; it is assigned to the closest category based on the overall organization of terrain.

evidence: Center to right of the painting: A building complex with red walls and green tiles is arranged layer upon layer on mountain-slope terraces; obvious red perimeter walls, terraces, and hierarchical structure are visible, showing the form of buildings set on terraces and distributed according to the slope. | Background of the painting: Green mountain ridges lie behind the buildings; the building bases correspond to the mountain-slope terrain, unfolding according to the mountain's form. | Lower right foreground of the painting: Dark trees screen the lower part of the buildings, revealing the upper-storey buildings, but the main body of the buildings still clearly presents a layout set on mountain terraces.
distinction: Although the foreground trees screen the buildings (concealment and revelation), the dominant spatial logic of the painting is that the buildings are arranged layer upon layer relying on obvious sloping terrace bases (terrain-responsive siting), rather than forming the scene mainly through concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower part and middle of the painted panel: the building complex (pavilions and gazebos) has clear platforms or bases, railings, and enclosing walls, laid out immediately adjacent to the shoreline, presenting a form that unfolds along the bank. | Left side of the painted panel: the buildings are backed by mountains and rocks and trees; the layout follows the junction zone between the mountain foot and the waterside, and the building site corresponds to the natural terrain.
distinction: Although the buildings are the visual center of the painting, their platforms and layout clearly follow the waterside and mountain-foot terrain; the spatial relation of siting according to the ground is more prominent than mere accentuation of a vista.

evidence: Lower right of the painting: A small bridge is set over a stream, and two people on the bridge are walking along the bridge surface toward the depth of the painting (in the direction of the thatched pavilion). | Middle left of the painting: The roof, railings, and base of a thatched pavilion are revealed amid screening bamboo grove, serving as the destination of the people walking on the bridge. | Right side of the painting: Mountains, rocks, and the stream form a natural spatial transition, connecting the bridge on the right with the built structure on the left, constituting an accessible clue for movement through the landscape.
distinction: Although the thatched pavilion in the painting is screened by the bamboo grove (C2), the bridge on the right and the movement line of the figures clearly constitute a process of traveling toward the built structure; C4 better summarizes the overall spatial organization logic.

evidence: Middle of the right bank of the painting: A wooden bridge is visible spanning between the two banks, connecting the waterside path. | Water surface at lower right of the painting: There is a small boat with a canopy and people aboard, positioned on the water beneath the bridge, presenting a spatial relationship of traveling by boat and passing through the bridge.
distinction: Although the bridge is built adjoining the waterside, the painting emphasizes more its role as a passage connecting the two banks and guiding boat travel; therefore C4 is more apt than C1.

evidence: Middle right: A large tree grows on a green sloping bank, and the sloping bank extends to the water's edge. | Lower left sloping bank: There is a very tiny figure on the sloping bank, seemingly walking or standing.
distinction: No clear built elements are visible in the painting, only landscape, trees, and scenic accent figures; therefore it is assigned to scenic accentuation based on the overall visible space.

evidence: Right-side water surface of the painting: Two small boats with sails are visible floating on the water, implying clues of water transport and movement through the landscape. | Lower and left parts of the painting: The water surface is open, connecting the nearby willow-lined sloping bank with distant mountains and rocks, creating a sense of spatial extension for travel.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built elements, but the water surface and the movement clues of the boats conform more to the spatial-process implication of C4 than to mere scenic accentuation.

evidence: Middle-upper left: Between the mountain foot and the trees, several blurred brown outlines are faintly visible, suspected to be low roofs or built structures, but the details cannot be reliably identified. | Left side: The painting presents an open water surface, distant mountains, and trees along the bank, with an overall sparse and open composition.
distinction: Because the built elements are extremely blurred, they can only be inferred to serve as scenic accents amid the landscape, lacking clear evidence of spatial organization.

evidence: Right-hand painted panel: only waterside, sloping ground, clumps of grass, and trees are seen; no traces of built elements such as buildings, bridges, or paths are seen. | Lower part of the right-hand painted panel: the sloping bank and water surface extend naturally, presenting a natural spatial organization that follows the water and terrain.
distinction: The painting has no built elements; on the basis of the natural extension of the overall waterside and sloping ground, it is assigned to the closest category, C1.

evidence: Lower right corner of the circular painted panel of the right leaf: between the slope rocks and the base of a pine tree is a very small dark form, suspected to be a tiny figure or built element, but the details are blurred and cannot be reliably identified. | Overall circular painted panel of the right leaf: the painting consists mainly of pines in the near foreground on the right, slope rocks, and hazy peaks in the distance on the left; no clear, sizable built entity is seen.
distinction: The painting lacks a clear screening relation of architecture; the tiny element serves only as an accent in the lower right corner, which is more consistent with the role of scenic accentuation.

evidence: Center of the painting: Several houses are screened within a dense pine forest, with only roofs and parts of walls revealed, forming a deep layering of concealment and revelation. | Right side of the painting: A pavilion is built atop a cliff, with some buildings obscured by foreground trees and mountains and rocks, presenting a spatial relationship of seeing houses through a screen. | Left side of the painting: Building outlines are faintly visible amid dense woods, interwoven with the natural environment, strengthening the visual effect of concealment and revelation forming a scene.
distinction: Although the buildings are built against the cliff, the painting emphasizes more the trees' screening and revealing of the buildings; the concealment-and-revelation relationship is the main means of composing the scene.

evidence: Right slope of the distant mountains in the right-hand painted panel: amid dense woodland screening, the roof and walls of a building are faintly revealed, presenting a half-hidden, half-exposed state. | Overall right-hand painted panel: the building is tiny in scale and recedes deep into the mountain forest, using the screening of trees to form a deep spatial layering.
distinction: The building is deeply screened by trees and tiny in scale; its role is to create deep layering through concealment and revelation, rather than to mark the vista as a conspicuous sign.

evidence: Below the mountains and rocks on the left side of the painted panel: the roof and structure of a house (water pavilion) are visible, partly blocked by the trees and mountains and rocks above, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relation. | Center and left of the painted panel: mountains and rocks and trees occupy the main space, and the built elements are hidden behind trees and rocks, forming a spatial layering in which the house is seen through a screen.
distinction: Although the built elements are situated at the mountain foot by the water, the painting mainly shows their faintly visible layering through screening by trees and rocks; the concealment-and-revelation relation is more prominent than the correspondence of layout to siting according to the ground.

evidence: Middle of the right-hand painted panel: between the pine grove and mountains and rocks, the roof and structure of a thatched hut are faintly visible, the building partly screened by natural scenery, forming layers of concealment and revelation. | Lower part of the right-hand painted panel: at the junction of the waterside and the mountain foot there is a winding shoreline and gaps between rocks, suggesting spatial clues leading into the depths.
distinction: In the painting the concealment-and-revelation relation of the thatched hut hidden behind pines and rocks is the most direct, while the clues of a path or water inlet leading to the thatched hut are relatively weak and blurred.

evidence: Lower part of the right-side painting: A small boat is visible moored at the edge of the waterside, immediately adjacent to several willow trees. | Right-side painting: The painting is dominated by the waterside, trees, and a moored boat; no clear houses or fixed buildings are visible.
distinction: The painting mainly shows the spatial placement of the boat moored alongside the waterside, rather than emphasizing a path or process of entering the depths.

evidence: Left side and upper part of the painting: The branches and needles of a huge pine tree extend, forming the main natural screening element and covering most of the painting's space. | Middle-lower part of the painting: A figure sits beside sloping rocks, with a railing-like structure visible nearby; situated beneath the screening pine branches, the pine needles and branches form a layering of obscuring and revealing the railing and the figure's area.
distinction: Although the railing is set according to the sloping rocks, the core of the painting's composition lies in the covering and screening of the built element (railing/figures) by the pine branches and leaves; the concealment-and-revelation relationship dominates the spatial expression.

evidence: Lower right: sloping bank, trees, and mountains and rocks are visible; there are tiny blurred traces but no clear built elements can be identified. | Overall painted panel: the painting sets natural scenery below against a dark background; no clear architectural forms are seen.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built elements; only natural scenery screening is seen, so assignment to C2 is the closest inference.

evidence: Lower center of the painting: A large hall building, whose front and lower parts are obscured by dense foreground branches (appearing to be plum trees), presenting a layering of seeing a house behind trees, with roof, eaves, and columns revealed. | Right side of the painting: Tall pine trees and mountains and rocks are located to the side-rear and right of the building, forming foreground-background screening and spatial layering with the building.
distinction: Although the building is large in volume and is the main subject of the painting, in spatial organization it mainly embodies a concealment-and-revelation relationship of being obscured and revealed by foreground trees and side mountains and rocks, rather than serving merely as an accent marking the landscape scenery.

evidence: Below the right round surface: Blurred horizontal structures and block-like surfaces are visible, suspected to be a building roof or base, located at the bottom edge of the painting. | Center of the right round surface: There are dark mountain-rock or tree forms, located above the suspected building, forming an upper-lower spatial relationship.
distinction: The suspected building is located below the mountains, rocks, and trees / by the water, presenting a layout relationship dependent on the terrain, rather than serving merely as a visual scenic accent.

evidence: Main subject of the right-side painting: The painting depicts steep cliffs, dense trees, and swirling clouds and mist; the composition presents typical features of a landscape scene. | Calligraphic inscription poem on the left: The poem's content 'The perilous cliff drops sheer, the trees lush and green; the winding goat path opens a single thread' directly describes the steepness of the mountains and rocks and the winding path in the painting, corroborating the landscape theme. | Label in the upper right corner: The label text 'Xiao Zhao's Traveling through Mountain Passes' indicates the painting's title and author; Xiao Zhao was a Southern Song painter renowned for landscape painting, further confirming it as a landscape painting category.
distinction: Although the title is 'Traveling through Mountain Passes' and the poem mentions 'travelers' and 'horse hooves', and there are indeed extremely tiny figures and horses as scenic accents in the lower right corner of the painting, the overall composition, focus of brushwork, and spatial expression are all dominated by natural mountains, rocks, and trees; it belongs to a typical landscape painting (C2), rather than a figure painting with figures as the main subject.

evidence: Middle-lower and right parts of the painting: Multiple ox carts/horse carriages and figures are visible advancing along a mountain road, forming clear clues of movement through the landscape. | Mountain area in the middle-upper part of the painting: A building roof is visible amid screening trees, located deep in the direction of the road's advance. | Overall composition: The cart-and-horse procession advances along the stream and mountain road toward the depths, forming a spatial connection of going from here to there and approaching the built structure in the mountain hollow.
distinction: Although the building is partly obscured by trees (a C2 feature), the core of the painting lies in the process of the cart-and-horse procession advancing along the path and tending toward the built structure in the depths, emphasizing more an accessible spatial organization (C4).

evidence: Right-hand painted panel: on the right are painted towering sheer cliffs, with a broad water surface below. | Lower-left water surface: on the water is a small boat with two people aboard, in the posture of drifting on the water. | Lower right: bare tree branches are painted, extending toward the water surface.
distinction: The painting has no clear built elements; only boating suggests a process of traveling, so on the basis of movement-through-the-landscape clues it is assigned to C4, but there is a lack of connection between built elements and the clues.

evidence: Middle left: A thatched-roof building is half hidden behind foreground rocks and withered trees, revealing the roof, eave columns, and figures inside, forming an obvious layering of concealment and revelation. | Lower right corner: A walkway with railings and pedestrians are visible, echoing spatially with the building on the left, but the building mainly forms the scene through the screening of mountains, rocks, and trees.
distinction: Although the walkway in the painting implies a path, the core composition lies in the building on the left forming layering through the screening and revealing by mountains, rocks, and trees; therefore C2 is more dominant than C4.

evidence: Among the mountains and rocks on the right: A corner of eaves is revealed behind mountains, rocks, and pine trees, forming a spatial layering of screening and concealment-and-revelation. | Waterside below the painting: A building is set at the waterside, echoing in height with the screened building above.
distinction: The painting emphasizes more the concealment-and-revelation relationship of buildings half hidden and half revealed by mountains, rocks, and trees, rather than mere placement according to terrain.

evidence: Lower right: A platform or stone couch is set beside the cliff face, with a person sitting upright on it; the platform is built according to the cliff's form, with water below. | Right side: Pine trees extend horizontally, screening the cliff face and platform, forming a commanding spatial relationship.
distinction: The platform is built against the cliff, mainly embodying the terrain-responsive siting relationship of site-responsive placement, rather than merely identifying the scenery.

evidence: Lower center: winding steps and platforms connect building areas at different heights, with figures walking on them, forming a clear touring path. | Left side and lower-middle: multiple arched bridges cross water surfaces or valleys, connecting the two banks and different building groups, providing access into the built structures. | Between building groups: corridors and paths wind among the pavilions, guiding the eye from the foreground toward the depths of the buildings in the middle and background.
distinction: Although the buildings are arranged according to the mountain terrain, the painting more prominently highlights the spatial process by which touring clues such as bridges, steps, and corridors guide the movement of figures and the deepening of the gaze.

evidence: Right side of the painting, mid-slope: a group of pavilion buildings is visible, their roofs and walls partly obscured by the mountains and rocks and trees in front, presenting a half-hidden, half-revealed state. | Around the buildings: the buildings are surrounded by dense trees and steep rocks, forming a spatial layering in which deep woods conceal houses.
distinction: Although the buildings are erected according to the mountain, the painting more emphasizes their concealment and revelation as screened by mountains, rocks, and trees, rather than mere conformity to terrain.

evidence: Lower left waterside: pavilions and attached buildings are visible built beside the water, their sites unfolding in accordance with the form of the shoreline and sloping rocks. | Right side cliff: the towering cliff and waterfall form the main natural terrain, and the buildings are located on the waterside below them, presenting a spatial relationship of nestling against the mountain and beside the water.
distinction: Although the buildings are located by the water, their layout clearly unfolds in accordance with the terrain of the shoreline and sloping rocks, rather than serving merely as isolated markers pointing out the scenery.

evidence: Lower right: a figure sits on natural mountain rocks, with an attendant boy beside him; no houses, pavilions, or other clear built structures are visible. | Right side: cliffs and pine trees occupy the right side of the painting, forming natural terrain, and the figure is placed leaning against the rocks.
distinction: There is no clear architecture in the painting; the figure sits against the rocks, only barely embodying a placement relationship relying on the terrain, and is therefore assigned to C1 rather than scenic accentuation.

evidence: Left side: mountains and rocks, trees, and waterside are visible, constituting the main area where the painting's scenery gathers. | Distance: pale ink outlines the contours of distant mountains, forming spatial layering with the foreground.
distinction: No clear built structures are seen in the painting; the natural scenery on the left serves to concentrate the gaze within the empty background, and is therefore tentatively assigned to this category.

evidence: Lower left and left side: multiple houses and courtyards are largely obscured by dense branches and leaves, with only parts of roofs, eaves, and walls exposed, forming an evident relationship of concealment and revelation. | Left side of the painting, middle ground: the building group is screened among the trees, its presence revealed through gaps and edges of the woodland, presenting rich spatial layering.
distinction: Although the buildings are built beside the water, the painting more emphasizes the screening and revealing of the buildings by the trees; the relationship of concealment and revelation is the core of the composition.

evidence: Right semicircular painted panel: on the left are mountains and rocks and pines, on the right a broad water surface, on which is a small boat with figures; no fixed built elements such as houses or pavilions are seen. | Right water surface: the lone boat and figures are on the broad water surface, marking the scene of fishing on a cold stream and becoming the visual focus of the painting.
distinction: There are no fixed built elements in the painting; only a lone boat marks the vista, so it is assigned to C3; there are no obvious path or entry clues pointing to C4.

evidence: Lower right and right side: multi-story pavilions and platforms cascade down level by level against the sloping bank, and the building sites and railings are arranged in accordance with the terrain's rises and falls. | Left side and above: the broad water surface and distant mountains form an expansive natural configuration, and the built structures open toward the water, presenting a placement relationship of building along the bank.
distinction: Although the buildings point out the waterside scenery, their cascading platforms and layout conforming to the sloping bank more directly embody a terrain-responsive relationship of placement according to the terrain and shoreline.

evidence: Left side and center of the painting: the main building (great hall) is largely obscured by branches and leaves of trees in the foreground and middle ground, with only the roof, eaves, and part of the walls exposed, forming an evident relationship of concealment and revelation. | Foreground of the painting: trees interpose in front of the building with luxuriant branches and leaves, giving the building a spatial layering of 'seeing houses within the woods.'
distinction: Although the building is the main subject of the painting, its relationship of screening and revealing with the surrounding trees (concealment and revelation) constitutes the main spatial layering, rather than serving merely as a marker indicating the scenery.

evidence: Whole painting: the painting depicts only two birds perched on flowering branches; no traces of mountains and rocks, water bodies, or built structures are visible.
distinction: There is no built structure in the painting and no spatial expressive relationship can be constituted; because the rule requires forced selection of one of four, it is assigned to C1.

evidence: Lower center of the circular painted panel of the right leaf: at the mountain foot by the water a thatched hut is visible, its walls and roof partly blocked by the trees and mountains and rocks in front, presenting a half-hidden, half-exposed state. | Left side and upper part of the circular painted panel of the right leaf: towering mountains and rocks and dense trees form the foreground and middle ground, screening the built elements behind them and forming a clear spatial layering.
distinction: Although the architecture is situated against the mountains and beside the water, the painting emphasizes more the layers of concealment and revelation formed by the screening and exposure of the architecture by trees, mountains, and rocks, rather than simply emphasizing its layout as built according to the terrain.

evidence: Lower left corner: a small boat with a mast or sail is faintly visible on the water, implying the process of traveling on water or crossing the water.
distinction: The main category is C4, and the closest alternative category is C3, but the boat more implies the process of traveling on water rather than merely marking the scenery.

evidence: Top of the right-side cliff: a slender vertical structure is visible, resembling a pagoda or pavilion, located high on the cliff, marking the mountain configuration there.
distinction: The structure is located at an exposed spot atop the cliff and mainly serves to mark the high point of the mountain terrain, rather than emphasizing a layered relationship screened by mountains, rocks, and trees.

evidence: Whole painting: the painting presents only rolling waves and a gentle sandy shore below; no buildings, bridges, paths, figures, or other traces of built structures are visible.
distinction: There is no visible built structure in the painting and no specific spatial relationship can be determined; it is assigned to the closest category based solely on the overall visible organization of landscape.

evidence: Left side: willow trees, rocks, and two figures walking along the sloping bank are visible, presenting a state of traveling. | Right side: a large area of unpainted space forms an open water surface or flat ground, creating spatial extension with the direction in which the figures on the left are walking.
distinction: No built structures are visible in the painting; based on the momentum of the figures walking along the waterside and the extension of open space, it is assigned to C4, which expresses the process of traveling.

evidence: Whole painting: the painting mainly consists of waterside, sloping rocks, withered trees, bamboo clumps, and distant mountains; no clear traces of artificial built structures such as houses, bridges, or paths are visible.
distinction: No built structures are visible in the painting; it is assigned to the closest category based solely on the overall organization of natural landscape.

evidence: Lower left: two figures sit facing each other on the sloping bank, surrounded by rocks, pine trees, and bamboo clumps; no built elements such as houses or bridges are visible. | Right side: open water surface and distant mountains, with no traces of built structures.
distinction: No clear built structures are visible in the painting; it is assigned to the closest category based on the overall visible space, lacking clear evidence of built structures.

evidence: Lower right near the water: a built structure (resembling a pavilion or bridge) is visible, partly obscured by the rocks and trees on the right, presenting a spatial layering of half concealment and half revelation. | Left side and center of the painting: mainly sloping banks, trees, and distant mountains; no other clear built structures are visible, and the overall space is dominated by the relationship of concealment and revelation among natural scenery.
distinction: The built structure mainly uses the screening and revealing by rocks and trees to indicate its presence and participate in forming the scenery, rather than serving as an independent marker pointing out a particular landscape.

evidence: Lower left, slightly toward center: a canopied boat is moored at the waterside, its position and orientation conforming to the trend of the rocks and sloping ground along the bank. | Left side: trees and rocks form the boundary of the waterside, and the boat is placed close against this natural boundary, presenting a relationship of arrangement according to the ground.
distinction: Although the boat is partly obscured by the bank rocks, its main compositional role lies in mooring in accordance with the waterside terrain, rather than forming the scenery solely through concealment and revelation.

evidence: Left center of the painting: tall pine trees and withered trees stand in front of the building, their trunks and branches obscuring part of the building's roof and walls. | Left center of the painting: the building's lattice windows, eaves, and part of the roof are revealed through gaps in the trees, forming an evident spatial layering of concealment and revelation. | Left side of the painting: the building is placed against sloping rocks and trees, but the visual focus lies in the secluded, deep mood formed by the mutual screening of trees and building.
distinction: The painting organizes spatial layering mainly through the obscuring and revealing of the building by trees; the relationship of screening is more prominent than the conformity of the building layout to the terrain.

evidence: Center of the painting: two donkeys laden with firewood and a pedestrian carrying fish are visible, walking from right to left along the sloping ground at the foot of the mountain. | Right side and above of the painting: rocks and withered trees are distributed, constituting the path environment for the movement of the figures and livestock, but no houses or artificial structures are visible.
distinction: There is no clear built structure in the painting; it presents only the process of figures and livestock moving among rocks and trees, and is therefore assigned to the closest category of touring clues.

evidence: Left side: beneath pine trees and rocks, a figure sits upright with an attendant boy standing; no houses or pavilions or other built structures | Right side waterside: a stone pedestal or object and flying birds are visible; no clear architectural entity or screening relationship is seen.
distinction: There is no clear architecture in the painting; the figures and stone platform serve more as markers concentrating the waterside scenery, rather than an architectural layout unfolding according to the terrain.

evidence: Lower part of the painting, slightly to the right: a building group is visible, comprising multiple roofs and wall structures. | Around the building group: the buildings are surrounded by dense trees, and most of the structures are obscured by branches and leaves. | Parts of the building group: only parts of roofs and eaves are exposed, presenting an evident relationship of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the buildings are located at the foot of the mountain by the water, the painting more emphasizes the screening and revealing of the buildings by trees; the relationship of screening is more prominent than placement according to the ground.

evidence: Lower right: a wooden bridge spans the water, with pedestrians on it, connecting the water surface and the built area on land. | Water surface below: a small boat carries two people, presenting a state of traveling, heading toward the bank. | Center, slightly right: built structures (houses) are located within the woods, forming a spatial relationship of entry and approach with the touring clues of the bridge and boat.

evidence: Lower part to center of the painting: a walkway (or bridge) with railings winds among the rocks and trees, with two people walking on it. | Beside the rocks on the left: the walkway extends along the edge of the rocks, forming a path clue leading from the foreground into the middle ground.
distinction: The core of the painting lies in the spatial process of the path guiding the figures' walking (access to secluded settings), rather than the static relationship of buildings placed according to the mountain (terrain-responsive siting), and no clear houses or buildings are visible.

evidence: Whole painting: the painting shows only multiple columns of calligraphic inscription and red seals; no landscape scenery or any traces of built structures are visible.
distinction: The painting entirely lacks the spatial organization of landscape and built structures; because forced classification requires assignment to this category, there is no actual visual basis supporting a specific category.

evidence: Right image, left side among sloping rocks and bamboo grove: a tiny architectural outline is faintly visible, partly obscured by trees and sloping rocks, the details blurred and difficult to confirm. | Right image, right side water surface: the water is open, with a small boat floating on it, forming a spatial echo with the bank scenery on the left.

distinction: Although the building nestles against the rocks, the painting more emphasizes the obscuring and revealing of the building by branches and leaves; the relationship of concealment and revelation is the main means of composing the scenery.

evidence: Lower part of the painting and at the pavilion base: a clearly visible paved stone path (or steps) extends from the bottom of the painting and connects directly to the pavilion base, forming a definite line of entry. | Pavilion on the right: the pavilion is located at the end of the path, with people sitting and reclining inside; together with the path it presents a spatial process that is reachable and habitable/strollable.
