evidence: Circular painted panel of the right leaf: the painting presents mountains and rocks, pines, a stream, and flying birds; no clear traces of built elements such as houses, bridges, or paths are seen.
distinction: The painting lacks visible built elements and cannot be clearly classified on the basis of the relation between architecture and nature, so it is assigned to the closest category on the basis of the overall landscape scenery.

evidence: Lower left to lower middle: a railed terrace base is visible, directly attached to the rocky slope and bank, extending in accordance with the terrain's trend. | Lower middle: a figure sits on rocks at the edge of the terrace; the boundary of the built structure is tightly integrated with the cliff edge, presenting a relationship of a terrace set against the cliff. | Left: pines grow beside the built structure; although covered by branches and leaves, the railing and steps of the built structure are clearly visible, set according to the heights of the rocks.
distinction: Although pines screen the built structure to some extent, the dominant spatial expression is the terrace and railing placed in accordance with the terrain of the rocky slope and bank, with the feature of terrain-responsive layout more prominent.

evidence: Middle ground on the right: through the pine grove a building roof is faintly visible, presenting spatial layering of concealment and revelation. | Left foreground: a huge pine occupies the left side of the painting, its trunk and branches forming a front-to-back screening relationship with the scenery behind.
distinction: Although a railing in the lower right hints at a path, the core built expression of the painting is the layering of concealment and revelation created by the mid-ground building screened by trees.

evidence: Round-fan painting on the right: the painting mainly depicts banks, trees, and flying birds; no definite built elements such as buildings, bridges, or paths are seen.
distinction: There is no visible built structure in the painting, so its mode of spatial expression cannot be judged; it is assigned to the closest category based on the overall landscape organization.

evidence: Lower middle and water surface on the right: multiple boats are visible, including a small boat being poled in the foreground, a passenger boat carrying people in the mid-ground, and a lone boat in the distance, distributed across the water surface. | Left side and right bank: willows are planted on the banks; the water surface is open, and the boats together with the shoreline and water surface form spatial cues for movement on the water and mooring.
distinction: The boats mainly serve as vehicles for movement on the water, participating in a spatial organization that is enterable and traversable, rather than merely serving as markers accenting a fixed scene.

evidence: Lower right: a building (pavilion) is half hidden among pines and mixed trees; the roof and columns are partly screened by branches and leaves, but the people inside and the railing are clearly visible, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Middle left: the towering mountain rocks and waterfall on the left form a spatial contrast of near and far, opening and closing, with the wooded building at the lower right.
distinction: Although the building is beside the water, the most distinctive feature of the painting is its layering of concealment and revelation, half screened by trees, rather than placement based purely on terrain.

evidence: Lower left: a two-story pavilion is placed close to the base of the towering cliff on the left and against the waterside rocks, its site tightly integrated with the terrain | Left: the building spreads out with mountains behind and water in front, presenting an arrangement against the rock and on the bank | Lower middle: foreground pines slant out, some branches and leaves overlapping the pavilion, but the main body of the building is clearly visible
distinction: Although the pavilion identifies the scenery at the waterside cliff, its placement tight against the rocky bank terrain is more prominent, so C1 is more apt than C3.

evidence: Lower right: an arched bridge spans the stream, with pedestrians on it, connecting paths on both banks and leading to the pavilion building on the shore, forming a definite line of entry and travel. | Mid-ground to distance: plank roads or bridges built along the mountain's trend wind through the gorge, connecting the lower built structures with the pavilions above and guiding the eye deeper. | Upper right: high buildings faintly appear amid clouds and mist and mountain forest, serving as the distant terminus of the travel route and reinforcing the sense of spatial depth.
distinction: Although the plank roads built along the mountain's trend embody C1, the painting as a whole places greater emphasis on the travel process that guides figures and the eye into the depth of the painting through cues such as bridges and paths, so C4 is dominant.

evidence: Top center: the grand main pavilion is built on the summit platform of the highest peak, its site closely corresponding to the form of the peak, standing high. | Middle right: the building complex is placed against the steep cliff and the recesses of the mountainside, presenting a layout of separate placement along the slope, following the mountain's undulations. | Lower right corner: another building is located on the slope at the mountain's foot, forming a staggered high-low arrangement with the buildings above, extending upward in accordance with the overall mountain trend.
distinction: Although the buildings are conspicuous and located at visual high points, their staggered layout mainly embodies compliance with and reliance on the mountain forms and terrain (setting houses on terraces, separate placement along slopes), rather than merely serving as markers identifying scenery.

evidence: In the pine grove at the middle right of the painting: among the extensive pine grove, the roofs and eaves of several buildings are faintly revealed; the main bodies of the buildings are screened by trees, forming a layering of houses hidden in the forest. | At the water's edge in the lower right corner: a pavilion/water-side hall stands at the water's edge, partly screened by the foreground bank and trees, forming a front-to-back screening relationship with the building complex in the pine grove behind.
distinction: Although the built structures identify the scenery deep in the pine grove, their most prominent mode of spatial organization is the construction of layering through the screening and revealing of trees, so C2 is more apt than C3.

evidence: Near the bank at the lower right: to the right of the willow roots a small boat is moored on the water surface, with one person sitting upright in the boat, echoing the willow on the left and the water surface. | Far bank at the upper right: the far-bank hills are gentle, forming an open space with the foreground water surface, with the small boat accenting it and identifying the waterside scenery.
distinction: The small boat and figure, as scenic accents, concentrate and identify the specific scenery of the willow-shaded waterside, rather than emphasizing the terrain-responsive relationship between buildings and terrain or layering of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower part of the painting: an arched bridge spans the water surface/stream, with pedestrians on it, forming a definite travel cue pointing to the opposite bank. | Middle-right of the painting: behind the dense trees, house structures (roofs and walls) are visible, located in the direction the bridge leads, presenting a village form surrounded by trees. | Overall composition: the bridge connects with the shoreline and gaps among the rocks, guiding the eye from the foreground water surface to the built structures in the depth, forming a spatial process of entering from here to there and approaching the village.
distinction: Although the built structures are screened by trees, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation (consistent with C2), the definite bridge and pedestrians in the lower part of the painting constitute a strong travel guidance, making the process of entry 'from here to there' (C4) the dominant spatial organization.

evidence: Left side and lower middle: several houses are surrounded by dense trees, with roofs and walls revealed from the grove, forming a clear layering of concealment and revelation. | Background: continuous mountain ranges lie in the distance, forming a front-to-back spatial relationship with the nearby grove and houses.
distinction: Although the houses are located on flat ground or on the bank, the most prominent spatial expression of the painting is the screening and revealing of buildings by trees, rather than emphasizing the correspondence between buildings and terrain undulations.

evidence: Lower part of the painting: several thatched huts are scattered between the waterside and the grove, with roofs and eaves clearly visible. | Lower middle of the painting: the built structures are partly screened by foreground trees, presenting spatial layering of interleaved concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the built structures are located at the waterside, their main compositional role lies in forming layering through the screening and revealing of trees, rather than emphasizing a layout built in response to terrain.

evidence: Lower right corner: between the waterside rocks and trees a pavilion and houses are visible, partly screened by trees and mountain rocks, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Middle ground left: at the slope and bank at the mountain's foot, several houses are faintly visible, screened behind the mountain's outline and slope rocks.
distinction: Although the built structures in the painting are set against mountains and beside water, the more prominent visual feature is the construction of spatial layering through the screening and revealing by trees and mountain rocks, rather than simply emphasizing placement in response to terrain.

evidence: Middle ground left: a multi-story pagoda stands, partly surrounded by clouds and mist and trees, presenting a half-hidden, half-visible state. | Lower right corner: a pavilion stands by the water, partly screened by the branches and leaves of foreground trees, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Lower middle: among the grove the roofs and structures of houses are faintly visible, screened by trees, with rich layering.
distinction: Although buildings such as the pagoda serve as scenic accents, multiple built structures in the painting (such as the pavilion and houses) more conspicuously construct spatial layering through screening and revealing by trees and clouds and mist, giving a stronger overall sense of concealment and revelation forming a setting.

evidence: Upper right corner: at the mountain's foot a house structure is visible, its roof and walls partly screened by mountain rocks and trees, presenting a screening relationship. | Lower right and middle ground: boats are on the water and people on the bank, forming a ferry-crossing scene, but the built structure is located at the distant mountain's foot and does not directly connect with the ferry landing.
distinction: The built structure mainly creates layering through screening and revealing by mountain rocks and trees, rather than merely serving as a marker identifying scenery.

evidence: Lower right corner: a stone arch bridge is visible spanning among the mountain rocks, connecting the waterside with the depths of the mountain body. | Right mountainside: above and behind the bridge a pavilion/house is visible, with two people inside, connected to the bridge by a path. | Water surface at the lower left corner: a small boat, with the figure facing the bank, hints at a travel cue of entering the mountains by transferring from water route to land route.
distinction: Although the pavilion is screened by trees, the stone arch bridge definitely constructs an entry path from the water surface to the mountainside building, giving a stronger sense of spatial process.

evidence: Lower left corner: a two-story pavilion building is visible, placed in separate layers according to the heights of the rocky slope and terrace, presenting a layout of setting houses on terraces. | Right side and center: flowering trees and mountain rocks extend toward the building; the building's site closely adjoins the rocky slope, embodying a relationship of placement in response to terrain.
distinction: Although screened by trees, the main body of the building is clear and its layered layout's correspondence with the terrain's slopes and terraces is more prominent, so terrain-responsive siting is primary.

evidence: Middle-right of the painting: behind and to the right of the main trunk of a pine, the roof of a building (apparently a pavilion or house) is visible, its structure faintly discernible. | Center to right of the painting: the main body of the building is partly screened by the trunk and branches and leaves of a tall foreground pine, forming spatial layering of trees in front and house behind. | Around the building: shrubs surround the base and surroundings of the building, further screening it, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation of a house seen in the forest.
distinction: Although the building at the waterside beneath the trees serves as a scenic accent, the screening and revealing of the building by the pines in the painting constitutes a more prominent spatial layering relationship.

evidence: Lower right: the built structure is placed tight against the rocky slope and bank, its base following the terrain's heights in a staggered manner, presenting a posture of setting houses on terraces and building along the slope. | Below: water flows past beneath the built structure; the building is tightly integrated with the mountain rocks and waterside, spreading out in accordance with the natural terrain.
distinction: Although the built structure is relatively conspicuous in the painting, its site's attachment to the rocky slope and bank is more direct and dominant, embodying the feature of placement in response to terrain.

evidence: Center and right: the main subject of the painting is layered mountain rocks and trees; no definite man-made built structures such as houses or pavilions are seen. | Slightly below center: in a gap among the mountain rocks there is a tiny figure; the rocks and trees form spatial layering of front-to-back screening.
distinction: The painting has no definite built structures, only natural layering and secluded depth formed by mountain rocks and trees; C2 is closer to this relationship of concealment and revelation without path guidance than C4.

evidence: Lower right: two houses are placed tight against the foot of the green rocky slope on the right; parts of the walls and roofs are screened by the branches of flowering trees above and by the mountain rocks beside them, presenting a layering relationship of half hidden and half revealed. | Middle right: the branches of luxuriant flowering trees extend downward, covering above the houses, creating an effect of natural scenery screening the built structure.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed at the mountain's foot, the painting places greater emphasis on the spatial layering formed by the screening and revealing of the houses by flowering branches and mountain rocks, rather than simple terrain correspondence.

evidence: Lower right: a multi-story pavilion building, partly screened by surrounding trees, with its roof and upper story exposed. | In front of the building to the lower left: definite steps or a path extend, with several figures ascending step by step, forming a travel cue leading to the building. | Around the building: trees surround the building, forming natural layering of screening and revealing.
distinction: The clear steps and pedestrian route in the painting emphasize the spatial process of approaching and entering the building, better embodying the guiding role of the travel cue than simple screening by trees.

evidence: Middle right: a group of buildings is partly screened by surrounding withered trees and willow branches; roofs and eaves appear faintly among the grove, forming spatial layering combining concealment and revelation. | Foreground and middle ground: weeping willows in the near view and a grove of withered trees in the middle ground surround the buildings, with the screening effect of the vegetation highlighting the buildings' sense of seclusion.
distinction: Although the buildings are conspicuous, their screening and revealing relationship with the surrounding trees is more prominent in the composition, not merely serving as scenic markers.

evidence: Whole painting: the painting is dominated by towering mountain rocks and a waterfall on the left and an open waterside and distant mountains on the right; no clearly discernible man-made built structures such as houses, pavilions, or bridges are seen.
distinction: The painting mainly presents the forms and opening-closing scenery of the landscape itself and lacks clear evidence of built structures, so it is assigned to the closest category based on the overall landscape organization.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: a huge natural rock is used directly as a stone table, with a figure leaning on it and objects placed on the table; the built arrangement (furnishings) is placed entirely according to the form and position of the natural mountain rock. | Lower left of the painting: beside the base of a plum tree there is a low bamboo fence, distributed along the terrain and tree roots, presenting a relationship of placement in response to terrain.
distinction: Although the stone table serves to identify scenery, its most distinctive feature is the direct use of natural mountain rock as site and furniture, embodying a terrain-responsive relationship of placement in response to terrain.

evidence: Upper center: the pavilion building has a railed terrace base, placed on high flat ground, presenting the feature of setting houses on terraces. | Right side and lower right: rows of banners and blue tents (or curtains) are arranged linearly along the undulating trend of the hillside, presenting a relationship of separate placement along the slope and unfolding in accordance with the terrain. | Left: ceremonial facilities and figures are located at the edge of the slope, distributed in accordance with the terrain.
distinction: Although the pavilion above is surrounded by trees, the built structures in the painting (especially the tents and banners below) mainly present a terrain-responsive layout arranged along the hillside, rather than being dominated by layering of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower right of the right-hand painted panel: pavilions and multi-storey buildings are blocked by the mountains and rocks and pines in the foreground, revealing only roofs, eaves, and some railing posts, forming clear layers of concealment and revelation from front to back. | Lower left of the right-hand painted panel: a group of house buildings is screened behind trees, with roof outlines visible, indicating that the built elements lie deep in the woodland and form a setting through screening by natural scenery.
distinction: Although the architecture is placed against the mountains and beside the water, the visual focus of the painting is the spatial layering formed by the screening and exposure of the architecture by trees, mountains, and rocks, rather than simply emphasizing the terrain's guidance of the layout.

evidence: Lower middle right of the painting: an open pavilion (ting) is built by the water, located beside trees and rocks, with two people sitting facing each other inside. | Background of the right side of the painting: the built structure faces an open expanse of water and distant mountains, situated at an open spot on the waterside, its position corresponding to the surrounding landscape space.
distinction: Although the built structure is placed by the water, the terrain is relatively flat; its main role is to point up the waterside viewing scenery rather than to display a complex terrain-responsive relationship.

evidence: Lower middle of the right-hand painted panel: the building base is immediately adjacent to the waterside, with railings and corridor columns, laid out following the water's edge, presenting a form of building by the water. | Left side of the right-hand painted panel: tall trees (willows) stand to the left of and behind the building, with dense foliage partly covering the upper part of the building, but the main body of the building is clearly visible. | Right side and background of the right-hand painted panel: in front of the building is a broad water surface, with faint mountain shadows in the distance; the building occupies a prominent position at the water-land boundary.
distinction: The main body of the building is fully exposed and immediately adjacent to the waterside; the layout feature of building according to the water (base and railings following the bank) is more dominant than the partial screening by trees (concealment and revelation).

evidence: Right-hand painted panel: the painting depicts withered trees on a plain and a figure on horseback; no clear architecture or built structures are seen.
distinction: There are no visible built elements in the painting; it is assigned only with difficulty on the basis of the overall open plain scene, lacking architectural evidence.

evidence: Lower left: built structures with tiled roofs are visible, arranged against the mountains and rocks and waterside, fitting naturally with the terrain. | Lower right: a stone table is set beneath an old plum tree, figures sit on the rocks, and the built elements and human activity unfold in accordance with the terrain.
distinction: The built elements in the painting are mainly placed in response to the terrain and topography, rather than serving purely as scenic markers.

evidence: Lower foreground: a party of figures on horseback and on foot carrying loads is visible moving along a path by the bank, forming a clear line of movement through the landscape. | Right cliff: a storied pavilion is built halfway up the mountain, with a stepped path winding below it and connecting to it, presenting a spatial relationship whereby one place leads to another and can be reached. | Left waterside: boats are moored by the water, and houses are distributed along the bank and partly screened by trees, suggesting a link between the ferry crossing and travel.
distinction: Although the painting has features of buildings placed according to mountain and water (C1), the marching party of figures below and the stepped path connecting the buildings place stronger emphasis on the spatial process of movement and entry, so C4 is more dominant.

evidence: Left side and upper part of the painting: tall willows and their hanging branches are in front of and above the waterside pavilion, forming pronounced foreground screening and enclosure. | Lower left to center of the painting: the roof, eaves, and colonnade of the waterside pavilion emerge through the willow shade, presenting a layered concealment and revelation and spatial depth of trees screening a building.
distinction: Although the waterside pavilion is built by the water and has terrain-responsive features, the pronounced screening and enclosure of the building by willows (concealment and revelation) is more dominant in the spatial organization.

evidence: Lower right of the painting: among the trees on the sloping bank appear the roof and part of the wall of a thatched hut, the building screened by trees, forming a layered spatial relationship of concealment and revelation. | Upper right of the painting: distant peaks faintly appear amid clouds and mist, together with the near-foreground trees screening the built elements forming a sense of deep space.
distinction: Although the thatched hut is built on the sloping bank, the painting emphasizes its concealment among the trees rather than a layout placed purely according to the terrain.

evidence: Lower middle: a bridge is visible crossing water or a ravine, connecting the path on the left with the built area on the right. | Lower right corner: a figure on horseback with attendants is moving toward the bridge and the built area, presenting a spatial process of entry and arrival. | Below the right cliff: built structures (houses) are screened among trees, connected to the outside space by the bridge and path.
distinction: Although the painting has a concealment-and-revelation relationship of trees screening built structures, the bridge and the figures' route form a clearer spatial line of entry, dominating the spatial organization of the painting.

evidence: Lower center of the right-hand painted panel: the roof and columned corridor of a water pavilion are partly blocked by the dense bamboo leaves and branches around it, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relation. | Lower part of the right-hand painted panel: in front of the water pavilion is a water surface covered with lotus leaves; the building is screened between the bamboo grove and the waterscape, forming layers.
distinction: Although the architecture is built facing the water, the painting highlights more the screening and exposure of the architecture by the bamboo grove; the role of concealment and revelation forming a setting is greater than siting according to the terrain.

evidence: Lower left: a wooden bridge is visible spanning a stream and ravine, its structure clear, connecting the two banks, with travelers crossing it. | Lower right: a figure on horseback is visible walking along a mountain path, the path winding, suggesting the movement of travelers and spatial extension. | Left and center: a waterfall flows down, and a winding path faintly appears among the mountains and rocks, together with the bridge forming a line of movement through the landscape into the depths of the scenery.
distinction: Although the bridge spanning mountain and water embodies terrain-responsive placement (C1), the core of the painting lies in the process of figures moving along paths and the bridge, emphasizing spatial connectivity from one place to another, so C4 is more dominant.

evidence: Upper right to center: a huge rock overhangs at a slant, vine plants hang beneath it, and a figure and a divine beast stand below. | Left and lower parts: withered trees, weeds, and slope rocks are visible; no traces of houses, bridges, or paths or other built elements are seen.
distinction: No built elements whatsoever are seen in the painting; the main figures and the divine beast are under the screening of rock and plants, with only a relationship of natural scenery screening, and no architecture to discuss.

evidence: Lower center: the roofs and walls of several houses emerge from dense woods, the trees clearly screening and concealing the buildings. | Lower left: the outline of another building is faintly visible, likewise screened by trees, reinforcing the layered sense of seeing houses deep in the woods.
distinction: Although the buildings are located at the foot of the mountain by the water, the painting emphasizes more their screening by trees, the spatial layers of half-hidden and half-revealed, rather than placement purely according to terrain.

evidence: Whole painting: only mountains and rocks, hanging branches and leaves, and a perched bird are seen; no houses, pavilions, bridges, paths, or other man-made built elements are visible. | Lower left corner: an inscription and seals are visible, belonging to the signature, not built elements within the pictorial space.
distinction: No built elements in the painting; assigned only tentatively on the basis of the overall organization of landscape and scenic-accent creatures, with no clear competing interpretation.

evidence: Right side of the painting: mountains and rocks, bamboo grove, a stream, and figures are visible; no clear houses, bridges, or other built structures are seen. | Lower part of the right side of the painting: a figure sits by the water, surrounded by sloping banks and plants, forming a scenic spot.
distinction: Because there are no clear built elements, its mode of spatial organization cannot be judged; assigned only tentatively as scenic accentuation on the basis of the figures' position, lacking architectural evidence.

evidence: Near foreground, slightly left: the roof of a pavilion or building emerges among a grove of willows, the building body and columns screened by trunks and branches, presenting layers of seeing a house in the woods. | Right foot of the distant mountain: houses are screened behind woods, only the roof and part of the walls exposed, forming a spatial relationship of seeing a house through a screen. | Central waterside in the distance: houses are distributed along the waterside, partly screened by trees, the concealment-and-revelation relationship participating in composing the scene.
distinction: Although the distant houses distributed along the waterside have terrain-responsive features (spreading along the bank), both the near-foreground pavilion and the distant houses markedly present a concealment-and-revelation relationship of being screened by woods with only roofs exposed; concealment and revelation forming a scene is more dominant in shaping spatial layers.

evidence: Lower middle: between trees and rocks, the roof and part of the columns of a building are visible, the building body screened by the branches in front and by the rocks, presenting a half-hidden, half-revealed state. | Right and center: dense trees and layered rocks form the foreground and middle ground, screening the building behind them, forming clear spatial layers.
distinction: Although the building is set against the rocks, the painting highlights more the screening and revealing of the building by woods and rocks; the feature of concealment and revelation forming a scene is more pronounced.

evidence: Center of the right side of the painting: several figures are visible standing on a stream bank between rocks and trees, facing distant mountains and flowing water; no houses, bridges, pavilions, or other built elements are seen. | Background of the right side of the painting: layered distant mountains, with rocks and trees nearby; the space is open, and the figures' position becomes the focus of viewing.
distinction: The painting presents a situation of figures pausing to view the scenery, similar to pointing up a scene, but lacks clear built entities, so C3 is taken as the closest classification rather than C4, which expresses an entry path.

evidence: Lower right: a figure is visible walking through a gap between slope rocks and trees, forming a line of movement extending into the depth of the painting. | Overall painting: dense woods and slope rocks occupy most of the space; no clear traces of buildings, bridges, or man-made built elements are seen.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built elements, but the figure's walking route forms a spatial process of penetrating deep into the woods, so under forced classification it is closest to the line-of-movement feature of C4.

evidence: Center of the painting: a group of houses stands in a mountain hollow, their roofs and walls partly screened by the dense pines and mixed trees around them, presenting a half-hidden, half-revealed state. | Middle ground to foreground: large trees in the foreground and woods in the middle ground form a natural screen layer, wrapping the building group within, constituting clear spatial layers and a concealment-and-revelation relationship.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed according to the mountain terrain, the painting emphasizes more the screening and revealing of the buildings by woods; concealment and revelation forming a scene plays a more prominent role than placement according to terrain.

evidence: Lower middle of the right side: the roof and part of the walls of a house are visible, its body partly screened by the trees and rocks in front, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Lower part and middle-right of the painting: withered trees and rocks in the foreground stand in front of the built structures, screening part of their structure as natural scenery, indicating front-to-back spatial layers.
distinction: Although the built structures are placed against rocks and sloping banks, the painting emphasizes more the spatial layers formed by the screening and revealing of the building by trees and rocks, rather than simple correspondence with the terrain.

evidence: Left side and lower left: dense trees screen the left wing and lower base of the building group, exposing only the upper-middle storied pavilion roofs and eave columns, forming spatial layers of trees in front and houses behind. | Center and right: the building body is layered, with red columns and green tiles clearly visible; the railed terrace on the right is relatively open, forming a contrast of concealment and revelation with the tree screening on the left.
distinction: Although the buildings have terraces and railings, the prominent spatial layers in the painting are mainly constituted by the screening of the buildings by trees (concealment and revelation), rather than a strong correspondence between building bases and natural mountain slopes and terraces.

evidence: Upper right: the roofs and railings of some buildings emerge from behind screening rocks and trees, as a potential destination for travelers. | Lower middle and left: two animal-drawn carts move along a path on sloping ground, forming a clear line of movement through the landscape. | Center of the painting: a winding path connects the carts in the foreground with the woods and buildings behind, presenting a spatial process from one place to another.
distinction: Although the buildings in the upper right present a concealment-and-revelation relationship, the line of movement formed by the carts and path runs through the composition, emphasizing more the spatial process of approaching the built structures.

evidence: Upper right: a small pavilion is built at the mountain summit, serving as the visual focus of the peak and marking the highest point of the mountain. | Lower right: travelers move along the slope at the foot of the mountain, forming a spatial high–low correspondence with the towering summit building above.
distinction: Although the building is located on the mountain, its main role is as a marker accentuating the summit (scenic accentuation), rather than emphasizing a terrain-responsive layout relationship between its base and the topography.

evidence: Lower left and lower middle: built structures (houses) are heavily screened by several withered trees in the foreground, only roofs and part of the structure exposed, presenting a typical layered concealment of houses in the woods. | Foot of the mountain, middle right: another built structure lies between rocks and trees, faintly visible, blending into the natural environment. | Lower right corner: figures walk along a path that leads toward the tree-screened area; although this suggests movement through the landscape, the built structures are mainly shown as screened by natural scenery.
distinction: Although the painting has a path and figures suggesting a process of movement (C4), the built structures are mainly screened by foreground trees, presenting a concealment-and-revelation spatial layer of 'seeing houses beneath the woods'; the screening relationship defines the composition more directly and dominantly.

evidence: Lower left corner: wooden railings and a plank walkway are visible extending along the edge of the sloping ground, with figures standing on them, the structures placed against the mountain rocks and sloping bank. | Right side: steep cliffs and a waterfall form the natural background, forming a correspondence and contrast in terrain with the man-made walkway on the left.
distinction: Although the plank walkway carries a sense of path, the painting mainly presents its placement along the sloping bank, rather than emphasizing a process of penetrating along a path.

evidence: Slightly below center: a pavilion is built on a flat sloping terrace base, presenting the form of a house set on a terrace. | Left side: a fence/railing winds along the edge of the rocks, embodying a site-responsive arrangement around the rocks. | Behind and around the pavilion: the built elements (pavilion and railing) occupy the terrace space, relying on the site conditions formed by the pines and rocks behind.
distinction: Although the pavilion is a visual focus (seemingly scenic accentuation), its base and the railing on the left are clearly placed in response to the terrain (the terrace and the edge of the rocks); the physical terrain-responsive placement is more concrete and prominent than the marking role of scenic accentuation.

evidence: Lower center: a small boat is moored on the water, with one person lying in it, suggesting movement and pause along a water route. | Right and upper parts: steep cliffs, pines, and a waterfall form a deep natural space. | Whole painting: no clear houses, pavilions, or other fixed built elements are seen.
distinction: Although the painting has no fixed built elements, the small boat as a line of movement suggests an accessible water-route space, closer to the spatial process of C4 than to merely pointing up a scene.

evidence: Lower part of the painting: two people sit on natural rocks; no houses, pavilions, or other man-made built elements are seen | Right side of the painting: towering peaks and a waterfall form the main landscape scenery | Left side of the painting: trees grow in clusters, adjoining the rocks
distinction: No clear built elements are seen in the painting; classified as the closest category on the basis of the overall spatial organization of landscape and scenic-accent figures

evidence: Lower right corner: a small bridge is visible crossing the water, connecting to a path on the bank, forming a clear line of passage. | Lower middle: trees, rocks, and figures on the bank, together with the bridge and path, form a traversable foreground space that guides the eye into the distance. | Middle right: a pavilion is screened in a pine grove halfway up the mountain, as a potential destination of the extended path or a scene in the depths.
distinction: Although the pavilion at middle right has a concealment-and-revelation relationship of tree screening, the bridge and path at the lower right corner build a clearer line of spatial travel from one place to another and into the depths, dominating the spatial organization of the painting.

evidence: Right side of the painting: the painting presents water surface, sloping bank, trees, and a figure herding an ox; no traces of built elements such as houses or bridges are seen. | Left side of the painting: calligraphic inscription, not an element of spatial composition within the painted panel on the right.
distinction: There are no visible built elements in the painting; it is assigned to the closest category on the basis of the overall landscape organization, with no clear architecture participating in the composition.

evidence: Upper right: the built structure is located on a high platform or sloping ground, its base clearly raised, presenting a layout of setting the house on a platform; two people stand on the platform/inside the house. | Overall painting: the built structure is high, while the foreground figures and Taihu rocks are low, forming through the platform base a high-low spatial relationship of separate placement according to the sloping platform, sited in response to the terrain. | Around the building: trees and mountains and rocks (Taihu rocks) are beside the built structure, and the building is arranged leaning on these features, forming a staggered high-low layering.
distinction: Although the building is in a woodland environment, the painting mainly presents its being built on a high platform and forming a high-low drop with the foreground (setting the house on a platform), rather than being dominated by concealment and screening (the building is fairly exposed and mainly arranged in front-back, high-low order).

evidence: Lower right of the painting: a group of buildings is visible, including a pagoda and several roofs, partly screened by the surrounding trees and mountains and rocks, presenting spatial layering of alternating concealment and revelation.
distinction: The buildings present their existence and layering mainly through screening and revelation by woodland and mountains and rocks, fitting the characteristic of concealment and revelation, rather than being merely sited according to terrain or serving as scenic markers.

evidence: Center of the painting: large lake rocks are seen adjacent to bamboo, trees, and flowers; the plants grow according to the rocky slope. | Lower right of the painting: a gentle sloping bank and water plants are visible, presenting natural terrain.
distinction: There are no clear built elements in the painting; only natural scenery arranged according to terrain is seen, so it is assigned to the closest category, terrain-responsive arrangement.

evidence: Behind the trees and shrubs on the middle-ground sloping bank on the left: extremely faint ink traces are faintly visible, suspected to be part of a house or pavilion, partly screened by trees and the sloping bank, with blurred form. | Overall painting: large areas of unpainted space represent the water surface or clouds and mist; the pines and rocks on the right and the distant mountains on the left form an opening and closing, and the suspected built structure on the left lies between concealment and revelation.
distinction: If the blurred ink traces on the left are regarded as built elements, they are more a matter of being hidden behind trees and rocks to form layering, rather than clearly pointing out a core scenic spot.

evidence: Whole painting: the painting depicts only a vigorous, gnarled pine tree and three birds perched on its branches; no traces of built elements such as houses, pavilions, bridges, or paths are seen.
distinction: Built elements are entirely absent from the painting, so the concrete spatial relationship between built elements and landscape cannot be expressed; it is assigned to the category only formally.

evidence: Right painting: only sloping rocks, twisted pines, and weeds are visible; no traces of artificial built elements such as buildings, bridges, or roads are seen. | Lower right: the sloping rocks and the ground form natural high-low undulations, and the pine roots grow clinging to the sloping rocks.
distinction: No clear built elements are seen in the painting; based on the natural placement relationship of the sloping rocks supporting the trees, it is barely assigned to C1.

evidence: Lower right: a building roof is faintly revealed among a cluster of trees, mostly screened by the branches and foliage in the foreground, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Center right: dense woodland and distant mountains create rich spatial layering; the building is hidden among the trees, using natural scenery to screen and compose the scene.
distinction: The building is mainly screened by trees, with emphasis on forming spatial layering through concealment and revelation, rather than serving as a conspicuous marker identifying a particular landscape scene.

evidence: Lower left: a small bridge can be seen crossing a water surface or ravine, connecting the sloping banks, implying a route of movement and spatial connectivity. | Right side: on the sloping banks there are trees, mountains and rocks, and figures in activity; the bridge together with these elements forms a traversable scene.
distinction: No clear building is seen in the painting, but the bridge, as an artificial structure, clearly expresses the relationship of spatial entry and connectivity, consistent with the definition of C4.

evidence: Right-hand painted panel: mountains and rocks, trees and several figures are visible, with no clear houses, bridges or other built structures seen.
distinction: The painting lacks built elements; assignment to the closest category is made on the basis of the overall visible organization of landscape and figures.

evidence: Whole image: the painting presents layered peaks and dense woodland, with finely rendered mountain and rock textures and deep spatial layering. | Lower center-right: at the interwoven trees and rocks there appear to be traces of a tiny structure, possibly a roof or platform, but the details are blurred and cannot be reliably identified as built elements. | Center: the mountain forms are steep and precipitous, with a waterfall visible flowing down; natural scenery predominates.
distinction: The painting emphasizes the deep layering of the woodland and the relationship of concealment and revelation; if any built elements exist, they should be within screening, rather than serving as an independent scenic marker.

evidence: Whole image: the painting shows only twisted tree trunks and dense branches; no houses, pavilions, bridges, paths, or any other built elements are seen.
distinction: There are no clear built elements in the painting, so no specific spatial relationship can be determined; it is assigned only to the closest category.

evidence: Left middle ground: a multi-arched bridge spans the water surface, connecting the two banks and marking the spatial opening, closing, and transition of the water surface. | Right foreground: sloping rocks and pine trees form the foreground, creating spatial layering with the bridge in the middle ground and the distant mountains; the bridge becomes a marker identifying the waterscape.
distinction: The bridge marks the waterscape scene, but the painting lacks clear path connections and a process of movement leading into the depths, so C4 is not selected.

evidence: Whole image: only bamboo, withered trees, and sloping rocks are seen in the painting; no traces of buildings, bridges, paths, or any other built elements are visible. | Lower center: bamboo clumps and withered trees grow alongside the mountain rocks, forming the visual center and natural scene of the painting.
distinction: There are no built elements in the painting; based on the overall organization of landscape, vegetation, and rocks, it is assigned with difficulty to scenic accentuation, with no other clear competing interpretation.

evidence: Right side: dense tall trees and weeping willows are painted on the right side of the painting; the ink at the tree roots and sloping banks is heavy and the structure complex, and there appear to be built elements (such as a house) screened by the trees, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Left side and distant view: the left side is open water, with mountain outlines in the distance, forming a spatial contrast with the dense trees, rocks, and sloping banks on the right, which sets off the layered pictorial depth on the right.
distinction: The suspected built elements are mainly located in the deep space screened by trees and rocks, emphasizing the layering created by concealment and revelation, rather than serving as a conspicuous landmark marking a particular landscape.

evidence: Lower right: a group of house buildings sits on the waterside bank, partly screened by the branches and foliage in the foreground, revealing roofs, eaves, and part of the walls. | Right lower center: trees and buildings form an obvious relationship of concealment and revelation; the buildings appear and disappear behind the woodland, constituting the spatial layering of the painting.
distinction: Although the buildings are built by the water, the painting emphasizes more the spatial layering formed by the screening and revealing of the buildings by the trees, so C2 is more apt than C1.

evidence: Right side of the painting: mountains and rocks, trees, and two figures are visible; the figures are shown walking and climbing, constituting a route of movement, but no houses, bridges, or other clear built elements are seen.
distinction: There are no artificial built elements in the painting; only figures moving among the mountains and rocks, so it is assigned to C4 according to the tendency of spatial organization.

evidence: Painted panel: the painting depicts an autumn suburban scene, with trees, sloping banks, flowing water and a herd of horses with figures visible; no clear built elements such as houses or buildings are seen. | Center and left side of the painted panel: the horses and figures are distributed according to the waterside and sloping ground; some drink in the water, some rest or run on the slopes, presenting a spatial relationship that unfolds along the bank and is arranged separately by slope.
distinction: The distribution of the horses according to the waterside and sloping ground conforms to the spatial organization logic of C1 terrain-responsive placement; although there are no buildings, this fits their dispersed layout better than the C3 scenic accentuation marker.

evidence: Left lower center, beside the waterfall: among the trees and rocks there is a small built outline, part of the structure screened by trees, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Left woodland area: dense pine forest surrounds the built structure, concealing it within the woods and forming spatial layering.
distinction: The built structure is mainly screened by woodland to present layering, rather than serving as a conspicuous node marking the scene.

evidence: Lower part of the painting: two figures, a table and chairs, books, an incense burner, and other objects are painted, with no landscape background or built structures. | Upper and middle parts of the painting: large areas of unpainted space, with only inscription and seals, no spatial layering or path clues.
distinction: The painting has no clear built elements or relationship with landscape; the combination of figures and furniture forms a visual focus within the unpainted space, so it is assigned to scenic accentuation.

evidence: Whole image: the painting mainly depicts figures and horses, with a blank silk background; no landscape terrain or built elements are seen.
distinction: No built elements are visible in the painting, so there is no competing interpretation.

evidence: Whole image: the entire painting depicts peonies, lotus, chrysanthemums, and various other flowers, leaves, and branches, with a plain background; no traces of houses, pavilions, bridges, or other built elements are seen.
distinction: The painting has no built elements and cannot form a typical spatial relationship between built elements and landscape; it is forcibly assigned according to the rules.

evidence: Whole image: the painting depicts only the overlapping forms of bamboo branches and leaves; no houses, bridges, paths, or any other artificial built elements are seen. | Upper left and lower left: inscriptions and seals are visible, which are ancillary information of the painting and do not constitute evidence of built elements within the picture.
distinction: The painting completely lacks built elements, so no substantive spatial relationship can be judged; it is assigned with difficulty based only on the visual layering of overlapping bamboo leaves.

evidence: Lower part of the painting: a rooster is seen standing on the ground, surrounded by grass. | Upper middle and right side of the painting: cockscomb, bamboo, and other plants as well as garden rocks are visible, with no traces of built elements.
distinction: There are no built elements in the painting; the scene is composed only of the rooster, plants, and rocks, so no spatial relationship of built elements can be judged; it is assigned with difficulty to scenic accentuation.

evidence: Center, slightly lower: the main subject of the painting is a huge garden rock, beside which grow withered trees and bamboo clumps, with a gentle sloping bank at the bottom. | Upper left: the characters 'Keshi Gumu' (garden rock and ancient trees) are inscribed, indicating that the theme of the painting is a scene composed of rock and trees.
distinction: The painting uses the garden rock and ancient trees as a visual focus to concentrate the scene; although there are no clear artificial built elements, their role as a scenic accent of natural scenery is stronger than a terrain-responsive relationship of built elements.

evidence: Painted panel (to the left of the calligraphy on the right section of the scroll): a thatched hut stands beneath/beside several large trees, its roof and eaves clearly exposed, its lower structure partly obscured by tree trunks and bank rocks, presenting a layering in which a house is seen within the woods. | Foreground of the painted panel: dense branches and leaves cover the built element above and to its side; the built element participates in the composition through the screening and revealing of the trees, forming foreground-background spatial layering.
distinction: Although the built element is placed according to the waterside, the concealment-and-revelation relationship formed by the trees covering and obscuring it is more prominent in the painting and dominates the spatial expression.

evidence: Lower part of the painting: a figure is seen leaning on a large rock to rest; above are large areas of unpainted space and an inscription; no buildings, bridges, or other built elements are seen.
distinction: There are no built elements in the painting, so there is no clear category of spatial expression; it is tentatively assigned to C3.

evidence: Lower center: an arched bridge spans the water surface, connecting the sloping bank on the left with the tree-covered slope on the right, forming a clear clue of passage and entry.
distinction: The bridge mainly serves to connect the two banks and guide the line of sight and the route of travel into the depths, rather than simply serving as a marker identifying a particular scene.

evidence: Lower left water surface: a small canopied boat is seen floating on the water surface, with faint outlines of figures inside. | Lower middle of the painting: the water surface is open, with trees and sloping banks on both sides; no clear traces of houses, bridges, ferry crossings, or other built elements are seen.
distinction: There are no clear built elements in the painting; only boating implies a process of travel, so in the absence of architectural evidence it is assigned with difficulty to C4, which expresses a spatial process.

evidence: Lower part of the painting: flowers and plants are visible, with no landscape or built elements | Upper part of the painting: inscription and seals are visible, with no buildings or paths
distinction: The painting consists only of flowers, with no relationship between built elements and landscape; assignment to this category merely satisfies the requirement of a forced choice.

evidence: Left side: the eaves, columns, and base of a built structure are visible, partly screened by the mountains, rocks, and trees in front, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Left side and center: figures gather inside and outside the screened building and among the trees and rocks, reinforcing the spatial layering of the built structure hidden within natural scenery.
distinction: Although the painting shows the building relying on mountains and rocks, the layering created by the screening and revealing of the building by trees and rocks is more prominent and dominates the spatial expression.

evidence: Lower middle of the right side of the painting: several figures carrying loads on poles and riding donkeys walk along the mountain slope; beneath their feet traces resembling a mountain path or steps are visible, implying a route of travel. | Upper right side and background of the painting: mountains, rocks, and trees form the background; no houses, pavilions, or other clear built elements are visible.
distinction: There are no clear built elements in the painting; only figures walking along a mountain path imply a route, so it is assigned to C4, which expresses the process of travel, but lacks complete evidence of built elements connecting with the path.

evidence: Upper left: a building with railings and a base is visible, presenting a form built on a high platform or slope, with figures seated within. | Lower center to right side: figures are active on the slope and beside the grass below the building, forming an obvious high-low spatial layering with the building, showing that the building is set on a platform. | Right side: the building is close to pine trees and mountain-rock slopes, placed in accordance with the terrain environment.
distinction: Although the building is adjacent to trees, its railings and base and its high-low relationship with the figures below more clearly demonstrate terrain-dependent placement on a platform, rather than being primarily about concealment and revelation.

evidence: Center: two figures walk along the ground, one pointing toward the mountain forms ahead, forming a clear route of travel and directional guidance. | Left side: old trees and pale-ink distant mountains create spatial depth, implying that the destination of travel is deep in the mountains.
distinction: There are no clear built elements in the painting; the dynamic movement and directionality of the figures are more consistent with the spatial process of access to secluded settings, rather than a static scenic marker.

evidence: Center and left of the painting: a towering main peak, continuous mountain ridges and sloping banks, and dense woodland are visible; on the right are an open water surface and distant mountains, constituting a complete landscape scene. | Whole image: no clear traces of houses, pavilions, bridges, roads, or other built elements are observed.
distinction: No clear built elements are seen in the painting; based on the scene form presented by the overall landscape composition, it is tentatively assigned to the scenic accentuation category, but lacks evidence of built elements.

evidence: Lower left: a pavilion is built on a protruding rock base by the water, presenting the form of a house set on a platform and standing by the water, with the base closely integrated with the rocky bank. | Upper left: multi-story towers are arranged in layers at the mountain waist and hollows, conforming to the undulations of the mountain, presenting a layout of placement according to the slopes. | Middle of the painting: other buildings are arranged according to the slope and form of the cliffs, corresponding to the high-low opening and closing of the natural terrain.
distinction: Although trees, mountains, and rocks screen some of the buildings, the building bases are clearly placed according to terrain conditions such as rocks and mountain waists; the spatial relationship of terrain-responsive placement is clearer and more dominant than mere layering of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Center, slightly right: the right and lower sides of the multi-story towers are partly screened by mountains, rocks, and trees, revealing roofs, eaves, and part of the walls, forming an obvious layering of concealment and revelation. | Right side of the painting: mountains, rocks, and trees extend from the foreground to the middle ground, screening the main body of the building behind.
distinction: Although the building is built on a platform base, the painting emphasizes more the half-screening of the building by the mountains, rocks, and trees on the right; the relationship of concealment and revelation is the dominant mode of composing the scene.

evidence: Left middle ground of the painting: on the broad water surface there is a small boat; no identifiable built traces such as buildings, bridges, or paths are seen. | Right foreground of the painting: the sloping bank is furnished with curious rocks and pine trees, with no built placement. | Distant view of the painting: gently rolling distant mountains meet the water surface, the space is open, with no built embellishment.
distinction: No built elements at all are seen in the painting; based on the overall openness and spatial extension of the water surface, it is tentatively assigned to the closest category C4, but there are no clues for entering built elements.

evidence: Center-left of the distant waterside: an extremely tiny built form with a roof outline is visible, situated at the junction of the foot of the distant mountains and the waterside. | Overall composition: the built elements unfold in response to the terrain of the mountain foot and the shoreline, presenting a placement relationship of leaning on water and flanking mountains, with no obvious path guidance or tree screening.
distinction: The built form is too small in scale and its details too blurry to serve a scenic-accentuating role of highlighting the scenery and unifying the painting; its placement characteristic of leaning on the waterside terrain is relatively more evident.

evidence: At the mountain foot in cloud and mist, center-left of the painting: a group of building roofs is visible, surrounded and screened by cloud, mist, and nearby trees, presenting a spatial layering in which buildings are seen through a screened view. | Lower-left corner of the painting: behind tall pine trees, part of a house wall and roof structure is exposed; the building is deeply hidden behind the woodland, forming a relationship of seeing a house within the woods. | Foreground to middle ground of the painting: the foreground pine grove and the middle-ground buildings form an obvious front-to-back occlusion relationship, and the cloud and mist further cut the space, strengthening the layers of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the buildings are located on flat ground at the mountain foot, the painting organizes spatial layers mainly through screening by trees and cloud/mist (concealment and revelation), rather than emphasizing the buildings' reliance on and use of terrain slopes and platforms (terrain-responsive siting).

evidence: Summit of the distant mountains: at the highest point of the ridge there is a row of tiny dark marks, blurry in form, suspected to be extremely small built elements or trees, located at the visual high point. | Main subject of the painting: dominated by cold woodland, sloping rocks, and water surface; figures are placed as accents at the lower left and on the right; no clear houses or buildings are seen.
distinction: If the marks on the summit are regarded as built elements, their location at the highest point mainly serves as a scenic accent marker, rather than displaying a complex layout relationship of siting according to terrain.

evidence: Left side: thick tree trunks and dense foliage occupy the left side of the painting, their roots extending into the water. | Lower right: on the water surface there is a small boat, with one person on board holding a pole; no built traces such as houses or bridges are seen.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built elements; only a lone boat and the wooded waterside are seen, and it is assigned to the closest category based on the overall visible space.

evidence: Right side: a multi-story pavilion is built in tiered layers following the mountain's contours, with a tall base platform and stairs at the bottom tightly integrated with the mountain rocks, presenting a relationship of siting according to terrain and suitability to the lie of the land. | Lower middle-right: the staggered heights of the buildings correspond to the forms of the mountain slopes and platforms; the built elements are placed according to site conditions.
distinction: Although the buildings and pine trees have a screening relationship, the painting's dominant expression is the grand layout of the pavilion following the mountain and being built in tiered layers, rather than primarily forming layers through concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower right: a small canopied boat is moored at the water's edge; the hull and the figures on board are partly occluded by the rocks on the right and the willow branches hanging down from above, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Left side and above: tall trees and weeping willows constitute screening elements in the foreground and middle ground, screening the small boat within them and creating a secluded spatial layering.
distinction: The painting mainly expresses the concealment-and-revelation relationship of the small boat screened by trees and rocks, rather than emphasizing the spatial process of entering the boat through paths or bridges.

evidence: Left side and above: several tall trees stand upright, with lush branches and leaves extending downward to the right, forming the main woodland setting. | Lower right: a thatched pavilion is built beside the trees; the pavilion's structure and the figures inside are clearly visible, within the area covered by the extending branches. | Overall composition: the branches and leaves of the trees form a covering gesture over the thatched pavilion from above and from the left; the thatched pavilion is exposed at the edge of the woods, presenting a spatial layering in which a house is seen within the woods.
distinction: Although the thatched pavilion is clearly visible and a visual focus, it is mainly beneath the covering and enclosure of the tall trees' branches and leaves, presenting a screening relationship of a house built among the woods, rather than simply serving as an identifying point of the landscape.

evidence: Lower middle: a thatched pavilion is built on the waterside rocks; its roof and pillars are half-hidden and half-exposed among the branches and leaves of the surrounding trees. | Left side and center: tall trees surround the thatched pavilion, with trunks and branches forming obvious occlusion of the pavilion body, building a spatial layering of seeing a house deep within the woods.
distinction: Although the thatched pavilion leans on rocks and flanks the water, the painting places more emphasis on the relationship of screening and exposure by trees; concealment and revelation forming scenery plays a greater role than simple reliance on terrain.

evidence: Overall painting: the foreground is sloping banks and trees, the middle ground is a broad water surface, and the distant view is rolling mountain ranges, presenting a spatial layering from near to far. | Lower middle of the painting: a blank space is left between the water surface and the mountain foot, suggesting a possible path for the line of sight to extend into the depths.
distinction: The painting lacks clear evidence of built elements, but the overall landscape composition presents a spatial progression from near to far and from the open water surface into the deep mountain ranges, closest to the mood of C4.

evidence: Middle-distant view on the right side: a multi-story pagoda and adjacent buildings are visible, situated among the sloping-bank woodland, with relatively clear outlines. | Overall composition: the building volume is tiny, located at the distant edge of the painting and contrasting in size with the huge ancient trees in the foreground, serving as a distant marker that highlights the scenery there and extends spatial depth.
distinction: Although the buildings are surrounded by woodland, their outlines are relatively complete and clear; their main role is as a distant marker highlighting the scenic spot (C3), rather than primarily creating concealment-and-revelation layers through severe screening relationships (C2).

evidence: Lower center and right bank: canopied boats are moored at the bank, with figures in the boats; another small boat and figure are beneath the trees on the right, forming mooring points for movement through the landscape on the water. | Center to distant view of the painting: the open water surface extends from the near bank toward the distant mountains, connecting with the boats and suggesting a route of movement through the landscape from here to there.
distinction: The boats and figures mainly present the process of movement, mooring, and the relationship of entering the water surface, rather than simply serving as static scenic accents identifying the landscape.

evidence: Middle ground of the painting: among the woods, a building's roof and fence wall are visible, half-screened and half-exposed by the surrounding trees, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Lower right of the painting: a person sits alone at the waterside, forming a near-far layering with the building screened by woodland in the middle ground.
distinction: Although the building leans on the mountain and flanks the water, its most prominent spatial expression is the layering of concealment and exposure through screening by woodland, rather than emphasizing placement according to terrain.

evidence: Center of the painting: the building complex (roofs, beams, and pillars) is surrounded and screened by dense trees, presenting a typical form of seeing a house within the woods, with only the upper structure exposed. | Lower middle of the painting: figures inside the open hall are clearly visible, but the building's base and surroundings are screened by groves, forming obvious layers of concealment and revelation. | Overall painting: the built elements are deeply hidden within the woodland, and the natural scenery (trees) forms the main screening-and-exposure relationship with the buildings, constituting a mood of secluded dwelling.
distinction: Although there are horse-riding figures and enclosing walls at the bottom of the painting hinting at an entrance and clues for movement through the landscape, the path is blocked by groves, and the visual focus is on the static layering of buildings screened by woodland, rather than a coherent process of entry.

evidence: Right side of the painting: a towering standing rock, with sloping rocks at its base and distant mountains, are visible; no clear built elements such as houses, bridges, or roads are seen. | Left side and edges of the painting: covered with calligraphic inscriptions and seals, with no pictorial traces of built elements.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built elements; only mountain and rock scenery is seen, and it is assigned to the closest category based on the overall visible space.

evidence: Lower middle: the building complex is half-hidden in the dense woodland, with only part of the roofs and walls exposed, forming obvious layers of concealment and revelation. | Mid-slope in the upper middle: buildings are placed against the cliff, partly occluded by rock faces and trees, presenting a spatial relationship of seeing a house behind the rock.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed according to the mountain's contours, the painting places more emphasis on the screening and exposure of the buildings by woodland and mountain rocks; the concealment-and-revelation relationship plays a dominant role in composing the scene.

evidence: Center-right and right side: multiple groups of houses and building complexes are built directly on the tiered platforms formed by the mountain rocks, with the building sites closely corresponding to the height of the mountain's contours. | Left side and lower left: houses are distributed along the bank and slopes, laid out following the terrain and the direction of the waterside. | Lower right: a waterside pavilion is placed relying on the bank rocks, forming an integration with the natural terrain.
distinction: Although the buildings play a role in highlighting the scenery, their most prominent visual characteristic is the layout relationship of following the mountain and being built on platforms, so C1 is more dominant than C3.

evidence: Center-left of the painting: a group of buildings clings to a rock platform halfway up a steep cliff, with the building sites closely fitted to the forms of the mountain rock, presenting the feature of setting houses on platforms. | Center-right of the painting: another group of buildings is placed on the gentle ground of the mountain-foot valley, unfolding in response to the mountain's contours and the woodland edge, with the layout determined by terrain. | Overall composition: the built elements in the painting are staggered in height, placed entirely according to the precipitous terrain of giant peaks and deep valleys, forming a clear corresponding relationship with the natural terrain.
distinction: Although the buildings have layers of screening by woodland and mountain rocks, their most core role in composing the scene is placement according to site conditions such as cliffs and valleys, so C1 is more dominant than C2.

evidence: Left side of the middle ground: between the rock face and the woodland, the eaves and structure of a pavilion are exposed, partly occluded by the mountain mass. | Right side of the middle ground: deep in the woods, the roof of a house is visible, screened behind the woodland. | Upper distant view: at the top of the cliff there are tiny buildings, hidden among the peaks according to the mountain's contours.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed according to the mountain's contours, the painting places more emphasis on the screening and exposure of the buildings by woodland and mountain rocks, forming spatial layers of interchanging concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower right side: several houses and buildings are visible, with parts of the walls and roofs occluded by the trees and mountain rocks in front, presenting a half-exposed state. | Lower middle: building outlines are faintly visible where the woodland grows densely; the buildings are hidden behind trees and rocks, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Mid-slope on the right side: buildings are screened among mountain rocks and vegetation, not fully exposed, participating in constituting the spatial layers of the painting.
distinction: In the painting, the buildings mainly present layers of half-concealment and half-revelation through the occlusion of trees and mountain rocks; the characteristic of concealment and revelation forming the setting is more prominent than simple placement according to terrain.

evidence: Mid-slope on the lower-left of the middle section: between the woodland and mountain rocks, building roofs are faintly visible, presenting a half-screened, half-exposed state. | Behind the grove on the lower right of the middle section: behind the screening trees, building eaves are exposed, forming spatial layers. | Water surface at the bottom of the painting: there is a small boat, suggesting a spatial clue for approaching the built elements or for travel.
distinction: In the painting, the built elements mainly present concealment-and-revelation layers through screening by woodland and mountain rocks; although a small boat suggests a path, concealment and revelation forming the setting is more prominent.

evidence: Middle-ground mid-slope and sloping platforms: several houses are placed in staggered fashion according to the mountain's slopes and platforms, with the building sites echoing the undulations of the terrain. | Among the woods on the right bank: houses are screened between trees and mountain rocks, laid out following the waterside and the woodland edge.
distinction: Although there is screening by woodland, the houses mainly present the spatial relationship of placement according to the sloping platforms and mountain contours, with screening as a secondary element.

evidence: Bottom of the painting: the building complex unfolds on the flat ground by the waterside, surrounded by trees, with a bridge connecting in front, presenting a layout of dwelling along the bank. | Lower center of the painting: a small pavilion-style structure is built on a protruding high rock platform, adjacent to where the waterfall flows down, presenting the feature of setting a house on a platform. | Center-left of the painting: several houses are distributed in staggered fashion according to the slopes of the mid-slope, screened among trees and rocks, presenting a relationship of separate placement according to the slopes.
distinction: Although the pavilion on the central rock platform plays a role in highlighting the waterfall scenery (similar to C3), the built elements throughout the painting present a multi-level distribution from the mountain-foot waterside and mid-slope slopes to the high rock platform, mainly embodying the placement logic of responding to terrain height, so C1 is more dominant.

evidence: Foreground at the bottom of the painting: a pavilion is built on a protruding stone-bank platform by the water, with railings and steps, a clear building site, presenting the form of setting a house on a platform and placing it by the water. | Waterside on the center-right of the painting: houses and buildings are distributed at the junction of the sloping ground and the waterside, placed according to the undulations of the terrain, presenting a relationship of unfolding along the bank or separate placement according to the slope. | Water surface in the center of the painting: an arched bridge spans the water connecting the two banks, with the bridge body following the water flow and shoreline positions, assisting in building the spatial connection between the banks.
distinction: Although the foreground pavilion is a visual focus, it is clearly built on a stone-bank building site and mainly embodies the terrain-responsive placement relationship of built elements conforming to the waterside terrain, rather than simply serving as an identifying scenic accent.

evidence: Lower-right corner: an arched bridge is visible spanning the water, connecting the foreground and middle ground, forming a path clue for entering the painting. | Middle-right mountain and lower-left part: houses and built elements are visible, screened among trees and mountain rocks; the bridge and shoreline guide the line of sight toward these built elements, presenting a spatial process from here to there.

evidence: Lower left corner: A simple wooden bridge (plank bridge) is visible spanning the water surface and connecting the two banks. | Middle ground and background of the painting: The painting consists mainly of mountains, rocks, trees, and distant mountains; no other clear houses or buildings are seen, and the bridge, as the only built element, suggests a path for movement through the landscape and entry.
distinction: The only built element in the painting is the bridge in the lower left corner, which provides a path across the water and into the painting, conforming to the characteristics of access to secluded settings rather than terrain-responsive siting, concealment and revelation, or scenic accentuation.

evidence: Left mountain slope: Winding steps/small paths connect the pavilion with the houses below, forming a clue for traversing the landscape. | Lower middle: The enclosing wall has a gate, suggesting an entrance and an accessible interior space.
distinction: The connectivity of paths and gates is more prominent in organizing spatial relationships than simply building according to the mountain terrain, emphasizing the process of entry.
