evidence: Lower left corner: A pavilion is built among the rocks and trees, with a stone bridge beside it crossing a stream and figures inside the pavilion, forming a clear stopping and entry point. | Lower right water surface: A small boat carrying figures travels on the water, forming a spatial echo and a clue to traversing the landscape with the pavilion on the bank. | Right middle ground: House roofs are faintly exposed behind the trees, suggesting a deeper habitable space.
distinction: Although the house on the right is screened, the pavilion, stone bridge, flowing water, and boat in the lower left corner together construct a more dominant clue to movement through the landscape and entry that runs through the spatial organization of the painting.

evidence: Middle of the painting, toward the right: The built elements (houses) sit on a rocky platform, partly screened by the surrounding trees and rocks, with only the roofs and part of the structure exposed, forming alternating layers of concealment and revelation. | Middle of the painting: The branches and foliage of the trees are lush and, together with the mountains and rocks, screen the buildings behind, making the buildings appear and disappear, enhancing the pictorial depth and sense of seclusion.
distinction: Although the built elements are sited according to the mountain, the painting places more emphasis on the screening and exposure of the buildings by trees, mountains, and rocks, forming the visual effect of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower part of the painting: A group of buildings unfolds along the waterside and the tree bases, with the houses staggered and adapted to the gentle terrain and shoreline. | Right side and upper middle of the painting: Multiple buildings are placed in layers according to the undulating forms of the cliffs and mountain hollows, presenting a layout of houses set against the rock and arranged separately along the slopes. | Middle of the painting: The buildings are embedded in valleys or terraces surrounded by mountains and rocks, and the building sites closely follow the contours of the mountain mass.
distinction: Although there is local screening of the buildings by trees, mountains, and rocks in the painting, the layout relationship of the buildings placed according to the undulations of the terrain and the mountain configuration is more prominent and pervasive, dominating the spatial expression.

evidence: Whole painting: The painting presents a purely natural landscape, including distant mountains, a broad water surface, sloping-bank trees on the left, and a small island in the water with dead trees in the middle ground; no houses, bridges, or other artificial built elements are seen. | Middle ground to background: Through the progressive recession of foreground trees, middle-ground islets, and distant mountain ranges, as well as the rendering of water mist, a profound spatial layering is formed.
distinction: There are no built elements in the painting; C2 focuses on the creation of spatial layering, while C3 focuses on built elements identifying scenery; here the natural layering is more prominent.

evidence: Left edge: A structure resembling a bridge or building screened by trees is faintly visible | Lower left corner: There are very few lines on the water surface, suspected to be part of a boat or waterside building
distinction: The built elements in the painting are very few and blurred, and the only remaining clues show a state of being screened by natural scenery, so it is assigned to C2.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: The roofs and walls of several buildings sit in a valley or on a mountainside surrounded by cliffs, screened in front by pines, mountains, and rocks, presenting a distinct concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Upper middle of the painting: The towering cliff (corresponding to the inscription 'Yuanzhu Terrace') serves as a backdrop, setting off the spatial layering of the buildings below hidden among the rocks and woods.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited according to the mountain terrain, the visual focus of the painting places more emphasis on their layering as screened by mountains, rocks, trees, and woodland and appearing faintly, rather than simple correspondence to the terrain.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: A wooden bridge spans between the two banks, with railings and supporting structures on the bridge. | On the bridge: A person riding a donkey (or horse) is crossing the bridge, forming a clear path of movement through the landscape and a spatial connection from one place to another. | Foreground on the left and right of the painting: The bridge connects the rocks and trees on both sides, guiding the line of sight across the water and suggesting an accessible spatial process of continuing to traverse the landscape.
distinction: Although the bridge serves as a scenic accent, the movement of the pedestrian on the bridge clearly emphasizes the sense of a passage and a path for traversing the landscape, rather than merely serving as a static scenic marker.

evidence: Lower middle: The house is partly screened by the foreground dead trees and mountains and rocks, with only the roof and wall surfaces exposed, presenting a layered effect of being screened among the woods. | Right side at the mountain foot: The buildings are arranged in a staggered manner following the mountain terrain and are revealed through the gaps between trees, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the buildings are arranged following the mountain terrain, the painting places greater emphasis on expressing the presence of the buildings and the spatial layers through the screening and revealing by woodland and mountains and rocks.

evidence: Waterside at the lower part of the painting: Moored boats and simple built forms leaning against the sloping rocks are visible, and the building site/base meets the waterside sloping rocks. | Bottom of the painting: The built structures and boats are distributed along the shoreline, presenting a spatial relationship of mooring against the bank and placement according to the terrain.
distinction: The built structures and boats are mainly moored and placed leaning against the waterside terrain, reflecting a relationship of terrain-responsive siting, rather than serving merely as isolated markers that identify the scenery.

evidence: Lower right of the painting: The thatched house is located among tall pine trees; the building itself is partly screened by thick trunks and branches and foliage, with only the roof, eaves, and some window lattices exposed, presenting a spatial layer of a house hidden in the woods. | Right side and center of the painting: Several tall pine trees stand in front of and beside the building, with dense pine needles forming a natural barrier that leaves the building in a half-screened state, reinforcing the relationship of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the building is placed by the water, the painting places greater emphasis on the relationship of screening and revealing of the building by the pine trees, rather than on a layout corresponding to the building's relation to terrain height.

evidence: Middle of the right side: A group of house buildings is visible, whose roofs and upper structures are partly screened by the branches and foliage of foreground trees, presenting a layered sense of houses revealed among the woods. | Lower part of the right side: The front porch and interior furnishings of the lower-level building are clearly visible, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation with the surrounding mountains and rocks and trees.
distinction: The relationship of concealment and revelation between the built structures and woodland is most prominent in the painting; spatial layers are constructed through the screening and revealing by trees, which dominates the presentation of the built structures, so C2 is more apt than C1.

evidence: Left side: Bamboo branches and the lines of the sloping bank below are visible, with no trace of built structures | Overall painting: Large areas are blank paper support with calligraphic inscription and seals; no buildings, bridges, or paths are seen
distinction: No built structures are visible in the painting; classification is assigned based on the bamboo, rocks, and sloping bank at the left as the closest scenic marker, with no other evidence of spatial organization.

evidence: Whole painting: The painting consists mainly of mountains and rocks, dead trees, and water surface; no clearly identifiable traces of man-made built structures such as houses, bridges, or paths are seen. | Among the mountains and rocks on the left: Some ink dots and texture strokes are present, but their forms are vague and cannot be confirmed as architectural structures.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built elements and takes natural landscape as its main subject; exact classification based on the relationship between built structures and landscape is not possible, so it is assigned to the closest category based on the overall visible space.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: The thatched house is built on the sloping ground at the mountain foot, placed in conformity with the terrain and blending with the surrounding mountains and rocks and trees. | Lower right corner of the painting: Tiny figures and a small boat moored at the bank are visible, implying a process of approach to the built structure by water route.
distinction: Although the painting contains a clue of access by water route, the relationship of the built structure being placed on the sloping ground at the mountain foot according to the terrain is more prominent, so C1 is dominant.

evidence: Lower center of the right-hand painted panel: several mountains and rocks emerging from the water, together with trees, are visible; no clear buildings | Upper right of the right-hand painted panel: a very small boat in the distance on the water, serving as a scenic accent
distinction: The painting lacks clear built elements; only water, mountains and rocks and a small boat are seen, and it is only tentatively assigned to the scenic accentuation category on the basis of the overall spatial organization

evidence: Upper middle of the right painting section: Distant mountain outlines and a few small boats on the water are visible, forming an open distant view. | Lower part of the right painting section: The near bank, mountains and rocks, and trees are visible, meeting the water surface to constitute the foreground.
distinction: No clear built structures are seen in the painting; natural scenery (distant mountains, near bank) identifies the openness and layers of the waterscape, so it is assigned to C3.

evidence: Center and lower right of the painting: The main subject of the painting is the open water surface and distant mountains; several small boats are in the center, and trees and figures are on the sloping bank in the lower right corner; no clear buildings are seen.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built structures; only boats and figures dot the water surface, serving to identify the scenery, so it is only marginally assigned to scenic accentuation.

evidence: Lower right corner: The roof and wall surfaces of a low house are revealed among trees and rocks; the built structure is partly screened by woodland and mountains and rocks, forming layers of concealment and revelation. | Middle of the left side: Distant mountains meet the water surface, with no built structures, setting off the partly screened scene in the lower right corner.
distinction: Although the built structure has a scenic accentuation role, its partly screened and partly revealed relationship with trees and rocks is more prominent and participates in constructing spatial layers.

evidence: Lower left of the painted panel: a built element (apparently a thatched pavilion) is visible, its roof and structure partly obscured by the surrounding trees and sloping bank, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Lower left of the painted panel: the built element, trees, mountains and rocks screen one another, forming foreground-background spatial layering.
distinction: Although the built element is placed according to the sloping bank, the painting places greater emphasis on the screening and revealing relationship between the trees and the built element, and constructs spatial layering through it.

evidence: Lower middle, slightly left: A thatched pavilion sits on the sloping bank/flat rock by the water, its building site/base fitting the terrain. | Left side: The thatched pavilion is adjacent to the dead trees and mountains and rocks on the left, placed leaning against natural scenery. | Lower middle: The thatched pavilion faces the open water surface and distant mountains, presenting a spatial placement by the water and against the bank.
distinction: Although the thatched pavilion has a scenic accentuation role, the painting places greater emphasis on its relationship of terrain placement leaning against trees and rocks and situated by the water against the bank.

evidence: Left side: Behind dense bamboo groves and trees, the roof, walls, and railings of a building are revealed, presenting a clear relationship of partial screening. | Right side: The open waterside and sloping rocks contrast with the dense woods on the left, setting off the secluded layers of the built structure within the woods.
distinction: Although the built structure is located at the waterside, the painting places greater emphasis on its relationship of screening and revealing by woodland, rather than on mere terrain placement.

evidence: Lower right: A group of multi-story pavilion buildings is built against the mountain rock and sloping platform, staggered in height, with the building site/base closely integrated with the mountain and rock terrain. | Lower left: Another waterside building is placed in conformity with the shoreline and sloping ground, connected to the surrounding terrain by a bridge.
distinction: Although the buildings have a role in identifying the scenery, their placement following the mountains and unfolding with the terrain's height is more prominent and constitutes the dominant spatial expression.

evidence: Center of the painting: Several figures on horseback or on foot, presenting a state of travel, with no buildings around. | Left side of the painting: Willows and a sloping bank constitute one boundary of the travel environment. | Upper right of the painting: Mountain rocks hang down, forming a spatial enclosure with the trees on the left.
distinction: There are no built structures in the painting; only traveling figures are seen, and it is only marginally assigned to C4 based on movement through the landscape, with no other competing interpretation.

evidence: Lower left: Dead trees and bamboo grow on the sloping bank. | Lower left toward center: Amid the screening of trees and bamboo, the roof and part of the structure of a pavilion are visible, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Background: Distant mountains and the water surface serve as the background, setting off the layers of the foreground woodland and pavilion.
distinction: Although the pavilion has a scenic accentuation role, the painting more prominently highlights the layers of concealment and revelation as it is screened by woodland and bamboo, so concealment and revelation is more dominant.

evidence: Lower right: A thatched pavilion is half-hidden between the pine trees on the right and the dead trees in the middle, with only the roof and some pillars exposed, presenting spatial layers of concealment and revelation among the woods. | Lower right to lower middle: The thatched pavilion sits on sloping rocks, surrounded by trees; the screening by vegetation clarifies the hidden position of the built structure.
distinction: Although the thatched pavilion is by the water and against rocks, the painting places greater emphasis on its relationship of screening and revealing by trees, rather than on a layout unfolded according to terrain.

evidence: Lower right: Two small boats and figures in them are visible, forming a clue of movement through the landscape on the water surface. | Lower left to center: Trees and mountains and rocks constitute the edge of the waterside, forming a spatially accessible relationship with the boats on the water.
distinction: There are no fixed built structures in the painting; only boats serve as a clue of movement through the landscape, presenting an accessible process of movement through the water space.

evidence: Middle right: The house is surrounded by dense trees, with only the roof, eaves, and railings exposed, forming clear layers of concealment and revelation. | Lower left: A small bridge spans the water surface, connecting the trees and rocks on both banks, but no clear path leading to the house is seen.
distinction: Although the painting contains a bridge as a clue of movement through the landscape, no clear path connecting to the built structure is seen; the built structure presents layers mainly through screening by woodland, so C2 is more apt.

evidence: Middle ground and right side: Multiple building complexes are extensively screened by dense pines, miscellaneous trees, and plants such as banana, with only parts of roofs, eave corners, and wall surfaces exposed, forming clear layers of concealment and revelation. | Middle ground on the left: Courtyard walls and a gatehouse loom behind the pine grove; branches and foliage interweave in front of and behind the buildings, reinforcing the screening relationship. | Lower foreground: A waterside pavilion is half-hidden in the grove, together with the water surface and arched bridge constituting a space enveloped by natural scenery.
distinction: Although the foreground bridge and boats imply paths, the core way in which buildings and landscape are composed in the painting is to create layers through the screening and revealing by woodland; the partly screened feature is more prominent and pervasive.

evidence: Lower right corner: A thatched pavilion is visible, built leaning against mountains and rocks; it is small in scale and serves as a visual foothold in the lower part of the painting. | Upper right to center: Bamboo branches hang down from above, forming a spatial echo with the mountains and rocks and thatched pavilion below, condensing the scene of secluded dwelling at the mountain foot.
distinction: Although the thatched pavilion leans against mountains and rocks, its main role in the painting is to condense and identify the scene of secluded dwelling at the mountain foot, rather than to emphasize the decisive influence of terrain on layout.

evidence: Lower middle and left side of the painting: House buildings are screened by dense trees (some with red color) and mountains and rocks, with only roofs and parts of wall surfaces exposed, presenting a state of being half hidden and half revealed. | Slightly below center of the painting: The building cluster is distributed deep in the valley and woods, revealed through the gaps between trees, forming rich spatial layers and a relationship of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the buildings are situated against mountains and by water, the painting places greater emphasis on the layered relationship in which the buildings are screened by trees and mountains and rocks and are half hidden and half revealed; the effect of concealment and revelation is more dominant than mere terrain adaptation.

evidence: Water surface at lower left: A small boat and figures in it are visible, implying a clue of movement by water. | Right side and far bank: Trees and sloping banks are visible, forming an open space for movement with the water surface.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built structures, but the small boat on the water provides an accessible, traversable spatial clue, so it is assigned to C4.

evidence: Lower right corner: A house with railings is visible, part of whose structure is screened by the branches and foliage of nearby trees. | Lower right corner: Trees and the building are closely adjacent, forming a screening relationship; the building is not fully exposed but half hidden and half revealed. | Overall painting: Through the screening by trees, the built structure in the lower right corner forms a foreground layer contrast with the open water surface, presenting a sense of houses seen among the woods.
distinction: Although the building is located at the waterside, the painting places greater emphasis on the relationship of screening and revealing of the building by trees, rather than on placement based solely on terrain.

evidence: Painted portion on the right side of the painting: The painting depicts dense woods, waterside, and a stream; figures and horses are seen gathered at the bank, and a small boat is on the water; no clear houses or built structures are seen.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built structures, but the waterside, boats, and traveling figures constitute spatial clues of a ferry crossing and movement through the landscape, so it is assigned to C4.

evidence: Middle ground on the left: Several houses are arranged in sequence along the sloping platform at the mountain foot and the edge of the waterside, their building sites/bases corresponding to the undulations of the terrain. | Lower right corner: Houses are built against mountains and rocks and woodland, partly screened by trees and arranged in conformity with the sloping ground. | Middle of the painting: The broad water surface separates the built structures and mountains and rocks on both banks; all built structures are placed close to the waterside or the foot of slopes.
distinction: The built structure in the lower right corner has a screening relationship, but what is more prominent in the left-side and overall built structures is placement leaning against the waterside and sloping-platform terrain; the feature of terrain-responsive placement is dominant.

evidence: Middle left: An arched bridge spans the stream mouth, connecting the paths on both banks and forming a spatial transition clue | Central water surface: A small boat carrying people moves along, constituting a dynamic clue of travel and approach | Right bank: A pavilion is built by the water, meeting the water surface and trees, serving as a potential node on the travel route
distinction: Although the pavilion has a scenic accentuation role, the bridge, boat, and pavilion together construct a clear travel route and process of spatial entry; C4 better summarizes the overall spatial organization.

evidence: Lower right: A small boat with one person in it is on the water, moored beneath the cliff and pine trees. | Right side: Steep mountains and rocks and pine trees occupy the right half of the painting, forming a cliff-and-bank landscape.
distinction: There are no fixed built structures in the painting; the lone boat, as a scenic accent element, identifies the scenery of the pine stream and waterside, rather than showing the relationship of buildings placed according to terrain.

evidence: Lower left: Amid the screening of pine trees and mountains and rocks, the roof structure of a thatched pavilion is visible, presenting a state of being hidden among the woods. | Overall composition: The built structure is partly screened by surrounding trees and mountains and rocks, and spatial layers are formed through the screening and revealing by natural scenery.
distinction: The painting focuses on the relationship of concealment and revelation in which the building is screened by woodland and mountains and rocks, rather than serving merely as a conspicuous landmark to identify the scenery.

evidence: Lower-middle of the painting: the foreground consists of slope rocks and several sparse trees; no houses, pavilions, or other built elements are visible. | Middle and distant parts of the painting: a large area of unpainted space represents the water surface; the distance consists of gentle, continuous mountain ranges, presenting an overall broad and open landscape prospect.
distinction: No clear built elements are visible in the painting; it presents only the spatial organization of natural landscape, with no other category competing.

evidence: Water surface in the lower-middle: a small boat can be seen moving on the water; no houses, bridges, or other clear built elements are visible. | Upper part and bottom: distant mountains and mist, together with woodland at the bottom, form an open natural landscape background.
distinction: The painting has no clear built elements; the small boat alone marks the waterside scene, so it is only marginally assigned to C3.

evidence: Central mountainside: building roofs and eaves emerge from dense pine forest, forming a typical concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Lower-left corner: the building group is arranged along the mountain foot and waterside, presenting a terrain-responsive siting.
distinction: The concealment-and-revelation relationship of the buildings at the central mountainside, screened by woodland (C2), has greater visual dominance and spatial layering than the buildings at the lower-left corner arranged along the waterside (C1).

evidence: Slightly right of center: a pavilion building can be seen, its lower part obscured by dense trees so that only the roof and upper structure are exposed, presenting the form of a house seen within woodland. | Middle and upper parts of the painting: mist and clouds coil among mountains and rocks and trees; the building stands amid the screening of cloud vapor and woodland, forming a spatial layering of a house seen through a screened scene.
distinction: Although the building is located at an open spot on the mountainside, the visually dominant relationship is the layer of concealment and revelation screened by woodland and mist, rather than its simply serving as a conspicuous scenic marker.

evidence: Slightly left of center: an arched bridge can be seen spanning a stream, connecting the trees on both banks and forming a clear clue to a route of movement through the landscape. | Water surface in the lower part of the painting: a small boat is located in the stream, implying waterway traffic and a direction of travel, and creating a connection with the bank space. | Waterside on the right side of the painting: built elements (houses or pavilions) can be seen built facing the water, their structures partly obscured by trees, together with the bridge and boat forming a spatial relationship that can be reached or entered.
distinction: Although the built elements are screened by trees, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship (consistent with C2 features), the movement clues of the bridge and boat in the painting are more prominent, constructing a spatial process of approaching the built elements by waterway or bridge; therefore C4 better explains their dominant role in the composition.

evidence: Lower left to lower middle: a group of houses is arranged in scattered fashion along the mountain-foot slope and waterside, with the building bases unfolding in response to the undulations of the terrain. | Lower part of the mountain rock on the right: the built elements are placed tightly against the bottom edge of a huge mountain rock, presenting a layout nestled against the rock and beside the water.
distinction: The built elements form a group unfolding in response to the terrain and waterside, primarily embodying a relationship of siting according to the ground, rather than serving merely as an isolated node marking a particular scenic spot.

evidence: Water surface in the lower-middle: a small boat with a canopy is moored on the water, with one person seated inside, the boat close to the right bank. | Right bank: strange rocks and trees are on the bank; the boat and bank connect with each other, implying a spatial link of reaching or leaving the bank from the water.
distinction: The boat primarily serves as a movement clue connecting the water surface and the bank, presenting a reachable spatial process, rather than simply a static marker identifying a landscape scene.

evidence: Left side: there is a huge mountain rock, surrounded by weeds and bamboo. | Center and right: a large stand of bamboo presents foreground and background layers, with bamboo leaves varying in density, creating a sense of space through screening and exposure. | Lower-right corner: waterside slope ground and several small rocks can be seen, with ripples on the water surface, but no buildings or paths are visible.
distinction: No built elements are visible at all in the painting; it is assigned to C2 solely on the basis of the foreground-background screening layers of natural scenery (bamboo and rocks).

evidence: Right-hand painted panel: the main body of the painting is a large area of unpainted water; there is a faint distant bank on the left and a little sloping bank and trees in the lower right corner; no clear built structures are seen. | Water slightly left of center: there is a very small ink mark, possibly a small boat, but it cannot be confirmed as a building or a clear clue to built elements.
distinction: The painting lacks clear evidence of built elements; the whole is composed of water and a minimal shoreline forming an open scene, and it is assigned to C3 as the closest description of the overall spatial accentuation.

evidence: Lower middle: building outlines are faintly visible between mist and the mountain foot, partly obscured by mountains, rocks, and woodland, presenting a layer that appears and disappears. | Lower left: at the mountain foot there is a form suspected to be a pavilion or house, screened among trees, rocks, and mist.
distinction: The buildings in the painting primarily create a profound spatial layering through being screened and revealed by mountains, rocks, mist, and woodland, rather than emphasizing their layout in response to the terrain.

evidence: River surface slightly left of center on the right page: a small boat can be seen floating on the open water surface | Lower-right corner of the right page: beside the sloping bank, trees, and rocks there is a tiny form of two figures seated facing each other | Upper part and distance of the right page: distant mountains are hazy, forming a broad and level space with the river surface
distinction: The painting is dominated by the river surface and distant mountains; the boat and figures mark the focal point of the scene. Although there are no clear buildings, their role as spatial markers is more prominent than the movement clues of C4.

evidence: Lower right: among the sloping bank, trees, and rocks, tiny figures can be seen as scenic accents, but no houses, bridges, paths, or other built elements are visible | Left and center: towering peaks and large areas of unpainted mist form an open landscape space; the scenic-accent figures in the lower-right corner echo the distant mountains
distinction: The painting has no clear built elements; only the figures in the lower right serve as scenic accents that crystallize the landscape mood, so it is assigned to the closest category of scenic accentuation.

evidence: Lower-left corner: a built structure (house/water pavilion) can be seen, its building body and windows partly exposed, half-screened by the dark-ink mountains, rocks, and trees in the foreground, forming layers of concealment and revelation. | From the lower-left corner to the center: the built structure is close against the left slope rocks and willow trees, facing the large area of unpainted water surface on the right, its secluded position suggested by the screening of the foreground trees and rocks.
distinction: Although the built structure is sited in response to mountains, rocks, and the waterside, the painting emphasizes more its concealment and revelation, half-hidden and half-visible behind the foreground trees and rocks, so C2 is more apt than C1.

evidence: Lower right: a scholar sits on a rock, facing the landscape on the left | Left: blue-green mountain peaks rise, with a waterfall flowing down among the mountains | Upper right and lower part: cliffs, pines, and miscellaneous trees are distributed, forming a natural scene
distinction: No clear built elements are visible in the painting; only the scholar as a scenic accent is seen, so it is assigned to scenic accentuation on the basis of the overall spatial organization, but it lacks evidence of built elements.

evidence: Lower left: on the foreground water surface there is a small boat and figures, implying movement on the water. | Middle ground to distance: the open water surface extends to distant mountains, and the waterside and woodland form layers, constituting a profound space that can be traveled through.
distinction: The painting has no clear buildings as scenic accents; the movement clue of the boat better embodies a sense of entering the space than merely marking the scene.

evidence: Lower center: a stone bridge can be seen spanning the water surface, connecting the left and right sloping banks and implying a path of crossing and passage. | Left, lower middle: behind the woodland there are faint lines, suspected to be a wall or building edge, but the details are blurred and cannot be confirmed as clear built elements.
distinction: The painting lacks a clear building mass to form a typical concealment-and-revelation scene, while the stone bridge, as a clear piece of transport infrastructure, more directly embodies the spatial relationship of path and entry.

evidence: Lower-right corner: a person can be seen sitting on the waterside fishing, with a small box-like object beside them; no clear building construction is visible. | Overall painting: the painting is dominated by water surface, mountains and rocks, and trees; the figure and the water surface form a scenic-accent relationship.
distinction: No clear built elements are visible in the painting; it is assigned to the closest category on the basis of the overall visible relationship between landscape and scenic-accent figures.

evidence: Left mountainside: a building group is screened within dense pine forest, with only part of the roofs and walls exposed, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Right mountain foot: multiple houses are scattered among the woodland, partly obscured by branches and leaves, presenting a clearly layered sense of space. | Lower foreground: a pavilion is hidden at the edge of a grove, screening and being screened by the surrounding vegetation.
distinction: Although the buildings are distributed in response to the mountain terrain, the painting lays more emphasis on creating spatial layers through the screening and exposure of woodland, so C2 is more apt than C1.

evidence: Middle ground, slightly right: a bridge spans the water surface, with one person standing on it, connecting the two banks and forming a clear movement clue. | Left middle ground: pavilion buildings are screened within the woodland, with part of the roofs and structures visible, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Foreground and middle ground: water surface and lotus leaves are distributed; the bridge guides the gaze to extend into the depth of the painting.
distinction: The bridge and figures constitute a clear path of entry and touring that dominates the spatial process of the painting, while the screening of the buildings on the left is a local feature.

evidence: Left sloping bank: a pavilion can be seen, hidden beside a grove, its base nestled against the waterside sloping bank, serving as a spatial node. | Right water surface: in the distance an arched structure (suspected to be a bridge) can be seen spanning the water surface, implying a connection between the two banks. | Lower-right water surface: a small boat and figures can be seen, the boat facing toward the pavilion on the left bank, forming a visual guide to approaching the built elements by waterway.
distinction: Although the pavilion is screened by trees and the painting is shrouded in mist and clouds with screening features, the presence of the small boat and suspected bridge constructs a clear movement route from the water surface to the built elements on the bank, giving the space a sense of entering from here to there; therefore C4 is more dominant.

evidence: Right side of the painting: the painting contains only mountains and rocks, trees, waterside, and a figure playing the qin; no buildings, bridges, paths, or other built elements are visible. | Center of the right side of the painting: the figure is in a natural environment surrounded by mountains, rocks, and trees, creating a sense of space extending into the depths of nature.
distinction: The painting has no built elements; on the basis of the secluded spatial sense of the natural environment in which the figure is placed, it is only marginally assigned to C4, which expresses a spatial process.

evidence: Right-hand painted panel: the painting mainly depicts sloping rocks, trees (bare branches and bamboo leaves) and distant water; no clear built elements such as houses or bridges are seen. | Left side: the left side is calligraphic inscription and does not constitute evidence of spatial expression within the painting.
distinction: No built elements are visible in the painting; assignment to the closest category is made on the basis of the overall visible organization of the natural landscape.

evidence: Lower right: a thatched hut is partly obscured by the foreground tree trunks and branches and leaves, with only the thatched roof and part of the building mass exposed, forming a layer of a house hidden in the woodland. | Lower right: through the gaps between the trees, figures can be seen active inside the house; the building is closely integrated with the surrounding mountains, rocks, and trees, forming a scene through the screening and exposure of natural scenery.
distinction: Although the building is sited against the mountain and beside trees, the painting emphasizes more the screening and exposure relationship of the trees to the building, and the visual effect of concealment and revelation forming a scene is more prominent.

evidence: Upper right of the painting: a group of buildings is scattered in response to the terrain of the mountain foot and waterside; the house bases have a clear correspondence with the mountain mass and the water's edge, presenting a layout that unfolds along the bank and places houses according to the ground. | Lower middle of the painting: a stream and gaps among mountains and rocks connect with a small bridge, on which there are pedestrians, implying a touring path leading into the depths and incidentally explaining the connection between the built elements and the natural terrain.
distinction: Although the small bridge and path at the lower part of the painting imply access to secluded settings, the most prominent feature of the main built elements in the painting (the building group in the upper right) is their placement in response to mountains and water and unfolding with the terrain; therefore C1 is more dominant.

evidence: Lower-right sloping bank: a white-walled, black-roofed house sits in a hollow of the sloping rocks, with the tree crowns behind and on both sides rising higher, branches and leaves hanging over the roof, and the building body exposed through gaps in the trees | Among the trees and rocks to the left of the lower-right house: tree trunks and branches slant across and screen the left half of the house, and among the trees and rocks another eave-like structure is half-exposed, forming layers of foreground-background concealment and revelation | Central-upper main peak and mist: the great peak and smoky clouds occupy the main body of the painting; the built elements appear only in one place among the woodland and rock edges at the lower right, in an enclosed and screened position rather than on an open face
distinction: Although the house sits at the foot of the slope, the painting organizes the layers of its existence through the concealment-and-revelation relationship of branches and leaves screening it and the roof and walls being exposed; the expression of siting corresponding to the terrain is less clear than the screening relationship

evidence: Lower left: two people are at the sloping bank below a willow tree, with objects beside them, presenting an appearance of waiting. | Right water surface: a boat carries several people, one poling, forming a spatial connection of crossing the river with the figures on the bank. | Whole painting: no houses, pavilions, or other fixed built elements are visible; the spatial organization unfolds mainly through the waterside and the ferry clue of the boat.
distinction: The interaction between the boat and the bank primarily expresses the movement process of a ferry crossing (C4), rather than simply serving as a scenic marker of the landscape (C3).

evidence: Lower right of the painting: a figure can be seen standing beside what appears to be a small path or wooden fence, facing the direction of the waterfall. | Right middle ground of the painting: a waterfall can be seen flowing down among mountain rocks, screened by trees around it, forming a secluded space.
distinction: No clear built elements are visible in the painting, but the figure and path imply a touring process of entering a secluded realm, so it is assigned to C4.

evidence: Right middle: an arched bridge spans a stream, connecting the two banks and forming a clear passage clue. | Left middle: among the screening woodland, house roofs can be seen; the path extending from the bridge seems to lead here, presenting a spatial process of going from here to there. | Overall composition: from the foreground stream and bridge, the path goes deep into the woodland to the houses, organizing a spatial sequence that can be traveled through.
distinction: Although the houses are screened by trees, the entry clue formed by the bridge and path is more prominent, dominating the spatial organizing process from outside to inside.

evidence: Left mountainside: a pavilion-style building is hidden among mountains, rocks, and trees, with only its top and part of its structure exposed, presenting a state of being screened by natural scenery. | Lower right: a group of house buildings is partly obscured by foreground trees and mountains and rocks, with roofs and eaves exposed, forming spatial layers screened by woodland.
distinction: Although the buildings mark the positions of the mountainside and mountain foot, the painting highlights more their concealment-and-revelation relationship through the screening and exposure of woodland, mountains, and rocks, so C2 is more apt than C3.

evidence: Lower left: a thatch-roofed pavilion (or thatched hall) is half-hidden in dense bamboo grove, its roof and part of its pillars exposed through the bamboo leaves, forming a clear layer of concealment and revelation. | Left and center of the painting: a large stand of bamboo covers the sloping bank, wrapping the built elements within it, and the natural scenery forms a strong screening and contrasting relationship with the building. | Right water surface: the water surface is open, with an arched bridge in the distance, forming a spatial contrast of opening and closing with the thatched pavilion screened by bamboo on the left.
distinction: Although the thatched pavilion is built along the sloping bank, the painting emphasizes more its concealment-and-revelation relationship, half-screened by dense bamboo grove; therefore concealment and revelation is more prominent than terrain-responsive siting.

evidence: Lower left: a small boat on the water surface suggests a clue to movement through the landscape | Center and distant view: mountains and rocks, trees and woodland interwoven with clouds and mist; no clear built elements visible
distinction: No clear built elements are visible in the painting; only the small boat on the water suggests a process of movement through the landscape, so it is classified as C4

evidence: Left mountainside: two pavilion buildings built against the mountain, partly screened by the surrounding pine trees, with only the roofs and eaves exposed, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Right mountainside: a thatched hut hidden behind mountains, rocks and trees, its existence and spatial layering indicated by partial exposure. | Lower waterside: a group of courtyard houses partly screened among dense woodland and the waterside, with buildings and natural scenery interwoven.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited against the mountain and beside the water (C1), the painting places greater emphasis on revealing parts of the buildings through screening by trees and rocks, thereby creating deep spatial layering (C2).

evidence: Center-right: a double-eaved roof and part of the building itself are visible, half screened by the dense foliage of surrounding trees, forming a clear layering of concealment and revelation. | Lower right corner: a pavilion or gatehouse structure with steps is visible, likewise screened among trees and rocks, with only part of its outline exposed.
distinction: Although the steps visible at the lower-right building suggest a path, the dominant spatial organization of the whole painting is the screening and exposure of buildings by woodland, rather than a coherent route of movement through the landscape.

evidence: Whole painting: mountains and rocks, several pine trees and a waterfall are visible; no explicit built elements such as houses or bridges are seen. | Upper left and upper right: there are inscriptions and seals, but these are not treated as evidence of built elements present within the painting.
distinction: No visible built elements in the painting; the closest classification is made on the basis of the overall mountainous terrain.

evidence: Left middle ground: the roofs and building bodies of several houses are visible, partly screened by the foliage of trees in front, forming a layering of alternating concealment and revelation. | Lower center of the painting: dense woodland lies across the front of the built elements, so that the buildings appear and recede within the woods.
distinction: In the painting the built elements form spatial layering mainly through screening and exposure by woodland; no clear evidence of terrain-responsive layout or path guidance is seen.

evidence: Lower central water surface: a person is seen riding a small boat on the water; there are no houses, bridges or other man-made built elements. | Left: a waterfall flows down among the mountains and rocks, joining the water surface below. | Right: ancient pines grow on the cliff bank, with luxuriant foliage.
distinction: No explicit built elements in the painting; only the figure in the boat as a scenic accent, the whole presenting a realm of traveling through landscape, so it is classified as C4.

evidence: Lower right: several figures sit facing the water on flat bank ground, close to a stream. | Left and above: pines and mountains and rocks surround them; no buildings such as houses or pavilions are seen.
distinction: There are no explicit built elements in the painting; only figures acting beside the waterside, which can barely be regarded as terrain-responsive placement, with no other obvious competing interpretation.

evidence: Lower right: a pavilion building is visible, partly screened by the foliage of trees in front, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Right lower center: mountains, rocks and woodland surround and lie behind the building, forming spatial layering. | Right: a waterfall and stream are beside the building, and building and natural environment partly screen each other.
distinction: Although the building stands beside water and against the mountain, the painting places greater emphasis on the screening and exposure of the building by woodland and rocks; the relationship of concealment and revelation forming the scene is more prominent than terrain-responsive placement.

evidence: Lower left foreground: a thatched hut is visible, its roof and building body clear, placed beside a sloping bank and trees (bare trees, bamboo). | Middle and distant view of the painting: a broad water surface and distant mountains form an open background, with the foreground sloping bank serving as the building site.
distinction: The built elements are placed primarily in response to the foreground sloping-bank terrain, rather than serving as a landmark node that draws together the middle and distant landscape.

evidence: Lower half of the painting: the painting mainly depicts overlapping peaks and mountains and rocks, the rocks of varied forms with a few trees interspersed; no clear traces of built elements such as houses, bridges or paths are seen. | Among the mountains and rocks: the arrangement of rocks forms a certain spatial layering and unpainted space, possibly suggesting water flow or a valley, but visual evidence related to built elements is lacking.
distinction: The painting is dominated by natural landscape with no visible built elements; on the basis of spatial organization by mountain-and-rock terrain, it is barely classified as C1 as the closest basis of spatial expression.

evidence: Right hillside: a building complex sits on a hillside terrace, with steps or a ramp visible below extending downward along the mountain, presenting a layout of separate placement by slope and houses set on terraces. | Around the right-hand buildings: the building bases correspond to the varied heights of the mountain slopes, and the layout follows the undulations of the terrain.
distinction: Although the buildings are partly screened by surrounding trees, their layout against the slope terraces and with steps more directly embodies the responsive relationship between the placement of built elements and the terrain, rather than mere layering of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Center-left: beneath the cliff face, building roofs and walls are faintly visible, partly screened by trees and rocks in front, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the building is placed against the mountain, the painting places greater emphasis on its layering of concealment and revelation behind mountains, rocks and woodland, rather than a terrain-responsive layout.

evidence: Lower right: an arched bridge spans the water, connecting the two banks and constituting a clear cue for entry and crossing. | Lower left: among screening pines, a small built structure (house) is visible, echoing spatially with the shoreline and flowing water. | Center to right: the winding shoreline meets the bridge, guiding the eye into the depth of the painting and presenting a traversable spatial process.
distinction: Although the lower-left built structure is screened by woodland, the cue for movement through the landscape formed by the bridge and winding shoreline is more prominent and dominates the organization of spatial entry.

evidence: Center-left of the painting: a building complex (mountain dwelling) unfolds terrace by terrace along the mountain, its bases closely conforming to the undulations of the terrain, presenting a character of terrain-responsive placement. | Left of the painting: the building complex is located where the waterside meets the hillside, placed in response to the natural configuration of the bank and terraces.
distinction: Although trees are interspersed among the buildings, the placement of the buildings unfolding along the slope terraces is more conspicuous, rather than their forming the scene mainly through concealment and revelation.

evidence: Right side of the painting proper: the painting depicts a sloping bank, trees, garden rocks and two figures; no clear built elements such as houses or bridges are seen. | Inscription at left: the inscribed poem contains the characters 'plank bridge', but no bridge or related built structure is clearly presented in the painting.
distinction: No identifiable built elements are visible in the painting; on the basis of the figures' movement through the natural landscape, it is barely classified as C4, but visible evidence linking built elements with a path is lacking.

evidence: Lower left of the painting: a building complex is visible, with red walls and roofs exposed, most of it screened by foreground trees and rocks. | Center and left of the painting: dense trees and rocks stand in front of the buildings, forming a clear screening relationship so that the buildings appear half hidden and half revealed.
distinction: The painting chiefly presents the concealment and revelation of buildings screened by trees and rocks, rather than emphasizing a terrain-responsive relationship in which buildings are placed against the terrain.

evidence: Upper left corner: a group of pavilion buildings is built against a mountainside terrace, the bases conforming to the mountain's outline, presenting a staggered layout in response to the terrain. | Lower middle and right of the painting: mountains and rocks, trees and flowing water occupy most of the picture, contrasting natural configuration with man-made built elements against the upper-left buildings.
distinction: Although the buildings are partly screened, the layout feature of their placement along the mountain is more conspicuous and dominates the relationship between built elements and nature.

evidence: At the left-middle waterside: an open pavilion stands beneath a weeping willow, whose hanging branches surround and partly screen the building, with only the roof and pillars clearly exposed, presenting a screened condition at the water's edge. | Among the trees and rocks at right: a house is hidden behind pines, miscellaneous trees and boulders, its roof and part of its structure visible through gaps between trunks, forming a spatial layering in which a house is seen within the woods and behind rocks.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed beside water and against slopes, the painting places greater emphasis on the screening and exposure of buildings by trees and rocks; the layering of concealment and revelation forming the scene is more dominant than mere correspondence to terrain.

evidence: Lower right: a figure riding a donkey and an attendant carrying a load are seen advancing along the waterside, suggesting a route of movement through the landscape, but no identifiable built elements (such as houses, bridges or ferry crossings) are seen connecting with it. | Above and left: the painting consists mainly of cliffs, waterfalls, streams and red-leafed trees forming a natural landscape space, with no visible man-made built elements.
distinction: No explicit built elements in the painting; only a suggested route of figures advancing. Because evidence of built elements is lacking, it is barely classified as C4 on the basis of the overall spatial organization.

evidence: Lower right: a city platform and pavilion buildings are built against rocky slopes and banks, the city wall extending along the undulations of the terrain, with buildings set at varying heights on the platform bases. | Upper left: the roof outlines of another building complex are faintly visible in mist and clouds, forming an interplay of solid and void with the substantial buildings below.
distinction: Although the upper-left buildings are veiled by mist and clouds, the dominant lower-right built elements more prominently show their layout of following the mountain and setting houses on platforms.

evidence: Lower right: the built elements on the sloping bank are partly screened by foreground tree foliage and trunks, with only the roof, railings and part of the walls exposed. | Right: trees and houses form foreground and background layers, presenting spatial depth through the screening and exposure of natural scenery.
distinction: Although the building is located on the sloping bank, the painting places greater emphasis on its layering as screened by trees and half hidden and half revealed, rather than mere placement in response to terrain.

evidence: Lower left: a house is located behind and below a large gnarled pine, markedly screened by pine branches and foreground miscellaneous trees, with only the roof, eaves and some beams and pillars exposed, presenting a spatial layering of a house hidden in the woods | Lower left: rocks and red shrubs surround the building base, further strengthening the effect of the built elements being wrapped and screened by natural scenery
distinction: Although a bridge and pedestrians at the lower right corner of the painting suggest a path, the connection between the path and the left-hand house is separated by water surface and mist, which is less direct and clear than the screening relationship between the house and the pines; thus concealment and revelation forming the scene is dominant.

evidence: Upper left corner: the roof and eaves of a pavilion are exposed between mountain rocks and trees, the building partly screened by rocks, presenting a layering of a house seen behind rocks. | Lower right corner: several thatched huts are visible beside slope rocks and a pine grove, their bodies and roofs partly screened by tree foliage, forming a spatial relationship of houses hidden in the woods.
distinction: In the painting the buildings present their relationship of concealment and revelation mainly through screening by mountains, rocks and woodland, rather than emphasizing terrain-responsive placement or path guidance, so C2 is most apt.

evidence: Upper left: a group of pavilion buildings is stacked layer upon layer against a cliffside terrace, the bases conforming to the steep mountain. | Right mountainside: several houses are distributed against the hillside and woodland, following the undulations of the terrain. | Lower right: a pavilion (waterside chamber) is built beside the water, its lower part supported on wooden pillars at the water's edge.
distinction: Although the built elements serve to point up scenery such as the mountainside and water's edge, their most prominent way of composing the scene is placement in response to the terrain of cliffs, terraces and waterside; the feature of terrain-responsive siting is more dominant.

evidence: Lower right of the painting: a person in red is seen sitting on slope rocks, with bamboo grove screening nearby; no clear houses or structures are seen. | Left and distant view of the painting: bare trees are painted at left, and pale-ink mountains in the distance, the whole presenting an open natural landscape space with no traces of buildings.
distinction: No identifiable built elements are visible in the painting, only figures and natural scenery; on the basis of the overall spatial organization it is classified in the closest scenic-accent category.

evidence: Right hillside: a pavilion building stands on the hillside, partly screened by trees, becoming the visual focus of the landscape there. | Whole painting: the building forms spatial layering with distant peaks and the nearby water surface, pointing up the scenery of this hillside on the right.
distinction: Although the building is screened by trees, its main role is as a scenic accent that draws together and emphasizes the scenery of the right hillside, rather than forming spatial layering merely through concealment and revelation.

evidence: Whole work: the painting presents only calligraphic inscriptions and seals; no landscape scenery or built forms are seen.
distinction: The painting has no landscape or built content, so no actual category distinction can be made.

evidence: Middle ground right: the roofs of several houses are visible among screening woods, showing that the built elements lie deep on the bank side. | Middle ground slightly right (left of the trees): a small bridge is visible spanning the water/low ground, connecting the left sloping bank with the right-hand built area. | Lower left to middle ground: the sloping shoreline winds and extends, and together with the bridge suggests a route of movement through the landscape and a process of entry toward the built area.
distinction: Although woods screen the houses (a C2 feature), the bridge and shoreline constitute a clear cue for entry and organize the spatial process from one point to another, so C4 is more dominant.

evidence: Lower left: a stream, a small bridge and two pedestrians are visible, forming a clear cue for movement through the landscape pointing into the depth of the painting. | Lower center: a thatched hut is visible among screening trees, connected with the bridge-and-path cue at the lower left, presenting a spatial relationship that can be entered and reached.
distinction: Although there is a relationship of concealment and revelation in which trees screen the thatched hut, the painting more prominently highlights the spatial process of entry to the thatched hut guided by the bridge path and pedestrians, so C4 is more apt.

evidence: From lower left to the middle of the painting, on the riverbank: a multi-storey tall pagoda stands among the trees on the sloping bank, accompanied by pavilions and buildings, its outline clear. | Overall composition of the painting: the tall pagoda rises upright before the broad river surface and distant mountains, becoming the visual focus, giving the open water-facing side a point of anchor and marking the riverbank scenery.
distinction: Although trees surround the building and produce partial screening, the main body of the tall pagoda is fully exposed and rises high; its main role is to point up and draw together the scenery on the open river surface, rather than dominating spatial layering through concealment and revelation.

evidence: Center and right of the right painting panel: a group of pavilions and waterside halls is built against the mountain and beside the water; the building base closely meets the rocky slope and bank on the right, presenting the form of houses sited against the mountain. | Lower part and waterside of the right painting panel: the building group unfolds in layers along the shoreline, rising and falling in staggered heights, and its layout forms a clear correspondence with the water surface and mountain forms. | Lower-right corner of the right painting panel: stone steps, a platform, and a small boat in the water are visible, further indicating the connection between the built structures and the landscape setting.
distinction: Although steps and a small boat suggest an entry path, the more central and prominent compositional role is the layered placement of the building group according to mountain forms and water configuration.

evidence: Whole painting: the painting contains only calligraphic text, with no visual pictorial elements such as landscape, trees, or built structures.
distinction: The painting has no actual visual image, so no effective distinction can be made on the basis of spatial relationships; it is assigned only by rule as a forced category.

evidence: Lower-middle part of the painting: two tiny figures are visible walking on a sloping bank, presenting a state of movement through the landscape. | Center-right part of the painting: ahead of the figures, a small bridge or path is faintly visible crossing water/low ground and connecting the two banks, suggesting a spatial clue for entry.
distinction: The painting lacks obvious built structures as scenic accents and mainly relies on tiny figures and faint clues of a bridge and path to organize a process of traversable space, so C4 fits more closely than C3.

evidence: Left of the middle ground: the roofs and walls of several houses are faintly revealed amid dense trees, forming a partly screened, partly visible effect. | Whole painting: trees and built structures interweave with each other, and the screening by trees highlights the buildings' sense of concealment and spatial layering.
distinction: Although the houses are built beside the water, the painting emphasizes more the relationship of screening and revealing of the buildings by trees, rather than siting by terrain alone.

evidence: Right half of the painting: the painting shows sloping rocks, trees, and open water; on the near-bank sloping rocks, two people sit facing each other, with no clear building forms such as houses or pavilions visible. | Overall composition: the figures' activity is placed on a waterside sloping bank, marking the scenic enjoyment at this place, but no built entity participates in the composition.
distinction: There is no clear built structure in the painting; the role of the figures as scenic accents is closest to the logic of scenic accentuation, but built entities are lacking.

evidence: Center-left sloping ground: behind the trees, the roof and columns of a building are faintly revealed, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship partly screened by woodland. | Foreground to middle ground: several sparse trees interweave with a gentle sloping bank, forming layered screening of the built structures behind by natural scenery.
distinction: Although the building is sited against the slope, the painting emphasizes more the screening and revealing of the building by trees; the concealment-and-revelation relationship is more prominent than placement according to terrain.

evidence: Right side of the painting: a sloping rock at the waterside is depicted, with withered trees and clustered bamboo growing on the rock, surrounded by calm water, and no trace of built structures is visible.
distinction: The painting shows only natural sloping rocks and trees, with no clear built structures; the whole is presented as a natural scene, hence C3 is chosen.

evidence: Lower-middle part to middle ground of the painting: a winding path (or stream) extends from the lower part of the painting, passes through woods and the foot of the mountain, and leads toward the depth of the painting. | Among the mountain rocks in the middle ground: a pavilion is located deep along the extension of the path, surrounded by mountains, rocks, and trees, forming the endpoint or deep destination of the path. | Lower left and lower right of the painting: village buildings are distributed at the foot of the mountain, connected with the winding path, constituting the starting point and intermediate nodes for entering the secluded deep-mountain setting.
distinction: Although the middle-ground pavilion has an effect of being screened by mountains, rocks, and trees (C2), the winding path connects the foreground village with the deep pavilion, and the resulting process of movement and entry (C4) plays a more significant governing role in the overall spatial organization.

evidence: Center-right of the painting: the roof and walls of a house are visible, partly screened by surrounding mountains, rocks, and trees, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Middle and distant mountain ridges of the painting: a pagoda is faintly visible on the ridge line, existing as a scenic accent in the distance.
distinction: The nearby house mainly uses screening by trees, mountains, and rocks to create spatial layering, rather than serving simply as a marker of a certain scene, so C2 is more apt than C3.

evidence: Lower-middle part of the painting: among the trees, the roof and walls of a house are faintly visible; the building is partly screened by trees, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Whole painting: distant mountains, open fields, woods, and water form the background; the building is hidden among the woods, presenting the spatial layering of a house seen within the forest.
distinction: The correspondence between the building and the terrain is less obvious than the concealment-and-revelation relationship of the building screened by trees, so C2 is more apt.

evidence: Lower center of the painting: a canopied boat is moored at the bank, with two people aboard; the boat touches the reeds and rocks at the bank. | Left side of the painting: red-leafed trees and sloping rocks are at the bank; the boat is moored at the bank beneath the trees, forming a stopping point for movement through the landscape where water and land meet.
distinction: The boat canopy serves as a clue to waterside dwelling and movement through the landscape, connecting the waterside and suggesting a process of roaming, emphasizing more than a mere scenic accent the enterability of space and its relationship to travel.

evidence: At the cliff on the center-right of the painting: a pavilion (or open hall) is built on a high platform/cliff edge where the rocks protrude, at a relatively high position, presenting the feature of a house sited on a platform, with the base corresponding to the cliff form. | At the hillside/waterside in the lower-left corner of the painting: a group of house buildings is distributed according to the terrain of the mountain hollow and the shoreline, surrounded by trees, with the layout following the undulations of the mountain, presenting placement according to the slope. | Overall composition: the high and low positions of the built structures (the pavilion on the high cliff and the houses below) follow the mountain forms and waterside, forming a clear correspondence with the natural configuration.
distinction: Although the built structures in the painting are partly screened by trees (possessing C2 features), the choice of their bases (high cliff and low slope) and the high-low layout are mainly arranged according to the terrain and topography; the logic of terrain-responsive siting is more dominant.

evidence: Lower right: a small boat is on the water with one person aboard, presenting a clue to movement on the water. | Left side: a densely wooded hillside meets the water; the small boat is located between the waterside and the open water, suggesting an enterable, traversable spatial relationship.
distinction: The small boat is not merely an ornament on the water but serves as a clue to movement through the landscape that guides the gaze into the depth of the painting, embodying the spatial process of access to secluded settings rather than merely identifying the scene.

evidence: Lower middle: in a gap in the woods, the roof and structure of a built entity are visible, partly screened by the branches and trunks of trees in front, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Overall composition: trees in the foreground and middle ground surround and screen the built structure, making it faintly appear within the forest and forming spatial layering.
distinction: Although the built structure identifies the scene within the woods, its concealment-and-revelation relationship of being partly screened by woodland is more prominent in the composition, so C2 is more apt than C3.

evidence: Middle ground on the right side of the painting: a small bridge is visible crossing the water and connecting the two banks, providing a clear clue for passage. | Lower left and middle ground of the painting: woods and water interweave, and together with the bridge they form traversable spatial layering.
distinction: The small bridge mainly serves to connect and guide entry, rather than merely identifying a certain scene.

evidence: Left side: mountains and rocks, bamboo clumps, and withered branches are visible, with a horizontal shoreline or water ripples at the bottom | Right side: a large area of unpainted space, with no built structures, bridges, paths, or clues to movement through the landscape
distinction: No built structures are visible in the painting; it shows only the scene of rocks, plants, and waterside, with no other clues for spatial organization that could be assigned.

evidence: Lower right: a wooden bridge crosses a stream and connects the earth banks on both sides; figures stand on the bridge and at the bank, forming a clear connection of crossing and entry. | Lower left and middle: a winding shoreline and earth banks form a natural path; figures are distributed along the slope, and in the lower-left corner the roof of a thatched hut is visible nestled against the terrain. | Overall composition: the bridge and shoreline path link the scattered areas of figure activity, presenting a process of spatial organization of moving from here to there and traversable space.
distinction: Although thatched huts against the slope embody placement according to terrain, the passage clues formed by the wooden bridge and winding shoreline are more prominent and dominate the sense of spatial connection and travel.

evidence: Whole painting: the painting shows only calligraphic inscription and seals, with no visual elements such as mountains and rocks, water bodies, trees, or built structures.
distinction: The painting has no actual landscape or built imagery, so no substantive judgment of spatial relationships can be made; it is assigned only as a forced category.

evidence: Lower-left corner: a thatched pavilion is built on a sloping platform piled with rocks; the columns rest on the rock surface, presenting the form of a house sited on a platform. | Lower left to middle ground: the pavilion is located at the edge of the waterside, placed according to the configuration of the sloping ground, and forms a waterside relationship with the open water in front. | Right foreground: tall trees stand on the sloping bank, adjacent to the pavilion, together constituting the sloping-platform terrain of the foreground.
distinction: Although the pavilion at the waterside serves to identify the scene (C3), it is clearly built on a rocky sloping platform, presenting the terrain-responsive placement of 'a house sited on a platform,' which conforms to the definition of C1.

evidence: Right cliff: the pavilion directly attaches to the steep rock face, and its base is closely integrated with the mountain rocks. | Center-lower right: a railed corridor or plank walkway winds and twists along the mountain form, connecting building parts at different heights. | Lower-left corner: a person stands at the waterside facing the cliff and buildings, suggesting a path of looking up from outside or approaching.
distinction: Although the plank walkway and figures suggest an entry path (C4), the most prominent spatial relationship in the painting is how the buildings attach to and follow the form of the steep cliff for their placement (C1).

evidence: Lower-middle part and right mountainside of the painting: many houses are screened by dense trees and mountain rocks, with only roofs, eaves, or parts of walls exposed, presenting the layering of 'houses seen within the forest' and 'houses hidden behind rocks.' | Lower-left corner: behind the trunk and branches and leaves of a large tree, building outlines are faintly visible, forming a screening relationship between foreground trees and background built structures. | Mountain hollows and valleys: buildings are scattered among gaps in the rocks and deep in the tree clusters; their existence is suggested through screening by natural scenery, increasing the painting's sense of seclusion.
distinction: Although the buildings are distributed following the mountain forms, the visual dominance in the painting lies in the screening and revealing of buildings by trees and rocks (the concealment-and-revelation relationship), rather than simply emphasizing layout according to terrain.

evidence: Center of the painting: a group of buildings is hidden in a valley and dense woods, with only parts of roofs and walls exposed, forming an obvious concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Lower right of the painting: a thatched pavilion and a house are surrounded and screened by pines and miscellaneous trees, revealing only partial structures. | Lower left of the painting: there are buildings at the waterside, partly screened by the branches and leaves of foreground trees, blending into the natural environment.
distinction: Although streams and paths in the painting connect various places, the sense of spatial layering created by the screening and revealing of built structures by trees and rocks is more prominent, so C2 is more apt than C4.

evidence: Center of the painting: a group of house buildings is surrounded and screened by dense trees and mountain rocks, with only roofs and parts of walls exposed, presenting the concealment-and-revelation layering of houses seen within the forest. | Lower-right corner of the painting: a pavilion is situated among a bamboo grove and trees, partly screened by plant branches and leaves, forming a hidden resting space. | Overall composition: natural scenery (mountains and rocks, trees) forms an obvious relationship of screening and revealing with the built structures, creating a profound sense of spatial layering.
distinction: The built structures in the painting are mainly screened by trees and rocks, emphasizing layering of concealment and revelation and the relationship of screening, rather than guiding a process of movement through the landscape through clear paths or bridges.

evidence: Left mountainside: a group of pavilion buildings is half-hidden in dense woods, with only parts of roofs and eaves exposed, forming an obvious layering of concealment and revelation. | Lower-left corner: at the waterside there are building bases and steps, partly screened by foreground sloping rocks and vegetation. | Lower-middle sloping ground: several thatched huts are scattered, interwoven with surrounding trees and sloping ground, blending into the natural scenery.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited against the mountain and beside the water, the painting highlights more the screening and revealing of buildings by trees, emphasizing the spatial layering formed by concealment and revelation, rather than simple correspondence with terrain.

evidence: Upper part of the mountain rock, toward the left: very faint ink lines outline something like a wall or building base, but the details are blurred and difficult to confirm as a complete built structure. | Center of the painting: the main subject is a huge mountain rock with trees growing on top; no clear spatial connecting clues such as roads, bridges, or waterside are visible.
distinction: The blurred structure at the top appears to be placed on the summit of the mountain rock, rather than presenting concealment-and-revelation layering mainly through screening by trees.

evidence: Whole painting: the painting shows only running-script calligraphic inscription and red seals, with no images of mountains and rocks, water bodies, or built structures.
distinction: The painting has no landscape or built content, so no actual judgment of spatial relationships can be made; it is assigned only by form.

evidence: Center of the left painting panel: the thick trunk of a pine and its dense needles screen most of the main body of the building behind, revealing only decorated columns and the edge of a wall. | Lower part of the left painting panel: the base of the building is adjacent to foreground lake rocks and weeds; the building forms a close relationship of concealment and revelation and of foreground-background layering with the rocks and trees.
distinction: The painting mainly presents the layering of concealment and revelation of a building screened by pines and rocks, rather than emphasizing the building's layout and placement according to terrain and waterside.
