evidence: Whole painting: the main subject is ink bamboo and sloping rocks, with no trace of any artificial built structures such as houses, pavilions, bridges, or paths.
distinction: There are no built elements in the painting; it is assigned only loosely on the basis of the overall bamboo-and-rock composition, lacking concrete evidence of built structures for judging C1-C4.

evidence: Lower middle, toward the left: the roofs and walls of a group of buildings are visible, partly screened by trees in the foreground and middle ground, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Lower-middle part of the painting: trees surround the buildings, revealing parts of the buildings through gaps in branches and leaves, forming spatial layering.
distinction: Although the buildings are arranged according to mountain forms, the painting emphasizes more their concealment-and-revelation relationship of being screened by trees and appearing faintly, rather than simple correspondence with terrain.

evidence: Lower right: a two-story pavilion is close against the foot of the cliff, revealing a double-eaved roof and parts of walls, placed against the rocks. | Right side and above: tree trunks and branches extend from the cliff, their foliage covering and screening the upper part and left side of the pavilion, forming an obvious relationship of screening and revealing. | Left side and center: a large area of unpainted space with water ripples forms a spatial layering of solid and void and of concealment and revelation with the rocks and trees on the right and the built structures screened among them.
distinction: Although the building against the cliff and beside the water has the feature of terrain-responsive placement, visually the relationship of screening and revealing of the building by rocks and trees is more prominent, emphasizing concealment and revelation as the setting.

evidence: Lower right: An arched bridge is visible between the trees and the sloping bank; the bridge spans a gully or stream and connects the paths on the two banks. | Lower left: At the edge of the waterside there is a contour suspected to be a low building or bridge, adjoining the sloping bank terrain. | Lower middle: The sloping bank and trees form the foreground; the presence of the bridge suggests a route of movement extending from the foreground toward the depths of the woods or the background.
distinction: Although the trees partially screen the bridge, its role in connecting paths and guiding entry into the space is more prominent than a mere layer of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: Building structures are visible, partly screened by trees and cloud and mist, with roofs and walls exposed, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Around the buildings: The buildings are surrounded by trees and mountains and rocks, forming a spatial layering in which buildings are seen within the woods.
distinction: Although the painting contains a bridge, figures and a small boat suggesting clues of movement (C4), the screened relationship between the buildings and the trees, clouds and mist (C2) is more direct and prominent in expressing the spatial layering of built structures and landscape.

evidence: Lower part of the painting, toward the right: The roof and walls of a built structure are visible, partly screened by the dense surrounding trees and mountains and rocks, presenting a layering in which a building is concealed within the woods. | Upper middle of the painting: The main peak rises, cut off below the mountainside by cloud and mist, forming a contrast of near and far, solid and void with the woodland and built structures below, reinforcing the sense of built structures being screened.
distinction: Although the built structure stands on sloping ground, its most prominent compositional role lies in using trees, mountains and rocks to create a relationship of concealment and revelation, rather than emphasizing siting that follows the mountain contours.

evidence: Lower left: Among the trees on the sloping bank, the roof and pillars of a pavilion building are visible, half screened by the surrounding trees, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Overall painting: The upper part has high mountains wrapped in cloud and mist; the lower part interweaves waterside sloping rocks with trees and woodland; the built structures merge into the natural scenery, forming layers.
distinction: Although the built structure serves to punctuate the waterside scenery, its screened relationship—surrounded by trees and half hidden, half revealed—is more prominent, so C2 fits better than C3.

evidence: Upper left, mountainside: A pavilion building is erected on a mountainside platform, its site fitting closely with the undulations of the mountain. | Lower left corner: Several houses are arranged in scattered fashion on the sloping ground at the mountain foot, unfolding in conformity with the terrain. | Lower right corner, waterside: A pavilion terrace is built on the rocky bank beside the water, forming a corresponding relationship with the water surface and bank rocks.
distinction: Although the built structures serve to punctuate locations such as the mountainside and the waterside, the painting more prominently highlights how their sites and layouts conform to and depend on mountain forms, sloping platforms and watersides; the feature of siting according to the ground is more pervasive and dominant.

evidence: Middle-ground mountain foot: A group of houses is hidden behind dense pine woods, with only roofs and parts of walls exposed, presenting a layering in which buildings are concealed within the woods. | Lower right corner, foreground: Houses are built beside a rock, partly screened by the trunks, branches and foliage of tall pines, forming a screened relationship of trees in front and houses behind.
distinction: Although the houses are set beside mountains and rocks and the waterside (C1), the painting more strongly emphasizes the screening and revealing of the buildings by trees, mountains and rocks (concealment and revelation), so C2 is more dominant.

evidence: Middle right of the painting, mountain foot: A group of courtyards unfolds on the sloping ground at the mountain foot, with roofs and walls arranged in conformity with the terrain. | Middle of the painting, mountainside: Houses are placed at differing heights against mountains and rocks and trees and woodland, their sites fitting the mountain forms. | Left side of the painting, mountainside: Buildings are set on a sloping platform, forming a corresponding relationship with the surrounding mountains, rocks and terrain.
distinction: Although there is screening by trees, mountains and rocks, the buildings mainly present a ground-responsive arrangement in which they are placed at differing heights according to sloping platforms and mountain forms, rather than being primarily composed as scenery through concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: A wooden bridge is visible spanning a stream, connecting the mountains and rocks on the two banks and forming a clear passage route. | Lower right and lower left of the painting: Figures walk or pause along the bank paths; their lines of movement, together with the bridge and stream, constitute spatial clues that can be entered and traveled through.
distinction: The bridge and paths mainly guide the gaze and the process of travel, emphasizing spatial entry and transition rather than merely siting buildings according to terrain.

evidence: Right side and center of the painting: A large tree occupies the main picture, its branches and foliage luxuriant, with faint ground lines below. | Lower left of the painting: A figure on horseback pauses beneath the tree, gazing up at the canopy; the person and the tree form a spatial relationship of screening and pausing.
distinction: There are no clear built elements in the painting, only a relationship of screening and pausing between figures and trees, so it is assigned to C2, but the evidence is extremely weak.

evidence: Upper middle, toward the right: The roof of a pavilion is revealed between cloud and mist and trees, presenting a half-screened relationship of concealment and revelation. | Middle ground: Extensive unpainted space and pale ink wash form cloud and mist, separating the distant trees and built structures into different layers.
distinction: Although the distant pavilion serves to punctuate the scenery, its screened relationship—obscured by cloud and mist and trees—is more prominent in the spatial layers of the painting.

evidence: Whole painting: The painting presents distant mountains and nearby sparse woods and sloping ground; no clear traces of built structures such as houses or bridges are seen. | Upper left: Inscriptions and seals are visible, but they are not treated as spatial evidence within the painting.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built elements; the closest classification is made on the basis of natural terrain and the distribution of trees and woodland.

evidence: Lower right: A domed thatched hut is visible, with a person seated inside; the hut itself is half screened by the surrounding mountains and rocks and trees. | Right side and lower middle: Dense trees and scattered mountains and rocks surround the thatched hut, forming a clear spatial layering of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the thatched hut is situated within the mountain woods, the painting more strongly emphasizes its screened relationship—obscured and revealed by trees, mountains and rocks—rather than simple conformity to terrain.

evidence: Right side, cliff: A pavilion is built on a projecting rock platform, the house set against the cliff, corresponding to the steep mountain forms. | Middle-ground mountainside: A group of buildings is located on a gentle part of the mountain slope, arranged separately according to the slope in conformity with the undulations of the mountain form. | Lower left corner: Houses are located on sloping ground at the mountain foot, sited in conformity with the terrain and adjacent to the surrounding mountains and rocks and trees.
distinction: The feature of buildings being sited according to site conditions such as cliffs and sloping platforms (e.g., the pavilion on the right set against the cliff, the middle-ground buildings following the slope) explains their spatial organization better than mere screening by trees and woodland.

evidence: Right side: A winding path runs among the mountains and rocks, with two people riding animals traveling along the road, presenting clues of movement. | Whole painting: The painting consists mainly of mountains and rocks, withered trees and paths; no clear built entities such as houses or pavilions are seen.
distinction: There are no clear built elements in the painting; it is assigned to the closest category, C4, solely on the basis of the sense of spatial extension of the travel route on the right.

evidence: Right part of the right-hand painted panel: a multi-storey pavilion complex is built on mountains, rocks and sloping banks, its base closely conforming to the undulations of the terrain, presenting a posture of buildings set on platforms and built according to the slope. | Middle of the right-hand painted panel: to the left of the buildings, trees grow on the sloping bank and together with the buildings form a spatial layering nestled against the mountain and beside the water, while the main body of the buildings is clearly exposed.
distinction: Although the buildings serve to mark the scene of watching the tide, their placement according to the mountains, rocks and sloping banks is more prominent in the painting and determines the correspondence between the built elements and the natural terrain.

evidence: Left side: The roofs, eaves and walls of several houses are visible, partly screened by the trunks, branches and canopies of trees in the foreground and middle ground, presenting alternating layers of concealment and revelation. | Right side: The water surface is open, distant mountains faintly appear, forming a contrast of solid and void with the village screened by trees and woodland on the left, reinforcing the spatial sense of scenery formed by screening.
distinction: Although the houses are built beside the water, the most prominent compositional mode in the painting is the screening and revealing of buildings by trees and woodland, rather than simply emphasizing the constraint of terrain on layout.

evidence: Right-hand painted panel: mountains, rocks and sloping banks, water and a figure standing on the slope in the lower right corner are visible; no clear traces of built elements such as buildings, bridges or paths are seen.
distinction: No built elements are visible in the painting; on the basis of the open viewing surface formed by the overall landscape and figure, it is assigned to the closest category of scenic accentuation.

evidence: Lower left: A thatched pavilion is built on sloping rocks, its site closely integrated with the terrain, presenting an arrangement of a house set on a platform. | Lower part and right side: Sloping rocks and withered trees surround the thatched pavilion, and the built structure unfolds in conformity with the local terrain.
distinction: Although the thatched pavilion serves as a scenic accent, its ground-responsive siting against the sloping rocks is more prominent, so C1 fits better than C3.

evidence: Lower left: Figures are visible walking along the bank, accompanied by travel items such as carrying poles, suggesting the existence of a path or a ford | Lower right: There is a stream and a waterfall, forming a spatial extension with the shoreline where the figures are | Center and upper part: Tall pines and mountains and rocks occupy the main body; no clear built structures such as houses or pavilions are seen
distinction: Although there are no clear built elements in the painting, the movement of the traveling figures and the shoreline path suggest an enterable spatial process, which fits the intent of C4 better than mere scenic accentuation.

evidence: Middle-ground mountainside: Pavilion buildings are visible, screened among mountains and rocks and trees, with only parts of roofs and eaves exposed, presenting a spatial layering of half hidden, half revealed. | Foreground waterside: Buildings at the waterside are hidden behind trees and rocks, using natural scenery to screen them and create pictorial depth.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited according to the mountain forms, the painting more strongly emphasizes the spatial layering formed by their being screened and revealed by mountains and rocks and trees, so C2 is more dominant than C1.

evidence: Lower left: A waterside pavilion building is partly screened by the branches and foliage of trees in the foreground and middle ground, with only the roof, railings and figures inside exposed, forming a layer of concealment and revelation. | Center: The trunk, branches and foliage of a tall pine run through the painting, screening part of the built structures and shoreline behind it as a foreground element. | Right side and water surface: Boats are moored or moving on the water, forming a spatial echo with the built structures screened by trees on the bank.
distinction: Although boats and figures on the bank suggest clues of movement, the most prominent compositional role of the built structures is to form spatial layers through screening and revealing by trees, rather than to emphasize a route of entry.

evidence: Lower middle: A thatched waterside pavilion built beside the water is visible, with a scholar inside; the lower part of the building is supported by wooden piles between water and rocks. | Lower middle and right side: The right side of the thatched house adjoins a steep mountain crag, and above and around it is surrounded and half screened by luxuriant branches and foliage, forming a clear layer of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the building is constructed beside mountains and water, the painting more strongly emphasizes its screened relationship—surrounded and half screened by mountains and rocks and trees and woodland—thereby constructing a deep and secluded spatial layering, so C2 is more dominant than C1.

evidence: Lower middle: An arched bridge spans the water, with two people walking on it, connecting the foreground waterside with the woods and mountains behind. | Middle ground to distance: Among the mountains and rocks and trees and woodland behind the bridge are distributed several pavilion buildings and terraces, extending upward layer by layer in conformity with the mountain forms, forming a route of entry from near to deep. | Middle ground: Eaves and walls of buildings are revealed in the gaps between trees and woodland and mountains and rocks, suggesting that the path leads to courtyards deep within.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited according to the mountain forms, the painting clearly constructs, through the bridge and the movement of figures, a spatial process of travel from outside to inside and progressively deeper; C4 summarizes its dominant compositional role better than mere ground-responsive siting.

evidence: Lower left corner: A small bridge is visible spanning a water surface or stream valley, with tiny figures on the bridge, forming a clear clue of movement that guides the gaze into the depths of the painting. | Lower right corner: Screened by pines and rocks, a thatched hut is faintly visible, as a built structure deep within that the clue of movement may reach or point toward.
distinction: The bridge and figures in the lower left corner provide a clear clue of entry and travel, giving the space a process of moving from here to there, which is more dominant than a mere relationship of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower half of the painting: Mountain peaks, cloud and mist, trees, streams and waterfalls are visible, constituting natural landscape scenery, but no clear built elements (such as houses, pavilions, bridges, etc.) are seen.
distinction: The painting consists mainly of natural landscape and lacks built elements, so the specific mode of spatial expression of built structures cannot be determined; it can only be assigned to the closest category on the basis of the overall landscape composition.

evidence: Right side: A bridge (or plank walkway) is visible spanning between mountains and rocks and trees and woodland, connecting the two banks and forming a clear clue of crossing and entry. | Lower middle of the right side: Gaps among the mountains and rocks and hints of flowing water below and around the bridge combine with the bridge to constitute a spatial process that can be traveled and entered deeply.
distinction: The bridge in the painting, as a clear clue of movement, dominates the relationship of spatial entry and connection, rather than mere siting according to terrain or screening and concealment and revelation.

evidence: Upper part of a cliff, slightly right of the painting's center: A thatched pavilion is visible built on the cliff top, with trees beside it. | Lower part to center of the painting: A winding path extends upward along the mountain forms, and a person is walking on the path, facing toward the thatched pavilion on the cliff top.
distinction: Although the thatched pavilion punctuates the scenery of the summit, the painting clearly depicts the figure and path ascending along the mountain path, emphasizing the spatial process of moving from here to there and approaching the built structure, so C4 is more dominant than C3.

evidence: Upper middle: A group of hall buildings is surrounded by dense pines and cloud and mist; roofs and eaves loom faintly in the gaps between the trees and woodland, forming a clear layer of concealment and revelation. | Lower right corner: Pavilion buildings on the bank are partly screened by the branches and foliage of trees in front, presenting a screened spatial relationship. | Middle of the left side: Parts of a pavilion building are faintly visible among the woods, obscured by trunks and leaves, indicating the spatial position of the building deep within the trees and woodland.
distinction: Although the buildings dot the landscape, the painting more strongly emphasizes the layering of buildings screened and revealed by trees and cloud and mist, rather than their serving merely as landmarks.

evidence: Lower middle: Deep in the valley, the roofs and walls of a group of buildings are visible, half screened by the surrounding rocks and trees. | Right side, mountainside and below: Buildings are distributed according to the mountain forms, partly screened by trees and mountains and rocks, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the buildings are constructed according to the mountain forms, the painting more strongly emphasizes the spatial layering of their being screened and revealed by mountains and rocks and trees and woodland, so C2 fits better.

evidence: Lower left corner: The roof and walls of a built structure are visible, partly screened by the dense trunks, branches and foliage in the foreground, presenting alternating layers of concealment and revelation. | Lower middle: Several tall trees run through the painting, forming screening in the foreground and middle ground so that the built structure in the lower left corner appears faintly among the woods.
distinction: Although the built structure is situated beside mountains and water, the painting more strongly emphasizes the spatial layering formed by the screening and revealing of the building by trees and woodland, rather than mere dependence on terrain.

evidence: Lower left: the roof, railing, and platform base of a waterside building are visible; the building is placed close against the water's edge and the rocks. | Left side and above the building: the branches and foliage of tall trees partly screen the building's roof and walls, forming a layered relationship in which the building is concealed within the woods.
distinction: Although the building is sited according to the water and rocks, the trees' screening and revealing of the building are more prominent in the composition and dominate the spatial layering.

evidence: Lower middle: the building complex is partly screened by the pine trees on the right and in the foreground, revealing only the double-eaved roof and part of the walls, forming a clear relationship of concealment and revelation. | Lower middle: the building sits encircled by mountains, rocks, and woodland, presenting a spatial layering in which it emerges through gaps in the trees. | Overall: the building is closely integrated with the surrounding mountains and rocks and trees, participating in the scenery through screening and revealing rather than being fully exposed.
distinction: Although the building is sited according to the mountain terrain, the painting places greater emphasis on the spatial layering and mood created by its being screened by woodland and half-hidden and half-revealed, rather than on a simple correspondence with the terrain.

evidence: Lower right: a waterside pavilion is partly screened by the pine and willow trees in front of it, revealing only the roof, railing, and steps, forming a layering of concealment and revelation. | Center to lower right: tall pines and weeping willows stand in front of the pavilion, their branches and leaves interweaving and screening the pavilion within the woodland.
distinction: Although the pavilion is built by the water, the painting places greater emphasis on the trees' screening and revealing of the pavilion; the relationship of concealment and revelation is the dominant factor in the composition.

evidence: Lower right: a thatched pavilion is built on sloping rocks, close to trees, its site closely integrated with the undulations of the terrain. | Middle ground, opposite bank: dwellings are faintly visible distributed along the sloping shoreline, placed according to the natural terrain.
distinction: Although the thatched pavilion serves as a scenic accent, the manner of its placement against the sloping rocks and trees more prominently embodies a building relationship established according to terrain.

evidence: Upper left: a storied building is constructed close against a steep cliff; figures lean on the railing, and the building site follows the trend of the rock face, presenting the appearance of a building set against the cliff. | Middle right: a pavilion sits on a protruding rocky platform, surrounded by woodland, its base firmly set on the rock platform, presenting a relationship of a building set on a platform. | Lower middle: a waterside pavilion is built by the water, its wooden base close to the waterside boulders and the rippling bank, unfolding in accord with the waterside terrain.
distinction: Although a winding stairway is visible on the right side of the painting and a boat in the lower left corner hints at a movement-through-the-landscape thread (C4), the most salient visual feature of the three main buildings is the close fit of their sites to the cliff, the rock platform, and the waterside, presenting a clear relationship of placement according to terrain.

evidence: Below: a thatched hut sits among the woods, its body partly screened by tree trunks; in front, a person is walking along a path toward the thatched hut, presenting a spatial process of approaching the built structure. | Lower middle: terraced fields, the waterside, and a winding path are visible, connecting the area of human activity below with the deep valley, forming an accessible thread of entry. | Center to upper: cliffs on both sides form a deep valley; the path and stream extend upward along the valley, suggesting that the space continues to turn inward toward the depths.
distinction: Although the thatched hut has a relationship of concealment and revelation through the screening trees, the painting places greater emphasis on the person walking along the path toward the thatched hut and on the path extending deep into the valley as an accessible process, so C4 is more dominant than C2.

evidence: Lower right: a thatched pavilion is half-screened among a bamboo grove, bamboo leaves screening part of the roof and the pavilion body, forming a clear layering of concealment and revelation. | Lower middle: large boulders together with trees and bamboo groves form the screening environment of the foreground, enclosing the thatched pavilion within it.
distinction: Although the thatched pavilion is set by the water, the painting places greater emphasis on the bamboo grove's screening and revealing of it, rather than on simple dependence on the terrain.

evidence: Lower left: a group of thatched huts and village dwellings is built nestling against the mountain and beside the water, unfolding along the slope and the waterside. | Lower center: a wooden bridge spans the stream, with two people crossing it; the bridge connects with paths and leads toward the built structures on the left. | Left side: a wooden fence and a path extend along the waterside, connecting the bridge and the village dwellings, forming an accessible spatial thread.
distinction: Although the built structures nestle against the mountain and beside the water, the bridge, path, and other movement-through-the-landscape threads in the painting clearly guide the eye into the village dwellings, and the compositional role of access to secluded settings is more prominent.

evidence: Lower middle: a group of open halls/waterside pavilions is built close against the waterside, with a platform extending into the water and human activity visible inside. | Lower left: a person on the water rides a boat (or stands on a shoal), facing the direction of the built structures; the water surface and shoreline form a clear movement-through-the-landscape route approaching the built structures. | Lower middle and surroundings: the buildings are surrounded by tall pines and miscellaneous trees, with roofs and eaves revealed among the woodland, forming a layering of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the buildings are clearly built by the water (C1), the guidance of the figure and the waterside in the lower left corner emphasizes more strongly the spatial process of approaching and entering the built structures (C4).

evidence: Middle right and lower middle of the painting: multiple groups of houses and courtyards are arranged in staggered fashion according to the mountain terrain; roofs, eaves, and wall bodies are partly screened by trees and rocks in the foreground and middle ground, forming a spatial layering of alternating concealment and revelation. | Center of the painting: the buildings are screened among woodland and rock faces; the revealed portions indicate the existence of the built structures and their position in depth.
distinction: Although the buildings are arranged according to the mountain terrain, the painting places greater emphasis on the trees and rocks screening and revealing the buildings; the relationship of concealment and revelation is the main means of composing the scenery.

evidence: Lower right corner: the building complex is built by the water, the houses arranged following the shoreline, their sites parallel to the water surface, presenting a layout unfolding along the bank. | Center of the painting, slightly left (below the waterfall): the buildings are placed on the sloping terraces at the foot of the mountain, relying on the rises and falls of the mountain terrain, presenting a form of staggered placement according to the slope and buildings set on platforms.
distinction: Although the buildings are located in an open waterside position and serve to point out the scenery, their layout clearly follows the waterside and the mountain terrain, placing greater emphasis on the spatial correspondence of placement according to terrain.

evidence: Upper left: distant mountain slopes and banks, densely grown with trees; ink rendering brings out the texture of the mountains and rocks. | Middle water surface: on the open water is a single small boat, with one person poling, forming a visual focus and a hint of movement through the landscape. | Below: pines stand upright with gnarled trunks and branches, grass dotted at their roots, occupying the lower space of the painting.
distinction: No clear house building is seen in the painting; it is assigned to C4 on the basis of the movement-through-the-landscape thread formed by the boat on the water and the sense of spatial extension; if the boat is regarded as a scenic accent element, it approaches C3.

evidence: Lower left: houses on the sloping bank are partly screened by the large trees in the foreground, their roofs and walls faintly visible, forming a clear relationship of concealment and revelation. | Middle right and upper right: multiple houses are visible on the mountainside and at the foot of the distant mountains, screened behind dense woods and rocks, presenting a richly layered sense of space.
distinction: Although the houses are placed according to the sloping bank, the painting places greater emphasis on the trees and rocks screening and revealing the buildings; the relationship of concealment and revelation is the main means of forming spatial layering.

evidence: Lower center and right of the painting: the trunks and needles of the tall pines in the foreground screen the building complex behind, revealing only roofs and eaves, forming a clear layering of concealment and revelation | Lower left of the painting: a cluster of houses is located on the sloping waterside ground at the foot of the mountain, surrounded and screened by trees, presenting a spatial relationship of houses seen within the woods
distinction: Although the houses are sited nestling against the mountain and beside the water, the prominent screening of the buildings by the foreground pines forms the main spatial layering, more consistent with the characteristic of concealment and revelation creating a setting.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: a group of storied buildings and houses is partly screened by the dense pine woods on the left and above, revealing only roofs and part of the walls, forming a layering of houses hidden within the woods. | Lower right corner of the painting: part of the base of a waterside pavilion on the water is obscured by the sloping bank and trees in the foreground, presenting a spatial relationship of being half-hidden and half-revealed.
distinction: Although the buildings point out the scenery, the painting mainly constructs spatial layering through the woodland's screening and revealing of the buildings; the relationship of concealment and revelation is more prominent than simple scenic accentuation.

evidence: Lower right and lower middle: multiple groups of houses and buildings are screened within dense woods; roofs, walls, doors, and windows are partly obscured by branches and leaves, forming a clear relationship of concealment and revelation and spatial layering. | Middle-ground mountainside: the building complex on the slope is surrounded by stretches of trees, faintly visible, using the screening of the woodland to create the scenery.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited nestling against the mountain and beside the water, the painting places greater emphasis on constructing deep spatial layering through the screening and revealing of the woodland; the relationship of concealment and revelation is more prominent than placement according to terrain.

evidence: Left middle sloping bank: the building complex is surrounded by dense trees, revealing roofs, eaves, and part of the walls, presenting a spatial layering of houses hidden within the woods. | Right middle mountainside: house roofs are faintly visible, screened by rocks and woodland, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation in which houses are seen across a barrier. | Distant mountain foot: building outlines are faintly visible at the foot of the mountain and among the woods, screened by natural scenery, indicating that the built structures lie at a deeper level.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed according to the sloping bank, the painting places greater emphasis on the trees and rocks screening and revealing the buildings; the relationship of concealment and revelation constitutes the main organization of spatial layering.

evidence: Lower left: several thatched huts are visible screened among the trees, with a clear path in front of the huts winding toward the water, forming a thread of entry to the buildings. | Lower right: a single small boat is on the water, with a person rowing, suggesting a route of approaching the waterside built structures by water. | Middle ground: building complexes are distributed between the foot of the mountain and the woods, together with the waterside and path in the foreground forming spatial layering with depth that can be traversed.
distinction: Although the thatched huts in the near ground have a relationship of concealment and revelation through the screening trees, the painting places greater emphasis on the spatial process of guiding the eye and the movement through the landscape into the built structures by means of the path and water route.

evidence: Lower left and lower middle of the painting: houses and buildings are surrounded and screened by dense trees and rocks, revealing only roofs, eaves, and part of the walls, presenting a layering of houses hidden within the woods. | Middle and upper parts of the painting, mountainside and right side: buildings are hidden among the mountain woods, forming a spatial relationship of being half-hidden and half-revealed through the screening of trees and mountain bodies, indicating the existence of the built structures and the level at which they lie.
distinction: Although paths and the waterside connect the buildings in the painting, the buildings mainly form layering through being screened and revealed by woodland and rocks; the characteristic of concealment and revelation creating a setting is more dominant than access to secluded settings.

evidence: Middle left: a small bridge is visible crossing the stream, with travelers on the bridge, forming a clear thread of an entry path. | Lower middle: houses and buildings are placed beside the waterside and on sloping ground, surrounded by bamboo groves and trees; paths and the shoreline guide the eye toward these built structures. | Below: the shoreline and moored boats suggest possible routes of water transport and arrival at the built structures.
distinction: Although the built structures are arranged along the waterside (C1), the accessible and traversable spatial threads (C4) formed jointly by the bridge, paths, and waterside in the painting are more prominent, organizing the viewer's line of sight and imagined route.

evidence: Slightly above center: a thatched-roof pavilion (or thatched hall) is partly screened by the surrounding bamboo and mountains and rocks, revealing only the roof and part of the pillars. | Center and right side: dense bamboo branches and steep mountains and rocks surround the building, forming a clear spatial layering of screening and revealing. | Lower left: two people stand gazing upward, their line of sight directed toward the screened building, further indicating the building's existence and the secluded depth in which it lies.

evidence: Slightly right of center: the painting consists mainly of mountains and rocks, bamboo, and trees; no traces of built elements such as houses or bridges are seen. | Left side: inscription and seals are visible, with no depiction related to buildings.
distinction: The painting has no clear built elements; the natural scenery is concentrated on one side of the painting to form a visual focus, and it can only barely be regarded as scenic accentuation.

evidence: Slightly above center: a group of houses is screened among trees and mountains and rocks, revealing only part of the roofs and structures, forming a layering of concealment and revelation. | Middle of the painting: the built elements are partly screened by the surrounding woodland and terrain, not directly and fully exposed, and merge into the natural scenery.
distinction: The built elements mainly present a concealment-and-revelation relationship of being screened by woodland and mountains and rocks, rather than serving merely as an isolated marker for scenic accentuation.

evidence: Foreground rocky-shoal platform slightly right of center at the lower edge of the fan: a piled-stone platform extends horizontally along the water, and at its flat left end stands an open pavilion, whose roof and pillars are distinguishable, the pavilion body opening toward the broad water surface to the left | Middle and right of the platform: withered trees and bamboo clumps stand on the slope rocks, and the slope rocks continue along the water's edge to the right as a low shoreline; the pavilion's building site falls exactly on the flat spot of the platform facing the water | Upper half of the fan and middle ground: distant mountains lie in a row on the far shore of the water, the middle-ground shoreline with sparse woods spreads flat, and the foreground pavilion and terrace face them across the water; the open water surface and low, flat sloping bank constitute the siting ground for the pavilion
distinction: The pavilion's position is determined first by the waterside platform and the configuration of the water's edge, and its building site is set according to the terrain; it does not serve as a marker to accentuate specific scenic nodes such as mountain ridges or valley mouths.

evidence: Platform on the right bank: the pointed roof and red railing posts of a thatched pavilion sit at the high edge where the bank slope turns, its footings set according to the slope, facing the open water surface at the center of the painting | Waterside slightly below center: a small canopied boat moored in shallow water, its bow pointing toward the bank slope that extends into the water from right to left, which slope is the edge of the terrace on which the pavilion stands | Left front of the pavilion on the right bank: willows and broadleaf trees take root among the rocks at the slope's edge, joining with the slope rocks into a single terrace, with the pavilion at its rear edge, the height of its building site corresponding to the unfolding shoreline
distinction: Although the boat is moored at the bank, no path, dock, or landing direction is seen connecting it with the pavilion, so a process of movement through the landscape does not hold; the pavilion's main visible relationship is that its building site is set facing the water according to the height of the bank slope, hence C1 is taken.

evidence: At the water's edge slightly below center of the fan: one person sits in a slender boat holding an oar, the boat body connected to the right with an arched canopy-like object (suspected to be a boat canopy or a small bank-side shelter), the whole appearing to approach the sloping bank on the right | Slope rocks on the right bank: two trees stand at the edge of the slope rocks, whose foot extends into the water, adjacent to the canopy-like object, constituting the landing place toward which the boat travels | Far shore in the left half: connected mountains and slope rocks unfold along the left bank of the water; at the end of the distant promontory only a very small dot is seen, which cannot be reliably identified as a house; the central unpainted water surface separates the two banks
distinction: The painting is led by the movement-through-the-landscape connection of a boat traveling to the bank, which fits the visible orientation and arrival relationship better than an interpretation of the canopy-like object as statically placed against the bank.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: a winding path extends from the slope rocks on the left toward the distant mountains on the right, and a person is walking on the path. | Summit of the distant mountains on the right: several buildings (pavilions or a temple) are visible on the mountains and rocks, serving as the distant goal toward which the path extends.
distinction: Although the buildings on the summit serve for scenic accentuation, the combination of the path and the walking figure in the painting more strongly expresses the spatial process of going deeper along the path and approaching the built elements, so C4 is more fitting.

evidence: Water surface slightly right of center of the painting: one person rides in a small boat, the boat body slender, near the trees and rocks on the right bank | Right side of the painting: mountains and rocks and dense trees (including willows) are present, with no clear building roof or wall seen | Water surface on the left side of the painting: lotus leaves and lotus flowers are depicted, with a grassy bank in the distance
distinction: No clear built elements are seen in the painting, only a small boat; the boat is regarded as a scenic accent element marking the waterside scenery, rather than expressing an entry path.

evidence: Middle left: an arched bridge spans the water, with figures riding on the bridge, constituting a clear clue of movement through the landscape and transition. | Lower right: the roof and structure of a thatched hut are visible under the screening of trees, located where the shoreline connected by the bridge extends. | Overall: the bridge and shoreline connect the mountain-and-rock path on the left with the built area on the right, presenting the spatial process of reaching the other shore from this shore and approaching the built elements.
distinction: Although the built elements are screened by trees (C2), the movement-through-the-landscape clue formed by the bridge and figures dominates the spatial organization of the painting, emphasizing the process of entry and arrival (C4).

evidence: Middle ground slightly left: an arched bridge is visible spanning the water and connecting the two banks, forming a clear clue of land passage. | Slightly left of center of the water surface: a small boat is present, with a figure rowing, suggesting travel by water and the process of approaching the bank. | Lower right corner: a house roof emerges among the pines on the sloping bank, serving as a potential stopping point for travel by water or land.
distinction: The movement-through-the-landscape clues formed by the bridge and small boat in the painting run across the water, guiding the eye from one place to another and toward the built elements at the bank, and dominate the spatial organization more than mere screening by woodland.

evidence: Center of the painting: a bridge spans the water, with pedestrians on the bridge, connecting the built areas on the left and right banks and forming a clear clue of passage and entry. | Right side and lower middle of the painting: several house structures are distributed between the woods and the mountain foot, connected to the outer space through the bridge and shoreline, presenting an accessible relationship of travel.
distinction: Although the built elements are sited against the mountains and beside the water, the presence of the bridge and pedestrians in the painting more strongly emphasizes the spatial process of connection and entry, so C4 is more dominant than C1.

evidence: Lower center and right side of the painting: blurred line structures are visible, suspected to be house roofs or bridge railings, screened or interwoven by the surrounding brushwork of trees and mountains and rocks. | Center of the painting: towering mountains and rocks occupy the main position, and the suspected built elements below are at their foot or screened by woodland.
distinction: The traces of built elements in the painting are blurred and screened by scenery, tending more toward a screening relationship rather than clearly accentuating a particular scenic spot.

evidence: Among the mountains, rocks, and trees on the left: blurred line structures are visible, suspected to be a house or fence, partly screened by trees and mountains and rocks
distinction: The suspected structures mainly present a concealment-and-revelation relationship of being screened by natural scenery, rather than a clear layout according to the mountains.

evidence: Lower middle slightly right of the painting: a small bridge is visible spanning the water and connecting the two banks, forming a clear clue of movement through the landscape. | Bank on the right side of the painting: a building roof is visible amid the screening of trees, and the direction in which the small bridge extends points toward this area, suggesting an accessible path.
distinction: Although the building has a concealment-and-revelation relationship of being screened by trees, the bridge in the painting, as a clear entry clue, more strongly highlights the traversability and accessibility of the space.

evidence: Water's edge at middle right of the fan: an open pavilion (thatched hall) is set facing the water, with pillar footings visible beneath the pavilion body resting on the bank-side shoal, and a figure sitting upright inside | To the right and lower right of the pavilion: several tall pines stand on the rocky terrace, and the pavilion is placed tight against the edge of the stone platform, the height of its building site meeting the slope rocks and shoreline | Middle and left half of the painting: a large area of unpainted water surface, with sloping banks and trees on the left shore and distant mountains in a row above; the pavilion opens toward the broad water surface, and no bridge, path, gate, or other movement-through-the-landscape clue is seen connecting with it
distinction: The placement relationship of the pavilion's pillar footings resting at the water's edge and tight against the edge of the stone platform is directly visible, embodying the participation of terrain and waterside in the arrangement of built elements; it is not merely an isolated pavilion used to mark some scenic spot at a mountain ridge or valley mouth.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: a figure is visible sitting beneath a pine, surrounded by mountains and rocks and trees, with no clear built structures such as houses or pavilions seen. | Overall composition: mountains and rocks, trees, and human activity unfold according to the fan's terrain, presenting the spatial organization of natural landscape.
distinction: There are no clear built elements in the painting, and human activity is arranged according to the terrain, so it is classified as C1; if the figure is regarded as scenic accentuation it approaches C3, but there is no architectural entity.

evidence: Sloping bank at lower right of the fan: a house reveals a gabled roof and part of a wall, with several pine trunks and slope rocks lying across in front, the building itself half screened and half revealed | Around the house at lower right of the fan: the house is embedded among the trees and slope rocks along the slope, with trunks and canopies separating the front and rear layers of the house | Valley in the middle of the fan: the valley between two mountains is filled with clustered trees and slope rocks, and no bridge, path, gate, or other movement-through-the-landscape clue is seen connecting with the house
distinction: The existence of the house is mainly indicated by the screening of tree trunks and slope rocks and the revealing of the roof and wall, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship constitutes the layering at this spot; although placement according to the slope is visible, it organizes this scene less directly than the screening relationship.

evidence: Upper right: a slender, slightly arched bridge spans the water, with bridge pillars visible below, its two ends resting respectively on the right bank slope and the central bank slope, connecting the two banks into a traversable relationship | Left half to center: weeping willows, peach groves, and slope rocks occupy the left part, and the shoreline extends toward the unpainted water surface at the center; the central bank slope reached by the bridge is hidden among the flowers and willows | Lower right: reeds stand in clumps beside the unpainted water surface; the water surface is broad and communicates with the open space beneath the bridge, suggesting waterside space that can continue to extend beyond the bridge
distinction: The bridge here presents a traversable and enterable process of movement through the landscape by having its two ends rest on the banks and connect the sloping banks of the two shores, rather than merely marking a scenic spot by its own form.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: the house building is partly screened by the surrounding branches and leaves of trees, revealing only the roof, eaves, and part of the lower supporting structure, presenting a clear concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Left side and center of the painting: the building leans against mountain-and-rock slopes and trees, with woodland surrounding it to form screening, placing the building in a spatial layering of half hidden and half revealed.
distinction: Although the building is sited according to the terrain of the sloping bank, the visual center of the painting more strongly emphasizes the screening and revealing of the building by woodland, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship dominates the spatial layering at this spot.

evidence: Center: a person walks with a staff along the sloping bank / waterside, suggesting a travel path. | Left and right sides: dense trees and sloping banks form a spatial enclosure, guiding the line of sight to extend into the depth.
distinction: No clear built elements are seen in the painting; only the walking movement of the figure and the extension of the sloping bank suggest a traversable spatial process, so it is barely classified as C4.

evidence: Top of the slope on the right: on the flat, open top of the terrace sits a solitary figure facing the broad unpainted space and distant mountains at the center; this terrace lies on the waterside open face and becomes the focal point on which the line of sight settles | Center: a horizontal band of woodland stretches across the middle ground, with distant mountains rising and falling behind it, forming an opening-and-closing relationship with the foreground terrace; the large central unpainted space constitutes an open water surface or open air | Left: bamboo groves on the sloping bank, their branches and leaves hanging down, screen the slope surface, but no identifiable house, eaves ridge, or wall is seen anywhere in the painting
distinction: The painting centers on the positional relationship between the open face of the terrace and the solitary seated figure who concentrates the scenery, rather than a layering relationship in which roofs and walls are revealed through screening; no built elements at all are revealed in the woods.

evidence: Center and left side of the painting: the painting depicts figures sitting on a sloping bank, surrounded by bamboo groves, banana plants, and unusual rocks, with a waterside in front; no clear built structures such as houses or pavilions are seen.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built elements; based on the spatial organization in which the figures and the sloping bank and waterside depend on one another, it is assigned to the closest category, C1.

evidence: Right side to center: several people walk along the ground, their movement line pointing toward the table beneath the trees on the left, forming a spatial process of approaching the built setting. | Slightly left of center: a table is placed among the trees, with one person standing beside it, serving as the destination or stopping point of the figures' movement through the landscape. | Left side and background: trees and distant mountains constitute the setting; the table is set according to the trees, and the figures walk from the open area into the woods.
distinction: The painting mainly expresses the process of approaching the table through the movement line of the walking figures, rather than emphasizing the table's dependence on the terrain.

evidence: Flat-topped rock platform to the left of the central main peak of the fan: a small pavilion stands on the level rock platform, its base flush with the platform surface, the platform edge projecting forward over the broad unpainted water surface; the pavilion's position and height are directly determined by the configuration of the platform | Between the central mountain rock and the mountain mass on the right, and at the mountain foot: a waterfall flows down the mountain ravine, with trees growing densely at the mountain foot; apart from the one pavilion on the rock platform, no other houses are seen, nor any bridge, path, gate, ferry, or other movement-through-the-landscape clue connecting with the pavilion | Pavilion on the rock summit: the pavilion's roof and pillars are exposed above the rock summit, unscreened by woodland or mountains and rocks, so no relationship of layering through concealment and revelation exists
distinction: The correspondence between the pavilion's building site and the configuration of the rock platform is directly visible, belonging to terrain-responsive siting by building on the platform; the pavilion is very small in scale and is not the focal point of the whole painting's opening and closing, so its role in scenic accentuation is weaker than its correspondence with the terrain.

evidence: Lower center of the painting: several clumps of trees are painted in dense ink, and among the trees and to their right are line structures suspected to be a house, outlined in light ink, with roof contours faintly visible. | Lower center slightly left of the painting: the suspected built elements are partly screened by the heavier ink of the trees on the left, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship and suggesting that they lie among or behind the trees. | Upper part of the painting: distant mountains are rendered in light ink, forming a foreground-background spatial layering with the foreground trees and the suspected built elements.
distinction: Although the built elements at the lower part of the painting serve as an embellishment, the layering of concealment and revelation (screening) formed by their being screened by trees is the main feature of the composition, rather than their serving merely as a landmark marker.

evidence: Slightly left of center of the painting: several house buildings are visible at the mountain foot by the water, their roofs and walls clearly distinguishable, embellishing the landscape. | Center of the painting: the houses are located where the mountains and rocks meet the water surface, giving the scenery at that mountain foot and waterside a point of settlement.
distinction: The houses mainly serve to embellish and mark the landscape scenery, rather than emphasizing a strict correspondence between their layout and the terrain.

evidence: Middle right of the fan, behind the large tree trunk: behind the trunk and dense leaf clusters, a window with straight lattice bars and part of a wall are revealed, most of the building itself screened by trees | Upper part to upper right of the fan: bamboo branches and leaves hang down from above, pressing over the side where the house stands, so that the house window is revealed only through the gaps in the trees | Water surface from center to lower left: fine brushwork ripples cover the water surface, a figure wearing a conical hat sits in a boat, and at the lower left bank a person with a staff stands among the grass; no bridge, path, or gate is seen connecting with the house
distinction: The staff-bearing figure and the boat merely show activity on the water and at the bank, lacking entry clues such as a path, bridge crossing, or gate leading to the house; the house, by contrast, has its window and wall revealed from behind the trees, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship is directly visible, so concealment and revelation is the main aspect.

evidence: Lower center: a small bridge spans the valley mouth, with one person on the bridge, forming a clear movement-through-the-landscape clue and connecting the two banks. | Cliff on the right: a pavilion is built high on the cliff, connected with the foreground through the bridge and the mountain configuration, presenting the spatial process of going from one place to another. | Right side: the building screened by trees echoes the bridge path, guiding the line of sight to extend into the depth.
distinction: The presence of the bridge and figures in the painting constitutes a clear movement-through-the-landscape clue, guiding the line of sight toward the building on the right and emphasizing the spatial process of entry and travel, which is more dominant than mere concealment and revelation.

evidence: Center of the painting: a vigorous pine tree occupies the main position, with dense branches and foliage extending in all directions. | Beneath the pine, among the rocks: between the tree roots and the rocks, a person lies on a felt blanket, half screened by the pine trunk and the mountains and rocks. | Left and right sides of the painting: mountains and rocks rise and fall, together with the central pine forming an enclosing and partly screened spatial layering.
distinction: The painting mainly forms layers of concealment and revelation through the screening of mountains, rocks, and trees, rather than showing a clear entry path or architectural clues.

evidence: Center-right of the painting: a person rides a donkey through the mountains, rocks, and trees, with clouds and mist swirling around, suggesting a route of movement and spatial extension. | Upper part and right side of the painting: pines and other vegetation are depicted, together with the mountains and rocks forming a mountain-forest setting, within which the figure is placed.
distinction: The painting mainly shows a figure riding a donkey among mountain forests, trees, and rocks, with a sense of movement through the landscape and spatial extension; although there are no explicit built elements, the movement-through-the-landscape clue dominates the spatial organization of the painting more than mere concealment and revelation layering.

evidence: Foreground: an embankment or small path extending along the waterside is visible, with two people walking on it, and a small boat on the water at the left. | Middle and far distance: the main subject of the painting is rolling mountains, clouds and mist, and rows of willow trees; no explicit houses, pavilions, or other built elements are seen.
distinction: There are no explicit built elements in the painting, but the embankment path and the figures' tracks in the foreground provide spatial clues for movement through the landscape, hence classified as C4.

evidence: Lower center of the painting: a small bridge spans a stream or valley, with a person walking to the right on it, constituting a clear clue of movement through the landscape and entry. | Right side of the painting: behind dense woods, the roof and wall of a built structure are faintly revealed; the direction of travel on the bridge points toward this place, presenting a spatial relationship of passing from here to there and turning into the depths.
distinction: Although the built structure on the right is screened by trees, the presence of the small bridge and the walking figure in the painting makes the accessible, reachable clue of movement through the landscape the dominant relationship organizing the space.

evidence: Among the trees on the lower-left bank: between the interlacing trunks and branches, a gable roof and the horizontal straight line under the eaves are revealed; most of the house form is obscured by branches and foliage, and only the roof and part of the frame are discernible | Water surface at lower center: a small boat on the open water, with two people aboard, one poling; between the boat and the house form on the left bank lies water, with no visible bridge, path, or shoreline connection | Upper part and right bank: pale-ink distant mountains and sandbar groves stretch across the top; the sloping rocks and groves of the right bank close off the water surface, placing the lower-left grove and the house form within it in the foreground layer
distinction: The house form is presented in layers mainly through concealment by the grove and the revealing of the roof; its correspondence with the slope's configuration is unclear due to the occlusion, so concealment and revelation take precedence over terrain-responsive siting

evidence: Center of the painting: a person sits on flat ground between mountains, rocks, and trees; no houses, pavilions, paths, or other built elements are seen anywhere in the painting.
distinction: The painting lacks built elements; the figure in the open area of the landscape serves as a scenic accent, closer to the compositional function of scenic accentuation than to terrain-responsive siting.

evidence: Lower center of the fan painting: a thatched-roof pavilion supported by several columns, whose bases rest on a waterside earthen platform and sloping bank outlined in pale ink; the platform and bank extend leftward into a large expanse of unpainted water | Right and lower right of the pavilion: sloping rocks, groves, and bamboo groves on the right bank grow from the same bank; the bank line supports the pavilion base, and the pavilion is set by the water following the terrain of the shore | Upper left: a row of low hills stretches across the opposite shore of the unpainted water, facing the shore occupied by the pavilion across the water; the pavilion faces the open water
distinction: The pavilion's site clearly sits on the waterside sloping platform and is placed following the configuration of the shore; the relationship in which terrain participates in the siting of the built structure is more directly visible than its role as a scenic marker

evidence: Upper center: a pavilion half hidden behind a huge tree trunk and mountains and rocks, with only part of its roof and columns revealed, forming a clear relationship of concealment and revelation. | Left side: a thatched hut hidden among dense groves and bamboo, its eaves and walls partly obscured by branches and foliage. | Right middle ground: a small red bridge spans between mountains and rocks, its body partly screened by foreground rocks and trees.
distinction: Although the built structures are placed beside mountains, rocks, and trees, the painting emphasizes constructing spatial layering through the screening and revealing by groves and rocks; the relationship of concealment and revelation is more prominent than terrain-responsive siting.

evidence: Lower left corner: two people ride horses along a small path; the path extends toward the upper right of the painting, forming a clue of movement through the landscape. | Among the mountains and rocks in the center and on the right: the roofs and walls of several buildings are visible, built against mountains, rocks, and trees, and partly obscured. | Overall painting: the path in the lower left corner points toward the buildings screened by mountains and rocks, presenting a spatial process of passing from here to there and approaching the built structures.
distinction: Although the buildings are screened by mountains, rocks, and trees, the clear travel path of the figures in the lower left corner guides the eye into the mountain buildings, emphasizing an accessible spatial process rather than merely static screening.

evidence: Center-right of the painting: a thatched pavilion half hidden between the bamboo grove and strange rocks on the left and the trees on the right, with only its roof and some eave columns revealed, forming a clear layering of concealment and revelation. | Center of the painting: dense bamboo and trees wrap around the built structure; the screening and revealing of the architecture by natural scenery participates in the spatial composition.
distinction: Although the thatched pavilion marks the scenery here, its half-screened, half-revealed relationship with the groves and rocks is more prominent in the composition and is the main means of forming spatial layering.

evidence: Right foreground: a built structure (pavilion) is visible between mountains, rocks, and pines; its roof and part of its structure are obscured by tree trunks and rocks, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Left-center of the painting: the water surface is open, dotted with several small boats, forming a foreground-to-background spatial layering with the groves and rocks of the right foreground.
distinction: Although the built structure serves as a scenic accent, the spatial layering formed by its screening and revealing through groves and rocks (screening) is visually more prominent.

evidence: Left center: several houses are visible among the trees on the bank; their roofs and walls are partly obscured by the surrounding bare trees, presenting a half-hidden, half-visible state. | Left side: the houses are placed beside the sloping bank and groves; the branches and foliage of the trees screen the front of the houses, constructing a spatial layering of foreground trees and middle-ground built structures.
distinction: Although the houses dot the bank, the relationship of concealment and revelation formed with the surrounding groves is the main means of pictorial composition, more prominent than serving merely as landmarks.

evidence: Center-right: the roof and wall of a house are visible between mountains, rocks, and trees, partly obscured by the rocks and branches in front, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Water surface below: a small boat on the water and figures on the bank form a spatial layering with the screened built structure behind.
distinction: Although the house is placed against mountains and rocks, the painting emphasizes more its layering of concealment and revelation screened by trees and rocks, so C2 is more apt than C1.

evidence: Central mountain summit: a pavilion is built atop a towering, steep mountain rock, with two people sitting facing each other inside; its conspicuous position makes it the visual center of the painting, marking the scenery at the peak. | Right slope: another house is hidden among blossoming flowering trees, with part of its roof and walls revealed, forming a screening relationship with the trees. | Lower right: a person stands beneath the flowering trees, with a horse nearby, suggesting an association between human activity and the built structure.
distinction: Although the pavilion is built following the terrain of the mountain summit, its main role as the visual focus at the highest point of the painting is to concentrate and mark the mountain configuration, rather than to show a complex terrain-responsive layout.

evidence: Center: an arched bridge spans a waterfall, with two people standing on it; the bridge body connects the mountains and rocks on both sides, forming a clear clue of crossing and passage. | Upper right: the right end of the bridge connects to a small path or platform between the rocks and the pine grove; the path extends into the depths of the mountain forest, guiding the eye into the interior of the painting. | Lower right: a structure resembling a bamboo fence or railing is visible, suggesting a man-made boundary or the continuation of a path.
distinction: Although the bridge is built following the water, the painting emphasizes more the process of the figures moving through the bridge and path into the depths of the mountain forest, rather than mere terrain-responsive siting.

evidence: Center-right mountainside: the roof of a small pavilion or building is visible, half hidden behind trees and mountains and rocks, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Lower part of the painting: faint traces of transverse timber structures or a bridge are visible, forming a foreground-to-background layering with the groves and rocks above.
distinction: The building's mass is tiny and obscured by groves and rocks; its main role is to form spatial layering rather than to serve as a conspicuous landmark concentrating the scenery.

evidence: Center: a figure is visible sitting on mountains and rocks, surrounded by pines and bamboo. | Right side: mountains, rocks, and trees are visible; no explicit houses, pavilions, or other built structures are seen.
distinction: No explicit built elements are seen in the painting; only a figure serves as a scenic accent among the mountains, rocks, and groves, hence classified as scenic accentuation rather than concealment and revelation.

evidence: Center-right of the painting: a thatched-house courtyard is visible; its roof, walls, and fence are partly obscured by the surrounding dense trees, forming a spatial layering of alternating concealment and revelation. | Left side and background of the painting: the left is an open waterside and distant mountains, forming a contrast of solid and void with the built structure screened by groves in the center, highlighting the mood of the built structure deeply hidden in the woods.
distinction: Although the built structure is located beside the waterside, the most prominent compositional means in the painting is the screening and revealing of the architecture by trees, rather than the direct terrain-responsive arrangement of the architecture to the waterside.

evidence: Center-right of the fan painting, to the right of the pine trunk: a white-walled house reveals its roof and part of its wall; the lower part of the building itself is obscured by the sloping rocks in front, and only the upper half is visible | Right half of the fan painting: groves and layered mountains and rocks enclose the surroundings of the house; the roof ridge is revealed from behind the rocks and between the gaps in the trees, forming a layering of concealment and revelation | Left half of the fan painting: a gentle waterside and distant mountains are laid out in pale ink; the only discernible built structure in the painting is concentrated where the trees and rocks screen it in the right half
distinction: Although the house sits among the sloping rocks, the dominant relationship in the painting is the layering of concealment and revelation in which the roof and walls are revealed after being screened by the sloping rocks and groves, rather than the correspondence of a site laid out following the terrain

evidence: Center and both sides of the painting: natural scenery such as mountains, rocks, and trees is visible; no explicit houses, bridges, paths, or other built elements are seen.
distinction: No explicit built elements are seen in the painting; based on the overall landscape organization, it is assigned to the closest category.

evidence: Lower right-center: between the tree trunks and branches and the mountains and rocks, the roughly outlined form of a house (roof and wall) is visible, presenting a relationship of being half screened and half revealed by natural scenery. | Overall painting: the central main peak and the trees on both sides form the foreground and middle ground; the house on the right is hidden behind the groves, forming spatial layering.
distinction: Although the house is located on the flat ground at the foot of the mountain, the painting emphasizes more its layering of concealment and revelation screened by trees, mountains, and rocks, rather than a correspondence of terrain-responsive arrangement.

evidence: Center-right of the painting: behind and in the gaps of the dark-ink grove, the outline of a roof faintly sketched in extremely pale ink lines is indistinctly visible, suspected to be a building screened by groves. | Center to right of the painting: a row of horizontally spread trees forms a screening layer between foreground and middle ground, half concealing and half revealing the pale-ink scenery behind (including the suspected roof).
distinction: The form of the suspected building in the painting is extremely blurred and largely obscured by trees, mainly presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation rather than clearly marking a particular scenery.

evidence: Left side and bottom: a natural waterside environment formed by sloping banks, trees, rocks, and water is visible; no traces of buildings, bridges, paths, or other built elements are seen. | Center and right of the painting: the water surface is open, with several egrets active, and reeds and other aquatic plants on the right; the whole is a purely natural landscape.
distinction: The painting consists entirely of natural landscape, flora, and fauna, with no built elements at all; based on the overall waterside spatial organization, it is barely assigned to C1, but lacks actual evidence of built structures.

evidence: Lower fan painting, center: a house is surrounded by trees and mountains and rocks, with part of its structure obscured by branches and foliage, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Lower fan painting, right side: the roof of a building is revealed behind mountains, rocks, and trees, forming a layering of seeing a house through a screen. | Upper fan painting, right side: the outline of a suspected building is visible amid the screening groves, merged into the natural scenery.
distinction: The buildings in the painting mainly form spatial layering and concealment-and-revelation relationships through screening by trees and rocks, rather than serving merely as isolated landmark scenic accents.

evidence: Upper fan painting, center-right: the roof and part of the wall of a house are visible, partly obscured by the surrounding branches and foliage, presenting a layering of seeing a house in the woods. | Upper fan painting, middle ground: the house is located between the mountains, rocks, and groves behind the waterside; the surrounding trees form a relationship of concealment and revelation, making the built structure faintly visible. |

evidence: Lower center: a thatched-roof house is partly blocked by the trees and bamboo grove in the foreground, with only the roof, part of the walls, and the doors and windows revealed, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Lower middle: behind and around the house are colorful woods and bamboo groves; natural scenery wraps the built structure within it, creating a layering of a house seen within the grove.
