evidence: Center-right lower part: a wooden bridge is visible crossing a stream valley and connecting the two banks, with figures walking on the bridge, forming clear clues of passage and entry. | Center-left upper part: the roof of a pavilion is revealed between the pine grove and the rock face, presenting a screening relationship, though it is not the sole dominant element of the painting. | Lower right corner and lower left: boats carrying people are on the water, and a traveling party is on the bank; together with the bridge, they reinforce a spatial organization that can be traversed and reached.
distinction: Although buildings in the painting are screened among the woods and rocks, the relationships of entry and connection formed by the wooden bridge, boats, and travel routes are more prominent and dominate the spatial organization.

evidence: Right side, middle-to-distant view: the roofs and eaves of a group of buildings emerge from the woodland, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship in which they are partly screened by trees. | Right-side waterside: the buildings are situated among the woods by the water, using natural scenery to form spatial layering, giving the built structures a sense of depth.
distinction: Although the buildings mark the distant scenery, the layering of concealment and revelation by which they are revealed through screening by the woodland is the most prominent mode of spatial organization in the painting.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting and the right-side mountainside: several people are visible walking along the sloping paths among the mountains and rocks, and one person on the right mountainside climbs along a small path, forming a coherent travel clue. | Left side: there is a thatched hut built structure, partly blocked by trees and rocks, revealing the roof, door frame, and figures inside. | Overall painting: the figures and paths link the foreground, middle ground, and distant mountains and rocks in sequence, presenting a spatial process that can be entered and traversed.
distinction: Although the built structure on the left has a screened appearance, the coherence of the figures and paths plays a more prominent role in organizing the spatial depth of the painting and guiding the eye.

evidence: Lower right: a simple wooden bridge or plank walkway structure supported by wooden piles is visible crossing the water surface and connecting the two banks. | Lower middle: two people stand at the water's edge facing the direction of the wooden bridge, suggesting the path connection for movement through the landscape and crossing the water surface.
distinction: The wooden bridge in the painting mainly provides a travel clue for crossing the water surface, rather than being a settlement built structure sited according to the mountain terrain.

evidence: Lower right: several trees grow on the sloped bank, and a pavilion is screened among the trees; the pavilion's roof and part of its structure are revealed through the trunks and foliage. | Right-side middle ground: the branches and foliage of the trees clearly block the pavilion, creating spatial layering of alternating concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the pavilion serves a scenic accentuation role, the painting places greater emphasis on the trees' screening and revealing of the pavilion, and the characteristic of concealment and revelation forming a scene is more prominent.

evidence: Lower left corner: beside the reeds on the waterside beneath the willow, a canopied boat is moored; as the only visible man-made object in the painting, it marks the waterside scenery. | Overall painting: the broad water surface and distant mountains form an open space, and the willow and boat in the foreground concentrate the scenic focus of the willow pond in spring water.
distinction: Although the boat may suggest travel by water, in the painting it mainly serves as a static visual focus marking the scenery of the willow pond in spring water, rather than emphasizing a path into the depths.

evidence: Water surface at the lower left of the painting: a small boat carrying one person is moored or drifting on the water, clearly visible as a man-made object (an extension of built elements). | Right side and lower part of the painting: old trees lean across, rocks below, and the boat is located in the open water between the trees and rocks and the distant mountains. | Overall composition: the boat and figure mark the scenery of traveling on the water or of reclusion, giving the open water surface and the trees and rocks on the bank a visual anchor and a concentration of mood.
distinction: Although the boat is a tool for movement through the landscape, the painting does not show a clear path or ferry crossing guiding entry; instead it directly marks the scenery with the boat, so C3 is more apt.

evidence: Center-right of the painting: a group of house buildings is partly blocked by the trees and rocks in the foreground, with only roofs and part of the walls revealed, presenting a layering of a house seen within the woods. | Center of the painting: tall trees have luxuriant branches and foliage that block most of the structure of the built elements behind, forming an obvious concealment-and-revelation relationship.
distinction: Although the houses are laid out according to the mountain terrain, the painting mainly expresses their existence and spatial layering through screening by trees and rocks; the concealment-and-revelation relationship is more pronounced than siting according to terrain.

evidence: Left side of the painting: several trees are visible standing on sloping rocks and earthen banks; no houses, bridges, or other built structures are seen. | Upper middle: there are inscribed characters and seals, but the painting itself does not present corresponding architectural forms.
distinction: No built elements are visible in the painting; it is only tentatively assigned to the basis of terrain-responsive siting based on the natural arrangement of sloping rocks and trees, lacking evidence of actual buildings.

evidence: Lower right water surface: a small boat with figures aboard is visible, in a state of traveling on the water, suggesting a process of movement through the landscape. | Left and center: mountains and rocks, trees, and water form a natural space; no clear architectural built elements are seen.
distinction: No clear buildings are seen in the painting, but the boat's traveling state suggests an enterable, traversable spatial process, so it is assigned to C4.

evidence: Upper middle of the left leaf's painted area, in a mountain hollow: the roofs, eaves, and railings of a group of buildings emerge from the notch where two mountains converge, the lower part of the buildings being screened by the sloping rocks in front and a row of trees | Middle of the left leaf's painted area, on the slope: below the buildings the slope is covered with a colonnade of pines and clusters of ink-dot trees, screening the building site at the hollow so that the buildings appear only by their tops above the trees and rocks | Lower part of the left leaf's painted area, at the stream bank: two figures stand on a level path among the slopes, and a single-arch bridge spans the ravine at lower right, but between the bridge and path up to the hollow buildings the way is interrupted by sloping rocks, and no continuous identifiable entry path is seen
distinction: Although the bridge, path, and traveling figures are visible, there is no identifiable connecting route between them and the buildings in the hollow; the buildings mainly suggest their layer of existence through screening by trees and rocks and the exposure of their roofs, so concealment and revelation is more apt than access to secluded settings.

evidence: Lower left corner: two small built structures (roofs and eave pillars) are visible, half screened among clusters of trees and the sloping bank, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Lower middle of the painting: foreground sloping rocks and trees dominate, the built elements recede to the edge, forming spatial layers through screening by natural scenery.
distinction: The built elements are tiny in scale and relegated to one corner; their main role is to form scenery through the screening of trees, rather than to point out or concentrate a core scenic spot.

evidence: Lower foreground: a thatched hut is partly obscured by the trunk and branches of a large foreground tree and by bamboo beside it, revealing only part of the roof, pillars, and figures inside, forming an obvious relationship of concealment and revelation. | Upper distance: a group of buildings in a mountain hollow is surrounded and screened by the surrounding slopes and woodland; some buildings are hidden behind trees, others exposed, presenting a deep layering.
distinction: Although the foreground thatched hut leans against an earthen slope, the painting emphasizes more the interpenetration and screening of the buildings by tree branches, constructing spatial layers thereby, so C2 is more dominant than C1.

evidence: Top of the central cliff: a pavilion and storied buildings are visible at the mountain summit, surrounded by trees, their roofs clearly visible, becoming the visual focus of the painting and marking the lofty point of the cliff. | Left water surface and right cliff: a large area of unpainted water and the steep cliff on the right form a contrast of opening and closing; the summit buildings concentrate the gaze and emphasize the scenery of that place.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed at the cliff top with the character of terrain-responsive siting, in the composition they mainly serve as a visual center marking the summit scenery, so C3 is more apt.

evidence: Lower right: a scholar and an attendant are seen sitting among bamboo grove and mountain rocks, with a stream and spring beside them, but no built structures are seen. | Whole painting: the painting is dominated by mountains and rocks, bamboo grove, spring water, and figures, with no traces of houses, pavilions, or other built elements.
distinction: There are no clear built elements in the painting; the figures together with the spring, rocks, and bamboo mark the scene of 'listening to the spring beneath bamboo,' so it is assigned to C3.

evidence: Lower left to bottom: a long bridge (multi-arched) spans the water, connecting the left and right shorelines, forming an obvious thread of movement through the landscape. | Right lower bank: the right end of the bridge connects to the bank, and house roofs are visible amid screening trees, showing the linkage of built elements with the bridge. | Upper right summit: building outlines are also present at the summit, obscured by trees and rocks, but the connection of the bridge below with the houses more prominently organizes the sense of spatial entry.
distinction: Although the houses screened by trees fit concealment and revelation (C2), the long bridge as a clear thread of movement connects the water surface with the bank built elements, more strongly expressing the spatial process of passing from one to the other (C4).

evidence: Lower right: a group of built structures (including pavilions and a pagoda) is placed close against the mountain rock, the site closely fitting the rock outlines, unfolding in staggered heights according to the mountain's form. | Center-right water surface: a small boat is on the water, echoing spatially with the bank rocks and built elements, but the built structures mainly present a siting relationship that follows the mountain's configuration.
distinction: Although the built elements serve to mark scenery, their most prominent feature is the site-responsive placement close against the rock face and arranged according to the mountain's heights, so C1 is more apt than C3.

evidence: Lower left corner: a water pavilion is built by the water, its site close against the water's edge, presenting a relationship of placement following the bank. | Middle of the painting, mountainside: houses are built on a protruding rocky platform, surrounded by trees, showing buildings set upon a platform. | Lower right to center: the building group unfolds in layers up the mountain foot and slopes, staggered in height, following the mountain's form.
distinction: Although paths and figures connect the various buildings, the correspondence of building sites with mountain forms, slope platforms, and the waterside (set upon platforms, following slopes, facing water) is more prominent and dominates the spatial layout.

evidence: Lower left: the built elements are located on the slope at the foot of towering mountain rocks, the site placed following the terrain, presenting a relationship of separate placement along the slope. | Around the lower-left built elements: the buildings are surrounded by trees, integrated with the rocky environment, the layout following the site conditions at the mountain foot.
distinction: Although the built elements are partly screened by trees, their placement alongside the slope at the mountain foot is clearer, mainly embodying site-responsive placement rather than a mere layer of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower right corner: a pavilion is built directly on the rocky shoreline by the water, its base supported by wooden pillars suspended over the water, the site forming a clear correspondence with the terrain and waterside. | Lower middle: building roofs and eave corners are visible half screened among pines and miscellaneous trees, arranged along the slope at the mountain foot.
distinction: Although the lower-middle buildings have a concealment-and-revelation relationship screened by trees, the site-responsive placement of the lower-right pavilion on the waterside rocks is more prominent, dominating the correspondence between built elements and natural forms.

evidence: Lower center of the painting: an open hall (thatched pavilion) is half hidden among clustered trees and sloping rocks, revealing only the roof, pillars, and figures inside. | Lower part of the painting: tree branches and mountain rocks partly obscure the building, presenting spatial layers of alternating concealment and revelation.
distinction: The building mainly forms a layer of concealment and revelation through screening by woodland to create scenery, rather than serving to mark or identify a macro landscape scenic spot.

evidence: Lower middle, slightly left: a multi-story building is built close against the edge of the slope platform of the right cliff, its site and layout arranged in layers following the mountain's heights. | Central ridge: tiny built structures are faintly visible among the ridge woodland, placed separately according to the mountain-slope terrain.
distinction: The buildings mainly present a form of layered placement following the cliff slope platforms; the determining role of terrain over layout is greater than a mere layer of tree screening and concealment.

evidence: Right: a slope extends into the water, with trees and scattered fine ink dots on it; no clear architectural forms are seen. | Left and center: the water surface is open, dotted with several mountain rocks; trees at the lower left corner; no traces of buildings. | Distance: distant mountains stretch in succession, with fine ink dots on the ridge line; no built structures are seen.
distinction: No clear built elements are seen in the painting; it is assigned to C1 based on the overall natural extension relationship of the landscape terrain and waterside.

evidence: Center and left of the painting: mountain rock outlines and the interwoven branches of several withered trees are visible; no traces of houses, bridges, or built elements are seen. | Lower right corner: there are inscribed characters and seals, but these do not constitute evidence of spatial built elements within the painting.
distinction: No clear built elements in the painting; only the natural forms of mountains, rocks, and trees are seen, and it is assigned to the closest category based on the overall visible space.

evidence: Left mountain rocks: on the left side of the painting are mountain rocks and pines, with a figure in red standing on the rock; no traces of any buildings, bridges, or built elements are seen.
distinction: No visible built elements in the painting; only figures and natural landscape, assigned only tentatively based on the overall spatial organization, lacking clear grounds for classification.

evidence: Lower left (at the foot of the waterside rocks): a small pavilion-type built structure is visible, placed close against the base of a huge rock and the water's edge, presenting a layout beside the rock and by the water. | Left and center: branches of purple-flowering trees extend from above the rock and cover the built structure; the building site unfolds following the natural forms of the rock and waterside.
distinction: Although the built structure marks the scenery of a corner of the waterside, its site-responsive placement against the rock foot and following the shoreline is more direct and dominant.

evidence: Upper middle left: a group of houses is partly obscured by tree trunks and branches, revealing only roofs, wall bodies, and window lattices, forming a layer of houses hidden in the woods. | Lower left: another building is hidden behind mountain rocks and tree clusters, with eaves and walls partly exposed, forming a front-and-back screening relationship with the foreground rocks and vegetation. | Left side overall: the built elements are not directly and fully exposed, but present a spatial depth of alternating concealment and revelation through the interpenetrating screening of trees and mountain rocks.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed by mountains and water, the painting emphasizes more the construction of spatial layers through the obscuring and revealing by trees and rocks; the concealment-and-revelation relationship is more prominent than site-responsive placement.

evidence: Upper middle and left of the painting: many houses are placed in staggered heights against mountain rocks and rock platforms, roofs and walls distributed following the mountain's form. | Middle of the painting: building sites are closely combined with rocky slope platforms, presenting a layout of buildings set upon platforms, suited to the configuration.
distinction: Although the buildings have layers of screening by woodland and rocks, their layout feature of being placed according to the terrain and the heights of rock platforms is more prominent, so C1 is more apt than C2.

evidence: Upper middle: through the tree clusters, horizontally arranged lines are visible, presenting the form of railings or steps. | Lower middle: between tree trunks and branches, vertical pillars and horizontal eave outlines are exposed, indicating buildings half screened by woodland. | Left: mountain rocks and trees surround the built elements, forming spatial layers of front-and-back screening.
distinction: Although the painting shows buildings placed according to the mountains, the obscuring and revealing of parts of the buildings by woodland and rocks (concealment and revelation) is the foremost visual feature organizing the spatial layers.

evidence: Left side of the painting: red trees (red leaves) are visible, with freehand brushwork, forming a color contrast with the green mountains on the right. | Right side of the painting: green peaks and trees are visible, the mountain rocks rounded in form, echoing the red trees on the left. | Lower right corner: there are inscribed characters and seals, mentioning an imitation of Mi Nangong's White Clouds and Red Trees, indicating the theme is landscape and trees.
distinction: The painting is mainly landscape and trees with no clear built elements; the red trees and green mountains constitute the main scenery, so it is assigned to the near category of scenic accentuation, but lacking evidence of built elements.

evidence: Whole painting: the painting consists mainly of mountain rocks, trees, and a waterfall; no clear houses, bridges, paths, or other built elements are seen. | Center: the waterfall flows down from above, surrounded by dense trees and rocks, presenting a natural landscape form.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built elements; based on the spatial organization of pure natural landscape, it is assigned to C1 as the closest description.

evidence: Left cliff edge: a suspected pavilion-type built structure with railings and a roof is visible, placed attached to the rocky terrain, with figures inside.
distinction: If regarded as a built structure, its placement attached to the cliff terrain (terrain-responsive) is more prominent than its mere role as a visual marker (scenic accentuation).

evidence: Left edge: part of a building (a textured roof or wall) is visible, partly obscured by the mountain rocks and trees on the left, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Below the left building: a figure is faintly visible below the building, further indicating the existence of built elements and their layered relationship with the surrounding woodland.
distinction: Although the building is located beside mountain rocks, the painting emphasizes more its layer of concealment and revelation through partial exposure screened by woodland, rather than a layout unfolding according to the terrain.

evidence: Lower left: through the gaps in the branches and leaves of foreground trees, line fragments resembling railings or a wooden frame are faintly visible, suspected to be built structures. | Center and left of the painting: thick ancient trees and luxuriant branches and leaves occupy the main space of the painting, forming obvious screening of the scenery behind.
distinction: The part suspected to be built structure is heavily screened by trees, mainly presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship through woodland screening and exposure, rather than serving as a clear visual focus to mark scenery.

evidence: Middle left: part of a built structure is visible, including walls, doors and windows, and eaves, with figures faintly visible inside. | Center to left of the painting: the thick trunk and dense branches and leaves of a foreground pine screen most of the built structure, forming an obvious relationship of concealment and revelation. | Upper left: withered branches further interpenetrate in front of the built structure, increasing the sense of spatial layering and screening.
distinction: Although the built structure is built against mountain rocks, the most dominant spatial expression in the painting is the revealing of the building through screening by foreground trees, forming layers, rather than emphasizing its site-responsive layout.

evidence: Lower right: a pavilion stands at the foot of mountain rocks; its building body and pillars are partly obscured by the trunk of a foreground pine and branches of red-leaf trees, revealing only the roof, railings, and figures inside the pavilion. | Lower middle to lower right: tall trees stand in front of the pavilion, forming foreground and middle-ground layers, so that the built structure appears partly screened in the woods, half hidden and half exposed.
distinction: Although the pavilion exists as a scenic accent, the marked screening of the pavilion by trees and the front-and-back layering in the painting better fit the spatial character of concealment and revelation, rather than serving merely as a landscape marker.

evidence: Upper middle of the painting: a dense grove of withered trees presents overlapping front-and-back spatial layers | Lower part of the painting: at the water's edge a figure rides an ox wading through the water, forming a spatial separation from the woodland above
distinction: No clear built elements are seen in the painting; it is assigned to C2 based on the front-and-back screening layers of the woodland.

evidence: Lower middle of the left bank: several groups of houses are placed in staggered fashion on the slope at the mountain foot, unfolding according to the terrain's rises and falls. | Middle-ground mountainside: buildings are set upon platforms, placed against the mountain's form and woodland. | Distant right bank: houses on the opposite slope are distributed following the shoreline, echoing the landscape's configuration.
distinction: Although there is tree screening, the buildings mainly present site-responsive placement following slopes, shoreline, and platforms, with screening secondary.

evidence: Left-middle: a pavilion is built on a steeply protruding rocky platform, with supporting structures visible below, presenting a form of setting a building against the cliff and building in response to the terrain. | Lower right: a bridge is visible spanning a stream valley and connecting paths, with figures walking on it, but the main visual focus is the correspondence between the cliff-set built structure on the left and the mountain forms.
distinction: Although there is a bridge and path guiding space in the lower right (C4), the pavilion on the left is built against the perilous cliff, and its close dependence of building site on the mountain-rock forms (C1) is more prominent and dominant in the composition.

evidence: Lower-middle of the painting: the house building is partly screened by the branches and foliage of surrounding tall trees, revealing only the roof, eaves, and part of the wall, presenting a layering of a house hidden in the woods. | Lower right corner of the painting: a fence-enclosed courtyard and small house are partly screened by trees, with figures active within, reinforcing the sense of spatial depth of built structures deeply hidden in the woods.
distinction: Although the painting has a fence and figures suggesting an entrance, it lacks a clear and continuous path leading into the depths; the dominant relationship remains the trees' screening and revealing of the building.

evidence: Lower left corner: the roof and upturned eaves of a pavilion-style building are visible, partly screened by the dense branches and foliage of surrounding trees, presenting a spatial layering of a house revealed in the woods. | Overall painting: mountains, rocks, and trees occupy the main space, while the built structure recedes to a marginal corner; its existence is hinted at through the screening and revealing of the trees, and the concealment-revelation relationship participates in the composition.
distinction: The building is located at the edge of the painting and screened by trees; it mainly enriches the spatial layering through concealment and revelation, rather than serving as a visual center that identifies a specific scene.

evidence: Left-middle: an arched bridge (or long embankment) is visible spanning the water surface/valley mouth, connecting the left bank with the building area on the right, forming a clear route for movement through the landscape. | Lower-middle: a building group (hall, waterside pavilion) is built beside the water, supported by colonnades, and spatially connected with the bridge path, presenting a relationship of moving from here to there and approaching the built structures.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited with mountains behind and water in front (C1), the arched bridge on the left and the waterside buildings form a clear entry path and process of movement, making the spatial organization of access to secluded settings (C4) more dominant.

evidence: Middle of the painting: several houses are partly screened by the trunks and foliage of tall pines in the foreground, revealing only roofs and walls, forming a concealment-revelation relationship. | Left-middle of the painting: building outlines are faintly visible behind mountains and rocks, presenting spatial layering through the screening of rocks. | Lower left of the painting: a waterside building (water pavilion) is built close to the bank, with mountains, rocks, and trees in the foreground partly screening it.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited with mountains behind and water in front, the painting places more emphasis on the screening and revealing of buildings by trees and rocks, thereby constructing profound spatial layering; therefore C2 is more dominant than C1.

evidence: Mountain hollow in the middle of the painting: a building group is screened behind a valley flanked by two mountains and behind trees, revealing only part of the roofs and walls, presenting an obvious screening-and-revealing relationship. | Bottom left and right sides of the painting: pavilions and towers are interspersed among dense trees and rocks, with parts of the buildings screened by trunks and foliage, forming rich spatial layering. | Along the stream in the lower-middle of the painting: buildings are distributed in staggered fashion along the stream and mountain forms, enveloped by the surrounding natural scenery, alternating concealment and revelation, reinforcing pictorial depth.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited with mountains behind and water in front, the painting places more emphasis on revealing buildings through the screening of trees, rocks, and mountains, using concealment and revelation to create profound spatial layering; therefore C2 is more dominant than C1.

evidence: Lower-middle of the painting: the roofs, eaves, and walls of several building groups are revealed through the dense pine branches and foliage of the foreground and middle ground, forming an obvious screening-and-disclosure relationship. | Left and right-middle of the painting: figures and railing details inside the buildings are visible through gaps in the trees, indicating that the buildings are surrounded by woodland and situated at different spatial levels.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited against mountains and rocks, the most prominent compositional method in the painting is to present the buildings' layering through the screening and revealing of pine branches and foliage; therefore C2 is more dominant than C1.

evidence: Right panel of the painting: the painting presents foreground sloping rocks and trees (including bare branches and leafy trees), an open water surface or unpainted space in the middle ground, and low mountains in the distance; no houses, bridges, paths, or other artificial built elements are seen. | Left panel of the painting: calligraphic inscription and seals, which do not constitute spatial evidence within the painted scene.
distinction: The painting completely lacks artificial built elements, showing only the layered unfolding of natural sloping rocks, trees, and landscape; based on the relationship between terrain and water surface, classifying it under C1 is closer to purely natural spatial organization than C3, which emphasizes scenic accentuation.

evidence: Left-middle: at the top of a sloping bank, a flat-roofed artificial built structure is visible, with a low wall or railing, sited directly according to the terrain of the rocky slope platform. | Left side: the building site and the steep rocky cliff below form a high-low correspondence of terrain-responsive placement.
distinction: This built structure mainly presents a placement relationship conforming to the sloping platform terrain, rather than serving as a visual marker that concentrates or identifies a specific landscape scene.

evidence: Right side: through the branches and foliage of trees in the foreground and middle ground, part of a waterside built structure (pavilion or waterside pavilion) is visible, with a seated scholar inside, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship screened within the woods. | Overall painting: dense woodland and sloping rocks form rich spatial layering; the built structure is placed behind the trees, and its existence is revealed through the screening of natural scenery.
distinction: Although the built structure is beside the water, the painting places more emphasis on its layered relationship of being screened and revealed by trees, rather than on its placement in relation to the waterside terrain.

evidence: Upper left of the painted panel: a multi-storey pagoda stands between distant mountains and woods, its outline clear. | Left and middle of the painted panel: a broad expanse of water and scattered boats form an open space, and the gaze naturally extends to the distant pagoda and mountains. | Upper left of the painted panel: the pagoda, as a high point in the distant view, marks and concentrates the landscape of the opposite shore.
distinction: The pagoda body is essentially fully exposed above the trees and mainly serves to mark the distant view, rather than being dominated by a layered relationship of screening and revealing.

evidence: Middle-left of the painting: behind the woodland, house roofs and railings are revealed, screened by tree branches and foliage, forming a concealment-revelation relationship.
distinction: Although the house follows the mountain forms, visually it presents layering mainly through the screening of trees, and the partly-screened characteristic is more dominant.

evidence: Center and left of the painting: sloping banks, bare trees, and weeping willows are visible, with mountains, rocks, and water in the distance; no clear built structures are seen. | Overall composition: natural scenery constitutes the main scene, lacking built elements such as buildings and paths.
distinction: The painting has no clear built structures; trees and sloping banks identify the waterside scene, so it is classified under C3.

evidence: Middle-right of the painting: the roofs of a group of houses emerge from dense pine woodland, with the building bodies screened by trunks and foliage, forming a spatial layering of houses hidden in the woods. | Right side of the painting: another pavilion-like built structure is likewise partly screened by trees, with only the roof outline visible, participating in the construction of the concealment-revelation relationship.
distinction: The built structures in the painting are mainly screened by woodland in the foreground and middle ground, with only roofs revealed to construct layers of concealment and revelation, rather than emphasizing the terrain-responsive correspondence between building site and landform.

evidence: Lower right: a thatched pavilion is built on a raised rocky platform, with the site integrated with the terrain, presenting a form of setting a building on a platform. | Middle left: pine roots interlace with sloping rocks, and vegetation grows according to the terrain. | Upper right: building outlines are faintly visible amid the pale shadows of distant mountains, blending with the forms of the distant mountains.
distinction: The thatched pavilion is clearly built relying on the rocky platform, presenting a terrain-responsive placement of setting a building on a platform, which emphasizes the correspondence between building site and terrain more than mere scenic accentuation as a visual focus.

evidence: Left-middle: a bridge is visible spanning between mountains and rocks, connecting the two banks. | Middle-right: a figure is under the trees, and together with the bridge suggests a route for movement through the landscape.
distinction: The bridge mainly serves as a route for movement through the landscape connecting the two banks and guiding spatial access, rather than merely identifying a single scene.

evidence: Center of the painting: several trees of varied forms (pine, bare tree, bamboo) interlace with mountains and rocks, forming foreground-background layering of natural scenery. | Whole painting: no houses, pavilions, bridges, or any artificial built elements are seen in the painting; only natural landscape and plants are present.
distinction: The painting lacks built elements and cannot constitute a strict C1-C4 classification; based on the visible interlacing layering of trees and rocks, it is tentatively classified under C2 as the closest form of natural spatial organization.

evidence: Left middle ground: the roof and columns of a pavilion are visible in the woodland, partly screened by surrounding tree branches and foliage, presenting a concealment-revelation relationship. | Right side and foreground: large trees screen the foreground sloping bank and, together with the woodland in the middle ground, form a natural layering that screens the built structures.
distinction: The built structure presents spatial layering mainly through the screening and revealing of woodland; no obvious path guidance or mere terrain-dependence relationship is seen.

evidence: Lower-middle right: the roof outlines of two connected buildings are visible, their lower parts completely screened by dense dark-ink tree clusters in the foreground, revealing only the upper portions. | Overall painting: the buildings are hidden behind tree clusters, and through the screening of trees and the revealing of roofs, a clear foreground-background spatial layering and concealment-revelation relationship is formed.
distinction: Although the buildings are located on a sloping bank, the most prominent spatial organization in the painting is the partial screening of buildings by trees, rather than emphasizing their terrain-conforming layout.

evidence: Center-right of the painting: behind a group of trees a thatched hut is partly screened, revealing only the roof and part of the structure, forming a layering of a house deeply hidden in the woods. | Left side and background of the painting: distant mountains and unpainted water surface set off the partly-screened relationship between the foreground trees and the thatched hut.
distinction: The thatched hut presents concealment-revelation layering mainly through the screening of trees, rather than serving as an isolated marker identifying a specific landscape scene.

evidence: Upper-middle: the painting is dominated by a towering main peak and distant pale-ink mountains, presenting scenery among the peaks. | Lower part: the foreground consists of sloping rocks and trees; no traces of houses, bridges, paths, or other built structures are seen.
distinction: No clear built structures are seen in the painting; the whole is dominated by natural landscape forms, so natural peaks serve as the main subject of scenic accentuation and it is classified under this category.

evidence: Lower-middle left: among the grove of wintry trees, the roof, walls, and fence of a house are revealed; the main building body is screened by trunks and foliage, presenting a concealment-revelation layering of a house hidden in the woods. | Lower right corner: a person stands beside a tree, with a railing-like structure nearby, suggesting a stopping point or path node.
distinction: The core of the painting lies in the concealment-revelation relationship of the house on the left screened by wintry trees, rather than emphasizing a process of movement from here to there.

evidence: Lower right corner: a group of houses is partly screened among woodland and rocks, with parts of the eaves, roofs, and walls visible, presenting a layering of being half-screened by natural scenery. | Right side: pines and mountain rocks surround the built structure, forming foreground screening and placing the building at a spatial level behind the woodland and rocks.
