distinction: The boat moored at the bank mainly serves a scenic accent and marking role, concentrating the visual focus of the shoreline and open water surface, rather than showing a complex terrain-based layout structure; mere adjacency is insufficient to determine C1.

evidence: Middle right of the painting: the roofs and eaves of several houses are visible, partially obscured by foreground trees and rocks, forming a concealment and revelation relationship. | Center to right of the painting: built elements are screened among trees and rocky banks; the exposed parts of the buildings indicate their existence and spatial layers.
distinction: Although the built elements are situated by mountains and water, the painting emphasizes more the spatial layers formed by their screening and revealing by trees and rocks, rather than mere terrain placement.

evidence: Center-right mountain foot: houses are located behind woods; roofs and walls are partially obscured by foreground tree branches and leaves, presenting spatial layers in which buildings are seen through intervening scenery. | Lower right corner: another built structure is hidden in dense pine woods, with only part of the roof visible, forming a concealment and revelation relationship through tree screening.
distinction: Although there is a bridge spanning the water in the painting, the built elements mainly present layers through occlusion relationships with trees, rather than emphasizing the process of entering via paths.

evidence: A band running across the middle of the fan: rows of dense-ink trees stand before the foot of the main peak, with crowns and trunks forming a screening band | Among the trees slightly right of center: a gabled roof and eaves emerge from gaps in the tree crowns; the building body is obscured by branches, leaves, and trunks | Slightly right of center, below: another roof is half-revealed behind trees, with only the sloped roof and eave line visible, indicating houses hidden within the woods
distinction: The height correspondence between houses and mountain slopes/terraces is not obvious; the main visible relationship is roofs revealed and concealed among rows of trees, so the screening layer is a better explanation than terrain placement.

evidence: Lower left: the roof and walls of a house emerge from foreground pines and miscellaneous tree clumps, forming a clear tree-screening relationship. | Middle left: parts of buildings at the mountainside are obscured by rocks and trees, with only part of the eaves visible, indicating the buildings' layers in space.
distinction: Although the buildings in the painting rely on rocks and trees, their faint appearance formed by tree occlusion is the main means of constructing spatial layers, so C2 is more appropriate than C1.

evidence: Lower right side: a small bridge is visible spanning a stream or valley, connecting the two banks, suggesting a route for movement and an accessible spatial relationship. | Center and left of the painting: distant mountains, clouds and mist, and trees are depicted, creating a sense of deep space; the presence of the bridge guides the gaze deeper into the painting.
distinction: No obvious houses or buildings are seen in the painting; the main built element is the bridge, whose role is to guide the gaze and suggest a movement path, conforming to the C4 characteristic of access to secluded settings rather than other categories.

evidence: Lower middle: a path between sloped banks and rocks is visible, with a figure on horseback and attendants traveling. | Middle of the painting: rocks and trees form a flanking space, guiding the gaze deeper.
distinction: No clear built elements are seen in the painting; based only on the visible traveling path and sense of spatial extension, it is assigned to the closest category of access to secluded settings.

evidence: Lower left: two simply drawn houses stand at the edge of a sloped bank, partly screened by willow and pine trees in front, presenting an alternating pattern of concealment and revelation in the spatial layering. | Left side of the painting: tall willow and pine branches droop or extend, forming a foreground-background screening relationship with the houses behind, creating a sense of secluded depth.
distinction: Although the houses are built on the sloped bank, the painting emphasizes the screening and partly screened effect of the trees on the houses rather than the decisive role of terrain in determining the architectural layout.

evidence: Full painting: the painting depicts a sloped bank, sparse trees, and distant mountains, with no clear traces of built elements such as houses or pavilions. | Center and left: multiple groups of trees are distributed on the sloped bank, with spreading forms that together with the water surface and distant mountains form a level-distance prospect.
distinction: The painting contains no explicit built elements, but the arrangement of the sloped bank and trees identifies a waterside scene, so it is assigned to C3; if the emphasis were on the terrain itself, it would approach C1.

evidence: Upper middle: a built element (pavilion/house) sits atop a mountain rock, screened by surrounding tall pines and mountain rocks, with only the roof and part of the walls exposed, presenting the layering of a house seen within the woods. | Left and center: dense pine branches extend around the built element, forming a natural screen that leaves the built element in a half-concealed, half-revealed state, participating in constituting spatial depth.
distinction: Although the built element is located in the mountains and serves as a scenic accent, the painting emphasizes more the concealment-and-revelation relationship formed by its screening by pines and rocks, so C2 is more apt than C3.

evidence: Lower right: one person with a staff is seen walking along the waterside; in the lower right corner there are a few brushstrokes resembling wooden posts or a fence, but no clear architectural built elements. | Middle ground: the broad water surface and distant mountains form an open space, and the direction of the figure's movement suggests a route of travel along the waterside.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built elements; there is only a figure walking along the waterside, presenting a certain trace of movement through the landscape, so it is only marginally assigned to C4.

evidence: Lower left of the mountain rocks on the left side of the painting: a simplified outline of a house is visible, situated amid the screening of towering mountain rocks and trees, presenting concealment-and-revelation relationships and spatial layering.
distinction: Although the building is located beside the mountain rocks, the painting mainly expresses, through screening relationships, its layering as hidden within the mountain forest, rather than emphasizing a correspondence of layout to terrain.

evidence: Lower middle of the right image: between the woodland and sloped rocks, faint dot-like traces of built elements are visible, half-screened by trees, presenting concealment-and-revelation relationships. | Upper middle of the right image: mountain rocks and clouds interweave, with no obvious built elements, mainly natural landscape layering.
distinction: The traces of built elements in the painting are faint and screened by woodland; the main effect is a partly screened relationship formed by screening with natural scenery to create layering, rather than clear terrain-responsive siting or scenic accentuation.

evidence: Right-hand painted panel: the painting consists mainly of mountains and rocks, trees and a waterside; no clear built elements such as houses, bridges or paths are seen.
distinction: The painting lacks identifiable built elements, and its mode of spatial expression cannot be determined precisely; on the basis of the overall landscape layering it is provisionally assigned to C2, but there is no actual evidence of built elements.

evidence: Lower part of the painting: several houses are visible, with roofs and wall bodies partly exposed, located behind trees. | Lower right of the painting: dark-ink trees stand in front of the houses, screening part of the buildings and forming an evident concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Upper part of the painting: mountain rocks rise, separated from the built elements below by unpainted space, forming foreground-background spatial layering.
distinction: The houses are mainly screened by trees in front, emphasizing the spatial layering formed by concealment and revelation, rather than simply being arranged according to terrain.

evidence: Lower right: through gaps in the woodland, the roof and supporting structure of a built element are visible, partly screened by tree trunks and branches, presenting concealment-and-revelation relationships. | Upper right: distant mountains are outlined in pale ink, forming foreground-background spatial layering with the woodland and built elements below.
distinction: The built element mainly relies on the screening and revealing by woodland to signal its existence and participate in forming the scene; no obvious clues of siting according to terrain, scenic accentuation, or path guidance are seen.

evidence: Right side of the painting: the right side of the painting depicts distant mountains, nearby sloped rocks, and several trees, with no clear built elements such as houses or bridges. | Left side of the painting: the left side contains calligraphic inscription and seals, with no landscape painting content.
distinction: No clear built elements are seen in the painting, so its mode of spatial expression cannot be accurately determined; it is only marginally assigned based on the overall landscape composition.

evidence: Center of the painting: the roofs and walls of several houses are faintly visible, screened and surrounded by the surrounding trees, forming the layering of a house seen within the woods. | Center of the painting: tree branches and leaves cover above and in front of the houses, and the evident concealment-and-revelation relationship participates in forming the space.
distinction: The built elements are mainly screened by trees to form spatial layering, rather than serving as a conspicuous marker to point out a specific scene.

evidence: Full painting: the painting shows only distant mountains, clouds, trees, and unpainted space representing water, with no identifiable traces of buildings or artificial built elements.
distinction: The painting is purely natural landscape, lacking evidence of artificial built elements, and cannot embody spatial organization such as terrain-responsive siting, concealment and revelation, or access to secluded settings.

evidence: Lower middle: an open thatched pavilion is built against the waterside and rocks, with a person seated inside, forming a stoppable node. | Left middle: a small bridge crosses a stream, forming a spatial connection with the area where the thatched pavilion is located, suggesting a route for entry or movement through the landscape. | Lower middle and right: trees and rocks surround the thatched pavilion, forming a relatively independent and secluded spatial layer.
distinction: Although trees partly screen the thatched pavilion, the movement-through-the-landscape and entry clues formed jointly by the small bridge on the left and the thatched pavilion are clearer and dominate the spatial organization.

evidence: Lower middle: a person sits alone on a rocky platform, facing the unpainted space to the left, in a leisurely posture | Right and upper parts: tall pines coil among the mountain rocks, occupying the main space of the painting; no built entities such as houses, pavilions, or bridges are seen | Overall composition: the painting takes the figure, pines, and rocks as its main subjects; the figure's position concentrates the visual focus, but there are no traces of artificial architecture
distinction: The figure sits on a rocky platform, which carries a sense of placement according to terrain, but there is no actual built entity; as a visual focus it accentuates the scene of a scholar viewing the landscape here, so assignment to C3 is more apt.

evidence: Water surface below: two small boats travel on the water, suggesting a clue of movement by water route. | Middle-right: a bridge spans a valley/stream, connecting the mountain rocks and buildings on both sides, forming a clear passage route. | Among the mountains: building groups are distributed along the mountain terrain, connected by bridges and implied paths, guiding the gaze to extend into the depths.
distinction: C4 emphasizes more the entry and movement-through-the-landscape clues formed by bridges, boats, and the like that organize the painting's space; C1 emphasizes only the dependent relationship between buildings and terrain.

evidence: Center-left: the roof and partial structure of a group of built elements (houses) are exposed among the mountain rocks and woodland, partly screened by the foreground and the mountain forms on both sides, forming an evident layering of concealment and revelation. | Left edge: the eaves and walls of another built element emerge from behind a cliff, signaling its existence through the screening of the mountain form.
distinction: Although the built elements are sited according to the mountain terrain, the painting emphasizes more the construction of spatial layering through the screening and revealing by mountain rocks and woodland, so C2 is more apt than C1.

evidence: Lower left: a house is partly screened by the branches and leaves of foreground trees, with only the roof, eaves, and supporting columns exposed, presenting the concealment-and-revelation relationship of a house seen within the woods. | Middle ground: the building group on the mountainside reveals only roof outlines, hidden behind mountain rocks and clouds, forming the spatial layering of a house seen through an intervening layer. | Overall: clouds and mist swirl between the mountain rocks and the built elements, strengthening the screening-and-revealing effect in which the buildings appear faintly and intermittently.
distinction: Although the building in the lower left corner is built against the waterside sloped rocks and has C1 features, multiple built elements in the painting (especially in the middle ground) mainly organize spatial layering through screening by clouds and trees; the concealment-and-revelation relationship is more dominant in the composition.

evidence: Upper left corner: faintly rendered outlines of distant mountains in pale ink | Lower left corner: waterside plants such as reeds and lotus leaves are depicted | Center and right of the painting: large areas of unpainted space, covered with red collector's seals, with no traces of built elements
distinction: No built elements are seen in the painting, and its mode of spatial expression cannot be determined; it is only marginally assigned based on the landscape arrangement.

evidence: In the valley slightly left of the painting's center: the roof of a building is visible, half-screened by the surrounding mountain rocks and trees, presenting spatial layering deeply hidden within the valley. | Lower part of the painting: a person with a staff walks between the mountain foot and the trees, suggesting a route of movement through the landscape, but the building itself mainly relies on the screening of mountain rocks to establish its position.
distinction: Although a figure walking in the lower part of the painting suggests a path, the central compositional role of the building is to be screened by mountain rocks and woodland, highlighting the concealment-and-revelation relationship rather than emphasizing the process of entry.

evidence: Lower left: a person stands on a small bridge; the bridge connects the two banks, forming a clear ferry or passage node. | Lower middle to right: a small path extends from beside the bridge, passing through gaps between trees and rocks, leading to the built elements on the right. | Right middle ground: at the water's edge stands a pavilion-style building with column bases and railings, and the path's endpoint points to this place, forming an enterable and reachable spatial relationship.
distinction: Although the building on the lower right is screened by trees, the core spatial organization of the painting is the process of movement through the landscape in which the bridge and path guide the figure toward the built elements, rather than a purely concealment-and-revelation layering.

evidence: Lower right: a bridge is seen spanning and connecting the two banks, implying a passage route. | Lower middle: traveling figures are seen moving along a path, pointing toward the depths of the painting. | Upper left and center: built elements are distributed according to the mountain terrain, partly screened by trees, forming spatial connections with the path and bridge.
distinction: Although the painting has built elements constructed according to the mountains, the entry clues formed by the bridge, path, and traveling figures are more prominent, emphasizing the spatial process of movement through the landscape.

evidence: Lower right: a house compound is partly screened by palm trees on the right and tall trees on the left, revealing only the roof, courtyard walls, and figures within the courtyard, forming a layering of concealment and revelation. | Lower middle to lower right: the built elements are hidden behind dense woods and foreground rocks, with the screening by woodland highlighting their secluded and hidden spatial position.
distinction: Although the houses face the water and lean against rocks, the painting emphasizes more the screening-and-revealing relationship of the woodland to the buildings, rather than placement solely according to terrain.

evidence: Lower part of the painted panel, slightly left: a thatched pavilion or small house is visible on a sloping rock, its roof outline clear, its walls or columns faintly visible. | Lower center and foreground of the painted panel: in front of the thatched pavilion, clumps of bamboo or reed-like plants screen it, and tall trees surround it behind and to the right; the main body of the building is partly obscured by plants, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | The painted panel as a whole: distant mountains in pale shadow, unpainted water in the middle ground, and sloping rocks and trees in the foreground screening the building, forming foreground-background spatial layering.
distinction: Although the building's position on the waterside sloping rock has a scenic-accent quality, what is visually more prominent is the screening layering formed by the building being obscured by foreground plants and trees, which conforms to the definition of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Middle right: a wooden bridge spans the water connecting the two banks, linking the foreground space with the wooded house area behind, suggesting a route of movement through the landscape. | Lower center: a thatched pavilion is built on a rocky jetty at the water's edge, with steps in front of the pavilion and a figure standing before it, presenting a state of approaching or pausing at the built element. | Center: a group of houses is hidden within dense woods, revealing only roofs, connected to the foreground by the bridge, forming spatial layering from light into dark and turning into the depths.
distinction: Although the houses in the center present a concealment-and-revelation relationship screened by woodland, the painting clearly constructs, through the bridge, steps, and figure positions, a traversable path leading from the foreground pavilion deeper toward the middle-ground houses; spatial connectivity and the sense of entry dominate the composition.

evidence: Upper right of the painting: house roofs and walls are visible, half-hidden behind dense woods and mountain rocks, presenting the concealment-and-revelation relationship of a house seen within the woods. | Lower right of the painting: a house stands at the waterside, forming foreground-background layering with the woods behind, serving as a partly screened element of the scene.
distinction: Although the houses accentuate the scene, the sense of spatial layering formed by their being half-screened by woodland and mountain rocks is more prominent and dominates the compositional method.

evidence: Lower part of the painting: a stream winds, a person walks along the stream bank, and the gaze and water flow lead toward the middle ground. | Lower middle of the painting: an arched bridge is built over the stream, connecting the two banks, and beyond the bridge leads to a courtyard with a fenced gate. | Lower middle courtyard of the painting: figures interact at the courtyard gate, and there are people inside the courtyard, presenting the spatial process of entering the built elements via the bridge, path, and gate.
distinction: Although the houses are sited against the mountains and beside the water, the painting emphasizes more, through the stream, small bridge, courtyard gate, and figure activity, the traversable process of entering the built elements from outside via paths.

evidence: Lower right: a wooden bridge is seen spanning a stream, with horseback travelers and a servant carrying a load on the bridge, proceeding toward the courtyard. | Middle right: the courtyard wall has an open gatehouse, with a person visible inside the gate, and behind the gate a building roof screened in the trees, forming an enterable spatial connection. | Middle left: the waterside and sloped rocks on the left form an extension of the path, guiding the gaze to converge toward the courtyard gate.
distinction: Although the painting has the concealment-and-revelation relationship of trees screening buildings, the entry-through-movement clues formed by the bridge, path, and gate are more prominent and dominate the painting's spatial organization.

evidence: Lower part of the painting: two figures (a scholar and a boy attendant) are seen walking upward along a winding mountain path and stone steps, forming a clear clue of movement through the landscape. | Upper middle of the painting: at a mountain cliff and valley mouth, built elements (a pavilion or house) are visible, and the direction in which the path extends suggests the spatial process of leading to this place. | Lower middle of the painting: dense woods and the mountain path interweave, strengthening the visual guidance from outside to inside and into a secluded setting.
distinction: Although the built elements are screened by woodland and mountain rocks (C2), the painting emphasizes more, through the action and path of the figures below moving deep along the mountain path, the enterable and reachable spatial process, so C4 is dominant.

evidence: Left: an arched bridge spans the water, with pedestrians on the bridge, forming a clear passage clue. | Lower right: a waterside building (water pavilion) is connected to the bank by a small bridge, and there are boats on the water, presenting a reachable and traversable spatial relationship. | Lower left: several houses are arranged in scattered fashion on the sloped ground at the mountain foot, forming spatial connections with the mountain rocks and waterside.
distinction: Although the painting has buildings sited against the mountains and beside the water, the movement-through-the-landscape clues formed by the bridge, pedestrians, and boats are more prominent, emphasizing the spatial process of going from here to there.

evidence: Middle ground: houses are screened within bamboo groves and tree clumps, revealing only roofs and partial structures | Right bank: a bridge is seen spanning the water, connecting the two banks | Lower part: at the water's edge a pavilion is built against rocks
distinction: The painting mainly organizes spatial layering through the screening and revealing of houses by woodland, rather than emphasizing an enterable path process.

evidence: Lower right of the painting: among dense trees and mountains and rocks, the roof and part of the wall of a house are visible, partly screened by the tree trunks and foliage in front. | Lower middle of the painting: the built structure is hidden deep among the trees, and through the screening of the foreground trees presents a spatial layering of intertwined concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although there are gaps among the trees and mountains and rocks in the painting, no clear movement-through-the-landscape clues such as a bridge, path, or gate are seen directly connecting to the built structure; the scene is formed mainly through relations of occlusion.

evidence: Lower left corner: a wooden bridge is visible spanning a stream, with pedestrians on the bridge, connecting to the path entering the painting. | Lower middle to right of the painting: the path winds upward, connecting the foot of the mountain with the houses at the mountainside and beside the rocks, forming an accessible route. | Mountainside and lower right: the houses are arranged against mountains and rocks and trees, connected to the external space through visible paths.
distinction: Although the houses are arranged according to the mountain terrain, the painting clearly constructs, through the bridge, path, and figures, spatial clues that are enterable and traversable, placing more emphasis on the process of entering the scene.

evidence: Center of the lower half of the painting: an arched bridge is visible spanning the water, connecting the slopes and building clusters on both banks, forming a clear clue of crossing and entry. | Both banks in the lower half of the painting: dense houses spread along the waterside and slopes, interconnecting with the bridge, paths, and water system, presenting a traversable spatial organization.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited against mountains and beside water, the movement-through-the-landscape clues formed by the bridge and the paths along the banks are more prominent in the painting, emphasizing the spatial process of passing from one place to another.

evidence: Lower right: a thatched pavilion is built on the waterside, with a person seen sitting upright inside; the pavilion itself is partly screened by the branches and foliage of the trees in front. | Lower left: a person walks along the waterside, moving toward the thatched pavilion on the right, forming a clear clue of approach and arrival.
distinction: Although the thatched pavilion identifies a scenic spot on the waterside, the painting, through the movement line of the figure below walking along the waterside toward the thatched pavilion, places more emphasis on the enterable and reachable spatial process.

evidence: Lower right of center: a thatched pavilion is built on rocks at the waterside, with a person seen sitting alone inside. | Lower center to right: the trunks and foliage of several trees interpose in front of and on both sides of the thatched pavilion, partially screening the pavilion itself, presenting a layered relationship of screening among the trees. | Lower part as a whole: through the screening of the nearby trees and the revelation of the open water surface behind, the thatched pavilion constitutes a pictorial depth of alternating concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the thatched pavilion identifies a scenic spot at the waterside, the clear front-to-back screening and concealment relation of the trees to the pavilion is more prominent in the composition, so it is classified as C2.

evidence: Lower left: a thatched pavilion is visible built on rocks of the sloping bank, with several people seated around inside. | Around the thatched pavilion at lower left: the thatched pavilion is partially screened by the trees and rocks of the foreground, presenting a spatial layering of half concealment and half revelation.
distinction: Although the thatched pavilion serves as a scenic accentuation, its relation of forming layers of concealment and revelation through trees and rocks and participating in the construction of the setting is more significant.

evidence: Lower left and lower right: at the lower left corner a thatched pavilion is built by the water, beside it a small bridge crosses a stream; at the lower right corner figures walk on the sloping bank, and a small boat carrying people is on the water, forming movement-through-the-landscape clues from water to bank and from path to pavilion. | Middle ground and right bank: storied buildings are visible between the mountainside and the rock face on the right, interpenetrating with the mountains and rocks and trees, suggesting spatial layers that can be explored deeply.
distinction: Although buildings are screened among the mountain forest, elements such as the boat, bridge, path, and pavilion together construct a clear process of entry and traversal, and the spatial orientation is more prominent.

evidence: Lower right: a wooden bridge spans a stream, with pedestrians on the bridge, connecting the two banks and forming a clear movement-through-the-landscape clue. | Lower left: the thatched pavilion has a platform and railings, with a lofty scholar inside; together with the bridge and the waterside it constitutes an enterable and traversable spatial organization. | Mountainside in the middle ground: storied buildings are faintly visible, suggesting a path along which the line of sight extends into the depth of the painting.
distinction: Although there is screening by trees, the connection of bridge, path, and buildings constitutes a dominant relation of traversal and entry rather than a mere layering of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Below the cliff on the lower right side: houses are located at the base of the cliff, partly screened by the branches and foliage of tall foreground trees; the eaves, walls, and people inside the houses are revealed, presenting a layering of seeing houses in the forest through concealment and revelation. | Waterside at the lower left corner: a small pavilion or shed structure stands by the water, adjacent to mountains and rocks and trees, as an accent at the waterside.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed against the cliff, the visual focus of the painting lies in the screening and revelation of the buildings by the foreground trees, forming spatial layers, so concealment and revelation (C2) is more dominant than terrain-responsive siting (C1).

evidence: Lower part of the painting: an arched bridge spans a stream, with pedestrians crossing on the bridge, constituting a clear movement route and spatial connection. | Left-center of the painting: among the pine woods halfway up the cliff, the roof of a building is faintly visible, presenting a layer screened by trees.
distinction: The bridge and pedestrians in the lower part of the painting constitute a clearly discernible path of entry and connection, whose organizing role as a movement-through-the-landscape clue is more prominent than the mere screening of the middle-ground buildings.

evidence: Middle left: a pavilion building is visible, with its roof and columns half screened by the surrounding trees and clouds and mist, presenting an evident relation of concealment and revelation. | Middle ground: a wooden bridge spans the water, with pedestrians on the bridge, but the direct connection between the bridge and the building is not clearly shown in the painting.
distinction: The building in the painting presents spatial layers mainly through screening by trees and clouds and mist (C2), rather than serving as a clear endpoint or entrance of a movement route (C4).

evidence: Bottom center: an arched bridge spans the water, with a pedestrian carrying a load walking on the bridge, connecting the paths on both banks. | Lower right corner: amid screening trees there is a gatehouse and courtyard walls, with figures pausing in front of the gate, forming an enterable node. | Left bank: figures walk along the waterside, and the path extends into the depth of the painting, suggesting a traversal route.
distinction: The waterside pavilion and the small pavilion on the mountainside serve as scenic accentuation, but the arched bridge at the bottom, the gatehouse on the right, and the figures' walking paths together constitute a clearer spatial process of entry and traversal, so C4 is more appropriate.

evidence: Lower left: a large waterside pavilion building, with railings and figures inside, its base extending to the water's edge. | Lower center: a flat bridge spans the water, connecting the pavilion on the left with the shoreline on the right, forming a clear passage. | Right bank: a small pavilion is visible amid screening trees, together with the bridge constituting a reachable endpoint or node of traversal.
distinction: Although the building is erected beside the water, the connecting role of the bridge in the painting is more prominent, clearly organizing the spatial process of entry and traversal from left to right and from one place to another.

evidence: Lower left: most of the thatched hut is screened by the branches and foliage of a large luxuriant tree, revealing only the eaves, part of the columns, and the people inside, forming an evident relation of concealment and revelation. | Lower left to center: the branches of the trees interlace with the roof of the thatched hut; natural scenery as foreground screens the main body of the built structure, indicating the spatial layer in which the building is situated.
distinction: Although the thatched hut is built on a rocky earthen platform against the mountain, the painting places more emphasis on the screening and revelation of the building by the large tree, and the concealment-and-revelation relation is the dominant spatial expression.

evidence: Whole painting: the painting consists mainly of mountain peaks, clouds and mist, pine trees, and a herd of deer; no traces of man-made built structures such as houses, bridges, or paths are seen.
distinction: There are no identifiable built elements in the painting, so no substantive judgment of spatial relations can be made; it is only tentatively assigned based on the overall deep and secluded woodland atmosphere.

evidence: Right center: houses are hidden behind the mountain foot and trees, revealing only the roof and part of the eaves, presenting a layering of seeing houses through intervening scenery. | Lower right corner: the building cluster is distributed along the slope, surrounded and screened by dense trees, forming a concealment-and-revelation relation of dwellings in the forest.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed on mountain slopes and platforms, the painting visually places more emphasis on the screening and revelation of the buildings by trees, mountains, and rocks, and the concealment-and-revelation relation is more dominant than the siting on the terrain.

evidence: Waterside at the lower left: a pavilion (or waterside pavilion) is built close to the shoreline, its lower platform meeting the water surface, extending in accordance with the waterside terrain. | Middle ground on the right: a building is faintly visible hidden between the slope platform and the trees, arranged according to the mountain terrain.
distinction: The built structure is clearly placed against the waterside terrain, presenting a correspondence of siting according to the ground, which is more dependent on terrain than mere scenic accentuation.

evidence: Lower middle: the main building cluster is heavily screened by several foreground trees (bare branches, pines), revealing only the roofs, eaves, and part of the walls, presenting a spatial layering of seeing houses through trees and houses hidden in the forest. | Upper middle: a building is placed in a recess embraced by mountains and rocks, which screen it, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relation of seeing houses behind rocks or among mountains. | Overall composition: the built structures form a tight relation of screening and revelation with the trees and mountains and rocks; natural scenery participates in dividing space, placing the buildings at a secondary or hidden level.
distinction: Although the buildings in the upper middle have the characteristic of being sited according to the mountain terrain (C1), the overall visual focus of the painting lies in the strong screening and revelation of the building cluster by trees and mountains and rocks, and the compositional role of concealment and revelation is more dominant.

evidence: Lower left: a thatched-roof pavilion is built on the water surface, supported underneath by wooden piles, placed directly according to the waterside and water-surface conditions. | Right lower middle: amid screening trees, a railed platform or part of a building is visible, arranged according to the mountain terrain and woods.
distinction: Although the thatched pavilion identifies the waterside scenery, its placement on piles in the water and built according to the bank highlights the correspondence between terrain and built structure, so C1 is more dominant than C3.

evidence: Lower center of the painting: a thatched hut is surrounded by tall withered trees and clumps of bamboo; the trunks and foliage screen part of the roof and walls, forming a concealment-and-revelation relation. | Inside the thatched hut: through the open doors and windows, the people inside are visible, showing the building revealing a scene of life amid natural screening.
distinction: The core of the painting lies in the layered relation of the building being screened and revealed by trees and bamboo groves, rather than placement according to terrain or guidance by paths.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: the building cluster (roofs, walls, and people inside are visible) is surrounded by several trees, presenting a layout of seeing houses in the forest. | Left of and above the buildings: the branches and leaves of tall pines extend over and in front of the buildings, forming an evident relation of screening and revelation with the built structures. | Right of the buildings: trees and buildings are adjacent and juxtaposed, and front-to-back occlusion enhances the spatial layers.
distinction: Although the buildings are one of the visual foci, the surrounding and screening of the buildings by trees (the concealment-and-revelation relation) is more prominent in organizing spatial layers, consistent with concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower left: a thatched hut or thatched pavilion is visible built close against the waterside and a rocky base, its roof and walls following the undulations of the terrain. | Beside the thatched hut at lower left: a small bridge connects the waterside with the platform where the thatched hut stands, and the building layout clearly unfolds according to the waterside and slope conditions. | Lower middle of the painting: figures stand on the platform, and together with the thatched hut and bridge they constitute a built ensemble arranged according to the terrain.
distinction: Although the bridge and figures in the painting suggest a path (C4), the placement of the thatched hut against the waterside rocks (C1) is the most principal feature determining its spatial relations.

evidence: Lower right corner: a pavilion (or waterside pavilion) is visible, revealing its roof, railings, and columns, its main body partly screened by the trunks and foliage of the foreground pines. | Center and right of the painting: tall pines occupy the main position, their foliage and trunks screening the pavilion behind, creating a spatial layering of seeing houses deep in the forest. | Lower middle: two people sit facing each other on a rocky platform, in front of the pine woods and the pavilion, further clarifying the front-to-back spatial relation of screening.
distinction: Although the pavilion serves to identify the waterside scenery, its partial screening by the pine woods and its spatial layering of alternating concealment and revelation are the most principal features of the painting's composition.

evidence: Left edge, slightly below center, behind the bamboo clumps and sloping rocks near the bank: a conical roof-cover-like object with radiating parallel lines emerges from behind the bamboo clumps; below it no column shafts, walls, or platform base are seen; suspected to be the roof of a thatched shed but cannot be confirmed | Water surface at lower center: a small boat with a curved bamboo canopy, one person in the boat holding a pole, the bow pointing toward the bamboo clumps screening the left bank; between the boat and the bank is unpainted water surface, with no dock or path seen connecting them | Upper far-bank terrace: a row of trees on a high, flat slope platform; no traces of built structures such as buildings or railings are seen on the terrace edge or the cliff face; the center is a large area of unpainted water surface
distinction: The suspected built structure appears through a concealment-and-revelation relation in which the roof is revealed and the lower body is hidden in the bamboo clumps, while the boat's movement clue is separated from it by water, with no discernible connecting or entry path, so the layering of concealment and revelation is closer to the visible relations than the process of traversal

evidence: Middle ground on the right: behind the trees and mountains and rocks, the roof of a building is faintly revealed, presenting a half-screened, half-revealed relation of concealment and revelation. | Water surface at the lower right corner: a small boat is on the water, as an accent of movement on the water.
distinction: Although the small boat in the painting suggests movement on the water, between the boat and the screened houses on the bank there is no clear entry path or connecting clue; the houses mainly form layers of concealment and revelation through trees, mountains, and rocks, so C2 is more appropriate.

evidence: Lower right and lower middle: the roofs, walls, and windows of several houses are half screened and half revealed among dense tree clusters, presenting evident spatial layers of concealment and revelation. | Lower left: at the edge of the woods on the left, a pavilion or bridge structure is faintly visible, likewise partly screened by branches and foliage, merging into the woodland setting.
distinction: Although there are clues of paths or bridges in the painting, the built structures construct spatial layers mainly through the screening and revelation of trees, and the characteristic of concealment and revelation is more prominent and dominant.

evidence: Lower left: an elaborate storied building is partly screened by the branches of foreground pines and by mountains and rocks, forming rich layers of concealment and revelation. | Middle ground: between mountain rocks and ravines, the roofs and walls of buildings are faintly visible, deeply screened by mountain forms and trees, revealing only parts. | Lower right: building roofs are revealed from behind withered trees and mountains and rocks, continuing the spatial organization of screening.
distinction: The primary category emphasizes the spatial layers formed by buildings being screened and revealed by mountains and rocks and trees; the alternative explanation emphasizes buildings placed according to terrain; in the painting multiple buildings are deeply hidden behind mountains, and the screening characteristic is more prominent.

evidence: Lower middle: a waterside pavilion stands at the water's edge supported on wooden piles, with figures seated upright inside. | Lower right side: between the rock face and the pines there is a clear small path/plank walk, with a person walking along it; the path connects toward the waterside pavilion, forming an enterable spatial clue.
distinction: Although the waterside pavilion is built against water and mountain and has C1 characteristics, the painting clearly depicts the movement-through-the-landscape clue of a figure walking along the path toward the built structure, emphasizing the process of entry and arrival, so C4 is more dominant.

evidence: Lower left middle: a thatched-roof building leans against the rocky sloping bank, part of its body and roof screened by the branches and foliage of a large tree hanging down from above, forming a concealment-and-revelation relation. | Left side: the platform in front of the building and the area of figures' activity are partly enclosed by the tree trunks on the left and the canopy above, presenting a spatial layering of seeing houses in the forest.
distinction: Although the building is erected against the mountain, the painting places more emphasis on the screening and revelation of the building by branches and foliage, creating spatial layers through concealment and revelation, so C2 is more appropriate.

evidence: Lower left middle: a group of houses is built beside the water, with supporting structures visible underneath extending into the water, the layout following the waterside terrain. | Lower left corner: two adults and a child stand on the bank facing the water and the buildings, suggesting a path leading to the buildings. | Right side and upper middle of the painting: mountains and rocks are layered, and waterfalls and flowing springs converge into the water surface below, providing the buildings on the left with an environmental background of mountains and water.
distinction: The terrain-responsive layout of the buildings erected beside the water is the clearest spatial relation in the painting; although the figures' path suggests enterability, as a compositional dominant it is less tight than the combination of buildings and terrain.

evidence: Lower middle: a wooden bridge spans the waterfall and stream, its deck fitted with railings; two figures stand or walk on the bridge, forming a clear crossing point over the water. | Middle right: to the right of the bridge, a winding mountain path with railings connects to it, the path extending along the lie of the mountain into the depths of the woodland on the right, suggesting a route by which the journey may continue. | Overall composition: the waterfall, stream, bridge and path connect with one another and, together with the figures on the bridge, form a spatial journey from this bank to the far bank and from the near to the deep.
distinction: Although the bridge is built in response to the water and has a terrain-responsive character, the painting places greater emphasis on the movement-through-landscape thread formed by the bridge and path and on the figures' activity within it, foregrounding an enterable, traversable spatial process; C4 is therefore more apt.

evidence: Lower right: a single figure sits alone on a rock facing the water, with pine branches extending beside him, forming the visual focus of the painting. | Main subject: tall mountains and rocks and dense pines occupy most of the space, while the unpainted space below represents the water surface, creating a contrast between openness and seclusion.
distinction: No built elements are clearly identifiable in the painting; the figure seated by the water defines the scene and, as the visual focus, serves to accentuate it rather than to show a terrain-responsive relationship between architecture and landform.

evidence: Middle left: a figure sits in a small boat moored by the waterside beside rocks and trees. | Upper part: a large area of unpainted space represents the water surface, with distant mountains stretching across, presenting an open lake-and-mountain space. | Lower part and right side: rocks and trees form the near-ground waterside, creating a spatial enclosure.
distinction: The painting contains no clear architectural entity; only the boat suggests movement through the landscape and entry onto the water, so it is classed as C4 rather than scenic accentuation.

evidence: Lower-middle flat slope: a single figure is visible sitting alone on a rocky flat by the water, facing the flying waterfall and high cliff to the right. | Beside the trees at lower left: another figure is visible standing next to broad-leaved plants (such as banana), echoing the seated figure. | Whole painting: the picture is dominated by high cliffs, flying waterfalls, pines and the waterside, and no clearly identifiable artificial built elements such as houses, pavilions or bridges are present.
distinction: The figures in the painting are placed in viewing positions, serving to define and concentrate the mountain-and-water scenery rather than to show path clues for entering into the depths.

evidence: Middle ground, right of center: the roofs of several houses are visible in a mountain hollow, partly screened by the surrounding trees and rocks, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Middle ground, left of center: buildings are also present, likewise screened by trees and not directly or fully exposed. | Overall composition: the buildings, through the screening and revealing of natural features such as rocks and trees, present spatial layering among the woods and behind the rocks.
distinction: Although a road with carts and horses runs through the lower part of the painting, the most prominent compositional role of the middle-ground buildings is the relationship of concealment and revelation formed with natural features, rather than an emphasis on a path of entry.

evidence: Middle left: a group of buildings is surrounded by dense trees, their roofs and walls looming faintly among the groves, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Middle right: houses are partly screened by trees, with only parts of their structure exposed, embodying the spatial layering of seeing houses within the woods. | Lower part: the houses and dock facilities in the near ground are likewise screened by trees, reinforcing the effect of concealment and revelation.
distinction: The painting creates spatial layering mainly through the screening and revealing of buildings by trees, rather than emphasizing a path of entry.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: two figures are visible seated by the water, surrounded by trees and rocks, but no clearly identifiable built structures such as houses or pavilions are present. | Right side: a waterfall and flowing water are visible, and the space shows a certain layering and relationship of concealment and revelation, but built entities are lacking.
distinction: No built elements are clearly identifiable in the painting; the classification is the closest category based solely on the overall spatial layering of landscape and figures.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: a winding red railing/bridge structure is visible, with a scholar standing on it, forming a clear movement-through-landscape thread. | Foreground to middle ground: the path/bridge extends from lower right toward upper left, passing beneath pines and guiding the eye into the depths of the landscape.
distinction: The painting organizes space through the winding bridge/path and the figures' movement, emphasizing the process of entering and journeying, in keeping with the characteristics of access to secluded settings.

evidence: Middle right of the painting: several houses are screened by trees and bamboo groves, with only roofs, eaves and parts of walls exposed, forming a clear layering of concealment and revelation. | Lower right: another building's roof is faintly visible amid screening trees, further reinforcing the sense of hidden houses in the woods.
distinction: Although the houses are built by the water, the painting presents their spatial layering mainly through screening and revealing by trees, so the feature of concealment and revelation is more prominent.

evidence: Lower left: a small canopied boat with figures aboard is visible floating on the water. | Right side and lower part: drooping willow branches and leaves and faint distant mountain silhouettes in pale ink are visible, with broad unpainted space representing the water.
distinction: No fixed built elements are present in the painting; only the boat serves as a scenic accent concentrating the waterscape, and no spatial path into architecture is presented.

evidence: Lower left to lower middle: a group of thatched huts is placed close against the foot of the great rocky slope on the left, the building outlines closely bound to the mountain-rock terrain, presenting the form of houses set against the rock. | Left side: the great mountain-rock slope extends from top to bottom, providing a clear base and support for the built structures below, which unfold with the lie of the mountain. | Right side and distance: towering cliffs and pines stand on the right, and the distance shows open water and distant mountains; no clear clues such as paths or bridges guiding entry are present.
distinction: Although the buildings are screened by trees, their terrain-correspondence in being placed tight against the rocky slope is more prominent, and no clear layering of concealment and revelation dominates the composition.

evidence: Lower center, left of center: between screening rocks and trees, the roof and part of the structure of a thatched hut are visible, partly screened by the surrounding features. | Right side and lower part: near-ground cliffs and dense trees screen and enclose the built structures below, creating a spatial layering of alternating concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the thatched hut lies among rocks, its most prominent compositional role is the relationship of concealment and revelation formed by screening with trees and rocks, rather than an emphasis on layout according to terrain.

evidence: Lower-left water: a figure is visible in a small boat on the water, defining the scenery of the open water area. | Lower-right edge: behind the trees there is a fragment that appears to be part of a building eave or wall, but it is heavily screened and incomplete, making it difficult to confirm as a complete built structure. | Left side: a gently sloping cliff bank meets the water, and no clear layout of built structures responding to the mountain terrain is present.
distinction: The painting lacks clear, complete built structures and mainly features a small boat on the water as a scenic accent, so it is classed as C3.

evidence: Middle-lower right: amid screening rocks and trees, a flat-roofed structure is visible with blurred outlines, suspected to be a pavilion or platform building, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Among the trees on the left: straight-line outlines are faintly visible behind the trees, suspected to be house buildings screened by vegetation.
distinction: The suspected built structures in the painting mainly present a layering relationship of being screened by rocks and trees, rather than a clear layout responding to terrain.

evidence: Lower right: a thatched pavilion is built on a stone platform at the waterside, with steps at the platform edge leading down to the water, presenting a layout of a building set on a platform and placed along the bank. | Lower right: the pavilion is surrounded by pines and other trees, but the main built structure is clearly visible, and the base forms a clear correspondence with the waterside terrain.
distinction: Although the pavilion serves as a scenic accent as a place of human activity, the painting more clearly shows the terrain-responsive placement of the built structure relying on the waterside terrace and setting steps down to the water, so C1 is more dominant.

evidence: Lower right: figures are active inside an open pavilion, which is partly screened by the bamboo grove in front and the tall trees on the right. | Middle-lower right: behind the pavilion, the roof of another building is faintly visible, screened amid dense groves, forming a front-to-back layering.
distinction: Although the pavilion is built on the rocky bank by the water, the painting emphasizes more the spatial layering formed by buildings being screened and revealed by trees and bamboo, rather than placement simply according to terrain.

evidence: Lower right: a large pavilion complex is set tight against the foot of the cliff on the right, unfolding level by level on platform bases, presenting a layout of buildings set against the cliff and built on platforms. | Lower left: pavilion structures sit on a slope, surrounded by trees, presenting a form of separate placement according to the slope. | Lower part of the painting: the building complex as a whole lies on the mountain-foot slope terraces and cliff edge, placed according to the terrain's height and the shoreline, corresponding to the natural configuration.
distinction: Although the buildings on the left are screened by trees, the buildings in the painting (especially the grand pavilion on the right) more markedly embody terrain-responsive layout against the cliff, along the slope and following the bank, rather than mainly relying on screening to form the scene.

evidence: Lower right: a stone arch bridge is visible spanning the stream, connecting the travelers' path with the built area on the right. | Lower center to lower right: a rider and a companion carrying a load travel along the path and cross the bridge, presenting a spatial process of approaching the built structures. | Right side: a courtyard wall and gatehouse are screened among trees, with figures active before the gate, serving as the destination of the travel thread.
distinction: Although the painting has a relationship of concealment and revelation in which trees screen the buildings, the process of entry formed by the bridge and the travelers' path is clearer and more dominant in organizing the spatial relationships.

evidence: Middle-lower right: a pavilion emerges from the woods, with its roof, columns and railed platform visible. | Right foreground: the branches and leaves of foreground pines screen part of the building's structure, creating a spatial layering of alternating concealment and revelation.
distinction: The building mainly forms layering through screening and revealing by trees, blending into the woods, rather than serving as a striking node that defines a particular scene.

evidence: Middle-upper left: a red-roofed building is visible, its building body and base partly screened by the dead-tree branches and mountain rocks in front, with only the roof and part of the eaves exposed. | Right side and center: towering rocks and a waterfall form the background; the building leans against the mountain configuration, forming a front-to-back spatial layering through the screening of foreground trees and rocks.
distinction: Although the building is set against the mountain, the painting emphasizes more its relationship of concealment and revelation, half-hidden and half-shown through screening by trees and rocks, rather than simple terrain compliance.

evidence: Lower part to center: a figure is walking up along a winding mountain path that passes through gaps between trees and rocks, forming a clear entry clue. | Center: in the middle section of the path, a wooden fence or bridge structure is visible, suggesting the path's continuation and a spatial transition. | Upper left: the path extends toward a building complex screened among dense woods and cliffs, with clearly visible roofs and walls, constituting the destination of the journey.
distinction: Although the painting contains a relationship of concealment and revelation in which buildings are screened by woods, the path guidance of figures going deep into the mountain forest along the trail toward the buildings is the core thread organizing the whole pictorial space.

evidence: Middle left bank: a stretch of wall rises and turns with the slope ridge, and the houses within the wall are placed level by level on slope terraces, their bases unfolding with the rise and fall of the bank slope | Middle right bank: a small pavilion is placed at the top of a promontory terrace jutting into the water, its platform base at the water's edge and the pavilion standing on the platform | Lower water's edge: a waterside platform and water pavilion are set close to the bank rocks, with a moored boat beside them, their position following the indentation of the shoreline
distinction: The relationship of walls and houses being placed according to the rise and fall of slope terraces and shoreline runs through the middle section of the composition, whereas the figures and boat in the lower part, though visible, do not form a continuous entry thread connected with the built structures

evidence: Middle right: the roof, gable and eaves of the main building are exposed amid dense pines and mixed trees, forming a spatial layering in which the woods screen the hall. | Left side: the terrace pavilion on the left is partly screened by tree branches and leaves, with buildings and trees interlocking, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Lower middle: the stone steps and platform in front of the building meet the surrounding trees, further reinforcing the visual effect of built structures hidden among the woods.
distinction: Although the painting has bridge-and-path clues, the built structures present their spatial layering mainly through screening and revealing by trees, so the role of concealment and revelation is more prominent.

evidence: Middle left: house structures are hidden in dense groves, with only parts of roofs and walls exposed, presenting an obvious relationship of screening by woods. | Middle right: behind the grove, a small bridge is faintly visible spanning the water, facing the built structures on the left across the water. | Lower middle: a small boat with a person aboard is on the water, defining the activity of movement through the landscape on the water.
distinction: Although a bridge and boat in the painting suggest a movement-through-landscape thread, the dominant compositional mode is the concealment and revelation layering formed by built structures screened by woods, rather than an emphasis on a path of entry.

evidence: Lower right: a building's roof emerges amid screening woods, its lower structure screened by trunks and branches, forming an obvious relationship of concealment and revelation. | Lower right to lower middle: the building is hidden behind the trees on the sloped bank, the front-to-back arrangement of the trees indicating the existence of the built structure and the spatial depth in which it lies.
distinction: The building relies mainly on screening by trees to form layering and participate in the scene, rather than serving as a visual focus to concentrate or mark a particular landscape scene.

evidence: Lower left: several house roofs emerge from the woods, their bodies screened by branches and leaves, presenting the concealment-and-revelation relationship of seeing houses within the woods. | Lower right: a pavilion-type structure stands on the sloped bank by the water, screened by trees beside it, forming layering with rocks and the waterside. | Lower middle: on the water, a tiny bridge or path connects the two banks, aiding spatial extension, but the main compositional feature remains the screening of built structures by woods.
distinction: The built structures in the painting present layering of concealment and revelation mainly through screening by trees, rather than emphasizing a layout corresponding to terrain and the waterside.

evidence: Lower center: an open waterside pavilion is surrounded by foreground pines and mixed trees, whose trunks and branches clearly half-screen the building's main body and the figures inside, presenting the layering of seeing houses within the woods. | Right middle ground: behind rocks and trees, parts of a pavilion's roof and eaves are exposed, the building's main body screened by natural features, constituting the concealment-and-revelation relationship of seeing houses across a screen.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed by the water, the painting emphasizes more the wrapping and screening of buildings by trees and rocks, with the concealment-and-revelation relationship playing a dominant role in the composition, rather than simple terrain compliance.

evidence: Lower left: two figures walk along a path on the sloped bank toward a waterside pavilion, presenting a clear relationship of progression and approach to built structures. | Middle ground left: a house is hidden among the pines, with a path and stream extending in front, suggesting an attainable travel clue. | Middle ground: the stream bank winds, and gaps between rocks and trees guide the eye into the distance, connecting different built nodes.
distinction: Although woods screen the houses, the painting more prominently foregrounds the figures walking along the path toward the pavilion and the journey guided by the stream bank leading the eye, so the organizing role of access to secluded settings is stronger.

evidence: Lower middle: the stream winds, with a flat bridge spanning it and tiny figures on the bridge, forming a clear movement and crossing thread. | Middle-lower left: amid screening trees and rocks, the roof and walls of buildings are faintly visible, indicating an attainable destination. | Overall composition: the stream rocks in the foreground, the bridge and figures in the middle ground, and the deep distant rocks together construct a spatial process from near to deep and from this side to the other.
distinction: Although the painting has a concealment-and-revelation relationship in which buildings are screened by woods, the movement thread formed by the bridge, stream and figures has a more significant and coherent guiding role in organizing the space.

evidence: Lower part, left of center: a simple wooden bridge is visible spanning the stream, with a staff-carrying figure crossing it, connecting the spaces of the two banks. | Upper middle: a waterfall flows down among the rocks and joins the stream below, together with the bridge forming a clue to spatial connection within the landscape.
distinction: No built entities such as houses are present in the painting, but the bridge and figures form a clear thread of movement and entry, so it is classed as C4.

evidence: Lower middle: The building complex is largely screened by tall pines and trees, with only parts of the roofs, walls, and window lattices exposed, forming a concealment-and-revelation layering in which buildings are seen deep within the forest. | Upper middle, mountainside: Several houses are faintly visible, screened among the mountains, rocks, and trees, presenting a half-concealed, half-revealed spatial relationship.
distinction: Although two people walk along the waterside in the lower part of the painting, no clear path or entrance clue connecting to the buildings in the forest is visible; the dominant compositional role lies in the trees' screening of the buildings rather than in guiding a route of travel.

evidence: Right middle: The roof and upper walls of a building emerge from behind the mountains, rocks, and trees, while its lower half is screened by natural scenery. | Overall painting: The building presents a concealment-and-revelation relationship through the screening of the mountain rocks, forming a clearly layered pictorial depth.
distinction: Although the building leans against the mountain and beside the rocks, its most prominent compositional role lies in the spatial layering created by its being half-screened by the mountain rocks, rather than in a layout simply unfolding according to the terrain.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: The roof and beam-and-column structure of a building are faintly exposed between the pine forest and the mountains and rocks, with the main body of the building partly screened by branches and foliage. | Left lower middle of the painting: A corner of a house is visible behind a cluster of trees, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship in which it is screened by the woodland.
distinction: Although the building is situated within the mountain forest, the most prominent spatial expression in the painting is the woodland's screening and revealing of the building, rather than an emphasis on its layout following the mountain terrain.

evidence: Lower center of the painting: The roofs and walls of several houses are visible, partly screened by the pines and mountains and rocks in front, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Middle right of the painting: A pavilion or house built against the mountain is faintly visible, mostly screened behind trees and mountain rocks.
distinction: Although the built elements are constructed according to the mountain terrain, the painting places greater emphasis on the layering and sense of seclusion created by their being screened and revealed by the woodland and mountain rocks, so C2 is more apt.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: Several figures are visible sitting on the ground on a gentle slope beside a stream, surrounded by mountains, rocks, and trees. | Right side and lower part of the painting: Dense bamboo groves and a winding stream bank are visible; no clear traces of built elements such as buildings, bridges, or paths are seen.
distinction: There are no clear built structures in the painting; based on the relationship between the figures' activity and the mountain-and-water terrain, it is assigned to the closest category of terrain-responsive placement.

evidence: Lower right: A thatched pavilion is built directly on a protruding rocky platform, its site closely conforming to the form of the mountain rocks. | Middle left: Several houses are arranged in staggered fashion against the sloping bank at the foot of the mountain, following the undulations of the waterside and terrain. | Lower left: A small bridge spans the water connecting the two banks, with two people on the bridge, implying connectivity between the shores.
distinction: Although a small bridge in the painting provides a clue for entry, the most prominent compositional role of the built elements (thatched pavilion, houses) lies in their terrain-responsive placement relying on the rocky platform and the sloping bank at the foot of the mountain, so C1 is more dominant than C4.

evidence: Upper middle: A corner of a house is exposed in a recess of the mountain rocks beside the waterfall, half-screened by the surrounding mountains, rocks, and trees. | Lower part: Many figures are scattered throughout a large pine forest, with sloping rocks and faint paths among the trees; no other obvious large-scale built elements are seen. | Overall: The visible built elements are deeply hidden among the mountain rocks and woodland, forming spatial layering through screening and exposure.
distinction: Although the building identifies the scenery at the source of the waterfall, its concealment-and-revelation relationship, heavily screened by mountain rocks and woodland, is more prominent in the painting.

evidence: Upper left: A pavilion or terrace building is visible between the mountain rocks and trees, partly screened by branches and the mountain body, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Lower middle: Two people play the qin by the water, surrounded by dense trees with water flowing around them; no clear guiding path or entrance is seen.
distinction: The built elements in the painting mainly present spatial layering through the screening of woodland and mountain rocks; no obvious clues of terrain-responsive placement or paths guiding entry are seen.

evidence: Lower center of the painting: A person sits on a rock on the stream bank, facing the water ahead and the waterfall above. | Upper middle of the painting: A waterfall flows down among the mountain rocks and joins the stream below, screened by trees around it. | Upper left of the painting: There are inscriptions and seals mentioning scenery such as the flying spring, but no clear buildings or boats are seen.
distinction: There are no clear built elements in the painting, only figures and landscape; the stream guides the gaze and can barely be regarded as identifying the scenery or as a clue for travel, but there is no architectural entity.

evidence: Whole painting: The painting mainly depicts ancient trees, mountains and rocks, and a cold spring; no clear traces of artificial built elements such as buildings, bridges, or roads are seen.
distinction: No built elements are visible in the painting; based on the overall visible organization of natural landscape, it is assigned to the closest category.

evidence: Lower left: A thatched pavilion is built at the foot of the cliff by the waterside, with figures inside, identifying this as a place for viewing the scenery by the water. | Lower middle of the painting: The thatched pavilion is surrounded by trees and faces the water in front, contrasting with the towering cliff and flying waterfall, concentrating the landscape scenery of this spot.
distinction: Although the thatched pavilion is built on the waterside, its main role is to identify and concentrate the landscape scenery of this spot, rather than to emphasize a complex relationship of terrain adaptation.

evidence: Lower left: A flat bridge is visible spanning the water, with pedestrians on it, connecting the cliff on the left with the trees and built area on the opposite bank, forming a clear entry path. | Lower right: A winding plank walkway or bridge structure is visible, extending along the waterside and guiding the gaze toward the depth of the painting and toward the built area. | Lower middle: The built elements (houses) are located amid screening trees, and through the clues of the bridge and walkway in front, a reachable spatial relationship is presented.
distinction: Although the built elements are screened by trees (conforming to C2 features), the prominent bridge and winding walkway in the lower part of the painting constitute a strong clue for movement through the landscape, emphasizing the spatial process of passing from here to there and approaching the built elements; therefore C4 is more dominant.

evidence: Middle of the painting, slightly left: The roofs and walls of a group of buildings are visible, partly screened by the surrounding trees and mountain rocks, appearing faintly visible. | Around the buildings: Dense trees and undulating mountain rocks form screening in the foreground and middle ground, placing the buildings in a spatial layer that is half hidden and half revealed. | Overall painting: The buildings are located deep in the valley, and through the concealment-and-revelation relationship of natural scenery, the spatial depth and sense of seclusion of the painting are enhanced.
distinction: Although the buildings are constructed on mountain terraces, the painting more prominently highlights the layering of their being screened and revealed by trees and mountain rocks, rather than simply emphasizing terrain correspondence.

evidence: Middle of the painting, slightly lower left: A pavilion house is built on a rocky platform beside the waterfall, its site directly relying on the mountain-rock terrain. | Middle of the painting, slightly right: Several houses are visible among the trees on the hillside, distributed in staggered fashion following the slope.
distinction: Although the buildings are partly screened by trees, their placement relying on the rocky platform and hillside terrain is more prominent and dominates the spatial expression.

evidence: Lower right: A waterside pavilion or terrace is built directly on the sloping rocks of the waterside, its site closely conforming to the water surface and shoreline, presenting a posture of building in response to water. | Lower left: The building complex is arranged against the sloping bank, with roofs and platforms following the undulations of the terrain, forming a terrain-responsive placement relationship with the surrounding mountain rocks and waterside. | Middle right: Parts of building roofs are exposed amid screening trees; although there is a concealment-and-revelation relationship, the overall painting more emphasizes the integration of built elements with the terrain and waterside.
distinction: Although the middle-ground buildings are screened by woodland, the integration of the foreground built elements with the terrain and waterside in response to circumstances is clearer and more dominant, so C1 is more apt.

evidence: Right middle at the cliff: Houses are located behind the mountain rocks and trees, with only roofs and parts of the structure exposed, presenting a layering of houses seen behind rocks. | In the woods at the lower right corner: Multiple houses are screened within dense clusters of withered trees, with mainly roofs visible, presenting a spatial sense of houses hidden in the forest. | Left middle hillside: Houses are built against the slope, surrounded by trees, forming a half-concealed, half-revealed concealment-and-revelation relationship.
distinction: Although the buildings are distributed according to the mountain terrain, the visual focus of the painting lies in the screening of the buildings by trees and mountain rocks; the concealment-and-revelation relationship is more dominant in the spatial expression than terrain-responsive placement.

evidence: Lower left: A person riding a donkey is crossing a bridge spanning the stream, forming a clear route of movement. | Right lower middle: A courtyard entrance with doors is visible behind the trees, implying an accessible space. | Upper right: Pavilions and terrace buildings are screened between the mountain rocks and trees in the mountain hollow, serving as an extension of or destination along the route of movement.

evidence: Left and center of the painted panel: along both banks of the gorge stream, several sections of plank walkways with railings and bridges are arranged, winding along the edges of the mountains and rocks. | Middle of the painted panel: the plank walkway crosses the stream and connects the two banks, forming a clear continuous path that guides the gaze into the depths of the gorge.
