evidence: Left-hand painted panel: the painting mainly depicts sloping rocks, withered trees and a bamboo grove; no built elements such as houses or bridges are seen.
distinction: There is no identifiable built structure in the painting, so its specific compositional role cannot be determined; it is assigned only to the closest category.

evidence: Lower left corner: a person carrying something walks along the slope, creating a sense of movement and an implied path leading deeper into the woods. | Main body of the painting: the pine forest is dense, with tree trunks staggered front and back and branches and leaves interlacing, creating a sense of secluded depth extending into the distance.
distinction: Although there is no identifiable built structure in the painting, the dynamism of the figure walking deeper accords better with the implication of a spatial process of access to secluded settings than mere screening by woodland.

evidence: Lower right: a thatched hut is half-hidden behind withered trees, with only its roof and part of its wall visible, showing a clear relation of screening by woodland. | Left middle ground: on a slope terrace are layered buildings, faintly appearing among clumps of trees and mountain rocks, forming a front-to-back spatial hierarchy of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the built structures follow the mountain terrain, the painting emphasizes more their layered relation of screening and revealing by trees and mountain rocks; thus C2 is more dominant than C1.

evidence: Lower right: a multi-arch bridge spans the water, with pedestrians and riders crossing it and boats moored or moving beneath it, forming a node of land and water traffic. | Center: a broad street or embankment extends into the distance, lined on both sides with shops and houses, and pedestrians come and go on the street, guiding the eye deeper into the painting. | Center left: a city gate tower with an arched passage stands beside the street, people pass through the passage, connecting the spaces inside and outside the gate.
distinction: Although the placement of buildings along the road and water embodies terrain-responsive siting, what the painting highlights more is the role of traffic and movement cues such as the bridge, road, and city gate in organizing and guiding space, giving the painting an accessible and explorable process.

evidence: Left side: greenish-blue hills and trees are visible, with no trace of any built structure | Right side: decorative ground pattern, with no pictorial-center content
distinction: No built structure is seen in the painting; it is assigned to the closest category based on the overall organization of landscape.

evidence: Left-hand painted panel: the painting shows mountain rocks, sloping banks, trees and water on the left, presenting natural undulations of terrain; no clear traces of built structures such as houses, bridges or paths are seen.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built elements; on the basis of the overall visible mountain-rock and sloping-bank terrain, it is assigned to category C1, which most likely reflects siting according to terrain.

evidence: Left middle ground: a multi-story pagoda building is visible, with its pagoda body and top partly exposed and its base blocked by foreground earthen slopes and vegetation. | Center and left of the painting: dense woodland is interspersed, with trunks and branches forming front-to-back layers that screen the pagoda building, presenting the relation of concealment and revelation of seeing a house within the woods. | At the junction of pagoda and trees: the exposed part of the pagoda contrasts with the surrounding dense branches, clearly indicating that the building lies deep in the woodland and participates in forming the scene through screening and revealing.
distinction: Although the pagoda is a visual focus, the painting emphasizes more the screening and revealing of the building by trees, forming a spatial hierarchy of seeing a pagoda deep in the woods, rather than simply identifying a scenic spot.

evidence: Lower right: two figures walk along the foot of a mountain-rock slope deeper into the painting, presenting movement. | Center to upper right: gaps and slope paths form between the mountain rocks and trees, implying an extendable passable route.
distinction: No identifiable built structure is visible in the painting, but the sense of an explorable path formed by the figures' movement and the gaps among the mountain rocks is stronger than mere screening by woodland.

evidence: Left side: mountain rocks, sloping banks, and withered trees are visible; no clear trace of built structures | Right side: blank paper and seals, with no pictorial content
distinction: No built structure is seen in the painting, only natural landscape; it is assigned only tentatively based on the overall spatial organization.

evidence: Right side: mountain rocks and trees grow densely, forming the main subject of the near view with prominent forms. | Distance: rolling mountains lie on the far shore of the water, forming a spatial correspondence with the near view. | Overall: the composition presents a configuration of near-view trees and rocks confronting distant mountains, focusing on presenting a particular mountain-ridge scene.
distinction: The composition focuses on presenting the form and spatial position of a particular mountain-ridge scene (scenic accentuation), rather than on expressing the layering of buildings screened by natural scenery (concealment and revelation).

evidence: Upper right: a tile-roofed house is built on a stone base, and the trunks and branches of several trees interpose in front of the house, blocking part of the pillars and walls, forming a relation of screening. | Center and right of the painting: trees and mountain rocks are distributed in front of and to the side of the house, forming a clear front-to-back spatial hierarchy with the house, giving the built structure the visual effect of a house revealed within the woods.
distinction: Although the house is built on a base, the screening and revealing of the building by trees is more prominent in the painting, dominating the spatial hierarchy between the built structure and the landscape.

evidence: Right center of the painting: a stone arch bridge spans between rocks and woodland, connecting the two banks and forming a clear route of passage and entry. | Right side of the painting: the bridge interweaves with the surrounding bamboo groves and mountain rocks, and the unpainted space beneath the bridge arch implies the flow of water or an extension of space, guiding the eye to explore deeper.
distinction: As the core built structure, the bridge's main role is to provide a spatial cue for crossing and entry, rather than merely depending on terrain (C1) or serving as an isolated scenic spot (C3).

evidence: Right of center in the painting: a conical thatched structure (a thatched hut) is situated among the pine forest and mountain rocks, with a person seated inside. | Around the building: pine trees and rocks block part of the building's outline, creating a half-hidden, half-revealed visual effect with an evident relation of concealment and revelation. | Overall painting: the building is wrapped by the natural environment, and through screening by woodland it presents a secluded spatial hierarchy.
distinction: The painting emphasizes more the layered sense of the building screened by trees and mountain rocks (concealment and revelation), rather than simple adaptation to terrain (terrain-responsive siting).

evidence: Upper right: the roof and eaves of a building emerge from dense bamboo groves, and the building is partly blocked by the bamboo. | Overall painting: the building is deeply hidden in a wooded valley, and through the screening of the bamboo groves it presents a relation of concealment and revelation, forming a secluded spatial hierarchy.
distinction: Although the building is located in a wooded valley, its main visual feature is being revealed through the screening of bamboo groves, emphasizing a spatial hierarchy of concealment and revelation, rather than serving merely as a marker identifying a scenic spot.

evidence: Right-hand painted panel: a group of built structures is arranged in front and rear, high and low, according to the mountain terrain; the taller building at the rear is partly screened by mountain rocks and withered trees, with only its roof and upper structure exposed. | Lower part of the right-hand painted panel: the lower hall building in front is more exposed, with figures and columns visible inside, forming a clear spatial layering of concealment and revelation with the screened building behind.
distinction: Although the buildings are arranged according to the height of the terrain, the painting places greater emphasis on the layering of concealment and revelation and the pictorial depth created by screening the rear building with trees and mountain rocks.

evidence: Lower left of the right side of the painted panel (near the waterside): a roof (built structure) is visible emerging through screening clumps of trees; the main body of the building is screened by trees, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship of a house seen among woodland. | Middle of the right side of the painted panel: cloud and mist lock across the mountainside, separating the peaks above from the trees and built structures below, forming a front-to-back spatial layering; the built structure lies in the secluded depths below the cloud and mist. | Upper part of the right side of the painted panel: the inscription 'Woyun Shi' (Chamber of Sleeping Clouds) is located in the upper right corner; although it is text, together with the cloud-wreathed scene of the painting it implies that the built structure lies deep in the clouds, reinforcing the mood of screening and concealment (note: judged mainly on the basis of the visually observed screening relationships of the trees).
distinction: The built structure in the painting is tiny in scale and screened by trees and cloud and mist, mainly presenting a spatial layering of 'concealment' and 'revelation' (C2), rather than serving as a conspicuous landmark that points out the scenery (C3).

evidence: Right center: a built structure (a house) is set between mountain cliffs, with its walls and roof partly blocked by the rocks and pines in front, presenting a relation of concealment and revelation. | Inside the built structure on the right: through an unblocked window/door opening, a person is visible seated inside, indicating the existence of the building and its internal spatial hierarchy. | Right foreground: withered branches and rocks in the foreground together with the pines behind form a screening of the built structure, placing the building within the pictorial depth.
distinction: Although the building is set against the mountain cliff, the most prominent spatial expression in the painting is the hierarchy formed by the blocking and revealing of mountain rocks and trees, rather than simply emphasizing the base-site relation of siting according to terrain.

evidence: Upper middle of the right side of the painting: the roof and walls of courtyard buildings are partly blocked by the surrounding dense tree branches and leaves, presenting a spatial hierarchy of concealment and revelation within the woods. | Lower left and bottom of the right side of the painting: stone bases or pond banks and wooden railings are visible, forming with the buildings above a staggered front-and-back, high-and-low relation of screening.
distinction: The painting emphasizes more the relation of concealment and revelation in which buildings are surrounded and screened by trees, rather than the terrain-responsive relation of siting simply according to slope terraces.

evidence: Lower right: a railed bridge or waterside path is visible with two people standing on it, forming a clear movement cue. | Right side: the path extends along the waterside, flanked by willows, pines, and slope rocks, presenting a spatial relation of movement along the water.
distinction: Although there is screening by trees, the railed path and the figures' activity constitute a more dominant cue of entry and movement through the landscape; thus C4 is more apt than C2.

evidence: Right center of the painting: an open roofed structure (a well pavilion) has a well mouth visible inside, with steps and a railing in front. | Lower right corner of the painting: a person carrying a water bucket is walking toward the opening in the railing in front of the building, forming a clear route of approach to the built structure. | Around the building: dense trees stand behind and to the left of the building, partly screening it, but the steps and the figures' movement line clearly lead to the building's entrance.
distinction: Although the building is partly screened by trees (C2), the figures carrying water toward the well pavilion and the arrangement of steps and railing emphasize more the spatial process of proceeding from one place to another and approaching the built structure (C4).

evidence: Right side of the painting: the roof and walls of a building emerge from behind woodland, presenting a half-hidden, half-exposed hierarchy. | Left side of the painting: there are buildings at the foot of the mountain by the water, partly blocked by mountain rocks and trees. | Center of the painting: on the mountainside and at the foot of the main peak, building outlines faintly appear among woodland and mountain rocks.
distinction: Although the built structures in the painting follow the mountains and water, what is more prominent is their layered relation of concealment and revelation as screened and revealed by woodland and mountain rocks, rather than simple emphasis on siting according to terrain.

evidence: Lower left: waterside houses are surrounded by trees on the left and behind, with roofs and walls emerging from the clumps of trees, forming a relation of concealment and revelation. | Lower right: a waterside pavilion is built on the water, screened above and to the right by dense tree canopies, with only part of the roof and supporting structure exposed.
distinction: Although the built structures are erected by the water, the painting emphasizes more the spatial hierarchy formed by the screening and revealing of buildings by woodland, rather than simple siting according to terrain.

evidence: Foot of the mountain on the left: a group of houses is arranged along the foot of the mountain, with roofs and walls emerging between woodland and the mountain mass, with a fence in front, presenting a hierarchy half-screened and half-covered by trees and the mountain's form. | Center of the painting: dense clumps of trees block part of the boundary of the built structure, making the building faintly appear among the woods, and the relation of concealment and revelation participates in forming the scene. | Shoreline at lower right: two people walk along the waterside, but no clear bridge, path, or gate is seen connecting to the built structure on the left, and the movement cue does not run through.
distinction: Although the built structure is sited at the foot of the mountain, the painting highlights more the screening and revealing of the building by woodland and the mountain mass, and the role of concealment and revelation in forming the setting is stronger than siting according to terrain.

evidence: Lower water surface and rocky bank on the right: the painting shows an open water surface with steep rock walls and trees on the right, and below there is a small boat carrying a person (holding a pole); distant mountains on the left are painted in pale washes; no clear houses, buildings, or other built structures are seen.
distinction: The boat, as a vehicle of movement through the landscape, implies the process of entering the water surface and a cue for exploration, which fits the spatial organization of movement through the landscape better than simply identifying a scenic spot.

evidence: Lower center of the painting: a small boat is on the water with one person aboard, near the trees on the left bank. | Whole painting: the painting consists mainly of distant mountains, water surface, near sloping banks, and withered trees; no fixed built structures such as houses or pavilions are seen.
distinction: The painting lacks clear architectural built structures; only a small boat is seen as a scenic accent, with no other evident competing interpretation.

evidence: Lower right: two figures are visible standing on sloped rocks at the waterside, facing the high mountain and flying waterfall to the left, forming a clear viewing line of sight. | Left: a flying waterfall drops within high mountains and a deep valley, constituting the core scenery of the painting.
distinction: No explicit built elements are seen in the painting, but the figures' act of pausing to view the waterfall serves to identify and focus this landscape scenery, so it is classified as C3.

evidence: Lower left: a wooden bridge is visible connecting the left bank with a waterside building, and one person is walking on the bridge, forming a clear entry path. | Left waterside: the base of the waterside building (water pavilion) is set above the water surface and directly connects with the bridge, presenting an accessible spatial relationship. | Lower right: a thatched hut is concealed among trees and mountain rocks, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation with the surrounding environment and helping to enrich the painting's layering.
distinction: Although buildings in the painting are screened by trees, the movement clue of the figure crossing the bridge toward the water pavilion on the left is more prominent and dominates the sense of spatial entry.

evidence: Lower left: a thatched pavilion/house is visible built at the waterside, screened by trees nearby. | Lower center: a small bridge spans the stream, connecting the near-bank house with the wooded hills on the opposite bank. | Lower right: a small boat and figures are on the water surface, implying waterborne travel and the possibility of landing.
distinction: The bridge, stream, and houses together construct clear clues of connection and entry, which better embodies a traversable spatial process than mere siting against the mountains.

evidence: Lower right: a thatched hut is visible, with lines resembling a small path or shoreline extending in front of it, and a person sitting quietly nearby, implying a spatial process of approaching built elements or of traversable space. | Left waterside: a building with a flagpole is set at the waterside on a sloped platform, embodying the integration of building and terrain.
distinction: Although the building on the left embodies the feature of terrain-responsive siting in relation to the water (C1), the combination of path, figure, and thatched hut in the lower right more clearly expresses the spatial process of moving from here to there and approaching built elements, so C4 is more fitting.

evidence: Lower left: parts of a house roof and walls are visible, screened by sloped rocks and trees, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation | Left center: an arched bridge on the water surface connects the sloped banks on both sides | Left water surface of the painting: several sailboats form a near-far layering with the waterside built elements
distinction: Although a bridge in the painting implies a path, the concealment and revelation of the house in the lower left through tree screening is more prominent in the composition, so concealment and revelation is taken as primary.

evidence: Left center: a thatched pavilion is faintly visible behind trees and rocks, with only the roof and some pillars exposed, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship screened by natural scenery. | Right water surface: an arched bridge spans the water, connecting the two banks and implying accessibility of space, but it is not the core built focus of the painting.
distinction: The concealment and revelation of the thatched pavilion screened by trees and rocks is the most prominent feature of the built elements in the painting; although the bridge implies a path, the role of concealment and revelation is more dominant.

evidence: Lower left: an arched bridge is visible crossing the stream, connecting the foreground with the sloped bank of the middle ground, forming a clear passage clue. | Right lower center: the roof and walls of a house building are visible amid tree screening, located in the direction in which the bridge path extends. | Overall composition: the bridge, water surface, and sloped banks together form a path guiding the line of sight, presenting a spatial process of moving from here to there and approaching built elements deeper within.
distinction: Although the built elements on the right are screened by trees (C2), the entry path formed by the bridge and water system is more prominent in organizing spatial relationships and dominates the visual experience of access to secluded settings (C4).

evidence: Lower center of the painting: dense vertical wooden piles are drawn beneath the thatched hut, showing that the building is raised on stilts over the water and placed in accordance with the terrain of the stream bank. | Left to center of the painting: the rocky sloped bank on the left extends to the right, and the thatched hut is arranged on the flat ground between the mountain foot and the waterside, with its site closely corresponding to the natural terrain. | Behind the thatched hut: a bamboo grove (vertical lines) is visible behind the house; the building backs onto woodland and unfolds in reliance on the natural environment.
distinction: The building body is clear and complete, mainly displaying its placement logic of being raised over water and nestled between mountains and water, rather than emphasizing a concealment-and-revelation layering heavily screened by trees.

evidence: Right near bank: trees, bamboo grove, and faint outlines of figures are visible; no clear built structures such as houses, pavilions, or bridges are seen. | Left and center: the natural landscape organization of distant mountains, sloped banks, and open water is presented, with no traces of built elements.
distinction: No explicit built elements are seen in the painting; based on the overall visible organization of natural landscape and sloped banks, it is assigned to the closest category.

evidence: Lower center: an arched bridge spanning the water is visible, with a figure walking on it, forming a clear movement clue. | Lower right: the roof and walls of a pavilion built against the mountain are visible amid tree screening, and the bridge and path visually guide toward this built area. | Right: the gaps between trees and mountain rocks imply an extension of the path, connected with the bridge, presenting a spatial process of entering deeper areas.
distinction: Although the painting has a screening relationship in which trees block the pavilion, the entry clues formed by the bridge, walking figure, and path more directly organize the painting's sense of spatial movement through the landscape.

evidence: Lower left: a thatched pavilion is built at the waterside, its site conforming to the waterside terrain. | Lower right: several thatched huts are distributed along sloped rocks and woods, their layout unfolding with the terrain.
distinction: Although the built elements are screened by trees, their sites and layout more notably embody terrain-responsive placement in accordance with the waterside and sloped terrain.

evidence: Upper left: the roofs of two thatched huts are clearly exposed, while the building bodies and bases are screened by trees and clouds and mist, forming a spatial layering of seeing houses through intervening scenery. | Lower left: a wooden bridge spans across, but it does not show a complete continuous path directly leading to the thatched huts and mainly serves as a foreground element.
distinction: The concealment and revelation of the thatched huts through clouds, mist, and trees (screening) is the main expression of built elements in the painting; although a bridge exists, it does not form a clear complete movement clue leading to the built elements.

evidence: Left mountain cliff: a plank walkway with railings winds upward closely against the steep rock face, conforming to the mountain's form. | Lower central rocks: the viewing platform and railings where two people sit are built directly on the edge of a protruding rock, following the mountain's configuration. | Lower left: stone steps extend upward with the mountain's form, connecting to the platform area, embodying the integration of terrain and built elements.
distinction: Although there are path elements such as the plank walkway and stone steps in the painting (C4), the most prominent feature of the built elements (walkway, platform, railings) is that they completely attach to and conform to the form and direction of the mountain rocks, so C1 is more fitting.

evidence: Lower left to center of the painting: a large expanse of reeds grows densely, screening a moored small boat, whose hull is partly blocked by the reeds, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Center to right of the painting: the water surface is open, with faint distant shorelines, and a bright moon in the sky, creating an overall tranquil atmosphere.
distinction: The painting has no fixed built elements; only a small boat is screened by reeds to form layering, so it is assigned to C2; if the small boat moored against the waterside is regarded as terrain-responsive placement, it would be close to C1.

evidence: Center-right: a flat platform base or paved ground is visible, with one person kneeling and sitting on it, surrounded by trees. | Background and both sides: the trunks of many trees stand behind and to the right of the platform base, their canopies covering above, forming a space within the woods.
distinction: The built element (platform) is mainly presented within the spatial layering of a wooded space surrounded by trees, rather than emphasizing a placement relationship responsive to terrain undulation.

evidence: Lower left: a figure is visible standing on rocks at the bank, facing the open water surface to the right. | Right: steep mountain rocks and pines are visible, forming a water passage with the left bank slope. | Center: a large area of unpainted space represents the open water surface, implying that space extends into the distance.
distinction: No explicit built elements are seen in the painting; based on the figure standing at the waterside and the sense of spatial extension of the water passage, it is assigned only with difficulty to access to secluded settings, but it lacks direct evidence of buildings and paths.

evidence: Left middle ground: a city platform and gate tower buildings are visible, with an arched gate opening below, serving as the directional target of the path. | Lower to middle of the painting: a winding path runs among the gaps in the mountain rocks, and a person carrying a load on a shoulder pole walks along the path, with movement directed toward the city gate. | Overall spatial relationship: the path and the city gate (built elements) connect with each other, presenting a spatial process of approaching the built elements from the foreground and moving from here to there.
distinction: Although weeping willows screen the gate tower to form layering, the movement of the path and pedestrians clearly establishes an entry relationship leading to the city gate, and the sense of spatial process is more dominant.

evidence: Left: a person is visible sitting on a stone platform, with trees nearby; no clear buildings or structures are seen. | Center and background: the main subject of the painting is layered mountain rocks, a multi-tiered waterfall, and a pool below, constituting a complete landscape scene.
distinction: There are no clear buildings in the painting; the combination of the figure and stone platform serves more as a scenic accent element focusing the landscape scenery, rather than showing the relationship of buildings placed according to terrain.

evidence: Center: a simple building with a thatched roof is visible, with one person sitting upright before a desk inside. | Foreground and right: the building is partly blocked by dead trees in the foreground and pine branches on the right, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Below and around: the base of the building is surrounded by mountain rocks and miscellaneous trees, presenting a spatial layering screened within the mountain forest.
distinction: The painting mainly constructs spatial layering through the blocking and exposing of the building by trees and mountain rocks, rather than emphasizing the building's dependence on terrain or its role as a scenic marker.

evidence: Whole painting: the painting consists mainly of layered mountain rocks, dead trees, and a stream and waterfall on the left; no clear traces of built elements such as houses, pavilions, or bridges are seen.
distinction: The painting lacks built elements and mainly presents natural landscape scenery; regarding spatial relationships, the gaps between the stream and mountain rocks have a certain sense of vertical extension, but there are no clear entry clues or built nodes.

evidence: Center-right of the painting: a thatched-roof pavilion is partly blocked by pine trees and miscellaneous trees in front, with only the roof, pillars, and part of the eaves exposed, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Inside the pavilion: through the gaps between trees and the pillars, a person is visible sitting cross-legged in the pavilion, indicating the building's spatial layering and interior activity. | Middle ground of the painting: foreground trees, middle-ground buildings, and background mountain rocks and water form foreground-to-background blocking, reinforcing the pictorial depth of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the building is nestled against the waterside and mountain rocks, the most dominant compositional technique in the painting is to use the screening and exposing by trees to present the building's spatial layering, rather than emphasizing its layout generated by terrain.

evidence: Lower left: a thatched hut is half hidden behind sloped rocks and woods, with only part of the roof and walls exposed, forming a clear layering of concealment and revelation. | Upper center: a person stands at the mountain peak, echoing in near-far relationship with the screened thatched hut below, but no direct path connects them.
distinction: Although the thatched hut is nestled against the mountain and beside trees, its most prominent spatial feature is that it is revealed through screening by trees and sloped rocks; the concealment-and-revelation relationship is more prominent than terrain-responsive placement.

evidence: Lower center: in the lower center of the painting a figure sits on a flat rocky platform, facing a layered waterfall; no houses, pavilions, or other clear built elements are seen. | Whole painting: the main subject is mountain rocks, waterfalls, and trees, and an inscription in the upper right indicates that this is a specific scenery.
distinction: The painting has no clear built elements; the figure sitting on the rock identifies the scenery, so it is assigned to C3; if the sitting place is regarded as placed according to terrain, it would be close to C1.

evidence: Lower center: on a flat platform surrounded by mountain rocks, two people sit facing each other, with a small object placed beside them; no clear house building is present. | Upper right: there is an inscription 'Dongyuan Shi' and seals, which belong to inscriptions and are not visible building entities in the painting. | Overall: the mountain rocks are jagged and the trees are scattered; the platform where the figures are located is enclosed by the surrounding mountain forms, forming an open face.

evidence: Left center of the painting: a person is visible sitting cross-legged on a rocky platform; no clear traces of built elements such as houses or pavilions are seen. | Whole painting: the painting is dominated by layered rocks, a multi-tiered waterfall, and woods, and the figure is placed on a rocky platform.
distinction: The painting has no clear built elements; only a figure is placed on a rocky platform, and based on the overall spatial organization it is assigned to the closest category of terrain-responsive placement.

evidence: Lower center: within the surroundings of dense woodland (red leaves and green trees) there is an open area, where two people are visible sitting facing each other with a stone table, and the surrounding mountain rocks and trees form spatial layering that screens in successive layers.
distinction: The painting mainly creates secluded layering within the woods through the screening and exposing by trees, rather than identifying a specific landscape node through built elements.

evidence: Lower left: on the mountain slope on the left side of the painting a person sits alone, facing the water surface and distant mountains, surrounded by rocks and dead trees. | Center to right: from the center to the right of the painting are distributed many dead trees, and on the right are an open water surface and distant mountains; no buildings or artificial facilities are seen.

evidence: Right side, slightly below center of the painting: on the open water surface there is a small boat with a person aboard, presenting a state of movement through the landscape on the water. | Around the right side of the painting: the painting consists of nearby cliff rocks, trees, and distant continuous mountain ranges and water surface; no fixed built elements such as houses or pavilions are seen.
distinction: There are no clear built elements in the painting, only a boat moving on the water; based on the movement clue it is assigned only with difficulty to C4, but it lacks a fixed entry connection.

evidence: Middle ground right: a group of buildings is distributed along the waterside and gentle slope, and the layout of the houses conforms to the undulation of the terrain, presenting a form built in response to the terrain. | Distant right hillside: a pavilion is built against the mountain at a higher position, corresponding to the mountain form. | Around the middle-ground building group: trees are distributed in front of the buildings, and some houses are screened by trees, but the overall layout still clearly shows their placement according to the sloped platform and waterside.

evidence: Lower right: behind the pine woods the roof and walls of a house are faintly visible, partly screened by trees, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Right center to lower right: many pine trees are arranged, forming foreground and middle ground, screening the built elements behind them and forming spatial layering.

evidence: Lower right: beside the mountain-rock cliff there is a small path, and figures can be seen traveling along it into the interior of the painting, forming a clear movement-through-the-landscape thread and an entry route. | Middle-ground right: a group of courtyard buildings sits on gentle sloping ground, surrounded by tall trees, with roofs and wall bodies partly exposed, and the path direction points toward this area. | Middle ground to far distance: open fields and water extend into the distance, connecting to distant mountains, and together with the foreground path create a spatial layering from near to deep that is walkable and livable.
distinction: Although the buildings have a concealment-and-revelation relationship with the trees (C2), the clear path and figures traveling in the lower right more dominantly organize the spatial process of entering from here and approaching the built structures.

evidence: Lower right: a storied pavilion building is partly screened by surrounding pines and vegetation, revealing the roof, upper-level railings and figures inside, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Lower right: trees interweave in front of, behind and to the sides of the building, giving the architecture a spatial layering of being screened within the mountain forest. | Middle of the painting and background: clouds and mist wreathe among the mountain peaks, and together with the foreground trees' screening they reinforce the sense of depth and seclusion of the scene.
distinction: C2 emphasizes the layering of concealment and revelation formed by trees screening; C1 emphasizes the determining role of terrain on layout; in this painting the enveloping and revealing of the building by trees is the core of the composition.

evidence: Upper right, far bank: an arched bridge can be seen connecting the two banks across snowy ground, forming a traffic thread crossing the water surface. | Center and right water surface: multiple boats are scattered across the open water, presenting the dynamics of travel and arrival. | Lower left: among the trees on the bank, building roofs and walls are revealed, connecting with the moored boats and the shoreline.
distinction: The movement-through-the-landscape thread formed by the bridge and boats runs across the open water and organizes the spatial process of entering from here to there, more dominant than the mere screening of buildings.

evidence: Center-left: an arched bridge spans the water, connecting the two banks, forming a clear passage thread | Right side and river surface: houses are distributed along the bank, and on the river several boats carry people back and forth, presenting a ferry-crossing traffic scene | Lower left: pedestrians gather on the bank, echoing the boats on the river, suggesting the movement-through-the-landscape process of crossing the river
distinction: The core of the painting lies in the ferry traffic and passage process formed by the bridge and boats, rather than simply emphasizing the placement relationship of buildings according to the waterside terrain.

evidence: Lower-middle of the painting: a stone arched bridge spans across, several people walk on the bridge, and behind the bridge a path with red railings winds upward along the hillside. | Upper-middle of the painting: the path connects to pavilions and storied buildings built against the mountain, presenting the spatial process of traveling from the bridge, going deeper along the path, and reaching the built structures.
distinction: Although the built structures are arranged according to the mountain terrain, the movement-through-the-landscape thread formed by the bridge and winding path in the painting is more prominent, dominating the entry and extension relationships of the space.

evidence: Top of the central hill: a tall pagoda and several houses are built at the highest point of the hill, striking in form. | Overall painting: the pagoda and building group at the hilltop become the visual center of the hill, marking out the scenery there and making the hill a focus of recognition.
distinction: The built structures are located at the hilltop, and their main role is to serve as a visual focus marking the scenery there, rather than showing an entry path or being concealed due to complex terrain.

evidence: Lower left: a wooden bridge spans a mountain stream, with riders and walkers on the bridge, forming a clear passage path. | Lower-middle of the painting: the bridge connects the two banks, guiding figures from the foreground toward the depths of the mountain rocks and trees on the right, presenting a spatial process of entering from here to there.
distinction: The bridge mainly serves as a movement-through-the-landscape thread crossing the water to guide figures into the depths of the landscape, rather than emphasizing the dependent relationship of the building site on the terrain.

evidence: Lower right: a building can be seen, with a clear roof, columns and railings, partly screened by foreground shrubs. | Around the building: pines and other trees are behind and to the left of the building, their branches and leaves extending above and in front of it, forming an obvious screening relationship. | Background: towering peaks and a waterfall serve as the background, forming a deep spatial layering with the foreground building screened by trees.
distinction: Although the building is against the mountain and beside the water, the painting emphasizes more the screening and revealing of the building by trees, constructing spatial layering through concealment and revelation, so C2 is more apt than C1.

evidence: Middle-lower right: a pavilion/waterside chamber supported by wooden columns is erected over the water, its platform and columns unfolding in response to the waterside terrain. | Lower left: sloping rocks and trees are adjacent to the waterside pavilion, and the building base forms a natural connecting relationship with the sloping bank and water surface. | Overall painting: the building is built beside the water, presenting a spatial placement relationship of siting the house by the water and adapting appropriately to the situation.
distinction: Although there are trees nearby, the main body of the building is clearly revealed, and its core compositional role lies in being built in response to the waterside terrain, rather than mainly concealment and revelation.

evidence: Right side: a pavilion is built facing the water, with supporting columns visible below, alongside willow trees and bank rocks, presenting a form of siting the house along the bank. | Left side: a small bridge spans the water connecting the two banks, arranged in response to the waterside terrain.
distinction: Although the building plays a scenic-accentuation role, its base and form more directly embody the placement relationship responding to the waterside terrain, so C1 is more apt.

evidence: Lower right: a sloping rock can be seen, with a person sitting on it, beside withered trees and pines, facing the large unpainted space on the left of the painting. | Upper left: several flying birds in the unpainted space, suggesting open water or sky space.
distinction: No clear built elements are seen in the painting; only a figure sitting alone on a sloping rock serves as a scenic accent, condensing the scenery of viewing the water at this spot, so it is classified into the closest category C3.

evidence: Lower left and lower-middle: a thatched hut and an extending bamboo fence can be seen, with an opening or gate left on the right side of the fence. | Lower right: a person is walking toward the opening in the fence, forming a clear moving line of entering the built courtyard.
distinction: Through the fence gate and the pedestrian's moving line, the painting emphasizes an accessible spatial process, rather than simply using a building to mark the distant mountain scenery.

evidence: Left side: a clearly visible house building with a snow-covered roof and a figure inside, serving as the visual focus of the painting. | Right side and behind: a large expanse of continuous snow mountains, contrasting with the house on the left, the house marking out the mood of the cold mountain snow scene.
distinction: Although the house is placed on the sloping bank, its main compositional role is as a visual focus and poetic anchor, marking out the snow scene, rather than emphasizing the terrain relationship of siting according to the ground.

evidence: Center-left of the painting: the building is partly screened by foreground trees and mountain rocks, revealing only the roof, walls and window lattices, forming a layered relationship of a house hidden in the woods. | Left side of the painting: a small path or steps are faintly visible amid the screening trees, connected to the location of the building.
distinction: Although the painting suggests a path, the concealment-and-revelation relationship of the building half-screened by trees and rocks is more prominent and dominates the spatial expression.

evidence: Lower middle: a pavilion sits on the waterside bank, its roof and columns partly screened by the branches and leaves of surrounding trees. | Right side: towering rocks are adjacent to the pavilion, together with the trees forming an enveloping and screening relationship around the building. | Center: several tall trees and weeping willows interweave in front of and behind the pavilion, forming a spatial layering of alternating concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the pavilion marks out a spot of scenery on the waterside bank, the painting emphasizes more the screening and revealing relationship of trees and rocks to the building, and the role of concealment and revelation creating a scene is more prominent.

evidence: Water surface below: a small boat carrying a person floats on the water, near the mountain-rock bank on the left, as the only man-made object in the painting marking out the waterscape. | Left side: huge mountain rocks and dense trees occupy the left half of the painting, forming a heavy foreground. | Right side and distance: the open water's unpainted space and distant mountains rendered in pale ink form an empty and deep space.
distinction: Only the small boat is seen in the painting as a scenic accent element indicating the water surface space and the secluded atmosphere; no clear entry process formed by fixed built structures connected with paths is seen.

evidence: Middle-lower right: between the mountain rocks and pines, the roof and walls of a building can be seen, partly screened by pine branches and rocks, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Right side: the foreground pines and the trees and mountain rocks behind layer upon layer, screening the built structures within, constituting spatial layering.
distinction: Although the building is arranged according to the mountain rocks, the painting emphasizes more the screening and revealing of the building by trees and mountain rocks, and the feature of concealment and revelation creating a scene is more prominent.

evidence: Overall painting: the painting presents only undulating peaks and wreathed clouds and mist; no traces of built structures such as houses, bridges, boats or figures are seen. | Lower left and lower right: red seals can be seen, which are attached marks of the painting, not built elements within the painting.
distinction: The painting completely lacks built elements; it is classified into the closest category based on the overall visible organization of the landscape space.

evidence: Lower left: amid the screening of dense willow trees, the roof and part of the structure of a built element are faintly revealed, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Middle-ground right: reeds and water surface interweave, dotted with small boats, enriching the layering of the waterside boundary.
distinction: The built element mainly relies on the screening and revealing by the foreground willows to indicate its existence and participate in the spatial layering, rather than serving as an isolated marker marking out some landscape scenery.

evidence: Overall painting: only the natural distribution of mountain rocks and trees is seen; no clear traces of built structures such as houses or bridges are seen. | Middle ground and foreground: the forms of mountain rocks and the growth of trees unfold according to the undulations of the terrain, presenting the spatial organization of natural scenery.
distinction: Because no built structures are seen at all in the painting, there is no competing interpretation from other built categories; it is classified into the closest category C1 based on the terrain distribution of natural scenery.

evidence: Lower right: among the pines and rocks there is a very indistinct ink mass, possibly a tiny built element or merely mountains and rocks; it cannot be confirmed as architecture. | Whole painting: the painting is dominated by an open water surface, distant mountains, and foreground pines and rocks; no clear built elements such as houses, bridges, or paths are seen.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built elements; on the basis of the overall landscape composition it can only tentatively be assigned to the scenic-accentuation category, but there is no definite visual evidence to support any specific category.

evidence: Lower left: beside the reeds there is a simple small bridge, with a figure walking on it, forming a movement-through-the-landscape thread crossing the waterside. | Central water surface: several sailboats dot the water surface, and together with the small bridge by the bank they suggest the traffic connection between the water route and the land route.
distinction: The bridge mainly serves as a movement-through-the-landscape thread guiding figures to cross the waterside, presenting a spatial process of entering from here to there, rather than simply being placed according to the terrain.

evidence: Right side: behind the trees and huge rocks, the outlines of a building's roof and walls are revealed, partly screened by the foreground natural scenery. | Right foreground: trees and rocks serve as the foreground, forming a front-back layering with the built structures behind, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship.
distinction: The building is mainly screened by trees and rocks, forming spatial layering through the concealment-and-revelation relationship, rather than serving as a striking marker marking out the scenery.

evidence: Upper right: behind the cliff and among the trees, houses and a pagoda finial are faintly visible, partly screened by the foreground mountain rocks and branches and leaves. | Middle left: below the cliff, on the waterside bank, there is a building, its base and roof partly revealed, forming a screening relationship with the surrounding sloping rocks and vegetation.
distinction: Although the building is against the mountain and beside the water, the painting emphasizes more the concealment-and-revelation layering of its being half-screened by mountain rocks and trees, rather than mere terrain adaptation.

evidence: Middle-ground right: behind the woods, the outline of a pitched roof is faintly visible, partly screened by the tree canopy. | Middle-ground left: a few roof-ridge lines of buildings are revealed in the gaps between trees, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship.
distinction: The painting's focus lies in the layering formed by the screening and revealing of buildings by trees, rather than emphasizing the layout relationship of buildings placed according to the terrain.

evidence: Lower-right tree cluster: beneath the screening branches and leaves, lines resembling a thatched roof or fence are faintly visible, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Lower-left water surface: a small boat floats, with the outline of a figure on the boat.
distinction: The painting is dominated by trees screening suspected built structures; although the boat suggests travel, it is not connected to clear built structures.

evidence: Center and left of the painting: two arched bridges span the river, with pedestrians walking on them, connecting the land and built structures on both banks of the river. | River surface: boats sail on the water, with people poling or riding, constituting waterway traffic and travel threads. | Foreground and middle-ground riverbank: the foreground walled courtyard and the middle-ground village among the woods are interconnected through the bridges and boats on the water, forming an accessible spatial network.
distinction: Although the built structures arranged along the waterside embody terrain-responsive siting, the traffic network formed by bridges, boats and pedestrians in the painting more strongly expresses the spatial process of entering from here to there and being able to travel through.

evidence: Middle of the left side: several houses are faintly visible among the trees by the waterside, revealing only part of their roofs and walls, half-screened by the trees. | Lower right: the buildings on the sloping bank are likewise surrounded by the surrounding trees, their eaves revealed among the branches and leaves, forming a spatial layering of alternating concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the built structures are placed beside the water and against the slope, the painting emphasizes more the screening and revealing relationship of trees to buildings, and the feature of concealment and revelation creating scenery is more prominent.

evidence: Lower left: a wooden bridge can be seen crossing the water, connecting to an earthen slope path extending into the depths of the painting. | Lower middle: on the path there is a pedestrian holding an umbrella, the moving line pointing behind the woods and the sloping bank, presenting an accessible and travelable spatial process. | Upper left: part of the railings and wall structure of a building can be seen, serving as a potential destination or environmental background for the path's extension.
distinction: The dominant thread of the painting is the travel moving line formed by the bridge, path and pedestrians, rather than the layout relationship of buildings placed according to the terrain.

evidence: Lower right: the built structure is located on the bank slope, surrounded by tall trees on the right and behind, with the roof and walls revealed from the trees, forming a layering of a house seen at the edge of the woods. | Right side: the branches and leaves of trees cross and screen with the built structure, and the partial concealment-and-revelation relationship participates in the composition, indicating the spatial layering in which the built structure is situated.
distinction: Although the built structure is beside the sloping bank terrain, the concealment-and-revelation layering formed by the surrounding trees is more significant, dominating the spatial expression of the built structure and the landscape.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: on the river surface there is a small boat with a canopy, and one person sits at the bow fishing | Right side of the painting: trees grow on the sloping bank, their branches extending | Upper part and distance of the painting: continuous distant mountains, shrouded in clouds and mist, with a broad expanse of water
distinction: Here the boat mainly serves as a scenic accent, marking the scene of fishing at the heart of the river and concentrating the mood of the empty water surface, rather than depicting a route of movement from one place to another.

evidence: Left middle: two people can be seen sitting on rocks on the sloping bank by the water, facing the open water surface and distant mountains. | Background: continuous blue-green mountain ranges and a broad water surface form an open, facing spatial setting. | Whole painting: no clear traces of built elements such as houses, bridges, or paths are seen in the painting.
distinction: Since there are no clear built elements, the spatial organization is identified by the figures pausing on the bank to indicate the viewing position, and is assigned to the closest category, scenic accentuation.

evidence: Whole painting: only calligraphic writing and red seals are visible in the painting; no landscape or built-element imagery is seen.
distinction: There is no visible relationship between built elements and landscape; based on the overall absence of imagery, it is assigned to the closest category.

evidence: Top of the central main peak: a pavilion is placed tightly against the top of a steep cliff, built following the mountain's form, showing the feature of setting a building according to height. | Central mountainside and left slope: houses are distributed along the slope and pine forest, placed separately according to the slope, corresponding to the form of the mountain body. | Lower right corner: a waterside pavilion is built directly on the rocks at the water's bank, opening out toward the water, with figures pausing within it, showing a relationship of arrangement following the bank.
distinction: Although an arched bridge in the painting hints at a path, several built elements (the summit pavilion, the mountainside houses, the waterside pavilion) strongly depend on terrain for placement, and the feature of terrain-responsive siting is more widespread and dominant.

evidence: Lower right, at the water's edge on the sloping bank: a thatch-roofed open pavilion stands on a flat terrace projecting leftward from the sloping bank; the terrace edge is the shoreline with water plants, the pavilion body faces the open water surface, and its site is placed according to the slope terrace and the bank's configuration | To the right of the pavilion, among the slope rocks: a slanting red-leaf tree and a pine grow from among the slope rocks, enclosing the right edge of the terrace; the pavilion's pillar bases rest on the terrace surface, their position and height defined by the terrace | Center-left water surface: two fishing boats pole along and hold rods on the broad river, with no visible bridge, path, or ferry crossing connecting them to the bank pavilion
distinction: The pavilion's site clearly falls on the waterside slope terrace, with its position and orientation set according to the bank's configuration; the relationship in which terrain participates in placement is more directly visible than its role as a scenic marker.

evidence: Left side of the painting: steep cliff walls, a falling waterfall, and swirling clouds and mist are visible, with no houses or artificial structures seen. | Right side of the painting: on the sandy bank there are three figures, some sitting and some standing, in a natural landscape setting, with no traces of built elements around them.
distinction: There are no visible built elements at all in the painting; based on the excursion context formed by the overall landscape and figures, it is barely assigned to category C4, representing the process of movement through the landscape.

evidence: Lower right: a waterside pavilion is elevated over the water, supported by wooden piles beneath, placed tightly against the shoreline, showing a posture of unfolding along the bank and being built according to the water. | Right side: the houses behind are built according to the slope terrain, forming a staggered high-and-low layout with the waterside pavilion in front, corresponding to the terrain of rocks and waterside.
distinction: Although the pine trees clearly screen the buildings (C2), the layout of the buildings elevated over water and built according to the mountain has a more fundamental and dominant correspondence with terrain conditions.

evidence: Center-left to center of the painting: a group of houses and a surrounding fence sit on a snowy slope and sandbar by the water; the house group unfolds from the left toward the middle, turning along the shoreline, with open sides and windows facing the broad water surface in front | Left-center sloping bank: the houses are backed against the foot of the left cliff slope, with bamboo clumps and withered trees ranged along the slope behind the houses; the site is placed on the slope terrace, and the layout rises and falls with the height of the sloping bank | Center-right water inlet: an arched bridge spans the inlet, connecting the sloping bank where the houses are located with the right bank, but no clear path beside the bridge leads to the house doors, and the movement-through-the-landscape thread is relatively partial
distinction: Although the bridge is visible, it does not form a clear entry sequence with the house doors and paths, whereas the correspondence of the house group's placement with the shoreline and slope terrace runs through the center-left composition; therefore terrain-responsive siting is primary.

evidence: Left page: the painting depicts reeds by the water and swimming waterbirds, with no buildings or traces of artificial construction seen. | Right page: the painting depicts bamboo branches, weeds, and flying birds by the water, likewise with no buildings or traces of artificial construction seen.
distinction: There are no visible built elements at all in the painting; based only on the distribution of the natural waterside and living things, it is barely assigned to category C1, following natural terrain.

evidence: Center-left of the painting: a thatch-roofed building is partly screened by withered trees in front, revealing the eaves, window lattice, and figures inside, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation. | High on the rocks on the right side of the painting: a small pavilion or thatched hut is half-hidden behind trees and rocks, with only the roof and part of the structure revealed, presenting a spatial layering of screening.
distinction: Although paths and figures suggest entry, the overall composition places more emphasis on the spatial layering formed by built elements being screened and revealed by trees, rocks, and mountains.

evidence: Upper right: a storied building built following the mountain is visible, with clearly defined window lattice; figures appear to sit facing each other inside, and the building is surrounded by pines and withered branches (possibly plum blossoms). | Center to lower left: a winding stone-step mountain path extends from the lower left corner up to the building above; a figure dressed in white is climbing along the path, and at the lower left corner there is a wooden plank walkway or small bridge. | Left side and foreground: dense pine forest is distributed on the left side and lower part of the painting, with slender, upright trunks, creating a deep mountain-forest setting.
distinction: Although the painting contains a clear building (a storied pavilion) and figure activity, the overall composition takes the natural landscape setting (pine forest, mountain path) as its main subject, with the building merged into the mountain's form, conforming to landscape-painting characteristics rather than being a ruled-line painting dominated by architecture or a figure painting dominated by figures.

evidence: Left slope: the building complex is surrounded by pines and large numbers of withered trees, with some roofs and walls revealed through gaps in the trees. | Center and right of the painting: trees loom and fade in the clouds and mist, forming a front-to-back spatial layering with the buildings on the left and reinforcing the screening relationship.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed according to the mountain, the core of the pictorial composition lies in the screening and revealing of the buildings by trees and clouds and mist, rather than emphasizing the determining role of terrain on building layout.

evidence: Center: the main building is built on a high stone platform by the water; the lower platform faces the water, and the upper level has a railed terrace, showing a form of setting a building according to a platform and building by the water. | Left to right: the building complex (including a long corridor, waterside pavilions, and houses) is arranged continuously along the curving shoreline, unfolding following the water's edge. | Right side: houses are distributed according to the slope and trees, rising and falling in height, embodying a layout of separate placement according to the slope.
distinction: Although a zigzag bridge and corridors provide clues for wandering, the dominant spatial expression is the layout of the building complex conforming to the waterside and slope terrain (unfolding along the bank, setting buildings according to platforms), rather than emphasizing a process of entry.

evidence: Lower middle to upper middle of the painting: a winding stone path extends from the lower part of the painting, passes through an archway among the bamboo grove, and leads to houses on the slope; the path is clear and continuous. | Left middle and lower right of the painting: figures walking are painted on the path, clearly indicating the spatial process of moving along the path and approaching the built elements. | Within the bamboo grove at the left middle of the painting: houses are half-screened by the bamboo, with roofs and parts of walls partially revealed, serving as the endpoint of the path, guided and revealed by the path.
distinction: Although the houses screened by bamboo have a C2 feature, the winding path running through the depth, with an archway and pedestrians, more strongly organizes an enterable spatial process; therefore C4 is dominant.

evidence: Lower center of the painting: a group of house buildings, with roofs and walls clearly visible, and figures active inside. | Behind and to the right of the buildings: towering rocks and dense bamboo grove form a background screen, presenting a layering in which houses are seen behind the rock. | Around the buildings: trees surround the buildings, with some branches and leaves screening the edges of the buildings, forming a spatial layering in which houses are seen within the woods.
distinction: Although the buildings are the visual center, the layering of concealment and revelation in which they are surrounded and screened by rocks, bamboo, and trees is more prominent, conforming to the feature of seeing houses within woods and behind rocks.

evidence: Left middle: a two-story storied building is built on a rocky slope terrace, surrounded by trees, with figures visible inside. | Lower middle: a clear small path winds upward from the lower part of the painting, leading directly to the building's base. | Lower right: a figure is walking along the small path toward the storied building, reinforcing the spatial connection of entry and arrival.
distinction: Although the storied building built on the rocky slope terrace embodies terrain-responsive siting, the painting more strongly emphasizes, through the winding path and the walking figure, an enterable and reachable spatial process; therefore C4 is more apt.

evidence: Right middle ground: a group of houses is surrounded by trees on the right and behind, with roofs and parts of walls revealed through gaps in the trees, forming a clear layering of concealment and revelation. | Upper left, distant view: tiny building roofs are faintly visible among rocks and trees, likewise showing a state of being partly screened by natural scenery.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed among the slope and trees, the painting more strongly emphasizes the layered relationship of their being screened by trees and partially revealed, rather than a layout unfolding simply according to terrain.

evidence: Left side: a timber bridge is visible spanning across, its body bearing red railing lines, connecting the two banks and forming a clear clue of crossing and passage. | Right side: willows, flowers and plants, and a pair of ducks by the water, together with the bridge on the left, form an excursion-able spatial scene on the waterside.
distinction: The dominant built element in the painting is the bridge, whose core role lies in providing a clue of crossing the water and a spatial connection, conforming to the feature of access to secluded settings, rather than being merely a scenic accent or screening.

evidence: Whole painting: only gnarled old trees, lake rocks, banana plants, flowers and plants, and flying birds are visible in the painting; no houses, pavilions, bridges, paths, or other artificial built elements are seen.
distinction: There are no built elements in the painting; based on the core scenery formed by the overall trees, rocks, flowers, and plants, it is barely assigned to scenic accentuation, but lacks built entities.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: a gentle shoreline and slope rocks are visible, with trees and red-flowering shrubs growing at the bank; the space unfolds horizontally along the waterside. | Upper part of the painting: distant mountains have gentle outlines, birds fly across the sky, and no traces of artificial built elements such as buildings, bridges, or paths are seen.
distinction: There are no clear built elements in the painting; based on the overall visible landscape organization, the level-and-distant unfolding relationship of the waterside and slope rocks is closest to C1's site-placement logic, but lacks actual evidence of built elements.

evidence: Whole painting: only rocks, trees, flying birds, and waterfowl are visible in the painting; no built elements such as houses, bridges, or paths are seen. | Lower left: waterfowl rest on the waterside, marking the natural scenery of this waterside spot.
distinction: There are no built elements in the painting; the waterside scenery is marked only by natural scenery and birds, so it is assigned to C3.

evidence: Whole painting: only foreground rocks, trees, and waterbirds, middle-ground water surface and reeds, and distant mountain ranges are visible in the painting; no traces of built elements such as houses or bridges are seen.
distinction: There are no clear built elements in the painting; if a building were assumed, it would most likely be at a layer screened by mountain forest, rather than serving as a scenic marker.

evidence: Center of the painting: one figure is visible sitting upright on a rock by the water; no built elements such as houses, bridges, or pavilions are seen. | Upper left corner: a golden inscribed poem and seals are visible, belonging to the painting's textual content and not taken as evidence of built elements.
distinction: There are no actual built elements in the painting; based on the overall landscape-and-figure composition, with the figure occupying the position on the water and rocks, it is closest to the spatial relationship of scenic accentuation.

evidence: Right side of the painting: the painting consists mainly of foreground pine trees and slope rocks and distant cliffs and forest, with no clear built elements such as houses, bridges, or paths seen.
distinction: The painting lacks visible built elements, so its spatial expression cannot be clearly judged; based on the overall composition it is barely assigned to the scenic-accent category, but the evidence is severely insufficient.

evidence: Lower left: the roof and part of the wall of a house are revealed among the trees, partly screened by the surrounding branches and leaves. | Lower left: the built element is hidden among the woods, presenting a spatial layering of concealment and revelation, with trees screening the building.
distinction: Although the built element is beside trees on level ground, its most striking compositional role is forming layering through the screening and revealing by trees, rather than emphasizing placement according to terrain.

evidence: Whole painting: the painting consists mainly of foreground slope rocks and trees, middle-ground water surface, and distant mountain ranges, with no clearly identifiable built entities such as buildings, bridges, or paths. | Foreground center: several foreground trees stand on slope rocks, concentrating the painting's visual focus as the foreground and forming a spatial contrast with the open water surface and distant mountains.
distinction: Because the painting lacks clear built elements, based on the overall landscape composition, the foreground trees serve to mark the foreground and concentrate the scenery, so it is assigned to C3.

evidence: Upper right: a storied pavilion is built atop a towering cliff wall, its building body partly shaded by the dense branches and leaves of surrounding trees, revealing only the roof and part of the eaves. | Lower center-left: a house is screened among the trees by the waterside, with trunks and branches screening part of the walls and roof, forming a front-to-back layering.
distinction: Although the upper-right storied pavilion marks the summit position, both built elements in the painting construct spatial layering mainly through screening and revealing by trees and rocks, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship is more prominent than mere scenic marking.

evidence: Lower right: a house stands beside trees, its roof visible, with part of the wall screened by branches and leaves, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Lower right to center right: multiple trees surround the house, giving the built element a spatial layering of being within the woods or seeing a house through a screen.
distinction: The house mainly uses tree screening to form a layering of concealment and revelation, rather than emphasizing a placement relationship according to terrain and sloping bank.

evidence: Left middle ground: behind a mountain rock the roof and wall of a house are revealed, partly screened by the mountain body and trees, presenting a layering of concealment and revelation. | Right foreground to middle ground: a faint path or stream extends through gaps between trees and rocks, but no clear entry clue connecting to the built elements is seen.
distinction: In the painting the built element mainly forms layering through screening and revealing by rocks and trees, rather than being entered mainly by path guidance.

evidence: Lower middle: at the water's edge there is a platform or waterside pavilion, whose site unfolds tightly against the waterside and slope rocks, showing a placement of setting a platform according to the water. | Lower middle, slightly right: one figure is visible sitting upright on the platform, positioned in the gap between tree roots and rocks, with the built element corresponding to site conditions. | Right side: the branches of a weeping willow hang toward the water surface and above the built element; the built element is arranged by means of the waterside terrain and gaps between trees, fitting the terrain appropriately.
distinction: Although there is tree screening in the painting, the built element is placed mainly according to the terrain conditions of the waterside and slope rocks, and the correspondence between the site and the natural configuration is clearer.

evidence: Lower-middle, toward the right: one house is visible, its roof, eaves, and part of its wall emerging from behind thick foreground tree trunks and rocks; one person can be seen inside the house. | Middle of the painting: dense tree branches and mountain rocks clearly screen the house, creating a spatial layering of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the house is placed against mountain rocks, the painting emphasizes more its partly screened concealment and revelation by trees and rocks, rather than mere topographic accommodation.

evidence: Right-middle: a built structure is faintly visible among the trees, partly screened by branches and leaves, presenting a relation of concealment and revelation.
distinction: The built element mainly forms spatial layering through the screening of trees, rather than serving simply as a marker that identifies a scenic spot.

evidence: Lower left: a pavilion-type building is visible, with its roof and part of its column structure exposed. | Center, toward the left: the branches and trunks of tall foreground trees interpose in front of the building, clearly screening its facade and presenting a relation of concealment and revelation. | Behind and to the right of the building: the building is placed against mountain rocks and a sloping bank, and the rocks and trees together enclose the spatial layering in which the building sits.
distinction: Although the building is placed against the sloping bank, the screening and revealing of the building by tree branches and trunks (concealment and revelation) is more prominent in the painting and is the dominant means of constructing the spatial layering here.

evidence: Center of the painting, toward the lower part: a thatched hut stands below a cliff, its roof and walls partly screened by the projecting rocks above and the hanging branches and leaves, presenting a layering of a house seen beneath the cliff. | Right side of the painting and around the thatched hut: trees surround the hut and, together with the mountain rocks, form a relation of screening and revealing of the built element. | Lower part of the painting: a sloping bank lies in front of the thatched hut and extends to the waterside, indicating the spatial position of the built element.
distinction: Although the thatched hut is placed against the sloping bank, the painting emphasizes more its partly screened concealment and revelation by rocks and trees, and constructs spatial layering by this means.

evidence: Right side, from the lower-middle to the middle: a clear winding path (or shoreline) extends from the lower right of the painting, linking the pavilion by the water, the houses among the trees, and the settlement in the distance. | Lower-middle and right side of the painting: multiple built elements (houses, pavilions) are distributed along this path, presenting a spatial progression of movement from one place to another and gradually deeper.
distinction: Although some built elements are screened among trees and woodland, the path thread running through the painting is clearer and more dominant in organizing the spatial relation of entry.

evidence: Lower-left corner: a small bridge spanning a stream is visible, with tiny human figures on it, serving as a starting clue for entering the space of the painting. | Lower-middle: a winding path extends from the bridgehead, passes through a pine grove, and leads to a house roof faintly visible behind the trees, forming a clear entry route. | Right-middle: a pavilion is built on top of the cliff, echoing spatially with the path and woodland below and implying the reachability and depth of the journey through the landscape.
distinction: Although the buildings are arranged according to the mountain terrain, the movement-through-the-landscape clues formed by the bridge and winding path are more prominent in the painting, clearly guiding the eye from outside to inside and deeper, in keeping with the character of access to secluded settings.

evidence: Lower-middle: two people walk along a mountain path deep into the gorge, forming a clear route of travel. | Both sides of the painting: towering mountain rocks and trees flank the way, leaving an open passage in the middle that extends into the depth.
distinction: No built elements are visible in the painting, but the spatial organization of the figures moving along the path deep into the gorge comes closest to the process of movement through the landscape of access to secluded settings.

evidence: Left middle ground: several thatched huts are distributed in staggered fashion against the foot of the mountain and the sloping land, close to the waterside, presenting an arrangement that unfolds according to the terrain and the waterside. | Left waterside: a simple wooden bridge connects the waterside in front of the built elements, further reinforcing the characteristic of buildings erected in reliance on the land-and-water terrain.
distinction: Although there is a small bridge and path in the painting, the most central compositional role of the built elements is their layout against mountain and water and following the slope, rather than emphasizing a process of entry along a path.
