evidence: From the lower left to the left side: a winding path extends from the lower part of the painting, and a walker is proceeding along the path into the depth of the painting; the path leads to a built element on the left screened by trees. | Left side: among the screening trees a built element (pavilion or house) is visible, with its roof and railing exposed; it is the destination or waypoint guided by the path.
distinction: Although the built element is screened by trees (C2), the clear path and walker in the painting emphasize more the spatial process of approaching or entering the built element via the path (C4).

evidence: Lower right: behind a cluster of trees the roof of a built element and a wall or platform with vertical railings are faintly exposed. | Right side and foreground: dense bare tree branches and foliage partly screen the built element at the lower right, forming a front-to-back layering. | Left side: the left side is open water and towering cliffs, forming a contrast of void and solid with the built element screened by trees on the right.
distinction: Although the built element faces the water, the painting emphasizes more its partly screened concealment and revelation by tree branches and foliage and its spatial layering, rather than its topographic placement against mountain and water.

evidence: Lower left: several houses sit on level ground on a slope at the foot of the mountain, backed by mountain rocks and trees, their layout unfolding in accordance with the terrain.
distinction: The houses mainly embody a relation of placement according to the terrain at the foot of the mountain, rather than serving simply as a marker of a visual focus.

evidence: Left side of the painting proper: the painting mainly depicts mountains, trees, and waterside; no clear built traces such as houses, pavilions, bridges, or paths are visible.
distinction: No clear built elements are visible in the painting; the closest classification is made on the basis of the overall natural landscape configuration.

evidence: Among the trees at the lower middle of the right side: part of a roof of a suspected built element (pavilion or house) is faintly visible, screened by the surrounding branches and leaves, presenting a relation of concealment and revelation
distinction: The painting mainly presents a relation of layering in which the built element is screened by trees, rather than emphasizing the correspondence of its building site to the mountain terrain; moreover, the details of the built element are indistinct.

evidence: Middle of the upper part, on the mountainside: a roof and eaves of a built element are visible, half hidden behind mountain rocks and trees and woodland, forming a relation of concealment and revelation. | Overall composition: by means of screening by the surrounding mountain forms and trees, the built element presents a clearly layered spatial depth and is integrated into the landscape scenery.
distinction: Although the built element is placed as an accent among the mountains, its partly screened relation with the surrounding rocks and trees is more prominent; its main role is to form spatial layering rather than simply to mark a particular scenic spot.

evidence: Lower left of the painting: a thatched pavilion is built directly on a rock platform extending into the water, its building site closely fitting the terrain of the bank rocks. | Lower-middle of the painting: the thatched pavilion is set facing the water, and its position and manner of unfolding follow the natural configuration of the waterside and rocks.
distinction: Although the thatched pavilion marks a waterside scenic spot, its placement against the rocks and facing the water more prominently embodies a terrain-responsive correspondence between the built element and the natural terrain (rocks, waterside).

evidence: Right side of the painting proper: the painting depicts distant mountains, middle-ground woodland, and a foreground waterside; no built elements such as houses or bridges are visible. | Overall composition: the space presents a broad, level, and open natural landscape, lacking traces of man-made intervention.
distinction: No built elements are visible in the painting, so no specific terrain-responsive, screening, or secluded-access relation can be formed; it presents only the natural landscape scenery itself.

evidence: Lower-middle of the painting: a clear path winds upward from the foreground sloping bank, passes through gaps between the trees, and extends into the depth of the painting. | Right middle ground of the painting: buildings are visible among the trees on the hillside, and the direction of the path implies a route of travel leading to these built elements. | Right side of the painting: the built elements are partly screened by trees and mountain rocks, presenting a degree of concealment and revelation layering, but the guiding role of the path is more prominent.
distinction: Although the built elements have a relation of screening, the clear path in the painting guides the eye into the depth and emphasizes a spatial process of entry and movement through the landscape, so C4 is more dominant than C2.

evidence: Lower-middle of the painting: several houses are screened among trees and mountain rocks, their roofs and walls partly exposed, forming a spatial layering of concealment and revelation. | Lower-middle of the painting, toward the left: foreground tree branches and foliage screen part of the buildings, placing the buildings amid the screening of woodland.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed at the foot of the mountain, the painting emphasizes more the screening and revealing of the buildings by woodland, and the characteristic of concealment and revelation forming a setting is more dominant.

evidence: Lower left: a built element (pavilion) is visible, its roof and walls partly screened by the branches and foliage of trees in front, presenting a state of being half hidden and half exposed. | Middle right: the outline of another built element is faintly visible among the screening trees on the mountainside, forming a layering with the rocks and woodland. | Lower right: the waterside, sloping rocks, and trees interweave, placing the built elements amid the surrounding natural scenery and reinforcing the relation of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the built elements mark the waterside scenery, the painting emphasizes more the spatial layering formed by the screening and revealing of the buildings by woodland, so C2 is more dominant than C3.

evidence: Lower right: several buildings are visible at the waterside, partly screened by foreground trees and mountain rocks, presenting a relation of concealment and revelation. | Lower middle of the right side: the buildings appear faintly among the woodland and mountain rocks, forming spatial layering through the screening of natural scenery.
distinction: Although the buildings stand beside the waterside, the painting emphasizes more the layering of concealment and revelation formed by screening by woodland and rocks, rather than mere topographic placement.

evidence: Left middle: a group of pavilion buildings is visible on the mountainside, their building bodies and part of their roofs screened by the branches and foliage of trees in front, presenting a spatial layering of being half hidden and half exposed. | Lower-left corner: two people walk along a path deep into the mountain forest, the path disappearing among the trees and rocks, implying a movement-through-the-landscape clue of entry into the built elements or deeper into the mountain forest.
distinction: Although a path implies entry, the built elements themselves mainly establish their spatial layering within the landscape through the screening and revealing of woodland, and the screening relation is more direct and prominent.

evidence: Lower-middle: a wooden bridge spans the water connecting the two banks, with two people walking on it; one end of the bridge connects to a winding path leading into the depth. | From the lower-right corner to the middle-left: a clear path extends from the lower-right corner, passes through gaps between the trees, and leads to the built area on the left; one person at the lower-right corner is walking along the path. | Left middle: the built elements (houses) are screened among clusters of trees, and the direction of the path and bridge clearly points toward them, forming an accessible spatial relation.
distinction: Although the built elements screened by trees have a C2 characteristic, the bridge, path, and movement of the figures together construct a clear route of entry and movement through the landscape, and C4 better captures the dominant role of this spatial organization.

evidence: Center of the painting: a path winding along a stream extends into the depth of the painting, with two pedestrians on it, forming a clear movement-through-the-landscape clue. | Left mountainside: pavilion buildings built against the mountain are visible, and the direction of the path and stream implies a spatial connection leading to them. | Among the trees on the right: houses screened among the trees are likewise within reach of the path or within sight.
distinction: Although the buildings on the right are screened by woodland, the dominant spatial relation in the painting is a process of entry and movement along the stream and path, rather than mere layering of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower-middle of the painting: the building stands between two large trees on the left and right; the foreground branches and foliage and trunks are in front of the building, forming a spatial layering of a house seen within the forest. | Foreground on the left and right sides of the painting: tall trees surround the building, and the screening relation establishes the building's middle-ground position, forming depth with the background mountains and waterfall.
distinction: Although a figure at the lower-left corner walking toward the building implies a path of approach, the dominant spatial organization of the painting establishes the building's layering through the front-to-back screening of trees, rather than emphasizing a complete route of movement through the landscape.

evidence: Lower-left corner: a group of houses is screened by dense foreground trees, with only the roofs and parts of the structure exposed, presenting a layering of houses hidden within the forest. | Left middle: an independent small structure is hidden at the edge of a grove, half screened and half exposed, forming a relation of concealment and revelation with the surrounding vegetation. | Water surface on the right and in the center: built elements are scattered on the waterside islets and sandbars, using cloud and mist and distant trees to form a separating view; some buildings are exposed, while others are screened by environmental elements.
distinction: In the painting, the built elements are mostly screened by trees and cloud and mist to form a pronounced layering of concealment and revelation (C2), rather than mainly emphasizing a correspondence of layout to the waterside terrain (C1); and although the buildings on the right follow the bank, the overall effect is predominantly one of screening.

evidence: Middle right: a pavilion is built on a stone platform, with figures visible inside. | Foreground and right side: dense bamboo and trees screen the lower part and sides of the pavilion, forming a relation of concealment and revelation. | Left side and background: tall pines and distant mountains form a front-to-back layering with the pavilion, setting off the sense of space in which the pavilion is screened among woodland and mountain rocks.
distinction: Although the pavilion is built on a stone platform, the painting emphasizes more its layering of concealment and revelation screened by bamboo and trees, rather than placement simply according to the terrain.

evidence: Middle ground, toward the left: a thatched hut is partly screened by the weeping willows and bamboo in front, with only its roof and part of its walls exposed, forming a clear relation of concealment and revelation. | Middle ground: trees and buildings interweave, the buildings hidden behind the woodland, presenting a spatial layering of a house seen within the forest.
distinction: In the painting, the relation of screening and concealment and revelation between buildings and trees is more prominent than their characteristic of relying on the terrain, and it dominates the organization of the spatial layering.

evidence: At the foot of the mountain, slightly left of the center of the painting: a small building (apparently a pavilion or thatched hut) is visible, with a roof and columns, partly screened by the surrounding trees and mountain rocks, appearing faintly visible. | Lower-middle of the painting: several pines stand upright, their branches and foliage spreading outward, forming a clear front-to-back layering and screening relation with the building behind. | Water surface at the lower right of the painting: there is a small boat with a person on board, on open water, with no clear connecting path to the buildings on the bank.
distinction: The primary label emphasizes the layering of concealment and revelation between the building and the trees and mountain rocks; the alternative interpretation emphasizes topographic placement, and the screening relation in which the building is screened by trees is more conspicuous in the painting.

evidence: Lower right: a wooden bridge spans the water, with pedestrians on it, connecting the two banks and forming a clear clue of crossing and entry. | Right middle ground and distant view: pedestrians at the edge of the waterside walk along a path into the depth of the painting, and the path, together with the water flow and mountain forms, guides the eye deep into the valley. | Left mountainside and distant valley: houses are distributed on the mountainside and in the distant valley, serving as the endpoint or waypoints along the movement-through-the-landscape clue and indicating an accessible space.
distinction: Although the houses stand against mountain and water, the dominant spatial organization of the painting is a process of movement through the landscape extending into the depth, formed by the bridge, waterside, and pedestrian paths, rather than mere emphasis on the dependence of buildings on the terrain.

evidence: Left middle-ground waterside: a group of houses is partly screened by the trees in front, with only the snow-covered roofs and part of the structure exposed, presenting a relation of concealment and revelation. | Left distant view, opposite bank: a row of houses is faintly visible screened among the distant snow-scene woodland, increasing the spatial layering of the painting.
distinction: Although the houses add an accent to the snow scene, their screening relation with the trees (concealment) is more prominent in the composition and forms a clear spatial layering, rather than serving simply as landmarks.

evidence: Lower-middle of the painting: a person riding a donkey is visible, accompanied by a servant boy, traveling along a faint shoreline or small path, presenting a thread of movement through the landscape. | Upper part and distant view of the painting: the distant mountains are gentle, the water surface is broad, and no identifiable houses, bridges, or other built elements are seen.
distinction: The painting lacks explicit built elements, but the thread of movement through the landscape formed by the figures and the path is, in terms of spatial organization, closest to the entering-and-traveling relationship of C4.

evidence: Lower left: a thatched hut is built on a sloping platform, and a person is visible sitting upright inside; the building site corresponds directly to the sloping-platform terrain. | Left and right sides: pine and willow trees surround the thatched hut, and the edge of the sloping platform extends downward, presenting a disposition toward the water or an open face. | Above: distant mountains and sloping banks extend into the distance, forming a topographical echo with the sloping-platform built elements in the foreground.
distinction: Although the thatched hut serves in the foreground to point up the scenery, its siting—house set on a platform and placed according to the slope—makes the terrain-responsive arrangement visually more direct and explicit.

evidence: Center of the painting: a small boat on the water, with one figure poling and one seated upright, presenting a state of movement through the landscape on water. | Lower part of the painting: the foreground consists of earthen slopes and weeping willows, with no traces of built structures. | Upper part of the painting: the background consists of gentle, continuous hills, with no built elements discernible.
distinction: No built structures are visible at all in the painting; only a boat serves as a clue to movement through the landscape, and it is only with difficulty assigned to access to secluded settings, but it lacks support from any physical building.

evidence: Central water surface: a lone boat floats on the open water, becoming the visual focus of the painting's middle ground. | Lower foreground: several trees grow on the sloping bank, and no houses or other built elements are seen. | Upper distant view: gently rolling distant mountains meet the water surface, and the composition is open.
distinction: There are no explicit built elements in the painting; the lone boat, as a scenic accent element, marks the scenery of the open water surface, and is therefore assigned to C3.

evidence: Lower right: a railed pavilion structure is visible, with two people sitting facing each other inside; the main body of the building is partly screened by the pine trees in front. | Center-right: a pine tree stands in front of the building, and its branches and trunk form an obvious screening relationship over the left side and top of the building. | Right side: the building backs onto a rocky slope bank; the rocks and pine trees together constitute the spatial layers in which the building is situated, presenting a visual effect of seeing the house through a screened view.
distinction: Although the building is placed according to the mountain terrain, the concealment-and-revelation relationship formed by the pine trees and the building is more prominent in the painting and is the main means of organizing the spatial layers at this location.

evidence: Right side: towering mountains and rocks and trees occupy the right side of the painting, with a water shoreline at the bottom. | Lower left: a small boat on the water, with several people aboard, presenting a state of movement through the landscape.
distinction: No explicit built elements are seen in the painting; there is only the thread of boat travel, and the closest category is assigned based on the overall visible relationship between the waterside and the boat.

evidence: Lower left of the painted panel: two figures riding donkeys are seen traveling beneath a cliff wall, presenting the dynamic of journeying or hurrying along a road. | Center and upper part of the painted panel: steep cliff walls and wreathing cloud and mist are depicted; no traces of built structures such as houses or bridges are seen.
distinction: There are absolutely no visible built elements in the painting; only figures travel through the landscape, and on the basis of the overall spatial organization it is assigned only tentatively to category C4, representing the process of movement through the landscape.

evidence: Lower center of the painted panel: several bare deciduous trees stand upright from the foot of the slope, their trunks and slanting branches pressing in front of the outline of the house, cutting off part of the building itself | Lower right of the painted panel: the roof, eaves and wall of the house emerge from behind the trees; a person is seen sitting upright at an open window in the house on the right, and the built structure appears through the relationship of concealment and revelation | Behind the house (center of the painted panel): rows of bamboo or reed-like brushstrokes lie horizontally above the roof, and the house is situated within the layering of screening trees and bamboo
distinction: The foot-of-slope line is gentle and the terrain's involvement in the placement of the house is weak, whereas the screening and exposure of the house by tree trunks and bamboo clumps runs through the main body of the painted panel; therefore concealment and revelation forming a scene is dominant.

evidence: Central lower slope: a gentle slope extends from lower left toward the center; three figures stand on the slope, an attendant carrying objects in front, and a scholar raises a hand pointing toward the upper part of the rock wall on the right, in the posture of pausing during travel | Left and right sides: withered trees and rock walls flank each other, with a misty opening formed by light-ink unpainted space in between; the slope surface continues around the right rock foot toward the lower right, suggesting that travel can continue deeper | Lower left and right slope: bamboo grows among the slope rocks at lower left, and a crane stands on the right slope, sharing the open sloping platform with the figures; no houses, walls, or bridges or corridors are seen
distinction: The painting presents the process of turning toward the depths behind the rock through the extension of the slope path and the figures' advancing and pointing, rather than marking a scenic spot with built elements; there are no built elements in the painting, so the spatial organization of travel into the landscape is taken as the closest classification.

evidence: Lower-left embankment end: an arched bridge spans the water below the embankment; on the bridge deck are a rider and pedestrians, and both ends of the bridge connect directly with the path along the embankment | Left middle to upper middle: the embankment road extends diagonally with the row of willows, and the figures and trees grow smaller and more distant, indicating the direction of travel continuing along the embankment | Lower-right water surface: a painted pleasure boat with sail and cabin lies diagonally on the water, a figure stands at the bow, accompanied by a small boat; ripples spread outward from the hull, presenting the dynamic of boat travel arriving
distinction: The main label is based on the process of crossing the bridge into the embankment and boat travel arriving, as presented by the bridge and embankment path and the boat and water-surface wake linking up, rather than the simple correspondence of the embankment and bridge being placed according to the waterside terrain.

evidence: Lower-left slope foot: several white-walled, orange-red-roofed houses sit as a group on the flat ground at the foot of the slope, backed by sloping hills and a row of vertical pine woods; the buildings are staggered front and back according to the slope | Lower left to center: in front of the house group is a dark sloping bank, and beyond the bank is open water rendered as unpainted space; the direction in which the houses spread is consistent with the trend of the bank slope | Slightly below center: a group of tall trees stands on a rocky bank, facing the house group across the sloping bank; no bridge, path, gate, or other travel clues connecting with the houses are seen in the painting
distinction: The pine woods are located behind the houses as a background, and the roofs and walls are fully exposed; the layers of concealment and revelation are weaker than the relationship of the houses being placed according to the slope foot and facing the waterside.

evidence: Right side: between huge mountains and rocks and trees, a built roof and eave corner are visible, partly screened by the branches and bamboo leaves in front. | Lower right: the built elements are arranged relying on the mountains and rocks, and through the front-back screening relationship of trees and rocks, spatial layers with concealment and revelation are presented.
distinction: Although the built elements are set according to the mountains and rocks, the painting emphasizes more their half-hidden, half-revealed relationship screened by trees and rocks, and in this way they participate in forming the scenery.

evidence: Center-left of the painted panel, at the foot of the cliff and to the right of the unpainted tree trunk: behind the dense-ink cliff wall and hanging branches is a square structure outlined in pale ink, suspected to be a house, of which only a partial outline is exposed, most of it screened by the cliff wall and tree shadows | Water at the lower right of the painted panel: a small boat carries several people, one standing at the stern poling; between the boat and the left bank no bridge, path, gate or landing is visible | From the center of the painted panel to the left bank: the cliff wall comes directly to the water, the shoreline unfolds in fine ripple lines toward the mid-ground rocks, and there is a semicircular pale-ink shadow in the middle of the water
distinction: The suspected house is indicated only by a pale-ink partial outline exposed from behind the screening cliff wall and hanging branches, which is its sole discernible compositional mode of concealment and revelation; the details of how the building site and layout correspond to the terrain are not visible, so terrain-responsive siting is not adopted.

evidence: Lower foreground of the painting: between the slope rocks and trees, the roof of a building is faintly visible, mostly screened by the tree trunks and branches in front. | Lower foreground of the painting: the building is screened by the foreground pines, miscellaneous trees, and slope rocks, presenting spatial layers of alternating concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the building leans on the slope rocks, its most distinctive spatial feature is the layers of concealment and revelation formed by the screening of trees, rather than simply emphasizing placement according to the terrain.

evidence: Middle left: the roofs and windowed walls of two houses emerge from the upper edge of the foreground earthen slope; the house foundations are obscured by the slope body, and no ground-level building site is seen | Center: a pine grows on the slope mound in front of the house; the trunk and the moss dots on the slope top form a band across the front of the right end of the house, and the pine's hanging branches and leaves cover the upper right of the house | Left side: small trees and clumping branches surround the left side and rear of the house; the house is sandwiched between the foreground slope mound, the pine, and the side-and-rear clumping trees, forming layers of front-back screening
distinction: The house foundations are hidden by the foreground slope mound and cannot be seen; the visible relationship is the layers of concealment and revelation in which the roofs and walls emerge from behind the slope mound and trees, rather than a correspondence in which the foundation height is placed according to the terrain.

evidence: Right side of the painted panel: the roof and windowed wall of the house emerge through gaps among many tree trunks, branches and leaves, with part of the building itself screened by foreground trees | Right foreground: red-leaf trees, pines and bare branches stand in front of the house, their trunks and branches slanting across and covering the roof and wall, forming a layering of concealment and revelation in which a house is seen among woodland | Center of the painted panel: a low, flat bridge trace crosses the stream gap between the rock ledges, but the path beyond the bridge is blocked by sloping rocks, and its connection with the house cannot be discerned
distinction: The house presents its layering mainly through screening and exposure by foreground woodland; the bridge trace in the center is short and has no continuing path, so it is insufficient to constitute an enterable process of movement through the landscape.

evidence: Upper-right hillside: pavilions and pagoda-style built elements are surrounded by pine woods and mountain rocks, with only the roofs, eaves, and pagoda body exposed, presenting an obvious relationship of concealment and revelation within the woods. | Lower water surface of the painting: a small boat carries people facing the wooded hills on the right, the line of sight pointing toward the screened direction of the built elements, but no clear physical entry path is formed.
distinction: Although the built elements point up the scenery of the mountain temple, their relationship of screening and revealing with the trees and rocks is more direct and prominent in shaping the spatial layers.

evidence: Left mountainside: a group of buildings is faintly visible between the mountain rocks and woods, with roofs and walls partly screened by trees, forming layers of seeing houses deep within the woods. | Lower-right waterside: buildings by the water are half-hidden behind weeping willows and mountain rocks, with only part of the roofs and structures exposed, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship of seeing houses through a screened view.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed according to the mountains and beside the water, the painting emphasizes more the layers of concealment and revelation in which they are faintly visible through the screening of trees and rocks, so C2 is more dominant than C1.

evidence: Lower right: on the slope below there is an open thatched pavilion surrounded by bamboo groves and trees, with the pavilion body revealed through the gaps in the grove. | Middle right: on the hillside above there is a house, whose roof and part of the structure are screened by dense tree crowns, presenting a half-hidden, half-revealed state. | Right side overall: the built elements form an obvious relationship of screening and revealing with the mountain rocks and woodland, and the distribution of trees constitutes the front-back spatial layers of the painting.
distinction: Although the built elements are placed according to the mountain terrain, the painting emphasizes more the spatial layers formed by the screening and revealing of the buildings by the woodland, so C2 is more dominant than C1.

evidence: Lower middle: an arched bridge is visible spanning between the trees and rocks, connecting the foreground with the hillside area on the right. | Right hillside: multiple house buildings are distributed on the hillside, their roofs visible and arranged according to the mountain terrain, connected to the foreground by the bridge. | Painting overall: the bridge, as a thread of movement through the landscape, guides the line of sight from the foreground toward the mountain town on the right, presenting a spatial process of entering from here to there.
distinction: The bridge provides a clear entry path and spatial connection, and explains the orienting relationship between the foreground and the built area better than simple placement according to the mountain (C1).

evidence: Lower left: houses are built at the waterside, and their building sites unfold tightly along the water bank. | Right mountainside and mountain foot: houses are arranged in a staggered way according to the mountain terrain and sloping platforms, their heights echoing the undulations of the terrain. | Center: the built elements are distributed along the hillside, and the layout follows the natural configuration of the mountain rocks and woodland.
distinction: Although there is a screening effect formed by tree cover, the terrain-responsive placement of the built elements according to the waterside, sloping platforms, and mountain terrain is more prominent and dominant in the composition.

evidence: Between the right mountain foot and the woodland: the roofs, thatched eaves, and fence walls of several buildings are visible, partly screened by trees and mountain rocks, presenting spatial layers of alternating concealment and revelation. | Lower-left corner: a person travels along the waterside or a path toward the depths of the painting, forming a spatial connection with the buildings screened within the woodland.
distinction: Although the figure and path in the lower-left corner suggest entry, the buildings themselves mainly construct the spatial layers through screening and revealing by the woodland and mountain rocks, and the feature of concealment and revelation is more dominant.

evidence: Among the pine woodland on the sloping bank at the right: a very small figure or tiny element can be seen dotted on the sloping bank, with no clear built structures such as houses or pavilions. | Center and left of the painting: a large area of unpainted space represents the water surface; mountains, rocks, and pines are on the left, pine woodland on a sloping bank on the right, and the whole is a natural landscape composition.
distinction: No clear built structures are visible in the painting; it is only with difficulty assigned to scenic accentuation on the basis of the tiny elements dotted within the overall landscape organization, but it lacks physical evidence of buildings.

evidence: Center of the painting: the upper half of a multi-story pagoda emerges from dense groves, the pagoda body half-screened by branches and leaves. | Lower middle of the painting: below the woods, roofs and walls of houses are faintly visible, hidden behind the trees. | Right side of the painting: the open waterside and distant mountains form a contrast, setting off the secluded depth of the built elements deep within the central woods.
distinction: Although the pagoda has a scenic-accent function, the painting emphasizes more its layers of concealment and revelation, screened by deep trees and occasionally revealed, so C2 is more apt than C3.

evidence: Rock top slightly right of the painting's center: a small pavilion-type built element is visible on top of the rock, tiny in scale, pointing up the scenery at the rock edge. | Far shore on the right side of the painting: at the end of the shoreline there is a tiny building outline, serving as a marker of the waterside scenery.
distinction: The built elements are extremely small in scale and isolated, mainly serving to accent and mark landscape nodes; no obvious relationship of terrain-responsive layout or spatial organization is displayed.

evidence: Left side: courtyard walls with stone foundations, gate openings, and building roofs are visible, arranged along the shoreline according to its trend and closely integrated with the terrain. | Left side: dense trees surround the buildings, and some buildings are screened by branches and leaves, forming certain layers of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the buildings have a screening relationship with tree cover, their terrain-responsive relationship of unfolding along the waterside terrain is clearer and more dominant.

evidence: Left middle-to-distant shore: faint groups of house buildings and a small bridge are visible, tiny in scale, dotting the shoreline where the distant mountains meet the water surface. | Overall composition: the foreground sloping bank with trees and the mid-ground open water rendered as unpainted space are broad, and the tiny built elements in the distance serve to point up the scenery on the opposite shore and to gather the line of sight toward the distant mountains.
distinction: Although there is a bridge on the left side of the painting, it does not form a clear travel clue guiding the viewer's line of sight deeper or into the built elements; the built elements mainly serve as distant scenic accents and markers of the scenery.

evidence: Center-right stream shoal: a traveler carrying a long staff with objects over the shoulder walks along the sandy stream bank toward the valley; the shoal is marked with fine-lined water channels and broken stones as a walkable bank path | Left and right sides: layered slope rocks and hanging branches on the left and an upright rock wall on the right flank each other to form a narrow valley opening; within the valley the stream-shoal path extends from the foreground toward the middle ground | Outside the valley mouth at upper middle: beyond the valley mouth, unpainted space represents open water and pale-ink distant mountains, forming with the foreground narrow valley layers of deepening from narrow to broad; no houses, bridges, corridors, gates, or other built elements are seen in the entire painting
distinction: The painting organizes the process of turning from the foreground into the valley and then toward the open water through the traveler and the stream-shoal bank path, which is closer to the visible spatial relationships than an explanation of scenic accentuation that merely frames the distant water with the rock opening.

evidence: Top of the mountain head on the middle-right side: a small house emerges among a row of small trees on the gentle slope top, its roof and eaves revealed from between the trees, and the lower part of the building itself falling between the slope top and the tree crowns | Middle of the painting: a large bamboo grove lies across the stream bank, located below and in front of the mountain head where the house is, placing the house in a distant layer behind a screened view | Foreground to middle ground: the stream runs through rock gaps toward the interior, with slope rocks and bamboo and trees flanking both banks, but no bridge, path, gate, or other clues connecting with the house on the mountain top are seen
distinction: The house is seen by its roof and eaves being revealed from among the trees on the mountain top, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship directly determines the layer in which it is presented; its mountain head is not a key node of the composition's opening and closing or of the convergence of the line of sight, and its scenic-accent role is weak.

evidence: Middle-ground right bank: among the trees on the sandbar, the outlines of low houses are faintly visible; the buildings and woodland interweave with each other, presenting a half-hidden, half-revealed state. | Lower middle of the foreground: willow groves screen a small building (appearing to be a pavilion or thatched hut), whose roof and partial structure are revealed through the branches, forming front-back layers.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed at the waterside, the painting emphasizes more the spatial layers formed by the screening and revealing of the buildings by the woodland, rather than highlighting the terrain-responsive correspondence between the buildings and the terrain.

evidence: Center-right: multiple buildings sit on terraced platforms with mortared-stone retaining walls; the building bases and eaves rise and fall in step with the terrace levels, and the retaining walls at the terrace edges and the slope foot are clearly visible | Middle-left to lower-left: several buildings spread out along the sloping bank, fences turn with the slope to enclose courtyards, and the ridge heights step down progressively with the slope | Below and lower-right: beneath the building terraces are paddy fields and sloping banks spread out along the shore, and the shoreline encircles the village building sites and forms the site boundary
distinction: Although the wooden bridge at upper left crosses the stream, there is no visible path or gateway connecting the bridge ends with the buildings, so it does not form an entry sequence; the dominant relationship in the painting is buildings disposed in layers according to the terrace and slope gradients

evidence: Left middle ground: a small bridge is visible among the mountains and rocks, with a figure on it, forming a spatial clue for entry or transition. | Whole painting: the painting consists mainly of mountains and rocks, trees, and waterside, and no clear houses or other built structures are seen.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built structures and mainly uses the bridge and path to suggest a spatial relationship of travel and entry, so it is assigned to C4.

evidence: Lower right: a four-cornered pavilion stands behind a withered tree; the pavilion roof and columns are partly obscured by the trunk and branches, forming a clear concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Foreground: the gnarled trunk and spreading branches serve as the foreground and half-screen the pavilion behind, participating in constructing the painting's spatial layers.
distinction: The pavilion and trees form a clear relationship of occlusion and exposure, and concealment and revelation is the core means of foreground composition, rather than mere placement according to terrain or use as a scenic marker.

evidence: Left middle slope gap: a thatched hut shows a hat-shaped straw roof and the upper part of its straw-woven wall; the lower half of the building itself is obscured by the moss-dotted line of the slope ridge passing in front, presenting a layer of a house seen behind the slope. | Left of the thatched hall: a slanting branch with leaf dots extends from the side of the house toward the left, its leaf dots covering the left shoulder of the house, and the branches and trees participate in screening and revealing the building itself. | Center to upper right: the central large tree and main slope occupy the main body of the painting, and the thatched hut recedes into a hollow on the left foot of the main slope, half-hidden behind the slope and branches, forming front-back spatial layers with the foreground bank.
distinction: The discernible relationship between house and slope consists mainly of the slope ridge and branches screening and revealing the building itself and indicating the layering of a house hidden behind the slope, rather than a siting correspondence in which the base layout unfolds with the slope form, so concealment and revelation is more apt than terrain-responsive siting.

evidence: Lower right: a flat bridge crosses the stream, connecting the two banks. | Lower middle, slightly right: a person stands on the bank beside the bridge, facing the stream and bridge, in a posture of traveling or pausing. | Overall: the painting consists mainly of landscape, trees, and a stream, and no clear houses, pavilions, or other built structures are seen.
distinction: No built structures are visible in the painting, but the bridge, stream, and figure form a clear clue to movement through the landscape and entry, so it is assigned to the closest category, C4.

evidence: Upper middle: a platform is built at the edge of a cliff, with two people standing on it; the platform base directly follows the projecting terrain of the cliff, presenting a relationship of a platform set according to the cliff. | Right: a thatched hut is visible among the mountains, rocks, and trees; the building itself is partly obscured by foreground elements, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship.
distinction: Although the thatched hut on the right presents a concealment-and-revelation relationship, the cliff-edge platform at the visual center of the painting, where the figures are, more prominently embodies the terrain-responsive relationship of built structures placed according to the cliff terrain, so C1 is dominant.

evidence: Water surface below: a small boat carries one person, its bow facing the bank/cave opening, forming a clear clue to movement through the landscape. | Center of the painting: a huge arched cave/rock opening forms a spatial entrance, connecting the outer water surface with the inner land. | Among the trees on the right: the roofs and walls of two thatched huts are visible, located deep in the space indicated by the cave and serving as the destination of the journey.
distinction: Although the built structures screened by trees fit the C2 characteristic, the painting constructs a strong path from outside to inside through the boat on the water and the central cave, and the process of spatial entry (C4) is more dominant.

evidence: Lower middle waterside: an open hall or pavilion is visible, its base level with the water surface, with columns set directly on the water's edge, presenting a layout of a building set facing the water. | Middle-ground water surface: in front of the built structure is an open water surface with several sailing boats visible, and the built structure forms a direct correspondence with the water surface. | Right and rear: trees and sloping banks lie behind and to the right of the built structure; the building is placed against the waterside terrain, and no clear path or bridge is seen leading to it.
distinction: Although the built structure marks the waterside scenery, its base layout level with the water surface more directly embodies the terrain-responsive relationship of placement according to the waterside terrain.

evidence: Lower-right water surface: a person is visible sitting in a small boat, floating on the open water, with no fixed buildings or bridges. | Lower left and right bank: clumps of reeds grow in the water, forming an open natural scene together with the distant mountains.
distinction: The painting lacks fixed built structures and uses only the lone boat on the water as the visual focus, marking the open waterside scene.

evidence: Upper right: a building complex is half-screened by dense trees, revealing part of the roofs, eaves, and walls, forming a layering of houses seen within the woods. | Lower left: an open pavilion is built on a rocky slope platform, echoing the surrounding mountain forms.
distinction: Although both buildings have the character of following the mountains, the concealment-and-revelation layering formed by the trees screening the upper-right buildings is more prominent in the painting and dominates the spatial expression.

evidence: Upper middle: a red-roofed built structure is half-hidden behind rock and withered trees, revealing only part of the roof and walls, forming layers of concealment and revelation. | Lower left: a house is obscured by foreground tree trunks and branches; through gaps in the trees the building itself and figures inside the windows can be seen, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Right and lower right: a figure riding a donkey is visible moving along a mountain path, and there is a small bridge in the lower-right corner, suggesting spatial extension, but this is not the dominant mode of composition.
distinction: Although the painting has paths and a bridge suggesting clues to travel, the built structures mainly construct spatial layers through relationships of screening and revealing with mountains, rocks, and trees, and the role of concealment and revelation is more significant.

evidence: Lower right: the roof and structural lines of a house are visible among the trees; the built structure is screened by foreground trees, presenting clear layers of concealment and revelation | Lower right: the built structure is located within or behind trees at the foot of the mountain, and the screening by woodland indicates its existence and spatial depth
distinction: The built structure mainly forms front-back spatial layers and a sense of seclusion through screening by woodland (C2), rather than serving as a visual marker to point out a specific landscape scene (C3).

evidence: Lower-left corner: a small pavilion (or thatched hut) is visible, with several clumps of bamboo beside it, small in scale and placed on the foreground sloping bank. | Painting as a whole: the built structure is tiny in scale and located at the edge of the painting, echoing the distant mountains on the left and the middle-ground slope rocks and withered trees in a near-far relationship, marking the secluded scene of the near bank.
distinction: There is a bamboo clump beside the pavilion, but the pavilion itself is basically fully exposed, and its main function is to mark the near-foreground position rather than to emphasize concealment-and-revelation layering.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: houses are visible among the trees at the foot of the mountain; the roofs and walls are partly obscured by foreground tree trunks and branches, presenting layers of concealment and revelation with houses seen deep in the woods. | Center, slightly below: the built structure is located in a sparse grove beside the waterside at the foot of the mountain; the building itself is screened by trunks, revealing only part of its structure, and the scene is formed through screening by woodland.
distinction: Although the houses are located at the waterside at the foot of the mountain, their most visually prominent feature is the concealment-and-revelation relationship formed by screening by trees, rather than an emphasis on their layout following the mountains.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: a group of built structures is placed against the sloping bank at the base of huge mountain rocks, and the base follows the undulations of the mountain foot and the rocks. | Lower left of the painting: to the left of the built structures is a bamboo grove and sloping ground, and to the right are scattered rocks, presenting a layout arranged according to the site.
distinction: The built structures mainly present a site-based relationship of placement following the sloping bank at the foot of the mountain, rather than relying on concealment-and-revelation layering or travel paths.

evidence: Upper bank of the painting: groups of buildings are arranged in rows from left to right along the winding shoreline, their ridge orientations turning with the shoreline, forming a village belt laid out along the shore | Upper-right water's edge: several buildings stand side by side close to the water's edge, their bases facing the water and aligned with the direction of the right-edge shoreline | Right-middle sandbar: several buildings are placed at the edge of the sandbar, facing the open water surface, and masts and trees on the sandbar gather along its shore
distinction: Some buildings are indeed screened by willow groves, but all groups of built structures in the painting are placed according to the shoreline and water's-edge configuration and spread out along the shore; the shore-water relationship runs through the composition and organizes the placement of built structures, and concealment and revelation is only a secondary layer

evidence: Upper half of the painting: the city wall winds and stretches horizontally along the edge of the sloping platform; gate towers and arched gate bases are set on high platforms, a pagoda stands on the slope line, and the heights of built structures correspond to the undulations of the slope | Middle left to right bank: multiple groups of buildings spread in rows close to the waterside; where the shoreline turns, the buildings are arranged accordingly, and their bases conform to the shoreline configuration | Center and lower right: an arched bridge crosses the water to connect buildings on both banks; the lower-right city gate opening stands according to the sloping bank, and on the bank a figure holding an umbrella walks along the bank path toward the gate opening
distinction: The bridge, gate opening, and pedestrians provide local entry clues, but the dominant relationship in the painting is that the city wall, gate towers, and building groups are placed and spread out according to the sloping platforms and shoreline terrain, and the travel clues do not run through and organize the composition

evidence: Upper opposite bank of the painting: city walls, city gates, and dense houses spread out along the water shoreline, with several wharves projecting into the water, presenting a layout built according to the water. | Center of the painting: houses and trees on a small island are distributed according to the island's terrain, with buildings dotting the sandbar and blending with the natural environment. | Left side of the painting: a building complex is arranged in layers along the sloping bank, rising and falling in height and closely integrated with the terrain.
distinction: Although the gate tower and island buildings have a scenic marking function, the painting as a whole emphasizes the distribution relationship of built structures (town, wharves, island houses) following the waterside and island terrain.

evidence: Right side and lower waterside of the painting: trackers are visible hauling boats along the waterside, and on the bank people ride horses or walk, forming a continuous water-and-land travel route. | Mountain foot at upper right of the painting: a large group of people and horses is visible moving along a curved path at the mountain foot, the route extending into the depth of the painting and guiding the eye. | Left sloping bank of the painting: multiple groups of houses are arranged against the slope platforms and willows, adjacent to the winding shoreline and the travel route.
distinction: Although the houses placed along the sloping banks embody terrain-responsive siting, the enterable and traversable spatial process formed by the towpath, bank paths, and traveling parties running through the whole painting is more prominent and dominates the overall composition.

evidence: Left bank and left edge: a row of houses is arranged closely in sequence along the winding shoreline; below is a long embankment or stepped structure connecting to an isolated building at the water's edge, presenting a clear layout spread out along the shore. | Upper-right bank: a building complex is distributed along the edge of the opposite-bank land, following the course of the shoreline, with house bases integrated with the bank terrain. | Lower near bank: a group of houses is located on elevated ground on the bank slope, with willows planted beside them, the layout following the undulations of the bank terrain.
distinction: Although some houses at upper right are screened by trees, the most prominent feature of the building complex in the painting as a whole is its winding distribution along the water shoreline, following the terrain, rather than a predominance of concealment-and-revelation layering.

evidence: Upper left: a building complex is arranged in staggered fashion on mountain slope platforms, roof heights following the terrain undulations. | Upper right: at the water's edge there is a structure resembling a wharf or trestle, extending into the water along the shoreline.
distinction: Although the wharf structure has the sense of a transportation node, the layout of the upper-left building complex following the mountains is more prominent and dominates the relationship between built structures and terrain.

evidence: Upper opposite-bank stretch along the shore: rows of buildings spread horizontally close to the winding shoreline, their bases set on the slope foot on the bank, the layout rising and falling with the turns of the shoreline | Middle-rear part of the upper village: the roofs of the rear row of houses rise above the front row of buildings and the tree belt, presenting a layered arrangement according to the heights of the sloping ground | Lower near bank: several buildings are laid out along the near-bank shoreline, their building bodies and roofs fully discernible, with groves mostly standing behind and beside the houses rather than screening the building bodies
distinction: Although the houses interpenetrate with woodland, most are fully exposed and spread in belts closely following the shoreline, and the organizing role of the waterside and sloping ground in placement is stronger than the layering formed by tree screening and revelation

evidence: Upper right: a temple complex sits atop a steep cliff, and its base forms a clear correspondence with the high-cliff terrain. | Middle left: a group of village houses is arranged in sequence along the edge of a waterside platform, spread out according to the sloping platform and shoreline. | Right cliff face: a stepped path is visible connecting the foot of the cliff with the temple at the top, further indicating that the buildings are placed according to the height difference.
distinction: The painting mainly shows the site-based arrangement of the village spreading along the waterside platform and the temple perched on the cliff top; the path is only a local connection, and following the terrain is dominant overall.

evidence: Middle-left sandbar of the painting: a stretch of buildings spreads in rows along the edge of the sloping bank outlined in ink lines, their bases set on the waterside slope platforms, the layout extending and contracting with the turns of the shoreline | Middle-lower-right sandbar of the painting: several buildings are placed on the top of a low sloping bank, backed by groves and facing the open water, their bases corresponding to the sandbar's slope form | Interior of the middle-left settlement: trees interpenetrate among the buildings, and some building bodies are half-covered by tree crowns, but most roofs and building bodies are fully visible, and concealment and revelation is only local interpenetration
distinction: The relationship of buildings spreading along the shore with bases placed according to the slope platforms runs through both sandbars and dominates the composition; tree screening is only a local phenomenon within the settlements and does not form layers of concealment and revelation constituting a scene

evidence: Upper-middle mountain top: a group of buildings (apparently a temple) is built directly on the highest point of the mountain top, placed according to the mountain forms. | Middle-right riverbank: dense village houses spread out with varying heights along the platforms and slopes of the waterside, following the terrain contours. | Lower-left near bank: scattered houses are placed on flat ground at the edge of the waterside, adjacent to the water surface and trees, built according to the site.
distinction: The buildings are laid out and spread mainly according to the undulations of the terrain and waterside, rather than serving only as isolated landmarks to point out a certain scene.

evidence: Left and lower left: a cluster of dwellings is densely arranged along the winding riverbank, with staggered roofs, presenting a clear layout spread out along the shore. | Right: a red-walled building complex is located on flat ground at the foot of the mountain, backed by mountains and placed according to the terrain. | Central water surface and bank: many boats are moored at the river estuary, their masts standing in profusion, connecting the water surface with the onshore built structures and conforming to waterside mooring.
distinction: Although the right-side buildings are larger in scale and striking in color, with a certain landmark quality, the many dwellings in the painting mainly present a distribution following the waterside and mountain-foot terrain, and the spatial organization of terrain-responsive siting is more dominant.

evidence: Upper middle and upper right: gate towers, barbicans, and attached houses are arranged in staggered fashion according to the rises and falls of the sloping platform terrain, with the highest building at the highest slope top and the remaining buildings spread out following the slope. | Right side of the painting: the building bases clearly rest on projecting earthen slope platforms, presenting a spatial relationship of houses set according to the platform and placed with the terrain.
distinction: The buildings are mainly placed and laid out according to the heights of the terrain and slope platforms, rather than serving merely as markers pointing out a certain landscape scene.

evidence: Center-right: a gate tower and city wall are built on a steep cliff facing the water, and the city wall winds and spreads following the mountain slope platforms. | Upper-right corner: a building sits directly on the rocks at the mountain top, placed according to the mountain form. | Left: a complex of pavilions and buildings is distributed in staggered fashion on the sloping ground of the mountainside, echoing the mountain form.
distinction: Although the built structures in the painting also serve to point out scenery, their most prominent feature is site-based placement according to the cliff, the slope, and the shore, so C1 is more accurate than C3.

evidence: Middle horizontal band of the painting: the city wall winds and turns from left to right along the ochre-colored bank platform; the wall base and the bank face rise and fall along the same line, with rocks placed below the bank, and the built structures spread out along the waterside platform | From the center to the right end inside the city wall: gate towers, gatehouses, and groups of buildings are arranged along the platform inside the wall; the right-end pavilion is set according to the platform, and roof heights change with the platform configuration | Upper left and middle left: several buildings on the mountain top are placed according to the summit slope platforms, and at middle left the village houses spread in groups along the sloping bank, their bases corresponding to the platform edges
distinction: Although the middle-left arched bridge and the city-wall arched gate suggest approach clues, they exist only locally and there is no connecting path outside the gate; the dominant relationship is the correspondence of the city wall and the inner and outer buildings winding and being placed according to the bank-platform configuration

evidence: Upper middle of the painting: the city wall winds along the mountain ridge line, with a pavilion built on the mountain top, presenting a layout built according to the mountain forms. | Middle of the painting: many houses are densely arranged along the waterside and sloping ground, spreading out along the shore following the terrain. | Lower-right corner of the painting: houses and boats are moored at the waterside edge, with built structures dwelling by the water, corresponding to the shoreline form.
distinction: The building complexes in the painting (city wall, houses) mainly follow the mountain forms and waterside layout, emphasizing the spatial relationship of site-based placement rather than serving merely as markers adorning the scenery.

evidence: Upper left: a group of houses is arranged in sequence along the curving shoreline contour, the layout following the direction of the waterside. | Upper middle of the painting: the houses are placed close against the edge of the sloping bank, presenting a spatial relationship of houses set according to the bank and placed according to the terrain.
distinction: Although the inscription labels the location, the houses in the painting are mainly laid out following the terrain of the shoreline; the spatial organization of terrain-responsive siting is more prominent than mere scenic accentuation.

evidence: Central mountaintop and ridge: multiple groups of buildings are distributed in rows along the ridgeline and the slope crest, the building bases rising and falling with the mountain's contours, and the clustered buildings unfold along the ridge line rather than spreading flat | Hillside down to the mountain foot slopes: pavilions are set in tiers according to the slope, and houses at the mountain foot spread laterally along the foot of the slope and the winding waterside, the settlement edge turning with the shoreline | Slightly above the right side of the ridge: a pale winding track runs up from the mid-slope building group to connect with the mountaintop buildings, only partly visible, and forms no continuous sequence of entry with the boats on the water or the bank landing
distinction: The ridge track only locally links the upper and lower groups of built elements, whereas the relationship of buildings being placed layer by layer according to the form from the summit through the mid-slope to the waterside runs through the whole painting, giving it a stronger organizing role

evidence: Upper left, foot of the slope: a group of houses and one taller pavilion gather on a flat slope between the foot of the hillside and the gully shoreline, the roof ridges rising and falling and spreading laterally along the slope terrace | Running across the middle of the painting to the lower left: a winding gully shoreline with double lines enclosing texture strokes runs horizontally from the turning point at the lower left of the house group toward the right, and the building bases of the house group directly face the terrace enclosed by the bend of this shoreline | Around the house group: willows stand among the houses and at the foot of the slope behind, the outlines and roofs of the houses fully exposed, and the screening relationship does not form a dominant layer
distinction: The built group mainly presents a relationship of placement and unfolding according to the slope terrace and facing the gully bank, rather than using built elements to mark a landscape feature such as a peak edge or valley mouth

evidence: Left and middle: the city wall and gate structures are built against the sloping ground and waterside, with steps below directly connecting to boats moored on the water. | Upper middle: the house clusters are distributed in a staggered high-and-low arrangement following the slope of the hillside, the layout following the undulations of the terrain. | Along the waterside: the building bases and wharf facilities unfold following the winding shoreline, presenting a form of houses set according to the water.
distinction: Although the painting includes transport elements such as the city gate, steps, and boats that suggest a movement route, the overall composition emphasizes more the layout relationship of the building clusters against the waterside and sloping ground, with placement according to terrain as the dominant expression.

evidence: Left side and middle of the painting: multiple groups of houses and boats are distributed along the winding river and earthen banks, the bases and layout following the twisting form of the waterside. | Lower part of the painting: wharves, boats, and houses are placed close against the shoreline, presenting a spatial relationship of unfolding along the bank and placement according to terrain.
distinction: Although there is screening of trees and houses in the painting, the dominant logic of spatial organization is that the built elements unfold in response to the winding of the waterside terrain, rather than being dominated by concealment and revelation.

evidence: Upper left: the city wall and gate towers extend along the high slope, set according to the high ground and following the undulations of the terrain. | Middle and lower parts: dense house clusters and wharf facilities unfold along the curving shoreline, the layout following the form of the water system. | Middle of the painting: a bridge spans the water connecting the built elements on the two banks, the route following the interval of the waters.
distinction: Although bridges and waterways suggest passage, the dominant expression is that the city wall, houses, and wharves are closely laid out according to the high ground and shoreline forms, presenting a clear relationship of terrain-responsive siting.

evidence: Lower part: a dense group of built elements (houses, courtyards) unfolds along the shoreline, the layout following the undulations and openings and closings of the bank terrain. | Left middle: a building with steps is placed against the sloping bank, partly screened by willows.
distinction: Although there is local screening, what the main building group below more prominently shows is the layout relationship unfolding according to the waterside terrain, rather than scenery formed purely by concealment and revelation.

evidence: Left middle to center: a grey-walled city terrace, multi-eaved pavilions, and rows of houses unfold along the diagonally sloping earthen bank of the river, the terraces and buildings rising and falling with the bank's contours in a bank-following arrangement | Center-left waterside: a row of timber piles with horizontal beams extends from the bank slope into the water, aligned with the direction of the shoreline, with several sailing boats moored alongside, showing that the built elements are set close to the water | Upper right: a red-walled building and several houses sit on the upper section of the bank slope band, distributed along the bank with the building bases corresponding to the bank slope, backed by rows of trees
distinction: Although the boats, waterside piles, and bank paths form a ferry-crossing movement thread, the whole painting is governed by the shoreline and slope terraces in the placement and unfolding of built elements, rather than emphasizing a process of entering from here to there

evidence: Lower center of the painting: the sluice-gate structure is precisely placed at the gap in the transverse earthen embankment, forming a strict spatial correspondence with the embankments on both sides and the waterway below, embodying a terrain-responsive relationship of building at a break in the terrain. | Above the earthen embankment: village houses and pavilions are separately placed following the direction and terrain of the earthen embankment, the layout following the undulating form of the embankment.
distinction: Although the painting includes a passage thread through the sluice-gate waterway, the core of the composition leans more toward the placement relationship adapted to local conditions between the sluice gate and the embankment gap, and between the village and the direction of the embankment.

evidence: Upper left: the house group is built against the steep earthen cliff terrace, presenting a form of houses set according to the terrace and separately placed according to the slope, with high and low staggered in correspondence with the terrain. | Middle right: dense houses unfold layer by layer along the shoreline, the layout closely fitting the direction of the riverbank and presenting a bank-following relationship. | Right side: a gate-tower building stands facing the water, with steps or wharf structures below connecting to the water surface, embodying the combination of building base and waterside terrain.
distinction: The painting mainly expresses the overall layout of the building clusters according to the slope terraces and along the shoreline and their correspondence with the terrain, rather than emphasizing a single movement path or a process of entering into the depths.

evidence: Upper left corner and above: the city wall extends according to the terrain and has an arched city gate, with a bridge connecting nearby, showing that the built elements are placed according to the terrain. | Middle to right of the painting: a large number of house clusters are densely arranged along an implied shoreline, presenting a bank-following layout that corresponds to the boats moored on the water. | Lower left corner: houses and trees are set facing the water, distributed following the bank terrain.
distinction: Although bridges and city gates provide entry clues (C4), the dominant spatial relationship is the settlement layout in which the house clusters unfold along the bank according to the waterside terrain (C1), rather than emphasizing the deepening process of a single path.

evidence: Lower middle: several thatched huts are scattered in a staggered arrangement, surrounded by dense willows, with roofs and walls partly obscured by branches, presenting a layer of concealment and revelation among the trees. | Right edge: another house is screened among willows and trees with red blossoms, only part of its building outline visible. | Upper right corner, distant view: the outlines of a city wall and gate towers are visible, forming spatial depth with the trees and houses in the near ground as a distant view.
distinction: Although the houses are scattered on flat ground, the core of their scenic composition lies in using the branches and leaves of the willows to form spatial layers of screening and exposure, rather than emphasizing placement according to terrain slopes and terraces.

evidence: Right middle, slope top: an open pavilion sits at the edge of the slope-crest platform, with railings set between the columns, the pavilion base fitting the flat rim of the slope crest, and the pavilion body facing the open water to the left, its base level determined by the turning of the slope crest | Lower right to middle right: the slope cliff rises from lower right to upper left with texture strokes, turning at the top into a gentle slope surface that supports the pavilion base, the slope and cliff edge directly participating in the pavilion's placement and orientation | Lower right, slope ridge: a figure walks on a pale gentle band of the slope ridge, facing the direction of the pavilion, with a diagonal stepped path connecting to it in front of the pavilion, forming a local arrival clue
distinction: The figure and stepped path are only local clues in the lower right corner, whereas the correspondence of the pavilion base, railings, and orientation with the slope-crest cliff edge and the open water runs through the right half of the composition, giving the terrain a stronger organizing role in placement

evidence: Lower middle: a waterside pavilion is partly screened by tree trunks and hanging willow branches in front, revealing only the roof, eaves, and figures inside, forming a clear layer of concealment and revelation. | Left and lower middle: trees grow densely on the sloping bank, screening the building among them; the building is not fully exposed but participates in the composition through the screening and exposure by the woodland.
distinction: Although the building is constructed against the waterside slope, the painting emphasizes more the spatial layers formed by the screening and exposure of the building by the trees, rather than simply emphasizing its layout as placed according to the terrain and waterside.

evidence: Lower right: one built element (a house) is visible, surrounded by trees, with open ground or a path in front. | Lower right and middle right: figures are near the built element, and boats are moored at the bank on the water, suggesting a spatial connection by which the built element can be reached by waterway or bank path. | Middle right, sloping bank: figures walk on the sloping bank, echoing the movement clues with the built element and water below.
distinction: Although the built element is partly screened by trees (C2), elements such as walking figures and moored boats more strongly suggest an enterable and reachable spatial process leading to the built element, so C4 is more apt.

evidence: Lower left: a multi-arched stone bridge spans the water, with figures carrying loads and holding umbrellas on the bridge and boats moored beneath, forming a clear movement clue and spatial transition. | Right middle: roofs and walls of buildings emerge amid screening trees, together with the stone bridge forming a spatial connection from the water to the built elements on the bank. | Upper right: a pagoda on the mountaintop appears faintly amid clouds and mist and trees, serving as the visual endpoint of the distant view and enhancing the sense of spatial depth.
distinction: Although there is a concealment-and-revelation relationship of trees screening buildings in the painting (C2), the stone bridge and the figures' activity on it form a more dominant movement clue, clearly expressing the spatial process of going from here to there and approaching the built elements (C4).

evidence: Left middle ground: a multi-story pagoda reveals its upper story and finial from behind autumn-colored trees, its base and lower section obscured by the canopy, presenting a layer of seeing the pagoda behind the trees | Among the trees below the pagoda, left middle: roof ridges and eaves are half-revealed amid mixed trees, the walls not visible, the existence of built elements indicated by the exposed roofs | Central water surface: an arched bridge spans the water with figures on it, the left end of the bridge landing at the foot of the sloping bank where boats are moored, and between it and the pagoda and houses among the trees there is screening by tree clusters with no directly connecting path visible
distinction: The pagoda and houses are presented by concealment and revelation among the trees, which determines their visible layers, while between the bridge end and the built elements there is blockage by tree clusters and no discernible entry connection, so the concealment-and-revelation relationship is closer to the painting's organization than the movement clue

evidence: Middle ground, right bank and right of the arched bridge: several water pavilions are raised above the water on dense timber piles, their bodies spreading laterally along the shoreline, the bases directly following the waterside configuration | Lower left foreground, sloping bank: a double-eaved pavilion is built on a river-facing slope terrace, its enclosing walls winding down with the slope, the building heights corresponding to the slope-terrace terrain | Middle ground, left bank, foot of the main peak: house clusters are placed on the slope at the mountain foot and on the bank-side terrace, roofs distributed with the undulations of the slope, corresponding to the mountain form and slope foot
distinction: Although the arched bridge and the ferry boat in mid-river are movement clues, they are only local elements; the built elements throughout the painting are organized by the correspondence of bases and modes of unfolding with the shoreline and slope terraces, so terrain-responsive siting is dominant

evidence: Lower left and lower middle: the roofs, eaves, and walls of a group of buildings appear faintly amid a large expanse of blossoming pink trees, forming a clear relationship of screening and exposure. | Left, mountain foot: the building group is placed against the mountain foot, screened layer upon layer by the blossoming trees of the foreground and middle ground, indicating the spatial layers in which the buildings sit.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed against the mountain foot and waterside, the most prominent mode of spatial organization in the painting is the use of screening by blossoming trees to present the layers of concealment and revelation of the buildings, rather than simply emphasizing placement according to terrain.

evidence: Right side and middle ground: houses are built following the mountain terrain, with clear stone steps and paths connecting the buildings below and above the mountain, figures walking along the paths, forming clear clues of entry and movement. | Lower part and middle ground of the painting: pack horses, bearers, and pedestrians advance along the road into the mountains, the path extending to the built elements on the right, expressing a spatial process of going from here to there.
distinction: Although the buildings are constructed following the mountain, the painting emphasizes more the guidance of the viewer's gaze by clear paths, steps, and advancing figures into the mountain built elements, highlighting an enterable and traversable spatial process.
