evidence: Lower right corner: part of a house is visible, including the roof and window frame, partly obscured by branches and leaves in the foreground and the sloping bank, presenting a half-concealed, half-revealed state. | Slightly left of center: a figure sits alone on the waterside slope, forming a spatial echo and layering with the screened built elements on the right. | Right side and center: tall trees interpose between foreground and middle ground, forming a clear relationship of screening and exposure with the built elements on the right.
distinction: Although the built elements are placed against the sloping bank, the painting mainly presents their spatial layers through the screening and exposure by trees, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship is more prominent.

evidence: Lower right: a pavilion is built facing the water, surrounded by pine trees, with figures inside, becoming the visual focus of the lower right of the painting. | Left middle: a group of house roofs is faintly visible among trees on the opposite bank, blending with the natural environment. | Lower left: a boat is moored on the water, forming a spatial echo with the pavilion.
distinction: Although the waterside pavilion has the appearance of terrain-responsive placement, its more main role in the painting is as a visual focus, marking out and concentrating the scenery of the waterside.

evidence: Middle right of the painting: a pavilion is partly obscured by the trunks and branches of pine trees in the foreground and by mountains and rocks behind, revealing only part of its roof and columns, forming spatial layers of alternating concealment and exposure. | Lower part of the painting: a small boat is on the water with a figure aboard, forming a line-of-sight or spatial echo with the pavilion on the bank, but not directly connected. | Right side of the painting: mountain rocks, sloping bank, and trees interweave, further setting off the state of the pavilion hidden among natural scenery.
distinction: Although the pavilion has a scenic-accentuating role, its concealment and revelation by trees and rocks is more prominent in the composition and fits the feature of concealment and revelation forming a setting.

evidence: Lower center of the painting: mountains and rocks, old trees, and a sloping bank are visible, with a figure sitting alone and a boat nearby; no clear houses or built structures are seen. | Right side of the painting: the water surface is open, distant mountains faint, with no trace of buildings.
distinction: There are no clear built structures in the painting; the figure and boat, as scenic accent elements, concentrate the scenery of the open waterside, so it is only tentatively assigned to C3.

evidence: Lower right: a small built structure with a roof is visible at the waterside, surrounded by trees and mountain rocks. | Left side: tall mountain rocks and dense woodland on the left form a spatial contrast with the open water on the right. | Lower right built structure: the built structure sits in an open area of the waterside, serving as the visual focus of the lower right of the painting and marking out the waterside scenery here.
distinction: Although the built structure is located at the waterside, its main role is to mark out a scenic spot between the open water and high mountains as a visual marker, rather than emphasizing its layout as built according to the terrain.

evidence: Right scroll, foreground lower bank: a figure in white stands leaning on a staff in a recess of the sloping bank, facing the open water to the left, in a posture of pausing during movement | Right scroll, middle ground: the water surface spreads laterally, islets and low banks interlace, and the shoreline extends from the near bank toward the mountain foot in the distance, forming a spatial sequence that can be continued onward | Right scroll, foreground right: several slanting pines stand on slope rocks, and the sloping bank extends from right to left into the water, defining a zone for passage along the bank
distinction: The painting organizes a traversable process through the staff-bearing figure and the extension of the shoreline and water surface, rather than the correspondence between terrain and building bases (the latter being entirely invisible).

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: a pavilion is visible, revealing its roof and columns, built on slope rocks | Around the pavilion: willows stand in front of the pavilion, their branches hanging down and obscuring part of the pavilion body; tall trees surround it on the right, forming layers of concealment and revelation in which woodland screens the built element
distinction: Although the pavilion is built on slope rocks, the painting mainly presents the pavilion's spatial layers through the screening and exposure by willows and tall trees, and the relationship of concealment and revelation forming a setting is more dominant.

evidence: Among the mountain rocks on the left: there are blurred ink traces, suspected to be tiny structures, but the details are unclear and cannot be confirmed as clear built elements. | Lower right shoreline: there are short vertical ink lines, suspected to be remnants of timber piles or a bridge, but lacking clear structural features. | Whole painting: the painting is dominated by mountains and rocks, trees, and clouds and mist, with no clearly discernible buildings, bridges, or paths.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built elements; it is assigned to C2 only on the basis of the natural spatial expression of clouds and mist screening and revealing the mountain forms.

evidence: Lower left and center: surrounded by mountains and rocks and trees, forming a winding waterside space | Lower right: a small boat is on the water, near the trees and rocks on the bank, presenting a movement clue
distinction: The combination of the boat with the water surface and bank trees emphasizes more a traversable movement relationship than serving merely as a scenic marker

evidence: Lower left waterside of the painting: a small open house is visible amid screening trees and rocks, with a figure seated inside, the main body of the building partly obscured by foreground trees and mountain rocks. | Left side of the painting: branches and leaves of trees and mountain rocks form the foreground, half-screening the buildings behind, presenting spatial layers of alternating concealment and exposure.
distinction: Although the building is set facing the water, the painting emphasizes more its concealment and revelation, half-screened by trees and rocks, rather than simply placement according to terrain.

evidence: Central isolated island in the river: a multi-storey pagoda stands above the tree canopy of the isolated island, its finial projecting vertically; it is the only conspicuous vertical built element in the open, expansive painting | Middle of the isolated island: several buildings and eaves are arranged around the pagoda base, screened among the island's trees, together with the pagoda forming the entire content of the isolated island | Water around the isolated island: beyond the island all is open river water, scattered with only a few small boats, with no other mountain banks or buildings; the view is concentrated on the central built isolated island
distinction: The trees half-screening the buildings are only a local concealment-and-revelation layer of the isolated island; the whole painting sets the built isolated island against the open river surface, and the pagoda gives cohesion and identity to a single scenic spot in mid-river, so the primary category is C3 rather than C2.

evidence: High on the mountains and rocks on the right side of the painting: a storied pavilion is built, its base clearly situated on a rocky platform, presenting the form of a building set on a terrace. | Beside the building: two pine trees and the building are placed together on the rocky terrace, the building unfolding in reliance on the terrain.
distinction: Although the building serves as a scenic accent on the right side of the painting, its spatial relationship of being placed in reliance on the rocky terrace (building set on a terrace) is visually clearer and dominant.

evidence: Lower left: a single-arch bridge spans a stream gorge, its deck connecting the wooded slope on the left bank with the sloping bank on the right, forming a traversable crossing cue | Middle right: a flight of stone steps rises diagonally from the lower bank terrace up to an open arched gatehouse, a standing figure visible within the gate opening, with another roof visible above and behind the gatehouse | Lower right: among the trees on the sloping bank there is another roofed archway with an open gate opening, which together with the middle-right gatehouse and the lower-left arch bridge indicates several entry mouths
distinction: The bridge, the steps and the gate openings form a progression from the outer bank through the gate into the deeper building complex, which explains the organization of the whole painting better than layering shown only through concealment by trees.

evidence: From the lower to the middle part of the painting: a long multi-arch stone bridge (long bridge) spans the water, its body extending continuously, with pedestrians walking on it and a pavilion built at its midpoint, forming a clear movement-through-the-landscape cue and traversable route. | Right side of the painting: the long bridge extends to the right and connects to the bank, where a pagoda and houses appear amid screening trees; the bridge serves as a cue guiding the eye and direction of travel toward these built elements, presenting a spatial relationship of passing from here to there. | Lower left and water surface: the water beneath the bridge is open, dotted with sailing boats; the bridge spans the water connecting the two banks, reinforcing the spatial process of passage and arrival.
distinction: Although the long bridge and pagoda have landmark character (C3), the painting emphasizes more the long bridge as a movement cue connecting the two banks and guiding pedestrians and the eye toward the deeper built elements (pagoda/houses) in a 'from here to there' spatial process, in accordance with the C4 definition.

evidence: Lower right: a stone arch bridge spans the water, figures walking visible on its deck, its two ends joining respectively the wooded slope of the right bank and the sloping bank of the central mountain mass | Right slope of the central mountain mass: a flight of step-like paths winds up from a pavilion house on the mountainside to the building complex at the summit, the path partly screened by trees | Central summit: a multi-storey pagoda and the roofs of several halls cluster on the peak, the destination to which the bridge and the steps lead
distinction: Although the pagoda standing on the peak has a scenic-accent role, the figures on the bridge and the steps on the mountain flank form an enterable sequence from the bank to the summit built elements; the movement linkage runs through the composition more than the identifying role.

evidence: Middle ground spanning the lake: a row of multi-arch long bridge-causeway crosses the water, joining houses on the bank at the left and connecting at its right end by another arch bridge to the hill on the right, tiny standing figures visible on the deck indicating passage | Lower-right hill: pale paths wind up the slope from the lower bank, successively linking a waterside pavilion, a mid-slope pavilion and a summit pagoda, presenting layering of ascent turning into the depths | Lower center-right: a gate-tower-style building sits at a bend in the shoreline, with a low wall extending along the bank beside it and joining the bank path, forming a portal cue for entering the lake shore within the painting
distinction: The bridge-causeway, mountain paths and gate tower link the scattered houses and pavilions around the lake into an attainable, ascendable process of travel, which explains the spatial organization of the whole picture better than C1, which would only describe the buildings as placed in reliance on the bank and slopes.

evidence: Lower right: a plank bridge spans a stream gorge, a person carrying a load on a pole walking leftward across it, the bridge end joining a pale open ground on the sloping bank | Center-right: an open pavilion stands at the edge of the open ground on the sloping bank, two figures standing beside it, the open ground extending from the bridge end to the front of the pavilion, forming an attainable connection | Between the central trees and the great rock on the left: roofs and eaves of buildings emerge among the slope rocks and trees behind and left of the pavilion, and white wall and eave lines also appear in the crevices of the great rock on the left, showing that beyond the bridge and pavilion there are deeper built elements to turn into
distinction: The figures on the bridge and beside the pavilion form an enterable, attainable movement linkage; although the screening and revealing of rocks and trees is present, it serves the process of passing from here to there rather than dominating the layering.

evidence: Lower-right valley: a flight of step-like paths extends upward from the valley mouth at the stream bank directly to the doorway of a small white-walled pavilion on the mountainside, forming an attainable, enterable movement cue | Right mountain hollow: among the rocks and trees above the small pavilion another building appears faintly, its position continuing the upward direction of the steps, suggesting that the journey may continue into the depths | Central main peak: an open pavilion is placed on a platform at the peak, facing the valley pavilion across the valley, at a position where the view along the valley-mouth path converges
distinction: The linkage of the steps with the mountain pavilion and the building among the rocks makes the painting present a process of approaching the built elements from the valley mouth and turning into the depths, which explains the organizing role of the built elements in the composition better than a single pavilion at the peak marking the scenery.

evidence: Left mountain foot: a group of houses is screened among trees and mountains and rocks, roofs and part of the walls exposed, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Upper-middle mountainside: building roofs are faintly visible behind mountains and rocks and trees, forming spatial layering through screening by natural scenery.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed in reliance on the mountain terrain, the painting emphasizes more their layered relationship of being screened and revealed by trees, mountains and rocks, rather than simple correspondence with the terrain.

evidence: Lower left: a wooden bridge is visible spanning between sloping banks, a person walking on it with a staff, forming a clear movement-through-the-landscape cue. | Lower-middle part of the painting: the bridge connects the open ground on the left with the pine-and-rock area on the right, implying the spatial process of the figure passing from here to there and advancing into the depths of the painting.
distinction: Here the bridge serves mainly as a path cue for the figure to cross the waterside and enter the depths of the pines and rocks, emphasizing the process of passage and travel rather than simply serving as an accent marking a scenic spot.

evidence: Middle right: two tiled-roof houses are staggered before a bamboo grove, the left end of the rear house and a fence disappearing into the bamboo; the houses emerge through gaps in the grove, forming a layering of houses seen within the grove | Behind and to the left of the houses on the right bank: dense bamboo rises behind and to the left of the houses, bamboo leaves hanging over the roofs, enclosing and screening the rear of the houses so that they appear half-screened by trees | Right of the houses: the houses are placed close against the rock wall on the right, the rock wall and bamboo grove together sheltering the houses, the open ground before the houses and the walls emerging in front of the rock and grove
distinction: The main compositional role of the houses is to present concealment-and-revelation layering through enclosure and screening by the bamboo grove and rock wall, rather than correspondence of base height, unfolding manner and slope-bank configuration.

evidence: Center of the painting: the house is partly blocked by the trees and bamboo grove in front, only the roof, part of the walls and a railing exposed, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Left and center of the painting: behind the built elements are mountains, rocks and a waterfall, in front are sloping banks and water, tree trunks and branches interweave before the house, enhancing the spatial layering.
distinction: Although the built elements rely on the mountains and water, the painting emphasizes more the layering of the house presented through screening and revealing by trees and bamboo grove, so C2 is more apt than C1.

evidence: Center-right of the painting: a flat great rock (white rock) juts out from the water, a person seated on it, with no clear houses, pavilions or other built elements around. | Left: layered mountains and rocks with a waterfall flowing down, forming an opening-and-closing space with the water on the right. | Right: a large area of unpainted space represents the water; the inscription identifies 'white rock', 'clear spring' and 'facing the water'; the figure and the white rock concentrate the landscape scenery here.
distinction: There are no clear built elements in the painting; the figure and the white rock are placed in reliance on the waterside, but their main role is to identify the scenery of sitting alone facing the water, so it is assigned to C3.

evidence: Water on the right: a small boat and figures in it are visible, presenting a state of movement through the landscape. | Middle and distant parts of the painting: the water is open, connecting the sloping bank in the foreground with the distant mountains, creating a sense of spatial extension.
distinction: The painting lacks fixed built elements, with only a small boat traveling on the water, presenting a traversable spatial process, so it is assigned to C4.

evidence: Left middle ground: the roof and columns of a group of buildings are faintly visible through the branches of the trees in front, presenting a layering of houses hidden within the grove. | Water in the right middle ground: a small boat and the figure in it are partly blocked by the branches and leaves of the trees in the right foreground, forming a screened-view-of-the-boat effect.
distinction: The core compositional device of the painting lies in the spatial layering formed by the screening and revealing of the buildings and boat by trees, rather than emphasizing following the mountains or path guidance.

evidence: Lower right: thatched buildings are visible, their walls and roofs partly blocked by the trees in the foreground and the bamboo grove in the middle ground, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Right: the built elements are screened among sparse trees and dense bamboo, presenting a spatial layering of a hut built within the grove.
distinction: Although the built elements identify the scenery on the right, the painting emphasizes more the spatial layering formed by their screening and revealing through trees, so C2 is more apt than C3.

evidence: Lower-left foreground: slope rocks and a terrace extend from the lower left toward the center, a withered tree entwined with vines standing at a turning point of the slope rocks, its root foot resting on the high ground of the sloping bank | Center to right bank: several stretches of sandbar and sloping bank unfold laterally along the water, their rises and falls meeting the unpainted water surface, on which there are only moss dots and earthen slopes, with no houses or walls visible | Distant view and the whole painting: pale-ink distant peaks stand behind the sandbars, the water surface open and unpainted; there are no identifiable roofs, eaves, bridges, paths, gates or other built elements or movement cues in the whole painting
distinction: In the visible organization, the conditions of the slope terraces and shoreline govern the corresponding placement of the foreground trees and rocks and the middle-ground sandbars, which is closer to terrain-responsive arrangement; but the painting lacks identifiable entry cues such as bridges, paths and gates, and shoreline extension alone is insufficient to constitute access to secluded settings.

evidence: Lower-right waterside: a group of buildings (pavilion/water-side belvedere) is visible placed close against the waterside, with supporting structures below facing the water, presenting a posture of buildings set by the water and unfolding along the bank. | To the left of and behind the buildings: the buildings are surrounded by withered trees and slope rocks, the base following the undulations of the terrain and forming a clear relationship of dependence on the natural sloping bank.
distinction: Although there are cues beside the buildings on the right of the painting that may be a bridge or plank walkway, the buildings' own character of relying on the water and being placed along the bank following the terrain is more prominent and dominant, so C1 is more apt than C4.

evidence: Lower right: a pavilion is built on a rocky bank by the water, its base directly relying on the natural shoreline and the mountains-and-rocks terrain. | Lower middle: trees and mountains and rocks are distributed along the waterside, and the pavilion unfolds its placement in conformity with this terrain.
distinction: Although the pavilion identifies the waterside scenery, its relationship of placement in reliance on the waterside terrain is more direct and prominent, in accordance with the characteristics of terrain-responsive siting.

evidence: Lower right: several withered trees are visible growing on an earthen slope, accompanied by slope rocks and clumps of grass. | Lower left: at the edge of the waterside a person sits on the slope holding a rod and fishing, with no traces of houses, bridges, paths or other built elements visible.
distinction: There are no clear built elements in the painting; only a figure sitting on the waterside slope rocks is seen, which barely corresponds to a spatial relationship of placement in reliance on the water.

evidence: Center-right of the painting: a pavilion sits within a grove of trees, its roof and columns partly blocked by the surrounding trunks and branches and leaves, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Left and lower parts of the painting: mountains and rocks and trees form the foreground, creating foreground-background layering with the pavilion behind, further enhancing the screened effect.
distinction: Although the pavilion serves as a scenic accent, the painting emphasizes more its spatial layering of being half-screened by trees, mountains and rocks, the concealment-and-revelation relationship being more dominant.

evidence: Lower right: between the waterside and a clump of trees a simple small wooden bridge is visible spanning and connecting the land on the two banks. | Whole painting: no clear houses or buildings are visible; the space consists mainly of water, distant mountains and near-bank trees, and the bridge provides an entry cue for crossing the water.
distinction: The painting lacks obvious layering of concealment and revelation of buildings, and the bridge at the lower right more directly provides a movement cue for crossing the water and entering the wooded bank, so C4 is more apt than C2.

evidence: Lower part of the painting: the right bank is painted with trees and a sloping bank; on the water at the left a small boat with a person lying in it, with no clear houses or other built elements visible. | Center-left of the painting: the small boat is moored at the edge of the waterside, presenting a state of stopping in reliance on the water.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built elements; only the small boat moored at the bank is taken as the closest classification of terrain-responsive placement.

evidence: Left mountain slope: several houses are built in reliance on the mountain, partly blocked by the mountains and rocks and dense trees in front, only roofs and part of the walls exposed, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Left and center: the houses are surrounded by trees, with branches and leaves interweaving with the buildings, reinforcing the spatial layering of built elements hidden within the grove.
distinction: Although the small bridge and figures on the right of the painting hint at a movement cue, the screened relationship of the house group on the left being screened by mountains, rocks and trees is more conspicuous and constitutes the main built situation of the painting.

evidence: Lower-middle right at the stream mouth: a plank bridge with supports spans the water, connecting the pine slope on the right bank with the shrubby sloping bank on the left | Middle of the right bank: a figure with a staff stands at the end of the bank path, the path running straight to the bridge end at the left, presenting an intention to cross the bridge | Left-middle sloping bank: a person sits on the waterside slope, the fine lines of the sloping bank joining the path on the right bank through the bridge, forming a continuous attainable shoreline organization; no houses, pavilions or other built elements appear in the whole painting
distinction: The painting organizes the spatial process of crossing from this bank over the bridge to the other bank through the bridge, the path and the movement of figures, rather than the corresponding placement of building bases with the terrain, so C4 is taken rather than C1.

evidence: Right sloping bank: a courtyard enclosed by white-walled houses and a grid-like fence sits on a waterside slope terrace, the fence turning and unfolding along the terrace edge, the base corresponding to the configuration of the sloping bank | Right front slope edge: a large tree grows at the slope edge and bamboo in the courtyard, the tree canopy over the roofs while the walls and windows of the buildings remain clearly visible, the built elements arranged following the high ground of the slope terrace | Lower-middle water edge: bank rocks and grassy flats at the foot of the slope extend into the water, an empty canopied boat moored at the bank, three people standing on the flat ground outside the end of the courtyard wall, the level bank ground connecting the water edge and the wall end
distinction: Although the boat and bank ground imply a relationship of arrival, no path or gate opening connecting the landing place with the courtyard gate is visible; the correspondence of the houses and fence with the sloping terrace and shoreline is clearer and runs through the right-hand composition.

evidence: Lower right corner: a person is visible sitting on slope rocks by the bank holding a rod and fishing, with no traces of houses, bridges or other built elements. | Whole painting: the painting consists mainly of open water, distant mountains and trees on the right, with no placement, screening or travel cues of any man-made buildings visible.
distinction: There are no clear built elements in the painting; only a figure serves as a scenic accent, and it is assigned to scenic accentuation only tenuously on the basis of the overall open spatial organization, but lacks built substance.

evidence: Upper right: the roof and part of the walls of a thatched house emerge through dense trees, a person seated inside visible, forming a layering of a house hidden within the grove. | Right and center: tall pines, bamboo and willows surround and partly block the built area on the right, placing the buildings in a spatial relationship of half-hidden and half-visible. | Lower middle: a bamboo-woven fence and courtyard gate connect the open ground in front with the thatched house behind, further reinforcing the boundary of the courtyard screened by trees.
distinction: Although the bridge and courtyard entrance hint at a travel path, the dominant spatial expression is the screening and revealing of the buildings by trees, rather than a coherent entry process.

evidence: Right half, top of slope: two groups of thatched houses, an open hall and an inner chamber, sit on a raised platform at the top of the slope, with masonry bases and step-like edges visible below the buildings, the base determined by the slope configuration | Center to lower left: the slope rises gradually from the stream bank at the lower left toward the upper right, supporting the house base, the slope in front of the houses descending broadly, the height of the house group corresponding to the slope-top platform | Behind and to the left of the houses: pine trunks and bamboo grow behind and beside the houses, but the walls and roofs are fully exposed, the screening relationship weak
distinction: The pines and bamboo stand only behind the houses as background while the buildings are fully exposed, so concealment and revelation do not form a layer; the correspondence of the terrace base with the slope-top platform is clear and runs through the right half of the composition, so terrain-responsive siting is taken as primary.

evidence: Center-right of the painting: a small boat with one person on it on the broad water, with no houses or other built elements | Upper part of the painting: several small islands in the distance, with trees painted on them, no buildings visible | Lower part of the painting: shrubs painted near the bank, the water ripples finely rendered
distinction: No clear built elements are visible in the painting; the small boat serves as a scenic accent on the broad water and does not present a movement cue connected with built elements.

evidence: Left middle ground: the roof and posts of a thatched pavilion emerge from behind willows and other trees, forming a clear relationship of concealment and revelation. | Overall painting: the built structure is partly screened by natural elements (trees), its presence suggested through the exposed portions, participating in constructing the painting's spatial layers.
distinction: Although the pavilion stands at the waterside, the painting emphasizes its layered concealment and revelation behind the trees rather than focusing on how it is sited according to terrain or the bank.

evidence: Left center: several white-walled, grey-roofed houses sit on a terraced slope; the building itself and the roof are partly covered by the trunks and foliage of several trees in front and behind, the houses emerging from among the trees | Around and above the houses: multiple tree trunks rise from the slope in front of and beside the houses, the crowns pressing over the upper part of the roofs, forming spatial layers of encircling woodland with alternating concealment and revelation | Lower right to center: a small plank bridge over a stream ravine connects the slopes of the two banks, a figure in red stands on the central bank, but no path is delineated between the figure and the houses, and the bridge connects only indirectly with the houses
distinction: The core of the houses' presentation lies in the layered concealment and revelation of roof and walls amid the encircling trees; although the bridge and figure suggest possible movement through the landscape, they form no directly discernible entering connection with the houses, so the screening relationship better matches the visible organization.

evidence: Left half to center: several huge trees take root on a pile of slope rocks by the waterside bank, the trunks distributed according to the height of the rocks, the foot of the slope meeting the water with scattered stones | Center-right: a flat terrace opens out toward the stream, on its surface two people sit facing each other and one stands holding a staff, the outer edge of the terrace dropping to the water in a steep bank | Right: among the rocks a waterfall pours into the stream ravine, the shoreline extending down-left along the terrace edge so that terrace, shoreline and water surface correspond
distinction: The visible relationship is mainly that the terrace and bank configuration carry and situate the only dwelling place in the painting, while discernible access clues such as bridges, paths, gates and crossings are absent, so C1 better matches the visible siting correspondence than C4.

evidence: Right-bank water's edge: a thatched-roof open pavilion is raised on several piles at the water's edge, its platform projecting over the water, the back of the pavilion pressed close to the foot of a rocky slope, the building site corresponding directly to the shoreline and slope-foot configuration | Right rocky slope and trees: the rocky slope descends from the right toward the water's edge, trees grow on the slope top and behind the pavilion, the pavilion set at the low waterside position at the slope foot, its height determined by the bank configuration | Junction of pavilion roof with rock and trees: the right end of the roof and the right side of the pavilion disappear into the rocky slope and foliage, forming partial screening, but the posts, platform and figures in the pavilion remain fully visible
distinction: The pavilion is raised on piles over the water with its back against the slope foot, its siting corresponding clearly to the bank configuration and determining its manner of existence; the screening by rock and trees only partly encloses it, the pavilion itself fully exposed, so concealment and revelation do not form a dominant layer.

evidence: Left to center: a long bridge spans the water, with pedestrians walking on it, directly connecting the left bank with the building complex on the right, forming a clear entry path. | Lower right: the building complex spreads along the waterside, with people active in front of courtyards and workshops, the end of the bridge pointing toward the entrance of the building area. | Center: tall trees partly screen some buildings, but the overall spatial layout clearly shows the path relationship from the bridge into the courtyard.
distinction: Although the buildings are built by the water, the long bridge, as a clear movement-through-the-landscape clue, dominates the spatial process of entering the building complex from outside, so C4 is more apt than C1.

evidence: Center and rear: the main hall complex lies deep in the valley, backed by high mountains, the building ground higher at the rear and lower at the front, arranged in tiers following the mountain configuration. | Left and right of the painting: the twin pagodas and the long rows of corridor buildings on both sides spread laterally along the open part of the valley, their layout corresponding to the valley's topographic form. | Overall composition: the vast building complex sits in a valley encircled by mountains, strict courtyards laid out on flat terrain, showing the character of siting according to the ground.
distinction: The building mass is enormous and its layout strict, mainly expressing an overall siting against mountains and beside the valley and a correspondence with terrain, rather than serving merely as an accent marking within the landscape.

evidence: Left to center: a grand long bridge across the water carries pavilions, pedestrians on the bridge and boats beneath forming clear clues of traffic and travel, connecting the spaces of the two banks. | Right: the waterside building complex connects to the bank by a zigzag bridge, boats moored and moving on the water, presenting an accessible water route. | Lower right corner: a flat bridge extends into the water, with figures walking on it, further reinforcing the enterable and traversable spatial relationships in the painting.
distinction: Bridges, water routes and shorelines form a movement-through-the-landscape route running through the composition, linking the various built nodes and emphasizing an enterable, traversable spatial process, more prominent than merely showing buildings' dependence on terrain.

evidence: Left and lower waterside: the building complex adjoins the water, with railings, steps and a jetty landing, boats moored at the bank, showing that the built structures are erected by the water. | Center to right: the main buildings are long corridor-houses and enclosed courtyards, unfolding along the winding shoreline, their layout corresponding to the forms of water surface and shoreline. | Around the buildings: trees interweave among the buildings, but the building sites and orientation are clearly placed according to the waterside terrain, presenting a disposition that follows the bank.
distinction: Although the jetty and boats suggest arrival, what dominates visually is the layout relationship of the building complex unfolding along the shoreline, rather than an emphasized process of in-depth path guidance.

evidence: Left and upper middle: a large building complex is distributed in irregular tiers over mountain slopes, roofs and wall bases unfolding in response to the terrain's undulations. | Left waterside: buildings and bridges are arranged along the shoreline, forming a close correspondence with the water surface and the land edge. | Right: the waterside building complex is placed against trees and the shoreline, showing the layout characteristic of buildings set according to the water.
distinction: Although connecting elements such as bridges appear, the core of the overall composition lies in how the building complex carries out a large-scale layout in response to mountain forms and shoreline, rather than emphasizing a single travel-and-entry path.

evidence: Upper center: a multi-story pavilion is built directly on the top of a steep cliff, the building site closely corresponding to the cliff-wall form, showing the character of buildings set according to the cliff. | Left: courtyards and houses are arranged in tiers according to the hillside terrain, with walls and paths unfolding along the terraced slopes. | Right waterside: pavilions and pagoda-type buildings are placed along the shoreline, forming a relationship of unfolding by the water.
distinction: Although the built structures also serve to mark the scenery, the painting more strongly emphasizes the dependence and correspondence of building sites on natural configurations such as cliffs, slopes and shoreline, with terrain-responsive siting as the more dominant characteristic.

evidence: Lower right and lower middle: several bridges (arched and flat) and winding paths are visible, connecting different courtyards and hills, with figures walking on the bridges and roads. | Center to right of the painting: paths and streams lead the eye through woods and hillsides toward the building clusters deep within and the pavilion on the summit, forming an enterable, traversable spatial sequence. | Left cliff: buildings are erected against the cliff, connected to the outside by a mountain path, integrated into the overall travel route.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited against mountains and beside water, the painting more strongly emphasizes leading the viewer through clues such as bridges and paths to enter and travel through the various scenic spots, with spatial connectivity dominant.

evidence: Upper part and background of the painting: the halls and long gallery complex are screened by several tall bare trees, only roofs, eaves and some gallery columns exposed, forming spatial layers of seeing houses through a screen | Lower left and foreground of the painting: a small pavilion is hidden behind dense bare trees and rockery stones, only its roof visible, presenting a relationship of houses concealed in the woods | Center of the painting: a platform enclosed by red railings separates the building area from the foreground woods, trees interweaving in front of the buildings, reinforcing the screening and revealing of built structures by natural scenery.
distinction: Although movement-through-the-landscape clues such as bridges and galleries are visible, the main visual structure is formed by the screening of buildings by foreground trees and rocks and background trees, emphasizing layers of concealment and revelation rather than the extension and sense of entry of a path.

evidence: Lower middle: a thatched pavilion is built on a steep rocky platform, the building site closely bound to the mountain-and-rock terrain, showing a placement of a building set according to the platform. | Lower left corner: a small bridge and figures on it are visible, forming a spatial relationship of differing heights with the rocky platform above.
distinction: Although a bridge suggests a path, the core composition lies in the terrain-responsive siting of the thatched pavilion against the rocky height, rather than emphasizing a process of entry.

evidence: Lower middle-right of the painting: the roof of an open pavilion thatched hall emerges from beneath the dense tree canopy above, the building itself and the space between its columns partly screened by several foreground trunks, figures and interior visible through the gaps between trunks, presenting layers of seeing a house among the woods | Right: stacked rock blocks press against the right wing of the building, one end of the eaves emerging from the side of the rock, the wall and roof ridge truncated by the rock | Lower left: railings enclose a flat court in front, one person leaning on the railing, on the same ground level as the thatched hall; no access clues such as bridge, path or gate connecting with the building are seen
distinction: The painting organizes the emergence of the thatched hall through the relationships of concealment and exposure of trunks, canopy and rocks, while the left railings merely enclose the court ground and form no discernible entry or arrival route, so concealment and revelation better fits than access to secluded settings.

evidence: Lower left: the white walls, window lattice and seated occupant of a thatched house emerge between several large foreground trunks, the upper part of the thatch roof screened by dark-ink canopy, a fence running along the edge of the waterside terrace in front of the house | Around the lower-left house: dense canopy covers above and to the right of the house, bamboo clumps beside it, trunks and distant woods behind, the house situated within layers of screening by woodland | Center-right: a bridge crosses the stream mouth, a pedestrian holding an umbrella walks leftward on it, the left end of the bridge falling behind slope rocks, with no path or doorway seen connecting to the house's fence
distinction: A travel clue on the bridge exists, but its landing place is cut off by slope rocks and no visible entrance links it to the fenced house; the house's presence and layers are mainly suggested by screening and revealing through canopy and trunks, so the screening relationship is more dominant.

evidence: Among the trees of the right-bank middle ground: a group of pale-ink horizontal and vertical lines forms something like a house or pavilion, partly screened by trunks and foliage in front and behind, only the top line and posts exposed, details unclear | Central main peak: the main peak stands at the center of the painting, pines and round boulders layered on its waist, another very small ink trace at the middle of the peak wall, possibly a scenic-accent structure but not reliably identifiable | Left and below: a waterfall between the left cliffs drops to the water below, cloud vapor cuts across between the main peak and the right bank, making the wooded clearing on the right bank the site of the concealment-and-revelation relationship
distinction: The visible relationship is a layer of concealment and revelation in which a house-shaped line structure is exposed beneath screening trees, rather than built structures marking a scenic spot at positions such as the peak edge or water mouth.

evidence: Upper right of the left half: a pavilion is built atop a cliff, below it a clear stepped path winds up following the rocky slope, connecting the pavilion with the waterside below, showing a layout of buildings set along the slope and ascending according to the terrain. | Left side and lower middle of the left half: houses are built against the left rocks and tree sites, an arched bridge in the lower-middle water connects the two banks, buildings and bridge placed in response to shoreline and terrain. | Center and left valley of the right half: several groups of houses are scattered irregularly between valley slopes and waterside, their sites following the terrain's undulations, presenting a settlement form laid out according to the ground.
distinction: Although a bridge and stepped path provide access clues, the terrain-responsive layout of buildings against mountains and beside water, placed according to the heights of slopes and terraces, is more prominent and runs through the whole, so C1 is more dominant than C4.

evidence: Lower left of the left panel: houses are visible arranged against the woods at the foot of the mountain, a winding path leading deep within, suggesting enterable space. | Lower right of the right panel: a corridor-house or waterside pavilion is built by the water, adjoining an arched bridge on its right, with pedestrians on the bridge, forming a clear travel clue of entering the house from the bridge. | Middle of the right panel: tall trees and rocks screen part of the built structures, forming spatial layers of alternating concealment and revelation, supporting the sense of an in-depth path.
distinction: Although trees and rocks screen the buildings in the painting (screening), the direct connection of bridge, path and waterside building in the right panel constitutes a more dominant traversable spatial process.

evidence: Center-right of the left page: boats are moored beneath pines, figures active on the bank, marking the riverbank scenery. | Lower part of the right page: a small boat is moored by the islet's water's edge, marking the islet scenery.
distinction: Although the boats may be regarded as ferry-crossing clues, the painting mainly presents static mooring and scenic accentuation rather than a strong process of entry or travel.

evidence: Center of the right panel: a waterfall pours down between the flanking cliffs on left and right, falling into the pebble-strewn stream bed below, the waterfall mouth forming the visual focus of the right panel | Right bank of the right panel: a flat terrace extends from the lower-right bank toward the stream ravine, a single figure standing at its end facing the waterfall mouth, several pines growing on the slope behind the terrace, forming a viewing point for the waterfall mouth | Entire left panel and slope surfaces of the right panel: the left panel shows only bamboo, orchid grass and slope rocks arranged on a flat slope, and on the right panel's slope and among the trees no clues of built structures such as roofs, walls, bridges or paths are seen
distinction: The dominant organization of the right panel is the gathering and viewing of the waterfall-mouth scene at the terrace end; although the slope ridge and stream bed suggest accessibility, they form no movement-through-the-landscape process connecting with built structures.

evidence: Lower left: houses and a waterside pavilion are built at the water's edge, their sites against the mountain foot and bank, presenting a form that unfolds along the bank with buildings set according to the water. | Upper right: a pavilion is built at the mountain-and-rock peak, placed according to the high terrain.
distinction: The building complex on the left unfolds along the waterside site, its relationship to terrain placement clear, dominantly expressing terrain-responsive siting rather than merely marking scenery.

evidence: Center of the right side of the painting: a wooden bridge spans the water, connecting the left stone bank with the right land, forming a clear passage clue. | Lower right corner of the right side of the painting: houses are built by the water, together with the bridge and shoreline forming an accessible, traversable spatial relationship. | Upper right of the right side of the painting: a pavilion is visible at the mountainside, suggesting that travel may continue deeper along the rocks and woods.
distinction: The connecting role of the bridge and the sense of a path guiding entry are very prominent, organizing a traversable spatial process, more dominant than mere siting against mountains and beside water.

evidence: Lower left: built structures are partly screened by tall foreground bare trees and rocks, only roofs and parts of the structure exposed, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Upper middle-left: another group of built structures is screened behind trees and rocks at the bank, presenting layers of seeing houses through a screen.
distinction: Although the built structures are sited against landscape, the painting more strongly emphasizes revealing buildings through the screening of trees and rocks, thereby forming deep spatial layers, so C2 is more apt than C1.

evidence: Lower right: a winding wooden bridge or plank walkway is visible extending into the water, tiny figures on the bridge, constituting a clear clue of travel and entry. | Right mountainside: a storied building is visible, spatially echoing and connecting with the path and bridge below. | Lower left: a thatched-roof building is visible, together with the bridge and path on the right organizing a traversable landscape space.
distinction: The winding plank walkway/bridge in the painting constitutes a clear movement-through-the-landscape clue, leading the eye inward and connecting the various built structures, better summarizing the painting's spatial organization than screening by woodland alone.

evidence: Lower center-left: a built structure is visible, its roof and part of its walls screened by surrounding trees and rocks, presenting a layered relationship of screening. | Lower center-left: figures are visible within the built structure, showing it revealed as part of the spatial layers.
distinction: The built structure is mainly screened by trees and rocks, only partly exposed, emphasizing a relationship of concealment and revelation rather than terrain-responsive siting, scenic accentuation or access to secluded settings.

evidence: Lower right corner: two small boats are visible on the water with people aboard, marking the open scenery of the waterside. | Left and below: the main subject of the painting is mountains and rocks, trees and sloping banks; no clear houses or fixed built structures are seen.
distinction: There are no fixed built structures in the painting, only boats as scenic accents, so it is classified as scenic accentuation; if the boats are regarded as activity structures placed according to the waterside, it is close to terrain-responsive siting.

evidence: Center-left: several tall masts are visible, clearly indicating the existence of a waterside ferry crossing or boat structures. | Lower middle to lower part: several groups of figures move along a winding path among woods and rocks, forming a clear movement-through-the-landscape clue pointing toward the waterside area. | Center-right: houses are located beneath a cliff, adjacent to the waterside built area to which the path extends, constituting the destination or backdrop of the travel.
distinction: The dominant spatial relationship of the painting is the figures' travel along the path toward the waterside ferry crossing, rather than merely showing buildings' layers of concealment and revelation among the woods.

evidence: Lower left corner: a figure is visible standing on rocks, gazing up at the pines and high cliff ahead; no clear built structures such as houses, pavilions or bridges are seen. | Upper middle of the painting: the towering cliff face and pines constitute the main landscape forms, the figure below the cliff serving to mark and focus the landscape scenery of this spot.
distinction: There are no clear built structures in the painting; the scenic figure emphasizes the landscape beauty, closest to the compositional role of scenic accentuation.

evidence: Lower left corner: a wooden bridge is visible spanning water/among rocks, serving as a movement-through-the-landscape clue connecting foreground and middle ground. | Lower center-left: a figure stands on a rock facing the direction of the bridge and buildings, suggesting an action of approaching or crossing the water. | Middle left: the building complex (pavilions and storied buildings) is built on a stone-faced high platform, located in the area to which the bridge leads, presenting a spatial relationship of entering from one to the other.
distinction: Although the buildings are built on a stone platform and have a C1 characteristic, through the linkage of bridge, figure and buildings the painting more strongly emphasizes the path toward the built structures and the process of entry, so C4 is dominant.

evidence: Upper-left hillside: a multi-story pagoda and the roof ridges of grouped halls rise in tiers along the slope, the building sites placed according to the hillside's height, the pagoda on the summit and halls on the slope face | Middle left bank: rows of houses and shops unfold tightly along the riverbank, extending with the shoreline's turns, boats densely moored on the water in front of the houses, the direction of building unfolding consistent with the water system | Middle of the right bank: small houses are placed on a bank platform, their foundations fitting the sloping bank terrain, facing the marketplace across the water
distinction: The sites and manner of unfolding of the hillside pagoda-temple and the riverside houses are all arranged according to slope configuration and shoreline, the relationship of terrain participating in placement running through the whole painting; screening by trees exists only locally and is insufficient to serve as the dominant compositional mode.

evidence: Lower left: In the woods, a built roof and railings are faintly visible, partly obscured by the branches and leaves of the surrounding trees, forming a relationship of concealment. | Lower waterside: The built structure sits between the woodland and the waterside, revealing partial structure through the screening of foreground trees, suggesting its spatial layering.
distinction: Although the built structure is placed near the water, the painting emphasizes more its half-hidden, half-revealed relationship screened by trees, thereby constructing pictorial depth; thus C2 is more apt than C1.

evidence: Right side of the painting: a plank walkway with railings is visible, built tight against the steep cliff face, its path winding and extending in response to the projections and recesses of the mountains and rocks. | Lower middle of the painting: the walkway starts from the rocks near the water surface and climbs upward following the lie of the mountain, showing the direct dependence of built elements on topographic conditions.
distinction: Although the plank walkway serves as a path guiding movement through the landscape, its most prominent visual feature is its placement tight against the cliff face and following the rise and fall of the mountain, so C1 is more dominant than C4.

evidence: Lower middle: A person is seen sitting alone on a rock by the stream, surrounded by trees and sloping rocks, with the stream flowing beneath the rock. | Overall painting: No clear houses, pavilions, bridges, or other built structures are seen, only natural landscape and figures.
distinction: There is no clear built element in the painting; the figure sitting alone on the stream rock marks the secluded scenery here, more directly than the path guidance of access to secluded settings.

evidence: Lower middle: The water surface is open, with a small boat carrying several people moving forward, suggesting spatial extension and a process of travel. | Middle ground: Sloping banks and trees interweave, forming spatial layers, but no clear houses or building sites are seen. | Lower left corner: Trees grow on the near-shore sloping bank, with no obvious traces of artificial built elements.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built structures to accentuate scenic spots; it mainly relies on the water surface and the small boat to guide the eye, presenting a sense of enterable space.

evidence: Lower left corner: A small bridge is seen spanning a stream valley, with a figure beside the bridge; no clear houses, pavilions, or other built structures are seen. | Lower middle: Towering cliffs and pine trees occupy the main subject, with a waterfall flowing down on the left, the whole presenting the deep and secluded scenery of natural landscape.
distinction: There is a small bridge and figures in the painting suggesting movement through the landscape, but no clear built structure is seen connecting with them as a destination; therefore C4 is not chosen, and the closest category, scenic accentuation, is selected.

evidence: Upper middle: Buildings are hidden within dense woods, with only part of the roofs and walls exposed, showing an obvious concealment and revelation relationship. | Lower middle waterside: Parts of buildings are exposed at the waterside, forming foreground-background layers with the surrounding sloping rocks and trees. | Right side: Behind the trees, door and window openings or wall structures of buildings are faintly visible, half-screened by the woodland.
distinction: Although the painting has a waterside and partial paths, the buildings mainly construct spatial layers through screening and exposure by trees, rocks, and mountains; the role of concealment and revelation in creating the setting is more prominent.

evidence: Upper middle mountain hollow: House roofs emerge from crevices in the rocks, obscured by surrounding rock bodies and trees, presenting the layering of seeing houses behind rocks. | Left middle woods: Deep in the woods, an open hall or pavilion is visible; multiple tree trunks in the foreground obscure the building itself, forming a spatial relationship of houses hidden in the woods. | Lower right waterside: There is a long building at the waterside, partly screened by foreground tree branches and leaves, with exposed walls and doors/windows indicating the presence of built elements.
distinction: Although there are figures riding donkeys traveling in the lower part of the painting, suggesting movement, the path does not clearly connect to a specific building entrance; the built structures mainly present concealment and revelation layers screened by trees, rocks, and mountains, rather than a clear process of entry.

evidence: Lower right corner: A corridor pavilion is built at the waterside, its base directly unfolding along the waterside terrain. | Lower middle: Thatched huts are built among trees on sloping ground, placed according to the rise and fall of the hillside. | Left middle section: A courtyard building complex is distributed along the slope terrace at the foot of the mountain, echoing the surrounding terrain.
distinction: Although there is a phenomenon of trees screening buildings in the painting, the built structures mainly present a layout relationship of following the mountains and being placed according to the terrain; thus C1 is more dominant.

evidence: Lower left: A wooden bridge is seen spanning the water, with pedestrians on the bridge, connecting paths on both banks. | Middle ground: A city gate opens in the city wall, suggesting entry into the city is possible here; houses are scattered inside and outside the city. | Lower right: A bamboo fence encloses the front of thatched huts, forming with the surrounding trees and waterside a local space that can be dwelt in and traveled through.
distinction: Although there are built structures placed according to water and mountains, travel clues such as the bridge, path, and city gate run through the composition, emphasizing more the spatial process of moving from here to there.

evidence: Left middle: A small boat floats on the open water surface, with a figure wearing a conical hat and a canopy structure on board, serving as a visual focus that marks the river scenery. | Lower right corner: The sloping bank and trees serve as foreground, forming spatial opening and closing and echoing with the lone boat in the middle ground, highlighting the boat's role in scenic accentuation.
distinction: The boat is on the open water surface and does not directly connect with travel clues such as shore paths or ferry crossings; it does not constitute a spatial process of entering deep into the scene, but rather condenses the scenery as an isolated focus.

evidence: Lower foreground: A waterside study with railings is surrounded and screened by the trunks and branches of several large trees, with only part of the roof, walls, and interior figures exposed, showing an obvious relationship of a house hidden in the woods. | Middle ground left: Among the trees at the foot of the mountain, the roofs and eaves of multi-story pavilions are faintly visible, the main building screened by trees and rocks. | Middle ground water surface: A flat bridge spans the water, connecting both banks, with the bridge body and surrounding reeds and trees forming layers.
distinction: Although the foreground study is built near the water, the painting emphasizes more the layered screening and exposure of the building by tall trees; the concealment and revelation relationship plays a dominant role in the composition.

evidence: Left middle: Buildings are hidden behind dense woods and rocks, with only roofs and part of the eaves exposed, presenting a layering of seeing houses through a screen. | Left side: Tree branches and leaves screen in layers, forming a spatial relationship of trees in front and houses behind, with obvious concealment and revelation.
distinction: The painting mainly expresses the concealment and revelation relationship of buildings screened by trees and rocks; although travel paths are faintly visible, they are less prominent than the screening relationship.

evidence: Lower part of the painting: a bridge is visible, with a figure riding a donkey and attendants on it, moving toward the interior of the painting and forming a clear cue for entry. | Middle of the painting: a pavilion stands on a terrace in front of a waterfall, and houses are arranged in staggered fashion following the lie of the mountain, connected with the bridge and path. | Overall composition: the bridge and the human activity connect the foreground with the built area in the middle ground, presenting a spatial process of moving from here to there and of being reachable.
distinction: Although the built elements follow the mountain terrain, the painting emphasizes the spatial process of entry and movement through the landscape via the bridge and figures, and C4 better captures this dynamic spatial organization.

evidence: Bottom of the painting: A wooden bridge spans a stream, with a person riding a horse with attendants crossing the bridge, forming a clear travel clue connecting the foreground and the right bank. | Right lower bank: Behind the woods, house roofs and walls are exposed, located at a reachable position along the bridge path, presenting a relationship of moving from here to there. | Upper middle valley: Mountain rocks, gorges, and streams form vertical depth; gaps between rocks suggest paths going deeper, connecting to pavilion buildings faintly visible among the woods deep in the valley.
distinction: Although there are built structures screened by woods (C2 feature), the clear bridge and figures traveling at the bottom constitute the main clue for entering the painting, and the rocks and streams guide the eye to extend into the depth, organizing an enterable spatial process; thus C4 is more dominant.

evidence: Lower left: a group of courtyard buildings is half-hidden behind a pine grove, with only the roofs and part of the walls exposed, presenting a layering of houses concealed within the woodland. | Right middle ground: buildings are arranged against the cliff and partly screened by tree trunks and branches in front, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship in which houses are seen through a screening layer. | Overall painting: the branches and foliage of trees in the foreground and middle ground repeatedly screen the built elements behind, making the buildings appear and disappear among the gaps in the woodland.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited according to the mountain terrain, the painting places greater emphasis on the spatial layering created by the screening and revealing of the buildings by the trees, so C2 is more dominant than C1.

evidence: Lower left side: A roof structure with diagonal line texture is visible, located below the mountain rocks. | Left side: Rocks and trees obscure most of the built structure, with only the roof exposed, forming a concealment and revelation relationship.
distinction: Although the built structure is placed according to the rocks, the painting emphasizes more the screening and exposure of the built structure by rocks and trees, highlighting the spatial layers of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Left middle: A tiled-roof house sits among sloping rocks, with raised earth mounds and stones in front of the building itself, the building base placed according to the rise and fall of the slope foot, and a resident seen sitting inside. | Left middle, slightly above: Behind the house is another group of buildings, below which a flat platform railing and terrace base are visible, built on the slope terrace, forming a two-level arrangement with the foreground house. | Center to lower right: Pine trees and sloping rocks are arranged in front of and to the right of the house; at the lower right, figures stand at a narrow pass on the sloping bank, but no clear path, bridge, or gate is seen connecting to the house.
distinction: The walls, doors/windows, and terrace base of the house are fully visible; pine branches only interpenetrate in front of the house without organizing layers through concealment and revelation; the correspondence between the layered heights of the built structures and the terrace base and slope foot is more direct.

evidence: Lower left and center: At the lower left corner of the painting there is an arched bridge with pedestrians; at the waterside there are steps and a dock connecting the water surface with houses on land. | Central mountainside: A stone-step path winds upward from the waterside at the foot of the mountain, passing through woods, leading to a temple complex at the summit; figures pause at a platform on the mountainside. | Center, slightly above: A building complex including a pagoda and multiple halls is built at the summit, connected via the stone-step path below to the waterside at the mountain foot, forming a clear route of entry and travel.
distinction: Although the buildings are built along the mountain (C1), travel clues such as the bridge, dock, and winding stone steps are extremely clear, linking a complete process of entry from the water surface to the summit temple; therefore C4 is more dominant.

evidence: Lower middle: A small boat with a canopy is seen floating on the water, with a person holding a pole on board, presenting a state of travel on water. | Left side and background: Water surface, near-shore trees, and distant mountains are visible, forming an open water space; no fixed buildings are seen.
distinction: There are no fixed built structures in the painting; only the boat serves as a clue for travel on water, so it is classified under C4.

evidence: Lower center: An arched bridge spans an unpainted water surface, with the bridge body and railings clear, connecting paths on both banks. | On and around the bridge: Figures (one with a staff, one carrying something) travel along the bridge or stand beside it, forming a clear travel clue. | Overall composition: The bridge and paths guide the figures' movement and the viewer's gaze, presenting a spatial passage relationship of moving from here to there and crossing the water surface.
distinction: Although the bridge is erected according to the water terrain, the core of the painting lies in the travel process of figures crossing the bridge and the path connection, rather than simply emphasizing the building's adaptation to terrain.

evidence: Lower left corner: Between the sloping rocks and the roots of a pine tree, a part of a built structure is visible, exposing a thatched roof and vertical supports or a fence below. | Left side and center: The trunk and dense needles of a huge pine tree extend from above, covering and obscuring most of the built structure below, forming a layered relationship of a house hidden beneath the trees.
distinction: Although the built structure is placed according to the slope, the painting highlights more its concealment and revelation relationship screened by pine branches and needles above, rather than emphasizing its terrain-responsive layout.

evidence: Lower left: two figures are visible standing among slope rocks and trees; no traces of building such as houses or pavilions are seen. | Left side, full view: the painting consists mainly of distant mountains, sloping ground, woodland, and figures, and lacks identifiable architectural structures or man-made facilities.
distinction: No built elements are visible at all in the painting; it is assigned only tentatively on the basis of the relationship between the overall natural landscape and the figures as scenic accents, with no clear competing interpretation.

evidence: Left-hand painted panel: the painting depicts distant mountains, water surface and a near-ground sloping bank with willow trees; no traces of man-made built structures such as houses or bridges are seen.
distinction: No built structure is visible in the painting, so no specific judgment of spatial relationships can be made; it is assigned only tentatively on the basis of the overall landscape organization.

evidence: Left side and center: Mountains and rocks, trees, and three pedestrians carrying luggage are visible, presenting a state of traveling, but no clear built structures such as houses or bridges are seen.
distinction: There are no clear built structures that figures can enter in the painting; there is only the clue of figures traveling through the mountains and wilds, so based on the overall spatial organization it is classified under the closest category, movement through the landscape.

evidence: Lower left: A person is seen rowing a small boat with a canopy on the water, forming a travel clue. | Around the painting: Reeds, dry branches, and distant banks are visible, the water surface is open, and no fixed built structures such as houses are seen.
distinction: There are no fixed built structures in the painting, only boat travel; based on the overall spatial organization, it is classified under the closest category, access to secluded settings.

evidence: Right foreground: An open pavilion is built against the rocks and trees on the right, its base closely integrated with the sloping rock terrain. | Middle ground, slightly left: A house is set at the waterside, placed along the shoreline. | Left background: Among the woods and sloping land, houses are faintly visible, distributed in staggered fashion according to the terrain.
distinction: Although there is local screening of buildings by trees in the painting, the correspondence of each built structure with the terrain of rocks and waterside is more clear and dominant.

evidence: Left painting: The painting presents the natural forms and trends of rocky sloping banks, with trees dotted about, but no clear traces of built elements are seen.
distinction: There are no visible built elements in the painting; based on the overall visible spatial organization of rocks and sloping banks, it is classified under the closest category C1, which arises from terrain.

evidence: Center of the painting: The main body of the thatched hut is largely obscured by the thick, curved trunks and needles of foreground pine trees, with only part of the thatched roof, pillars, and eaves exposed. | Center, slightly left: Through the gaps in the pine trees and the open eaves, a scholar is seen sitting inside at a desk, forming spatial layers of alternating concealment and revelation. | Right side: The right half of the thatched hut is further screened by clumps of bamboo and sloping rocks, strengthening the visual effect of the building hidden within the woods.
distinction: Although the building is constructed according to the rocky sloping ground, the core spatial organization of the painting is the use of pines and bamboo to interpenetrate and screen the building to create layers, rather than emphasizing its terrain-responsive layout.

evidence: Left middle of the painting: The house complex is partly obscured by dense trees and rocks, with only roofs and part of the eaves exposed, forming a sense of layering of seeing houses deep in the woods. | Right middle of the painting: Pavilions and houses at the waterside and in mountain hollows are screened behind trees and rocks, their spatial positions indicated by partial exposure. | Right side: Built structures are distributed in staggered fashion among the mountain forests; through the screening of foreground trees and middle-ground rocks, a deep concealment and revelation relationship is created.
distinction: Although the built structures also follow the terrain, the painting emphasizes more the layers of concealment and revelation formed by screening by trees and rocks, rather than simply emphasizing the correspondence between building bases and terrain.

evidence: Lower left corner: A stone-paved platform, railings, and steps are visible, placed close to the waterside, forming a clear entry point or stopping place for travel. | Left side: Dense bamboo groves grow above the platform; the built structure is combined with natural scenery, suggesting a path entering the woods or waterside. | Right side and background: On the right side of the painting there are rocks, a waterfall, and bamboo groves, echoing spatially with the built structure at the lower left and guiding the eye to extend into the depth.
distinction: C1 emphasizes the placement of built structures according to terrain, while C4 emphasizes more the built structures (such as steps and railings) as travel clues guiding entry into or deeper into the spatial process of the painting. In this painting, the entry features of the stone-paved platform and steps are more prominent.

evidence: Lower middle, slightly left: Through the branches and canopy of the foreground pines, a thatched roof, a wooden fence, and figures inside the building are visible; the built elements are partly screened by woodland. | Lower middle: The pine grove and the built elements form a foreground-background occlusion relationship, and the exposed eaves and parts of the walls indicate the spatial layering of the built elements deep within the woods.
distinction: Although the painting contains a path and human activity, their main compositional role lies in the screening and revelation of the built elements by woodland, rather than in strong route guidance.

evidence: Center of the painting: A relatively large complex of buildings is built following the mountain's contours, tier upon tier and well arranged in staggered levels, showing the features of setting houses on terraces and placing them separately according to the slopes. | Center, slightly left: The building complex is distributed along the rises and falls of the mountain body and the slope terraces, forming a close correspondence with the natural terrain. | Right side of the painting: A small number of buildings in the distance also dot the mountain ranges, likewise conforming to the mountain's contours.
distinction: Although the building complex also has a partly screened effect of being occluded by mountains and rocks and trees, its features of following the mountains and adapting to the terrain, with layout varying with the undulations of the land, are more prominent and dominant.

evidence: Lower-left foreground: The courtyard buildings are partly screened by pines, with only the eaves, wall surfaces, and figures beneath the veranda exposed, forming a foreground layer of concealment and revelation. | Middle and distant valleys: The roofs of a large building complex loom faintly between the groves and the mountain forms, revealing a sense of deep spatial recession through the screening of woodland and mountain masses. | Overall composition: The built elements do not occupy the absolute center but participate in the composition through their screening and revelation by mountains and rocks and woodland, presenting a layering in which houses are seen within the woods and behind the rocks.
distinction: Although the buildings are distributed following the mountain's contours, the painting emphasizes more the screening and revelation of buildings by woodland and mountain masses, thereby constructing a deep spatial layering, rather than stressing placement according to the terrain alone.

evidence: Lower-left corner: Parts of a building can be seen connected to an arched bridge, with a figure riding a donkey beside the bridge, forming a clear clue of entry and progression. | Upper-middle valley: Deep within, a continuous stretch of roofs of a building complex is visible, screened by foreground pines and mountains and rocks, indicating that the line of sight extends into the depth. | Center of the painting: The foreground pine grove, mountains and rocks, and the bridge together organize a spatial path leading from the foreground to the built elements in the depth.
distinction: Although the painting contains the layering of buildings screened by trees (C2), the bridge and figures in the lower-left corner clearly construct a process of movement from the foreground toward the building complex in the depth, making C4 the dominant mode of spatial organization.

evidence: Left waterside: A small bridge can be seen spanning the water and connecting the land, with pedestrians on the bridge, and a path on the bank extending toward the built area. | Lower-left and right waters: Boats on the water approach the bank, and at the edge of the village on the right figures can be seen moving along the waterside or paths, suggesting accessibility. | Middle and right of the painting: Houses and pavilions are scattered among the slope terraces and woodland, forming a coherent spatial organization of movement through the waterside, paths, and bridges.
distinction: Although the built elements are placed nestling against mountains and beside water (C1), the clues of movement through the landscape—bridges, boats, and human activity—are more prominent in the painting, emphasizing the spatial process of entry and movement through the landscape.
