evidence: Lower-left corner: A wooden bridge spans a stream, and one person carrying an object crosses the bridge, moving toward the buildings on the right. | Right side: Inside an open hall two people sit facing each other, with steps in front of the hall connecting to the ground, forming an accessible entrance. | Middle of the painting: Although trees form a screen in front of the buildings, the bridge and the movement lines of the figures clearly establish a path from the outer stream, across it, and toward the built elements.
distinction: Although the buildings are screened by trees, the bridge and the movement lines of the figures in the lower-left corner clearly construct an entry path leading to the buildings, and C4 better accounts for this spatial connection from one point to another.

evidence: Left-hand painted panel: the painting mainly depicts thick old trees, mountain rocks and distant mountains behind; no traces of built structures such as houses or bridges are seen. | Right side: this is decorated mounting or unpainted space, with no painted-area content.
distinction: There is no built structure in the painting; only the natural layering and screening relationships of trees and mountain rocks are seen, so it is assigned to C2, the closest to natural spatial organization.

evidence: Lower center: A wooden platform (or bridge) with railings spans the water, connecting the cliff on the left with the sloped bank on the right, with figures standing on it. | Lower center, slightly right: At the edge of the platform, a structure of steps or a ramp extending downward is visible, suggesting that one may step down to the water or cross to the opposite bank.
distinction: Although the platform is built beside the water (C1), as a passage crossing the water and a node for figures to move through the landscape and pause, it more prominently expresses the spatial process of passing from one point to another and of accessibility (C4).

evidence: Lower left: An open pavilion is built on a sloped bank, surrounded by dense trees. | Lower left: The thick branches of an ancient tree pass in front of the pavilion, and the canopy covers and screens part of the roof, forming a clear layering of concealment and revelation. | Left side and background: The pavilion faces open water, with gentle mountain ranges in the distance, and the building becomes the visual focus of the foreground amid the screening of trees.
distinction: Although the pavilion facing the water serves as a scenic accent, the interpenetrating and screening relationships among tree branches and the building's roof and columns are more prominent in the painting and dominate the spatial layering of this area.

evidence: Whole painting: The painting contains only calligraphic text and a cloud-and-dragon patterned silk border on the right, with no landscape or built imagery visible.
distinction: The painting has no landscape or built elements, and no actual judgment of spatial relationships can be made; it is assigned only by form.

evidence: Left-middle on the bank: An open thatched-roof building is placed directly beside the waterside and level ground, with figures active inside, and its building base is closely integrated with the terrain. | Right side and rear of the painting: Other houses on the bank can be seen connected to a road with carts and horses, and the built elements overall show a layout unfolding along the bank and placed according to the terrain.
distinction: Although the painting contains a great deal of movement of figures and traffic of carts and horses, the most prominent feature of the built elements themselves is their placement beside the waterside terrain, rather than an emphasis on the spatial process of leading into the depth through paths.

evidence: Upper right: A wall winds and extends along the contours of the sloped land and the waterside, conforming to the trend of the terrain. | Middle of the painting: Halls and small pavilions are placed beside the waterside and earthen slopes, surrounded by trees and mountains and rocks, and their building bases are closely integrated with the terrain. | Lower right: A cluster of houses is built facing the water, unfolding in conformity with the shoreline and the distribution of vegetation.
distinction: Although trees screen buildings in the painting, the siting and layout of the built elements more prominently show their placement in conformity with natural configurations such as slope terraces and the waterside.

evidence: Below the painted portion on the right: On the waterside stands an open pavilion (or xuan), inside which scholars sit facing each other, surrounded by trees and mountains and rocks; it is small in scale. | Overall painted portion on the right: The pavilion is located at the junction of open water and mountains and rocks and trees (at the water's edge), and as the main man-made built element in the painting it becomes the visual focus. | Spatial relationship: The presence of the built element gives the waterside space a point of anchorage, identifies the specific scenery of the riverbank, and concentrates the space of landscape and human activity.
distinction: Although the pavilion is placed beside the waterside, its main compositional role is as an identifier of the scenery and a visual point of convergence (scenic accentuation), rather than emphasizing the conformity of the building layout to complex terrain (terrain-responsive siting).

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: A winding bamboo fence runs across the sloped land, with an open small gate set in the middle, clearly dividing inside and outside space and providing a clue for entry. | Upper middle of the painting: The house is located on high ground on the slope behind the fence, surrounded by dense pines, and through the guidance of the fence and gate a spatial process is formed of entering from outside to inside and turning into the depth. | Right side and upper part of the painting: Dense pine branches and foliage screen part of the house's roof and walls, increasing the sense of seclusion of the built elements and reinforcing the deep layering after 'entry into the setting.'
distinction: Although the painting contains trees screening the house in a relationship of concealment and revelation (C2), the bamboo fence running across the painting and the clear small gate constitute a strong spatial boundary and entry clue, organizing an accessible relationship from the outer natural sloped land to the inner built elements; thus access to secluded settings (C4) is more dominant.

evidence: Left-hand painted panel: the painting presents a waterside, distant mountains, pine trees and figures in the lower left corner; no clear man-made built structures (such as houses or bridges) are seen.
distinction: The painting is dominated by natural landscape and figures and lacks evidence of built structures; it is assigned to the closest category on the basis of the overall visible space.

evidence: Center-left island islet: A pagoda stands on the island top, and houses and pavilions are distributed down the island slope to the water's edge, with the buildings' heights corresponding to the configuration of the island mound | Lower-right sloped bank: A stretch of houses unfolds along the bank following the rises and falls of the bank slope, with roofs arranged in staggered levels according to the sloped land | Right cliff top: A pavilion stands on a platform at the cliff top, facing open water, its building base corresponding to the configuration of the cliff
distinction: The screening and revelation of pavilions and houses by pines is only local, whereas the building bases and the high-and-low layout of the built elements throughout the scroll are all placed according to the configuration of the island slopes and bank slopes; the relationship of terrain-based placement runs more pervasively through the composition

evidence: Left-middle portion: A large building complex unfolds along the waterside, with rows of columns or platform structures visible at its base, showing clear features of arrangement along the bank and of setting houses beside the water. | Middle to right, among the mountains: Many pavilions and towers are placed at the foot of mountains, on slope terraces, or in valleys surrounded by mountains and rocks, with their layout separately arranged according to the heights of the mountain contours, corresponding to the terrain. | Lower middle, slightly right, and lower right: Arched bridges and plank roads connecting paths are visible; although they provide clues for movement, the built elements overall are more broadly manifested as placed according to the waterside and mountain forms.
distinction: Although the painting contains bridges and boats that provide clues for movement through the landscape (C4), the built elements are broadly laid out according to the waterside, mountain feet, and slope terraces (for example, the waterside pavilion on the left follows the bank, and the mountain house follows the slope); the relationship of terrain-based placement is more widespread and dominant than that of entry paths.

evidence: Center, slightly right: Behind mountains and rocks and trees, building structures are faintly visible, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation screened by natural scenery. | Lower middle of the painting: A bridge can be seen connecting the two banks, with figures active on the bank and on the bridge, suggesting the accessibility of the space. | Left cliff: Two people sit facing each other on a platform of mountains and rocks, echoing the surrounding trees and mountains and rocks.
distinction: The buildings mainly rely on the screening of mountains and rocks and trees to present spatial layering; although a small bridge and path suggest movement through the landscape, the feature of forming a setting through concealment and revelation is more prominent.

evidence: Right-hand painted panel: multiple groups of pavilions and storied buildings are scattered among woodland and mountain rocks, their roofs and eaves faintly visible behind the tree crowns, forming a clear relationship of concealment and revelation. | Waterside and woodland of the right-hand painted panel: through the screening and exposure of the buildings by trees and sloping rocks, a richly layered sense of space is presented, rather than being fully open or simply arranged according to terrain.
distinction: Although the buildings serve as scenic accents, the painting places greater emphasis on the spatial layering and concealment-and-revelation relationships formed by the mutual screening of buildings, woodland and mountain rocks.

evidence: Right river surface: A small boat carrying two people can be seen floating on the river surface, presenting a state of movement through the landscape, but no houses, bridges, or other built elements connect with it. | Right sloped bank: Pines and a sloped bank are visible, with no traces of buildings such as pavilions or houses.
distinction: No clear built elements are visible in the painting; only a small boat moving through the landscape is seen. Because there is no built entity, it is assigned only with difficulty to C4 based on the overall space of movement, but it lacks evidence of built elements.

evidence: Lower left and along the bank: Boats at the water's edge, figures, and paths along the bank are visible, suggesting a starting point for entering the painting or landing from the water. | Middle and right valleys of the painting: Built elements (houses, towers, pagodas) are scattered among mountains and rocks and woodland, connected by small paths and bridges, forming clues for movement through the landscape. | Overall composition: The handscroll format, combined with elements such as the waterside, mountain paths, and bridges, guides the line of sight to shuttle between landscape and built elements, presenting a spatial process of passing from one point to another.
distinction: Although the built elements are placed nestling against mountains and beside water (C1), the painting emphasizes more the guidance of the viewer, through clues of paths, bridges, and the waterside, into and through the entire space (C4).

evidence: Right side: A thatched hut is screened among trees and mountains and rocks, with its roof, eaves, and figures inside the window exposed, forming a clear layering of concealment and revelation. | Lower middle: Two people on the bank walk along a small path toward the built elements on the right, and a clue for movement through the landscape exists. | Left side: A large expanse of water and distant mountains left as unpainted space, forming a contrast of sparseness and density with the dense woodland and built elements on the right.
distinction: Although there are pedestrians and a small path pointing toward the built elements, the most prominent compositional role of the built elements themselves is to present spatial layering through their screening and revelation by woodland and mountains and rocks.

evidence: Lower left: A group of houses is screened among trees, with only the roofs and parts of the walls exposed, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Middle and distant view: Water and distant mountains form an open background, setting off the layering of the foreground woodland and houses.
distinction: Although the houses are located beside the waterside, the painting mainly expresses spatial layering through trees screening the houses, and the relationship of concealment and revelation is more prominent than terrain-based placement.

evidence: Right side of the painting, at the mountain foot and waterside: A building complex (a city wall or village) is visible in an open area embraced by mountain ranges and at the water's edge, identifying the scenery of that place. | Middle section of the painting, on the river surface and far bank: Boats dot the river surface, pointing toward tiny buildings on the bank, suggesting a correspondence between nodes of human settlement and the positions where the landscape opens and closes.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed nestling against mountains and beside water, in the handscroll composition they mainly serve as scattered visual nodes marking the scenery along the way, rather than emphasizing a close borrowing between a single built layout and the terrain.

evidence: Left side, middle-lower portion: Several houses are situated between the sloped bank and woodland, with roofs and wall surfaces partly screened by trees, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Left-middle: Behind the houses are distant mountains, and in front are sloped rocks and water, with trees forming natural screening and layering around the buildings.
distinction: Although the houses nestle against mountains and beside water, the painting emphasizes more the spatial layering formed by the screening and revelation of the buildings by woodland, rather than terrain-based placement alone.

evidence: Whole painting: The painting mainly shows distant mountains, water, and nearby mountains and rocks and trees, with no clear built elements such as houses, pavilions, bridges, or paths visible.
distinction: The painting is dominated by natural landscape and lacks visible built entities or clear entry clues; it is assigned to the closest category based on the overall visible space.

evidence: Lower left: A built structure with a roof and columns can be seen, situated on a sloped bank and immediately adjacent to several tall trees. | Left side: The built element is placed beside a sloped bank and trees, facing open water and distant mountains, presenting a relationship of terrain-based placement.
distinction: Although the building is adjacent to trees, the painting mainly shows its placement beside a sloped bank and facing the water, rather than emphasizing the layering of concealment and revelation formed by screening.

evidence: Lower left to middle ground: A wooden bridge is built over the water, connecting the foreground sloped bank with the middle-ground land, forming a clear path of crossing and entry. | Middle-ground left: The bridge extends toward the settlement houses among the woods behind, constructing a spatial layering from near to deep that can be traveled and entered. | Upper-middle hillside: The roof of a house looms faintly among the hillside woods as a potential destination for the extension of the path, reinforcing the directional quality of entry into the setting.
distinction: Although the hillside houses have a relationship of concealment and revelation through screening by trees, the guiding role of the coherent path and entry process constructed by the bridge in the painting is more prominent for the overall spatial organization.

evidence: Left side, middle-lower portion: A house can be seen, with its roof and wall surfaces partly screened by the pines and mountains and rocks in front, presenting a state of being half hidden and half revealed. | Center of the painting: A large expanse of pine grove interlaces with mountains and rocks, forming rich foreground-background layering and wrapping the built elements within it.
distinction: Although the house is placed on the mountain slope, the painting emphasizes more the layering of its screening and revelation by the pine grove and mountains and rocks, so C2 fits better than C1.

evidence: Lower middle: Through the gaps between the branches of the foreground trees, the roof of a pavilion is visible, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation through screening by woodland. | Foreground: Several bare trees and sloped rocks are located in front of the painting, forming natural screening of the pavilion behind and constructing spatial layering.
distinction: The built elements construct the pictorial layering mainly through the screening and revelation of trees, rather than simply serving as a marker identifying a certain landscape.

evidence: Middle ground: a wooden bridge spans the stream, with figures, cattle and horses crossing over it, linking the two banks and forming a clear line of passage. | From the lower-middle to the upper-right of the painting: the stream and the winding path connect the thatched hut in the foreground, the bridge in the middle ground, and the storied building built against the mountain at the upper right, presenting an enterable, traversable spatial depth. | Lower right: boats and figures are on the waterside, serving as nodes of the water route and further enriching the accessible, transferable lines of traffic and travel in the painting.
distinction: Although built structures are placed against the mountain in the painting, the coherent travel line formed by the bridge, stream and paths plays a more dominant role in organising the overall spatial depth.

evidence: Lower left: a thatched hut, courtyard wall and door leaf are visible, with figures active inside the gate, constituting a clear destination. | From the lower right to the lower middle: an arched bridge is visible crossing the stream, with a path extending beside the bridge, and a figure walking along the path towards the courtyard gate. | Lower middle: the bridge, path, gate and thatched hut form a coherent visual and spatial line, presenting a process of movement through the landscape that is enterable and reachable.
distinction: Although the built structures are sited against the mountain and beside the water, the painting emphasises more the dynamic spatial process of guiding the eye and the figures through the bridge, path and gate into the built structures, rather than merely displaying a static relationship of placement according to terrain.

evidence: Lower part: a thatched pavilion is built on a stone platform/sloping bank by the water, its base integrated with the terrain, presenting a relationship of building on a platform and siting by the water. | Right side: to the right of the thatched pavilion a small bridge/path connects it, further indicating its spatial connection with the bank. | Middle-ground valley: houses are faintly visible among the trees in the valley, distributed according to the slope and following the terrain.
distinction: Although the thatched pavilion is the visual focus, its placement against the mountain and beside the water, built on rock, is more prominent, embodying the correspondence between the built structures and the terrain and waterside.

evidence: Middle, slightly left, valley: pale-ink buildings and corridor railings are concealed behind clustered broadleaf trees and slanting pines, with only roofs and parts of walls exposed, forming a layering of buildings seen behind woodland | Right bank, middle section, among the cliffs: beneath the eaves and platform railings exposed at a gap in the cliff, several slanting thin poles resemble scaffolding, the built structures half-screened by rock walls and woodland | Lower water surface and valley mouth: an open expanse of unpainted water extends upward from below into the valley where the buildings behind the woodland are located; boats are moored on the water, but no bridge, path, gate or other direct link to the buildings is visible
distinction: The built structures participate in the composition and run through the middle of the painting mainly through the concealment-and-revelation relationship of roofs exposed behind woodland and rock, whereas the unpainted water surface and boats only indicate mooring and the direction of view, lacking discernible connective clues for entry

evidence: Lower part, slightly right of centre: an arched bridge spans the stream, with two people on horseback or on foot on the bridge, forming a clear line of movement through the landscape. | Lower part, slightly left of centre: beside the bridge is a pavilion or thatched hut, with figures active nearby, together with the bridge constituting an enterable spatial node. | Lower part overall: the bridge, path, built structures and figures at the foot of the mountain by the water connect with one another, presenting a spatial process of passing from one place to another and approaching the built structures.
distinction: Although the built structures are sited by the water, the painting emphasises more the line of movement through the landscape and the relationship of entry formed by the bridge, figures and built structures, so C4 is more apt.

evidence: Lower centre: a person is visible sitting on a rock by the water, surrounded by water ripples and mountains and rocks. | Upper part and left side: the trunks and leaves of old trees are visible, as well as the mountains, rocks and sloping bank in the middle, with no buildings or man-made structures seen.
distinction: No clear built structures are seen in the painting, only figures and landscape; it is assigned to the closest category on the basis of the overall visible space.

evidence: Left side, middle: a thatched-roof pavilion is built on a rock platform with wooden railings, clearly placed on the rocky sloping platform. | Left side, lower part: below the pavilion steps extend downward to a platform where figures stand, presenting a layout distributed according to the heights of the terrain. | Painting overall: the built structures unfold closely against the cliff and sloping bank on the left, and the base forms a clear correspondence with the natural terrain.
distinction: Although steps guide the way in the painting, the core visual relationship is the placement of the building according to the terrain of the rock platform, rather than an emphasis on the extension of a travel path.

evidence: Lower left: an arched bridge is visible, with pedestrians on it; behind the bridge a path connects, leading to the area of mountains, rocks and buildings, forming a clear clue for entry. | Lower right: buildings are erected against the cliff, partly obscured by trees and connected with the path and bridge system below, implying an accessible spatial relationship. | Middle: boats are by the waterside, and houses are faintly visible among the trees on the opposite bank, implying a connection between water-route traffic and the built structures and further indicating the extended spatial process.
distinction: Although the buildings partly screened by trees embody a concealment relationship, the clues of the bridge, path and pedestrians are more prominent in the painting, clearly organising the traversable spatial process of passing from one place to another, so C4 is closer to the dominant expression than C2.

evidence: Lower left: a roofed pavilion or waterside chamber is visible, supported below by columns, with figures faintly visible inside. | Lower left and centre: the building is partly obscured by the thick trunks and foliage of foreground pines, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Left side and background: mountains, rocks and trees surround the building behind and around it, further emphasising the spatial layering of the building amid the screening of woodland and rocks.
distinction: Although the building is sited against the mountain and beside the water, the painting emphasises more its concealment-and-revelation relationship, half exposed as it is obscured by pines and rocks, and constructs spatial layering thereby, so C2 is more apt than C1.

evidence: Lower right: a multi-storey building and its attached structures are surrounded by several trees; the building itself, eaves and steps are revealed through the trunks and foliage, forming a distinct layering of concealment and revelation. | Lower left: a courtyard building complex is screened behind the sloping bank and clusters of trees, with parts of the walls and roofs visible, forming a relationship of concealment and exposure with the natural environment. | Lower middle: waterside, sloping ground and trees interweave, with the built structures placed among them, presenting spatial depth through the screening of the woodland.
distinction: Although the built structures are placed beside the waterside and sloping ground, the relationship of concealment and revelation of the buildings by trees is more prominent in the painting, constituting the main spatial layering and mode of scene-making.

evidence: Lower-middle part of the painting: a fishing boat is visible floating on the water with figures aboard, but there are no fixed buildings | From the lower left to the centre of the painting: willows extend in the near ground, their branches and leaves hanging towards the water | Upper part of the painting: distant mountains loom faintly in cloud and mist, and the water surface is open
distinction: There are no fixed built structures in the painting, only a fishing boat as a scenic accent, so it is assigned to C3 to reflect its role in defining the waterscape

evidence: Lower-middle part of the painting: two boys are visible on a sloping rock and three sheep below the slope, with no houses, bridges or other clear built structures seen. | Right side and upper part of the painting: mainly luxuriant trees and sloping rocks, with no traces of buildings.
distinction: No clear built structures are seen in the painting; it is assigned to the closest category solely on the basis of the spatial organisation of the overall landscape and the scenic accent figures.

evidence: Lower-middle part, slightly right: an open-sided pavilion is built on the waterside, its structure clearly visible | Lower-middle part: the pavilion stands between the trees and the waterside, facing the towering cliff and open water in the distance | Overall composition: the pavilion stands where the water surface is open, forming a visual correspondence with the distant mountains and marking the position for viewing the waterside scene
distinction: The pavilion mainly serves to mark the waterside scenery and concentrate the gaze, making it an identifier of the landscape, rather than emphasising adaptation to complex terrain (such as following a slope or winding around rocks).

evidence: Lower-left corner: a figure sits alone on a rock beneath a pine; to his left, by the water, a blurred vertical and horizontal linear structure resembling a bridge or railing is visible, implying a waterside connection. | Lower-middle part of the painting: tall pines and steep mountains and rocks occupy the main body, with the figure dotting beneath the pine, forming the spatial focus of a scholar sitting alone. | Left side and upper part of the painting: the mountains and rocks are tall, water winds at the foot of the mountain, and inscription and seals are distributed across the upper part and both sides of the painting.
distinction: The suspected bridge structure in the lower-left corner, as a clue for movement through the landscape (C4), is closer to its function of connecting the waterside and implying a path than as a mere scenic marker (C3), even though the built element is extremely faint.

evidence: Lower-left corner: houses are largely obscured by the dense foreground pine grove, with only the building's front face and window lattice exposed, presenting a typical state of buildings hidden in woodland. | Upper-middle part: a storied building is placed among the rocky gullies of the mountainside, surrounded and screened by mountains, rocks and trees on both sides, forming a deep layering; the exposed eaves and railings indicate its presence. | Middle, right side: a pavilion stands atop a cliff rock, its base concealed behind the rock body and merging with the surrounding mountain forms, presenting a relationship of exposure on the rock.
distinction: Although the bridge and figures in the lower-right corner imply entry, the path does not directly and coherently connect with the built structures, whereas the concealment-and-revelation relationship between the buildings and the woodland and rocks runs through the painting and more dominates the organisation of spatial layering.

evidence: Lower right: the roof and walls of a house are exposed behind trees, presenting a layered relationship of being screened by woodland. | Lower left: a building outline is faintly visible among the waterside trees, screening and being screened by the natural environment.
distinction: The painting mainly presents the concealment-and-revelation relationship of built structures screened by trees, rather than emphasising their layout according to terrain.

evidence: Lower part of the painting: a person is walking on a bridge spanning the stream; the bridge connects the two banks, forming a clear clue for movement through the landscape and a path into the space. | Upper-middle part of the painting, mountainside: the roofs and parts of the walls of buildings are visible among trees and rocks, together with the bridge and path below constituting an accessible deep space.
distinction: Although the buildings have a screened appearance, the clear bridge and pedestrians in the lower part of the painting constitute a strong process of spatial entry and travel, making access to secluded settings the dominant expression.

evidence: Lower right: the roofs and walls of several buildings are visible, partly obscured by the trunks and crowns of foreground trees, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Lower left: a bridge spans the water, connecting the sloping bank on the left with the building area on the right, implying a path of entry. | Lower middle: dense trees surround the building complex, placing the buildings within the woodland and enhancing the spatial layering and screening effect.
distinction: Although a bridge in the painting implies a path of entry, the concealment-and-revelation relationship of the buildings screened by trees is visually more prominent and dominates the spatial expression of the painting.

evidence: Lower half of the painting: sloping rocks, several tall withered trees and shrubs are depicted, with no houses or other built structures seen. | Among the trees and rocks in the lower right of the painting: a figure carrying something and holding a staff stands on a faint path in a walking posture, implying spatial extension and a relationship of entry.
distinction: There are no built structures in the painting; it is assigned to C4 on the basis of the spatial organisation of the figure walking along the path, with no other obvious competing interpretation.

evidence: Upper-left corner: a building is visible on the mountain slope, its roof and wall structure clear, partly obscured by surrounding trees, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Upper middle: there are faint traces on the mountainside suspected to be buildings, but the details are unclear and difficult to confirm.
distinction: Although the building in the upper-left corner serves as a scenic accent, its concealment-and-revelation relationship with the trees is more significant, mainly presenting the characteristic of concealment and revelation forming a scene.

evidence: Lower centre: a figure playing the qin is visible sitting beneath a willow, surrounded by mountains, rocks and vegetation, with no houses or structures seen. | Middle ground: a large area of drooping willow branches forms a screen, creating a foreground-background spatial layering with the water surface and distant mountains behind. | Distant view: mountains rise and fall, with no visible building bases or man-made structures.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built structures, but the layering of concealment and revelation formed by the figure and the willows is closest to a spatial organisation of concealment and revelation forming a scene.

evidence: Lower-middle part of the painting: a house is surrounded and obscured by the tall red-leaf tree on the left and the banana plants and bamboo grove behind. | Centre, slightly right of the painting: the roof, walls and open doors and windows of the house are revealed through the gaps in the trees, forming a distinct layering of concealment and revelation. | Overall composition: the screening by woodland and the exposure of the building together constitute the spatial relationship of buildings seen in woodland, with the built structures integrated into the natural scenery.
distinction: The painting mainly presents the layering formed by the screening and exposure of the buildings by trees, rather than simply using buildings to mark a certain landscape scene.

evidence: Lower-left corner: a figure leaning on a staff is visible standing before mountains and rocks, facing the high mountain and withered trees to the right. | Whole painting: the painting consists mainly of mountains and rocks, withered trees and figures, with no traces of houses, bridges, paths or any other man-made built structures seen.
distinction: No built structures at all are seen in the painting; on the basis of the figure's posture of contemplating the landscape, it is assigned only with difficulty to C4, which expresses a sense of spatial entry, but there is a lack of actual evidence of built structures and paths.

evidence: Lower-middle part: two people are visible sitting facing each other on a rocky platform, surrounded by pines and distant mountains, with no houses, pavilions or other built structures seen. | Lower-right corner: another person is on a rock by the water, and there are no traces of bridges, paths, buildings or other man-made built structures in the painting.
distinction: No visible built structures in the painting, only scenic accent figures, so it is assigned to the closest category on the basis of the overall landscape organisation.

evidence: Lower-middle part: the lower-middle part of the painting shows a water surface, reed beds and a small moored boat with one person aboard, with no clear houses, pavilions or other built structures seen. | Upper part: the upper part of the painting depicts a bright moon and clouds, with much unpainted space, and there are inscriptions and seals.
distinction: No clear built structures are seen in the painting, only a small boat moored among the reeds; it is assigned only with difficulty to C2 on the basis of the reeds screening the boat, but it lacks typical evidence of buildings.

evidence: Lower-middle part of the painting: the built structures (a group of houses) are heavily surrounded by dense pine woodland, with only roofs, eaves, doors and windows and parts of the walls exposed, presenting a spatial layering of buildings hidden in woodland. | Left side of the painting and around the buildings: the branches and foliage of tall pines clearly screen the building structures, expressing a secluded dwelling environment through the concealment-and-revelation relationship, with trees and buildings interweaving to form foreground and background layering.
distinction: Although a bridge and fence in the painting imply a path, the dominant visual relationship is the screening and exposure of the built structures by woodland, forming concealment and revelation forming a scene, rather than emphasising the process of entering through the bridge and path.

evidence: Lower right: a canopied boat is moored at the edge of the waterside with several people aboard, becoming the visual focus in the lower part of the painting. | Lower middle: the boat is closely integrated with the surrounding trees, sloping bank and water surface, marking the specific scene of mooring on the river bank.
distinction: Although the boat is moored at the waterside, its main compositional role is to mark and concentrate the river-bank scene there, rather than to emphasise a layout relationship following the mountain and terrain.

evidence: Middle, slightly right: an open-hall thatched pavilion sits on a platform at the cliff edge, with two people sitting facing each other inside; the thatched roof ridge and left eave are partly obscured by clusters of pine needles hanging down from above, and the roof and eaves are exposed from beneath the pine shade | Right side to centre: a thick pine trunk slants out and coils from the right cliff, spreading over the thatched pavilion to form a cover; the right roof corner of the pavilion is screened by the pine trunk and rock wall, constituting a layering of buildings seen behind rock and amid woodland | Lower left: the front edge of the platform on which the thatched pavilion stands is the foot of the downward slope and cliff, below which a stream winds among the rocks, and cloud and mist separate the thatched pavilion from the distant pine woodland and peaks into foreground and background layering
distinction: The roof and eaves of the thatched pavilion are mainly exposed from beneath the covering of the coiling pine branches and the rock wall, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship runs through the composition and dominates the scene-making; although the sloping platform base is visible, its correspondence with the terrain is less prominent than the screening relationship of pines and rocks

evidence: Lower part, slightly right of centre: the roof and bright open building of a house are exposed between the trunks of a pine grove, with figures visible inside the house, the building itself being vertically interrupted by several trunks in front | Above and on both sides of the lower house: dense tree crowns cover the upper edge and surroundings of the house, the roof line appearing intermittently through the gaps in the branches and leaves, forming a layering of buildings seen in woodland | Lower foreground: the sloping bank and rows of trunks lie across in front of the house, acting as foreground scenery that pushes the built structures into the depths of the woodland
distinction: The built structures present spatial layering mainly through screening and exposure by woodland; although there is open ground and a standing figure in front of the house, no discernible travel clues such as a bridge, path or gate connecting with it are seen, so C4 is not adopted

evidence: Bottom and lower right of the painting: courtyard walls, gate openings, a winding waterside walkway and a bridge crossing the water are visible, constituting a clear path of entry and connection. | Lower-middle part of the painting: the building complex advances layer by layer along the waterside and mountain slope, with figures standing on the bank-side walkway, presenting an accessible, traversable spatial relationship. | Right side, upper-middle part of the painting: a winding path is visible along the mountain-slope woodland, connecting the halls on the mountainside and the pagoda at the summit, continuing the upward travel clues.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited against the mountain and beside the water, the painting emphasises more the travel process of guiding the viewer through clues such as bridges, paths and gates deep into the courtyard and the mountain temple.

evidence: Upper middle: pavilions are built against the mountain, partly obscured by clouds, mist and mountain rocks, presenting a half-hidden, half-revealed layering. | Middle left: buildings are screened behind trees and mountain crags, with only part of the roofs and walls exposed. | Bottom center: a waterside pavilion is set at the water's edge, surrounded by trees, forming a relation of concealment and revelation with the natural setting.
distinction: Although the built elements nestle against mountain and water, the painting places greater emphasis on creating spatial layering through the screening of mountain rocks, trees and mist, so the relation of concealment and revelation is more prominent than terrain-based siting.

evidence: Lower left: a two-storey pavilion is partly screened by the branches and foliage of surrounding tall pines, with only part of the roof, railings and figures exposed. | Lower right: a waterside pavilion platform abuts the bank, its roof and structure screened by pine trunks and canopy in the foreground. | Middle ground, left of center: a small pavilion is half-hidden among trees, with only the roof and part of the eaves exposed.
distinction: Although the buildings stand by water and against the slope, the painting places greater emphasis on the layer-by-layer screening and exposure of the buildings by woodland, and the relation of concealment and revelation dominates the spatial layering.

evidence: Middle ground: a red arched bridge spans and links the two banks, acting as an obvious movement-through-the-landscape cue that leads the eye deeper into the painting. | Lower left and lower right: clear covered walkways, steps and railings are painted around the building complex, forming an accessible, traversable path system. | Overall composition: the built elements connect with the landscape space through bridges, walkways and paths, presenting a spatial process of moving from here to there and approaching the hall.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited against mountain and water, the movement cues of bridges, covered walkways and steps are more conspicuous in the painting, strongly organizing an accessible, traversable spatial relationship.

evidence: Lower half, left: palace buildings are disposed in staggered fashion along the mountain foot and slopes, closely integrated with the mountain's contours | Lower half, right: a large building complex is built on artificially constructed high platforms and bases, unfolding along the edges of the shoreline and mountain rocks | Middle ground, left: pavilions and terraces emerge from behind mountain rocks, their bases attached to the natural terrain
distinction: Although trees and mountain rocks partly screen the buildings, the overall layout of buildings nestling against mountain forms and shoreline and placed on platforms is more prominent and dominates the spatial organization.

evidence: Lower middle: a person leans between mountain rocks and tree roots, the figure's posture closely bound to the rocky terrain. | Lower right corner: another person squats beside mountain rocks, with tea utensils placed nearby, the activity space entirely reliant on the natural rocks and ground. | Whole painting: trees and mountain rocks are the main compositional elements; no houses, pavilions or other man-made structures are seen, and the figures' activities unfold by relying on the natural terrain.
distinction: There is no identifiable architecture in the painting; the figures' dependence on rocks and trees comes closest to the spatial logic of terrain-responsive siting, but there is no evidence of physical built structures.

evidence: Middle left, at the mountain foot: a roof and outline of a built structure faintly emerge between woodland and mountain rocks, partly screened by the surrounding scenery, forming a relation of concealment and revelation. | Below, near the water's edge: a small boat is moored, adjacent to the bank's trees and rocks, but it does not constitute the main body of a fixed built structure.
distinction: The painting mainly presents the layering of a house screened among woodland and mountain rocks, rather than emphasizing a spatial process of entering the built setting via cues such as bridges or paths.

evidence: Lower center, slightly right: a built structure is visible among the trees, its roof and right wall partly screened by the trunks and foliage of surrounding tall trees. | Lower center: the front porch of the built structure is open, and two people are seen sitting facing each other; the main body of the building is half-hidden behind the woodland, forming an obvious layering of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the built structure stands by the water's edge below the waterfall, the painting places greater emphasis on the screening and exposure of the building by trees, and the relation of concealment and revelation is the principal means of composing the scene.

evidence: Left side of the island: the wall and roof of a building are seen emerging from behind trees and mountain rocks, in a half-hidden, half-revealed state. | Top of the island: a corner of a roof appears above the tree cluster, indicating a built structure at the height, mostly screened by woodland. | The island as a whole: the built structures form a screening relationship through the dense woodland and mountain rocks on the island, hinting at their existence and spatial layering through exposed partial components.
distinction: Although the buildings are located on the island, the painting places greater emphasis on the relation of concealment and revelation in which they are screened by woodland and rocks and only partly exposed, rather than on showing their layout as sited according to terrain.

evidence: Middle of the painting: a hall-style building is surrounded by dense trees (pines and miscellaneous trees) to the left, right and above, its roof, eaves and columns partly obscured by branches and foliage, only partly exposed. | Inside and in front of the building: through gaps in the trees and openings in the building, two people sitting facing each other and an attendant are clearly visible, presenting a spatial layering of seeing a house within the woods and viewing figures across the scenery. | Foreground left and right: tall trunks and luxuriant foliage form a foreground frame, wrapping the building within it and creating a strong contrast of screening and exposure.
distinction: The core visual structure of the painting lies in the layer-by-layer screening and partial exposure of the building by woodland, constructing the layering of a deep, secluded dwelling in the woods, rather than emphasizing a coherent movement route or a process of entry guidance.

evidence: Lower right: a house is partly screened by bamboo and trees in front, with only the roof and part of the walls exposed, forming a relation of concealment and revelation in which a house is seen within the woods. | Below: a person is walking along a small path toward the house, providing a cue for movement through the painting.
distinction: The painting contains both screening and path cues, but the screening and exposure of the house by bamboo and trees constitutes the more prominent spatial layering, so concealment and revelation in forming the scene predominates.

evidence: Lowest section, over the stream: a small plank bridge crosses the stream surface; on the right bank stand two figures with staffs moving through the landscape, facing up toward the bank above | Lower middle, level bank at the water's edge: an open pavilion thatched hall is built at the water on an earthen platform; inside, a person sits before a couch, and the bank line in front slopes gently down to meet the line of the bridge and walkers | Middle left bank slope and middle-upper mountain col: an empty pavilion is set on a projecting point of the slope, and further up a roof emerges among the ridge trees in the mountain col, forming with the thatched hall below a series of successively higher points of arrival
distinction: The bridge, the walkers and the continuous shoreline string the thatched hall, the slope pavilion and the buildings in the mountain col into a sequence that can be reached and penetrated further, which explains the organization of the whole painting better than static siting alone on platforms by the water

evidence: Lower left to upper middle: a winding plank road/mountain path spirals upward along the mountain's form, with conspicuous railings, and figures riding horses or walking on it, forming a route of movement through the landscape that runs through the painting. | Middle right: a bridge crosses the stream and waterfall, linking the mountain paths on both sides and strengthening the sense of spatial connectivity and extension into depth. | Lower foreground: figures stand on a platform enclosed by railings, apparently the starting point or a node of the path, connecting with the mountain road behind, presenting a here-to-there relationship.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited against the mountain, the winding plank road, bridges and railings in the painting form the dominant movement cues, strongly leading the eye from bottom to top and from outside to inside, emphasizing the sense of spatial process rather than terrain-based siting alone.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: a house is surrounded and screened by pines, withered trees and bamboo groves, with only the roof, eaves and part of the walls, doors and windows exposed, figures inside the house, presenting a layering of a house hidden in the woods. | Lower right corner: another small building (a pavilion or open hall) is partly screened by trees and rocks, with only one corner of the roof visible, forming a screening relationship with the main house. | Overall composition: the built structures lie deep in the woodland, hinting at their existence and level through the screening and exposure by natural scenery, and the relation of concealment and revelation participates in forming the scene.
distinction: Although there are staff-bearing figures and a stream, the painting lacks a clear, coherent path leading into the built structures; the built structures are presented mainly through the screening and exposure by woodland to convey spatial layering.

evidence: Left and middle: pavilions, terraces and a long gallery are obscured by dense trees and mountain rocks, with only the roofs, eaves and part of the walls exposed, forming an obvious layering of concealment and revelation. | Middle, mid-slope: buildings are hidden behind tree clusters and rock faces, faintly visible, presenting spatial depth through screening by natural scenery. | Lower right corner: there is a small bridge beside the waterfall and stream, but the built structures overall appear mainly wrapped and screened by mountain forest.
distinction: Although the buildings are arranged according to the mountain's form, the painting places greater emphasis on the screening and exposure of the buildings by trees and mountain rocks, and the relation of concealment and revelation dominates the spatial layering.

evidence: Middle left of the painting: a group of halls is built on a rocky mountain terrace, with a railed platform in front serving as a spatial node. | Right side and below: a winding mountain path, wooden bridge and plank road are visible, with figures walking along the path, forming clear movement cues. | Overall: paths and built structures connect with one another, leading the eye from bottom to top and from outside to inside, presenting an accessible and reachable spatial process.
distinction: Although the built structures are sited according to the mountain's form, the winding paths, bridges and figures' traces in the painting constitute a strong movement guidance, making the spatial process of access to secluded settings dominant.

evidence: Lower center, slightly right: a small bridge crosses the water, linking the two banks and forming a clear cue for passage. | Lower left: a small path and tiny figures walking along it are visible, leading the eye toward the depth of the painting and toward the waterside pavilion. | Lower right, at the water's edge: a pavilion/waterside pavilion with a platform is built at the water, serving as the endpoint of the path or an accessible node.
distinction: Although the buildings are built according to the water-and-rock terrain, the painting places greater emphasis on the accessible, traversable spatial process formed by the bridge, path and guidance by figures.

evidence: Middle ground: a building complex is arranged in layers along the cliff and on both sides of the waterfall, disposed in staggered fashion according to the terrain's height. | Below: buildings are set at the water, with platforms or plank roads extending to the water surface, unfolding along the bank. | Overall: the layout of the built structures corresponds closely to the direction of the mountain form, the waterfall's drop and the position of the water, showing the characteristics of terrain-based disposition.
distinction: Although the buildings are partly screened among woodland and mountain rocks, their layout features—nestling against the cliff, following the terrain and being built at the water—are more prominent and dominate the spatial relationships in the painting.

evidence: Right cliff: buildings are distributed in layers along the cliff face, in the form of structures placed on platforms and disposed separately according to the slope, corresponding to the height of the mountain. | Lower shoreline: pavilions and houses are set at the water, unfolding along the bank, their bases integrated with the shoreline terrain. | Left mountain foot: buildings are seen adjacent to trees and mountain rocks, sited according to the slope.
distinction: The buildings are clearly laid out in accordance with the terrain features of the cliff and shoreline, showing a terrain-based siting relationship, rather than serving merely as isolated visual foci to highlight the scenery.

evidence: Middle ground right: a pagoda and halls are partly screened by pine forest, with only the roof and part of the walls exposed, presenting a spatial layering of concealment and revelation within the woods. | Foreground left: pavilions and gallery buildings emerge from behind dense pine forest and mountain rocks, buildings and natural scenery screening each other. | Distant high point: a small pavilion stands on the cliff; though exposed, it is small in scale and serves as a high-point supplement within the overall screening relationship.
distinction: Although some buildings are sited according to the terrain, the painting places greater emphasis on the screening and exposure of the buildings by woodland, and the relation of concealment and revelation dominates the organization of spatial layering.

evidence: Lower middle: a small bridge is seen crossing the water surface or stream mouth, linking the left and right banks and forming a movement cue. | Lower left corner: the roof of a house is visible amid screening trees, located at one end of the bridge, implying a reachable built structure. | Lower right corner: a tree cluster is adjacent to part of a building (a roof), together with the bridge forming an accessible spatial scene at the bank.
distinction: The bridge in the painting clearly links the bank and the house, emphasizing a here-to-there, reachable spatial process, which is more organizational than mere tree screening (C2).

evidence: Lower left: two people are seen sitting facing each other among mountain rocks and trees, with no traces of built elements such as houses, bridges or paths around them | Whole painting: the painting consists mainly of mountain rocks, trees, figures and calligraphy on the right; no clear man-made architectural structures are seen
distinction: There are no identifiable built elements in the painting, only figures active in nature, with no evidence of buildings for concealment and revelation, scenic accentuation, or terrain-based siting

evidence: Lower left corner: a house and pavilion built at the water's edge are visible, with figures inside or nearby. | Lower left to lower middle: an arched bridge crosses the water, linking the built structures with the opposite bank, with pedestrians on the bridge. | Lower middle to lower right: behind the bridge a small path extends deep into the woods, with a figure carrying a load walking along it, presenting a spatial process of movement into the landscape.
distinction: Although the built structures are set by the water, the painting places greater emphasis on guiding the viewer through bridges, paths and figures' movement into a secluded depth, and the organizing role of the access-to-seclusion cues is more prominent.

evidence: Lower left and below: a wooden bridge crosses the stream in the lower part of the painting, with pedestrians on it, forming the starting point for entering the painting. | Lower middle to left: along the stream and mountain rocks, a winding stone-step path leads upward, connecting the bridge below with the building complex on the mid-slope. | Left mid-slope: roofs and walls of buildings are visible among the trees, one of the destinations reachable by the extending path.
distinction: Although the buildings are built against the mountain, the coherent movement route formed by the bridge, stream and stone steps in the painting more prominently displays the spatial process of moving from here to there and penetrating into a secluded setting.

evidence: Middle left: a building complex (houses, enclosing walls) is placed tight against the shoreline, its layout following the shape of the bank, showing a tendency to unfold along the shore. | Building bases: the built structures are located on the sloping bank, facing water in front and backed by trees, their disposition corresponding closely to the shoreline terrain.
distinction: Although a bridge and boats suggest transport connections, the layout feature of buildings extending along the shoreline (unfolding along the shore) is more prominent and dominates the spatial relationship between built structures and landscape.

evidence: Lower right: through the interlacing withered branches, the roof and beam-and-column structure of a house are faintly visible, the building largely screened by trees, forming a layering of concealment and revelation. | Lower left: houses are built beside a rocky slope bank, with a figure standing nearby, the buildings half-screened behind trees and rocks, screening each other with the natural setting. | Overall: the built structures do not occupy a conspicuous position but are screened by dense foreground woodland and mountain rocks, presenting the spatial depth of seeing houses within the woods and behind crags.
distinction: The core of the painting lies in the layering of concealment and revelation and the spatial depth formed by buildings through woodland and rocks, rather than emphasizing path cues that guide the viewer in.

evidence: Upper middle and mid-slope: numerous pavilions and terraces are placed along cliffs and peak flanks, their bases resting on rocky platforms, in the form of structures placed on platforms and disposed separately according to the slope, following the steep mountain form. | Left valley and middle: buildings unfold along the direction of the mountain and the valley floor, staggered in height, corresponding to the undulations of the mountain, showing terrain-based disposition. | Lower part: village houses are laid out along the shoreline and level ground, surrounded by trees, unfolding according to the terrain and echoing the mountain dwellings above in height.
distinction: Although mist and woodland screen the buildings to form a layering of concealment and revelation (screening), the layout relationship in which buildings nestle against cliffs, rest on platforms and follow the mountain form (terrain-responsive) is more fundamental and determines the overall spatial structure.

evidence: Middle ground: two building complexes are surrounded by dense woods, with only roofs, eaves and part of the walls exposed, presenting an obvious layered relationship of woodland screening and exposure. | Middle ground, slightly right: there is a waterfall to the right, with a bridge spanning above it and linking the rocks on both sides, but the relation of concealment and revelation between the middle-ground buildings and the woodland is more prominent. | Lower left corner: a pavilion and waterside pavilion are built at the water, partly screened by foreground trees, likewise embodying the screening effect of natural scenery on built structures.
distinction: Although the building complexes are sited on mountain terraces, the layered relationship in which woodland half-screens and half-reveals the buildings, with concealment and revelation generating each other, is more prominent and dominates the mode of composing the scene.

evidence: Lower right: a stone arch bridge spans the ravine, with a red-robed walker and two companions on it; the bridge end meets the bank slope, forming the starting point for movement into the mountains | Right middle to middle: a railed plank road winds upward along the cliff face, with a person walking on it; the plank road joins the open hall in the middle and continues around the cliff to the pavilion at the cliff top above | Lower middle left: halls and houses are built on constructed high platforms, with a railed platform in front facing the stream, the platform base meeting the slope rocks and shoreline
distinction: Although the buildings are placed on platforms and cliffs, the whole painting uses bridges, railed paths and plank roads to string numerous built structures into a continuous process that can be reached from below and turned into the depths; the organizing role of movement cues runs through the composition and is stronger than terrain-based siting alone

evidence: Middle right of the painting: the roof and upturned eaves of a group of buildings are visible, most of the structure screened by dense pine forest and mountain rocks, with only the top exposed. | Overall: the built structures are hidden deep in mountain forest, forming spatial layering through the screening by trees and the exposure of roofs, presenting a relation of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the buildings follow the mountain form, the painting places greater emphasis on the layering of concealment and revelation in which they are screened by woodland and rocks with only roofs exposed, rather than on the corresponding layout of bases and terrain.

evidence: Middle left, foot of the waterside cliff slope: a row of houses unfolds along the shoreline, the front facing the water, with a plank bridge crossing the stream mouth beside them and a small boat moored at the bank, the house bases laid out along the slope-foot shoreline | Middle right, mountain col: a pavilion, houses and a railed platform are disposed at three levels along the slope, the direction of the stepped layout consistent with the slope of the mountain col | Upper left, valley edge: a tiered pagoda stands on a high platform among the valley-slope woodland, with a waterfall pouring down from the valley mouth beside it, the pagoda base set on the valley platform
distinction: The building bases and mode of unfolding follow the slope and shoreline directly (a row along the shore, three levels along the slope); concealment and revelation are merely an incidental effect of the surrounding woodland and do not serve as the main means of indicating existence and layering

evidence: Lower right: a red-railed wooden bridge is visible spanning across, with two people on the bridge, forming an initial clue for entering the upper built area from the lower landscape area. | Middle: a white wall encloses the boundary of a courtyard; children play outside the wall; the form of the wall implies a path relationship leading from the outer open ground to the inner main house. | Upper part: the main house is open, with figures seated around within it, located deep along the visual path guided by the bridge and enclosing wall, presenting spatial depth from here to there.
distinction: Although trees partly screen the edges of the houses, the painting constructs a clear sequence of entry from outside to inside through the bridge, enclosing wall, and human activity; the spatial orientation of access to secluded settings is more dominant than mere concealment and revelation layering.

evidence: Lower left: a wooden bridge spans the water, connecting the left slope bank with the right mountains and rocks, forming a clear line of passage. | Lower right: amid screening trees, the roof, walls, and doors and windows of houses are visible; the route of the bridge points toward this built structure.
distinction: Although there is a concealment-and-revelation relationship in which trees screen the houses, the bridge at the lower left clearly establishes a traveled path leading to the built structure, making the enterable spatial process dominant.

evidence: Lower left: Houses are located on a gentle slope at the foot of the mountain, sited in accordance with the mountain's form and surrounded by trees. | Right side, mountainside: Another house is set on the mountainside according to the mountain's form, echoing the shape of the mountain body.
distinction: The houses are mainly sited in accordance with the terrain at the foot and on the mountainside, presenting a relationship of placement according to the ground, rather than primarily relying on screening and revelation to form scenery.

evidence: Whole painting: the picture consists of distant mountains and waterside in the upper section and foreground slopes, rocks, and trees in the lower section, separated by unpainted water surface in the middle; no traces of built elements such as houses or bridges are seen. | Upper left: an inscribed poem mentions 'renjia' (people's homes), but the corresponding area of the painting shows only mountains, rocks, and trees, with no actual depiction of buildings.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built elements, showing only the natural distribution of landscape; therefore it is tentatively assigned to C1 based on overall spatial organization, with no other obvious competing interpretation.

evidence: Left middle ground: thatched-roof buildings are placed against a slope platform and waterside, with the building base closely integrated with the terrain. | Lower foreground: courtyards or houses are built against the slope, surrounded by trees and slope rocks, with the layout following the natural terrain. | Lower left corner: a pavilion or house is screened among trees and rocks at the waterside, showing the feature of setting houses according to the ground.
distinction: Although the buildings have a screening relationship with trees, mountains, and rocks, the painting more prominently highlights the layout feature of buildings placed according to terrain conditions such as slope platforms and waterside, so C1 is more dominant than C2.

evidence: Left middle mountainside: the roofs and walls of several houses are visible, partly blocked by surrounding mountains, rocks, and trees, presenting a half-hidden, half-revealed state. | Overall painting: the built structures are hidden within mountain forest, using the screening of trees and mountain rocks to form spatial layering; no obvious path guidance or scenic-accent marking function is seen.
distinction: Although the buildings are built against the mountain, the painting more emphasizes their concealment and revelation by woodland and mountain rocks, rather than highlighting their placement in accordance with the terrain.

evidence: Lower middle and right of the painting: houses and buildings are partly blocked by dense trees and clouds and mist, with only roofs and parts of walls exposed, forming spatial layering of alternating concealment and revelation. | Left middle of the painting: house outlines are faintly visible behind clusters of trees, using woodland screening to hint at the presence of built structures.
distinction: In the painting, the concealment-and-revelation relationship between built structures and trees, clouds, and mist constitutes the main spatial layering, more prominent than mere placement according to terrain.

evidence: Lower right: a house is half hidden behind a cluster of trees, with only part of the roof and walls exposed, presenting the layering of a house hidden in the forest. | Middle-ground left: a building is located among trees on a sloping bank, using the screening and revealing by trees to form spatial depth.
distinction: Although the building faces the water and follows the slope, the painting more emphasizes the relationship of screening and revealing of the building by woodland, with concealment and revelation forming the scene as the main feature.

evidence: Upper central part: the main peak stands upright, with layered mountains and rocks, its form prominent | Lower right: a sloping bank rises, with dense woodland; among the trees a tiny dot-like object resembles a figure, and no clear buildings are seen | Middle of the painting: a large area of unpainted water surface separates distant and near landscape, forming an opening-and-closing scenery
distinction: No clear built elements are seen in the painting, but the landscape layout is intended to present a corresponding scenery between the main peak and the foreground, so it is assigned to C3; if the emphasis were on the sloping bank terrain, it would be close to C1.

evidence: Whole painting: the picture is divided into upper, middle, and lower sections of landscape scenery, separated by water surface and sloping banks, with no clear built elements seen. | Lower section: the foreground is rocks and trees, with mountains and rocks on the right, and no houses or bridges.
distinction: No clear built elements are seen in the painting; it is assigned to the closest category based on overall landscape spatial organization.

evidence: Middle, slightly left: houses are partly blocked by trees and mountains and rocks, with only roofs and parts of walls exposed, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Right cliff: buildings are built against the mountain, partly screened by the mountain mass and vegetation, appearing faintly. | Lower right foreground: houses are half hidden among woodland, with parts of the buildings visible through gaps between trees.
distinction: Although the buildings are arranged according to terrain, the painting more emphasizes presenting the spatial layering and mood of the buildings through the screening and revealing by natural scenery.

evidence: Middle ground, slightly right: A group of buildings is arranged beside the waterside and at the foot of the mountain, with the building site fitting closely to the terrain. | Middle ground, slightly left: A pavilion is built facing the water, with its columns and roof clearly visible, extending along the edge of the waterside. | Overall painting: The built elements are all located in the gentle zones where mountains and rocks meet the water surface, presenting a spatial relationship of placement according to the ground and suitability to the terrain.
distinction: Although the built elements punctuate the waterside scenery, their siting beside the terrain and their placement of buildings by the water is more prominent and dominant than mere scenic accentuation.

evidence: From the mountainside to the summit on the right of the distant peak: there are very faint brush and ink traces, whose form resembles tiny building or pavilion structures, attached to the mountain and rock outlines, but the details are blurred and difficult to confirm as built elements. | Foreground and middle ground of the painting: mainly slope rocks, willows, pines, and other vegetation; no clear roads, bridges, or definite built entities are seen.
distinction: The suspected built structure is located among high mountains and rocks, very small in scale, mainly serving to accent and mark the scenery of the peak, rather than displaying a clear terrain-responsive layout structure.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: a thatched house is partly blocked by the tall trunks and branches and leaves of foreground trees, with only the roof, eaves, and parts of the walls and figures under the corridor exposed, forming a spatial layering of seeing the house through a screen. | Right of the building: bamboo grove and mountains and rocks surround the rear and sides of the building, further participating in the screening relationship, so that the built structure presents a half-hidden, half-revealed state.
distinction: Although the building is placed against a waterside slope platform, the painting's composition mainly relies on the blocking and revealing of the building by foreground trees to organize spatial layering; the visual feature of concealment and revelation forming the scene is more dominant.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting, lake-center island: there are several houses on the island, located in the middle of the open water, surrounded by trees, becoming a visual focus and marking the scenery in the lake. | Lower right hillside of the painting: there is a tall multi-story pagoda and houses beside it, standing against the slope, striking in form, serving as a shore landmark to mark space. | Upper part of the painting, summit of distant mountains: tiny buildings (resembling a pagoda or pavilion) are faintly visible on the summit, echoing the built structures below and marking the position of the distant mountains.
distinction: Although the built structures are placed according to terrain (such as island houses and slope pagoda), in a composition with large areas of unpainted space, their role as visual focus and landmark (especially the tall pagoda and lake-center island) in scenic accentuation and marking is more dominant, rather than simply showing a relationship of compliance with terrain.

evidence: Left mountainside: A pavilion terrace is built on a protruding rocky platform, placed according to the heights of the mountain's form, presenting a relationship of setting a house on a platform. | Left, at the foot of the mountain by the water: A pavilion is built facing the water, its building site meeting the bank rocks and the waterside, presenting a form arranged along the shore. | Right, in the sloping woodland: House roofs emerge above the tree clusters, distributed in accordance with the slope's terrain.
distinction: The buildings are mainly sited according to the cliff platform and the waterside terrain (setting a house on a platform, building facing the water); screening is only a local secondary feature, and the dominant relationship is terrain-responsive siting.

evidence: Middle right, mountainside: The building group is half-hidden behind rocks and pine woods, with only part of the roofs and walls exposed, forming a clear layering of concealment and revelation. | Left, in a mountain hollow: A pavilion terrace is partly obscured by the trees and rocks on the left, faintly visible, strengthening the sense of deep seclusion in the space.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited according to the mountain's form, the painting emphasizes more the screening and revealing of the buildings by trees, rocks, and mountains, and the relationship of concealment and revelation plays a dominant role in the composition.

evidence: Lower left: an arched bridge is visible, with figures beside it, forming the starting point of a movement-through-the-landscape clue. | Lower middle: a thatched pavilion sits on a platform surrounded by trees and rocks, serving as the destination guided by the path. | Right and background: trees and mountains and rocks screen layer upon layer, working with the bridge and thatched pavilion to form spatial layering from outside to inside.
distinction: The bridge and figures in the painting provide a clear entry clue, guiding the eye to the thatched pavilion; this emphasizes an enterable spatial process more than scenic accentuation as a mere visual focus.

evidence: Upper right: a complex of red-walled buildings is stacked layer upon layer according to the slope of the mountainside, with roofs rising and falling in irregular heights, following the undulations of the mountain form. | Middle: pavilions and buildings are built on a platform in a mountain hollow, with the base closely fitting the surrounding slope. | Left: a stone bridge spans a stream, connecting the sloping banks on both sides, embodying the connection between built structures and terrain.
distinction: Although screened by woodland, the layout relationship of buildings following the mountain and being distributed according to the slope is more conspicuous and dominates the spatial expression.

evidence: Whole painting: the picture depicts waves and multiple groups of figures (arhats, attendants, etc.); no houses, pavilions, or other built elements are seen. | Bottom: rocks/land are painted at the bottom, with figures sitting or standing against the rocks, marking the shore scenery.
distinction: The painting has no clear built elements; it is assigned to C3 based on the distribution and scenic-accent role of the figures within the landscape (waves, rocks).

evidence: Lower right side: built structures are located behind foreground trees and mountains and rocks, with only parts of eaves, walls, and doors and windows exposed, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship screened by natural scenery. | Left middle ground: mountains and rocks rendered in light ink and trees screen and reveal, echoing the buildings on the right in spatial layering.
distinction: Although the buildings are located at the waterside, the most prominent scene-composing method in the painting is to use foreground trees and mountains and rocks to block the buildings, forming layering of concealment and revelation, rather than emphasizing their placement according to the ground.

evidence: Lower middle valley: A group of buildings is placed on the flat valley floor between two mountains, extending in accordance with the terrain. | Lower left corner, waterside: Houses are built beside a sloping bank, their building sites closely integrated with the terrain. | Middle, among clouds and mist: A storied building appears faintly in the clouds and mist on the mountainside, presenting a relationship of placement according to the heights of the mountain's form.
distinction: Although the buildings have layering screened by trees and clouds and mist, the painting emphasizes more the layout relationship in which the building groups are placed according to natural terrain such as valleys, slope platforms, and watersides.
