evidence: Upper middle, mountainside: The house group leans against the mountain's form, partly screened by rocks and trees, presenting a half-screened, half-exposed state. | Middle mountain hollow and left slope: Several houses are hidden behind woods and rock walls, with only roofs or parts of walls exposed, forming a layering of alternating concealment and revelation. | Lower right and lower left corners: Pavilions and houses are interspersed among trees, mountains, and rocks, screened by natural scenery rather than standing out in isolation.
distinction: Although the built elements are distributed according to the mountain's form, the painting emphasizes more the screening and revealing of the buildings by trees, rocks, and mountains, and the relationship of concealment and revelation plays a dominant role in the composition.

evidence: Lower part, slightly left of the painting: a thatched house is visible amid screening trees at the mountain foot, with a gentle sloping bank in front connecting to the water surface. | Lower part, slightly right of the painting: a flat bridge spans the water connecting the two banks, linking the right sloping bank with the area where the left thatched house is located. | Lower center of the painting: the bridge and thatched house are visually and spatially connected through the waterside and stream, presenting a traveled clue that allows entering deep into the scene.
distinction: Although the thatched house is placed against the mountain and beside the water, the movement-through-the-landscape clue formed by the bridge and path in the painting is more prominent, emphasizing the sense of spatial entry from here to there.

evidence: Lower middle foreground sloping bank of the painting: a thatched pavilion (or thatched hall) sits on slope rocks, its building itself and columns partly blocked by several trees in front, with only the roof and part of the lower structure exposed. | Foreground sloping bank and trees: the branches and trunks of the trees and the forms of the slope rocks screen in front of the thatched pavilion, making the built structure present a half-hidden, half-revealed state and constituting a clear front-to-back spatial layering.
distinction: Although the thatched pavilion marks the scenery of the foreground sloping bank, the blocking and revealing relationship of the trees to the building in the painting is more prominent and is the main way of organizing the spatial layering of this local area.

evidence: Lower left: a thatched pavilion/thatched house is half hidden behind trees, with only part of the roof, eaves, and columns exposed, blocked by leaves and branches. | Left and lower middle: trees and the thatched pavilion form front-and-back layering, with a clear concealment-and-revelation relationship, integrating the building into the woodland environment.
distinction: The painting mainly presents the layering relationship of the building being screened and revealed by trees, consistent with concealment and revelation forming the scene; there are no obvious clues of terrain-responsive placement or path guidance.

evidence: Lower left corner: A tiny structure suspected to be a small pavilion or thatched hut is set by the bank, with figures beside it, located at the water's edge in the foreground, seemingly a stopping point or starting point. | Center to upper part of the painting: A waterfall and stream flow down along the mountain gorge, forming a clear vertical visual cue that suggests a spatial path extending from the foreground into the deep valley. | Foreground and middle ground: Rocks and trees organize the form of a valley entrance; together with the direction of the water flow, they create a spatial momentum of entering from outside and turning into the depths.
distinction: Although the structure at the lower left is suspected to be built by the water, the overall composition of the painting emphasizes more guiding the viewer's gaze deep into the valley through the stream and the mountain's form, presenting a sense of the process of access to secluded settings rather than simply showing buildings sited according to terrain.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: A small bridge crossing the stream is visible, connecting the two banks and forming a clear passage. | Middle and upper parts of the painting: Several stone steps and platforms are built according to the mountain's form, connecting different areas of human activity in layers and presenting a spatial process of gradual penetration into the depths. | Lower part of the painting: A traveling party (riding horses, carrying loads on shoulder poles, carrying sedans) is advancing along the path into the painting, suggesting a route of entry and movement through the landscape.
distinction: Although the built elements are arranged according to the mountain's form, the painting emphasizes more the process of movement through the landscape in which bridges, paths, and steps guide figures into different scenes, rather than mere placement according to terrain.

evidence: Middle-left waterside: a pavilion is built against the rocky sloping bank by the water, with the base closely integrated with the terrain, presenting the feature of terrain-responsive siting. | Lower waterside: two people (one on horseback, one walking) travel along the waterside path, interacting spatially with the water surface and mountains and rocks.
distinction: The pavilion's placement against the water and beside the rocks is the most prominent spatial expression of built structure in the painting; although the route of the figures below implies spatial extension, its direct connection with the built structure is less clear than the relationship of placement according to the ground.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: figures sit on a stone platform in front of a huge rock, with a small table placed on the left, the whole arranged against the huge rock and a bamboo grove base. | Left and middle of the painting: tall bamboo grove and huge rocks form the background and support of the figures and furnishings, presenting a layout relying on rocks and beside bamboo. | Lower part of the painting: the stone platform is adjacent to the waterside, and the furnishings and figures unfold according to the natural forms of the waterside and stone platform.
distinction: Although the bamboo grove and huge rocks provide some screening of the figures, the painting more prominently highlights the terrain-responsive relationship in which the figures and furnishings are placed relying on site conditions such as huge rocks, bamboo grove, and waterside.

evidence: Whole painting: the picture depicts reeds, lotus leaves, waterfowl, and a full moon in the upper left corner; no built elements such as buildings, bridges, or roads are seen.
distinction: No built elements exist in the picture; based on the overall visible organization of landscape, flowers, and birds, it is assigned to the closest category.

evidence: Lower right and lower middle of the painting: multiple groups of houses and courtyards are arranged in a staggered manner according to the mountain slopes and terraces, and the building sites closely conform to the undulations of the mountain body. | Left side and middle ground of the painting: thatched huts and trees are distributed along the hillsides and the edges of the slopes, presenting a layout relationship placed according to the terrain.
distinction: Although trees partially screen the buildings in the painting, the layout feature of built structures spreading in a staggered manner according to terrain slopes and terraces is more prominent and dominates the spatial organization.

evidence: Middle, slightly right: a section of plank walkway or small bridge with railings is visible, with pedestrians on it, connecting the mountain body and forming a clear touring path. | Lower part: figures play a board game on a platform beneath trees, and at the lower right a figure sits beside a railing, implying an activity space that can be stayed in and entered.
distinction: The man-made structures in the painting (plank walkway, railings, platform) mainly serve to guide movement through the landscape and provide activity space, rather than simply displaying a layout of buildings following the mountain.

evidence: Lower right corner: the roof, eaves, and columns of a group of houses are visible, partly screened by foreground pine trees and surrounding woodland, forming a spatial layering of concealment and revelation. | Lower middle of the painting: dense trees and mountains and rocks envelop the built structures; the houses are not fully exposed but rather, through the screening of natural scenery, hint at their existence and location.
distinction: Although the built structures are located beside the waterside, the core of their pictorial composition lies in forming layers through the screening and revealing by trees, rather than emphasizing placement according to terrain height.

evidence: Center of the painting: a figure riding an ox and a figure leading an ox are visible moving along the waterside, presenting a dynamic thread of movement through the landscape. | Lower right corner: a mudflat or waterside edge with vertical lines and ripples is visible; no clear built structures such as buildings, bridges, or fords/ferries are identifiable.
distinction: No clear built elements are identifiable in the painting; it is only tentatively assigned to C4 on the basis of the thread of figures moving along the waterside, with no other obvious competing interpretation.

evidence: Lower left: a thatched hut is surrounded by dense trees, bamboo groves, and mountains and rocks; the roof and the building itself are partly screened by branches and leaves, with only parts exposed, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship of seeing the house within the woods. | Center, slightly left: the branches and leaves of a large foreground tree extend above and in front of the thatched hut, forming natural screening and placing the built structure within a screened spatial layer.
distinction: Although the thatched hut is placed beside mountains, rocks, and trees, the visual focus of the painting lies in the layers formed by the screening and revealing of the building by trees, rather than simply emphasizing that the building conforms to the terrain.

evidence: Right side and lower part: natural scenery such as slope rocks, withered trees, and bamboo clumps is visible; no identifiable traces of built structures are seen. | Left side: calligraphic inscription and seals, which are not evidence of spatial built structures in the painting.
distinction: No clear built structures are seen in the painting; it is assigned to the closest category based on the overall landscape organization, and no specific built-structure relationship can be discerned.

evidence: Lower right corner: the roofs, walls, and fences of multiple houses are visible, partly screened by the dense branches and leaves of surrounding trees, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Right side, lower middle: behind the grove, a taller pavilion-style building is revealed, using the screening of trees to hint at its spatial layer.
distinction: Although the buildings are beside the waterside, the painting mainly organizes the spatial layers of the buildings through the screening and revealing by trees; the feature of concealment and revelation forming a setting is more prominent.

evidence: Lower center: a pavilion (or waterside chamber) is built directly at the water's edge, with its base meeting the water surface, presenting a layout built alongside the water. | Left middle ground: building eaves are faintly visible, placed among the hillside woods, set according to the undulations of the terrain.
distinction: Although there is tree screening, the direct combination of the foreground pavilion with the waterside is more prominent, mainly embodying a terrain-responsive siting relationship placed according to the terrain and waterside.

evidence: Left middle ground: a thatched hut is half-hidden among dense trees and mountains and rocks; its roof and eaves are clearly visible, and there are people inside, presenting a state of being screened by woodland. | Right middle-to-far ground: the roof of another building emerges from dense groves, with most of the building itself screened by trees, forming a deeply hidden layer.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed according to the mountain terrain, the painting more strongly emphasizes the spatial layering of buildings screened by trees, half-hidden and half-revealed, so C2 is more dominant than C1.

evidence: Lower left: a waterside chamber is set on a sloping bank beside the water; beneath the house, rows of pillars are visible supporting it at the water's edge, and the building itself faces the open water surface | Center, slightly lower: a group of multi-roofed houses extends horizontally along the waterside, with rows of short pillars beneath the base set on the bank and mudflat, corresponding to the water level | Center-right: a building likewise has pillar feet set at the water's edge, facing the central house group across the water, together forming a layout distributed along the shore
distinction: All the houses have pillar feet set at the waterside and extend along the shoreline, and the correspondence of building bases to the waterside configuration runs through the whole work; tree screening only leaves individual houses half-hidden and is less comprehensive than waterside placement in organizing the composition

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: a person carrying a tool on the shoulder walks along a mountain path, presenting a dynamic of moving toward the depth of the painting. | Beneath the mountain rock on the right: a person sits cross-legged on the mountain rock, in a secluded environment screened by woodland.
distinction: There are no clear buildings in the painting, but the figures' walking and resting constitute a spatial process that can be traveled through, so it is assigned to C4.

evidence: Left middle to lower middle: multiple houses are arranged along the shoreline, some buildings having platforms or pillars extending toward the water surface, presenting a layout spreading along the shore and dwelling beside the water. | Left side: a small bridge connecting the waterside is visible; the buildings are distributed according to the terrain and water system, corresponding to the natural configuration.
distinction: Although there are bridges and paths in the painting, the placement relationship of the building group spreading along the waterside terrain is more prominent and dominates the spatial expression.

evidence: Center-left of the painted panel: an arched bridge spans a ravine, a figure with a staff walks on the bridge, and the stream below flows out toward the lower part of the painting, forming the starting point of movement into the valley | Center of the painted panel: a stepped plank walkway is visible on the mountain ridge, a figure in red is climbing up along the walkway, and the walkway turns and rises with the mountain terrain | Lower right of the painted panel: a city-wall-type wall extends diagonally along the foot of the mountain, an arched gate opening is set in the wall, a multi-eaved storied building stands on top of the wall, and the sloping-bank open ground in front of the gate opening meets the direction of the ravine
distinction: The bridge, walkway and gate opening constitute a process of movement that can be crossed, climbed and entered, with the storied building connected to the gate as the arrival point; C1 only explains the correspondence of the building site where the wall and building are placed according to the slope, and does not cover the entry clues running through the painting.

evidence: Middle of the right page: a waterfall drops from the edge of a flat slope above and pours into a stream pool below, flanked by pine branches and rock walls, forming the core of the whole scene | Lower part of the right page: beside the water is a stone platform with a straight edge, on which two figures stand, one raising a staff facing the waterfall, the platform edge meeting the water surface | Upper middle of the right page: two figures sit at the flat sloping bank above the waterfall source, the bank line extending diagonally to the waterfall mouth, echoing the stone platform below
distinction: The painting concentrates a scenic spot at the waterfall mouth, the waterside stone platform, and the waterfall-viewing figures, rather than organizing an enterable process of movement through clues such as bridges, paths, and gates

evidence: Middle of the right page: the thatched roof and eaves of a pavilion are revealed from beneath drooping bamboo leaves, with the upper edge of the roof partly screened by bamboo groves | Right side of the right page: multiple bamboo stems interpenetrate in front of and beside the pavilion; the pavilion's railing and the figure seated upright within are visible through the gaps between the bamboo stems, forming a layer of seeing the pavilion within the grove | Lower right of the right page: beneath the pavilion, several pillars support it on the sloping rocks of the stream bank; the sloping rocks and clustered rocks extend leftward to the open water surface
distinction: Although the pavilion is set on the sloping bank by the water, the right half of the composition is dominated by the concealment-and-revelation layering in which bamboo groves cover the roof and the pavilion body is revealed through the bamboo stems; the terrain only supports the base and does not form a layout correspondence unfolding with the situation.

evidence: Center of the painted panel, slightly left, on a sloping terrace: several houses sit side by side on a level terrace at the foot of the mountain, their foundations extending along the edge of the sloping terrace, backed by tall trees and bamboo clumps | Lower center of the painted panel: another group of houses is located on a lower level of sloping ground, forming a two-level terrace arrangement with the upper group of buildings, with large trees and a rocky slope in front defining the slope surface | Right bank of the painted panel: houses and a plank bridge are distributed along the waterside, the houses extending along the shoreline, and a rocky slope at the water's edge separating the water surface from the building foundations
distinction: Although the houses are partly screened by trees, their building sites and high-low levels are clearly arranged according to the sloping terraces and the waterside, and concealment and revelation are not the main means of organizing the composition.

evidence: Center of the right page: a farmer supports a plow while an ox pulls a harrow, cultivating in a paddy field; the fields are enclosed by winding field ridges, and no buildings such as houses, pavilions, bridges, or gates are seen | Upper middle to lower left of the right page: the field ridges turn and stack according to the slope, enclosing several levels of fields descending in height, and the way the man-made field banks unfold corresponds to the slope form | Upper right and lower left: trees and pale-ink slope rocks enclose the fields from both sides; the field surface is open, with no concealment-and-revelation layering or clues of entry through movement
distinction: Although the field ridges connect in layers, no figures move along them and there are no arrival clues such as bridges, gates, or paths, so they do not constitute a process of entering; the visible organization is mainly the correspondence of field plots placed in layers according to the slope, so it is assigned to C1

evidence: Upper left: a house is built on a rocky platform projecting from a cliff, presenting the form of a house set on a platform. | Lower left: a pavilion is placed at the waterside, its base meeting the waterside terrain. | Overall: the built structures are distributed at high and low positions, attached respectively to the high cliff and the waterside, and the layout conforms to the natural terrain.
distinction: The buildings in the painting are clearly attached to the cliff platform and the waterside terrain, and the terrain-placement relationship is more dominant in the overall spatial layout than local tree screening.

evidence: Lower right: a fenced house courtyard is built beside the waterside; to its left front, a pillared plank bridge spans the water surface, one end reaching the courtyard bank and the other connecting to the path on the left bank | Upper part: two groups of houses are arranged on a terrace at the top of the slope; a pale-ink path is left on the slope surface, and several farmers carrying tools walk on it, the path leading toward the houses at the top of the slope | Lower left: on the shoreline path, an adult stands with a child and a bearer of carrying poles walks forward, extending along the shore to the right toward the bridge and courtyard
distinction: The bridge, paths, and figure movement lines directly connect with the house courtyard and present a process that can be reached and further traveled through, which explains the main compositional role better than houses merely placed along the sloping bank.

evidence: Middle, slightly left: the roofs and eaves of a pavilion and houses are revealed through the gaps of slanting pine branches and needles, with the lower part of the building body screened by pine trees and groves | Middle, slightly right: several roof ridges float above mist and groves, with only roof outlines visible; walls and bases are not visible | Lower center: a staff-bearing figure and a boy stand before the sloping bank, and between them and the buildings above no discernible connecting clues such as paths, bridges, or gates are seen
distinction: Although the buildings are located on the mountainside, the painting organizes spatial layers through the concealment-and-revelation relationship in which pine branches and groves screen the building body and only roofs and eaves are exposed, which runs through the composition more than the correspondence of bases to terrain

evidence: Center, slightly right, of the painting: a person sits upright on a projecting flat rock platform, backed by a large tree, becoming the visual focus. | Lower right corner of the painting: two people stand beside a rock, seemingly attending or conversing, forming a spatial echo with the figure above. | Left side of the painting: towering fantastic peaks and mountain rocks contrast with the rock platform on which the central figure sits, setting off the openness of the platform.
distinction: No clear buildings are seen in the painting; the figures' activity mainly serves to point out this mountain-rock platform as a scenic spot for rest and viewing, rather than emphasizing a spatial process of entering buildings through paths.

evidence: Lower center of the right half: an arched bridge spans a stream gap; on the bridge a person walks with a staff, and the path at the bridge end points toward the wall gate at the upper right | Middle right of the right half: a gatehouse with an arched doorway connects to a courtyard wall; the doorway is open, and beyond it up the slope are layered houses and a double-eaved pavilion | Upper left of the right half: on a cliff platform above a band of clouds stands an open pavilion, forming with the gate courtyard below a spatial sequence from low to high
distinction: The painting organizes space through the walker on the bridge and the connection between the bridge and the doorway, emphasizing the process of entering through this gate and turning into the depths, rather than merely the correspondence of buildings placed according to the height of sloping terraces.

evidence: Upper left of the painted panel: two thatched roofs emerge from behind a diagonal sloping bank and pale-ink mist, the building itself cut off by the slope and mist, with only the roofs and eaves visible, indicating that the built structure lies in a layer behind the slope | Center-right to lower right of the painted panel: two figures wearing hats ride donkeys downslope to the left along the bank, and between them and the roof at the upper left lies a large expanse of blank cloud and mist, with no visible path connecting the two | Bottom edge of the painted panel: a row of column-like or masonry-like structures runs horizontally along the bottom (resembling a bridge or embankment), meeting the bank that the travelers traverse, but it is not shown extending toward where the houses are located
distinction: Although the travelers and the bottom bridge-stones carry a sense of movement through the landscape, no entry clue connecting them with the houses is seen; the houses are mainly presented through the layering of concealment and revelation in which the slope and mist cut them off and the roofs are half-exposed, so concealment and revelation forming a scene is closer to the visible relationships.

evidence: Lower left to middle left: an open-hall-style pavilion sits on the top surface of a rock projecting into the water; there are no walls between the columns but railings are set, and several people lean on the railing inside, facing the water surface to the right. | Right half and center: a large expanse of surging water unfolds; at the upper right a boat carrying people travels amid the waves, echoing the orientation of the figures in the pavilion, and the scene of the open waterside face is concentrated at the pavilion. | Beneath the pavilion base and at the lower right: waves beat against the rock on which the pavilion base sits and against the reef at the lower right; among the reefs several mast-like thin branches are exposed, indicating that the pavilion is at an open waterside node.
distinction: Although the pavilion base is set on the rock top, the painting has the figures in the pavilion leaning on the railing and gazing at the boat in the waves, with the open face toward the great water, giving the open waterside scene a concentrated anchor; the organizing role of scenic accentuation runs through the relationship between pavilion and water and is more dominant than mere terrain correspondence.

evidence: Left side: the pavilion building is partly screened by the branches and trunks of pine and withered trees, with only the roof, window lattices, and part of the walls exposed, forming a concealment-and-revelation layer. | Water surface on the right: a boat floats on the water, forming a spatial echo with the screened building on the left. | Lower right corner: a person stands on the bank facing the water surface and the direction of the building, strengthening the layer of pictorial depth.
distinction: Although the building is set by the mountain bank, the painting more strongly emphasizes the screening and revealing of the building by trees, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship dominates the composition.

evidence: Lower left: a pavilion (waterside arbor) is set directly over the water surface on wooden pillars, adjacent to the sloping bank and tree roots on the left, with its base and layout fully conforming to the terrain conditions of the waterside. | Center-right: on the distant water surface a flat bridge connects the two banks, likewise placed according to the direction of the waterside.
distinction: Although there are trees beside the building, its most core compositional role is to be set over the water surface relying on the waterside terrain, rather than mainly relying on the screening and revealing by trees to form layers.

evidence: Lower left and central waterside: a small boat is visible on the water, and on the bank a bridge connects the two shores, forming clear movement clues between water and land. | Lower middle and right side of the painting: the building group is distributed along the waterside and the mountain foot, connected to the water surface and external space through paths and bridges, presenting an enterable relationship of being reachable. | Mountainside on the right: some buildings are hidden behind woodland and mountain rocks, with screening increasing the depth of space and the layers of entry.
distinction: Although there is a screening relationship, the coherent entry clues formed by bridges, boats, and paths in the painting are more prominent and dominate the overall sense of spatial movement through the landscape.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: a two-story pavilion sits on a gently sloping waterside bank; it is large in scale with clear details and is the visual center of the painting. | Overall painting: the pavilion lies in a transitional zone between the open foreground face and the towering mountains in the background, identifying the landscape scenery here and becoming the core marker that identifies and concentrates the painting.
distinction: Although the building is built by the waterside, the terrain is gentle, and its role as a visual focus and scenic marker (C3) far exceeds the feature of being placed according to terrain undulation (C1).

evidence: Left side: a pavilion beside the waterfall is half-hidden behind trees and rocks, with its roof and eave pillars exposed | Mountainside on the right: several houses are screened among the woods in a mountain hollow, with only parts of the roofs exposed | Lower right corner: a fence and figures are surrounded by mountain rocks and woodland
distinction: Although the built structures are placed according to the terrain, the painting more strongly emphasizes the concealment-and-revelation layers formed by their screening and revealing by mountain rocks and woodland

evidence: Right side of the painting, among the trees: beneath the screening trees a stone table (or desk) is revealed; no clear house or building is visible. | Center and left of the painting: pine trees and miscellaneous trees surround a sloping ground; the figures and objects are situated amid the screening and revealing of the trees, forming layers.
distinction: No clear building is visible, but the objects and figures form a half-hidden, half-revealed layering through the trees, coming closest to concealment and revelation forming a setting.

evidence: Whole painting: the picture shows distant mountains, water surface, sloping banks, willow trees and horses; no houses, pavilions, bridges or other built elements are visible.
distinction: There are no built elements in the painting, so it cannot strictly correspond to any of the category definitions; based on the overall sense of scenic accentuation it is assigned to C3.

evidence: Lower middle: a figure can be seen walking along a railed path beside the water, the path extending into the depth of the painting and connecting the foreground with the middle ground. | Lower left and lower middle: a waterside building complex is sited at the water's edge, with supporting timber piles visible at its base; the path connects with the building complex, forming an accessible starting point of space. | Middle: on the mountainside buildings are screened among trees and rocks, and the direction in which the path extends points toward this spot, presenting a thread of movement turning into the depths.
distinction: Although the buildings sited by water and mountain embody terrain-responsive siting, the clearly depicted path, railings and walking figure more strongly organize the spatial process of moving from one point to another and penetrating into the painting.

evidence: Lower left corner: a traveling figure on horseback and on foot can be seen advancing along the waterside, suggesting the starting point of the route. | Lower left to middle left: a flat bridge spans the water surface, connecting the shoreline where the travelers are with the opposite bank, providing a clear clue to crossing and entry. | Lower right and middle right: at the foot of the mountain a timber plank road/bridge extends along the lie of the mountain, and in the middle right a courtyard house is visible, forming a built space that can be reached.
distinction: Although the courtyard on the right is partly screened by trees, the continuous entry route formed by the bridge, plank road and traveling figures is more prominent and dominates the spatial organization.

evidence: Central summit: a stone-built high platform is built on the mountain ridge summit, its platform wall dropping from the ridge among clustered trees, the platform top enclosed by a balustrade and overhanging the open water surface to the right | On the platform: two figures stand by the platform railing facing the vast empty water and low distant mountains to the right; the platform gives the open, water-facing aspect of the summit a point of rest and focus | Lower left: between cliff crevices there are stone steps and a walking figure ascending, the path disappearing upward behind a huge rock, with no visible connecting segment between it and the summit platform
distinction: Although the platform base is sited following the lie of the cliff, the composition uses the platform and the figures leaning on the railing to mark and focus the open, water-facing scenery of the summit; the siting correspondence itself does not dominate the picture's organization

evidence: Waterside, lower middle-left of the painting: an open pavilion (roof and columns discernible) sits at the end of a flat-sloped stone terrace extending toward the water, the pavilion base pressed against the terrace edge and facing the open water to the left | Sloping rocks from center to lower right: the sloping rocks descend gradually from the right-side mountain rock to the water's edge to form a terrace, the pavilion following this slope and ending at the shore, its base height corresponding to the terrace surface | Around and above the pavilion: bamboo behind the pavilion and a withered tree on the right surround it, but the pavilion roof and columns are largely fully exposed; screening does not constitute a major spatial layer
distinction: The pavilion's base sits directly on the waterside sloping terrace and follows the slope to end at the shore; the relation of terrain participating in siting is more concretely visible than mere scenic marking

evidence: Lower left foreground: the walls and roofs of several orange-roofed houses are partly blocked by the trunks and crowns of the front row of trees, the house bodies revealed through gaps in the trees | Central middle-ground tree belt: many orange and grey roofs are revealed above the tops of dense tree crowns, only roofs and parts of white walls visible, the house bodies hidden within the trees | Middle-ground left shoreline: an obliquely placed plank bridge crosses the water, but no discernible path connects it with the houses among the trees
distinction: The houses are presented mainly through the screening by rows of trees and the revealing of roofs, forming a layering of concealment and revelation; the terrain is flat, the correspondence with the shoreline weak, and the bridge forms no accessible connection with the built structures

evidence: Center of the painting: the gnarled trunk of a withered tree and its interlacing branches can be seen, forming a front-to-back layering with the sloping rocks and distant mountains behind. | Lower part of the painting: sloping rocks and bamboo are screened and revealed, constituting a foreground spatial relation of blocking and exposure.
distinction: No clear man-made built elements are visible in the painting; based only on the front-to-back screening and spatial layering of natural scenery (trees and rocks), it is assigned to the closest category, C2.

evidence: Lower middle, where the water surface meets the right bank: an open pavilion is set on a platform extending from the foot of the rock, the platform's left end reaching into the water, the pavilion body backed against mountain rock, its base sited following the lie of the shore and rock foot | Above the right rock edge: a stretch of railing turns and ascends along the rock face, its course following the undulations and turns of the rock surface, corresponding to the mountain form | Above and to the right of the pavilion: willow branches and withered trunks hang down from the rock top to cover the pavilion roof, the pavilion eaves lower than the tree roots at the rock foot, the built height corresponding to the sloping terrace
distinction: Although the railing on the rock shows a thread of movement, it is cut off from the pavilion by the rock mass with no discernible entry connection; the correspondence of the pavilion platform's base to the shore-hugging, rock-backed setting runs more directly through the painting

evidence: Middle right: a thatched hut is raised on a platform supported by a row of posts, the platform at the water's edge extending from the rock foot, the hut backed against the cliff face and the waterfall pouring down, facing the open water to the left, its base height following the lie of the bank slope | Right side: the right end of the house is pressed under the foot of a huge foreground rock slope, the house body embedded between rock crevices, but the roof, eaves, railing and supporting posts are all clearly discernible | Left half and foreground: on the left are a broad flat water surface, distant mountains and grassy sandbars, the bank slope where the house stands extending into the water, broken stones and grass at the slope foot, with no bridge, path or other movement clue connecting to the house
distinction: The house is raised on a post platform at the waterside rock foot, backed by cliff and facing water; the correspondence of base to terrain and shoreline is concretely visible; the right rock screening the house is only marginal blocking, and concealment and revelation is not the main line organizing the composition

evidence: Lower left to center: the roots and trunk of an old pine grow from among the sloping rocks at lower left, occupying the sloping terrace and extending diagonally across toward the center following the slope, the pine's base and the sloping rock forms supporting each other. | Lower part: broken stones on the bank and a pale shoreline extend along the lower edge, with an isolated rock standing at the shore in the lower right; no bridge, path, gate, ferry crossing or other movement clue is visible. | Background: pale-ink cliff faces recede at upper left and on the right, forming a front-to-back layering with the foreground pine and rocks; no trace of roofs, eaves, walls or other built elements is visible throughout.
distinction: The dominant organization of the painting is the sloping terrace supporting and guiding the placement and unfolding of the pine and rocks, whereas the object of concealment and revelation required by C2 is built structures; no houses are revealed at all in the painting, so a screening relation does not hold.

evidence: Central slightly left, cliff top: a thatched-roof open pavilion stands at the end of a tongue-shaped flat rock platform jutting over the river, the platform edge being a sheer cliff, the pavilion base set facing the water following the shape of the terrace | Upper right summit: a red-walled storied pavilion and attached buildings are built on the summit slope terrace, pine woods encircling the slope, with steps and walls following the slope visible among the trees, the built heights unfolding with the lie of the peak | Lower left river surface and shore: sails and sandbar masts gather in the water below the cliff platform, the cliff-top pavilion forming a high-low correspondence with the riverbank water, the shoreline participating in the siting of built structures
distinction: The bases and heights of the pavilion and storied building are directly determined by the cliff-top platform and the summit slope; the siting correspondence runs through the whole painting; the role of marking the scenery is more localized, and the storied building is screened among the trees with weak identifying effect.

evidence: Middle right: a railed arch bridge spans the waterfall ravine, with a rider and walking attendants crossing the bridge | Lower right to below the bridge: a railed zigzag path winds upward among the sloping rocks, joining the bridge end, forming a continuous walkable route | At the cliff on the right end of the bridge: the other end of the bridge disappears into the cliff face and behind the side of the waterfall, the route vanishing here and showing a tendency to turn into the depths
distinction: Although the bridge and plank road are arranged following the cliff and shore, the picture's focus is the continuous process of entry—path, bridge, travelers, disappearing behind the cliff—rather than the correspondence of base layout to terrain

evidence: Lower left: an arched doorway is opened at the foot of an earthen slope, within the opening door leaves and plank partitions are visible, the door facing the open ground on the right bank of the stream, forming an entrance into the realm above the slope | Lower middle: a staff-bearing figure stands on a small path among the rocks at the stream bank, facing the doorway and houses to the left, the pale ground at the shore winding left to connect with the slope foot | Middle left and left edge: among the trees on the terrace above the doorway the roof, eaves and columns and railings of houses are revealed, and at the left edge another house body is half hidden behind trees
distinction: Although the houses are half revealed among the trees, the picture forms a sequence of approach to the built structures through the bank path, the staff-bearing figure and the slope gate; the connection of gate and path runs through the composition more than the layering of concealment and revelation

evidence: Middle right: a fenced courtyard is provided with an open brushwood gate, within which women and children can be seen leaning out and the courtyard space, a wooden pole leaning obliquely beside the gate, the spaces inside and outside the gate connected | Open ground outside the gate, middle right: an old man leaning on a staff stands on the level open ground outside the brushwood gate facing the paddy fields, forming with the figures inside the gate a positional relation of arrival outside the gate and welcoming within | Lower middle to lower left: beneath the feet of the laborers in the paddy fields a plank crosses the water, the field ridges and bank slopes linking the waterside labor area and the open ground before the gate into a continuous passable transitional ground
distinction: Although the houses are partly crossed and blocked by tree trunks, the fence, brushwood gate and roof as a whole are clear, and concealment and revelation is not dominant; the picture organizes a sequence of arrival from the waterside and entry into the courtyard through the open brushwood gate, the staff-bearing figure outside the gate and the connected open ground, so C4 is taken

evidence: Central slightly lower: a timber bridge spans a stream valley, its posts set in the valley, the two ends of the bridge deck joining the left and right banks respectively, linking the passable shorelines of the two banks | Middle-ground left bank: a line of figures is arranged along the sloping bank toward the bridgehead, the shoreline extending from the blue-green sloping rocks at lower left to the left end of the bridge, suggesting the passage relation from bank to bridge | Foreground to middle ground: the foreground paddy fields and the middle-ground stream bank are linked by an oblique field-ridge shoreline, the bank and large trees behind the bridge extending toward the upper part of the painting, forming a spatial layering of turning into the depths after crossing the stream valley
distinction: C4 fits the process, formed jointly by the bridge, shoreline and field ridges, of crossing the stream to arrive and turning into the depths; C1 requires built bases sited following the terrain, but the painting has no house-type built structures on which to base this.

evidence: Lower right to lower middle bank: a pole-carrier, an accompanying boy and a basket-carrier stand at the water's edge, the basket-carrier raising a hand and pointing into the distance, the figures in a posture of advancing and pointing, the shoreline extending from right to left | Lower left waterside: a frame-like structure of horizontal beams on upright posts with blue-green clumps on top, possibly a trellis or a ferry-side facility, but the structural details are unclear and it cannot be confirmed as a house | Between the middle-left field slope and the foreground shore: an open water surface and a bend in the shoreline separate two layers of sloping bank, front and back, with another stooping laborer in the fields, the space showing a layering of depth from foreground into middle ground
distinction: What dominates the painting is the process of travel and penetration suggested by the figures advancing along the shore and pointing, rather than the correspondence of built bases to terrain and shoreline; the suspected frame-like object also shows no arrangement relation of resting on a terrace and following a slope

evidence: Middle to lower left: a stone retaining wall unfolds in a turn along the slope foot, enclosing a level terrace, the wall base height varying with the slope, with figures working on the terrace surface | Middle right: a white-walled house is backed against an earthen slope and set at the edge of the terrace, its roof descending with the slope, its walls and straight-bar windows clearly visible | Right side: the crown of a large tree covers in front of the house roof and walls, the house revealed through gaps in the tree, the covering limited to the local area before the house
distinction: The overall layout of the stone terrace walls and houses turns with the sloping ground and encloses the terrace, the relation of terrain participating in siting running through the middle of the painting; this is more dominant than the local relation of tree crowns screening the house

evidence: Central slightly right of the painting: a thatched roof and part of a timber structure can be seen, partly screened by the thick pine branches and needles above and to the left. | Right and center of the painting: the thatched hut is adjacent to mountain rocks and a sloping bank; the rocks and pines together constitute the surrounding and screening of the built structure, forming a spatial layering of alternating concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the built structure is erected against the mountain rocks, the picture emphasizes more the relation of the pine branches and rocks screening and revealing the thatched hut, and the role of concealment and revelation forming a setting is more prominent.

evidence: Whole painting: only mountain rocks, willow trees, water birds, egrets and two figures are visible; no houses, bridges, roads or any other built elements appear. | Lower right: a figure lies on a rock or prostrate on the ground, which belongs to human activity, not architectural building.
distinction: Built elements are entirely lacking in the painting; it is assigned to the closest category on the basis of the overall spatial organization of natural landscape and figures as scenic accents.

evidence: Right side: an arch bridge can be seen spanning across, connecting the right bank with the central area of trees and houses, forming a clue to land passage. | Lower left: a small boat on the water suggests water transport and ferry crossing, echoing the shore space. | Lower middle: pavilions are built at the waterside, houses faintly appearing behind the woods, linked by the shoreline, bridges and boats, presenting a spatial sequence that can be toured and dwelt in.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited against mountains and beside water (C1), the transport elements such as the bridge and boat in the painting clearly construct a movement path and entry relation, so C4 is more dominant.

evidence: Lower middle slightly right of the painting: a red bridge spans the water surface, connecting the wooded area on the right with the bank on the left where the built structures are, with pedestrians on the bridge, constituting a clear entry path. | Middle left of the painting: a group of houses is arranged along the shoreline, surrounded by dense trees, roofs and walls partly revealed, the left end of the bridge pointing toward this area. | Lower right corner of the painting: a fence and a small hut can be seen, with a figure standing within, facing into the painting, helping to suggest the direction of travel and approach to the built structures.
distinction: Although there are trees screening the built structures (C2), the red bridge and figures constitute a clear physical movement clue, giving the painting a spatial process of entering the built structures from this bank, so C4 better explains its role in spatial organization.

evidence: Lower right side: a pavilion is built at the waterside, and to the right of the pavilion a small bridge connects to the land on the bank. | Lower right corner: a figure is on the bank, whose posture and position suggest the path leading to the waterside pavilion. | Whole painting: the bridge, shoreline and figures together constitute a spatial movement clue by which the built structures can be entered and reached.
distinction: Although the pavilion has a scenic-accentuating role, the painting clearly depicts the clues of the bridge and the figures' movement, emphasizing more the enterable spatial process, so C4 is more apt.

evidence: Lower right: a small red bridge spans the water connecting the two banks, with a mounted figure and attendants advancing along a path beside the bridge. | Lower left to middle left: the path winds along the shore toward the buildings among the trees on the left. | Middle left: parts of a pavilion or house are revealed among the trees, connecting with the shore path.
distinction: Although the buildings are screened by trees, the movement clues formed by the bridge and path lead the figures toward the buildings, emphasizing more the spatial process of entering from here to there.

evidence: Lower right: a clear winding path extends upward along the lie of the mountain, passing through the trees, forming a clear clue to entry and travel. | Central slightly upper: a pavilion is built on a protruding rock, becoming the visual goal in the direction the path extends. | Lower left: houses are screened among the pine woods, together with the mountain path forming a reachable built setting.
distinction: Although there is a relation of trees screening the houses, the winding mountain path at the lower right runs through the spatial process of entering the painting, and its organizing role in the composition is more coherent and dominant.

evidence: Right side of the painting: a stream, sloping bank, pine trees and two figures seated facing each other can be seen; no houses, pavilions, bridges or other built elements are visible. | Center of the right side of the painting: the pine trees and figures are on the sloping ground by the stream, marking the stream-and-mountain scenery here and forming a visual focus.
distinction: There are no clear built elements in the painting; only natural scenery and figure activity mark the streamside scenery, so it is assigned to C3.

evidence: High on the cliff, upper middle: the roof and veranda columns of a building can be seen, located above the source of the waterfall and partly screened by the surrounding trees and rocks. | Around the building: the building is hidden behind trees and rocks, presenting an evident relation of concealment and revelation and forming spatial layers.
distinction: Although the building is located high up, its relation of concealment and revelation through the screening of trees and rocks is visually more prominent, so C2 is more apt than C1.

evidence: Right mountainside: a building is screened among pine trees and rocks, only part of its roof and structure revealed, forming layers of concealment and revelation. | Lower right near the shore: a building stands at the waterside, with a bridge and small boat beside it, adjacent to the surrounding trees and rocks.
distinction: The mountainside building forms scenery mainly through being screened and revealed by trees and rocks; although there is a bridge below, the whole emphasizes more the layered relation of screening rather than a clear travel path.

evidence: Right side of the painting: the picture shows mountain rocks, trees, a stream and a waterfall; no clear houses, bridges or other built objects are visible. | Lower right: two figures can be seen standing at the waterside, present as scenic-accent figures.
distinction: There are no clear built elements in the painting; on the basis of the overall relation of landscape and figures as scenic accents, it is assigned only with difficulty to C3.

evidence: Lower right corner: amid the screening of trees and sloping rocks the roof and railing of a building are revealed, presenting a spatial layering of half concealment and half revelation. | Middle ground of the painting: the foreground trees and the rocks on the right form a blocking relation, directing the gaze toward the built structure hidden in the depths.
distinction: Although the building is sited against the sloping bank, the picture emphasizes more its relation of concealment and revelation through screening by trees and rocks, rather than mere placement according to the ground.

evidence: Lower right: several house roofs and structures are faintly visible between the trees and the sloping bank, partly screened by the surrounding trees. | Right side at the mountain foot: the built structures are screened behind mountains and rocks and thickets, presenting spatial layering of concealment and revelation alternating.
distinction: Although the built structures are located at the mountain foot, their concealment and revelation through screening by trees and mountain rocks is more prominent than their siting simply according to the terrain.

evidence: In the pine grove at the center-right of the painting: the roof and wall of a building emerge from the dense pine grove, forming a clear concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Lower center of the painting: a stone-built structure (or bridge-gate) with an arched doorway is visible, connected with the surrounding mountains, rocks, and path.
distinction: Although a bridge-gate and path below suggest entry, the most prominent presentation of built elements in the painting is the building deeply hidden within the pine grove, forming spatial layering through screening and revelation by the woodland; thus C2 is more dominant.

evidence: Right page, slightly right of the middle ground: the roofs and light-colored walls of several houses emerge from behind a stand of flowering trees, with the lower parts of the buildings screened by the tree crowns | Right page, lower-left sloping bank: a small house roof is faintly visible among the flowering trees on the green slope, with the trees screening most of the building itself | Right page, middle horizontal band: unpainted space and lightly tinted cloud mist run across the painting, dividing the distant mountains from the middle-ground woodland and houses into foreground and background layers, with the woodland and houses situated between the near slope and the distant mountains
distinction: The houses are presented primarily through roofs revealed from among the flowering trees while the building itself is screened by the thickets, forming a concealment-and-revelation layering, rather than being dominated by a relationship of siting according to slope and bank configuration with base elevation.

evidence: Right-hand painted panel: the painting depicts continuous blue-green mountain peaks and wreathing cloud and mist; no traces of built structures such as buildings, bridges or paths are seen. | Left-hand painted panel: the left side is calligraphic inscription, which does not count as evidence of spatial built structures in the painting.
distinction: No built elements are seen at all in the painting, and the specific way in which they participate in the landscape composition cannot be clearly determined; it is assigned only tentatively on the basis of the overall pure landscape composition.

evidence: Left side of the painting: the house is partly screened by foreground trees and bamboo, with only the roof, eaves, and part of the wall revealed, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Right side of the painting: the house is situated behind a bamboo grove and trees, surrounded by a fence, presenting spatial layering in which the house is seen through a screen. | Overall painting: the built elements use the screening and revelation of trees and bamboo thickets to hide the architecture within the natural scenery, creating a visual effect of concealment and revelation forming a setting.
distinction: The painting primarily emphasizes the layering of concealment and revelation formed by the architecture screened by trees, rather than highlighting a correspondence in which the architecture is sited according to the terrain and banks.

evidence: Right page, lower register, lower left: a small pavilion with a pyramidal roof stands at the water's edge, red railings enclosing its base, with a figure inside leaning on the railing and facing the open water surface to the right | Right page, from center to right: a large expanse of unpainted space representing water runs across the painting, with a willow thicket and bank in the middle ground and blue-green distant mountains above lying flat and open, forming an expansive level-and-distant waterscape, which the pavilion directly faces | Left of the pavilion and below it: sloping rocks and a large tree are arrayed to the left of the pavilion, whose base sits on the bank slope at the water's edge, the pavilion body and roof fully revealed with no significant screening
distinction: Although the pavilion sits at the bank edge, the terrain undulation is weak and the siting relationship is local; its waterside position and the figures within the railing give the expansive waterscape a point of vantage, and its role as a scenic accent runs more through the composition.

evidence: Left side of the painting, middle ground: a house is partly screened by the surrounding trees and shrubs, with only the roof, eaves, and part of the wall revealed, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Center and right of the painting: tall pines and other vegetation surround the architecture, reinforcing the spatial layering of the building hidden within the grove.
distinction: The painting primarily presents the layering of concealment and revelation of the architecture screened by woodland; although a fence and flower beds suggest a courtyard, the guiding role of an entry path is less prominent than the concealment-and-revelation relationship.

evidence: Center of the right half of the painted panel: among the blue-green mountain ridges, unpainted space represents a ravine, winding down from between the ridge and the mountain rocks, and the valley passage pierces the gap deep into the mountains | Lower part of the right half of the painted panel: the streams converge in the open, pale-colored water surface of the foreground, and the shoreline and sandbars are low and flat, forming an opening through which one can go up the valley from the water surface | Entire right half of the painted panel: only mountain rocks, moss-dot tree clumps and flowing water are seen; no traces of built structures such as houses, pavilions, bridges or gates are seen
distinction: What runs through the composition is the process of going upstream and penetrating deeper, guided by the ravine passage, rather than a correspondence of built structures placed according to sloping terraces and watersides (in the latter, no built structures at all are visible).

evidence: Lower center: in a valley embraced by mountains, the roofs and walls of several tiny buildings are visible, partly screened by the mountain forms. | Lower right corner: at the mountain foot by the water's edge, part of a building is revealed, forming front-and-back layering with the surrounding mountains and rocks.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited according to the mountain forms, the painting more prominently highlights their concealment and revelation, half-hidden and half-revealed by the mountain forms, rather than simply being arranged according to the terrain.

evidence: Below the pine grove on the right: on the sloping bank a tiny human figure or extremely blurry trace is visible, but there are no clearly discernible buildings, roofs, or wall structures. | Overall painting: the left side is water surface and scattered sloping rocks, the right side is pines and sloping bank, and no clear spatial organizing relationship between built elements and natural scenery is seen.
distinction: The painting lacks clear evidence of built elements; the pines and sloping bank on the right form a relatively independent natural scene, so it is assigned to C3 as the closest category.

evidence: Lower center, slightly right: the roof and wall of a building are revealed through gaps in the thicket, the building partly screened by woodland, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Middle ground of the painting: trees in the foreground and middle ground surround the building, placing it within a layer of woodland screening and increasing the spatial depth.
distinction: The building participates in the construction of spatial layering mainly through screening and revelation by the trees, rather than serving as a core marker that identifies a particular landscape scene.

evidence: Left side: the roofs and eave corners of pavilions and other buildings emerge from the dense thickets, forming a clear concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Left side: the buildings are surrounded and screened by mountains, rocks, and trees, presenting spatial layering of woodland screening.
distinction: Although the buildings identify the scene on the left, they participate in the composition mainly through the concealment-and-revelation relationship of being screened by trees and mountains and rocks, rather than simply serving as striking landmarks.

evidence: Lower right at the bank edge: a group of thatch-roofed houses stands on rows of wooden posts at the foot of the slope at the water's edge, the building itself close against the foot of the rock spur, spreading laterally along the shoreline | Right side, main mountain: huge rocks and dense woodland drape down from above the houses, their bases placed exactly at the water's edge at the end of the rocky slope-terrace, rising and falling with the foot of the slope | Middle ground, far bank: among the tree shadows of the far bank, low houses are arranged in a line along the water's edge, consistent with the direction in which the level, distant shoreline unfolds
distinction: The outlines of the houses and the post-supported bases are fully revealed at the foot of the slope at the water's edge, and the relationship of terrain support and waterside unfolding runs more through the composition than the concealment-and-revelation relationship of being half-screened by tree shade.

evidence: Lower center of the painting: at the water's edge near the roots of two large pines, a tiny figure sits on an object resembling a small boat or simple platform, immediately adjacent to the water's edge. | Overall painting: the painting is dominated by natural landscape, including the near foreground sloping bank and pines, the middle-ground water surface, and the distant opposite-bank woodland and mountains, with no clear buildings, pavilions, or bridges visible.
distinction: The painting lacks clear buildings; only a tiny structure (or boat) at the water's edge is sited in conformity with the bank, barely fitting terrain-responsive siting, with no other obvious compositional relationship.

evidence: Behind the woodland on the right: through the tree branches and trunks, part of a roof structure is visible, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship screened by woodland. | Center-left water surface of the painting: a person rides in a small boat, serving as a scenic accent element on the water surface.
distinction: The building forms layering mainly through screening by trees, rather than serving as a striking visual focus that identifies the scene.

evidence: Lower left corner: a small boat is moored at the bank, with a person seated in it, immediately adjacent to the water surface and bank rocks. | Center and right of the painting: the open water surface extends to the distant mountains and woodland, forming a transparent, unobstructed space.
distinction: The small boat, moored at the bank as a means of movement through the landscape, suggests the thread and process of waterborne movement through the landscape, which fits the intention of access to secluded settings better than simply identifying the scene.

evidence: Lower center of the painting: a rectangular flat-slab bridge spans the mouth of the stream, its two ends meeting the foot of the slopes on the left and right, with a figure standing on the bridge facing upstream toward the stream valley. | Middle ground, slightly right, green mossy slope-terrace: two figures sit on the slope-terrace facing the central waterfall; the right side of the terrace meets the pine grove and grassland, forming a place to linger by the stream. | Center to upper part: the waterfall cascades down level by level through gaps in the mountains and rocks into the stream, and the stream extends toward the bridge at the lower part of the painting, with the slope gaps on both banks forming a depth passage from below upstream.
distinction: The painting provides an accessible process of crossing the stream from the foreground and going upstream to view the waterfall through the bridge crossing and the figures' movements and pauses, rather than concentrating or marking the waterfall scene through some single structure.

evidence: Lower right: a group of waterside buildings is built against a steep cliff and sloping bank, some of the buildings supported by wooden posts reaching directly into the water, their layout conforming to the turns of the shoreline and the rise and fall of the terrain. | Lower right to center: in front of the buildings, a stone-step path meets the water surface, connecting the sloping bank with the building bases, reflecting a direct correspondence between the buildings and the waterside site.
distinction: Although a stone-step path below suggests a process of entry, the most striking spatial organization of the buildings overall is the direct conformity of their bases, elevation, and manner of unfolding to the shoreline and cliff terrain; thus C1 is more dominant than C4.

evidence: Lower part to middle ground of the painting: a winding path (or stream bank line) extends from the foreground into the depths of the middle-ground woodland, forming a clear visual guiding thread. | Center-right of the painting: through the screening woodland, the roof and fence of a building are visible, and the path's direction points toward this built area, presenting a spatial process of entering from here to there. | Overall painting: the path threads among the mountains, rocks, and trees, linking the built elements of the foreground and middle ground, creating a sense of deep, expansive space that can be entered and traveled through.
distinction: Although the buildings are screened by trees (C2), the spatial process in which the winding path guides the eye deep into the grove and approaches the built elements (C4) is more prominent, constituting the dominant mode of spatial organization.

evidence: Center of the painted panel, slightly left: an open thatched hall is built on level ground at the top of a waterside slope, with railings and an elevated platform in front of the house supported by posts on the waterside slope, its building site and manner of unfolding determined by the configuration of the sloping terrace and the waterside | Center of the painted panel, slightly right: behind red-leaf trees and sloping rocks another house is placed on low ground behind the slope, forming a corresponding relationship with the main house in which they are set at different heights according to the slope | Center of the painted panel, slightly lower left: among the sloping rocks a small plank bridge crosses a ravine and connects the bank slopes; the bridge is short, and no continuous discernible route is seen between the staff-carrying traveler on the bank below and the bridge
distinction: The building sites, platforms and relative heights of the whole group of built structures are all arranged according to the sloping terraces and the waterside, and the terrain correspondence runs through the entire group of buildings; the bridge is only one short clue and does not constitute an entry process running through the painting.

evidence: Lower right: among the woodland on the sloping bank, parts of roofs and walls are revealed, the built elements partly screened by tree branches and leaves, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Middle ground to distant view: the nearby woodland, water surface, and the distant peaks and waterfall form front-and-back spatial layers, with the built elements within the screening of the near-ground woodland.
distinction: Although the built elements are located on the sloping bank, the most prominent compositional mode in the painting is the screening and revelation of the houses by woodland, rather than emphasizing their layout following the mountains and terrain.

evidence: Lower center of the painting, slightly right: a low flat-slab bridge spans a narrow point at the stream mouth, two people stand on the left bank at the bridge, and the right end of the bridge lands at the foot of the right bank slope | Lower right corner: among the thickets on the right-bank slope, the roof and red wall railing of a house are revealed, situated on the bank land that the right end of the bridge connects to, reachable upon crossing the bridge | Middle of the painting: the stream valley winds and narrows from the bridge toward the upper part of the painting, with the foot of the slopes and the shoreline on both banks continuous, helping to present the extension from near to deep
distinction: The bridge and the figures crossing the stream constitute an accessible clue approaching the house on the right bank; the screening and revelation by thickets is merely the manner in which the house is presented, so the primary label is access to secluded settings.

evidence: Center-right sloping bank: a thatched pavilion stands at the end of a gently sloping terrace at the water's edge, the terrace edge neat and unfolding toward the water, the pavilion base placed according to the configuration in which the bank slope descends to the water surface | Behind and to the right of the pavilion: the slope descends gently from the foot of the mountain on the right toward the water on the left, several bare trees extend from the sloping bank, their branches covering above and behind the pavilion, which stands where the foot of the slope meets the water surface | Lower right near bank: a canopied boat is moored at the rocky bank, several trees stand on the bank, and between it and the pavilion in the middle ground lies an open water surface, with no bridge, path, or other connecting clue visible
distinction: The pavilion's base falls on the waterside slope-terrace and is appropriately placed following the bank configuration, with the terrain and shoreline directly participating in its siting; its role as a waterside marker is secondary to this relationship of arrangement according to the terrain.

evidence: Lower left, middle ground: a pavilion-house is built at the edge of the sloping bank, its base conforming to the slope terrain, presenting a relationship of placement according to the slope. | Around the building: the building is backed by trees and mountains and rocks and fronts onto the open water surface (unpainted space), showing its layout on a terrace facing the water.
distinction: The building is clearly placed according to the sloping bank terrain, presenting a spatial relationship of arrangement according to the site, which is more concrete than a mere role as a visual focus or scenic accent.

evidence: Middle horizontal band of the painting: between the trunks and crowns of rows of trees, the roofs, eaves, and white walls of several groups of houses are revealed, the buildings partly screened by the trees, presenting layering in which houses are seen within the grove | Center, slightly left, at the water's edge: in front of the waterside houses, tree trunks pass through, roofs are revealed through gaps in the grove, and the building bases are hidden behind the trees | Center-right: behind the thickets, house roofs emerge in succession, with parts of the walls visible, and figures walk in the clearings among the trees
distinction: Although the houses are situated on the flat ground between the mountain foot and the bank, the painting organizes the built elements through the concealment-and-revelation relationship of screening by woodland and roofs revealed, lacking a clear placement corresponding to the terrain such as differences in elevation according to slope or houses set on terraces.

evidence: Lower right: a person rides a donkey forward along the water's edge, suggesting a route of movement through the landscape | Center to upper right: snow mountains, trees, and a river form a natural landscape space, with no obvious artificial built elements visible
distinction: No clear built elements are visible in the painting; there are only figures traveling, so it is assigned to C4 on the basis of the travel route, but the evidence is insufficient.

evidence: Center of the right side: the built elements (thatched huts) are largely screened by dense tree branches and leaves, with only the roof and part of the walls revealed, presenting spatial layering of houses hidden within the grove. | Lower right corner: two people walk along a path at the mountain foot, the path disappearing among the woodland and rocks and pointing toward where the built elements are located.
distinction: Although a path and figures in the painting suggest movement through the landscape, the built elements form spatial layering mainly through screening and revelation by trees, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship is more prominent than the guiding of the path.

evidence: Lower right: a bridge spans the stream mouth, and on the bank path above the bridge two pedestrians carrying objects walk upward, forming the starting point of movement through the landscape by crossing the bridge into the setting | Middle, slightly right: along the right edge of the ravine's rocky shoal, a pale slope path leads upward to connect with the terrace where the open ravine-side pavilion stands, and to the rear right of the terrace another zigzag stepped path leads up to the mountain pass above | Center: the green-roofed open pavilion opens toward the ravine's rocky shoal, with someone seated inside, and is a node reachable along the movement thread
distinction: The bridge, bank path, stepped path, and open structure connect to form a process of movement through the landscape that is reachable and turns into the depths, organizing the space of the whole painting more than a relationship of buildings placed on terraces according to the slope.

evidence: Center: an open pavilion stands on a flat waterside slope, its white base at the water's edge, two people seated facing each other inside; the pavilion faces the open water surface at the lower left, above which a waterfall feeds into this water surface via the ravine, and the pavilion is placed exactly to one side of the open surface at the point where the water channels converge | Lower right: the roofs of a group of buildings emerge from among the tips of the densely planted pines, rising and falling along the woodland belt on the sloping bank | Center of the right side: a railed bridge or plank walkway spans among the sloping rocks, only partly visible, with no complete path visible connecting it to the central pavilion
distinction: Although the pavilion has its base set at the water's edge, the painting is mainly concerned with the pavilion gathering the open surface of the waterfall and pool and giving that waterscape a point of focus, rather than with its base elevation or manner of unfolding responding to the terrain.

evidence: Central mountaintop terrace of the painting: multiple temple halls unfold in staggered layers along the mountain ridge platform, their building bases rising and falling with the edge of the terrace, supported below by slope surfaces and rows of trees | Right flank of the monastery: steps are set along the slope connecting the upper halls with the lower small hip-roofed houses, the direction of the steps turning and descending with the slope | Lower left front slope: a small path skirts a huge rock toward the front-slope houses, and between the houses and the mountaintop building complex above there is no continuously visible road surface
distinction: Although the path, pavilion, and steps suggest ascent, the connections in the middle section are largely interrupted or omitted; the main relationship running through the composition is the layered placement of the temple halls according to the mountaintop terrace and slope configuration.

evidence: Center: a green-tiled main hall, a side room on the left and a small pavilion on the right sit on a mountain platform enclosed by surrounding peaks; the main hall backs onto the foot of the main peak's slope, the buildings spread laterally along the terrace, and a level courtyard of open ground is left in front of the terrace | Center-right: a large boulder stands close against the right end of the building group, the small pavilion is placed at the edge of the rock, and the rock body together with the mountain mass behind forms a natural screen for the courtyard buildings | Lower right: a light-colored mountain path with incised step lines winds upward from the lower right to join the right edge of the platform; several people stand or sit at the edge of the terrace within the courtyard
distinction: The mountain path is only a partial clue in one segment at the lower right, whereas the placement of the courtyard buildings backing onto the mountain and spreading out along the rock corresponds to a formation that runs through the center of the painting and organizes the enclosure of the surrounding peaks; therefore terrain-responsive siting is primary.
