evidence: Center: multiple tiers of flat-topped rock terraces stack up to form the main peak; pines cluster on the terrace top, and surrounding unpainted space and cloud qi lift it, making the summit platform the concentrated focus of the whole painting | Center-right: a waterfall pours down from a lateral gap in the rock terrace and falls into a large area of unpainted space below, marking the position and opening-and-closing of the peak body | Lower left: atop an isolated stone pillar is a lump-like form (possibly a person or an unusual rock, details unclear), facing the central cluster of peaks; no buildings, pavilions, bridges, paths or other built elements are seen anywhere in the painting
distinction: No clues of built placement, concealment and revelation, or movement through the landscape can be discerned; only the spatial organization in which the summit terrace and the waterfall concentrate a single scenic spot comes closest to scenic-accentuation composition.

evidence: Center-right: a tower-like structure built of flat stone slabs stacked in horizontal layers stands erect among vertical peak rocks; its layering is regular and its form differs from the surrounding natural peak rocks, suggesting artificial stacking, but the details are unclear | Upper right: several figures sit or recline gathered on the flat top of a slope terrace, facing the central forest of peaks; no buildings, pavilions or walls are seen on the slope terrace | Center to lower left: multiple groups of vertical stone-pillar peak forest rise from unpainted space of cloud and mist; the tower-like structure is located precisely at the open spot in a gap in the peak forest, becoming the only layered focal point among the peak rocks there
distinction: The tower-like structure shows no building site, layout, or corresponding placement relationship with the slope terrace or waterside; its role is closer to standing at the edge of the peaks with a prominent form to mark the forest-of-peaks scenery there.

evidence: Within the recessed hollow embraced by the central great cliff: a group of halls and houses sits in the hollow below the cliff; roofs and walls emerge from among interwoven pines, and the overhanging cliff face above and the rock slopes on both sides form screening edges | On both sides of the hollow's mouth and the slope rocks in front: stretches of pine forest stand at the mouth and on the slope, their crowns screening the lower parts and flanks of the buildings inside the hollow, creating a layer of concealment and revelation in which houses are seen among the trees | At the rock edge in the middle of the right bank: a pavilion is half hidden behind a rock slope, with only its roof and part of its walls showing, indicating that there is another layer of built structures behind the rock
distinction: Although the covered bridge over the stream provides a clue for entry, the path from behind the bridge to the hollow is cut off by slope rocks and trees and is not drawn; the focus of the painting remains the layer of concealment and revelation of the buildings enclosed by cliff walls and pine forest.

evidence: Center-right: a double-eaved round pavilion and an adjacent building stand on a mid-slope terrace; the terrace edge is enclosed by an arc-shaped railing, and the stone base beneath is laid following the winding slope; two people stand within the railing | On the slope ridge at center to lower right: a four-pillar memorial gateway stands on the ridge, with several steps below it facing down toward the approaching path from below, and the slope surface above it leads directly up to the pavilion terrace | From lower right to middle right: a group of buildings spreads along the slope bank and walls; to the right of the trees and buildings, a stone stepped path extends upward along the slope toward the ridge where the gateway stands
distinction: The gateway and the multiple flights of stone steps string the buildings below the mountain and the mid-slope pavilion into an accessible entry sequence; terrain-responsive placement only explains the siting of the terrace and cannot account for the organizing role of the gateway and stepped path running through the lower half of the composition.

evidence: Middle left: a flight of stepped path on a mountain ridge extends upward along the slope, its top disappearing into a mountain pass, forming a climbing clue leading from the foreground into the depths | Lower center: two buildings have steps and door openings in front, a light-colored mountain path winds to connect with the open ground before the houses, and at the edge of the open ground stone steps lead into the interior of a bamboo grove | Center: two people stand on the open ground embraced by the bamboo grove; above and behind the open ground, the roofs of a multi-story tower emerge in layers, situated at the deep endpoint of the bottom-to-top movement-through-the-landscape sequence
distinction: The stepped path, door steps and stone steps among the bamboo link the stream mouth, the buildings and the deep tower into an accessible process that can be further explored; although the concealment and revelation of the bamboo grove is prominent, the tower's outline is fully exposed, and the partly screened effect is subordinate to the deep presentation within the entry sequence.

evidence: Upper middle and left mid-slope: multiple buildings and towers are half hidden behind dense trees and mountain rocks, with only roofs or partial eaves corners exposed, forming rich layers of concealment and revelation. | Right mountain recess: a pagoda and halls are partly screened among tree clusters; architecture and natural scenery interpenetrate, highlighting the front-to-back depth of space. | Overall painting: built structures are not placed in isolation or abruptly, but rather their existence is suggested through the screening and revealing by mountain rocks and trees, participating in forming a deep and secluded mountain-forest mood.
distinction: Although the buildings are also arranged following the mountain terrain (C1), the painting emphasizes more the screening and revealing relationship of trees and mountain rocks to the buildings, and the feature of concealment and revelation forming scenery is more dominant.

evidence: Right half, lower middle slightly right: a bridge with red railings crosses a branch of the stream; two people stand on the bridge, and on the slope bank at the left end of the bridge a porter carrying a load walks along the bank | Right half, lower center: several buildings stand on a bank platform, and the bank land extending to the right from the platform joins the left end of the bridge, forming a walkable connection from the buildings to the bridge | Right half, middle ground right: the bank land joined at the right end of the bridge leads upward to a slope terrace, at whose edge a group of houses is arranged, surrounded by tree clusters with roofs emerging from among the trees
distinction: The bridge and the people crossing it and walking the bank string the buildings on both banks into an accessible sequence that can be further traveled through, exceeding the relationship in which the houses are merely placed according to the rise and fall of the bank terrace.

evidence: Lower right: at the bank a small wooden bridge (or plank walkway) extends to the water's edge; one person stands on the bridge, connecting the trees and mountain rocks on the bank with the water space. | Water surface of the painting: several small boats on the water, together with the small bridge at the bank, form spatial clues for wandering and crossing the water.
distinction: Although the small bridge depends on the bank slope, its main compositional role is to provide clues for figures to pause and for entering the water space, rather than simply showing architecture placed according to terrain.

evidence: Lower right: figures and horses appear along the riverbank; one person leads a horse in the water, while two people stand on the bank, forming a horse-washing scene. | Middle right: willows and other trees grow on the earthen slope along the bank; the river is broad, with distant mountains on the opposite bank. | Left side: the inscription includes 'Qujiang Tou' and 'washing horses', identifying the subject and location of the scene.
distinction: Although the figures are active along the waterfront, they mainly function as scenic accents that echo the theme of the inscription, rather than illustrating the layout of buildings.

evidence: Right middle of the painting: a thatched house (built structure) stands on level ground surrounded by tree clusters, with its roof and eaves and the people inside visible, showing it as a destination. | Lower middle of the painting: a red arched bridge crosses the water, connecting the foreground bank with the area where the built structure is located, forming a clear passage clue. | Lower right corner of the painting: figures on horseback and on foot travel along the waterside, their movement line pointing toward the bridge, presenting the spatial process of approaching the built structure from here to there.
distinction: Although the built structure is placed according to the waterside and mountain foot (a C1 feature), the bridge and the movement line of the figures form an entry path running through the painting, emphasizing more the spatial process of access to secluded settings.

evidence: Middle ground right: several thatched houses stand within a grove, partly screened by branches and leaves, with only roofs and eaves exposed. | Middle ground: the built structures form a concealment-and-revelation relationship through the screening and revealing of trees, presenting a spatial layer of houses seen within the grove.
distinction: The houses mainly form layers through tree screening, rather than emphasizing a corresponding relationship of placement according to terrain.

evidence: Lower right: a pavilion structure is built over the water surface, with supporting wooden piles visible beneath, placed close against the base of the mountain rocks and pines on the left, sited in conformity with the waterside terrain. | Center slightly right: the pavilion is located at the junction of the mountain foot and the water surface, its layout unfolding with the mountain forms and water edge, showing the feature of placement according to terrain.
distinction: Although the pavilion is partly screened by pines to form a concealment-and-revelation relationship, its placement relationship, erected according to the waterside and mountain-foot terrain, is clearer and more dominant in the composition.

evidence: Middle-left islet: several pines lean across and cover it; among the trees the roof and eaves of a small pavilion are exposed, its body partly screened by the tree trunks in front | Lower-right islet: a thatched house is placed behind tree clusters, with only the roof and part of the walls showing; a thatched pavilion stands at an open spot on the slope bank, with willow branches hanging beside it | Central water surface: the water is open, with a boat traveling across it; between the boat and the built structures on the banks there are no discernible linking clues such as bridges, paths or gates
distinction: The built structures mainly suggest their existence and the layer they occupy through the screening and revealing of trees; the islet and bank slopes are gentle, and the correspondence between the base layout and the rise and fall of terrain is weaker than the concealment-and-revelation relationship.

evidence: Lower right corner: a pavilion and thatched house are built on the waterside, placed in conformity with the waterside terrain, with trees around. | Center and upper part of the painting: a broad water surface and distant mountains; the built structures at the lower right corner are set according to the water.
distinction: The built structures are placed according to the waterside terrain, embodying a relationship of placement according to terrain; although they also serve as scenic accents, the feature of terrain-responsive siting is more direct.

evidence: Right side and upper part: mountain rocks, pines and distant mountains; no buildings are seen. | Lower left: trees and rocks on the bank. | Center of the water surface, slightly lower: a small boat with a person aboard, serving as a scenic accent in the painting.
distinction: There is only a small boat in the painting and no clear buildings; the small boat, as a scenic accent element, highlights the water scenery rather than emphasizing an entry path.

evidence: Left middle of the painting, among trees at the mountain foot: built structures (houses) are surrounded and screened by pines and withered trees, with roofs, eaves and window leaves (with people visible inside) exposed, presenting a layer of concealment and revelation in which houses are hidden in the grove. | Lower part of the painting, waterside: pedestrians on horseback and on foot travel along the waterside/ice surface, forming a clue for movement through the landscape, but the path extends horizontally and no connection leading directly to the built structures is drawn.
distinction: Although there is a clue of pedestrian movement along the waterside in the lower part of the painting, the path extends along the waterside without clearly linking to the entrance of the built structures, while the concealment-and-revelation relationship by which the built structures are screened and revealed by trees is more dominant in the composition.

evidence: Left mid-slope: buildings are constructed according to the mountain, partly screened by pine forest and mountain rocks, appearing half hidden and half revealed. | Right waterside: houses are surrounded and screened by dense trees, with only roofs and part of the structures exposed, hidden within the grove.
distinction: Although the buildings on the left have a tendency of following the mountain, the most prominent feature of the two groups of built structures in the painting is forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship through trees and mountain rocks, constituting spatial layers; therefore C2 is more dominant.

evidence: Whole painting: the painting mainly depicts mountain rocks, trees, cloud and mist, and deer; no clear built elements such as houses, pavilions, bridges or paths are seen. | Lower middle: mountain rocks and trees interweave to form a deep and secluded natural space, but there are no identifiable artificial entry clues.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built structures and is classified into the closest category based on the overall organization of deep and secluded natural space.

evidence: Lower right: several trees and mountain rocks at the waterside, among which the roof, railings and platform of built structures are exposed, appearing half screened and half concealed by trees and mountain rocks. | Middle ground: the broad water surface separates the foreground trees and built structures from the continuous mountain ranges behind, forming front-to-back spatial layers.
distinction: Although the built structures are erected facing the water, the painting emphasizes more their concealment-and-revelation relationship as screened and revealed by foreground trees and mountain rocks, rather than highlighting their placement in conformity with terrain.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: a thatched-roof built structure sits on a rocky slope bank by the water, its roof and part of its walls clearly visible. | Right side and center of the painting: the branches and leaves of several trees screen the right side and part of the front of the built structure, forming a layer of concealment and revelation in which the house is seen behind trees. | Overall painting: the foreground trees and rocks and the built structures screen one another, forming a front-to-back spatial contrast with the open water surface and distant mountains of the middle and far distance.
distinction: Although the built structure marks out a scenic spot at the waterside, the layer of concealment and revelation formed by the explicit screening of its walls and flanks by trees is more prominent in the organization of the foreground space.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: a small bridge crosses a stream, connecting the tree-and-rock slope bank on the left where the figures are with the bamboo-grove slope land on the right. | Left side of the painting: two people stand beneath a tree, facing the stream and the bridge, forming a guide for the line of sight. | Right side of the painting: the slope bank and dense bamboo grove form a deep space, connected to the foreground by the bridge, suggesting an accessible path.
distinction: The painting mainly organizes a wanderable spatial process through the bridge and the bank path, rather than emphasizing the concealment-and-revelation relationship of buildings screened by natural scenery.

evidence: Right mid-slope: a multi-story tower is built according to the mountain, mostly screened by foreground pines and mountain rocks, with only part of the eaves and floors exposed, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Lower middle: several thatched houses are partly screened among withered trees and shrubs, with roofs and walls partly revealed, forming spatial layers with the surrounding trees. | Lower left corner: some houses are screened by trees and slope land, with only partial roofs visible, blending into the natural scenery.
distinction: Although there are paths and figures on the right side of the painting pointing toward the tower, the overall composition mainly relies on the screening and revealing of buildings by trees and mountain rocks to create layers, and the partly screened relationship is more prominent than the movement-through-the-landscape clues.

evidence: Central main island of the painting: building groups are scattered across the island, with a large number of roofs and walls screened by the branches and crowns of trees, presenting an obvious concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Lower middle of the main island: houses are half hidden among sparse trees, their existence suggested through exposed eaves and structures, forming rich spatial layers. | Right bank slope of the painting: buildings are likewise partly screened behind pine forest, only partially visible, continuing the compositional method of screening through borrowed scenery.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed according to the mountains and beside the water, the most prominent visual feature of the painting is the screening and revealing of buildings by trees, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship dominates the creation of the spatial mood.

evidence: Left side and lower middle: multiple towers and halls cling closely to the steep cliffs and slope land on the left, their building sites and layouts stacked layer upon layer following the rise and fall of the mountain terrain. | Between the building groups and the mountain body: the roofs, eaves and walls of the buildings interweave with the outlines of mountain rocks, presenting a spatial relationship of placement according to terrain and suitability following the forms. | Between buildings and trees: foreground and middle-ground trees partly screen the building groups, but the overall posture of the buildings being constructed according to the mountain remains clearly visible.
distinction: Although there is a partly screened relationship between buildings and trees, the layout feature of buildings stacked layer upon layer according to the mountain terrain is more prominent and dominates the spatial organization of the painting.

evidence: Left waterside: several houses are distributed along the waterside, partly screened by surrounding trees, with only roofs and part of the walls exposed, forming a partly screened relationship. | Right lower middle: a group of houses is hidden within a dense grove, mostly screened by leaves with only roofs exposed, presenting a layer of houses hidden deep in the forest. | Right upper middle: a multi-story tower stands among mountain rocks and trees, half screened by cloud and mist and trees, highlighting a spatial sense of alternating concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the buildings are arranged according to the waterside and mountain forms, the painting emphasizes more the screening and revealing of buildings by trees and cloud and mist, forming rich layers of concealment and revelation, and the effect of concealment and revelation forming scenery is more prominent and dominant.

evidence: Center: a winding light-colored band-like form (resembling a path or stream) passes through rocks and groves, extending into the depths of the painting, forming a visual guide. | Surroundings: dense trees and mountain rocks interweave, forming layer upon layer of screening and creating a deep and secluded spatial layer.
distinction: Although the tree-screening relationship is obvious, the winding clue at the center emphasizes more the spatial process of guiding the line of sight into the depths, in keeping with the momentum of access to secluded settings.

evidence: Center slightly left of the painting: the house built structure is largely screened by dense weeping willows on the left, trees on the right and bamboo clusters in the foreground, with only the roof, part of the walls and the figures inside the doors and windows exposed, presenting an obvious tree-screening relationship. | Middle ground of the painting: the building is hidden behind trees and rocks, its existence suggested through partially exposed eaves and walls, forming a spatial layer of alternating concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the building is placed according to the mountains and beside the water, the most prominent compositional technique in the painting is to use the screening and revealing of trees to create layers, rather than emphasizing a layout unfolded according to terrain.

evidence: Lower right foreground: a thatched house is seen built facing the water, with a small bridge beside it; a pedestrian on the bridge is walking toward the thatched house, forming a clear entry path. | Right middle ground: a group of buildings is arranged according to the mid-slope and trees, connected by paths or platforms, presenting an accessible layer. | Upper left far distance: a village building group in a valley, scattered according to the waterside and terrain.
distinction: Although there is tree screening of buildings in the painting, the interaction of the bridge and the pedestrian at the lower right corner forms a clear entry clue that dominates the sense of spatial wandering; therefore C4 is more fitting.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: a thatched house and fence are partly screened by surrounding trees (especially the large tree on the right and the tree clusters on the left), with only the roof, eaves and fence exposed, forming an obvious layer of concealment and revelation. | Middle to rear of the painting: tall cliffs and mountain rocks embrace the built structures, hiding the houses deep within the valley and grove, and using natural scenery as screening to form scenery.
distinction: Although the built structures are located on level ground in a mountain hollow, the visual center of gravity of the painting lies in the screening and revealing relationship of trees and mountain rocks to the houses, rather than simply emphasizing the corresponding placement of the base and terrain.

evidence: Middle ground at right: behind the sloping terrace and trees, the roof and parts of the wall of a building are faintly revealed, partly screened by the branches and trunks of trees in front and by mountains and rocks. | Overall painting: the building is not fully exposed; rather, through the screening of pines and mixed trees in the foreground and middle ground, it forms spatial layers of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the building stands on a sloping terrace, the painting emphasizes more the layered relationship of its being screened by trees, mountains, and rocks and thus half-revealed, rather than focusing on showing its layout unfolding according to the terrain.

evidence: Central mountain hollow of the painting: the roofs and eaves of a group of houses emerge through gaps in the trees in the valley, the building itself half-screened by trees before and behind | Lower middle-right: the roof, white walls, and railings of a building emerge from behind a row of trees, with crowns and branches screening its upper part and surroundings, forming a layering of seeing houses through the woods | Stream below: several bridge-pier-like structures are visible on the stream flats, but behind them they are cut off by slanting slope rocks and trees, and no continuous path leading to the houses is seen
distinction: Although the bridge piers are visible, they are cut off from the houses by slope rocks and the connection of access cannot be discerned, while both built structures are presented through the screening and revealing of trees in spatial layers, with the concealment-and-revelation relationship running more pervasively through the whole painting

evidence: Foot of the mountain at lower right: a group of houses and courtyard walls is partly screened by trees and rocks in front, with only the roof, eaves, and part of the wall revealed. | Right side of the painting: the towering cliffs and the trees on the slopes form screening in the foreground and middle ground, giving the architecture spatial layers of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the architecture nestles against the mountain and beside the water, the painting emphasizes more the relationship of screening and revealing of the architecture by trees, mountains, and rocks, rather than simply emphasizing the correspondence of building sites arranged according to the terrain.

evidence: Lower left: several white-walled houses are arranged in staggered fashion at the foot of the slope, their bodies and roofs partly screened by trunks and crowns in front and behind, with only parts of the walls, windows, and eaves revealed | Lower middle-right: the roof and the columns beneath the eaves of a building emerge above dense trees, the crowns screening its base and surroundings, presenting a layering of seeing houses within the woods | Lower half: rows of trees along the slopes and mounds form a continuous screening band, and both built structures are surrounded by trees, with the concealment-and-revelation relationship running through the lower composition
distinction: Although the houses stand at the foot of the slope, what is visible is chiefly the layering of concealment and revelation formed by tree crowns screening the building bodies and roofs, rather than the correspondence between building sites, heights, and terrain arrangement

evidence: Lower left: a small thatched-roof hut is half-hidden behind withered trees and slope rocks, with only part of the roof and wall revealed. | Left side: the branches and trunks of withered trees in the foreground interpose in front of the hut, forming a clear layering of screening and revealing.
distinction: Although the hut is built against the slope, its main compositional role is to form a layering of concealment and revelation through the screening of trees and slope rocks, rather than to emphasize a layout unfolding according to the terrain.

evidence: Lower right: a built structure is visible among the trees on the sloping bank, its roof and wall outlines partly screened by branches and leaves, presenting a relationship of partly screened concealment.
distinction: The built structure is chiefly screened and revealed by trees; no obvious path guidance or emphasis on placement according to the terrain is seen, so C2 is the most fitting.

evidence: Lower middle-right: a red-walled built structure is visible, partly screened by pines and mixed trees in front, with only the roof, walls, and doorway revealed, forming a layering of houses hidden in the woods. | Right side of the painting: branches and leaves together with mountains and rocks form the foreground and middle ground, screening the built structure within them and presenting a spatial relationship of seeing houses across a screen.
distinction: Although the built structure leans against mountains and rocks, the most prominent compositional means in the painting is the screening and revealing of architecture by trees, rather than emphasizing its layout unfolding according to the terrain.

evidence: Upper middle: the roof and part of the walls of a building are visible, partly screened by surrounding mountains, rocks, and trees, presenting a state of half-hidden, half-revealed. | Middle left: part of the structure of a building is visible, screened behind trees and rocks, forming spatial layers.
distinction: Although the building is situated amid mountains and woods, the painting emphasizes more the concealment-and-revelation relationship of its being screened and revealed by mountains, rocks, and trees, rather than a close attachment and correspondence to the terrain and topography.

evidence: Middle right: the roof and walls of a building are visible on the hillside, partly screened by surrounding trees and slope rocks, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Among the trees in the lower middle: architectural structure is faintly visible between dense foliage and slope rocks, further strengthening the spatial layering of built structures screened by trees.
distinction: Although the building is placed against the mountain, the painting emphasizes more the screening and revealing of architecture by trees and rocks, and the role of concealment and revelation in forming a setting is more pronounced.

evidence: Lower right corner: a pavilion building with flying eaves and a flagpole beside it are visible, located at the edge of the waterside in the near ground. | Middle and far distance: large areas of unpainted space depict water surface and cloud vapor, distant mountains are hazy, and the building at the lower right corner becomes the visual anchor of the near ground.
distinction: The building is located at the edge of an open waterside, and its main function is to punctuate the near ground and focus the composition; no obvious clues of screening or path guidance are seen.

evidence: Lower center: houses are built facing the waterside, their bases conforming to the slope and the configuration of the bank, presenting a state of following the bank and relying on the slope. | Lower right: trees surround a towering rock mass/mountain rocks, and on or beside the rock top there appears to be a building/pavilion, presenting a tendency to set houses on high ground. | Upper left: building outlines are faintly visible among mountains, rocks, and trees, distributed according to the mountain configuration and integrated with the terrain.
distinction: The architecture is chiefly sited according to the waterside and rock-terrace terrain (terrain-responsive), and although trees surround it, the concealment-and-revelation relationship is less dominant than the relationship of terrain-based placement.

evidence: Lower middle and right of the painting: dense pine woods and mountains and rocks interweave, forming a layered relationship of foreground and background screening, but no clear built elements such as roofs, walls, or paths are seen. | Upper right of the painting: cliffs rise high, with trees dotting the rock faces, presenting the screened state of natural landscape, with no trace of buildings attached.
distinction: The painting consists entirely of natural scenery and lacks evidence of built elements; it is only tentatively assigned to C2 on the basis of the concealment-and-revelation layering of mountains, water, and trees.

evidence: Lower middle, slightly left: the sloping roof, eaves, and columns of a pavilion are visible, with two slender tree trunks passing in front of the pavilion, cutting off parts of the eaves and columns | Around the pavilion: bamboo clumps and pines and broadleaf trees stand beside and behind the pavilion, the roof emerging through gaps in the branches and leaves, forming a layering of seeing houses in the woods | Lower middle foreground: an upright boulder lies across the front left of the pavilion, screening the lower left part of the pavilion body, so that only the upper half and the right side are exposed
distinction: The pavilion body is partly cut off by tree trunks, bamboo clumps, and the upright rock while the roof emerges from the woods, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship organizes the near ground; the correspondence of the sloping terrace to the placement is less clear than this screening layering

evidence: Lower left: a group of houses with roofs and walls in outline (void-outline), with a section of vertical railing connected beside them, placed at the converging point of the left end of the foreground slope and at the bank edge facing the open unpainted water in the middle | Lower middle to lower right: the foreground slope tilts and extends from lower right to lower left, its surface dotted with rows of clustered small trees and several large trees, the slope stopping at the waterside where the houses are at the left end | Middle: a large expanse of unpainted water runs across the painting, and the slope rocks at the foot of the far mountain extend into the water, facing across the water the foreground bank where the houses are located
distinction: The bases and manner of unfolding of the houses and railing are defined by the slope end and water's edge, presenting terrain-based placement; they do not serve as markers giving definition to a particular peak or water mouth, so C1 is taken rather than C3

evidence: Among the cliffs of the main peak in the upper middle: between pine clumps and rock terraces is a vertical rectangular block of dense ink, slightly wider at the top as if covered, suspected to be a pavilion or small hut, half-screened by trees and rocks, with unclear outline and details | Foreground lower left to center: the sloping bank is built up of boulders extending into the water on the right, and pines, bamboo, and broadleaf trees on the bank are layered in groups, screening the space behind the bank | Middle ground and right side: the water surface spreads out in fine ripples, and gaps of unpainted space remain between the middle-ground trees and the sloping bank, with no clues of movement through the landscape such as bridges, paths, or gates seen
distinction: The suspected built structure suggests a layering among the rocks by means of a partial exposure half-screened by pine clumps and rock faces, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship is more discernible than the correspondence of base to terrain, so C2 is taken rather than C1.

evidence: At the foot of the mountain slightly left of center: a tiny outline of a built structure is visible, with the basic form of a roof and walls, half-hidden behind mountains, rocks, and trees. | Middle ground of the painting: tree trunks and slope rocks in the foreground screen the built structure behind, presenting spatial layers of alternating concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the built structure nestles against the mountain and beside the water, its most conspicuous compositional role in the painting is to form a screening layering through the occlusion of trees, mountains, and rocks, rather than to emphasize a layout relationship of terrain-based placement.

evidence: Lower left corner: sloping bank, trees, and houses are painted in darker ink as the near ground, with house outlines visible. | Middle: long strip-like roof lines are painted among the woods, suggesting houses or a covered bridge, screened among the trees. | Upper part: distant mountains are painted in light ink wash, with rounded mountain forms, depicting a scene wreathed in mist and clouds.
distinction: The painting is chiefly a natural landscape, depicting mountains, streams, and trees in ink technique, with architecture appearing as scenic accents, consistent with the characteristics of a typical landscape painting.

evidence: Lower right of the left page: within screening woods, the outline of a simple built structure is faintly visible, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Right page: mainly mountain ridges, mist and clouds, and woods, with no clear built elements seen.
distinction: Built elements in the painting are very few and screened by trees, mainly embodying a screening relationship in which natural scenery is borrowed to screen and form spatial layers.

evidence: Upper middle of the left page: buildings are located on a rocky platform on the mountainside, arranged in staggered heights following the mountain configuration. | Upper middle of the right page: pavilions and houses are arranged in the valley and on the mountainside, their bases adapted to the forms of the surrounding mountains and rocks. | Overall painting: the layout of built elements corresponds closely to mountain forms and sloping terraces, presenting a relationship of terrain-based arrangement and fitting according to the configuration.
distinction: Although there is screening by trees, the correspondence and placement relationship between the architecture and the terrain (platforms, mountainside) is more prominent and dominant.

evidence: Left picture area: peaks, pines, and mountains and rocks are visible, with no trace of buildings or man-made built elements. | Right picture area: upper mountains and rocks and lower waterside withered trees are visible, with no trace of buildings or man-made built elements.
distinction: The painting presents purely the natural scenery of mountains, water, trees, and rocks, with no clear participation of built elements in organizing space.

evidence: Center-right of the right page: the roofs and outlines of several houses are faintly visible between mountain rocks and trees, partly screened by natural scenery. | Overall right page: built structures, through the screening and revealing of mountains, rocks, and trees, present spatial layers of interwoven concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the built structures are located among the mountain rocks, the painting emphasizes more the concealment-and-revelation relationship of their being half-screened by trees, mountains, and rocks, rather than merely terrain-based placement.

evidence: Middle-ground mountainside: pavilions or houses are visible, built according to the mountain configuration and sloping terraces, their bases closely fitting the mountain rock faces and the undulations of the terrain, presenting a form of setting houses on terraces. | Right mountain hollow: house outlines are faintly visible in the gaps between woods and rocks, forming screening and revealing through natural scenery.
distinction: The terrain-based relationship of the middle-ground built structures placed according to the mountain configuration and sloping terraces is more prominent and dominates the spatial organization of the painting, while the screening and revelation on the right is a secondary manifestation.

evidence: Right side of the painting: there are extremely faint ink dots at the junction of the mountain foot and the waterside, but they cannot be confirmed as clear built structures; the whole is dominated by natural landscape. | Entire painting: mountains, rocks, and pines on the left, and continuous mountain ridges and open water on the right, with no clearly identifiable buildings, bridges, or roads seen.
distinction: The painting lacks clear evidence of built elements; it is only tentatively assigned to the landscape-organizing logic of scenic accentuation on the basis of the opening-and-closing forms of peaks and water surfaces in the landscape itself.

evidence: Left panel: the painting presents gentle mountains and rocks, water surface, and trees, with no clear traces of built elements such as buildings or paths seen. | Right panel: the painting presents steep rock faces, a waterfall, and trees; mountains, rocks, and woods form foreground and background layers, but no discernible built elements are seen.
distinction: The painting as a whole is dominated by the layering and screening relationships of natural scenery; because there are no clear built elements, it is assigned to the closest category on the basis of overall spatial organization.

evidence: Upper part of the right page: houses are built at the edge of the cliff top, placed relying on the flat terrain of the summit, presenting a form of setting houses on terraces. | Middle of the right page: a pavilion stands on a protruding rocky platform on the mountainside, forming with the houses above a layout of separate placement along the slope, staggered according to the heights of the mountain configuration. | Overall right page: the built elements (houses, pavilion) are clearly placed level by level according to the terraces and slope configuration of the cliffs, forming a correspondence with the natural terrain.
distinction: The built elements mainly embody a layout relationship of level-by-level placement according to mountain terraces (terrain-responsive), rather than merely serving as isolated marker points for a particular scene (scenic accentuation).

evidence: Lower right corner of the right picture: the roof and part of the walls of a building emerge between woods and rocks, the building partly screened by foreground trees. | Lower middle of the right picture: multiple layers of rocks and trees form foreground and background layers, and the building appears faintly in the gaps of the woods, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the building is located at the foot of the mountain beside the water, the painting emphasizes more the layered relationship of its being screened and revealed by trees, rather than prominent features of terrain-based placement.

evidence: Summit of the left page: at the summit outline there are extremely tiny line structures resembling roofs, suspected to be buildings. | Lower right corner of the right page: there are horizontal lines at the junction of water and rocks, suspected to be a bridge or water-mouth structure.
distinction: The suspected structure at the summit mainly serves to accent the mountain configuration, rather than clearly showing an accessible path connection.

evidence: Upper middle of the right page, on the mountainside: a corner of a roof with a yellowish tone emerges between woods and rocks, the main body of the building screened by natural scenery, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Left page: the entire page is mountains, rocks, trees, and water, with no clear built elements seen, dominated by natural landscape organization.
distinction: The building on the right mainly forms a half-screened layering through woods and rocks, rather than serving as a conspicuous landmark to punctuate the scene.

evidence: Middle of the painting and right bank: rows of houses are distributed along the sloping bank and the shoreline, unfolding and arranged according to the terrain's heights and the course of the riverbank. | Middle of the painting: the house bases are located between the sloping terrace and the waterside, presenting a layout relationship of relying on the slope and nestling beside the water, placed along the riverbank.
distinction: The houses mainly unfold and are arranged according to the riverbank slopes, embodying a settlement form of terrain-based placement, rather than serving as a single marker to punctuate a specific scene.

evidence: Middle-ground mountain foot of the right page: several roofs are visible, screened between mountains, rocks, and trees, presenting spatial layers of concealment and revelation. | Left page: mainly mountains, rocks, trees, and water, with no clear built elements seen.
distinction: The built structures present layering mainly through the screening and revealing of trees, mountains, and rocks, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship is more prominent than terrain-based placement.

evidence: Upper-middle and middle of the left side of the painting: among the mountains, rocks, and sloping banks are distributed several buildings with roofs and post-and-beam structures, arranged at varying heights according to the mountain terrain, presenting a placement relationship of resting against rock and leaning on slope. | Right side of the painting: mainly depicts rock caves, water surface, and pine trees; no clear built structures are seen.
distinction: The built elements visible in the painting are mainly expressed as arrangements at varying heights that conform to the rocky mountain terrain; no obvious concealment and revelation or movement-through-the-landscape clue is seen to guide the view, therefore C1 is most fitting.

evidence: Lower-middle and lower-right of the left panel: building roofs emerge among the trees on the waterside, and the built elements and trees form a concealment-and-revelation relationship of mutual screening | Middle of the right panel: building roofs emerge between the mountains, rocks, and trees, borrowing natural scenery for screening to present spatial layering
distinction: The built elements in the painting mainly form scenery by being screened and revealed by trees and mountains and rocks, emphasizing layers of concealment and revelation, rather than highlighting their correspondence to terrain-based placement.

evidence: Right mountain slope: a building is half-hidden behind a massive rock body, with only part of the eaves and wall revealed, forming a layer of a house hidden behind rock. | On the waterside in the right middle ground: several houses are partly blocked by foreground trees and sloping rocks, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship of seeing houses through intervening scenery. | Lower-right corner: parts of built structures are faintly visible in the gaps between woods and rocks, forming screening with the surrounding natural scenery.
distinction: Although there is a bridge in the lower-right corner of the painting, the built elements mainly construct spatial layering through being screened and revealed by mountains, rocks, and trees, rather than emphasizing a path of entry.

evidence: Near ground to middle ground: the lower part of the painting depicts willows, miscellaneous trees, and shrubs growing by the water. | Distant ground: the upper part of the painting depicts gentle mountain outlines. | Whole painting: no clear traces of built structures such as houses, bridges, or paths are seen in the painting.
distinction: No clear built elements are seen in the painting; it is assigned to the closest category based on the overall visible organization of trees and landscape.

evidence: Upper-middle of the left page: pavilions and houses can be seen arranged at varying heights according to the forms of the mountains and rocks; the building bases are closely integrated with the mountain rocks, presenting a posture of houses set against rock. | Middle of the left page: the buildings are placed along the undulations of the mountain terrain and the distribution of rock masses, at varying heights, conforming to the natural terrain.
distinction: Although the buildings are partly screened by mountains, rocks, and trees, their main feature is layout relying on the rocky mountain terrain, rather than forming layers purely through screening.

evidence: Whole painting: the main body of the painting is calligraphic inscription; no landscape scenery or built traces are seen.
distinction: The painting has no landscape built elements, so spatial-expression classification cannot be carried out; it is forcibly assigned according to the rules.

evidence: Right side of the main peak ridge in the upper right half: the roof and eaves of a house are revealed at the edge of a cliff in a mountain hollow; the building itself and its base are blocked by the mountain ridge, and only the upper structure is visible | Among the trees on the sloping bank in the lower right half: the roof and part of the wall of a house emerge from between the woods and the sloping bank, surrounded by pines and miscellaneous trees, with the lower half of the building obscured | Middle of the right half: the upper and lower sections are separated by unpainted space and cloud qi, and both built elements are embedded into the layers of mountains, rocks, and trees by means of partial revelation
distinction: The building bases and the way they unfold with the terrain are mostly obscured and unclear; what the painting highlights is the layer of concealment and revelation in which roofs emerge from mountain ridges and groves, so concealment and revelation as compositional effect is more fitting than terrain-responsive siting

evidence: Middle of the right page: rows of tree trunks and layered horizontal-dot tree crowns are distributed on the slope; the mountainside is cut off by a large area of unpainted space and cloud mist; treetops and slope surfaces are half-hidden and half-revealed, forming spatial layers organized by concealment and revelation. | Lower part of the right page: a horizontal waterside and unpainted space of water surface unfold; grass and low trees on the bank form patches, and no artificial traces such as houses, bridges, paths, or gates are seen. | Upper part of the right page: the main peak rises through ink washes of dense and pale tones, and cloud mist below the peak separates the middle-ground slope trees; no recognizable roofs, eaves, or walls are seen in the entire work.
distinction: The pictorial space mainly relies on cloud mist and groves to block and reveal and thereby organize layers, rather than an entry process via bridge-and-path movement-through-the-landscape clues, so it is assigned to the category closest to concealment and revelation as compositional effect.

evidence: Lower right: within the screening of trees, a pavilion-house is visible; its roof and posts are revealed and partly blocked by foreground trees, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Right side: surrounded by tall pines and miscellaneous trees, the built structure is wrapped within the woods, presenting a spatial layer of seeing a house within a grove.
distinction: The painting mainly expresses the blocking and revealing of the building by trees to form layers, rather than emphasizing the correspondence of the building's placement to the terrain.

evidence: Middle-lower right: a group of houses is placed closely against the foot of the cliff on the right; the bases conform to the turn of the mountain foot and the shoreline, presenting a placement mode of leaning against the cliff and beside the water. | Right side: the built elements unfold along the waterside, forming a clear relationship of placement according to the terrain with the mountains, rocks, and sloping banks, and do not exist in isolation from the terrain.
distinction: Although trees and rocks partly screen the houses, what the painting highlights more is the placement relationship in which the houses lean against the cliff and beside the water and unfold in conformity with the terrain; therefore C1 is more dominant than C2.

evidence: Lower middle: the roof of a building is faintly revealed in the grove, partly blocked by the branches and leaves of foreground and surrounding trees, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Waterside at the lower right: among the trees on the waterside there are tiny dark brushstrokes, suspected to be another built structure or a bridge, likewise within the screening of the woods.
distinction: Although the building sits on the sloping bank, the painting highlights more its layered relationship of being screened by woods with only the roof revealed, rather than emphasizing its layout conforming to the terrain.

evidence: Slightly right of center in the painting: the roof and wall of a house are visible below the cliff wall, partly blocked by trees. | Center of the painting: the house is located between the woods and the cliff, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship and forming spatial layering.
distinction: The house is mainly blocked and revealed by trees and mountains and rocks to form layers, rather than emphasizing layout according to terrain.

evidence: Middle right: a group of buildings is visible with roofs, walls, and posts; their lower halves are blocked by foreground tree trunks and branches and sloping rocks, forming a screening relationship. | Right side: the buildings are close to the towering cliff face and dense woods on the right, and the cliff face and trees constitute the screening boundary at the rear and top of the buildings. | Center foreground: gnarled pines and miscellaneous trees extend forward, further blocking the building bases and strengthening the spatial layer of built structures deeply hidden within mountain forests.
distinction: Although the buildings lean against mountains, rocks, and waterside, the most prominent compositional method in the painting is to create layers by means of the screening and revelation of the buildings by foreground trees and the side cliff face, so C2 is more dominant than C1.

evidence: Right mountainside and mountain foot: several houses can be seen arranged at varying heights on the mountain slopes and terraces, unfolding along the terrain, with the bases corresponding to the mountain slope surfaces. | Middle-right of the painting: the buildings are screened among mountains, rocks, and trees and placed in conformity with the mountain forms, presenting a relationship of placement according to terrain.
distinction: Although the buildings are screened by trees, mountains, and rocks, their most conspicuous feature is arrangement at varying heights conforming to the sloping mountain terrain, and the relationship of terrain-based placement is more prominent.

evidence: Top of the central main peak: within the outline of the peak there is an extremely small ink-brush structure with vertical strokes and horizontal lifts, resembling a pavilion or the tip of a pagoda, but the details are unclear and it cannot be reliably confirmed as a built structure | From the center to both sides of the entire work: the main peak rises and stands in the center, embraced by ridges and pine groves on both sides, and the composition takes the peak area as its point of convergence | Foreground and middle-ground valleys: sloping rocks, miscellaneous trees, and valley openings are visible, but no other built elements or movement-through-the-landscape clues such as houses, walls, bridges, or paths are seen
distinction: The suspected structure at the peak top is located at the highest peak area of the whole painting, and its recognizable role is to mark the position of the main peak, rather than to display the correspondence between building bases, layout, and slope-terrace terrain

evidence: Upper-middle mountainside: several simplified building outlines can be seen, attached among the mountain rock and slope surfaces | Upper middle: the buildings are partly blocked by the surrounding mountains, rocks, and trees, presenting spatial layers of alternating concealment and revelation
distinction: Although the buildings are placed according to the mountain terrain, the painting emphasizes more their half-hidden, half-revealed concealment-and-revelation relationship with the mountains, rocks, and trees, rather than highlighting the base forms placed according to terrain.

evidence: Whole painting: the painting presents distant mountains, clouds and mist, pine groves on sloping banks, and waterside trees and rocks in the near ground; no clear traces of built structures such as houses, pavilions, bridges, or paths are seen.
distinction: The painting lacks visible built elements and is only assigned with difficulty based on the spatial organization of the overall natural landscape, with no clear competing interpretation.

evidence: Below the mountains and rocks slightly right of center: below the waterfall there are tiny ink dots, suspected to be a very small distant structure or figure, but the details are blurred and cannot be confirmed as a built structure. | Overall painting: the painting is dominated by mountains and rocks, trees, and waterside; no clear traces of built structures such as houses, bridges, or paths are seen.
distinction: The painting lacks clear evidence of built elements and is only assigned with difficulty to C2 based on the overall landscape layers and concealment-and-revelation relationships.

evidence: Whole painting: the painting mainly consists of distant mountains, water surface, foreground rocks and trees (including red-leaf trees and pines), and a steep cliff on the right; no clear built elements such as houses, bridges, or paths are seen.
distinction: The painting lacks visible built elements and its compositional method cannot be clearly judged; it is assigned with difficulty to scenic accentuation based on the overall landscape organization, but there is no actual building serving as an accent.

evidence: Lower right: a building is visible with roof and wall structure; its left side and front are partly blocked by the branches, leaves, and trunks of several trees. | Center right: the rear of the building is close to mountains, rocks, and a waterfall, with woods in front, forming spatial layers in which the building is hidden among woods, mountains, and rocks. | Waterside at the lower right: the building base is near the water surface, leaning against the mountain foot and closely integrated with the surrounding natural environment.
distinction: Although the building is placed against the mountains and beside the water, the layer of concealment and revelation formed by the clear screening of the building by trees in the painting is more prominent and dominates the spatial expression.

evidence: Right half of the painting: mountains and rocks, trees, and a stream are visible; no fixed built structures such as houses or pavilions are seen. | Water surface at the lower right: there is a small boat and a person in it, which are a mobile carrier, not a fixed built structure.
distinction: The painting lacks fixed built structures, and the boat on the water surface tends more toward embellishing the scenery than providing a path into a fixed built structure.

evidence: Slightly left of the center of the painting: several houses can be seen built by the water; one is a water pavilion with wooden piles visible beneath supporting it on the water surface, and another has a stone base close to the waterside, presenting a layout placed according to the water conditions. | Right side and foreground of the painting: there are sloping banks and trees in the foreground and continuous distant mountains in the background; the built elements are located at the open waterside between mountains and water, forming a relationship of terrain-responsive arrangement with the natural environment.
distinction: Although the built elements mark the waterside scenery, their form of being built by the water with the water pavilion rising over the waves more prominently embodies the feature of terrain-responsive siting in which placement is carried out according to the waterside terrain conditions.

evidence: Mountain valley in the middle of the right page: a white-walled, yellow-roofed house sits in a valley hollow between two mountains, and in front of the house a pale winding path extends down the valley | Lower middle of the right page: a yellow-roofed open pavilion stands on a foreground earth slope, and at the lower left of the pavilion, in a ravine gap, a roofed corridor-bridge-like structure is visible | Lower to middle part of the right page: the winding path links the foreground slope, the pavilion, and the house in the deep valley hollow, forming a movement-through-the-landscape clue from bottom to top that can reach the house
distinction: Although the house and pavilion are placed according to the slope and hollow, what runs through the composition is the winding path connecting the foreground pavilion slope and the valley house into an enterable and reachable sequence; the connecting role of the path is more dominant than simple terrain-responsive arrangement

evidence: Near the bank at the lower right: two thatched houses are built by the water, and parts of the buildings are blocked by the branches and leaves of foreground trees, presenting a half-hidden, half-revealed state. | On the mountainside in the right middle-distant ground: behind groves and mountains and rocks, the roofs and walls of houses are faintly visible, using natural scenery for screening to form deep spatial layers.
distinction: Although the buildings lean against mountains and beside water, the painting highlights more the relationship of screening and revelation of the buildings by woods, mountains, and rocks, and the feature of concealment and revelation forming scenery is more dominant.

evidence: Slightly left of the center of the painting: the roof, eaves, and walls of a thatched house are revealed between several tall tree trunks; the trunks stand in front of the house and block part of the building | Around the house: groves and dense woods enclose the rear and sides of the house, and a fence in front of the house extends along the sloping bank; the house is within layers screened by woods | At the water's edge below the sloping bank: a person stands on the bank and a boat is moored on the water surface, but no recognizable entry clues such as bridges, paths, or gates are seen between the person and boat and the house
distinction: Although the house is located on the sloping bank by the water, the clearest relationship in the painting is the layer of concealment and revelation in which tree trunks and groves screen the house and the roof emerges from the woods, rather than the correspondence between base layout and terrain forms

evidence: On the mountainside at the left of the middle ground: the roof and part of the wall of a storied pavilion building are visible, partly blocked by foreground trees and mountains and rocks, presenting a half-hidden, half-revealed state. | Near ground at the lower-right corner: a house is built against the sloping bank and trees, and the building and trees interweave, forming layers of mutual foreground-background screening.
distinction: Although the near-ground house has the tendency of leaning against mountains and beside water, the painting as a whole emphasizes more the screening and revelation of buildings by woods, mountains, and rocks, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship dominates the spatial layers.

evidence: Top of the earth slope in the middle of the right page: a large tree with dry branches extends slanting across from the slope top, its trunk and twigs covering above and in front of the house, forming a foreground screening layer | To the middle right of the right page, behind the tree: a thatched-roof house is revealed through the gaps between trunk and branches; white walls, eaves, and window lattice are distinguishable, a seated figure is seen inside, and the left end of the building is cut off by branches | At the foot of the slope at the lower right of the right page: a figure holding a staff stands at the side of the slope; only moss dots and grass strokes are seen on the slope surface, and no recognizable path, bridge, or gate connects to the house
distinction: Although the house is located at the slope top, the dominant relationship is the foreground-background layer formed by the screening and half-revelation of the house by the large tree's trunk and branches, rather than the placement correspondence between base layout and slope forms and water conditions

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: the outlines of roofs and walls of several houses are visible, partly blocked by foreground trees and sloping rocks. | Slightly right of the center of the painting: branches and leaves of trees interweave with mountains and rocks, screening the built structures behind, forming a visual layer of half concealment and half revelation.
distinction: The painting emphasizes more the concealment-and-revelation relationship and spatial layers in which built structures are screened by woods, mountains, and rocks, rather than simply showing their layout conforming to the terrain.

evidence: Whole painting: the painting presents distant mountains, a middle-ground water surface, and foreground sloping rocks and trees; no clear traces of built structures such as houses, pavilions, bridges, or paths are seen. | Left side: there are inscriptions and seals, but they do not serve as evidence of built structures.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built elements and the specific category of spatial expression cannot be determined; it is assigned with difficulty based on the overall landscape composition.

evidence: At the edge of the sloping rocks at the lower right of the fan surface: pale ink outlines the roof, walls, and window lattice of a house; its left end meets the foot of a round rock slope in front and is cut off there, while behind and to the right it is further enclosed by sloping rocks and groves | Slightly below the center of the painting: the main slope is composed of piled round rocks and clustered trees, and the rock bodies and tree crowns screen the space behind the slope; the house is revealed from the right edge of this slope, forming a layer of seeing a house at the forest edge behind rocks | Upper part and left side of the fan surface: distant mountains and flat banks are arrayed horizontally in pale ink, and a large area of the water surface is left as unpainted space; only one recognizable built structure appears at the lower right of the whole painting, and its existence is suggested by the concealment-and-revelation relationship among sloping rocks and woods
distinction: The house is mainly suggested as being at its layer by the half-screening and half-revelation of sloping rocks and woods, rather than by the correspondence between the height of its base or its layout and the forms of the sloping bank

evidence: Middle-lower right: Between partly screening mountain rocks and trees, the roofs and wall outlines of several houses are faintly visible, appearing half-hidden and half-exposed. | Overall painting: The trees and mountain rocks of the foreground and middle ground noticeably screen the built elements on the right, constructing the painting's spatial layers through concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the built elements are placed at the foot of the mountain rocks, what the painting emphasizes more is the spatial layers formed by the screening and revelation of the buildings by trees and mountain rocks, rather than stressing a terrain-responsive correspondence between buildings and landform.

evidence: Center and right of the painting: Ink-rendered distant mountains, clumps of trees in the middle ground, and a near waterside are visible, presenting the front-to-back layers of a natural landscape. | Left side of the painting: Multiple columns of inscription are visible, but no forms of artificial built elements such as buildings, bridges, or paths can be seen.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built elements; based on the overall front-to-back screening and layering of the landscape, it is assigned to the closest category of spatial organization.

evidence: Lower-middle of the painting: The roofs and walls of several houses are visible, partly screened by the dense surrounding trees and mountain rocks, presenting spatial layers of alternating concealment and revelation. | Right side of the painting: The houses are arranged along the mountain foot and tree clumps; eaves and doors and windows appear through gaps in the trees, strengthening the visual effect of concealment and revelation forming a scene.
distinction: Although the houses nestle against the landscape, the painting emphasizes more the relationship of screening and revelation between trees and mountain rocks and the buildings, rather than mere placement by terrain.

evidence: Center-lower foreground: A sloped rock rises from the unpainted water surface, its top leveling into a flat terrace that opens toward the water, with the slope foot extending toward the lower-right water surface | Among the trees on the sloped terrace: Several tall trees and one weeping willow stand on the terrace top; between the trunks are pale ink horizontal strokes suspected to be eaves or pavilion pillars, but the forms are unclear in detail and cannot be reliably identified as built elements | Upper-middle: A band of mountains lies across the water on the far bank, facing the foreground sloped terrace across the water, forming a configuration of open water corresponding to the far shore

evidence: Right side of the painting: Roofs and eaves of buildings appear amid screening trees, presenting a half-hidden, half-exposed relationship of concealment and revelation. | Center to right of the painting: Dense trees and mountain rocks interweave, wrapping the built elements within, forming spatial layers of seeing houses deep in the woods.
distinction: Although the painting follows mountains and water, the most prominent scenic role of the built elements is to form layers through the screening and revelation of trees, rather than simply emphasizing placement according to terrain.

evidence: Center-left of the painting: Several houses are outlined in fine lines with gabled roofs and eaves; the building bodies are screened by a row of dark-ink trunks and dotted leaves in front, with only the roofs emerging above the treetops | Center of the painting: A small pavilion or roof with upturned corners emerges between tree clumps and sloped rocks, on the same level as the roofs on the left, suggesting the built elements are hidden behind the woods | Lower-middle: Dark-ink tree clumps and houses are placed together on a transverse sloped bank, below which unpainted space is water; houses and tree clumps overlap vertically to form front-to-back layers
distinction: Although the houses sit on the sloped bank, their visibility mainly comes from the layers of concealment and revelation in which roofs emerge from the tree clumps; the terrain placement relationship is weaker than the screening relationship of the trees.

evidence: Whole painting: The painting depicts distant mountains, clouds and mist, middle-ground woods, and foreground sloped-bank trees; the composition presents a complete landscape scene, with no clear built elements such as houses, bridges, or paths.
distinction: The painting is purely a presentation of landscape scenery with no clear participation of built elements; based on overall spatial organization it is assigned to the category of scenic accentuation as the closest match.

evidence: Lower-middle of the painting: The roofs and walls of several houses are visible, partly screened by surrounding tree branches and leaves, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Lower left and lower right of the painting: The built elements are scattered among the sloped banks and woods, forming spatial layers through the screening of tree clumps.
distinction: Although the buildings follow mountains and water, the most prominent scenic method in the painting is the screening and revelation of buildings by trees, rather than emphasizing the determining role of terrain in building layout.

evidence: Lower part and left side of the painting: Sloped-bank lines extend into the depth of the painting, forming the boundary between waterside and land, suggesting a space along which movement is possible. | Lower-left corner: There are blurred ink marks, resembling a figure or animal on the sloped bank, suggesting a clue to movement through the landscape, but no clear built elements. | Center and right of the painting: Trees grow on sloped-bank rocks, organizing front-to-back spatial layers, but no screening of buildings is seen.
distinction: The painting mainly consists of the natural organization of sloped-bank trees; the blurred ink marks in the lower-left corner suggest a route of movement rather than scenic accentuation buildings, so it is assigned to C4 rather than C3.

evidence: Upper-middle right of the painting: Amid encircling mountain rocks and screening trees, the roof and wall outlines of house buildings are visible; the buildings are partly screened by natural scenery, forming layers of concealment and revelation. | Middle of the painting: Clumps of trees and sloped rocks interweave, further screening the space behind and setting off the position of the buildings, which appear faintly visible.
distinction: Although the buildings follow the mountain terrain, the visual focus of the painting is the screening and revelation of the buildings by mountain rocks and trees, rather than emphasizing the site relationship of their terrain-based arrangement.

evidence: Lower right: The roofs and part of the walls of houses are visible, partly screened by trees and mountain rocks in front, appearing faintly visible. | Middle and left: Mountain rocks and trees occupy most of the painting, forming the foreground and middle ground and creating layers of concealment and revelation with the built elements at the lower right.
distinction: Although the built elements are located at the mountain foot, the painting emphasizes more the screening and revelation of the built elements by trees and mountain rocks to form spatial layers, so C2 fits better than C1.

evidence: Lower-middle of the painting: The roofs and walls of several houses are visible, partly screened by tree branches and leaves of the foreground and middle ground, presenting spatial layers of alternating concealment and revelation. | Background of the painting: Behind the houses are continuous mountain ranges, and woods surround the built elements, strengthening the visual effect of concealment and revelation forming a scene.
distinction: Although the houses are placed at the mountain foot, the painting highlights more the relationship of screening and revelation between trees and buildings, rather than emphasizing the determining role of terrain in layout.

evidence: Left and lower left: Behind the pine trees, roof and wall lines of houses are visible; the buildings are partly screened by trees, presenting layers of seeing houses in the woods. | Right: Behind the large trees, roof structures of buildings are faintly visible, screened by branches and leaves, forming a relationship of separated scenery. | Center: Several large trees stand on sloped ground as the foreground, screening the built elements behind, so that the relationship of concealment and revelation participates in forming the scene.
distinction: The painting mainly shows the screening and revelation of houses by trees to form spatial layers; although the sloped-ground lines below have a guiding feel, they lack a clearly identifiable movement route connecting to the built elements.

evidence: Right middle ground: A multi-story pavilion is screened behind pine trees, with only part of its eaves and upper structure exposed, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Upper distant view: Several houses on the waterside are screened by tree clumps and mountain rocks, with roofs and door-opening structures faintly visible. | Left middle ground: House outlines are faintly visible among the woods on the sloped bank; buildings and woods interweave with each other.
distinction: Although the built elements follow mountains and water, the painting emphasizes more the screening and revelation of buildings by trees and mountain rocks, creating spatial layers through concealment and revelation, so C2 fits better than C1.

evidence: Center and right of the painting: Many trees grow in clumps, their trunks and branches interweaving, forming front-to-back spatial layers | Lower part of the painting: Sloped-bank lines extend horizontally, meeting the water surface | Upper part and left of the painting: Distant mountains are rendered in pale ink, their outlines blurred
distinction: The painting mainly presents the front-to-back layers of screening between woods and sloped banks; although there are no built elements, the spatial organization is closer to a relationship of concealment and revelation than to emphasis on a single scenic node.

evidence: Center-left: Two buildings (pavilion/house) are hidden in a clump of withered trees, with roofs and walls partly exposed, presenting layers of screening in the woods. | Middle ground right: A small path leads to an arched-door-like structure, suggesting a route, but the building body is still wrapped by its surroundings. | Right and foreground: Huge mountain rocks and trees form a visual barrier, setting off the hiddenness and concealment-and-revelation relationship of the central buildings.
distinction: Although the painting has a path and an arched opening suggesting entry (C4), the buildings mainly form the scene through their relationship of concealment and revelation with woods and mountain rocks (C2); concealment and revelation forming a scene is more dominant.

evidence: On the mountain-hollow slope left of center: Rows of house roofs spread in staggered heights along a gentle slope; the building site lies on a sloped terrace clearing flanked by two mountains, with rows of pine woods encircling both sides and the rear | Left middle-section sloped bank: One house is placed alone on the sloped bank, with open water below the slope; the house base is set according to the slope | Lower-left rock: Behind the rock, a thatched roof and a vertical pole are exposed; the house stands at the rock's edge, facing the water
distinction: The houses are mainly characterized by placement spreading in staggered heights along the sloped terrace and by sitting by the bank and against the rock; the roofs are clearly exposed in rows rather than revealed through screening by woods, so C1 is chosen rather than C2.

evidence: Lower-middle: A low stone wall runs across the painting, its body partly screened by the trunks and branches and leaves of multiple trees, forming front-to-back layers. | Center: A rectangular door opening is set in the center of the wall; the opening appears among the trees, and a hexagonal stone platform is visible within. | Lower left: A wooden fence gate is set by the roadside, enclosing an interior space together with the stone wall.
distinction: Although the painting has a door opening and a fence gate suggesting entry, the core of the composition lies in the front-to-back screening and revelation between trees and the wall; the relationship of concealment and revelation forming a scene is more prominent.

evidence: Lower-middle to right of the painting: A winding path with a stone-revetment slope extends from the lower left; tiny figures are visible on the path, which clearly leads to the building group on the right. | Right side of the painting: Multiple buildings with roofs and courtyard walls are visible; the path connects directly to this building area, forming an accessible spatial relationship.
distinction: Although the buildings are partly screened by trees, the clear path guidance and the route of figures moving in the painting more prominently express the spatial process of proceeding from here to there and approaching the built elements.
