evidence: Center-left: A walled courtyard and its main hall sit on a level terrace; another platform below the terrace edge extends toward the water, and the wall outline turns according to the terrace edge | Upper left to center: The mountain slope extends diagonally from the upper left to behind the courtyard; scattered rocks at the slope foot stop behind the courtyard wall, and the buildings are placed with their backs against the slope foot | Waterside below: The edge of the terrace base directly faces the water; waves lap the bank, a boat is moored on the water below the terrace base, and the gate house in the courtyard wall opens toward the waterside
distinction: Although the boat and gate house suggest that arrival is possible, the painting lacks a continuous path linking them into a process of entry; the dominant relationship is the terrain-based placement of the courtyard on layered terraces according to the slope and the waterside.

evidence: Center-left mountain slope: The roofs and walls of a group of built elements emerge from dense pine woods, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation in which they are half-screened by the woods. | Lower-right waterside: A pavilion is built between bank rocks and trees, with part of its structure screened by branches and sloped rocks.
distinction: Although the built elements are arranged according to the mountain terrain, the painting emphasizes more the screening and revelation of buildings by trees, forming spatial layers through concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower-left-middle valley: A group of gray-roofed buildings lies behind withered trees and sloped rocks; roofs and part of the walls emerge through gaps in the branches, with branches in front screening the building bodies horizontally | Center-right slope: A house with ochre walls and a gray roof is placed among rows of pine woods, its body surrounded by trunks and canopies in front and behind, appearing as a house revealed in the woods | Middle slope: Rows of trees are distributed along the slope ridge lines and slope surfaces, separating the hollow where the houses lie and the forest gaps into several front-to-back layers
distinction: Although the houses sit in slope hollows and forest clearings on the slope, the painting mainly relies on woods and sloped rocks screening and then revealing roofs and walls to indicate the presence and layers of built elements; the concealment-and-revelation relationship organizes the built elements more directly than terrain correspondence.

evidence: Among the mountain rocks at the upper middle-right: A small building is visible, nestled in a recess of the mountain rocks and partly screened by the surrounding rocks, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Right-side mountain rock structure: The mountain rocks encircle the building, forming the screening and revelation of the built elements by natural scenery and constituting spatial layers.
distinction: Although the building is placed according to the mountain terrain, its half-screened, half-exposed relationship of concealment and revelation with the mountain rocks is visually more prominent and dominates the way the scene is composed.

evidence: Lower-middle of the painting and the middle water surface: Several short vertical lines are faintly visible, suspected to be masts or wooden posts, but their forms are extremely blurred and cannot be confirmed as clear built elements. | Overall painting: The painting is dominated by distant mountains, misty waves, and moonlight, and lacks clear built forms such as buildings, bridges, or paths.
distinction: The painting contains only extremely blurred short lines suspected to be waterside structures, with no clear built elements; based on the overall space they are regarded as faint elements accentuating the waterside scenery and assigned to C3.

evidence: Lower-middle: A stone arch bridge spans the water, with pedestrians on the bridge, connecting the left and right banks and forming a clear passage route. | Lower right: A village building group is distributed along the waterside and woods, connected to the opposite bank by the bridge, presenting an accessible spatial relationship. | Left mountainside: A small number of houses are placed in staggered heights according to the mountain terrain, echoing mountain paths or the waterside.
distinction: Although there are elements built according to the mountains, the movement clues and sense of entry organized by the bridge and village are more prominent and dominate the spatial expression.

evidence: Lower left to center-left mountain path: A line of riders and walkers proceeds uphill along a narrow mountain path, which winds around the foreground sloped rocks deep toward the mountain ridge. | Center-left among the pine woods: A roof is half-exposed among pine branches, located right beside the turning point where the mountain path goes uphill. | Upper-left mountain top: A multi-story, multi-eaved pavilion stands on the ridge, its lower part screened by tree canopies, located above the direction in which the mountain path extends.
distinction: The travelers and the winding mountain path link the half-hidden pavilion with the pavilion above, constituting a process of approaching the built elements from below the mountain and turning into the depths; although concealment and revelation are visible, they are only a partial mode of presenting the built elements and play a less organizing role than the movement clues running through the lower half of the composition.

evidence: Left middle among the tree clumps: A house reveals its roof, eaves, white walls, and pillars; most of the building body is screened by trees in front and behind, presenting layers of seeing a house in the woods | Upper center-left ridge: In the diagonal vegetation of the ridge, a pointed-roof pavilion- or pagoda-like built structure is half-exposed; only the top and eaves are visible, the rest hidden in the slope vegetation | Lower-right stream gully: A bridge with railings spans the stream; a pedestrian is on the bridge, both ends of which disappear into trees and rocks, with no visible path connecting to the built elements on the mountain
distinction: Although the bridge and pedestrian suggest movement, no discernible connection between them and the built elements on the mountain is seen; the built elements mainly form spatial layers through screening by trees and half-exposure, so concealment and revelation forming a scene is primary.

evidence: Left-middle sloped bank: Multi-story pavilion buildings are placed in tiers on the slope; roofs, eaves, and railings emerge from the tree clumps in front and behind, and the lower parts of the building bodies are screened by the canopies in front, forming layers of seeing houses in the woods through concealment and revelation | Lower center: An arch bridge spans the stream; the left end of the bridge disappears into the lower-left tree-clump sloped bank, and no clearly discernible path connection with the pavilions is seen | Right-middle slope: A person on horseback proceeds uphill along the mountain path on the right slope, the path extending into the valley, with no direct connection to the pavilions on the left bank
distinction: Although the bridge and mountain path provide clues to movement, they do not form a discernible entry connection with the pavilions; the pavilions mainly form spatial layers through screening by tree clumps and the exposure of roofs, so C2 is primary.

evidence: Left side and middle ground of the painting: Houses and fences are visible on the left bank; in the middle ground a small bridge spans the water, connecting the two banks. | Lower foreground of the painting: A thatched pavilion stands in the foreground, with a figure herding cattle in front of it, forming a coherent movement clue with the sloped bank and small bridge in the lower-left corner. | Overall painting: The stream winds through the painting; the bridge, thatched pavilion, and paths suggest an accessible, explorable spatial process.
distinction: Although the built elements are arranged along the waterside, the bridge and thatched pavilion emphasize more the movement routes and the spatial process of entering the depths, rather than mere terrain adaptation.

evidence: Lower-middle to right of the painting: Multi-story pavilions and attached buildings rise in tiers according to the mountain slope, with tall platform bases and stairways at the bottom, unfolding in accordance with the undulations of the terrain. | Lower left to lower middle of the painting: A city wall is built winding along the mountain terrain, connecting building nodes at different elevations, presenting a spatial form of defense by terrain advantage and terrain-based arrangement. | Right side of the painting: Pagodas and pavilions are distributed in staggered positions at different places on the mountain slope; the building sites form a clear correspondence and dependence relationship with mountain rocks and sloped terraces.
distinction: Although the buildings are large in scale and landmark-like (C3), their tiered platform bases, the alignment of the city wall, and the overall layout's compliance with and use of the mountain slope (C1) are the more dominant logic of spatial organization.

evidence: Left side of the central main peak, midway up the slope: a single house sits on a sloping terrace at a recess in the mountainside of the main peak; the building itself and its roof are fully exposed, and the building site conforms to the shape of the recess | Right side, upper-middle ridge: the roof of the building extends along the ridge line, the lower half of the building itself is submerged behind the sloping bank and trees, and its placement rises and falls with the height of the ridge | Lower foreground sloping bank: the foreground is a sloping bank with clusters of trees; a single figure is visible in the lower right corner, but no bridge, path, gate, or other movement clue connecting built elements is seen
distinction: The building sites and heights of the two built structures are both placed according to the mountain terrain's recessed terraces and ridge lines, and the relationship of terrain participating in the layout runs through the whole painting; the right building being half-hidden in trees is only local concealment and revelation, insufficient to serve as a dominant explanation

evidence: Center-left: a group of houses is arranged in tiers on mountain slope platforms, presenting a layout of houses set on platforms and separately placed according to the slope, closely integrated with the terrain. | Upper right: at the mountain top, a building base and roof are visible, placed according to the towering mountain form. | Lower right: in the waterside woodland there is a pavilion, arranged against the water bank and terrain.
distinction: Although some built elements are screened by trees, the correspondence between multiple built elements in the painting (especially the house group at center-left) and the mountain forms and slope platforms is more prominent and widespread, so C1 is dominant.

evidence: Among the cliffs at upper center: the top and body of a multi-story pagoda emerge from behind the cliff and pine trees, forming a clear relationship of concealment and revelation. | Center of the painting: the foreground pines and the cliff behind form layer upon layer of screening around the pagoda, placing the built structure within deep spatial layers.
distinction: Although there are figures and a faint path in the lower part of the painting, they lack a clear connecting and entering relationship with the pagoda above; the dominant expression remains the screening of built elements by mountains, rocks, and trees.

evidence: Lower center: a multi-story pavilion and covered corridor are surrounded by trees in the foreground and middle ground; the building itself and railings are partly obscured by leaves, forming a clear relationship of concealment and revelation. | Left: a platform building is hidden behind tree clusters, figures move on the platform, and the building and trees form a spatial layering of foreground-background screening. | Upper right: behind mountains, rocks, and trees a building roof is faintly visible, further enriching the layers of screening.
distinction: Although the buildings are set against mountains and beside water, the painting mainly constructs spatial layers through the screening and revealing of buildings by trees; the characteristic of concealment and revelation forming a setting is more dominant.

evidence: Lower center to right: clear plank-road and bridge structures are visible extending along the cliff and water bank, connecting different areas. | Lower center of the painting: pedestrians and horses advance on the plank road, presenting a spatial process of moving from here to there, approaching built structures, or turning into the depths. | Left hillside and right cliff: houses, pavilions, and other built elements are visible, linked with the plank road and travel route.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed according to mountain forms, the painting more strongly emphasizes the spatial process of guiding the eye and path into pictorial depth through the plank road and travel clues.

evidence: Right hillside: a multi-story pagoda and halls rise in tiers according to the mountain form; the base closely fits the slope platforms and rocks, presenting a layout built according to the mountain. | Lower center of the painting: a covered bridge spans the water surface, connecting the mountain rocks on both sides; its direction follows the opening and closing relationship of the water bank and terrain.
distinction: Although the painting contains travel clues such as bridges and paths, the overall characteristic of built elements following the mountain and unfolding with the terrain's height is more significant and dominates the spatial organization.

evidence: Central main peak summit: a multi-story pagoda and several hall roof ridges are arrayed on the flat summit of the rounded peak; the base is placed according to the summit platform, flanked by tree clusters on both sides | Left middle-lower slope: several groups of houses are arranged downslope along the slope ridge line, the building bases rising and falling with the slope | Lower central mountain foot: a walled courtyard with an arched gate and a double-eaved pavilion occupy a gentle slope platform at the mountain foot, surrounded by trees in front; on the right, a winding stream path is also seen climbing the slope to the upper-right house
distinction: The summit pagoda courtyard certainly has the effect of marking the peak, but built elements from summit to slope ridge to mountain foot are all placed according to the heights of the terrain; terrain correspondence runs through the entire painting and explains the main spatial organization better than a single scenic marker

evidence: Lower-left corner: faint traces of tiny figures and what appear to be a thatched hut or pavilion are visible at the mountain foot by the water, but their form is blurred due to damage to the painting. | Whole painting: the painting is dominated by high mountains, waterfalls, and woodland; there are many creases and flaking, and no other clearly identifiable built structures are seen.
distinction: The traces in the lower-left corner are too blurred to confirm any layered relationship of screening by trees, mountains, and rocks; they can only be regarded as a tiny accent within the grand landscape.

evidence: Middle-ground left: built elements are partly obscured by trees, with only the roof and part of the wall exposed, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Foreground center: built elements are screened behind several large trees; eaves and partial structures emerge through gaps in the branches and leaves. | Middle-ground right: screened by mountains, rocks, and trees, two figures stand among them, suggesting spatial layers.
distinction: Although the built elements are placed beside water, the painting more strongly emphasizes the spatial layers formed by the screening and revealing of built elements by trees, rather than mere placement according to terrain.

evidence: Lower left: thatched buildings are visible; their roofs and walls are partly obscured by foreground trees, presenting a layer of houses revealed within the woods. | Center right: in the clouds and mist on the hillside a building outline is faintly visible, screened by trees and mist, appearing indistinct.
distinction: Although the buildings are set against mountains and beside water, the painting more strongly emphasizes the screening and revealing of buildings by trees and mist, forming spatial layers of alternating concealment and exposure, rather than simply emphasizing placement according to terrain.

evidence: Lower right: a bridge is visible connecting the water bank with a pavilion, forming a clear entering and transitional space. | Lower left: a courtyard is arranged according to the mountain foot and pine woods, forming a terrain-responsive relationship with the surrounding mountains, rocks, and trees. | Middle ground and lower right: pavilions are built on the hillside and at the water's edge, together with the bridge and water bank forming a traversable spatial clue.
distinction: Although the built elements set against mountains and beside water embody terrain-responsive siting, the guiding role of the bridge and path is more prominent, emphasizing the process of movement from here to there.

evidence: Lower center of the painting: groups of figures sit around tables among trees and mountains and rocks; no fixed built structures such as pavilions or halls are seen. | Upper right of the painting: between bamboo grove and mountains and rocks two people sit facing each other, likewise with no building screening or support. | Whole painting: figure activity is directly scattered among natural landscape, woods, and trees, relying on trees and mountains and rocks to form spatial layers.
distinction: No clear built elements are seen in the painting; figures and scenery are directly combined, with layers formed by the screening of trees and mountains and rocks, so it is assigned to C2.

evidence: Lower right: a small bridge is visible spanning across, connecting foreground and middle ground, forming a clear passage clue. | Lower left: a building group built against the mountain is visible, with a path or open ground in front echoing the direction of the bridge. | Lower center: figures are visible near the path or bridge, suggesting a process of movement through the landscape and entry into the building space.
distinction: Although the painting has buildings arranged according to mountain forms (C1), the combination of bridge, path, and figures more strongly expresses the spatial process of moving from here to there and approaching built structures (C4).

evidence: Lower center: a platform or plank road supported by multiple wooden posts is visible, erected between the stream and mountains and rocks, with two people sitting on it. | Left and center: the platform is set against mountains, rocks, and trees, placed according to the waterside terrain, presenting a terrain-responsive arrangement.
distinction: Although the platform has figures as scenic accents, its post-supported structure clearly depends on the waterside and mountain-rock terrain, and the characteristic of terrain-responsive placement is more prominent.

evidence: Middle-lower slope to the right: a person on a donkey advances to the right along a path on the slope, while another walking attendant carrying an object follows at lower left; the path turns out from among the lower-left slope rocks and crosses the slope, constituting a movement clue | Slope foot below the middle-lower path: a row of thin vertical wooden fencing or hedges is set along the slope foot parallel to the path, indicating artificial enclosure beside the path, but no identifiable houses are seen within the enclosure | Middle to left slope: sparse woods and withered trees densely cover the slope; the path passes between the forest edge and slope rocks, and the gaze follows the figures from the foreground into the depths of the forested ravine
distinction: The dominant feature of the painting is the process, constituted by the path and traveling figures, of turning into the depths and approaching the enclosure, rather than forming a scene through roofs and eaves concealed and revealed by trees

evidence: Whole painting: the painting consists mainly of mountains and rocks, trees, and sloping ground; no clear houses, bridges, paths, or other artificial built elements are seen. | Center-left of the painting: a cluster of red trees contrasts with the surrounding green mountains and rocks, becoming the visual focus of the painting.
distinction: No built elements are visible in the painting, so its mode of spatial organization cannot be determined; it is only tentatively assigned to C3 on the basis of the visual focal role of natural scenery.

evidence: Upper left: a group of pavilion buildings is placed at the edge of a protruding rocky platform, the base adjoining the mountain rock. | Lower center: a courtyard building is partly obscured by the twisting ancient pine branches in the foreground and by trees on the right, with only part of the roof, eaves, and walls exposed, forming layers of concealment and revelation. | Foreground and middle ground: foreground boulders and trees form a foreground-background screening relationship with the lower-center buildings, which are half-hidden among woods, mountains, and rocks.
distinction: Although the left pavilion has the characteristic of being placed on a mountain platform, the screening and revealing relationship formed by the lower-center courtyard with trees, mountains, and rocks is more prominent and dominates the painting's spatial layers.

evidence: Right center: a group of buildings (pavilions and houses) is arrayed along the water bank line, with supporting posts or bases visible at the bottom facing the water, presenting a layout unfolding along the bank and conforming to the waterside terrain. | Lower water surface: a boat is located in the waters below the painting, its bow pointing toward the upper-right buildings; although this suggests waterway transport, the building layout mainly reflects placement beside the water. | Left and above: mountains, rocks, and trees are located to the left of and above the buildings; the buildings stand in the open area of the mountain-foot water bay, arranged according to the terrain.
distinction: Although a boat suggests waterway access pointing toward the buildings, the layout characteristic of the buildings themselves unfolding along the water bank (the waterside-pavilion form) is more significant, and there is no clear physical connection between boat and buildings (such as a bridge or dock directly linking them), so C1 is more apt than C4.

evidence: Lower center of the painting: an elder and a youth are seen walking along the waterside slope, presenting a state of movement through the landscape. | Whole painting: the painting consists of mountains and rocks, trees, water, and figures; no traces of houses, bridges, or any other built elements are seen.
distinction: There are no built elements in the painting; it is assigned to the closest category solely on the basis of the movement clue of figures walking along the water bank.

evidence: Right-center woodland: through the screening of trees, lines resembling a roof and building structure are faintly visible, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Left: towering peaks and rocks, with no obvious built elements. | Below: slope rocks, withered trees, and water surface, with no obvious built elements.
distinction: The building is mainly obscured by trees to form spatial layers, rather than serving as a conspicuous scenic marker.

evidence: Middle-lower left: a group of house buildings is visible, arranged against the mountain and beside water, surrounded by trees. | Right middle-lower: a bridge spans the water surface, with a figure painted on it, forming a clear movement clue connecting the opposite bank with the building area. | Whole painting: bridge, water bank, and buildings together form a spatial relationship of moving from here to there that can be entered and traveled through.
distinction: Although the buildings are screened by trees, the movement clues of the bridge and pedestrians are more prominent and dominate the painting's sense of spatial entry.

evidence: Lower left: a wooden beam bridge crosses the stream diagonally, its right end resting on flat ground on the stream bank; two figures stand on the flat ground, and the bank ground rises to connect with a masonry-platform building, forming a clue to approaching built structures by crossing the stream | Center left: the building group is built on a tiered masonry platform; at the foot of the slope to the lower right of the platform base is a small roofed gatehouse-style pavilion with figures inside, seemingly a node for entering the platform courtyard | Center to upper center: the stream valley opens upward beside the buildings into a gentle water surface, and a group of pavilions emerges faintly in the mist, linking with the foreground bridge and midground buildings into a depth sequence running from near to far and turning into the deeper recesses
distinction: The bridge, bank ground, gatehouse, and the valley's extension link into a process of movement through the landscape that is reachable and can turn into the deeper recesses, with built structures organizing the whole picture as sequence nodes; although the placement of the platform base against the slope and beside the stream is visible, it only accounts for the local form of the built structures and does not cover the connecting role of the bridge and the pedestrians' route

evidence: Lower center of the painting: several people are seen around a long table; in the background are banana plants and lake rocks, and no clear houses or pavilion buildings are seen. | Right and center of the painting: banana leaves and lake rocks form a foreground-background screening relationship; the figures are between plants and mountains and rocks, presenting a certain spatial layering.
distinction: No clear buildings are seen in the painting, only a courtyard scene formed by plants, mountains and rocks, and figures; on the basis of the overall spatial layers it is tentatively assigned to concealment and revelation forming a setting, but lacks evidence of actual buildings.

evidence: Lower center of the painting: figures and an ox cart are seen advancing along a path beside the water bank, presenting a movement clue. | Right side of the painting: a stream winds along, creating a sense of spatial extension with the direction of the figures' advance.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built elements, but the advancing relationship of figures and path is closest to the spatial organization of access to secluded settings.

evidence: Center of the painting: a group of house buildings is half-screened by trees and mountains and rocks, with only part of the roofs, eaves, and walls exposed, forming clear spatial layers of concealment and revelation. | Center-right of the painting: through gaps in the trees a small bridge is faintly visible, connecting the two banks and helping to convey the spatial depth of the setting. | Lower-center water surface: a boat with an awning cabin is moored or moving on the water, echoing the screened buildings on the bank.
distinction: Although the painting contains movement clues such as a bridge and boat, the concealment-and-revelation relationship in which the central building group is screened by woods, mountains, and rocks and then revealed is more central and dominates the painting's spatial composition.

evidence: Right-hand painted panel: pine trees, sloping rocks, distant mountains and a boat moored by the water are visible; no clear built structures such as houses or bridges are seen. | Left-hand painted panel: the painting is essentially blank, with only seals, and no built structures or landscape details.
distinction: There is no clear built structure in the painting; only natural landscape, scenic-accent figures and a boat are seen, so it is assigned to scenic accentuation on the basis of the overall scenery.

evidence: Left-hand painted panel: the painting mainly depicts huge mountain rocks and moss dots, with a few tree branches and leaves in the upper left corner; no clear built structures such as houses or bridges are seen.
distinction: No built structure is visible in the painting; it is assigned to the closest category on the basis of the overall visible forms of the mountain rocks.

evidence: Left middle ground: house outlines are faintly visible among tree clusters, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation beneath the screening of woodland. | Right middle-lower: outlines of house roofs and walls are visible, surrounded by trees, mountains, and rocks, forming layers of screening. | Overall painting: multiple built elements are scattered among mountain forests and sloping ground, mostly obscured by vegetation, with details somewhat blurred because the painting's tones are relatively dark.
distinction: Although the buildings are distributed according to mountain forms and sloping ground, what is more visually prominent is the spatial layering formed by the screening and revealing of buildings by trees, mountains, and rocks.

evidence: Lower-left corner: a figure is seen standing on mountains and rocks, facing the cliff and waterfall to the right, with no building or path connected. | Right and center: mainly cliffs, waterfall, and protruding pines; no traces of built elements are seen.
distinction: The painting has no clear built elements; figure activity alone marks the waterfall-viewing scenery, so in the absence of building evidence it is assigned to C3 on the basis of overall spatial organization.

evidence: Left middle-lower: a pavilion is built on a stone base, screened above and around by tree branches and leaves, revealing eaves, pillars, and figures inside the pavilion, presenting a layer of seeing a house within the woods. | Right center: in mist or open space a pavilion roof outline is faintly visible, creating a deep sense of spatial depth through seeing a house across a barrier.
distinction: Although the pavilion being built on a stone base has the characteristic of terrain-responsive siting, the painting more strongly emphasizes the screening and revealing of buildings by trees and mist, constructing spatial layers through concealment and revelation.

evidence: Whole painting: The picture consists mainly of pine branches, mountains and rocks, plum blossoms, and birds; no traces of built structures such as houses, pavilions, or bridges are visible.
distinction: No built elements are visible; the closest placeholder classification is based only on the overall composition.

evidence: Lower left: A thatched hut is partly screened by the mountains and rocks and trees in front of it, with only the roof and part of the building itself exposed, forming a relation of concealment and revelation. | Lower right: Another building is partly screened behind the trees and rocks on the right, merging with the natural environment. | Middle distance: The vague outlines of a sailboat or building can be faintly seen, half-hidden among clouds, mist, and trees, increasing the painting's spatial depth.
distinction: Although there is a clue in the lower part of the painting of a figure riding a horse across a small bridge, the overall painting emphasizes more the deep spatial layering created by buildings screened by mountains, rocks, and trees, rather than stressing the process of entering along a path.

evidence: Whole painting: The picture depicts pine trees, mountains and rocks, water ripples, and a flock of cranes; no houses, bridges, paths, or other man-made built elements are visible. | Lower middle: Mountains and rocks and flowing water are distributed according to natural forms; cranes perch on the rocky bank, presenting a natural ecological scene.
distinction: The painting lacks evidence of man-made built elements; it is reluctantly assigned to C1 based on the distribution of natural scenery over the terrain, with no other manifestation of built space.

evidence: Whole painting: The picture consists mainly of cliffs, withered trees, flying birds, flowing water, and birds in the lower left corner; no clear built elements such as houses or bridges are visible. | Upper middle: The forms of the mountains and rocks are prominent, with a flock of flying birds on the right, forming an open natural scene. | Lower left: Birds and plants with red leaves can be seen as accents of the natural scene.
distinction: The painting lacks evidence of built elements; it is reluctantly assigned to C3 based on the overall opening and closing of the landscape and the presentation of natural scenery, with no other clear built clues competing.

evidence: Lower left middle: Beneath the cliff, the roof and pillars of a built structure are visible, placed close against the sloping bank at the foot of the mountain. | Lower left to lower right: A clear path extends along the waterside and the mountains and rocks; on the path are pedestrians and a person riding a donkey, forming a clear clue to movement through the landscape. | Left side: The path connects with the built structure on the left and is led along the mountain forms into the depth of the painting, presenting a spatial process of moving from here to there.
distinction: Although the built structure is placed at the foot of the mountain, the path and the figures' movement run through the spatial organization more prominently, emphasizing an enterable process of travel.

evidence: Whole painting: The picture depicts plum blossoms, camellias, mountains and rocks, and various birds; no houses, bridges, paths, or any other man-made built structures are visible.
distinction: There are no built elements in the painting, so C1-C4 cannot be distinguished according to the definitions; by rule it is forcibly assigned to C3.

evidence: Lower middle: A building is visible, its structure and the figures inside clearly discernible, with its left edge partly screened by the mountains and rocks and trees in the foreground. | Around the building: Mountains and rocks and trees on the left and pines on the right surround the building, forming screening and revealing of the built structure by natural scenery and presenting a spatial layering in which the house is seen through a screen. | Upper part and background: A towering cliff stands behind the building; the building is placed beneath the cliff and partly screened by natural scenery.
distinction: Although the building marks the scene beneath the cliff, the painting emphasizes more the spatial layering formed by its screening and revealing through the surrounding trees and mountains and rocks, so C2 is more apt.

evidence: Center-left of the painting, behind tree trunks: The faint outline of something like a roof or building structure is visible, partly screened by trunks and foliage, its details blurred and unclear. | Overall painting: Dominated by old trees, reeds, waterfowl, and flying birds; no clearly discernible built structures, paths, bridges, or other man-made features are visible.
distinction: The painting lacks clear evidence of built elements; only behind the tree trunks is there a very blurred suspected screened structure, so it is reluctantly assigned to concealment and revelation, but this cannot be confirmed.

evidence: Lower-left foreground: A stone arch bridge spans the water, with several people standing on it gazing into the distance, forming a clear clue to movement through the landscape and a starting point for entering the painting. | Mid-ground mountainside: Among trees and mountains and rocks, a pavilion, a gazebo, and a pagoda are visible, serving as the endpoint of the gaze of the people on the bridge and the destination of the journey. | Center of the mid-ground: A stream flows out from among the mountains and rocks, connecting the foreground water with the mid-ground buildings and helping to explain the extension and deepening of space.
distinction: Although the mid-ground buildings have a layering of concealment and revelation, the bridge and figures in the foreground form a stronger guidance for movement through the landscape, making the painting present a spatial process of moving from here to there.

evidence: Lower part to left middle of the painting: In the lower part, a figure carrying something walks upward along the rocky sloping bank, forming a discernible line of movement through the landscape that points toward the rocky platform in the upper left where two people sit facing each other. | Left middle of the painting: Two people sit talking on a rocky platform, a potential arrival point of the line of movement, constituting spatial layering and process.
distinction: Through the line of movement of the figures walking along the mountain path, the painting expresses a reachable spatial process, rather than merely marking a scene in isolation with figures or scenery.

evidence: Upper middle: Between the mountains and rocks and the trees, a vague building outline or roof is faintly visible, partly screened by natural scenery. | Foreground: A figure riding a donkey and an attendant walk among the trees, surrounded by trees and mountains and rocks, forming foreground and background layering.
distinction: Although the figures have movement, no clear path or clue is visible directly connecting to that vague built structure, so concealment and revelation is closer to the visible relation of screening than access to secluded settings.

evidence: Bottom: A bridge with railings (or a plank walkway) spans the water, connecting the left and right banks, with pedestrians crossing on it. | Right cliff: The right end of the bridge connects to the towering cliff on the right, on which there are trees and a partial, suspected building, forming a path extending into the depths.
distinction: Although there is a partial building on the right cliff screened by trees and mountains and rocks (C2), the bridge at the bottom, as a clear clue to movement through the landscape, dominates the painting's spatial organization of moving from here to there and toward the depths, so C4 is more apt.

evidence: Left middle: Among the trees, the roof of a building is faintly revealed, half-screened by the surrounding withered branches and woodland, forming a spatial layering of concealment and revelation. | Lower part of the painting: Two people walk through gaps between the mountains and rocks and the trees, suggesting a path leading into the depths.
distinction: The concealment and revelation of the building through the screening of the woodland is clearer than the faint path below, which does not form a coherent clue for entering.

evidence: Lower middle, slightly right: A white plank bridge spans a stream gorge; the left end of the bridge connects to an open flat area that leads directly to the front courtyard of the building in the lower left. | Lower left: A thatched pavilion and a tile-roofed building are placed beside the open space; two or three figures walk on the open ground in front of the building, facing toward it. | Middle to middle left: A stream waterfall pours down from a mountain hollow and extends along the sloping rocks to the stream gorge beneath the bridge; among the clouds and mist in the hollow a small pavilion is revealed, forming with the foreground bridge and path a sequence of turning from outside into the depths.
distinction: Although the building is surrounded by trees and rocks, its main body is openly exposed on the front courtyard reached by the bridge path; the painting is dominated by the process of crossing the bridge to approach the building, rather than layering of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Center-left of the mid-ground: Between the huge rock and the dense trees, parts of an eave and wall lightly outlined in pale ink seem to be exposed, mostly screened by leaves and the rock mass, leaving only a blurred outline. | Lower center: A figure in red sits alone at the edge of the sloping bank, facing the open unpainted water to the left, with no bridge, path, gate, or other clue to movement through the landscape beside them. | Between the upper part and the mid-ground: The main mountain and the mid-ground rocks and trees are separated by a large area of unpainted space; the mid-ground trees and the huge rock pile into layers of screening.
distinction: The suspected built structure exists only as a partly exposed form after being screened by trees and rocks; concealment and revelation is its only discernible compositional function. The correspondence of the building site with the sloping platform and the waterside cannot be discerned here, so C1 is not chosen.

evidence: Upper-right hillside: A thatched pavilion sits on a gently sloping platform formed by a turn in the mountain forms; the pavilion's pillars are set according to the high and low points of the slope, and the building site corresponds to the way the slope surface unfolds. | Slightly below the upper-right pavilion: A waterfall flows down step by step along the slope from the mountain gorge beside the pavilion; the pavilion's placement is adjacent to and echoes the configuration of the gorge stream and waterside. | Lower-middle open ground by the stream: Three people stand on the open stream bank, one raising a hand to point into the mountains, but no path, bridge, gate, or other clue for entering connecting the figures to the pavilion is visible in the painting.
distinction: The pavilion has its pillars set on the sloping platform and corresponds in site to the mountain forms and the adjacent gorge stream; its compositional function lies in terrain-responsive placement. By comparison, its role in marking a landing point at a certain peak edge or valley mouth is less clear than the correspondence with the terrain.

evidence: Left middle, among the trees: Through the screening of the woodland, a roof with vermilion eaves and a platform-like horizontal line beneath it are revealed; the building itself is screened by trunks and foliage, with only the roof and eaves visible. | Left edge middle, sloping bank: At the edge of the trees and sloping bank, a corner of a building and a railing-like structure are also visible, on the same level as the roof in the woods, forming a relation in which the house is seen through a screen. | Lower center valley: The unpainted stream valley winds from below upward, flanked by sloping rocks on both banks, but no bridge, path, gate, or other clue to movement through the landscape directly connects with the house in the woods.
distinction: Although the valley path below has a tendency to extend inward, no bridge, path, or gate connects it to the building; the building mainly suggests layering through screening by woodland and exposure of the roof, so concealment and revelation is more apt than access to secluded settings.

evidence: Upper-left ridge: A roof with upturned ridges and eaves is revealed from behind the sloping bank and trees; the lower part of the building itself is screened by the slope surface and leaves, with only the upper part visible. | Slightly below and right of the upper-left main house: Another small patch of roof is obliquely revealed among the trees on the slope, on the same screened level as the main house. | Middle to foreground of the painting: Clusters of trees, large rocks, and banana leaves occupy the mid-ground, forming a layer of screening; the building at the left edge can be seen only through gaps in the slope trees.
distinction: The visible relation is mainly that of roofs revealed from screening by slope trees, suggesting layering of concealment and revelation; the correspondence of the building site with the form of the sloping platform (platform base, layout along the slope) is less clear in the painting than the relation of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower left: A two-story pavilion stands on the cliff top overlooking the river; the lower part of the building itself is supported on the precipice by dense pillars, and the building site fits closely with the configuration of the cliff bank. | Lower right to middle right: Several groups of buildings are placed level by level along sloping platforms and mountain ridges, their roofs rising and falling with the mountain forms; at the bottom, a roofed corridor building follows the sloping bank and connects with the buildings on the platform. | Middle-right cliff top: A freestanding pavilion is set at the edge of a projecting platform, its base seated on the platform surface, facing out over the great expanse of unpainted river water to the left.
distinction: The corridor building at the bottom serves only as a local connection, whereas the building sites and heights of the many built structures throughout the painting are arranged according to the cliff tops, sloping platforms, and riverbanks, and the relation of terrain-responsive placement runs through the composition.

evidence: Left of the painting's center: Multiple roofs and eaves galleries are revealed in layers behind dark tree clusters; the lower part of the buildings is screened by the foreground woodland and sloping rocks, presenting a layering of houses seen among the woods through screening and exposure. | At the rocks to the right of the painting's center: A small house is half-hidden in a gap behind a huge rock jutting out diagonally, with only its roof and one wall exposed, appearing through the screening of the rock face. | Lower part of the painting: A plank bridge spans a stream gorge, with one person standing on the bridge; the end of the bridge disappears into sloping rocks and is cut off from the mid-ground house among the woods by the diagonally projecting huge rock, with no discernible path connection.
distinction: Although the buildings sit on a mountain-hollow platform, the composition is dominated by their half-screened, half-revealed layering by woodland and rock faces; the relation of concealment and revelation runs through more clearly than the correspondence with terrain.

evidence: Left half: A multi-story pavilion stands on a stone-built high terrace and flat platform; the platform base, front terrace, and railings are built up and descend level by level with the slope, and the pavilion's building site corresponds to the height of the terrace. | Lower middle to lower right: A railed stairway and a zigzag covered bridge extend level by level from the platform base toward the right, their ends reaching toward a large area of unpainted water; the built structures unfold along the direction of the waterside. | Upper part to right side: Low, flat distant mountains lie across the unpainted space, forming an open water surface and sky; the pavilion is placed facing this open water, with trees and slope foot at the lower left supporting the platform base.
distinction: Although the stairs and covered bridge provide a clue for ascending and approaching, in the painting they mainly serve as parts of the platform base unfolding along the slope and facing the water; the placement of the pavilion on the terrace overlooking the water runs through the composition more than the process of entering.

evidence: Lower scroll, middle-right foreground: A flat-roofed thatched pavilion stands on a waterside flat platform on several pillars; the platform surface is level, and the pavilion faces the water area at the lower right. | Lower left: Sloping rocks pile upward from the lower left to form a terrace, with several withered trees growing at its edge; the pavilion's building site corresponds directly to this platform surface and the enclosing sloping rocks. | Middle distance, foot of the far bank: Several small houses are placed in a recess of the sloping bank, with a flat beach and stones in front and the sloping bank and withered trees behind; the layout unfolds along the shoreline.
distinction: The connection of the pavilion's pillars to the terrace and sloping rocks is clear, and the building sites are arranged according to the height of the bank terrace, rather than merely marking a scene with isolated volumes.

evidence: Left middle: Several houses are placed in layers along the sloping platform at the foot of the mountain, their foundations rising and falling with the slope and backed against the steep cliffs and mountain rocks. | Lower left: In front of the houses is a gentle slope and a large area of unpainted water; the houses face the open side, corresponding to the configuration of the bank slope. | Center-left mountain hollow: Between the rocks and on the slope, another building outline is visible set among the sloping platforms, corresponding to the undulations of the mountain forms.
distinction: The walls and roofs of the houses are largely exposed, and the correspondence of the building sites to the height of the sloping platforms is clear; concealment and revelation is not the main way the composition is organized, so terrain-responsive siting is chosen rather than concealment and revelation.

evidence: Middle right, on the water: A small boat carrying two people floats on the unpainted water, one person standing and poling; the boat moves crosswise between the near bank and the far bank, forming a clue to movement through the landscape by crossing the water. | Lower foreground: Sloping rocks, willow trees, and bamboo form the near bank; the shoreline extends from the lower left toward the water on the right and connects with the water where the boat is. | Upper part: The main peak of the distant mountains and the trees on the sloping bank face the foreground across a large expanse of water; no traces of built structures such as houses, walls, eaves, or bridge corridors are visible throughout the scroll.
distinction: The only discernible clue for entering in the painting is the boat crossing the water and connecting the shorelines of the two banks, presenting a reachable process; while built sites placed according to the terrain are entirely invisible, so C1 is not chosen.

evidence: Center-right, among the pines on the islet: A double-eaved pavilion is revealed from among the trunks and branches of the pines; the upper roof and projecting eaves are clearly discernible, while the lower part of the building itself is partly cut off by trunks and foliage. | Center, sloping bank islet: Several pines stand in a group on the rocky beach bank, their trunks crossing and slanting, forming a screening layer in front of the pavilion. | Left middle, on the water: The water is broad and empty, with only two boats floating; no bridge, path, gate, or other clue to movement through the landscape connecting to the pavilion on the islet is visible.
distinction: The pavilion is presented with its roof and eaves cut off by the pine woods and partly exposed, creating a layering of concealment and revelation, rather than serving as a striking marker that points out an open scene; thus the relation of screening is closer to the visible organization than scenic accentuation.

evidence: Lower center, slightly left: A figure sits alone on the sloping ground near the bank, facing the mid-ground water and distant mountains, forming a fixed viewing point. | Center to upper middle: Open water runs across the middle of the painting, with layered peaks of distant mountains encircling it, constituting the most important open scenic surface in the whole painting. | Foreground center to right: The sloping bank, rocks, and several trees of varying ink density frame the foreground, focusing the gaze on the junction of the mid-ground water and the mountain edge.
distinction: The main label focuses on the open water and the main peak being drawn together by the near-bank viewpoint into a scenic landing; the relation of screening of built structures required for C2 is not visible in the painting, and screening occurs only among trees, rocks, and landscape.

evidence: Center to right of the sheet: Vertical columns of cursive ink writing run from the top of the sheet through to the bottom, with continuous flow between lines; the last stroke of the final line is drawn out and extended, forming a continuous linear clue from top to bottom. | Left middle: Several columns of smaller characters are arranged parallel to the main columns; the whole sheet is ink writing on paper, with no scenery such as mountains and rocks, water bodies, or trees. | Lower left middle and lower left corner: Several red seals are distributed; throughout the sheet no traces of built structures such as houses, bridges, paths, or gate corridors are visible.
distinction: The only continuous organization in the painting is the continuous extension of the vertical flow of the writing, somewhat close to C4's emphasis on the process of moving from here to there, while the terrain correspondence, layering of concealment and revelation, or scenic marking required by the other categories are entirely absent.

evidence: Lower center: A clearly outlined standing rock with texture strokes occupies the lower middle of the painting, with another small rock adjoining it at its lower right, constituting the only site-like element in the painting. | Lower middle, slightly right: The bundled stem bases of a clump of narcissus grow close in front of the right foot of the large rock; the long leaves extend horizontally to the left and overlap the rock surface, presenting an arrangement placed according to the rock's foot and unfolding horizontally with the rock's form. | Upper center: Flower clusters and stems gather above the top of the large rock and rise along its right edge, forming a relation of attachment and correspondence with the rock; throughout the sheet no houses, walls, bridges, paths, or other built or movement clues are visible.
distinction: The leaf clump lies in front of the rock and screens its surface, rather than the main subject being partly revealed after screening by the rock, so the layering of concealment and revelation does not dominate; the visible relation is that the clump of leaves is placed according to the rock's foot and unfolds around the rock, closer to terrain-responsive placement.

evidence: Center of the painting: The roof and walls of an open pavilion and an adjacent house are intersected and screened by the trunks and hanging branches of the foreground willows; the figures and couch-table inside the pavilion are visible only through gaps in the trees. | Center, slightly upper right: A group of double-eaved roofs is hidden behind the hanging strands of the willows, with only the roof and eaves exposed, suggesting another layer of houses behind the willow shade. | Center, slightly right: The fence wall and the lower part of the houses are screened by the earthen slope and the grove; the built structures are half-exposed along the edge of the sloping bank.
distinction: Although the houses are placed by the water, the painting mainly organizes the layering of the built structures through the screening of willow branches and trunks and the exposure of roofs and eaves; the correspondence of building sites to the terrain is less prominent than the relation of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower left: A white wall, gray-tiled roof, and open veranda are revealed through a gap between the bamboo clump and the sloping rocks, with the lower part of the building itself cut off by the foreground rocks. | Lower middle, slightly left: A clump of green bamboo stands in front of the house; the bamboo branches and leaves press over the roof, placing the house on another spatial level behind the bamboo grove. | Middle-right stream bank: Two people sit facing each other on a platform by the stream; between the platform and the house is a gap of stream-bank rocks, and no bridge, path, gate, or other enterable connecting clue is visible.
distinction: The house mainly reveals its layering through the exposure and screening of its roof and walls among the bamboo clump and sloping rocks, rather than being dominated by a placement relation in which the building site unfolds according to the height of the slope.

evidence: Lower right of the right half: above the tree cluster is a group of oblique parallel short lines, resembling a stepped ramp or bridge deck, extending from the right edge toward the lower left and disappearing behind the trees | Right-half central ridge: a tiny figure stands at a platform in a gap between rocks; below it, the direction roughly connects with the oblique path at the lower right, suggesting an ascent along the mountain gap and the possibility of continuing to move through the landscape | Upper right edge, at the cliff: between the pine branches and the rock wall are several parallel horizontal ink lines, possibly eaves or a railing, but the details are unclear and cannot be reliably identified as built elements
distinction: The main spatial organization of the painting is the process of entry and ascent formed by the lower-right stepped path and the figure on the ridge, which is closer to the visible relationships than the concealment interpretation supported by the very weak suspected exposure at the cliff edge

evidence: Center to lower center: an obliquely standing rock occupies the middle of the painting; its body is textured with light ink washes and outlined with dark ink moss dots, screening the branches and foliage behind it. | Behind and beside the rock (upper center, center right, center left): hibiscus blossoms and bamboo leaves emerge from behind and beside the rock; only flowers and leaves are visible, not roots or stems, forming a layered front-and-back concealment and revelation with the orchids at the slope foot in front of the rock. | Whole painting: apart from the inscription and seals at the upper right, only flowers, bamboo, rock, and grass are visible; no houses, pavilions, bridges, paths, gates, walls, or any other built elements appear.
distinction: The visible organization is dominated by the layering of concealment and revelation, in which the rock screens and the flowers and leaves are revealed from behind it, rather than by an placement relationship in which the building base corresponds to terrain height; it is therefore classified under concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower-center water surface: a small boat carrying one person is moored near the lower-right sloping bank, the boat facing the shore; a net-like canopy mat is placed on the boat, presenting a relationship of arrival from the open water toward the sloping bank | Lower-right sloping bank: bank rocks and reeds layer and extend into the painting; beside the tree trunk another person sits at the water's edge, connecting across the tree with the person in the boat, suggesting landing and a transition to behind the slope | Gaps between trunks in the center: several tall trees grow from the sloping bank, leaving gaps between the trunks that lead toward the water and the boat; the shoreline extends inward along the lower right, further indicating continued spatial depth
distinction: The main category is based on the movement-through-the-landscape thread of the boat meeting the bank, arriving from the water and being able to turn behind the slope; the alternative interpretation sees only partial screening by trees and rocks of the figure at the water's edge and the canopy mat, and lacks any object of built concealment and revelation forming a scene.

evidence: Bottom of the painting, running across the entire scroll: a series of low earthen slopes and mounds rise and connect, dotted with bamboo clumps at their tops, forming the only ground base and terrain organization in the entire scroll | Middle and upper parts of the painting: the main subject is a group of figures—officials, attendants, ghosts and monsters, and a tiger rider—arranged horizontally on flat ground behind the slopes; no houses, pavilions, walls, or other built elements are visible | Beneath the seated figure on the left: only a seat (chair or couch) supports the figure, which is an object rather than architecture; the entire scroll has no bridges, paths, gates, fords, or other movement-through-the-landscape clues
distinction: The only discernible spatial organization in the entire scroll is the foreground slope serving as a base that supports the unfolding of the subjects, approximating a site relationship of placement according to the slope; no concealment and revelation, scenic accentuation, or accessible clues act on any built elements.

evidence: Lower center: the thatched pavilion roof spreads horizontally, cut off in front by the upright tree trunk in the foreground; the pavilion pillars stand behind the trunk, forming a layering of tree in front and pavilion behind | Right of the pavilion and above its roof: a right-leaning trunk and hanging bamboo branches and leaves press over the front of the right part of the pavilion roof; the eaves are revealed through gaps in the branches and leaves | Lower left and lower right: the pavilion base adjoins unpainted water and a low shoreline on the left, and gentle sloping rocks on the right; the bank rises and falls only weakly, with no clearly visible arrangement following the height of the terrain
distinction: The visible screening of the roof by the trunk and bamboo branches makes concealment and revelation the main way the painting is organized, while the gentle bank and the weak correspondence between building base and terrain make concealment and revelation rather than terrain-responsive siting the appropriate choice

evidence: Over the stream, center-right: a slightly arched plank bridge with bridge piers spans the ravine, its right end meeting the shrubby slope of the right bank and its left end falling toward the sloping bank where the central house stands, forming a thread of crossing the stream | Among the central trees: through gaps in branches, leaves, and hanging bamboo, the sloping roof, eaves, and white walls and colonnade of the house are revealed; the house base is cut off by dark foreground shrubs, and the bank where it stands is precisely where the left end of the bridge points | Right-half water surface: between the large unpainted water surface on the right and scattered distant islets, the bridge is the only structure spanning the water, connecting the right bank and the central shore into a traversable space
distinction: The bridge links the two banks and points toward the house among the trees, so that the painting presents a process of crossing the bridge to approach built elements, and this organizing role runs through the right half and the center; concealment and revelation only explains the partial screening of the house and does not account for the relationship of arrival established by the bridge

evidence: Entire painting: the painting is a mounting surface fully covered with brocade patterns, with a vertical blank paper label pasted at the center; the lower end of the label bears a number written in ink, and no mountains, water, trees, bridges, paths, or built images are visible. | Central paper label strip: apart from a few stains and the number at the lower end, the label surface is blank with no image, and does not constitute spatial content within the painting proper.
distinction: The painting does not present the content of the painting proper; evidence for built elements and landscape is entirely absent, none of the four categories has direct support, the main label is a forced assignment, and there is no obvious competing interpretation.

evidence: Lower-left water surface: a boat carries several people, its bow facing the lower-left sloping bank, in a position of advancing toward the shore | Lower-left sloping bank: an earthen slope extends into the water, several pines stand upright on the slope, and the shoreline can extend behind the slope; no houses, pavilions, corridors, bridges, gates, or other built elements are visible on the slope or around the water | Upper right to center right: a waterfall falls among the cliffs into the open water below, and a large area of unpainted space in the middle of the painting forms an expansive stretch of water and mist
distinction: The boat, sloping bank, and open water present a relationship of approach and landing, which is closer to the visible spatial organization than an interpretation that merely marks one scenic spot with an isolated point

evidence: Center right of the painting: two thatched-roof pavilion buildings, one higher and one lower, stand on a slope terrace to the right of the central huge rock; their pillar bases rest on the slope surface, their eaves spread toward the lower right following the slope, and in front they adjoin the unpainted water at the lower center of the painting | Center left: another small thatched pavilion roof is revealed between trees and sloping rocks, its base placed against the left-bank slope | Center to lower right: the foot of the huge rock and the moss-dotted sloping bank form the edge of a terrace, and the pavilion buildings are set precisely at this terrace edge, their heights corresponding to the slope line
distinction: The main pavilion's building body and pillar bases are clearly seen standing on the slope terrace and opening toward the water, and the terrain's participation in the base and heights runs through the composition more than the layering of concealment and revelation; the left pavilion's revealed roof is only partial screening and is not enough to dominate

evidence: Center left: two thatched houses are staggered front and back; the right half of the front house's roof is covered by the branches and leaves of a large central tree, and the building body and eaves are revealed from behind the trunk and branches | Left side: the rear house adjoins a stand of bamboo on its left, with a row of bamboo closely behind its ridge; the houses are surrounded by trees rather than in an exposed clearing | Lower center: below and to the left of the front house, sloping rocks are piled up, and a trunk slants out from among the rocks and lies across in front of the house, forming layers of mutual screening among rock, tree, and house
distinction: The correspondence between the building base and the slope terrace is gentle and not prominent; the painting mainly organizes the layering of built elements through the screening and revealing of roof and eaves by tree crowns, trunks, and bamboo groves, so concealment and revelation is closer to the visible evidence than terrain-responsive siting

evidence: Lower center: an ochre earthen slope terrace supports a group of buildings, their roofs arranged at heights following the rises of the slope top, the building base corresponding to the form of the terrace | Lower right: several houses descend in layers along the slope foot toward the water's edge, the lowest building body supported on pillar bases at the slope edge and projecting over the water | Right side and upper right: between the open water surface and the distant slope stretching across, the terrace where the buildings stand projects at a turn of the shoreline, forming a position of occupying the terrace and facing the water
distinction: The placement of the buildings according to the heights of the slope terrace and their waterside position runs through the main composition; the trees at the slope top stand only behind the houses and do not form a dominant role in organizing layers through concealment and revelation

evidence: Center right, at the slope waist beneath the flowering tree trunk: a corner of a roof and eaves is revealed, the building body screened by the slope surface and the slanting trunk, with only the upper half of the roof visible | Center-right, in a hollow of the slope mound: a section of courtyard wall with a crenellated top lies across between the slope mounds, both ends disappearing into the mounds, the lower half of the wall screened | Lower left, from the water's edge to the slope foot: a boat and standing figures are arranged along the shore, the shoreline connecting through grass to the slope foot, with no bridges, paths, gates, or other movement-through-the-landscape clues linking to the built elements on the slope
distinction: The built elements only suggest a layer behind the slope and beneath the trees through a screened roof and wall top, and the relationship of concealment and revelation is more clearly visible than the correspondence between base layout and terrain

evidence: At the end of the flat bank, lower center-left: a pointed, internally blank mass is suspected to be a thatched hut, closely adjoining the edge of the low sloping shoreline and facing the open water, its base meeting dense dark grass, the details of the hut form unclear | Left side to center: sloping rocks and bamboo groves descend in layers from the left bank toward the water, and the shoreline in the center turns into a gentle slope extending into the water, forming the site configuration of the slope foot and water's edge | Center to right: a large unpainted water surface and low distant-bank hills stretch across; no bridges, paths, gates, fords, or other movement-through-the-landscape clues are visible, nor is there layered screening of the suspected hut by trees
distinction: The suspected hut closely adjoins the slope-foot shoreline and is placed in correspondence with the bank configuration, rather than being at a peak edge or an open face as a scenic marker; the clue of placement according to the bank is stronger than the clue of scenic accentuation.

evidence: Center of the painting: a hall with a surrounding wall occupies a valley; the courtyard gate is open, and within the gate opening figures in the courtyard and hanging objects are visible, forming spatial depth from outside the gate to inside | In front of the gate, lower center: two people stand on the sloping ground before the gate, facing the open door and connecting with the courtyard within, presenting a sequence of approach from outside and entry into the built structure | Foreground below and surroundings: the sloping bank before the gate meets the water-line pattern at the lower edge, forming a transitional ground for reaching the gate; dense woods and mountain rocks surround the rear and both sides of the house, and a pine branch at the front right slants over the roof, but does not cut off the entering relationship at the gate
distinction: Although surrounded by trees, the house body and courtyard wall are fully and clearly revealed, so the tension of concealment and revelation is weak; the open gate, the figures before it, and the depth within form a discernible process of entry, so access to secluded settings is dominant

evidence: Center left: a multi-story building with eaves and a flat-balcony railing is revealed through the tops of the pines, the lower part of the building body screened by trunks and foliage | Lower right: several white-walled houses sit among trees on a slope terrace, their roofs and walls partly screened by foreground trees | Lower center: a stepped stone path extends obliquely along the slope, with a tiny dark dot on it resembling a traveler, both ends of the path disappearing into the terrace and trees
distinction: The existence and layering of built elements are mainly suggested by the concealment and revelation relationships of the pine forest and tree clusters; the stone path is only a partial section and is cut off by the slope surface, and does not constitute a process of entry running through the painting

evidence: Among the trees at the lower right of the right half of the painting: the roof, white walls, and railing-like structures of buildings are revealed behind the trees, most of the building bodies screened by trunks and foliage | Lower middle of the right half of the painting: a row of dense trees runs between the water surface and the mountain foot, forming a screening layer, with built elements located behind this row of trees and only partially visible | Lower-left water's edge of the right half: the water surface is open, with a small boat moored; the shoreline is low and flat, and no paths, bridges, gates, or other entry clues leading to the buildings are visible
distinction: The buildings are mainly suggested to exist and to have layering by roofs and walls revealed behind the screening trees, rather than primarily by the correspondence of base layout with the heights of the sloping bank, so C2 rather than C1 is taken

evidence: Lower right of the right page: an open thatched-roof pavilion sits on the sloping bank at the mountain foot; figures are visible seated facing each other inside, and the roof, eaves, and pillars are revealed between tree trunks, hanging branches, and sloping rocks | Center to right side of the right page: a large tree slants out from among the sloping rocks, its branches and leaves dense and fine twigs hanging down, covering above and around the pavilion; branches and leaves overlap in front of the pavilion roof outline, forming a layer of seeing the building through branches | Lower left of the right page: a spring flows down from a gap in the rocks at the mountain foot, and bank grass continues to near the pavilion base; no bridges, paths, gates, or other movement-through-the-landscape clues connecting with the pavilion are visible
distinction: Although the pavilion is close to the sloping bank by the water, the way the painting organizes its appearance is through the screening and revealing by the dense shade of the large tree and hanging branches, and the layering of concealment and revelation runs through the composition more than the correspondence with terrain

evidence: Among the slope trees at the lower right of the painting proper: an umbrella-shaped pavilion roof and several slender pillars are revealed through gaps between trunks, the building body partly screened by the foreground trunks and sparse branches and leaves | Near foreground at the bottom of the painting proper: several bare-branched trees grow from sloping rocks, their branches crossing in front of the pavilion, forming a foreground screening layer | Center of the painting proper: unpainted water stretches across, distant mountains behind it; the pavilion and trees are on the near waterside, and no bridges, paths, gates, or other movement-through-the-landscape clues are visible
distinction: The pavilion is mainly presented as a woodland layer through the screening and revealing of the foreground trunks and branches, rather than as a striking node that concentrates or marks a particular landscape

evidence: Lower slope bank of the right leaf: several trunks lean together in a cluster, branches and leaves covering above the sloping bank; between the tree roots and rocks is a very small dark rectangular outline, suspected to be a house or pavilion base, but its form is blurry and the details unclear | Middle of the right leaf: open water is represented by unpainted space, separating the near-bank slope trees from the pale-ink peaks above into front and back layers, with the tree cluster forming a near-foreground screening layer | Water's edge at the lower right of the right leaf: two very small seated figures sit facing the water; beside them no bridges, paths, gates, boat crossings, or other movement-through-the-landscape clues linking to built elements are visible
distinction: The suspected building trace is suggested to exist by being half-screened by trees and rocks and partly revealed; no corresponding layout is visible in which its base unfolds with the height of the sloping bank, so the relationship of concealment and revelation is closer to the visible organization than terrain-responsive placement

evidence: Lower middle of the right half of the painting: multiple roof ridges and eaves are revealed between sloping rocks and a pine grove, the building bodies partly screened by the mountain rocks and tree crowns in front, with the built elements presented in the middle-ground layer by way of concealment and revelation | From lower left to lower middle of the right half of the painting: mountain rocks and clustered trees are densely distributed on the obliquely rising sloping bank, forming layers of mutual screening front and back with the hollow where the buildings are located | Lower right of the right half of the painting: a small boat with a mast is moored at the water's edge; the shoreline is flat and extends behind the sloping rocks, but no paths, bridges, or gates connecting with the buildings are visible
distinction: The buildings mainly reveal their layer through screening by trees and rocks, and the relationship of concealment and revelation dominates their presentation; traces of placement according to the slope are visible but do not run through as clearly as the screening relationship, and the boat mast and shoreline lack any discernible entry connection.

evidence: Among the mountains on the right side of the right half of the painting proper: a thread of waterfall falls from a mountain hollow, meeting the unpainted water and several round rocks below, forming the vertical focus of the right half of the painting | On the sloping bank below the right half of the painting proper: two people stand beside the grass on the sloping bank, one of them raising an arm and pointing toward the distant mountains and waterfall | Middle of the right half of the painting proper: a large slanting tree and sloping rocks occupy the middle ground, branches and leaves dense, with open unpainted space behind; no roof, eaves, walls, or other built outlines are visible in the entire painting
distinction: The painting organizes the scene by concentrating it at a single waterfall and making it explicit through a pointing figure, which is closer to the visible relationships than a movement-through-the-landscape process lacking discernible entry clues such as bridges, paths, or gates

evidence: Center-left of the right leaf, at the slope foot by the water beneath the cloud band: pale-ink low building forms are arranged horizontally along the junction of slope foot and water surface, their bases adjoining the shoreline | Middle of the right leaf: a cloud band cuts across the mountain waist, and the sloping bank extends from beneath the cloud toward the water, forming a gentle bank foot; the building forms are placed on this terrace-like bank foot | Lower right of the right leaf: the near-bank slope has a flowing spring and grass, defining the high-low direction of the shoreline; the water surface is open, with boats moored at the slope foot
distinction: The suspected built elements unfold closely along the slope-foot shoreline and their bases correspond to the water surface and the terrace, which explains their placement better than the layering formed by screening through trees
