evidence: Right side of the right half of the painting proper: a vertical rock wall hangs down from above, its surface dotted with dark ink leaf dots, and a flat slope clearing is left at its foot | Lower right of the right half of the painting proper: a figure in white sits on the ground on the flat slope before the foot of the rock wall, with a long strip-like object placed horizontally in front; no houses, wall eaves, platforms, or other built elements are visible in the entire painting | Center to lower part of the right half of the painting proper: a bare-branched tree with red dots slants out from the sloping rocks below, its trunk stretching horizontally through the middle of the painting; round rocks and grass are also at the slope foot, and the figure and tree both take their positions according to the configuration of the rock wall and sloping rocks
distinction: The visible relationship is mainly that the figure and tree are placed according to the configuration of the rock wall and sloping rocks; although a gap is enclosed between branches and wall, there is no layer of screening and revealing of built elements, so terrain-responsive placement is chosen rather than concealment and revelation

evidence: Middle of the right half: a low railing extends horizontally, its left end hidden behind the seated figure, suggesting an enclosed space on one side of the banana plant and rock | Center-left of the right half: a huge lake rock and banana leaves occupy the upper half of the painting, screening the space behind them; two people sit facing each other in the clearing before the rock | Lower right: an oblique sloping bank strip extends from the right edge toward the lower left, dotted with grass, forming front and back layers with the flat ground before the rock
distinction: The railing is revealed from between the banana plant, rock, and figures, and the relationship of concealment and revelation constitutes the main spatial layer; no discernible entry clues such as gates, paths, or bridges appear in the painting, so it does not lead to the movement-through-the-landscape process of C4

evidence: Center to upper right of the right page: a large tree slants out from the right bank, its dense branches and leaves and hanging tendrils covering most of the painting, its roots meeting the rocky slope at the lower right | Lower middle of the right page: a figure wearing a conical hat sits in the hollow between the tree roots and the rocky slope, the lower body and seated place partly screened by foreground reeds and the rocky slope, with only the upper body and head revealed | Left side of the right page: a large area of unpainted space serves as water, with two birds flying above; no houses, pavilions, corridors, bridges, door openings, or other traces of built elements are visible in the entire painting
distinction: The dominant relationship in the painting is the layer of screening and revealing of the bank setting and the figure by the tree crown, hanging tendrils, reeds, and rocky slope, rather than a corresponding relationship in which the building base is placed according to terrain height

evidence: Center-left of the right page: a horizontal railing with posts, or a bridge, spans the stream banks, connecting the empty bank on the left with the sloping ground where the figures are on the right | Center-right of the right page: a staff-holding scholar and an attendant stand on the sloping bank beneath a bare tree, facing the side with the bridge railing, in the posture of pausing during movement through the landscape | Right edge of the right page: a brown thatched-looking slanting roof structure is revealed behind tree trunks and sloping rock, suspected to be a roof but with walls and eaves indistinguishable
distinction: The bridge railing and the staff-holding figure form a movement-through-the-landscape sequence from the other bank to this bank, which runs through the spatial organization of the painting more than the screened revelation of the suspected roof at the right edge

evidence: Among the trees on the lower-right sloping bank: the roofs and eaves of several houses are revealed through gaps in the dense treetops, most of the building bodies screened by the foreground trees, and the relationship of concealment and revelation constitutes the main way the built elements are identified | Toward the lower part of the right edge: the roof surfaces arranged obliquely along the slope are more fully revealed, forming front and back layers with the foreground tree cluster; the revealed roofs indicate the depth at which the built elements lie | At the water's edge, center left: a low, flat arched bridge lies across the stream bank, with no clear paths extending from either end toward the lower-right house area, making this movement-through-the-landscape clue isolated
distinction: Although the houses are staggered along the slope, their existence and layering are mainly suggested by screening through trees and revealing of roofs, and the organizing role of concealment and revelation is stronger than the correspondence between building base and slope form

evidence: Lower center-left: a small bridge with railings spans the ravine, connecting the left foreground sloping bank with the sloping ground beneath the middle-ground woods, forming a movement-through-the-landscape clue of crossing the bridge and entering the middle ground of the painting | Top of the right-bank slope: an open pavilion is supported on pillars with a roof above, standing at the top of an earthen slope by the water, its body opening toward the water at the left front | Between the middle ground and the right bank: the shoreline is continuous between the sloping ground beneath the middle-ground woods and the earthen slope beneath the pavilion, with no water barrier, so after crossing the bridge one can walk along the bank to reach the earthen slope where the pavilion stands
distinction: The bridge and the continuous shoreline link the foreground, the middle-ground woods, and the waterside open pavilion into an accessible movement-through-the-landscape sequence, which runs through the lower half of the composition more than the pavilion's placement according to the slope alone

evidence: Center-left: a large moss-dotted rock occupies the main body of the painting; a pine trunk emerges from behind the rock, its middle section screened by the rock face, with only the upper and lower sections revealed, forming a clear layer of concealment and revelation | Above and to the right: pine branches and needles hang down from the top of the painting and slant out from the right, overlapping the rock top and the blank background, further strengthening the spatial relationship of mutual screening front and back | At the slope foot below: bamboo clumps, fine twigs, low sloping rocks, and grass at the slope foot screen one another; no houses, pavilions, bridges, corridors, or any other traces of built elements are visible throughout the painting
distinction: The actual organization of the painting is the layer of concealment and revelation in which the rock screens the pine trunk and the branches cover the rock face, which is closer to the visible relationships than a scenic-accentuation interpretation that would require built elements as markers

evidence: Lower left: a bridge deck with piers spans the ravine, its right end landing on the foreground sloping bank and connecting with the bank surface where the pavilion stands | Lower center: the pointed roof and pillars of the thatched pavilion are clear, standing on the flat part of the foreground sloping bank and facing the open water to the left | Behind and to the right of the pavilion: bamboo groves and several tree trunks are arranged around the rear side of the pavilion; the pavilion body is fully revealed and unscreened
distinction: The bridge crosses the stream and connects to the sloping bank where the pavilion stands, forming an accessible movement-through-the-landscape link to the pavilion, which is closer to the visible spatial organization than merely using the pavilion to mark a waterside scene

evidence: Lower right near bank: a pavilion with upturned eaves sits among clustered trees on the sloped bank, its building itself and the people in the window clearly visible, while its base and the slope foot are screened by broadleaf groves in the foreground | In the lower-right tree cluster: another roof shows only its ridge line and tile surface between the treetops, the building itself wholly hidden in the woods, forming a concealment-and-revelation layering of a house seen within the forest | To the left of the pavilion: two pines stand beside the pavilion, their trunks and branches slanting out toward one side of the pavilion eaves, the pavilion body emerging from the enclosure of pine trunks and clustered trees, facing the open river surface
distinction: Although the pavilion is set by the waterside bank, the slope is gentle and the correspondence to terrain is not marked; the built elements mainly use the tree cluster to screen the base and the ridge revealed at the forest edge to form layering, and the screening relationship runs through the foreground more than terrain-responsive siting does

evidence: Left middle among sparse woods: a pitched-roof house and white wall emerge through gaps between tree trunks, the building itself partly interrupted by the trunks and foliage in front, presenting a house seen within the forest | Center of the painting: a slanting giant rock and the clustered trees atop it lie across the right-front of the house, together with the tree trunks forming a barrier, placing the house at a layer behind the rock and behind the woods | Right half water surface and sloped bank: before the open unpainted water surface and the gentle distant slope, no bridge, path, gate, or other movement-through-the-landscape clue connecting to the house is visible; the house's existence is mainly hinted by a roof revealed through a forest gap
distinction: The house enters the painting through the concealment-and-revelation layering of a roof revealed through a forest gap and a body hidden behind the rock, rather than being dominated by a siting relationship corresponding to terrain such as resting on a terrace or following the bank

evidence: Lower right: an arched bridge with railings spans the stream, its body extending rightward beyond the painting edge, the bridge end joining the stream bank | Lower bank center-right: a figure wearing a conical hat rides a donkey, an attendant with a staff following, moving along a path on the stream bank toward the bridge | Middle ground to lower bank: the stream flows gently across, the shoreline continuing from the lower-left sloped bank to the bridge end, beyond which the slope cuts off the path, implying crossing the bridge to enter deeper
distinction: The painting expresses a process that can be reached and continued through movement through the landscape via the bank path, bridge, and traveling figures, rather than merely presenting a static correspondence of structures placed according to the waterside terrain

evidence: Right upper ridge among trees: the upper roof and eaves of a storied pavilion emerge from the treetops, the lower wall body and corridor hidden behind trunks and foliage, only partly visible | Left edge of the right-upper tree cluster: a small gate-pavilion or building outline half-revealed among the trees, largely obscured by branches and foliage | Right-upper slope top: the building mass is wrapped by the surrounding canopy, only the revealed roof and intermittently visible wall body hinting at its spatial position in a layer behind the woods
distinction: Although the storied pavilion occupies a high point on the slope top, the painting mainly uses tree screening and the revealing of roof and wall body to hint at the built elements' existence and layering, rather than marking a landscape node by a conspicuous position

evidence: Center-lower right among the willows: the roof and wall body of a thatched hut emerge through gaps in the drooping willow branches and leaves, the lower part and both sides of the house surrounded and interrupted by the canopy | In front of and to the left of the house: foreground willow trunks slant out and drooping leaves sweep down, lying across the front of the house, placing the house in a layer behind the trees | Lower-left bank slope: two travelers walk rightward along the waterside slope, with slope rocks and tree clusters between them and the house, and no continuous path or gate or bridge connection visible
distinction: The house's existence and layering are mainly hinted by willow screening and a revealed roof; although the travelers face the tree cluster, no visible path connects to it, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship runs through more clearly than an entry relationship does

evidence: Center-right: a red-walled gate tower with an arched gate emerges among the trees, the gate opening transparent; below and to its right a light-colored small bridge is built over the ravine, its bridgehead joining the open ground before the gate tower | Lower-right stream bank: a figure stands on the stream bank slope facing the ravine and small bridge, the stream flowing from the lower painting toward the middle ground | Upper-left peak top: a multi-story pagoda stands on the peak top, and to its lower left a balustraded storied pavilion is placed on the cliff top, forming with the middle-ground gate tower and small bridge a depth sequence from near to far
distinction: Although the pagoda marks the peak top, the painting links the stream-bank figure, small bridge, and gate tower with its arched gate into an approachable and enterable process of movement through the landscape, and the movement linkage runs through the composition more than mere marking does

evidence: Lower left: a thatched pavilion is supported on multiple piles above the water surface, two people seated within, its building site directly determined by the waterside condition | Center-right: a two-story storied pavilion is built facing the water, with a balustraded platform and steps in front descending to the water's edge; behind it, on a slope terrace, another house sits high among the tree clusters | Center-left: a stretch of enclosing wall extends diagonally along the sloped bank and undulates with the slope, separating the slope houses above from the water below, the slope houses placed according to the slope top
distinction: Although trees half-screen part of the building bodies, the building sites, heights, and manner of unfolding of each built element all follow the sloped bank and water surface, and the terrain correspondence runs through the whole scroll more than concealment-and-revelation layering does

evidence: Center-lower: the roof and white wall of a small house emerge through gaps in the slanting pine trunks and needles, the building itself partly obscured by the trunk in front | Lower left: an open pavilion is placed beneath overhanging pine branches, its roof screened by trunks and needles, figures visible within | Right side: a railed plank bridge spans the stream, its left end resting on slope rocks, with no clearly drawn path connecting it to the house or pavilion
distinction: Although the bridge is identifiable, its ends lack a discernible entry connection with the buildings, whereas the pavilion and house both organize spatial layering by being screened and revealed by the pine woods, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship runs through the composition

evidence: Lower center: a two-story storied pavilion stands above dense tree clusters, the lower part of its base screened by treetops, revealing only the double eaves, flat-platform balustrade columns, and figures within, presenting the appearance of a house revealed above the forest | Lower left and lower center: two roof ridges and tile surfaces emerge through gaps in the canopy, the building bodies wholly hidden within the woods, forming with the central storied pavilion a layering of concealment and revelation within the forest | Right-upper sloped bank: among the slope's trees and rocks a pale-ink roof is faintly revealed, the house form half-screened behind clustered trees
distinction: Although the storied pavilion faces the water surface, the painting organizes the existence and layering of multiple built elements through tree screening and revealed roof ridges, rather than using built elements to mark some peak-edge or water-mouth scenery

evidence: Center: a dense-ink canopy lies across the front of a house, the building body obscured, only the gray-tile roof and eaves emerging between the treetops, forming a layering of house behind trees | Lower left: a pale-ochre wall and an open gate opening are revealed through gaps in trunks and foliage, the roof behind the wall half-revealed beneath the canopy | Center-right: a waterside thatched shed has most of its body blocked by an earthen slope and tree clusters, only the shed roof and posts slanting out above the slope rocks
distinction: The concealment-and-revelation relationship runs through the three built elements at lower left, center, and center-right, while before the gate opening there is no path or crossing connection, the entry process only locally implied, so concealment and revelation into a setting predominates

evidence: Right middle: a multi-story storied pavilion is placed close against the cliff slope, supported below by a stone-built base and platform, the building body tiering with the mountain's height, the cliff face and slope directly participating in its site and manner of unfolding | Below at the water's edge: a small waterside pavilion is supported on posts above the water at the bank, set facing the water, corresponding to the shoreline configuration | Center-left stream bank: clustered houses are scattered along the sloped ground of the stream bank, roofs distributed with the undulations of the slope and tree clusters, and a low flat plank bridge spans the stream linking the two banks
distinction: Although the middle-ground houses are half-revealed above the treetops, the main pavilion rests on a stone platform against the cliff and the water pavilion is raised over the water, so the participation of terrain and waterside in siting runs through the composition more than concealment-and-revelation layering does

evidence: Upper-middle ridge: the roof and a small part of the building body of a pavilion emerge between the treetops of sparse woods, the lower part of the building body obscured by woods and the slope top | Right middle: the wall body and roof of a thatched hut lie behind a large foreground tree and foliage, only partly visible, with a fence wall and open ground in front | Lower right and center-left: a plank bridge at lower right crosses a stream bend, a pole-carrying figure at center-left walks on a mountain path, the path rising and vanishing among slope rocks and woods, not directly joining the houses or pavilion
distinction: Although the bridge and mountain path are visible, they do not form a continuous, discernible process of arrival with the built elements; the built elements mainly form a concealment-and-revelation layering through roofs revealed at treetops and walls revealed behind trees

evidence: Center-right ravine: a railed wooden bridge spans the water, its two ends joining the sloped banks, forming a movement-through-the-landscape clue across the water | Right of the central mountain ridge: behind the bridge a flight of stepped stone pathway can be seen slanting upward along the slope, leading to the storied pavilion eaves revealed at the mountainside | Lower-left and lower-right water surface: figures are within a waterside thatched pavilion, railings set beside it; on the water a boat is poled to shore by a figure, forming an arrival relationship with the bank pavilion and railings
distinction: The bridge, stone pathway, and boat crossing connect from the lower waterside up to the mountainside built elements, presenting a spatial process that can be reached and continued upward; although terrain-responsive siting of the built elements is visible, it is subordinate to the organization of this entry clue

evidence: Right middle at the base of a tree trunk: squarely layered block-like objects are arranged in terrace form with flat tops, suspected to be an artificial stone platform or base, but the details are unclear and it cannot be confirmed as built elements; beside it on the ground is another small rectangular object. | Right side to center: a sloped bank extends diagonally from right to lower left, the platform at its foot carrying trees, rocks, and seated or reclining figures, the block-like objects suspected to be a base placed according to the height of the slope foot, corresponding to the sloped bank and the trend of the shoreline. | Lower left and lower right: two water buffalo occupy the bank edge and the waterside respectively, with a horizontal sandbar and water gaps spread below; no clear architecture such as houses, pavilions, bridges, corridors, or gates is seen in the whole painting.
distinction: The main label focuses on the suspected base being placed with the slope-foot terrace and corresponding to the sloped bank and shoreline as a terrain-responsive relationship; the painting has no peak edge, valley mouth, or open face requiring marking, and the scenic-accentuation role of C3 lacks any visible footing.

evidence: Center and lower center of the painting: three capped riders on white horses proceed one after another down a gentle earthen slope toward the lower left, the horses' direction of step consistent, forming a continuous traveling column | Right side and upper part: several large tree trunks and branches slant out, foliage covering the upper painting, below the trees an open slope, and in the whole scroll no houses, walls, bridges, paths, or gates or crossings are seen | Bottom: the foreground is raised rocks and clustered bamboo and grassy slope, the slope surface extending gently upward and joining the middle-ground open ground, with no trace of built sites on the ground
distinction: The only spatial movement line in the painting is the process of the figures and horses traveling along the slope and able to continue beyond the painting, which is closer to the organizational mode of access to secluded settings than the entirely absent relationships of built siting, concealment and revelation, or marking

evidence: Lower-right bank edge: a tiered stone platform projects from the cliff foot above the open water, on it a figure seated facing the water, the seated position set according to the configuration of the waterside slope terrace. | Center-left: a flowing spring winds down through gaps in the mountain rocks and joins the large rippled water surface in the foreground, the rock gaps and shoreline organizing the painting's opening and the water's coming and going. | Right side: the cliff face rises steeply, pines slanting out from the cliff over the stone platform, the platform site at the slope where the cliff foot meets the water.
distinction: The visible relationship is mainly the terrain correspondence of the seated position being placed according to the waterside stone platform and set facing the water, rather than some structure acting as a marked point to identify scenery; the painting has no houses or other built elements that could serve a scenic-accentuation role.

evidence: Left edge: a waterside storied pavilion partly enters the painting, its double eaves, flat platform, and columns visible, a boat moored at the water below, its mast leaning beside the pavilion, forming a connection approaching this built element by waterway | Center-lower-left sloped bank: among the tree cluster on the sloped bank stand several slender straight masts, the boat bodies hidden behind the bank, hinting at a ferry crossing point of mooring and landing at the bank | Central water surface: on the open water a sailing boat travels, together with the moored boat at left continuing the clue of movement along the water that can be further traveled
distinction: The waterside storied pavilion is not only adjacent to the shoreline but directly connected with mooring boats and traveling boats and other ferry clues, organizing a waterway process that can be reached and continued, while the terrain correspondence is instead incomplete owing to the cropping at the painting edge

evidence: Lower left to lower center water surface: a double-eaved storied pavilion stands on a long bridge corridor spanning the water, the bridge body with rows of piles, extending diagonally from the lower-left sloped bank to the pavilion and continuing from the pavilion's right to the willow-planted bank islet at lower center, forming a continuous passage from bank to pavilion and then across to the opposite bank | At the water below the bridge to the right of the water pavilion: covered boats and small craft are moored on the water beside the bridge, joining the bridge corridor, hinting at waterway ferry clues for reaching the water pavilion | At the small islet at the water's edge center-left: on the fenced and protected islet stands a water pavilion, a small boat moored beside the islet, together with the foreground bridge and pavilion forming a sequence of nodes for waterside stopping that can be crossed and reached
distinction: The foreground long bridge spans the water connecting the water pavilion and extending to the opposite bank islet, presenting a process of movement through the landscape that can be reached and traversed, which runs through the composition more than the terrain correspondence of the middle-ground houses placed according to the slope, and better explains the main scenic role of the built elements

evidence: Lower center-right: two red-railed wooden bridges span the stream valley, their decks and railings clear, connecting the foreground grassy slope with the middle-ground sloped bank, the bridge ends joining the passage between the slopes | Right side to center-right: a column of mounted and walking figures proceeds in single file upward along the passage between the slopes and valleys, continuing from lower right through the center-right sloped ground to the right-upper mountain edge, small advancing figures still visible at the ridge, presenting a continuous process of turning into the depths | Lower left: a stretch of red-railed bridge plankway is set at the stream bank, leading to the group of people and horses resting on the slope terrace, joining the slope opening
distinction: The role of the bridges and railed walkways lies in connecting the marching column and guiding the turn from the foreground stream valley into the mountains, rather than merely expressing the correspondence of structure sites with terrain

evidence: Left half of the painting to the center: dense canopy and drooping branches cover the slope rocks over a large area, trunks extending from rock gaps, foliage screening the rock faces, forming a layering of concealment and revelation front and back | Lower center to lower right: giant rocks and slope stones pile up, red-leaf branches emerging from stone gaps and behind the rocks, the stone surfaces partly interrupted by branches and foliage | Whole painting: no roof, eaves, wall body, bridge or path, or any other discernible built element or movement-through-the-landscape clue is seen; the pale silk surface at right is blank at the scroll end and is not counted as space within the painting
distinction: The dominant relationship in the painting is the layering of screening and revealing of the rocky slope by woodland, rather than terrain-responsive siting of built elements; because no built elements are visible, it is classified by concealment-and-revelation organization into the closest C2 rather than C1

evidence: Right-upper mountain col: a column of mounted figures proceeds in order upward along a narrow gap path between two mountains, the column head and tail joining, the path extending behind the mountain, presenting a traveling sequence turning into the depths | Center to center-left valley: in the open valley multiple groups of mounted figures and banners are scattered, their direction of travel roughly toward the gap in the right-upper mountain col, forming with the mountain gap path a sense of linkage that can be further traveled | Center-right dense woods: within the woods only red vertical strip-like objects (like banner flags) are seen, and in the whole picture no houses, eaves, bridges, gates, or other clear built elements appear
distinction: The main label rests on the process of turning into the depths presented by the mountain-col path and the figures and horses' entry sequence running through the painting; C2 relies only on one revealed object in the woods that cannot be confirmed as built elements, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship does not constitute the main spatial organization

evidence: Lower center-right sloped bank: a group of houses and a double-eaved storied pavilion are situated on the terraced slopes of undulating earthen mounds, the building bases tiering with the slope mounds, the layout corresponding to the sloped bank configuration | Lower right: the house group unfolds in order close against the water shoreline, the front houses facing the water, the arrangement direction extending with the trend of the shoreline | Lower left to center-left mountain group: houses, a pagoda, and storied pavilions are placed between mountain cols and ridges, the built elements' high and low positions distributed with the mountain slopes and foothills
distinction: The settlement sites and directions of unfolding clearly follow the slope terraces, shoreline, and mountain-foot configuration, running through the lower part of the painting; the screening by trees and slope mounds is only local, and concealment and revelation do not constitute the main compositional layering

evidence: Upper and left: pine branches and needles hang down from the upper edge of the painting, the left trunks and bamboo clusters dense, screening the upper part and left edge of the middle-ground sloped bank, forming a foreground screening layer. | Center to lower right: a blue-green colored sloped bank extends diagonally from center-right to lower left, a narrow gap left between the slope foot and the left bank, the lower stream drawn with fine lines in swirling water patterns. | Whole scroll: the painting shows only trees, bamboo, slope rocks, water patterns, and three birds (one standing on a rock below, two flying in the blank at right), with no trace of houses, roof eaves, bridges or paths, or other built elements; the red seals are collectors' seals and are not counted as spatial evidence.
distinction: What runs through the composition is the layering of screening and revealing of the sloped bank and water mouth by pine and bamboo branches and foliage, and although the swirling stream hints at extension, there are no discernible entry clues such as bridges, paths, gates, or crossings, so the concealment-and-revelation layering is closer to the visible organization than access to secluded settings is

evidence: Lower left to center: a diagonal slope terrace extends from the left cliff to the center of the painting, forming a flat platform surface, two people seated or reclining on it leaning against the slope, the platform edge unfolding along the turn of the lower-right bank edge. | Upper-center cliff edge: pines slant out from among the cliff rocks, trunks and red hanging threads covering above the platform, the tree roots placed following the trend of the sloped cliff. | Right side: outside the right of the platform is a gentle shoreline and open water, the shoreline extending to the upper right and forming a high-low correspondence with the slope terrace; in the whole scroll no houses, bridges, paths, gates, or other built elements are seen.
distinction: The relationship in which the slope terrace and shoreline receive the main figure's placement runs through the composition, and is closer to site-specific spatial organization than the local screening of the figure by pine shade

evidence: Center-lower-left at the mountain-foot waterside: a group of houses and corridor buildings unfolds horizontally along the water bank, the site close against the blue-green mountain slope foot, the roof ridges staggered front and back, placed according to the slope-foot and shoreline terrain | Central mountain foot: dark-green tree clusters cover the mountain slope, the house group on the waterside flat ground below and in front of them, revealed as a whole rather than revealed by screening | Lower-left water surface: a small boat floats on the open water, with no visible bridge, path, gate, or other connecting clue between it and the houses
distinction: The house group is fully revealed on the slope-foot waterside zone and unfolds with the shoreline, the concealment-and-revelation relationship is weak, and the dominance of terrain and shoreline over the site layout is more obvious

evidence: Center-right cliff slope: a pale zigzag stepped path climbs in segments along the rock face, its top ending at a tiny dark dot-like object at the cliff edge, suspected to be a figure or very small built element, not reliably identifiable | Left to center: blue-green layered rocks pile upward from the lower left, a waterfall pouring down through the rock gaps, constituting the main near-view force | Upper part: open water crosses the painting, distant mountains low and level in a row, forming an opening-and-closing contrast with the tall near-view cliffs
distinction: The zigzag stepped path climbs in segments along the cliff face and points to the cliff-top endpoint, presenting a spatial process that can be reached and continued upward; the scenic accentuation built element required by C3 at the cliff top is only an indistinguishable small dot, lacking a discernible relationship that identifies a piece of scenery

evidence: Left edge: a multi-story pagoda body emerges above the treetops of dense woods, the pagoda base and lowest story screened by the canopy | Lower-left sloped bank: the roof and eaves of houses are revealed among the tree clusters, part of the red building bodies obscured by branches and foliage front and back | Center and upper right of the painting: open water and rolling waves occupy the main body, the built elements not unfolding along the waterside but retreating and hidden within the lower-left tree belt
distinction: Both the pagoda base and the building bodies are screened by the canopy, with only the upper pagoda body and roofs revealed, and the concealment-and-revelation layering is clearer and more discernible than the correspondence of built elements placed according to the sloped bank configuration

evidence: Center to upper right: a gnarled pine rises from the sloped ground, trunks and pine canopy layering to cover the upper part of the painting, forming upper and lower layering organized by tree screening | Center-lower: a robed figure stands in the gap left by the embrace of a curved trunk, the trunk, pine canopy, and shrubs framing a concealment-and-revelation relationship before and behind the figure | Below and center-right: slope rocks, grass, shrubs, and red-leaf trees layer front and back, a distant mountain at upper left half-hidden in pale ink, the whole painting arranging front and back space through relationships of screening and revealing
distinction: What dominates the painting is the layering of screening and embracing of space by woodland and slope rocks, and no discernible movement-through-the-landscape entry clues such as bridges, paths, gates, or crossings appear, so the concealment-and-revelation layering is taken rather than access to secluded settings

evidence: Left-middle slope top among trees: behind snow-covered trunks and slanting branches a black railing, posts, and a stretch of white wall are revealed, the house body hidden behind the trees, only wall, posts, and railing exposed | Upper left to center: layered snow-covered canopy and trunks shelter the upper part of the house, the eaves roof not visible, the concealment-and-revelation relationship forming a layering of foreground slope, middle-ground trees and house, and distant landscape | Center to lower-right water surface: the snow slope descends gently to the water, a small boat on the water, facing the slope-top house across the water, but no bridge, path, gate, or other entry clue connecting with the house is seen
distinction: The house's existence is mainly hinted by the wall, posts, and railing revealed through tree gaps, the concealment-and-revelation layering dominating the composition; the slope-top placement is merely the site's position, and no correspondence of layout unfolding with the slope trend is seen

evidence: Left-middle cliff edge: storied pavilion buildings stand on a flat-platform balustraded terrace set against the cliff face, the platform unfolding horizontally along the cliff edge, below it a steep cliff face, the site's height corresponding to the mountain configuration | Upper-left cliff top: pine branches and tree clusters slant out from the cliff top over and behind the architecture, but the roof, eaves, and balustrade outlines are fully revealed, screening limited | Lower-right water edge: a bridge or plankway with posted railings spans the water and extends along the bank, but no discernible path connects it with the cliff-top architecture
distinction: The relationship in which the architecture is placed along the cliff edge on a cliff-hugging platform with balustrades and the house is set on the platform is the most concrete and clear, and although trees surround it the building body is fully revealed, concealment-and-revelation layering not dominating the scenery

evidence: Lower left: a flat wooden bridge with posts spans a gap in the stream; its deck is divided into two sections sloping upward to the right and connects to the sloping bank on the right, with the post feet set into the waterside inlet at the bank's edge. | Lower-right sloping bank: on the bank at the bridge's right end stands a figure holding a staff; behind and to his right another figure carries an object and walks along the slope; the two figures are directly adjacent to the bridge end, forming a sequence of crossing the bridge, landing on the bank, and continuing onward. | Middle ground to far distance: unpainted water surface and distant mountains lying across separate the near and far layers; no houses or other built elements are visible in the middle and far distance; the foreground bridge and the figures on the sloping bank are the only identifiable man-made structures and points of connection for movement in the painting.
distinction: The bridge's key role lies in connecting with the sloping-bank path and the figures' movement, presenting the process of crossing the bridge, landing on the bank, and passing from here to there, rather than merely showing the topographic correspondence of the bridge base set according to the bank's form.

evidence: Left center: the roofs, eaves, and walls of a group of buildings emerge from behind foreground pine trunks and branches; figures are visible inside; the right part of the building group is cut off by blue-green sloping rocks in front | Center-right far bank: among trees on the far bank across the water, the outlines of a storied pavilion and roof ridges faintly appear, with only the tops exposed, forming a distant layer of buildings seen at the edge of woodland | Lower right: a rider and accompanying servants walk along the shoreline; their path forms no identifiable entrance or path connection with the buildings on the left
distinction: Although the buildings adjoin the sloping rocks, the composition conceals the building bodies with pine trunks and rock masses and uses the exposed roofs and walls to suggest layers; the topographic correspondence is less clearly continuous than the concealment-and-revelation relationship.

evidence: Right to upper right: a double-eaved storied pavilion and connecting galleries are arranged in layers from high to low along blue-green rock slopes and terraces, with the building bases and terrace foundations resting directly on the slope surfaces and rocks | Lower left: a railed platform and zigzag steps project toward the water; water ripples are visible beneath the platform; the lower foundation of the built elements corresponds in height to the shoreline | Center: pine trunks and bamboo clumps interpenetrate among the buildings and terrace bases; the building group descends with the slope rather than spreading out on flat ground
distinction: Although pines and bamboo partly screen the eaves and create layers, what determines the overall layout is the height correspondence of the building bases with the sloping terraces and waterside; concealment and revelation are only a local effect.

evidence: Lower scroll, center to lower left: a narrow long boat is moored among reeds; the boat's bow and planking are exposed; the lower edge of the hull is partially cut off by foreground reed leaves | Lower center, slightly right: a reclining sleeping figure on the boat, along with a conical hat and straw rain cape, emerges from the grass, covered and screened above by dead branches extending horizontally from the right bank | Upper half of the scroll: a large expanse of empty water and a flock of flying geese; throughout the scroll no traces of houses, pavilions, walls, bridges, or paths are visible
distinction: In the near view, reeds and dead branches screen and reveal the boatman, forming a concealment-and-revelation layer, while the flat waterside has no high-low foundation or topographic correspondence that would allow a C1 determination.

evidence: Lower left among the slope trees: a pale-ink gable roof emerges from behind the trees, its ridge line and two slopes visible; the building body and eaves are cut off by trunks and foliage | Lower left to center: miscellaneous trees grow from the sloping rocks, their branches and foliage extending up and to the right, covering the area above and to the right of the roof, forming layers of screening and partial exposure | Lower-right water surface: a small boat with one person poling; it faces the buildings on the bank across the water, with no identifiable connecting clues such as a bridge, path, or gate between them
distinction: The roof is half-exposed because of tree screening, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship dominates the scene; the correspondence between the building base and the sloping bank terrain is obscured and unclear, so C1 is not selected.

evidence: Right center: the roof ridge, upturned eaves, and the red bracket sets and flat balustrades beneath the eaves of a storied pavilion are clearly exposed; the lower half of the building body is screened by the dense pine canopy in front | Right center-lower, in front of the pavilion: broad masses of pine branches and foliage lie across and overlap beneath the pavilion, forming a concealment-and-revelation layer in which the roof shows above the treetops and the base is hidden below the trees | Lower slope, slightly right: a rider and walking attendants travel on the slope; between them and the pavilion are trees and the slope surface, and no path, bridge, or gate is visible connecting them
distinction: The clearest relationship in the painting is the concealment-and-revelation layer in which the pine grove screens the building body and the roof emerges above the treetops, rather than the correspondence of base, layout, and sloping-terrace terrain.

evidence: Lower right: a small boat is moored on the water; a person sits reading in the boat; a woven canopy is set behind the person; the hull is close against the lower-right sloping bank and bamboo clumps. | Right side: plum branches extend diagonally and spread horizontally from the right bank; bamboo leaves hang down and overlap the top of the boat canopy, forming a layer of partial screening and exposure over the canopy top. | Upper part and left half: distant mountains lie across the upper part of the painting in pale ink; the left half is open water and unpainted space; no outlines of houses, pavilions, galleries, bridges, or paths are visible.
distinction: The only concealment-and-revelation organization in the painting is the screening layer formed by the plum and bamboo on the right bank over the boat canopy; the boat is moored still on the water, with no connecting clues such as a bridge, path, gate, or ferry landing, so C4 is not selected.

evidence: Right center-lower to lower right: a group of buildings and galleries spreads horizontally along the mountain-foot sloping bank; roof ridges rise and fall with the slope, and the red-pillared walls are set close against the waterside rocky slope foundation | Right center, mid-slope: another group of buildings is set on a cliff terrace, with balustrades enclosing the terrace edge; its base is clearly higher than the mountain-foot group and corresponds to the turn of the cliff slope | Center, slightly right: slanting pines and rocky slopes stand in front of the building group, yet the main group remains fully exposed, showing its layered arrangement rising with the mountain terrain
distinction: The bases and heights of the two building groups are both arranged in layers according to the cliff-slope terrain, and the terrace balustrades follow the cliff; terrain-responsive arrangement runs through the entire building group. The pine-grove screening of roofs is only local concealment and revelation, not the main way of organizing the built elements.

evidence: Right bank, center-lower: gable roofs and white walls emerge among pines and blue-green trees; the building bodies are partially screened by foreground trunks and foliage, forming a concealment-and-revelation layer of buildings seen in the woods | Center, slightly lower: another white mass among the trees resembles a screened roof, but the details are unclear and it is not counted as primary evidence of built elements | Lower stream bank and sloping ground: no identifiable path, bridge, or gate connects the waterside and slope with the buildings; there is a lack of accessible movement clues
distinction: Although the buildings sit among trees on the sloping bank, the compositional emphasis is on the concealment-and-revelation layer in which they are half-screened by the pine grove and trees, revealing only roofs and walls, rather than on the correspondence between building bases and terrain height.

evidence: Lower left: waterside buildings stand at the foot of the bank slope; beneath them, rows of wooden post supports extend out over the water; one person sits inside facing the water; the building bases are set according to the bank slope and water level | Center, slightly left: a small pavilion with a pyramidal roof stands on a platform on a projecting rock head; the pavilion base contracts according to the form of the rock top, and a waterfall drops through a rock crevice beneath it; the pavilion's height corresponds to the rock terrace | Lower left to center-left: pine trunks and branches extend diagonally from the bank slope and lie across in front of the buildings and rocky slope, partially screening roofs and eaves, but the building bodies, post supports, and pavilion remain fully discernible
distinction: Although pine branches lie diagonally before the buildings, the architectural bodies and bases are clear and complete, and concealment and revelation do not form the main layers; the dominant relationship is the terrain-corresponding placement of the waterside buildings on posts along the bank and the pavilion on the rock top.

evidence: Left to center: a large tree rises from the lower-left sloping rock; its canopy covers the left half of the scroll and cuts off the middle-ground shoreline; water surface and distant mountains emerge to the right of the canopy and through gaps in the branches, forming front-and-back layers of screening and exposure. | Middle ground: open water and sandbars spread horizontally; the shoreline extends from behind the tree to the right edge; scattered rocks appear on the water; no traces of houses, walls, bridges, or galleries are visible. | Foreground sloping bank: a herd boy holding a rope faces an ox, standing on level ground on the sloping bank; the ox steps along the slope; no roof, eaves, or building base is identifiable anywhere in the scroll.
distinction: What runs through the composition is the concealment-and-revelation layer in which the tree canopy cuts off the middle ground and the water and distant mountains emerge from behind the tree; the figure leading the ox moves toward outside the painting and forms no connected process of passing from here to there via clues such as a bridge, path, gate, or ferry landing.

evidence: Lower left to center: a section of slanted bamboo railing runs up along the foot of a grassy slope and turns; on the slope stand garden rocks and broad-leaved plants with red flowers; the direction of the railing foundation corresponds to the slope-edge line | Center to right bank: a horizontal bamboo railing runs level along the rear edge of a platform; low trees are faintly visible beyond the railing; within the railing is a level paved platform, enclosing a raised terrace | Lower platform: the folded-line edge of the platform floor aligns with the junction and corner turn of the slanted and horizontal railings; the platform forms a height correspondence with the sloping ground and garden rocks outside the railing
distinction: The railing and platform bases are placed according to the turning edges of the sloping terrace and correspond in height to the rocks outside the railing; terrain directly participates in the built layout. No identifiable entry clues such as gates, paths, or bridges are visible in the painting, so access to secluded settings is not selected.

evidence: Center to upper part: a large tree extends diagonally from the sloping bank, its hanging branches and dense foliage covering the middle ground downward, forming a large screening surface | Center-right sloping bank: two figures, one seated and one standing, are beneath the hanging branches and beside the sloping bank, revealed through gaps in the branches and foliage, forming front-and-back layers with the pale mountains behind the tree | Lower part: the foreground waterside and grassy slope spread horizontally; the water surface is unpainted; no traces of houses, bridges, galleries, or walls are visible
distinction: The layers visible in the painting are organized mainly by the concealment-and-revelation relationship between the screening hanging branches and the exposed sloping bank, not by terrain-corresponding placement of building bases (no building bases are visible in the entire painting).

evidence: Center-right of the painting: the front slope of the roof of an open thatched hall emerges through gaps in the dense tree canopy; the rear part of the roof is screened by branches and foliage, leaving only eaves and a gable fragment visible | Right side: a thick tree trunk extends diagonally over the top and rear of the building; dense foliage presses on the eaves; the building body is half-hidden in tree shade; the concealment-and-revelation relationship determines how the building is visible | Lower left to lower center: a weeping-willow sloping bank faces the water and the water surface is open; no identifiable connecting clues for movement, such as a bridge, path, or gate, are visible on the slope in front of the building
distinction: Although the building sits on a waterside slope, the right half of the painting is organized by the concealment-and-revelation layer in which the canopy screens the eaves and the building is seen through gaps in the trees; topographic correspondence is weaker than the screening relationship.

evidence: Lower-right sloping bank: among pine trunks and branches, an arched, ribbed roof-like structure is revealed; its lower edge is cut off by pine trunks and sloping rocks, presenting a concealment-and-revelation layer of tree in front and roof behind | Upper left: a towering cliff face drops straight to the water; the cliff foot is closed off by stacked rocks, a sloping terrace, and grass, meeting the open water in the center | Central water surface: a canopied boat carries several people, with one person poling; it travels on the unpainted water between the cliff wall and the right bank, connecting with no structure on shore by path or bridge
distinction: Although the boat carries a sense of movement, it connects with no identifiable built element or path; the only identifiable relationship in the painting between built elements and scenery is the layer in which pine trunks screen and reveal the roof-like structure, so C2 is selected rather than C4.

evidence: Lower left: a wooden bridge spans a stream gorge; to the right of the bridge a person riding a donkey travels right along a pale-ink dotted path; the path extends toward the buildings and banner in the center | Lower center: a person carrying a shoulder pole stands by the water, beside which slanted stone steps lead up to the open ground in front of the buildings, connecting the waterside with the built structures | Center, slightly right: an open hall and a group of buildings are set on level ground by the stream bank; people sit around a table inside the hall; a banner stands before the eaves; this becomes the destination of the movement clues
distinction: Although trees interpenetrate among the buildings, the open hall and the human activity are fully exposed overall, and concealment and revelation are not dominant; the bridge, path, rider, and stepped path form a continuous process of approaching the built structures, and their role in organizing the composition is more continuous.

evidence: Center, slightly lower: a rider on a white horse leads a dog by a rope; the horse's hooves stand on level ground before the slope; horse and rider are in motion | Right side to upper right: a slanted bank and rock wall enclose the foreground open ground from top to bottom; the ground at the slope foot extends down and left, forming an open passable band | Entire scroll: no houses, walls, bridges, gates, paths, or ferry crossings or other built elements and movement facilities are visible; only mountains and rocks, hanging branches, and grass
distinction: With no built elements visible, the only spatial organizing clue in the painting is the movement of horse and rider along the open ground at the slope foot and the extension of the ground, which is closer to the visible relationship than the built-element/terrain correspondence, concealment-and-revelation layers, or marker relationships required by C1–C3.

evidence: Center, slightly right, hillside: the roofs and walls of multiple building groups are arranged in layers along the slope, rising and falling with the mountain terrain; their bases rest on sloping terraces | Center of the painting: several buildings are placed according to sloping terraces and rock crevices; their orientation follows the direction of the slope; trees beside them grow along the slope without cutting off the sequence of buildings | Lower slope foot, waterside: the slope foot opens toward the water; a boat and people are visible at the bank; above them the building group rises step by step from the slope foot, forming an overall sequence arranged according to the slope
distinction: The buildings are spread across the slope overall and rise and fall in layers with the slope; tree screening serves only as local embellishment; the dominant relationship is terrain participating in placement rather than concealment and revelation forming layers.

evidence: Lower left: a simple wooden frame structure stands at the water's edge, with two posts, a crossbar, and a top beam, resembling a bridge pier or the remnant section of a trestle, extending beyond the left edge of the painting | Center, slightly lower: a rider wearing a conical hat and an umbrella-holding attendant both move left; their direction faces the wooden structure and shoreline at lower left, forming a moving sequence of travel | Lower part of the painting: an ink-washed waterside runs across the lower part; the wooden structure is set at the water's edge and meets the rider's path by the water, suggesting a connection for crossing the water or continuing onward
distinction: The composition's emphasis is on the reachable process suggested by the figures' direction of movement connecting with the waterside wooden structure (a bridge/ferry type), rather than the placement correspondence between the wooden structure and terrain height, so C4 is selected rather than C1.

evidence: Left side to upper part: a thick-trunked willow extends diagonally from lower left; its slender hanging branches cover the upper half of the painting, screening the space beneath | Lower-center sloping ground: the slope surface is rendered with parallel diagonal lines; a boy holding a scroll stands facing a rider; the rider sits on a donkey on the slope; all figures are beneath the covering hanging branches | Right center, behind the rider: a pale-ink broken line emerges from behind the rider and donkey and extends horizontally to the right with a turn; its form resembles the top of a wall or a remnant of a railing edge, but it is extremely pale and incomplete and cannot be reliably identified
distinction: The dominant relationship in the painting is the concealment-and-revelation layer formed by the covering hanging branches and the pale line revealed behind the figures, while reachable movement clues such as bridges, paths, gates, or ferries are not identifiable in the painting, so the screening layer is closer to the visible organization than the movement process.

evidence: Right side and upper part: a large tree extends diagonally from the right bank; its thick trunk occupies the right edge; branches and foliage spread horizontally and cover the upper half of the painting, forming a layer of screening and exposure over the bank-side space | Center, slightly lower: a figure in a red robe rides a deer and stops on the surface of a slanted bank terrace; a boy stands facing him to his right; shrubs and rocks dot the bank edge and slope foot | Center-left and far view: open water lies across; in the distance low flat sandbars and rocky-bank shrubs form horizontal rows; no traces of houses, walls, bridges, galleries, gates, or ferry crossings are visible anywhere in the scroll
distinction: The spatial organization running through the composition is the layer of screening and exposure formed by the large tree and bank vegetation, while the figures' movement and stopping connect with no identifiable path, ferry crossing, or opening into depth, so the screening layer is closer to the visible relationship than access to secluded settings.

evidence: Center of the painting, slightly lower: a thatched-roof pavilion; the umbrella-shaped thatch roof has a tied-grass knot at its apex; several posts supporting it are visible beneath the roof; the pavilion body has no walls. | Around and in front of the pavilion: numerous leafless dead trees surround the pavilion; one trunk passes in front of the pavilion; fine dense branches lie over the thatch roof; the roof and posts are revealed through gaps between trunks and branches, forming a concealment-and-revelation layer of a pavilion seen in the woods. | Upper part and middle ground: distant mountains are low and gentle; a large unpainted area in the center resembles water surface or mist; the near ground is a gentle slope; the pavilion stands among trees on the slope; no movement clues such as bridges, paths, or gates are visible, nor is there a terrace base or terrain-corresponding layered arrangement following the slope.
distinction: The pavilion is presented mainly through the screening and exposure created by the interpenetrating dead trees, forming a concealment-and-revelation layer in the woods; its position is among a flat slope in a cold forest, not at a scenic node such as a peak edge or waterside outlet that could serve as scenic accentuation.

evidence: Left waterside: the bottom of an open hall is supported on a row of post feet above the shoal bank; the platform projects toward the water; the building body backs onto the sloping bank and trees; the base corresponds directly to the shoreline | Right center: a two-story storied pavilion stands on a high stone-built terrace; the terrace base descends in layers with the slope; the pavilion faces the open water in the center | Center and far view: a large area of unpainted water runs across the heart of the painting; distant mountains are gentle; the two building groups on left and right face each other across the water, each placed according to its bank or terrace rather than connected into a route
distinction: Trees are mostly placed behind and beside the buildings as foils; building bodies, eaves, and posts are fully exposed, and concealment and revelation do not dominate the layers; the correspondence of post feet and terrace bases with the water surface and sloping bank directly determines the placement of built elements, so C1 is more apt.

evidence: Upper right: an arched bridge spans the water; a line of figures crosses the bridge in procession; both ends of the bridge connect with bank paths and building groups on the slope | Center of the painting: an arched bridge crosses a stream gorge; two people pass over it; the bridge body connects the storied-pavilion courtyard on the left with the path on the right slope | Lower center to lower right: a red-railed bridge, steps, and galleries link the waterside with multiple storied pavilions on the slope; figures walk along steps and galleries; boats carry people back and forth on the water, forming reachable movement clues
distinction: Movement clues such as bridges, paths, galleries, and boats run through the entire painting and connect the building groups, making the process of entry and travel dominant; although the buildings are arranged according to sloping banks and terraces, the topographic correspondence is less significant in organizing the painting than the movement clues.

evidence: Left-bank waterside: an arched canopied platform is set close against the rock foot of the bank wall; rows of wooden piles are visible along the platform's lower edge extending into the water; its position is determined by the sloping bank's waterline | Beside the left-center bank wall: a small poled boat lies close to the bank wall, sharing the recess embraced by the bank wall with the canopied shelter below | Center of the painting: a large tree extends diagonally from the left-bank sloping rock and crosses the water; its root foot meets the bank rock, defining the boundary between the bank edge and the open water
distinction: The placement relationship between the bank-side canopied shelter and the bank wall's waterside is more directly visible than clues of boat arrival; the poled boat only locally approaches the bank edge and does not form a continuous entry route.

evidence: Lower left: an open hall building stands on the sloping bank; one person sits inside; attendants, horses, and cart wheels outside the hall form a stopping and reception point on the bank | Center, slightly lower: a boat approaches the sloping bank, its bow close to the bank edge; a standing person on the boat points toward the bank and echoes the figures on shore, forming a connection of landing from the water | Left center: the roofs and eaves of the building extend from beneath the dense canopy; trunks stand on the sloping bank in front of the building; the front edge of the building directly faces the waterside where the ferry boat moors
distinction: The boat approaching the bank, the exchange between figures, and the carts and horses on shore form a movement process of landing from the water and reaching the built structures; although tree screening is present, the building body is openly exposed, and concealment and revelation are not the dominant compositional mode.

evidence: Right center-lower: a multi-story storied pavilion stands on a high brick-and-stone terrace that turns diagonally; the terrace base tapers and turns with the hillside; the stories and terrace base correspond in height | Left center: waterside buildings are raised on a base above the water bank; the building bodies spread horizontally along the shoreline, backed by sloping rocks and trees | Right edge: pine branches extend from among the mountain rocks and cover one side of the pavilion roof, but the pavilion body, terrace base, and eaves remain clearly discernible
distinction: Pine branches only locally cover the roof while the architectural body is fully exposed; concealment and revelation do not dominate the composition; the terrain-responsive placement of the terrace base turning with the slope and the buildings raised along the shoreline runs more through the painting.

evidence: Center: two figures stand on level ground, with a screen-like rock lying across behind them as a background barrier; the figures are fully exposed in front of the rock | Upper left and right side: dead branches extend diagonally into the painting from the edges, their branches interweaving above the central scene and, together with the rocks in the lower center, enclosing the central open ground | Lower left: two sheep lie on the ground at the slope foot, behind them sloping rocks and dead trees; no traces of houses, walls and eaves, bridges, paths, gates, or ferry crossings or other built elements and movement clues are visible in the entire scroll
distinction: The enclosure and screening framework of trees and rocks around the central scene runs through the composition and is more dominant than the topographic correspondence of the figures placed against the sloping rocks, so the concealment-and-revelation/enclosure category is selected.

evidence: Center to center-left: a small boat lies diagonally across the water; a low table and vessels such as a bottle and dish are placed in the boat; one person sits in the boat looking up; another bends at the boat's end holding a long pole | Lower left: a projecting sloping rock stands in front of the boat, cutting off the hull and the lower part of the tableware; the bottle vessel emerges from behind the rock top | Upper left to center: dense bamboo hangs down from the bank edge over the boat; the boat and figures are in a layer between the bamboo and the sloping rock
distinction: The cutting off and revealing of the boat, vessels, and figures by the sloping rock and bamboo grove form layers running through the entire painting, while the poling, though suggesting movement, has no visible destination or connecting node.

evidence: Lower center, slightly right, waterside: a small canopied boat is moored on the water at the end of the sloping bank; its bow faces the open water and is adjacent to a figure holding a pole on the bank, forming a waterside connection between bank and boat | Lower left: the sloping bank and trees extend from lower left into the water; the shoreline ends at the water's edge in the middle ground, forming a transition zone from land to water | Whole scroll: apart from the waterside canopied boat and the figure on the bank, no clear built elements such as houses, pavilions, bridges, or galleries are visible; the center-right is open water and reefs; the far view is continuous mountain ranges
distinction: C4 is closer to the reachable and navigable connection suggested by the shoreline, moored boat, and open water; C3 treats the canopied boat only as a static scenic marker and does not reflect the entry connection formed by bank and boat.

evidence: Center-left: between the pine trunk and the branches and foliage, a gabled roof and eave lines are exposed, while most of the building itself is screened by the trunk in front and the sloping bank, with only part of the roof visible | Lower area to center: the foreground sloping bank, reeds, and clustered trees spread horizontally, and the building is placed behind the bank and grove, forming a layered front-to-back effect of screening and revelation | Center-right water surface: on the open water a single small boat, its occupant wearing a conical hat, faces the building on the bank across the water; no bridge, path, or gate is seen connecting to the building
distinction: The building is dominated by the concealment-and-revelation relation in which its roof emerges from among the trees; the correspondence between its site and the sloping terrain is not evident, so concealment and revelation is chosen rather than terrain-responsive siting

evidence: Center-lower, toward the right, on the waterside sloping bank: an open pavilion is set on the sloping rocks, its roof pressed down by the dense canopy above, its body emerging from the edge of the grove, with railings and figures inside the pavilion visible | Above and to the right of the pavilion, at the edge of the slope: only the roof and part of the lattice-walled building itself are exposed, the rest screened by trunks, leaves, and rocks, presenting a layered effect of seeing the building among trees and behind rocks | The lower-right sloping bank as a whole: the bank's rocks rise and several dense trees cover them; both the pavilion and the building are embedded amid screening trees and rocks, contrasting with the open water on the left as concealment against openness
distinction: Although the built site rests on the slope by the water, in the painting the building is presented mainly by partial exposure of roof and wall beneath the screening of trees and rocks; the organization of concealment and revelation plays a stronger role than the correspondence between site and terrain elevation

evidence: Lower middle of the right bank: a hall with white walls and black tiles sits on a terrace on the waterside slope, below which another lower tier of roofs and a white-walled courtyard step down the slope, and further to the right there is a higher platform with figures, their high and low placement corresponding to the slope | Left-center slope hollow: a small pavilion building is set on a terraced slope within a mountain hollow, its site rising with the slope, surrounded by pine forest | Center-left waterside: a stretch of building roofs spreads horizontally along the sloping bank, distributed following the shoreline, backed by the slope and facing the water
distinction: Although the built elements on the right bank are partly screened across by pine trunks and branches, the hall, buildings, and courtyard walls step up and down along the terraces and open toward the water; the organizing role of terrain and shoreline in placement runs through more of the built elements across the painting than the concealment and revelation by woodland

evidence: Upper left: bamboo branches, chrysanthemum leaves, and a pendent flower overlap and screen down from the upper edge of the painting, the foliage screening from front and back so that only the flower head and part of the leaf surfaces are exposed | Lower right: a cluster of flowers enters diagonally from the lower-right corner, branches and leaves pressing over one another with red and white flowers, forming a layer of concealment and revelation at the edge | Center: the middle of the painting is a large area of unpainted space, with only flying insects and grass insects scattered within it; there are no traces of built elements whatsoever—no buildings, walls and eaves, bridges or paths, or doorways
distinction: No built elements are visible anywhere in the work; the only discernible spatial organization is the screening and revealing layers of foliage at the edges, so concealment and revelation is the closest category; terrain-responsive siting, scenic accentuation nodes, and movement clues are all absent

evidence: Lower right near the bank: a person sits on a flat waterside rock platform facing the open water; around the platform there are only miscellaneous trees and sloping rocks, with no buildings, pavilions or galleries visible | Center to upper right: the main peak and secondary peaks stand beyond the water, separated by cloud and mist; on the ridges and at the mountain foot only rows of horizontal dotted tree clusters are seen, with no recognizable building outlines | Lower left to middle-ground water: open water runs across the painting, a middle-ground grove forms an islet dividing the near water from the distant mountains, and an empty boat is moored on the water at lower left
distinction: The waterside rock platform and seated figure occupy an open near-ground plane and, corresponding to the main peak across the water, become the focal point of the scene; the painting lacks any recognizable access connection such as a bridge, path, gate, or ferry, with only the water surface extending, so access to secluded settings is not selected.

evidence: Lower left: at the end of the pine-covered sloping bank by the water there is a roofed built structure, with a horizontal eave line beneath an arched roof, several short columns under the eaves standing at the bank's edge at the water, its site hugging the edge of the sloping bank and facing the open water | Lower right: a small boat carrying people on the water, facing the waterside structure at lower left across the water, with no recognizable connecting line such as a dock, jetty, or path between them | Upper middle: two ink-washed peaks and faint distant mountains lie across the broad open water; the lower-left sloping bank is the only sloping terrace shoreline in the painting that provides a built site
distinction: The correspondence between the built site and the waterside at the end of the sloping bank is clearly visible, but between the boat and the built structure there is no recognizable access connection; the entry process is less evident than the terrain-responsive placement relation

evidence: Center: a porous rock or tree-trunk-like main subject running vertically through the painting, connected below to an earthen slope, forming the structural framework of the entire picture. | Lower left, middle right, upper right: cabbage, flowers and plants, bamboo shoots and bamboo culms are placed close against the foot of the slope, the sides, and the slope terrace of this main subject, organized as separately arranged according to the slope and spread out around the rock. | Whole painting: no built elements or movement-through-landscape clues such as buildings, walls and eaves, bridges, paths, or gates and crossings are identifiable; only frogs, lizards, and insects are interspersed among the plants.
distinction: The visible organization is primarily plants arranged according to the force of the central slope and rock and spread out around the rock, rather than a built hierarchy screened by concealment and revelation suggested through concealment-and-revelation relations; therefore it is assigned under the relationship of arrangement according to circumstance.

evidence: In a hollow on the left ridge: a pavilion with a pyramidal roof exposes its roof and eave columns; the right half of its terrace base and the column feet are screened by the mountain-shoulder rocks and dotted-leaf groves in front, so the pavilion body lies in a layer behind the mountain rocks | On the left shoulder of the central main peak: the main peak's shoulder slopes down across in front of the pavilion, its dotted-leaf groves screening the pavilion's lower right, forming a concealment-and-revelation relation between foreground mountain rocks and background built elements | At the stream bank at the bottom center: a plank bridge and a staff-bearing figure stand at the bank's edge, but no visible path connects upward to the ridge pavilion, and the movement clues are not linked to the built elements
distinction: Although the pavilion base is built on a terrace, the painting mainly signals the built presence through the concealment-and-revelation layering by which the mountain shoulder and groves screen its right half and expose its roof and columns; the terrain correspondence is less clearly sustained than the screening relation

evidence: Center-lower part of the painting: the roof of a main hall and the openly exposed figures inside are visible; the front part of the building itself is blocked by a towering dark boulder, and above the roof ridge it is covered by a dense canopy, presenting a layered effect of seeing the building behind rock and within the grove | Upper right: a storied pavilion exposes only its upper eaves and flat-balcony railing, its lower part lost among the groves and mountain rocks | Upper-right stream ravine: a small bridge spans the ravine, and the path beside it disappears into sloping rocks and groves, with no recognizable continuous route between it and the central building
distinction: Although the bridge and the figures at the bank hint at movement, there is no recognizable access connection; both built structures are presented through concealment-and-revelation relations of rock screening and grove screening, and the screening function runs through the composition more dominantly

evidence: Center-left valley: the roofs and eaves of a group of storied pavilions emerge from behind groves and sloping rocks, the lower part of the building bodies screened by woodland, forming a layered effect of seeing buildings among the trees | Upper-right mountain hollow: several buildings and pavilions are half hidden among the ridge woodland, exposing only roofs and part of the walls, their sites cut off by the foreground hillside | Center-left sloping bank: several buildings are hidden behind the groves on the sloping bank, exposing walls and roofs, with the stream ravine and sloping rocks in front cutting off their lower parts
distinction: The built elements are all signaled and given spatial layering by roofs and eaves exposed after being cut off by woodland and mountain rocks; the concealment-and-revelation relation runs through all three built structures; the slope-responsive correspondence of sites is visible but largely screened, making it less explanatory

evidence: Center-left valley of the painting: a pagoda, storied pavilions, and a group of buildings are arranged in tiers along the valley floor and terraces, their bases rising and falling with the ridges and valley, the layout spreading with the mountain terrain | Right bank edge: a group of buildings is arranged and unfolded along the waterside slope, the roof orientation consistent with the configuration of the sloping bank | Around the central building complex: the outlines of buildings and courtyards are fully and recognizably visible, only partly half-screened by cloud mist and foreground sloping rocks, with the main mass exposed on the valley platform
distinction: The building complex is dominated by the correspondence of base elevation and manner of unfolding with the valley and terraces; building bodies and courtyards are fully exposed, and layering is not organized by screening and revealing, so C1 is chosen rather than C2.
