distinction: The only prominent spatial organization in the painting is the layering of screening and exposure among trees, slope rocks, and the peak foot, which is closer to the visible relations than the terrain placement of C1, the scenic accentuation of C3, or the movement clues of C4

evidence: Lower section: Between the slope rocks, a curved ochre-colored band-like structure threads through the crevices of the rocks, forming a winding, interconnected configuration that resembles a streambank or a path clue | Middle section: Gaps and openings are left between the withered trees, red trees, bamboo clumps and the horizontally cut-off cloud vapor, forming a layered passage through which one can move from below upward | Upper section: Blue-green peaks rise above the gaps in the woodland of the middle section, and together with the curved band below and the opening in the middle form a spatial sequence from near to deep
distinction: The main label is taken from the penetrable process suggested by the curved band below and the woodland opening, rather than merely the concealment-and-revelation layering of trees and cloud vapor

evidence: Center-right of the painting: Faint ink lines resembling a building roof or structure are dimly visible between the mountains and rocks and the trees, partly obscured by the foreground trees and rocks. | Left side and center of the painting: Multiple withered trees and the mountains and rocks on the right form foreground-background layers, screening the dimly visible buildings within them.
distinction: The buildings primarily present a concealment-and-revelation relationship of being screened by trees and rocks, rather than clearly displaying a layout sited according to the terrain.

evidence: Center-left of the painting: Several houses stand clustered on a flat slope terrace where the mountain foot extends into the water, their building bases pressed close to the shoreline, backing onto the mountain and facing the water | Central house cluster: The houses spread out laterally along the waterside, staggered front and back and arranged according to the flat shoal terrain, the layout consistent with the direction of the shoreline | Center-right to upper section: The mountain-foot slopes descend step by step into the water, forming the waterside flat shoal on which the houses sit, and the siting of the built structures corresponds directly to this terrain
distinction: The outlines of the houses are fully exposed on the waterside flat slope, with the cold woodland beside them merely encircling rather than covering the building itself; the concealment-and-revelation layering is weaker than the correspondence between building base and bank configuration

evidence: Lower left: A wooden bridge spans the water, its end meeting bank rocks and a bamboo-fence gate, within which are waterside houses and moored boats, constituting a clue for entering the village from outside | Center-left: A bridge with railings spans the stream mouth, linking the waterside house cluster with the slope on the opposite bank, with houses and fences arranged continuously along the shoreline | Center-upper: A plank-road bridge with posts is built across the mountain ravine, above which a winding path climbs along the valley and gradually disappears into the gullies at the summit, suggesting a movement-through-the-landscape route extending into the depths
distinction: The bridge, fence gate, plank road and winding mountain path together form a traversable process leading from the waterside village houses into the depths of the ravine, which runs through the entire composition more than the terrain correspondence of houses sited along the bank

evidence: Right-central ridge (at about sixty percent of the painting's vertical axis): At the turning point of the ridge, a gallery-road or railing-like structure composed of parallel horizontal lines and diagonal braces is visible, erected against the ridge, its ink dark and details unclear | Lower-right slope: Between the slope rocks and tree clumps, the outlines of houses with roofs and walls are visible, their positions rising and falling with the slope, some edges merging into the dark mountains and rocks | Lower left and upper left: Pine trees stand on the slope rocks at lower left, above which a large area of unpainted space contrasts with the mountain mass extending diagonally on the right; the suspected built structures are all located on the ridge line and slope foot of the right half of the mountain mass
distinction: Although the central gallery-road-like structure resembles a movement-through-the-landscape clue, its connection with the houses and paths cannot be reliably identified; the correspondence of the suspected built structures being sited according to the rise and fall of the ridge and slope terraces is closer to the visible layout

evidence: Center-left: The roof and eaves of a thatch-roofed pavilion are covered in multiple layers by the large tree trunk slanting out from the lower left and its dense foliage, with the building itself emerging through the gaps in the trees | Center-left: The reclining figure on the couch inside and the floor before the couch are visible through the open building itself, and the edge of the platform in front of the building is half-hidden by foreground branches and leaves | Lower right: A fence and a brushwood gate enclose the boundary of the courtyard; beside the gate stands an attendant boy holding a broom; the open ground inside the gate connects with the flat ground before the pavilion, but no continuous path is seen extending onward
distinction: Although the brushwood gate and fence suggest an entrance, the movement-through-the-landscape clue stops at the static figure beside the gate and does not form a continuous process approaching the pavilion; the existence and layering of the pavilion are mainly suggested by the screening and revealing of the tree trunk and foliage, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship runs through the middle of the painting

evidence: Lower-middle valley: Several houses and a railed platform sit on the flat ground of a valley flanked by two mountains, the buildings spreading out at varying heights along the direction of the valley | Lower-middle valley mouth to foreground slope bank: The building bases of the house cluster are placed step by step according to the slope terraces of the valley, and the open space at the valley mouth connects downward to the foreground slope bank and the grassy stream bank | Right-middle woodland: Behind the treetops another group of pavilion roofs emerges, with only the eaves and ridges visible, constituting a partial concealment clue
distinction: The valley houses are relatively completely visible in the open space of the valley and their layout unfolds along the slope terraces and valley configuration; the terrain-siting relationship explains the main compositional mode of the built structures better than the partial woodland concealment and revelation

evidence: Middle-ground left sandbar: Extremely faint traces of houses appear among the trees on the sandbar, with roofs emerging from beneath the tree shadows, their outlines blurred | Right-bank middle: Behind the reeds and bank slope, a pale-ink horizontal ridge-like structure is seen, partly obscured by the reeds | Full-width water surface and foreground: The foreground slope bank's large trees and the open water surface occupy the main composition, with three boats distributed on the water; no bridges, paths, gates or other land-based movement-through-the-landscape clues are seen
distinction: The visibility of the suspected houses mainly depends on screening and revealing by the tree clumps and reeds, rather than on a correspondence of height with the slope terraces and waterside, so concealment and revelation is taken rather than terrain-responsive siting

evidence: Center-left lower: An open pavilion with railings and a rolled blind is built on the waterside bank slope; inside, two people sit facing each other before a table, and the pavilion opens toward the stream surface to the right front | Lower right: A bridge with railings spans the stream ravine; on the bridge a person carrying a crane walks toward the open pavilion to the left | Among the slope rocks at lower center: The left end of the bridge rests on the bank slope below the pavilion's platform base, and the gaps between the slope rocks and shoreline link the bridge deck with the platform before the pavilion, forming a sequence of crossing the bridge and landing to approach the pavilion
distinction: The bridge and the crane-carrying walker form a movement-through-the-landscape sequence arriving at the open pavilion, which organizes the spatial process of the lower half of the painting more than the correspondence of buildings to the slope base

evidence: Center-right mountain hollow: A red-walled hall and another roof on a lower level sit at the upper edge of a concave valley, their bases and lower parts obscured by a patch of dark dense trees, with only the roof, eaves and upper wall exposed | Right of the central giant peak: The left side of the buildings presses close to the rock face and slope rocks extending from the giant peak, and the rock mass and tree clumps form a foreground screen, placing the buildings in a spatial layer behind the rock and within the woodland | Lower slope road in the painting: Riders and walkers proceed leftward along the mountain-foot slope road, which does not extend into the concave valley where the buildings are located, and no visible path links the two
distinction: The buildings mainly reveal the layering of roof and walls through the screening and revealing of woodland and rock, while the horse-and-figure path below forms no identifiable entry connection with the buildings, so concealment and revelation fits the visible relationship better than access to secluded settings

evidence: Bottom: At the bottom of the painting is a bridge, on which are walkers and a person riding a donkey, presenting the dynamics of traveling and crossing the bridge. | Right side: Among the cliffs on the right, a building is visible, below which a clearly winding mountain path or stone steps extends upward, connecting to the building. | Overall composition: The bridge at the bottom and the mountain path on the right form a coherent movement-through-the-landscape clue, guiding the eye from the foreground toward the built structures in the depths.
distinction: Although the right-side building is screened by cliffs, the movement-through-the-landscape route formed by the bridge, walkers and winding mountain path is more prominent, dominating the process of spatial entry.

evidence: Center of the painting: The conical roof of a pyramidal-roofed pavilion emerges between bamboo clumps and slanting pine branches, and the pavilion body below the eaves is partly screened by pine branches and bamboo leaves, presenting a layering of seeing a house within the woodland | Middle-ground center: A railed bridge-plank road with balustrade posts runs horizontally across the painting, its left end meeting the brick platform foundation on the left bank, positioned below and in front of the pavilion | Lower left: One balustrade post stands at the edge of the slope bank, the shoreline extends diagonally, and two figures stand on the bank in the foreground
distinction: Although the bridge railing runs across the middle ground, its connection with the pavilion is discontinuous and no clear arriving relationship is seen; the pavilion mainly uses the screening and revealing of pines and bamboo to suggest its layer, so concealment and revelation fits the visible evidence better than access to secluded settings

evidence: Lower left: A plank bridge with supports is built among the stream shoals and rocky islets, its deck running horizontally, meeting the slope-bank shoal rocks on the left and leading on the right to the open ground before the pavilion | Lower-right middle: A thatched pavilion stands between two clumps of trees, with a figure seated upright inside; the bank ground before the pavilion is continuous with the right end of the bridge, forming an arriving relationship of crossing the bridge to approach the thatched hall | Center-left: Above the cloud vapor and earthen mounds emerge the double eaves and flat balcony of a pavilion, and to its right another small pavilion roof is half-hidden in the trees, suggesting a deeper layer of built structures
distinction: The bridge and stream bank provide the traversable, reachable movement-through-the-landscape connection to the thatched hall, organizing the lower space more dominantly than the concealment-and-revelation layering of encircling tree clumps

evidence: Center-left of the painting: A group of houses and an open pavilion gather at the water's edge, with dense tree canopies running across above them; the rear half of the roofs and the building bodies are obscured by branches and foliage, with only the roof ridges, eaves and veranda columns exposed | Among the tree clumps at center-left: A roof emerges through the gaps in the treetops, its building body almost entirely hidden behind the woodland, suggesting another layer of built structures concealed within the trees | Before the central main house: The foreground open pavilion is relatively fully exposed, but its upper left is still partly obscured by slanting branches and foliage, forming a foreground-background concealment-and-revelation relationship with the half-hidden main house behind
distinction: The obscuring and revealing of roofs and building bodies by trees runs through the entire group of built structures and constitutes the main spatial layering, while the waterside line is bland and no clear correspondence of slope terraces or height differences with building bases is seen, so the evidence for terrain-responsive siting is weaker than the concealment-and-revelation relationship

evidence: Lower center-right: On the stream ravine a slightly arched bridge deck and square balustrade posts at both ends are visible, the bridge meeting on the left the front edge of the slope terrace where the figures stand and on the right the foot of the right-bank cliff, forming the linking element for crossing the stream | Lower-central slope terrace: Two figures stand on a flat boulder, one holding a staff and pointing upward; the place where they stand is connected via the bridge with the right bank and with the lower edge outside the painting | Left edge to upper right: A pale vertical line descends from the upper part among the cliffs on the left edge, resembling a waterfall; pine branches extend horizontally from the right bank and screen the upper half of the painting; the bridge together with the shoreline and the gaps of the stream ravine together organize the orientation from crossing below into the waterfall-viewing spot
distinction: The visible relationship emphasizes the reachable, crossable process presented by the bridge's linkage with the slope terrace and shoreline, rather than using built structures to mark a particular scenic spot such as the waterfall or the peak tops

evidence: Right side to center: Two giant willows slant out from the lower-right slope terrace, their trunks leaning along the slope and extending toward the upper left, their hanging branches draping down to the middle of the painting, their roots corresponding to the configuration of the slope terrace | Lower slope bank: A cowherd riding an ox leads, followed by several oxen, spreading out laterally from right to left along the flat, continuous slope-bank line, the arrangement of the motifs constrained by the shoreline | Lowest section: Stream-ravine scattered rocks and water ripples define the lower limit of the waterside, and withered trees and shrub clumps transition between the slope bank and the water surface; no houses, bridges, paths, gate corridors or other built elements are seen
distinction: The lower composition uses the slope bank and waterside to determine the placement and unfolding of the trees and oxen, which fits the visible relationship more closely than C4, which has only the herd's direction of travel but lacks bridges, fords and arrival targets

evidence: Lower part of the painting: Figures (a lofty scholar and an attendant boy) are seen pausing on a rocky platform, before them a structure resembling wooden posts or a simple fence, with no clear houses or pavilion buildings visible. | Upper-middle part of the painting: Tall pines and the waterfall on the right form the main landscape scenery, and the figures' position directly faces this scenery.
distinction: The painting has no clear buildings, but the platform where the figures pause and the simple fence constitute a viewing node, identifying the scenery of pines and waterfall, so it is assigned to C3.

evidence: Whole painting: The painting depicts bamboo branches, plum blossoms, peonies and various birds, with no buildings, bridges, roads or other man-made built elements seen.
distinction: The painting has no built elements; it is assigned to the closest category based on the overall visible space.

evidence: Middle of the painting: An open pavilion is built on a platform base with railings and post supports, several people sit around inside, and the pavilion body spreads out laterally along the platform surface | Center-right to lower right: The platform, railings and platform base drop level by level, their stacking corresponding to the configuration of the bank slope | Center-left: Another building with lattice windows is located on a higher platform surface, staggered in arrangement with the central open pavilion
distinction: Although tree canopies cover the rear upper part of the roofs, the building bodies, platform bases and railings are fully exposed; the dominant relationship is the buildings being placed in stacked levels according to the rise and fall of the slope terraces, rather than forming a setting through concealment and revelation

evidence: Center to right: two groups of figures riding beasts travel across a horizontal stretch of open ground among a pine grove; the central rider turns his head to the right, forming a sequence of passage from right to left | Upper part and both left and right sides: several thick pine trunks are staggered front and back, pine needles cluster over the upper part, and the gaps between the trunks leave a passable woodland clearing and depth | Lower center: slope rocks and dense moss dots gather on the ground, defining the lower edge of the woodland clearing, with the figures and beasts traveling on the level slope above
distinction: The painting presents, through figures riding beasts advancing along a woodland clearing, a process of moving from here into there and of being able to continue deeper, whereas the concealment-and-revelation relationship required by C2, in which roof eaves of houses are revealed amid the screening of trees, is entirely absent

evidence: Upper center-left: Behind the reed islets emerge the arched mat-awning top and the upper body of an angler beneath the awning, the lower part of the awning obscured by reeds, with only the top exposed above the clumps of grass. | Center-left: On a long boat is erected a flat-topped shelter with posts, people sit around beneath the shelter, the shelter frame and boat hull pressed close to the side of the reed islet, the rear half screened by the front edge of the reed clumps. | Left edge: Between the slope-bank rocks and the reeds, several masts and woven-pattern awning tops are exposed, and the moored boat group is half-hidden behind the bank rocks and vegetation, with only partial components showing.
distinction: The obscuring and revealing of awning tops and shelter frames by the reed islets constitutes the layering relationship running through the left half of the painting, which fits the visible concealment-and-revelation organization more closely than the travel clues suggested by boats being towed and coming to shore.

evidence: Center-left mountain hollow: The roofs of several houses emerge in the depression between two mountains, their bases arranged according to the sunken configuration of the mountain-hollow slope | Lower-left cliff edge: A single-story pavilion is built against the cliff terrace, its white walls and roof projecting from the slope according to the cliff height, its lower part directly adjoining the rocky slope | Lower-central slope terrace: An open hall sits on the flat ground of the slope terrace, its colonnade and platform base spreading along the slope, the heights of the eaves corresponding to the surrounding slope configuration
distinction: Although there are traveling figures on the bridge at center-right and on the lower-right bank, no continuous path connecting with the houses is seen; the bases and heights of the three built structures are all arranged according to the configuration of the slope terraces and mountain hollow, and the relationship of siting according to terrain runs through the composition more fully

evidence: Lower-center foreground: Several large trees in dense ink stand on the slope rocks, their trunks and foliage partly screening the outlines of figures standing with staffs and sitting at rest beneath the trees, the figures emerging from among the trees | Middle-ground right bank: On the earthen mound, clumps of dotted-leaf trees screen the slope surface, their canopies and the mound's outline emerging from the unpainted space of the water surface, forming a foreground-background concealment-and-revelation layering with the foreground tree clumps | Upper right: A tree-covered hill hangs down from the upper right, the rock face and tree group on its side half-hidden in the dim silk color; no identifiable outlines of houses, bridges, corridors or other built structures are seen in the whole painting
distinction: The dominant relationship in the painting is the half-screened, half-revealed layering among the tree clumps, earthen mound and figures; the movement-through-the-landscape clues consist only of figures pointing at the water surface and standing along the bank, lacking identifiable bridges, paths, gates, fords or other entry connections.

evidence: Left side to center: Cliff faces overlap and screen one another with slanting pines and dense-leafed tree clumps, forming multiple foreground-background concealment-and-revelation relationships | Lower right: Withered wood slants across before the slope rocks, its branches partly screening the slope surface, forming a progressive layering with the middle-ground snow slope and distant mountain shadows | Full width: No houses, eaves, walls, bridges, paths, gates or other built elements or movement-through-the-landscape elements are seen, and the painting closes with large areas of unpainted space and distant mountain shadows
distinction: The only compositional organization running through the painting is the concealment-and-revelation layering of woodland and cliff rocks screening one another, closest to the spatial mechanism of C2; C1's terrain siting, C3's scenic-marking nodes and C4's movement-through-the-landscape clues have no identifiable counterparts

evidence: Lower right: A building raised on posts on the waterside bank slope, its roof, eaves, railings and interior figures clearly identifiable, with open water and flat ground before it | Lower center-left: A railed bridge path runs diagonally from the left bank down to the right, with figures standing near the bridgehead, their direction pointing toward the bank ground where the lower-right building is located | Lower middle: A roofed corridor-bridge-like structure spans the stream-valley slope, its right end joining the bank rocks on the side of the lower-right building and, together with the railed bridge, forming a clue for descending to arrive at the building
distinction: Although the building is raised on a platform at the waterside, the painting links the building with railed bridges, a corridor bridge and a descending path, forming a reachable, enterable movement-through-the-landscape sequence, so C4 is taken rather than only describing terrain siting as in C1

evidence: Lower-left slope: Several houses are placed step by step downward along the slope, their bases staggered with the rise and fall of the slope, the slope foot ending at the waterside | Lower center-left: A group of houses is arranged close to the edge of the rocky slope terrace, facing the open water surface on the right, their bases corresponding to the terrace and shoreline | Center: Red-leaf canopies cover above the slope-terrace houses, but the roofs and walls of the houses remain fully identifiable, the screening reaching only the upper part of the eaves
distinction: The correspondence of house bases with the slope terraces and waterside runs through the lower left to lower center, while the trees merely cover above the houses and do not form a relationship organizing layering through concealment and revelation, so terrain-responsive siting is taken rather than concealment and revelation

evidence: Lower middle: The main hall sits on the slope terrace of a mountain hollow, below it a level platform base and a railed platform enclosure, its base corresponding to the slope configuration | Center right: A pavilion is erected on the cliff rocks with a flat balcony railing projecting into the air, and below it a corridor building drops diagonally along the rock slope to connect with the houses below, the building heights rising with the mountain configuration | Center left: Another group of houses is arranged along the woodland edge of the slope bank, their roofs emerging with the rise and fall of the slope, their unfolding consistent with the direction of the bank slope
distinction: Although pine branches and rock blocks partly obscure the houses, the main bodies, platform bases and railings of the hall and pavilion are fully visible, and the relationship of their bases and heights being placed according to the slope terraces and cliff banks runs through the lower half of the painting; the concealment and revelation is only a local effect rather than the main compositional mode

evidence: Lower left: A group of houses and a long corridor are erected on a waterside platform base, the posts and platform directly facing the water, the layout unfolding along the shoreline | Center: A pavilion is embedded in the slope of a hollow valley squeezed between two mountains, its building body rising above the withered trees and slope rocks in front according to the slope, its base corresponding to the mountain-hollow configuration | Lower right: Several houses are distributed at varying heights along the stream-bank slope, beside them a small bridge spans the stream, and the house bases are placed according to the bank slope
distinction: Although there are movement-through-the-landscape clues such as the mountain-hollow plank-road railings and the stream bridge in the painting, the built structures in each place are mainly placed according to the mountain hollows, waterside and slope terraces, and the terrain correspondence runs through the whole painting, explaining its main compositional role better than the entry process

evidence: Center: The bases of a group of houses and pavilions are arranged close to the pond bank, with platforms and plinths set before the houses facing the water, spreading laterally along the water surface | Left side: Enclosing walls and houses extend along the rise and fall of the slope bank following the bank, the wall bases turning with the height of the slope, consistent with the direction of the shoreline | Lower right: A pavilion is erected at the edge of a slope terrace, below which a raised base and steps connect with the slope, the pavilion body facing the open water surface
distinction: The field-ridge path and riders on the right are only local scenic accents and do not form a continuous entry sequence with the built structures; while the correspondence of house bases, enclosing walls and pavilion platforms to the waterside and slope terraces runs through the whole painting, so terrain-responsive siting is taken as primary.

evidence: Middle of the right side: An open-fronted house emerges among the tree clumps, with its roof, eaves and seated figures inside visible, the building body partly obscured by the tree trunks and foliage in front and behind | Right side: The house is surrounded by dense woodland (withered branches, red-leaf and green-leaf trees), canopies and trunks lying across before the house, forming a concealment-and-revelation layering | Left front of the house: A section of slanting fence extends along the slope bank to beside the house, resembling a hedge or bridge railing, but it does not form a continuous, identifiable movement-through-the-landscape path
distinction: The existence of the house is mainly suggested by the layering of woodland screening and revealing, and the fence clue is brief and does not constitute an enterable process, so concealment and revelation fits better than access to secluded settings

evidence: Center of the painting, slightly right, among the pine grove: the roof and eaves of a small pavilion emerge from between pine trunks and needles; the body of the pavilion is partly overlapped by trunks in front and behind, producing a layering in which a building is seen within the grove | Behind the trees on the right slope: the roof and walls of a building emerge from behind a dark mass of foliage in the foreground; the roof surface is half-concealed by branches and leaves, indicating that the built structure is hidden behind the grove | Entire width, middle ground: the mountain forms and pine grove create multiple layers of foreground and background; both built structures stand amid screening trees, and no bridge, path, gate, or other movement cue is seen directly connecting to them
distinction: Although the building on the right is placed on a slope, the built structures across the whole painting signal their existence and their level within the scene by being screened and revealed by trees; this concealment-and-revelation relationship runs through the composition more than the correspondence between building sites and terrain.

evidence: Right center: an open pavilion stands on a level slope encircled by a pine grove; several figures sit inside the pavilion, and its roof and eave pillars are fully visible | Lower, somewhat right: a plank bridge spans a slope ravine; one figure carrying a staff walks across the bridge, and the bridge's right end connects to a pale, level open ground in front of the pavilion | From the foreground to the pavilion: after crossing the ravine by the bridge, one goes up along the open ground and directly reaches the pavilion base; grassy slope, bridge, open ground, and pavilion form a continuous, reachable sequence
distinction: Although the pavilion stands among pines, its roof and body are open and fully visible, so concealment and revelation are not the main layering; the bridge and walker connect directly to the open ground before the pavilion, presenting the process of movement through the landscape of crossing the bridge to reach the pavilion, hence the primary code is C4.

evidence: Center of the fan, slightly low: a building shows its roof, eaves, and pillars and railing; the right part of the building body is occluded by a large tree trunk and foliage close against it, so only the left half and the structure beneath the eaves are visible | To the right of and behind the building: dense large trees, bamboo clumps, and mixed trees surround the building; the canopy presses over the top of the roof, and the building emerges from gaps in the grove, producing a layering in which a building is seen within trees | Left side and lower-right bank: level distant banks and far mountains spread to either side; no discernible bridge, path, gate, or other movement connection is seen before the building
distinction: The building forms the scene chiefly through being screened by the grove and revealing its eave pillars, and this concealment-and-revelation relationship runs through the composition at this location; its site's correspondence to the bank terrain is weaker and less clear than the screening layers.

evidence: Lower left, where the water meets the sloping bank: a row of four or five arched canopy-top structures is arranged tight against the water's edge; below them a low, level baseline extends a thin line to the left, resembling moored canopy boats or waterside sheds, the two being difficult to distinguish reliably | Center right to lower right: an earthen slope juts from right to left into the water; several weeping willows grow in groups on the slope, and the foot of the slope is outlined with horizontal strokes and moss dots as the shore edge; the arched canopy-top structures lie exactly at the water's edge at the end of this slope foot | Upper center to left: pointed peaks of far mountains stretch across the background; the mountain feet are washed in pale ink into sloping mounds; a large area of the water is unpainted space, and at lower left several birds skim the water
distinction: The canopy-top structures lie tight against the water's edge at the foot of the slope and unfold along the shoreline, embodying the correspondence between placement and the configuration of the shoreline; the painting shows no discernible bridge, path, gate, ferry, or other access connection, so access to secluded settings is not selected.

evidence: Upper middle right, in a mountain hollow: several hall-style roofs stand on a level terrace hemmed between two mountains, backed by a screen of mountains and encircled by ridge slopes on left and right; the buildings spread laterally along the terrace surface | Middle left, waterside: a group of storied pavilions and buildings is placed on a level bank facing the water, with open water and the shoreline at the slope foot before them; the buildings are arranged laterally following the bank | Middle right, at the slope edge: the site of a white-walled building falls on level ground among slope rocks, partly hidden and partly visible among the trees according to the rise and fall of the slope
distinction: The dominant relationship of the built structures is their placement corresponding to terrace, waterside, and slope configuration; concealment and revelation appear only in local buildings and do not run through the composition as a means of forming the scene.

evidence: Upper right, mountain top: a double-eaved storied pavilion and buildings sit on an enclosed terrace at the summit, the terrace edge enclosed by curved lines, and the buildings placed at different heights according to the terrace | Middle left, waterside: a group of buildings and storied pavilions spreads along a sloping bank facing the water, the line of roof ridges roughly following the shoreline, with slope rocks and trees in front | Middle right, sloping ground: several buildings are placed on a level slope at the mountain foot, their walls and roofs exposed according to the sloping ground and joining the slope of the mountain behind
distinction: Although the buildings are locally screened and revealed by trees and rocks, the correspondence of the summit terrace, waterside shoreline, and mountain-foot slope to their sites and manner of unfolding runs through the whole painting; terrain's role in placement is more dominant than the layers of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower foreground, slightly left of center: a group of white-walled, grey-roofed buildings sits on a level slope; the building bodies and roofs are partly occluded by several white-trunked, dense-leaved trees in the foreground, producing a layering in which a building is seen behind trees | Middle section, left side, amid clouds: several roofs emerge from between cloud mist and slope hollows; their bases are hidden by cloud vapor and vegetation at the slope foot, so only roofs and eaves are seen | Between the upper main peak and the middle section: a waterfall dropping from the main peak pours into a band of cloud vapor that runs across the painting; the cloud band separates the peaks and the two built structures into layered spaces, screened front and back
distinction: Although the buildings adjoin the bank, the painting organizes the built structures through the concealment-and-revelation relationships of buildings revealed behind trees and roofs revealed amid clouds, rather than chiefly through the placement corresponding to the height of sites and the configuration of the terrain.

evidence: Center of the painting: the ridge and eaves of an open hall emerge from between several pine trunks and pine branches; figures and a table are visible inside the hall, and the left end of the building body is occluded by broad-leaved trees | Slightly below center: a courtyard wall and a gate house in the wall run across in front of the hall; the wall body is cut vertically by foreground pine trunks, producing a layering in which a walled courtyard is seen behind the grove | Lower section of the painting: slope rocks pile up in front of the courtyard wall and, together with the pine grove, form a foreground screening layer; the buildings as a whole stand in the middle ground behind trees and slope rocks
distinction: Although the buildings sit on a mountain-waist slope, the dominant relationship is the layering of concealment and revelation formed by pine trunks, branches, and slope rocks screening and revealing the roofs, eaves, and courtyard wall, rather than the correspondence of site layout to terrain.

evidence: Middle right, beside where the waterfall falls into the stream: a double-eaved pavilion shows its roof and part of its wall; the building body is cut and screened by bamboo branches and leaves in front and on both sides, appearing through gaps in the bamboo | Middle right, somewhat low, on the stream bank: a pavilion stands on a stone-built base; the lower part of the base is occluded by slope rocks and bamboo clumps in front, and bamboo clumps press close behind the pavilion, forming front and back layers | Lower right: behind slope rocks and dense bamboo only a roof and eaves are revealed, indicating another built structure behind the grove
distinction: Although the built structures adjoin the stream and occupy platforms, the viewer chiefly perceives their existence and level within the scene through roofs and eaves revealed among bamboo groves and rocks; the concealment-and-revelation relationship dominates the composition more than terrain placement.

evidence: Lower-left corner: an open pavilion or thatched hall with a pale roof, pillars, and railing emerges from behind and beside foreground slope rocks and a pine grove; its roof, eaves, and part of the pillar framework are visible, while its right half is occluded by slope rocks and tree trunks. | Lower center to right: the foreground earthen slope rises, pines grow in a grove on the slope, and rocks at the slope foot lie across the right front of the pavilion, placing the pavilion in a layer behind slope rocks and trees. | Center to upper part: the main peak and successive mountain-foot groves occupy most of the painting; the mountain mass narrows downward to the foreground slope body, and the pavilion stands in a low, level hollow at the side of the remaining slope at the mountain foot, enclosed by trees.
distinction: Although the pavilion is close to the slope foot, the visible evidence consists chiefly of the layering formed by slope rocks and pines screening and revealing the roof and eave pillars, rather than a correspondence in which the site and layout unfold according to the configuration.

evidence: Lower-left corner: a building shows its roof surface, eave pillars, and figures within the railing; its right end and lower edge are cut off and occluded by foreground slope rocks and pine trunks | Lower center: a group of pines and slope rocks lie across in front of the building; the tree canopy and slope top form a foreground screening layer, and the building emerges through gaps in grove and rocks | Middle right: beside the unpainted space of the stream bank is a low horizontal structure resembling a bridge or dike, but no path or gateway connecting it to the lower-left building is seen
distinction: Although the building stands at the slope foot by the water, the clearest compositional relationship is the layering of foreground pines and rocks screening and revealing it, rather than a placement corresponding to how the site unfolds with slope, platform, and waterside.

evidence: Center: a large rock occupies the middle of the painting; its surface is outlined and washed in pale ink, with dark ink moss dots on top, and no trace of buildings, eaves, walls, or other built elements is seen | Slightly right of center, behind the rock: several bamboo stalks extend from behind the rock; bamboo leaves are concentrated above and to the right of the rock, and the rock body screens the bamboo's roots and lower section, forming a layer of concealment and revelation | Lower left: at the slope foot to the lower left of the rock, more bamboo leaves extend from the rock's side, forming a front-and-back screening relationship with the rock body
distinction: The dominant relationship in the painting is the layer of concealment and revelation in which the rock body screens and the bamboo branches are revealed, rather than a correspondence in which objects are placed according to terrain height or waterside location.

evidence: Lower-left water surface: a small boat with a woven-pattern canopy carries one person and floats on open water; the boat is low and level, and it is the only visible movement or ferry-type cue in the painting | Center to right bank: an ochre-colored slope foot extends from beneath the mountain rocks of the right bank into the water, meeting the ripples that fill the water surface, forming a bank cliff and slope platform approachable from the water | Upper right and top of the bank: mountain rocks are layered and large trees slant across and cover the top of the bank; the space behind is screened; no buildings, pavilions, bridges, galleries, gates, or other built elements are seen in the whole painting
distinction: The boat, together with the open water and the slope foot extending into the water, forms a spatial relationship in which the bank cliff can be approached and movement through the landscape can continue; this is closer to the only visible movement cue in the painting than reading it as placement according to the bank configuration alone.

evidence: Upper-left distant water surface: a pale horizontal band-like structure crosses the water, with evenly spaced thin vertical posts along it, resembling a level bridge or trestle railing, connecting the level slope at left with the middle-ground islet | Lower foreground: slope rocks, bamboo clumps, withered trees, and pine trunks form a near-shore islet, and the shoreline opens toward the unpainted water of the middle ground | Middle right: hill slopes, mixed trees, and dotted leaves layer behind the waterside, with no discernible roofs, eaves, or walls
distinction: The only discernible man-made cue is the reflection or form of a bridge crossing the water, indicating an access relationship by which one crosses the water to reach the far bank; evidence of building placement, concealment and revelation, or scenic accentuation is not visible.

evidence: Lower center: a figure wearing a hat and white clothing stands at a gap in the slope ridge; the slope surface extends obliquely at his side, in the manner of moving along the slope | Lower left to lower right: a sloping bank runs across the lower edge of the painting; pink-dotted flowering trees and green leaves are distributed in a band along the slope ridge, leaving a gap like a narrow path where the figure stands | Left side and upper right: a high cliff drops from the upper left to meet the sloping bank; in the large unpainted area at upper right there is only a round moon, with no trace of any buildings, walls, eaves, bridges, or galleries
distinction: The painting shows a walker and a flowering path along a slope ridge that suggest a process of advancing and going deeper, yet it entirely lacks roofs or walls revealed through screening flowers and trees; it is therefore classified under the movement-through-the-landscape organization closest to access to secluded settings, rather than concealment and revelation.

evidence: Center, slightly low, on the water: a small canopy boat lies across the unpainted water; one person in the boat holds an oar, and the boat faces the bank rocks at lower left | Left side: sloping rocks and jetty rocks layer outward into the water, and the shoreline breaks in the middle, forming a gap open to the water | Right side: several withered trunks and leafy trees stand on the bank at the water's edge, facing the left bank across the water, and the two banks are connected by blank water
distinction: The painting suggests a crossable, reachable process of movement through the landscape by means of the boat and oar, the shorelines of the two banks, and the unpainted water, rather than identifying a scenic spot with a particular structure, so access to secluded settings is selected rather than scenic accentuation.

evidence: Middle right, among the slope rocks: a figure in blue sits behind a rock, the lower half of the body occluded by the slope rock, facing the open water to the left | Left side and upper part: a large area of unpainted water and a pale-ink far bank form an open waterside space, and the seated figure faces directly into it | Right bank: the sloping bank unfolds from right to left along the water, with weeping willows, clumps of grass, and rocks on it; the seated figure is at the point where slope rocks meet the water
distinction: A single human presence at the water's edge gives the open water scene a point of focus; its organizing role is greater than the local layering of concealment and revelation created by the rock.

evidence: Lower right: a white stream winds down from a mountain gap, gathering into a waterfall-like water outlet and forming a passage-like blank extending into the depth of the painting | Center: a pine tree slants out from the foreground slope rocks and spreads across; behind it are a middle-ground sloping mound and pale-ink far mountains; no buildings, pavilions, bridges, galleries, or other built elements are seen in the whole painting | Lower left to middle ground: foreground slope rocks and the middle-ground slope surface are separated by unpainted space; the slope surface has only dotted clumps of trees, with no discernible path or gateway
distinction: The primary label is based on the access cue of the stream and mountain gap extending into depth, while the terrain-responsive built structures required by C1 are entirely invisible in the painting.

evidence: Center to lower right: a sloping bank unfolds obliquely from lower left to upper right; a figure in blue sits on the slope ridge; the slope surface is washed in pale ink and dotted with moss, forming the only site baseline in the painting | Right side: a red-leaf tree bends and slants out from the right end of the slope ridge, following the slope configuration, its crown extending over the large unpainted area at upper left, its roots joining directly with the slope surface | Lower left: a standing rock rises at the slope foot, its body marked with dark ink moss dots, joining the lower end of the slope surface and forming the terminal close of the bank
distinction: The painting's organization is carried through by the oblique configuration of the slope terrace, which determines the high and low placement of trees, rocks, and figure; this is closer to a spatial relationship arranged according to configuration than merely marking a scenic spot with a single point, but since the whole painting has no built elements, the classification is only the closest analogy.

evidence: Center of the painting: a garden rock textured with dark ink occupies the middle; no buildings, eaves, walls, bridges, paths, or other built elements are seen in the whole painting | Behind and to the right of the rock: several bamboo stalks extend from behind and beside the rock; branches and leaves rise above the top of the rock and spread to the right, forming a front-and-back layering in which the rock screens and the bamboo is revealed | At the rock foot and lower left: more bamboo leaves emerge below the rock foot, screening and being screened by the main rock above and below; unpainted space is concentrated above the rock and at upper right
distinction: The visible organization in the painting is the layering of concealment and revelation in which the rock body screens and bamboo branches are revealed, rather than using a particular element to mark a scenic position such as a peak edge or water outlet; concealment and revelation is therefore closer to the visible relationship than scenic accentuation.

evidence: Center, slightly left: the gate opening of a walled courtyard gate house stands open; figures stand and interact inside and outside the gate, and behind the gate storied pavilions and side rooms recede layer by layer, forming a spatial connection from outside to inside | Lower left to center foreground: sedan chairs and horses, an honor guard, and crowds of figures gather on the open ground before the courtyard gate; the procession faces the gate house, showing movement toward arrival at and approach to the built structure | Lower right: an arched bridge spans the stream bank; pedestrians cross the bridge, and the bridge road extends along the open sloping ground toward the middle of the painting, joining the figures moving in the direction of the courtyard
distinction: The open gate, the procession arriving before the gate, and the pedestrians on the bridge and path form a process that can be entered and reached, and this runs through the composition more than the local concealment-and-revelation relationship of tree canopies screening buildings.

evidence: Upper middle: a stone arch bridge crosses a river branch; people and sedan chairs pass over the bridge deck; both ends of the bridge connect to roads along the bank, and the road continues to the right past buildings and the sloping bank. | Middle, somewhat low and right: before the group of red-pillared, black-tiled halls is a gate hall and steps; figures stand and walk inside and outside the gate; at the left front it joins an open gallery building, beneath which a passable passage is formed. | Lower left: boats come to shore, masts stand at the bank, and crowds spread from the wharf toward the open ground on the bank, which faces the central hall complex.
distinction: Bridge, road, gate, steps, and ferry form a movement cue of arrival at the built structures that runs through the painting, while the screening and revealing by trees is only an accompanying phenomenon; the main architectural bodies are complete and conspicuous, and concealment and revelation do not dominate the scene.

evidence: Upper part of the painting, along the bank: houses and shops are densely distributed along the riverbank and the edge of the earthen slope, showing a layout that unfolds along the bank and is placed in dependence on the terrain. | Middle and lower-right water surface: many boats moor or sail according to the water, their positions corresponding to the shoreline, embodying a relationship of placement according to the water. | Upper right and left-side groves: some buildings are hidden behind trees or adjoin woodland, arranged according to the undulation of the terrain and the direction of the shoreline.
distinction: Although the painting has cues of traffic and flow formed by roads and boats, the overall spatial structure chiefly embodies the lateral unfolding and placement of built structures along the waterside terrain, rather than emphasizing a route of travel turning into depth.

evidence: Upper-left area: a group of houses is arranged in tiers according to the slope terrain, their sites at differing heights, showing a clear layout of separate placement according to the slope. | Upper middle and riverbank: buildings (such as sheds) and crowd activity unfold along the blue earthen slope and the shoreline, placed in accordance with the terrain outline. | Lower water surface and bank: boats moor at the bank, and buildings and facilities are distributed in accordance with the form of the current and the shoreline.
distinction: Although the painting has paths and boats forming a scene of traffic, the layout of the built structures chiefly shows a terrain-correspondence relationship of separate placement according to the slope and unfolding along the bank, rather than emphasizing the deep guidance of a single access route.

evidence: Left center: a stone arch bridge spans the river channel; crowds pass back and forth over the bridge deck, connecting the left bank with the dense street market on the opposite bank; boats pass beneath the bridge | Middle riverbank: many boats moor at the bank; people go on and off between boat and bank and load and unload goods, forming a connection between ferry landing and the street market on the bank | Along both banks of the river: crowds stream along the roads on the banks, linking houses, sheds and stalls, and market stalls, presenting a continuous spatial sequence that can be traveled and reached
distinction: The painting links built structures and riverbanks with movement cues such as bridge, ferry, and bank roads, emphasizing the process of reaching from one place to another, rather than merely the terrain correspondence of houses placed along the bank.

evidence: Upper and lower sides of the painting and the areas along the river: large numbers of houses and buildings are densely arranged, chiefly unfolding linearly along both banks of the river in the middle (or a broad waterway) and along the roads, showing a clear pattern of arrangement along the bank and along the road. | Right side of the painting: a large arch bridge spans the water connecting the two banks; buildings join closely with the bridge and the waterside, their sites placed in accordance with the terrain and the water's edge. | Upper left and middle of the painting: buildings are distributed in dependence on trees and terrain; some have houses set by the water, others are arranged along ramps, embodying placement according to the ground.
distinction: Although the painting contains traffic cues such as bridges and roads, the overall spatial organization of the buildings chiefly embodies a linear unfolding along the waterside and terrain (unfolding along the bank), rather than singly emphasizing the process of being guided by a route into depth.

evidence: Center, somewhat low: people and horses pass through the arched city gate opening in the city wall; on both sides outside the gate, street sheds and crowds are arranged along the road, forming a passage through the city gate into and out of the city | Lower right: a stone arch bridge spans the water; people and horses come and go on the bridge, and the road at the bridge end joins the street market and shops along the bank | Center to upper right: the city wall runs obliquely across the painting, with a gate tower on the wall platform; on the oblique face of the wall a line of figures can be seen going up along a ramp, and another arch gate opens in the city wall at upper right, with a boat before the gate opening, indicating movement cues by water and land
distinction: Although the gate tower is the focal point of the painting, the composition organizes space through the passage connections of gate openings, bridge, and streets, presenting a process of going from one place to another, rather than using built structures to mark a scenic spot in the landscape.

evidence: Upper-left corner: an arch bridge can be seen connecting spaces, and a red storied pavilion stands near the bridgehead, forming a clear spatial node and suggesting an entrance. | Middle and lower parts of the painting: a broad street (path) runs through the painting, with shops and houses densely arranged on both sides, and crowds bustling along the street, presenting strong cues of movement and flow. | Buildings on both sides of the street: shopfronts open onto the street, and figures are active beneath the eaves, showing that the built structures connect closely with the path, presenting a relationship that can be entered and reached.
distinction: Although the painting contains a bridge suggesting the waterside, the overall spatial organization chiefly relies on the street (path) to connect built structures and the flow of people, rather than chiefly placing them according to natural terrain (mountain forms, slope terraces).

evidence: Lower and middle parts: a broad street or square gathers large crowds, serving as the main movement cue (path), connecting the shops and building entrances on both sides and guiding the eye into the depth of the painting. | Upper-middle building complex: dense buildings are interconnected by gate towers, enclosing walls, and corridors, forming courtyard structures and presenting a spatial process of going from one place to another and penetrating layer by layer. | Overall layout: trees are interspersed among the buildings, but the spatial organization chiefly depends on the connectivity of streets and building entrances, rather than on reliance on natural terrain or on screening by trees alone.
distinction: Although trees are interspersed among the buildings in the painting, the dominant spatial relationship is the network of enterable paths formed by streets and gate corridors, rather than chiefly relying on screening by trees to form layers of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower left and lower part of the painting: an arch bridge can be seen spanning the water, connecting roads on both banks, with pedestrians and carts and horses passing on the bridge and along the banks. | Middle and upper parts of the painting: dense buildings unfold along both sides of the streets and the river channel, and large numbers of pedestrians come and go on the streets, forming clear passage routes. | Throughout the painting: building facades and corridors connect directly with the streets, and crowds are active inside and outside buildings and on the roads, presenting a spatial relationship that can be entered and traveled.
distinction: The painting chiefly represents a route of urban travel formed by bridges, roads, and river channels connecting buildings, rather than emphasizing a natural terrain relationship in which buildings follow the lie of the mountains.

evidence: Center and both sides of the painting: a broad street (path) runs through the painting, with dense buildings (shops, houses) on both sides facing and lining the street; figures and carts and horses move along the street, forming a movement-through-the-landscape thread of approaching the built elements along the path. | Lower left: pavilion structures are built beside the water and have steps leading down to the water surface, showing the linkage between built elements and the waterside (ferry crossing) and supporting the spatial access relationship. | Lower right: boats can be seen moored at the bank, with buildings on the shore, suggesting a thread of land-and-water transport and the connectivity of the built structures.
distinction: Although waterside buildings conforming to terrain-responsive following of the bank are visible at the lower left and edges, the main space of the painting is organized by the street (path), and the role of the path in connecting the built elements and guiding movement through the landscape is more prominent.

evidence: Center-left and lower left: tall gate towers, city walls and wall gates can be seen; figures are entering and exiting through the gates, connecting the waterside outside the city with the street markets inside the city. | Lower left and center-right: an arched bridge can be seen spanning a river, with figures walking or pausing on the bridge; the bridge serves as a key node connecting the spaces on either bank. | Whole painting: dense shops and houses line the streets and riverbanks, with figures moving through and gathering among them, forming a continuous route of urban movement.
distinction: Although the gate towers and bridges have a landmark function (C3), the painting places greater emphasis on connecting different areas (outside the city, inside the city, bridgehead, street markets) through gates, bridges and roads, presenting the process of figures moving through and spatial transitions, so C4 is more dominant.

evidence: Right: two groups of tall pavilions are built on lofty terraces, clearly displaying the form of buildings set upon terraces, with the built layout corresponding to the artificial terraced platforms. | Lower right: buildings are arranged close to the waterside, with bridges connecting them, presenting a spatial relationship unfolding along the bank. | Left: a building complex is arranged according to the city wall and high ground, with figures gathering in the plaza below the city wall, showing that the built elements are placed according to the terrain.
distinction: Although large numbers of trees screen the buildings to create layering (C2), the terraced buildings on the right clearly display a built relationship in which buildings are placed according to terraced platforms, conforming to the definition of "buildings set upon terraces" within terrain-responsive siting.

evidence: Right: the building complex includes multiple levels of platforms and broad steps; figures gather going up and down the steps, clearly showing the spatial path from the ground-level plaza into the terraced buildings. | Lower part: a perimeter wall running across the painting has a gate-tower structure, with figures active inside and outside the gate opening, marking the boundary of the site and the point of entry, connecting the spaces inside and outside the wall. | Center to right: on the open ground, ranks of figures and a mounted procession are arranged or advancing toward the buildings on the right, forming a momentum of approach to the built elements and a visual guide.
distinction: Although the buildings are the visual focus on the right side of the painting, the basis for coding lies mainly in the clear process of entry and arrival constructed by the steps, the wall gate opening and the movement lines of the figures, rather than their serving simply as a marker of landscape or scene.

evidence: Left and upper left: a building complex (including red-walled houses and pavilions) is distributed according to the mountain slopes and the foot of the slopes, presenting a layout of varying heights, reflecting placement according to slope. | Lower left and left of center: houses are placed along the edges of mountains and rocks and woodland, with the building sites integrated with the terrain, presenting a form arranged around rocks or beside trees.
distinction: Although the painting shows paths and streams of people displaying a spatial process, the layout of the buildings on the left mainly reflects dependence on the mountain forms and slopes (placement according to slope), rather than simple guidance of entry by paths.

evidence: Upper left: a building complex sits on level ground in a mountain hollow, surrounded by mountains and rocks and trees, with building sites placed in conformity with the depressions of the terrain. | Right: multiple groups of buildings are distributed at varying heights along the mountain slopes, extending from courtyards at the foot of the mountain up to pavilions on the mountainside, presenting a layout of placement according to slope. | Overall: the built elements can be seen to be placed according to the mountain forms and terrain and do not exist independently of the natural terrain; the layout corresponds to the natural configuration.
distinction: Although figures and horses travel along routes past the buildings, the most prominent compositional feature of the buildings themselves is their distribution at varying heights according to the mountain slopes, rather than emphasis on the spatial process of guided entry through paths, gates and bridges.

evidence: Upper left on the mountainside: a red tower and pavilions are placed at different heights according to the mountain forms, the tower on high ground at the peak and the pavilions on lower ground among the trees, presenting the form of buildings set upon terraces. | Lower part of the painting: a dense building complex (houses, an opera stage, etc.) unfolds along the mountain foot/base, situated on the open level ground in front of the mountain and forming a layout with the mountain mass behind as support.
distinction: Although the buildings serve to indicate the locations of the mountainside and the mountain foot (appearing to be C3), the overall layout more mainly reflects a relationship of terrain-based placement according to the height of the mountain forms (upper left) and the terrain at the mountain foot (lower part).

evidence: Lower right to center: an arched bridge spans the water, connecting the paths on either bank, with figures coming and going on the bridge and boats moored or moving beneath it, constituting a clear node of transport and entry. | Center: the built area has a perimeter wall and a gate tower, with figures gathering, conversing or entering and exiting at the gate, showing an accessible courtyard space. | Lower left to center along the bank: there is a clear path along the riverbank, with figures walking, leading horses or pushing carts along it; the path points toward and encircles the central built complex, forming a thread of movement through the landscape.
distinction: Although the built elements are distributed according to the mountain forms, the painting places greater emphasis on the spatial process of guiding figures to enter and move through the built area by means of threads such as bridges, paths and the waterside, rather than simple adaptation to terrain.

evidence: Lower right: a stone bridge can be seen connecting the riverbank with the land, with figures crossing on horseback and on foot, forming a movement-through-the-landscape thread leading to the building area on the right. | Right: the building complex has steps, gate porches and courtyards, with figures gathering or entering and exiting at the gateways, clearly displaying an accessible spatial relationship. | Lower part and center: boats carrying people move on the river, and winding paths with walking figures and cattle on the slopes constitute a network of paths for land-and-water transport and movement through the landscape.
distinction: Although some buildings are placed according to the mountains and beside the water (C1), the threads of movement through the landscape—bridges, paths, boats and gate porches—are denser and run through the composition, mainly emphasizing the spatial process of figures passing from one place to another and approaching the built elements.

evidence: Lower right side: the roof and supporting columns of a pavilion or thatched hut emerge from behind trees and mountains and rocks, with the lower part of the building screened by rocks in the foreground. | Lower center of the painting: withered trees, pines and rocks in the foreground form a screen, so that the buildings behind present a spatial layering of seeing the house through intervening scenery.
distinction: The buildings are mainly screened by foreground trees and rocks and only partially revealed, emphasizing the layered relationship created by concealment and revelation rather than focusing on displaying a layout placed according to terrain.

evidence: Lower right: the roof and columns of a thatched pavilion can be seen, located behind several withered trees and pines. | Lower part: tree trunks and rocks screen part of the structure of the thatched pavilion, forming a spatial layering of foreground-background screening.
distinction: Although the thatched pavilion has a scenic-accent function, the painting places greater emphasis on the relationship of screening and revealing between the trees and rocks and the building, and the feature of concealment and revelation forming a scene is more prominent.

evidence: Lower center and right of the painting: on the near-bank slope can be seen trees in red, yellow, green and other colors, serving as foreground accents and forming a spatial layering with the gentle mountains and open water surface in the distance. | Whole painting: no clear traces of man-made built structures such as houses, bridges or paths are seen in the painting; it consists mainly of natural landscape, mountains and water, and vegetation.
distinction: There are no clear built elements in the painting; based on the overall visible organization of mountains and water, the foreground trees serve to indicate the scenery (autumn scenery), so it is provisionally assigned to C3.

evidence: Upper center: gate towers and city walls are built according to the ridge and rock platforms, with the building sites closely fitted to the outlines of the mountains and rocks, presenting a relationship of terrain-based placement by setting up defenses according to natural strongpoints. | Left of center: steps can be seen extending upward along the slope of the mountain mass, connecting built sections at different elevations and echoing the undulations of the terrain. | Lower right: on the slope there is a path and a memorial gateway, serving as the starting point of the transition from the mountain foot up to the built elements on the mountain, helping to indicate the rise of the terrain.
distinction: Although the painting has paths that guide movement, the core compositional role of the built elements lies in their layout closely attached to the rocky mountain terrain, rather than simple emphasis on the process of entering through movement.

evidence: Lower center: an arched bridge spans a ravine, connecting the two banks and forming a clear thread of passage. | Right of center in the painting: roofs and walls of buildings can be seen on the mountainside, surrounded by surrounding trees and mountains and rocks. | Overall composition: the alignment of the bridge and the valley guides the eye into the distance, suggesting the spatial process of approaching the built elements.
distinction: Although the buildings have a relationship of concealment and revelation through tree screening, the clear bridge thread at the lower part of the painting more strongly emphasizes the spatial organization process of being enterable and traversable.

evidence: Lower center: houses are screened by the branches and trunks of tall foreground trees, revealing only roofs and parts of walls, presenting a layering of houses concealed within the woods. | Right mountainside: houses are located behind tree clusters, screened by trees and forming a foreground-background screening relationship with the mountains and rocks. | Left mountainside: houses are hidden among dense woodland and mountains and rocks, faintly visible, their presence indicated by the exposed eaves.
distinction: Although the buildings are distributed according to the mountain forms, what is more visually prominent is that they are obscured by dense woodland to form a layering of concealment and revelation, rather than simple emphasis on the correspondence of terrain placement.

evidence: Right center of the painting: a group of buildings stands on an islet in the water, surrounded by willow trees, with roofs and walls visible. | Water surface in front of the buildings: a winding wooden bridge (plank walkway) extends from the building base, connecting the islet with the bank and forming a clear entry path.
distinction: Although the buildings are screened by trees to form a layering of concealment and revelation (C2), the winding wooden bridge, as a clear thread of movement through the landscape, more directly expresses the spatial process of passing from one place to another and approaching the built elements (C4).

evidence: Right center-lower: a waterside building complex (water pavilion) with railings and colonnades is built directly at the water's edge, presenting an arrangement unfolding along the bank and built beside the water. | Left center: there are houses by the water at the foot of the mountain, with a bridge beside them connecting the land and the buildings, placed according to the waterside and the mountain forms. | Upper left distant mountains: houses are faintly visible on the mountainsides of the distant mountains, distributed at varying heights following the mountain forms.
distinction: Although there is a bridge connecting to the buildings on the left of the painting, the overall composition places greater emphasis on the placement relationship of multiple built elements according to the waterside and mountain feet (terrain-responsive), rather than solely emphasizing the process of entry guided by paths.

evidence: Painting as a whole: the painting mainly depicts mountains and rocks, woodland and the water surface on the left; no clear traces of built structures such as houses, pavilions, bridges or paths are seen.
distinction: The painting lacks identifiable built elements, and its compositional mode cannot be determined with certainty; it is assigned only loosely on the basis of the overall organization of mountains and water.

evidence: Left middle ground: the two-tiered roof and eaves of a building emerge from behind a large mass of mountains and rocks on the left, forming a spatial layering of foreground-background screening. | Right and middle ground: the tree clusters and sloping rocks on the right occupy the main foreground, forming a screening relationship with the buildings revealed on the left, placing the built elements in a condition of being half concealed and half revealed.
distinction: The painting mainly displays the layering of concealment and revelation in which buildings are revealed only at the roof after being obscured by mountains and rocks, rather than emphasizing the correspondence between building sites and terrain slopes and banks.

evidence: Center-right of the painting: a wooden bridge spans the water, connecting the rocky slopes on either bank, with tiny figures on the bridge, forming a clear thread of crossing and entry. | Left center and upper center areas: multiple houses are placed at varying heights according to the mountain slopes and terraces, presenting the form of buildings set upon slopes. | Lower center area: houses are half concealed behind foreground trees, adjoining the surrounding waterside and sloping ground.
distinction: Although the houses are placed according to the mountain forms (C1), the bridge connecting the two banks and the figures in the painting constitute a strong thread of spatial entry and movement through the landscape, dominating the spatial organization of the painting.

evidence: Lower right water surface: a wooden bridge (or plank bridge) extends from the water surface on the right, pointing toward the shore at the foot of the mountain, providing a starting point for entering the painting. | Center-left mountain foot: a path winds upward along the mountain rocks, with a figure wearing a bamboo hat walking toward the interior of the mountain on the path, suggesting access to the depths. | Left and upper-left mountainside: multiple groups of buildings are distributed at varying heights according to the mountain forms, serving as reachable goals guided by the paths and the bridge.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed according to the mountain, the painting places greater emphasis on the process of entry and movement through the landscape formed by the bridge, the path and the walking figures, rather than simple correspondence to terrain.

evidence: Lower left: a bridge spans above the water surface, connecting the two banks and forming a clear thread of passage. | Lower center-left: houses are built on the sloping bank and connect with the shoreline where the bridge is located, suggesting they can be reached via the bridge. | Center-right: another house emerges faintly behind a tree cluster, together with the foreground sloping bank and bridge forming a deeper layering of the painting.
distinction: Although there is placement according to the mountains and beside the water, the combination of bridge and houses places greater emphasis on the spatial process of entering and moving through the landscape by way of paths.

evidence: Lower center-right: a person can be seen sitting on a rock, with trees nearby; no building components such as roofs or walls are seen. | Lower left: a crane can be seen standing at the water's edge, with the water surface and distant mountains forming an open horizontal space. | Whole painting: the painting consists mainly of mountains and water, trees, figures and a crane, and lacks identifiable built structures and threads of movement through the landscape.
distinction: There are no clear built elements in the painting; only the figure and the crane are placed beside the waterside rocks, so among the four options it is assigned only loosely to C1, conforming to terrain and waterside, with no other more fitting competing explanation.

evidence: Lower center: a person is walking on a small bridge spanning a water gap; the bridge connects the waterside on the left with the area of mountains, rocks, trees and woodland on the right, forming a clear entry path. | Right mountainside: the roof of a red-roofed building is revealed amid screening trees, suggesting reachable built elements within the mountain. | Right foreground: mountains and rocks, trees and the bridge together enclose a spatial opening extending into the depths, guiding the line of sight and the route of movement deeper into the mountain forest.
distinction: Although the buildings have a relationship of concealment and revelation through tree screening, the painting places greater emphasis on the spatial process of guiding entry deep into the mountain forest through the bridge and the movement-through-the-landscape thread of the figures.

evidence: Lower right corner to right center: a winding wooden plank walkway (or bridge) extends from the foreground sloping bank, passes through lotus leaves/the water surface, and connects to the pavilion at the water's edge. | Right: the pavilion (water-side pavilion) is built at the water's edge beneath willow trees, and the plank walkway leads directly to the pavilion, forming a clear entry path. | Upper right: tall willow trees cover the pavilion, but the plank walkway establishes the spatial connection from the foreground to the built elements.
distinction: Although the pavilion is screened by willow trees (conforming to C2), the clear winding wooden bridge in the painting provides a clear thread of movement through the landscape, guiding the eye from one place to another to approach the built elements, making the spatial process (access to secluded settings) dominant.

evidence: Left cliff: a winding stone-step path can be seen extending upward along the mountain forms, leading to a pavilion situated among pine trees. | Upper center: roofs and eaves of buildings are revealed amid screening woodland, suggesting the presence of built elements deep in the mountain hollow.
