distinction: Although there are buildings screened by woodland in the painting (C2), the clearly visible stone steps up the mountain and the pavilion on the left constitute a clear route of movement through the landscape, placing greater emphasis on the spatial process of entering from one place to another (C4).

evidence: Lower left: the roof of a building is revealed behind mountains and rocks, with clear tile ridges, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation through screening by mountains and rocks. | Center-right: withered trees and clumps of bamboo grow on a rocky slope, together with the mountains and rocks on the left forming the natural environment that screens the buildings.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed according to the mountains and rocks, the most prominent spatial expression in the painting is the layering of concealment and revelation in which mountains and rocks obscure the building itself and only the roof is revealed, so C2 is more fitting than C1.

evidence: Left mountainside: houses are placed at varying heights according to the mountain slopes and terraces, presenting a layout of buildings set upon slopes. | Middle-ground waterside: the built elements are distributed following the shoreline, with building sites corresponding to the terrain. | Right water surface: a small bridge can be seen connecting the waterside, helping to indicate the linkage between the built elements and the terrain.
distinction: Although the painting has path threads such as bridges, the layout feature of the built elements being placed according to the mountains and beside the water and following the undulations of the terrain is more prominent and dominates the spatial organization.

evidence: Left and central mountains and rocks: houses are placed at varying heights according to the rocky slopes and terraces, with roofs echoing the undulations of the mountain forms, presenting a layout of buildings set upon terraces and placed according to slope. | Right water surface: the shoreline meets the base of the mountains and rocks, and the building sites extend to the water's edge in conformity with the terrain.
distinction: The built elements mainly conform to the placement on mountain forms and terraces, rather than serving simply as isolated markers indicating the scenery.

evidence: Lower left beside the bank: roofs and walls of several houses can be seen, partly screened by trees and the sloping bank, presenting a half-hidden, half-visible condition. | Right mountainside: the roof of a building is revealed amid screening trees, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation with the surrounding woodland.
distinction: Although the built elements are placed according to the mountains and beside the water, the painting places greater emphasis on the layered relationship in which they are obscured and revealed by woodland, mountains and rocks, so C2 is more dominant than C1.

evidence: Under the tree on the right, on the rock: one person is visible sitting alone on the rock, surrounded by trees and mountains and rocks; no identifiable buildings such as houses or pavilions are seen. | Left and center: the painting is mainly water surface, distant mountains, and sloping banks, with no traces of built elements.
distinction: No identifiable built elements are seen in the painting; there is only a figure as a scenic accent, assigned to the closest category based on the overall visible space, with no clear evidence of built elements.

evidence: Lower-middle waterside: a person is walking across a small bridge spanning the water, the bridge connecting the open waterside with the mountain-and-rock and woodland area on the right. | Among the mountains, rocks, and trees on the right: a red-roofed building (pavilion or house) is partly screened, and the direction of the bridge and the walking figure points toward the depth of the space where this building is located.
distinction: Although the building is screened by trees, the clearly depicted small bridge and walking figure in the lower part of the painting constitute a movement clue for entering this space, making the process of access to secluded settings dominant.

evidence: Left middle: a building roof emerges from behind trees and mountains and rocks, presenting a spatial layering of seeing the house through intervening scenery | Left lower: pavilion buildings stand beside pine trees, with parts of their structure obscured by branches and leaves
distinction: The painting mainly presents a concealment-and-revelation relationship in which buildings are obscured by trees and mountains and rocks with only roofs exposed; path clues are weak and no clear entry guidance is formed.

evidence: Left: houses are built on a distinct sloping platform/earthen slope, with the building base raised above the surrounding ground, presenting the form of setting houses on a platform, corresponding to the undulations of the terrain. | Lower middle: beside the pavilion-style building is connected a long strip-shaped fence or field ridge, extending horizontally in accordance with the terrain, embodying terrain-responsive arrangement.
distinction: Although the houses are located at the woodland edge, the painting mainly presents their layout relationship of being placed according to the sloping platform, rather than a concealment-and-revelation layering formed by screening with trees.

evidence: Right hillside: a group of built roofs and parts of walls are visible, half-screened by the surrounding dense trees and mountains and rocks, presenting an evident concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Center of the painting: between the large rock on the left and the built elements on the right, spatial layering is formed through clouds and mist and woodland, and the built elements are in a relatively deep pictorial depth.
distinction: In the painting the built elements mainly reveal parts of themselves through screening by trees and mountains and rocks, forming spatial layering, without emphasis on path guidance or a specific scenic-accent marking role.

evidence: Lower left: a person is visible walking upward along a stone-step path, the path winding between mountains and rocks and woodland. | Lower middle: a bridge spans a stream, connecting the paths on both banks, forming a clear clue of crossing and passage. | Right mountainside: a group of house buildings is visible hidden behind woodland, and the direction of the path and bridge implies the spatial process leading to this place.
distinction: Although the painting has a concealment-and-revelation relationship in which buildings are screened by woodland, the walking figure at the lower left and the bridge at the lower middle constitute clearer clues of movement and entry, dominating the spatial organization.

evidence: Lower left: among dense trees the roofs and columns of pavilions and houses are exposed, presenting a layering of houses hidden in woodland. | Middle right: through gaps in the trees, house buildings are faintly visible, half-screened, indicating the presence of built elements through partial exposure. | Overall: built elements in several places are obscured by foreground or middle-ground trees, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship participates in composing the scenery, forming spatial depth.
distinction: Although the houses are placed according to the mountain terrain, the painting emphasizes more the screening and revealing of buildings by trees, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship is more prominent than terrain-responsive placement.

evidence: Lower center of the painting: a wooden bridge spans the water, connecting the bank rocks on the right with the courtyard area where the built elements on the left are located, forming a clear entry path. | Lower middle of the painting: the courtyard has a gatehouse and enclosing walls, with houses visible inside, the whole surrounded by trees and connected to the external water system by the bridge.
distinction: Although the built elements have a concealment-and-revelation relationship of being screened by trees, the small bridge in the lower part of the painting clearly provides a movement clue for entering the built elements from the water, and the sense of spatial entry is more prominent.

evidence: Lower left: the roof, columns, and interior figures of a building are visible, partly obscured by the foreground sloping bank and trees, presenting a half-hidden, half-exposed state. | Middle-left mountainside: between woodland and mountains and rocks the outline of a small pavilion or hut is faintly visible, screened by natural scenery, indicating the spatial layering of the middle ground. | Middle-right waterside: the form of a bridge is faintly visible at the waterside, interpenetrating with the surrounding trees and sloping bank, increasing the layering of pictorial depth.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed by mountains and water, the painting emphasizes more the concealment-and-revelation layering formed by the screening and revealing of buildings by woodland, mountains, and rocks, so C2 is more apt than C1.

evidence: Lower left: a group of house buildings is arranged against the mountain foot and waterside, with the building base extending in accordance with the terrain and the water's edge. | Left lower middle: mountains, rocks, and sloping bank adjoin the buildings, and the building layout follows the direction of the mountain terrain and waterside.
distinction: The buildings mainly present an arrangement relationship of being set against mountains and water, rather than serving merely as an isolated marker indicating a certain scenic spot.

evidence: Lower middle: roofs and walls are faintly visible between woodland and mountains and rocks, presenting a half-screened state. | Center-left: tree branches and leaves obscure parts of the building structure, forming a spatial layering of alternating concealment and revelation.
distinction: The painting mainly expresses the concealment-and-revelation relationship of built elements screened by woodland, mountains, and rocks, rather than emphasizing path guidance or scenic-accent marking.

evidence: Lower left and middle ground: dense trees and willow trees in the foreground, gentle sloping banks and clusters of trees in the middle ground, and mountain ranges in the distance. | Center and right of the painting: large areas of unpainted space suggest water surface or clouds and mist, separating and connecting foreground, middle ground, and distance, forming a profound spatial layering.
distinction: No built elements are seen in the painting; only the natural spatial organization of mountains, water, and trees is seen, creating a profound space that can be traversed through unpainted space and layers of scenery, so it is assigned to the closest category, C4.

evidence: Center-right: an arched bridge spans the water, connecting the left and right banks, forming a clear clue of crossing and entry. | Right: houses are built against mountains and rocks, and the route of the bridge points toward this built area, presenting an accessible spatial relationship.
distinction: Although the houses are placed against mountains and rocks, the spatial organization more prominently presented in the painting is the process of movement in which the bridge connects the two banks and leads to the built elements.

evidence: Lower middle: two thatched-roof buildings side by side, with dense vertical lines painted at their base (resembling piles or supporting structures), located at the junction of the mountain foot and the waterside, with water ripples visible in front, presenting a waterside elevated layout. | Lower middle, slightly left: the buildings back onto the foot of the mountain-and-rock slope on the left and extend along the shoreline, embodying the relationship of placing built elements according to the terrain and water conditions.
distinction: Although the buildings mark a mountain-dwelling scene, their pile structure at the base and waterside position more clearly demonstrate the 'terrain-responsive' characteristic of elevated placement according to the waterside terrain, rather than serving merely as a scenic-accent marker.

evidence: Middle of the left hillside: a pavilion is visible, its roof and eaves emerging from the screening of mountains, rocks, and trees, forming a spatial layering of alternating concealment and revelation. | Left mountain body and trees: dense trees and undulating mountains and rocks form a natural screen around the pavilion, highlighting the characteristic of built elements creating a setting through screening by natural scenery.
distinction: Although the pavilion is built according to the mountain, the painting emphasizes more its layered relationship of being screened and revealed by mountain woodland and trees, rather than merely terrain-responsive placement.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting, slightly left: the roof and eaves of a built structure are visible, half-hidden behind dense woodland and mountains and rocks. | Lower middle of the painting: foreground and middle-ground trees and mountain rocks form an evident screen in front of the built elements, presenting a spatial layering of alternating concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the built elements are located in a mountain hollow, the painting emphasizes more the layered relationship of their being screened by woodland, mountains, and rocks and thereby revealed, rather than focusing on expressing their terrain-responsive layout.

evidence: Lower center, slightly right: dense tree branches and leaves obscure and reveal the thatched hut's roof and structure, presenting a layering of seeing the house within woodland. | Lower center: the built elements are nestled between rocks and clusters of trees, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship through the screening of natural scenery.
distinction: Although the house is placed against mountains, rocks, and trees, the visual focus of the painting emphasizes more the spatial layering formed by the screening and revealing of the house by branches and leaves, rather than merely emphasizing arrangement according to terrain.

evidence: Left middle: a pavilion is built on a protruding sloping rock at the waterside, with the building base following the waterside terrain, presenting the form of setting a house on a platform. | Upper right: a pagoda body is revealed among the woodland on the mountainside, placed against the mountain slope. | Lower left: a small bridge spans a stream connecting the bank slopes, assisting in presenting the adjacent relationship between the waterside terrain and the built elements.
distinction: Although the pagoda on the mountainside is screened by woodland (C2), and there is a bridge beside the waterside pavilion (C4), the two main built elements in the painting (the waterside pavilion and the pagoda) are both evidently placed relying on site conditions such as mountain forms and the waterside, and the characteristic of terrain-responsive siting covers more comprehensively.

evidence: Center of the painting, water surface: a small boat carrying one person floats on the water, serving as a movement clue connecting the spaces of the left and right banks. | Left and right of the painting: the cliff on the left and the bamboo and trees on the sloping bank on the right form an open water space, with the small boat in between, presenting a process of movement from one place to another.
distinction: The small boat is not merely an ornament on the water but serves as an accessible, traversable clue organizing the spatial relationship of the two banks, so C4 is more apt than the mere scenic accent of C3.

evidence: Lower center, pine woodland: the roofs of two buildings are faintly revealed in the dense pine woodland, the main bodies of the buildings obscured by trunks and branches, presenting a layered relationship of houses hidden in woodland. | Left woodland edge: a roof is revealed from the edge of the tree cluster, forming a concealment-and-revelation contrast with the surrounding dense trees.
distinction: Although the buildings are located in the woodland at the mountain foot, the most prominent spatial organization in the painting is the screening and revealing of buildings by trees, rather than emphasizing the dependent relationship of buildings on terrain and sloping banks.

evidence: Lower middle: the roof and parts of the walls of a group of buildings are visible, partly obscured by tall foreground trees and mountains and rocks, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Foreground and middle ground: trees and mountains and rocks as foreground and middle-ground elements screen the built elements behind, creating a spatial layering of seeing houses within woodland.
distinction: Although the buildings are set by mountains and water, the painting emphasizes more the concealment-and-revelation layering of their being screened by trees, mountains, and rocks, rather than a merely terrain-responsive placement relationship.

evidence: Top of the high cliff on the right: tiny ink marks are visible, suspected to be pavilion built elements, located at an extremely high place | Lower middle of the painting: paired pines and rocks are depicted, forming the foreground and creating spatial depth with the distant bank
distinction: The suspected built elements are located at the cliff top and mainly serve to indicate the scene of the high cliff, rather than emphasizing a complex relationship of terrain-based layout

evidence: Lower middle, left: a building complex extends along a sloping bank or platform, with dense supporting structures or railings visible below, presenting the form of setting houses on platforms and extending along the bank, with figures active among them. | Upper middle: built elements (pavilions and houses) are visible in several places on the mountainside and among trees and rocks, placed in staggered heights according to the mountain terrain, presenting a layout of separate placement according to slopes. | Overall composition: the built elements are distributed layer by layer following the mountain terrain, from the lower sloping bank to the upper mountainside, with the building bases corresponding to the terrain.
distinction: Although some built elements are screened by trees, mountains, and rocks (C2), the dominant relationship in the painting is the layer-by-layer placement of built elements according to mountain forms and sloping platforms (C1), and the screening is only a partial layer.

evidence: Lower water surface: a small boat carrying a person moves across the water, with a person at the bow holding a pole, presenting a spatial process of movement and going deeper onto the water. | Upper-right cliff: a corner of a building eave is revealed among trees and rocks, indicating the presence of built elements on the bank.
distinction: Although the building at the upper right has the manner of creating a setting through screening, the movement clue of the boat below more clearly organizes the spatial entry and extension relationships of the painting.

evidence: Middle of the painting: an earth road or sloping ground runs across the painting, with figures distributed along this path, in a state of advancing or pausing | Background: rocks and trees form a natural background; no trace of any building, bridge or other built element is visible
distinction: The painting has no built elements, only a path and figure activity; it is closest to the spatial cue of access to secluded settings, but lacks built elements to connect with

evidence: Overall painting: the painting depicts three figures, a tiger and a flying bird, with rocks and trees in the background; no clear built elements such as houses or bridges are visible. The rocks and trees form the natural environmental layers within which the figures are active.
distinction: The painting has no built elements; the rocks and trees mainly surround the figures as background and do not show a clear role of scenic accentuation.

evidence: Lower-middle part of the painting: several figures move horizontally among rocks and trees, in a state of traveling or walking. | Whole painting: the background consists of rocks and trees; no clear man-made structures such as houses, bridges or paths are visible.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built elements and shows only the dynamic movement of figures through the landscape, so it is assigned only tentatively to C4, which expresses the process of movement through the landscape.

evidence: Lower right corner: a thatched-roof house can be seen, partly obscured by the branches and leaves of trees in the foreground and middle ground, with only the roof and part of the wall exposed. | Right and center: tall willows and other mixed trees are densely distributed, screening the house in the lower right corner and creating a spatial layering in which a building is seen deep in the woods.
distinction: Although the house is located on the bank, the painting places greater emphasis on the relation of concealment and exposure of the house by trees, rather than on the terrain-responsive placement of the house in relation to the sloping bank.

evidence: Left foot of the mountain: several houses screened by pine forest are placed on the sloping ground at the foot of the mountain, marking the scenery of the valley at the foot of the mountain. | Right mountaintop: a pavilion is built high on the mountaintop, becoming a marker of the mountaintop scenery and concentrating the space there.
distinction: The houses on the left have the characteristic of being placed according to the mountain terrain, but overall the houses at the foot of the mountain and the pavilion on the mountaintop serve more importantly as scenic accents that mark and concentrate the scenery at the foot of the mountain and on the mountaintop, rather than simply emphasizing placement according to terrain.

evidence: Left mountainside: houses are built on cliff terraces, arranged in staggered heights conforming to the mountain terrain. | Central valley: the built elements are distributed separately according to the slope, and the layout corresponds to the forms of the mountain slopes and terraces. | Lower right and right foot of the mountain: houses are arranged following the mountain terrain and the gaps between trees, presenting a relation of placement according to terrain.
distinction: Although there is screening by woodland, the built elements mainly present a relation of terrain-responsive placement on terraces and along slopes, and screening is not the dominant compositional method.

evidence: Lower-middle and right of the painting: the trunks, branches and leaves of two huge ancient trees occupy the main part of the painting, and behind the trees a building roof with tile lines is faintly exposed. | Center of the painting, slightly right: the main body of the building is obscured by tree trunks and canopy, and the existence of the built elements is indicated only by the exposed part of the roof, forming a clear layering of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the building is behind the trees, what is mainly expressed is the relation of concealment and revelation under the screening of trees, rather than a marker identifying the scenery of a particular place.

evidence: Lower-middle part of the painting: a row of houses is arranged along the shoreline, and on the right a structure resembling a bridge or boardwalk extends into the water, presenting a layout unfolding along the bank. | Left of the middle ground: several houses are placed beside the water and willows, their sites closely integrated with the water surface and trees. | Right of the middle ground: houses are built facing the water, forming with the surrounding water surface and trees a situation of dwelling beside the water.
distinction: Although the built elements in the painting are screened by trees, their layout unfolding along the shoreline and their construction beside the water are more prominent features, embodying a relation of placement according to terrain.

evidence: Middle slope on the right: a building group is located on gently sloping terraces below the cliff, arranged at different heights conforming to the slope, presenting a layout of separate placement along the slope. | Lower right: the building sites are integrated with the mountain-slope terrain, surrounded by trees but without major screening, mainly embodying placement according to terrain.
distinction: The built elements mainly present a layout relation of placement on slope terraces; although adjacent to trees, this is a front-and-back arrangement rather than a notable layering of screening and concealment.

evidence: Middle right of the painting: the roofs and walls of a group of houses are exposed from behind dense woods and rocks, forming a clear relation of occlusion and exposure. | Center and right of the painting: tall trees and dense branches and leaves partly obscure the built elements behind, making the buildings appear faintly among the woodland and constituting rich spatial layering.
distinction: Although there is a bridge in the lower left of the painting, the overall composition gives greater prominence to the screening and concealment-revelation relation of the houses by woodland and rocks, rather than emphasizing a path of entry.

evidence: Right middle ground: several houses are hidden behind withered woods, with only roofs and parts of walls exposed, presenting a layering in which houses are hidden deep in the woods. | Lower left corner: a small bridge spans a stream, connecting the two banks and implying a route of movement through the landscape.
distinction: The core of the painting lies in the occlusion and exposure of the houses by woodland, forming a deep and secluded spatial layering; although the small bridge hints at a path, it is not the dominant compositional method.

evidence: Below the rocks on the right: houses are partly obscured by pine trees and bamboo groves, with only snow-covered roofs and parts of walls exposed, forming a layering in which buildings are seen behind rocks. | Center foreground: a house with a round doorway is surrounded by withered trees and rocks, and figures are visible within the doorway, presenting a spatial relation in which a house is hidden among the woods. | Overall composition: the built elements are distributed in staggered fashion among trees and rocks, their existence and level indicated by concealment and exposure through natural scenery.
distinction: Although the houses are placed against the mountain and beside the water, the painting places greater emphasis on the layering of concealment and revelation formed by the occlusion and exposure of the houses by trees and rocks, rather than on mere adaptation to terrain.

evidence: Lower left and middle ground: village houses, figure activity, and the small bridge and mountain path connecting the houses with the outside can be seen, forming clear cues of departure and travel. | Right middle ground: a wooden bridge spans the stream, with figures crossing it, connecting the space on the two banks and guiding the eye and the route of travel to extend into the depth of the painting. | Upper part and left middle-ground ridge: pavilions and terraces are built on steep peaks and ridges, serving as distant goals or nodes of the travel route and, together with the paths and bridges below, constituting a complete process of spatial entry.
distinction: Although some buildings are placed according to terrain, the more prominent feature of the painting is that bridges, paths and crossings link the various built elements together, emphasizing a spatial process that can be entered and traveled through.

evidence: Right side, from the mountainside down to the lower-middle: a clear winding path extends upward from the woodland below, leading directly to the pavilion at the mountain hollow, forming an explicit clue for movement through and entry into the landscape. | Lower right and lower-middle, among the trees: houses are built concealed within the woodland and beside the waterside; the gaps between the path and the waterside help indicate that the space extends into the depth, presenting a traversable layering. | Left side, mid-slope: a pavilion is built on a platform and, as an elevated node, echoes the deep space guided by the path below, together forming a scene of dwelling in the mountains and moving through it.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed according to the mountain terrain and platforms (C1), the winding mountain path in the painting runs through the upper and lower parts as a clue for movement through the landscape, placing greater emphasis on the spatial process of moving from here to there and turning into the depths (C4).

evidence: Left side of the painting: a large porous mountain rock blocks the left half of the thatched hut, revealing only the roof and the window lattice on the right. | Right side and center of the painting: several large trees with dense foliage screen the right half of the thatched hut; through the gaps in the leaves a round doorway and wall are visible. | Center of the painting: the roof, windows, and doorway of the thatched hut are revealed in the gap between the mountain rock on the left and the trees on the right, forming a clear layering of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the building in the painting is built against mountain rocks and trees, the screening and revealing of the building by rocks and trees (the concealment-and-revelation relationship) is the primary means of composing the scene, rather than a simple emphasis on the building being placed according to the terrain.

evidence: Upper area and the riverbank on the right: a large number of building complexes are distributed closely along the winding shoreline, showing a clear character of unfolding along the bank | Lower left and around the hill below: the built elements (village) are located at the foot of the green mountain or on gentle slopes, placed according to the mountain terrain | Overall painting: the built elements form a clear correspondence with the water system and mountain forms, demonstrating geographical attachment.
distinction: Although the buildings exist as landmarks, their distribution is mainly driven by terrain (waterside, mountain foot), emphasizing layout according to circumstances rather than simply identifying scenic spots.

evidence: Right-side slope: houses are distributed at different heights according to the mountain terrain, their layout following the undulations of the ground, showing a relationship of separate placement according to slope. | Lower middle and lower left waterside: building groups are densely arranged along the shoreline, with continuous roofs, showing a layout character of unfolding along the bank. | Right-center: an arched structure (bridge or water gate) spans the water surface connecting the embankments, its base relying on the waterside terrain, with pavilions and human activity above.
distinction: Although the painting includes transport elements such as a bridge and boats that suggest movement through the landscape (C4), the overall composition places greater emphasis on the layout relationship in which building groups are widely distributed according to the shoreline and mountain-slope terrain (C1), rather than a single path guiding entry into the depths.

evidence: Left side, beneath the pines: two people are seen sitting facing each other, surrounded by pine trees and mountain cliffs; no houses, bridges, or other built structures are visible | Overall painting: dominated by pine trees, mountains and rocks, and distant mountains; the human activity identifies the scene of sitting facing each other beneath the pines.
distinction: No explicit built elements are visible in the painting; only figures as scenic accents, so it is assigned to scenic accentuation as the closest category.

evidence: Lower-middle of the painting: sloping rocks, several bare trees, and bamboo clumps are visible; there are no traces of houses, pavilions, or other built structures | Upper left corner: there are an inscription and seals, which are not built elements in the painting.
distinction: No built elements are visible in the painting; it is assigned to the closest category based on the overall visible organization of natural landscape.

evidence: Lower left corner: between the waterside sloping rocks and trees, the roof and wall body of a small built structure are visible, partly screened by foreground trees. | Overall painting: the built structure is small in scale, hidden behind woodland and mountain rocks, its presence indicated through partial revelation, forming a spatial layering of alternating concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the built structure is located at the waterside, the painting mainly emphasizes its relationship of being half-screened and half-revealed by woodland, slopes, and rocks, rather than its layout characteristics of conforming to the terrain.

evidence: Center-left: an arched bridge spans a stream/valley, with pedestrians on the bridge, forming an explicit clue for movement through the landscape. | Lower/lower-middle: built elements (houses) are located beside the waterside, logically connected to the bridge through the stream and shoreline, suggesting they can be reached or departed from. | Overall composition: bridge, stream, and built elements combine to present a spatial process of moving from the foreground dwelling into the deep mountains (the main peak above).
distinction: Although the built elements are screened by trees (a C2 characteristic), the bridge and pedestrians provide a more dominant clue for travel and a sense of spatial entry, matching the definition of access to secluded settings.

evidence: Lower right: house buildings are visible half-hidden behind mountain rocks and trees, showing a concealment-and-revelation relationship | Upper-right mountainside: built elements appear faintly among woodland and mountain rocks, forming spatial layering.
distinction: Although the built elements are placed according to the mountain, the painting places greater emphasis on their concealment-and-revelation relationship with mountain rocks and woodland, rather than simply being arranged according to the ground.

evidence: Middle ground, slightly right: several houses are separately placed according to the mountain slopes and platforms, their roofs at different heights, the layout following the mountain contours and platform terrain. | Lower center: a building (pavilion or tower) is placed on a rocky platform/slope projecting at the waterside, its base combined with the rock, showing a disposition according to the platform and along the bank. | Distant mountain top/mountainside: buildings can be faintly seen placed according to the rock; although screened, their positions follow the high points of the mountain.
distinction: Although trees screen the buildings to form a layering of concealment and revelation (C2), the building bases clearly rely on mountain slopes, platforms, and waterside rocks (separate placement according to slope, houses set on platforms); the determining role of terrain in layout and placement is more prominent and matches the typical definition of C1.

evidence: Lower right: a pavilion is built on a high point of the mountain rocks, placed according to the mountain-top terrain and closely integrated with the mountain form. | Upper middle: a pavilion is built at the waterside, set facing the water, its base echoing the shoreline. | Upper right: houses are visible at the edge of the cliff, arranged according to the cliff terrain.
distinction: Although the built elements serve to identify scenic spots, the painting places greater emphasis on the correspondence in which buildings are placed against natural terrain such as cliffs and watersides, so C1 is more appropriate.

evidence: Center-left of the painting: between trees and mountain rocks, the roof of a building is faintly revealed, half-screened by the surrounding woodland. | Middle ground of the painting: the building is hidden deep in dense woods, revealed through gaps in the branches and leaves, forming a spatial layering of alternating concealment and revelation.
distinction: The building is presented mainly as a secluded dwelling hidden among the trees, forming a layering of concealment and revelation, rather than as a visual center identifying an open scene or a landmark.

evidence: Center of the painting: a scholar is seen standing beside mountain rocks, facing the open water surface and sky to the left; no explicit built entities such as houses or bridges are visible. | Right side of the painting: there are sloping banks, lake rocks, and trees as the background for the figure's stance; no combination of buildings with terrain or relationship of screening is presented. | Left side of the painting: a large area of unpainted space represents the water surface and distant sky, with a bright moon above; the whole presents an open, level distant scene.
distinction: There is no clue of a figure entering a building in the painting, only a posture of gazing over the water, so access to secluded settings is excluded.

evidence: Right-center: most of a group of buildings is screened by dense willow trees, revealing only the roof and part of the walls, showing a clear concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Left and center willow grove: several roofs appear faintly among the willows, using the screening of the trees to indicate the presence of buildings and spatial layering. | Center of the painting: a small bridge is visible among the willow grove, helping to indicate the water-and-land space, but the main mode of presenting the buildings is screening by trees.
distinction: Although there is a bridge in the painting, the most prominent scenic-composition feature of the buildings themselves is the layering formed by concealment and revelation through willow trees, rather than an emphasis on an enterable path.

evidence: Upper-middle, top of the cliff: courtyards and pagoda-style buildings are placed directly on the edge of the steep cliff and on projecting rock platforms, their bases conforming to the terrain. | Left cliff: building groups are distributed against the mountain rocks, their layout corresponding to the rises and turns of the cliff.
distinction: Although the buildings serve a scenic-accent role, their direct attachment to and conformity with the cliff terrain is more prominent; the dominant manifestation is terrain-responsive siting.

evidence: Right side: a figure is seen sitting leaning against a pine tree on mountain rocks, surrounded by pine needles, branches, and sloping rocks; no houses, bridges, or other built structures are visible. | Left side: a large area of unpainted space and an extending sloping bank, with no traces of buildings or paths.
distinction: There are no explicit built elements in the painting; it is assigned to the closest category based on the overall visible relationship between landscape and figures as scenic accents.

evidence: Upper left: a person sits on a projecting rocky platform, fishing facing the open water surface. | Right side: a group of figures gathers among sloping rocks and woodland, forming a spatial relationship of facing across the water with the left side.
distinction: There are no explicit buildings in the painting, but the human activity is clearly arranged relying on rocky platforms, emphasizing attachment to terrain more than simple scenic accentuation.

evidence: Left-side slope: several houses are placed according to the mountain slopes and platforms; below, steps or a small path extend downward along the mountain body, showing a layout of houses set on platforms and separately placed following the slope. | Overall painting: the bases of the built elements correspond to the mountain terrain at different heights, demonstrating a relationship of arrangement according to the ground.
distinction: The houses mainly embody a relationship of arrangement according to the ground, placed according to mountain forms and slopes, rather than making the screening and revealing by woodland and mountain rocks the dominant means of composing the scene.

evidence: Whole painting: the painting consists mainly of distant mountains, water surface, sloping banks, and trees; no explicit built elements such as houses or pavilions are visible. | Lower-middle water surface: a small boat is painted, with one person sitting in it, presenting a state of moving over the water and suggesting an enterable path. | Foreground and right side: pines and mixed trees grow thickly on the sloping banks and mountain rocks, forming an opening-and-closing relationship with the water surface.
distinction: The boat as a clue for movement through the landscape suggests a relationship of entry and travel (close to C4), rather than simply serving as a fixed marker identifying a scenic spot (C3).

evidence: Left mountainside: a group of houses with dark roofs is arranged according to the mountain slopes and platforms, their bases placed conforming to the undulations of the terrain. | Middle ground of the painting: clouds and mist surround the mountainside; the built elements are located on the slope revealed above the mist, forming a clear relationship of attachment to the mountain.
distinction: Although the built elements serve to identify the mountainside scene, their terrain-responsive placement following the mountain and conforming to slopes and platforms is more prominent, so C1 is more appropriate than C3.

evidence: Middle ground: a stone bridge spans the water surface, with pedestrians on the bridge, connecting village houses on both banks and forming an explicit passage clue. | Foreground and middle-ground water surface: boats are moving on the water, with a fisherman poling a boat nearby and a sailboat in the distance, suggesting the connectivity of the water route and the process of travel. | Lower right and middle left: waterside pavilions and houses along the bank are spatially connected through the water surface and bridge, guiding the gaze to extend into the depth of the painting.
distinction: Although the buildings built facing the water embody terrain-responsive siting, the coherent travel clues formed by the bridge, boats, and water surface in the painting are more prominent, emphasizing the enterability of the space.

evidence: Lower left of the painting: a small bridge spans the water surface, connecting the external path with the waterside pavilion building on the right, forming an explicit entry route. | Lower middle of the painting: the waterside pavilion/hall has its doors and windows open, with human activity inside; the small bridge connects with the building, presenting a spatial relationship that is reachable and traversable. | Upper middle of the painting: a pavilion stands deep in the mountain hollow, surrounded by mountain rocks and trees, suggesting a path leading deeper into the mountains.
distinction: The pavilion in the upper middle of the painting has a screening effect, but the entry and travel clues formed by the waterside pavilion and small bridge in the lower part of the painting are more explicit and dominate the spatial organization of the painting.

evidence: Left side, lower-middle: the roof and part of the structure of a small built element are visible, screened by the trees and mountain rocks in front, presenting a half-hidden, half-revealed state. | Center and right side of the painting: tall mountain rocks and dense trees form the foreground and middle ground, creating spatial layering and a screening relationship with the built element on the left.
distinction: Although the built element serves a scenic-accent role, its main function in the painting is to form spatial layering through being screened by woodland and mountain rocks; the feature of concealment and revelation creating the scene is more dominant.

evidence: Center-left of the painting: between mountain rocks and dense woodland, the roofs and eave corners of a group of pavilion buildings are faintly revealed, presenting a state of being screened and hidden by natural scenery. | Lower part of the painting: there is a small boat and figures on the water surface, but no explicit path or entrance directly connecting to the building on the left is shown.
distinction: Although there is a boat moving on the water in the painting, there is a lack of enterable clues such as bridges, paths, or doors that directly link the boat's movement with the building; the building exists more as a scene screened by woodland and mountain rocks.

evidence: Lower right corner: a wooden bridge is visible connecting the waterside, serving as a clue for movement through the landscape. | Left water surface: there is a small boat with a person on board, forming a transport connection with the bridge and waterside.
distinction: The bridge and boat mainly express the process of transport and entry, rather than simply being placed according to the terrain.

evidence: Left side: an open pavilion is screened among pine woods and mixed trees, its roof and pillars partly blocked by branches, with figures visible inside the pavilion, presenting a layering of seeing a house within the woods. | Center-right: behind dense clumps of trees, the roof or fence structure of a building is faintly visible, partly screened by foreground trees. | Right side: behind distant clumps of trees there is a small building, also in a half-screened state.
distinction: Although the pavilion is built according to the terrain, the painting more prominently highlights the relationship of screening and revealing of the buildings by woodland; the effect of concealment and revelation forming the scene is greater than simple correspondence with terrain.

evidence: Center: the thatched pavilion is partly screened by banana leaves and the rockery on the right, revealing the roof and part of the structure, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Right side: another building is screened by the branches and leaves of foreground trees, with window lattice and eaves faintly visible, presenting a layering of seeing a house through a screen. | Left side: an enclosing wall and an arched gate form the boundary of the space, enclosing a courtyard space together with the plants and increasing pictorial depth.
distinction: The painting mainly presents the concealment-and-revelation relationship of buildings screened by banana plants, trees, and rockery, rather than emphasizing buildings placed according to natural terrain.

evidence: Center-right: between the middle-ground woodland and sloping bank, geometric outlines resembling roofs or walls are faintly visible, but the details are blurred and cannot be definitively identified as built elements. | Overall: the painting consists mainly of mountains, clouds and mist, trees, and streams; the spatial layering is deep, and there are clear relationships of screening and revealing among the natural scenery.
distinction: The painting lacks clear evidence of built elements; it is assigned to the closest category based only on the overall visible screening relationships of landscape and suspected outlines.

evidence: Lower right to lower middle: a winding path and trees are visible, guiding the gaze to extend into the depth of the painting. | Lower left to center: a small bridge or stone beam connects the mountain rocks on both sides, forming a node of crossing and entry. | Right cliff: a clear stepped path is painted on the cliff face, extending upward along the mountain, presenting a spatial process of climbing and going deeper.
distinction: Although the path and steps are built according to the mountain terrain, the core of the painting lies in using these clues to guide the viewer to enter and travel through, rather than simply showing the placement relationship between buildings and terrain.

evidence: Lower left and lower middle: multiple building groups are arranged at different heights along the waterside and sloping ground; courtyards and enclosing walls unfold following the undulations of the terrain, closely connecting with the surrounding water surface and mountain foot. | Right side of the painting: terraced fields are present at the waterside, following the curved form of the shoreline, further reflecting the correspondence between built elements and site conditions.
distinction: Although the buildings occupy an important position in the painting, their layout's relationship of conformity to terrain and waterside is more prominent and dominant than simply serving as scenic markers.

evidence: Lower center: the roof, walls, and door of a house are visible, partly screened by the trunk and branches of a tall pine on the left. | Right side: the branches of a withered tree on the right extend toward the center of the painting, together with the trees on the left forming a relationship of concealment and revelation around the house.
distinction: Although the house is built on sloping rocks, the painting mainly presents the spatial layering of the house through the screening and revealing by the trees on the left and right; the concealment-and-revelation relationship is more prominent.

evidence: Cliff at the upper center-right: a striking red building (a pavilion) sits on a projecting part of a steep cliff, becoming the visual focus. | Below the red building: steps or a mountain path can be seen connecting to the building, showing its precipitous position. | Right mountainside: there are winding paths and tiny figures, which set off the height of the cliff and the scenic-accentuation role of the building.
distinction: Although the building is placed according to the mountain terrain, its vivid color and prominent position on the cliff top make its main role that of defining and concentrating this precipitous scenic spot, rather than simply displaying siting according to the terrain.

evidence: Left middle ground: several groups of houses are distributed in scattered fashion along the waterside and slopes, their layout unfolding with the rises and falls of the terrain. | Lower center: at the base of the mountain mass is an arched opening through which water passes, forming a spatial passage. | Distant water surface: a few houses dot the waterside, echoing the open water surface.
distinction: The layout of the house cluster on the left, set against water and slope, occupies the main visual weight and clearly shows the relationship between built elements and terrain, while the opening below, though passage-like in nature, is more like a single node.

evidence: Lower left-center, at the foot of the main peak: a building with red walls and black tiles is clearly visible, situated on flat ground between the mountain foot and the waterside, with a few trees around it. | Center of the painting: the towering main peak occupies the main body of the painting; the building is located at its foot, forming a vertical echo with the peak and defining the specific scenery at the mountain foot.
distinction: Although the building is at the mountain foot, the painting emphasizes its role as a visual focus marking the scenery at the mountain foot, rather than a complex terrain-adaptive layout.

evidence: Right middle: a group of multi-storied buildings is screened by dense woodland, with only the roofs and parts of the building bodies exposed, presenting a spatial layering of houses hidden within the woods. | Lower left: a thatched pavilion by the water is partly screened by foreground trees and rocks; figures are inside the pavilion, forming a relationship of foreground screening and background.
distinction: In the painting the buildings mainly form spatial layering through screening and revealing by trees, rather than serving simply as isolated markers defining a particular landscape.

evidence: Left and center: several trees are visible, including withered trees and weeping willows, growing on sloping banks. | Right and background: distant mountains rise and fall, with unpainted space for the water surface; there are no traces of built elements such as houses, bridges, or paths.
distinction: No built elements are visible in the painting, so an exact classification based on the relationship between built elements and landscape is not possible; it is assigned to the closest category only on the basis of the overall landscape composition.

evidence: Lower part: several figures can be seen walking along a sloping bank, forming a dynamic cue of movement toward the depth of the painting or toward the mountains and rocks above. | Upper middle: mountains and rocks and a waterfall form a deep spatial background; the direction in which the figures move suggests a path into this landscape setting.
distinction: There are no explicit built elements in the painting, but the figures' tracks provide spatial cues for entry and movement through the landscape, so it is assigned to the closest category, C4.

evidence: Whole painting: the painting is dominated by hills, pines, and clouds and mist; figures are visible at the bottom and on the mountainside, and no clear traces of built elements such as houses, pavilions, or bridges are seen. | Upper middle: the mountain terrain rises and falls, with patches of pines distributed on the summit and mountainside, forming a natural visual focus. | Center: clouds and mist run horizontally across, separating the front and rear mountain masses and forming spatial layering.
distinction: The painting lacks identifiable built elements; it is assigned to the closest category only on the basis of the natural opening and closing of the landscape forms and the visual focus.

evidence: Center-left of the painting: building roofs and eave corners are visible above the cliff bank, partly screened by foreground pines and mixed trees, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Right side and foreground: dense pine groves and dotted-leaf trees form a foreground layer that screens the buildings in the middle ground, creating spatial depth.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed against the cliff, the painting emphasizes the layering of concealment and revelation, with roofs half exposed and screened by woodland, rather than simple correspondence to terrain.

evidence: At the mountainside slightly right of center: a group of houses is distributed in staggered fashion along the slope terraces of the mountain, the building bases set in accordance with the direction of the mountain's rock and slope. | Right waterside and mountain foot: some buildings or structures are placed tightly in the gaps between the waterside and the rocks, showing a layout that follows the bank and winds around the rocks.
distinction: Although the built elements are screened by woodland, their most distinctive feature is that the houses are placed in staggered fashion according to the mountain's forms and slope terraces; the role of terrain in the built layout is greater than that of simple concealment-and-revelation layering.

evidence: Right side of the painting: the painting depicts a mythological figure treading on clouds, surrounded by cloud vapor and stars, with grasses, trees, and branches painted below; no buildings or traces of artificial construction are seen.
distinction: The painting lacks explicit built elements, so an effective distinction based on the relationship between actual buildings and landscape cannot be made; it is assigned only by forced classification under the rules.

evidence: Center and upper part of the right-hand painted panel: a large tree has a thick trunk and luxuriant branches and leaves that screen part of the sky, and a figure leans beneath the tree. | Lower part and sky of the right-hand painted panel: the figure is beside the tree roots, with grass painted around, and a full moon and constellations are painted in the sky; no built structures such as houses, pavilions or bridges are seen in the entire painting.

evidence: Distant opposite bank in the upper part of the painting: a long city wall can be seen extending horizontally along the terrain of the opposite bank, with gate towers on the wall and dense roofs behind, presenting a form arranged along the bank. | Foreground in the lower part of the painting: mainly sloping rocks and trees, with no clear buildings, forming a spatial contrast of near and far with the distant city.

evidence: Lower center-right of the painting: through the branches of trees and the screening of mountains and rocks, the roof and part of the structure of a built element are visible, presenting a half-hidden, half-exposed state. | Middle ground of the painting: dense trees and mountains and rocks form screening elements in the foreground and middle ground, hiding the built elements behind natural scenery and creating spatial layering.
distinction: The built elements are mainly screened by woodland and mountains and rocks, emphasizing the spatial layering formed by concealment and revelation, rather than serving as a striking node defining the scenery.

evidence: Lower right: a figure can be seen leaning against tree roots, facing the open water surface and distant mountains; there are no traces of building or construction. | Middle ground and background: the water surface and layered mountain ranges form an open landscape space; the figure, as a scenic accent, concentrates the contemplation of this landscape.

evidence: Right-hand painted panel: the painting depicts undulating sloping ground, clumps of grasses and trees, and drifting clouds above, presenting a spatial layering of natural scenery; no traces of built structures such as houses, bridges or roads are seen.
distinction: There is no built structure in the painting; it is assigned to the closest category solely on the basis of the overall visible spatial organization of the natural landscape.
