distinction: There are no explicit built elements in the painting, only figures moving through landscape and clouds and mist; it is barely assigned to access to secluded settings to represent the spatial process.

evidence: Right-hand painted panel: the painting mainly depicts overlapping, interlaced rocky mountain forms; no clear traces of man-made built structures such as houses, bridges or paths are seen. | Left-hand painted panel: this is calligraphic inscription, which does not count as a built element of the spatial representation of the painting.
distinction: There is no clear built structure in the painting, only the forms of mountain rocks are seen; it is assigned to the closest category on the basis of the overall visible space.

evidence: Right-hand painted panel: the painting depicts rocks covered in ice and snow and ground cracked by drought; no traces of built structures such as buildings, roads or bridges are seen.
distinction: There are absolutely no built elements in the painting, only natural mountain-rock landforms are presented; therefore it is assigned only tentatively to the closest category of terrain representation on the basis of the overall spatial forms.

evidence: Lower center of the painting: several thatched huts are surrounded by masses of pink flowering trees and green willows, with roofs and eaves emerging from among the branches and leaves. | Right side: two connected houses are mostly screened by tree trunks and flowering branches, with only parts of the building structure exposed, forming a layering of houses seen through a screen. | Left side: a small hut is likewise screened behind pink blossoms and green trees, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship.
distinction: The painting mainly constructs spatial layering through the screening and revealing of the houses by trees, rather than emphasizing the decisive role of terrain and topography in the building layout.

evidence: Lower center: a wooden bridge spans a stream, with a person carrying a load walking across it, connecting the two banks and forming a clear cue for movement through the landscape and a path into the painting. | Right mountainside: a building with red columns and a roof is visible half-hidden behind trees, together with the bridge below suggesting a reachable destination. | Overall composition: the bridge guides the eye deep into the valley, and together with the cloud-wreathed mountain ranges presents a spatial process of passing from here to there and turning into the depths.
distinction: Although the building on the right has the character of concealment and revelation, the combination of the bridge and the walking figure in the painting more strongly expresses an enterable, traversable spatial process, so C4 is dominant.

evidence: Right side: a building is largely screened by the dense branches and leaves of foreground and middle-ground trees, with only the green roof and parts of the eaves and columns exposed. | Right side and middle ground: the screening by trees forms clear spatial layering, giving the building a visual effect of alternating concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the railings and path in the lower left corner hint at entry, the core compositional role of the painting is the concealment and revelation of the building by trees, rather than emphasizing the extension of a route of travel.

evidence: Left side: a red-walled building is partly screened by trees and mountains and rocks, with only the roof and part of the walls exposed, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Right side: beside the mountains and rocks is a small bridge, its arch faintly visible, forming layering with the surrounding scenery.
distinction: The building presents spatial layering mainly through screening and revealing by trees and mountains and rocks, consistent with the characteristics of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower left corner: the house building is largely screened by the dense branches and leaves of a huge foreground willow, with only the roof and part of the walls exposed, presenting a typical state of a house hidden in the woods. | Center: a pavilion on a hill is surrounded by trees, and a horizontal band of mist (unpainted space/light ink) on the mountainside separates it, giving the pavilion a layering of a house seen through a screen, half hidden and half exposed.
distinction: Although the buildings present a terrain-responsive layout placed separately according to the slope (the pavilion high, the house low) (C1), the painting actively screens the buildings through the dense willows and the horizontally cutting mist; the concealment-and-revelation relationship is more dominant in constructing spatial layering and expressing the theme of "forest mist."

evidence: Left side: a waterside pavilion is built by the water, supported by columns below, with a gentleman playing the zither inside; the building base meets the bank slope and the water surface. | Center to right: a flat bridge (plank walkway) extends from near the pavilion across the water surface, connecting to the opposite bank and forming a clear cue for passage.
distinction: Although the buildings are built along the water, the extension of the flat bridge in the painting clearly constructs an enterable route of travel across the water and connecting the two banks, making the spatial process (C4) dominant.

evidence: Right side and center: the building is partly screened by foreground pines, Taihu rocks, and weeping willows, with only the eaves, window lattices, and door leaves exposed, forming clear layering of concealment and revelation. | Left side: a wall with a circular moon gate connects with plants in the courtyard, further enriching the relationships of spatial screening and revealing in the courtyard.
distinction: The painting mainly represents the layering of concealment and revelation of the building screened by trees and mountains and rocks, rather than emphasizing the building's placement according to specific terrain and waterside.

evidence: Left side: most of the building is screened by foreground boulders and pines, with only the roof, eaves, columns, and the figure inside the window on the left exposed, forming a clear concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Center to right of the painting: a red-railed winding path/bridge threads among the mountains, rocks, and trees, together with the screened building forming a richly layered space.
distinction: Although there is a winding path guiding the way in the painting, the most prominent spatial expression of the building itself is that it is screened by trees and rocks; the concealment-and-revelation relationship dominates the composition.

evidence: Center and right side: the red columns, green columns, doors, and windows of the building are partly screened by the trunks, branches, and leaves of two large foreground trees, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Left side and center: artificial rockery and trees screen the building's platform base and sides, increasing the sense of layering in the courtyard space.
distinction: Although the painting shows the building set against a pond and artificial rockery, the interpenetration and screening of the building facade by trees is the most prominent mode of spatial organization in the composition.

evidence: Lower right-center: the roofs and gable walls of two buildings emerge from dense woodland, with the roof ridges and tile surfaces clearly visible, but the main bodies of the buildings are screened by branches and leaves. | Right side: the buildings form a clear concealment-and-revelation relationship with the surrounding trees; the woodland screens the houses, presenting a clearly layered sense of space.
distinction: The painting mainly emphasizes the concealment-and-revelation relationship of the buildings screened by woodland and then revealed (concealment and revelation), rather than the correspondence of buildings placed according to terrain (terrain-responsive siting).

evidence: Lower left: on flat ground beside the mountains and rocks and the banana plants is a seat, on which one person sits while another stands, placed against the rocky bank.
distinction: The seat is placed on the flat ground against the rocky bank, presenting a relationship of sitting according to the ground, rather than serving as a striking marker defining a particular landscape scene.

evidence: Lower right corner: a stone arch bridge spans across, its railings clearly visible, extending into the painting as a path and suggesting a connection between land and water. | Lower left corner: on a canopied pleasure boat, three people pole and row, presenting the process of traveling by boat on the water and its accessibility. | Upper left corner: a pavilion is built on high ground among the mountains and rocks, serving as a node in the distant scene and forming a spatial echo with the water-borne travel.
distinction: The bridge and the boat constitute a clear route of movement and a dynamic process, dominating the painting's sense of spatial entry and travel relations rather than serving merely as static scenic markers.

evidence: Lower right to center right: a clear winding path extends upward from the lower right corner of the painting, passes through woodland, and connects to a group of buildings in a mountain hollow on the right. | The mountain hollow on the right: multiple houses gather on the flat ground of the valley, and the path clearly points toward and enters this area, presenting an accessible spatial relationship. | Center-left: beside a mountain waterfall stands an arch bridge, echoing the mountain forms and the path, suggesting a travel clue of crossing and passage.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed according to the mountain terrain, the travel clues formed by the winding path and the bridge in the painting are more prominent, dominating the spatial process of entering from outside to inside and going from one place to another.

evidence: Right center-lower part: a group of red-walled buildings (a main hall and a gate tower below) is hidden among pine woods and trees, with only roofs, eaves, and parts of the walls exposed. | Right foreground to middle ground: tall pines and dense woodland screen the buildings in front and behind, creating a spatial layering of seeing houses deep in the woods. | Below the buildings: stone steps or a bridge structure are visible beneath the gate tower, meeting the unpainted space (water/cloud) in the foreground and suggesting a partial relationship of entry.
distinction: Although there are path clues below the buildings, the painting emphasizes more the spatial layering formed by the buildings' screening and revelation through the woodland; the effect of concealment and revelation forming a scene is greater than the travel process of access to secluded settings.

evidence: Right side: along the stream and the foot of the mountain runs a clear path (or embankment) connecting village houses distributed along the mountain, and it extends deep toward the upper right of the painting, forming a clear travel clue. | Left middle ground: a red pagoda and a group of hall buildings are partly screened among trees and mountains and rocks, with paths or terraces connected to them, situated within the embrace of the mountain forest. | Lower center: waterfall water falls from among the mountains, together with the water system and path on the right forming the painting's sense of spatial connectivity.
distinction: Although the buildings on the left have screening characteristics, the clear path system on the right connects the building groups and guides the eye deeper, making the spatial process of access to secluded settings more dominant.

evidence: Left side of the painting: a group of buildings is built on a stone masonry base, backed by mountain rocks and a bamboo grove, placed in accordance with the terrain. | Left side to center of the painting: the buildings open out toward expansive water, presenting a layout relationship of nestling against the mountain and facing the water, with houses set on a terrace.
distinction: Although the buildings indicate a waterside scene, their placement on a terrain-following terrace and their correspondence with the mountain rocks and bamboo grove behind are more prominent, dominantly manifesting terrain-responsive siting.

evidence: High on the left slope: a building is half hidden behind mountain rocks and trees, with only its roof and part of its walls exposed, presenting a state of being screened by natural scenery. | At the valley mouth and water bay in the center-right of the painting: a group of buildings is blocked by pine trees in front and a huge mountain rock on the right, with eaves and walls revealed in the gaps between woodland and rocks, forming front-to-back layering. | Beside the water on the right: a sailboat is moored beside a protruding rock, together with the screened building group forming pictorial depth at the land-water boundary.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed according to the mountain terrain, the painting emphasizes more the spatial layering formed by the screening and revelation of the buildings by woodland and mountain rocks, so C2 is more dominant than C1.

evidence: Lower left corner: part of a building is visible (roof and supporting structure), arranged immediately beside flowing water and rocks, presenting a placement relationship of nestling against water and beside rocks. | Lower center of the painting: water flows among rocks and woodland, and the built elements in the lower left corner unfold in accordance with the waterside terrain.
distinction: Although the building is only partially visible, its main characteristic is its integration with the terrain of the waterside rocks, rather than emphasizing the layering of concealment and revelation screened by woodland and mountain rocks.

evidence: Center-left: a thatched pavilion stands beside a curved large tree trunk and beneath a bamboo grove; the pavilion roof is partly obscured by branches extending above, presenting a layering of seeing a house beneath the trees. | Left side and behind the pavilion: mountain rocks, dead trees, and a bamboo grove surround the pavilion, forming screening in the foreground and background and placing the built structure within the embrace of natural scenery.
distinction: Although an arch bridge on the right side of the painting suggests a travel clue, there is no discernible road or watercourse connection between the bridge and the pavilion to form a clear process of entry, whereas the screening relationship between the pavilion and the trees is visually more direct and close.

evidence: Lower right: a figure leading livestock along a path is visible; the path extends toward the left of the painting and into the depth, constituting a clear travel clue. | Lower center to center-left: a long plank walkway or railing structure (dense vertical lines) is visible, winding along the mountain terrain and the stream bank, helping to explain the path's extension and entry relationship. | Upper left: a group of building roofs is visible on the mountainside, serving as a built node in the depth to which the path leads, giving the travel process a destination.
distinction: Although the walkway and houses are placed according to the mountain terrain (C1), the painting emphasizes more, through the figures' movement and the winding path, the spatial process of going from here to there and turning into the depth (C4).

evidence: Center-left of the painting: a pavilion sits among mountain rocks; around and in front of it, branches of luxuriant flowering trees (appearing to be plum) extend, partly screening the pavilion's columns and base, forming a layering of alternating concealment and revelation. | Lower left to center of the painting: a figure is walking along a sloping path among the mountain rocks toward the pavilion, the path threading between flowers, trees, and rocks, enhancing the sense of a spatial process of approaching the built structure, though the pavilion itself is mainly screened by flowers and trees to form a scene.
distinction: Although figures walk along the path toward the pavilion, embodying a clue of access to secluded settings, the pavilion's main compositional feature in the painting is its half-screened, half-revealed relationship with the flowering trees and mountain rocks, so C2 is more apt.

evidence: Valley to the center-left of the painting: a small house is half screened by surrounding trees and mountain rocks, with only part of its roof and walls exposed. | Mountainside at center-right of the painting: a larger pavilion building is built against the mountain, partly obscured by the mountain mass and trees in front, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Deep in the distant valley of the painting: building groups are faintly visible, obscured by distant mountains and clouds and mist, increasing the painting's spatial layering.
distinction: Although the buildings are built against the mountain, the painting emphasizes more the buildings' concealment and sense of layering through the screening of mountain rocks and trees, rather than simply emphasizing the determining effect of terrain on building layout.

evidence: On the waist of the mountain rock at center-right of the painting: a two-story building is half hidden in a grove, with only the upper roof, railings, and part of the lower eaves exposed. | Around the building: pink flowering trees and dark trees surround and screen the building's walls, forming an obvious concealment-and-revelation relationship and spatial layering. | Right side of the painting: a tall mountain rock serves as background, and the building is embedded between mountain rocks and woodland, presenting a deep and secluded mood behind the rock and within the woods.
distinction: Although the building is placed against the mountain rock, the painting emphasizes more its spatial layering of being screened by woodland and half exposed, half hidden, rather than mere correspondence to terrain.

evidence: Lower left corner: a thatched-roof pavilion is built at the top of a protruding rocky slope terrace, its site following the terrain's height, presenting a form of setting a house on a terrace. | Left foreground: the built position is waterside and elevated, together with the adjacent trees forming a placement at the edge of a sloping bank, corresponding spatially to the open water on the right.
distinction: Although the pavilion serves to indicate a waterside scene, its form of being built atop a rocky slope terrace more directly matches the terrain-responsive placement characteristic of setting a house on a terrace, emphasizing the correspondence between built structure and terrain.

evidence: Center-left: the corner of a building roof is revealed between mountain rocks and dense trees, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship of being half screened by natural scenery. | Lower right corner: beside reeds on the water, there is a small boat with an angler, serving as a scenic accent on the water and not forming a clear travel-path connection with the shore.
distinction: Although the building nestles against the mountain and faces the water, the painting mainly presents its faintly visible layering through the screening of trees and mountain rocks; the concealment-and-revelation relationship is more prominent than placement according to terrain.

evidence: Upper left-center: a pavilion is built on a protruding rocky terrace on the mountainside, its site closely integrated with the mountain form, presenting a placement relationship of setting a house on a terrace. | Overall painting: the built structures follow the mountain's rises and falls in scattered arrangement; no obvious path guidance or deep woodland screening is seen, mainly manifesting the characteristic of placement according to terrain.
distinction: Although the pavilion is in a conspicuous position, its dependence on and placement upon the rocky terrace is more direct and dominant, rather than its serving merely as an isolated marker indicating scenery.

evidence: Lower left: a simple wooden bridge spans the water, connecting the flat ground on the left with the sloping bank on the right; on the bridge a person holding a staff is walking toward the depths of the woodland. | Right side: dense woodland grows beneath towering mountain rocks, and the direction of the bridge suggests a path leading into the depths of this mountain forest.
distinction: Although there are no obvious built entities such as houses in the painting, the combination of bridge and pedestrian clearly constructs an accessible, traversable spatial clue, most consistent with the characteristic of access to secluded settings.

evidence: Lower right: a pavilion is erected on a waterside rock or wooden piles, built at the water's edge, presenting a form of setting a house on a terrace. | Center: a long corridor or waterside pavilion is placed in the gaps among mountain rocks and by the water, spanning between the rocks on the left and right and unfolding in accordance with the terrain. | Overall layout: the building groups (pavilion, waterside pavilion) are mainly placed according to the shoreline and the distribution of mountain rocks, presenting a relationship of placement according to terrain and suitability to the lie of the land.
distinction: Although buildings on the upper right are screened by woodland (a C2 feature), the placement of the core buildings in the center-lower part according to water and mountain rocks (placement according to terrain) is more significant and dominates the painting's spatial organization.

evidence: Left bank: houses are visible on the bank, partly obscured by trees, with a small bridge beside them connecting the waterside. | Water surface at lower center: a small boat carries two people, moving toward the shore, expressing a path approaching the built structures. | Left shoreline: the shoreline, trees, and bridge form a coherent clue of entry, guiding the eye toward the buildings on the bank.
distinction: Although the buildings have a concealment-and-revelation relationship with trees obscuring them, the painting emphasizes more the travel process of boating on the water and entering the bank via the bridge; the organizing role of access to secluded settings is more prominent.

evidence: Right side: a house is partly screened by a bamboo grove and miscellaneous trees, with only the roof, eaves, and part of the walls exposed, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Inside the window of the house on the right: a figure can be seen sitting within, indicating the spatial layering and presence of the built structure. | Around the house on the right: fences and trees surround the built structure, making the building hidden among woodland and participating in the forming of the scene.
distinction: The painting mainly presents the spatial layering formed by the built structure's screening and revelation through woodland, rather than emphasizing its correspondence to terrain-based placement.

evidence: Left mountainside: a small building (pavilion or house) is visible, built according to the mountain terrain, with supporting structures below, close against the rock face. | Central ridge: two small buildings are visible, scattered on the slope, following the mountain's undulations and the gaps in the woodland. | Right distant shore: the water surface is expansive; the far shore has low woodland and faint building outlines, forming a spatial contrast with the towering mountain rocks on the left.
distinction: Although the buildings are partly adjacent to woodland, their core characteristic is placement according to the terrain of mountain rocks and slope terraces, rather than mainly relying on screening to form layering.

evidence: Lower left foreground: the roofs and walls of several houses are partly obscured by the dense foliage of willow branches, presenting a layering of houses hidden in the woods. | Mid-ground hill in the painting: a red-roofed tower is built on the ridge and mountainside; its lower half and surroundings are screened by mountain rocks and tree clusters, with only the top exposed, creating the effect of seeing a house across a screen. |
distinction: Although the building on the mid-ground peak serves to mark the mountain peak, the buildings in the foreground and middle ground are generally screened by trees and mountain rocks, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship runs through and dominates the composition more.

evidence: Lower right foreground: multiple houses are arranged in scattered tiers following the rising and falling terrain of the slope, unfolding against the slope terraces and trees. | Left middle ground: building groups are distributed along the foot of the slope and the shoreline, presenting a placement relationship of following the bank and nestling against the slope. | Middle-ground water surface: a small bridge spans the water connecting the sloping land on both banks, helping to explain the connection between buildings and terrain.
distinction: Although the buildings are screened by trees, the painting emphasizes more the layout of the building groups in accordance with the terrain of the slope and shoreline; the relationship of placement according to terrain is more dominant than the layering of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower left: at the foot of the mountain by the water's edge is a group of houses, with a small bridge in front connecting to the waterside path. | Lower center: a person fishes by the water, positioned on the bank line extending from the small bridge that connects to the buildings, forming a travel clue.
distinction: Although the buildings nestle against the mountain and face the water, the clues of entry and travel constituted by the small bridge and the shoreline path are more prominent, dominating the spatial organization.

evidence: Upper center-left: on a cloud-and-mist-wreathed mountainside, a building structure resembling a roof or railing is faintly revealed, half screened. | Lower left: in the gaps of dense foreground tree clusters, the roof and supporting structure of a simple building are revealed. | Lower right: beneath the screening of waterside grass and trees, the roof outline of another building is visible, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship with the natural environment.
distinction: Although the buildings dot the landscape, their main visual characteristic is being revealed while screened by clouds and mist and trees, emphasizing spatial layering and the concealment-and-revelation relationship rather than serving merely as markers indicating landmarks.

evidence: Lower right: in the reeds/grass, a simple hut or platform is revealed, with the hut roof structure visible and a person sitting within. | Lower right: the built structure is half screened by the surrounding dense grass, forming a spatial layering of alternating concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower center: the roofs and walls of several houses are partly obscured by trees in the foreground and middle ground, presenting a layering of houses hidden in the woods. | Upper center mountainside: buildings on the mountainside are half screened by mountain rocks and red-leafed trees, revealing parts of eaves and roofs. | Lower right: two people stand beside trees, suggesting the space is accessible, but no clear coherent clues such as bridges, paths, corridors, or gates are seen.
distinction: Although the buildings are distributed according to the mountain terrain, the most prominent compositional method in the painting is forming a layering of concealment and revelation through the screening and revelation of trees and mountain rocks, rather than emphasizing the terrain correspondence of placement according to terrain.

evidence: Right middle ground: a house building is partly obscured by a huge mountain rock (or tree root) in the foreground and by trees in the middle ground, with only the roof, side walls, and a latticed window exposed. | Behind and around the house: a bamboo grove and trees surround the building, forming a screening relationship; a figure visible inside the window indicates the building's presence and the layer it occupies.
distinction: Although the building is built against the slope, the painting emphasizes more the screening and revelation of the building by foreground mountain rocks and trees, forming a layering of concealment and revelation, rather than simply emphasizing the correspondence between terrain and layout.

evidence: Lower center-right: a small bridge is visible; on the bridge a figure is walking toward the buildings on the right, forming a clear clue of movement. | Lower right: a group of buildings is located at the end of the path, connected with the bridge and the figure's movement, presenting an accessible spatial relationship. | Upper left mountainside: another group of buildings is hidden among the mountain forest; though farther away, it is also within the traversable landscape space.
distinction: Although buildings are screened by trees, the painting clearly organizes, through the bridge, figures, and path, the spatial process of entering the buildings; C4 describes this dynamic travel relationship more accurately than C2.

evidence: Lower center of the painting: multiple foreground trees and middle-ground mountain rocks form front-to-back layering, but no houses or artificial built structures are seen. | Lower right corner: a figure sits on a rock, with no sign of buildings. | Overall: the painting consists mainly of mountain rocks, trees, and figures, lacking built elements.

evidence: Center and left of the painting: clusters of bamboo, trees, and sloping rocks are visible, forming the natural scenery that constitutes the main subject of the painting. | Right side and background: gently sloping shoreline lines extend, forming a spatial contrast with the sloping rocks and trees in the foreground.

evidence: Lower center: a wooden bridge spans a stream, with travelers crossing on it, constituting a clear thread of crossing and connection. | Deep in the valley at the upper right: a house is faintly visible, located deep along the extending path, suggesting a destination or a waypoint along the route. | Overall composition: the stream and bridge guide the gaze from near to far, extending into the interior of the valley, presenting a spatial process of moving from here to there.

evidence: Lower right: a pavilion is built beside a bamboo grove on the waterside, with a clear base, facing the water. | Lower right of center: a small canopied boat is moored at the bank in front of the pavilion, its hull meeting the shoreline, with a mast standing upright. | From lower right to lower center: the boat and pavilion form a water-land connection, constituting a ferry-landing relationship and suggesting that the bank-side built elements can be reached from the water.

evidence: Overall painting: the painting consists mainly of bare trees, a wintry forest, waterside, and distant mountains; no clear traces of built elements such as houses, pavilions, bridges, or paths are seen. | Center and both sides: tree branches interlock, forming spatial layers of foreground and background screening, but no buildings are concealed or revealed within them.
distinction: The painting is dominated by the screening layers of natural scenery, and no built elements identify a particular scene, so C3 is not selected.

evidence: Upper-middle mountain ridge: a row of small, blurred vertical brushstrokes can be seen, suspected to be a miniature wooden fence or simple built element, but its specific form cannot be reliably identified. | Whole image: the main subject of the painting is a multi-tiered waterfall and surging water; the water flows from top to bottom through the painting, forming a strong sense of depth and flow.
distinction: Because the built element is extremely blurred and its spatial function cannot be confirmed, it is only on the basis of the overall spatial momentum of the water flowing from far to near and from top to bottom that it is tentatively assigned to C4, which suggests a movement-through-the-landscape route.

evidence: Lower center, slightly right: a group of houses is partly screened by the branches and leaves of foreground trees, with only part of the roof and walls exposed, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Left middle ground: building outlines are faintly visible, likewise screened by trees along the bank, suggesting spatial layering.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed in response to the waterside slope, the painting emphasizes more the screening and revealing of the buildings by trees to construct spatial layering, so C2 is more apt.

evidence: Left side: mountains and rocks and a waterfall flowing down can be seen | Right side and lower part: pine trees, bamboo clumps, and a person sitting on a rock can be seen, with a long strip-shaped object placed beside them | Whole image: no clear built entities such as houses, pavilions, or bridges are seen in the painting
distinction: There are no clear built elements in the painting; only a figure and landscape with trees, with no buildings participating in the composition

evidence: Upper middle of the painting: a group of buildings is screened by mountains and rocks and trees, with only part of the roof and eave corners exposed, presenting a layer hidden in the mountain forest. | Lower right of the painting: another building is screened behind the mountain rocks on the right and the foreground woodland, with water flowing below, forming a spatial relationship in which a house is seen through a screened view.
distinction: Although the built elements are placed in response to the mountain terrain, the painting emphasizes more their concealment-and-revelation relationship and spatial layering as revealed through screening by mountains, rocks, and trees, so C2 is more dominant than C1.

evidence: Whole image: the painting mainly depicts mountains and rocks, trees, and waterside; no clear built elements such as houses, pavilions, bridges, or paths are seen. | Upper right corner: there is an inscription, but according to the rules it is not treated as spatial evidence within the painting.
distinction: No clear built elements are seen in the painting; the closest category is chosen on the basis of the overall visible landscape organization (the natural distribution of mountains and rocks, trees, and waterside), and clear evidence of built elements is lacking.

evidence: Lower part of the painting: a clear small path winds through a pine forest, and two figures are walking along the path, connecting the houses at the lower left with the elevated terrace building on the right. | Lower left and lower right of the painting: the two ends of the path respectively connect to the house group built against the mountain and the pavilion on the waterside high terrace, forming a clear route of movement and entry.
distinction: Although the buildings are laid out in response to the mountain terrain, the painting emphasizes more the spatial entry process linking different buildings through the path and the figures' movement through the landscape, so C4 is more dominant than C1.

evidence: Upper middle: a pavilion is placed high on mountains and rocks, surrounded by trees, becoming the visual focus of the upper part of the painting. | Lower and middle parts: the lower part of the painting contains a stream, sloped rocks, and trees; the mountains and rocks layer upward, and the pavilion identifies the scene at the high point of the mountains and rocks.
distinction: Although the pavilion is screened by trees, it is placed high on mountains and rocks, and its main role is to identify and concentrate the scene at the high point, rather than forming the scene solely through concealment and revelation.

evidence: Center of the foreground: a person can be seen sitting on a rock, facing the waterfall and mountain ranges to the left rear; no buildings such as houses or bridges are seen. | Left side of the painting: there is an inscription in the upper left corner, but the painting itself does not present any physical building structure corresponding to the text.
distinction: There are no entry clues such as man-made paths or bridges in the painting, only natural landscape and a figure, so C4 is excluded; because there are no buildings, assignment to C3 is only the closest inference of spatial organization in the absence of evidence of built elements.

evidence: Lower right of the painting: a building (a hall or lodge) is partly screened by several trees in front, with only the roof, columns, and the people inside exposed, forming an obvious layering of concealment and revelation. | Lower middle of the painting: trees and buildings interlock; the buildings are hidden behind the woodland, presenting a spatial relationship in which a house is seen within the woods.
distinction: Although the building is placed in response to the mountain terrain, the painting emphasizes more its concealment-and-revelation relationship of being screened by woodland and partly exposed, so C2 is more apt than C1.

evidence: Water surface at lower right: a small boat and a person fishing on it can be seen, surrounded by reeds and flying birds | Lower left and distant view: trees, reed thickets, and the far bank are depicted, and the water surface is open
distinction: No fixed built elements such as houses are seen in the painting; only a fishing boat identifies the autumn-pond scene, so it is assigned to scenic accentuation.

evidence: Lower left: a thatched hut can be seen, with part of its roof, eaves, and walls exposed, but most of it is screened by the trunks and branches of the twisted old trees in front. | Center to right: thick old trees with dense branches occupy the main body of the painting, forming obvious screening over the built elements behind and constituting a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Left side: a steep cliff serves as the background, together with the trees enclosing the hidden spatial layering in which the built elements are situated.
distinction: Although the built elements are located below the cliff, the painting mainly constructs spatial layering through the partial screening and revealing of the house by trees, and the effect of concealment and revelation is more dominant.

evidence: Lower part to center of the painting: a winding path extends from the lower part of the painting into the depths of the mountains, rocks, and trees, guiding the eye to explore inward. | Upper left of the painting: the inscribed poem mentions "a temple with a row of windows," implying the existence of built elements, but no specific building form is seen in the painting.
distinction: No clear buildings are seen in the painting, but the guiding role of the path is most prominent, suggesting an enterable spatial process rather than a mere relationship of screening.

evidence: At the mountain ridge, upper middle slightly left: a small building (a pavilion or house) can be seen hidden among mountains and rocks and pine trees, with only part of the roof and eaves exposed, half-screened by natural scenery. | Overall painting: mountain peaks rise and fall, pine trees grow in clusters, and the building blends into the mountain forest, forming spatial layers of alternating concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the building is located high on the mountain ridge, its main compositional role is to be screened by trees, mountains, and rocks, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship, rather than emphasizing a layout unfolding in response to the terrain.

evidence: Water surface at lower right: a small boat can be seen, with two people on board, one seemingly holding an oar or fishing rod, floating on the open water. | Left side and middle ground: trees grow in clusters on the sloped bank, and the shoreline winds and extends into the water, forming an opening-and-closing space. | Distant view: mountain ranges rise and fall, wreathed in clouds and mist, forming near-and-far layering with the foreground water surface.
distinction: The small boat, as one of the visual foci of the painting, identifies the specific scene of the "misty boat"; although it carries a sense of movement through the landscape, the painting has no fixed built elements or connecting paths to present a process of approaching built elements, so the emphasis is on scenic accentuation.

evidence: Lower right and middle right: at the lower right of the painting, a waterside wooden railing and a flat bridge can be seen extending toward the upper right and connecting to a pavilion among the pine forest, forming a clear clue of movement and entry. | Lower left: houses faintly appear among the trees and mountains and rocks at the lower left, with a sloped bank and a small path in front, implying an accessible route. | Whole image: the bridge, wooden railing, sloped bank, pavilion, and houses connect with one another, organizing a spatial journey from outside to inside and from the waterside into the mountain forest.
distinction: Although the built elements are screened by pines and rocks, the painting emphasizes more the spatial process of guiding the eye into the built elements through clues such as the bridge and railing, rather than a mere layering of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower left: a person walking with a staff along the sloped bank, presenting a momentum of movement through the landscape | Center to right: old trees, rocks, and distant mountains form a natural space; no clear buildings or bridges are seen
distinction: There are no man-made built elements in the painting; there is only the movement-through-the-landscape clue of a figure walking in nature, so it is assigned to the closest category of access to secluded settings.

evidence: Upper left: a multi-story pavilion built on a cliff platform, sited in dependence on the mountain's form. | Center to lower part: a small path made of stone steps starts from the waterside in the foreground and winds upward through mountains and rocks and trees. | Middle ground of the painting: the stone path extends deep into the mountains, forming a spatial guiding thread leading from the foreground to the rear cliff.
distinction: The winding upward stone-step path in the painting constitutes a clear entry thread for movement through the landscape, emphasizing the spatial process of passing from here to there, and dominates the spatial organization more than treating the pavilion alone as a high landmark.

evidence: Lower right: a person sits upright inside an open pavilion; the pavilion itself is partly screened by the bamboo grove in front and the trees on the right, presenting a half-hidden, half-revealed layering. | Left: a cliff waterfall flows down and joins the water surface in front of the pavilion; the water surface spatially links the mountains and rocks on the left with the built elements on the right.
distinction: Although the pavilion is built facing the water, the painting emphasizes more its screening and revealing by bamboo and trees; the effect of concealment and revelation forming a scene is greater than mere topographic siting.

evidence: Upper middle, slightly right: a tiny figure stands on a rocky platform at the summit of a peak; no houses, pavilions, or other built elements are visible. | Upper left: there is inscription text mentioning climbing to gaze at cloud peaks; the painting takes continuous mountain ranges and pine trees as its main subject.
distinction: No clear built elements are seen in the painting; only a figure stands at the summit, marking the scene of climbing high, so it is assigned to C3 as the closest spatial expression.

evidence: Lower left: a small bridge is visible crossing a stream and connecting the two banks, forming a clear entry thread. | Lower middle: on the sloped bank there is a building with an arched gate, with a path or open ground in front, giving a sense of spatial connection with the bridge on the left. | Middle ground, slightly right: in the depths of the valley, parts of pavilion roofs emerge amid screening trees and woodland, suggesting a spatial layer that can be entered and explored.
distinction: Although the middle-ground buildings have a screened effect, the bridge and path in the lower-left corner clearly construct a thread of movement from outside to inside, making access to secluded settings the dominant mode of spatial organization.

evidence: Lower left to center: a figure stands on a sloped bank; in front, a winding path (or stone steps) extends toward the upper right, passing beside pine trees. | Center, slightly right, mid-slope: the path connects to a pavilion (or open gallery) at the mid-slope, forming a clear line of travel. | Among the mountains and rocks on the right: houses are visible in the screening of mountains and rocks above and behind the pavilion, and the path suggests access to these depths.
distinction: Although the built structures are screened by mountains and rocks, the painting, through the connection of the figure, the winding path, and the pavilion and houses, emphasizes more the process of movement from here to there.

evidence: Right, upper middle: the building complex is distributed according to the mountain's form, but most of it is blocked by the foreground pine trees and mountains and rocks, revealing only roofs, eaves, and parts of walls, presenting the layering of seeing houses within the woods. | Right, middle: another building (appearing to be a waterside pavilion) is screened by pine branches and leaves, producing the effect of seeing a house through an intervening layer, with an evident concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Lower-right corner: red railings or a bridge structure are visible crossing a stream, suggesting the existence of space, but the main visual focus is the screening of the buildings by trees.
distinction: Although the buildings are distributed according to the mountain's form (matching the C1 feature), the painting chiefly constructs spatial layering through the extensive screening and revealing of the buildings by foreground pines and mountains and rocks; the visual effect of concealment and revelation forming a scene is more dominant.

evidence: Lower-right corner: a stone bridge crosses a stream, with a pavilion built on the bridge; the bridge, together with the stream and mountains and rocks, constitutes a clear entry path. | Center, slightly right: a building with red columns is built on a cliff, positioned in the direction in which the stream-and-bridge path extends, suggesting an accessible spatial relationship. | Right, upper middle: the roof of another building is faintly visible amid screening trees and woodland, forming with the buildings and bridge below a progressively layered thread of movement through the landscape.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited against the mountain and beside the water, the combination of bridge, stream, and buildings in the painting emphasizes more a continuous, enterable path of movement through the landscape, so C4 fits better than C1.

evidence: Lower right: the building complex is built on an evident stone masonry base, arranged in staggered tiers following the mountain's form, showing the features of houses set on terraces and distributed according to the slope. | Upper right: another building is located high on the mountainside, sited according to the terrain and integrated with the surrounding mountains and rocks and trees. | Lower-left corner: a winding path extends, but the core of the painting lies in the way the buildings are sited on terraces relying on the mountain's form.
distinction: The form of buildings built on terraces against the mountain and distributed according to the slope is more prominent, directly embodying the correspondence between built structures and terrain; although a path exists, its main compositional role is to display the combination of buildings and mountain form.

evidence: Right: mountains and rocks, sloping ground, and trees are painted on the right side of the painting; no houses, pavilions, or other built elements are visible. | Left: calligraphic inscription and seals are on the left side of the painting, with no spatial clues of built structures.
distinction: The painting has no clear built elements; it presents an overall natural scene of mountains and rocks and trees, and is only tentatively assigned to scenic accentuation.

evidence: Right: a group of gallery buildings unfolds in staggered heights and zigzag fashion following the slope of the hillside; at the bottom, stone retaining walls built according to the mountain's form are visible, showing the feature of siting according to the terrain. | Right, upper middle: the building complex is partly screened by the surrounding bamboo grove and trees, concealed and revealed within the mountain forest.
distinction: Although the buildings and woodland have a screening relationship, their terrain-responsive arrangement, unfolding in staggered heights along the slope and terraces, is more central and prominent in the composition.

evidence: Lower right of the painting: a curved path or bridge with railings is visible, extending into the depth of the painting and forming a thread of movement through the landscape. | Right, middle of the painting: two buildings are built on a stone masonry base, with steps in front, connecting with the path space below. | Right of the painting: trees and mountains and rocks surround the buildings, and the path guides the eye toward the built area.
distinction: The railed path/bridge in the lower part of the painting constitutes a clear thread of movement through the landscape, guiding entry into the building area, and emphasizes the enterable spatial process more than mere building on terraces against the mountain.

evidence: Lower part, slightly right of center: a pavilion building is built on a waterside terrace, with an evident building site and steps or a platform extending in front, showing the form of houses set on terraces and unfolding along the bank. | Right, middle: a house building is sited against the mountainside slope, between mountains and rocks and trees, showing a layout distributed according to the slope. | Overall painting: the two built structures are distributed according to the high and low configuration of the waterfall's flow, from the mountainside to the waterside, and their building sites form a clear correspondence with the terrain (waterside, sloped terraces).
distinction: Although the buildings serve to mark the water outlet and the mountainside scenery (C3), their reliance on and siting according to the terrain (waterside, hillside) is more specific and dominates the spatial expression.

evidence: Upper right: a pavilion is built on a towering rocky platform, sited in reliance on the steep mountain form. | Lower right: a group of gallery buildings unfolds along the shoreline, with building sites laid out according to the waterside terrain. | Center: water flows through a gorge of mountains and rocks, and the buildings are distributed at the upper and lower ends of the water flow, showing a relationship of staggered heights and siting according to the terrain.
distinction: Although the buildings are partly screened by trees and woodland, the correspondence of their building sites and layout with terrain conditions such as rock and waterside is more prominent, dominating as terrain-responsive siting.

evidence: Upper part of the right side of the painting: a two-story pavilion building sits on a platform at the top of mountains and rocks; the building site is level and corresponds to the terrain, showing the form of houses set on terraces. | Edge of the right side of the painting: part of another building group is visible, arranged in tiers according to the hillside terrain, forming with the main building a relationship of distribution according to the slope. | Middle of the right side of the painting: the base of the buildings interlocks with the contours of the mountains and rocks, sited in accordance with the rise and fall of the mountain's form.
distinction: Although trees and woodland screen the buildings, the site relationship of being built on a high terrace and the layout distributed according to the slope are clearer, dominating the spatial correspondence between built structures and terrain.

evidence: Center, slightly right: dense bamboo grove and pine trees are painted slightly right of center, with faint traces among them, screened and revealed by the branches and leaves of the trees, forming layers. | Left: sloped rocks and water surface are painted on the left, forming an opening-and-closing relationship with the woodland on the right.
distinction: The painting organizes space through the concealment and revelation of woodland; no landmark built structure that clearly marks a scene is visible.

evidence: Right side and center of the painting: rocks and sloped banks are visible, with bamboo growing according to the rocks and beside the slope, showing a posture that follows the natural terrain. | Bottom of the painting: the waterside boundary is visible, and bamboo and rocks are distributed along the sloped bank; the overall spatial organization conveys a sense of siting according to the terrain.
distinction: There are no clear built elements in the painting; it is assigned to the closest category only on the basis of the spatial organization of bamboo and rocks following the sloped-bank terrain.

evidence: Center, slightly lower: a small boat is on the water surface with two people aboard, one appearing to pole the boat, constituting a thread of movement through the landscape. | Left: mountains and rocks and pine trees occupy the left side of the painting and extend to the water surface, forming a bank scene.
distinction: The painting has no clear buildings; only a boat serves as a thread of movement through the landscape, so it is assigned to C4.

evidence: Middle left: behind mountains and rocks and pine trees, the roofs of several houses emerge, partly screened by foreground scenery. | Right: behind miscellaneous trees and mountains and rocks, another house emerges, with window lattice visible, presenting the layering of seeing a house through an intervening layer. | Overall: the built structures, through the screening and revealing by woodland and mountains and rocks, form a concealment-and-revelation relationship that participates in the composition.
distinction: The painting chiefly emphasizes the layers of concealment and revelation in which houses are screened by trees and mountains and rocks, rather than the layout relationship of buildings sited according to the terrain.

evidence: Lower left: house buildings are hidden behind dense pine forest and mountains and rocks, with only roofs and parts of structures revealed, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Lower left to lower middle: tall trees and undulating mountains and rocks form a foreground barrier that wraps the built structures within, enhancing the layering and secluded depth of the space.
distinction: Although a bridge in the lower right of the painting suggests a path, the core compositional role of the main built structures (houses) lies in forming a scene through screening by woodland and mountains and rocks, rather than emphasizing the process of entry.

evidence: Lower right: beneath a pine, a lofty scholar faces the layered sloped banks on the right, suggesting a space for movement through or lingering in the landscape. | Right: in the distance there are layered sloped banks and clumps of trees, creating a sense of spatial extension.
distinction: No clear built elements are seen in the painting; there are only figures and natural scenery. On the basis of the layout of the figure and the sloped banks suggesting an enterable space, it is assigned to C4.

evidence: Center, slightly right, top of the cliff: houses are surrounded by dense pine forest, with only roofs and parts of walls revealed, presenting the concealment-and-revelation layering of seeing houses within the woods. | Center, slightly right, top of the cliff: houses sit on a terrace at the top of the cliff, sited according to the terrain, but the screening effect of the trees is significant.
distinction: Although the houses are built on the cliff terrace (C1), the painting emphatically depicts the screening and revealing of the houses by the pine forest; the relationship of concealment and revelation forming a scene is more prominent in the composition.

evidence: Lower right: a building is visible among the woodland at the foot of the mountain, with its roof and parts of its structure screened by tree branches and leaves and by mountains and rocks, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Left: a thatched hut stands at the waterside, surrounded by trees, contrasting with the open water surface. | Center, slightly right: the towering mountain mass and the foreground trees and buildings form front-to-back layers, with the buildings screened within the natural scenery.
distinction: The screening relationship between the building on the right and the woodland, mountains, and rocks is more prominent, emphasizing the spatial layering formed by concealment and revelation, rather than simply marking a particular scene.

evidence: Middle ground on the right side of the painting: a group of house buildings is partly screened by the withered tree branches of the foreground and middle ground, revealing roofs and parts of walls, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Right half of the painting: trees and built structures interweave, with branches threading in front of the houses, so that the buildings appear faintly among the woodland, presenting a clearly layered sense of space.
distinction: Although the built structures are sited against the mountain and beside the water, the most prominent compositional mode in the painting is the screening and revealing of the buildings by trees, rather than simply emphasizing the constraint of the terrain on the building sites.

evidence: Left: a small bridge is visible crossing a stream and connecting to a thatched pavilion on the bank, forming a clear thread of passage and entry. | Right: building roofs are visible amid screening trees and woodland at the foot of the mountain, suggesting an accessible dwelling in the depths. | Central waterside: two people sit facing each other at the waterside; together with the bridge and shoreline, this presents a spatial process of moving through the landscape and pausing. |
distinction: Although the painting has layers in which buildings are screened by trees, the connection of the small bridge on the left with the thatched pavilion and the waterside path emphasize more the enterable, explorable spatial thread, so C4 is more dominant.

evidence: Center, slightly upper: a corner of a roof emerges between mountains and rocks and trees, indicating that a building is hidden behind the mountain crags and woodland. | Lower right: part of a house is visible among the waterside trees and shrubs, partly screened by foreground trees, forming layers. | Lower left: village houses are arranged on level sloping ground, surrounded by trees, presenting a half-hidden, half-revealed appearance.
distinction: Although the village houses at the lower left have the feature of following the mountain's configuration, multiple built structures in the painting present spatial layering mainly through screening and revealing by woodland, mountains, and rocks, and the screening relationship is more dominant.

evidence: Center, slightly lower in the painting: the roof and walls of a house are faintly visible among the woodland, partly screened by trees, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Middle ground of the painting: the built structure is hidden within the thicket, presenting spatial layering through the screening of the woodland.
distinction: The built structure presents layering mainly through screening by woodland, rather than being clearly sited according to terrain slopes and banks.

evidence: Right bank: a group of houses is arranged along the shoreline, parallel to the water surface, presenting a layout unfolding along the bank. | Center: building components (such as a fence or gallery) are visible among mountains and rocks and pine trees, sited in reliance on the mountains and rocks.
distinction: The main label emphasizes the siting relationship in which houses unfold according to the waterside terrain; the alternative explanation focuses on the houses as markers of the waterside scene, and the former better fits their form of being arranged along the shoreline.

evidence: Center, slightly right: house buildings are partly screened by the lush trees on the right and the mountains and rocks in front, revealing only roofs and parts of walls, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Left: beneath screening weeping willows there is a small bridge connecting the water surface with the bank slope where the buildings are located. | Overall composition: the built structures are deeply hidden among woodland and mountains and rocks, presenting spatial layering through the screening and revealing of natural scenery.
distinction: Although a bridge in the painting suggests a path, the concealment-and-revelation screening relationship between the buildings and the surrounding trees, mountains, and rocks is more prominent and dominant in the composition.

evidence: Upper middle of the painting (summit area): tiered, horizontally stacked structures are visible, extending upward according to the mountain's form, presenting in form the layout features of terraces built against the mountain or building sites of houses. | Overall composition: the mountain's form is closely combined with the suspected built tiered structures, presenting a spatial relationship of proceeding up the slope and siting according to the terrain.
distinction: The tiered structures in the painting mainly present a layout following the mountain's form (C1); although located at a high point, their form emphasizes more the correspondence between building site and terrain, rather than serving merely as a point marker (C3).

evidence: Lower right: a thatched hut is screened behind trees and rocks, revealing only the roof and parts of the structure, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship.
distinction: Although the thatched hut is sited according to the terrain, its concealment-and-revelation relationship, screened by trees and rocks, is more prominent and constitutes the spatial layering of the painting.

evidence: Lower center: at the place where the figure in red stands there are horizontal lines, suspected to be a stone bank or a simple platform, directly facing the waterfall and mountain rocks, indicating the viewing position. | Left side: at the base of the pine trees/bamboo grove, linear structures suspected to be a fence or low wall are visible, distributed along the sloping ground, suggesting an artificial boundary.
distinction: The suspected built elements in the painting (platform/fence) mainly serve to mark the waterfall-viewing scenery, rather than emphasizing their structural relationship to the terrain.

evidence: Right side: the house is screened by dense trees, with only part of the roof and wall body exposed, presenting a concealment relationship of a house hidden in the woods. | Left side: the house is built at the foot of the mountain by the waterside, with mountains in the background; although relatively exposed, it is also embraced by mountain forest.
distinction: The concealment-and-revelation relationship between the house on the right and the trees is very typical and dominates the spatial layering of built elements and natural scenery, so C2 is more apt than C1, which emphasizes siting beside mountains and water.

evidence: Center-right: behind the trees a row of continuous arched structures is visible, partly screened by branches, presenting a faintly visible layering. | Center: several bare trees stand on the sloping bank, their branches extending forward and covering the built structures behind, forming an obvious concealment-and-revelation relationship.
distinction: The painting mainly shows the concealment-and-revelation relationship of built structures screened by trees, rather than clear path guidance into the interior.

evidence: Center-right lower part of the painting: a thatched pavilion is built on sloping rocks, with figures visible inside; it becomes the visual focus of the painting and marks the landscape scenery of this place. | Upper part and left side of the painting: mountains and rocks and pine trees surround the thatched pavilion, forming an opening-and-closing space, in which the thatched pavilion plays a role of gathering and marking.
distinction: As a scenic-accent structure, the thatched pavilion clearly marks a place amid the landscape that can be visited and dwelt in, rather than mainly expressing terrain-responsive siting or concealment relationships.

evidence: Middle ground, left: a small pavilion or thatched hut is visible, its roof and part of its structure partly screened by surrounding trees and the sloping bank, presenting alternating concealment and revelation in the layering. | Right side and background: trees and the sloping bank surround it, further setting off the spatial relationship of the middle-ground built structure hidden among the woods.
distinction: The built structure forms spatial layering mainly through its screening relationship with the surrounding trees, rather than serving simply as a visual focus or landmark.

evidence: Lower fan, center-right: a group of house buildings is surrounded by dense trees (such as bamboo and pine), with roofs and walls partly exposed, presenting the spatial layering of houses seen within the woods. | Upper fan, right side: the outline of a house is present among the trees, partly screened by branches and leaves, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship.
distinction: Although the houses are sited beside mountains and water, the painting emphasizes more the screening and exposure of the buildings by trees, forming the layering of houses hidden in the woods, rather than simply emphasizing terrain siting.

evidence: Lower left corner: pale ink outlines a structure suspected to be a waterside house or a boat, with simplified lines, located in an open area of the waterside. | Overall painting: distant mountains and water occupy most of the space, and the built elements are very small in scale and located at the margins, echoing the river-scene mood of the inscription.
distinction: Although the built elements are located by the water, the terrain features are not obvious; they serve more as scenic accents marking the river scene, rather than emphasizing a correspondence with site-specific layout.

evidence: Center-right of the painting: the roofs and wall bodies of several houses emerge from dense willow and pine woods, forming an obvious concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Middle of the painting: the branches and trunks of weeping willows screen part of the buildings, giving the built structures a spatial layering of being deep within the woods.
distinction: The screening and exposure relationship of the houses by trees in the painting constitutes the main spatial layering, more prominent than siting simply beside the waterside terrain.

evidence: Lower left to center: several houses are distributed along the shoreline, closely adjacent to the willows on the bank and the boats moored on the water, presenting a layout unfolding along the bank. | Right-side cliff: the houses are arranged at different heights according to the cliff, some at mid-slope and some at the foot, sited in response to the mountain terrain. | Overall composition: the distribution of the building group is clearly guided and constrained by the waterside on the left and the mountain forms on the right, presenting terrain-responsive layout.
distinction: C1 emphasizes the topographic relationship of the building layout conforming to the waterside and mountain forms, whereas C3 emphasizes buildings as isolated focal points marking specific scenery; in the painting the buildings unfold in groups along the terrain, so C1 is more apt.

evidence: Left side: mountain rocks, sloping banks, pines, and mixed trees are visible, with trees growing according to the rocky sloping ground. | Right side: the outline of distant mountains and nearby sloping rocks and bamboo leaves are visible, with unpainted space in the middle representing water surface or open ground.
distinction: No built elements are visible in the painting; it is only approximately assigned to the terrain-responsive siting category based on the natural layout of mountains, water, and banks.

evidence: Lower right corner: the roof and wall outlines of a house building are visible, partly screened by trees and mountain rocks rendered in dark ink in the foreground, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Right side: the built structure is located where woods and mountain rocks interlock, using the screening of natural scenery to form the spatial layering of 'a house seen within the woods.'
distinction: The painting mainly presents the layering relationship of the house screened by woods and mountain rocks (concealment and revelation); although a small boat in the lower left corner suggests waterside space, it does not form a clear path connection leading to the built structure (access to secluded settings).

evidence: Lower left corner: several house buildings are visible, sited beside the waterside/slope edge, presenting a layout unfolding along the bank. | Lower part of the painting: the building site corresponds to the waterside configuration in the unpainted space below, presenting a terrain-responsive siting relationship.
distinction: The houses mainly present a layout relationship beside the waterside terrain (following the bank), rather than serving as a visual focus to accentuate a specific scenic spot.

evidence: Right side: the roof and eaves of a house are exposed between mountain rocks, bare trees, and a bamboo grove; the building is partly screened by natural scenery, forming concealment-and-revelation layering. | Left-side water: on the large area of unpainted water there is a small boat, forming a spatial contrast with the screened house on the right, but they are not directly connected.
distinction: The house in the painting mainly presents a concealment-and-revelation relationship screened by trees and mountain rocks, rather than emphasizing a layout unfolding according to the terrain and bank.

evidence: Center-right to the right mid-slope of the painting: a winding stepped path is visible extending upward along the hillside, connecting the foot of the mountain with the built structure at mid-slope, forming a clear climbing route. | Lower middle of the painting: a flat bridge spans the water, connecting the two banks and providing a clue for crossing the water to enter the inner space. | Left side, right mid-slope, and lower right corner: houses are distributed at various heights according to the mountain forms, linked by movement clues such as paths and bridges, presenting an accessible touring relationship.
distinction: Although the built structures are sited according to the mountain forms, the movement clues formed by the winding mountain path and the bridge across the water are more prominent and dominate the process of entry and connection in space.

evidence: Lower right: the house is sited immediately beside the waterside and the foot of the rocky slope, its base unfolding in response to the terrain, presenting a layout beside water and against rock. | Lower middle of the painting: the shoreline extends toward the house, and the built structure forms a direct siting correspondence with the sloping platform and the water's edge.
distinction: Although trees and mountain rocks surround the house, the house mainly presents a siting relationship beside the waterside terrain, rather than being dominated by concealment-and-revelation layering.

evidence: Right-side mountain mass: houses are distributed layer upon layer from mid-slope to the summit according to the mountain forms, presenting a layout of separate placement by slope and houses set on platforms, corresponding to the steep mountain forms. | Lower waterside: houses are located on the slope by the water, adjacent to the small boat moored at the shoreline, presenting a siting mode unfolding along the bank. | Overall composition: the high and low positions of the built structures closely match the undulations of the mountain forms and the direction of the shoreline, embodying a terrain-responsive spatial relationship.
distinction: Although trees in the foreground screen the houses (concealment and revelation), the feature of buildings distributed at different heights along the mountain forms (separate placement by slope) is more prominent in the main body of the painting and better explains the overall layout.

evidence: Middle ground, left: the building group is placed close to the waterside and sloping ground, with houses at different heights unfolding in response to the terrain. | Foreground center: on the sloping bank a house is hidden among trees, with a small bridge beside it connecting the two banks.
distinction: The foreground buildings have a concealment-and-revelation relationship, but the terrain-responsive siting of the middle-ground building group beside water and slope is more prominent and dominant in the painting.

evidence: Left side and central mid-slope: houses are placed at different heights according to the mountain slopes and platforms, presenting a layout of houses set on platforms and separately placed by slope. | Right waterside: the building group unfolds along the waterside and the edge of the bamboo grove, forming a corresponding relationship with the terrain and shoreline.
distinction: Although there is screening by trees, the siting relationship in which built structures follow the mountains and unfold with the terrain is more prominent and systematic in the composition.

evidence: Top of the mid-ground cliff: several small, blurry vertical brushstrokes are visible, suspected to be extremely simplified trees or tiny built structures, but the specific forms cannot be reliably identified. | Right side and foreground: clear bamboo clumps and mountain rocks are visible, forming the front-to-back layering of natural scenery.
distinction: The painting lacks clearly identifiable built elements; the closest classification can only be made based on the layering relationships of natural scenery.

evidence: Lower center of the painting: a small bridge is visible spanning a stream and connecting the sloping ground on both banks, forming a clear clue of crossing and entry. | Lower left to center-left of the painting: faint traces of a path follow the stream and bank, linking the foreground water surface with the houses screened among the woods in the middle ground. | Center-left of the painting: the roofs and eaves of several house groups are half-hidden and half-exposed among trees and mountain rocks, indicating the destination toward which the path leads.
distinction: Although the built structures clearly have a concealment-and-revelation relationship with the woods, the bridge and stream-bank path in the lower part of the painting constitute clearer movement clues, organizing the spatial process from outside to inside; therefore C4 is more dominant than C2.

evidence: Left side: lake rocks and bamboo are painted, the lake rocks rugged in form and the bamboo leaves sparse | Center: an elderly man wearing a crown is painted facing the lake rocks on the left, hands raised as if making a bow | Right side: a boy is painted standing in attendance holding a large ceremonial fan, with an inscription beside him
distinction: The core of the painting is the figure facing the lake rocks, emphasizing the scenery of the rocks (bowing to the rock); although there are no built elements, the compositional intent approaches scenic accentuation; C2 emphasizes concealment-and-revelation layering, but here concealment is not the dominant spatial relationship.

evidence: Between the mountain rocks and trees on the right: the roof and part of the structure of a thatched hut are visible, partly screened by the pines and mountain rocks in front, forming spatial layering with alternating concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the building is sited according to the mountain rocks, the painting more prominently shows its layering of being screened and exposed by woods and mountain rocks, rather than emphasizing its layout unfolding with the natural terrain.

evidence: Center of the painting: flowers and branches and leaves are painted within the fan, with no traces of mountain rocks, water bodies, or built elements
distinction: The painting has no built elements and no landscape, so the spatial expression classification cannot be applied; per the rules it is force-assigned

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: a wooden bridge is visible spanning and connecting the left and right banks, with a figure walking on the bridge, constituting a clear movement clue. | Overall painting: the path extends via the bridge from the left foreground to the trees and rocks in the right middle ground, presenting a spatial orientation of proceeding from here to there and moving into the depth.
distinction: Although there is no clear house-type built entity in the painting, the movement clue constituted by the bridge and figure dominates the spatial organization and best matches C4's expression of entry and spatial process.

evidence: Right side: a steep cliff and pines growing from the cliff face occupy the right half of the painting. | Left-side water: a small boat floats on the water, with a person wearing a bamboo hat and holding a pole and a seated person aboard, and a water bird standing at the bow.
distinction: There are no fixed built elements in the painting; the small boat, as a scenic accent, gathers the scenery of the open water surface, so it is assigned to C3.

evidence: Left album leaf: mountain rocks, trees, and a stream are visible, and in the mountain hollow there are extremely blurry tiny traces suspected to be houses, but the details are unclear. | Middle album leaf: line-drawn flowers, with no built elements. | Right album leaf: calligraphy work, with no built elements.
distinction: Because traces of built elements are extremely weak and the natural forms of landscape predominate, if a classification is forced, scenic accentuation is less dependent on specific terrain correspondence than terrain-responsive siting.
