evidence: Left side of the middle painting: houses are built on sloping ground, surrounded by woods, with a stone enclosure wall below extending in response to the terrain. | Lower right of the middle painting: a pavilion is built on a rocky waterside outcrop, set facing the water, its base closely corresponding to the natural terrain. | Overall middle painting: the building group is distributed according to the sloping platform and waterside terrain, presenting a layout relationship of houses set on platforms and unfolding along the bank.
distinction: Although enclosure walls and paths suggest touring clues, the layout relationship of the buildings following the slope and beside the water and responding to the terrain is more dominant in the composition.

evidence: Right side of the middle painting: a hexagonal pavilion is built on a protruding stone platform or high ground, overlooking open space below, presenting the form of a house set on a platform. | Lower part and left side of the middle painting: a stone-built long embankment or revetment extends from the foreground, and the main building and pavilion are distributed beside this waterside and according to the terrain, presenting a layout unfolding along the bank. | Left side of the middle painting: the main building (hall) is sited beside trees and sloping ground, bounded by enclosure walls, its base closely integrated with the natural terrain.
distinction: Although in the painting a long embankment/path connects the buildings, the positions of the buildings are mainly determined by the high platform and waterside terrain (set on platform, following the bank), and the determining role of terrain on layout is stronger than the guiding and entering role of paths.

evidence: Right middle: the lower half of the two-story pavilion is screened by dense bamboo grove, with only the roof and upper-story eaves exposed, presenting the layering of a house hidden in the woods. | Lower middle of the painting: banqueting figures are placed in a clearing in the bamboo grove, surrounded by bamboo and trees, forming a screened space, with built elements and natural scenery forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Lower right corner: a rider advances along a path on the sloping bank, the path extending to the edge of the bamboo grove, but the built structure is mainly shown as screened by woods rather than directly connected by the path.
distinction: Although a path points toward the depths of the bamboo grove, suggesting a touring process, the path does not directly connect to the entrance of the built structure, and the built structure is mainly manifested as a concealment-and-revelation relationship screened by the bamboo grove, so C2 is more apt.

evidence: Upper right corner: a pavilion and pagoda are built on the summit, standing prominently on the mountain top and becoming the visual focus of the distant view, marking the scenery of this peak. | Left middle: a thatched hut is built on the waterside, beside trees, marking the waterside village scenery of the near bank and echoing the lotus-gathering activity on the water.
distinction: Although the thatched hut beside mountains and water embodies terrain-responsive siting, the pavilion and pagoda on the summit more strongly emphasize the role of a landmark marking the summit scenery, and overall scenic accentuation is dominant.

evidence: Among the mountain cliffs on the left: two tiers of buildings are visible, arranged unevenly following the mountain's contours, with platforms and railings. | Slightly left of center in the painting: a long bridge or covered corridor bridge spans across, connecting the two banks and leading toward the building area on the left. | Lower left: a figure is walking along a small path toward the bridge and buildings, forming a touring thread that leads into the painting.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited against the mountain, the painting places greater emphasis on the process of guiding the viewer, through the bridge and the figures' routes of travel, into the space where the buildings are located.

evidence: Center-left of the painting: the roofs and eaves of several houses emerge from among the trees and mountains and rocks, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Center of the painting: dense trees and mountains and rocks surround the houses, partly screening the main body of the buildings and suggesting spatial layering.
distinction: The houses participate in the composition mainly through being screened and revealed by trees and mountains and rocks, rather than emphasizing path guidance or a specific correspondence with the terrain.

evidence: Lower-middle of the painting: several groups of buildings are distributed unevenly; the pavilion in the foreground is fully revealed, while the storied pavilion in the middle ground is partly screened by the surrounding branches and leaves of trees, forming foreground-to-background layering. | Upper-middle of the painting: a distant waterside pavilion building is half hidden between the towering cliffs on either side and the unpainted space (mist/water surface), presenting a sense of depth in which buildings are seen across a screen. | Right side and center of the painting: dense trees interweave among the building groups, screening part of the roofs and walls, so that the built elements present a spatial relationship of alternating concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although there are paths and human activity in the painting, the relationship of screening and revelation (layers of concealment and revelation) formed by buildings interwoven with mountains and rocks and trees occupies a dominant position in the composition, and better summarizes the spatial organization of the painting than the touring path alone.

evidence: Upper part of the painting: a green-domed building is largely screened by dense groves, revealing only its top, presenting a relationship of screening in which the top is revealed amid the woods. | Center and right side of the painting: the red columns and eaves of the main building are partly screened by the branches and leaves of trees in the foreground and at the sides, forming foreground-to-background spatial layering. | Lower-right corner of the painting: a small pavilion is screened by bamboo groves and trees, revealing only part of its structure, consistent with the feature of buildings seen across a screen.
distinction: In several places in the painting (the distant roof, the nearby pavilion, and the edges of the main building) buildings are markedly screened by trees, forming layering amid the woods; although steps below connect to the platform, the relationship of concealment and revelation is more continuous and dominant in organizing spatial depth.

evidence: Center-left: a long bridge with red railings spans the water, connecting the waterside pavilion on the left with the shoreline on the right, forming a clear connecting thread. | Lower part and lower right: a procession of carts and horses advances along the path, forming a clear movement line that points toward the right side of the painting and into the depth. | Upper right and center-right: the roofs of storied buildings and the tips of pagodas emerge among the mountain woods; though screened by trees, they echo, through the bridge and paths, the movement thread in the foreground, suggesting built elements in the depth that can be reached.
distinction: Although the buildings on the right are screened by trees, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation (a C2 feature), the bridge and the route of the carts and horses in the painting constitute a more dominant spatial guidance from here to there, emphasizing the process of approaching the built elements.

evidence: Lower left to center: a stream winds, mountains and rocks are scattered, and the line of sight extends along the water and the mountain contours toward the deep valley on the left, forming spatial depth | Lower middle-right: two people sit and stand beneath a large tree beside rocks on the stream bank, in a spatial position that can be reached or lingered in
distinction: Although the painting has focal figures, the course of the stream and the depth of the valley place greater emphasis on the accessibility and extending process of space, and there is no clear built entity serving as a node of scenic accentuation

evidence: Upper-left corner: the inscription mentions "taking the trees as pillars, sweeping leaves to make a hall," defining trees and fallen leaves as the pillars and hall of the built elements, implying siting according to natural conditions. | Lower-middle of the painting: figures are located among woods and mountains and rocks; one sits on a rock and one holds a broom sweeping, their positions corresponding to the space of "making a hall" in the inscription, presenting a layout of dwelling according to trees and rocks.
distinction: The inscription explicitly emphasizes "taking the trees as pillars," focusing on the terrain-responsive relationship in which natural things (trees) serve as the structure of the built elements, rather than simply the screening and revelation of trees.

evidence: Right side and center: a long gallery-style building complex extends along the waterside and the sloping ground, with wooden piles visible supporting its base; the layout bends in response to the terrain, presenting a form that unfolds along the bank and is distributed according to the slope. | Lower-left corner: courtyard buildings are sited on level ground, surrounded by trees, with figures active within the courtyard, the building site corresponding to the site conditions.
distinction: The main building (the long gallery on the right) clearly shows a layout that responds to the waterside terrain; siting according to terrain dominates its spatial form and position more than the screening of trees.

evidence: Lower-middle and center of the painting: a long covered corridor connects different pavilions and storied buildings, figures walk along the corridor, and the corridor extends to a waterside platform. | Center of the painting: broad steps and a platform lead directly to the water, figures gather on the platform, forming clear spaces for entry and lingering. | Right side and upper-left of the painting: the buildings are interconnected by corridors and paths, presenting a spatial sequence that penetrates layer by layer and is suitable for touring and dwelling.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited by the water (C1), the painting places greater emphasis on the spatial process of guiding figures through corridors, steps, and platforms to enter and tour (C4).

evidence: Right side and center: a large storied building is sited by the water; at its base, multiple tiers of steps and a white stone-railed platform (bridge/gallery) extend to the water surface, forming a clear transitional entrance. | Central platform: several figures walk on the white stone-railed bridge/platform, their direction pointing toward the buildings on the right, presenting a clear path and movement of 'approaching the built elements.' | Lower left and water surface: a small boat with figures rowing on the water, and on the bank figures sit on a red platform, forming, together with the buildings, parallel touring threads by water and by land and a spatial connection.
distinction: Although the buildings are arranged along the waterside (consistent with a C1 feature), the painting clearly organizes, through bridges, steps, and boats, the figures' direction of movement and the path of approaching the buildings, placing greater emphasis on the spatial process of touring and entering (C4).

evidence: Center-left: the outline of a thatched hut (or thatched pavilion) appears faintly behind reeds and trees, its roof and part of its walls screened by vegetation. | Right side and center: dense trees and clumps of reeds form the foreground and middle ground, wrapping the built elements on the left within them, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Lower left: the water surface and wooden piles/fences extend to near the built elements, but the built elements are mainly screened by vegetation.
distinction: The painting places greater emphasis on the screening and setting off of the buildings by trees and reeds, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation, rather than simply emphasizing the siting of buildings according to terrain.

evidence: Left side: a thatched hut is hidden behind groves and slope rocks, revealing only its roof and part of its walls, presenting a screened state. | Right side: another building is likewise screened by trees and mountains and rocks, revealing only the outline of its roof, forming layers of concealment and revelation with the surrounding scenery.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited according to the mountain contours, the painting places greater emphasis on the relationship of screening and revelation between the woods and mountains and rocks and the buildings; the effect of concealment and revelation forming a setting is more prominent.

evidence: Lower middle-right: below the waterfall a bridge is visible spanning across, and beside the bridge steps or a path extend upward along the mountains and rocks | Right mountainside: a complex of buildings is visible among trees and mountains and rocks, distributed unevenly following the slope | Foreground to middle ground: the stream, bridge, and path connect, forming a visual guiding thread from the water surface in the foreground into the mountain buildings
distinction: Although the buildings are arranged according to the mountain contours, the bridge and path clearly construct a touring thread leading from the foreground into the mountain buildings, and the sense of spatial entry is more dominant.

evidence: Lower right: buildings are erected on a flat area projecting at the waterside, the building site closely integrated with the shoreline and waterside terrain. | Center-left: houses are distributed on slope terraces according to the mountain contours, responding to the undulations and direction of the mountains and rocks. | Upper right: built elements are located high on the cliff beside the waterfall, sited according to the strategic high point, corresponding to the steep terrain.
distinction: C1 emphasizes how the building site and layout of the built elements respond to the terrain and waterside, whereas C3 only emphasizes their role as visual markers; in the painting the relationship in which terrain participates in siting is more dominant.

evidence: Right mountainside: within a huge rock cave a complex of storied buildings is painted, sited according to the space of the cave, presenting a form of setting houses against the rock. | Lower part and left bank of the painting: several houses and pavilions unfold along the shoreline, built beside the water, echoing the form of the river. | Beside the cliffs and waterfall: buildings are distributed according to the height of the mountain contours, such as the pavilion on the cliff top and the houses beside the waterfall, embodying siting according to the ground.
distinction: Although trees and mountains and rocks screen the buildings (screening), the siting of the buildings (such as within the rock cave, on the cliff top, and on the waterside) more prominently highlights the terrain-responsive relationship of being placed according to terrain conditions.

evidence: Lower-middle of the central mountain mass: an obvious arched stone gate or bridge opening is visible, connecting to a stone-step path leading upward, forming an entrance into the mountain mass. | Upper-middle of the central mountain mass: the path winds upward along the mountain contours, connecting to building complexes on the mountainside and summit screened among the woods, presenting a spatial process of passing from here to there and turning into the depth. | Lower-left corner of the painting: houses and trees also appear at the waterside edge, facing the central isolated mountain across the water; a boat is on the water, suggesting a path thread of crossing the water to arrive.
distinction: Although the buildings are arranged tier upon tier according to the mountain contours (C1), the most prominent spatial organizing thread in the painting is the clearly visible entrance, stone steps, and path guiding the line of sight deep into the mountain, emphasizing an accessible touring process; therefore C4 is more dominant.

evidence: Lower-left corner: a building complex is visible, arranged along the mountain foot and the waterside; in front an arched bridge spans the flowing water, connecting the path and the buildings, presenting a clear relationship of entry. | Right mountainside: building roofs emerge amid screening woods, suggesting spatial layers in the mountain that are suitable for dwelling and touring. | Lower-right corner: a pagoda stands on the waterside rocks, marking the waterside scenery.
distinction: Although the painting has the terrain-responsive siting feature of buildings placed against the mountain and beside the water, the connection between the bridge and the building complex in the lower-left corner more prominently expresses the spatial process of passing from here to there and of accessible touring; therefore C4 is more dominant.

evidence: Upper-middle and left cliff face: plank roads cut according to the mountain contours and winding small paths are visible, with a group of travelers on them, forming a touring thread that penetrates deep into the gorge. | Bottom of the right gorge: flowing water and a small boat are visible, indicating the traveling relationship of a water route and crossing. | Whole painting: no clear houses, pavilions, or other built structures are identifiable; the painting consists mainly of mountains and rocks, plank roads, paths, and flowing water.
distinction: The painting has no clear buildings, but the plank roads, small paths, and water route constitute a strong spatial process of entering and penetrating deep into the gorge; therefore it is classified under C4.

evidence: Island slightly above center: mountains rise steeply, a pagoda-like or pavilion-like high structure is built on the summit, houses are visible on the mountainside, buildings alternate with trees, and the whole is surrounded by the lake surface. | Lower part and central water surface of the painting: the broad water surface has fine ripples and is scattered with many sailboats and small boats, some heading toward the island. | Right edge: a long causeway or bridge structure is visible extending into the water, with figures walking on it or carrying goods.
distinction: Although boats and the long causeway suggest travel and approach, the core of the painting lies in the marking and condensation by the island buildings of this specific scenic site, Dongting Lake (Junshan), rather than emphasizing a winding, penetrating spatial process.

evidence: Center-right waterside: two small pavilion buildings stand against mountains and rocks and trees, built directly on the flat ground at the waterside, closely integrated with the terrain. | Upper-right mountainside: a building complex unfolds upward along the slope, clearly arranged according to the height of the mountain contours. | Lower-left slope: buildings are faintly visible, built according to the mountain contours and echoing the slope terrain.
distinction: Although the buildings are screened by trees, their compositional role of being placed against the mountain and beside the water and sited according to the terrain is more significant and dominant.

evidence: Central mid-river island: a building complex is arranged tier upon tier according to the mountain contours; at its base stone-built foundations and steps extend directly into the water, and a tall pagoda is built on the summit; the overall layout closely fits the island terrain and the waterside. | Upper-right mountain foot: a group of houses unfolds tightly against the mountain foot and the shoreline, sited according to the edge of the terrain. | Lower-right foreground slope: buildings are distributed unevenly along the undulations of the slope, mutually dependent with the mountains and rocks and trees.
distinction: Although the buildings on the central island serve to mark the mid-river scenery (C3), the painting places greater emphasis on depicting how the building complex is concretely sited and unfolded according to the mountain forms, slope terraces, and waterside (C1); the compositional logic of terrain-responsive siting is more prominent.

evidence: Top of the distant mountain in the upper-left corner: a group of buildings is located at the highest point of the peak, marking the summit position and becoming the visual focus of the distant mountain. | Right middle-ground mountainside: a group of buildings is arranged on the mountainside according to the mountain contours, marking the spatial layering of the mountain there. | Lower part of the painting: a large area of water ripples occupies the lower half of the painting, contrasting with the mountains and rocks and buildings above and setting off the marking role of the buildings on the summit and mountainside.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited against the mountain, their positions on the summit and mountainside mainly serve to mark and emphasize specific landscape scenery, rather than simply displaying the layout relationship of siting according to the ground.

evidence: Central island of the painting: several groups of houses are distributed unevenly according to the height of the mountain contours, embedded between the rocks and sloping ground, the layout responding to the undulations of the terrain. | Right side and mountainside of the island: the building groups unfold along the natural outline and terraces of the mountain mass, presenting the features of setting houses against the rock and distributing them according to the slope.
distinction: Although there is screening by trees, the height correspondence and dependence between the buildings and the mountain terrain are more prominent and dominate the spatial organization.

evidence: Center-right slope of the painting: several house buildings are visible, their roofs and walls emerging from among dense trees and mountains and rocks. | Around the buildings: the built elements are surrounded and screened by woods, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation and presenting spatial layers of houses seen amid the woods. | Slightly right of center of the painting: the buildings are located on the valley slope to the right of the twin peaks, existing by being screened by natural scenery, without abruptness.
distinction: Although the buildings mark the mountainside scenery, their main compositional role is to form spatial layers through screening and revelation by woods and mountains and rocks; the relationship of concealment and revelation is more prominent.

evidence: Center and right mountainside of the painting: several house roofs and partial eaves are visible, the building bodies mostly screened by dense trees and mountains and rocks, presenting layers of houses seen amid the woods and behind the rocks. | Throughout the valleys of the painting: the built elements are scattered among the mountain ranges, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation through the screening and revealing by natural scenery, blending into the deep and secluded landscape.
distinction: Although streams or paths extend through the valleys in the painting, the built elements present spatial layers mainly through their screening relationship with the woods and mountains and rocks, rather than emphasizing the process of entering the buildings through paths.

evidence: Right mountainside down to the mountain foot: a building complex is distributed tier upon tier along the slope terrain, unfolding according to the height of the mountain contours, presenting the layout feature of distribution according to the slope. | Among the mountains and rocks in the upper-middle: pavilion buildings are placed at gaps in the rocks or on platforms, leaning against the rock faces, the building sites corresponding to the forms of the mountains and rocks. | Right edge: pagoda silhouettes and houses are sited according to the edge of the mountain contours, echoing the outline of the mountain mass.
distinction: Although trees screen the buildings considerably (possessing a C2 feature), the layout feature of the building complex being distributed tier upon tier along the mountain contours (distribution according to the slope) is more significant, embodying the correspondence between the built elements and the terrain forms; therefore C1 is more dominant.

evidence: In the mountain hollow slightly left of the lower-middle of the painting: extremely small and blurred ink marks are present, suspected to be the outline of built elements, but their form and specific spatial relationship with the landscape cannot be reliably identified.
distinction: The painting is mainly landscape; the suspected built elements are extremely inconspicuous and serve only as tiny accents amid the landscape, so it is classified under scenic accentuation, but the evidence is insufficient.

evidence: Lower middle-right: a building stands on a waterside terrace, surrounded by railings, partly screened by the trees on the right, with its roof and walls revealed. | Upper middle-right: another building is hidden behind dense woods and mountains and rocks, revealing only part of its roof, forming obvious layers of concealment and revelation. | Center of the painting: turbulent water runs through the gorge; the built elements on the right, through the screening and revealing by mountains and rocks and woods, blend into the landscape scenery.
distinction: Although the built elements are placed against the mountain and beside the water, the painting places greater emphasis on the screening and revelation of the buildings by woods and mountains and rocks; the relationship of concealment and revelation constitutes the main spatial layering.

evidence: Upper-middle: house buildings are placed on the terrace at the top of a projecting cliff, the building site closely integrated with the terrain of the mountains and rocks, presenting a layout of setting houses on the terrace. | Upper-middle: the buildings unfold along the edge of the cliff, rising and falling, embodying a spatial relationship of siting according to the ground and adapting appropriately to the contours.
distinction: Although the buildings are screened by trees, their core compositional role lies in being sited according to the cliff terrace; the feature of terrain-responsive siting is more significant than concealment and revelation forming a setting.

evidence: Center-left: the roof of a small built element emerges amid screening woods, presenting spatial layers of half hidden and half revealed. | Whole painting: multi-tiered waterfalls and mountains and rocks dominate; the built elements blend into the natural scenery through the screening of trees.
distinction: The built elements are tiny in scale and screened by woods, mainly embodying layers of concealment and revelation rather than marking the macro scenery.

evidence: Middle of the cliff on the right: a small building (pavilion) sits on a protruding rock platform, presenting the form of a building set on a platform, corresponding to the mountain terrain.
distinction: The building is tiny in scale and has the sense of a scenic accent, but its layout of being built on a platform clearly shows the placement relationship between the built structure and the terrain platform, so C1 is more fitting.

evidence: Lower middle-right: several pavilion buildings are built against the cliff, partly obscured by the branches and foliage of foreground trees, presenting a half-hidden, half-revealed state. | Middle right: the buildings interweave with steep rocks and dense woodland, forming rich spatial layers through the screening of natural scenery. | Lower right: protruding rock platforms support part of the building bases, and the buildings reveal roofs and eaves from behind the rocks and among the trees.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed against the cliff, the painting emphasizes more the screening and revealing of the buildings by trees and rocks; the concealment-and-revelation relationship constitutes the main spatial layering.

evidence: Left of center in the painting: the building is partly obscured by surrounding trees and rocks, revealing only the roof and part of the wall, forming spatial layers of alternating concealment and revelation. | Center and right of the painting: dense woodland and undulating rocks surround the building, reinforcing the partly screened relationship in which the building is hidden among natural scenery.
distinction: Although the building marks the scenery here, the painting focuses more on presenting the building's spatial layers through the screening and revealing by trees and rocks; the role of concealment and revelation is more dominant.

evidence: Lower right: a building (terrace) is built against rocky slopes and stones, its base closely adjoining the rock, placed in response to the uneven heights of the terrain. | Right: towering rocks and the sloping rock terraces below form the natural terrain; the buildings unfold according to this terrain, presenting a relationship of placement according to the ground.
distinction: Although the building marks the scenery here, its placement closely against the rock face and in response to the sloping terrace terrain is visually more prominent and dominates the spatial expression.

evidence: Lower middle-right of the painting: most of a multi-storey pavilion is obscured by foreground tree branches and foliage and by the lake rocks to the left, revealing only part of the roof, flying eaves, and upper structure. | Left and foreground of the painting: towering lake rocks and dense trees serve as the foreground, forming a clear front-to-back screening and concealment-and-revelation relationship with the pavilion behind, constituting spatial layers.
distinction: Although the pavilion is built among rocks beside the water, the most dominant spatial expression in the painting is the revealing of the pavilion through screening by foreground trees and rocks, emphasizing layers formed by concealment and revelation rather than focusing on how the building unfolds in response to the terrain.

evidence: Center of the painting: a group of pavilion buildings is built on a rocky terrace, with railings and steps, arranged in tiers according to the terrain, presenting the form of buildings set on a platform. | Lower right of the painting: a pavilion is placed at the edge of the hillside, set according to the slope and echoing the mountain terrain. | Upper part of the painting: among the peaks and rocks, buildings are faintly visible placed in dependence on the mountain forms, echoing in height with the terraced buildings below.
distinction: Although the buildings are the visual focus and serve as scenic accents, their close integration with the rock terrain through platforms, railings, and placement by slope more dominantly embodies the spatial relationship of terrain-responsive siting.

evidence: Upper middle-right hillside: two built structures are visible, placed in staggered arrangement according to the heights of the hillside terrain—a pavilion above and a building with a platform below—presenting a layout of buildings set on the slope and unfolding with the terrain. | Among the trees and rocks on the right: the building bases are closely integrated with natural features such as the hillside and trees, embodying a spatial relationship of placement according to the ground.
distinction: Although the buildings are screened by trees, their main compositional logic lies in placement according to the heights of the mountain terrain; the concealment-and-revelation relationship is a secondary feature subordinate to the terrain arrangement.

evidence: Middle ground on the right: a building (terrace pavilion) is hidden among the trees on the hillside, revealing only the roof and part of the wall, partly obscured by branches and foliage. | Foreground to middle ground on the right: dense trees and rocks form the foreground, half-screening the buildings behind, creating spatial layers of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the building is built against the mountain, the painting emphasizes more its spatial layers of being screened by trees and alternating between concealment and revelation, rather than a simple relationship of terrain placement.

evidence: Upper middle of the painting: a group of multi-storey pavilion buildings sits in an open area surrounded by mountains and wreathed in clouds and mist, becoming the visual focus of the painting. | Around the building group: peaks rise on all sides, trees surround it, and clouds and mist set the buildings apart, marking the core position of this scenic landscape.
distinction: Although the buildings are screened by trees and clouds, their main role is to mark and concentrate the surrounding landscape as the core scenery, rather than merely forming layers through concealment and revelation.

evidence: Mid-slope and summit in the upper part of the painting: building roofs and structures are visible screened behind rocks and dense woodland, presenting a clear concealment-and-revelation relationship | Upper middle of the painting: the built structures are faintly visible, their presence and the deep spatial layers they occupy indicated through the screening of trees
distinction: The buildings mainly present a concealment-and-revelation relationship screened by trees and rocks (C2), rather than emphasizing the correspondence between building base and terrain layout (C1).

evidence: Lower right: in a hollow embraced by rocks, a group of buildings (pavilions) is visible, with roofs and walls partly visible. | Lower right to center: flowering trees with twisting branches (pink blossoms) grow from the rocks, their branches extending and covering above and around the buildings, forming a clear relationship of screening and revealing (buildings seen in the trees/behind trees).
distinction: Although the buildings are placed in response to the rock terrain (terrain-responsive), the pronounced obscuring and surrounding of the buildings by tree branches (screening) constitutes a more prominent spatial layering and concealment-and-revelation relationship.

evidence: Center of the painting: roofs of several buildings emerge amid clouds and mist, presenting spatial layers of buildings seen across a screen, indicating the screened building group. | Lower part of the painting: tree branches and foliage obscure the enclosing wall and gate tower (memorial archway), forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship among the trees and leaving the buildings half-hidden. | Upper part of the painting: a terrace building stands on the rocks, which surround and obscure its base, presenting layers of a building seen behind rocks/on the mountain.
distinction: Although the upper terrace on the summit is landmark-like (close to C3), the painting as a whole organizes spatial layers through the successive screening and revealing of the building group by clouds and trees (especially the center, where only roofs are visible); the feature of concealment and revelation is more dominant.

evidence: Lower middle-right of the painting: pavilion buildings directly adjoin the cliff slopes and terraces, their bases closely integrated with the rock terrain, presenting a placement mode of buildings set on a platform. | Middle right of the painting: trees grow around the buildings, and some eaves and walls interweave with rocks and trees, embodying a layout in which the buildings respond to the natural terrain.
distinction: Although the buildings have a screening relationship with the trees, the terrain-responsive placement of the buildings against the cliff slopes and terraces is more evident and dominant.

evidence: Central main peak: tiny buildings are visible on the waist and summit of the towering peak, attached to the rocks, set on platforms and responding to the mountain forms. | Lower left and lower right: houses are distributed along the foot slopes and water's edge, placed by slope and unfolding along the bank, corresponding to the terrain.
distinction: Although the buildings serve to mark the peak, their layout emphasizes more the placement relationship following the mountain forms and banks, rather than serving simply as visual landmarks.

evidence: Hillside and rock face on the right: a group of multi-storey pavilion buildings is distributed in staggered arrangement according to the heights of the mountain, with building bases and platforms placed tier upon tier upward in response to the mountain's slope. | Lower middle-right: the way the building group unfolds is closely integrated with the distribution of rocks and trees, presenting a form of placement according to the ground.
distinction: Although the buildings are conspicuous in scale, their most essential compositional logic is placement at different heights in response to the mountain slope and rock forms, rather than serving simply as isolated landmarks marking a particular scenic spot.

evidence: Lower right: houses are built at the foot of the mountain by the water's edge, with a stone-faced embankment visible in front; the layout responds to the waterside terrain | Middle left: roofs emerge among the trees on the sloping bank, placed according to the terrain beside the water
distinction: Although there is screening by trees, the placement relationship in which the buildings follow the water in building the embankment and respond to the terrain is clearer

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: roofs, eaves, and walls of several building groups emerge through gaps in the trees (such as willows and miscellaneous trees) of the foreground and middle ground. | Lower right of the painting: waterside corridors and pavilions are partly obscured by branches and rocks in front, forming front-to-back spatial layers. | Center of the painting: parts of pavilions are visible amid screening trees; the concealment-and-revelation relationship is clear and contributes to the painting's pictorial depth.
distinction: Although the buildings in the painting are set against mountains and beside water, the screening and revealing of the buildings by trees (the concealment-and-revelation relationship) is more prominent and dominant in organizing spatial layers.

evidence: Upper middle, toward the right of the painting: the roof and eaves of a building are visible, partly obscured by surrounding pines and rocks, presenting a half-hidden, half-revealed state. | Right bank of the painting: pines and rocks surround the building, forming foreground and middle-ground layers; the building appears and disappears among the trees.
distinction: Although the building marks the scenery, the painting emphasizes more the spatial layers formed by its screening and revealing through trees and rocks; thus concealment and revelation (C2) is more dominant than scenic accentuation (C3).

evidence: Lower middle: an arched bridge spans the stream, connecting the two banks and forming a clear passage cue. | Middle right and behind the bridge: pavilions are screened among trees and rocks; another building is faintly visible behind the bridge, presenting spatial layers leading from here to there. | Bottom: the gaps between the stream and rocks guide the eye deeper into the painting, working with the bridge to form a traversable path.
distinction: Although there is screening of buildings by trees, the passage and penetration cues formed by the arched bridge and stream are more prominent and dominate the spatial organization.

evidence: Lower right: built structures (pavilions/houses) sit among clustered rocks, obscured by foreground trees, revealing only parts of roofs and structures. | Foreground/center-right: the trunks and branches of withered and miscellaneous trees interpose in front of the built structures, forming clear layers of screening and revealing, presenting a relationship of buildings seen across a screen.
distinction: Although the buildings sit on rocks and have some terrain-responsive placement features, the painting mainly presents the spatial layers of the built structures through the obscuring and revealing by tree trunks and branches; the screening relationship is visually more prominent.

evidence: Slightly right of the painting's center: a group of large pavilion buildings unfolds along the mountain terrain and the waterside; the building bases fit closely to the terrain, presenting a layout that leans on the water and relies on the mountains, arranged following the rises and falls of the terrain. | In the lower foreground of the painting: pavilions and terraces are placed against mountains and rocks and trees; the lower parts of the buildings meet slopes, platforms, and rocks, reflecting a placement relationship suited to the situation. | In the upper-middle part of the painting: beside the mountain ravine where a waterfall flows down, buildings extend in accordance with the gorge and the direction of the water flow, reinforcing the correspondence between built elements and the natural configuration.
distinction: Although trees in the painting partially screen the buildings, the main layout of the building group emphasizes more its terrain-responsive relationship of leaning on mountains and facing water and being arranged following the rises and falls of the terrain, rather than being dominated by layers of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Upper middle of the cliff on the right: a group of built structures (houses and pavilions) is built on a protruding terrace of the cliff; the base is level, and the layout responds to the terrain at the cliff edge, presenting the feature of buildings set on a platform. | Around the built structures: pines are painted growing in dependence on the mountain forms; the built structures are placed according to the high and low forms of the cliff, corresponding to the natural site conditions.
distinction: Although trees surround the buildings, their main spatial feature is being built on a cliff terrace; the correspondence between building base and terrain (buildings set on a platform) is more dominant than the screening and revealing by trees.

evidence: Lower right and lower middle of the painting: a red bridge and plank walkway are visible crossing the stream, connecting the two banks and leading to the building group at the foot of the mountain. | Lower middle-right of the painting: a group of pavilions is built against the mountain and beside the water, connected to the surrounding environment by bridges and paths, presenting a spatial relationship that is enterable and traversable.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed against the mountain and beside the water (C1), the red bridge and paths in the painting clearly guide the eye and the route of movement into the building area, emphasizing more the spatial process of access to secluded settings.

evidence: Summit of the peak on the right: a pavilion is built on the top of a protruding rock, becoming the visual focus and landmark of this peak. | Waterside in the lower middle of the painting: a building with railings is built beside the water, together with the surrounding rocks and trees forming a scenic spot.
distinction: The pavilion on the summit mainly serves to mark and concentrate the scenery of the peak, rather than simply being placed in response to the terrain.

evidence: Right bank: a pavilion building with railings and steps is visible; figures gather in front of the building and on the path along the bank, and the path connects with the building, presenting a spatial relationship that is enterable and traversable. | Left bank and middle ground: houses are visible amid screening trees; figures walk along the water's edge and paths, forming a movement cue from near to far. | Overall in the painting: the river, shoreline, paths, and buildings connect with one another, guiding the eye and the figures' activity deeper into the scene.
distinction: Although the buildings mark the scenery, the painting emphasizes more the enterable, traversable spatial process formed by the connection of paths, waterside, and buildings.

evidence: Middle section of the right bank: a group of buildings (pavilions/towers) is partly obscured by the sloping bank and dense grasses, revealing only roofs and parts of walls, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Lower left and lower middle: waterside buildings are screened by the branches and foliage of luxuriant foreground trees (willows/reed-like plants), presenting spatial layers of buildings seen among the trees. | Middle ground of the painting: a bridge spans the water connecting the two banks, surrounded by trees and grasses, further reinforcing the screening and layering among the scenery.
distinction: In the painting, the built structures mainly form rich layers of concealment and revelation through obscuring by foreground trees and middle-ground grasses; the role of concealment and revelation is more prominent than path guidance.

evidence: Lower right to middle left: a traveler wearing a conical hat walks along a small path deeper into the painting; the path guides the eye toward the thatched hut on the left and the distant mountains. | Lower left: the thatched hut lies in the direction in which the path extends, half-screened by trees, serving as one of the path's destinations. | Middle-left slope: another traveler is walking up the slope, further reinforcing the spatial process of advancing deeper into the scene.
distinction: Although the thatched hut in the lower left is screened by trees, the painting emphasizes more the process of travelers moving deeper into the painting along the path; the guiding role of the path is more dominant in the overall spatial organization than the simple concealment-and-revelation relationship.

evidence: Waterside in the lower middle: a pavilion on a stone base (water pavilion) is built there, with figures seated facing each other, serving as a near-ground stopping point and starting node. | Center of the painting: a winding zigzag bridge or stepped path is visible passing through the trees, connecting the foreground with the middle and rear ground areas, forming a clear spatial guiding cue. | Middle ground of the right bank: several people walk along the bank toward the screened house cluster behind, suggesting a process of movement from here to there and approaching the built structures deeper in the scene.
distinction: Although there are terrain-responsive features in the pavilion placed by the water and rocks and the houses placed according to the ground, the winding paths/bridges and the movement lines of walking figures more dominantly organize the spatial structure of moving from here to there.

evidence: Slightly left of the middle ground: a stone arched bridge spans the stream, connecting the left and right banks, forming a clear cue of crossing and entry. | Right bank of the middle ground: several people walk along the waterside path, heading toward the bridge and the opposite bank, suggesting a spatial process of reaching and continuing to travel. | Left bank and distant view: there is a pavilion house beside the trees on the left, and houses are faintly visible on the distant mountainside, together with the bridge and path forming an enterable landscape environment.
distinction: Although there is screening of buildings by trees, the bridge and the figures' routes of movement are more central in organizing the sense of spatial entry, so C4 is more fitting than C2.

evidence: Middle ground on the right: houses and fencing are visible, partly obscured by trees and rocks, located behind the waterside. | Right waterside: a fence or path extends along the water's edge, guiding from the foreground toward the built structures in the middle ground, forming an enterable spatial cue. | Foreground to middle ground: figures in the foreground are active by the water, and the line of sight and path extend along the waterside toward the houses in the middle ground, presenting a movement relationship from here to there.
distinction: Although there is screening of the houses by trees and rocks, the path/fence extending along the waterside more clearly organizes the spatial process of entering from the foreground into the middle-ground built structures.

evidence: Left side of the painting: houses, enclosing walls and a fence gate are visible; the building base adjoins the waterside and is laid out along the sloping terrain. | Lower-middle part of the painting: the shoreline is clear, and the layout of the built elements forms an explicit correspondence with the water's edge and the sloping platform, presenting an arrangement that unfolds along the bank.
distinction: Although natural features such as willow trees stand adjacent to the buildings, the painting mainly shows the buildings' placement in relation to the waterside and the sloping platform terrain, rather than a layered composition dominated by concealment and revelation.

evidence: Middle of the painting: a bridge spans the stream, connecting the paths on both banks, with figures walking on the bridge | Lower part to middle of the painting: the path combines with the waterside and the field ridges, guiding the figures from the foreground fields toward the depth of the painting | Overall composition: the stream and path form an S-shaped course, which together with the bridge constitutes a movement-through-the-landscape thread leading from here to there
distinction: Although the paddy fields in the lower part of the painting are distributed according to the terrain, no clear houses or buildings are visible, whereas the access thread for movement formed by the bridge and path is more prominent and organizes the spatial process.

evidence: Lower right: an arched bridge is painted over the stream, connecting the foreground rocks with the opposite bank, forming a clear crossing thread. | Middle right: houses and buildings are visible behind the woodland, with roofs and walls partly exposed, located in the depth toward which the bridge points. | Overall composition: the bridge and the course of the stream guide the eye toward the depth of the painting, pointing to where the built elements are located and suggesting a movement-through-the-landscape path from here to there.
distinction: Although the painting shows trees partly screening the houses (C2), the bridge at the lower right clearly constitutes a movement-through-the-landscape thread leading to the built elements, placing greater emphasis on the spatial process from here to there (C4).

evidence: Lower left corner: a group of houses with enclosing walls is visible, placed on the gentle ground where the mountain foot meets the stream/waterside, with the layout conforming to the terrain. | Left side: trees are dense around the built elements, and the building base relies on the mountain mass and slope behind it, presenting a placement that leans on the slope and adjoins the water.
distinction: Although a path with figures walking appears on the central ridge, this path mainly leads to the summit platform rather than directly connecting to the built elements at the lower left; the main expression of the built elements therefore remains placement according to terrain (C1), rather than guidance by a movement-through-the-landscape thread (C4).

evidence: Middle ground, slightly right: a group of courtyard-style built elements with enclosing walls and roofs, surrounded by dense deciduous trees. | Middle ground: the roofs, wall bodies and doors and windows of the buildings are revealed through the gaps between tree trunks, forming a spatial layering of alternating concealment and revelation. | Left of the middle ground: two people carrying loads on shoulder poles walk along a dirt road toward the courtyard gate; the path and trees together set off the state of the built elements hidden among the woods.
distinction: Although a path leads to the courtyard gate, the built elements are mainly presented through their screening and revealing by trees, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship is more prominent than the movement-through-the-landscape thread.

evidence: Left side: a building is partly blocked by bare trees in the foreground, revealing its wall body, window lattice and base, presenting a half-hidden, half-revealed state. | Right middle ground: a roof emerges from behind dense bamboo grove, screened by bamboo leaves.
distinction: The most prominent compositional feature of the painting is the spatial layering formed by the screening and revealing of buildings by trees and bamboo groves, rather than a direct correspondence between buildings and the terrain and topography.

evidence: Middle right and center of the painting: the roofs and eaves of several buildings are partly blocked by dense branches and leaves of bare trees, with only portions exposed, forming a clearly layered concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Center of the painting: through gaps between the trees, an open hall and figures seated facing each other inside are visible; natural features serve as foreground and side scenery, participating in the framing and screening of the built space. | Left side and upper part of the painting: clouds and mist weave between the buildings and the mountain woods, further blurring the boundaries of the built elements and enhancing the spatial depth of concealment and revelation forming a setting.
distinction: Although the buildings are distributed in staggered fashion according to the mountain terrain, the most dominant compositional technique in the painting is the use of screening and revealing by trees and clouds and mist to present the spatial layering of the buildings, rather than simply emphasizing their terrain-responsive placement.

evidence: Overall painting: the painting mainly depicts a winding waterside, stretches of bare trees and flocks of flying birds; no clear built elements such as houses, bridges or paths are visible. | Upper-middle and lower-right parts: the shoreline extends naturally, and trees grow along the bank, presenting a purely natural landscape.
distinction: No built elements are visible in the painting; it is assigned to C1 only tentatively on the basis of the overall natural waterside and terrain distribution, but evidence of man-made built elements is lacking.

evidence: Right middle: a group of buildings is surrounded by dense trees; roofs and wall bodies appear indistinctly among the woodland, presenting an obvious relationship of screening and revealing. | Right lower-middle: the front-to-back layering of the houses is expressed through the blocking by trees, forming a spatial depth in which houses are seen within the woods.
distinction: Although the buildings lean on the mountain and adjoin the water, the painting mainly expresses the spatial layering of the buildings through screening and revealing by trees, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship is more dominant than terrain-responsive placement.

evidence: Central mountain mass: a clear stone-step path extends downward from the mountainside, connecting to the pavilion platform in the middle ground, forming a clear movement-through-the-landscape thread. | Middle ground, slightly left: a pavilion sits on a rocky platform, serving as the endpoint of the stone-step path and presenting an accessible spatial relationship. | Lower right corner: a group of houses is screened among trees and the waterside, echoing the surrounding water flow and terrain.
distinction: Although the pavilion serves to point out the mountain scenery, the prominent stone-step path in the painting constitutes a strong access and touring thread, making the spatial organization of access to secluded settings more dominant.

evidence: Right panel: the painting mainly depicts mountains and rocks, a stream and trees; no clearly identifiable building is visible. | Upper left: an inscription reads 'Guanshui Yan' ('Water-Viewing Rock'), naming the scene, but no corresponding building is visible.
distinction: The painting contains no clearly identifiable built elements and names the scene 'Guanshui Yan' solely through its inscription. It is therefore assigned to C3, although there is no evidence of a physical building.

evidence: Lower right: a group of houses is built adjoining the water, with the base conforming to the sloping waterside ground and laid out parallel to the water surface. | Center: a large expanse of water meets the rocky sloping bank, and no clear bridge or path is visible that would lead the eye directly to the building group in the lower right corner.
distinction: The buildings in the painting mainly present a placement relationship adjoining the waterside terrain, and there is a lack of clearly identifiable movement threads such as bridges or paths that would connect them with the surrounding landscape into an access process.

evidence: Upper-middle recess in the mountain rock: roofs and railings are exposed, half screened by the surrounding rocks and clouds and mist | Among the central cliffs: pavilion buildings are visible, embedded among the rocks | Lower right valley: several houses are screened behind woodland and rocks, presenting layers of concealment and revelation
distinction: Although some buildings are arranged according to the mountain terrain, the dominant spatial expression in the painting is the built elements' use of screening and revealing by rocks, woodland and clouds and mist to form a multi-layered spatial mood.

evidence: Right side of the painting: the painting presents only natural features such as mountains and rocks, woodland and clouds and mist; no identifiable traces of built elements such as buildings, roads or bridges are visible.
distinction: There are no clear built elements in the painting; it is assigned to the closest category on the basis of the overall visible organization of natural landscape.

evidence: Center of the right pictorial area: a stream winds among the rocks, forming a natural thread of spatial extension. | Overall right pictorial area: the painting is mainly composed of rocks, trees and waterside, and no clear built forms such as houses or bridges are visible.
distinction: There are no clear built elements in the painting; it is assigned to C4 on the basis of the sense of spatial extension guided by the stream.

evidence: Right pictorial section: the main subject of the painting is layered, unusual rock formations and pine trees; no traces of any man-made built elements such as houses, paths or bridges are visible. | Upper right: an inscription identifies 'Lion Rock', and the painting concentrates on expressing the formal characteristics of this mountain rock.
distinction: No built elements are visible in the painting; it is assigned tentatively to C3 on the basis of the overall mountain-rock formation as the visual core, but direct evidence of buildings participating in the composition is lacking.

evidence: Lower-middle waterside of the painting: a small pavilion sits on the flat ground where the mountain foot meets the water surface, in a transitional position between the enclosure of the rocks and the openness of the water. | Right side and center of the painting: cliffs rise steeply, and the pavilion is located at the water's edge below them, pointing out the waterside scenery beneath the mountain rock and becoming a visual focal point.
distinction: The pavilion mainly serves as a scenic accent marking a spatial node at the mountain foot and water surface, emphasizing its role of pointing out the scenery rather than focusing on expressing the complex terrain-responsive layout of a building group.

evidence: Lower right corner: there are houses and buildings, clearly structured, with roofs and walls
distinction: The main category C1 indicates that buildings are clearly visible, and its difference from C2 (buildings visible but not clear) lies in the clarity and recognizability of the buildings.

evidence: Lower left corner: a pavilion and an adjacent small bridge (or path) structure are visible, connecting the built elements with the external space and forming an access thread. | Middle right: the built elements are located deep in the mountainside, screened by trees and rocks, as the destination of the spatial extension. | Overall: the foreground bridge and pavilion and the middle- and far-ground built elements form, through mountain forms, water flow and unpainted space, a touring thread leading from here to there and turning into the depths.
distinction: Although the painting shows a concealment-and-revelation relationship in which the built elements are screened by trees and rocks, the connection between the bridge/path at the lower left and the built elements expresses more clearly an enterable, tourable spatial process.

evidence: Right middle: a house is visible, with trees and the waterside immediately to its left. | Middle of the painting, slightly right: in front of the house a small bridge spans the water surface, connecting the opposite bank. | From the middle of the painting extending to the upper left: the bridge, shoreline and small path together form a touring route leading into the mountain woods in the depth of the painting.
distinction: Although the house is placed leaning on the mountain and adjoining the water, the painting places greater emphasis on guiding the eye into the depth through the bridge and path, and the connectivity of the path and the touring process are more dominant than simple terrain-responsive placement.

evidence: Middle right: between the rocks and trees, the eaves and wall body of a building are faintly visible, partly screened by natural features, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Middle right, mountainside: a winding small path or steps are visible, suggesting a path leading into the depth.
distinction: Although a path is suggested in the painting, the spatial layering created by the building screened by rocks and trees is more intuitive and dominant.

evidence: Lower left bank: a house is located beside a clump of trees, with part of its building body and roof blocked by branches and leaves, presenting a half-hidden, half-revealed state. | Middle-ground mountain foot: a group of built elements is hidden among rocks and dense woods, with only the roof outline exposed, forming a layering in which houses are seen through a screen. | Overall painting: mountains overlap, woodland is dense, and built elements are interspersed among them, mainly using the screening of natural features to indicate their existence and spatial position.
distinction: Although the built elements are located at the water's edge and the mountain foot, the painting places greater emphasis on their concealment-and-revelation relationship as screened by trees and rocks, rather than simply displaying their terrain-responsive layout.

evidence: Lower right: between the stream and the rocks, a wooden bridge (or plank walkway) supported by multiple vertical posts is visible spanning the water surface, connecting the two banks. | Center: the bridge is located at the entrance to the gorge, guiding the eye along the water flow and mountain forms into the depth of the painting, forming an enterable spatial thread.
distinction: The bridge mainly serves as a path thread guiding touring and entry into the gorge, rather than a static building simply placed according to the terrain.

evidence: Left middle: a pavilion is half hidden behind sloping rocks and trees, with only the roof and part of the columns exposed, forming an obvious relationship of screening and revealing. | Right upper-middle: in the depths of a mountain hollow, a building outline is faintly visible, deeply blocked by the surrounding rocks and dense woods, presenting a sense of secluded depth.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed according to the mountain terrain, the painting focuses more on showing the concealment-and-revelation layering of the buildings through the blocking of woodland and rocks, rather than simply emphasizing placement according to the terrain.

evidence: Lower left: a small bridge spans the stream, connecting the two banks and constituting a path thread that allows entry and touring. | Whole painting: no obvious buildings such as houses or pavilions are visible; only the bridge participates in the spatial organization as a built element.
distinction: The only visible built element in the painting is the bridge, which clearly provides a spatial process of crossing the stream and going deeper into the painting, with no obvious other built threads.

evidence: Upper right rock face: a small building is placed close against the steep cliff, presenting a spatial relationship of being built against the rock and suspended on the face. | Lower right foreground: a building roof is visible on the sloping bank, placed in reliance on the waterside and the wooded terrain.
distinction: Although the foreground buildings are screened by trees, the painting places greater emphasis on the buildings' terrain-responsive placement close against the steep rock face and adjoining the waterside, so C1 is more dominant.

evidence: Upper-middle part of the painting: between the rocks and woodland, part of a building's roof and wall body are exposed; the building is half screened by the surrounding natural features. | Center of the painting: the arrangement of trees and mountain rocks forms front and back layers, and the building is situated in a deeper layer, participating in the composition through concealment-and-revelation relationships.
distinction: Although the buildings are located in the mountains, the painting places greater emphasis on their layering as screened and revealed by woodland and rocks, rather than on a specific placement according to terrain slopes and platforms.

evidence: Middle-ground waterside: several houses are placed adjoining the waterside and sloping ground, with the building bases echoing the undulations of the terrain. | Lower left corner: a building is erected adjoining the water, unfolding in conformity with the form of the waterside. | Upper right mountainside: houses are placed according to the mountain terrain, partly screened by trees and rocks.
distinction: Although some buildings have screening relationships, overall the terrain-responsive placement of the buildings in reliance on the waterside and sloping ground is more prominent and widespread.

evidence: Middle of the right cliff: there are faint vertical and horizontal short lines on the rock face, suspected to be traces of a plank walkway or small structure arranged against the cliff face.
distinction: The traces are too faint to be confirmed as a marker pointing out scenery, and tend more toward a weak built thread following the form of the cliff.

evidence: Middle of the right rock face: there are layered horizontal linear structures among the rock face, suspected to be stone steps or platforms arranged according to the form of the mountain mass, but the details are faint and difficult to confirm as clear built elements.
distinction: The suspected structures mainly present a form close against the rock face and layered with the mountain terrain, lacking a clearly identifiable continuous travel path or access relationship.

evidence: Top of the isolated peak at the left of the painting: a tiny pavilion building sits atop the summit of the peak; its volume is extremely small, forming a contrast with the surrounding sea of clouds and mountains and rocks. | The painting as a whole: the building serves as the visual focus on the isolated peak, identifying the mountain scenery at that spot and making this peak a recognizable specific scenic feature within the painting.
distinction: Although the building is located on the summit, the painting mainly emphasizes its role as a marker identifying the scenery, rather than showing in detail the layout relationships it develops in response to the terrain.

evidence: Right side and center of the painting: layered, towering mountain rocks and trees are depicted; the gaps between the mountains and rocks and the unpainted space form winding paths or stream forms. | Overall composition: the unpainted path/stream winds upward from the foot of the mountain in the foreground and extends into the depth, constituting a visual sense of guidance and entry. | Whole painting: no clearly identifiable houses, pavilions, bridges, or other built structures are seen; there are only mountains and rocks, trees, and paths.
distinction: The inscription suggests the specific scenic feature 'Yiqiyan' (Chess-Playing Rock); if there is a tiny scenic accent it may belong to scenic accentuation, but visually there is a lack of clear built markers, while the sense of entry formed by the path (access to secluded settings) is more immediate.

evidence: Lower middle: within the valley, a group of pavilion buildings with red columns and green tiles is visible, arranged in staggered fashion according to the mountain terrain. | From the lower right to the center: a clearly defined stone-step path extends upward from the right waterside/edge of the clouds and mist, connecting directly to the building group in the valley, forming a clear route of entry. | Slightly left of center: in front of the buildings there are pines and mountain rocks screening them, forming a certain spatial layering, but the guiding role of the path is more prominent.
distinction: Although the building group is arranged according to the mountain terrain (C1), the clearly visible winding stone-step path in the painting guides the eye deep into the valley, strongly expressing an enterable, traversable spatial process, so C4 is more dominant.

evidence: At the mountainside slightly above center in the painting: red-roofed buildings are screened by dense trees and mountain rocks, with only the roofs and parts of the walls exposed, presenting the spatial layering of houses hidden in the woods. | At the lower-left waterside: small buildings are concealed behind clusters of trees, sited beside the water, forming a partly screened relationship with the surrounding trees.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed according to the mountain terrain, the painting places more emphasis on the screening and revealing of the buildings by trees and mountain rocks; the relationship of concealment and revelation constitutes the main spatial layering.

evidence: Lower middle: a bridge spans the stream, connecting the two banks, forming a clear line of passage. | Lower right corner: building roofs and walls are visible on the mountain slope; the bridge and stream guide the eye toward this area. | Right middle: a waterfall flows down among the mountain rocks and trees, and together with the stream and bridge below forms a sense of spatial extension.
distinction: Although the buildings are partly screened by trees, the bridge, as a clear line of movement through the landscape, places more emphasis on the spatial process of going from here to there and approaching the built structures.

evidence: Lower middle: the courtyard compound adjoins a gentle slope; the long enclosing wall follows the lie of the terrain in a winding extension, presenting layout characteristics of disposition according to the slope. | Upper middle: the building group is located among the trees in the mountain hollow, placed in staggered fashion according to the height of the mountain forms and merged with the mountain terrain. | Right side as a whole: the built structures are distributed from the foot of the mountain to the mountainside, unfolding in response to the site conditions of the right-side mountain terrain and the left-side waterside (mountain foot).
distinction: Although the upper-middle buildings clearly show the feature of tree screening (C2), the layout in which the enclosing wall of the compound below unfolds along the slope, and the overall placement in response to the mountain terrain (C1), are clearer, embodying the dominant logic of siting according to the terrain.

evidence: Upper-right mountainside: part of a red-roofed pavilion is visible, partly screened by the pines and mountain rocks in the foreground, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Lower-right valley: a group of houses is partly screened behind slope rocks and withered trees, with roofs and parts of the walls exposed. | Lower-left waterside: a corner of a waterside house is visible, screened by the foreground bank and trees.
distinction: Although the painting contains an arched bridge and shoreline hinting at paths, the relationship of concealment and revelation between the built structures and the mountain rocks and trees is more prominent in the composition and dominates the organization of spatial layering.

evidence: Mid-ground mountainside: houses are visible half-hidden behind mountain rocks and trees, with only parts of the roofs and eaves exposed, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Lower-right corner waterside: a group of buildings sits by the water, partly screened by the foreground trees and mountain rocks, presenting a clearly layered spatial relationship. | Lower-left corner: a path or stream is visible winding along, guiding the eye, but the built structures primarily create the scenery through being screened by and revealed among the mountain rocks and trees.
distinction: Although the painting contains path clues, the built structures present spatial layering mainly through being screened and revealed by mountain rocks and trees; the feature of concealment and revelation forming the setting is more dominant.

evidence: Lower middle: an arched bridge spans the water surface, connecting the foreground earth slope with the opposite bank, forming a clear line of passage and entry. | Lower-left corner: a path or small bridge structure is visible beside the houses, hinting at a spatial connection leading to the built structures. | Center: long narrow houses extend along the waterside slope, echoing the surrounding water system and potential paths, constituting nodes of movement.
distinction: Although houses placed along the waterside embody terrain-responsive siting, the lines of movement through the landscape constituted by the arched bridge and paths more strongly dominate the sense of spatial entry and connectivity in the painting.

evidence: Right of center: the building group in the mountain hollow is partly screened by mountain rocks and pine woods, with only the roofs and parts of the walls exposed, forming a clear layering of concealment and revelation. | Lower-left corner: pavilions and buildings at the waterside are arranged in staggered fashion according to the mountain terrain, partly screened by the foreground rocks and trees. | From lower right to center: a winding path is visible on the mountain slope, threading among the trees and rocks and connecting spaces at different heights.
distinction: Although the painting contains path guidance, the pronounced relationship of concealment and revelation created by the central building group through the trees and mountain rocks is the core of the scenic composition, conforming more to the definition of concealment and revelation forming the setting.

evidence: Whole painting: on the right side of the painting only line-drawn textures of water ripples or clouds and mist are seen; the left side is calligraphy; no built elements such as buildings, bridges, or roads are seen.
distinction: Built elements are entirely absent from the painting, so no clear spatial relationships among C1 to C4 can be constituted; it is assigned to the closest category only by rule.

evidence: Lower right: a thatched hut is built on flat ground at the foot of the mountain, backed by a cliff (with a waterfall visible flowing down), with a rocky bank in front, presenting a placement beside mountains and water. | Left side: dense bamboo groves grow on the slope, immediately adjacent to the left side of the building; the building is placed beside the woodland. | Upper right: the cliff waterfall and the buildings below form a relationship of height correspondence, and the buildings unfold in response to the terrain.
distinction: Although the building is surrounded by bamboo groves and mountain rocks, it mainly presents a relationship of siting according to the terrain, adjoining the mountain foot, bamboo grove, and bank; the main body of the building is clearly visible, rather than emphasizing the layering of screening and concealment.

evidence: Whole painting: the painting is a pure calligraphy work; only Chinese characters and seals are seen, with no visual imagery of landscape or built structures.
distinction: The painting has no actual landscape or built content, so no substantive distinction of spatial relationships can be made.

evidence: Right middle: a thatched hut sits beside mountains and water, built on flat ground on the mountain slope, backed by mountain rocks and facing an open water surface. | Right side: the rocky bank rises and falls, forming a natural terrace, and the thatched hut is placed in response to the terrain. | Beside the thatched hut on the right: trees stand beside the hut, together with the mountain rocks forming the natural environment of the built structure.
distinction: Although the thatched hut is accompanied by trees, it is on the whole fairly exposed; its placement according to the mountain terrain is more prominent than any relationship of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower right: slope rocks are seen meeting the waterside; the forms of the rocks are natural, and no artificial building base or structure is seen. | Upper right: vegetation is distributed on the far bank, birds fly over the water surface, with no trace of built structures.
distinction: No clear built structures are seen in the painting; based on the natural forms of the waterside slope rocks throughout, it is assigned with difficulty to C1, with no other category in competition.

evidence: Whole painting: the painting consists of vertically arranged calligraphic text and seals, with no image elements such as landscape, trees, or built structures.
distinction: The painting has no image elements, so categories of spatial expression cannot be distinguished.

evidence: Lower middle and right mountain foot: multiple groups of house compounds are placed in staggered fashion according to the mountain terrain and slopes, with their building sites closely fitted to the topography, presenting a layout of siting according to the terrain. | Left mountainside and among the trees: some buildings are partly screened behind mountain rocks and trees, with roofs or walls exposed, forming a spatial layering of concealment and revelation. | From the lower-left corner to the mid-ground: a winding path is visible connecting the slope bank and the buildings in the mountains, hinting at a line of movement through the landscape from here to there.
