distinction: Although the painting contains path guidance, the feature of built structures following the mountains and being placed according to the rises and falls of the terrain is more notable and dominates the overall spatial organization.

evidence: Lower-right water surface: a small canopied boat floats on the open water surface, with people in the boat, serving as a scenic accent that condenses the mood of spring-water excursion. | Left side and mid-ground: pines, peach blossoms, and mountain rocks surround; the unpainted water surface is broad, and the boat is dotted among it, identifying the scenery.
distinction: Although the boat hints at excursion, the painting does not show a clear entry path or a spatial process of turning into the depths; it mainly serves the role of scenic accentuation and marking the scene.

evidence: Lower-left corner: multiple houses are arranged along the shoreline, with water pavilions and bridges built, unfolding in response to the waterside terrain. | Lower middle: a pavilion is built on a rocky terrace, surrounded by trees, with the building site corresponding to the mountain-rock terrain. | Bottom center: a house is built on a protruding rocky platform, presenting a manner of placement of setting a house on a platform.
distinction: Although the central pavilion is screened by trees, several buildings in the painting (the waterside houses, the house on the rocks) more prominently display the relationship of terrain-responsive siting beside mountains and water and placed according to the terrain.

evidence: Slightly below center: a two-story pavilion sits at the open spot where the clouds and mist part on the mountainside, becoming the visual focus of the painting and identifying the scenery of this mountainside. | Foreground and mid-ground: pines are distributed in front of and on both sides of the pavilion, with towering peaks behind; the building stands on the open face embraced by the mountain body.
distinction: Although the building is screened by trees, its main role is to serve as a marker at the open spot on the mountainside and to concentrate the scenery, rather than forming the scenery solely through a relationship of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: multiple arched bridges (such as a white stone bridge) are visible spanning the water surface and connecting the building groups, with pedestrians crossing on the bridges, constituting clear land-transport nodes and entry paths. | Central building group of the painting: dense palaces and houses are connected by a clear network of streets and squares, with clear pedestrian circulation, presenting a complex spatial organization that is enterable and traversable. | Lower left and lower waters of the painting: boats are visible traveling and mooring; wharves or pavilion facilities are set along the banks, connecting with the buildings, forming clues of waterway entry and connection.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed beside mountains and water (a C1 feature), the transport network constituted by bridges, roads, and waterways in the painting is more prominent, strongly emphasizing the enterability of the space and the connective relationships among the building blocks (C4).

evidence: Left middle: city walls and dense house groups are arranged in winding fashion along the mountain foot and the shoreline, presenting a layout form unfolding along the bank and beside mountains and water. | Upper-middle mountains: pavilions and buildings are placed layer upon layer according to the height of the mountain terrain on the mountainside and among the rocks, presenting relationships of disposition according to the slope and setting buildings on platforms. | The painting as a whole: the bases and distribution of many built structures (city, villages, pavilions) closely correspond to the rises and falls of the mountain forms and the direction of the water flow, placed according to the terrain.
distinction: Although city gates, bridges, and paths (C4 elements) are visible in the painting, the layout of built structures dependent on mountain forms and waterside (C1) runs through the whole painting and determines the overall spatial positions of the buildings, while the lines of movement through the landscape are more scattered and do not constitute a single dominant entry sequence.

evidence: Lower right: a stone bridge is visible spanning the stream, connecting the paths on the two banks. | Lower middle: an enclosing wall and gate tower are visible, constituting a clear entrance to the building complex. | Whole painting: paths and streams wind along, linking the built structures from the mountain foot to the mountainside, forming a tendency toward penetrating into the depths.
distinction: Although the buildings are distributed according to the mountain terrain, the entry sequence constituted by the bridge, gate, and paths is more prominent and dominates the spatial process of going from here to there.

evidence: Lower-left corner: there is human activity inside a pavilion building; below the building, a zigzag staircase with railings extends downward, forming clear path guidance. | Lower-right corner: an arched bridge spans the stream, connecting the two banks, serving as a crossing clue guiding spatial entry. | Left mountainside: the building group is distributed layer upon layer according to the mountain terrain, echoing the mountain paths and presenting a spatial layering of turning into the depths.
distinction: The lines of movement through the landscape in the foreground of the painting, such as the bridge and staircase, connect closely with the built structures and strongly express the spatial process of going from here to there and approaching the built structures, which is more dominant than mere placement according to the mountain.

evidence: Mid-ground: a long causeway runs across the water surface; bridges and pavilions are built on the causeway, connecting the land on the left and right and forming a clear line of land-based movement through the landscape. | Water surface: multiple boats are distributed, hinting at waterway transport and crossings, forming accessible relationships with the banks and the causeway. | Lower-right corner: a stone bridge is visible crossing the waterway, connecting the trees and buildings on the two banks and further strengthening spatial connectivity.
distinction: Although buildings are scattered as scenic accents in the painting, the lines of movement through the landscape constituted by the bridges, long causeway, and boats run through the composition, placing more emphasis on spatial connectivity and the process of excursion from here to there.

evidence: Lower-right corner: a water pavilion is built directly on the waterside slope rocks, supported by columns at the bottom, with its building site closely fitted to the waterside terrain. | Left-bank mid-ground: several houses are distributed on a slope screened by woods, placed in staggered fashion in response to the terrain.
distinction: Although the water pavilion identifies the waterside scenery, its relationship of terrain-responsive siting, with columns erected on the waterside slope rocks, is more direct and prominent.

evidence: Central mountain hollow of the painting: the building group is arranged in staggered fashion on the flat ground of the mountain hollow according to the mountain terrain, unfolding in response to the topography. | Right mountainside of the painting: pavilions are built clinging to the slope of the mountain body, conforming to the forms of the mountain rocks. | Lower-right waterside of the painting: a pavilion is set facing the water, its building site combined with the bank terrain.
distinction: Although trees screen the buildings, the painting more prominently highlights the layout relationship of the buildings placed beside mountains and water and according to the terrain.

evidence: Lower middle of the right mountain body: the building group is distributed in staggered fashion according to the height of the mountain terrain, placed in response to the direction of the ridges and gullies, presenting the feature of siting according to the terrain. | Left waterside: a small number of buildings are built close against the waterside rocks, with building sites closely combined with the terrain. | Right valley: houses extend along the deep direction of the valley, their layout constrained and guided by the terrain.
distinction: Although some buildings are screened by woods, what the painting more prominently highlights is the layout relationship of the building group as a whole in response to the mountain forms and terrain, rather than mere layering of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Among the trees on the mid-ground mountainside: a red-roofed building group is visible, partly screened among the pine woods. | Near-ground right side and the waterside below: pavilion buildings and a waterfall outlet are visible, with layered mountain rocks. | Main body and upper part of the painting: the main peak towers high, rendered in blue-green coloring, wreathed in clouds and mist, displaying deep spatial depth.
distinction: The painting takes natural mountains and rivers as its main subject, with buildings as auxiliary, belonging to the typical landscape painting, distinct from categories dominated by figures or flowers and birds.

evidence: Lower middle: a building group is placed at the mountain foot, with a stream and a small bridge connecting in front, forming a clear entry path. | Lower right: buildings are set according to the slope, merging with the surrounding mountain rocks and trees and hinting at an reachable space. | Left mountainside: buildings are partly screened among the trees and rocks, increasing the layering and depth of the space.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed beside mountains and water (C1), the guiding role of the bridge and stream in the painting is more prominent, emphasizing an enterable and traversable spatial process (C4).

evidence: Center of the painting, slightly lower: a group of houses is placed against the foot of the mountain, surrounded by trees; the roofs and walls are clearly visible, presenting a layered effect screened among the woods. | Right side of the painting, lower middle: houses are hidden behind dense pine woods and mountains and rocks, with only part of the roofs and structures exposed, forming spatial depth through occlusion. | Upper right of the painting: buildings are arranged according to the mountain terrain and partly obscured by trees and woodland; the exposed eaves indicate the presence of built elements and their spatial level.
distinction: Although the built elements are sited according to the mountain terrain, what the painting emphasizes more is the spatial layering and the relationship of concealment and revelation formed by the buildings being screened and revealed by trees and mountains and rocks.

evidence: Bottom of the painting, slightly left: an arched bridge spans the water, connecting the two banks; there are pedestrians on the bridge and boats beneath it, forming a clear entry path and spatial transition. | Bottom and lower right of the painting: pavilions, terraces and houses are built by the water, closely connected with the bridge and the waterside, forming an entrance space that can be traveled and lived in, guiding the gaze to extend into the depth of the painting. | Middle of the painting: a river winds into the distance, with villages, trees and mountains and rocks distributed along both banks; together with the bridge and waterway, it presents a spatial process of passing from here to there and turning into the depths.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited against the mountains and by the water, the painting, through the movement-through-the-landscape clues formed by the bridge, waterway and waterside buildings, more strongly organizes the spatial process of passing from here to there and going deep into the landscape.

evidence: Lower left and lower middle waterside: multiple houses and courtyards can be seen distributed along the waterside and woods, with a bridge connecting the two banks, forming clear clues for passage and entry. | Lower middle of the painting: built elements interweave with the stream, sloping banks and trees, presenting a spatial process of gradually going deeper along the waterside and paths to reach the built elements.
distinction: Although the built elements are sited against the mountains and by the water, the connections among the bridge, waterside and paths in the painting emphasize more the spatial process of entry and travel, rather than siting solely according to the terrain.

evidence: Lower left to the middle: figures can be seen walking along a path; the path connects the built elements in the lower left corner with the mountains and rocks and the bridge in the middle, forming a clear travel clue. | Among the mountains and rocks in the middle: bridges or plank roads connect the mountains and rocks, implying the accessibility of the space and its extension into the depths. | Right waterside: boats are moored by the water, echoing the path on the bank and the built elements in the distance, forming entry clues for land and water transport.
distinction: Although the built elements are sited against the mountains and by the water (C1), the travel clues formed by the paths, bridges and figure activity in the painting are more prominent and dominate the spatial organization.

evidence: Middle, slightly left: a pavilion is built facing the water, its base closely adjoining the waterside and unfolding with the water's direction. | Lower left corner: thatched huts are placed against the bank's sloping ground and among trees and rocks. | Lower right corner: boats are moored on the water near the bank, echoing the shoreline.
distinction: Although the built elements are screened by trees, their placement facing the water and against the slope, and their correspondence with the terrain and waterside, are clearer and dominant.

evidence: Lower right: a wooden bridge spans a stream valley; two figures (apparently wearing bamboo hats and carrying staffs) are crossing the bridge toward a thatched hut behind a large tree, forming clear clues for movement through the landscape and entry, connecting the foreground with the built elements. | Left side, lower middle: a small boat is on the water near the waterside pavilion, implying a waterway crossing and an accessible relationship with the built elements. | Middle right and upper valley: many houses are screened behind trees and rocks, with only roofs or parts exposed; together with the mountain paths, this implies that the space extends into the depths and can be further traveled.
distinction: The built elements in the painting indeed have extensive concealment and revelation through trees and mountains and rocks (C2), but the clear bridge and figure activity in the lower right corner and the boats on the water more strongly emphasize the spatial process of approaching the built elements through travel clues and passing from here to there, so C4 is more dominant.

evidence: Right middle: the roofs and walls of several houses are partly blocked by the trees and mountains and rocks in front, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Overall painting: the built elements are placed behind the mountains and rocks and trees and woodland on the right, using natural scenery for screening to form spatial layering.
distinction: The painting emphasizes more the blocking and revealing of the houses by trees and mountains and rocks, rather than mainly showing how the buildings are sited according to the terrain.

evidence: Middle-ground mountainside: several roofs and eaves can be seen emerging through gaps in the mountains and rocks and trees, presenting a layered effect of being half-hidden and half-revealed by the mountain forest. | Lower right foreground waterside: a building has part of its building itself blocked by several tall trees, with only the roof and part of the structure exposed, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship through the trees and woodland.
distinction: The painting organizes spatial layering mainly through the screening and revealing of buildings by trees and woodland and mountains and rocks; no clear travel clues such as bridges, paths or crossings guiding entry are seen, so C2 fits the visible relationships better than C4.

evidence: Lower right: a small canopied boat is on the open water, marking the scenery of the water area as a human-made object. | Center to left: ink-rendered mountains and rocks and trees are distributed vertically, forming a spatial opening and closing with the unpainted water surface on the right; the small boat falls within the open area.
distinction: The small boat does not show a layout relationship of being placed according to complex terrain or the waterside; rather, it serves as a scenic accent in the open water area, giving the landscape a point of focus.

evidence: Lower left corner: a bridge spans the water, with two people walking on it, forming a clear travel clue. | Lower middle: the path connected by the bridge leads to a group of buildings surrounded by trees, presenting a spatial process of passing from here to there and approaching the built elements. | Lower middle: pavilions and terraces are sited against the mountains and by the water and connected to the outside through paths, making the painting present an accessible and travelable relationship.
distinction: The entry clues formed by the bridge and paths run through the lower part of the painting, clearly guiding toward the buildings, and play a greater role in spatial organization than the concealment-and-revelation relationship alone.

evidence: Center of the painting, slightly right: beneath pine trees and among mountain rocks, a pavilion or waterside structure with railings and a roof is visible, with figures seated facing each other inside; the main body of the building is partly blocked by the surrounding trees and mountains and rocks, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Left mountainside of the painting: tiny figures or scenic accents are faintly visible amid the screening of mountains and rocks, echoing the central built elements from far and near, enhancing the sense of spatial layering.
distinction: Although the building is placed among mountains and rocks, the painting emphasizes more its layered concealment and revelation, screened by pines and rocks and appearing indistinctly, so C2 is more dominant than C1.

evidence: Lower right: the roof, walls and window lattice of a building are visible, partly blocked by the trunks of pine trees and bamboo clumps in front. | Right side, lower middle: the building is hidden behind pine woods and mountains and rocks; the exposed parts indicate its existence and its spatial level.
distinction: Although the building is placed against the terrain, the painting presents the building's spatial layering mainly through screening and revealing by trees and woodland and mountains and rocks, and the feature of concealment and revelation forming a setting is more dominant.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: a bridge spanning the water and paths connecting the two banks can be seen, linking the foreground water surface with the middle-ground mountain forest. | Right side of the painting: along the waterfall and mountain terrain, a winding upward walkway or mountain path guides the gaze into the depths. | Lower left and right side of the painting: pavilions and terraces and other built elements are distributed, and together with the bridge, paths and water flow they form a progressive space that can be traveled and lived in.
distinction: Although the built elements are sited against the mountains and by the water, the painting emphasizes more the travel process of guiding the gaze deep into the mountain forest through clues such as bridges, paths and water flow, so C4 is more dominant than C1.

evidence: Right middle of the painting: the roof of a thatched pavilion appears indistinctly among dense tree trunks and foliage, and a person is faintly visible inside the pavilion. | Right side and middle of the painting: trees in the foreground and middle ground interlock, forming an obvious blocking and revealing relationship with the thatched pavilion and constructing a spatial layering in which the pavilion is seen deep in the woods.
distinction: Although there is a bridge in the lower left corner, the main visual focus and the expression of built elements lie in the concealment-and-revelation relationship of the thatched pavilion screened by trees and woodland, rather than emphasizing the path process of entry.

evidence: Right water surface and bank: a small boat is moored beside the sloping bank and trees; the boat body is clear, with figures and a simple shelter structure on board. | Overall composition: the open water surface and distant mountains form a large area of unpainted space; the boat, as a human-made object, is placed within it, condensing the scenery of traveling on the water and indicating the mood of boating.
distinction: There are no typical fixed buildings in the painting; only the boat serves as a scenic element, acting as scenic accentuation, with no obvious clues of terrain-responsive siting, concealment and revelation, or access to secluded settings.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting, at the foot of the mountain: several houses can be seen placed against the base of the mountain terrain, presenting a relationship of being sited according to the mountain. | Right waterside of the painting: a small building can be seen placed facing the water, unfolding along the shoreline.
distinction: The buildings are mainly placed against the foot of the mountain and the waterside terrain, embodying siting according to the ground, rather than simply serving as visual focal accents in the landscape.

evidence: Lower left corner: beside the waterside at the base of a pine tree there is an extremely small ink-mark structure, suspected to be a thatched pavilion or shed, surrounded and blocked by pine branches and slope rocks. | Middle of the painting: pine trees and miscellaneous trees grow on the slope rocks, forming the main layers of natural scenery.
distinction: If the tiny structure in the lower left corner is regarded as a scenic accent, it would be C3, but since it is amid the screening of trees and rocks, it better matches the concealment-and-revelation relationship feature of C2.

evidence: Left side of the painted panel: the roof and structure of a house faintly emerge from behind a grove of trees, the built structure screened by the trees, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Center of the painted panel, slightly right: a small boat is moored at the waterside with people in it, forming a spatial connection with the distant embankment and path, but the built structure is mainly manifested as screened among the woodland.
distinction: Although there are a waterside and path in the painting, the most prominent feature of the built structure (the house) is that it is screened by woodland, presenting a layering in which a house is seen in the woods, rather than emphasizing an entry path.

evidence: Upper middle and middle mountainside of the painting: many pavilions and terraces appear indistinctly among the pine woods and mountains and rocks; their roofs and eaves appear indistinctly under the screening of trees, forming rich layers of concealment and revelation. | Right middle ground of the painting: a group of buildings is situated in a mountain hollow, partly blocked by foreground mountains and rocks and trees, presenting a spatial relationship in which houses are seen through a screen. | Lower left and lower middle of the painting: the woods and woodland are dense, and buildings are screened within them, together with mountains and rocks and clouds and mist forming profound layers.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited according to the mountain terrain, the painting emphasizes more the spatial layering and concealment-and-revelation relationships formed by their screening and revealing through trees and woodland and mountains and rocks.

evidence: Lower middle: the building group is distributed in an irregular, staggered manner according to the mountain valley, rising and falling, and sited in conformity with the terrain. | Right hillside: a large number of figures go up along the slope, and the path follows the mountain terrain toward the pavilion on the mountainside. | Left side: buildings beside the waterfall are placed against the cliff and water flow.
distinction: Although there is an obvious figure travel path on the right hillside, what the overall building group more prominently displays is the siting relationship of following the mountain and adapting to the terrain's rises and falls, and C1 is more comprehensively dominant.

evidence: Upper middle mountainside: pavilions and terraces are placed in a staggered manner according to the mountain slopes and terraces, and their building bases follow the rises and falls of the mountain body. | Right mountain foot: houses are placed against the hillside terrain, corresponding to the direction of the mountains and rocks. | Lower left corner waterside: thatched huts are built facing the water, their bases closely adjoining the waterside slope.
distinction: Although the built elements serve to accentuate the mountainside scenery, their siting according to site conditions such as slope terraces and the waterside is more prominent and dominant.

evidence: From the lower part to the upper middle of the painting: a winding road passes through the foreground valley, goes past a pavilion, extends upward along the mountain terrain, and connects to the city gate and building group in the upper right. | Lower part of the painting: pedestrians, carts and horses travel on the road, reinforcing the road's function of passage and entry. | Upper right: the road finally leads to a city wall with an arched gate opening and the buildings inside, forming a clear destination.
distinction: Although the upper right building group is built against the mountain, what runs through the entire painting and dominates the spatial organization is the path clue that guides the gaze and travel, rather than mere siting according to the terrain.

evidence: Whole painting: The painting depicts mountains and rocks on the left, sloping rocks at the bottom, and various autumn flowers interspersed among them; no built elements such as houses, pavilions, or bridges are seen. | Lower left: There is an inscription, "Autumn Blooms Convey Auspiciousness," which identifies the painting's theme as an autumn flower scene.
distinction: There are no built elements in the painting; the flowers and mountains and rocks together form the autumn scene, and can only barely be regarded as elements that identify the scenery.

evidence: Lower left: a pavilion is built at the waterside, its base closely adjoining the rocks at the waterside and unfolding with the water's direction | Lower middle: houses are placed beside huge rocks and pine trees, rising and falling in accordance with the sloping terrace terrain | Right mountainside and upper right mountain summit: the building group is distributed layer by layer according to the hillside, and the summit buildings are placed on the peak, with their layout corresponding to the direction of the mountain terrain
distinction: Although the built elements serve to accentuate local scenery, many buildings in the painting are clearly sited according to specific terrain such as the waterside, slope terraces and mountain summits, and the relationship of siting according to the ground is more pervasive and dominant.

evidence: Lower left: a waterside pavilion is built facing the water, with a platform or column-base structure visible below, presenting a building-base relationship of unfolding along the bank and setting the house on a platform. | Upper right: the building group is distributed according to the mountainside slope terraces, with roofs at different levels, and the layout follows the rises and falls of the mountain terrain. | Middle left: houses are located on the gentle ground of a mountain hollow, placed relying on the terrain and adjacent to the surrounding mountains and rocks and trees.
distinction: Although the foreground pine trees obviously block the lower right building (consistent with the C2 concealment-and-revelation relationship), the bases and layouts of many built elements in the painting (the lower left waterside pavilion and the upper right hillside buildings) more notably embody the corresponding relationship of being sited against the mountains and by the water and according to the ground, so C1 is more dominant.

evidence: Lower left: a waterside pavilion is built on a stone bank beside the water, spreading out along the waterside and sloping rocks, its site closely integrated with the natural terrain. | Lower middle-right: a pavilion is screened among woods and trees and mountains and rocks, placed in conformity with the mountain forms and sloping platforms. | Upper middle-right: pavilions cling to the edge of a steep cliff, built in a commanding position and corresponding to the mountain shapes.
distinction: Although there is screening by woods and trees in the painting, the terrain-responsive placement of built structures beside the waterside, on sloping platforms and against cliffs is clearer and more dominant.

evidence: Lower left and left: a bridge, carriage and horses, and pedestrians are visible, forming a clear starting point for movement and a clue for entering the painting. | Center to upper right of the painting: winding mountain paths and a stream run through the composition, guiding the eye and the traveler deep into the painting and upward. | Upper middle and lower right: a group of pavilions on the mountainside and village houses in the valley bottom are located at the end of or along the path, as reachable spatial nodes.
distinction: Although the buildings have a screening relationship in which they are concealed by trees, mountains and rocks, the clues of movement running through the whole painting, such as the bridge, path, carriage and horses, are more prominent and dominate the enterable spatial organization.

evidence: Lower right: a bridge is visible spanning across, connecting the sloping banks and forming a clear clue for a path entering the painting. | Lower center: the bridge leads toward the waterside and the pavilions on the sloping platform, presenting a spatial process of going from here to there and approaching the built structures. | Upper middle: pavilions are visible on the mountainside and summit, implying a clue of going deeper upward along the mountain forms.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed according to the mountain forms, the painting strongly guides the eye through the bridge and bank paths to enter and move through the depths of the landscape, and the clue of access to secluded settings is more prominent.

evidence: Right: a thatched pavilion is partly screened by the huge mountains and rocks behind it and the branches of plum trees in front, revealing only the roof, posts and figures inside. | Right and center: plum branches interweave in front of the pavilion and together with the mountains and rocks behind form multiple layers of screening and revealing of the built structure, creating a clear spatial layering.
distinction: Although the thatched pavilion points up the scenery of human activity, the painting emphasizes more the screening and revealing relationship of the building by mountains, rocks and trees, and the characteristic of concealment and revelation forming a setting is more dominant.

evidence: Overall painting: the painting consists of water and distant mountains on the left and foreground mountains and rocks, pines and mixed trees on the right; no clear built elements such as houses, pavilions, bridges or paths are visible. | Right: mountains and rocks are layered, with a waterfall flowing down, lush branches and leaves, dotted with red flowers and fruits, purely a combination of natural scenery.
distinction: The painting lacks built elements and cannot form terrain-responsive, screening or secluded-access relationships; it presents only the natural landscape itself, so it is only tentatively assigned to scenic accentuation as the closest spatial presentation.

evidence: Right mountain foot: two levels of built structures (pavilions) are visible, their walls and lower structures partly screened by the branches of foreground trees and by mountains and rocks, presenting a half-hidden, half-visible state. | Center to right of the painting: many tall trees (pines, etc.) stand in front of and beside the built structures, their branches and leaves interweaving with the built structures, forming a spatial layering in which houses are seen within the woods. | Above the built structures on the right: the roofs and upper railings are revealed, indicating that they are amid the screening of mountains, rocks and woods and trees, rather than fully exposed in open ground.
distinction: Although the built structures are placed at the foot of the mountain (C1), the obvious screening and revealing of the built structures by trees (concealment and revelation) in the painting constitutes a more dominant spatial layering relationship.

evidence: Center-left of the painting: two figures are visible sitting facing each other among pines and mountains and rocks; no built elements such as houses or pavilions are visible | Left: huge mountains and rocks occupy the left side of the painting, forming the main composition together with the pines | Background: distant mountains rendered in pale ink, with no traces of buildings
distinction: No clear built elements are visible in the painting, only figures as scenic accents, so it is assigned to scenic accentuation as the closest category

evidence: Middle ground right: a long row of buildings spreads out along a sloping platform in conformity with the mountain forms, with supporting structures visible below, their sites closely corresponding to the mountain terrain | Lower right: a pavilion-type building is set on rocks, its roof harmonizing with the forms of the surrounding mountains and rocks
distinction: The built structures mainly show a terrain-responsive relationship of placement relying on the terrain, rather than simply serving as markers pointing up the scenery

evidence: Left: a person sits beside mountains and rocks, surrounded by trees and distant mountains; no built entities such as houses or bridges are visible. | Right and center: pines, mixed trees and mountains and rocks are depicted, forming a natural landscape scene.
distinction: The painting has no clear built elements, only figures as scenic accents, so it is assigned to C3 on the basis of the overall relationship between landscape and figures.

evidence: Lower center of the painting: a pavilion building is partly screened by tall foreground trees and flowering branches extending from the right, revealing only the roof and part of the columns, presenting a layering of a building hidden within the woods. | Left and central foreground: multiple trees stand in front of the building, trunks and branches interweaving, creating a clear relationship of screening and revealing with respect to the building.
distinction: Although the building identifies the woodland scenery, the painting mainly constructs spatial layering through the foreground trees' screening and revealing of the building, and the feature of concealment and revelation forming a setting is more pronounced.

evidence: Among the trees and rocks on the right: a figure is visible standing beneath a tree, with several vertical lines to its left, possibly a simple fence or enclosure, but the details are blurry and difficult to confirm as definite built elements. | Overall painting: the painting is dominated by mountains and rocks, pines, red-leafed trees, and a stream; the figure and the possible fence are located in the lower right among screened trees and rocks, identifying the scenery here.
distinction: The possible built element (fence) and the figure are surrounded by trees and mountains and rocks, serving to identify the scenery, but a relationship of concealment and revelation also exists; because the evidence for built elements is extremely weak, scenic accentuation predominates.

evidence: Center-left of the painting: a thatched hut is partly screened by the trees and mountains and rocks in front, revealing only the roof, eaves, and part of the columns, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Center of the painting: tall trees and foreground rocks are located in front of the thatched hut, screening the building among trees and mountains and rocks, presenting clear spatial layering.
distinction: Although the building is located among mountains and rocks and trees, the most prominent compositional method in the painting is the foreground trees and rocks screening and revealing the building, rather than emphasizing its placement according to the terrain.

evidence: Water surface on the right: on the open water at the right of the painting there is a small boat with a person aboard, identifying the space of the water surface and becoming the visual focus of the waterscape. | Left and center: the left and center consist of mountains and rocks, trees, and reeds, forming a contrast of solid and void and of density and sparseness with the boat on the water at the right, highlighting the openness of the water surface.

evidence: Right middle ground: several houses are partly screened by the pines, red-leafed trees, and mountains and rocks in front, revealing only the roofs and walls, forming a layering of seeing houses through a separating screen. | Right foreground to middle ground: trees and mountains and rocks serve as foreground, half-screening and half-revealing the built elements behind, highlighting the relationship of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the buildings are located among mountains and rocks and trees, the most notable spatial organization in the painting is the foreground trees' screening and revealing of the buildings, rather than emphasizing terrain-responsive layout of the buildings.

evidence: Left middle: a pavilion is built tight against the steep cliff face, its base closely integrated with the cliff surface, presenting a placement that follows the mountain. | Right middle: at the water's edge a railed corridor bridge or waterside structure is built, extending along the shoreline and connecting to the right bank rocks, with figures upon it. | Overall painting: the built elements (pavilion and waterside structure) are respectively placed against the cliff and along the bank, their layout heights corresponding to the mountain forms and waterside.
distinction: Although the pavilion serves a scenic function, its placement tight against the cliff and the waterside structure extending along the bank, placed according to the site, is more fundamental and prominent in the composition.

evidence: Center-right waterside: a small plank bridge is visible connecting two land masses, forming a passage clue across the water. | Overall painting: the bridge connects the sandbar with the opposite bank, implying a spatial process of entry and travel.
distinction: The only built element in the painting is the bridge, whose role is to connect land and provide a passage route, rather than screening, scenic accentuation, or terrain-responsive building placement.

evidence: Right foreground: among dense willow groves, red-roofed white-walled houses are revealed, the building masses screened by trunks and branches, presenting a layering of seeing houses within the woods. | Left middle ground opposite bank: a row of houses is arranged along the waterside, screened at intervals by trees, with a long fence in front, producing an effect of seeing houses through a separating screen.
distinction: Although the buildings are distributed along the waterside, the painting more emphasizes the trees' screening and revealing of the buildings, forming layers of concealment and revelation, rather than simply emphasizing placement according to terrain.

evidence: Center of the painting: the roof, eaves, and porch of a thatched hut emerge from the gaps between the pines and bamboo clusters on the left and the trees on the right, presenting a half-hidden, half-revealed state. | Right of the painting: the roof and body of another building are partly screened by the foreground strange rocks and bamboo grove, revealing only parts. | Middle ground of the painting: the built elements are surrounded by the surrounding mountains and rocks and trees, forming spatial layering through the screening and revealing by natural scenery.

evidence: Lower left-center: a house is largely screened by dense wind-and-rain vegetation (reeds or bamboo clusters), revealing only the roof and part of the walls, forming a clear relationship of concealment and revelation. | Overall painting: diagonal wind-and-rain lines and bending vegetation wrap the built elements within them, reinforcing the spatial layering created by borrowing natural scenery to screen and form a setting.
distinction: The painting mainly expresses the vegetation and wind and rain screening and revealing the house, rather than emphasizing the house's placement according to the terrain and waterside.

evidence: Lower left to center right: a wooden bridge spans the water, with a figure carrying a load on the bridge, connecting the left waterside with the right built-up area, forming a clear entry route. | Center right: there is figure activity in front of the house courtyard; the bridge and shoreline guide the gaze and the route of movement directly to the front of the built entrance, presenting a spatial relationship that is enterable and reachable. | Center right and surroundings: the built elements are surrounded by many weeping willows, and the bridge, path, and buildings together form a clue for traveling deeper into the scene.

evidence: Lower center: a wooden bridge spans the water, with two people walking on it, connecting paths on both banks. | Lower to right: a clear waterside path extends from beside the bridge, winding along the foot of the mountain toward the red pavilion deep in the painting. | Left and upper right: the path links the waterside village on the left with the building complex in the mountain hollow on the right, forming an enterable and traversable spatial sequence.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed with mountains behind and water in front, the most prominent spatial organization in the painting is the movement-through-the-landscape clue formed by the bridge and winding path, guiding the gaze deep into the painting.

evidence: Middle ground slightly left: a red-walled building complex is located at the foot of the mountain, partly screened by the pine grove in front, revealing the roof and upper walls, presenting a layering of seeing houses within the woods. | Left and around the building: towering blue mountains and rocks are immediately to the left of the building, together with the surrounding trees forming screening and enclosure of the built elements, reinforcing the relationship of concealment and revelation. | In front of the building: two people stand on the flat ground outside the enclosing wall, surrounded by trees, the building being surrounded by natural scenery.
distinction: Although a gate and figures in the painting suggest approach to the built elements, the buildings are mainly surrounded and screened by mountains and rocks and trees, and the spatial layering formed by concealment and revelation is more dominant, lacking an obvious path-guided movement line for entry.

evidence: Left and central mountainside: a winding path with red railings starts from the left foot of the mountain and spirals upward along the mountain body, clearly guiding the gaze toward the buildings on the mountain. | Lower center: the path passes through an arched bridge spanning a water gap, connecting the lower and upper parts of the mountain body, forming an enterable and traversable spatial clue. | Summit and mountainside: red-walled gray-tiled pavilions and city walls are arranged in layers according to the terrain, as the final destination guided by the path and bridge.

evidence: Lower right to center right: a winding stone-step path extends upward from the lower right corner of the painting, passing through gaps in the woods and mountains and rocks, directly reaching the built elements at the mountainside on the right. | Right mountainside: a built element with a red roof (pavilion or house) is visible, serving as the endpoint or node of the path, implying a reachable spatial relationship. | Lower center: two people walk along the foreground path, further reinforcing the movement-through-the-landscape clue and sense of entry in the painting.
distinction: Although the built elements are built according to the mountain, the dominant spatial expression in the painting is the winding mountain path guiding the gaze and the process of movement, emphasizing the sense of entry from here to there, rather than simple terrain placement.

evidence: Lower center of the painting: a stream or path winds forward, leading directly to the built-up area in the valley, forming a visual and spatial guiding line. | Center-left of the painting: a person is walking along the path toward the gate tower of the built elements, clarifying the action process of approaching the built elements from here to there. | Center of the painting: the built elements include a gate tower, enclosing wall, and houses, located deep in a valley embraced by two mountains, the gate tower serving as the entrance connected to the external path.
distinction: Although the built elements are placed with mountains behind and water in front, the painting more strongly expresses the spatial process of entering the built elements through the figure walking toward the gate tower and the clear guidance of the path/water flow; therefore C4 is more apt than C1.

evidence: Lower right: the roofs and walls of several houses are visible, partly screened by the branches and leaves of foreground and middle-ground trees and by mountains and rocks, presenting spatial layering of alternating concealment and revelation. | Center right: tall pines and other trees surround the built elements, forming natural screening so that the built elements appear faintly among the woods.
distinction: Although a bridge on the left of the painting implies a path, the main compositional role of the built elements in the painting is to form layering through the screening of trees and mountains and rocks, rather than emphasizing an enterable travel clue.

evidence: Left mountain rocks: a white path winds upward along the mountain, with two figures walking on the path, forming a clear movement-through-the-landscape clue. | Overall painting: the path extends from the lower left corner to the mountainside, guiding the gaze to move deep into the painting, presenting a spatial process from here to there.
distinction: No definite built elements are visible in the painting; the enterable and traversable spatial relationship is mainly expressed through the mountain path and figures walking, so it is assigned to C4.

evidence: Upper left: city walls and gate towers are built winding along the mountain ridge terrain, the gate base situated at the foot of the mountain by the waterside, presenting a layout of building the city according to the mountain and extending along the bank. | Lower right and center: large tracts of fields are distributed in layers following the slope terrain, with ridge paths winding and extending according to the terrain. | Waterside below the city gate: houses and boats are arranged along the shoreline, the placement of built elements closely corresponding to the water boundary.
distinction: Although the gate towers are identifying, the painting more highlights the placement of city walls and houses following terrain conditions such as mountain ridges, slopes, and waterside; therefore C1 is more dominant than C3.

evidence: Left: a high platform is built against mountains and rocks, with railings, and a figure sits on the platform, presenting the feature of a building placed on a platform. | Center: a long corridor and enclosing wall are built on an obvious stone-built high base, with steps in the middle connecting the ground and the interior, embodying placement according to the slope platform. | Right: a pavilion stands on a stone-built base, accompanied by mountains and rocks beside it, showing a spatial relationship of arrangement around the rocks.
distinction: Although the painting includes movement-through-the-landscape clues such as corridors, gates, and steps, all the main built elements are prominently built on stone platforms or immediately adjacent to mountains and rocks, and the terrain-corresponding relationship of buildings placed on platforms and arranged around rocks is more dominant in the composition.

evidence: Lower and lower left: a winding path extends along the waterside, a person is walking along the path toward the built-up area in the center of the painting, and a wooden bridge on the left connects the two banks, forming a clear entry and connection clue. | Upper center and right bank: multiple houses are arranged in a staggered manner beside the sloping bank and waterside, and the path and bridge connect these built elements with the external waterside space, showing a reachable and traversable spatial relationship.
distinction: Although the built elements placed beside water and slope embody terrain-responsive siting, the coherent movement-through-the-landscape clue formed by the path, figures, and bridge in the painting is more prominent, dominating the spatial process of approaching the built elements.

evidence: Left: stone-built slope platforms, stairs, and houses are arranged layer by layer upward following the mountain slope terrain, the base closely fitting the mountain forms. | Lower center: a stone-built embankment or wall extends according to the waterside, with a water gate in the middle through which the water flows, and a platform above for people to rest. | Overall: the built elements in the painting (houses, stairs, stone platforms, water gate) are all placed according to the site conditions of the left mountain slope and the waterside below, presenting a relationship of placement according to the site.
distinction: Although the water gate and paths in the painting imply a travel clue, the terrain-responsive layout in which the built elements unfold layer by layer attached to the mountain slope and waterside terrain is more prominent and dominant.

evidence: Center of the painting: a long row of houses is erected on the water surface between cliffs, supported below by dense pillars, extending horizontally along the trend of the cliff face. | Lower left: two smaller houses cling to the edge of a steep rock face, likewise placed beside the waterside by means of pillar-supported elevation.
distinction: Although the built elements serve to identify the waterside and cliff scenery, their most core compositional logic is placement by means of elevation according to the mountain cliff and water conditions, embodying a relationship of placement according to the site.

evidence: Overall painting: the painting consists mainly of mountains and rocks, trees, and water surface, with no clear traces of artificial built elements such as houses or bridges. | Middle ground and distance: mountains and rocks and trees interweave, forming spatial layering of front-to-back screening.
distinction: The painting lacks definite built elements; based on the spatial layering formed by the mutual screening of the overall landscape elements, it is assigned to the closest category, C2.

evidence: Whole painting: the painting depicts layered mountain peaks, multi-tiered waterfalls, and a foreground water surface, with no traces of any artificial built elements such as houses, pavilions, or bridges. | Lower left corner: two red seals are visible, which are painting identifiers, not built elements within the painting.
distinction: The painting is purely a natural landscape, with no identifiable built elements; therefore it is assigned to the closest category based on the spatial organization of the overall natural forms.

evidence: Center of the painting: a clear white stone-step path winds upward from the stone-built base below, passing through the valley and woods. | Upper center to summit: the path passes the red gate-tower building at the mountainside and continues to extend toward the pagoda and pavilions at the summit, forming a coherent upward clue. | Lower center: the path starts at an obvious stone-built wall/platform structure, implying the starting point for entering deep into the mountain.
distinction: Although the buildings are distributed according to the mountain terrain (C1), the clear long path in the painting links the buildings from the mountain foot to the summit, forming a clear entry and travel clue, with a stronger sense of spatial process.

evidence: Lower to upper right: a clear stepped path winds upward from the lower part of the painting, passing the mountainside (with a person walking) straight to the pavilion between the mountain gorges at the upper right, forming a clear travel-entry clue. | Lower right: a group of courtyard buildings is hidden among the woods, echoing the mountain forms and path system, serving as a spatial node reachable or passed by the path. | Upper right: a multi-story pavilion is visible between the mountain gorges, serving as the endpoint or high target of the winding path, reinforcing the spatial process from bottom to top and from outside to inside.
distinction: Although buildings in the painting are screened among woods and mountains and rocks, the winding path running through the painting and the entry relationship it guides are more prominent, dominating the spatial organization.

evidence: Lower foreground of the painting: beneath several withered trees a thatched hut is screened, its roof and part of the walls obscured by interwoven branches, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Middle water surface of the painting: on the open water there is a small boat, forming a near-far layering with the foreground trees and thatched hut.

distinction: Although the houses are located at the water's edge, the painting places greater emphasis on the relationship of screening and exposure between the grove and the houses, rather than on the terrain-responsive layout of buildings and landform.

evidence: Center left: several houses are partly screened by trees and mountains and rocks, with only the roofs and parts of the walls exposed, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Lower right center: houses are screened behind pine trees and cliffs, using woodland cover to create spatial layering.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited according to the mountain terrain, the painting places greater emphasis on the layers of concealment and revelation formed by screening with trees, mountains, and rocks, so C2 is more apt than C1.

distinction: Although the buildings are sited beside the water and along the bank (C1), the winding embankment, paths, and bridges in the painting constitute strong visual guiding lines, clearly showing a travel route connecting the various built nodes and making the space present a process of entering from one place to another; therefore access to secluded settings (C4) is dominant.

evidence: Lower right center: a building group (a house and a long corridor) is arranged along the waterside and the foot of the mountain, presenting a layout that unfolds along the bank and is distributed according to the slope. | Right background: the buildings are backed by undulating hills and face an open water surface, with their sites forming a close correspondence with the terrain and waterside. | Distant left: a few buildings on the far bank are also sited against the mountain and beside the water, echoing the overall spatially organized terrain-responsive arrangement.
distinction: The painting mainly displays the layout relationship of buildings unfolding in accordance with the waterside and mountain terrain, rather than emphasizing a spatial process of entry guided by bridges and paths.

evidence: Lower center of the painting: an arched bridge spans the water, connecting the two banks and forming a clear passage clue. | Upper right of the painting: a building group is arranged according to the mountain terrain and surrounded by trees; it is the destination to which the bridge guides the viewer's gaze and path. | Water area on the right of the painting: the water surface, together with the bridge and shoreline, constitutes a spatial process by which the built elements can be entered and reached.
distinction: Although the building group being arranged according to the mountain terrain has C1 characteristics, the bridge in the painting serves as a clear movement clue, guiding the viewer's gaze and path into the mountain villa, and the access-to-secluded-settings role of C4 is more prominent.

evidence: Lower right: buildings are built on a rocky terrace bank, with the site raised and steps leading down, presenting a form of buildings set on a terrace and sited along the bank. | Center right: a group of buildings is located among trees at the foot of the mountain, arranged according to the sloping ground, with steps or paths connecting in front. | Lower center: a small pavilion is located on flat ground near the waterside, forming an adjacent relationship with the surrounding mountains, rocks, and stream.
distinction: Although path clues such as steps are visible in the painting, the buildings mainly present a relationship of placement on terraces and according to slopes, and the determining role of terrain in the layout is more significant.

evidence: Lower middle right of the painting: between the red-leaf trees and pines, a house (or pavilion) is visible, with its roof and part of its walls exposed and partly screened by foreground trees. | Right side of the painting: the built structure is located within woodland screening, forming spatial layering in which the house is seen through a screen, with an obvious concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Lower right corner of the right side of the painting: a figure stands on the bank or a rock, facing toward the built structure, but there is no clear, continuous path or bridge connection between the two.
distinction: The built structure mainly presents layers of concealment and revelation screened by trees (C2); although there are figures at the waterside, there is no clearly discernible entry path or bridge directly connecting to the built structure, which is insufficient to determine access to secluded settings (C4).

evidence: Lower middle to center of the painting: a winding path extends from the foreground, passes through grass and rocks, and leads directly to the walled entrance of the building group in the middle ground. | Center right of the painting: the building group includes pavilions, halls, and walls; the path clearly leads into its interior, presenting a spatial process that can be entered and traveled through.
distinction: Although the buildings are arranged according to the terrain, the winding path leading to the building entrance in the painting is more prominent in organizing spatial relationships, emphasizing the process of entry.

evidence: Lower right to lower center: a red bridge spans a shallow stream, connecting the foreground bank with the flat ground on the opposite bank. | Middle ground: the bridge leads to a walled courtyard on the opposite bank and a pavilion among trees, forming a visual path of entering from one place to another and approaching the built structures. | Background and middle ground: green mountains and dense trees surround the built structures; the courtyard and pavilion are placed on flat ground at the foot of the mountain, backed by the mountain and facing the water.
distinction: Although the built structures are sited against the mountain and beside the water, the bridge in the painting serves as a clear movement clue, guiding the gaze across the water to approach the built structures and emphasizing the spatial process of entry.

evidence: Right middle ground of the painting: the roofs and walls of several building groups emerge from dense trees, forming a layered relationship of screening and exposure by woodland. | Right waterside of the painting: the building group is distributed along the waterside and sloping ground, blending into the natural scenery through the screening of surrounding trees.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited beside the water and along the slope, the painting places greater emphasis on the spatial layers of their concealment and revelation among the trees, rather than simply emphasizing a layout built according to the terrain.

evidence: Lower left: a pavilion is built by the water, with wooden piles visible supporting its base, sited at the water's edge, presenting a form of building set over the water. | Lower right: a building group is distributed along the waterside rocks, built beside the water, with the houses closely joined to the shore rocks, presenting a layout unfolding along the bank. | Center right: a building group is located in front of a bamboo grove at the foot of the mountain, placed on flat terrain, backed by the mountain, presenting a relationship of distribution according to the slope.
distinction: Although connecting elements such as plank roads are present in the painting, what dominates visually is the layout relationship of buildings placed according to terrain conditions such as the waterside and the foot of the mountain, rather than emphasizing the deep process of a travel route.

evidence: Lower middle: a figure can be seen standing on a path among mountains and rocks, surrounded by trees and mountains and rocks, presenting spatial clues that can be traveled through. | Overall: the painting consists mainly of landscape, trees, and figures; no clear built structures are visible, but the gaps among the mountains and rocks and the paths suggest an extension of space.
distinction: No clear built elements are visible in the painting, but the combination of the figure and the rocky path suggests an accessible spatial process, so it is assigned to C4.

evidence: Lower right: a small bridge can be seen spanning a stream, with pedestrians on the bridge, connecting paths on both banks and forming clear clues for entry and travel. | Center left: several houses are arranged in a staggered manner on the mountain slope, surrounded by trees and fences, unfolding according to the terrain. | Center right: an independent house stands on high ground by the waterside, forming a spatial echo with the waterside and bridge below.
distinction: Although the houses being arranged against the mountain and beside the water embodies terrain-responsive siting, the connection of bridges and paths in the painting more prominently organizes an accessible, travelable spatial process, so C4 is dominant.

evidence: Left mid-slope: a group of buildings is located in a mountain hollow, screened by pines and mountains and rocks, with only the roofs exposed, presenting layers hidden among the trees. | Right mid-slope: another group of buildings is located on the mountain slope, surrounded by pines, with part of the walls and roofs visible, forming a screening relationship with the mountain. | Overall painting: the built structures are not in a fully open place but are embedded in the mountain forest, forming spatial layers through screening by trees and the mountain.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited according to the mountain terrain, the painting places greater emphasis on revealing the buildings through screening by trees, mountains, and rocks, forming spatial layers of concealment and revelation, rather than simply emphasizing the correspondence between sites and terrain.

evidence: Left: a built complex (houses, walls) can be seen, including a clear courtyard gate that serves as a spatial entrance and exit connected to external paths. | Center right: a stone arched bridge can be seen spanning across, connecting the land on the left with the wooded, rocky area on the right, constituting a clear passage clue. | Center of the painting: a path/shoreline extends from the courtyard gate on the left, passes through trees, and leads to the bridge on the right, forming a travel sequence of entering from one place to another.
distinction: Although the built structures on the left are screened by trees (C2 characteristic), the painting places greater emphasis on the coherent travel path and sense of spatial entry constructed through the courtyard gate, path, and arched bridge (C4).

evidence: Center left of the painting: a thatched pavilion is built on a gentle terrace, with two people seated facing each other inside; its form is fully exposed, identifying the scenery of this open mountain spot. | Right side of the painting: on the right are towering cliffs, trees, and a waterfall, forming a spatial contrast with the gentle terrace where the central thatched pavilion is located; the thatched pavilion becomes a marker that concentrates the landscape of this place.
distinction: Although the thatched pavilion is built on a terrace, its main role is to serve as a visual center that identifies and concentrates the landscape scenery of this place, rather than emphasizing its layout relationship with the undulations of the mountain.

evidence: Upper center of the painting: a pavilion sits on a protruding rocky terrace, its site closely integrated with the terrain of the mountains and rocks. | Center of the painting: the pavilion is surrounded by trees, and the building is placed according to the rises and falls and heights of the mountain rocks.
distinction: Although the pavilion has the role of identifying the high point of the mountain rocks, its most distinctive feature is the terrain-responsive placement of being built against the rocky terrace, so C1 is more apt than C3.

evidence: Lower left corner: there are boats and figures on the water, in a posture of moving or mooring, constituting a movement clue | Left edge: there are a few ochre-red patches, suspected to be parts of a building, but extremely incomplete | Center to right: willows form shade, mountains and rocks are scattered, and the boat faces toward the willow bank and the suspected building direction
distinction: The painting mainly uses the boat as a movement clue to suggest the process of approaching the bank, rather than emphasizing the layout relationship of buildings placed according to the terrain

evidence: Center and lower right: thick tree trunks and lush foliage are located in front of the building, markedly screening the middle of the xuan, revealing only the roof, the right-side wall, and the left-side railing, creating a concealment-and-revelation layering of seeing the house within the woods. | Building interior and left side: through the gaps in the trees and the railing, figures can be seen sitting and reclining inside the xuan, and the bamboo grove and railing on the left extend along the slope, further heightening the spatial depth of the built structure being surrounded and screened by vegetation. | Distant view: distant mountains are outlined in pale ink at the upper part of the painting, forming a near-far contrast with the dense foreground trees and building, and setting off the secluded setting in which the built structure is situated.
distinction: Although the railing and figures on the left side of the painting suggest a movement-through-the-landscape path (C4), the core composition lies in the marked screening and revelation of the building by the large foreground trees, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship (C2) is more dominant in visual hierarchy and theme ( gazing at the branches ).

evidence: Lower left: a pavilion building is half-hidden between cloud and mist and trees, with the eaves and base partly revealed, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Lower middle: dense woodland and swirling cloud and mist together screen part of the building's structure, strengthening the sense of spatial layering and seclusion.
distinction: Although the building serves an accenting role in the painting, its most prominent feature is being screened by cloud, mist, and trees to form layers, rather than serving purely as a landmark scenic accent.

evidence: Lower left corner: a built structure with an arched doorway is visible, its base closely abutting the sloping bank and tree roots, sited in conformity with the terrain. | Left side: trees and rocky slopes form the natural terrain, and the built structure stands alongside them, presenting a relationship of placement according to the site.
distinction: The built structure is placed alongside the sloping bank, with no obvious path leading into it or concealment-and-revelation relationship, so C1 is most apt.

evidence: Lower right: between pines and rocks, figures can be seen walking along a small path into the depth of the painting, forming a clear travel thread. | Middle left: among the screening trees, a building roof is faintly revealed, suggesting the deep built structure to which the path may lead. | Middle of the painting: the gaps between rocks and stream imply an extension of space, helping to explain the process of passing from the foreground into the depths.
distinction: Although the painting has a concealment-and-revelation relationship in which buildings are screened by trees, the action of the figures at the lower right moving deeper along the small path more strongly organizes an enterable, traversable spatial process, so C4 is dominant.

evidence: Right-side mountainside and mountain foot: multiple houses and pavilions are distributed according to the mountain terrain, marking the scenery among the mountains | Right-side waterside: built structures are placed facing the water, echoing the sailboats on the water surface, emphasizing the waterside space | Among rocks and trees: some buildings are half-revealed behind trees and rocks, participating in the organization of landscape layers
distinction: Although there is a concealment-and-revelation relationship, the main role of the built structures is to mark and concentrate the various landscape scenes, rather than to form the setting purely through concealment and revelation

evidence: Right-side water surface: a small boat can be seen moored on the open water, with people aboard. | Center and lower left of the painting: towering rocky slopes and foreground trees are visible, forming a waterside space.
distinction: The painting has no clear fixed built structures, only a lone boat on the water suggesting the spatial process of travel and mooring, so it is assigned to C4 rather than scenic accentuation.

evidence: Left side and left-middle waterside: multiple groups of houses and thatched pavilions are built directly on the waterside terraces and at the mountain foot, their bases unfolding in conformity with the shoreline. | Middle ground: courtyards and houses are laid out on the flat ground at the mountain foot, with fences on the outer side, forming a supporting relationship with the mountain mass behind. | Foreground island in the water: a thatched pavilion is built on the sloping rock projecting at the water's edge, sited in conformity with the terrain.
distinction: Although boats on the water suggest travel threads, the most prominent scenic role of each built structure lies in its manner of placement abutting the waterside and the terrain at the mountain foot, rather than emphasizing the path process of entry.

evidence: Lower left of the painting: a house is hidden behind the pine grove on the left, its roof and walls partly obscured by tree branches and leaves, presenting a layering of seeing the house within the woods. | Left middle of the painting: a red-pillared open xuan sits at the foot of the rocks, screened in front by dense trees (including branches with red leaves), forming a spatial relationship of seeing the house through a separating screen.
distinction: Although the built structure is placed at the mountain foot (C1), the painting more markedly creates secluded layers through the screening and revelation of the building by trees and rocks (C2).

evidence: Upper middle: houses are built halfway up a high cliff, directly attached to the steep rock face, presenting a relationship of placement according to the site by establishing houses against the cliff. | Lower middle: several houses are scattered among the trees at the mountain foot, their layout conforming to the gentle terrain and harmonizing with the surrounding trees and rocks. | Lower left: at the edge of the waterside there is a small bridge connecting the two banks, implying the height differences of the terrain and the presence of flowing water.
distinction: Although the houses at the mountain foot have a concealment-and-revelation relationship, the close dependence of the cliff buildings on the terrain is the most dominant scenic feature in the painting.

evidence: Middle left: a roofed built structure is visible, its building itself, columns, and platform partly obscured by the bamboo grove and boulders in front, with only parts revealed. | Center and right of the painting: tall pines and bamboo groves screen the front and back of the building, forming obvious front-back spatial layers and rendering the building half-hidden and half-revealed. | Middle right: a stretch of fence or enclosure wall is visible, likewise partly obscured by trees and foliage, continuing the spatial relationship of screening.
distinction: Although the building is placed against the sloping rocks, the most dominant compositional method in the painting is to use trees, bamboo, and rocks to screen the building so as to form layers of concealment and revelation, rather than emphasizing the posture of siting according to terrain.

evidence: Lower center, slightly left: several simple house roofs and walls are hidden among the sloping bank and withered trees, presenting a half-hidden, half-revealed state. | Right-side middle-ground mountain foot: the built structures are partly obscured by rocks and trees, with only parts of the roofs and structures revealed, forming front-back spatial layers.
distinction: Although the built structures are located on the sloping bank at the mountain foot, the painting emphasizes more their concealment-and-revelation relationship as obscured and revealed by trees and rocks, rather than placement purely according to terrain.

evidence: Middle left: a thatched hut is built against the water and backed by the mountain; its roof, white wall, and round window are revealed against the rocks and bamboo grove behind, but the building itself is partly obscured by the branches and leaves in front. | Center to right of the painting: a great many tree trunks and leaves interweave through the foreground and middle ground, markedly screening the rocks and thatched hut behind, creating spatial layers of alternating concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the thatched hut being placed against the water and backed by the mountain embodies the features of C1, the painting more prominently highlights the layered relationship formed by the screening and revelation of the built structure by trees and rocks, so C2 is more dominant.

evidence: Water surface in the lower middle of the painting: several small boats with sails can be seen traveling on the water, presenting travel threads | Left side of the painting: rocky slopes and trees extend to the water's edge, with no clear houses or pavilion buildings visible
distinction: The painting contains only the travel thread of boats and no clear buildings; it is assigned to C4 only with difficulty on the basis of the overall spatial organization

evidence: Left side: a thatched-roof pavilion is half-hidden in the dense bamboo grove, with only the top and some columns revealed. | Right side: a fenced building stands behind large lake rocks and pines, with withered tree branches interweaving and screening in the foreground, forming front-back layers.
distinction: The painting emphasizes more the layers of concealment and revelation formed by the building being screened by bamboo grove, lake rocks, and trees, rather than placement purely according to terrain.

evidence: Lower right: the roof and columns of the thatched hut are revealed from behind the withered tree branches and rocks in the foreground, forming an obvious relationship of screening and layering. | Left-side middle ground: a plank bridge is half-hidden behind the sloping bank and trees, and the junction of the bridge body and the water surface is partly obscured. | Right side: dense trees and bamboo grove further wrap and screen the rear of the thatched hut, strengthening the visual effect of the built structure hidden among the woods.
distinction: Although there is a plank bridge in the painting as a path clue, the core of the overall composition lies in the layer-by-layer screening and revelation of the thatched hut and bridge by trees and rocks, rather than emphasizing a coherent process of travel and entry.

evidence: Lower middle: several houses are partly obscured by foreground pines, miscellaneous trees, and bamboo groves, with only the roofs and parts of the walls revealed, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Lower middle: tree branches and leaves interweave with the house buildings, placing the built structures within layers screened by woodland.
distinction: Although the houses are built on the sloping bank, the painting emphasizes more the spatial layers formed by the screening and revelation of the buildings by woodland, so C2 is more apt than C1.

evidence: Upper middle, slightly right: a group of house buildings is visible, with clear roofs and lower supporting structures, placed on a hillside terrace in conformity with the undulations of the terrain. | Left side and lower part of the painting: on the left are sloping rocks and trees, and below is open water with willows and a small boat on the bank, forming with the built structures on the slope above a relationship of landscape terrain with high and low interlocking.
distinction: Although the built structures are within a mountain-forest setting, their overall outline is clearly revealed, mainly manifesting a terrain-responsive relationship of placement according to the sloping terrace, rather than being dominated by concealment and revelation through woodland screening.

evidence: Lower center: a person sits alone on the sloping rocks at the waterside, facing the open water, becoming the visual focus of the painting. | Right side: a cliff rises steeply, with trees hanging down, enclosing the space with the water and setting off the spatial position of the solitary sitting place.
