distinction: No clear artificial buildings are visible in the painting; only figures serve as scenic accent elements marking the scene of solitary sitting, so it is assigned to C3; the painting has no enterable spatial clues such as paths or bridges, so C4 is not selected.

evidence: Lower part to middle ground of the painting: a clear small path winds upward along the hillside, connecting the waterside with the built area on the hillside. | Right-side hillside of the painting: two pavilion houses are visible on the hillside, and the direction in which the small path extends points toward these built structures, forming enterable spatial clues.
distinction: Although the built structures are laid out according to the mountain terrain, the winding small path's role in guiding and connecting space is more prominent in the painting, emphasizing the process of travel and entry.

evidence: Lower middle, slightly left: a house is surrounded and screened by foreground and middle-ground trees, with only part of the roof and walls revealed, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Right edge: the roofs of some buildings are faintly visible, likewise screened by trees.
distinction: Although the houses are placed according to the mountain terrain, the painting emphasizes more the spatial layers formed by the screening and revelation of the buildings by woodland.

evidence: Middle right of the painting: an open pavilion is built directly at the edge of a waterside rock terrace, its base sited in conformity with the form of the waterside cliff. | Right side of the painting: behind the pavilion are towering boulders and trees, and the built structure unfolds attached to the natural terrain of rocks and waterside, presenting a relationship of placement according to the site.
distinction: Although the pavilion serves to mark the waterside scenery, its most core compositional logic is placement in conformity with and attachment to the terrain of the waterside rock terrace, so C1 is more dominant than C3.

evidence: Lower right: a small bridge spans the water, connecting the right-side earthen slope with the opposite bank, and behind the bridge a path or platform can be faintly seen extending into the woods. | Lower left: a small boat is on the water, implying that the water surface is passable. | Right middle: trees are dense, screening the space behind the bridge and creating a secluded visual effect.
distinction: The painting mainly uses the small bridge and path to guide the eye into the depths of the woods, emphasizing an enterable spatial process rather than a mere concealment-and-revelation relationship.

evidence: Middle right of the painting: a thatched hut is surrounded by dense blossoms and branches (a plum grove) in the foreground and middle ground, the lower part of the building itself obscured by branches, with only the roof and part of the walls and the figures inside revealed. | Left side to center of the painting: tall pines and the plum grove below together constitute the foreground and middle ground, wrapping the built structure within them and forming obvious spatial layers of woodland screening and revelation.
distinction: The painting mainly emphasizes the concealment-and-revelation relationship formed by the surrounding and screening of the thatched hut by woodland, rather than serving purely as a marker to identify a certain landscape scene.

evidence: Middle ground of the painting, slightly right: the house is half-screened and half-revealed by the surrounding dense trees and rocks, with only part of the roof, columns, and interior figures revealed, forming obvious layers of concealment and revelation. | Middle ground of the painting: tree branches and leaves and rocky slopes surround the building, wrapping the built structure within natural scenery and strengthening the spatial effect of concealment and revelation forming the setting. | Lower part of the painting: the water surface, boats, and the bridge at the lower left corner suggest spatial extension, but the core of the painting still focuses on the screened house in the middle ground.
distinction: Although the bridge and boats below suggest travel threads, the concealment-and-revelation relationship formed by the middle-ground house with the woodland and rocks is more prominent and dominant in the composition.

evidence: Right-side lower middle: a thatched hut sits at the waterside, its building itself and roof partly obscured by the surrounding dense bamboo grove, presenting a layering of a house revealed within the woods. | Overall painting: a large expanse of bamboo grove is distributed along the waterside and hillside, and the natural scenery forms an obvious screening relationship with the built structure.
distinction: Although the thatched hut is built facing the water, the painting emphasizes more the screening and revelation of the building by the bamboo grove, and the role of concealment and revelation forming scenery is greater than that of mere terrain conformity.

evidence: Lower left corner: a person stands at the bank or on a dike bridge, facing the water surface and the middle ground, forming a clear starting point for travel and a guide for the line of sight. | Middle-ground waterside: a group of village houses unfolds horizontally along the waterside, forming a spatial relationship of arrival and entry with the figure at the lower left corner. | Lower right corner: a foreground house is hidden behind pines, and together with the shoreline and stone path forms an enterable local spatial layer.
distinction: Although the foreground buildings are screened by trees, the guiding role of the figure and path at the lower left corner runs through the composition, emphasizing more the spatial process from here to there, so C4 is more dominant than C2.

evidence: Lower left corner: a thatched hut is built against the earthen slope and trees, its roof echoing the undulations of the terrain. | Right-side middle ground: houses are screened among sparse woods, their bases unfolding in conformity with the gentle sloping land. | Lower right corner: a small pavilion-type building is placed at the edge of the sloping land, naturally connecting with the surrounding terrain.
distinction: Although there are bridges and paths guiding the procession in the painting, the built structures themselves more prominently exhibit a relationship of placement according to the slope and living along with the trees, rather than serving purely as nodes of the travel route.

evidence: Upper left: a red-walled building is located on an earthen terrace, its base raised, with steps in front connecting to the sloping land below, presenting a manner of placement by establishing the house on the terrace. | Left side and center: trees surround the building, the sloping bank extends below, and figures' activities unfold along the sloping land, the built structure forming a corresponding relationship with the terrace terrain.
distinction: Although there are movement lines of figures active toward the building in the painting, there is a lack of clear travel clues such as bridges and paths connecting them, and the terrain relationship of the building being placed on the sloping terrace is more direct and dominant.

evidence: Middle left and upper right areas: several houses have part of their building itself obscured by dense willows or are located behind groves, presenting a concealment-and-revelation layering of seeing the house within the woods. | Lower left area: houses are located under the willows on the sloping bank, screened by trees, with only the roofs and part of the walls revealed. | Overall composition: willows, as the main natural scenery, surround the houses, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship that echoes the mood of 'graceful willows' in the inscription, making screening participate in forming the scenery.
distinction: Although the houses distributed along the field ridges (sloping terraces/waterside) have the feature of terrain-responsive placement, the screening and surrounding of the houses by willows are more conspicuous in the visual hierarchy, constituting the main concealment-and-revelation relationship.

evidence: Right side of the painting: rows of willows and gentle sloping land are visible, and several people ride horses through the sloping land and woods. | Center to right of the painting: the figures and horses move in a direction pointing into the depths of the woods, presenting spatial extension and a process of travel.
distinction: The painting has no clear built structures, but the route of the figures entering the woods along the sloping land embodies a spatial process, which is closer to C4 than mere terrain placement.

evidence: Lower left: an arched bridge is visible crossing the water surface, connecting the two banks and forming a clear circulation cue. | Lower center: on a sloped terrace stands a small red hut, located on the bank side toward which the bridge points, surrounded by trees. | Right side: fields and distant mountains extend into the depth, forming with the foreground bridge and hut a spatial layering from near to far.
distinction: In the painting, the bridge as a circulation cue and the built structure (the hut) connect spatially, emphasizing the spatial process of passing from this bank to the far bank and approaching the built structure; this fits the definition of access to secluded settings better than merely identifying a scenic spot.

evidence: Lower-middle to middle ground of the painting: a winding bank path extends from the foreground into the middle ground, with travelers walking on it, connecting different islets and groves. | Left and right middle ground of the painting: the extending direction of the path points toward or connects to groups of waterside houses, presenting a spatial relationship that is enterable and reachable.
distinction: Although the houses are sited by the watery islets, the painting places greater emphasis on the process of guiding travelers through the winding path into the pictorial depth, and the organizing role of the path is more prominent.

evidence: Center-left: house roofs emerge between clouds and trees, presenting the layering of seeing houses through a screen of scenery | Lower left: stone steps and parts of buildings are obscured by trees, faintly visible
distinction: Although the painting has a cue of stone steps, the built elements mainly organize space through screening and revealing by clouds and trees, emphasizing concealment and revelation rather than path guidance.

evidence: Lower left: an arched small bridge is visible crossing a stream; on the sloping ground beside the bridge, several house roofs are screened among the trees, forming a spatial cue of entering the village from the bridge. | Middle-ground left bank: on the opposite sloping ground there are also scattered houses interspersed with trees, forming with the water surface a layer of movement that faces across the bank. | Center of the painting: the broad water surface connects foreground and distance; on the water is a small boat, suggesting a route of travel on the water.
distinction: Although trees screen the houses, the combination of the small bridge and the dwellings in the lower-left corner clearly constructs a circulation cue of moving from here to there, and its organizing role in access to secluded settings is more prominent.

evidence: Left-middle of the painting: a pavilion building is visible situated on the mountainside, its lower half obscured by clouds and foreground trees, with only the roof and part of the building itself exposed. | Lower-middle of the painting: the foreground withered trees and pine grove form layers with the middle-ground clouds and mist, partly screening and partly revealing the mountains and rocks and the buildings behind, constituting a relationship of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the building identifies the mountainside scenery, the painting emphasizes more its layered relationship of being screened and revealed by clouds and woodland; therefore C2 fits better than C3.

evidence: Whole painting: the picture consists mainly of layered mountains, trees, and rocks; no traces of built elements such as houses, pavilions, or bridges are seen. | Lower-right corner: mountains and rocks meet the water flow here, forming an inward-recessing cove or valley mouth, suggesting the extension and deepening of space.
distinction: There are no built elements in the painting; only the opening formed by the waterside and mountain configuration in the lower-right corner presents a sense of space guiding the gaze inward, so it is only marginally assigned to C4.

evidence: Center-left: among the screening trees and rocks there are very faint ink outlines, suspected to be the top of a building, but the details are blurred and hard to identify with certainty. | Whole painting: the picture consists mainly of mountains and rocks and woodland, with interlocking layers and no clearly identifiable cues of paths or bridges.
distinction: The suspected built elements are hidden behind trees and rocks, and the relationship of concealment and revelation is more significant than identifying a scenic spot.

evidence: Lower right: an arched bridge and figures on it are visible; behind the bridge it connects to a winding path extending into the depth of the painting. | Center-left: the path leads to a pavilion building between mountains and rocks and trees, the building partly obscured by branches and leaves. | Overall: the bridge, path, and figures form a clear circulation cue, guiding the gaze from the foreground into and toward the built elements deep in the painting.
distinction: In the painting, the circulation cue formed by bridge, path, and people runs from the foreground to the middle ground, clearly guiding entry toward the built structures; this has a stronger spatial organizing role than a mere layering of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower left: a group of courtyard buildings is partly obscured by the trunks, branches, and leaves of the foreground pine grove, presenting the layering of houses hidden within the woods. | Center-left: on the mountainside there is a pavilion, leaning against the rock face and hidden among trees and rocks, its existence and spatial position indicated through partial exposure. | Right side: the open water surface and far bank serve as background, setting off the sense of depth of the built structures screened by mountains, rocks, and trees on the left.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited according to the mountain terrain, the painting emphasizes more the spatial layering formed by the screening and revealing of the buildings by woodland and mountains and rocks; therefore C2 is more dominant than C1.

evidence: Lower-middle of the painting: the building complex is surrounded and obscured by dense pines and mountains and rocks, with only roofs and parts of walls exposed, presenting the typical spatial layering of seeing houses within the woods and houses hidden behind rocks. | Lower-right corner of the painting: structures resembling railings or a bridge, and figures below, are visible, suggesting the front-back relationship of space, but the path cues are interrupted by vegetation.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited on mountain slopes and terraces according to the terrain (a C1 feature), visually the screening and revealing of the buildings by vegetation (concealment and revelation) is more prominent and dominates the expression of spatial layering.

evidence: Left slope: a group of houses is arranged in sequence along the slope gradient and contour lines, presenting the form of houses set according to the slope. | Right mountainside: a pavilion building is placed in staggered fashion on the slope according to the mountain configuration. | Distant mountaintop: a pagoda stands at the summit, placed in accord with the highest point of the mountain.
distinction: Although the pagoda and pavilion serve to mark the mountaintop and mountainside, the most prominent feature of the built group in the overall painting (especially the village on the left) is the layout unfolding in accord with the sloping terrain; the terrain-responsive siting feature is more comprehensive and dominant.

evidence: Lower half of the painted panel: the painting depicts near-ground sloping rocks, bamboo clumps, withered trees and pines, as well as a pale-ink water surface and distant trees in the mid- and far ground; no traces of man-made built structures such as houses, pavilions, bridges or paths are seen.
distinction: There are absolutely no visible built elements in the painting, so its mode of spatial representation cannot be accurately determined; it is assigned only tentatively on the basis of the distribution of natural scenery.

evidence: Lower-middle of the painting: the house buildings are obscured by the dense foreground weeping willows and bamboo grove, with only roofs, eaves, and parts of walls exposed, presenting the layering of houses hidden within the woods. | Left and center of the painting: drooping willow branches and interlacing bamboo leaves form multiple screens, placing the buildings in a half-hidden, half-visible state and strengthening the spatial relationship of concealment and revelation. | Right side of the painting: towering mountains and rocks together with the trees below surround the buildings, further heightening the secluded living environment and making the concealment-and-revelation relationship participate in forming the scene.
distinction: The core visual relationship of the painting is the screening and revealing of the buildings by tree branches and leaves, forming rich spatial layering, rather than mainly emphasizing a close correspondence between building sites and terrain slopes and banks.

evidence: Right-middle: house buildings are faintly visible between rocks and trees, partly obscured by natural scenery, presenting the layering of seeing houses through a screen of scenery. | Left-middle: a corner of a roof emerges from behind bank-side trees and shrubs, the building half-hidden behind the woodland, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation.
distinction: The painting emphasizes more the concealment-and-revelation relationship by which buildings are screened by trees and rocks to form spatial layering, rather than focusing on the terrain-responsive correspondence between buildings and sloping banks.

evidence: Lower part: a wooden bridge/plank walkway and two standing figures are visible, connecting the path and suggesting an entry node into the built structures in the woods. | Lower-middle: a shepherd boy rides an ox winding along a dirt road, the path pointing toward the built area above the slope, forming a land-route travel cue. | Middle water surface: a small boat travels on the water, echoing the pavilion screened by willows on the bank and providing a water-route cue for reaching the built structures.
distinction: Although in the painting many trees screen the built structures (a C2 feature), circulation cues such as the bridge, path, and boat run through the composition, clearly organizing the spatial process of going from the foreground deeper into the built structures; therefore C4 is more dominant.

evidence: Lower-middle of the painting: mountains and rocks, pines, water ripples, and several figures (immortals, attendant youths, etc.) are visible active on rocks by the water; no clear architectural built elements are seen. | Overall painting: the figures are combined with mountains and rocks and the water surface, identifying this spot of scenery and carrying a sense of scenic accentuation.
distinction: There are no clear architectural built elements in the painting; figures combined with landscape identify the scenery, so it is assigned to the closest category, C3.

evidence: Middle-ground right: several roofs and wall bodies faintly emerge among the trees, the buildings half-screened by woodland, forming a spatial layering of concealment and revelation. | Lower-left corner: part of a bridge is visible, suggesting a path along the waterside, but it is not the dominant circulation cue of the painting. | Lower-right corner: a stone-revetted embankment is clearly visible, establishing the boundary of the waterside, but no obvious buildings unfolding according to the terrain are seen.
distinction: Although a bridge in the painting suggests a path, the built structures are mainly presented through the screening of woodland to create spatial layering, rather than emphasizing an enterable process of travel.

evidence: Lower part and center: a stream flows from below upward, passing through gaps between rocks and flowing toward the waterfall and woods, forming a visual guide. | Left side and center: steep cliffs and the trees on the right form a gorge-like space; the water flow and gaps among mountains and rocks suggest extension into the depth of the painting.
distinction: The painting mainly guides the gaze into depth through water flow and gaps among mountains and rocks, presenting a spatial process rather than emphasizing the layering of concealment and revelation of built structures.

evidence: Lower left: several houses are screened among trees and mountains and rocks, roofs and walls partly obscured, presenting a spatial layering of alternating concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the houses are located at the foot of the mountain, the painting emphasizes more their layered relationship of being obscured by woodland and mountains and rocks and appearing faintly, rather than mere placement according to terrain.

evidence: Lower-right corner: in the near ground, a gate or fence structure screened by trees is visible, suggesting an entrance or boundary. | Center of the painting: on the water is a small boat, forming a travel cue moving toward the depth of the painting or toward the built structures on the left. | Center-left: houses are built where the mountain meets the water, forming a relationship of spatial echo and arrival with the water surface and the boat.
distinction: Although the houses on the left are sited against the mountain and beside the water (C1), the painting, through the gate in the lower-right corner, the boat in the middle ground, and the extension of the waterside, emphasizes more a spatial process that is enterable and traversable (C4).

evidence: Lower left: an arched bridge is visible spanning the water, with a path or shoreline extending behind the bridge into the depth of the painting. | Lower right: the path or shoreline connects to a house building, forming a spatial cue of entering from the bridge and arriving at the house. | Center-right: the house is partly obscured by foreground pines and mountains and rocks, but a clear reachable relationship is established through the path and bridge.
distinction: Although the house has a layering of being screened by trees, the cue of entry and arrival formed by the bridge and path more dominates the spatial organization of the painting.

evidence: Lower-middle of the painting: a house building is visible, its roof and part of its walls obscured by the branches and leaves of the trees in front, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Left mountainside of the painting: another roof is faintly visible screened behind mountains and rocks and trees, suggesting spatial layering.
distinction: Although the built structure is located on sloping ground at the foot of the mountain, the painting emphasizes more the screening and revealing of the house by woodland, with the concealment-and-revelation relationship participating in forming the scene, rather than simply emphasizing placement according to terrain.

evidence: Right-page painting: the picture depicts mountains and rocks, trees (bamboo and withered trees), and a figure seated on a rock; a pale moon is in the sky, and no traces of built elements such as houses or pavilions are seen.
distinction: There are no clear built elements in the painting, only figures as scenic accents; it is assigned to the closest category based on the overall visible space.

evidence: Upper center of the painting: at the valley mouth between two cliffs, the roofs and wall bodies of several houses are visible, partly obscured by the mountains and rocks and trees on both sides. | Lower left and lower right of the painting: stone banks and water surface are nearby, and no obvious path or bridge connecting to the built structures above is seen.
distinction: Although the built structures are located at the valley mouth, their half-screened, half-revealed relationship with mountains and rocks and trees is more prominent in the painting and constitutes the main spatial layering, rather than serving merely as a conspicuous landmark.

evidence: Lower left: a small bridge is visible spanning a stream and connecting the two banks; behind the bridge a small path extends into the mountains. | Lower right: there is a group of house buildings surrounded by trees and paths, forming a connected relationship with the waterside and bridge below. | Upper left and right mountainside: pavilion buildings are visible on the cliffs and mountainside, combined with mountains and rocks and woodland, suggesting a route by which one may travel up to a high point to view the scenery.
distinction: Although in the painting buildings are screened by trees and rocks, the bridge and path in the lower-left corner clearly guide the gaze and travel route into the depth of the painting, and the cue of access to secluded settings is more prominent.

evidence: Lower part of the painting: a small bridge is visible spanning a stream, connecting the paths on the two banks. | Lower right of the painting: a figure stands on the path leaning on a staff, presenting a state of traveling, approaching, or traversing. | Center-left of the painting: house buildings on the cliff are placed according to the mountain configuration, together with the path and bridge below forming an enterable landscape space.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed according to the mountain configuration (C1), the combination of bridge, path, and traveling figure more strongly expresses the spatial process of moving from here to there and being traversable (C4).

evidence: Lower right of the painted panel: a built structure is visible between mountain rocks and trees, its roof and part of its wall exposed, with the rest screened by the foreground mountain rocks and woodland, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Right side of the painted panel: towering mountain rocks and sparse trees surround the built structure, reinforcing the spatial layering in which the built structure is hidden among mountain forests and rocky valleys.
distinction: Although the built structure is placed according to the mountain terrain, the painting places greater emphasis on its relationship of half concealment and half revelation by mountain rocks and woodland, through which the spatial layering is constructed; therefore C2 is more apt than C1.

evidence: Lower-center, slightly right: a waterside pavilion is obscured by the tall trees and lake rocks on the right, with only part of the roof, eaves, and the figures inside the pavilion exposed, forming a clear layering of concealment and revelation. | Lower-left corner: a person stands at the edge of a platform extending into the water, facing toward the pavilion, forming a spatial echo with the pavilion screened behind trees and rocks.
distinction: Although the painting has the platform and the figure's line of sight in the lower-left corner pointing toward the pavilion, the concealment-and-revelation relationship by which the pavilion itself is screened by trees and rocks is the dominant way of composing the scene, rather than emphasizing a coherent travel route.

evidence: Lower-middle: a roofed pavilion building is half-hidden behind the foreground pines and bamboo clumps, with only the roof, eaves, and parts of the columns exposed. | Inside the pavilion in the lower-middle: through gaps in the trees, two people are visible sitting facing each other; the screening by trees establishes the spatial layering in which the building is situated.
distinction: Although the building is sited by water and rocks, the most prominent composition technique of the painting is the use of pine and bamboo screening and revealing to present the layering of concealment and revelation of the building, rather than emphasizing its layout unfolding according to terrain.

evidence: Middle-ground mountainside: a group of houses is placed according to the mountain configuration on a rocky terrace, the layout echoing the undulations of the mountain body. | Beside the waterside in the lower part: a roofed pavilion is built facing the water, its base closely adjoining the waterside rocks, presenting the characteristic of arrangement following the bank.
distinction: Although trees and mountains and rocks screen the built structures to some extent, the painting more highlights the correspondence by which the built structures are placed according to mountain forms and waterside terrain.

evidence: Mid-left hillside: Roofs and eaves emerge from behind dense tree clusters and mountain rocks, forming a partly hidden, partly revealed layering. | Lower left corner: The building is partially screened by foreground tree branches and foliage, with only parts of the wall and roof exposed. | Lower right corner: An open hall is built at the waterside, surrounded by trees and mountain rocks, with figures seated inside, mutually screening and revealing with the natural environment.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited according to terrain, the painting emphasizes more the spatial layering formed by buildings being screened and revealed by trees and rocks, so C2 is more dominant than C1.

evidence: Lower-middle of the painting: A group of buildings' roofs and walls are visible, partially screened by foreground and middle-ground tree branches and foliage, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Building interior: Through gaps in the trees, a figure in red can be seen inside the building, further indicating the spatial layering and sense of seclusion of the built elements. | Right and center of the painting: Dense pines and miscellaneous trees surround the built elements, creating a visual effect of tree screening, causing the buildings to be hidden within the mountain forest.
distinction: Although the buildings are located at the foot of the mountain, the dominant spatial expression in the painting is the layering of concealment and revelation formed by tree screening, rather than emphasizing layout relations sited according to terrain.

evidence: Lower right: The roofs and columns of two built structures are visible, partially screened by foreground trees and sloping rocks, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Center-left: Dense ink trees and sloping rocks are positioned in front of the built elements, forming a screen that places the built elements in a spatial layer behind the trees and rocks.
distinction: Although the built elements are adjacent to the waterside, the painting emphasizes more their layering of being screened and revealed by trees and rocks, rather than a layout unfolding according to terrain.

evidence: Left side: the inscription includes the phrase 'Let the path wind as it will', explicitly referring to the presence and winding course of a path. | Lower part: a sloping bank or path-like lines extend horizontally along the bottom of the painting; together with the bamboo grove, they suggest a space extending into the woodland. | Center and right: trees and rocks form a landscape of sparse trees and slender rock forms; the path appears to lead deeper into this setting.
distinction: The inscription and the lines at the bottom of the painting emphasize the guiding role of a path and a sense of entry into a secluded setting, rather than simply emphasizing trees screening built elements.

evidence: Lower-middle, slightly right: A building with an arched doorway is visible, its roof and doorway partially exposed, half-screened by surrounding tall trees and bamboo clusters on the right. | Center and right of the painting: Dense tree canopies and bamboo leaves form screens in the foreground and middle ground, giving the building a spatial layering of alternating concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the building is situated among mountain rocks and trees, the core compositional role in the painting is to reveal the building through screening by trees and bamboo clusters, forming layers of concealment and revelation, rather than emphasizing its placement in relation to a specific terrain slope or bank.

evidence: Lower-middle of the painting: In an open area of mountain rocks are four figures, two standing as if conversing and two seated on the ground, forming the visual focus of the painting. | Right and upper parts of the painting: The mountain slope extends with dense trees, using ink tonality to express the texture of mountain rocks and spatial layering.
distinction: The figures' placement on the mountain rocks has C1 characteristics, but the main role of the gathered figures is to mark this as a gathering scene, so it is classified under C3.

evidence: Lower right bank: Behind the pines, the top of a thatched pavilion is visible, partially screened by tree trunks and foliage, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Lower left waterside: A small boat floats on the water, echoing in near-far correspondence with figures and buildings on the bank, but the buildings are mainly screened by trees.
distinction: Although the thatched pavilion has a scenic-accentuating role, its concealment-and-revelation relationship of being screened by pines is more prominent and constitutes the spatial layering of the painting, so C2 is more apt.

evidence: Mid-right hillside of the painting: A group of buildings is visible, their roofs and walls partially screened by pines and mountain rocks in front, forming an obvious concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Mid-right of the painting: Trees and built elements interweave, and the screening by trees gives the buildings a spatial layering of receding behind the woods, participating in the composition.
distinction: Although the buildings are constructed according to the mountain terrain, the screening and revealing relationship of trees to buildings is more prominent in the painting and is the main mode of composition.

evidence: Lower-middle: A thatched pavilion is hidden among sloping rocks and dense tree clusters, with only the roof, eaves, and part of the columns exposed; one figure can be seen inside. | Lower-middle: The pavilion is screened by sloping rocks in front and trees on both sides, forming an obvious concealment-and-revelation relationship that integrates the building into the layers of natural scenery.
distinction: Although the pavilion marks a scenic spot, its concealment-and-revelation layering, revealed through screening by trees and rocks, is the most dominant spatial expression in the painting.

evidence: Lower part of the painting: Figures are depicted seated on sloping rocks, with trees nearby; the figures' posture suggests a sightseeing attitude, and the sloping rocks and trees imply a space where one may linger. | Whole painting: The painting is dominated by mountains, trees, sloping rocks, and figures; no clear buildings, pavilions, bridges, or other built elements are identifiable.
distinction: There are no clear built elements in the painting; the figures seated on rocks viewing scenery present an attitude of traveling and entering the setting, which is closer to a sense of spatial entry than to scenic accentuation as a fixed marker.

evidence: Lower scroll, right side: A pavilion is built at the edge of a rocky high platform, with its column bases resting on the rock surface, presenting the form of a building set on a platform. | Upper scroll, center-right: A thatched house is built on flat ground at the waterside, adjacent to reed clusters, sited by the water.
distinction: The building site clearly relies on a rocky platform and waterside terrain (set on a platform, by the water); the relationship of terrain support and placement is more specific than mere scenic marking.

evidence: Lower foreground: A thatched pavilion sits on sloping rocks, surrounded by trees, marking the scenery at the waterside. | Middle-ground water surface: A small boat floats on the water, echoing the thatched pavilion in the foreground and together forming the main landscape node of the painting.
distinction: Although the thatched pavilion sits on sloping rocks, it does not display strong characteristics of being arranged according to complex terrain changes; it serves more as a visual focus and landscape marker in the foreground.

evidence: Whole painting: The main subject is mountain rocks, trees, and water; no houses, pavilions, or other clear built elements are identifiable. | Lower water surface: In the near-ground water, a small boat carries one seated figure, presenting a state of movement through the landscape and implying the accessibility of the space. | Middle and distant views: Space is guided visually from the foreground trees and bank through the water surface toward distant mountains, extending into depth.
distinction: There are no clear built elements; only a boat serves as a clue to movement through the landscape, with an intention of spatial extension into depth, so it is classified as C4; if the boat were regarded as scenic accentuation it would approach C3, but the boat is not a built element and C4 emphasizes the spatial process more.

evidence: Lower-middle of the painting: A built structure (pavilion or house) is visible, its roof and part of its structure exposed, but its main body is screened by pines and mountain rocks to the right and in front, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Right and foreground of the painting: Pines and sloping rocks painted in dense ink are positioned in front of the built structure, forming a foreground screening layer that places the built structure amid tree screening.
distinction: Although the built structure marks a scenic spot in the mountains, its concealment-and-revelation layering, half-screened by pines and rocks, is the most prominent mode of spatial organization in the painting, so C2 is more apt than C3.

evidence: Center of the painting: Buildings on a sloping platform are partially screened by trees and the slope body, with only the roof and parts of the walls exposed, forming layers of concealment and revelation. | Lower left of the painting: Waterside buildings are screened by foreground trees and rocks, presenting a spatial relationship in which buildings are seen within the woods and behind rocks.
distinction: Although the built elements are sited according to terrain, the painting emphasizes more the screening and revealing of built elements by trees and mountain rocks; the concealment-and-revelation relationship is the dominant mode of composition.

evidence: Left side: Behind a group of trees, the roof and walls of a house and a fence in front are exposed; the building is partially screened by tree trunks and foliage. | Center-left of the painting: Built elements are hidden within tree clusters, their existence indicated by exposed partial forms, forming a spatial layering of front-back screening with the surrounding trees.
distinction: The painting mainly emphasizes the concealment-and-revelation relationship of built elements within the woods to form scenery, rather than highlighting their placement alongside specific terrain or waterside.

evidence: Right hillside: A group of buildings is distributed in staggered fashion along cliffs and slopes, with the site and layout closely conforming to the undulations of the mountain terrain and the direction of the rocks. | Left lower-middle waterside: A building is constructed by the water, sited according to the waterside terrain. | Lower right corner: A small bridge is visible among trees and mountain rocks, connecting the waterside and the mountain path.
distinction: Although some buildings in the painting have a concealment-and-revelation relationship screened by trees, the most prominent feature of the main building group on the right hillside is siting according to the mountain and following its forms, so C1 is more dominant than C2.

evidence: Lower-middle of the painting: A group of houses is largely screened by dense tree clusters (rendered with ink dots), with only roof outlines exposed, presenting a spatial layering of houses hidden in the woods. | Bottom of the painting: A hall-style building is located between a pine grove and bamboo clusters; eaves, colonnades, and tree foliage interweave, forming a front-back screening relationship.
distinction: Although the built elements are located on the sloping ground at the foot of the mountain, the visual focus of the painting is the screening and surrounding of buildings by trees, rather than the buildings' layout conforming to terrain slopes and platforms.

evidence: Left middle: A small house is built at the foot of the mountain, partially screened by mountain rocks and trees, presenting a half-hidden, half-exposed state. | Lower right corner: A pavilion is surrounded and screened by foreground pines and bamboo clusters; figures inside the pavilion are faintly visible, forming a layering of houses hidden in the woods.
distinction: Although the built elements in the painting also serve scenic accentuation, the dominant factor constituting pictorial depth is the spatial organization of being screened layer upon layer by mountain rocks and trees, with alternating concealment and revelation, which more closely matches concealment and revelation.

evidence: Below: At the bottom of the painting a small bridge is depicted, on which a figure holding an umbrella stands, facing the waterfall and deep mountains above, forming a clear clue for movement through the landscape and visual guidance. | Middle-ground left: Between trees and mountain rocks, the outlines of a building's roof and walls are faintly visible, half-screened among tree clusters.
distinction: Although buildings in the middle ground are screened among the woods, the bridge and figure below form a stronger clue of entry and travel, dominating the spatial process of the painting.

evidence: Center-left water surface: A small boat with a canopy floats on the open water, echoing the winding shoreline and distant mountains. | Overall composition: The painting is dominated by natural landscape; the small boat, as the only clear man-made object, marks the scenic travel over the water.
distinction: There is only a boat traveling on the water in the painting; no clear spatial clues such as bridges, paths, or fords that allow entry or turning into depth are visible, so C4 is not selected.

evidence: Lower left: A thatched pavilion is built on a stone platform by the water, its site closely corresponding to the form of the rocky bank, presenting a relationship of a building set on a platform. | Upper middle: Houses are arranged in staggered fashion on hillside slope platforms, conforming to the undulations of the mountain terrain, presenting a layout sited according to terrain.
distinction: The built elements mainly embody placement on stone platforms and along the hillside, corresponding to the terrain, rather than simply serving as visual markers to mark scenery.

evidence: Upper-middle, slightly right of the painting: A group of buildings is located in a dense pine forest; roofs and walls are partially screened by branches and leaves, presenting a layering of houses hidden in the woods. | Center of the painting: Foreground pine branches slant across, screening the buildings behind, forming an obvious front-back screening relationship.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited according to the mountain terrain, the painting emphasizes more the screening and revealing of buildings by trees; the feature of concealment and revelation is superior to terrain-responsive siting.

evidence: Lower-middle, slightly left: A building complex is hidden behind mountain rocks and dense trees, with only roofs, eaves, and some railings exposed, forming an obvious layering of screening and revealing. | Lower right side: A bridge spans the water, connecting the two banks and assisting in constructing spatial depth.
distinction: Although a bridge in the painting implies a path, the half-screened, half-revealed relationship between the main building complex and the mountain rocks and trees is more prominent, dominating the expression of spatial layering.

evidence: Lower-middle of the painting: A small boat on the water is moving toward the bank, with a person poling, forming a clear clue of movement toward the built elements. | Center of the painting: A thatched house is visible amid tree screening, its roof and lower structure half-hidden and half-exposed, located along the visual extension of the boat's movement.
distinction: Although the built elements have a concealment-and-revelation relationship screened by trees (C2), the painting emphasizes more the dynamic process of the boat approaching the thatched house and its accessibility; C4 better summarizes its role in spatial organization.

evidence: Lower-middle: Several figures on horseback move through gaps between mountain rocks and woods, implying the existence of a path and the direction of travel. | Overall composition: Autumn woods and mountain rocks flank each other, leaving a passage for people and horses to pass through, presenting a spatial process of turning into depth.
distinction: There are no clear built elements in the painting; it mainly depicts the process of people and horses moving through a mountain path in the woods, so it is classified as C4.

evidence: Center of the painting: A group of houses (built elements) is located behind a dense grove of bare trees; roofs, eaves, and window lattices are faintly visible through gaps in the branches, forming an obvious spatial layering of deep woods hiding houses with alternating concealment and revelation. | Lower-middle waterside: A small boat is moored at the bank, near the woodland and house area, but the main built subject is mainly screened by foreground trees; the visual focus is the trees' screening of the buildings rather than direct connectivity by path.
distinction: The core of the painting lies in the screening and revealing of houses by trees (concealment and revelation); although a boat implies the possibility of arrival, the concealment-and-revelation relationship is more prominent and dominant than the clue of movement through the landscape (access to secluded settings).

evidence: Mid-right hillside of the painting: A small pavilion or house is built on a platform protruding from a cliff, presenting the form of a building set on a platform. | Right middle of the painting, at the foot of the mountain: A group of houses is situated in a relatively open and gentle part of the valley, placed alongside the mountain terrain and woods. | Lower-middle col of the painting: Houses conform to the undulations of the mountain and the terrain of the col, presenting a layout distributed according to the slope.
distinction: The buildings mainly present a placement relationship dependent on terrain (set on cliff platform, at the foot of the mountain), emphasizing arrangement according to terrain rather than simply serving as visual markers to mark specific scenery.

evidence: Left cliff: An obvious zigzag stairway or plank road winds upward, connecting the foot of the mountain area with buildings or pavilions higher up, forming a strong upward guiding clue. | Lower right corner: A bridge is visible spanning across, connecting the waterside with the building group on the right, providing a clear path for crossing and entry. | Below and among the middle-ground woods: A small path is faintly visible passing through gaps between trees and mountain rocks, connecting the buildings at the foot of the mountain with scenery in depth, implying an extensible space for travel.
distinction: Although the buildings are distributed according to the mountain terrain (matching C1 characteristics), the prominent long stairway and bridge in the painting form a coherent clue of movement through the landscape, emphasizing the spatial process of going from here to there and deep into the mountains, so C4 is more dominant.

evidence: Lower right corner: Roofs and walls of houses are visible, partially screened by foreground tree branches and foliage, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship.
distinction: Although the built elements serve to mark scenery, their concealment-and-revelation relationship screened by trees is more prominent in the composition, more closely matching the feature of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower left to lower center: a stream winds, with a bridge above connecting the two banks, guiding the eye deeper into the painting. | Lower center, slightly left: a pavilion is built by the water, forming together with the stream and bridge a route for movement through the landscape. | Lower right and center left: houses are partly screened among dense woodland, connected to the outer space by paths or the waterside.
distinction: Although houses are partly screened in the woods, the entry and movement cues formed by the bridge, stream and pavilion are more prominent and organize the spatial layers of the painting.

evidence: Lower left: a thatched pavilion is built between sloping rocks and a bamboo grove, with a railing beside it, becoming the visual focal point of the waterside and sloping-rock scenery there. | Right side and upper area: tall trees with distant mountains and water form an open background, setting off the role of the thatched pavilion in the lower-left corner as a scenic accent.
distinction: Although the thatched pavilion is placed in reliance on the sloping rocks, its main role in the painting is as a scenic accent that concentrates and marks the specific scenery of bamboo, rock and waterside in the lower-left corner.

evidence: Foreground at the bottom of the painting: several houses are partly screened among trees and rocks, with only part of their roofs and walls exposed, forming an evident relation of concealment and revelation. | Middle ground on the right side of the painting: a pavilion is built on a projecting rocky platform, surrounded by mountains, rocks and trees, half hidden and half revealed. | Distant view in the upper-right corner of the painting: a group of buildings on the ridge looms faintly among mountains, rocks and woodland, increasing the spatial layers of the painting.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited according to the mountain (C1), the painting places greater emphasis on the spatial layers and sense of seclusion created by the buildings being screened and revealed by trees and mountains and rocks (C2).

evidence: Center right: behind mountains and rocks or tree clusters rendered in dense ink, two small roofs are exposed, showing an evident relation of screening and revelation and indicating that the buildings lie within the pictorial depth. | Lower right: a pavilion stands on the waterside, its lower part screened by foreground masses of tree ink, creating a layer in which a house is seen through a screen. | Lower-left foreground: pines and a railing (or bridge railing) serve as foreground elements, forming a front-to-back spatial layer with the buildings screened behind ink masses, reinforcing the effect of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed by the water and against the mountain (a C1 feature), the painting places greater emphasis on the layer-by-layer screening of the buildings by dense-ink mountains, rocks and trees and on the exposure of their roofs; the concealment-and-revelation relation constitutes the main spatial layers, so C2 is more dominant.

evidence: Lower area: a small boat carrying several people on the water, presenting a state of movement through the landscape. | Lower center: unpainted space between mountains and rocks and the water surface suggests spatial cues for the boat's travel or entry.
distinction: The painting has no explicit buildings; only the boat and the water space imply the process of traveling through the landscape, so it is assigned to the closest category, C4.

evidence: Middle of the painting, mountainside: a group of buildings is distributed in staggered fashion following the mountain's contours, placed level by level in accordance with the mountain's slopes and terraces, with the roof lines echoing the outlines of the mountains and rocks. | Left side of the painting, mountainside: pavilions and terraces are arranged relying on the mountain rocks and trees/woodland, staggered high and low, closely integrated with the steep mountain terrain. | Lower right corner of the painting, waterside: houses are built facing the water, their building sites/base conforming to the bank's terrain, merging into one with the surrounding trees and mountains and rocks.
distinction: Although the buildings have a partly screened effect of being partially concealed by trees, their characteristics of following the mountain and adapting to the terrain, being placed in accordance with the terrain's terraces, are more prominent and dominant.

evidence: Center of the painting: a sailing boat is hidden in dense reeds, with only its mast and sail exposed, forming an evident relation of concealment and revelation. | Foreground and both sides: dense reeds serve as foreground and middle ground, naturally screening the boat behind them and building front-to-back spatial layers.
distinction: The boat is mainly screened by reeds to create layers, rather than serving as a marker to point out a specific landscape scene.

evidence: Lower half, slightly left of center: a thatched hut, whose roof and the space above it are covered and screened by branches extending from the right. | Lower half, right side: several old trees with gnarled, twisting trunks and branches extending toward the upper left, forming a relation of screening and revealing the thatched hut.
distinction: The painting mainly presents the relation in which the branches and leaves of trees cover and screen the thatched hut, rather than emphasizing the placement of built elements according to mountain forms and slopes.

evidence: Center of the lower half of the painting: a multi-story pagoda stands, its lower part screened by dense-ink trees in the foreground and middle ground, with only the upper part of the pagoda body exposed. | Slightly right of center in the lower half of the painting: to the right of the pagoda is a red-roofed building, likewise partly screened by the trees on the right, with only its roof and part of its walls exposed, presenting a layer in which a house is hidden in the woods. | The lower half of the painting as a whole: heavy tree ink surrounds and screens the lower parts of the built elements, forming evident front-to-back spatial layers and a relation of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the built elements lie among mountains and water and serve as scenic accents, the painting mainly creates spatial layers through the screening of the pagoda and the lower parts of the buildings by dense-ink trees; the feature of concealment and revelation forming a realm is more prominent than mere scenic accentuation.

evidence: Lower half of the painting: depicts faint distant mountains, a broad water surface, nearby red-leaved trees and grass, with a figure standing in the lower right facing the water. | Whole painting: the upper half consists only of plant branches and leaves (reeds or bamboo), and no explicit traces of built elements such as houses, pavilions or bridges appear in the lower half's mountains and water.
distinction: The painting has no explicit man-made built elements; the figure stands under a tree by the bank, and although there are traces of human presence, they do not form an evident path or entry cue; compared with C4, C3 is closer in a broad sense to the figure's role as an accent to the landscape scenery.

evidence: Lower right and lower center: the roofs, eaves and walls of several groups of houses are exposed from behind tall foreground pines and mountains and rocks, forming an evident relation of concealment and revelation. | Center-left lower area: a small building is half hidden behind mountain rocks and trees, with only part of its roof structure exposed. | Center-right upper area: building outlines are faintly visible on the mountain slope, partly screened by the mountain mass and vegetation.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited according to the mountain's form, the painting places greater emphasis on the screening and revealing of the buildings by woodland, mountains and rocks, and the role of concealment and revelation forming a realm is more prominent.

evidence: Lower center: a thatched pavilion is surrounded and screened by luxuriant trees, with only the pavilion roof, pillars and the people inside exposed, forming a spatial layer in which a house is seen in the woods. | Left edge: parts of a multi-story pavilion building are visible, its lower part screened by foreground trees, presenting a relation of concealment and revelation.
distinction: The relation in which trees screen and reveal the buildings is more prominent in organizing the painting's spatial layers than mere placement according to terrain.

evidence: Water surface below: a person wearing a bamboo hat is visible sitting in a small boat, holding a fishing rod, near the bank. | Upper center: steep cliffs with a waterfall flowing down and swirling clouds and mist; no buildings such as houses or bridges.
distinction: The painting has no explicit built elements; the small boat and figure mark the waterside scenery, so it is assigned to C3.

evidence: Lower center: a stone bridge spans the stream, with figures walking on it, connecting the paths on the two banks. | Middle ground to upper right: a winding mountain path extends along the stream valley, with several groups of figures and pack animals traveling along the road, forming an evident cue for movement through the landscape. | Upper left and center-left lower area: there are pavilions on the mountain slope, with a pavilion among tree clusters screening it, serving as spatial nodes after the path leads deeper.
distinction: Although there are buildings screened by woodland in the painting, the continuous mountain path, bridges and traveling figures form a strong guide for movement through the landscape, making access to secluded settings the dominant mode of spatial organization.

evidence: Lower center: a figure is visible sitting between pines and mountains and rocks; no explicit built structures such as houses or bridges are seen. | Overall painting: the painting is dominated by towering peaks and dense pines, with the figure as a scenic accent concentrating the painting's visual focus.
distinction: No explicit built elements (such as houses) are seen in the painting; the figure, as a scenic accent, gives the landscape scenery a resting point, so it is assigned to C3; if the concealment-and-revelation relation between the figure and the pines and rocks is regarded as the main mode of composing the scene, it approaches C2.

evidence: Lower part of the painting: a lofty scholar stands, a servant boy walks, and a donkey (or horse) is visible; the figures and animal present the dynamics of traveling or touring, implying activity of moving through the landscape. | Bottom of the painting and among the mountains and rocks: unpainted ground and the edges of mountains and rocks form an implied passage space, which together with the figures' movement constitutes a path cue for movement through the landscape. | Center to upper part of the painting: tall pines and the sloping bank on the right form the main natural environment, with the figures active beneath the trees and beside the mountain, presenting a sense of spatial process from here to there.
distinction: Although the painting has no man-made built elements, the traveling dynamics of the figures and the donkey and the organization of ground space emphasize more the process and path of movement through the landscape (C4), rather than merely pointing out a single static scene (C3).

evidence: Lower center: a group of houses is partly screened by the dense branches and leaves of surrounding trees, with roofs, doors and windows and people inside revealed through gaps in the woodland, forming evident layers of concealment and revelation. | Upper center: above the source of the waterfall is a group of buildings, half hidden behind mountains, rocks and trees, with only part of their roofs and outlines exposed.
distinction: Although the built elements accent the area beside the waterfall and in the deep mountains, the painting places greater emphasis on the spatial layers formed by the screening and revealing of the buildings by woodland, mountains and rocks, rather than their serving merely as landmarks.

evidence: Upper center and right mountain slope: groups of houses are distributed irregularly following the mountain slopes and the terrain of the mountain hollows, presenting a layout placed according to the slopes and unfolding along the mountain. | Upper-right mountain top: a pavilion is built on the mountain-top platform, placed according to the high terrain and corresponding to the form of the peak. | Lower center: there are also built elements at the mountain foot and near the water, the whole arranged level by level with the height of the mountain form, reflecting a relation of placement according to the ground.
distinction: Although trees partly screen the houses, the dominant feature of the built elements is being arranged level by level in conformity with the mountain slopes and the terrain of the mountain hollows, rather than using concealment and revelation as the main means of composing the scene.

evidence: Slightly left of center in the painting: behind trees and mountains and rocks, horizontal and vertical lines sketched in pale ink are visible, suspected to be house or fence structures, partly screened by foreground woodland. | Center of the painting: mountains, rocks and trees are interwoven, forming front-to-back spatial layers; the suspected built elements are hidden among the woods and rocks, presenting a relation of concealment and revelation.
distinction: The suspected built elements in the painting are mainly screened by woodland, mountains and rocks, presenting a layered relation in which a house is hidden in the woods, rather than clearly showing a layout placed according to terrain.

evidence: Slightly right of center in the painting: a group of buildings is partly screened by foreground trees and the sloping bank, with only roofs and walls exposed, forming spatial layers of concealment and revelation. | Left side of the painting: a small bridge spans the water surface, connecting the two banks and implying a path leading to the buildings.
distinction: Although a bridge in the painting implies a path, the concealment-and-revelation relation of the buildings among the woodland is more prominent and constitutes the painting's main spatial layers, so C2 is more apt than C4.

evidence: Center-left mountain slope of the painting: the roof and part of the walls of a house are visible screened by woods, presenting a half-hidden, half-revealed state. | Waterside on the right side of the painting: through gaps in the trees, a person sits on a platform or bank facing the water, forming layers with the surrounding woodland.
distinction: Although the house is on the mountain slope, the painting places greater emphasis on its layered relation of being screened and revealed by woodland, rather than merely emphasizing its placement according to terrain.

evidence: Right side: behind mountain-slope trees, the roof and part of the walls of a house are visible, partly screened by branches and leaves and mountains and rocks | Lower right: in front of the house is a low fence or low wall, interwoven with the surrounding vegetation
distinction: The painting's emphasis lies in the sense of layers formed by the screening and revealing of the buildings by trees, mountains and rocks, rather than emphasizing the correspondence of buildings placed according to terrain.

evidence: Right part of the right fan: several thatched huts are visible, part of their bodies and roofs screened by the trees and sloping bank in front, presenting a half-hidden, half-revealed state. | Left part to center of the right fan: cliffs, waterfalls and trees occupy the main space, forming a front-to-back layered contrast with the built elements on the right.
distinction: Although the thatched huts are built on the waterside slope, the painting places greater emphasis on the screening of the buildings by trees and the sloping bank, building spatial layers through the concealment-and-revelation relation, so C2 is more apt than C1.

evidence: Lower part of the painting, toward the right: a waterside pavilion or kiosk is visible built directly on the waterside, its base structure conforming to the shoreline, presenting a form of setting a house by the water. | Lower center of the painting: the built elements form a direct spatial correspondence with the broad water surface and the mountain-rock sloping bank on the left, the layout relying on the natural terrain.
distinction: Although the built elements serve to mark the waterside scenery, their placement in reliance on the water and in conformity with the shoreline is more prominent, so C1 is more apt than C3.

evidence: Lower left: among the waterside tree clusters are very pale lines, suspected to be the outlines of a tiny pavilion or waterside kiosk, but the details are blurred and hard to confirm. | Overall: the painting is dominated by mountains and rocks, trees and the waterside, with built elements extremely indistinct; only in the lower-left corner are there suspected traces of a scenic accent.
distinction: The suspected built elements are located in an open waterside spot and, if present, serve as a scenic accent; no other evident cues for spatial organization.

evidence: Whole painting: the painting consists mainly of cliffs, waterfalls, woods and distant mountains; no explicit built elements such as houses, pavilions, bridges or paths are seen.
distinction: The painting consists purely of natural landscape, with no identifiable built elements participating in spatial organization; it is assigned to the closest category based on the overall visible space.

evidence: Center-right lower area: behind the trees, the roof and pillars of a thatched hut are visible, partly screened by leaves and branches, forming a relation of concealment and revelation. | Lower-left corner: a small boat on the water with two people aboard, serving as scenic accents. | Slightly right of center: dense trees occupy the foreground, with the building hidden behind the tree clusters, presenting a spatial layer in which a house is seen in the woods.
distinction: The building participates in composing the scene mainly through its screening-and-revealing relation with the trees, forming spatial layers, rather than serving merely as a conspicuous landmark accenting the landscape.

evidence: Left middle ground: a group of buildings is half screened by dense trees, with only part of the roofs and wall structures exposed, forming a relation of concealment and revelation. | Right edge: part of another building is revealed, screened by a large foreground tree, increasing the painting's spatial layers.
distinction: Although there is a bridge in the painting, it does not form an evident touring route guiding entry to the built elements; the buildings participate in composing the scene mainly through the screening of trees.

evidence: Lower left to lower center: a stone-step path is visible extending from the lower-left corner, following the sloping bank toward the water. | Lower-center waterside: a waterside pavilion is built by the water, its lower part supported by pillars standing in the water, the path's endpoint pointing to this built structure, forming an accessible spatial connection.
distinction: Although the built elements are placed facing the water, the painting places greater emphasis on the spatial process of guiding the eye and the touring route through the stone-step path toward the building, rather than merely emphasizing its layout built according to the terrain.

evidence: Middle ground: the roofs of a group of buildings emerge from dense woods, their walls and bases screened by trees, forming an evident relation of concealment and revelation. | Upper right: a pavilion stands on a mountain ridge, surrounded by trees and mountains and rocks, part of its structure screened by scenery. | Left side: a small bridge over the stream connects the two banks, implying spatial connectivity, but the main visual focus lies in the screening interplay between the buildings and the woodland.
distinction: In the painting, the concealment-and-revelation relation between the buildings and the woodland (screening) is more prominent and dominant than the guidance of paths (access to seclusion); the middle-ground buildings are entirely hidden in the woods with only their roofs exposed, a typical concealment and revelation forming a realm.

evidence: Center-right of the painting: the roofs and walls of several houses emerge from behind dense trees and rocks, showing a clear concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Left side of the painting: the water surface meets the woodland, and pale-ink mountain peaks appear in the distance, setting off the layering of the built elements screened by the foreground trees.
distinction: Although there is a clue resembling a small bridge on the left side of the painting, the most prominent compositional role of the built elements is the layering formed by their concealment and revelation by trees and rocks, rather than an emphasis on a path of entry.

evidence: Lower right: a small canopied boat (or a small waterside structure) is moored at the water's edge, beside which a single person sits fishing, identifying the waterside scenery here. | Upper middle: the pale silhouettes of distant mountains and the trees on the sloping bank form an open expanse of water, and the canopied boat in the lower-right corner becomes the visual anchor.
distinction: Although the canopied boat sits beside the waterside, its main role is to serve as a scenic accent that concentrates the visual focus in the lower-right corner of the painting, rather than to emphasize a building layout arranged according to the terrain.

evidence: Central water surface: there is a small boat with several people aboard, one punting with a pole, situated on the open water, forming the visual focus of the painting. | Upper left and lower right: pine trees, willow trees, and clumps of reeds are painted on the two banks, forming a lakeside landscape and creating an opening-and-closing relationship with the water surface.
distinction: Although the small boat carries a sense of movement through the landscape and points toward the bank, the painting lacks a clear built structure as a destination or as a link to a path; it functions mainly as an identifying scenic accent of the lake view.

evidence: Lower-right corner: built elements (a pavilion and a water-side pavilion) sit on the bank, largely screened by dense trees (weeping willows) and rocks, with only the roof, eaves, and part of the structure exposed, forming a clear layering of concealment and revelation. | Lower-right corner: branches and leaves cover and surround the buildings, leaving the built elements in a half-hidden, half-visible state, so that natural scenery participates in forming the scene through screening.
distinction: The relationship of screening and revealing between the trees and the buildings (concealment and revelation) is more prominent than the correspondence between the buildings and the terrain, and dominates the spatial layering.

evidence: Lower left and lower center: a small boat is moored on the water, with dense reeds and shrubs in the foreground; the hull is behind or beside the vegetation, forming a local layering of screening and revelation. | Right side: tall autumn-forest trees occupy the right side of the painting, their branches and leaves extending toward the upper left, forming a front-to-back spatial relationship with the small boat on the water; the built elements stand on the waterside bank screened by trees.
distinction: The small boat is mainly surrounded and screened by the foreground reeds and the trees on the right, presenting a spatial layering of concealment and revelation, rather than serving merely as an isolated marker identifying a particular peak or valley mouth.

evidence: Lower right: a water-side pavilion is built on waterside sloping rocks; its roof, columns, and the people inside are clearly visible, and the building base is directly against the waterside and the sloping rocks. | Lower right to middle right: the trunks, branches, and needles of several foreground pine trees interpose in front of the water-side pavilion, clearly screening and revealing the building and constituting a spatial layering of concealment and revelation. | Middle left: a small boat is on the river surface, echoing the built elements on the right bank across the water space, but no clear path connecting to the shore is visible.
distinction: Although the building is constructed against the waterside sloping rocks, the interposing and screening relationship of the pine trees to the building is more prominent in the painting, dominating the way the built elements and nature form the scene.

evidence: Lower right: two people are active in a bamboo grove, beside which is level ground or the start of a small path, suggesting the beginning of a journey. | Middle left: a clear stepped path is painted among the mountain rocks and sloping bank, winding upward. | Upper left: the stepped path leads to the mountainside, where the roofs and walls of a building group are visible, forming the endpoint of the path.
distinction: Through the winding stepped path, the painting clearly connects the figures below with the buildings on the mountain, emphasizing an enterable and reachable process of movement through the landscape; the guiding role of the path is more significant than mere placement according to the mountain.

evidence: Center and left mountainside of the painting: dense pine forest and huge rocks screen the built elements over a large area, revealing only the roof of the central multi-story building (pagoda/pavilion) and the eaves on the left mountainside, presenting a typical spatial layering of houses hidden in the forest and houses seen behind the rocks. | Lower-right corner of the painting: waterside houses, a bridge, and a path with people walking are visible, but the main large-scale built elements of the painting lie deep in the pine forest, their existence suggested mainly through the screening and revelation by the trees rather than directly connected by a path.
distinction: Although the lower-right corner contains a path and bridge hinting at a movement-through-the-landscape thread, the main large-scale built elements of the painting construct spatial layering mainly through screening and revelation by the pine forest and rocks; the feature of concealment and revelation forming the scene is more dominant in compositional proportion and visual focus.

evidence: Middle ground, slightly left: the pavilion building is screened on its left side and behind by several tall pine trees, exposing the roof, eaves, and railing, presenting a screening relationship of a house seen in the forest. | Middle ground: clouds and mist swirl around the building, forming a layer of spatial separation that further emphasizes the concealment-and-revelation relationship, making the built elements faintly visible. | Lower-right corner: although there is a wooden bridge and figures walking, the path does not directly connect to the pavilion building, being cut off by the pine forest and mist, so no clear route entering the built elements is formed.
distinction: Although there is a bridge and path with figures moving through the landscape in the lower part of the painting, the main built elements (the pavilion) lack a directly visible connection with the path; their concealment-and-revelation relationship, screened by trees and mist, is more prominent and independently forms the scene.

evidence: Lower middle: two people walk along a path beside a stream, the path winding toward the waterfall and mist in the depth of the painting, forming a clear movement-through-the-landscape thread. | Lower-left corner: houses are built following the mountain terrain, partly screened by trees and rocks, serving as a possible destination of the path or scenery along the way. | Overall composition: the stream, path, and the distant waterfall and mist echo one another, guiding the eye from near to far into the mountain forest and presenting a spatial process of proceeding from one place to another.
distinction: Although the houses in the lower-left corner have the feature of concealment and revelation forming the scene, the movement-through-the-landscape thread of the figures following the path deep into the mountain forest is more prominent and dominates the sense of spatial entry.

evidence: Left side and lower part of the painting: trees, rocks, and shoreline are painted, with no fixed built elements such as houses visible. | Central water surface of the painting: a small boat is visible, with a person aboard, forming the main man-made element in the painting. | Right side of the painting: the water surface is open, with faint brushstrokes on the distant shore, and the space is expansive.
distinction: The painting has no clear built elements; the small boat, as a scenic accent, marks the water space and, although it hints at a water route, does not present a movement-through-the-landscape thread connecting to built elements, so it is classified as scenic accentuation.

evidence: The painting as a whole: it mainly depicts pine trees, rocks, flowers and plants, and several flying birds, with no houses, bridges, or other man-made built elements visible. | Left side and center: rocks and plants form the natural scenery, with birds perching and flying among them, and no buildings participating in the spatial organization.
distinction: The painting has no built elements and consists solely of natural scenery and birds; it is therefore classified as scenic accentuation, as the closest expression of natural space.

evidence: Lower center: the houses are partly screened by the trunk, branches, and leaves of a large foreground tree, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship | Middle right: the houses are screened within the woodland, with only part of the roof and walls exposed | Overall: the built elements rely on screening and revelation by trees and other natural scenery, presenting spatial layering within the forest
