distinction: Although the houses are built against the mountain, the painting emphasizes more the spatial layering formed by the screening and revelation of the houses by trees.

evidence: Middle-lower right: amid dense pine forest and mixed trees, the roof, eaves, and part of the wall of a pavilion are revealed, the building deeply hidden behind the woodland. | Middle left, slightly low: where rocks and trees interweave, the roof of a pavilion or small hut is faintly visible, partly screened by foreground pine branches and rocks. | Overall painting: neither group of built elements is fully revealed; instead, they rely on the surrounding dense trees and rocks to form layering of screening and revelation, presenting the pictorial depth of houses seen in the forest.
distinction: Although a stream, a small boat, and a small bridge in the lower part of the painting hint at a movement-through-the-landscape thread, the main role of the built elements in the composition is to form spatial layering through screening by trees and rocks, rather than to serve as the endpoint or entrance of path guidance.

evidence: Lower right: an arched bridge spans the stream, and a person holding a staff stands on the bridge or at its head, forming a clear crossing point and starting point of movement through the landscape. | Lower middle to left side: the stream bank and path wind toward the depth of the painting and to the left, connecting the bridge with the woodland houses, forming a visual guide from one place to another. | Middle left: houses (thatched huts) appear faintly behind pine trees and rocks, serving as the direction in which the path extends and presenting an approachable spatial relationship.
distinction: Although the houses on the left are screened by trees (a C2 feature), the painting constructs a stronger movement-through-the-landscape thread and process of entering the depths (C4) through the bridge, figures, and winding path, which dominates the spatial organization.

evidence: Lower-left corner: the roofs and eaves of houses are visible, partly screened by the surrounding trees and sloping rocks, presenting a screening relationship. | Lower middle of the painting: pine trees and rocks form the foreground, creating a spatial layering of concealment and revelation with the built elements in the lower-left corner.
distinction: Although the built elements follow the mountain terrain, the painting emphasizes more the layering relationship formed by the screening and revelation of the built elements by trees.

evidence: Lower right, slightly center: an arched bridge is visible spanning the water surface/valley, with pedestrians on the bridge connecting the paths on both banks and forming a clear thread of entry and movement through the landscape. | Left middle ground: a pavilion is screened behind trees and rocks, serving as a potential destination toward which the path extends. | Distant mountain ridges: the outlines of pavilions are faintly visible among the ridges, suggesting spatial layering extending into the depths.
distinction: Although the pavilion on the left has the feature of concealment and revelation forming the scene (C2), the movement-through-the-landscape thread formed by the bridge and path runs through the foreground and middle ground and dominates the enterable spatial organization, so C4 is more appropriate.

evidence: Center-right: a group of pavilions and covered corridors is arranged directly against the cliff and sloping bank on the right, unfolding in response to the waterside terrain. | Lower center: wooden piles supporting the built elements are visible beneath them, raising them above the water surface, and the building base forms a clear correspondence with the water body and shoreline. | Left side: foreground trees and the right cliff form a flanking enclosure, and the built elements sit at the valley mouth beside the water between the two, placed according to the terrain.
distinction: Although the trees form some screening, the core compositional role of the built elements lies in their terrain-responsive placement directly against the cliff and waterside, rather than in layering of concealment and revelation as the main feature.

evidence: Center-right mountainside: a group of houses is half-hidden behind rocks and woodland, with only the roofs and part of the walls exposed, forming a clear layering of concealment and revelation. | Lower foreground: a building sits on waterside rocks, surrounded and screened by dense trees, presenting a spatial relationship of houses seen in the forest. | Left mountainside: a small pavilion is hidden in the sloping-bank woodland, with only its top exposed, forming the scene through screening by trees.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed against the mountain and beside the water, the painting emphasizes more the spatial layering formed by the buildings' screening and revelation by trees and rocks, so C2 is more dominant than C1.

evidence: Lower left to middle left: a small boat is on the water, the person aboard facing the shore, where a wooden bridge connects the water and the land, forming a clear thread of landing and entry. | Center to right side: behind the wooden bridge a small path extends through dense bamboo grove toward a half-revealed thatched hut on the right, presenting a spatial process of moving from outside to inside and approaching the built elements. | Behind the bamboo grove on the right: the thatched hut is screened by the bamboo grove, with only the roof and part of the posts exposed, serving as the endpoint of the movement-through-the-landscape thread and suggesting a reachable dwelling.
distinction: Although the thatched hut has a concealment-and-revelation relationship through screening by the bamboo grove, the painting highlights more the entry route linked by boat, bridge, and path, making C4 a better fit for the overall spatial organization than C2 screening alone.

evidence: Middle ground, slightly right: behind the woodland a thatched roof is revealed, the main body of the building screened by trees, forming a layering of a house seen across a spatial separation. | Middle ground, slightly lower left: within a dense clump of willow trees, a wooden bridge or plank walkway with red railings is faintly visible, the bridge half-screened by branches and leaves.
distinction: Although the bridge in the painting suggests passage, its main visual role, together with the thatched hut, is to be screened by trees, emphasizing the layering of concealment and revelation forming the scene, rather than showing a complete process of movement and entry.

evidence: Right middle ground: a simply drawn small bridge on the water connects the two banks, forming a path across the water surface. | Lower-left foreground: a person sits at the waterside on a projecting plank or small bridge, suggesting a stopping point and entry point at the waterside. | Upper-left middle ground: houses are built against the mountain on the mountainside, serving as a possible destination of the path or a node along the way.
distinction: Although the mountainside houses are placed according to the mountain terrain, the path thread formed by the small bridge over the water and the foreground waterside platform is more coherent, emphasizing the process of movement through the landscape from one place to another.

evidence: Middle left of the painting: a group of pavilion buildings is supported by dense vertical wooden piles and built directly between the water surface and the mountain hollow, placed in response to the waterside terrain. | Right side of the painting and around the buildings: the rocks and trees on the right partly screen the buildings, but the relationship of the building base to the mountain and water remains clearly discernible.
distinction: Although the buildings are partly screened by rocks and trees, their terrain-responsive placement, with houses built on piles over the water, is more prominent and dominant.

evidence: Top of the hill on the right: a multi-story pagoda stands above the ridge woodland, prominently positioned, becoming the visual focus of that hill. | Middle-right of the painting: the pagoda echoes spatially with the open water surface and distant mountains on the left, identifying the scenic character of the hill beside the water.
distinction: The pagoda, as a landmark building, identifies and concentrates the scenery of that hill; no clear path guidance or layering of concealment and revelation is visible.

evidence: Center-right: two thatched-roof buildings are partly screened by the branches of foreground withered trees, exposing the roofs and part of the walls and corridor columns. | Right side: a huge rock on the right screens the right side of the buildings, forming front-to-back layering and leaving the buildings in a half-hidden, half-revealed state.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed against the mountain and beside the water, the most prominent spatial expression in the painting is the layering of concealment and revelation formed by screening with trees and rocks, rather than an emphasis on their layout in relation to the terrain.

evidence: Middle-lower right: a group of houses is visible, their roofs, walls, and railings partly screened by foreground tree branches and leaves, presenting a half-hidden, half-revealed state. | Lower center: dense woodland and rocks screen the built elements behind them, forming a clear front-to-back spatial layering.
distinction: Although the buildings are built against the mountain, the painting emphasizes more the spatial layering formed by the screening and revelation of the buildings by trees, so C2 is more appropriate than C1.

evidence: Right slope: a thatched hut is visible, partly screened by trees and bamboo in front of it. | Lower center of the painting: there is a small bridge, on which a figure is walking toward the thatched hut on the right. | Overall composition: the small bridge, the figure, and the thatched hut on the right slope form a recognizable movement-through-the-landscape thread, expressing a spatial process of proceeding from one place to another and approaching the built elements.
distinction: Although the thatched hut has a concealment-and-revelation relationship through screening by trees, the clear route of travel and the relationship of entry formed among the small bridge, figure, and thatched hut are more prominent in the composition, so C4 is more appropriate than C2.

evidence: Lower left: a thatched-roof pavilion is half-hidden behind the sloping bank and trees, with only the roof and part of the columns exposed, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Right mountainside: another building (appearing to be a water-side pavilion) clings among the rocks, partly obscured by the ink tones of the mountain, forming spatial layering. | Lower-right water surface: a small boat echoes the built elements on the bank, but its main compositional role still lies in the screening of the buildings by the mountain forest.
distinction: Although boats and the sloping bank hint at a movement-through-the-landscape thread, the built elements participate in forming the scene mainly through screening and revelation by trees and rocks, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship is more prominent.

evidence: Middle right: a small pavilion or building is visible among the trees on the slope, of small size. | Right side: a winding path or ridge line extends upward from the lower-right of the painting toward the pavilion, forming a movement-through-the-landscape thread. | Overall composition: the path connects with the built elements, presenting a spatial process of proceeding from one place to another and approaching the built elements.
distinction: Although the pavilion also serves as a scenic accent, the clear path guidance in the painting emphasizes more the enterable spatial process, so C4 is more appropriate.

evidence: Right side and center of the painting: large expanses of reeds grow thickly, and a flock of wild geese swims, rests, or flaps their wings in the water, forming the main subject of the painting. | Upper part of the painting: several wild geese fly in the air in various postures. | Left side of the painting: the water surface is open, with reeds rendered in pale ink in the distance, and an inscription and seals in the upper-left corner.
distinction: No built elements (buildings, bridges, etc.) are visible in the painting, only the natural scenery of reeds and geese; it is classified as C3 because the gathering of the geese serves to identify the autumn river scenery and, though not built elements, is the closest available category in the absence of built elements.

evidence: Center-left of the painting, on the water surface: a small boat carrying two people is moving toward the built elements on the right side of the painting, forming a clear travel clue. | Right side of the painting, waterside: a thatched-roof pavilion is built on wooden posts at the water's edge, serving as the destination and visual anchor of the boat's movement. | Right side of the painting, behind the pavilion: woodland screens the area behind the pavilion, adding a sense of spatial layering, but does not change the main dynamic of the boat guiding toward the built elements.
distinction: Although the built elements are sited by the water, the painting places greater emphasis on the travel process of the boat approaching the built structures, so C4 is more dominant than C1.

evidence: Lower left and center: the roof and parts of the wall of a house are visible, partly blocked by trees and mountains and rocks in the foreground and middle ground, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation. | The painting as a whole: the built elements appear intermittently among the woodland and mountains and rocks, creating spatial layering through screening and exposure, rather than being fully open or an isolated scenic accent.

distinction: Although the plank walkway and houses also embody placement nestling against mountains and water (C1), the painting constructs a strong process of travel from the foreground deep into the background through the bridge, figures, and long plank walkway; C4 better captures this spatial organization.

evidence: Foreground sloping bank: tiny figures and horses are visible among the trees, suggesting a route of travel on land. | Middle-ground water surface: a small boat is on the open water, suggesting waterborne transport and a thread of travel. | Overall composition: the painting extends from the foreground sloping bank, rocks, and trees to the middle-ground water surface and distant mountain ranges, forming a traversable spatial layering.
distinction: The painting lacks identifiable built structures to punctuate or concentrate a particular scene, but the figures and boat provide parallel land and water travel threads, presenting a sense of spatial process from here to there; hence C4 fits better than C3.

evidence: Middle ground, slightly left: a multi-storey pavilion is built tier upon tier on a mountainside terrace according to the mountain's form, its base corresponding to the slope's shape, presenting a state of setting houses on a platform. | Lower right and foreground: the building group is arranged by the waterside, with steps leading down to the water, staggered according to the heights of the slope, presenting an unfolding along the bank and distribution along the slope. | Overall layout: the built structures extend from the water's edge to the mountainside, and the buildings' heights and manner of unfolding form a clear corresponding relationship with the mountain forms and waterside.
distinction: Although the foreground trees clearly screen the buildings (a C2 feature), the core of the painting lies in the building group's high-and-low layout conforming to the mountain forms and waterside; the determining role of terrain for the placement of the built structures (C1) is stronger than a mere relationship of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower left: a group of houses is visible, including roofs and walls, with a horizontally arranged linear structure in front (appearing to be a fence, steps, or waterside); the buildings are placed on this base on the slope at the mountain foot. | Lower middle of the painting: the buildings are located below/beside tall pines and rocks, laid out in conformity with the terrain at the mountain foot, presenting a form of setting houses on a platform/along the slope.
distinction: Although trees screen the buildings nearby, the building bases (fence/terrace) and layout are clearly visible, chiefly expressing a relationship of placement according to terrain rather than relying solely on screening to signal their presence.

evidence: Center to upper-middle of the painting: a clearly winding stone-step path extends upward from the mid-slope courtyard directly to the pavilion at the summit, forming a definite route of entry and ascent. | Lower-middle and lower-left corner of the painting: several built elements (the mid-slope courtyard, the houses in the lower-left corner) echo one another through paths and terrain, presenting spatial layers that can be traveled through and reached. | Upper-middle of the painting: the summit pavilion, as the end point of the path, is surrounded by mountains, rocks, and trees, reinforcing the sense of a destination deep in a secluded setting.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed according to the mountain terrain, the continuous path in the painting links buildings at different elevations, emphasizing the process of moving from one to another and going deep into the mountains; therefore C4 is more dominant than C1.

evidence: Lower-right to lower-middle of the painting: a group of buildings is surrounded by dense pines and mixed trees; roofs, eaves, and walls are partly visible and partly hidden among the branches and leaves, forming a clear layering of concealment and revelation. | Left-middle of the painting: several houses are visible on the mid-slope, distributed unevenly according to the mountain terrain, some screened by rocks and trees, presenting a state of being screened by woodland and rock. | Overall painting: the built elements are not fully exposed but are screened by the dense trees of the foreground and middle ground, merging the buildings into the natural scenery and constituting a deep spatial layering.
distinction: Although the buildings are arranged according to mountain and water, the painting places greater emphasis on constructing spatial layers through the screening and revealing by trees, rocks, and mountains; the feature of concealment and revelation is more dominant.

evidence: Lower-middle: a wooden bridge spans a stream, with pedestrians on the bridge; behind the bridge it connects to a small path leading into the depth of the painting. | Middle ground, slightly left: steps ascending along the mountain terrain are visible, with figures walking on them, connecting the foot of the mountain with higher ground. | Middle ground right and lower-right corner: building groups and pavilions are distributed on the mid-slope and by the bank, connected to the foreground through paths and bridges, forming a spatial sequence that can be traveled through.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed according to the mountain terrain, the painting places greater emphasis on guiding the eye and the travel route through bridges, steps, and paths, giving the space a dynamic process of entry and deepening.

evidence: Middle-right: a group of buildings is screened behind pines and rocks, with only parts of the roofs, eaves, and bases exposed, forming a clear layering of concealment and revelation. | Left-middle mid-slope: building outlines are faintly visible amid the screening trees, indicating the presence of built elements deep in the space. | Foreground to middle ground: dense pines and undulating rocks form a foreground barrier that partly screens and partly reveals the buildings behind, strengthening the pictorial depth.
distinction: Although the buildings are arranged according to the mountain terrain, the painting places greater emphasis on the relationship of screening and revealing between the trees, rocks, and buildings; the role of concealment and revelation in forming the setting is more prominent.

evidence: Lower-middle and left of the painting: multiple groups of houses and villages are scattered among the slopes and woods; roofs and walls are partly screened by branches and leaves, presenting a layering of partial concealment and partial exposure. | Lower-middle of the painting: the houses are distributed according to the mountain terrain and woods, and the screening by trees creates a spatial depth of alternating concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the painting has bridges and paths connecting the houses, the built elements are mainly merged into the natural environment by being surrounded and screened by trees; the relationship of concealment and revelation is more prominent in the composition.

evidence: Middle-right mountain hollow: the partial structure of a building is faintly revealed between the rocks and the trees, partly screened by natural scenery. | Lower-middle among the trees: two people sit facing each other before a table, in a semi-open space surrounded by trees and rocks, forming a layering of building beneath the trees.
distinction: The built elements mainly construct spatial layers through the screening and revealing by rocks and trees, rather than emphasizing the responsive correspondence between their sites and the terrain.

evidence: Lower-middle right of the painting: two houses and a fence are visible, partly screened by the surrounding trees and slope rocks, presenting spatial layers of alternating concealment and revelation. | Right bank of the painting: the buildings are half hidden behind the trees, with roofs and walls revealed through the gaps in the foliage, using natural scenery to create a visual effect of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the buildings face the water and back onto the mountain, the painting places greater emphasis on the layered relationship of their being screened and revealed by trees and slope rocks, rather than on placement by terrain alone.

evidence: Upper-middle: a thatched hut is hidden among the rocks and trees, with only the roof and part of the structure exposed, presenting a layering of seeing a house within the woods through concealment and revelation. | Lower-left to middle: dense trees and rocks surround the built elements, forming a clear relationship of screening and revealing.
distinction: Although there is a stone-step path in the lower-left of the painting that guides the eye deeper, the built elements themselves are mainly presented through the screening of trees and rocks as a layering of concealment and revelation, and the path does not directly and clearly connect to these built elements.

evidence: Lower-right: a two-story pavilion is placed tight against the cliff on the right, with eaves and structure clearly visible. | Lower-right: an arched bridge spans the water, connecting the right bank where the pavilion is located with the wooded slope on the left, forming a definite passage route. | Lower-middle: unpainted space is left on the water surface and the bank; together with the arc of the bridge, it suggests spatial extension from this bank toward the pavilion.
distinction: Although the pavilion is built against the cliff, the painting clearly constructs a travel path through the bridge that connects the two banks and leads to the building; therefore the guiding role of access to secluded settings is more prominent.

evidence: Lower-right: one person sits alone on a slope rock beneath a tree | Lower-left: one person on a slope rock appears to be walking or pausing | Upper part of the painting: distant mountains, a waterfall, and flying birds are visible, with no trace of buildings
distinction: The painting has no identifiable built elements; the figures' activity within the landscape suggests a spatial process of traveling into the setting, so it is classified as C4.

evidence: Whole painting: only pine branches, a full moon, plum blossoms, bamboo leaves, and slope rocks at the bottom are visible; no buildings, bridges, or traces of artificial construction are seen. | Lower-middle: pine, bamboo, plum, and rocks screen and combine with one another, forming a purely natural landscape of plants and rocks.
distinction: The painting contains no built elements at all; based on the overall visible combination of natural scenery, it is only barely assigned to C3 as scenic accentuation, but it lacks actual evidence of buildings accentuating the scenery.

evidence: Lower-right side: several houses are located among the pines and rocks; roofs and walls are partly exposed and screened by the foreground rocks and pine branches and leaves, forming a layering of houses hidden in the woods. | Lower-center: tall pines stand upright, their branches and needles covering part of the buildings, so that the built elements appear half hidden and half exposed.
distinction: The painting focuses on the layering of concealment and revelation formed by trees and rocks screening the houses, rather than on a spatial process of entry guided by paths or fords.

evidence: Middle ground right: a group of buildings (pavilions and towers) is partly screened by trees and clouds and mist; the exposed roofs, eaves, and bases indicate their presence, forming spatial layers of concealment and revelation. | Lower part to middle ground of the painting: paths and figures are visible; the path extends toward the buildings in the middle ground, suggesting a spatial relationship of entry.
distinction: The buildings form the scene mainly through screening and revealing by trees and clouds and mist; the relationship of concealment and revelation is more prominent than the guiding role of the path.

evidence: Middle-ground right mid-slope: houses are distributed unevenly according to the mountain terrain, placed level by level in response to the slope. | Middle-ground left mountain: village houses gather on the gentle ground at the foot of the mountain, coordinated with the surrounding mountain forms and waterside. | Lower-left and lower-right corners: buildings are built facing the water or against rocks and trees, presenting features of unfolding along the bank and siting houses according to the ground.
distinction: Although some buildings are screened by trees, the painting places greater emphasis on how the building groups as a whole are laid out according to natural conditions such as mountain forms, slope terraces, and the waterside.

evidence: Left mountainside (slightly left of the painting's center): a group of buildings is distributed in overlapping layers following the mountain's form, showing a clear characteristic of separate placement according to the slope, with the building bases closely corresponding to the mountain's slope terraces. | Lower left corner: several houses are sited facing the waterside or on level ground, their layout unfolding in conformity with the terrain. | Overall composition: the uneven heights of the built structures correspond to the rises and hollows of the mountain form, presenting a spatial relationship of siting according to the ground and attaining suitability by following the terrain.
distinction: Although trees screen the surroundings of the buildings (consistent with C2 concealment), the layout characteristic of buildings being separately placed according to the slope and sited in conformity with the mountain terrain (C1) is more dominant in the spatial organization.

evidence: Right mid-slope: the building group is screened among dense pines and rocks; roofs and walls are faintly visible, forming a clear layering of concealment and revelation. | Lower-left and lower-middle: waterside houses and bridges are partly screened by the branches and leaves of foreground trees, presenting a spatial relationship of seeing houses through a screen. | Middle of the painting: several houses are scattered among the mountains and woods, their presence revealed through the screening of rocks and trees.
distinction: Although the built elements are also placed according to mountain and water, the painting places greater emphasis on the relationship of concealment and revelation and the spatial layers in which buildings are half screened by trees and rocks; therefore C2 is more apt.

evidence: Lower-right: an arched bridge is visible spanning the water, connecting the two banks; one end of the bridge leads to a waterside pavilion or kiosk, forming a definite entry path. | Lower-left: several houses are arranged at the foot of the mountain and among the woods, merging with the surrounding waterside and trees, suggesting a space for dwelling and travel. | Lower part of the overall painting: built elements, bridges, water, and rocks together organize a landscape space that can be entered and traveled through.
distinction: Although the built elements' placement according to mountain and water reflects terrain-responsive siting, the combination of bridges and waterside buildings more strongly emphasizes spatial clues of entry and travel; therefore C4 is more dominant.

evidence: Lower-left: a courtyard building group is half hidden behind slope terraces and trees, with only parts of the roofs, eaves, and walls exposed, forming spatial layers of foreground-background screening. | Lower-middle: a freestanding house is partly screened by the branches, leaves, and trunks of foreground trees, presenting a screening relationship of a house hidden among the woods. | Lower-right: a stream and rocks are visible, but no definite bridge or path directly connecting to the above built elements is seen.
distinction: Although the built elements also respond to the slope-terrace terrain, the painting places greater emphasis on the relationship of screening and revealing between the buildings and the trees, thereby constructing pictorial depth and layering.

evidence: Lower-left to lower-middle of the painting: a bridge spanning the water is visible, connecting the land on both banks and forming a definite passage clue. | Middle ground to distant right bank: several houses and villages are distributed along the waterside and slopes, extending deeper in response to the water flow and mountain terrain. | Slightly left of the painting's middle ground: pavilions are on the islets by the water, forming reachable nodes together with the bridges and shoreline.
distinction: Although the built elements are placed according to mountain and water, the painting places greater emphasis on the process of travel in which bridges and shorelines guide the eye deeper into the villages and valleys.

evidence: Middle, slightly left mid-slope: the building group sits on a protruding rock terrace, adjacent to a waterfall on the left, with the site corresponding to the terrain terrace, presenting houses set on a terrace. | Lower-right corner waterside: the house group unfolds along the low waterside, responding to the flat terrain, presenting a layout unfolding by the water. | Lower-middle among the rocks: a winding mountain path (steps) is visible passing through the rocks and connecting the lower and upper spaces, helping to embody the terrain's undulation and the separate placement of buildings at different heights.
distinction: Although mountain paths connect the built elements, the buildings are mainly placed according to the mid-slope terrace and waterside terrain (houses set on a terrace, unfolding by the water); the determining role of terrain on layout is superior to the guiding role of paths.

evidence: Lower left corner: a group of buildings is erected facing the water, with supporting posts visible at the base, presenting a form sited along the waterside. | At the foot of the cliff, slightly right of the painting's center: a cluster of houses is distributed on level ground at the mountain's foot, its building-site layout conforming to the mountain terrain. | Overall composition: the built structures are mainly distributed along the water's edge and at the foot of the cliff, presenting a spatial relationship of siting according to the ground and attaining suitability by following the terrain.
distinction: Although there is a clue of a bridge in the lower part of the painting, the main visual characteristic of the buildings is adaptation to terrain by being set against the mountain and beside the water, rather than emphasizing the process of an access path.

evidence: Left middle ground: a pavilion sits on a protruding rock terrace, partly screened by the surrounding tree branches and leaves, revealing its roof and eaves. | Lower-right foreground: houses are faintly visible behind the sloping bank and dense trunks and foliage; walls and roofs are half hidden and half exposed. | Overall painting: several built elements form spatial layers through the trees of the foreground and middle ground; the relationship of concealment and revelation participates in composing the scene.
distinction: Although the left pavilion has the terrain-responsive feature of being set on a terrace, buildings throughout the painting generally form layers of concealment and revelation through trees and rocks; the role of concealment and revelation is more prominent.

evidence: Lower-left: the buildings are largely screened by dense tree branches and leaves, with only parts of the roofs and structure exposed, presenting a clear layering of concealment and revelation. | Right lower-middle: two houses are placed on the slope at the foot of the mountain, surrounded by trees and sloping banks, merged into the natural scenery. | Upper-middle: building structures are faintly visible on the mid-slope, half screened by rocks and trees, increasing the sense of spatial depth.
distinction: Although some buildings are placed at the foot of the mountain, the relationship of screening and revealing between the buildings and the trees and rocks (layering of concealment and revelation) is more prominent and dominates the creation of the spatial mood.

evidence: Middle right: the building group is placed at different heights on the mountain slope terraces, its layout responding to the mountain form, presenting a state of unfolding by slope. | Lower-left corner: the building group is placed by the waterside, its site meeting the water surface and bank rocks, presenting a tendency to unfold along the bank. | Overall composition: the building sites clearly correspond to the mountain form and waterside; they are placed according to the terrain, not merely adjacent.
distinction: Although the buildings are screened by trees (C2), the painting more conspicuously displays the layout relationship of buildings by mountain and water, unfolding by slope and along the bank; terrain's participation in the placement of built elements is clearer and runs through the composition.

evidence: Upper-middle of the painting: parts of roofs and walls are revealed between the mid-slope rock face and the trees, presenting a state of being half hidden and half visible. | Middle of the painting: several houses in the mountain hollow are arranged unevenly according to the mountain terrain, some screened by the trees and rocks in front. | Lower-right corner of the painting: houses are by the waterside, screening and being screened by the surrounding trees and rocks.
distinction: Although the buildings are arranged according to the mountain terrain, the painting places greater emphasis on the layered relationship in which buildings are screened by trees and rocks and partly exposed; therefore C2 is more apt than C1.

evidence: Lower left corner: houses are built facing the waterside cliff, with dense vertical lines painted at the base (resembling wooden piles or a supporting structure), presenting a form of buildings set according to the waterside/terrace and clearly adapted to the steep waterside terrain. | Middle-right valley: a cluster of houses is distributed on the gentle ground between the valley's mountain foot and the riverbank, unfolding along the bank in conformity with the mountain form and water flow. | Lower right corner: a small bridge is painted connecting the rocks and the shoreline; although a clue of movement through the landscape exists, the main visual characteristic of the built structures in the painting is placement according to terrain.
distinction: Although a bridge in the painting suggests a path (a C4 clue), the wooden-pile supports of the waterside pavilion in the lower left and the along-bank distribution of the middle-right settlement more strongly embody the dominant relationship of built structures being sited according to terrain and waterside (C1).

evidence: Lower-right: a waterside pavilion or water-side kiosk, supported at the bottom by posts, is erected directly over the waterside and rocks; its site layout closely corresponds to the water surface and rock terrain. | Lower-middle: rocks and trees are distributed in front of and around the buildings; the buildings unfold against these natural features, presenting a placement relationship of being against rock and facing water.
distinction: Although the buildings are partly screened by the branches and leaves of foreground trees, producing a screening effect, their site-placement relationship of being by water and against rock is more central and definite in composing the scene.

evidence: Middle ground: multiple building groups are distributed along the shoreline and the edges of sandbars, presenting a layout that unfolds along the bank in response to the winding terrain. | Lower-right corner: buildings are placed against the rocky bank and water's edge, their sites closely integrated with the bank terrain, presenting a form of houses set according to the bank. | Overall layout: the height and density of the built elements are placed according to the configuration of the waterside, not placed in isolation, embodying a relationship of placement according to the ground.
distinction: The buildings in the painting are mainly distributed in response to the waterside terrain (unfolding along the bank); although surrounded by trees, the relationship of concealment and revelation is less dominant than the terrain-correspondence relationship.

evidence: Mid-slope at the left of the painting: the building group is surrounded and screened by dense foreground pines and rocks, with only roofs and parts of walls exposed, presenting spatial layers of houses hidden in the woods and seen through a screen. | Lower center and lower-left corner of the painting: the branches and leaves of tall pines and rocks block the view behind; the buildings in the lower-left corner are screened behind trees and rocks and adjacent to a bridge, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the buildings are laid out according to the mountain slope terraces, the painting more conspicuously highlights the buildings' presence through screening by foreground trees and rocks; the relationship of concealment and revelation dominates the spatial expression.

evidence: Middle of the painting: a row of houses sits at the edge of a protruding long strip of rock terrace, presenting a layout of houses set on a terrace, closely corresponding to the cliff terrain. | Upper-middle of the painting: the building cluster is located in the hollow of the mid-slope and among the slopes, distributed unevenly according to the mountain and woodland terrain, presenting separate placement by slope. | Lower-left corner of the painting: houses sit on the flat ground beside the waterside, their sites adjacent to the water surface, presenting a tendency to unfold along the bank.
distinction: Although the upper-middle buildings are screened by trees and woods, several buildings in the painting (especially the central terrace and the lower-left waterside) more conspicuously embody the feature of being placed according to terrain conditions such as terraces, mountain forms, and waterside; the determining force of terrain on layout is stronger than the relationship of concealment and revelation alone.

evidence: Lower central part of the painting: behind trees and sloping rocks, the roofs and walls of built structures are revealed, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship in which they are half-hidden by natural scenery. | Lower left of the painting: a small bridge is visible by the water, but between the bridge and the built structures behind it there is no clearly discernible movement path connection.
distinction: Although there is a bridge in the painting, it lacks a clear entry path connecting to the built structures; the built structures mainly rely on the screening of trees and sloping rocks to suggest their presence and to constitute spatial layering.

evidence: Middle-ground mountain foot, slightly left: several roofs and walls are visible, half-screened by trees and rocks, presenting a layering of houses hidden in the woods | Foreground lower right corner: faint traces of small built structures appear among sloping banks, trees, and rocks, mutually screening with the natural environment
distinction: Although the built structures are placed according to the mountain foot and sloping bank, the painting emphasizes more the spatial layering formed by their concealment and revelation through trees and rocks, rather than simply siting according to terrain.

evidence: Lower center: a thatched pavilion is hidden between pine and willow trees, with only its pyramidal roof and some pillars exposed, half-screened by the surrounding branches and leaves. | Lower center to right side: tall pines and weeping willows surround the thatched pavilion, forming foreground and middle-ground layers, giving the building a visual effect of concealment and revelation among the woods.
distinction: Although the thatched pavilion marks the scenery among the woods and by the water, the painting emphasizes more the relationship of screening and exposure between trees and architecture; the feature of concealment and revelation forming a setting is more prominent.

evidence: Lower left: a small wooden bridge is visible spanning between mountain rocks and a valley mouth, with a path behind the bridge connecting and extending deep into the woods. | Lower center: streams and gaps among rocks combine with the bridge, suggesting a spatial extension that is enterable and can be further traveled.
distinction: The entry relationship formed by the bridge and path in the painting is clear and dominates the spatial organization of the foreground, while no obvious concealment-and-revelation relationship of buildings is seen.

evidence: Lower middle and right side of the painting: multiple house compounds are blocked by tall pines and rocks, with only roofs, eaves, and parts of walls exposed, forming obvious layers of concealment and revelation. | Left mountainside: a small house is screened behind trees and rocks, faintly visible. | Overall composition: the built structures are deeply hidden among dense pine forests and valleys; the screening and exposure of buildings by natural scenery constitute the main spatial layering of the painting.
distinction: Although bridges and paths suggest entry, the visual focus lies in the deep layering formed by the screening and exposure of houses by pine forests and rocks; the screening relationship is more dominant than the travel clues.

evidence: Lower middle: willow trees, the waterside and a cowherd riding an ox are visible in the painting; no definite houses, bridges or other man-made built elements can be seen. | Lower left corner: there are a few strokes resembling planks or rocks, but they are insufficient to constitute clear evidence of built elements.
distinction: The painting lacks definite built elements; only a cowherd riding an ox among willows and along the waterside is seen, carrying a sense of movement through the landscape, and it is therefore only tentatively assigned to C4.

evidence: Lower part: several groups of figures are visible walking on an open flat area, presenting a dynamic of traveling or advancing into the depths of the landscape. | Left side: on the left are towering cliffs and a vertically falling waterfall, constituting the main landscape background of the painting. | Right side: on the right are sloping rocks covered with pines, forming a spatial enclosure with the left cliff, with figures walking between them.
distinction: No clear built structures are seen in the painting, but the walking movement of the figures suggests the process of entering the landscape space, so it is classified as C4.

evidence: Right side and center: huge pine branches extend, with lush foliage covering the pavilion from above and the right, forming a significant screening relationship. | Lower right: the pavilion (thatched roof, colonnade, with figures inside) is located within the screening of pines, exposing the building itself, presenting a spatial layering of seeing a house beneath trees, with pine shade participating in the scenery. | Bottom of the lower-right pavilion: wooden stakes are painted beneath the pavilion, showing it is built by the water, but the main spatial relationship is being enveloped and screened by the form of the pines.
distinction: Although the pavilion is built by the water (wooden stakes visible, with C1 terrain-responsive siting features), the envelopment and screening of the pavilion by the huge pines (concealment-and-revelation relationship) is more dominant in composition and mood (pine shade), conforming to concealment and revelation forming a setting.

evidence: Left middle: a two-story pavilion is surrounded by trees of alternating red and green, with roofs and some walls revealed through branches and leaves. | Slightly below center of the painting: a group of houses is built against the mountain, mostly blocked by pines and miscellaneous trees in the foreground and middle ground, with only roof outlines exposed. | Lower right corner: a waterside pavilion or platform is partially blocked by pine branches extending from the foreground, presenting a layering of seeing houses through intervening scenery.
distinction: Although there is placement against mountains and by water, the painting emphasizes more the screening and exposure of buildings by trees; the concealment-and-revelation relationship dominates the composition.

evidence: Full view: only mountains and rocks, trees, and an inscription and seals in the upper left corner are visible in the painting; no traces of built elements such as buildings, bridges or paths can be seen.
distinction: The painting has no built elements; on the basis of the overall landscape forms it is only tentatively assigned to C3, but it lacks any actual built entity for scenic accentuation.

evidence: Right middle: house buildings are half-screened by surrounding trees and rocks, with only parts of roofs, walls, and window lattices exposed, forming obvious spatial layers of concealment and revelation. | Lower left: a pavilion is built by the water, partially blocked by pine branches and leaves in the foreground, with figures active inside the pavilion, mutually screening with the natural environment.
distinction: Although the lower-left pavilion has the sense of being built by the water, the screening and exposure relationship between buildings and trees/rocks in the painting is more prominent, dominating the spatial layering of the painting.

evidence: Lower part of the painting: a simple wooden bridge spans the water, with two people holding umbrellas walking on it, facing the direction of the buildings in the middle of the painting, forming a clear entry path. | Slightly right of center: a group of buildings is located on the sloping bank by the water, partially blocked by trees on the left and mountain rocks on the right, exposing roofs and building bodies. | Right side of the painting: huge mountain rocks closely adjoin the right side of the buildings, together with the trees on the left forming screening and spatial enclosure of the buildings.
distinction: The bridge and the figures' travel route clearly constitute the spatial clue for entering the built structures, presenting a process of arrival, which is more dominant than mere screening layers.

evidence: Left mountainside: a winding stepped path is visible, connecting the lower area with houses on the left-middle slope, forming an upward travel clue. | Right mountainside: a group of houses is screened among trees and rocks, with roofs exposed, suggesting spatial layering. | Lower foreground: houses are set at the waterside, with a path extending beside them, echoing the mountain path.
distinction: Clear path clues in the painting connect built structures at different locations, emphasizing the spatial process from here to there, which is more dominant than mere screening relationships.

evidence: Lower left: house buildings are largely blocked by the branches, leaves, and trunks of tall foreground trees, with only roofs and parts of walls and fences exposed, presenting a state of houses hidden in the woods. | Lower center: another group of house buildings is surrounded by surrounding groves and sloping rocks, half-hidden and half-exposed, forming a tight enveloping relationship with the natural environment. | Overall foreground: built structures are deeply placed among trees, rocks, and mountains; through the screening and exposure by natural scenery, a spatial layering of 'seeing houses in deep woods' is formed.
distinction: Although winding streams/paths in the painting suggest depth (a clue to secluded access), the foreground built structures mainly rely on the screening and exposure by trees (concealment-and-revelation relationship) to construct the layering of deep dwelling beneath the woods, rather than emphasizing the connectivity and entry process of paths.

evidence: Right mountainside: the building complex is arranged layer upon layer upward following the mountain terrain, with roofs staggered in height, presenting obvious features of distributed placement according to slope. | Central mountainside: the built structures are located on a platform surrounded by cliffs and trees; the building base is tightly integrated with the mountain rock terrain, with houses set on the platform. | Slightly left of center: water (waterfall/stream) is visible flowing down the mountain; the built structures are located on a platform beside the water, reflecting placement according to terrain and waterside.
distinction: Although the built structures are surrounded by dense pine forests and have screening features (C2), the form of buildings layered and staggered according to the mountain slope (distributed placement according to slope) is more prominent and dominates the spatial expression.

evidence: Lower left corner: a thatched hut built structure is visible, with two people facing each other inside; the building is partially blocked by surrounding rocks and pines, with only parts exposed. | Lower middle of the painting: dense pine forests and undulating rocks half-screen the built structure in the lower left corner, forming obvious spatial layers of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the built structure is placed against the mountain and beside trees, the painting emphasizes more the screening and exposure relationship of trees and rocks to it, rather than simply corresponding to terrain placement.

evidence: Lower left: a pavilion is surrounded by tall, dense pines and woodland, with only parts of the roof, pillars, and figures inside exposed, presenting an obvious screening relationship among the woods. | Middle ground to distant view: mountains and dense forests layer upon layer, further strengthening the deep, hidden spatial layering, setting off the pavilion's scenery of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the pavilion marks a scene among the woods, its screening and exposure relationship with surrounding trees is more prominent and is the main way of constituting the spatial layering of the painting.

evidence: Left middle of the painting: a building complex (pavilions and towers) is partially blocked by dense foreground pines and background mountain rocks, with only roofs and parts of eaves exposed, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Left and center of the painting: pine branches and leaves interweave in front of and behind the buildings, strengthening the spatial layering of buildings hidden in the woods.
distinction: Although figures walking in the lower part of the painting suggest a path, the most prominent compositional feature of the buildings is being screened by trees and rocks; the concealment-and-revelation relationship is more prominent than path guidance.
