evidence: Lower middle: a hexagonal pavilion is built on a stone platform by the water; the platform has railings, with weeping willows beside it, and the built structure is directly adjacent to the water surface. | Left of the pavilion: the platform extends left as a bank path; several people walk along the path toward the pavilion, forming a clear movement clue and dynamic of approaching the built elements. | Left side: houses are screened among trees, with a fence in front, connected to the bank path system, suggesting the connectivity of garden space.
distinction: The dynamic of figures walking along the path toward the pavilion and the direct connection between the platform and the built elements emphasize an enterable process of traversal, rather than serving merely as a location marker.

evidence: Lower left to midground: a small bridge crosses the water connecting the two banks; on the sloping bank there are paths and figures riding, forming a movement clue extending into the depth of the painting. | Left midground: houses are arranged along the sloping bank, partially screened by trees, and spatially connected with the foreground waterside and small bridge through the shoreline and paths. | Lower right water surface: moored boats suggest arrival by waterway, and together with the bridges and paths on the bank constitute a process of entering by water-land connection.
distinction: Although the houses have a concealment-and-revelation relationship of being screened by trees, the connection of bridges, paths, figures, and waterside in the painting more prominently presents an enterable and traversable spatial process.

evidence: Lower left waterside: several thin upright poles and lines resembling a fence or simple structure are visible, attached to the rocky bank, but their form is blurred and difficult to confirm as a definite building. | Lower right water surface: a small boat with two people, belonging to scenic figures and a boat, not fixed built elements.
distinction: The painting lacks clear and definite fixed built elements; in the lower left corner there are only extremely faint traces of suspected human work attached to the waterside, so it is tentatively assigned to C1, but the evidence is seriously insufficient.

evidence: Right sloping terrace: several houses are arranged in staggered fashion according to the sloping terrace, their sites conforming to the undulations of the terrain, presenting a form of houses set according to the terrace. | Lower right waterside: a small bridge is visible connecting the waterside with the sloping land, and figures are crossing the bridge toward the built area. | Around the built elements: the houses are screened among the trees on the slope, merging with the surrounding landscape.
distinction: Although the painting has a bridge and figures suggesting an entry route, the most prominent feature of the built elements is their staggered placement according to the sloping terrace terrain, which dominates the spatial expression.

evidence: Lower right among mountains and rocks: tiny figures are visible walking along a mountain path; the path extends into the mountains, suggesting an enterable spatial process. | Lower center slightly left: courtyard buildings are hidden behind clouds and trees, forming a spatial layering of entering from outside to inside. | Upper right among cliffs: a corner of a roof is half-hidden by mountains, rocks, and trees, suggesting further built elements in the depths.
distinction: Although there is obvious screening by woods and clouds, the figures walking on the mountain path point toward buildings in the mountains, emphasizing more an enterable and traversable spatial process, so C4 is more dominant than C2.

evidence: Center-right mountainside: a pavilion is built on a prominent rocky high platform, its site clear, presenting a form of houses set according to the platform. | Lower and right slopes: houses are distributed according to the slope and the foot of the mountain, the layout staggered with the height of the mountain, presenting a relationship of separate placement according to the slope. | Overall composition: the high and low positions of the built elements correspond to the mountain forms and sloping platforms, embodying the feature of placement according to the ground.
distinction: Although the buildings in the painting have a screening relationship of being obscured by trees (such as the houses on the right), the layout feature of buildings distributed according to high platforms and slopes is more prominent, directly embodying terrain-responsive siting.

evidence: Lower left corner: thatched houses are built on the sloping land by the water, with fences and platforms, connected to the bank path, presenting an reachable recreational node. | Middle right among mountains and rocks: a clear stepped path extends upward according to the mountain terrain, with pedestrians climbing, clearly expressing a path entering deep into the mountains. | Lower right corner: boats and figures on the water echo the bank path, suggesting a movement clue connecting water and land.
distinction: Although the buildings are arranged according to the terrain, the painting more strongly organizes an enterable and traversable spatial process through clear steps, waterside paths, and figure activity.

evidence: Lower right: houses are visible amid screening trees, with a stream and a small bridge in front of them. | Lower middle: a cowherd and cattle on the grass, near the stream and small bridge, forming the foreground. | Overall: the small bridge and stream connect the foreground cowherd scene with the background houses, constituting an enterable and reachable spatial clue.
distinction: Although the houses are screened by trees, the small bridge and stream clearly constitute a path clue connecting the foreground with the houses, emphasizing the process of entry and traversal, so C4 is more appropriate than C2.

evidence: Lower left: a group of house compounds is built beside the waterside, enclosed by fences. | Lower middle slightly right: a small bridge crosses the water connecting the two banks; beside the bridge a person is walking along the path toward the houses. | Overall: the bridge, path, and built elements are connected, forming a clear spatial clue of entry and arrival at the built elements.
distinction: Although the houses are placed by the waterside, the combination of the small bridge, path, and pedestrians more prominently highlights the spatial process of proceeding from here to there and approaching the built elements.

evidence: Lower left corner: a wooden bridge with railings connects the foreground land with the stone bank where the midground built elements are located, constituting a clear physical connecting passage. | Lower center: riders and walkers are proceeding toward the bridge, forming a movement clue pointing toward the built elements and presenting a process of approaching them. | Midground: on the stone bank there are fence walls and buildings; the bridge lands toward the courtyard area, suggesting a spatial relationship of entering the courtyard from here.
distinction: Although trees have an obvious screening effect on the buildings, the painting clearly constructs, through the foreground bridge and the direction of figure movement, a path and process of approaching and entering the built space from outside, so access to secluded settings is more dominant.

evidence: Lower right to central mountainside: a clear travel group (figures and horses) is visible proceeding along a winding mountain path; the path passes between mountains, rocks, and woods, presenting a traversal clue extending into the depths. | Lower left corner: at the foot of the mountain, pavilion buildings are screened among trees and clouds, serving as a node that the travel path may reach or pass. | Left middle: a group of village buildings sits on the slope, combined with surrounding trees and terrain, constituting the landscape layering on the left side of the painting.
distinction: Although the buildings are distributed according to the mountain terrain, the clear travel path and figure activity in the painting emphasize more an enterable and traversable spatial process, rather than mere placement according to the ground.

evidence: Lower left: a wooden bridge is visible crossing a stream, connecting to a path leading to the built elements in the woods. | Lower center: a forest path connects to houses screened among trees, and pedestrians walk on the path, presenting an enterable spatial process. | Lower right: a water pavilion with railings is built by the water, connected to the bank by a path, forming a traversable waterside space.
distinction: The painting links the various built elements through movement clues such as bridges, paths, and water pavilions, emphasizing a spatial process of entering from outside to inside and traversable space, rather than mere screening or scenic accentuation.

evidence: Right mountainside to waterside: multiple groups of pavilions, houses, and pagodas are arranged in layers according to the mountain terrain, extending from high places to the water's edge, staggered with the height of the terrain. | In the right building group: buildings are partially obscured by mountains, rocks, pine trees, and clouds, presenting a spatial layering of alternating concealment and revelation. | Lower water surface of the painting: several boats travel on the water, approaching the buildings on the bank, suggesting waterway transport and an entry path.
distinction: Although the buildings have a screening relationship, their feature of following the mountain and being arranged according to the height of the terrain is more prominent and dominant.

evidence: Upper half of the painting: the city wall winds and extends along the natural undulations of the mountain ridge, conforming to the topographical trend. | Upper middle and upper left of the painting: two gate towers are built on high platforms according to the mountain situation, their sites corresponding to the form of the mountain body.
distinction: Although the lower part of the painting has bridges and figures suggesting movement clues, what occupies the dominant position in the painting is the layout of the city wall conforming to the mountain terrain, so C1 is more appropriate.

evidence: Middle left: several thatched huts are arranged in sequence along a curving waterbank and earthen slope, their building sites following the undulations of the terrain. | Lower right: a waterside pavilion is built at the water, close against the bank, its layout corresponding directly to the water's edge. | Middle ground, slightly right: houses are placed along a gentle slope and the edge of woodland, presenting the form of buildings sited according to the slope.
distinction: Although trees screen the houses and create layers, the most prominent feature of the several groups of built elements in the painting is their placement against the waterbank and slopes; the guiding effect of terrain on layout is greater than a simple concealment-and-revelation relationship.

evidence: Lower right: the house buildings are surrounded and screened by bare trees and evergreen trees in the foreground, with only the roof and part of the wall body exposed (a person is visible inside the house), presenting a concealment-and-revelation layering of houses hidden in woodland. | Right middle ground: pavilion roofs are faintly visible among the level, distant woodland, using the screening of trees to form a spatial depth of houses seen across a barrier. | Overall composition: the main built elements (mountain dwelling, pavilions) are not directly exposed in open areas but rely on the screening of the cold-forest snow scene to merge into the landscape, forming foreground-background layers.
distinction: Below the painting there are figures traveling and a bridge suggesting a movement-through-the-landscape thread (C4), but the core relationship between the main built elements and the landscape is expressed as concealment-and-revelation layering screened by trees (C2), and the visual connection between paths and buildings is less direct and prominent than the screening relationship.

evidence: Lower left: a person is walking on a wooden bridge with railings, the bridge spanning between mountains and rocks, forming a clear thread of crossing and progression. | Middle left: a railing structure resembling a plank walkway or bridge is visible, extending along the mountain configuration, suggesting connectivity and a route of travel through the space.
distinction: The painting is dominated by movement-through-the-landscape threads such as bridges and plank walkways, presenting a spatial process of passing from here to there; no obvious screening of buildings or scenic-accentuation function is seen.

evidence: Lower middle-right of the painting: a multi-storey pagoda stands amid a pine grove, its body partly screened by pine branches and needles, with only some storeys and the pagoda top exposed, forming a clear relationship of concealment and revelation. | Right side of the painting: the steep cliff and the pines below together form the natural background, and the pagoda is sited amid the screening pine grove, its spatial layering suggested by the cover of the woodland.
distinction: Although the pagoda serves as a scenic accent, the painting places greater emphasis on the screening and revealing of the pagoda body by the pine branches, and the spatial layering of concealment and revelation is more prominent.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: an arched bridge is visible spanning the water and connecting the two banks, forming a clear passage thread. | Lower part of the painting: behind the bridge there are house buildings, partly screened by trees and vegetation, suggesting a reachable destination. | Very bottom of the painting: boats are on the water, and figures on the bank are towing them, reinforcing the spatial process of moving along the water and passing from here to there.
distinction: The bridge, boats, and figures together form a clear movement-through-the-landscape thread and relationship of entry, emphasizing the sense of spatial process more than mere screening of buildings.

evidence: Lower right: a zigzagging wooden bridge extends into the water surface, with two people standing on it, constituting a clear movement-through-the-landscape thread and a path entering the painting. | Middle ground, right bank: a group of buildings is built at the water, serving as a potential destination or scenery along the way for the gaze guided by the bridge path. | Middle ground, left bank: a pavilion is built among mountains and rocks, forming a spatial echo and sense of connectivity with the water surface and the foreground bridge.
distinction: Through the prominent zigzagging bridge and figures at the lower right, the painting clearly constructs a movement route that guides the gaze toward buildings in the depth, emphasizing a process of spatial entry more than mere placement against mountains and water.

evidence: Lower left: the building group is arranged along the shoreline, with dense wooden piles or column bases visible supporting it at the bottom, presenting a layout that unfolds along the water and follows the bank. | Middle left to lower left: the built elements are located in a water inlet below a cliff and waterfall, with houses staggered in height, placed in accordance with the terrain junction between the mountain foot and the water surface.
distinction: Although the buildings beside the waterfall may have a scenic-accentuation role, their long, strip-like arrangement along the shoreline and against the mountain foot more prominently embodies terrain-responsive siting.

evidence: Lower left: the roof and wall body of a building are faintly revealed among trees, partly screened by branches and leaves, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Lower part of the painting: the water surface is covered with lotus leaves, and there is a small boat, which together with the screened houses on the bank forms a secluded layering.
distinction: Although the houses are at the water, their layering of being screened by tree branches and leaves, half hidden and half revealed, is more prominent in the painting, so C2 is more apt than C1.

evidence: Lower middle: the roofs and wall bodies of several built elements are partly screened by the foreground woodland, presenting a layering of houses hidden in woodland. | Lower left and lower middle: a stone bridge, a winding path, and pedestrians and riders moving along the path are visible, connecting the exterior with the built elements in the woodland.
distinction: Although paths and bridges guide the gaze, the built elements present their spatial layering mainly through screening and revealing by woodland, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship is more prominent.

evidence: Lower right to middle: two people tow a boat along a waterside path, forming a clear route of progression and spatial guidance into the painting. | Middle left to middle right: the arched bridge on the left echoes the sailing boats moored and navigating on the river, constructing threads of water-and-land transport and travel. | Middle left: thatched huts are hidden behind willow trees, forming part of the riverbank scenery and dotting the travel route.
distinction: Although the thatched huts are screened, the dominant spatial organization of the painting is the process of travel and entry formed jointly by the boat-towers' path, the bridge, and the boats, rather than mere concealment-and-revelation layering.

evidence: Upper middle: a cluster of houses is distributed according to the gentle terrain at the mountain foot, interspersed among woodland, presenting a layout divided according to slope. | Lower middle: a group of houses is built at the water, unfolding along the shoreline, with building sites adjacent to the water surface. | Lower left: houses are located at the foot of mountains and rocks, placed according to the terrain, forming a relationship of reliance on the surrounding mountains and rocks.
distinction: Although trees surround the houses, the painting mainly presents the overall layout of houses distributed according to terrain conditions such as the mountain foot and waterbank, rather than emphasizing the concealment-and-revelation layering under woodland screening.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: a group of houses is screened by the tall tree trunks and shrubs in the foreground, with only the roof, eaves, and part of the wall body exposed, presenting a layering of houses hidden in woodland. | Distant upper part of the painting: several house outlines are faintly visible behind mountain peaks, screened by the mountain mass, forming a spatial relationship of houses seen across a barrier.
distinction: The painting mainly expresses the concealment-and-revelation layering of built elements screened by trees and mountains and rocks; although there is a bridge-arch-like structure at the lower left, it does not form a clear travel thread leading to the built elements.

evidence: Whole painting: the picture consists mainly of mountains and rocks, pines, miscellaneous trees, and a waterfall at the bottom; no clear built elements such as houses, pavilions, or bridges are seen. | Upper left: there is an inscription and seals; the inscription mentions a studio name, but the corresponding building is not depicted in the painting.
distinction: No clear built elements are seen in the painting; based on the overall landscape composition it is tentatively assigned to scenic accentuation, since the painting itself presents a complete landscape scene.

evidence: Lower left: on the sloping bank the roof and columns of a built element (such as a thatched pavilion or house) are visible, partly screened by the trunks and branches of bare trees in the foreground, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Middle ground: the water surface is open, separating the screened built elements in the foreground from the mountains and rocks in the distance, strengthening the spatial layering.
distinction: The built element forms layering mainly through screening and revealing by trees (screening), rather than serving purely as a conspicuous marker identifying a particular landscape spot (scenic accentuation).

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: the roof and eaves of built elements emerge from behind pines and rocks, presenting an evident relationship of screening and revealing. | Lower left of the painting: there is a built element at the water, with a platform base and roof, forming foreground-background layering with the surrounding mountains, rocks, and woodland.
distinction: Although the built elements are set against mountains and water, the painting emphasizes more the concealment-and-revelation layering of buildings revealed through screening by woodland and mountains and rocks, rather than purely emphasizing terrain-based placement.

evidence: Lower left: thatched huts are partly screened by trees (bamboo, pines, etc.) on the left and behind, with only part of the roof, eaves, and building body exposed; one person is visible inside, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Lower left to lower middle: in front of the thatched huts there are a fence and water surface; trees are interspersed between the buildings and the foreground mountains and rocks, enhancing the spatial layering.
distinction: Although the thatched huts are built at the water, the painting emphasizes more their layering of being screened and revealed by trees, so C2 is more apt than C1.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: a group of houses is partly screened by foreground trees and mountains and rocks, with only the roof and part of the wall body exposed, presenting an evident concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Middle left of the painting: houses appear faintly on the mountainside between mountains and rocks and woodland, forming layering through natural scenery. | Distant right of the painting: scattered cottages are faintly visible among the waterside woodland, screening and being screened by the natural environment.
distinction: Although the painting also shows buildings placed according to the mountains, the sense of spatial layering formed by the screening and revealing of buildings by woodland and mountains and rocks is more prominent and dominates the compositional method.

evidence: Upper half, right side: a thatched pavilion sits at the edge of a sloping bank, its building site adjoining grassland and sloping-rock terrain, presenting a placement of buildings according to the slope. | Lower half: waterside trees and rocks and a sloping bank, with no clear built elements seen, existing only as natural scenery.
distinction: Although the thatched pavilion has a role in identifying the scenery, its main visual feature is placement against the sloping-bank terrain; the relationship of terrain-based arrangement is more prominent than mere scenic accentuation.

evidence: Lower center: figures are walking on a small path or bridge crossing a stream, forming a movement-through-the-landscape thread. | Right side: a stepped path winds upward along a cliff, leading toward the depth of the painting and guiding the gaze. | Overall composition: paths, bridge, and stream combine to present a spatial process of passing from here to there and turning into the depths.
distinction: The path and bridge mainly serve to guide travel and connect spaces, presenting an enterable process rather than merely displaying the form of buildings placed according to mountain configuration.

evidence: Foreground: sloping banks and clustered trees are visible, the terrain extending gently into the water | Middle and distant ground: the water surface is open, distant mountains layered, presenting the undulation and opening-and-closing of natural terrain
distinction: No clear built elements are seen in the painting; it is assigned to the closest category solely on the basis of the spatial organization of natural landscape unfolding according to terrain

evidence: Middle-right of the painting: the roofs and eaves of pavilions and houses emerge from behind dense tree crowns and mountains and rocks, presenting an evident half-screened, half-hidden state. | Around the built elements: tree branches and leaves and rock masses screen the building bodies, with only part of the structure exposed, constructing a spatial layering of woodland-and-rock screening.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed according to the mountain configuration, the painting emphasizes more their concealment-and-revelation layering formed by screening and revealing through woodland and mountains and rocks, rather than mere terrain correspondence.

evidence: Lower left: a small bridge spans the water, connecting the two banks, serving as the starting point for entering the painting. | Middle left to center: a winding path extends from beside the bridge, rising along the slope and pointing toward the built elements behind the woodland. | Middle left: a house is visible behind the woodland, and the extension of the path suggests a spatial process by which that built element can be reached.
distinction: Although the built elements are partly screened by trees, the continuous small bridge and winding path in the painting emphasize more the travel process of passing from here to there and approaching the built elements, so C4 is more dominant.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: water surface, sloping banks, and rows of trees are visible, presenting a layered distribution of natural waterside, with no traces of built elements such as houses, bridges, or paths. | Upper part of the painting: distant mountains are painted with Mi-dot texture strokes, wreathed in clouds and mist, purely a natural landscape scene.
distinction: No visible built elements in the painting; based on the overall spatial organization of the landscape following the waterside slopes, it is assigned to the closest category, C1.

evidence: Lower right: a waterside pavilion is built on the bank, with figures visible inside and trees screening it nearby. | Right side: a clear small path winds along mountains and rocks and the waterbank, connecting to and leading toward the pavilion on the right, presenting an enterable spatial thread. | Middle ground: the roof of a building is revealed in the woodland, forming layering with the surrounding trees.
distinction: Although the middle-ground buildings have screening features, the enterable, travelable spatial organization formed by the lower-right pavilion and the winding path is more prominent and dominates the spatial expression of the painting.

evidence: Lower right: several houses are distributed on the sloping ground by the bank, surrounded by dense pine woodland, with some roofs and walls revealed from the trees. | Right mountainside: several cottages are faintly visible among the mountain-slope woodland, buildings and woodland screening each other and forming foreground-background layering.
distinction: Although the houses are placed against mountains and water, the painting emphasizes more the relationship of screening and revealing of buildings by woodland; the feature of concealment and revelation forming scenery is more prominent than mere terrain-based placement.

evidence: Upper left: the roofs and columns of two houses are revealed from dense pine woodland and trees, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Upper left: the houses are surrounded and screened by woodland on all sides, presenting a spatial layering of houses seen in woodland.
distinction: Although the houses are built on sloping ground, the painting presents their existence mainly through screening and revealing by woodland; the feature of screening and revealing forming a scene is more prominent than terrain-based siting.

evidence: Lower left: a bridge is visible spanning a stream, connecting the paths on the two banks and forming a clear thread of entry. | Center, slightly left: the building group is staggered according to the mountain configuration, partly hidden behind woodland, and the gaps between stream and mountains and rocks guide the gaze into the depth. | Lower right: houses are built at the water, corresponding to the stream and mountains and rocks, suggesting a reachable spatial relationship.
distinction: Although there is a concealment-and-revelation relationship in which woodland screens buildings, the travel thread formed by bridges, streams, and paths runs through the whole more, dominating the spatial organization.

evidence: Right middle ground: several houses are arranged along the sloping bank at the mountain foot, following the undulations of the terrain and together with the adjacent trees and rocks forming a situation of dwelling at the water. | Lower right foreground: at the waterbank houses are placed against mountains and rocks and trees, naturally connecting with the base of the towering cliff on the right.
distinction: Although the houses are accompanied by trees, their main feature is placement according to the terrain of the mountain foot and waterbank, rather than emphasizing a screened concealment-and-revelation relationship.

evidence: Lower center, slightly right: a thatched hut sits on a sloping-rock terrace by the water, its roof covered with snow, placed against the waterbank and sloping rocks. | Lower right: a small boat is moored at the edge of the sloping rocks beside the thatched hut, unfolding together with the built element according to the waterside terrain.
distinction: Although the thatched hut is screened by woodland, its terrain-based relationship of sitting on a sloping terrace and being placed along the waterbank is more prominent, so C1 is more apt than C2.

evidence: Left and center: the painting is filled with cold-forest bare trees and mountains, rocks, and sloping banks; tree trunks interlace and mountains and rocks are layered, forming rich foreground-background spatial layering. | Lower part: water winds among mountains and rocks and trees, enhancing the sense of depth and seclusion in the painting.
distinction: Although water and sloping banks suggest spatial extension, no clear built elements connected with paths are seen, so C4 is not selected; the spatial layering formed by the screening of trees and rocks is closest to the scene-forming feature of C2.

evidence: Lower left: a plank bridge is visible crossing a stream, and behind the bridge a path extends into the depth of the painting. | Mid-ground mountain hollow: the path connects several houses distributed according to the mountain terrain, forming an enterable and reachable spatial relationship. | Overall painting: the plank bridge and mountain path serve as movement-through-the-landscape clues, guiding the gaze from the foreground into the built area of the mid-ground.
distinction: Although the houses are distributed according to the mountain terrain, the entry and travel clues formed by the plank bridge and path are more prominent and dominate the spatial organization of the painting.

evidence: Lower-middle of the painting, toward the left: a thatched hut is surrounded by tall pines and deciduous trees; the roof and walls appear through gaps between trunks and branches, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Left side of the painting: a fence surrounds the thatched hut, and trees interlace in front and behind, giving the built structure a spatial layering situated deep within a sparse grove. | Right side and background of the painting: open water and distant mountains set off the foreground, making the thatched hut screened by trees the visual focus and strengthening the effect of seeing the house through a screening layer.
distinction: The painting mainly presents the layers of screening and revealing of the thatched hut by trees, rather than emphasizing a spatial process of entering the built structure through paths or bridges.

evidence: From the lower part to the lower-middle-left of the painting: a winding line (resembling a path or shoreline) extends from the foreground, passes through the roots of pine trees, and continues into the depth of the painting. | Behind the pine grove at the left-middle of the painting: lines resembling house roofs and walls are faintly visible where pines and rocks screen them, and the direction of the path seems to point toward this place.
distinction: The path/shoreline in the lower part of the painting guides the gaze deep into the grove, emphasizing an enterable spatial process, which is more dominant than a simple concealment-and-revelation relationship.

evidence: Lower center and right side of the painting: several thatched huts are arranged beside the water's edge and on sloping ground, presenting a layout of houses set by the water and separately placed according to the slope. | Lower left and center of the painting: the building sites are closely connected with the water surface and sloping banks, unfolding in response to the terrain.
distinction: Although the built structures are partly screened by groves, the layout feature of their placement beside the waterside and on sloping ground is more conspicuous and dominates the spatial expression.

evidence: Mid-ground water surface of the painting: there is a small boat and the figure of a person on it, dotting the open water surface | Lower left corner of the painting: clumps of trees are painted, and the distance shows gently sloping shorelines rendered in pale ink
distinction: No built elements are visible in the painting; only the small boat on the water identifies the open water scene, so it is assigned to scenic accentuation as the closest category.

evidence: Lower right corner: a group of multi-story buildings is visible; dense trees (with heavier ink tone) are around and in front of them; the building roofs and parts of the walls are exposed, while the lower parts are obscured by or merged with the trees, presenting a layering of seeing houses within the grove. | Right side and lower part of the painting: the buildings are located at the foot of the mountain by the waterside, screened by foreground trees and the sloping bank, forming a spatial relationship of seeing the house through a screening layer, and creating foreground-background layering with the towering main peak and clouds behind.
distinction: Although the buildings exist as a scenic accent, their main visual characteristic is being screened within the grove (a concealment-and-revelation relationship), rather than serving as a conspicuous landmark identifying the main peak or core landscape form (the accentuation role is not significant).

evidence: Lower left corner: a small pavilion is visible, located on mountains and rocks or by the waterside. | Middle of the right side: a simple bridge is visible spanning the water and connecting the two banks, implying a movement-through-the-landscape route.

evidence: Lower right: between the grove and the mountains and rocks, the outline of a built structure is visible; its roof and walls are partly obscured by foreground trees and rocks, presenting a half-hidden, half-exposed state. | Right side: the built structure relies on the hillside and woodland, forming spatial layering through the screening of natural scenery.
distinction: The built structure is mainly obscured by trees and mountains and rocks, emphasizing a concealment-and-revelation relationship and spatial layering, rather than serving as a conspicuous landmark identifying a specific scene.

evidence: Right-side mountain peak, mid-slope and foot: several tiny buildings dot the space between the towering extraordinary peaks and the sloping bank; their volume is extremely small, and they serve as visual anchor points that concentrate the landscape scenery. | Overall right side of the painting: the built structures correspond to the surrounding mountain and rock forms, identifying the specific scenery among the mountains and by the waterside, so that the painting gains recognizable scenic markers.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed according to the mountain terrain, their main compositional role is to identify and concentrate the landscape scenery through their tiny volume, rather than emphasizing a layout relationship of placement according to the terrain.

evidence: Left side: dead trees grow on the sloping bank, their branches extending toward the water; no building sites or artificial structures are visible. | Right side and distance: reeds, rocks, and the outlines of distant mountains are visible; there are no traces of built elements such as houses, bridges, or paths in the painting.

evidence: Lower left: several thatched huts sit at the roots of a pine grove; their roofs and walls are partly obscured by trunks and pine branches, presenting a half-hidden, half-exposed state. | Left side: tall pines interweave with mountains and rocks, wrapping the buildings below within them, forming a spatial layering of seeing houses deep within the grove.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed at the foot of the mountain, the painting emphasizes more the relationship of screening and revealing of the buildings by the grove, rather than a simple correspondence to terrain.

evidence: Lower center of the painting: where the clouds and mist meet the mountain ridges, there are faint, tiny brushstrokes suspected to be the outlines of houses or pavilions, but their forms are blurred and difficult to identify with certainty. | Overall painting: the painting is dominated by a sea of clouds and mountain peaks; the suspected built structures are half-hidden and half-screened by clouds and mist and the mountain body, presenting a layering that appears and disappears.

evidence: Among the mountains and rocks of the mid-ground: the roofs and eaves of buildings are faintly exposed behind the mountains and rocks and the grove, presenting a layering of houses hidden behind rocks. | Lower right corner, waterside: a pavilion is built on the rocky bank by the water; part of its structure is obscured by foreground mountains and rocks, forming an adjacent relationship with the water surface.
distinction: The mid-ground buildings form concealment-and-revelation layers through the screening of mountains and rocks and the grove, conforming to C2; although the pavilion in the lower right corner is built by the waterside and has a C1 feature, the overall composition emphasizes more the appearing and disappearing relationship of buildings within the natural scenery.

evidence: Lower center of the painting: a dense cluster of houses (white roofs) is distributed between dark trees and slope/cloud areas rendered in ink, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship of seeing houses within the grove. | Middle of the painting: horizontal clouds and mist (unpainted space and pale ink) interweave between the mountain ridges and the village, obscuring part of the scenery and forming a spatial layering of seeing houses through a screening layer. | Around the village: the houses are surrounded by vertical tree brushstrokes and fences; some buildings are obscured by foreground trees and rocks, with only roofs or eaves exposed.
distinction: The painting mainly creates the spatial layering of a 'misty village' through the obscuring and revealing of the house cluster by clouds and mist and trees, rather than emphasizing a strict dependent relationship between building sites and specific terrain (such as slopes, terraces, or waterside).

evidence: Right side: steep cliffs and trees in heavy ink are visible; at the foot of the mountain there are rows of tree trunks or scenic accents, but no clear houses or building forms are visible. | Center: mountains and rocks and the unpainted space of the water surface form an open space, lacking identifiable built structures.
distinction: No clear built elements are visible in the painting; it is assigned to C3 on the basis of the overall opening and closing relationships of the landscape.

evidence: Upper right: the roof, eaves, and columns of a building emerge from the bamboo grove and trees behind it, forming an obvious relationship of screening and revealing. | Right middle: dense trees in the foreground and mid-ground obscure the lower half of the building and its courtyard, exposing only partial structures, indicating the spatial layering in which the building is situated. | Lower right: the sloping ground and trees in front of the building guide the gaze, but the main body of the building presents its existence mainly through the screening of trees.
distinction: Although the building is constructed according to the slope, the painting emphasizes more the screening and revealing of the building by trees; the concealment-and-revelation relationship is the main compositional mode.

evidence: Middle of the right side: among the trees, the roof and eaves of a building are faintly visible, half-screened by branches and leaves. | Overall right side: distant mountains and nearby sloping banks, trees, and rocks form foreground-background layering, and the building is situated within the screening of the grove.
distinction: The building participates in forming the scene mainly by means of the concealment-and-revelation layering created by the grove, rather than serving as a marker identifying a specific landscape scene.

evidence: Lower center: a small bridge is visible spanning the water, connecting the nearby sloping bank with the house area in the distance, forming a clear entry clue. | Right side and mid-ground: several groups of houses are scattered along the waterside, screened among willow trees and sloping banks, and connected to the foreground through the waterside and the bridge.
distinction: Although trees screen the houses in the painting, the path formed by the small bridge and the waterside guides the gaze deep into the painting, emphasizing more an enterable spatial process.

evidence: Lower-middle of the painting, toward the left: layered building roofs are visible, partly obscured by dense trees and mountains and rocks in front, with only the eaves and top structures exposed. | Lower-middle of the painting: the buildings are hidden behind the grove, forming a spatial layering of trees in front and houses behind, with an obvious concealment-and-revelation relationship.
distinction: Although the buildings identify the scenery, the concealment-and-revelation layering created by trees and mountains and rocks screening them is the main compositional mode of the painting, more prominent than simple scenic accentuation.

evidence: Lower right: a group of houses is arranged beside the sloping bank and the waterside, unfolding along the terrain, with some houses extending to the water's edge. | Lower right-middle: there is a bamboo grove beside the houses, providing a certain screening of the building group, but the overall layout is still mainly in response to the waterside terrain.
distinction: Although there is screening by the bamboo grove, the built structures mainly present a placement relationship of leaning on the slope and beside the water and unfolding along the shore; screening is not the dominant mode of spatial organization.

evidence: Lower right: house roofs and partial structures are exposed amid the screening of groves and shrubs, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Right side: tall red-leaf trees and pines are located in front of the built structure, naturally screening the buildings and participating in the construction of spatial layering.
distinction: The painting mainly presents the concealment-and-revelation layering of buildings screened by the grove, rather than merely serving as markers identifying the scenery.

evidence: Right-side waterside: a small boat is visible moored by the water, together with the rocks on the bank and the water surface forming a mooring node. | Left-center of the painting: bamboo clumps grow on the waterside, with a large expanse of reeds above, and several birds flying past, creating a desolate and empty spatial atmosphere.
distinction: The painting lacks clear building structures; only a small boat appears as a scenic accent, so it is assigned to C3 on the basis of the focal point of the overall desolate mood.

evidence: Right side: mountains and rocks and pines are painted on the right side of the painting; no traces of built elements such as houses or bridges are visible.
distinction: There are no built elements in the painting; the scene is formed only by natural mountains, rocks, and trees, and it is only tentatively assigned to scenic accentuation.

evidence: Right side: the building group is partly obscured by foreground sloping rocks and trees, with only roofs, eaves, and parts of the walls exposed, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Middle-right: the clump of dead trees and the buildings on the right form foreground-background layering; the branches and leaves screen the buildings, indicating the spatial depth in which the buildings are situated.
distinction: Although the buildings are located by the waterside, the painting emphasizes more the spatial layering formed by their being obscured by trees and mountains and rocks, rather than focusing on their placement by the water or by the slope.

evidence: Upper left: pines grow on steep cliffs; the roof and railings of a small building appear faintly among the pines, partly obscured by the grove. | Right side and lower part: a large area of water surface or distant mountains rendered in pale ink contrasts with the solid scenery on the left, highlighting the layering of the building screened by the grove in the upper left corner.
distinction: Although the building is located high up and serves as a scenic accent, its visual relationship of being surrounded by pines and half-hidden and half-exposed is more prominent and dominates the spatial expression.

evidence: Lower-middle of the right side: the roof and eave structures of houses are visible, but they are partly obscured by the pines and other trees in front, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Right side: dense trees and mountains and rocks surround the built structures, forming a clearly layered spatial screening effect.
distinction: Although the built structures lean on the mountain and are beside the water, the painting emphasizes more the screening and revealing of the buildings by the grove; the concealment-and-revelation relationship is the main compositional mode.

evidence: Right side: a thatched hut is visible, with a person sitting and reading inside; part of the building's facade and the edge of the roof are obscured by foreground tree trunks. | Center-right: several slender tree trunks stand in front of the building, forming a foreground-to-building layering relationship, so that the building presents a half-hidden, half-exposed state. | Left side: banana plants and Taihu rocks occupy the left half of the painting, forming a left-right spatial distribution and a pictorial-depth contrast with the screened building on the right.
distinction: Although the human activity in the building serves as a scenic accent, the concealment-and-revelation layering formed by the foreground trees obscuring the building is more conspicuous in the composition and dominates the spatial expression.

evidence: Lower left: houses are partly obscured by foreground pines and rocks, with only roofs and parts of the walls exposed, presenting a screening relationship. | Center-right: a group of houses sits on flat ground at the foot of the mountain, surrounded by the mountain body and grove behind and to the side, forming a half-hidden, half-exposed layering. | Right-side mountain mid-slope: buildings high up nestle into recesses of the steep mountain rock and are obscured by the mountain's outline, indicating a distant spatial position.
distinction: Although the built structures are placed in dependence on the terrain, the painting emphasizes more the screening and revealing of buildings by mountains, rocks, and the grove, constructing spatial layering through the concealment-and-revelation relationship, so C2 is more dominant.

evidence: At the waterside toward the lower left of the painting: a small covered boat is moored among reeds and weeping willows; the lower part of the boat is obscured by dense vegetation, with only the boat's canopy exposed, forming a relationship of screening and concealment-and-revelation of the built element by natural scenery.
distinction: The boat is mainly obscured by vegetation to form a concealment-and-revelation layering, participating in creating a deep and secluded mood, rather than serving as a conspicuous marker identifying a specific landscape node.

evidence: Lower-middle, toward the left: between the mountains and rocks and the grove, beside the waterside, the partial outline of a built structure is faintly visible, seemingly with an eave structure, but most of it is obscured by foreground trees and mountains and rocks. | Right side and center of the painting: dense trees form the foreground and mid-ground, screening the space behind and possible built structures, constituting a concealment-and-revelation relationship.
distinction: Although there are waterside and gaps between mountains and rocks in the painting, no clear movement-through-the-landscape clues such as bridges, paths, or gates are visible connecting to the built structure; the existence of the built structure is mainly suggested by the screening of trees and mountains and rocks, so C2 is more apt than C4.

evidence: Foreground right: a combination of slope rocks, willow trees, and bamboo is visible, occupying the main position in the painting and identifying the waterside scenery. | Middle ground: a large area of unpainted space represents the water surface, connecting the foreground and the distant view. | Distant view left: continuous sloping banks and rocks, among which there are blurred block-like outlines, but these cannot be confirmed as built elements.
distinction: The painting takes trees, rocks, and the waterside as its main subject; no clear built elements are seen, so natural scenery serves mainly as scenic accentuation.

evidence: Behind the trees on the left: through the bare branches, the roof and wall structure of a building can be faintly seen, presenting a half-hidden, half-revealed state. | Behind the waterside rocks on the right: parts of the building's columns and eaves emerge from behind the rocks, screened by terrain and vegetation, forming spatial layering.
distinction: Although in the lower left of the painting figures walk along a small path, implying a route, the buildings themselves are mainly presented through the concealment and revelation created by trees and rocks screening them, establishing their layering within the landscape, rather than emphasizing a process of entry.

evidence: Lower right to middle ground: a winding mountain path starts from the waterside on the right, passes through gaps between woods and rocks, and extends into the depth of the painting; traveling figures can be seen on the path. | Lower left corner: a wooden bridge is visible spanning a stream, connecting to the path leading into the mountains, forming the starting point for entering the painting. | Upper right hilltop: a pavilion is built on the summit, serving as the endpoint of the mountain path's extension and as a visual focus, forming an accessible spatial connection with the path below.
distinction: Although woods screen the buildings in the painting, the mountain path, bridge, and hilltop pavilion running through the composition constitute a clear process of travel and entry, and their role in spatial organization is stronger.

evidence: Lower center: a small boat is moving on the water, with ripples at its stern, suggesting that its direction of travel is toward the peach-blossom bank in the middle ground. | Middle ground: where the water surface extends, there is land covered with pink flowering trees, forming a visual destination. | Whole painting: no fixed built elements such as houses, pavilions, or bridges are seen in the painting, only natural landscape and boats.
distinction: The painting lacks fixed built elements, but the boat's trajectory of travel suggests a process of journeying toward the depths of the peach blossoms, so it is assigned to C4; if the peach-blossom island is regarded as a scenic marker, it approaches C3.

evidence: Left middle-lower part: a pavilion is built at the water's edge, with wooden piles or bridge structures supporting its base, sited in response to the waterside terrain. | Lower right corner: figures are active on the hillside and at the waterside, suggesting passable space, but the built elements mainly present a posture of being built alongside the water.
distinction: The built elements are clearly sited according to the waterside terrain, presenting a relationship of placement according to the site; the dominant manifestation is terrain-responsive siting.

evidence: Whole painting: only slope rocks, bamboo clumps, bare trees, and distant mountains are seen in the painting; no artificial built structures such as houses, pavilions, or bridges are visible. | Upper left: several lines of inscription and seals are present, which are textual information of the painting, not evidence of spatial built elements.
distinction: There are no built structures in the painting; it is assigned to the closest category based on the overall visible organization of the natural landscape.

evidence: Central hill: pavilions and buildings are layered according to the mountain's form, arranged in staggered fashion from the foot of the mountain to the summit following the terrain's height. | Mountain foot and riverbank: some buildings extend to the water's edge and meet the shoreline, responding to the waterside terrain. | Right side: a city wall extends along the high ground, following the terrain's undulations.
distinction: Although the buildings are the visual center, their layout closely conforms to the mountain's form and terrain; the relationship of placement according to the site is most prominent, so C1 is more accurate than C3.

evidence: Left center: houses are built hidden among mountains, rocks, and dense woodland, with only roofs and parts of eave walls revealed, forming a clear layering of concealment and revelation. | Lower left: another smaller built structure is likewise partly screened by trees and terrain, blending into the mountain-forest environment.
distinction: Although there are bridges and clues of travelers in the lower part of the painting, the most prominent compositional role of the built elements themselves is to form spatial layering through screening and revealing by woods and rocks, rather than serving directly as the endpoint or entrance of a path.

evidence: Middle-left valley: house buildings can be seen screened by the surrounding dense pine forest and mountain forms, with only parts of roofs and walls revealed, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Painting overall: the buildings are deeply hidden behind woods and rocks, their existence suggested through the screening of natural scenery, forming spatial layering.
distinction: Although there are streams and boats in the painting, the main compositional role of the built elements is to present layering through screening by woods and rocks, rather than emphasizing clues of a path of entry.

evidence: Lower left corner: a bridge is visible connected to a path, the path extending along rocks and the waterside, forming spatial clues of entry. | Upper right: buildings are built on terraces following the mountain's form, connected to the mountain path on the right, suggesting accessibility.
distinction: Although the buildings at the upper right have the characteristic of siting according to the mountain (C1), the bridge and path at the lower left and the mountain path on the right more strongly guide the viewer's gaze and travel route, making access to secluded settings the dominant mode of spatial organization.

evidence: Left mountainside: pavilions or pass-like structures are built against the cliff and following the mountain's form, presenting a form of placement according to strategic terrain/against the rock. | Lower middle and lower right: building groups (pavilions, halls) are distributed at different heights along the slope at the mountain foot, and unfold closely along the shoreline. | Lower right waterside: platforms or waterside pavilions extend from the building bases to the water, with boats moored nearby, showing a relationship of arrangement following the bank.
distinction: Although the buildings identify the scenery of the mountain foot and waterside, their layout—distributed according to the slope and unfolding along the bank—more directly embodies the corresponding siting relationship between built elements and natural terrain (mountain form, waterside).

evidence: Lower right water surface: a small sailboat and a small skiff are visible on the water, suggesting clues of movement on the water. | Lower part near the bank: reeds are painted, contrasting with the open water surface and defining the waterside space. | Upper distant view: distant mountains depicted in pale ink meet the water surface, constituting an open visual space.
distinction: There are no clear buildings in the painting; only boats suggest water transport and a process of movement, so it is assigned to C4.

evidence: Upper panel: the painting depicts reeds and flying geese; no traces of buildings or artificial built elements are seen. | Lower panel: the painting depicts sloping banks, bare trees, distant water, and flying geese; no built elements such as houses or bridges are seen.
distinction: There are no clear built elements in the painting; it is assigned to the closest category based only on the visible organization of sloping-bank waterscape.

evidence: Among the trees in the lower-middle part of the painting: a roof outline tinged with pale red is faintly visible, partly screened by branches and leaves, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Lower right corner of the painting: roof or eave lines outlined in ink are revealed beside shrubs, indicating that built elements lie behind the vegetation.
distinction: The built elements form spatial layering mainly through roofs revealed behind screening trees, rather than serving as a conspicuous marker identifying a particular scene.

evidence: Lower painting, bottom center-left: several small ink blots are visible, whose forms are suspected to be house or bridge structures, but they are extremely blurry and cannot be clearly identified | Upper painting, full frame: depicts willow trees and lake rocks; no architectural structures are seen
distinction: The main category C2 refers to architectural structures that are blurry or uncertain; here the lower painting's bottom appears to have tiny buildings but this cannot be confirmed; it differs from C3 (no buildings) in that traces of buildings still remain, and differs from C1 in that they are not clear.

evidence: Upper painted panel: The roof and wall sections of the thatched hut are partly screened by the bamboo clumps and Taihu rocks in the foreground, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Lower painted panel: The left side and rear of the waterside studio are screened by withered trees, pine branches, and mountain rocks, with the building half-hidden among the natural scenery.
distinction: The painting's emphasis lies in the mutual screening and revelation between the buildings and the trees and rocks that form the scene, rather than in stressing the placement of buildings depending on specific terrain.

evidence: Upper right: a small boat and two people are visible; no fixed built elements (such as houses, bridges, etc.) are seen. | Left side and center: earthen slopes, trees, and reeds are visible; the water surface is open, with no sign of buildings set against mountains and water or screened among them.
distinction: There are no clear built elements in the painting; only boats dot the open water surface, so it is assigned to scenic accentuation based on the overall spatial conception.

evidence: Lower left corner: a group of houses nestles against the mountain foot and is arranged along the shoreline, presenting a layout that unfolds along the bank and is sited in response to the terrain. | Left middle: the mountain is steep, and the houses lie between the slope at the mountain foot and the water's edge; the building site forms a corresponding relationship with the natural sloping bank. | Lower middle: a wooden bridge and pedestrians are visible, connecting the two banks and helping to explain the connectivity of the waterside space, but the main building group is manifested as built according to the terrain.
distinction: The layout of houses arranged along the shoreline (unfolding along the bank) is the main relationship between built elements and terrain; although a bridge exists, it serves more as a local connection and does not create a strong dominant sense of a journey turning into the depths.

evidence: Right center: a group of pavilion buildings stands on sloping ground, surrounded by trees | Right side: an arched bridge connects the land on the right with the sloping ground where the buildings stand, forming a path clue | Lower left and lower middle: several fishing boats are on the water, suggesting movement and travel on the water surface
distinction: The bridge in the painting clearly connects the built area and provides a path clue from here to there, emphasizing the accessibility of the space and the process of travel more than mere screening by woods.

evidence: Left painting, lower-middle to middle mountainside: multiple groups of house buildings are layered on terraces following the mountain's form, extending from the waterside all the way to the mountainside, their layout responding to the terrain's undulations. | Left painting, center: the building bases are closely integrated with the slope's outline, presenting a spatial relationship of distribution according to the slope and unfolding with the terrain.
distinction: Although woods and buildings are adjacent in the painting, the buildings mainly present a layout of layered placement in response to mountain terraces; screening and concealment are not their dominant compositional mode.

evidence: Middle ground, slightly left: an open hall is visible, with two people seated facing each other inside; the building is partly screened by bare trees and bamboo clumps in front and woodland behind, revealing only the roof, eave columns, and interior space. | Center of the painting: dense trunks and branches interweave in front of the building, forming obvious visual screening and giving the built elements a layered relationship of being half-hidden, half-revealed. | Right side: a huge rock and the woodland on the left together enclose the middle-ground space, further setting off the state of the built elements hidden among woods and rocks.
distinction: Although the building identifies the scenery within the woods, the painting emphasizes more the screening and revealing of the building by woods and rocks; the relationship of concealment and revelation is the main way this space is organized.

evidence: Lower left corner: several houses are visible set beside the water, surrounded by trees, serving as the starting or ending point of a path. | Center-left to mountainside: a clear stepped path winds up along the mountain's form, connecting the waterside at the mountain foot with the depths of the mountains. | Overall composition: the path guides the gaze from near to far and from bottom to top into the painting, presenting an accessible, traversable spatial process.
distinction: The stepped path winding along the mountain's form clearly guides the process of journeying into the mountains; this role in spatial organization is more prominent than mere screening by woods.

evidence: Right mountainside: the roofs and eaves of a group of buildings emerge from the dense pine forest, forming a layered relationship of houses hidden deep in the woods. | Lower right corner: a winding path and small accent figures are painted among the rocks, echoing spatially with the buildings screened by woods above. | Lower left and bottom: low building groups are distributed at the waterside and mountain foot, forming a near-far contrast with the buildings in the woodland on the right.
distinction: Although there are mountain paths and figures in the painting, the core compositional role lies in the spatial layering formed by the buildings on the right through screening and revealing by woods, rather than emphasizing a path guiding entry.

evidence: Lower left: houses are built at the waterside, with boats moored nearby, forming an accessible node | Lower center: a small bridge spans the water, connecting the two banks and providing a clear clue of passage | Right mountainside: buildings are faintly visible distributed according to the mountain's form, forming layering with the space below the mountain
distinction: The connecting role of the bridge and paths in the painting is more prominent, guiding the gaze and travel route, rather than merely emphasizing the corresponding placement of buildings and terrain.

evidence: Left middle ground: the roofs and eaves of a group of buildings appear indistinctly behind sparse woods, partly screened by trunks and branches, forming layering of concealment and revelation. | Among the rocks and bamboo grove on the right: building outlines are faintly visible behind rocks and dense bamboo leaves, screened by foreground scenery, suggesting a deeper spatial layer.
distinction: Although a bridge and path are implied on the left of the painting, the buildings themselves establish their spatial presence mainly through screening and revealing by woods and rocks, rather than emphasizing a process of entry.

evidence: Upper part of the right slope: a pavilion is built at the edge of a steep slope, with visible column support structures below, sited in response to the mountain's height and presenting the feature of buildings set according to the slope. | Left cliff, lower part near the water: a building (apparently a pavilion or waterside structure) is visible arranged against the rocky bank at the mountain foot, combined with the rocky terrain and waterside, presenting a relationship of placement according to the site.
distinction: Although the buildings serve an accenting role in the painting, their support structures and positions more directly embody adaptation and attachment to the steep terrain and waterside; the feature of terrain-responsive siting is more significant than mere scenic accentuation.

evidence: Right water surface: several sailboats dot the broad water surface, echoing the distant mountains and clouds. | Lower right corner: sloping banks and trees are painted, serving as a foreground setting off the water surface and distant mountains. | Upper-middle part of the painting: clouds and mist swirl, distant mountains are faintly visible, creating an open expanse of water.
distinction: No clear building-type built elements are seen in the painting; sailboats as accent elements mark the water space, so it is assigned to C3.

evidence: Lower-middle part of the painting, slightly right: the roof and beam-column structure of a house are faintly revealed behind trees and a sloping bank, presenting a half-hidden, half-revealed state. | Center of the painting: a clump of dark-ink trees screens the built elements behind, forming foreground and middle-ground layering.
distinction: Although the built elements lie beside the sloping bank, their main compositional role is to form layering of concealment and revelation through screening by trees, rather than emphasizing a corresponding relationship of placement according to terrain.

evidence: Left side and center: the painting is mainly composed of mountains and rocks, trees, and streams; rocks are layered and streams wind, presenting the trend of natural terrain. | Right side: mountain ridges rise and fall, echoing the scenery on the left, forming an open layout of mountain-and-water space.
distinction: No clear built elements are seen in the painting; based on the natural forms and layout of rocks and flowing water, it is closest to a spatial organization arising in response to the terrain.

evidence: Lower right: a house is built at the edge of sloping ground by the water, with visible column supports at its base, presenting a form of elevation built over the water in response to the waterside terrain. | Left side and center: a large area of trees and sloping bank extends to the lower right; the house lies at the junction where the end of the sloping bank meets the water, its layout settled in response to the terrain.
distinction: Although the house is partly screened by the sloping bank and trees in front, its form of columns set according to the water more directly embodies the logic of siting in response to terrain conditions.

evidence: Right and center: The painting mainly depicts reeds, large-leaved plants (resembling lotus leaves), and round-leaved duckweed; the brushwork is light and elegant, representing waterside vegetation, with no architectural structures. | Lower part: Faint water ripples and swimming fish (or aquatic plants) are painted, representing the pond surface; no bridges, embankments, or other man-made facilities are visible. | Left side: An area for an inscribed poem and seals; the text mentions 'Pu Tang' (Reed Pond), corroborating that the scene is a natural pond landscape, with no architectural depiction.
distinction: The main category is judged as C3 (no architecture identifiable), because the painting consists entirely of natural aquatic plants, water scenery, and inscription, without any man-made buildings or structures, which is entirely distinct from categories containing clear or faint architecture (C1/C2).

evidence: Right center-lower: Between the mountains and rocks and the trees, the roofs and walls of several buildings are revealed; the buildings are partly screened by the trees and rocks in front, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Right side overall: Dense trees and mountains and rocks form the foreground and middle ground, with built elements faintly appearing among them, presenting a spatial layering of houses seen within the woods.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited against the mountains and beside the water, the painting emphasizes more their layered relationship of being screened and revealed by trees and rocks, rather than placement solely according to terrain.

evidence: Painting overall: The painting depicts banana plants and flowers in snow; no built elements such as buildings, bridges, or paths are visible.
distinction: There are no built elements in the painting; it is assigned to the closest category based on the overall visible space.

evidence: Center-right: A thatched-roof open pavilion stands on the sloping bank, its columns clearly rendered, serving as the endpoint or resting place of the path. | Center-left: A person holding a staff walks along a small path on the sloping bank, the movement line clearly pointing toward the thatched pavilion, forming a movement-through-the-landscape thread approaching the built elements. | Lower part and left side: The sloping bank meets the water surface (unpainted space), and the path extends along the waterside, guiding the line of sight and the direction of travel toward the pavilion.
distinction: The movement line of the figure walking along the path toward the thatched pavilion constitutes a clear relationship of entry and arrival, which governs the spatial expression more than placement according to terrain alone.

evidence: Center of the painting: A small boat carrying two people can be seen moving across the broad water surface, forming a visual guide. | Right side: Trees and sloping banks are visible, but no fixed built elements such as houses or pavilions are seen.
distinction: There are no definite built elements in the painting; only a small boat moving on the water, which barely corresponds to an enterable spatial process.

evidence: Center-left: A figure can be seen lying on the mountains and rocks, with a waterfall flowing down nearby; no trace of architecture. | Whole painting: The painting consists mainly of mountains and rocks, trees, a waterfall, and figures; no built elements are visible.
distinction: No built elements are visible in the painting, so it cannot be definitively classified according to the relationship between built elements and landscape; it is assigned to the closest category based solely on the overall landscape composition.

evidence: Lower left: A house with a thatched roof and an arched doorway is partly screened by the tall pine trunks and branches and foliage in front, with only the roof and part of the walls revealed. | Center-lower part of the painting: The house is surrounded by sloping ground and sparse woods; the screening by trees gives the built elements a layered relationship of being half hidden and half revealed.
distinction: Although the house is sited on the hillside, the painting emphasizes more the relationship of screening and revelation of the house by trees, and the feature of concealment and revelation into a scene is more prominent.

evidence: Left bank: Above the sloping rocks, the roof of a building is visible, half screened behind trees and rocks. | Central pine woods: Deep within the pine woods, the colonnade structure of a pavilion is faintly visible, partly screened by tree trunks and foliage. | Overall composition: The built elements, through the screening and revelation by mountains, rocks, and trees, present spatial layering of concealment and revelation in the woods and behind the rocks.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited along the sloping bank, the painting emphasizes more their layered relationship of concealment and revelation screened and revealed by trees, mountains, and rocks.

evidence: Lower right bank edge: Simple wooden posts or a platform stand at the water's edge, with a person wearing a conical hat sitting on it, a fishing line beside them entering the water, placed close against the waterside and the base of the willow trees. | Right side: A broad expanse of weeping willows covers the sloping bank; the built elements are hidden in the willow shade at the water's edge, unfolding along the natural shoreline.
distinction: The built elements are placed close against the waterside terrain, showing the feature of a platform set according to the water, rather than serving merely as a distant landmark.

evidence: Bank in the center-right of the painting: Two people can be seen sitting on rocks, facing the open water surface, with no traces of built elements such as buildings, bridges, or roads around them. | Left side of the painting: Mountains, rocks, and trees are naturally distributed, with no man-made built elements attached to or screened among them.
distinction: There are no definite built elements in the painting, only natural landscape and figures as scenic accents; the figures indicate the viewing position on the bank, so it is barely assigned to C3.

evidence: Left side of the painting: The contours and textures of the rocky sloping bank are visible, forming natural terrain. | Right side of the painting: There is a large tree, beneath which two people sit on the ground; no buildings or structures are visible.
distinction: No built elements are visible at all in the painting; based on the natural spatial organization of the overall landscape and the figures resting, it is barely assigned to the closest category of terrain relationship.

evidence: Lower right: A dense cluster of buildings is distributed among the trees and mountains and rocks, with roofs and walls partly screened by branches and foliage, presenting a clear layering of concealment and revelation. | Center-left: A small number of buildings can be seen on the waterside terraces, interspersed with the surrounding trees and terrain, blending into the natural scenery.
