evidence: Slightly right of center: a small bridge spanning the water surface is visible, with a person walking on it, connecting the foreground water surface with the woods and village in the middle ground and forming a clear entry path. | Lower left: several houses are distributed at varying heights according to the mountain terrain and trees and woodland, their roofs and walls clearly visible, serving as the destination of the path's extension or as scenery along the way. | Foreground to middle ground: the water surface, lotus plants, shoreline, and bridge together form a traversable visual thread that guides the eye deep into the painting.
distinction: Although the houses built against the mountain embody the characteristics of C1, the movement-through-the-landscape clues of the bridge and pedestrian are more prominent, organizing the spatial process of entering from one place to another, so C4 is more apt.

evidence: Upper right: the building complex is placed tightly against a steep cliff, stacked layer upon layer following the slope, with houses at varying heights, their layout following the undulations of the terrain. | Lower left: a small pavilion is placed beside a rocky platform by the water, built against the rock and closely integrated with the surrounding pine-and-rock terrain. | Right mountainside: a stepped plank walkway winds down along the rock face, connecting the built structures above with those below, showing the adaptation of paths and building layout to the mountain terrain.
distinction: Although the painting contains a plank walkway connecting upper and lower levels (a C4 clue), the characteristic of terrain-based arrangement—the building complex distributed layer upon layer against the cliff and the pavilion built against the rock—is more dominant, emphasizing the correspondence between the built elements and the terrain.

evidence: Left middle ground: a group of buildings is arranged at varying heights on hillside terraces, with roofs rising and falling in accord with the form of the mountain. | Lower-right foreground: a waterside pavilion is built on the bank by the water, with steps extending from the sloping bank down to the water surface and connecting to the building's base.
distinction: Although the waterside pavilion at lower right has steps that embody an access relationship, the building group on the left, distributed according to the slope, is larger in scale, and overall the siting relationship of the built elements conforming to the terrain is more prominent.

evidence: Center of the painting: a clear flight of steps/mountain path winds upward from the foot of the mountain, passing through woods and mountains and rocks and connecting building groups at different heights. | Left mountainside and mountain foot: there are multi-storey buildings on the mountainside and waterside buildings at the mountain foot, and the stepped path links them, forming a movement-through-the-landscape thread from bottom to top and from outside to inside. | Right mountain foot: houses are visible screened among trees and mountains and rocks, echoing the overall mountain terrain and path system and indicating an accessible space.
distinction: Although the buildings are arranged at varying heights according to the mountain terrain, the stepped path running through the painting has a strong guiding function, making the accessible, traversable spatial process dominant.

evidence: Lower right, middle-to-lower part: a group of houses is visible built overlooking the water, with wooden piles or stone foundations at the bottom supporting them at the edge of the waterside, unfolding in accord with the waterside terrain. | Lower right: a multi-storey building is visible arranged at varying heights according to the rocky terrain, its building base closely integrated with the form of the mountains and rocks.
distinction: Although trees are adjacent to the built elements in the painting, the built elements mainly present a terrain-responsive layout relationship of placement relying on specific terrain conditions such as the waterside and mountains and rocks, rather than forming layering primarily through screening and revelation.

evidence: Upper-right mountainside: the building complex is placed on a mountainside terrace, arranged following the undulations of the mountain, presenting a state of houses set on terraces. | Lower-right bank: houses are built overlooking the water, situated on flat ground by the bank, with a fence structure alongside, presenting an arrangement following the bank.
distinction: Although there is screening by trees, the correspondence between the buildings' siting on terraces and by the water and the terrain is clearer and more dominant.

evidence: Lower left and lower-middle part: the building complex is partly screened by withered trees and pine woods in the foreground and middle ground, with only roofs and parts of walls exposed, presenting a layering of buildings seen within the woods. | Right mountainside and upper right: houses are arranged at varying heights according to the mountain terrain, and the pavilions at upper right are hidden behind mountain rocks and trees and woodland, forming a screened relationship of buildings hidden behind rocks.
distinction: Although the built elements are placed according to the terrain, the painting more strongly emphasizes the screening and revealing of buildings by trees and woodland and mountains and rocks, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship is the primary means of composing the scene.

evidence: Lower right: a railed pavilion and attached buildings are built on a sloping terrace, with a person standing leaning on the railing inside the pavilion. | Upper left and distant view: a large area of unpainted space represents the open water surface or sky, with a bright moon at upper left and faint mountain silhouettes in the distance. | Overall painting: the building serves as the visual focus of the foreground, forming a relationship of mutual gazing with the distant landscape, water, and bright moon, and marking out the prize viewing spot.
distinction: Although the building is built on a sloping terrace, its more primary role in the composition is as a viewing focus, concentrating and marking out the scenery of gazing afar at the landscape, water, and bright moon.

evidence: Left: the branches and leaves of trees cover above the thatched hut's roof, with the tree trunks in front of the house, forming an evident screening relationship. | Slightly left of center: a person can be seen lying inside the thatched hut, and the building itself is partly screened by trees and the reeds in front, presenting a layering of concealment and revelation. | Right: the water surface and reed beds form a front-to-back spatial relationship with the thatched hut, setting off the environmental layering in which the hut is situated.
distinction: Although the thatched hut is built overlooking the water, the painting more strongly emphasizes the screening and revealing of the roof and building itself by tree branches and leaves, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship rather than emphasizing the determining role of terrain in the layout.

evidence: Lower middle, near the water: a pavilion/house sits on a sloping bank, with a clear path extending alongside it, and a figure is walking along the path toward the building, presenting an accessible, reachable spatial process. | Left mountainside: a group of houses is arranged according to the mountain terrain, partly screened by trees, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship with the mountain. | Right water surface: a small boat is on the distant water, suggesting a movement-through-the-landscape clue on the water.
distinction: The pavilion, figure, and path at the lower middle of the painting form a clear relationship of travelling and entering, which more strongly dominates the spatial organization of the painting than the mere screening of the houses on the left.

evidence: Right mountaintop: a pavilion is set on the summit of a high rocky peak, placed toweringly according to the mountain terrain. | Middle-ground waterside: several houses unfold along gentle sloping ground and the shoreline. | Lower left: buildings are screened among rocks and trees and woodland, following the local undulations of the terrain.
distinction: Although the built elements accent the landscape scenery, their layout more prominently highlights the correspondence of terrain-based placement according to site conditions such as mountain forms, terraces, and the waterside, rather than serving merely as isolated markers.

evidence: Lower right: the roof and posts of a thatched pavilion are visible among trees and rocks, partly screened by foreground branches and leaves and mountains and rocks. | Foreground: trees and sloping rocks interlock, screening the thatched pavilion and presenting a spatial layering of alternating concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the thatched pavilion marks out a corner of the foreground, its primary scenic-composition role lies in forming layering through the screening and revealing by trees and rocks, so C2 is more apt than C3.

evidence: Lower-middle part of the painting: a group of building bases sits directly on a waterside terrace, with supporting posts or an elevated structure visible at the bottom, unfolding in accord with the waterside terrain. | Middle-right part of the painting: behind the buildings are trees and woodland and sloping rocks, and the layout of the built elements is set against the waterside and sloping ground, presenting a relationship of terrain-based placement.
distinction: Although the buildings are partly screened by trees and woodland, their characteristic of being sited by the water and against the slope and placed in conformity with the terrain is more prominent and dominates the spatial expression.

evidence: Lower left: several thatched huts are distributed at varying heights along the sloping bank at the mountain foot and the bamboo grove, presenting a layout of houses set on the ground and unfolding with the slope. | Left middle ground: the building complex is placed at the water's edge, forming a spatial correspondence of terrain-based arrangement with the distant mountains and the waterside.
distinction: Although the buildings are screened by bamboo groves, their primary scenic-composition role lies in placement according to site conditions such as the sloping bank and the water's edge, rather than forming layering simply through concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower right: a small bridge is visible by the water connecting the two banks, suggesting a traversable path | Left and lower left: houses are arranged at varying heights along the mountain foot and rocks, linked by paths or the waterside | Right center: a group of houses is screened among trees and woodland and mountains and rocks, forming layering
distinction: Although the built elements form layering through screening by trees and woodland and mountains and rocks (C2), the connection by the bridge and waterside paths more strongly emphasizes the accessible, traversable spatial process (C4).

evidence: Lower right: the roofs and walls of several buildings emerge among the woods, the buildings partly screened by trees and mountains and rocks, forming a layering of concealment and revelation. | Center, slightly lower right: a pavilion or waterside pavilion outline is visible at the water's edge, partly screened by foreground tree branches and leaves.
distinction: Although the buildings are beside the water and against the mountains, the painting mainly emphasizes the screening and revealing relationship of the buildings by trees and woodland, rather than simply terrain-based placement.

evidence: Lower-left corner: a flat bridge is visible spanning a stream, with tiny figures of people or livestock on the bridge, connecting the paths on the two banks and forming a traversable clue. | Right mountainside: among the screening trees and rocks there is a very tiny building outline (possibly a pavilion or house), suggesting dwellings in the mountains, but the details are blurry. | Lower-middle part of the painting: the gaps between the stream and mountains and rocks form a space extending into the depths, and the bridge at lower left acts as a node guiding the eye and the movement-through-the-landscape route into the painting's interior.
distinction: The bridge at lower left clearly constitutes a path clue for movement through the landscape and entry (C4), while the tiny building on the right mountainside, though having screening characteristics (C2), is less prominent than the bridge's role in spatial organization, which is also consistent with the description of the bridge and pedestrians in the inscription.

evidence: Lower middle, slightly right: a small boat is on the open water surface, with people aboard, its bow pointing toward the lower-left bank, constituting a movement-through-the-landscape clue. | Lower left: a thatched pavilion is built on the sloping ground by the bank, with trees alongside, serving as the landing rendezvous point for the boat. | Left center: below a huge mountain rock, an arched doorway and stone steps are visible, showing a built entrance set against the mountain rock and suggesting a path leading deeper.
distinction: Although the painting contains a concealment-and-revelation relationship of buildings screened by mountain rocks (C2), the small boat, thatched pavilion, and entrance below the rock together constitute a continuous spatial process of approaching by boat and turning into the depths, and C4 better captures this movement route.

evidence: Middle-right water surface of the painting: a small boat with figures aboard is visible, floating on the open water surface. | Lower left to center of the painting: the foreground consists of sloping banks and miscellaneous trees, forming a spatial transition with the middle-ground water surface. | Distant view of the painting: distant mountains stretch continuously, with woods at the mountain foot, forming a deep spatial layering with the water surface.
distinction: No clear built elements are visible in the painting, but the water surface and the small boat suggest an accessible, traversable spatial process, so it is assigned to the closest category, C4.

evidence: Lower left: a thatched hut is built on the sloping bank by the water, screened by the branches and leaves of trees in front and by sloping rocks, with only the roof and parts of the walls exposed, forming a layering of a house hidden within the woods. | Lower right: a bridge and pedestrians are visible, suggesting a movement-through-the-landscape path, but the scenic-composition role of the main built element (the thatched hut) lies in its screened state by natural scenery.
distinction: Although the painting contains movement-through-the-landscape clues, the concealment-and-revelation relationship of the thatched hut at lower left, partly screened by trees and sloping rocks, is more prominent and dominates the spatial expression of the built elements and the landscape.

evidence: Left mountainside: a group of buildings is arranged at varying heights in conformity with the hillside terrace terrain, the building bases closely integrated with the slope of the mountain. | Upper-right peak: a pavilion is placed on the summit of the highest peak, built relying on the terrain of the mountain top. | Upper-middle mountain hollow: several buildings are hidden in the recess of the mountain, placed following the undulations of the mountain.
distinction: Although the pavilion on the peak has a scenic-accentuation role, the layout of the multiple building groups following the mountain terrain is more prominent, and overall a relationship of terrain-based placement is presented.

evidence: Lower-middle of the painting: a bridge and paths are visible connecting the waterside with a village at the foot of the mountain; there are pedestrians on the bridge, and the path extends into the depth of the painting. | Middle of the painting, mountainside and valley: several houses are scattered, forming a coherent travel route with the paths and bridge, guiding the eye from near to far into the mountains. | Lower left foreground of the painting: a pavilion and railings are built at the waterside, serving as the starting point or node of the path, connecting with the bridge and village in the middle ground.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited against the mountain and beside the water, what the painting emphasizes more is the enterable, traversable spatial process linked by the bridge and paths, rather than mere placement according to terrain.

evidence: Center-left mountainside: a group of houses built against the mountain is visible, presenting clear built structures. | From the lower part to the center of the painting: a winding, zigzagging path extends upward from the valley at the bottom of the painting, connecting directly to the building group on the mountainside. | Overall composition: the path and built structures form a clear connection, guiding the eye from the foreground deep into the dwelling on the mountainside, presenting an enterable, reachable spatial process.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed against the mountain, the winding upward path in the painting connecting the foreground with the buildings has a more prominent role as a clue guiding movement and entry, dominating the spatial organization.

evidence: Top of the main peak, upper center: a pavilion sits atop the highest peak, marking the peak's edge and becoming the visual focal point and identifier of the towering mountain mass. | Lower left, mountain foot and waterside: a walled building group is arranged against the mountain foot and waterside, marking the human settlement scenery at the mountain foot. | Central mountainside: stairs or paths are faintly visible winding among the mountains and rocks, connecting the scenery above and below.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed according to terrain, the main role of the hilltop pavilion and the building group at the mountain foot is to mark and emphasize specific scenery at the peak and at the mountain foot, serving an identifying function.

evidence: Lower middle: a bridge is visible spanning a stream, and behind the bridge it connects to houses hidden among trees, forming a clear relationship of passage and arrival. | Center-left mountainside: an archway or pass-type structure is visible, with a winding mountain path spiraling up below it, presenting a spatial process of moving from here to there.
distinction: Although the houses are screened by trees, the connection of movement clues such as the bridge, mountain path, and gateway is more prominent in the painting, dominating the enterable spatial organization.

evidence: Lower left and middle ground: a bridge, stepped paths, and figures are visible, winding upward along the mountain terrain and waterside, forming clear movement clues. | Upper middle and upper left: pavilions are visible on the mountainside and at the summit; the paths guide the eye toward these built structures, presenting a reachable spatial relationship.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed against the mountain, what is more prominent in the painting is the process of movement guided by the bridge and paths and the sense of spatial penetration.

evidence: Lower left and lower middle: a stream winds along, accompanied by paths, a small bridge, and moving figures, forming clear movement clues leading into the depth of the painting. | Center-left: built structures are placed on mountain-slope terraces, enclosed by fences, serving as a destination or waypoint guided by the paths and stream.
distinction: The clear paths, stream, and figure-movement clues in the painting constitute a strong process of entry and movement, which characterizes the overall spatial organization better than mere placement against the mountain.

evidence: Upper-left ridge: several houses placed according to the mountain terrain are visible, located high on the mountain mass. | From the center to the upper left of the painting: a winding, zigzagging mountain road spirals up from the mountainside, connecting directly to and leading toward the built structures at the summit. | Right mountainside: pedestrians are visible walking on the mountain road, reinforcing the enterable and traversable quality of the path.
distinction: Although the built structures are placed according to the mountain terrain, the winding, spiraling mountain road in the painting serves as a clear movement clue, dominating the spatial entry process from the foot of the mountain up to the built structures above; therefore C4 is more apt than C1.

evidence: Lower left: a city is built at the mountain foot and waterside, its wall following the undulations of the terrain, presenting a layout of defense based on the site. | Right middle to lower right: village houses are densely distributed along the river shoreline, unfolding along the bank and forming a close relationship of reliance on the water surface. | Upper center: houses are placed separately on slopes among the mountains, with a mountain road winding to connect them, reflecting placement according to mountain terrain.
distinction: Although the painting contains movement clues such as mountain roads and bridges, the built structures (city, village) mainly present a placement relationship of relying on the mountain and water and unfolding along the bank, with the feature of terrain-based arrangement more prominent.

evidence: Lower left and middle-right water surface: two canopy boats and figures are visible, floating on the open water between reed beds and distant mountains | Overall composition: the water surface has extensive unpainted space, and the distribution of boats suggests movement routes on the water and spatial extension
distinction: The boats mainly present the dynamic process and path suggestion of movement on the water, rather than statically marking a fixed landscape scenery.

evidence: Lower left: a figure is visible sitting upright on a slope rock, surrounded by low shrubs and a gentle sloping bank | Right side: tall trees, bamboo clumps, and jagged lake rocks are visible, forming a natural space with the left sloping bank
distinction: The painting has no artificial buildings; it mainly shows a figure sitting against natural slope rocks, closest to a posture of placement according to terrain, rather than scenic accentuation by architecture.

evidence: Left side: several thatched huts are located behind large trees, their roofs and walls partly blocked by trunks and branches, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Lower right corner: a long bridge spans the water surface, its body faintly visible, suggesting spatial extension.
distinction: Although the painting has a bridge suggesting passage, the layers of concealment and revelation formed by the left thatched huts screened by trees are the core of the composition, more consistent with the feature of concealment and revelation forming a scene.

evidence: Center-left of the painting: two figures are visible walking among cloud-and-mist-filled mountains, presenting a movement toward traveling into the depth of the painting. | Overall painting: the painting mainly consists of mountains and rocks, trees, clouds and mist, and waterfalls; no clear built elements such as houses, pavilions, bridges, or artificial paths are seen.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built entities, but the walking movement of the figures suggests a spatial process of entering deep into the landscape, so in the absence of obvious built structures it is assigned to the closest category, C4.

evidence: Right bank: the roof and walls of a thatched hut are partly blocked by the branches and leaves of trees and slope rocks in front, presenting a screened relationship of concealment and revelation. | Left side of the painting: a small boat and figures are on the river, serving as movement clues, but they do not form a direct spatial connection with the built structures on the right.
distinction: Although the painting has boat movement, the most prominent compositional feature of the right thatched hut is the layering formed by screening by trees and slope rocks, rather than emphasizing the entry relationship of paths.

evidence: Center and left of the painting: a large number of pine trees are densely arranged, with upright trunks and luxuriant, interwoven branches and leaves, forming deep layers of woodland and a sense of screening. | Upper left corner: among distant mountains and clouds there are very faint building outlines (possibly roofs), appearing indistinct, presenting a state screened by clouds and mist. | Lower right: a figure pushes a cart on flat ground in front of the pine forest, forming a front-and-back spatial layering with the dense pine forest behind.
distinction: The main label C2 emphasizes the concealment-and-revelation relationship in which built structures (houses) are screened by pine forest and clouds and mist (houses hidden in the forest); the alternative explanation C4, although it has figure-movement clues, lacks a clear connection between paths and built structures in the painting to show a process of entry.

evidence: Left side: a towering city wall or embankment is visible extending along the waterside terrain, with trees painted on top, presenting a form of defense based on the water and arrangement according to the site. | Center-right: a sailboat is on the water surface, forming a land-and-water spatial relationship with the city wall on the left, but the sailboat itself is not a fixed built structure.
distinction: The city wall extends and is placed along the waterside terrain, mainly embodying a terrain-responsive siting relationship, rather than simply marking a particular scenery.

evidence: Upper-middle summit: a pavilion is built at the highest point of the mountain ridges, surrounded by trees, in a conspicuous position. | Right mountainside: faint stepped traces are visible among the mountains and rocks, suggesting the undulations of the mountain terrain. | Lower part of the painting: a large expanse of water surface with low sloping banks and trees sets off the height of the mountain ridges above.
distinction: Although there are suspected path traces on the right side of the painting, they do not form a clear, coherent clue of entry, whereas the pavilion at the summit clearly serves the function of marking the peak's edge and focusing the scenery.

evidence: Below the waterfall on the left cliff: a thatched-roof built structure (pavilion or house) is visible, its roof and part of its structure partly blocked by surrounding mountains and rocks and withered trees, presenting a half-hidden, half-exposed state. | Center-left of the painting: the built structure forms front-and-back layering with the surrounding trees and mountain rocks; its existence is suggested through the screening and revealing of natural scenery, participating in constituting the spatial depth of the painting.
distinction: The built structure mainly forms layers of concealment and revelation through screening by surrounding mountains, rocks, and trees, rather than serving as an isolated marker to point out a specific scenery.

evidence: Left middle ground: a thatched hut is built at the edge of a grove, presenting a layout of dwelling by the forest. | Lower right corner: a pavilion is built facing the water, with railings or a platform, conforming to the waterside terrain. | Upper right, at the foot of distant mountains: houses are faintly visible distributed along the mountain foot, echoing the form of the mountain mass.
distinction: Although the buildings have a scenic-accentuation role, their layout by the forest, facing the water, and at the mountain foot more prominently highlights spatial relationships of placement according to terrain.

evidence: Lower left: the roof, columns, and railings of a built structure are visible, partly blocked by the branches and leaves of foreground trees, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Lower left: two figures are walking toward the built structure, which is hidden among trees and mountain rocks.
distinction: Although the painting has a tiny path and figures walking toward the built structure, the dominant spatial expression is the layering of concealment and revelation formed by tree screening, rather than emphasizing a deep path process.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: a corridor building with red railings is partly blocked by tall trees on the left and a bamboo grove on the right, revealing only the roof, eaves, and part of the walls, presenting an obvious concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Left and right sides of the painting: tall trees on the left and dense bamboo grove on the right together constitute natural screening of the building in the middle, placing the building amid screened woodland.
distinction: Although the building relies on the natural environment, the most prominent spatial organization in the painting is the layering of the building presented through tree screening and revelation, rather than emphasizing its layout as placed according to terrain.

evidence: Center-right middle ground of the painting: a tiny house-like structure (seemingly with a roof) is faintly visible, located between the middle-ground tree clumps and the horizontal clouds and mist, presenting an indistinct state. | Overall space of the painting: distant mountains are continuous, the foreground is an open waterside, and the middle ground forms obvious spatial separation and screening layers through clouds and mist and trees.
distinction: The suspected built structure is very small in size and merges into the screening relationship of clouds, mist, and trees, mainly embodying layers of concealment and revelation, rather than serving as a conspicuous independent marker to point out specific scenery.

evidence: Lower left: a two-story building is visible, with clear roof and walls, partly blocked by surrounding trees and mountain rocks, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Lower middle of the painting: foreground trees have luxuriant branches and leaves, forming front-and-back layering with the building behind, enhancing the screening effect.
distinction: Although the building is placed at the mountain foot, the painting emphasizes more its screened relationship with surrounding trees and mountain rocks, forming spatial layers.

evidence: Left, lower middle: several trees stand in the foreground, their branches interlocking, blocking the houses behind. | Left, lower middle: the houses reveal their roofs, part of their walls, and the fence in front, presenting a layered relationship of seeing houses through trees.
distinction: The focus of the painting is the layering formed by the screening and revealing of houses by trees, rather than how the houses are placed in conformity with the terrain.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: several houses are built against the mountain and beside rocks, partly blocked by foreground pine trees and mountain rocks, revealing only roofs and part of walls, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Right waterside of the painting: a pavilion sits on a sloping bank, surrounded by trees, presenting a half-hidden, half-exposed spatial layering.
distinction: Although the built structures are placed according to terrain, the painting emphasizes more the screening and revealing of buildings by trees, rocks, and mountains; the concealment-and-revelation relationship plays a dominant role in organizing spatial layers.

evidence: Whole painting: the main subject is a gnarled tree, its roots coiled in the slope rocks and grass in the lower left corner, its branches extending toward the upper right; no artificial built elements such as houses, pavilions, or bridges are seen.
distinction: There are no clear built structures in the painting, so no spatial relationship can be judged; based on the compositional feature of the painting with the tree as the visual focus, it is provisionally assigned to C3.

evidence: Lower left: a thatched-roof building is visible, its building itself partly blocked by the trunk, branches, and leaves of a tall pine tree on the left. | Lower middle: the pine tree and thatched hut form front-and-back layering; the building presents a concealment-and-revelation relationship through the screening and revealing of trees.
distinction: The building mainly forms layers of concealment and revelation through trees to create scenery, rather than emphasizing the corresponding relationship of placement according to terrain and sloping bank.

evidence: Center-right of the painting: a pavilion is located behind several tall trees; trunks and branches block part of the pavilion's structure, revealing only the roof and part of the columns. | Middle ground of the painting: foreground trees and the middle-ground pavilion form obvious front-and-back screening layers, creating a sense of space screened within the forest.
distinction: Although the pavilion faces the waterside, the most prominent compositional technique in the painting is the screening and revealing of the pavilion by trees, rather than emphasizing its placement according to terrain.

evidence: Right side of the painting, center-left: between mountains, rocks, and trees there are indistinct ink masses, suspected to be buildings or pavilions, but the details are unclear, screened by natural scenery. | Right side of the painting, upper part: there are brief brushstrokes at the edge of the cliff, possibly suggesting structures at the summit, but they cannot be definitely identified.
distinction: Because the built parts are extremely indistinct, it cannot be determined whether they serve a scenic-accentuation role, but their faintly revealed state among mountains and forests is more consistent with the feature of concealment and revelation forming a scene.

evidence: Right-hand painted panel: The painting depicts distant mountains, an expansive water surface, several sailboats, and withered trees nearby, with no clear houses or built structures. | Center of the water surface: Only sailboats dot the water surface, serving to highlight the waterscape.
distinction: There are no clear built elements in the painting, only sailboats as scenic accents, so it is assigned to C3 as the closest spatial expression.

evidence: Upper part: the Great Wall winds and undulates along the ridge, clearly built following the mountain terrain. | Left side: a building group is arranged on the sloping ground at the mountain foot, with stone bases visible below conforming to the terrain. | Lower right: buildings are built facing the water, with a stone platform and steps in front extending directly to the waterside.
distinction: The Great Wall and building group in the painting mainly present a placement relationship conforming to natural terrain such as ridges, mountain foot, and waterside; although the lower-right buildings have steps facing the water, the overall emphasis is more on terrain-based arrangement than on a process of entry guided by paths.

evidence: Top of a hill in the middle-to-far distance: a pagoda stands at the highest point of the hill, with a clear outline, becoming a visual focus in the open background and identifying the scenery of this peak. | Right waterside: a pavilion is built by the water, partly screened by the branches and foliage of foreground trees. | Lower-left bank: several buildings are distributed beside rocks on the bank, adjoining the waterside.
distinction: Although the pavilion on the right has a partly screened relationship, the most dominant built element in the painting (the hilltop pagoda) mainly serves to mark and concentrate the distant mountain scenery, rather than being primarily defined by levels of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Middle-upper hillside: buildings are half-hidden by pine woodland and mountain rocks, with only part of the roofs and walls exposed, presenting a spatial layering of houses concealed within woodland. | Lower-right waterside: a waterside pavilion is built close against the rock face, forming a tight relationship of screening and exposure with the surrounding mountains and rocks. | Lower left: figures on horseback travel along the foot of the mountain, increasing the painting's depth and sense of travel, but the concealment-and-revelation relationship between buildings and nature is more prominent.
distinction: Although the waterside pavilion at lower right shows the feature of being built in response to water, the concealment-and-revelation relationship between the buildings (especially those on the middle-upper hillside) and the pines, rocks, and rock faces is more significant and dominates the construction of spatial layering.

evidence: Center-left: an arched bridge spans the water, with a porter carrying a load crossing it, connecting the left bank with the right sloping bank and forming a clear cue of crossing and entry. | Upper-right hillside: houses are built following the mountain, screened among trees and mountain rocks, serving as a potential destination for the path's extension. | Right sloping bank: gaps between the sloping bank and mountain rocks suggest a natural path, guiding the gaze from the bridge toward the buildings deep in the upper right.
distinction: Although the painting has a layering of buildings screened by trees (C2), the crossing and penetrating path formed jointly by the arched bridge, the figures, and the sloping bank more prominently organizes the spatial process of moving from here to there (C4).

evidence: Right: a pavilion appears amid the screening of pines and miscellaneous trees, with figures visible inside, showing a clear relationship of concealment and revelation. | Left: the building complex on the hillside is partly blocked by the grove in front, arranged in reliance on the mountain's form. | Lower right: a thatched hut and fence by the waterside stand behind trees and rocks, blending into the natural scenery.
distinction: Although the buildings adjoin the mountain and water, the painting places more emphasis on the screening and exposure of the buildings by trees and woodland, forming spatial layering through the relationship of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower right: a group of buildings is arranged along the sloping bank, with houses staggered in height and unfolding in conformity with the terrain. | Middle ground: a small pavilion is set on the hillside, echoing the form of the mountain. | Lower left: the roots of old pines coil over sloping rocks, closely integrated with the terrain.

evidence: Lower right corner: a two-story pavilion stands between pine trees and rocks, close to the waterside, serving as the visual focus of the foreground. | Overall painting: the pavilion together with the pines and rocks forms a waterside scene, serving to identify and concentrate the landscape of this place.
distinction: The pavilion mainly serves to identify the waterside scene of pines and rocks (C3); although it stands beside rocks, it is a single building, and no complex terrain-responsive layout or obvious building-on-a-platform relationship is seen (C1).

evidence: Lower right and center: a winding wooden bridge is visible spanning the water, connecting the two banks and pointing toward the houses on the shore, forming a clear entry path. | Left and center: multiple houses and pavilions are distributed along the waterside and slopes, connected by faint paths or shoreline, guiding the gaze deeper into the painting. | Overall composition: the built elements together with the bridge, waterside, and other elements organize a traversable spatial cue, giving the painting a spatial process of moving from here to there and gradually deeper.
distinction: C4 emphasizes the accessible, traversable spatial process brought by the bridge and paths, whereas C1 only emphasizes the placement of buildings according to terrain; in the painting the guiding role of the bridge and paths is more prominent.

evidence: Top mountain peak: at the highest point of the summit, a tower or pavilion is built, set high and conforming to the apex of the mountain. | Middle ground, mountain foot: a cluster of houses is distributed in staggered fashion according to the mountain slope, the layout rising and falling with the slopes and terraces. | Right and left shorelines: some houses unfold along the waterside, placed close to the water surface, corresponding to the direction of the river.
distinction: Although a bridge connects on the left side of the painting, the built elements as a whole more conspicuously present a terrain-responsive placement against mountain and water, high and low in staggered arrangement, rather than being dominated by a single movement-and-entry cue.

evidence: Lower left: the building complex nestles against the mountain and beside the water, with fences, courtyards, and houses placed according to the sloping terraces of the terrain, the layout corresponding to the natural configuration. | Right mountain cliff: houses are built on the cliff, likewise following the mountain, reflecting the characteristic of terrain-responsive placement.
distinction: Although a bridge suggests a path, the close correspondence between the buildings and the terrain is more prominent and dominant.

evidence: Left mountain foot: a group of houses is partly blocked by trees and mountain rocks, with only roofs and some walls exposed, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Lower-middle waterside: a pavilion building is screened behind trees and rocks, located at a projecting position by the water. | Overall composition: buildings interweave with mountains and rocks and trees, forming a multi-layered sense of space, composed by the screening and revealing of natural scenery.
distinction: The buildings not only identify the waterside scene but, through the screening by trees and mountain rocks, form rich layers of concealment and revelation; the characteristic of concealment and revelation forming the setting is more prominent.

evidence: Left: a steep mountain cliff, with pines growing at its top and the water below the cliff. | Lower left by the water: a person stands alone, facing the open water and distant mountains. | Center and right of the painting: a large area of unpainted space represents the water surface, with continuous pale-ink mountain ranges and flying birds in the distance.
distinction: There are no identifiable built elements in the painting; only a figure identifies the mood of viewing the scenery by the water, so it is classified as C3.

evidence: Left middle ground: several pavilions and houses are screened among rows of willow trees, with only roofs and partial structures exposed. | Lower right corner: a house is surrounded and blocked by dense willows, revealing its roof, eaves, and figures inside, forming a layering in which the house is seen through a screen. | Bottom center: several house roofs appear behind clumps of trees, forming a front-back screening relationship with the foreground willows.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed along the waterside, the painting more prominently highlights the screening and revealing of the buildings by woodland, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship dominates the spatial layering.

evidence: Lower left: a flat bridge spans between the water surface and the rocky bank, connecting foreground and middle ground and forming a clear movement-path cue. | Right center: houses and built elements are located on high ground by the waterside, echoing the bridge through the continuous shoreline and suggesting the spatial process of reaching the built elements from this bank. | Around the built elements: the houses are partly blocked by tall trees on the right and clumps of trees in front, which together with the path cue create a layering of secluded setting opening into greater depth.
distinction: Although the painting has a concealment-and-revelation relationship in which trees screen the buildings, the bridge at the lower left establishes a clear movement cue and a spatial orientation from one point to another, making the accessible path relationship dominant.

evidence: Left mountainside: a multi-story tower hugs the steep cliff face, with a railed platform at its base, placed in layers according to the cliff configuration, presenting the form of a building set on a platform. | Right mountain hollow: other built elements are placed in conformity with the valley terrain, located above the waterfall and matching the forms of the mountains and rocks. | Overall layout: the building sites in the painting, with their high and low staggering, rely closely on the mountain forms and sloping terraces, presenting a relationship of terrain-responsive placement suited to the configuration.
distinction: The most conspicuous feature is the main built element on the left hugging the cliff face and being placed in layers according to the configuration, which dominates the relationship between built elements and terrain; although there is a stone path on the right, the spatial organization of the main built elements leans more toward terrain-responsive placement than path guidance.

evidence: Upper right mountain ridge: a group of tower buildings is distributed along the ridge line, following the rise and fall of the mountain, high and low in staggered fashion, presenting a layout placed separately according to the slope. | Right mountainside: the building bases cling to the mountain slope, layer upon layer, closely integrated with the forms of the mountains and rocks.
distinction: The building layout closely follows the direction and gradient of the mountain ridge, embodying a configurational relationship of terrain-responsive placement rather than merely serving as an accent as a visual focus.

evidence: Lower-middle woodland: deep in the trees there are blurry dark dot-like objects, suspected to be tiny built elements or figures, but the details cannot be clearly discerned. | Foreground and middle ground: the main body of the painting is sloping rocks and dense woodland, with water and distant mountains beyond; no clear houses, bridges, or path structures are seen.
distinction: Because clear architectural forms are lacking, the screening relationship cannot be confirmed; it is regarded as scenic accentuation because the dark objects in the trees serve to concentrate the visual focus.

evidence: Center-left: multiple buildings are placed in layers against the steep cliff and sloping terraces, high and low in staggered fashion, their sites closely fitting the mountain and rock terrain. | Lower left corner: a stone-step path is visible winding along the mountain, connecting the lower waterside with the upper building area, following the undulations of the terrain. | Lower right corner: houses are also built by the waterside according to the terrain, forming a natural transition with the surrounding withered trees and sloping bank.
distinction: Although the painting has paths and a small bridge, the most conspicuous feature of the building group is the terrain-responsive placement unfolding in layers against the cliff and sloping terraces, rather than simply emphasizing the process of travel and entry.

evidence: Lower left corner: houses are half screened by dense bamboo grove, revealing roofs, walls, and fences, presenting a layering in which houses are seen within the grove. | Center-right mountainside: several houses are screened among bamboo and trees, with only parts of the roofs exposed, forming a relationship of screening and revealing through natural scenery. | Upper mountainside: a few buildings are blocked by trees, faintly visible, participating in the composition.
distinction: Although the buildings are distributed according to the mountain configuration, the painting more emphasizes the spatial layering formed by the screening and revealing of the buildings by bamboo and trees; concealment and revelation forming the setting is more prominent.

evidence: Lower left slope: a flock of white sheep is visible moving about on the slope, concentrating the scenery of this place as a scenic accent element. | Whole painting: the painting mainly consists of mountain ranges, withered trees, and sloping banks; no clear traces of buildings, bridges, or artificial built elements are seen.
distinction: The painting lacks clear artificial built elements and has only animals as scenic accentuation, so it is assigned to the closest category based on the overall visible space.

evidence: Whole painting: the painting mainly consists of distant mountains, water, middle-ground hills, foreground sloping banks, trees, mountains and rocks, and animals; no houses, bridges, or other artificial built elements are seen. | Middle ground to foreground: woodland and mountains and rocks form front-back layers, presenting a screening relationship of natural scenery, but no built elements participate.
distinction: No built elements are visible in the painting; it is assigned to the closest category based on the overall landscape layering and screening relationships.

evidence: Left center: between the mountain foot and the pine grove, the roofs and walls of several buildings are faintly visible, partly blocked by trees, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Overall painting: dense pines and undulating mountains and rocks form the foreground and middle ground, screening the buildings within them and creating a richly layered sense of space.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed at the mountain foot, the painting more prominently highlights the layered relationship in which they are screened and revealed by woodland, mountains, and rocks, rather than emphasizing their terrain-responsive layout.

evidence: Lower right side: a multi-story tower and houses are arranged in staggered heights according to the mountain configuration, their sites clearly relying on the slope and rocks. | Lower right side: the buildings form a screening relationship with the surrounding trees, mountains, and rocks, with parts of roofs and walls blocked.
distinction: Although the buildings are screened, their layout feature of being placed at different heights according to the mountain configuration is more prominent and dominates the spatial expression.

evidence: Upper right: the building complex is stacked layer upon layer according to the mountain forms and sloping terraces, the sites closely fitting the direction of the mountain configuration. | Center mountainside: houses are placed separately according to the slope, distributed in staggered fashion among woodland and mountains and rocks. | Lower part near the water: pavilion buildings are built close to the water, unfolding in conformity with the waterside terrain.
distinction: Although there is screening by woodland, the terrain-responsive relationship in which the built elements are placed layer upon layer according to mountain forms and sloping terraces is more prominent and dominant.

evidence: Lower right corner: a small boat is moored on the water, with figures active on the bank, forming a ferry-crossing entrance that suggests the starting point of a journey. | Lower middle and left center: a wooden bridge is visible spanning the stream path, and on the left a covered bridge/pavilion bridge crosses the waterfall stream, connecting mountain roads and guiding the gaze deeper. | Right center and lower left: towers are built on the mountainside and thatched huts stand among the trees, connected to the outer ferry crossing through paths and bridges, presenting an accessible spatial relationship.
distinction: Although the painting shows the placement of buildings against mountain and beside water (C1), more conspicuous is the journey linked by the ferry crossing, bridges, and paths from the waterside to the deep-mountain towers, emphasizing the entry into and extension of space (C4).

evidence: Right center: a group of tower buildings is built tightly against the towering giant rock cliff, the eaves and walls closely fitting the contours of the mountains and rocks, presenting a placement relationship of buildings set against the rock. | Lower middle of the painting: below the buildings are sloping banks and water; the buildings are against the mountain and beside the water, their sites unfolding in conformity with the terrain.
distinction: Although the buildings are screened by trees, their placement tightly against the giant rock cliff and following the mountain is more prominent and is the dominant spatial expression.

evidence: Right center: a building complex is arranged layer upon layer according to the mountain configuration, roofs high and low in staggered fashion, closely fitting the slope terrain. | Lower left corner: a pavilion is built by the water, its base close to the waterside, conforming to the terrain. | Upper right: a pavilion is located at the summit of a distant mountain, set high.
distinction: Although there is screening by woodland, the terrain-responsive relationship in which the built elements are placed according to the height of the mountain and the winding of the waterside is more prominent and dominates the overall spatial organization.

evidence: Left mountain cliff: several houses are built on projecting terraces of the steep cliff face, presenting an obvious form of buildings set on platforms, with sites closely corresponding to the mountain forms. | Central main peak and right slope: buildings are placed separately according to the rock levels and slopes, high and low in staggered fashion, following the mountain layout. | Lower waterside: houses are placed close to the water or at the mountain foot, presenting a posture of unfolding along the shore or being built according to the slope.
distinction: The buildings mainly embody placement reliant on terrain platforms and slopes (terrain-responsive), rather than merely serving as isolated accents identifying the scenery (scenic accentuation).

evidence: Lower left: two people are walking toward a small bridge spanning the water, the bridge connecting the two banks and forming a clear entry cue. | Lower middle and right bank: houses are arranged in staggered fashion along the waterside and mountain foot, with a small boat on the water, suggesting access by water route. | Right mountain hollow: a group of houses rises layer upon layer according to the mountain configuration, forming a continuous traversable space with the mountain paths and waterside.
distinction: Although the built elements are against the mountain and beside the water (C1), the clear bridge, figures walking, and small boat on the water together construct a strong accessible, traversable spatial process, so C4 is more dominant.

evidence: Right bank middle ground: the building complex is hidden behind mountains, rocks, and woodland, with only parts of roofs and walls exposed, forming an obvious layering of concealment and revelation. | Lower left corner: houses are built against mountains, rocks, and trees, partly blocked by foreground trees, presenting a spatial relationship of houses seen within woodland. | Middle-ground waterside: a small bridge is visible spanning the water, connecting the two banks and helping to build pictorial depth, but the built elements are mainly screened by woodland, mountains, and rocks.
distinction: Although the built elements are against the mountain and beside the water, the painting more emphasizes the screening and revealing of the buildings by woodland, mountains, and rocks; the concealment-and-revelation relationship is the dominant factor in the composition.

evidence: Center-right: a house with a tiled roof is largely blocked by tall foreground trees and by the bamboo grove and lake rocks on the right, with only parts of the roof, walls, doors, and windows exposed, forming an obvious concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Left: a stretch of bamboo grove and a low wall further define the spatial boundary of the courtyard, setting off the building environment screened within it. | Middle-ground ground: a figure in red faces toward the house screened by trees, suggesting the spatial position of the building deep in the woodland.

evidence: Lower right: a thatched-roof pavilion is built on a rocky bank, partially screened by the trunks and branches of pine trees in front, appearing half-hidden and half-revealed. | Lower center: pines and rocks are arranged around the pavilion, forming layers of screening and revelation of the built structure by natural scenery.

evidence: Lower center-right: a thatched hut is visible, surrounded by trees, with three figures active in front of it. | Lower part of the painting: a winding stream and stone path extend from the bottom of the painting toward the location of the thatched hut. | In front of the thatched hut: figures stand on the path, presenting a state of walking along the path, approaching or lingering at the built structure.
distinction: Although the thatched hut indicates the mountain-dwelling scenery, the winding stream, path, and human activity in the painting more strongly emphasize the spatial process of moving from one place to another and approaching the built structure, so C4 is more appropriate.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: a wooden bridge is visible spanning the water, connecting the two banks, with a path leading to a group of houses on the slope, forming clear clues of entry and movement. | Middle of the painting: a pavilion stands on the waterside, with a path extending beside it, forming spatial connection and guidance with the mountains, rocks, and trees behind. | Lower left and lower middle of the painting: multiple groups of houses are scattered between the sloping terraces and the waterside, linked by winding paths and bridges, presenting an accessible spatial organization.
distinction: Although some houses are screened by trees, rocks, and mountains, the painting more prominently highlights the spatial process through which bridges and paths link dispersed built structures into an enterable and explorable space.

evidence: Lower right corner: a group of buildings is surrounded and screened by several trees in the foreground, with only parts of roofs, eaves, and walls exposed, presenting a spatial layer of houses hidden in the woods. | Mid-left mountainside: buildings are placed according to the mountain terrain, partially obscured by rocks and trees, creating a half-hidden, half-visible visual effect. | Mid-left waterside: buildings are located behind trees and rocks, faintly visible, their existence and position indicated through the screening of natural scenery.
distinction: Although the mountainside buildings have the characteristic of being built against the mountain, multiple buildings in the painting (especially in the foreground) rely more strongly on the screening and revelation by trees and rocks to construct spatial layers, and the concealment-revelation relationship is more prominent.

evidence: Upper left: a pavilion is built on a platform at the top of a towering cliff, presenting a relationship of placing a building on a terrace. | Lower left: a group of buildings is arranged in a staggered manner against the slope and waterside, with building sites corresponding to the undulations of the terrain. | Right side and lower right: buildings are either placed against the woods at the foot of the mountain or spread out along the waterside, presenting a layout that follows the bank and slope.
distinction: Although the pavilion on the mountain top serves to mark a high point, multiple built structures in the painting (lower left, lower right, right side) mainly present a terrain-responsive placement according to slope, waterside, and cliff; C1 better summarizes the overall correspondence between built structures and terrain.

evidence: Upper middle, slightly left: several pavilions and halls are built according to the mountain terrain, placed on ridges and sloping terraces, with building sites corresponding to the undulations of the mountain. | Lower part of the painting: streams, pines, and figures are visible, but there is no clear and coherent movement path connecting them with the built structures above.
distinction: Although the buildings indicate the mountainside scenery, their placement on terraces and conformity to terrain undulations are more prominent.

evidence: Left side of the painting proper: pines, rocks, and sloping ground are visible; no clear built elements such as houses, pavilions, or bridges are seen. | Right side: mounting silk borders and seals, not content within the painting space.
distinction: No clear built elements in the painting; only the natural terrain of rocks and trees is presented, with no features of the other categories.

evidence: Left mountain hollow: houses are built according to the mountain terrain, partially obscured by rocks and trees, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Central wooded area: pavilions and halls are screened within dense woods, with only roofs and parts of eaves exposed. | Right waterside: houses are built by the water, surrounded by trees, forming a spatial layer of partial screening.
distinction: Although paths and bridges guide the viewer in the painting, the spatial layers formed by built structures screened by trees, rocks, and mountains are more prominent and widespread.

evidence: Left side: a thatched pavilion is built on flat ground at the foot of the mountain, surrounded by trees, serving as the visual focus of the foreground. | Lower center: a small boat with two sails is moored by the waterside, dotted beside the reeds.
distinction: Although the thatched pavilion is placed at the foot of the mountain, its independent position on the open bank emphasizes marking and focusing the scenery there rather than the constraint of terrain on layout.

evidence: Middle ground, slightly left: a group of walled buildings sits on a waterside sloping terrace highland, its layout conforming to the undulations of the terrain, presenting the characteristic of placing buildings on a terrace. | Lower foreground: houses are arranged against huge blue-green rocks and the base of a cliff, presenting a form of winding around rocks or being placed at the mountain foot. | Right side and lower right of the painting: scattered buildings and pavilions are distributed along the shoreline and mountain foot, interspersed with trees and rocks, presenting a tendency to spread along the bank.
distinction: Although the buildings serve to indicate the human dwelling scenery, their specific physical correspondence with sloping terraces, rocks, and waterside (on terraces, around rocks, along banks) is more visually significant and concrete in the organization.

evidence: Left side: on a cliff terrace below a waterfall is a group of houses, placed according to the mountain terrain and landform. | Center: roofs and walls of houses are visible among rocks and trees, distributed in conformity with the undulations of the rocks. | Right side: the water surface is open, with trees and faint traces of built structures on the distant shoreline, echoing the mountain terrain on the left.
distinction: The building group on the left is clearly located on the terrace below the waterfall, placed in conformity with the terrain; the characteristic of terrain-responsive siting is more dominant than mere screening.

evidence: Lower left corner: a group of houses is surrounded and screened by dense tree branches and leaves, with only roofs and parts of walls exposed, presenting a layer of seeing houses in the woods. | Center of the painting: behind/beside a huge rock is a flat-roofed building structure (or platform), partially obscured by foreground tree branches and rocks, creating a visual effect of houses hidden behind rocks.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed against rocks, the visual focus of the painting is on the screening and revelation of buildings by trees and rocks; the concealment-revelation relationship is more prominent than placement according to terrain.

evidence: Left side: pavilions are built among rocky slopes and terraces, with obvious stairs connecting upper and lower levels, presenting a form of separate placement according to slope and buildings on terraces. | Lower middle: a group of houses is distributed along the mountain foot and the edge of woods, with building sites echoing the undulations of the terrain. | Right side: a pavilion is built on a rocky platform, placed relying on the mountain terrain.
distinction: The built structures in the painting not only serve to mark the scenery but more prominently display a layout relationship of placement according to mountain forms, sloping terraces, and other terrain conditions.

evidence: Central mountainside: a plank road or path cut along a steep cliff is visible, connecting the waterside at the mountain foot with the mountain, forming movement clues. | Lower part and lower left of the painting: multiple boats and figures on the water echo the plank road at the mountain foot, presenting a process of water-land transportation from one place to another.
distinction: No clear buildings are seen in the painting, but the plank road and water route clearly present an enterable and explorable spatial process, so C4 is chosen.

evidence: Lower middle: roofs, eaves, and walls of houses are visible, partially obscured by surrounding trees and rocks, forming spatial layers of concealment and revelation among the woods. | Lower left corner: parts of other building roofs are exposed, likewise forming a screening relationship with trees and rocks.
distinction: Although the buildings are arranged according to the mountain terrain, the painting more strongly emphasizes the spatial layers formed by the screening and revelation of buildings by trees and rocks, so C2 is more dominant.

evidence: Right side of the painting proper: overlapping rocks, pines, bamboo groves, and mist are visible; no clear built elements such as houses, bridges, or paths are seen. | Overall composition: natural scenery presents layers of foreground-background screening, lacking the participation of artificial built structures.
distinction: No clear built elements; assigned to the closest category based on the overall landscape layers.

evidence: Lower left corner: between trees and the sloping bank there are very few blurry lines, suspected to be parts of built structures, but their form and spatial relationships cannot be reliably identified. | Main body of the painting: large areas of unpainted space represent water surface, with continuous mountains in the distance and sloping banks and trees in the foreground; no clear movement clues such as bridges, paths, or gates are seen.
distinction: The painting lacks clear evidence of built structures; based only on the extremely blurry suspected traces in the lower left corner and the waterside position, it is barely assigned to the closest category.

evidence: Lower left side: a group of buildings is built by the water, with dense wooden piles visible underneath as support, placed directly according to the terrain conditions of the waterside and sloping rocks. | Left side: the building group spreads along the shoreline, with roofs and walls interlocking with surrounding trees and rocks, presenting a layout arranged according to the site.
distinction: Although the buildings are partially screened by trees, their main compositional role is to be placed in conformity with the waterside terrain, rather than forming scenery solely through concealment and revelation.

evidence: Left side: houses are visible, their roofs and walls partially obscured by foreground trees and terrain, presenting a layer of houses hidden in the woods. | Left middle side: houses are surrounded by dense trees; the buildings reveal parts through the screening of woods, forming a spatial relationship of screening and revelation.

evidence: Left side: a building group is distributed in layers along the sloping ground at the mountain foot, placed in conformity with the undulations of the terrain. | Right side: houses lean against the sloping bank and trees and rocks, with fences, placed at the edge of high ground. | Center, slightly left: a pavilion is located on flat ground by the water, forming a correspondence with the surrounding water surface and trees.
distinction: Although the buildings dot the landscape, their layout more prominently embodies a placement relationship conforming to terrain conditions such as slopes and waterside, rather than merely marking specific scenery.

evidence: Lower left: a building group is distributed along the waterside and sloping ground, with houses staggered in height, building sites matching the terrain, presenting characteristics of spreading along the bank and placing buildings on slopes. | Center: a pavilion is built on flat ground among the mountains, placed in conformity with the terrain, surrounded by rocks and trees. | Overall: the layout of built structures corresponds to mountain forms and waterside, embodying the characteristic of placement according to the site.
distinction: Although there is screening of buildings by trees in the painting (concealment and revelation), the terrain-responsive relationship of buildings placed according to landform and waterside is more prominent and dominant.

evidence: Right middle-lower part: walls and roofs of houses are exposed among rocks and trees, presenting spatial layers of concealment and revelation.
