evidence: Left edge: the partial outlines of two small boats are visible, moored at the water's edge. | Center and upper part of the painting: a large area of unpainted space represents the water surface; in the distance are low, flat sandbar or land outlines; no houses or other built elements are seen.
distinction: The painting has only boats as scenic accents, with no visible paths for entry or architectural clues, so C4 is not selected.

evidence: Painting as a whole: the painting consists mainly of mountains and rocks, trees, a stream, and figures; no explicit artificial built elements such as houses or bridges are seen. | Upper center: a figure leans against a rock platform, surrounded by trees and layered rocks, forming a deep and secluded sense of space. | Lower stream bank: a figure is active by the stream, implying a spatial process that can be entered and traveled through.
distinction: The painting lacks explicit built structures, but the deep, secluded space formed by the rocks and water flow, together with the figures' activities, implies a process of entry and travel, so it is assigned to C4.

evidence: Main body of the painting: the painting consists mainly of mountains and rocks, moss dots, and distant mountains; no explicit built forms such as houses or pavilions are seen. | Left side: there are inscriptions and seals, but the inscription content is not used as direct visual evidence for identifying built elements.
distinction: No explicit built elements are seen in the painting, so no visual relationship distinguishing between categories can be made.

evidence: Middle of the painting: a pale, winding path extends from the foot of the rocks on the left and connects to the area where the figures are on the right, forming a clear travel route. | Right side of the painting: two people carrying a sedan chair proceed along the path, reinforcing the path's directionality and sense of spatial entry.
distinction: No built elements are visible in the painting, but the path and the figures' movement together constitute a clear travel clue, presenting a spatial process of moving from one place to another, so C4 is selected.

evidence: Left mountainside: the building complex is arranged in layers according to the mountain form, with the roof heights corresponding to the undulations of the slope, presenting a form of setting houses on platforms. | Lower left: the waterside building complex is arranged along the shoreline, with building sites close to the water surface, presenting a layout unfolding along the bank. | Overall: the layout of the built structures clearly conforms to the natural forms of the mountain and shoreline, forming a corresponding relationship with the site conditions.
distinction: Although the painting has clues of bridges and paths, the placement relationship of the built structures themselves, nestled against the mountain and beside the water, is more prominent and dominant.

evidence: Center and left: a high platform enclosed by railings is visible; on the platform are a screen, a table, and figures; below the platform are steps, presenting the layout characteristic of setting a house on a platform. | Lower part: mountains and rocks, flowers and plants are visible below the platform base, serving as the site environment of the building and setting off the building's elevated placement. | Left side: the trunk of a large tree stands at the edge of the platform, its branches and leaves covering the area above, forming a front-to-back adjacent relationship with the building's railings.
distinction: Although trees partially screen the railings in the painting, the overall layout emphasizes more the building's placement on the platform base (setting a house on a platform), rather than relying mainly on concealment and revelation.

evidence: Upper right: a pavilion is built on a waterside platform base, surrounded by withered tree branches; part of its eaves and walls are screened by the trees, forming a spatial layering of alternating concealment and revelation. | Lower left to center: a figure walks along the waterside; ahead is a large area of unpainted water surface, and no clear bridge or path is seen directly connecting it to the pavilion on the opposite bank.
distinction: Although the pavilion marks the waterside scenery, its relationship of concealment and revelation with the surrounding trees is more prominent in the composition, so C2 is more apt than C3.

evidence: Left and center: mountains and rocks, withered branches, bamboo leaves, and a sloping bank are visible; on the right are water ripples and sloping rocks; no explicit built elements (buildings, bridges, paths, etc.) are seen in the painting.
distinction: The painting consists mainly of natural landscape scenery with no visible built elements, so it is assigned to scenic accentuation as the closest category, but it lacks evidence of built structures.

evidence: Left edge: a storied building is visible attached to a steep cliff, with its roof and structure placed in accordance with the mountain form. | Upper-middle mountainside: building outlines are faintly visible among the rocks and woodland, distributed in accordance with the terrain.
distinction: Although some buildings are screened by woodland, the painting emphasizes more the terrain-responsive relationship in which the buildings cling to the steep cliff and are placed according to the terrain.

evidence: Left painting area: the painting depicts undulating earthen slopes, trees of various forms (such as pines and red-leafed trees), and distant mountains and a shoreline, presenting a typical landscape composition; no artificial buildings such as pavilions or storied buildings are seen. | Right area: mounting silk with pale cloud/ floral patterns and a large area of blank paper are visible; this is part of the handscroll's mounting and contains no painting content.
distinction: The main body of the painting is natural landscape and trees, a depiction of scenery, distinguished from ruled-line painting or figure-activity scenes that take buildings as the main subject.

evidence: Left edge: a short section of wooden fence and a dirt road are visible, with a figure carrying a shoulder pole walking along the road. | Painting as a whole: the painting consists mainly of a sloping bank, trees, and paths; no explicit main built structures such as houses or pavilions are seen.
distinction: The painting lacks explicit built structures; only a path and figures are seen, which can barely be regarded as a travel clue, but there is no architectural connection.

evidence: Left side: the main subject is the single calligraphic Chinese character shang ('appreciation'); there are no landscape or built elements. | Right side: the right side consists of a patterned silk mounting border and contains no painted content.
distinction: The image contains no landscape or built elements, so no substantive judgment of spatial relationships can be made; the category assignment is merely formal.

evidence: Left middle: tree branches and leaves interweave, and between them part of a built roof and structure are revealed, presenting a state of being half screened by woodland. | Lower left: in front of the built structure is a figure facing the tree-screened building, indicating the building's existence and location. | Left side of the painting: mountains and rocks with trees form the foreground and middle ground, and the built structure is hidden among them, forming clear spatial layering and a relationship of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the painting hints at a path leading to the building, the core compositional method is the screening and revealing of the building by woodland, rather than emphasizing the penetration of a travel route.

evidence: Lower middle and lower left of the painting: several tiny house buildings are visible scattered among the mountains and rocks, some screened by mountain bodies or trees, presenting a half-hidden, half-visible relationship of concealment and revelation. | Left side of the painting: partial building outlines are revealed among the screening mountains and trees, forming front-to-back spatial layering.
distinction: Although the buildings are distributed according to the mountain form, the painting emphasizes more the spatial layering formed by the screening and revealing of the buildings by mountains, rocks, and trees, so C2 is more apt than C1.

evidence: Lower middle: between the mountains, rocks, and woodland, building structures with red roofs and walls are visible, partly screened by natural scenery. | Upper middle: mountains and rocks are layered, forming a front-to-back spatial layering of screening with the buildings below.
distinction: Although the buildings are built against the mountain, the painting emphasizes more their relationship of concealment and revelation as screened and revealed by the mountains, rocks, and trees, rather than simple conformity to terrain.

evidence: Lower left and lower middle: amid the screening woodland, house roofs and wall structures are visible; the buildings are partly screened by foreground trees, forming front-to-back layering. | Middle-right mountainside: traces of buildings are faintly visible among the mountains, rocks, and trees, presenting a spatial relationship of houses hidden behind rocks or within the woods.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed against the mountain and beside the water, the painting emphasizes more the spatial layering formed by the screening and revealing of the buildings by woodland and rocks, rather than simple correspondence to terrain.

evidence: Middle of the right cliff: a pavilion is built on a projecting rock, presenting the form of setting a house on a platform and corresponding to the precipitous mountain form. | Left mountainside: storied buildings are arranged in layers according to the slope terrain, presenting a layout of separate placement along the slope. | Lower left corner and middle-ground river valley: house clusters are distributed along the shoreline, parallel to the river's course, presenting a relationship unfolding along the bank.
distinction: Although the painting has a bridge and boats providing travel clues, the built structures are widely distributed across different terrain levels such as cliffs, slopes, and banks, emphasizing more the placement relationship of adapting to local conditions, rather than a single penetrating touring path.

evidence: Lower right: a wooden bridge spans the water surface, with figures riding horses and walking on the bridge, forming a clear clue for entry and transition. | Lower left: houses are built on the sloping waterside bank; the opposite bank connected by the bridge points to this area, implying an reachable path. | Middle right: multi-storied buildings are faintly visible among the mountain forest, and a winding path at the foot of the mountain on the right extends upward, suggesting a process of traveling deep into the mountains.
distinction: Although the middle-right storied buildings are screened by woodland, the painting constructs stronger clues of spatial entry and travel through the bridge, figures, and mountain path, so C4 is dominant.

evidence: Lower left to lower right: in the lower left corner of the painting is a small bridge connecting to a winding path; the path passes the thatched hut and bamboo fence at the lower right, forming a clear travel route. | Among the middle-ground mountains, rocks, and bamboo grove: steps are painted between the middle-ground rocks and the bamboo grove, suggesting that the path extends into the depth of the painting and guides the eye into a more secluded area. | Lower right and middle ground: the thatched hut, bamboo fence, and the faintly visible storied buildings in the middle ground are connected by paths and steps, presenting spatial layering that can be reached and traveled through.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed against the mountain and beside the water (C1), the travel clues of the painting—bridge, path, steps, etc.—are very clear and dominate the spatial entry process from near to far and from outside to inside, so C4 is more apt.

evidence: Middle-ground mountainside on the left: a pagoda is visible standing on the mountain ridge, marking the scenery high on the mountainside. | Middle-ground slope on the left: storied buildings built according to the mountain form are visible, with roofs revealed, marking the slope's position. | Lower right corner waterside: a pavilion is visible built beside the water, marking the waterside scenery.
distinction: Although the buildings are arranged according to the mountain form, their main role in the painting is as scattered nodes marking the scenery at different locations such as the mountainside, slope, and waterside, giving the grand landscape concrete points of reference.

evidence: Left and lower parts: a waterfall is visible flowing down from the mountains and merging into the stream below, forming a water-flow guide. | Lower left corner: a tiny figure sits beside a rock facing the landscape, implying a position for viewing or traveling.
distinction: There are no explicit built structures in the painting; the water flow and the figure's position imply a process of spatial entry and travel, so it is assigned to C4 rather than C3, which only marks scenery.

evidence: Right side of the painting: a group of house buildings is hidden behind mountains, rocks, and woodland, with only roofs and parts of walls revealed, forming a clear relationship of screening and revealing. | Middle-right part of the painting: the buildings interpenetrate with the surrounding mountains, rocks, and pines, screened by natural scenery, presenting spatial layering within the woods and behind rocks.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed according to the mountains and rocks, the most prominent compositional technique in the painting is the layering of concealment and revelation formed by screening with mountains, rocks, and woodland, rather than emphasizing a layout unfolding according to terrain.

evidence: Lower left and lower part: houses are partly screened by foreground tree branches, with roofs and walls faintly visible, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Right mountainside: the building complex is screened behind dense woods and mountains and rocks, with only parts of roofs and structures revealed, with deep layering. | Overall composition: the built structures are integrated into the mountain forest, participating in the scenery through the screening and revealing by woodland, mountains, and rocks, without appearing abrupt.
distinction: The primary label emphasizes that the built structures form spatial layering through screening by woodland, mountains, and rocks, while the alternative label emphasizes conformity to terrain; the feature of forming scenery through concealment and revelation is more prominent in the painting.

evidence: Lower middle to right side of the painting: a winding mountain path and a plank road with railings are visible, extending upward along the mountain form, forming a clear travel clue. | Upper center of the painting: a group of storied buildings is visible on the mountainside; the direction of the path and plank road implies a spatial relationship by which this built structure can be reached. | Middle ground of the painting: dense pine forest and mountains and rocks partly screen the built structures, but the connectivity of the paths gives the painting a process of turning into the depths.
distinction: Although the built structures are screened by woodland, mountains, and rocks, the clearly visible paths and plank roads in the painting constitute strong clues of entry and travel, making the spatial organizing role of access to secluded settings more prominent.

evidence: Middle ground, left of center and above: figures ride horses along a path; the path leads to a wooden bridge spanning a ravine, and the bridge connects the road extending to the village built structures in the distance, forming a clear spatial clue of entry into the depths. | Foreground right and waterside: a figure carrying a shoulder pole walks along the waterside path; the path connects to the built structure (thatched hut) in the lower right corner, presenting a travel relationship from one place to another. | Central water surface of the painting: boats travel on the broad water surface, implying a water transport clue and helping to explain the reachability and connectivity of the space.
distinction: Although the built structures are distributed along the waterside and flat ground (C1), the clear paths, bridges, and figures' travel activities in the painting constitute a stronger relationship of spatial entry and depth organization (C4).

evidence: Lower right: In front of the waterside building, a small bridge crosses the stream, connecting the paths on both banks; figures walk on the bridge and along the bank, forming a clear route of entry. | Left, upper-middle: A group of courtyard buildings is arranged along the slope and the waterside, with fences and paths on the periphery; figures can be seen moving along the paths, showing an accessible relationship. | Lower-middle of the painting: The winding shoreline and footpaths link together the trees and buildings of different areas, guiding the line of sight and the direction of travel.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed by water and by slope, the painting places greater emphasis on the spatial process of guiding figures to enter and travel through the built environment by means of bridges and paths.

evidence: Lower left: In front of the building complex are a wooden bridge, steps, and a platform; figures move on the platform, forming a clear route of entry | Lower middle: A waterside pavilion/platform extends over the water and, combined with trees and rocks, guides the line of sight into the building area | Valley at upper right: Building roofs are faintly visible, screened by rocks and trees, echoing as a distant view
distinction: The main label emphasizes travel clues such as bridges and steps guiding entry into the buildings, whereas the alternative interpretation attends only to screening relationships

evidence: Lower right: A wooden bridge crosses the stream connecting the two banks; on the bank two people (one riding a donkey) walk along the road, forming a clear travel clue for entering the painting or heading toward the built elements. | Left mountainside: A winding plank road or stairway passes through cloud and mist and climbs along the mountain, providing a spatial path from lower to higher ground into the depths. | Lower middle and lower left: Houses are scattered among bamboo groves and slopes, connected to the outer space by the shoreline and paths, presenting an accessible layout.
distinction: Although the built elements are heavily screened by bamboo groves, consistent with C2 features, the clear bridge, winding plank road, and traveling figures in the painting constitute strong clues of entry and travel, making access to secluded settings the dominant mode of spatial organization.

evidence: Center-right of the painting: Multiple groups of buildings are placed beside the waterside and slopes; a covered bridge winds along the water surface, and pavilions and towers are set at different heights according to the terrain. | Center of the painting: The waterside corridor and the bank buildings connect naturally through the terrain and water surface, presenting a spatial relationship that unfolds along the bank and is arranged according to the site. | Left-center of the painting: Houses are screened among trees and slopes, their bases following the edge of the land and forming a relationship of reliance on the surrounding water and rock environment.
distinction: Although the painting has covered bridges and paths connecting the buildings, the dominant expression is how the building complex is sited in response to the waterside terrain, rather than emphasizing a single process of travel and entry.

evidence: Center-lower part of the painting: A sailboat navigates the surging waves, becoming the visual focus at the water mouth and gorge mouth. | Right middle ground of the painting: At the boundary between the mountain bank and the grove there are extremely small blurry traces, possibly structures but not confirmable as built elements.
distinction: The painting lacks clearly identifiable buildings; the sailboat, as a scenic accent, condenses the scenery of the gorge-mouth water passage, and it is therefore classified as C3.

evidence: Lower middle, slightly left: Several houses are screened within dense woodland; roofs and walls are partly obscured by trunks and foliage, presenting a spatial layering of concealment and revelation. | Lower middle: Trees surround the built elements; through the interleaving of foreground and middle-ground trees, the houses are set deep within the woods, strengthening the visual effect of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although figures and paths at the lower part of the painting hint at travel clues, the chief compositional role of the built elements in the painting is to present spatial layering through the screening and revealing of trees, rather than to emphasize the process of entry.

evidence: Main subject of the painting: The painting consists mainly of the trunk, branches, and needles of an old pine; no built elements such as houses, bridges, or paths are seen. | Upper middle: Behind the screening pine branches a full moon is painted; below are an inscription and seals, the whole presenting a composition of natural scenery and unpainted space.
distinction: There are no clear built elements in the painting; the old pine, as the main subject, condenses the scenery of the painting, and it is therefore assigned to the closest category, C3, according to overall spatial organization.

evidence: Whole painting: The main subject of the painting is a cold shoal, withered willows, reeds, and water birds; no clear traces of artificial built elements such as buildings or bridges are seen. | Lower part and middle ground: The natural undulation and vegetation distribution of the waterside shoal are visible, presenting the organizational relationship of the natural landform.
distinction: No visible built elements in the painting; based on the overall spatial organization of the natural waterside, it is only tentatively assigned to the closest category.

evidence: Lower left corner: A pavilion is built on a sloping bank, partly screened by the surrounding plum trees and pines, with only the roof and part of the columns exposed, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Lower middle of the painting: The trunks and branches of pines and plums interlace, screening the pavilion within them, increasing the sense of spatial layering.
distinction: Although the pavilion marks the scenery, the relationship of screening and revealing by the trees is more prominent in the composition, emphasizing the spatial layering of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Water surface below: A small boat carrying two people travels along the water toward the interior of the painting, forming a visual guide from outside to inside. | Center of the painting: A small bridge crosses the stream, with figures walking on it, connecting the water surface with the building complex on the right bank. | Lower middle-right: The building complex lies in the direction in which the stream and bridge extend, surrounded by plum blossoms and bamboo groves, constituting the destination of the travel clues.
distinction: Although the buildings are screened by trees, the painting constructs a clear route of entry through the waterway, the small boat, and the bridge, which dominates the spatial process of access to secluded settings.

evidence: Lower middle, slightly right: An open thatched hut is half-screened by the lush foliage of the trees to its right and above, with figures visible inside, forming a spatial layering of concealment and revelation. | Upper left: A thatched pavilion is set on the mountainside, arranged according to the mountain terrain and the waterfall, surrounded by railings and trees.
distinction: Although the thatched pavilion at upper left embodies siting according to the mountain terrain, the relationship of screening and revelation formed by the thatched hut below and the surrounding trees is more prominent and dominates the spatial layering of the painting.

evidence: Left middle: An arched bridge spans the stream; on the bridge two people (a scholar with a staff and a boy servant) are walking toward the plum grove on the right, constituting a clear travel clue. | Lower right: On a stone base by the water stands a house (a study), partly screened by plum trees, located at the extension of the route traveled on the bridge and implying a reachable destination. | Upper middle: Beside the rocks and waterfall a pavilion is built, with a person inside, forming spatial connection and echo with the stream and bridge below through the waterside and the mountain terrain.
distinction: Although the house at lower right shows an obvious relationship of screening by trees, the bridge and the movement of the figures establish the painting's structure of travel "from here to there," making access to secluded settings the dominant spatial expression.

evidence: Whole painting: The painting consists mainly of pines, bamboo leaves, rocks, sloping banks, and a full moon; no identifiable built elements such as buildings, bridges, or paths are seen.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built elements; based on the overall visible spatial organization of natural scenery, it is only tentatively assigned to C2, which expresses layering relationships, but there is no actual evidence of built elements.

evidence: Center: Dense pine forest screens the main body of the building, exposing only the roof and railings, presenting the spatial layering of a house hidden in the woods. | Upper part: A huge mountain rock encircles and screens the left side of the tower, forming a relationship of seeing the tower behind the rock. | Lower right: A pavilion is placed amid screening bamboo groves; bamboo branches screen part of the eaves and walls, creating a sense of seclusion.
distinction: Although buildings can be seen sited on mountain platforms, the more conspicuous feature is the screening and revealing of the buildings by trees, rocks, and mountains, building up front-to-back layering thereby.

evidence: Upper and middle parts of the painting: Towering peaks are covered with accumulated snow (jisu); the rock textures are clear, clouds and mist swirl around, and they occupy the main portion of the painting. | Lower center of the painting: Dense pine forest and red-leaf trees surround a thatched hut, inside which a person is seen sitting upright; the building merges with the natural scenery. | Foreground at the lower part of the painting: A stream winds past, with rocks on the bank and a calm water surface, forming spatial depth with the mountain forest behind.
distinction: The main subject of the painting is snow-covered rocks and trees; the thatched hut and figures serve only as scenic accents, consistent with the features of a landscape painting (C1), rather than a figure painting centered on human activity.

evidence: Left middle: Thatched huts and pavilions are built among rocky slopes and platforms, partly screened by the trunks and foliage of foreground trees, exposing roofs and railings, presenting the layering of seeing houses within the woods. | Left lower-middle: Another thatched hut stands beside a grove at the foot of the mountain; its walls and roof are faintly visible, forming an obvious relationship of concealment and revelation with the surrounding rocks and trees.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed beside rocky slopes and platforms, the painting places greater emphasis on the screening and surrounding of the buildings by lush trees, forming a secluded layering of controlled concealment and revelation; thus concealment and revelation dominate more than terrain-responsive siting.

evidence: Lower center: A thatched hut on the waterside is half-screened by the foliage of foreground trees, forming a layering of concealment and revelation in which the house is revealed within the woods. | Middle-ground left valley: A tower building is faintly visible on the mountainside, screened by the mountain mass and trees, presenting the spatial depth of seeing a house through a screened view.
distinction: Although the thatched hut is sited by the water, the painting places greater emphasis on the spatial layering formed by the screening and revealing of the buildings by trees; thus C2 is more apt than C1.

evidence: Center-right of the painting: A thatched hut is visible, and to its right an arched bridge crosses the stream, forming a path connecting the two banks. | Lower middle of the painting: A figure wearing a conical hat is walking along the waterside path, presenting the dynamic of traveling toward the depth of the painting or toward the built elements. | Center of the painting: The bridge, path, and thatched hut are connected, constituting a clear spatial clue of entry and arrival.
distinction: Although the thatched hut has a relationship of concealment and revelation amid trees and rocks, the combination of bridge, path, and figures in the painting makes the clues of enterability and travelability more prominent, dominating the spatial organization.

evidence: Middle-ground right: A group of houses is arranged in tiers along the mountain slopes and platforms, with bases fitting the contours of the mountain mass. | Lower left and lower right: Houses are placed beside the waterside and sloping rocks, presenting a layout that unfolds along the bank and sets houses according to the site. | Whole painting: The distribution and staggered heights of the built elements in many places correspond to natural terrain conditions such as mountain forms, slopes and platforms, and the waterside.
distinction: Although there is screening by trees in the painting, the correspondence between the built elements and the terrain—sited beside mountains and water and placed according to the site—is more prominent and dominant.

evidence: Lower left: A small bridge is visible at the water surface, connecting the two banks and hinting at the starting point or transition of a travel route. | Lower right: At the foot of the mountain several houses are scattered along the sloping bank, forming an accessible spatial relationship with the surrounding trees and rocks. | Middle right: A group of buildings faintly appears among the trees on the mountainside; through the screening of rocks and trees, it suggests a visual guide toward traveling into the depths.
distinction: Although there is screening by trees, the painting places greater emphasis on the spatial process of enterability and travelability formed by the linking of bridge, shoreline, and houses, rather than on mere layering of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Foot of the mountain at left-center of the painting: The roofs and walls of a group of buildings are half-hidden behind trees and rocks, presenting a spatial layering of concealment and revelation. | Middle ground of the painting: The buildings are not fully exposed but rather hint at their existence through the screening of surrounding trees and sloping rocks, creating the visual effect of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited at the foot of the mountain, the painting places greater emphasis on the relationship of concealment and revelation in which they are revealed through the screening of trees and rocks, rather than on mere correspondence to terrain.

evidence: Left middle ground: A group of tower buildings is visible on the mountainside, surrounded and screened by pine forest, located where the mountain terrain opens out. | Lower right corner: A group of thatched huts stands on the waterside, set beside the water with bamboo and trees around, marking the scenery of the waterfront.
distinction: The tower at left has screening features, but the main role of the two built elements overall is to mark the specific scenery of the mountainside and the waterfront, serving as points of anchorage in the landscape composition, rather than merely emphasizing layering of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower middle: Houses are visible, their roofs, eaves, and walls partly screened by the trunks and foliage of tall pines in front, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Lower middle, slightly right: The houses are built on rocky sloping ground, surrounded by trees and rocks; the buildings are hidden among the trees and rocks, presenting spatial layering.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited according to the mountain terrain, the strong relationship of concealment and revelation and the spatial layering (screening) formed by the pines and the buildings in the painting are its most prominent compositional means.

evidence: Center of the painting: The central painted area depicts a towering main peak; the mountain mass is covered with trees and rocks, and no traces of built elements such as buildings, roads, or bridges are seen.
distinction: The painting presents only a natural landscape main peak, with no built elements involved; it is therefore assigned to the category of marking the main scenery as the closest designation.

evidence: Middle right: Pavilion roofs faintly emerge from dense woods, presenting the spatial layering of a house hidden in the woods. | Lower right corner: Houses are screened by foreground rocks and trees, with only part of the structure visible, forming a front-to-back relationship of screening. | Left middle: Houses are built on a sloping bank; although relatively clearly revealed, they are surrounded by trees and separated in space from the mountain mass behind.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited beside mountains and water (for example, the house at left set on a platform), built elements in many places in the painting are screened by trees and rocks, and the relationship of concealment and revelation plays a more significant role in building spatial layering and a sense of secluded depth.

evidence: Upper middle: Layered rocks form a high platform or terrace, on which buildings (houses/pavilions) sit, presenting the form of setting houses on platforms, placed in accordance with the mountain terrain. | Around the buildings: Trees surround the built elements, which are closely integrated with the rock structures. | Lower left and lower right: There is an arched bridge on the water at lower left, and stone steps or a revetment structure at lower right, as foreground elements, but they do not form a complete continuous path leading to the built elements on the mountain.
distinction: Although the painting has a bridge and stone steps hinting at travel clues, the most conspicuous feature of the built elements is that they sit atop a rocky high platform; the determining role of terrain in the placement of the built elements (setting houses on platforms) is more direct and dominant than path guidance, and there is no discernible continuous entry link between the paths and the built elements.

evidence: Right mountainside: A house building exposes its roof and part of its walls, screened by red-leaf trees and rocks, presenting the layering of seeing a house behind rocks. | Among the rocks at left: A pavilion-like structure is hidden in green trees, exposing only its top structure, forming a relationship of a house hidden in the woods. | Whole painting: The built elements are surrounded and screened by rocks and trees; the relationship of concealment and revelation participates in the composition, and they are not arranged fully in the open.
distinction: Although there are clues of steps or a path leading to the house on the right, the main visual feature of the built elements is the layering of concealment and revelation formed by screening by trees and rocks, and the building at left has no clear path connection; thus concealment and revelation are more dominant.

evidence: Center and left of the central painted area: Outlines of rocks and trees sketched in pale ink are visible; their forms are damaged and blurry, presenting landscape layering. | Lower left corner of the central painted area: There is a patch of heavier ink, possibly a building roof or wall, located below the trees and rocks, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation screened by the scenery above, but the details cannot be clearly distinguished.
distinction: The suspected built element is located amid screening by trees and rocks, emphasizing layering of concealment and revelation, and is therefore classified as C2; if regarded only as a scenic marker point in the landscape it would be classified as C3, but because the relationship of concealment and revelation (though blurry) better matches the screening feature, it fits the concealment and revelation characteristics.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: A house is built on flat sloping-bank ground; its base is clear and placed in accordance with the terrain. | Center and right of the painting: The house is laid out beside the trees behind it and the rocks to its right, presenting a relationship of placement along the slope/bank that is appropriate to the situation.
distinction: Although the house serves to mark the scenery, its placement beside the sloping bank and trees and rocks places greater emphasis on the spatial relationship of siting according to the site; thus C1 is more apt than C3.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting, slightly right: An arched bridge crosses the stream, connecting the right shoreline with the area at the foot of the mountain on the left, constituting a clear travel clue. | Left and lower left of the painting: Groups of houses are distributed at the foot of the mountain and on the mountainside; the bridge, together with the shoreline and stream, implies a path that turns through the bridge into the depths of the mountain forest, pointing toward these built elements. | Overall composition: The line of sight is guided from the open water surface on the right, through the bridge, to the secluded mountain forest on the left, presenting the spatial process of moving from here to there and approaching a mountain dwelling.
distinction: Although the houses at the lower left corner being placed beside the sloping ground at the foot of the mountain is consistent with terrain-responsive siting (C1), the clues formed by the bridge and stream in the painting place greater emphasis on the process of enterability from the water surface into the depths of the mountain forest (C4).

evidence: Lower left: The waterside pavilion is placed against the slope terrace and grove of trees, its building site conforming to the undulations of the waterside edge. | Center-left: Houses are built on a level slope beside the water, merging with the surrounding trees and terrain. | Center-right: Houses are distributed in a staggered manner on the slope at the mountain's foot, their heights conforming to the mountain's contours.

evidence: Lower-middle of the painting: a group of thatched huts is arranged in staggered fashion against slope platforms and tree clusters, with roof heights conforming to the undulations of the terrain. | Lower-right corner of the painting: a pavilion is built beside the water, its base closely abutting the waterside and sloped rocks. | Left middle and far distance of the painting: houses are faintly visible, unfolded along gentle slopes and the shoreline.
distinction: Although the buildings have the effect of accentuating the scenery, their most prominent spatial feature is placement conforming to natural terrain such as slope platforms and the waterside; therefore C1 is closer than C3 to the dominant expression.

evidence: Lower part of the painting: a bridge or walkway with railings is visible, spanning among the rocks and connecting the left and right sides of the painting. | Lower-middle of the painting: beside the bridge, a railing-lined path extends, implying an accessible and journeyable spatial thread.
distinction: Although pines and plum blossoms serve as scenic accents in the painting, the clear bridge and path below constitute a strong journeying thread guiding spatial entry; therefore C4 is more dominant than C3.

evidence: Left mountainside: a group of houses is arranged horizontally along a mountain slope platform, presenting a layout of separate placement according to the slope, with bases fitting the terrain. | Above, slightly right of the summit: a pavilion is located high beside the peak, set on a platform, corresponding to the height of the mountain's form. | Below, in the foreground slightly right: a pavilion is built on sloped ground at the waterside, surrounded by trees, its position conforming to the waterside terrain.
distinction: Although woodland screens the buildings (such as the foreground pavilion), the distribution of buildings in the painting from the water's edge and mountainside to the summit more predominantly embodies a terrain-responsive relationship of placement according to slope platforms.

evidence: Lower left: a thatched hut is visible, with a person inside; the hut's roof and walls are partially screened by bamboo and tree branches in front. | Lower-middle of the painting: tall pines and miscellaneous trees surround the thatched hut and its front, forming foreground and middle-ground layering and rendering the thatched hut half-hidden and half-exposed.
distinction: Although the thatched hut is sited against rocks and trees, the painting emphasizes more the screening and revealing relationship of woodland to buildings, forming a spatial layering of well-modulated concealment and revelation; therefore C2 is more fitting than C1.

evidence: Lower left: a pavilion is located deep among surrounding sloped rocks and trees; the morphology of the sloped rocks in front implies a path that can be ascended step by step, presenting a process of approaching the built structures. | Right center: at the boundary of the cliff and waterside, a form resembling a small arched bridge is visible; as a ford/crossing cue, together with the shoreline it implies a journeying connection of moving from one place to another.
distinction: Although the pavilion exhibits the feature of buildings set on platforms and placed according to terrain, the journeying cues implied by the bridge and slope path in the painting make the spatial organization more focused on the accessible process of entering and approaching the built structures.

evidence: Lower-right corner: a wooden bridge spans the water surface/stream gully, connecting the right bank with the left slope, forming a clear journeying thread pointing toward the built structures. | Lower left: built structures (houses) sit on a slope platform, with railings and step structures in front, echoing the direction in which the bridge extends, presenting an accessible and enterable spatial relationship. | Center-left: tall pines stand in front of the built structures; although they form foreground screening, the main body of the built structures is clearly visible and connected to the external space via the bridge, constituting the terminus or node of the journeying route.
distinction: Although the pines screen the built structures and form layering (consistent with C2 features), the bridge at the lower-right corner clearly constructs a path of entry into the built structures from outside, making the spatial process of 'moving from one place to another' (C4) the dominant organizing method.

evidence: Center and foreground of the painting: a red building complex stands among the trees and woods of the valley, screened by the huge pine branches in the foreground and the surrounding cedars; only the roofs, eaves and parts of the red walls are exposed, forming a pronounced concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Around the buildings: the buildings are arranged in tiers following the mountain terrain, yet are tightly wrapped by the natural environment, presenting a spatial layering of houses hidden in the woods and buildings seen across intervening scenery. | Lower right and lower left of the painting: a wooden bridge and the shoreline of a stream are visible; although there is a sense of spatial extension, the path does not connect directly through to the buildings, which mainly appear screened by trees and woodland.
distinction: Although the bridge and stream in the lower part of the painting hint at a movement-through-the-landscape thread, the main body of the buildings is heavily screened by the huge pine branches in the foreground and the surrounding trees, presenting a pronounced layered screening of houses hidden in the woods and buildings seen across intervening scenery; the concealment-and-revelation relationship is more dominant than the access path.

evidence: Lower-middle and foreground of the painting: the building complex (houses, pavilion, enclosing wall) is screened by the huge weeping willow in the foreground and the pine grove on the right; only the roofs, eaves and parts of the walls are exposed, forming a spatial layering and concealment-and-revelation relationship of houses seen in the woods. | Left side and foreground of the painting: the dense willow branches hang down, screening the base of the buildings and the waterside, producing the effect of buildings seen across intervening scenery, so that the screening relationship participates in forming the scene. | Right side of the painting: the pavilion is hidden at the edge of the pine grove; the screening by the trees indicates its existence and the level at which it sits, forming an interaction of screening and exposure with the surrounding trees.
distinction: Although the buildings are laid out along the waterside (possessing C1 characteristics), the pronounced screening of the buildings by the foreground willows and surrounding pine grove, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship (exposed roofs and walls), are visually more dominant, matching the definition of concealment and revelation forming the scene.

evidence: Bottom of the painting: the building complex is partly screened by the foreground tree branches and mountains and rocks; roofs and walls are revealed amid the screening, forming spatial layering. | Left side of the middle ground: a pavilion is built on a cliff platform, surrounded by trees, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship.
distinction: Although the pavilion in the middle ground, built on the cliff, embodies terrain-responsive siting, the pronounced screening and exposure relationship between the building complex at the bottom of the painting and the trees and mountains and rocks constitutes a more dominant spatial layering, so C2 is more apt.

evidence: Middle right: the building complex is placed against a steep cliff; wooden piles are visible beneath some of the houses, presenting the site characteristics of being near the water or perched on the cliff. | Middle right and rear: the layout of the houses follows the mountain terrain, with a pine grove surrounding them behind, and the buildings form a correspondence with the mountains and rocks and the waterside, nestling against the mountains and beside the water.
distinction: Although the buildings are surrounded by trees, their wooden-pile supports and cliff-side layout more prominently demonstrate the adaptation of the built structures to topographic conditions, rather than forming layering mainly through screening.

evidence: Lower right corner: a group of corridor buildings is surrounded and screened by the dense trees of the foreground and middle ground; only the roofs, corridor pillars and the figures inside are exposed, forming a clear spatial layering of concealment and revelation. | Left mountainside: a small pavilion is built against the mountains and rocks and trees, half hidden among the woods, its existence indicated by the screening of the trees. | Overall painting: the built elements are not in fully open places, but organize the pictorial depth and layering of the painting through the screening and exposure by trees and woodland.
distinction: The main label emphasizes the concealment-and-revelation layering relationship between the buildings and the woodland, while the alternative label emphasizes the dependent relationship between the buildings and the terrain; in the painting, the screening and exposure of the buildings by the trees is visually more prominent.

evidence: Lower-middle right of the painting: several houses are half hidden among the mountains and rocks and the dense pine grove; roofs and walls are partly exposed, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Lower center-right of the painting: a thatched pavilion is built against trees on the sloped bank of the waterside, partly screened by branches.
distinction: Although the built structures nestle against the mountains and beside the water, the painting more strongly emphasizes the screening and exposure of the buildings by the trees and mountains and rocks, with clear layering, so C2 is more apt than C1.

evidence: Middle of the painting: a group of houses is surrounded and screened by dense pines and miscellaneous trees; only the roofs and parts of the walls are exposed, presenting the layering of houses hidden among the woods. | Lower part of the painting: the houses in the lower right and lower left corners are likewise screened behind thickets and mountains and rocks, with the building itself visible through gaps in the branches and leaves. | Overall composition: mountains and rocks and trees overlap in layers, wrapping the buildings within them and producing a deep, secluded visual effect of being hidden deep among mountain forests and the bends of the water.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed according to the mountain terrain and the bends of the water, the painting chiefly creates a deep, secluded mood through the layered screening and exposure by trees and mountains and rocks; the concealment-and-revelation relationship is more prominently dominant than the correspondence to terrain.

evidence: Left middle: a clear stepped path can be seen winding upward, connecting the foot of the mountain with the group of houses on the mountainside, forming a definite clue to entry into the built structures. | Lower left corner: the building complex is laid out at the foot of the mountain, with trees screening it in front, but a path or waterside extension beside it hints at an accessible relationship. | Overall painting: the gaps among the mountains and rocks, the stream and the paths together help explain the extension of space, guiding the eye from the foreground into the depths, approaching the screened built structures.
distinction: The clear path clues in the painting (C4) emphasize the process of moving from here to there and approaching the built structures, and better summarize the dynamic spatial organization of the painting than a mere description of the buildings being placed according to the mountain terrain (C1).

evidence: Middle of the painting: the buildings (halls) are surrounded by dense bamboo groves and trees; the bamboo leaves screen the roof edges and the sides and rear, presenting the layering of houses seen in the woods. | Lower-middle of the painting: an enclosing wall and gate tower stand in front of the buildings, and foreground tree branches interpose between the buildings and the viewer, forming a spatial relationship of screening front and back. | Upper to middle part of the painting: the slopes and banks of mountains and rocks extend downward, joining the bamboo grove behind the buildings; the natural scenery wraps around and sets off the location of the built structures.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed at the foot of the mountain, the visual focus of the painting is the surrounding and partial screening of the buildings by the dense bamboo grove and trees, emphasizing the layering of concealment and revelation forming the scene rather than mere dependence on terrain.

evidence: Left middle: a building complex sits at the edge of a flat terrace projecting from the mountainside, with a steep cliff or unpainted space below, presenting a typical form of houses set on a terrace. | Lower right and lower left: many houses are distributed on the mountain slopes, in gaps in the woods and at the foot of the mountain, following the rises and falls of the terrain in a staggered layout, presenting an arrangement by slope. | Overall painting: the layout of the built structures is placed according to the undulations of the mountain forms, and the building sites form a clear correspondence with natural forms such as terraces and slopes.
distinction: Although the bridge in the lower part of the painting and the steps on the right mountainside provide clues for movement through the landscape, the building complex mainly presents a placement on terraces and along slopes; the determining role of terrain for the layout and its weight in the composition are more prominent.

evidence: Upper mountain summit: a slender multi-storey pagoda stands at the highest point of the peak, prominently placed, becoming the visual focus and marker of the mountain form. | Lower waterside: an arched bridge spans the junction of water and land, with a pavilion built on the bridge, identifying a particular scenic spot beside the open water (such as the Broken Bridge). | Mountainside and among the woods: several houses are distributed; although partly screened among trees and rocks, the pagoda and the bridge pavilion, as landmark built structures, serve in the composition to concentrate the mountain-and-water scenery.
distinction: Although the houses on the mountainside present a concealment-and-revelation relationship (C2), the towering pagoda and the bridge pavilion spanning the waterside serve as visual centers, chiefly playing the role of marking landmarks and concentrating the scenery, i.e. scenic accentuation.

evidence: Foreground lower left to center: a waterside building connects with a stone bridge; two figures are on the bridge, and the bridge spans the water, connecting the building with the banks and mountains and rocks, forming a clear clue for movement through the landscape and entry. | Middle-ground right: the roof and walls of a storied pavilion emerge among the trees on the mountainside, forming a front-to-back layering with the surrounding trees. | Overall painting: the bridge, buildings, water and mountains and rocks in the foreground together organize a spatial process from near to deep, reachable and traversable.
distinction: Although the middle-ground pavilion has a concealment-and-revelation relationship of concealment and revelation forming the scene, the accessible and traversable spatial clues formed by the foreground bridge, buildings and figures are more coherent and dominate the organization of the painting, so C4 is more apt than C2.

evidence: Central mountain hollow: the building complex is arranged in tiers descending along the slopes and valley, with staggered roofs, presenting a form arranged by slope. | Right cliff edge: a hexagonal pavilion is built at the edge of a cliff terrace projecting over the water; the building site corresponds closely to the cliff-bank terrain, presenting houses set on a terrace. | Lower right waterside: a group of houses is arranged along the shoreline, screened by surrounding trees, presenting a layout extending along the bank.
distinction: Although the buildings are screened by trees and mountains and rocks to form layering, their arrangement in tiers following the mountain terrain and their layout perched on the cliff and beside the water more prominently display the characteristics of siting according to the ground and adapting to the configuration.

evidence: Lower-middle of the painting: the roofs, eaves and courtyard walls of the built structures emerge through gaps in the dense trees and bamboo groves, presenting a clear layering of concealment and revelation. | Lower-middle of the painting: the branches and leaves of the woodland screen large areas of the main body of the buildings; only partial structure is exposed, forming the scene through screening by natural scenery.
distinction: Although the buildings nestle against the mountains and beside the water, the painting more strongly emphasizes the screening and exposure relationship between the woodland and the buildings, rather than siting based purely on terrain.

evidence: Lower middle: a building complex (several houses) is surrounded by dense trees and mountains and rocks; roofs and walls are partly exposed, presenting the spatial layering of houses hidden in the woods. | Middle-upper right: on the mountainside a house shows its roof, screened by the mountain body and trees in front, forming a screening relationship of buildings seen across intervening scenery. | Middle, slightly left: buildings can faintly be seen screened behind trees and rocks, with only partial outlines exposed, participating in forming a pictorial depth of alternating concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the buildings are laid out according to the mountain terrain, the painting more strongly emphasizes the layered relationship of the buildings being screened and exposed by trees and mountains and rocks, rather than mere adaptation to terrain.

evidence: Middle-right mountainside: several groups of house compounds are interspersed among the mountains and rocks and the trees and woodland; eaves and walls are partly exposed and partly screened by trees and rocks, forming a clear layering of concealment and revelation. | Lower left corner: houses are screened behind the foreground thickets, with only parts of the roofs and structures exposed, embodying the relationship of forming the scene through screening by woodland. | Left distance: a faint cluster of houses is visible at the foot of the mountain on the opposite bank, merged into the mountain forest, further enriching the spatial layering of the scenery in the painting.
distinction: Although the built structures in the painting are built according to the mountain, the more prominent compositional device is the use of trees and mountains and rocks to screen and expose the buildings, thereby creating a deep spatial layering, so C2 is more dominant than C1.

evidence: Lower left corner: a pavilion is built on the rocks by the water, placed according to the terrain of the waterside rocks. | Middle-right mountainside: a group of houses is built on a flat terrace, houses set on a terrace, arranged by the mountain slopes and terraces. | Left middle ground: a corridor-bridge-type structure stands by the water, extending along the shoreline and integrated with the terrain.
distinction: Although paths and bridges in the painting hint at a movement-through-the-landscape thread, the placement of buildings on terraces and along the waterside at different heights (houses set on terraces, arranged by slope) is more prominent and dominates the spatial relationship between the built structures and the landscape.

evidence: Middle ground, slightly right: a pavilion is visible among the woods, half screened by red trees and mountains and rocks. | Lower half of the painting: a stream and a stone path extend from the foreground into the middle ground, the path leading toward the pavilion in the woods. | Lower right corner: two figures walk along the stream bank, forming a movement-through-the-landscape clue of going deep along the path and approaching the built structures.
distinction: Although the built structures have a layering of screening by trees, the clues of entry and arrival formed jointly by the stream, stone path and figures are more prominent and dominate the spatial organization.

evidence: Middle-ground mountain hollow: a group of houses is distributed in a staggered way on the sloped ground at the foot of the mountain, arranged following the undulations of the terrain. | Distant mountainside: a pagoda stands high on the mountain ridge, echoing the outline of the mountain body. | Lower left and lower right: houses are placed against the waterside and mountains and rocks, presenting the characteristics of following the bank and being set against rocks.
distinction: Although the built structures play a role in identifying the scenery, their layout more prominently demonstrates placement that follows natural forms such as mountain slopes and the waterside.

evidence: Lower left: a pavilion terrace is built on a sloped bank, partly surrounded and screened by the surrounding pines and vegetation. | Center: the corner of a thatched roof emerges from behind mountains and rocks and trees, presenting a clear spatial layering of concealment and revelation. | Middle-upper water surface: a small boat with a canopy is on the water, hinting at a movement-through-the-landscape clue on the water.
distinction: In the painting, the layering of concealment and revelation formed by the thatched house and pavilion terrace screened by trees and mountains and rocks is more prominent, dominating the spatial organization of the built structures and natural scenery, while the movement-through-the-landscape clue (the boat) is relatively secondary.

evidence: Lower left to center: the building complex of pavilions, long corridors and so on extends linearly along the lakeside embankment, alternating with the trees on the bank and laid out along the bank following the trend of the waterside. | Upper-left distant mountains: a tall pagoda is built on the summit, with houses distributed on the mountainside, placed according to the height of the mountain terrain; the pagoda occupies the highest point, presenting a relationship of houses set on terraces and arranged by slope.
distinction: Although the tall pagoda on the summit has the scenic-accent role of marking the peak, the large building complex in the lower part of the painting mainly presents a layout extending along the bank, and the buildings on the mountain are also built according to the terrain; overall this emphasizes the adaptation of the built structures to the topography and the configuration of the waterside.

evidence: Right shoreline: the building complex is distributed along the curved shoreline, presenting a layout extending along the bank and following the trend of the bank. | Middle-right pavilion terrace: the pavilion has a base and steps extending into the water, embodying the placement of houses set on a terrace and built beside the water.
distinction: Although the stone pagoda on the water and the waterside pavilion terrace have a scenic-accent role, the characteristic of the building complex as a whole being laid out along the waterside terrain (extending along the bank, houses set on terraces) is more prominent and dominates the spatial relationship between the built structures and the landscape.

evidence: Lower middle: the building complex is arranged tightly along the shoreline, with enclosing walls, courtyards and trees, presenting a form of houses set by the water and laid out along the bank. | Middle-upper hillside: houses are distributed in a staggered way according to the mountain terrain, placed following the undulations of the terrain. | Lower right corner: an arched bridge and a pavilion join with the trees on the bank.
distinction: Although trees screen the buildings in the painting, the most prominent characteristic of the built structures is the placement and layout following the terrain of the waterside and hillside, so C1 is more apt than C2.

evidence: Center: the roofs and eaves of storied pavilions and pavilions emerge from the dense willow thickets, forming a clear layering of concealment and revelation. | Lower part: the building itself of the waterside building complex interweaves with the surrounding willows; parts of the walls and platforms are screened by willow branches. | Overall: the built structures are not fully open, but their existence and spatial level are indicated by the surrounding and screening of the willows.
distinction: Although the arched bridge in the painting provides a movement-through-the-landscape clue, the screening and exposure relationship of the buildings' roofs and walls by the willows is visually more pervasive and dominant, constituting the main spatial layering.

evidence: Upper left to center: the city wall/long wall winds along the mountain ridge line, following the undulations of the mountain terrain, presenting a layout extending along the mountain. | Left mountainside and foot of the mountain: house clusters are placed in layers according to the slope terrain, interspersed with trees, embodying arrangement by slope. | Right mountainside: a temple complex is distributed in a staggered way according to the mountain terrain, with an enclosing wall defining the space in front, and the building site corresponding to the terrain.
distinction: Although the temple complex on the right has pronounced screening by trees and woodland (C2), the terrain-responsive layout of the city wall winding along the mountain ridge and the houses distributed by slope is more continuous and prominent throughout the painting.

evidence: Lower-middle of the painting: a simple wooden bridge can be seen spanning a stream; one person riding a donkey and two attendants are crossing the bridge from left to right, forming a clear movement-through-the-landscape clue. | Lower-middle to right side of the painting: the bridge connects with the path under the figures' feet, guiding the eye toward the right side of the painting and expressing the spatial process of moving from here to there and continuing the journey.
distinction: No fixed built structures such as houses are seen in the painting; the spatial organization relies mainly on the journey process constituted by the bridge and the figures' route, so it is assigned to C4 rather than other categories involving the placement or screening of buildings.

evidence: Upper summit of the painting: a pagoda stands at the highest point of the peak, embodying placement at a height and corresponding to the apex of the mountain form. | Middle mountainside and foot of the painting: pavilion terraces and house clusters are distributed according to the slope terrain and the lakeshore line, presenting a layout of arrangement by slope and extension along the bank. | Lower waterside of the painting: an arched bridge and a pavilion stand by the waterside, placed following the waterside terrain and connecting land and water space.
distinction: Although the bridge in the lower part of the painting hints at a movement-through-the-landscape clue, the built structures overall (pagoda, pavilions, house clusters) are mainly laid out according to the height of the mountain terrain and the shoreline (e.g. a pagoda on the summit, houses along the bank); the characteristic of terrain-responsive placement runs through the whole picture.

evidence: Middle ground, slightly left: an arched bridge can be seen spanning a stream, connecting the two banks and guiding the eye toward the storied pavilion in the middle ground. | Middle-ground center: a multi-storey pavilion sits among the pine grove, linking spatially with the bridge and stream. | Near foreground, lower right: a thatched house is visible hidden among the thickets and the sloped bank, together with the foreground trees and path forming an entrance space that can be dwelt in and wandered through.
distinction: Although buildings in the painting are placed against the mountains and beside the water, the accessible and traversable clues formed jointly by the bridge, stream and buildings are more prominent, so C4 is more apt than C1.

evidence: Whole painting: the city wall and mountain pass are laid out in winding fashion along the ridge lines and valleys, the building sites and layout fully following the undulations of the mountain forms and terrain. | Middle left: building complexes such as Juyong Pass are built against the mountains and into the valleys, advancing in tiers, embodying the spatial relationship of defense by strategic terrain and siting according to the ground. | Middle-upper and lower right: the Great Wall and beacon towers extend along the steep slopes and rock ridges, highly consistent with the direction of the natural terrain.
distinction: Although paths and the mountain pass in the painting hint at entry, the layout of the built structures following the mountains and taking shape according to the terrain is the most important compositional mode running through the whole picture.

evidence: Lower right to middle-upper: a clear stone-step path winds upward along the mountain terrain, passing through the pine grove and connecting spaces at different heights. | Middle right: the path passes a house half screened among the woods, showing an accessible spatial node where one can enter and pause. | Top: the path finally leads to the temple and tower complex on the summit, forming a movement-through-the-landscape clue from bottom to top and from outside to inside.
distinction: Although the buildings are screened among the pine grove, the winding stone steps running through the painting clearly organize an accessible and reachable spatial process; the path clue is more dominant than the mere concealment-and-revelation relationship.

evidence: Upper-left mountainside: a group of houses is arranged in a staggered manner on the slope terraces following the mountain's form, with their sites corresponding to the undulations of the mountain body. | Lower-middle waterside and among the trees: houses spread out along the waterside and the terrain, sited in accord with the natural topography.
distinction: Although the layering formed by tree concealment is present, the built elements are mainly placed according to the mountain's form, slope terraces, and the waterside; the relationship of siting according to the terrain is more prominent.

evidence: From the right side to the upper-middle: a clearly winding path (stone steps) extends upward from the lower right near the water, passes the pavilions on the right mountainside, and continues toward the building group higher up, forming a clear route of travel. | Lower-middle: a bridge spans the water/ravine, connecting the two banks and, together with the path, forming an accessible, reachable spatial connection. | Multiple places (lower left, central mountainside, right mountainside): several building groups are distributed in a staggered manner following the mountain's form, visually linked in series by paths and bridges, presenting a spatial process of passing from one to another and turning into the depths.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited following the mountain's form (C1), the path and bridge clues running through the painting more strongly organize a traversable spatial process, so C4 is dominant.

evidence: Lower right: a bridge spans the water, with two people walking on it, forming a clear route of movement through the landscape into the painting. | Left middle: a pavilion is built atop a protruding rocky platform, forming a spatial correspondence with the surrounding mountains, rocks, and trees. | Lower-middle of the painting: the bridge and pavilion are connected by mountains and rocks, trees, and a faint path, guiding the eye from near to far and presenting an accessible spatial process.
distinction: Although the pavilion built against the mountain embodies terrain-responsive siting, the route of movement through the landscape formed by the bridge, figures, and path is more prominent, emphasizing the spatial process of entering and traveling.

evidence: Lower-middle: the roofs and eaves of houses emerge from dense branches and foliage, their walls screened by foreground trees, forming a spatial layering of houses concealed within the woods. | Lower right: a pavilion stands on rocks, its roof visible, surrounded by withered trees and mountains and rocks, presenting a clear relationship of screening and revelation. | Left waterside: a built structure stands by the waterside below a waterfall, surrounded and screened by trees, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation with the mountains and rocks.
distinction: Although the built structures are placed along the water and thus exhibit terrain-responsive siting, the visual focus of the painting lies in the screening and revealing of the built elements by the dense woodland; the relationship of concealment and revelation plays a more dominant role in constructing spatial layering.

evidence: Left middle and lower left: house clusters are distributed along the sloping ground at the foot of the mountain, presenting a layout of separate placement by slope, with building sites following the undulations of the mountain. | Lower center: a group of buildings is built beside the water, its form and position unfolding along the shoreline, embodying placement following the bank. | Overall composition: the built elements are mainly placed in gaps among mountains and rocks, on slope terraces, and on flat ground by the waterside, arranged high and low in a staggered manner, corresponding to the opening and closing forms of the natural terrain.
distinction: Although a winding path on the right side of the painting leads into the depths of the woods (a C4 feature), the main building groups (the village on the left and the waterside pavilion below) more prominently display a layout relationship of placement according to terrain (slope, bank), rather than mere path-guided entry.

evidence: Lower left: a zigzagging wooden plank bridge (or covered walkway) extends from the left side of the painting, connecting to a pavilion built on waterside rocks, forming a clear entry clue. | Lower middle: two people walk on a path by the bank, presenting a movement line of traveling along the waterside, approaching the built elements, or turning into the depths. | Lower-left pavilion: figures sit and rest inside the pavilion, serving as a stopping point or node of the travel route, giving the spatial process a destination.
distinction: Although the pavilion built along the waterside has terrain-responsive siting characteristics, the travel clues formed by the plank bridge and the figures' route run through the foreground, more strongly emphasizing the spatial process of passing from one to another and approaching the built elements.

evidence: Left mountainside: a clearly visible stepped path winds upward, connecting the foreground area with the building group on the middle-ground mountainside, forming a clear entry route. | Right stream: an arched bridge spans the water, connecting the two banks, implying the possibility of passage and the extension of space. | Slightly left of center: the building group (temple) lies deep along the path's extension, surrounded by mountain forest, presenting a spatial process of being led in by the path and passing from one to another.
distinction: Although the buildings are screened by trees, mountains, and rocks (a C2 feature), the clear stepped path and bridge in the painting constitute a strong route of movement through the landscape, organizing the spatial process from the foreground into the built elements, so access to secluded settings (C4) is more dominant.

evidence: Middle-ground left: a pavilion-type built structure is half-hidden behind dense trees and slope rocks, with only its roof and part of its columns exposed. | Middle-ground right: a multi-tiered eave building hugs the rock face, partly screened by the trunks, branches, and foliage of pines in front. | Upper-middle mountainside: several houses are staggered following the mountain's form, screened among mountains, rocks, and trees, presenting alternating layers of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the built elements are arranged following the mountain's form, the painting more prominently highlights the screening and revealing relationship of trees, mountains, and rocks to the buildings, thereby constructing spatial layering, so C2 is more dominant than C1.

evidence: Lower left: a building is placed close to the waterside, its site adjoining the water's edge, presenting a layout unfolding along the bank. | Left middle: a pavilion is built on a protruding rocky platform, relying on the terrain's height difference to form a posture of building on a platform. | Upper-middle mountainside: a building is placed on a mountainside slope terrace, surrounded by pines, presenting a form of separate placement by slope.
distinction: Although trees partly screen the buildings in the painting, the correspondence of the buildings' sites to mountains and rocks, slope terraces, and the waterside is clearer and runs through the whole painting, dominantly manifesting placement according to terrain rather than mere concealment and revelation forming scenery.

evidence: Lower-middle to middle of the painting: winding plank walkways and mountain paths are visible extending upward along the mountain's form, connecting the mountain foot with the building groups on the mountainside. | Lower part and lower right of the painting: there are a ferry crossing and a bridge at the waterside, with travelers passing through the bridge and paths into the mountain area, forming a clear entry clue. | Middle of the painting: the temple building group on the mountainside is connected by paths and plank walkways, presenting an accessible and deep spatial layering.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited following the mountain's form, the painting more strongly emphasizes guiding the eye and the process of travel through paths, bridges, and plank walkways into the deep mountains, and the organizing role of access to secluded settings is more prominent.

evidence: Upper-left mountainside: houses are placed in a staggered manner on slope terraces following the mountain's form, their sites fitting the mountain's contours. | Right mountainside: houses are arranged following the undulations of mountains and rocks, conforming to the terrain's heights and lows. | Lower waterside: pavilions and thatched huts are built beside the water, unfolding on the rocky platforms by the bank.
distinction: Although some buildings are screened by trees, the overall emphasis is more on the placement relationship of buildings relying on mountain forms, slope terraces, and the waterside; screening is not the dominant means of composing the scene.

evidence: Central mountain hollow of the painting: a group of houses is distributed layer by layer following the valley terrain, placed separately by slope, with the layout's heights corresponding to the mountain's directional trend. | Lower right of the painting: a pavilion is set by the waterside, its site placed according to the water's edge. | Lower left of the painting: houses are placed against mountains, rocks, and trees, conforming to the terrain by the bank.
