evidence: Left mountainside and cliff: pavilions and houses are visible placed on rocky platforms and steep mountain terrain, presenting forms of building on platforms and separate placement by slope. | Right and lower waterside: building groups unfold along the shoreline, placed beside the water, corresponding to the water surface and sloping ground. | Overall composition: the built elements are scattered high and low in a staggered manner, strictly conforming to the mountain's undulations and the waterside's windings, embodying a relationship of placement according to terrain and suitability following the trend.

evidence: Lower left to middle: several houses are placed against snow-covered sloping banks, their sites undulating with the slope terraces, presenting a layout of separate placement by slope. | Below: a waterside pavilion is built beside the water, unfolding on the waterside rocks, forming a corresponding relationship with the cold stream's surface. | Upper left: a pavilion is located on a recessed platform high among mountains and rocks, placed according to the mountain's form and the rocks' shapes.

evidence: Lower left: an arched bridge spans the stream, with two people standing or walking on it, connecting the two banks and forming a clear path of crossing and entry. | Upper middle: a small house is built atop a mountain rock, with a flagpole beside it, placed according to the high cliff's terrain.

evidence: Lower right: the roof and part of the walls of a built structure are visible, partly screened by foreground pines and shrubs and by the woods behind, forming a clear relationship of concealment and revelation. | Middle ground of the painting: a figure sits alone on the left bank, facing the built structure in the lower right across the water; the built structure is hidden behind trees, mountains, and rocks, enhancing the spatial layering and sense of seclusion.

evidence: Lower left: houses are built on a stone platform by the water, their sites closely integrated with the terrain | Middle ground: houses are placed separately according to the mountain slope's terrain, conforming to the mountain's form | Below: a bridge spans the stream, connecting the waterside with the built elements

evidence: Lower-middle of the painting: a large building group unfolds along the shoreline and sloping ground, with enclosing walls, covered walkways, and pavilions arranged following the terrain's undulations and the waterside's windings. | Lower right of the painting: a stone arch bridge spans the water, connecting the two banks and providing a path clue for entering the building group. | Middle of the painting: the building group is surrounded by trees, with some roofs and walls revealed among the woodland, forming layering, but the overall layout's unfolding according to terrain is more prominent.

evidence: Left mountainside: a clearly visible white path winds upward along the mountain's form, passing through woods and extending from near the building group in the lower left toward the depths of the painting, forming a clear travel clue. | Right waterside: an arched bridge spans the water, connecting the bank with a small waterside building (waterside pavilion/pavilion), providing a path for crossing and approaching the built elements. | Lower left: a building group is located at the mountain foot by the water, with paths connected to it, implying an accessible spatial relationship.

evidence: Middle right: a pavilion is partly blocked by foreground pine branches and leaves and by mountains and rocks behind, presenting a half-hidden, half-revealed state. | Slightly left of center: a group of buildings is distributed between a mountain hollow and the waterside, with some houses screened by surrounding trees and slope rocks. | Lower right corner: the near-ground building has a courtyard wall, screened by trees on its left and behind, forming front-to-back layers.

evidence: Lower left corner: a thatched hut stands at the foot of a cliff, partly screened by the branches and foliage of tall foreground trees and by rocks, revealing only the roof, eaves, and side walls, presenting a spatial layering of seeing the house within the woods/beneath the rock. | Left side and center of the painting: the built element (thatched hut) is enclosed and screened by natural scenery (rocks, trees); the dense foreground trees with variegated foliage and the mountain wall behind together constitute a relationship of concealment and revelation toward the building.
distinction: Although the house built on the terrace at the mountain foot has a certain terrain-responsive character, the composition places greater emphasis on the screening and revealing of the house by foreground trees and rocks, and the relationship of concealment and revelation dominates the spatial expression of the built structure.

evidence: Left side and central main body of the painting: a grand palace complex leans against the foot of the rocky mountain on the left and is mainly built upon a high terrace (sloped platform) enclosed by multiple tiers of white balustrades, presenting a layout of buildings set upon a terrace and unfurling according to the terrain. | Upper right of the painting: beside a gentle distant waterside an arched bridge spans across, and houses are distributed along the bank, showing the extension and correspondence of the waterside to the built layout. | Lower middle of the painting: the building group unfolds tier upon tier on the high terrace by means of steps and covered corridors, and the base sites form a close correspondence with the high and low levels of the terrace.
distinction: Although there are path elements such as bridges and steps suggesting relations of entry (C4), the dominant spatial logic is the placement of the building group according to the high terrace (sloped platform) and mountain terrain (buildings set upon a terrace), and the terrace base constitutes the primary spatial foundation.

evidence: Left middle ground: several houses are half hidden behind woods, revealing only part of their roofs and walls, forming layers of concealment and revelation | Right middle ground: buildings are screened among rocks and trees, their spatial position indicated through partial exposure | Lower right foreground: a pavilion sits on a sloped bank screened by trees and rocks, forming a relationship of foreground-background occlusion with the surrounding scenery
distinction: Although the built elements are placed against the mountain and beside trees, the painting places greater emphasis on constructing spatial layers through the screening and revealing by woods and rocks, rather than simply stressing the constraints of terrain on layout.

evidence: Lower middle and left mountainside of the painting: multiple building groups are distributed tier upon tier along the mountain foot and slopes, placed in accordance with the undulations of the mountain terrain, presenting a relationship of separate placement according to the slope. | Right mountain foot: a group of houses is located on relatively flat ground beside a bamboo grove, unfurling against the terrain. | Lower waterside of the painting: buildings adjoin a winding embankment bridge, presenting a layout unfurling along the bank, with base sites corresponding to the natural configuration.
distinction: Although path and zigzag bridge cues are visible in the painting, the building groups are extensively placed against mountain forms and sloped terraces, and the feature of siting according to terrain is more prominent and runs throughout the whole than the movement cues.

evidence: Lower right: a building group is arranged in zigzag fashion along the shoreline, presenting a layout unfurling along the bank, and is placed against the foreground rocks. | Left middle: houses are located at the edge of the waterside slope, with level base sites, parallel to the shoreline, and set according to the water. | Upper middle: a storied pavilion is located on gentle ground behind the woods on the opposite bank, placed according to the waterside terrain; although screened by trees, its base site is visible.
distinction: Although the buildings are screened by trees (a C2 feature), their zigzag arrangement along the shoreline (unfurling along the bank) and placement around rocks more directly embody the correspondence between built elements and terrain (waterside, rocks), and dominate the spatial placement.

evidence: Left middle: a tall gate tower and city wall, with the gate open and figures entering and exiting, serving as a clear entrance (gate) into the town. | Middle and lower parts: streets extend among dense houses, with figures walking within them; over the stream below a stone bridge connects the two banks, forming a passable network of paths (paths, bridges). | Overall composition: through the linking of city gate, streets, and bridges, the painting presents a spatial process of entering from the foreground waterside through paths into the depths of the town.
distinction: Although the houses are laid out according to the waterside and streets (C1), the movement cues (C4) formed by the city gate, bridges, and streets are more dominant in organizing the sense of spatial entry and connectivity.

evidence: Bottom center: stone steps and a bridge structure span between two cliffs, connecting the foreground with the middle-ground water area, forming a clear entry passage and movement cue. | Left middle: houses are placed against the mountain rocks, beside them a winding path extends downward, connecting with the path system below and guiding the gaze to move into the depth. | Lower right corner: water pours down from among the rocks, adjacent to the stone-step structure, helping to explain the connectivity and extension of space.
distinction: Although the houses placed against the mountain embody a relation of siting according to terrain, the stone-step bridge and winding path in the lower part of the painting constitute a strong movement guide, making the spatial process of passing from here to there dominant.

evidence: Lower middle: multiple house courtyards are arranged tier upon tier along the mountain-foot sloped terraces, unfurling in accordance with the undulations of the terrain. | Center-left and center-right: buildings are placed in staggered fashion among pine woods and rocks, their base sites fitted to the forms of the slopes. | Lower foreground: buildings also stand in a row at the waterside, forming with the houses built against the mountain behind a spatial organization that follows the high and low of the terrain.
distinction: Although there is screening by trees, the dominant expression of the painting is the terrain-responsive placement of the building groups according to the mountain-foot slopes and gaps in the woodland.

evidence: Lower part of the painting: a multi-arch stone bridge spans the water surface, connecting the group of houses on the right bank with the sloped bank on the left, forming a clear circulation cue. | Lower right waterside: houses are placed against the mountain foot by the water, connected with the stone bridge, presenting a spatial relationship that is reachable and enterable. | Top of the central cliff: a pagoda and houses are built on the cliff top, marking the scenery on high, but the bridge and paths below constitute the main movement guide of the painting.
distinction: Although the pagoda and buildings on the cliff top mark the peak, the connectivity and entry relations formed by the bridge and shoreline in the lower part of the painting are more prominent and dominate the spatial organization.

evidence: From the lower middle to the upper middle of the painting: a clear winding mountain path extends from the lower part of the painting, passing through the courtyard and bridge at the lower right corner, then upward through the mountain hollow and storied pavilion in the center, leading to the courtyard at the summit, forming a clear route of movement. | Lower right corner: a courtyard building can be seen connected with a bridge; the bridge spans a stream and serves as the starting point or node of the path, guiding the gaze into the depth of the painting. | Left mountainside: a pavilion is set beside the mountain path as a stopping point or viewing spot on the path, reinforcing the enterable, traversable spatial relationship.
distinction: Although the built elements are placed according to the mountain terrain (C1), the role of the winding path in linking the various buildings and guiding the gaze into the depth is more prominent, constituting the main thread of spatial organization.

evidence: Lower left to center: a winding path (or a small path accompanying a stream) extends upward from the mountain-foot foreground, passing through gaps between woods and rocks, forming a clear visual guiding line. | Mountainside (center-left): the path leads to a group of buildings built against the mountain; the buildings are located at the extension of the path, presenting a spatial connection of entering and approaching the built elements from here. | Summit: a pavilion is set on the highest peak, echoing in height with the mountainside buildings and implying a process of movement in depth from the mountain foot through the mountainside to the summit.
distinction: Although the buildings placed on the mountain slope accord with terrain-responsive siting (C1), the long winding path running through the composition and guiding the gaze from the mountain foot deep into the mountainside buildings places greater emphasis on the process of access from here to there (C4).

evidence: Lower middle cliff: a pavilion is built at the edge of the cliff, with a clear small path winding past beside it. | From the center to the upper left of the painting: the small path extends upward along the mountain terrain, passing the houses on the mountainside and finally leading to the building group and tall pagoda at the upper left, forming a continuous movement cue. | Upper left: a pagoda and houses are arranged tier upon tier against the mountain, located at the end of or beside the path, serving as the arrival point of the movement route.
distinction: The winding small path running through the upper and lower parts of the painting connects the pavilion, the mountainside houses, and the summit pagoda, emphasizing the process of moving from here to there, which is more dominant than placement according to the mountain alone (C1).

evidence: Lower middle: a gate tower, dwellings, and a stone bridge are arranged close to the shoreline, with house base sites unfurling in accordance with the riverbank terrain. | Bottom: a group of houses is arranged in staggered fashion against the waterside and slopes, the layout echoing the contours of the terrain. | Center-left: a storied pavilion sits among trees by the water, its base site combined with the local terrain.
distinction: Although there is a relationship of concealment and revelation in which willows screen the pavilion, the multiple building groups throughout the painting generally exhibit the feature of terrain-responsive layout according with the waterside and slopes, and C1 better summarizes their dominant mode of spatial organization.

evidence: Upper middle mountainside: a building group is stacked tier upon tier according to the mountain terrain, with roofs and walls unfurling in accordance with the undulations and orientation of the slope. | Waterside below: a pavilion terrace is built facing the water, its base site resting directly on the sloped rocks of the waterside. | Lower left sloped bank: houses are placed against the slope, merging with the surrounding trees and terrain.
distinction: Although there are paths connecting the buildings in the painting, the core feature of the built elements is the close correspondence of their base sites and layout with site conditions such as mountain forms and the waterside; the paths are more a result dependent on the terrain than a dominant movement cue.

evidence: Upper middle: pavilion-type buildings can be seen on the mountainside, placed according to the mountain slopes and terraces | Right side: houses are placed separately on the cliff slopes, following the high and low of the terrain | Lower foreground: houses by the waterside are built against the water and beside rocks, echoing the shoreline terrain
distinction: Although there is screening by trees, the painting places greater emphasis on the correspondence between building base sites and mountain forms and the waterside, rather than on layers of mere concealment and revelation.

evidence: Central mountainside: a group of buildings is built against the mountain, partly screened by trees and rocks, with steps connecting upward. | From the lower middle to the center of the painting: a clear stone-step path winds up from below the mountain directly to the mountainside buildings, forming a clear entry route. | Lower right corner: a gentle sloped bank and the extending trend of the path can be seen, implying the starting point and direction of movement.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed according to the mountain terrain, the winding stone-step path rising upward in the painting constitutes a strong spatial guide and process of entry, making access to secluded settings the dominant spatial expression.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: the roofs and eaves of a group of built structures emerge from behind dense pine woods and rocks, forming a clear relationship of concealment and revelation. | Lower right of the painting: another built structure is screened among the pines and sloped rocks on the right, only partially visible, increasing the layering of space.
distinction: Although the built elements are arranged according to the mountain terrain, the painting places greater emphasis on the screening and revealing of the buildings by woods and rocks, and concealment and revelation forming a realm is the dominant expression.

evidence: Lower right corner: a stone bridge, pavilion, and figures crossing the bridge can be seen; the figures walk on the bridge toward the pavilion and the mountain forest, forming a clear entrance and starting point of movement. | Middle-ground water surface: an arched bridge spans across connecting the two banks, implying a path to the buildings in the mountain hollow behind, linking the foreground with the deeper space. | Overall composition: through the foreground bridge, the middle-ground arched bridge, and the shoreline, the gaze is guided from near to far deep into the building group in the mountain hollow, presenting a spatial process of passing from here to there.
distinction: Through the foreground bridge and figures and the middle-ground arched bridge, the painting constructs a clear movement route and process of entry, which better summarizes its dynamic role in spatial organization than simply describing the buildings placed against the mountain (C1).

evidence: Left middle mountainside: a pavilion is placed on a protruding rocky terrace, its base site level, arranged according to the platform terrain. | From the lower left to the center of the painting: rocks stack up to form sloped terraces, and the built elements are set upon this terrace, facing the open water surface on the right, presenting a relationship of terrain-responsive placement.
distinction: Although the pavilion serves to mark the mountainside scenery, the correspondence between its base site built upon the terrace and the terrain is more direct and dominates the spatial expression.

evidence: From center-left to lower right of the painting: a winding mountain road extends downward from the left mountainside, connects with the wooden bridge in the middle ground, and leads toward the lower right of the painting. | On the mountain road and the bridge: multiple groups of figures riding horses, carrying loads, and walking are distributed along the road, forming a clear movement line that guides the gaze into the depth of the painting.
distinction: The painting takes the continuous mountain road and bridge as its dominant thread, presenting an enterable and traversable spatial process; no obvious architectural scenic accents or screening relationships are seen.

evidence: Lower left: an arched bridge spans a stream, connecting the two banks, forming a clear circulation cue. | Center-left: behind the bridge a path extends along the mountain foot, leading to houses half screened by trees, presenting a spatial process of passing from here to there. | Lower right: houses can be seen behind trees, which together with the foreground bridge and path constitute an enterable, traversable landscape space.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed according to the mountain terrain, the movement cues formed by the bridge and path in the painting are the dominant mode of spatial organization guiding the gaze into the built structures in the depth.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: a tall pagoda and attached halls are built on the top of a small hill, located at a protruding point of the waterside, forming a spatial correspondence with the open water surface and distant mountains and becoming a visual focal point. | Lower right corner of the painting: a multi-arch bridge can be seen spanning the water surface, connecting the shoreline and implying cues of traffic and movement. | Lower left and mountain foot of the painting: village houses are distributed, arranged against the waterside and the mountain foot, and there are also buildings on the left mountainside screened among trees.
distinction: The pagoda and building group are located on the summit of a waterside hill and mainly serve to mark and focus the scenery there (scenic accentuation), making it a recognizable landscape marker, rather than simply displaying terrain-responsive placement (C1).

evidence: Right mountain foot: a group of houses is surrounded and screened by pines and miscellaneous trees, revealing only roofs and parts of walls, presenting a layering of seeing houses within the woods. | Left sloped waterside: houses are screened by bamboo groves and trees, forming a spatial relationship of viewing houses across a screen. | Left middle pine woods: an arched structure (perhaps a gate or pavilion) is faintly visible, screened by pine branches, increasing the variations of concealment and revelation in space.
distinction: Although the buildings are distributed against the waterside and mountain foot (consistent with C1 features), visually the painting places greater emphasis on the screening and revealing of buildings by woods and rocks, constructing spatial layers through concealment and revelation, rather than simply displaying the accordance of layout with terrain.

evidence: Right middle: an arched stone bridge can be seen spanning a stream/path, directly connecting the foreground slope with the entrance area of the building group behind. | Right building group: houses are distributed in staggered fashion along the mountain slope, with stone steps, enclosure walls, and courtyard structures visible, presenting clear relations of entry. | Below and foreground: the winding stream and gaps between rocks form a path guide, and the gaze passes via the stone bridge and steps toward the built structures in the depth, constituting a spatial process of passing from here to there.
distinction: Although the layout of the buildings according to the mountain terrain embodies terrain-responsive siting (C1), the movement cues formed by the stone bridge, steps, and stream in the painting are more prominent, emphasizing the spatial process of entering the building group through paths (C4).

evidence: Lower middle: a plank bridge spans a stream, and on the bridge a figure riding a donkey with attendants is crossing, forming a clear entry cue. | Right middle ground: a stepped path can be seen winding upward along the mountain terrain, connecting the foreground with the space in the depth. | Right mountainside: storied pavilion buildings can be seen screened among trees, serving as the destination of the path's extension or the built structures in the depth.
distinction: Although there are buildings screened among woods and rocks in the painting, the continuous movement cues formed by the plank bridge, figures, and mountain path are more prominent and dominate the sense of spatial entry.

evidence: Middle, slightly lower part of the painting: in front of the building group a broad rectangular high terrace base is built, with steps or balustrade structures visible at its edge, set facing the water, presenting a layout of buildings set upon a terrace and unfurling along the bank. | Middle of the painting: the building group is distributed along the mountain foot in staggered fashion, backed by rocks and woods, its layout following the terrain and forming a placement relationship of backing onto the mountain and facing the water.
distinction: Although the buildings are located in an open valley area and serve to mark the scenery, the layout of their high terrace base facing the water and backed by the mountain more notably embodies the terrain-responsive relationship of placement according to terrain conditions.

evidence: Center-right: an open pavilion is built on flat ground on the mountain slope, its base site following the terrain, surrounded by trees. | Lower right: a stone bridge spans a stream, connecting the foreground bank with the middle-ground area, implying a path leading to the pavilion. | Right cliff: a waterfall flows down and joins the stream, and the stream and bridge together constitute spatial cues guiding movement.
distinction: Although the pavilion marks the scenery, the bridge and stream in the painting clearly constitute enterable, reachable spatial movement cues, so C4 is more apt.

evidence: Lower left: a pavilion is built on a waterside rock or wooden-pile base, placed according to the waterside terrain, presenting a form of building set upon a base. | Upper middle: a waterfall flows down between two mountains and joins the water area beside the pavilion, providing the landscape configuration on which the built elements are based. | Left side: pines grow beside rocks, adjacent to the pavilion, together constituting the foreground waterside space.
distinction: Although the pavilion facing the waterfall has a certain sense of scenic accentuation, the painting carefully depicts its form placed on a waterside base, and the spatial relationship of terrain-responsive siting (building set upon a base) is more direct and prominent.

evidence: Lower middle: a pavilion with a four-corner pyramidal roof sits on a sloped bank by the water, surrounded by trees and bamboo groves. | Lower middle: the pavilion's columns and part of its eaves are screened by foreground tree trunks and foliage, forming spatial layers of interleaved concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the pavilion is placed facing the water, its relationship of concealment and revelation, half hidden and half revealed by woods, is more prominent in the composition and dominates the mode of interaction between the built structure and nature.

evidence: Lower left to lower center: a stone bridge, waterside paths, and building groups distributed along the slope are visible, forming a line of approach extending from the water's edge inland. | Center: an arched bridge connects the two banks and, together with the gaps among the mountains and rocks and the arrangement of courtyards, implies a spatial relationship of crossing and penetrating deeper. | Upper left: a pagoda and pavilions rise tier by tier against the cliff and, together with the paths and bridges below, constitute a process of moving deeper into the landscape.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited against the mountains and beside the water (C1), the clues of bridges, paths, and watersides run through the composition, placing greater emphasis on an accessible and traversable spatial process.

evidence: Lower center of the painting: a prominent group of pavilions and towers is built in the middle of the water surface, becoming the visual focus and marker of the open expanse of water. | Right side and rear waterside: houses, bridges, and moored boats are distributed along the shore and, together with the encircling mountains, set off the central water scenery. | Overall composition: the arrangement of built elements clearly marks out the scenery of the lake center and the waterside, giving the open water space a point of focus.
distinction: Although the shore buildings have a disposition of leaning on mountains and facing water, the most central compositional role is the way the central water pavilion identifies and concentrates the scenery of the lake center.

evidence: Lower center of the painting: a figure playing the qin on a flat rock beneath a pine, together with an attendant boy, can be seen; no houses, pavilions, or other identifiable built elements are visible. | Left side and center of the painting: towering cliffs and a waterfall form the main natural scenery; the area of human activity is set beside mountains and rocks, among pines.
distinction: No built elements are clearly identifiable in the painting; only figures sit on a flat rock beneath a pine, placed in response to the natural configuration, and it is therefore only marginally assigned to C1, with no other evident built clues.

evidence: Center-left: a multi-story pavilion is built tight against the cliff and waterfall, its base closely integrated with the rock face and the water, presenting a manner of placing a house against the cliff. | Lower center, slightly right: a waterside pavilion/booth is built at the water's edge, supported by the rocks on the bank, forming a layout that leans on the water and rests against the rocks together with the water surface and woodland. | Overall composition: the built elements in the painting are all placed in conformity with the rises and falls of the mountain terrain and the line of the waterside; no isolated buildings detached from the natural terrain are seen.
distinction: Although trees partially screen the buildings in the painting, the most prominent feature of the built elements is the close correspondence between their sites and the conditions of the terrain such as cliffs and watersides, rather than relying solely on concealment and revelation to form the scenery.

evidence: Lower right: a wooden bridge spans a stream, and a person is walking on the bridge, forming a clear clue of movement through the landscape. | Lower left: houses are built on the hillside and connected to the bridge by a path, guiding the eye to extend into the depth. | Overall painting: the bridge, path, and figures together construct a spatial process of moving from here to there and approaching the built elements.
distinction: Although the houses are built against the mountain, the clue of movement formed by the bridge and figures more prominently expresses an accessible and traversable spatial relationship.

evidence: Left center: several houses are arranged horizontally along a gentle slope and the edge of the waterside, presenting a layout that unfolds along the shore and is distributed according to the slope, in conformity with the level-and-distant terrain. | Lower right corner: a group of houses is placed on the sloping ground at the foot of the mountain, in conformity with the rises and falls of the mountain and the distribution of woods, with their sites corresponding to the natural terrain. | Overall composition: the built elements are mainly distributed in the level-and-distant area on the left and at the foot of the mountain on the right, forming with the towering peaks on the right a terrain-responsive relationship of "flanked by level-and-distant ground."
distinction: Although trees surround the houses (possessing a partly screened character), the painting places greater emphasis on the layout relationship of the houses leaning on the level waterside and the sloping ground at the foot of the mountain (e.g., unfolding along the shore); the participation of terrain in their placement is stronger than that of mere concealment and revelation.

evidence: Directly below the painting: a stone arch bridge spans the stream, and two people on the bridge (one riding a donkey, one accompanying on foot) are advancing into the depth of the painting. | Lower-left mountain hollow: the bridge and path extend toward a group of courtyard buildings surrounded by trees and rocks, presenting an accessible and enterable spatial connection. | Water surface in the center of the painting: a lone boat on the river joins the bridge and paths on shore to form a clue of movement through landscape by both water and land.
distinction: Although the courtyard buildings are screened by woodland, the core spatial organization of the painting lies in the process of entering and travelling established by the bridge, path, and the route followed by the figures.

evidence: Mountainside in the center of the painting: a group of pavilions and towers is placed tier by tier on rock-face terraces, following the rises and falls of the mountain in a staggered manner, embedded within the mountain. | Waterside at the bottom of the painting: a water pavilion is built at the water's edge, its base resting on the rocky bank, with wooden piles visible below supporting it into the water, presenting an arrangement along the shore. | Lower right corner of the painting: houses are placed against the hillside and woodland, closely integrated with the terrain.
distinction: Although trees and rocks screen the buildings and create layers (C2), the dependence of the buildings on the mountain forms, terraces, and waterside (placement according to terrain) is more pronounced and dominates the spatial expression.

evidence: Among the trees in the lower center of the painting: the roofs and structures of built elements are faintly visible behind several trees; the built elements use the woodland to form layers of screening and exposure, presenting a relationship of houses seen within woodland.
distinction: The built elements lie in a layer screened by trees and mainly participate in the scenery as a concealment-and-revelation relationship, rather than serving as a striking focus that identifies a particular landscape scene.

evidence: Lower center: several houses are screened behind pines and mountains and rocks, with only roofs, eaves, and parts of the beam-and-column structure exposed. | Lower center, slightly right: tree trunks and foliage in the foreground clearly screen the buildings behind, presenting a spatial layer of houses seen deep within the woodland.
distinction: Although the built elements lean against mountains, rocks, and waterside, the painting places greater emphasis on the screening and exposure relationship of woodland to buildings, thereby constructing pictorial depth.

evidence: Lower center and right side: the trunk and branches of a huge pine extend from the right, with pine needles covering the roof of the building, forming a clear screening relationship and presenting a layer of a house seen beneath a tree. | Left side and rear: on the left of the building are a bamboo fence and bamboo grove, and behind it leans against mountains and rocks; the natural scenery encloses the building, placing it in a state of concealment and revelation. | Main body of the building: the front half of the building (columns, figures, table) is clearly exposed, while the roof and rear are screened by pine and rocks, constituting a partial concealment-and-revelation relationship.
distinction: Although the building identifies the courtyard theme (C3), the concealment-and-revelation layers formed by pine branches covering the roof and by the enclosure of bamboo and rocks (C2) are more prominent and specific in the spatial organization of the painting.

evidence: Center: a person sits on a rocky slope, surrounded by trees. | Lower right: a person and a cart are located on a path at the foot of the mountain, implying a clue of movement through the landscape.
distinction: No built elements are clearly identifiable in the painting, but the figures and cart in the lower right corner constitute a clue of movement, coming closest to a spatial organization of access to secluded settings.

evidence: Lower left: a stone arch bridge spans the water, and two people on the bridge are walking toward the depth of the painting, forming a clear clue of entry. | Lower right: a thatched pavilion and a low wall are built by the water, adjacent to the waterside and trees, serving as a stopping point along the route of movement. | Upper left and center right: pavilions and houses are screened among woodland and cliffs, suggesting that the eye can continue to travel deeper along the water flow and mountain forms.
distinction: Although the buildings have a screened appearance, the painting, through the linking of bridge, figures, and waterside buildings, places greater emphasis on an accessible and traversable spatial process.

evidence: Lower center: a stone arch bridge spans the water, with two people standing on it, connecting the field ridges and paths of the two banks and forming a clear crossing node. | Left center: a flat bridge connects the waterside with the opposite bank, with figures passing over it, and the path extends along the riverbank toward distant houses. | Lower right to lower left: winding field ridges and small paths run through the painting, connecting farmland, woods, and scattered houses; a rider and a farmer advance along the paths, presenting a traversable spatial process.
distinction: Although the houses are distributed along the waterside, the clue of movement constituted by the bridges and paths in the painting is more prominent and dominates the accessibility and narrative movement of the space.

evidence: Center of the painting: a scholar reclines on the twisted roots of a tree, his bodily posture corresponding to the form of the roots | Lower left and lower right: two boys and utensils such as tea wares and a water jar are placed directly on the rocks of the waterside
distinction: There is no clear architecture in the painting; the figures and utensils are placed naturally in response to the waterside and tree roots, coming closest to a spatial relationship of placement according to the terrain.

evidence: Lower part of the painting: a person and a horse are visible standing among pines and mountains and rocks; no clear built elements (architecture) are visible | Upper part of the painting: towering cliffs and pines occupy the main area of the painting, with no trace of architecture
distinction: No built elements are clearly identifiable in the painting; the figures and horse identify the landscape scenery, and it is therefore assigned to C3

evidence: Lower part: a wooden bridge spans a stream; figures cross the bridge on horseback and on foot and advance along a winding mountain path pointing toward a group of buildings deep in the painting. | Center: the building group is interconnected by covered galleries and platforms, with a waterside pavilion at the water's edge, and figures active in the galleries or pavilions, forming a traversable spatial sequence. | Right side and upper part: pavilions and towers are distributed against the mountains and beside the water, with steps and paths connecting buildings at different heights, guiding the eye to extend toward the distant water surface and mountains.
distinction: Although the buildings lean on the mountains and face the water (C1), the bridge, path, and route of the figures below, together with the connecting galleries in the center, more strongly express a spatial process of moving from here to there that is traversable (C4).

evidence: Lower center and right side of the painting: the building group is placed tight against the cliff on the right, using multiple tiers of foundations, steps, and covered walkways to unfold in conformity with the terrain's differences in height, presenting a layout against the mountain and on terraces. | Left side and lower center of the painting: courtyards and halls advance tier by tier along the sloping terraces, and the building sites form a clear correspondence with the surrounding sloping ground and waterside.
distinction: Although steps and paths are present, the core expression is how the building group is placed as a whole against the mountains and beside the water and in conformity with the terrain's differences in height, rather than emphasizing a single process of movement and entry.

evidence: Middle ground: three literati and an attendant boy sit in a circle on a rocky platform; no houses or other built structures are visible. | Lower right: a traveler carrying a load walks along a path among mountains and rocks; the path leads to the platform in the middle ground, presenting an accessible spatial connection.
distinction: There is no clear architecture in the painting, but the path among the mountains and rocks and the traces of the figures constitute an accessible and reachable spatial process, and it is therefore assigned to C4.

evidence: Left center: a pavilion-style building occupies a prominent rocky high platform, presenting a clear relationship of a house placed on a terrace. | Lower left: a building group is built by the water and against the slope, with a stream/waterfall passing beside it, presenting a layout distributed along the shore or according to the slope. | Mountainside on the right: houses are placed according to the terrain among the woods on the mountainside, in conformity with the form of the mountain.
distinction: Although a bridge and pedestrians below provide a clue of entry (C4), the direct correspondence between the buildings and terrain such as high platforms and watersides (on terraces, at the water's edge) is more prominent and dominant in the main composition on the left of the painting.

evidence: Mountainside at center left: a group of pavilions is piled tier upon tier, closely attached beside the steep cliff and waterfall, its layout unfolding vertically with the mountain, presenting a form of houses placed against the cliff. | Waterside at center right: a pavilion is built on a flat, prominent base at the water's edge, set by the water and forming a direct relation of reliance on the water surface. | Sloping bank below: a house is built on a gentle slope, placed according to the slope, its base matching the form of the sloping ground.
distinction: Although a winding path at the foot of the mountain on the left leads to the mountainside pavilions and provides a certain sense of entry, multiple built elements in the painting (mountainside pavilions, waterside pavilion, and slope-bank house) more generally and prominently embody the placement relations of against the cliff, at the water's edge, and according to the slope; the determining role of terrain in the layout of the built elements is superior to that of a single clue of movement.

evidence: Lower left: a flat bridge spans the water, connecting the left bank with the area below the rock face in the middle ground, forming a clear path of crossing and entry. | Left middle-to-far ground: a group of houses is built at the water's edge, leaning against distant mountains and willows, lying in the direction of extension pointed to by the bridge. | Right side and center: towering rock faces and foreground trees constitute the main barrier of the painting, while the bridge and houses on the left form an accessible spatial opening.
distinction: Although the waterside placement of the houses embodies terrain-responsive siting, the connecting role of the bridge in the painting is more prominent and dominates the accessible and traversable spatial organization.
