evidence: Upper-middle and upper-right, among the distant mountain woods: several houses reveal only their roofs, surrounded and screened by dense trees, presenting a spatial layering of houses hidden in the woods.
distinction: Although the houses are located at the edge of the woods at the mountain foot, what is visually conveyed is mainly the layering formed by the screening and revealing of the roofs by trees, rather than the correspondence of site layout to terrain banks and placement relationships.

evidence: Lower left to center: In the lower-left corner, two people walk along a small path at the water's edge toward the depth of the painting, forming a clear movement-through-the-landscape cue. | Middle-ground water surface: An arched bridge spans the water, connecting the foreground path with the opposite bank and guiding the eye toward the built area. | Right side: Houses and courtyards are built against the slope, surrounded by bamboo groves and flower beds; this is the reachable destination toward which the path and bridge lead.
distinction: Although the built elements are arranged against the mountains and beside the water, the movement-through-the-landscape cue formed by the bridge and path is more prominent in the painting, dominating the sense of spatial entry from one place to another.

evidence: Left-center: An open pavilion is half-hidden among dense woodland, with only its roof and part of its columns exposed, creating a layering in which a building is concealed within the woods. | Lower right: A waterside pavilion is built over a stream, surrounded and screened by tall trees; the buildings and woodland form a clear relationship of screening and revelation.
distinction: Although the painting shows buildings placed beside the water and nestled among the trees, the dominant visual relationship is the layer-by-layer screening and concealment-and-revelation of the buildings by the woodland, rather than a simple emphasis on the decisive role of terrain in determining building sites.

evidence: Middle ground of the painting, at the water's edge: a pavilion-style building is set directly over the water surface, its base closely corresponding to the shoreline, presenting a placement relationship of being built alongside the water. | Upper right and distant view of the painting: thatched huts and groups of haystacks are distributed along the slope and the woodland edge, the building layout conforming to the undulations of the terrain and the vegetation boundary. | Upper left of the painting, far bank: several houses are partly screened among trees and earthen slopes, sited along the edge of the land, forming a layout arranged according to local conditions together with the surrounding fields and water.
distinction: Although there are field ridges, paths, and figures in the painting, what is mainly expressed is how the built elements are sited according to site conditions such as the waterside and slopes, rather than emphasizing a spatial process in which paths guide the viewer into deeper movement through the landscape.

evidence: Lower left: A pavilion is built beside the water, and next to it a small bridge spans the stream, forming a clear cue for passage and entry. | Lower right: A structure is hidden behind trees and rocks, forming a spatial extension and connection with the stream and mountain path in the foreground. | Center: A stream winds through the painting, connecting the pavilion and bridge in the foreground with the mountains behind, guiding the eye on a journey into the depth.
distinction: Although the buildings are arranged against the mountains and beside the water, the painting places greater emphasis on cues such as the bridge and stream that guide the viewer on a journey into the depth of the painting, rather than on simple terrain-responsive siting.

evidence: Whole painting: The painting consists of mountains and rocks, bamboo groves, sloping banks, and water surfaces, with no identifiable built elements such as buildings, bridges, paths, or fords.
distinction: No built elements are visible in the painting, so its specific compositional mode cannot be determined; it is assigned to the closest category based only on the overall landscape composition.

evidence: Left side and lower-middle of the painting: A temple complex and a pagoda are built against the foot of the mountain and according to the mountain's configuration, their layout following the undulations of the terrain. | Upper-middle of the painting: Numerous houses are distributed along the mountain slope at varying heights, clearly sited according to the mountain's form. | Overall painting: The built elements are closely integrated with the form of the mountain mass, presenting a spatial relationship of staggered placement along slopes and terrain-responsive arrangement.
distinction: Although the buildings and trees have a screening relationship, the overall layout more prominently features terrain-responsive siting, in which the buildings follow the mountain's configuration and are staggered in height.

evidence: Upper slope of the painting: The roofs and eaves of multiple buildings emerge from dense tree canopies, appearing half-hidden and half-revealed. | Middle of the painting: Red railings (of a bridge or plank walkway) thread among the pine grove and mixed trees, partly obscured by branches and leaves. | Lower-right corner of the painting: A city-wall gate tower and the dense building cluster below it are surrounded and screened by trees in the foreground and middle ground, creating spatial layering.
distinction: Although the painting shows buildings distributed according to the mountain's configuration, the most prominent visual feature is the profound layering created by the woodland's screening and revelation of the buildings, so C2 is more dominant than C1.

evidence: Center: A hexagonal pavilion is built on a stone base in the water, extending to the right through a long winding corridor (or bridge) to connect with the willow trees on the shore, forming a clear movement-through-the-landscape cue. | Right side: A hall building is erected on a stone-built raised platform, with broad stone steps and a railed terrace in front, forming a reachable path from the building toward the waterside. | Lower right: A small pavilion is screened by trees, with a wall winding below it, forming a high-low spatial connection with the buildings above and suggesting an extension of the viewing route.
distinction: The prominent winding bridge/corridor and steps in the painting form a clear movement route, emphasizing the spatial process of entering the water from the shore and moving from one place to another (C4), rather than merely displaying a static siting layout in which buildings respond to the water and the platform (C1).

evidence: Mid-slope at the center of the painting: The roofs and walls of several buildings emerge from a dense pine grove, partly obscured by the surrounding trees. | Middle of the painting: The pine grove surrounds the buildings, forming a spatial layering of trees in front and buildings behind, with buildings concealed within the woods; the concealment-and-revelation relationship is evident.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited according to the mountain's configuration, the painting places greater emphasis on the layered relationship created by the pine grove's screening and revelation of the buildings.

evidence: Left side and center of the painting: Multiple houses and pavilions are half-hidden behind dense groves and mountain rocks, with only parts of their roofs, walls, and bases exposed, forming a clear layering of concealment and revelation. | Upper right of the painting: A bridge with red railings and a pavilion thread among the trees, partly obscured by tree canopies and slopes, presenting a spatial relationship of concealment within the woods. | Lower part of the painting: Walls and a gate tower wind along the slope, partly screened by the branches and leaves of foreground trees, reinforcing the pictorial depth and sense of entry.
distinction: Although the built elements are arranged according to the mountain's configuration, the painting places greater emphasis on building spatial layering through the screening and revelation of trees and rocks; the concealment-and-revelation relationship is more prominent than simple terrain compliance.

evidence: Right side: Tall city walls and a gate tower are built against the high-bank terrain, the walls extending in accordance with the undulations of the terrain. | Left bank and middle bank: Several groups of houses are distributed in staggered fashion along the riverbank, their bases close to the water's edge, presenting a layout unfolding along the bank. | Overall painting: The built elements (dwellings and city walls) are all sited in response to the waterside and sloping platform terrain, forming a corresponding relationship with the natural configuration.
distinction: In the painting, the built elements mainly present a layout relationship unfolding along the waterside and terrain, encompassing the overall organization of both dwellings and city walls, rather than serving merely as isolated markers that identify a scene.

evidence: Upper-middle of the painting: City walls wind along the mountain ridge, laid out in accordance with the undulations of the mountain mass; both the gate tower and the high pavilion at the summit are sited according to the terrain's height. | Lower-middle of the painting: A clear path and bridge structure are visible extending from the water surface, connecting to the city walls and the village within, presenting a spatial organization against the mountains and beside the water.
distinction: Although path cues guiding entry (C4) exist in the lower part of the painting, the overall siting relationship in which the city walls and building clusters follow the mountain terrain (C1) is more central and prominent in the composition.

evidence: Middle ground on the right side of the painting: Multiple buildings are screened within dense groves, with only parts of their roofs, eaves, and walls exposed. | Middle-right of the painting: The branches and leaves of trees clearly screen the buildings, presenting spatial layering in which concealment and revelation alternate.
distinction: Although the buildings are built according to the mountain's configuration, the painting places greater emphasis on the relationship of screening and revelation between the trees and the buildings; the effect of concealment and revelation forming a scene is more prominent.

evidence: Lower left: A two-story pavilion is built on a stone-built base on a sloping bank enclosed by red railings, facing an open expanse of water and surrounded by woodland. | Upper-middle of the painting: Two sailing boats navigate the broad water surface, with blue-green rocky islands ringed by waves in the distance, forming an open water scene.
distinction: Although the pavilion is built on a waterside platform, its main compositional role is to serve as a visual anchor in the foreground, identifying and concentrating the scene of 'all waters paying homage' that faces the broad water surface, rather than simply emphasizing a terrain-siting relationship.

evidence: Lower-left corner: A group of buildings is arranged tier upon tier along the sloping ground at the foot of the mountain, with staggered roofs, presenting a layout of staggered placement along the slope. | Middle of the right side: A red-walled arched structure (resembling a gate or bridge) is erected against the terrain of mountain rocks and woodland, following the undulations of the terrain. | Upper left and upper right: Scattered buildings are sited according to the mountainside or high ground among the woods, corresponding to the mountain's varying heights and showing a distribution from the valley floor up to the higher reaches of the mountain.
distinction: Although some buildings on the right side and upper part of the painting show a concealment-and-revelation relationship in which they are screened by woodland (a C2 feature), the overall composition places greater emphasis on the systematic layout of buildings according to the mountain's height and sloping platforms (such as the slope-following building cluster in the lower-left corner and the overall staggered heights); therefore C1 (terrain-responsive siting) better summarizes its dominant mode of spatial organization.

evidence: Middle ground and distant view: The roofs of numerous houses loom faintly among clouds and mist and trees, forming rich layers of concealment and revelation. | Middle-right: A gate tower and city wall extend according to the mountain's configuration, partly obscured by trees, presenting a spatial relationship of seeing buildings through a screen. | Lower-left corner: Courtyards and houses are surrounded by trees, screened within the woods.
distinction: Although the gate tower in the middle-right serves as a scenic accent, the numerous built elements (the village) in the painting mainly express spatial layering through the screening of clouds, mist, and trees; the screening relationship runs through the whole painting and is more dominant.

evidence: Center of the painting: A winding embankment or plank walkway extends from the foreground into the depth of the painting, with a figure walking on it, forming a clear journey cue. | Left side and lower left of the painting: Multiple building clusters are distributed in staggered fashion according to the mountain's configuration and the waterside, connected to the central embankment through paths and watercourses. | Lower right of the painting: A pavilion is built at the water's edge, serving as an endpoint or waypoint along the path, reinforcing the reachable spatial relationship.
distinction: Although the buildings on the left are clearly arranged against the mountains and beside the water (C1), the winding long embankment at the center of the painting and the walking figure form a strong visual guide and organize the journey from one place to another, so C4 is more dominant.

evidence: Center: A multi-story pavilion is built on a high rocky platform, its base closely fitting the form of the rocks, presenting a relationship of placing a building on a platform | Upper right: A pavilion is sited against a steep rock face, standing by borrowing the momentum of the mountain rock | Waterside at the lower right: A long gallery building unfolds along the shoreline, its layout corresponding to the water surface and bank rocks
distinction: Although there is screening by woodland, the painting more prominently features a terrain-responsive arrangement in which the built elements are sited according to terrain conditions such as rocky platforms, rock faces, and the waterside.

evidence: Overall painting: The painting mainly depicts a large expanse of water, reed marshes, and rocks on the right side; a single small boat is in the upper right, with no clear buildings, bridges, or other built elements. | Lower-left corner: There is an inscription, 'Wan Ting Lu Yue' (Moon over the Reeds at Wand Ting), indicating that the painting's theme is the moonlit scene of a reed marsh.
distinction: No clear built elements are visible in the painting; the scene is composed only of natural landscape and a small boat, and it is only tentatively assigned to scenic accentuation based on the overall spatial atmosphere.

evidence: Middle-right: A building complex stands within dense woodland, its walls and roofs partly obscured by the trunks, branches, and leaves in the foreground, appearing faintly visible and then hidden. | Overall painting: Trees, as the main elements of the foreground and middle ground, wrap around the buildings, forming a clear concealment-and-revelation relationship and spatial layering.
distinction: Although the stream and sloping ground on the left of the painting suggest spatial extension, the core visual relationship is the layering created by the buildings being screened by woodland, rather than a clear path guiding entry.

evidence: Left-center: The roofs and gallery columns of a building group are visible on the mountain slope, partly obscured by trees | Lower right: A person is walking along a winding path or bridge with railings, pointing toward the depth of the painting | Lower left: A small bridge over the water connects the two banks, suggesting a passable route
distinction: Although the buildings are screened, the painting places greater emphasis on the process of guiding the eye into the space through bridges and paths, rather than a simple concealment-and-revelation relationship.

evidence: Whole painting: The painting depicts an open waterside, sandbars, trees, and a flock of wild geese flying in the sky, with no clear traces of built elements such as buildings, bridges, or roads. | Lower-left corner: There is an inscription, 'Wan Dian Gui Yan' (Ten Thousand Dots of Returning Geese), which identifies the painting's thematic scenery, but no built elements correspond to it.
distinction: The painting lacks built elements and is assigned to the closest category based on the open natural scenery it presents as a whole.

evidence: Mid-slope, center-right: A built structure is half-hidden behind a rock face and woodland, with only parts of its roof and walls exposed, presenting a layering in which it is screened by mountain rocks. | Middle-ground sloping platform on the right: A group of buildings sits on a sloping platform, surrounded and screened by red-leafed trees, their eaves revealed through gaps in the trees.
distinction: Although the buildings dot the landscape, their main compositional role is to form spatial layering through the screening and revelation of mountain rocks and trees, rather than serving merely as markers identifying a particular scene.

evidence: Right-side mountain slope: Building clusters rise tier upon tier according to the mountain's configuration, arranged in stepped fashion along the slope, their layout closely corresponding to the terrain. | Distant mountain ridge: City walls wind along the ridgeline, following the trend of the mountain's form. | Left-side waterside: Houses are built beside the water, some with bases or platforms extending into the water, unfolding along the bank.
distinction: Although there are paths and figures in the painting, the most striking feature of the overall composition is the large-scale layout of building clusters in response to the mountain's form and the waterside, rather than an emphasis on a single movement-and-entry cue.

evidence: Right-hand slope toward the water: a winding white band, resembling a path or stream, extends from distant woodland toward the water, providing a cue of spatial extension. | Left and center: dense woodland, described by the inscription 'Myriad Trees in Dense Array', and rocks dominate the painting; no clearly identifiable houses or built structures are visible.
distinction: Given the dense woodland, any built elements could be screened by trees; however, no building is currently visible. Only the path or stream suggests entry or spatial extension, so the image is assigned to C4.

evidence: Left side and left-center of the painting: Several houses are partly obscured by tall trees in the foreground and middle ground, with only their roofs and parts of their walls exposed, forming a layering in which a building is concealed within the woods. | Middle of the painting: Trunks, branches, and leaves interpose in front of the houses, clearly constituting a relationship in which foreground trees screen the built elements behind.
distinction: Although the houses are built on level ground, the most prominent spatial relationship in the painting is the screening and revelation of the houses by trees, rather than an emphasis on their siting according to terrain.

evidence: Lower half: Depicts mountains and rocks, plum trees, a study, and distant mountains; on the left is an inscription reading 'Plum Blossom Study... after the brush idea of Song and Yuan masters,' forming the main body of the ink landscape painting. | Upper half: Transcribes a poem in running script, 'Imperially composed: Inscribing Zou Yigui's Twelve Views of Shucheng, using its rhymes...', and bears seals; this is calligraphic inscription addressed to the painting.
distinction: The main category is determined to be painting (C2), as distinct from pure calligraphy (C1). Although the upper half of the painting contains a large amount of imperially composed inscribed poetry and calligraphy, the lower half is the core painting 'Plum Blossom Study,' and the inscribed poem is closely tied to the painting ('using its rhymes'); the whole belongs to the album-leaf format, so painting is taken as primary.

evidence: Center: The main building cluster is tightly surrounded by a large number of flowering trees, with only roofs, eaves, and walls exposed, presenting a layering in which buildings are concealed within the woods. | Lower part and left side: Scattered houses and walls are obscured by trees and mountain rocks, forming a spatial relationship of foreground-background screening. | Overall: The density of trees (dotted with pink/purple) is high, covering most of the buildings' bases and surroundings, reinforcing the compositional role of screening and revelation.
distinction: Although a gate tower and bridge in the lower part of the painting suggest path guidance (C4), the buildings are mainly tightly surrounded by trees, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship (C2) is more significant in terms of visual area and compositional focus.

evidence: Lower center and left side of the painting: Multiple houses are obscured by tall trees, with only roofs, eaves, and parts of walls exposed, forming a clear concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Lower right of the painting: A wall and gate connect the houses, but the main body of the buildings remains hidden behind trees and sloping ground, presenting a layering of seeing buildings through a screen.
distinction: In the painting, the buildings mainly create spatial layering through the screening of trees; the feature of concealment and revelation forming a scene is more prominent than siting according to terrain.

evidence: Lower half of the painting, slightly left of center: An open pavilion (waterside pavilion) is erected directly on the bank, with supporting wooden piles visible at its base; its base closely hugs the waterline and unfolds in response to the waterside terrain. | Lower half of the painting, slightly right of center: Behind the open pavilion is connected a white-walled house; the building complex as a whole is sited according to the natural terrain of the earthen slope and large trees on the right. | Foreground of the lower half of the painting: The water surface in front of the building is covered with lotus leaves, and the building's waterside position forms a direct corresponding relationship with the water scene.
distinction: Although the buildings identify the waterside scenery, their compositional core lies in the close attachment of the base, column grid, and shoreline water dynamics to the water, so C1 is more dominant than C3.

evidence: Lower right: A house (a study) is surrounded and screened by dense bamboo groves, with only the roof and part of the beam-and-column structure exposed, presenting a layered relationship of a house concealed within the grove. | Foreground and lower area: A fence encloses a courtyard space, within which plants are set on trellises, forming with the bamboo grove and house behind a spatial layering of front-to-back screening and exposure. | Left side and background: Mountains, rocks and a waterfall (flowing water) are located to the left rear of the house, serving as a natural background that sets off the woodland dwelling setting.
distinction: Although the painting contains fence and path cues suggesting an entrance, the built elements are mainly deeply screened by the dense bamboo grove; the concealment-and-revelation relationship (partly screened) is visually more prominent and dominant than the process of entry (access to secluded settings).

evidence: Whole painting: The painting contains only calligraphic text; no mountains and rocks, water bodies, trees, or any traces of built elements are seen.
distinction: There is no actual landscape built-element relationship; selected due to the mandatory classification requirement, with no actual distinguishing significance.

evidence: Lower left: A house building is screened by dense trees, with only the roof, part of the wall, and a round doorway exposed, presenting a layering of a house concealed within the grove. | Right side: A pavilion in the distance across the water stands among trees, surrounded and partly screened by branches and leaves, faintly visible. | Lower left: Mountains, rocks and a bridge are in the foreground, but the main building body relies chiefly on the screening of trees to form spatial depth.
distinction: Although a bridge is visible in the lower-left corner suggesting a path, both the house and the pavilion in the painting mainly present a concealment-and-revelation relationship screened by trees, mountains and rocks; the feature of concealment and revelation is more pervasive and dominant than path guidance.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: A group of buildings (with clearly visible roofs) lies embraced by pine groves and mountains and rocks; pine trees in the foreground and surroundings screen part of the walls and bases, presenting a layering of houses seen within the grove. | Lower-left corner of the painting: A small house (with a visible arched doorway/wall) is half-hidden behind dense pines, with only the roof and upper structure exposed, forming an obvious screening relationship. | Whole painting: Large numbers of pines and mountains and rocks are intermingled, wrapping the buildings within them, and organizing the spatial depth in which the buildings sit through the front-to-back screening and exposure of the trees (concealment and revelation).
distinction: Although the buildings are situated in valley terrain (consistent with C1's siting according to terrain), the layer-by-layer screening and exposure of the buildings by the dense pines (concealment and revelation) in the painting is more prominent and constitutes the main visual spatial layering, so C2 is more apt.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting, slightly left: A thatched hut is screened by several tall trees, with only the roof, part of the wall, and veranda columns exposed, presenting a half-hidden, half-exposed state. | Lower middle of the painting, slightly right: Another thatched hut is partly screened by trees and an earthen slope in front, with the roof and doors and windows exposed, forming a layering with the surrounding woodland. | Whole painting: Multiple groups of trees surround the buildings; through the screening and exposure of branches and leaves, the built elements are integrated into the grove, forming a spatial relationship of concealment and revelation.
distinction: The painting mainly emphasizes the layered concealment formed by the buildings being surrounded and screened by trees, rather than highlighting their correspondence to terrain slopes and banks.

evidence: Lower left of the painting: A group of house buildings is visible screened by trees, with clear roof and wall structures. | Middle ground, slightly right: A small bridge is visible spanning among the mountains and rocks, connecting to a path and forming a spatial cue for entry. | Whole painting: Houses, bridge, mountain paths and the landscape setting connect with one another, presenting a spatial relationship of moving from here to there and of being able to travel through.
distinction: The connecting relationship between the bridge and path and the houses in the painting is clear and dominates the enterable spatial organization, so C4 is most apt.

evidence: Right side and center of the painting: A complex of buildings with halls and verandas is visible, its base adjoining the water, with water (waterfall/stream) passing below, the buildings closely connected with the water. | Front of the buildings/center: A bridge spans the water, connecting the building platform with the mountain-and-rock area on the left, forming a clear physical connection. | On the bridge: Two people stand, in a posture of traveling or conversing, implying a spatial process of approaching the built elements via the bridge or turning into the depths.
distinction: Although dense trees around the buildings form a relationship of concealment and revelation, the bridge and the figures' activity clearly construct a travel path from here to there, approaching the built elements, making the spatial process of access to secluded settings the dominant expression.

evidence: Upper-middle hillside: The building complex is arranged along the ridge and the slope-top line, following the undulations of the mountain, presenting a layout distributed according to the slope. | Right side and lower middle: Buildings are located at the junction of the mountain foot and the waterfront, their bases relying on the terrain, distributed in staggered heights. | Overall composition: The built elements are placed according to site conditions such as hillsides and terraces, and the layout forms a corresponding relationship with the natural configuration.
distinction: Although there are foreground stepping stones guiding the eye, the main feature of the building complex is its layer-by-layer arrangement following the hillside terrain; the terrain-responsive layout relationship is more prominent and dominant.

evidence: Middle ground left: A group of house buildings is distributed in staggered fashion along the slope at the mountain foot, arranged following the undulations of the terrain. | Middle ground, slightly right: A bridge spans the water, connecting the spaces on the two banks. | Lower-right corner: Two thatched huts are located at the edge of the woodland, integrated with the surrounding environment.
distinction: The most prominent feature in the painting is the staggered arrangement of the buildings according to the mountain configuration; although a bridge exists, it mainly serves as an auxiliary connection, and the whole emphasizes siting according to terrain.

evidence: Lower-right corner: A pavilion is built on a rocky platform at the water's edge, its base following the bank terrain, presenting a form of a house set on a platform, standing by the water. | Right side and behind the pavilion: Trees grow around the pavilion, but the main body of the pavilion is clearly visible, mainly attached to the rocky bank base.
distinction: Although the pavilion has a scenic-accentuation role, its form of being built against rock and beside water, set on a platform, more prominently demonstrates the correspondence between the built element and the terrain (waterside rock), so C1 is more apt than C3.

evidence: Lower-left corner: A stone bridge is visible spanning the water, connecting the two banks, forming a clear cue for entry. | Middle-right of the painting: Several built elements (pavilions, towers) are concealed and revealed among the trees, with roofs and eaves exposed; the paths and bridge imply an accessible relationship.
distinction: Although the built elements form layered concealment through the screening of trees (C2), the bridge in the lower-left corner and the extending path more strongly emphasize the spatial process of moving from here to there and of enterable travel, so C4 is more dominant.

evidence: Lower left to center: A stream winds among the mountains and rocks, forming a visual guide extending into the depths. | Whole painting: The painting consists mainly of mountains and rocks, pines and flowing water; no clear traces of built elements such as buildings, bridges or paths are seen.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built elements; the overall space is dominated by the sense of extension through the water flow and the gaps among mountains and rocks, so it is assigned to C4 rather than C1, which emphasizes siting according to terrain.

evidence: Lower right: A house is partly screened by trees, with the roof and part of the structure exposed, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Center: A house is faintly visible among the trees, hidden within the grove. | Lower left: A pavilion stands on rock, surrounded by trees, forming a layering with the mountains and rocks.
distinction: Although the buildings adjoin mountains and water, the painting more strongly emphasizes their layered concealment and revelation among the woodland and rocks.

evidence: Left side, middle-lower: Amid the screening trees, a red arched doorway or wall is exposed, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation.
distinction: The building is mainly screened and revealed by trees, presenting a layering of a house concealed within the grove, rather than emphasizing arrangement according to terrain.

evidence: Center and lower part of the painting: Layered mountains and rocks, waterfalls and flowing springs, and pines are visible, constituting the main landscape scenery. | Below the waterfall in the lower-middle of the painting: Among the rocks there is a blurred arc-shaped structure, suspected to be a bridge opening or stone hole, but the details are unclear and it cannot be confirmed as a definite built element.
distinction: The painting mainly presents a complete landscape scene; the suspected bridge-opening structure is extremely unclear and insufficient to constitute a clear cue for travel and entry, so it is classified as scenic accentuation.

evidence: Right side, middle-lower: A built element with roof and walls is visible, partly screened by mountains, rocks and trees, presenting a half-hidden, half-exposed state. | Middle of the painting, slightly left: Another built element's roof is faintly visible among trees and rocks, forming a layering with the surrounding natural scenery.
distinction: Although the buildings attach to mountains and rocks, the painting more strongly emphasizes the spatial layering formed by their screening and exposure by trees, mountains and rocks, so C2 is more apt than C1.

evidence: Middle ground left: A tower is placed against mountains and rocks, its body partly screened by flowering trees around and in the foreground, presenting a spatial layering of a house seen among rocks and grove. | Foreground slope bank: A thatched pavilion is set among flowering trees on the slope bank, surrounded and screened by trees on all sides, with only the roof exposed, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Overall painting: The built elements (tower, thatched pavilion) all stand in a relationship of screening and exposure with the mountains, rocks and woodland (flowering trees), forming spatial layering through natural scenery.
distinction: The painting mainly presents the layered concealment and revelation of the built elements screened by flowering trees and mountains and rocks; although there are brushstrokes in the lower-left corner resembling railings or vegetation, the travel cues are unclear or intermittent, insufficient to dominate the spatial process of access to secluded settings.

evidence: Middle-left of the painting: A building with an arched doorway is visible, placed close against the slope bank at the mountain foot, while another tower on the mountainside above is arranged in staggered fashion according to the mountain configuration. | Center of the painting: The bases of the built elements are closely integrated with the mountain rocks and slope terraces, presenting a layout distributed according to the slope and unfolding with the highs and lows of the terrain.
distinction: Although trees and mountains and rocks in the painting screen the buildings to some extent, the terrain correspondence of the built elements being placed according to the mountain configuration and slope terraces is clearer and dominant.

evidence: Left side, upper-middle: Two houses are located on the mountainside, surrounded by woodland rendered with ink dots; roofs and walls are visible, presenting a form of dwellings within the grove. | Left side overall: The houses are located behind and above-side of a huge foreground mountain rock, using the rock and woodland to form front-to-back spatial layering, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship of houses seen behind rock.
distinction: The houses mainly present the layered concealment and spatial depth of being surrounded by mountains, rocks and woodland (C2), rather than serving as a visual focus to mark or concentrate a particular landscape scene (C3).

evidence: Left side of the painting: The painting mainly depicts layered mountains and rocks, sloping banks, and trees; no clear built elements such as houses, pavilions, or paths are seen. | Left inscription: Inscribed with the characters 'Xiuyun Bi' (Embroidered Cloud Wall), indicating that the landscape here is a specific scenic feature.
distinction: The painting has no clear built elements, but the form of the mountains and water coalesces into the scenery of a 'wall,' so it is classified as C3; if regarded as purely natural mountain and rock forms, it would be close to C1.

evidence: Right side, middle-to-far distance: A group of houses is visible, their roofs and walls partly screened by trees and mountains and rocks in the foreground and middle ground, presenting a half-hidden, half-exposed state. | Overall painting: The layered arrangement of woodland and mountains and rocks screens the built elements within them, forming spatial layering through the screening and exposure of natural scenery.
distinction: The built elements present spatial layering mainly through the screening and exposure of woodland and mountains and rocks, rather than emphasizing siting according to terrain, marking a specific scene, or providing an entry path.

evidence: Center of the painting: Mountains and rocks are layered, with water flowing from top to bottom through the gaps in the rocks, forming a deep, secluded spatial layering | Lower left and center of the painting: Trees screen the view, a stream winds along, presenting a sense of a natural path that can be entered deeply
distinction: Although the painting has no clear built elements, the depth organization of mountains, rocks and water more strongly emphasizes an enterable process of travel rather than mere layered concealment and revelation.

evidence: Middle, slightly left: A building complex is placed on a flat terrace enclosed by mountains and rocks, presenting a layout of houses set on a platform, with the base corresponding to the terrain. | Upper right: A small building is attached beside a towering rocky peak, placed according to the highs and lows of the mountain, presenting a relationship distributed according to the slope. | Overall: The layout of the built elements unfolds with the undulations of the mountain form; the building bases form a clear relationship of terrain-responsive placement with site conditions such as slope terraces and mountain rocks.
distinction: Although the buildings mark the scene of a mountain dwelling, their feature of being set on platforms and placed against rock in a terrain-responsive layout is more prominent and dominates the spatial expression.

evidence: Middle ground, slightly left: A built element (pavilion/house) is visible in a mountain hollow, surrounded by trees and partly screened by them. | Lower-left corner: A small bridge spans the water, connecting the bank with the path leading to the built element, expressing an enterable spatial process.
distinction: Although the built element in the painting is screened by trees, the small bridge and path in the lower-left corner clearly guide the eye and the travel route toward the built element, more strongly emphasizing the spatial process of 'access to secluded settings'.

evidence: Left side: A house building is partly screened by the bamboo grove in front, with only the roof and part of the wall exposed, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Left center: The bamboo grove is dense, screening the built elements behind it within, presenting a spatial layering of houses seen within the grove.
distinction: Although the waterside and paths in the painting imply access, the concealment-and-revelation relationship between the buildings and the bamboo grove is more prominent and dominates the spatial expression.

evidence: Waterfront at the lower middle of the painting: A small pavilion is visible, located on flat ground between slope rocks and sparse trees, set by the water. | Overall painting: A large area of unpainted space represents the water surface; the distant mountains are level and far-reaching; the pavilion, as the main built element in the painting, marks the scenery at the waterside, giving the level, far-reaching landscape a visual resting point.
distinction: Although trees surround the pavilion, they do not form a strong layered concealment; its main role is to mark the scenery in the open waterside scene and concentrate the gaze, rather than emphasizing a concealment-and-revelation relationship.

evidence: Center and right: Red-leaf trees and mountains and rocks are distributed, forming the main visual scenery | Left side and upper center: Mountains and rocks are layered, with a waterfall flowing down, constituting the landscape space
distinction: No clear built elements; assigned to scenic accentuation based on the organization of the landscape scenery

evidence: Center, slightly left: A two-story tower and attached buildings are built on the hillside; the building bases follow the undulations of the mountain, presenting a form of houses set on a platform. | Center: Trees are distributed around the buildings, and some buildings are screened by trees, forming a certain relationship of concealment and revelation. | Overall composition: The buildings are located high on the hillside, echoing spatially with the peak on the left and the water surface on the right, marking the scenery at a high point in the mountains.
distinction: Although the buildings mark the mountain scenery, their layout feature of being built according to the mountain configuration is more prominent and is the main means of composing the scene.

evidence: Upper-middle rocky area: The roof and walls of one built element are half-hidden behind mountains, rocks and pines, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Among the pines on the lower right: The roof and part of the structure of another built element (pavilion or house) are screened by the trunks and branches of foreground pines, forming a layering.
distinction: The built elements in the painting form spatial layering mainly through the screening of the pine grove and mountains and rocks, rather than emphasizing an entry path or process.

evidence: Middle of the painting, slightly right: A thatched pavilion is hidden among withered trees, with only the roof and part of the eave-column structure exposed, screened by dense trunks and branches, forming a spatial layering of a house concealed within the grove. | Water surface on the left of the painting: A small boat floats on the water, its body small, keeping distance from the trees on the bank, with no clear landing path shown connecting to the thatched pavilion in the grove.
distinction: Although a boat on the water implies a travel cue, there is a lack of a clear path or transition connecting the waterside with the thatched pavilion in the grove; the concealment-and-revelation relationship of the built element screened by woodland is more prominent.

evidence: Lower right: a group of houses is partly screened by foreground trees and rocks, with only the roofs and part of the walls exposed, forming a clear layering of concealment and revelation. | Center left and distant mountains: dotted structures are faintly visible among the distant mountains and woodland; buildings are seen across the intervening scene, suggesting spatial depth. | Overall: the built elements mostly lie behind woodland or at the foot of the mountains, using the screening and exposure of natural scenery to participate in the composition.
distinction: Although a bridge beside the lower-right buildings hints at a path, the screening relationship in which the buildings are obscured by trees and rocks is visually more prominent and dominates the layered organization of buildings and environment.

evidence: Lower-right slope bank: a group of houses is built against the slope; the building bodies, roofs and fences are partly exposed and partly screened by foreground tree branches and foliage. | Middle ground and distant view: the broad water surface, the woodland on the opposite bank and the distant mountains form an open background, setting off the concealment and revelation layering of the built elements amid the screening foreground trees.
distinction: Although the houses adjoin the slope bank and waterside, the painting emphasizes more the spatial layering formed by the screening and exposure of the buildings by trees, so C2 is more dominant than C1.

evidence: Lower foreground: the waterside built structure (water pavilion) is supported directly on the water's edge by wooden piles; the building base corresponds closely to the junction of water and land, showing a placement relationship of building in relation to water. | Middle ground right: a wall or embankment winds along the hillside terrain, its course conforming to the undulations of the mountain, showing a feature of layout following the slope.
distinction: Although the foreground built elements are screened by woodland, the core spatial organization of the painting lies in the direct correspondence of the building bases to the waterside and the slope-terrace terrain, rather than being dominated by concealment and revelation layering.

evidence: Lower right and lower center: a small path winds upward from the bottom of the painting, passing through trees and fences and leading to the group of houses on the right. | Left waterside: a stone arch bridge connects the two banks, with figures at the bridgehead, hinting at a route across the water into this area. | Right slope terrace: houses are built against the slope and enclosed by fences; the small path clearly leads to these built elements, presenting an accessible spatial relationship.
distinction: Although the houses are placed on the slope terrace, the painting emphasizes more the guiding of the eye and movement route into the built area through clues such as the bridge and path; the connecting role of the path is more prominent.

evidence: Lower to central painting: a winding white path extends from the foreground, passes through woodland and leads to the courtyard entrance in the middle ground. | Center of the painting: the end of the path connects to an enclosing wall with a door, clearly indicating a passage into the built elements. | Middle ground of the painting: several roofs emerge behind the enclosing wall, surrounded by trees, presenting the scene seen after penetrating deeper along the path.
distinction: Although the painting has a concealment and revelation relationship in which trees screen the houses, the connection between the winding path and the door forms a clear spatial access clue and dominates the sense of movement through the painting, so C4 is more apt than C2.

evidence: Lower center: a group of houses is half screened by dense trees and sloping ground, with roofs, walls and window lattices exposed, forming a clear spatial layering of concealment and revelation. | Left and center of the painting: trees interweave before and behind the built elements, screening part of the building structures so that the built elements appear and disappear among the woodland.
distinction: Although the built elements are arranged according to the mountain terrain, the painting emphasizes more the spatial layering formed by the screening and exposure of the buildings by woodland, rather than mere correspondence to terrain.

evidence: Lower center: several houses and pavilions are partly screened by foreground trees and slope rocks, with roofs and eaves exposed, forming a layering of concealment and revelation. | Center right: trees interweave among the buildings, branches and foliage screening the building bodies, placing the built elements within the woodland layers.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed waterside, the relationship of screening and exposure of the buildings by trees and slope rocks is more prominent in the composition and dominates the spatial layering.

evidence: Lower center: an open pavilion or kiosk with clear structure (roof and railings visible), placed on flat ground at the waterside. | Right and rear: dense tree clumps (dot-leaf method) and tall rocks form the background, establishing a front-to-back positional relationship with the pavilion. | Left and distant view: open water and pale-ink distant mountains; the pavilion stands on the open side at the foot of the mountain by the water, becoming the visual anchor of this space.
distinction: Although the pavilion adjoins the tree clumps, its main body is fully exposed and it appears mainly as a front-to-back arrangement rather than a clear screening and concealment relationship; its role is more to identify the scenery of the mountain foot and waterside.

evidence: Center of the painting: a winding white ribbon-like feature (possibly a mountain path or stream) passes through clouds and mist, with tiny dark dots upon it, connecting the upper and lower waterfall areas and forming a clue extending deep into the mountains. | Lower part of the painting: two waterfalls flow down, forming vertical spatial continuity with the ribbon-like feature above, suggesting a layer that can be entered or traveled through.
distinction: The painting emphasizes the sense of entry and deep spatial recession guided by the path/stream, rather than the layering of concealment and revelation in which buildings are screened by woodland.

evidence: Lower center: an open four-cornered pavilion is clearly visible, located on a slope by the water, accompanied by several tall trees. | Overall painting: the pavilion serves as the visual focus of the foreground, identifying a scenic spot on the waterside and forming a spatial echo with the open water and distant mountains.
distinction: Although trees stand beside the pavilion, its main body is fully exposed and does not form a clear layering of screening and concealment; its main role is to identify and concentrate the scenery of this place.

evidence: Lower to central painting: a broad stream or path lies in the foreground, the eye extending upward along it past slope rocks and trees on both sides toward the built elements in the mountain hollow of the middle ground. | Center-left of the painting: in the mountain hollow is a group of built elements including houses, courtyard walls and a courtyard gate; the path connects directly to the gate, forming an reachable spatial relationship. | Right of the painting: a winding path and flowing water among the mountains further strengthen the clue of movement deep into the mountains.
distinction: Although the built elements are placed according to the mountain terrain, the painting emphasizes more the process of penetrating deep into the mountains along the stream path and reaching the built elements, so C4 is more dominant than C1.

evidence: Lower center: a stone arch bridge spans the stream, the bridge opening and water surface forming a clear passage. | Middle ground: the water surface extends along the bridge into the depth of the painting, connecting to the water pavilion and the waterside building complex, forming an accessible spatial circulation. | Left and middle ground: trees and rocks screen the buildings, but through the guidance of the bridge and water route the eye can clearly reach the location of the built elements.
distinction: Although the painting has a concealment and revelation relationship in which trees screen the buildings, the entry clue formed by the stone arch bridge and water route is the dominant mechanism organizing the spatial depth of the painting.

evidence: Upper center to center: a winding mountain path descends from the mountains above and connects directly to the courtyard houses at the center of the painting. | Center: built elements with courtyard walls and roofs are visible, serving as the terminus or waypoint of the mountain path, presenting an reachable spatial relationship. | Lower part: stream and trees surround, and together with the mountain path above they construct a clue of movement deep into the painting.
distinction: Although the built elements are placed among the mountains, the painting highlights more the process of movement in which the winding mountain path guides the eye and connects to the built elements, rather than simply emphasizing terrain-responsive placement of the buildings.

evidence: Middle ground: a bridge spans the stream, connecting the two banks, forming a clear clue of passage and entry. | Middle ground right: a cluster of houses is visible behind the bridge, hinting at the deep space reachable across the bridge. | Foreground lower right: a pavilion is set by the water, and together with the water surface and bridge it organizes an traversable spatial layering.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed by the water, the painting emphasizes more the entry process in which the bridge and stream guide the eye toward the distant village, so C4 is more dominant than C1.

evidence: Center to upper center of the painting: a clear winding mountain path passes through the valley between two mountains and extends into the depths of the painting; tiny figures can be seen walking on the path. | Lower center-right of the painting: behind the trees the roofs and walls of houses are faintly exposed, forming a spatial echo and relationship of arrival with the mountain path. | Overall painting: the mountain path, stream and gaps among the rocks together organize a clue of movement from near to far, penetrating deep into the valley.
distinction: Although the houses on the right have a concealment and revelation relationship of being screened by trees, the mountain path running through the painting and its spatial process of guiding the eye inward play a dominant role in the composition and better fit the definition of access to secluded settings.

evidence: Upper center of the painting: a group of houses is distributed in staggered fashion along the hillside terrain, roofs and walls conforming to the undulations of the terrain, presenting a layout following the mountain. | Overall composition: the building group is on the valley slope between two mountains, and the building bases have a clear relationship of dependence and correspondence with the mountain slopes and terraces.
distinction: The buildings mainly embody a settlement layout conforming to the terrain slope, emphasizing placement according to the ground rather than simply serving as a marker to identify a particular scenic spot.

evidence: Middle right, mountainside: the building group is distributed in layers according to the hillside terrain, the arrangement of roofs conforming to the undulations of the mountain, presenting a layout divided according to the slope. | Lower left corner: thatched huts are set by the waterside and flat fields, their position corresponding to the waterside terrain. | Overall composition: the building bases and their high and low distribution are clearly placed according to the mountain forms and terraces and the waterside conditions.
distinction: Although trees surround the built elements forming a certain concealment and revelation relationship (C2), their layout in rows along the mountain ridge and their waterside placement more directly embody the dominant relationship of placement according to terrain (C1).

evidence: Left waterside: a small bridge is visible spanning the water, connecting to the path on the bank. | Lower center and right of the painting: several houses are screened among trees and rocks, and the path appears to lead to these built elements.
distinction: Although there is a screening relationship, the bridge and path on the left form a clear clue of entry and movement and dominate the spatial organization.

evidence: Lower left corner: a group of buildings is placed close against the foot of the waterside slope, part of the structure supported on the water surface by posts, the layout corresponding closely to the shoreline terrain. | Middle ground right: several houses are arranged against the right hillside and woodland, conforming to the undulations of the terrain.
distinction: Although the right-hand houses are screened by trees, the placement relationship of the lower-left waterside buildings to the terrain and waterside is clearer and dominant, so C1 is more apt than C2.

evidence: Lower left: an arch bridge is visible spanning the water, with a figure on it, forming a clear passage node. | Lower right: houses are visible screened by woodland, with a winding path in front of them extending into the depths and connecting to the buildings. | Left mountainside: the roof of a small pavilion emerges among the trees, forming a spatial echo with the surrounding slope and woodland.
distinction: Although the painting has a concealment and revelation relationship in which woodland screens the houses, the coherent movement clue formed by the bridge, path and figures is more dominant, emphasizing an accessible and traversable spatial process.

evidence: Center right of the painting: a round-roofed pavilion stands, its base partly screened by clouds and mist and treetops below, presenting a half-hidden state. | Lower center-right of the painting: two long rectangular buildings show only roofs and ridges, their walls completely screened by clouds and mist and woodland, forming a layering of buildings seen across an intervening scene. | Foreground right and around the buildings: dense woodland and swirling clouds and mist screen the bases and lower parts of the buildings, strengthening the sense that the buildings are deeply hidden within the forest and clouds.
distinction: Although the pavilion's prominent position gives it a certain scenic-accentuating significance, the painting mainly constructs spatial layering through the screening and exposure of the buildings (especially the lower buildings of which only roofs are exposed) by clouds and trees; the concealment and revelation relationship is more dominant.

evidence: Lower part of the painting: a person stands beneath a pine, beside a winding stream or small path extending toward the upper right of the painting. | Middle ground to distant view of the painting: clouds and mist divide the space, bamboo groves and hills recede layer by layer, forming a visual guide into the depths.
distinction: No clear built elements are seen in the painting, but a stream or small path and figures can be seen forming a clue of movement extending into the depths of the painting, so it is assigned to the closest category, access to secluded settings.

evidence: Lower right: a pavilion is built on a rocky bank by the water, with stone steps (a path) winding upward beside it. | Lower right: beside the stone steps a figure is climbing, presenting the spatial process of approaching and entering the pavilion. | Upper center-right: houses are faintly visible among distant woodland, forming spatial layering with the nearby pavilion.
distinction: Although the pavilion is built by the waterside, the combination of stone steps and figures in the painting more strongly highlights an accessible and reachable movement clue, so C4 is more apt than C1.

evidence: Lower right and central foreground: tall pines interweave and screen part of the walls and bases of the halls, exposing only roofs and upper structures, presenting a layering of buildings seen within woodland. | Middle ground: numerous continuous roofs emerge between clouds and tree clumps, forming a spatial layering of buildings seen across an intervening scene and indicating the presence of distant built elements. | Upper right distant view: a storied pavilion appears above the clouds and mist, forming a near-far correspondence of concealment and revelation with the foreground buildings.
distinction: Although the buildings are arranged along mountain terraces, the painting more strikingly uses layer upon layer of screening by woodland and clouds to make the buildings appear and disappear, constructing a deep spatial layering and a concealment and revelation relationship.

evidence: Lower right: a small built structure is visible between rocky slope bank and trees, partly screened by natural scenery, presenting a concealment and revelation relationship. | Middle ground right: mountains and clouds interweave, forming rich spatial layering in which the built elements appear and disappear.
distinction: Although the built elements are placed according to the rocks and mountains, their main compositional role lies in using the screening and exposure of woodland and rocks to form spatial layering, rather than emphasizing a layout relationship of placement according to the ground.

evidence: Center right of the painting: a building complex is surrounded by dense woodland to the left, right and rear; roofs, eaves and walls are partly exposed, presenting a spatial layering of buildings seen within woodland. | Lower center of the painting: trees and rocks screen the front of the built elements, with mountains and waterfalls behind, forming a clear concealment and revelation relationship and layering of pictorial depth.
distinction: Figures and a winding shoreline at the lower part of the painting carry a sense of guiding the eye toward the houses, but the path does not clearly connect to the building entrances, whereas the screening and surrounding of the houses by trees is more prominent, mainly constituting a relationship of screening.

evidence: Lower left to center: a winding path extends from the lower left of the painting, passing through trees and rocks and leading to the building complex. | Center-right: the building complex has a courtyard gate and steps connected to the path, forming a clear entry path. | Behind the buildings: the buildings back onto high mountains, with terraces arranged according to the mountain terrain, together with the path forming a spatial sequence.
distinction: Although the buildings are arranged according to the mountain terrain, the path relationship in which the winding path guides the eye into the courtyard gate is more prominent in the painting, emphasizing an accessible spatial process.

evidence: Right-hand painted panel: The painting depicts several horses moving across open flat plains and a waterside, with willow trees, distant mountains, and nearby sloping rocks, and no clear built elements such as buildings or bridges.
distinction: There are no clear built elements in the painting; the herd of horses as the main subject highlights the scenery of the flat plains and waterside, and it is assigned to C3 only with difficulty.

evidence: Center-right: a double-eaved pavilion is built on an obvious terrace, with steps in front connecting to the ground, presenting a form of building placed on a terrace. | Left rear: buildings are placed against the background hillside terrain, their walls meeting the slope. | Lower left and right: on the left of the courtyard, stone balustrades protect the waterside; on the right, large artificial rockery stones are arranged; the building layout unfolds in response to the waterside and rocky setting.
distinction: Although stone balustrades and a walled gateway are visible in the painting, the visual focus is on the site-specific layout of the building complex according to terraces, hillside, waterside and artificial rockery, rather than emphasizing an entry process guided by a path.

evidence: Lower-left foreground: figures gather in activity beneath pines on the slope bank; traces of a path are visible beside the bamboo grove on the left, hinting at a movement clue. | Right and middle ground: the water shoreline and gaps among the rocks form spatial extension, helping to indicate an accessible or continuing relationship of movement. | Whole painting: no clear built elements such as houses, pavilions or bridges are seen, only figures and natural scenery.
distinction: The painting suggests a process of movement and a sense of spatial entry through the path and shoreline (C4), rather than relying on buildings to identify a particular scenic spot (C3), although both lack clear evidence of built elements.

evidence: Center-right of the painting: the roof and walls of a house emerge between a cluster of trees and mountains and rocks; the building is partly screened by natural scenery, forming a spatial layering of concealment and revelation. | Lower part of the painting: a stream and a stone bridge guide the eye toward the depth of the painting, but the built elements mainly rely on the screening and revealing by trees and mountains and rocks to present their sense of presence.
distinction: Although the painting has a stream and stone bridge providing a cue for entry, the most core compositional role of the built elements is to form spatial layering through the screening by trees and mountains and rocks, rather than emphasizing a traversable path process.

evidence: Right side: mountains and rocks and dense trees are depicted; the mountain terrain meets the water; no houses or pavilions are seen. | Left side and center: a large area of water with ripples on the surface; in the distance there are clouds and mist and faint mountain shadows; no boats or bridges. | Whole painting: the painting is mainly a natural landscape scene, with no clear traces of built elements (buildings, paths, etc.).
distinction: The painting is mainly natural landscape with no clear built elements, so based on the overall landscape composition (presenting a particular landscape scenery) it is classified as scenic accentuation.

evidence: Lower middle-right: a group of storied buildings is built against the mountain and beside the water; the building site/base unfolds following the sloping bank terrain, presenting a situation of placement according to the terrain. | Right foreground and water surface: in front of the buildings there are sloping banks and trees; on the left water surface there is a small bridge; the overall layout echoes the mountain-and-water configuration.
distinction: Although the buildings are partly screened by trees, their placement against the slope and beside the water, following the terrain, is the most prominent spatial organizing relationship in the painting, so C1 is more fitting than C2.

evidence: Middle-ground right: the house building is situated within a surround of trees; the trunk and branches and leaves of the tall trees on the left screen the left part of the building, and the cluster of dead trees on the right also screens the right end of the building, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Building main body: the roof, eaves and part of the walls of the building are revealed through gaps in the trees, indicating that it is within a layer screened by woodland. | Transition between foreground and middle ground: in front of the building there are trees and stone platforms, and behind it there are distant mountains and clouds and mist; the building is clamped between natural scenery, presenting a spatial layering of seeing a house among trees.
distinction: Although the building is beside the water and has a stone-built base, the painting more emphasizes the screening and surrounding of the building by trees, and the building layout is square rather than clearly following complex terrain, so concealment and revelation (C2) is more dominant than terrain-responsive siting (C1).

evidence: Lower left to center: a thatched hut is placed against the bank slope and trees, with a fence gate in front, following the terrain of the bank. | Middle right: a pavilion is built on high ground on the waterside slope, with a long plank walkway or bridge below connecting to the water surface, presenting a layout of setting a pavilion according to the bank. | Distant middle: a trellis or thatched pavilion is located at the edge of the paddy fields, arranged following the direction in which the field ridges and water bank unfold.
distinction: Although the painting has a plank walkway and human paths, the built elements (thatched hut, pavilion, trellis) mainly present a distribution layout following the water bank and field-ridge terrain; the feature of placement according to the terrain is more dominant than a single process of movement through and entry.

evidence: Center of the painting: a stream runs across the painting; on the stream is a small bridge, on which a person is walking, connecting the paths on the two banks. | Lower left and upper right of the painting: houses are distributed on the two banks; the paths and bridge imply an accessible and traversable route from the foreground to the houses in the background.
distinction: Although trees screen the houses, the combination of bridge, paths and pedestrians more emphasizes the connectivity of space and the process of movement through the landscape, so C4 is more dominant.

evidence: Center to upper right of the painting: multiple groups of buildings are distributed in staggered heights according to the mountain terrain, extending from the mountain foot to the mountainside, presenting a clear layout of placement according to the slope, with the building site/base following the mountain-slope terrain. | Lower part of the painting and around the buildings: there are paths winding upward connecting the mountain foot with the building groups; the buildings are surrounded by trees and clouds and mist, and some buildings are above the clouds and mist.
distinction: The layout of buildings stacked layer upon layer according to the mountain terrain (C1) constitutes the main skeleton and main spatial relationship of the painting, and is more prominent and dominant than the process of path-guided entry (C4).

evidence: Right side of the painting: mountains and rocks, trees, clouds and mist and human activity are visible; the figures sit or stand among the mountains and rocks; no clear buildings are seen. | Center-right of the painting: the figures are in a mountain-and-forest environment, with a sense of path or spatial extension, implying accessibility or movement through the landscape.
distinction: No clear built elements are seen in the painting; there are only figures active among the landscape, and the spatial organization presents a sense of movement through the landscape, so it is classified as C4, but the evidence is insufficient.

evidence: Middle right of the painting: a courtyard building group is arranged in a flat courtyard; the building site/base and the square tree pits of several pine trees form a regular corresponding and placement relationship. | Lower right of the painting: enclosure walls and a gate tower unfold along the edge of the courtyard, forming a spatial boundary with the cluster of willow trees below.
distinction: Although the buildings and trees screen each other, the painting more emphasizes the regular layout and placement of the building group according to the courtyard site and tree pits, rather than being dominated by concealment-and-revelation relationships.

evidence: Lower left and lower middle: tall pines and jagged mountains and rocks are in front of the building group, screening the lower half of the buildings and the interior of the courtyard, forming foreground screening. | Center and right: the roofs, eaves, corridors and red window lattices of the buildings are revealed through gaps between trees and rocks, presenting a spatial layering of seeing a house through a screen. | Background: distant mountains are shrouded in clouds and mist; the buildings are in the middle ground, set off by the foreground natural scenery (trees and rocks), strengthening the concealment-and-revelation relationship.
distinction: Although the buildings are large in scale, their main compositional mode is to create layering through the screening and revealing by foreground trees and rocks, rather than simply serving as a marker that points out the scenery.

evidence: Middle left of the painting: a group of pavilions and storied buildings is built on mountains and rocks, partly screened by the foreground pines and mountain crags, with only the roofs, eaves and part of the walls revealed, presenting a spatial layering of half concealed and half revealed. | In front of the middle-left buildings: the buildings extend out a platform, on which figures stand; below the platform are waves or a sea of clouds; the buildings take part in the composition through the screening and revealing by trees and mountains and rocks.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed according to the mountains and rocks, the painting more emphasizes the screening and revealing relationship of trees and mountains and rocks to the buildings; the effect of concealment and revelation forming a setting is more dominant.

evidence: Center-right of the painting: a water pavilion is built on a stone bank at the water's edge, with a platform extending into the water, becoming the visual center and scenic marker of the painting. | Behind and to the left of the water pavilion: behind the water pavilion there are enclosure walls and a doorway, and on the left there are trees screening, defining the spatial extent. | Foreground and waterside: in the foreground there is a small bridge and walking figures, and one person sits alone at the water's edge, together with the water pavilion forming a scenic accentuation scene.
distinction: Although there is a small bridge and the movement line of figures in the foreground implying entry, the role of the water pavilion as a visual center pointing out the fine scenery at the water's edge is more dominant.

evidence: Middle right of the painting: a figure stands on a protruding rock platform; no clear houses, pavilions or other built structures are seen. | Right side of the painting: mountains and rocks, woodland and a stream form a scene of deep valleys and high cliffs; the position where the figure stands points out this high vantage point for viewing the scenery.
distinction: There are no clear built elements in the painting; the rock platform on which the figure stands points out the scenery of high cliffs and deep valleys, so it is classified as C3.

evidence: Lower middle: a stone bridge with railings spans and connects the two banks, forming a clear passage cue and guiding the eye toward the depth of the painting. | Lower left corner: a bridgehead or pavilion building directly connects with the stone bridge, serving as the starting point or node of movement through the landscape. | Upper middle and upper right corner: groups of pavilions and storied buildings and a white pagoda on the mountain top are located in the direction in which the bridge path and water bank extend, implying that one can go deep along the cues to reach them.
distinction: The connectivity of the bridge and paths organizes the spatial depth and the process of movement through the landscape in the painting, and is more dominant than a simple scenic-marker role.

evidence: Center-left of the painting: a simple thatched hut (or fishing shed) is hidden amid a large expanse of reeds/water plants; inside the hut a person is visible holding a rod and sitting; the roof and the surrounding plant forms blend together, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Around the painting and at the center: a large area of reeds/water plants surrounds and partly screens the central thatched hut, forming a spatial layering of seeing a house among trees/grasses.
distinction: The thatched hut mainly presents a hidden layered relationship through the screening of reeds, rather than serving as a striking node that points out a specific landscape scenery.

evidence: Lower middle: an arched bridge spans the water surface or path, connecting the foreground with the built area in the middle ground, forming a clear passage cue. | Middle-ground left and left hillside: houses are arranged in staggered fashion against the mountain cliff; on the high left there is a pavilion, connected with the foreground through the bridge and implied paths, implying an accessible spatial sequence.
distinction: Although the built elements are arranged according to the mountain terrain (C1), the clear bridge in the painting and the line of sight and path relationships guided by it more emphasize the process of movement from here to there and turning into the depths, so C4 is more dominant.

evidence: Center of the painting: a thatched pavilion is placed on a terrace extending from the towering mountains and rocks on the left; the building site/base follows the high and low terrain, presenting a layout of setting a house according to the terrace. | Left side to center of the painting: the way the thatched pavilion unfolds corresponds with the trend of the mountains and rocks on the left and the sloping terrace; the building is closely integrated with the natural terrain.
distinction: Although the thatched pavilion is partly screened by mountains and rocks, its main compositional role lies in being placed following the mountain-and-rock terrace, rather than relying solely on the concealment and revelation of trees, mountains and rocks to form layering.

evidence: Lower left corner: a small boat is on the water surface, with figures in the boat, implying a cue of movement through the landscape or returning home. | Lower right corner: a small bridge spans the stream, connecting the foreground with the middle-ground sloping bank, providing a path cue. | Right hillside: house buildings are visible on the hillside; the lines of the stream and sloping ground guide the eye from the boat and bridge in the foreground toward this place.

evidence: Lower left: A group of buildings is placed against the mountain foot and the stream; the building site unfolds in conformity with the rises and falls of the sloping land. | Lower left: To the left of the building, steps or a ramp are visible, connecting the waterside below with the main body of the building, presenting a relationship of siting houses according to the slope and arranging them along the bank.

evidence: Left-side mountain mass: The city wall and pass wind upward along the steep ridge and mountain slopes, their direction closely following the rises and falls of the mountain terrain. | Lower left and bottom: At the foot of the mountain, built structures such as the city wall and watchtowers are visible, placed against the mountain foot and sloping land, forming a continuous line of defense.

evidence: Lower foreground hillside: Several houses are distributed in staggered fashion according to the slope and terraces of the hillside, presenting a form of distribution according to the slope and siting houses on terraces. | Middle-ground water surface and distant mountains: The unpainted water surface separates the foreground sloping-land built structures from the rocks behind, highlighting the foreground buildings' conformity to the local terrain.
