distinction: Although the painting implies paths, the screening and revealing of buildings by the bamboo grove (partly screened) is the primary means by which the scenic layers of this place are constituted.

evidence: Upper center: a small bridge crosses the water, connecting the two banks and providing a definite thread of passage. | Lower left corner: a pavilion stands beneath willow trees at the waterside, together with the water surface and a small boat forming a spatial node that can be traveled through.

evidence: Lower center of the painting, below the waterfall: the roof of a built structure (pavilion or house) is visible, half screened by surrounding trees and rocks, presenting spatial layers of alternating concealment and revelation. | Lower left of the painting: another faint outline of a house is hidden among trees, likewise forming a relationship of screening and revealing through woodland.
distinction: Although the built structure lies below the waterfall, its most visually striking feature is the concealment-and-revelation relationship in which roofs are exposed while screened by trees and rocks, rather than a correspondence between base and terrain siting.

evidence: Lower left corner: between the sloping bank and the waterside the roof and supports of a thatched pavilion or thatched hall are visible, its base relying on the terrain. | Upper left corner: a steep cliff rises, forming with the sloping bank and buildings below a staggered arrangement of heights nestling against the mountain and beside the water. | Left middle: bamboo clumps and trees surround the buildings, which are sited in response to the sloping bank terrain.
distinction: Although the buildings dot the scenery, their integration with the terrain of the sloping bank and cliff more prominently highlights the terrain-responsive siting relationship of placement according to local conditions, rather than mere scenic accentuation.

evidence: Foot of the mountain, middle right: a group of buildings is surrounded by dense pines and miscellaneous trees, roofs and wall bodies emerging through gaps in the trees, forming a distinct layering of concealment and revelation. | Left mountainside: a winding path leads to a small pavilion at the mountainside, the pavilion half hidden among sloping rocks and trees.
distinction: Although the path on the left leading to the pavilion embodies access to secluded settings, the main building group in the painting constructs spatial layers mainly through the screening and revealing of trees, and the feature of concealment and revelation forming a setting is more dominant.

evidence: Center-right of the painting: in a dense bamboo grove the roof, part of the wall bodies and a fence of a building are exposed; the main body of the building is screened by bamboo leaves and culms, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Lower part of the painting: sloping banks and flowing water surround the bamboo grove, but the building is mainly hidden deep within the grove and neither directly faces the water nor shows an evident path connection.
distinction: Although the building stands on a sloping bank, the most prominent spatial relationship in the painting is the screening and revealing of the building by the bamboo grove, rather than a correspondence between building and terrain relief.

evidence: Lower left: houses are hidden behind the hillside and flowering trees, with only roofs and part of the wall bodies exposed, presenting layers screened by woodland. | Lower right: a group of buildings is surrounded and screened by dense white flowering trees, roofs emerging through gaps in the canopy, forming a spatial relationship of seeing houses across a barrier. | Middle right: pines and flowering trees interlace, buildings faintly visible deep within the woodland, reinforcing the visual effect of concealment and revelation forming a setting.
distinction: The dominant visual relationship in the painting is the screening and revealing of buildings by woodland and flowering trees, rather than emphasis on the way buildings are sited in response to terrain and banks.

evidence: Left middle: a group of houses is arranged in a winding line along the shoreline, backed by woodland, presenting a layout extending along the bank, with bases corresponding to the shoreline forms. | Lower center: houses sit among trees at the waterside, with a wooden bridge beside them connecting land and the built area, showing that the built structures are sited against the waterside.
distinction: The layout feature of the house group on the left arranged along the shoreline (C1) better dominates the explanation of the spatial relationship between built structures and terrain than the local screening of the lower houses by trees (C2).

evidence: Overall painting: the painting presents sparse woods, sloping banks and water surface, with no definite traces of houses, bridges, paths or other built elements. | Lower left corner: the inscription 'Sparse Woods, Evening Mirror' is visible, but it is not taken as spatial evidence within the painting.
distinction: The painting lacks identifiable built elements, so it is assigned to the closest category based on the overall visible spatial organization of woodland and water surface.

evidence: Lower center: a waterside pavilion building stands at the edge of dense woods on the left, part of its body and roof screened by overhanging branches, presenting layers revealed beneath the trees. | Lower center to right: the building is built facing the water, with open lotus-pond water in front and surrounded behind and to the left by tall trees, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship.
distinction: Although the building faces the water and relies on the bank, its front-and-back screening relationship with the tall trees on the left, revealed beneath the trees, is more prominent in the composition, so it is assigned to concealment and revelation forming a setting.

evidence: Middle ground, left of center: an arched bridge crosses the water, with pedestrians on the bridge, forming a definite thread of crossing and connection. | Right: a building group is arranged along the waterside, with double-eaved roofs and covered corridors, connected to the path by the shoreline and the bridge. | Middle-ground waterside: moored boats and wooden posts along the bank imply water-land transport and routes of entry into the built structures.
distinction: Although the buildings are screened by bamboo groves, the movement threads formed by the bridge and paths more prominently organize the spatial process of entering the built structures.

evidence: Whole painting: the painting mainly depicts peaks, waterfalls, clouds and mist and trees, with no clearly identifiable traces of houses, pavilions, bridges or other built elements. | Center: a towering peak takes an arch-like form, with a waterfall flowing down from it; the forms of the rocks are prominent and constitute the painting's main spatial structure.
distinction: The painting is purely natural scenery, with no definite built structures participating in the composition; all categories lack direct evidence; based on the dominance of mountain forms and water flow, it is formally assigned to terrain-responsive siting.

evidence: Lower left to lower center: a group of houses and enclosing walls is partially screened by branches and leaves of foreground and middle-ground trees, roofs, wall bodies, doors and windows emerging through gaps in the trees, forming a distinct layering of concealment and revelation. | Lower center of the painting: the built structures sit on flat ground between the foot of the mountain and the waterside; weeping willows at the water's edge on the right further enrich the screening spatial relationships.
distinction: Although the built structures are sited against mountains and beside water, the painting emphasizes more the spatial layers formed by their screening and revealing through trees, so C2 is more apt than C1.

evidence: Whole painting: the painting consists mainly of layered rocks, multiple waterfalls and open water below, with no definite houses, pavilions or other built structures. | Lower right: a tiny figure sits facing the water at the waterside as a scenic accent, suggesting a path by which the viewer's gaze enters among the water and rocks.
distinction: The painting lacks physical built structures, but the deep space formed by the waterfalls and water flow guides the gaze inward, so in the absence of built elements it is assigned to the closest category of spatial process.

evidence: Middle-upper mountain hollow: a group of built elements is visible, with roofs and walls clearly discernible, situated among the valley woodland. | Lower right to center: a clear path passes through the foreground pine grove and extends into the depth of the painting, pointing toward the built elements. | Lower-middle part of the painting: dense pine woodland surrounds the path, forming spatial layers that lead from outside to inside and toward the built elements in the depths.
distinction: Although the painting has a concealment-and-revelation relationship in which trees partly screen the buildings, the clearly defined path below forms a strong cue for entry and movement through the landscape, making access to secluded settings the dominant mode of spatial organization.

evidence: Lower left to center: an arched bridge spans the water, connecting the two banks and forming a clear cue of crossing and entry. | Mountain area on the right: a stream and gaps among the mountains and rocks form a path that guides the eye toward the buildings in the mountain hollow. | Left middle ground: building groups are arranged along the waterside and the sloping ground, forming an accessible relationship with the bridge and the water surface.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited according to the terrain, the accessible, traversable spatial process formed by the bridge, waterside, and mountain path in the painting is more prominent, dominating the relationship between the built elements and the landscape.

evidence: Water surface at lower right: a person is visible traveling across the water in a small boat, presenting a cue of movement through the landscape. | Overall painting: the painting is composed of near-bank trees, reeds, water surface, and distant mountains; no houses, bridges, or other clear built elements are visible.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built elements; only the boat journey implies a spatial process of movement through the landscape, so it is only barely assigned to C4.

evidence: Lower center: a wooden bridge spans the water, connecting the two banks and forming a clear cue of passage and entry. | Lower left corner: a red-robed figure stands on the bank beneath a tree near the bridgehead, implying the starting point or direction of movement through the landscape. | Right middle: built elements are situated among willows on the sloping bank, connected to the bridge path via the shoreline, presenting a spatial relationship of reaching from one place to another that is accessible.
distinction: The bridge and shoreline in the lower part of the painting form a clear movement route, guiding the eye and the figure's movement toward the built elements, emphasizing an accessible spatial process rather than mere concealment and revelation through tree cover.

evidence: Right side: a figure walks along a sloping path among the mountains and rocks, showing a cue of movement into the depths of the mountain forest. | Center to lower part of the painting: the mountains, rocks, and stream form a natural spatial opening and closing that guides the eye into the depths.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built elements, but the momentum of the figure walking along the path constitutes an accessible spatial process, so C4 is chosen as the closest expression.

evidence: Lower middle: the roof, eaves, and walls of built elements are partly obscured by foreground tree branches and leaves and by mountains and rocks, only partially revealed. | Right middle: a bridge structure appears faintly between the trees and the cliff on the right, presenting a spatial layering in which buildings are seen through screening. | Lower left to lower middle: a path enclosed by red railings connects to the built elements, but the building mass as a whole is deeply hidden amid the screening trees.
distinction: Although the painting has paths and a bridge, the most dominant spatial expression is the layering formed by the screening and revealing of the built elements by trees, mountains, and rocks, rather than emphasis on the process of entry.

evidence: Lower right to beneath the central cliff: a group of buildings is placed close against the cliff slope, with vertical supporting structures visible below, the building site/base following the mountain slope and terraces. | Central mountainside: a small building is set on a terrace according to the mountain's configuration, interspersed with mountains, rocks, and trees. | Left waterside: a bridge is visible spanning the water and connecting to land, helping to explain the linkage between terrain and built elements.
distinction: Although trees partly screen the buildings, the dominant relationship is the siting of built elements according to the configuration of the slopes and cliff; concealment and revelation is not the main compositional mode.

evidence: Upper left: buildings are set on a high cliff, their building site/base corresponding to the mountaintop terrain, surrounded by trees. | Lower left: a building complex unfolds in successive tiers along the mountain slope, arranged according to the terraced terrain, presenting a form of distribution according to the slope. | Left side overall: the built layout is staggered in height, forming a close correspondence with the steep cliff and sloping terrain, presenting a relationship of siting according to the ground.
distinction: Although paths and figures in the lower right corner of the painting present cues of movement through the landscape, the main built elements on the left more conspicuously present a terrain-responsive relationship of siting according to cliff and terraces, dominating the spatial expression.

evidence: Left side: a group of houses is sited beside woodland and a sloping bank, the building site/base closely integrated with the undulations of the terrain, presenting a layout of houses set on terraces and distributed according to the slope. | Lower right: a small house sits on flat ground by the water, naturally connecting with the surrounding trees and sloping bank.
distinction: Although the small house on the right is screened by trees, the layout of the house group on the left unfolding according to the terrain and sloping bank is more conspicuous, dominating the spatial organization of the painting.

evidence: Upper middle: roofs and walls of pavilions are visible in the mountain hollow, partly obscured by woodland and mountains and rocks. | Lower right to center: a zigzag plank walkway with red railings winds upward along the cliff face, forming a clear cue of movement through the landscape. | Center: the end of the walkway connects to a mountain path and a fence, pointing toward built elements screened in the depths, presenting an accessible spatial process.
distinction: Although there is a concealment-and-revelation relationship in which trees screen the buildings, the zigzag walkway runs through the painting as a cue of movement and guides entry into the depths, and is the more dominant mode of spatial organization.

evidence: Upper left and upper right: the roofs of several houses emerge among trees and reeds, partly obscured by vegetation, presenting a layering in which buildings are seen through screening. | Left middle and lower left: houses are located behind trees or below the sloping bank; trunks and branches obscure part of the building walls, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited against the mountains and beside the water, the painting constructs spatial layering mainly through the screening and revealing of buildings by trees, and the relationship of concealment and revelation is more prominent.

evidence: Lower left corner: a small boat is on the water, with two people traveling in it toward the gorge in the depths of the painting. | Center and right: steep cliffs and trees flank each other, forming a water channel leading into the depths.
distinction: The painting has no clear built elements; the boat's direction of travel implies a spatial process of entering the depths of the landscape, so it is assigned to the closest category, C4.

evidence: Left and upper part: tall willows with dense, drooping branches and leaves cover the upper and left spaces of the painting. | Middle left: a pavilion (waterside pavilion) is located beneath the willows; the pavilion roof and the space above are obscured/surrounded by willow branches and leaves, while the pavilion body and figures are revealed. | Overall: the built elements borrow the screening of the trees, forming layers of foreground trees and middle-ground architecture; the concealment-and-revelation relationship beneath the tree shade participates in the composition.
distinction: Although the pavilion is built beside the water (possessing terrain-responsive siting characteristics), the covering and surrounding of the pavilion by the huge willow on the left forms a conspicuous screening layer, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship beneath the tree shade dominates the spatial organization of the painting more than mere siting according to terrain.

evidence: Lower left: a building group with red pillars and black tiles is partly obscured by dense foreground tree branches and leaves, with only roofs and parts of walls exposed, presenting a layering of houses hidden in the woods. | Right middle: a pavilion-style building is half-hidden behind mountains, rocks, and pines, with only part of its roof and supporting columns exposed, using screening elements to create spatial depth. | Overall composition: the built elements do not occupy the main body of the painting but are scattered among the cliffs and woodland, their existence indicated through partial revelation; the concealment-and-revelation relationship participates in the composition.
distinction: Although the buildings identify the scenery at the mountain foot and mountainside, the painting places greater emphasis on the spatial layering and concealment-and-revelation relationship formed by buildings partly revealed after being screened by trees, mountains, and rocks.

evidence: Lower right foreground: a boat is moored beside a reed-grown waterside, with one person seated in the boat facing the bank. | Beside the boat at lower right: at the bank rocks there is a brown flat-roofed object (suspected to be a pavilion, shed, or other artificial structure), half-hidden by grass, forming a mooring relationship with the boat. | Overall composition: against the background of open water and distant mountains, the boat and person imply a spatial process of water-route travel and approach to the bank.
distinction: Although there is a suspected building obscured by grass, the core of the painting lies in the ferry-crossing movement cue formed by the boat and the momentum of landing, rather than mere concealment-and-revelation layering.

evidence: Right middle ground: behind trees and a bamboo grove, the roof and columns of a thatched pavilion are revealed; the main body of the building is partly obscured by foreground trunks and branches. | Right side of the painting: foreground trunks and branches form a screen over the built elements behind, presenting a spatial layering of houses hidden in the woods.
distinction: Although the thatched pavilion serves to accentuate the scenery, its half-screened, half-revealed concealment-and-revelation relationship with the tree branches and leaves is more prominent in the painting and dominates the expression of spatial layering.

evidence: Whole painting: the painting is composed mainly of mountains and rocks, withered trees, sloping banks, and distant mountains; no clear traces of houses, bridges, or other built elements are visible.
distinction: No clear built elements are visible; based on the overall landscape composition it is barely assigned to scenic accentuation, but it lacks actual architectural evidence.

evidence: Upper middle: a pavilion is built on a platform at the summit of a towering, steep cliff, set on the high cliff. | Lower foreground: a house is built on sloping ground at the mountain foot, sited according to the terrain.
distinction: Although trees screen the house, the core of the overall composition lies in the pavilion and the house being respectively sited on the high cliff and on sloping ground at the mountain foot, emphasizing a corresponding relationship of placement according to the ground, rather than forming scenery purely through concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower left foreground: the corner of a blue-gray roof (of a pavilion or small house) is revealed among trees on the sloping bank, half-screened by tree trunks and slope rocks. | Middle-ground far bank: there are tiny traces among the trees on the far bank, suspected to be a building or bridge, forming a near-far layering with the water surface.
distinction: The foreground built elements are mainly screened by trees and slope rocks, with only the roof revealed, emphasizing the spatial layering of concealment and revelation rather than serving merely as a conspicuous focal point for scenic accentuation.

evidence: Lower right to center: a winding path extends from the lower right of the painting, passes through withered trees, and leads to a building on the mountain slope. | Slightly left of center: a building stands on the mountain slope, partly obscured by surrounding trees and mountains and rocks. | Lower left: a waterfall flows down among the mountains and rocks, together with the path and building forming spatial layering.
distinction: The clearly defined path in the painting guides the eye toward the building, emphasizing a spatial process of movement from one place to another and approach to the built elements, which is more dominant than a mere concealment-and-revelation relationship.

evidence: Middle ground, slightly right: a building complex is screened amid dense trees, with only roofs and parts of walls exposed, presenting a spatial layering in which houses are seen in the woods. | Lower center: a pavilion sits among weeping willows; willow branches surround and obscure part of the pavilion body, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship.
distinction: The built elements in the painting (houses and pavilion) are conspicuously screened and surrounded by trees, revealing roofs or parts, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship constitutes the main spatial layering, rather than serving merely as an isolated marker identifying the scenery.

evidence: Right and center: a towering main peak occupies the main position of the painting, with clear mountain and rock textures and vegetation dotted among them. | Left and lower left: a sloping bank extends, with several pines painted, upright in posture. | Lower right corner: a thatched hut (or pavilion) is painted by the waterside, with a clear structure, serving as a scenic accent.
distinction: The painting takes high mountains and pines as its main subject and is a typical small landscape scene, with architecture serving only as an accent, distinguishing it from ruled-line painting (jiehua) in which architecture is the main subject.

evidence: Lower right: a wooden bridge spans the water, connecting the two banks and, together with the surrounding pines and mountains and rocks, forming a crossable cue of movement through the landscape. | Left lower middle: a row of houses is arranged along the mountain foot and the stream bank, presenting a form built according to the configuration.
distinction: The houses on the left embody terrain-responsive siting against the mountains and beside the water, but the bridge in the lower right corner provides a clearer cue of the spatial process of crossing and entry, dominating the painting's sense of movement through the landscape.

evidence: Middle ground, slightly left: a small pavilion is built on top of a slope rock, surrounded by withered trees, becoming the visual focus and marker of the landscape at this spot. | Overall composition: the pavilion is located at a high point among the mountains and rocks, identifying this scenic spot and giving the surrounding landscape forms a point of anchorage.
distinction: Although the pavilion is built according to the mountain's configuration, its role as a visual focus and scenic marker is more prominent, rather than merely emphasizing siting according to the ground.

evidence: Lower middle: a wooden bridge spans the water, connecting the slope rocks and trees on the two banks, and tiny figures are visible on the bridge. | Overall composition: the bridge, together with the trees and slope rocks on the banks, forms a clear passage cue, guiding the eye and the movement route across the water and into the depths of the painting.
distinction: The only clear built element in the painting is the bridge, which mainly serves to connect the two banks and provide a passage, conforming to the characteristic of access to secluded settings, rather than being built against the mountains, screened, or serving as a scenic accent.

evidence: Lower-middle part of the painting: a small bridge spans the stream, and behind the bridge a path extends, connecting to houses among the trees on the left, presenting clear cues of entry and movement through the landscape. | Lower left of the painting: houses are screened between trees and the sloping bank, forming an accessible spatial relationship with the bridge-and-path cue below. | Upper-middle part of the painting: a building is built on a cliffside platform at the mountainside, set at a strategic point, echoing the lower part in height.
distinction: The buildings in the upper-middle part of the painting embody the C1 characteristic of siting according to the mountain's configuration, but the combination of bridge, path, and houses in the lower part more clearly constructs an accessible, reachable spatial process of movement through the landscape, so C4 is dominant.

evidence: Right mountainside: houses are built on mountain and rock terraces, close beside a waterfall, sited according to the mountain's configuration. | Lower left corner: houses are located on the waterside at the mountain foot, surrounded by trees, arranged according to the waterside slope. | Lower center: a small bridge spans the water, connecting the two banks, helping to explain the spatial relationship between the waterside and the built elements.
distinction: Although the bridge in the painting implies a cue of movement through the landscape, the built elements mainly present a placement relationship of siting against the mountains and beside the water and setting houses on terraces, and the characteristic of terrain-responsive siting is more dominant.

evidence: Middle-right mountainside: several small buildings sit on a mountain-slope platform, with roofs and parts of walls visible. | Middle-right mountainside: the buildings are partly obscured by surrounding red-leaf trees, forming a spatial layering of alternating concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited according to the mountain's configuration, the relationship of screening and revealing of the buildings by trees is more prominent in the composition.

evidence: Lower left: a section of city wall with crenellations and a gate tower is visible, extending horizontally along the terrain below, with the building site/base matching the direction of the terrain. | Lower-middle part of the painting: the left side of the city wall connects to the sloping bank and trees, and the right side extends to the foot of the mountains and rocks, presenting a spatial relationship of placement according to the ground and unfolding according to the configuration.
distinction: The built elements mainly present a layout unfolding according to the terrain, and their role in screening or scenic accentuation is less conspicuous than the characteristic of siting according to the ground.

evidence: Lower center of the painting: a thatched hut is surrounded by the flowering branches and trunks of trees on both left and right, with the building body, roof, and figures inside revealed through gaps between trees and rocks. | Behind the thatched hut: huge rocks and mountain forms serve as background and, together with the foreground trees, wrap the built elements in natural scenery, forming a clear layering of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the built elements are sited according to the mountains and rocks, the painting places greater emphasis on the screening and revealing of the built elements by trees and mountains and rocks, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship is the dominant mode of composition.

evidence: Left-center waterside: a small boat is moored at the bank, with a person aboard, forming a connection for approaching the built elements on the bank by water. | Lower-right waterside: two people stand at the bank, with a path nearby extending toward built elements half-screened by trees, presenting an accessible spatial relationship. | Multiple places in the painting: built elements connect with movement clues such as bridges, paths, and ferry crossings, giving the painting a spatial process of moving from one point to another and approaching the built elements.
distinction: Although the painting has concealment relationships, the mooring of the boat and the movement clues of the figures on the bank more clearly organize an accessible spatial process, so C4 is more apt than C2.

evidence: Center-right: a group of houses is arranged against mountain rocks and a stream, following the terrain's rises and falls in a staggered manner. | Lower-right: buildings extend along the waterside and slopes, their building sites tightly integrated with the surrounding natural terrain of rocks and trees.

evidence: Lower left: a group of village houses is partly blocked by foreground tree branches and foliage, presenting a half-hidden, half-revealed state. | Center-right: a pavilion is located behind midground mountains and rocks, with only its roof and part of its structure exposed, using the rocks to create concealment. | Right: behind the woods on the right bank, the roofs and walls of houses are visible, obscured by tree trunks and branches, forming layers.

distinction: Although the houses have concealment relationships, the continuous movement clues formed by the bridge and stone steps are the dominant factor organizing the painting's space.

evidence: Lower-left corner: a group of thatched houses is visible, arranged against the waterside and slopes. | Lower center of the painting: between two large pines, a small bridge is visible spanning a stream, connecting the two banks. | Lower part of the painting: the stream and shoreline guide the eye, together with the bridge and thatched houses forming an accessible, traversable spatial path.
distinction: Although the thatched houses are built according to the terrain, the clearly visible small bridge and stream together form a definite movement path and entry relationship, making C4 more dominant than terrain-responsive siting alone.

evidence: Left slope: the building complex is distributed in a staggered manner following the undulations of the slope and the varying heights of the terraces, presenting a layout arranged according to the slope. | Upper-center mountainside: a storied pavilion is placed in the gaps between mountain rocks and trees, extending upward in response to the mountain form. | Right waterside: waterside buildings extend along the sloping bank and the base of the woodland, their building sites corresponding to the terrain and waterside.

evidence: Left center-distance: a building complex is distributed along the waterside and gentle slopes, presenting a pattern of unfolding along the bank and arranged according to the slope. | Lower center: several houses are arranged below a massive rock face and on the slope in front of it, their building sites corresponding to the terrain's undulations and the positions of the rocks. | Among the midground rock faces: some houses are placed against steep rock walls and in gaps between trees, showing the feature of buildings sited according to the rocks.

evidence: Lower left and center: a building complex sits at the foot of the mountain, surrounded by dense trees; roofs, walls, and fences are revealed through gaps in the trees, forming an obvious relationship of screening and revealing. | Right mountainside: the roof of another building protrudes from behind the tree canopy, using the woodland's screening to indicate its existence and spatial layering.
