evidence: Middle left: House roofs emerge from dense woods, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation | Middle right: Houses are surrounded by trees, with parts of walls visible, reflecting the layers of dwellings in the woods | Lower right: Houses are close to the water's edge, screened by trees around them
distinction: Although the houses are distributed according to the mountain terrain, the painting emphasizes more the screening and revealing of the houses by trees, creating a layered sense of seeing houses within the woods, so C2 is more dominant than C1.

evidence: Lower right corner: The roofs and walls of several houses emerge from the foreground bushes, forming layers of concealment and revelation screened by trees. | Lower left water surface: A lone sail floats, contrasting with the open water surface and distant mountains, but it is a mobile carrier rather than a fixed built structure.
distinction: Although the houses are located at the waterside, the core of the painting's composition lies in the screening and revealing of the architecture by trees, rather than emphasizing the layout relationship of buildings unfolding according to the terrain and sloping bank.

evidence: Lower middle: The main subject of the painting is a large field planted with vegetables, laid out following the gentle sloping terrain. | Lower middle: Two figures are active in the field, but no clear man-made built structures such as houses, bridges, or paths are visible.
distinction: No clear built elements are visible in the painting; only fields cultivated according to the terrain are seen, so it is assigned to C1 according to the closest relationship of site attachment.

evidence: Lower right corner: An arched bridge is visible, with pedestrians on it and a waterfall and trees beside it, forming a spatial clue that can be entered.
distinction: The bridge and pedestrians constitute a clear travel clue, guiding the eye into the depth of the painting rather than merely identifying the scene.

evidence: Lower left: A wooden bridge spans the water connecting the two banks, with two people walking on it, clearly indicating the route into the waterside village. | Left and right sides: Thatched houses are distributed along the waterside and woods; the houses on the right are half-hidden behind tall trees, implying spatial layers leading deeper into the woods. | Central water surface: The open water surface together with the distant arched bridge and small boats forms an extendable space that can be traveled through, guiding the eye to explore deeper.
distinction: Although the houses on the right are screened by trees, the painting as a whole emphasizes more the process of entry and travel constructed through the bridge, waterside, and pedestrians, and C4 better summarizes this spatial organization.

evidence: Full image: The painting consists mainly of sloping rocks on the left and woods on the right and in the center; no clear traces of houses, bridges, paths, or other built elements are visible. | Center and right: Trees interweave front and back, forming a certain spatial layering, but no buildings are screened within them.
distinction: No built elements are visible in the painting; it is barely assigned to C2 on the basis of the front-to-back layered relationship of the overall trees and sloping rocks, but it lacks evidence of built entities.

evidence: Lower center: A small boat on the water, with a figure wearing a bamboo hat in it, presenting a state of travel | Right side: Trees, bamboo clumps, and sloping rocks on the bank form the near-shore shoreline | Above: Gentle, continuous hills in the distance form an open space with the large expanse of water
distinction: No clear buildings are visible in the painting; only the boat and figure traveling on the water present an enterable spatial process, so it is classified as C4 rather than scenic accentuation

evidence: Middle right of the painting: a thatched-roof house is partly screened by pine trees and mixed trees in the foreground, revealing its eaves and wall body, forming a relation of concealment and revelation. | Lower left and center left of the painting: another group of thatched huts is half hidden behind dense bamboo groves and shrubs, with only the roof and partial structure visible, presenting layers through plant screening. | Middle ground of the painting: houses are scattered among the trees and woodland, figures are active in the open space in front of the houses, and buildings and natural scenery interpenetrate, constituting the sense of seclusion of a woodland village.
distinction: Although the houses are arranged according to the sloping ground, the painting places more emphasis on the screening and revealing of the buildings by trees and bamboo groves; the effect of concealment and revelation forming the scene is greater than that of mere siting according to the terrain.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: the city wall extends following the ridge line and slope of the hills, and the building bases are closely integrated with the terrain. | Left mountain summit: a high terrace/tower is placed at the highest point of the mountain, highlighting the correspondence between terrain and built structures. | Among the mountain forest on the right: multiple groups of buildings are distributed along the hillsides and woods, presenting a layout that unfolds with the terrain.
distinction: Although there is a relation of concealment and revelation in which trees and woodland screen the buildings, the feature of the city wall and buildings as a whole conforming to the mountain forms and terrain is more prominent and runs through the entire composition.

evidence: Right side and lower middle of the painting: multiple houses are scattered among the trees and woodland, with roofs and wall bodies partly screened by trunks and foliage, forming distinct layers of concealment and revelation. | Left side of the painting: water surface, shoreline, and a small bridge are visible, but the main built structures are concentrated in the mountain forest on the right, forming scenery through the screening of trees.
distinction: Although the houses are situated against the mountains and beside the water, the most prominent compositional method in the painting is the mutual screening of buildings and woodland, rather than simply emphasizing the determining effect of terrain on building sites.

evidence: Right side and center: the white-walled building is partly screened by the dense foliage of trees in the foreground and background, revealing eaves, walls, and the figures' activity inside the building, forming distinct layers of concealment and revelation. | Left side and center: mountains, rocks, and trees surround the building; the screening by woodland makes the building appear indistinct and participates in constituting the pictorial depth of the painting.
distinction: The painting mainly presents the relation of concealment and revelation and the spatial layers of the building under the screening of woodland, rather than emphasizing its placement according to the mountain terrain.

evidence: Lower center of the painting: the roof, eaves, and wall body of a group of buildings are visible, with figures under part of the corridor, and the main body of the building is surrounded by the surrounding scenery. | Left and right sides and above the building: the branches and foliage of dense pines extend from the foreground and middle ground, screening part of the building's roof and walls, forming a relation of seeing houses within the forest through concealment and revelation. | At the boundary between buildings and trees: trunks and foliage interpenetrate in front of and behind the buildings, giving the built structures spatial layers screened by natural scenery.
distinction: Although the building is arranged according to the terrain at the foot of the mountain, the visual focus of the painting lies in the screening and revealing of the built structures by dense woodland; the relation of concealment and revelation dominates spatial expression more than siting on the terrain.

evidence: Lower right middle: line structures suspected to be a bridge or plank walkway are visible, crossing the water surface or connecting the banks, suggesting a route of movement. | Lower right to center of the painting: the shoreline and stream forms extend into the depth of the painting, together with screening by clouds and mist, forming a suggestion of space turning into the depths.
distinction: The suspected bridge on the right side of the painting mainly serves as a movement clue guiding the gaze inward (C4), rather than primarily displaying the terrain-responsive correspondence between building sites and terrain (C1).

evidence: Lower right and lower center: figures sit on the ground among pines and rocks, accompanied by tea utensils; no physical built elements such as houses or pavilions are visible. | Left side: the inscription 'Tea Conversation in the Pine Breeze' identifies the pine grove as a setting for an elegant tea gathering.
distinction: Although no physical built elements are present, the space enclosed by pines and rocks brings the tea-drinking scene into focus, which better matches the subject than concealment alone.

evidence: Middle right of the painting: a roofed long corridor or waterside pavilion building is screened in front and behind by the trunks and foliage of several trees, revealing only part of the roof, columns, and figures seated facing each other inside. | Right side of the painting: tall mountains and rocks and dense groves lie behind the building, further wrapping it in natural scenery, forming distinct layers and a relation of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the building faces the water, the core of the pictorial composition lies in the screening and revealing of the building by woodland, rather than emphasizing its placement according to the waterside terrain.

evidence: Middle right: the waterside pavilion building is largely screened by the dense foliage of weeping willows on the right, revealing only part of the roof and the figures inside the pavilion, forming a distinct relation of concealment and revelation. | Center: the left side of the waterside pavilion adjoins mountains, rocks, and mixed trees; the main body of the building is hidden behind rocks and woodland, presenting spatial layers screened by forest and rock. | Lower right: below the waterside pavilion, wooden pile structures supporting it on the water surface are visible, and the building is half hidden among the willows and lotus leaves in the foreground.
distinction: Although the building faces the water and leans on rocks, the painting places more emphasis on its layered relation of being screened by willow branches and mountain rocks and half revealed, rather than mere placement conforming to the terrain.

evidence: Middle right of the painting: the roof, eaves, and wall body of the thatched hut are partly screened by branches above and bamboo leaves around it, presenting a distinct relation of concealment and revelation. | Right side and upper part of the painting: dense trees and bamboo groves surround the thatched hut, placing the built structure within the forest and forming spatial layers of seeing the house through a separating screen.
distinction: The focus of the painting lies in the layers formed by the screening and revealing of the thatched hut by trees and bamboo groves, rather than emphasizing the corresponding placement of built structures with the sloping bank terrain.

evidence: Lower right: a small boat with a canopy is moored at the water's edge, and figures can be seen inside the boat. | Middle right to lower right: the branches and trunks of several weeping willows screen part of the boat's hull and canopy, so that the boat is half hidden and half revealed among the gaps in the woodland.
distinction: Although the boat is moored at the waterside, the painting places more emphasis on the screening and revealing of the boat by willow foliage; the relation of concealment and revelation is the dominant factor in the composition.

evidence: Left side and lower part: a tree-covered sloping bank meets the water surface, forming the edge of a wild pond. | Water surface at upper right: several small boats and figures in them can be seen floating on the water surface covered with duckweed.
distinction: There are no fixed built structures in the painting, only small boats dotting the water surface; based on the overall spatial relations, it is only with difficulty assigned to scenic accentuation, but it lacks architectural evidence.

evidence: Whole painting: the painting mainly consists of sloping rocks, mountain ridges, and dense bamboo groves; no identifiable buildings, bridges, paths, or other built entities are seen. | Lower left and upper right: inscriptions and seals are present, but according to the rules they are not used as visual evidence for identifying built structures in the painting.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built entities, so no specific spatial relation can be determined; it is assigned to the closest placeholder category only on the basis of the overall forms of landscape, sloping rocks, and rocks.

evidence: Right side: one person plays the qin and one listens, placed on flat ground under a tree; the qin table and figures form the focal point of the painting. | Left side and above: parasol trees, bamboo, and rocks surround them, forming a clear and secluded environment that sets off the theme of qin-playing.
distinction: The painting has no clear architectural built structures; the figures and qin table indicate the scenery of 'Qin Interest in the Shade of Parasol Trees', so it is assigned to C3.

evidence: Lower right corner: an arched bridge spans the water surface, connecting the earthen banks and trees and rocks on both shores; the bridge body and railings are clear, forming a definite passage route and spatial connection. | Water surface on the left: a canopied boat carrying people travels, with a boatman rowing at the stern, serving as a clue of crossing and movement, embodying movement on water and the process of travel.
distinction: Although the boat and bridge serve to indicate the scenery, the painting places more emphasis on the bridge's connecting route and the boat's dynamic travel, conforming to the definition of movement clues in access to secluded settings.

evidence: Center-right of the painting: an open pavilion sits on flat ground beside the water, surrounded by pine forest and mixed trees. | Left side of the painting: mountains, rocks, and trees form the foreground and, together with the pavilion in the center, form a complete waterside landscape.
distinction: Although the pavilion is placed according to the waterside, its main role in the painting is as a visual focus, indicating and concentrating this scenery of forest and spring, rather than emphasizing a complex relation of conforming architecture to terrain.

evidence: Left side and lower middle: sloping banks, withered trees, and reeds can be seen extending along the waterside; a large area of unpainted space on the right represents the water surface, birds fly across the sky, and no clear built structures are seen in the entire painting.
distinction: The painting lacks built entities; it is only with difficulty assigned to C1 on the basis of the natural layout of the sloping bank conforming to the waterside.

evidence: Left side and lower middle: multiple boats are moored alongside the sloping bank with mangrove trees and at the water's edge; the boat bodies form a close dependent relation with the shoreline and water surface. | Right side: house buildings sit on the sloping bank beside the water, surrounded by trees, with the building sites matching the terrain.
distinction: Although the boats and houses indicate the theme of 'Night Mooring' (C3), the painting more prominently presents how these built elements are placed according to natural terrain such as the waterside and sloping platforms (C1).

evidence: Right side of the painting: a thatched hut is visible, its roof and part of its walls screened by pine trees and mixed trees in front, with a bamboo fence enclosing the area in front of the house. | Inside the thatched hut on the right side of the painting: through gaps in the trees and the fence gate, a person can be seen standing leaning against the door, presenting spatial layers of alternating concealment and revelation.
distinction: The painting mainly constructs spatial layers through the screening and revealing of the thatched hut by trees; no obvious clues of layout according to terrain or path guidance are seen.

evidence: Right hillside: a multi-story pagoda stands high on the hillside; the lower half of the pagoda body is screened by pine trees and shrubs in the foreground, revealing only the upper half and the top of the pagoda. | Middle ground on the right: dense woodland is distributed around and in front of the pagoda, forming spatial layers in which the building is hidden within the forest.
distinction: Although the pagoda indicates the scenery of the right hillside, its clear relation of screening and revealing with the foreground woodland (concealment and revelation forming the scene) is more prominent in the painting, so C2 is more apt than C3.

evidence: Middle ground on the right: a pavilion-type built structure can be seen sitting on a mountain rock platform, surrounded by trees. | Right side of the painting: the built structure is situated in the open face formed by mountains, rocks, and woodland, indicating the scenery of the landscape there.
distinction: Although the built structure is screened by trees, its role as a marker and visual focus of the open face on the right side of the painting is more prominent, so C3 is more apt than C2.

evidence: Whole painting: distant mountains, middle-ground woodland and foreground banks and streams are shown; no clear traces of buildings, bridges or paths are visible. | Lower left: the inscription 'Cloud Bands over Lianxi Stream' and a signature are visible, but there are no related built elements in the image.
distinction: No built elements are present, so the closest category is assigned on the basis of the visible natural configuration of the landscape as a whole.

evidence: Right side: the roof and walls of a group of buildings are partly screened by dense trees (including bamboo and broadleaf trees), presenting layers of seeing houses within the forest. | Middle ground: a small pavilion or hut is surrounded by trees, with a person nearby sweeping fallen leaves, and the building appears indistinct among the woodland. | Left side: mountains, rocks, and woods form the background and create a front-to-back spatial relation with the screened buildings on the right.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed according to the terrain, the painting places more emphasis on the screening and revealing of the buildings by trees, forming spatial layers of alternating concealment and revelation, so C2 is more apt than C1.

evidence: Lower-left and lower-central bank: several thatched cottages or sheds are placed close to the waterside and sloping ground, with figures nearby. | River and bank on the right: a small boat carrying people heads toward the bank, where figures stand or walk, forming a clear ferry-landing scene and approach route. | Lower left: the inscription 'Evening Crossing by a Country Ferry' identifies the theme of a ferry landing and boating, reinforcing the sense of spatial transition and arrival.
distinction: Although the buildings stand beside the water, the central spatial organization is the relation of approach and transition created by the boat reaching the bank and the movement of figures, rather than siting in response to the terrain alone.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: a pavilion is surrounded by pines and mixed trees, revealing only its pyramidal roof and part of its columns, presenting the form of a house hidden within the forest. | Center of the painting: dense branches and foliage clearly screen the pavilion, placing the built structure in spatial layers of being half hidden and half revealed.
distinction: Although the pavilion is located in the mountain forest, its most distinctive spatial feature is the layers of concealment and revelation formed by screening by trees, rather than simply serving as a conspicuous landmark.

evidence: Bottom center, slightly left: the roof outline of a built structure can be seen, partly screened by trees and mountain rocks in front, presenting a relation of concealment and revelation.
distinction: The painting mainly presents the layers of built structures screened by woodland and mountain rocks, rather than emphasizing their layout according to the mountains.

evidence: Center-left of the painting: between mountain rocks and pines, the roof and red eaves of a building are revealed, while the main body of the building is screened by mountains, rocks, and woodland. | Middle ground of the painting: the building is hidden behind peaks and groves, its presence suggested by partial revelation, forming spatial layers of screening from front to back.
distinction: Although the building indicates the scenery of a mountain temple, its most prominent compositional method in the painting is forming layers through screening and revealing by woodland and mountain rocks, so C2 is more apt than C3.

evidence: Lower center: a thatched pavilion can be seen, with two people seated facing each other inside; the pavilion body is surrounded and half screened by the dense trunks of the surrounding woods. | Lower middle of the painting: the built structure (thatched pavilion) is deep within the woodland, forming a relation of concealment and revelation through the screening of trees, presenting spatial layers hidden under the forest.
distinction: Although the thatched pavilion indicates the scenery beneath the trees, the painting more prominently highlights the surrounding and half-screening relation of the trees to the pavilion, rather than its simply serving as a visual focus marking the scenery.

evidence: Whole painting: the composition consists mainly of old trees, sloping banks, grasses and birds flying in the sky; no human-built features such as buildings, bridges or roads are visible. | Left side: the inscription 'Ancient Trees and Circling Crows' identifies the natural subject: a scene of old trees and returning crows.
distinction: Only natural features are depicted, with no built elements involved, so no clear category of spatial expression is supported; the old trees and flock of crows simply identify the scene.

evidence: Lower center of the painting, slightly left: a small canopied boat is on the water surface, the top of the canopy covered in white, consistent with the snowy tones of the surroundings. | Lower part of the painting: the small boat is located between the open water and the foreground mountain rocks on the right, forming a visual anchor point on the empty river surface. | Lower right of the painting: the boat's hull is near the rocks at the bank, but it mainly appears as an isolated element on the river surface, concentrating the mood of the snowy river.
distinction: Although the boat is moored at the waterside, its position on the empty river surface mainly serves to concentrate the scenery and indicate the river landscape, rather than emphasizing a complex terrain-responsive correspondence between built layout and terrain.

evidence: Left to center: groups of houses are placed in staggered fashion on terraces according to the mountain slopes, rising and falling, with building sites fitting closely to the terrain. | Right: a bridge is visible crossing a stream, with figures active on the bank, but the overall layout of the village still mainly conforms to the sloping ground.
distinction: The placement of village buildings in accordance with the mountain terrain runs through the main body of the painting and is more dominant than the localized bridge and path on the right.

evidence: Lower center, slightly right: the main building is surrounded by a large expanse of flowering trees, with only part of the roof, walls, and one open window revealed. | Lower center: the branches and blossoms of the trees form a screen in front of the building, revealing parts of it through gaps in the foliage, creating layers of concealment and revelation. | Right side and above: the building is backed by mountains and rocks, which together with the trees form the natural setting that screens the building.
distinction: Although the building is sited against mountains and rocks, the most prominent spatial expression in the painting is the building presented through the screening and revealing of trees; the concealment-and-revelation relationship dominates the composition.

evidence: Upper center and left: the building sites are stacked in layers, with a row of crenellated city-wall battlements visible extending on the left; the buildings are placed against the elevated platform/city wall terrain, presenting a layout of houses set upon a platform. | From the lower part to the center of the painting: the dense pines below and the buildings above are separated by a large expanse of cloud mist/unpainted space, forming high and low spatial layers and suggesting that the buildings stand on an elevated slope terrace or city wall.
distinction: Although the buildings occupy a visually high position and are identifiable, their clear connection with the crenellated wall on the left and the tiered platforms more directly embodies the spatial characteristic of being sited according to the site (elevated platform/city wall), rather than serving merely as scenic accents.

evidence: Lower center: a group of figures (leading an ox, riding a horse, carrying banners, etc.) is visible moving across open countryside, forming a lateral travel thread. | Whole painting: the painting consists of trees in the foreground, the moving procession in the middle ground, and gentle mountains in the distance; no clear built elements such as houses, bridges, or pavilions are seen.
distinction: No built elements are visible in the painting, only the route of the figures' movement; on the basis of the overall spatial organization it is only marginally assigned to the category representing the process of movement through the landscape.

evidence: Middle ground and right: a large number of houses are arranged along the shoreline, with dense wooden piles painted beneath them, showing buildings extending along the water following the bank, forming waterside pavilions or stilted houses. | Upper distance: houses are distributed in staggered fashion according to the slope, rising and falling in layers, presenting a layout set out according to the slope and corresponding to the terrain behind. | Lower-left foreground: houses are placed against earthen slopes and trees, with a stepped path on the left connecting the sloping bank and the buildings, showing the combination of building sites with the sloping terrain.
distinction: Although a path in the lower-left corner hints at entry, the overall composition mainly displays the settlement form of the building group distributed along the waterside and slopes (market streets and lanes); the terrain-responsive siting (following the bank, relying on the slope) is more dominant than the movement thread.

evidence: Center-right: thatched huts and haystacks are partly screened by the trunks and branches of several trees, with roofs and walls appearing and disappearing. | Center, slightly lower: figures are active in the open space between the trees and the houses, showing spatial layers of concealment and revelation. | Overall: the building group is scattered among the woods, forming spatial layers through the screening and revealing of the trees.
distinction: Although the buildings are located on sloping ground, their main compositional role lies in the screening relationship with the trees, rather than emphasizing terrain-responsive placement according to the rise and fall of the land.

evidence: Lower left to center: paddy fields and field ridges distributed according to the water and sloping ground are visible, along with figures wearing conical hats at work; no clear houses or buildings are seen. | Center to the right bank: willows grow on the sloping waterside, and one person sits beneath a tree; no visible man-made structures or path-connecting facilities.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built elements; on the basis of the overall visible organization of sloping banks and paddy-field space, it is provisionally assigned to the closest category.

evidence: Left center and center: two houses are partly screened by the trunks and crowns of deciduous trees; through the branches, roofs, eaves, and figures active inside the houses are visible, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Lower-right corner: a pavilion or open hall is screened by the branches and leaves of pines, with only part of the roof and the figures inside revealed, presenting spatial layers of houses seen among the woods.
distinction: The painting mainly emphasizes the screening and revealing relationship between buildings and trees to form the scene, rather than highlighting terrain-responsive siting of buildings against the mountains.

evidence: Lower-left corner: a plank bridge is visible crossing the water, with pedestrians on the bridge connecting the paths on both banks. | Lower center: three figures walk along a small path, heading toward the built elements on the right. | Lower-right corner: a house (built element) stands beside trees, forming an accessible spatial connection with the bridge, path, and figures.
distinction: Although the house is partly screened by trees, the core of the painting lies in the movement through the landscape in which the plank bridge and small path lead the figures toward the built elements, rather than simply emphasizing layers of screening.

evidence: Lower-right corner: a gate tower and enclosing wall are visible, with the gate leaves open, forming a visual entrance and boundary into the courtyard. | Center of the painting: the courtyard space unfolds inside the wall, with figures standing in the courtyard, connecting the entrance with the building on the left and presenting spatial depth. | Left: figures sit together inside the open hall building, which serves as the deep scene of the spatial sequence and echoes the entrance.
distinction: Although there are waterside and trees in the painting, the entrance formed by the gate tower and enclosing wall and the depth relationship of the courtyard are more dominant, emphasizing the spatial process of entering and arriving rather than mere conformity to terrain.

evidence: Lower center: a thatched pavilion is built overlooking the water, its site close to the bank or extending over the water surface, presenting a layout extending along the bank and corresponding to the inscription 'overlooking the stream.' | Left: the house group is placed against the foot of the mountain and the edge of the woods, with roofs staggered, showing a relationship of being set out according to the slope and arranged according to the ground. | Right: houses are placed against mountains, rocks, and the roots of trees, closely integrated with the natural terrain.
distinction: Although trees screen the houses in the painting (concealment and revelation), the built elements (thatched pavilion, house group) are mainly laid out according to the waterside and the mountain foot (terrain-responsive), and the thatched pavilion as the visual center is not heavily screened, so terrain-responsive siting is more dominant.

evidence: Lower right: a wooden plank bridge crosses the stream, with a cowherd leading a water buffalo across the bridge, forming a clear passage route. | Whole painting: the bridge connects the two banks, guiding the eye and movement from the grassland on the right across the bridge to the waterside on the left, presenting an accessible, traversable spatial process.
distinction: The painting centers on the bridge and the action of crossing, highlighting the spatial connection of passage and entry; no other significant built elements participate in the composition.

evidence: Lower right: a wooden bridge crosses the water, with two people carrying staffs crossing it, forming a clear thread of movement through the landscape. | Left center: the roof and posts of a thatched pavilion emerge from a bamboo grove, screened among the trees. | Overall: the bridge, stream, and sloping bank guide the eye from the lower right toward the depths of the bamboo grove on the left, presenting an accessible spatial process.
distinction: Although the thatched pavilion is screened, the painting emphasizes the spatial process of entry and movement through the bridge and the figures' movement lines.

evidence: Lower-left corner: thatched huts are visible, situated beside a sloping bank surrounded by trees, with level ground or traces of a path in front. | At the stream in the center of the painting: a small bridge crosses the water, connecting the built-up area on the left bank with the peach-blossom, mountain-and-rock area on the right bank. | Overall composition: the stream and bridge link the residential area on the left with the depths of the peach-blossom grove on the right, presenting a spatial process of moving from here to there and turning into the depths.
distinction: Although trees screen the houses (C2 characteristic), the small bridge crossing the stream together with the built elements constructs a clear travel route, making spatial connectivity (C4) the dominant factor organizing the painting.

evidence: Lower center of the painting: there is a small bridge, on which a person is walking toward the built elements in the depths of the painting, forming a clear entry route. | Center, slightly right: several thatched huts are arranged in staggered fashion on level ground, connected to the bridge route in the foreground by the water surface and shoreline, presenting an accessible spatial relationship. | Right side: mountains and trees surround the built elements but do not completely screen them; the path and water surface maintain spatial connectivity.
distinction: Although trees surround the thatched huts in the painting, the presence of the bridge and pedestrians emphasizes the accessible, traversable spatial process rather than mere layers of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Right middle ground: a group of buildings is placed at the foot of the mountain, with an arched bridge in front connecting the two banks and pedestrians on the bridge, presenting a clear entry route. | Water surface at the bottom of the painting: a small boat travels on the water, suggesting that the area can also be reached by water, reinforcing the traversability of the space.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited against the mountain and beside the water, the painting emphasizes the spatial process of entering the place by bridge and boat rather than mere adaptation to terrain.

evidence: Right mountainside: buildings are half-hidden behind mountains, rocks, and trees, with only part of the roofs and walls revealed, forming layers of concealment and revelation. | Lower-right corner: the building group is partly screened by the branches and leaves of foreground trees, presenting a spatial relationship of houses seen among the woods. | Left distant bank: buildings along the waterside alternate with trees, screened at the edge of the woods.
distinction: Although there are paths and pedestrians in the painting, the built elements mainly construct spatial layers through screening and revealing by mountains, rocks, and trees, rather than emphasizing entry route clues.

evidence: Upper center: the roofs, walls, doors, and windows of the courtyard buildings are partly screened by the trunks and branches of the surrounding tall pines, presenting spatial layers in which parts of the buildings are revealed amid the screening of the woods. | Right: dense tree trunks are arranged in front of and beside the buildings, reinforcing the visual effect that the buildings are deeply hidden in the woods.
distinction: Although the buildings stand on level ground, the painting mainly organizes space through the screening and revealing of the buildings by trees, rather than emphasizing their placement in relation to specific terrain or waterside.

evidence: Left: house buildings are screened by dense willows, with only roofs and part of a fence revealed, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship of houses seen in the woods. | Lower center: a fishing hut is set up among the grasses on the waterside, with willow branches hanging down over and around it, screening it together with the trees. | Overall: willows are distributed along the bank, and the built elements (houses, fishing hut) all stand within or at the edge of the grove, forming spatial layers through the screening of the trees.
distinction: Although the built elements are arranged along the waterside, the painting more strongly emphasizes the screening and revealing of the houses and fishing hut by dense willows; the concealment-and-revelation relationship plays a more prominent role in forming the scene.

evidence: Lower right: the roofs and walls of a group of built elements emerge from behind blooming pink flower trees and mountains and rocks, forming clear layers of concealment and revelation. | Lower left: a small amount of built elements along the waterside is partly screened by foreground trees and the sloping bank.
distinction: Although the built elements are sited against the waterside and mountains and rocks, the painting mainly constructs spatial layers through the screening and revealing by flowering trees and rocks; the feature of concealment and revelation forming the scene is more prominent.

evidence: Water surface below: a small boat carrying two people is heading toward the right bank, forming a clear thread of movement through the landscape. | Right bank: several thatched huts are visible, with a path or steps on the bank suggesting that one can land and enter. | Lower-left corner: a pavilion is built on a stone platform by the water, serving as a stopping point along the waterside.
distinction: Although the thatched huts on the right are screened by trees, the boat's route in the lower part of the painting more strongly emphasizes the spatial process of approaching and entering the built elements, so C4 is more dominant than C2.

evidence: Upper-left corner: a group of village houses is partly screened by the branches and leaves of trees, with roofs and walls showing a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Lower center: an open pavilion-house is markedly screened by the trunk and crown of a large tree, with several people active in front of the tree. | Left: a plank bridge crosses the stream, connecting the two banks and leading to the sloping ground and village houses in the distance.
distinction: Although a plank bridge provides a route in the painting, the marked screening of several built elements by trees and the concealment-and-revelation relationship constitute the more dominant spatial layers and visual focus.

evidence: Lower left: a group of people carrying loads on shoulder poles proceeds to the right along a small path or bridge, forming a clear thread of movement through the landscape pointing toward the right side of the painting. | Right middle ground: a gate-tower structure is set up in front of the built elements (houses), with one person standing inside the gate, suggesting a relationship of entering the built elements from here. | Center to right: the path goes around the base of the tall tree in the center and leads to the built elements on the right, presenting a spatial process of approaching from outside and entering.
distinction: Although the built elements are partly screened by trees (C2), the painting, through the figures' route and the gate-tower structure, more strongly emphasizes the spatial process of approaching and entering the built elements from outside (C4).

evidence: Left: house buildings are partly screened by foreground dead trees and a bamboo grove, revealing roofs, eaves, and parts of walls, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Left center: the bamboo grove and tree trunks form a visual screen in front of the buildings, giving the buildings spatial layers of being in the woods and seen as a screened scene.
distinction: Although figures are in front of the buildings in the painting, there are no clear movement threads such as bridges, paths, or gates leading into the buildings; the buildings are composed mainly through the screening and revealing by vegetation.

evidence: Upper center: several thatched huts are surrounded by dead trees, whose trunks and branches screen part of the roofs and walls, forming layers of foreground-background screening; the exposed eaves and windows indicate the presence of the buildings. | Left: a thick tree trunk stands in front of the houses, screening a corner of the building on the left, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship between foreground trees and middle-ground buildings. | Right: a double trunk stands to the right front of the buildings, forming spatial layers of houses seen through a screened scene with the houses behind.
distinction: Although stepping stones in the foreground hint at a path (C4 clue), the screening relationship between the buildings and trees in the upper half of the painting is denser, constituting the main spatial layers and compositional method.

evidence: Left and center: thatched huts stand among tall pines, with the trunks and branches of foreground pines screening part of the roofs and walls, forming layers of houses seen in the woods. | Behind and beside the thatched huts: a bamboo grove is painted behind the huts, wrapping the built elements together with the pines and enhancing the sense of screening. | Front of the thatched huts: the doors and windows are open, revealing figures seated inside, contrasting concealment and revelation with the external screening by trees.
distinction: Although figures on the right side of the painting walk toward the thatched huts, suggesting a process of approach, no clear path is depicted, while the screening and revealing of the built elements by pines and bamboo is more prominent in the composition, constituting the main spatial layers.

evidence: Lower right to lower center: houses are partly screened by several foreground dead trees; through gaps in the branches, roofs, eaves, walls, and figures inside windows are visible, forming clear layers of concealment and revelation. | Upper-left corner: on distant sloping ground there are two haystacks or small huts covered in snow, echoing the near houses at a distance.
distinction: Although the houses are within the scene, the core of their composition lies in the screening and revealing of them by trees, rather than serving merely as markers identifying the landscape.

evidence: Left center of the painting: a thatched hut is half-enclosed by a thick large tree on the left and extending plum branches on the right, with the eaves and part of the walls screened by branches and leaves. | Inside the thatched hut: through the open doors and windows, figures can be seen sitting around a stove, forming spatial layers revealed after being screened by natural scenery. | Behind the thatched hut: mountains, rocks, and more trees serve as background, further wrapping the building in the natural environment.
distinction: Although the building is sited against the terrain, the painting more strongly emphasizes the screening and revealing relationship between the branches and leaves of trees and the building, with concealment and revelation forming the scene as the dominant feature.

evidence: Left side of the painting: the thatched-hut building is partly screened by the trunks and branches of several large foreground trees, revealing only the roof, part of the walls, and the table inside, forming a clear concealment-and-revelation relationship and spatial layers. | Center and left of the painting: trees serve as foreground and middle ground, separating the buildings behind from the figures' activity in front; the revealing of the buildings depends on gaps between the trees, embodying the feature of forming the scene through screening by woods.
distinction: Although the building stands on level ground among the woods, the painting more strongly emphasizes the screening and revealing relationship of trees to the building to create layers, rather than highlighting the terrain-responsive placement of the building in relation to slopes and banks.

evidence: Right: a long bridge crosses the water connecting the two banks, with a pavilion-like structure at the bridge end, constituting clear passage and entry clues. | Water surface in the lower center: a boat is moored in the water beside houses on the bank, suggesting a ferry-crossing relationship of reaching the built elements by water. | Left and central shoreline: houses are distributed against the mountain and beside the water, linked in sequence by the shoreline, bridge, and boats, presenting a spatial organization of movement through the landscape from here to there.
distinction: Although the houses sited against the mountain and beside the water embody terrain-responsive siting, the movement thread formed by the bridge and boats is more prominent in the painting, dominating the accessibility of the space.

evidence: Lower left and center-right bank: several small boats with canopied tops are visible, moored or tied at the water's edge screened by willow trees, serving as scenic accent elements. | Distant view: gently sloping distant mountains and a broad water surface form an open space, and the boats indicate the mooring place at the waterside.
distinction: The painting contains only moored boats, with no discernible paths, bridges, or clear access connections, so it does not belong to access to secluded settings; rather, the boats indicate the waterside scenery.

evidence: Lower left: a small bridge spans the stream, connecting the two banks; beneath the bridge, flowing water and bridge piers are visible, presenting a traversable movement-through-the-landscape cue. | Center-left: a group of red-roofed buildings sits in a mountain hollow, partly screened by trees, with a path or open ground in front implying accessibility. | Lower right: densely distributed dwellings in the valley, with houses staggered along the mountain contours, among which winding paths are visible, implying the possibility of deeper excursion.
distinction: Although trees screen the buildings, the bridge, stream, and mountain paths together form clear cues for entry and excursion, making the spatial process of access to secluded settings more prominent.

evidence: Lower left to center: a wooden bridge crosses a stone-strewn water surface (or tidal flat), connecting the sloping bank with the foreground trees to the flat ground with the midground houses, forming a clear entry path. | Right: a pavilion is built on a waterside terrace, with steps beside it extending down to the rocky shore, providing a cue of waterside accessibility. | Center and right: the houses and pavilion serve as linking points for movement cues such as the bridge and steps, presenting a spatial relationship of passage from one place to another and of accessibility.
distinction: Although pines and bamboo screen the buildings (e.g., tree trunks obscuring the building bodies), the movement path formed by the bridge and steps more clearly organizes the spatial entry and connectivity between the foreground and the built elements.

evidence: Lower right: an arched bridge spans the river, connecting the two banks and guiding the eye toward the group of houses behind the woods on the opposite bank. | Lower left: two people walk along a dirt road; a fenced gate stands ahead, and the path leads directly to cottages screened by trees. | Center-right and distant view: cottages are distributed with mountains behind and water in front, connected to the foreground through the shoreline, bridges, and implied paths.
distinction: Although the houses are sited with mountains behind and water in front (consistent with C1 features), the bridge, paths, and fenced gate in the painting form clear movement cues that guide the figures and the viewer's gaze into the built area; C4 better captures this spatial process of passage from one place to another.

evidence: Lower left to lower center: houses are staggered along the sloping ground, with a stone arched gate/bridge opening visible on the left, and the building bases follow the sloping terrace terrain. | Right: a pavilion is built atop the projecting promontory, and a waterside pavilion is built at the water's edge below, presenting a layout that sits against the rock, faces the water, and unfolds along the bank. | Overall foreground: the building group extends naturally along the waterside and sloping ground, rising and falling in height, forming a clear correspondence with the terrain.
distinction: Although the promontory pavilion on the right serves as a scenic accent, the building group as a whole mainly presents a terrain-responsive arrangement along slopes, against the promontory, and following the bank, so C1 better captures its dominant compositional mode.

evidence: Right-side water surface: a wooden bridge spans the water, connecting the two banks and providing a clear path across the water to the built elements on the opposite bank. | Left and central sloping ground: houses are sited against terraces and trees, with open water in front and hills behind, forming together with the bridge a spatial organization that is enterable and traversable.
distinction: The presence of the bridge strongly implies a spatial process of crossing and entry, making access to secluded settings the dominant expression, beyond mere terrain-responsive siting.

evidence: Upper center of the painting: a group of red-walled buildings is nestled among the mountains, partly obscured by the rocks and trees in front, with only roofs and parts of walls exposed, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Center-left of the painting: a building is half-hidden behind rocky slopes and sparse woods, its eaves partly revealed through the screening trees. | Lower right of the painting: a building at the waterside is partly obscured by the foliage of red-leafed trees in the foreground, forming foreground-background layering.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited according to the mountain contours, the painting places greater emphasis on the screening and revealing of buildings by mountains, rocks, and trees, constructing spatial layering through concealment and revelation, so C2 is more apt.

evidence: Midground right: a group of red-walled buildings (possibly a temple) is partly screened by pines and slope rocks in front, with only parts of roofs and walls exposed, forming layers of concealment and revelation | Right waterside: village houses are screened among groves and sloping ground, presenting a spatial relationship of seeing houses through intervening scenery | Midground left at the mountain foot: a pavilion appears faintly among pines and rocks, its presence revealed through the screening trees
distinction: Although there is a wooden bridge at the lower part of the painting, it does not directly connect to the main building group; the dominant compositional role is still the layering of concealment and revelation formed by the built elements screened by trees and rocks, rather than a clear movement route of entry.

evidence: Lower center to center of the painting: a winding path (or stream) extends upward from the bottom of the painting, passes through the valley, and leads directly to the building group on the mountainside. | Center of the painting, mountainside: a group of red-walled buildings is sited according to the mountain contours, serving as the terminus of the path's guidance, presenting a spatial relationship of accessibility. | Right of the painting, cliff top: a pavilion is set on the cliff top, likewise at a high point of the mountain terrain, echoing the overall mountain scenery.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited according to the mountain contours (C1), the clear path in the painting guides the viewer's gaze and excursion route into the mountain buildings, emphasizing the spatial process of being enterable and accessible, so C4 is more dominant.

evidence: Lower left: a hexagonal pavilion stands on the waterside sloping bank, its body partly obscured by plum branches in front, and two people are visible sitting facing each other inside. | Lower right, slightly toward center: a group of houses on the mountainside, their roofs and walls half-screened by dense plum branches around them, presenting layering of houses hidden in the woods. | Right: mountain rock faces interweave with the plum grove, and buildings recede among the rocks and flowering trees, with concealment and revelation participating in the composition.
distinction: Although the pavilion marks a waterside viewing node, the layered, interwoven relationships of partial screening and concealment and revelation among the buildings, the plum grove, and the rocks are more pervasive and dominant in the painting.

evidence: Right and lower center: a large stand of willow trees, with luxuriant branches and foliage, forms clear tree screening and spatial layering. | Lower center waterside: a lone figure sits fishing at the water's edge, facing the open water to the left, with no houses or other built elements visible. | Left and distant view: open water and continuous distant mountains form a contrast of opening and closing with the near-ground willow grove.
distinction: The painting has no built elements, only figures as scenic accents; it is classified as C2 because the screening of the willow grove constitutes the main spatial layering, whereas C3 usually refers to buildings accentuating scenery.

evidence: Right of the painting: a group of buildings is built at the water's edge, with a waterside pavilion in front whose base is supported by wooden piles standing directly on the lotus-covered water surface, connected behind to houses on land, presenting a layout sited according to the water conditions. | Left and background of the painting: willows, sloping banks, and distant mountains on the left, with open water; the built elements unfold close to the waterside, forming a clear correspondence with the natural terrain.
distinction: Although the buildings accentuate the waterscape, their placement according to the waterside terrain, rising over the water on wooden piles, is the most core and specific spatial organization in the painting, so C1 is more apt than C3.

evidence: Center-left: a white-walled, black-tiled house is extensively obscured by dense bamboo leaves, exposing only the roof, parts of the walls, and figures inside the windows, presenting a typical layering of a house hidden in the woods. | Lower left: the enclosing wall and gatehouse below the house are screened by dense bamboo stalks and foliage in the foreground, forming obvious foreground-background depth and concealment-and-revelation relationships. | Whole painting: the main subject is covered by the dense shade of myriad bamboos, and the built elements are fully merged into the screening of the bamboo grove, establishing their spatial position through the screening of natural scenery.
distinction: Although the bridge and pedestrians at the lower right imply movement cues, the built element (the bamboo house) is mainly deeply screened by the dense bamboo grove, and the static spatial layering of concealment and revelation is more dominant than the dynamic path of access to secluded settings.

evidence: Left: a high cliff with a flying waterfall pouring down, grand in momentum, is the core scenery of the painting | Lower right: three figures stand on rocky sloping ground gazing into the distance, their line of sight directed toward the waterfall | Overall: no clear houses, bridges, or other built structures are visible; the scenery is indicated mainly through the figures and the forms of the mountains and rocks
distinction: The painting has no clear built elements and indicates the waterfall scenery mainly through the positions of the figures and the forms of the landscape, so it is classified as C3.

evidence: Lower left and lower center: thatched huts/fishermen's dwellings stand at the waterside, supported by wooden piles and built among the reeds at the water's edge, with their bases directly corresponding to the water surface and bank slope. | Midground right: another small built structure at the waterside, likewise set facing the water and unfolding along the shoreline.
distinction: The built elements mainly present a siting relationship of resting on the water and bank, rather than serving merely as isolated markers indicating a particular landscape.

evidence: Center-left of the painting: two houses are surrounded by several tall trees, their roofs, eaves, and walls revealed through gaps between trunks and foliage. | Slightly left of center: furniture is visible inside an open house, with two people standing in front; the house forms layered screening with the surrounding trees and the lake rocks on the left.
distinction: Although the houses are built on flat ground, the painting organizes the spatial layering of the built elements mainly through the screening and revealing by trees, rather than emphasizing their siting relationship to specific terrain (such as terraces or waterside).

evidence: Upper center, slightly right: a pavilion sits on rocks, surrounded by red-leafed trees. | Upper center, slightly right: part of the pavilion's structure is obscured by branches and leaves in front, forming an obvious concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Center of the painting: the pavilion, together with the surrounding rocks and trees, forms a spatial unit with foreground-background layering.
distinction: The pavilion indeed accentuates a spot of scenery in the mountains, but the composition places greater emphasis on its layered concealment and revelation among the trees and rocks.

evidence: Lower center of the painting: a courtyard building group is partly obscured by several tall trees, exposing roofs, walls, and doors and windows, forming layering of seeing houses in the woods. | Lower right of the painting: Taihu rocks and a small gatehouse stand to the right of the buildings, with branches and foliage screening the edges of the buildings.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited at the mountain foot, the painting places greater emphasis on the screening and revealing of the buildings by trees, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship dominates the spatial expression.

evidence: Center-left: a group of multi-story pavilions, terraces, and courtyard walls sits at the junction of sloping ground and waterside at the mountain foot, arranged in staggered heights following the terrain. | Center-left to center: the building bases and manner of unfolding cling to the edge of the mountain body, forming a clear relationship of resting against the mountain and beside the water with the water ripples. | Lower right: a mounted procession advances along the waterside, helping to set off the built elements' spatial position at the land-water boundary.
distinction: Although there is a travel route at the lower part of the painting, the core compositional role of the building group itself lies in its terrain-responsive arrangement along the mountain forms and waterside, rather than emphasizing the excursion process of entering the buildings.

evidence: Lower left: a wooden bridge spans the water surface or valley, with a figure carrying a shoulder pole walking on it, forming a clear route of travel. | Lower right: the roof, eave columns, and walls of a built structure appear through screening trees, with figures active inside; it is the destination toward which the route points. | Lower center of the painting: the bridge and the built structure on the right are connected through the waterside and sloping ground, presenting a spatial process of entering the setting from the bridge and approaching the built elements.
distinction: Although the built structure at the lower right has a concealment-and-revelation relationship with the screening trees, the bridge and the figures' movement line at the lower left clearly construct the excursion process leading to the built elements, and the sense of spatial entry is more prominent.

evidence: Lower left side: a multi-story pavilion and an extending platform are visible, the platform fitted with railings and several people standing on it, with the building bases arranged in layers against the rocky sloping bank on the left. | Left cliff: the built elements cling to the mountain terrain, and the staggered heights of the pavilions and platforms echo the form of the mountain body, presenting a layout of houses set against the cliff and built according to the terrain.
distinction: Although the built elements are one of the visual foci of the painting, their layered arrangement against the cliff and sloping bank, with platforms extending according to the terrain, more prominently reflects the close correspondence between buildings and topographic conditions, so C1 is more apt than C3.

evidence: Lower left: a city-gate-type built structure is visible, with a path extending below it, and several figures walking along the path, forming a clear movement line of entry and excursion. | Center-left waterside: a row of waterside pavilions unfolds along the shoreline, their bases supported over the water by wooden piles, presenting a layout that follows the bank. | Left mountainside: the roof of a house appears amid screening rocks and trees, presenting a layered relationship of partial concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although there are several built elements sited with mountains behind and water in front, the city gate below and the path along which the figures walk constitute the most conspicuous spatial cue of entry and excursion, governing the painting's sense of movement.

evidence: Lower center: a stone-step path and several pedestrians are visible, presenting a movement-through-the-landscape cue of entering the mountains along the path | Whole painting: the main subject is mountain peaks, clouds and mist, and trees; no houses, pavilions, or other clear built elements are visible
distinction: The painting lacks clear buildings, and only paths and figures' movement cues are visible, so it is classified as C4 based on the sense of spatial entry.

evidence: Lower right: a thatched hut is partly obscured by the withered tree on the right and the dense trees on the left, with its roof and eaves exposed. | Lower right: tall fantastical rocks stand behind the thatched hut, further constituting spatial layering in which the built element is screened by natural scenery. | Lower right: several people are active in front of the house, in the open ground between the trees and the built element, reinforcing the depth between concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the built element rests on flat ground, the core compositional mode of the painting is to present the layering of the thatched hut through the screening and revealing by the surrounding trees and fantastical rocks, rather than emphasizing its terrain-responsive relationship to the mountain.

evidence: Lower center: several people sit together inside an open thatched hut (or pavilion), which is partly obscured by the withered tree on the left and the trees and bamboo clumps on the right, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Foreground and both sides: rocks in the foreground and trees on both sides surround the built element, forming spatial layering and placing the built element amid the screening of trees and rocks.
distinction: Although the built element rests against the terrain, the painting places greater emphasis on its layered relationship of being screened and revealed by trees and rocks, and the role of concealment and revelation is more prominent.

evidence: Lower right corner: two people walk along a small path, with a small bridge beside them connecting the two banks, forming a clear entry path. | Center-right: several houses appear amid screening trees; they are the destination guided by the path and bridge. | Overall composition: the small bridge and the figures' walking path direct the viewer's gaze toward the built elements in the center, presenting a spatial process of passage from one place to another.
distinction: Although the houses are screened by trees, the entry relationship formed by the small bridge and the figures' path is clearer and more dominant.

evidence: Lower left: a wooden bridge spanning the water surface is visible, with two people walking on it, forming a clear cue of entry and transition. | Right: a winding stone-step path extends upward along the hillside, with a figure carrying a shoulder pole beside it, expressing the spatial process of advancing along the path. | Center-left and upper right: a village building group enclosed by fences on the left, and an isolated thatched hut on the upper right hillside, serving as destinations or waypoints along the path.
distinction: Although the village is sited with mountains behind and water in front, the movement cues formed by the bridge, stone-step path, and figures' activity are more prominent and dominate the spatial organization of the painting.

evidence: Upper right: a pavilion is built on the waterside sloping ground, with wooden posts supporting it visible below, presenting a siting mode that follows the bank and rests on the terrace, responding to the water conditions and terrain. | Lower left: a courtyard building is arranged against a huge Taihu rock and enclosing walls, with its base closely fitting the form of the rocks. | Lower center and lower right: a hall and a thatched pavilion are respectively located in an open flat area and beside a plum grove, with the buildings scattered according to the opening and closing of the site and the distribution of vegetation.
distinction: Although there are buildings screened by trees in the painting (such as the small house at the upper left and the thatched pavilion at the lower right), the main buildings (the waterside pavilion at the upper right and the hall at the lower center) are clearly revealed and emphatically show their siting according to terrain conditions such as the waterside and rocks (e.g., on stilts, against rocks), so terrain-responsive siting (C1) is more dominant than concealment and revelation (C2).

evidence: Right: a thatched hut sits between trees and a bamboo grove, its roof and walls partly obscured by branches and foliage, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Inside the thatched hut on the right: several people are visible sitting together, seen through the open door and windows, indicating the presence of the built element and its interior space. | Left: the open water and distant mountains form a contrast, setting off the secluded layering of the thatched hut screened in the woods on the right.
distinction: Although the thatched hut is near the water, the painting places greater emphasis on its layered relationship of being screened and revealed by trees, rather than the correspondence between terrain and building layout.

evidence: Left: a two-story pavilion is partly obscured by pink flowering trees in the foreground and luxuriant trees in the midground, exposing only the roof, upper-story window frames, and lower-story doors, forming obvious spatial layering of concealment and revelation. | Center-left of the painting: branches and foliage interweave with the building, which recedes among the woods, its presence and level indicated through the screening and revealing by natural scenery.
distinction: Although the building is built against the sloping bank, the relationship of screening and revealing of the building by trees is more prominent in the composition and dominates the expression of spatial layering.

evidence: Right and left of the painting: a large stand of bamboo grove is visible distributed along the waterside, with bamboo roots scattered unevenly on the slope and bank. | Center and distance of the painting: the stream and sloping banks extend into the distance, presenting natural terrain contours and unpainted space on the water surface.
distinction: No identifiable man-made built structures appear in the painting; it is assigned to the closest category solely on the basis of the natural distribution of bamboo grove and stream banks.

evidence: Right side: a group of houses is visible, with an arched bridge in front; on the bridge are pedestrians holding umbrellas, forming clear circulation and entry cues connecting the bank with the buildings. | Waterside at center-right: a water pavilion is sited against the waterside, its base elevated above the water surface, adjoining the surrounding willow trees and sloping bank. | Overall composition: water surface, shoreline, bridge and houses together form spatial layers that can be traversed and reached, guiding the eye from the bridge into the setting.
distinction: Although the buildings are screened by trees, the combination of arched bridge and pedestrians more prominently expresses the spatial process of entering the built setting via a path, so C4 is more apt than C2.

evidence: Lower center of the painting: a wooden bridge spans the stream/channel, connecting the right bank slope with the farmland area at left/center, forming a clear crossing passage. | Lower right of the painting: a herd boy rides an ox along the grassy bank, his movement and position suggesting path cues toward the bridge or for movement along the waterside. | Middle ground of the painting: a farmer labors in the farmland; the bridge, as an artificial structure, spatially links the foreground bank slope with the middle-ground fields, presenting a relationship of passing from one to the other.
distinction: Although the bridge is placed in response to the waterside terrain, the herd boy's riding movement and the bridge together reinforce the spatial process of passage and entry, so C4 is more apt than C1, which merely denotes siting according to terrain.

evidence: Overall painting: the painting presents cloud-and-mist-wreathed mountains, with outlined cloud vapor at the bottom; no traces of houses, bridges or other built elements are visible. | Right main peak: the towering peak on the right stands out amid the sea of clouds, forming a visual focus, but there is no architectural accent.
distinction: The painting has no explicit built elements; based on the overall opening and closing of the landscape and the mountain form set off by clouds and mist, it is tentatively assigned to the landscape-organization logic of scenic accentuation, but architectural evidence is lacking.

evidence: Left side: a zigzag plank bridge/railing extends from the left bank into the water, forming a clear cue for a path onto the water surface. | Lower center and right bank: a pavilion is built on the water, supported by wooden piles, surrounded by lotus leaves, forming a reachable node for movement through the landscape. | Water surface at lower right: a boat carrying people moves among the lotus leaves, reinforcing the spatial process of traversing the water surface.
distinction: Although the structures are built against the water, the painting emphasizes more the process of entering the water space via the plank bridge and boats rather than mere placement according to terrain.

evidence: Lower left: houses are visible built on the waterside, supported underneath by wooden piles, sited in response to the waterside terrain, presenting the form of houses set against the bank. | Right side: a small wooden bridge is visible connecting the two banks, with pedestrians on it, and extensive farmland to the right.
distinction: Although the painting contains a bridge and path hints suggesting movement through the landscape, the terrain-responsive relationship of the houses at lower left sited against the waterside is more prominent and dominant.

evidence: Lower left: behind the trees a slender structure spanning the water is faintly visible, its form resembling a small bridge. | Center-right: several sailing boats are moored on the water near the bank-side trees, suggesting travel and mooring cues of a ferry crossing or anchorage.
distinction: The suspected bridge and boats suggest more the entry cues of travel and mooring (C4) rather than merely serving as a marker for a visual focus (C3).

evidence: Lower center of the painting: the pavilion stands in an open spot between the mountain rocks on the right and the water surface on the left, gathering the landscape space as a visual focus. | Inside the pavilion: a figure sits in the pavilion facing the water, making the built structure a marker for viewing and for identifying the scenery at the water's edge and mountain foot. | Right side: mountain rocks and trees serve as background foil, forming an opening-and-closing relationship with the open water at left, with the pavilion in between marking the scenic spot.
distinction: The pavilion primarily serves as a visual center marking the scenery at the landscape's opening (C3), rather than emphasizing a complex layout responsive to terrain (C1).

evidence: Lower right and lower center: thatch-roofed built structures (pavilion or house) are visible, their roofs and part of their structures screened by foreground willow and miscellaneous trees, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship of a house revealed within the grove. | Middle and far distance: mountain rocks, woods and clouds form multiple spatial layers; the built structures lie screened by foreground trees, forming foreground-background pictorial depth with the landscape behind.
distinction: Although the built structures mark the waterside scenery, the painting emphasizes more the spatial layers formed by the trees' screening and revealing of the built structures, so C2 is more apt than C3.

evidence: Lower right: a pavilion structure is screened within a dense pine grove, only its roof and part of its columns exposed, with several people visible inside, forming a clear concealment-and-revelation layering. | Lower center-left: beneath the rock cliff is a natural cave, in which two people sit facing each other, forming a spatial relationship of screening and revelation with the water and pine grove outside.
distinction: Although the building is set against mountain and water, the most prominent compositional device in the painting is the use of the pine grove's screening and revealing of the building to create spatial layers, rather than emphasizing a layout built in response to terrain.

evidence: Right side: the house structures are largely screened by dense willow trees and vegetation, only the roof, eaves and parts of the wooden framework exposed, presenting layers of a house seen within the grove. | Lower right to center: weeping willow branches hang down and interweave with the buildings, forming a rich screening effect that hides the buildings within the woodland.
distinction: The painting's focus is on the trees' screening and revealing of the buildings, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship, rather than mainly emphasizing the buildings as landmarks marking the scenery.

evidence: Waterside at lower center of the painting: a pavilion/water pavilion is built at the water's edge, its base and part of its structure screened by foreground trees and rocks, presenting a half-hidden, half-revealed state. | Slope platform at center of the painting: a pagoda stands on the slope, surrounded by trees, with the pagoda body and woodland forming a screening relationship. | Left side of the painting: roofs and walls of houses are faintly visible among the trees, screened by dense trees, forming deeply hidden layers.
distinction: Although the water pavilion built at the water's edge embodies siting according to terrain, the more prominent compositional device across the whole painting is the screening and revealing of multiple built structures by trees, rocks and mountains, forming rich spatial layers.

evidence: Lower center, slightly left: a boat with a canopy is moored by the waterside, with several people visible inside; the hull and canopy are partly screened by the thick foreground willow trunk and hanging branches, forming a clear concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Left side and upper part of the painting: dense bamboo grove and trees surround the boat, with branches and leaves interweaving before and behind it, giving the boat a spatial layer of being hidden beneath the grove at the water's edge.
distinction: Although the boat is the painting's visual focus, its concealment-and-revelation relationship of being heavily screened by branches and leaves (screening) is more dominant in the spatial organization than its serving merely as an isolated landmark marking the scenery.

evidence: Center-right of the painting: the main house structures are surrounded by trees, with roofs and walls revealed through trunks and branches, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Lower right of the painting: the roof of another structure emerges from behind trees and mountain rocks, further reinforcing the spatial layers of screening.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited at the waterside, the composition focuses more on the trees' screening and revealing of the buildings, with concealment and revelation as the dominant effect.

evidence: Lower left: the top of a small canopied boat emerges from reeds/grasses, the hull screened by the grasses, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Overall painting: distant mountains, clouds and mist, and the nearby willow trees and waterside form layers; the small boat is hidden among the bank-side grasses, presented through screening by natural scenery.

evidence: Lower right corner: an arched bridge connects the waterside with the land, with figures active on and near the bridge, forming a clue for entering the painting from the water-land junction. | Center and lower part of the painting: a street runs through the market, shops are arranged along the street, and figures come and go, forming a spatial path extending into the depths. | Upper left: the city gate is open, the city wall winds along the mountain forms, and the gate tower is located at a high point, with figures entering and exiting, suggesting a spatial transition from the market into the city or to higher ground.

evidence: Lower right corner: a moon gate and figures are visible, suggesting an entrance and the starting point of travel. | Lower middle: a small bridge with red railings spans the water, connecting the pavilions and paths on the two banks. | Among the mountains and rocks on the left: winding stone steps ascend along the mountain forms toward a pavilion at a high point, forming a clear climbing route.
