evidence: Lower center of the painting: an arched bridge can be seen spanning the water, with a figure walking along a path beside it, connecting the foreground with the mountains-and-rocks area of the middle ground. | Lower left corner: thatched huts are built on the waterside, with a small wooden bridge connecting the two banks, forming a movement-through-the-landscape cue unfolding along the shore. | Right side and lower right: courtyards and pavilions are distributed at the mountain foot and mid-slope, among which paths and steps are faintly visible, suggesting accessibility into the depths of the mountains.

distinction: Although pine trees partly obscure the buildings, the main bodies of the buildings are clearly visible, and what is chiefly expressed is the relationship of the buildings being placed in accordance with the mountain-and-rock terrain, rather than a dominance of concealment and revelation or partly screened effects.

evidence: Lower-middle waterside: a pavilion is built on a raised platform of level ground by the waterside, unfolding in conformity with the shoreline, with the building site corresponding in height to the water surface. | At the foot of the mountain on the right: houses are arranged at the foot of the mountain, backed by the hillside, their layout conforming to the mountain's form and the foot of the slope.
distinction: Although a bridge connects in the lower part of the painting, the built elements chiefly present a relationship of terrain-responsive siting by the water and against the mountain (following the bank, relying on the slope), rather than emphasizing a deep, far-reaching path process of moving from here to there.

evidence: Lower left: a thatched pavilion is half hidden behind tall trees and shrubs, with only the thatched roof and some pillars revealed, presenting a layering of a house concealed in the woods. | Middle-ground opposite bank: white buildings are surrounded by trees bearing red blossoms and by pine woods, their walls and roofs emerging through gaps in the trees, producing an effect of seeing houses across a screening layer. | Lower right: a waterside building is partly blocked by flowering trees slanting out in the foreground, its eaves and platform base faintly visible, reinforcing pictorial depth and the relationship of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the built elements are by the water or on the slope, the painting places greater emphasis on their layered relationship of being screened and revealed by trees and woodland, rather than on mere placement according to terrain.

evidence: Right middle: a waterside pavilion terrace is built at the water's edge, supported on wooden piles and adjoining the water surface and the bank, with figures inside. | Center and lower left of the painting: several boats move across the water, carrying passengers or boatmen, linking the spaces of the two banks. | Lower right corner: a facility resembling a ferry archway or open pavilion stands on the bank, with pedestrians beside it, forming a ferry transport link with the boats on the water.
distinction: Although the painting includes pavilions built by the water, its core lies in the transport and excursion cues formed by the ferry crossing, boats, and pedestrians, displaying an accessible spatial process of moving from here to there; thus C4 summarizes its dominant spatial expression more accurately than C1.

evidence: Right: a flat bridge over a stream connects the two banks and leads to the white-walled building on the right, forming a clear entry route. | Lower middle: an open hall is built by the water, directly adjoining the waterside, presenting a reachable spatial relationship. | Left: a house with a moon gate is placed beside mountain rocks and plants, forming with the surrounding environment a staggered spatial layering.
distinction: Although some buildings in the painting are screened by trees and mountain rocks, the connecting and guiding cues formed by the bridge and the waterside are clearer and dominate the traversable spatial organization.

evidence: Right mountain-rock platform: a lofty scholar is visible seated on the rock playing the qin, surrounded by pine trees, vines, and bamboo clumps; no clearly identifiable buildings or structures are visible. | Left and center: a stream and distant mountains are present on the left side of the painting, the whole presenting a natural landscape setting, and the figure's activity marks the secluded scenic quality of this spot.
distinction: The painting has no identifiable built elements; the figure playing the qin marks the landscape scenery of this spot, so it is classed as C3; if regarded as a process of entering this secluded place it would approach C4, but path cues are lacking.

evidence: Left: a group of buildings with round lattice windows and white walls is partly blocked by dense bamboo groves and by mountain rocks on the left, with only roofs, eaves, and part of the wall bodies revealed. | Right middle: a pavilion or small structure is screened behind bamboo groves and mountain rocks, presenting a layering of seeing houses across a screening layer. | Lower right corner: a flat bridge connects to the waterside, assisting the extension of space, but the buildings chiefly achieve their scenic effect through the concealment and revelation relationship of the bamboo groves and mountain rocks.
distinction: Although a bridge and shoreline in the painting hint at an excursion path, the most conspicuous scenic-compositional role of the built elements is to form spatial layering through screening and revealing by bamboo groves and mountain rocks, so C2 is more dominant than C4.

evidence: Center of the painting: an arched bridge spans the water, connecting the two banks and forming a clear circulation path. | Lower left and lower middle of the painting: a stone slab bridge and stone steps connect the waterside with the waterside pavilion, providing cues for entering the built elements. | Right side of the painting: a red railing extends in a winding line along the waterside, connecting the pavilion at the lower right corner with the building group behind.
distinction: Although the built elements are sited by the water and rocks, the movement-through-the-landscape cues of bridges, steps, and red railings are more prominent and dominate the spatial organization.

evidence: Right mountainside of the painting: white-walled, gray-tiled houses are visible, partly blocked by the surrounding dense pine woods and mountain rocks, with only roofs, walls, and windows revealed, forming a layering of houses concealed in the woods. | Middle-right of the painting: pine trees and mountain crags surround the built elements, and through the screening of branches and leaves and the mountain body the buildings are faintly visible, participating in forming the spatial depth of the painting.
distinction: Although the buildings mark the scenery of the mountainside, their concealment and revelation relationship of being screened by pine woods and mountain rocks is more prominent in the painting and dominates the expression of spatial layering.

evidence: Left: a group of courtyard buildings is surrounded by tall parasol trees and other vegetation, with trunks, branches, and leaves blocking part of the walls and eaves. | Left center: the building roofs, the railings of the second-story pavilion, and the ground-floor window lattices emerge through gaps in the trees, forming a clear layering of concealment and revelation. | Overall in the painting: the density of the woodland contrasts with the white walls and gray tiles of the buildings; the buildings are hidden in the woods, presenting a spatial relationship of seeing houses deep in the forest.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited within the natural environment, the painting places greater emphasis on the screening-and-revealing relationship of the woodland to the buildings as a way of constructing spatial layering, rather than highlighting a layout set according to terrain.

evidence: Upper middle of the painting: a pavilion-type building sits directly on the base of a steep, projecting cliff rock, its building site closely corresponding to the precipitous terrain. | Lower left of the painting: a thatched house is built by the water, sited against the sloping bank and trees, with figures visible inside.
distinction: Although the thatched studio at the lower left corner is screened by trees, the building on the cliff in the upper middle of the painting more prominently displays the terrain-responsive relationship of being placed against precipitous terrain, and dominates the spatial built-feature character of the painting.

evidence: Left lower middle: a thatched house is hidden behind dense pine woods and miscellaneous trees, with only the roof, part of the wall bodies, and the door and window structure revealed. | Left half of the painting: foreground tree trunks, branches, and leaves clearly block the buildings behind, constituting a spatial layering of alternating concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the building stands among mountain rocks and woodland, the painting places greater emphasis on the screening-and-revealing relationship of the trees to the building, rather than on how the building is sited in conformity with the terrain.

evidence: Lower right to center: a stone bridge spans the water, connecting the sloping bank on the right with the built area on the left, forming a clear entry path. | Lower left: built elements such as a thatched hut, courtyard wall, and granary stand on sloping ground at the foot of the mountain and are linked to it by the stone bridge and shoreline, presenting a reachable spatial relationship.
distinction: Although the built elements are arranged at the foot of the mountain, the spatial process in which the stone bridge and path lead into the built area is more prominent, so C4 is more apt than C1.

evidence: Lower left corner: a house is built at the edge of a sloping platform/high ground, its building site placed according to the terrain | Lower left corner to lower middle: a fence extends along the sloping ground/field ridges, conforming to the site boundary and the lay of the land | Left: trees surround the house, whose main body is clearly visible, presenting a layout of separate placement according to the slope
distinction: Although trees surround the house and form a certain degree of screening, the features of the house being placed on the sloping platform and the fence conforming to the terrain are more conspicuous, chiefly embodying terrain-responsive arrangement rather than scenic composition purely by means of screening.

evidence: Lower left and slightly below center: a building group with red walls and gray tiles is partly blocked by dense trees in the foreground and middle ground, with only roofs, flying eaves, and part of the wall bodies revealed, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Right middle-to-distant ground: two buildings are half hidden among clumps of trees and curling cloud vapor, whose screening indicates their spatial layering and presence.
distinction: The dominant relationship in the painting is that the buildings form a layering of concealment and revelation through trees and cloud vapor, rather than serving as markers to point out a particular landscape scene.

evidence: Left and center: a courtyard compound stands beside tall trees and mountain rocks, the tree crowns extending over and above the roofs; the main bodies of the buildings are revealed among the woodland, forming a layering of screening. | Foreground center: flowering branches slant across in front of the enclosing wall, blocking part of the wall and the ground, constituting a foreground spatial relationship of seeing houses across a screening layer.
distinction: Although an open courtyard gate and figures' activity in the painting hint at an entry circulation line, the buildings are chiefly blocked by the large trees on the left and the flowering branches in the foreground, and the screening relationship of concealment and revelation is more conspicuous in the composition.

evidence: Lower left: a thatched hut is partly blocked by the trees, bamboo clumps, and mountain rocks in front of it, with only the roof, part of the wall bodies, and the figures inside revealed, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Left and lower left: dense trees and bamboo groves surround the thatched hut, reinforcing the spatial layering of the building hidden among natural scenery.
distinction: Although the thatched hut is sited against the mountain and beside the water, the painting places greater emphasis on presenting its reclusive spatial layering through screening by the surrounding trees and bamboo groves, rather than merely displaying a layout sited according to terrain.

evidence: Lower right: a pavilion with red walls and black tiles is visible, situated among stone peaks and woodland. | Lower right: the building itself and the base of the pavilion are partly blocked by foreground trees and mountain rocks, with only the roof and part of the wall bodies revealed, forming a spatial layering of alternating concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the built element marks the waterside scenery, the painting places greater emphasis on its concealment-and-revelation layering as screened and revealed by trees and mountain rocks, so C2 is more apt than C3.

evidence: Left: an open hall with a tiled roof is surrounded and screened by the lake rocks on its left and by the luxuriant flowering trees behind and above it, with only part of the roof, the pillars, and the table inside revealed. | Left and center: tree trunks, branches, and leaves form screening in front of and above the building, presenting a spatial layering of a house concealed in the woods and of seeing houses across a screening layer.
distinction: Although the building is constructed against the rocks, the painting places greater emphasis on the screening-and-revealing relationship of the flowering trees to it; the role of concealment-and-revelation in forming the scene outweighs terrain-responsive placement.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: a thatched pavilion sits among a stand of weeping willows, whose drooping branches hang low and encircle the pavilion body; two people are visible sitting facing each other inside, and the pavilion roof and pillars are revealed through the willow branches. | Foreground and middle ground of the painting: numerous weeping willows are arrayed, their drooping branches forming a screen and enclosing the pavilion deep within the willow grove, presenting a spatial layering of built elements screened by woodland.
distinction: Although the pavilion marks the scenery of the embankment, the painting chiefly presents the encircling and screening of the pavilion by weeping willows, emphasizing a screening relationship of seeing a house within the woods rather than a mere scenic marker.

evidence: Lower left foreground: several houses are placed against the mountain and rock slopes and woodland, presenting a form of separate placement according to the slope. | Opposite bank on the right: a large number of houses are arrayed in an unbroken line along the shoreline and the foot of the distant mountains, their roofs staggered, presenting a clearly bank-following layout. | Overall composition: the distribution of the built elements (the village) conforms to the waterside and the trend of the terrain, forming a spatial organization of linked villages and adjoining households.
distinction: Although a screening relationship exists between the houses on the opposite bank and the trees (C2), the dominant expression of the painting is the layout of the village as a whole unfolding continuously along the waterside and the foot of the mountain, which better matches the bank-following unfolding defined in terrain-responsive built features (C1).

evidence: Right middle ground: a built structure is half screened within a dense bamboo grove, with only the roof, eaves, and part of the base revealed, and figures visible inside. | Lower middle of the painting: a large expanse of bamboo grove surrounds a stream and wraps the built elements on the right, forming a clear layering of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the built elements mark the scenery, their half-screened concealment-and-revelation relationship with the bamboo grove is more prominent in the composition and dominates the expression of spatial layering.

evidence: Lower middle: a stone arch bridge spans the stream, with an umbrella-holding pedestrian on the bridge and a figure wearing a conical hat below it, forming clear circulation and excursion cues. | Right: a pavilion roof and wall body are revealed amid the screening of a bamboo grove, hinting at the deep space to which the bridge path leads. | Overall composition: the stream and stone bridge together organize a spatial process extending from the foreground toward the depths of the bamboo grove, presenting a here-to-there relationship of entry.
distinction: Although the buildings on the right are screened by a bamboo grove (C2), the guiding role of the movement-through-the-landscape cues formed by the stone bridge and figures in the spatial organization is more central, clearly expressing an accessible, traversable process.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: a courtyard building group is surrounded by dense bamboo groves, its roofs and walls faintly visible under the screening of bamboo leaves, forming a rich layering of concealment and revelation. | Upper right of the painting: a pagoda and a gate tower are built against the mountain and partly blocked by mountain rocks and trees, presenting a sense of space deeply hidden within the mountain forest. | Lower right corner of the painting: a building is half hidden between the bamboo grove and the sloping ground, with only the roof and part of the wall bodies revealed, reinforcing the visual effect of concealment and revelation forming the scene.
distinction: Although the buildings are distributed according to the lie of the mountain and the bamboo groves, the most prominent scenic-compositional method in the painting is organizing spatial layering through the screening and revealing by bamboo groves and mountain rocks, rather than merely emphasizing terrain-responsive placement.

evidence: Right middle ground: several thatched huts are surrounded by dense bamboo groves, their building bodies and roofs faintly visible among the bamboo leaves, forming a clear spatial layering of concealment and revelation. | Center to right of the painting: a small path passes through the bamboo grove, connecting the figure carrying firewood with the thatched huts on the right, the path faintly appearing among the woodland.
distinction: Although a path connects the figure with the thatched huts, the most dominant visual feature of the painting is the layering formed by the built elements being extensively screened and revealed by the bamboo grove, rather than an emphasis on the process of entry.

evidence: Slightly right of center in the painting: an arched-roof built structure (a fishing shed) has its lower part blocked by the surrounding dense bamboo grove, with only the roof and parts of the structure revealed, presenting a layering of a house concealed in the woods. | Middle ground of the painting: the built structure and an angler are hidden between the bamboo grove and the waterside, their presence and the spatial depth in which they lie indicated by the screening and revealing of the bamboo clumps in front of and behind them. | Lower and right of the painting: although a wooden bridge and boats are distributed, the built structure is chiefly encircled and wrapped by the bamboo grove, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship constitutes the main mode of spatial organization in the painting.
distinction: Although the painting contains movement-through-the-landscape cues such as the bridge and boats, the built structure chiefly forms layering through screening and revealing by the dense bamboo grove, and the scenic-compositional role of concealment and revelation is more conspicuous than that of the entry path.

evidence: Lower right: a thatched pavilion sits within a bamboo grove, its roof, eaves, and part of the pillars revealed through the bamboo, with a single person visible seated upright inside. | Middle-right of the painting: a dense bamboo grove surrounds the built elements, forming a clear relationship of screening and revealing, so that the pavilion presents a spatial layering of being hidden in the woods.
distinction: Although the pavilion marks a scene on the waterside, the painting places greater emphasis on the screening and revealing of the pavilion by the bamboo grove, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship is the dominant scenic-compositional method.

evidence: Middle ground, slightly right: the roofs and parts of the walls of several houses emerge from dense bamboo grove, presenting a spatial layering of houses concealed within the grove. | Lower left corner: an open pavilion is built on sloping rocks at the waterside, surrounded and screened by tall bamboo, with a figure seated inside, forming a partly screened, partly revealed relationship. | Overall painting: extensive bamboo grove covers the mountain foot, the waterside, and the area around the buildings; the built elements all stand screened or partly screened by the bamboo grove, and the relationship of concealment and revelation is pronounced.
distinction: Although a bridge on the right side of the painting provides a path clue, the foreground pavilion and middle-ground houses are mainly screened and surrounded by dense bamboo grove, so the visual characteristic of concealment and revelation forming a setting is more dominant.

evidence: Upper right: the roof of a building appears between bamboo grove and mountain rocks, presenting a partly screened, partly revealed layered relationship | Lower middle: there is a small bridge and figures within the bamboo grove, but the main building is screened by dense bamboo and mountain rocks
distinction: The main building presents a layering of concealment and revelation through the screening of bamboo grove and mountain rocks; the bridge and path serve only as a local accent, not the dominant spatial expression

evidence: Lower left: two figures stand on a flat bridge; the bridge connects to the waterside and serves as an entry clue to the built area of the painting. | Middle ground: a winding embankment path crosses the water surface; two figures walk along the path, and sightline and path together lead toward the thatched hut cluster in the distance. | Lower right: the buildings are linked by stone paths, courtyard gates are open, and figures move inside and outside, presenting a clear relationship of accessibility and movement through the landscape.
distinction: Although the buildings are arranged according to the waterside slope, the painting strongly guides the sightline through the bridge, the winding embankment, and the courtyard paths, emphasizing the spatial process of moving from one place to another and approaching the built structures; thus C4 is more dominant than C1.

evidence: Middle left: two thatched-roof houses are built close to the water, with supporting structures visible at the base, together with the hills behind and trees to the left forming a countryside scene. | Lower middle of the painting: a spring-welcoming ceremonial procession advances along a road and passes in front of the built elements, which serve as the background identifying the rural setting in which the procession is situated.
distinction: Although the built elements take a form of facing the water and occupying a platform, in the painting they mainly serve as a background marker for the route of the spring-welcoming procession, identifying the rural scenery, rather than emphasizing their layout relationship to the terrain.

evidence: Lower left corner: a thatched shed is placed against the roots of a large tree on the left and the foot of the slope, serving as a base facility for the scene. | Right and center: the ground shows gentle slope undulations; figures, flower stalls, and tables are distributed along the slope, and the built elements and activity areas unfold in accordance with the terrain.
distinction: The thatched shed is mainly placed against the tree roots and at the foot of the slope, embodying a terrain-responsive arrangement rather than merely serving as a visual focus to mark distant landscape scenery.

evidence: Distant middle ground: a row of thatched houses is arranged in an orderly line along the waterside high ground, presenting a layout that unfolds following the shore, with the building sites corresponding to the waterside configuration. | Right: a red-walled, blue-tiled building (a shrine/temple) is placed on a sloping bank, presenting a relationship of separate placement according to the slope, with steps connecting to the sloping ground. | Lower left corner to middle ground: a wooden bridge and embankment path extend in accordance with the waterside configuration; people advance along the embankment, embodying built elements (embankment/path) set according to the water's configuration.
distinction: Although the painting has bridge paths and crowd movement clues (approaching C4), the built elements (village, shrine, embankment) mainly present the macro-layout characteristics of being arranged along the waterside and placed according to the slope; the terrain correspondence is more dominant.

evidence: Right and lower middle: thatched huts are arranged in scattered fashion according to the mountain-foot slope and the edges of terraced fields, with building sites echoing the undulations of the terrain | Left waterside: a small red building is placed on the waterside slope, forming a terrain-responsive relationship with the surrounding trees and waterside
distinction: Although there is a field ridge path in the painting, the built elements mainly unfold according to the configuration of farmland, slopes, and waterside, rather than emphasizing a path-guided entry process

evidence: Center and right of the painting: the main body of the hall building is partly screened by the tall pine trees on the right and the banana leaves in front, revealing only the roof, veranda columns, and part of the walls, forming a clear relationship of concealment and revelation. | Center of the painting: three figures stand in front of the building; steps in front of the building connect to level ground; branches and leaves of the trees interweave before and behind the eaves, enhancing the spatial layering.
distinction: Although the building is erected on a sloped platform, the painting more strongly emphasizes the screening and revealing of the building by the pine trees and plants; the layered relationship of concealment and revelation is more prominent than the terrain-responsive placement.

evidence: Center-left of the painting: beneath a large tree a figure stands leaning against the trunk, facing the open water surface to the right; no houses, bridges, or other built elements are visible. | Right and distant view: a gentle waterside extends into the distance, with low distant mountains, presenting an open, level, and expansive scene.
distinction: No clear built elements are seen in the painting; only figures serve as scenic accents, so based on the overall spatial organization it is barely assigned to the scenic accentuation category, but there is a lack of evidence for built elements.

evidence: Center: two figures stand in the center of the painting; on the left are two cranes; on the right are bamboo and rocks; the whole presents an open natural space, with no clear built elements such as houses, bridges, or paths visible.
distinction: No clear built elements are seen in the painting, but the presence of figures and cranes suggests a spatial conception that can be moved through, so it is barely assigned to C4, though in fact it lacks concrete clues of movement through the landscape.

evidence: Middle ground, slightly right: a figure sits on a stone platform by the water, with an attendant beside them, surrounded by pine trees and chrysanthemums, identifying the landscape scenery of this place. | Left: a waterfall flows down from the mountain rocks, with chrysanthemums dotted around, forming a specific natural landscape.
distinction: There are no clear built elements in the painting; the figures' activities identify the scenery of chrysanthemums and spring, so it is assigned to C3.

evidence: Center-right of the painting: the hall building is built directly on a towering rocky sloped platform, with the building site closely integrated with the mountain-rock terrain. | Center-left of the painting: in front of the building extends a stone-paved platform and railings that follow the terrain; figures move on the platform, showing a layout suited to the configuration.
distinction: Although pine trees provide local screening of the building, the terrain-responsive relationship of the building being erected on the mountain-rock platform is more fundamental and dominant in the spatial organization.

evidence: Lower left and center: dense woodland, earthen slopes, and three figures walking along a small path are visible | Right and background: steep cliffs and cloud vapor are visible; beneath the cliff one person bends over; the painting presents a sense of a path extending into depth
distinction: No clear built elements are seen in the painting; only the path and the figures' movement dynamics are present, embodying a spatial process of traveling into depth, so it is barely assigned to C4.

evidence: Mid-slope on the left-center of the painting: two groups of double-eaved buildings (pavilions/towers) are surrounded and screened by dense dotted-leaf trees, revealing only the roofs and eaves, forming a spatial layering of houses seen within the grove. | Lower middle-left of the painting: the walls of the lower houses are partly screened by tree branches and leaves, forming a clear foreground-background relationship of concealment and revelation with the surrounding mountain rocks and trees.
distinction: Although the buildings are distributed according to the mountain configuration, the visual focus of the painting lies in the screening and revealing of the buildings by trees; the relationship of concealment and revelation forming scenery is more prominent than mere terrain placement.

evidence: Lower and central parts of the painting: figures, carts and horses, and banners are visible advancing through the valley, forming a clear route of travel or procession. | Right mountainside: a structure suspected to be steps or a plank road extends upward along the mountain configuration, suggesting a spatial process of entering or climbing.
distinction: The painting lacks clear architectural entities, but the advancing route of figures, carts, and horses and the mountain paths constitute a strong sense of spatial guidance and entry, so it is assigned to C4.

evidence: Lower middle, slightly left of the painting: a person stands at the edge of a flat rocky platform, facing right | Right side of the painting: towering peaks and a hanging waterfall | Overall composition: the place where the figure pauses and the distant mountains and waterfall face each other, identifying the orientation and scenery of the viewing point
distinction: No typical architecture is seen in the painting, but the rocky platform on which the figure stands serves to identify the viewing position and focus the sightline, so it is assigned to C3.

evidence: Upper left: a group of pavilions, terraces, and towers together with a pagoda is hidden behind dense woodland, revealing only the roofs and the pagoda body, presenting a spatial layering of concealment and revelation within the grove. | Middle left: rows of trees extend along the waterside or path, screening the buildings behind them, forming a foreground-background screening relationship of seeing houses through a separating layer.
distinction: Although the buildings are located in the distance and serve as scenic markers, the painting emphatically expresses the dense screening and revealing of the buildings by trees; the relationship of concealment and revelation is more prominent than mere marking.

evidence: Lower middle: farmhouses are placed against trees and rocky banks, unfolding according to the waterside terrain. | Upper right: several houses are scattered among sloped platforms and tree clusters, with layout following the undulations of the terrain. | Left and center: terraced fields and field ridges outline the terrain contours, and the built elements form a terrain-responsive relationship with farmland and waterside.
distinction: Although trees screen and create layering, the overall layout relationship of the houses following the terrain, waterside, and sloped platforms is more prominent and dominates the spatial organization.

evidence: Lower left corner: a person holding an umbrella crosses a small bridge; the bridge connects to a path leading to the houses on the right, forming a clear entry clue. | Right: houses are screened among trees and bamboo grove; the path over the bridge points toward this place, presenting a spatial process of moving from one place to another.
distinction: Although trees screen the houses, the figure crossing the bridge and the bridge in the lower left corner constitute strong spatial guidance, making 'access to secluded settings' the dominant spatial expression.

evidence: Left and center: multiple buildings are arranged in scattered fashion according to mountain-rock sloping banks, rising and falling, presenting a form of houses set on platforms and separately placed according to slopes. | Lower left to center: stone steps connect with the winding wooden-railed waterside, linking the land buildings with the water space, embodying a layout that unfolds following the shore. | Lower right corner: a hexagonal pavilion is built in the water, echoing the weeping willows and rocky bank on the shore, placed relying on the waterside terrain.
distinction: Although stone steps and winding railings suggest a travel path, the characteristic of buildings being arranged in scattered fashion according to the terrain slopes and banks is more prominent and dominates the overall spatial organization.

evidence: Upper middle mountain summit: an open pavilion is built high on the mountain ridge; two people sit facing each other, with an open sea of clouds in front; the pavilion identifies the specific scenery of ascending high and gazing afar. | Lower middle among the pine grove: pedestrians climb upward through gaps in the mountain rocks, providing a travel background for ascending to the summit pavilion.
distinction: Although the painting has a mountain-climbing path, the pavilion, as the visual focus, serves primarily to mark the viewing position high on the mountain summit rather than to emphasize the process of entry.

evidence: At the junction of the right mountain slope and the left plain: several mounted riders and walking hunters advance along the mountain foot toward the depth of the painting, forming a clear travel clue. | Lower left corner at the plain edge: there are indistinct earthen mounds or thatched-grass-like forms that cannot be reliably identified as built elements.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built elements, but the path clue of the figures advancing along the mountain foot is the most prominent, so it is assigned to C4.

evidence: Center of the painting: a wooden bridge spans the water surface; a person carrying a load on a pole walks toward the thatched hut area on the right, forming a clear advancing route. | Right and lower middle of the painting: several thatched huts are arranged along the waterside and sloping ground, with paths and steps in front of the houses, connected to the bridge and the figures' movement lines, presenting an accessible spatial relationship. | Right side of the painting: bamboo fences and flower beds surround the thatched huts, and figures work in the garden, reinforcing the built elements' attribute as a destination and a place that can be traveled through.
distinction: Although the thatched huts are partly screened by trees, the painting more strongly emphasizes the spatial process of guiding the viewer's sightline through the bridge and the figures' movement lines into the built area, so C4 is more dominant than C2.

evidence: Lower part: a multi-arch bridge spans the stream, and a mounted figure is advancing on the bridge, constituting a clear passage clue. | Upper center: the path behind the bridge extends deep into the valley, leading to several houses surrounded by trees, presenting a spatial process of moving from one place to another. | Middle-ground valley: houses are arranged in scattered fashion according to sloping ground, serving as the endpoint of the path's extension, reinforcing the travel relationship of accessibility and reachability.
distinction: Although the houses are arranged according to the mountain configuration, the painting more strongly emphasizes the spatial process of guiding figures through the bridge and path into the depths of the valley.

evidence: Lower right to middle ground: a winding mountain road is clearly visible, with pedestrians, a donkey rider, and a mule-and-horse caravan on it, presenting a spatial process of advancing along the road. | Lower left corner: near the starting point of the mountain road, some building roofs are visible, suggesting a connection between the route and built elements. | Upper right mountain summit: a pagoda finial appears amid screening pine grove, serving as a distant target in the direction of the path's extension.
distinction: Although woodland screens the buildings (pagoda and houses), what dominates the composition is the entry and travel process shown by the winding mountain road and the traveling caravan.

evidence: Lower part to center of the painting: a clear small path extends from the foreground toward the gate in the enclosing wall of the middle-ground building complex. | Center, slightly left of the painting: after passing through the gate, the path connects to the internal houses and tall pavilion, forming a clear entry route. | Upper left of the painting: the tall pavilion is located at a high point at the end of the path, with figures inside, serving as the endpoint guided by the path.
distinction: Although the buildings are arranged according to the mountain configuration, the clear path and gate in the lower part of the painting constitute strong visual guidance, emphasizing the spatial process of moving from one place to another, so C4 is more dominant.

evidence: Lower right corner: several thatched huts are distributed among the withered tree grove; roofs and walls are partly screened by trunks and branches, presenting a layering of concealment and revelation of houses seen within the grove. | Left and center of the painting: a large area of unpainted space on the river; a small boat is on the river and figures are on the bank, forming a near-far spatial contrast with the built elements in the lower right corner, but the built elements themselves are mainly screened by trees.
distinction: Although the built elements identify the scenery of a riverside village, their relationship of concealment and revelation with the grove is visually more direct and concrete, so it is assigned to concealment and revelation forming a setting.

evidence: Lower right corner: a pass-like structure is built on the mountain ridge, with a clear stepped path winding upward below it, leading directly to the structure. | Lower middle to lower right corner: a camel caravan and mounted figures advance along the path, presenting a spatial process of moving toward the pass and about to enter.
distinction: Although the pass identifies the location of the mountain pass, the clear path and advancing caravan in the painting more strongly emphasize the spatial process of entering the pass, rather than mere scenic marking.

evidence: Lower left: foreground thatched huts are built against sloping ground; the building lines fit the direction of the slope, presenting a form of placement according to the slope. | Middle right and upper part: background thatched huts and courtyards are located on relatively level ground at the edge of the woodland, forming a layout of separate high and low placement relative to the foreground slope. | Overall: the building complex unfolds according to the terrain conditions of the lower-left slope and the rear woodland edge; bamboo-fenced courtyards enclose according to the terrain.
distinction: The main bodies of the buildings in the painting are clear and complete, not deeply screened by woodland; they mainly embody layout according to the sloping terrain rather than being dominated by a relationship of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower left: two thatched huts sit flat at the edge of the fields, constituting the main built nodes of the painting | Lower right to center: a figure draws water at the waterside; a simple plank bridge is visible at the right edge, forming a clue extending from the waterside toward the interior | Center to middle left: a figure carrying a load on a pole walks along a field path; the path points toward the thatched huts, presenting a relationship of accessibility and reachability
distinction: Although the thatched huts are placed against the fields, the painting more strongly emphasizes the travel process toward the huts organized jointly by the figures, the waterside, and the plank bridge.

evidence: Middle right of the painting: several thatched cottages are arranged in a staggered manner following the course of the waterside and the slope, their building sites closely integrated with the terrain. | Left side and lower part of the painting: the sloping bank and fields extend along the waterside, together with the houses on the right forming a layout that relies on the water and is sited on the slope.
distinction: Although there are trees around the houses, they do not form a distinct layered relationship of screening and revelation; what is mainly expressed is the layout of the houses sited according to the terrain and waterside.

evidence: Lower left corner: willows, rocks, and wooden posts (resembling stepping stones or a bridge) are depicted, forming the starting point of a path along the waterside and hinting at a clue for entry. | Lower center: a figure carrying wine jars on a shoulder pole walks along the open ground toward the house courtyard, forming a dynamic movement clue approaching the built structures. | Center: the house courtyard is open, with figures active within it (moving jars, brewing wine), presenting the spatial relationship of entering the inner built space from the outer path.
distinction: Although the painting has bamboo groves behind the houses and trees on the right providing screening, the clues of the bridge and path at the lower left and the figure carrying wine toward the courtyard are clear, constituting a definite spatial process of entering the village shop from the waterside (approaching the built structures), which dominates the spatial organization of the painting.

evidence: Lower to middle part of the painting: a winding mountain path extends upward from the bottom of the painting, with figures riding a donkey and carrying loads traveling along the path, forming a clear clue of entry and journeying. | Mid-upper mountainside of the painting: a thatched hut is visible on the mountainside, and the direction in which the path extends suggests a spatial process leading to this built structure or deeper into the landscape.
distinction: Although the thatched hut has a layer of screening by trees, the mountain path running through the upper and lower parts of the painting and the traveling figures more strongly organize the spatial process of moving from here to there, so C4 is dominant.

evidence: Left side and center: a pavilion and its connected terrace are surrounded by colored auspicious clouds and pine branches, and the lower part and edges of the building are obscured by clouds and mist, presenting a clear relationship of concealment and revelation. | Overall painting: clouds, mist, and pine trees serve as foreground and middle ground, wrapping the building within them and forming rich spatial layers, so that the building seems to appear and disappear within a fairy realm.
distinction: Although the building is eye-catching, the painting focuses more on creating layers and mood through the screening of clouds, mist, and pine trees, rather than simply serving as a marker identifying some natural landscape.

evidence: Upper left corner: a pavilion stands on the mountainside, surrounded by pine trees and mountains and rocks, presenting a half-hidden, half-revealed state. | Center-left of the painting: a group of buildings (roofs and canopies visible) stands on the slope of a mountain hollow, obscured by trees and mountains and rocks in front, forming a spatial layer of seeing houses within the woods. | Lower center of the painting: there are paths and figure activity, forming a certain spatial connection with the screened building group in the center.
distinction: In the painting, the relationship of concealment and revelation in which buildings are obscured by woodland, mountains, and rocks (C2) is more direct and prominent than the process of entry guided by paths (C4).

evidence: Lower left: a wooden bridge spans the water, connecting the courtyard on the left with the central sandbar, forming a clear passage route. | Left side: the courtyard is enclosed by a fence and trees, figures stand on the bank, and the path extends along the waterside. | Right side: a group of thatched cottages is screened among the trees, with figures active in front of the houses, echoing the left side through the water surface and path.
distinction: Although the built structures are arranged along the waterside, the painting emphasizes more the traversable, enterable spatial process constructed through bridges, paths, and figure activity.

evidence: Middle-right sloping bank: a standing figure is visible, with no traces of built elements such as houses, bridges, or pavilions around them | Overall painting: the painting is dominated by natural scenery such as blue-green mountain peaks, clouds and mist, waterfalls, and pine trees, with no spatial interaction between man-made buildings and the landscape visible
distinction: There are no identifiable built elements in the painting, only figures as scenic accents; it is tentatively classified as scenic accentuation based on the overall landscape composition, but lacks support from any architectural entity

evidence: Lower center of the painting: a bridge is visible between the pine forest and mountains and rocks, spanning a stream and connecting the two banks. | Lower center of the painting: the bridge, together with the stream and mountains and rocks, constitutes a traversable, enterable spatial clue.
distinction: The bridge, as a clear clue for movement through the landscape, mainly serves to guide the eye and provide access into the space, rather than simply using trees for screening to form layers of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower-left foreground: a multi-story pavilion is built on the sloping bank, its building site relying on the terrain, presenting an arrangement of houses set on a terrace. | Lower-middle part of the painting: the pavilion faces a broad expanse of water, its layout following the shoreline and embodying a posture of being built facing the water. | Around the pavilion: the sloping bank and trees surround the base of the pavilion, with natural scenery participating in constituting the site environment of the built structure.
distinction: The pavilion clearly relies on the sloping-bank terrain for its siting, embodying a logic of terrain-responsive building, rather than serving merely as an isolated visual marker adorning the landscape.

evidence: Right-side hillside: pavilions and terraces with railings are arranged in staggered heights according to the mountain's contours, with terraces extending outward in response to the mountain terrain. | Center-right of the painting: the building sites match the form of the hillside, presenting a spatial relationship of siting according to the ground.
distinction: Although the buildings mark the scenery here, their siting relationship—following the mountain and unfolding with the terrain—is more prominent in the painting.

evidence: Left side and upper part: a gnarled ancient pine occupies the main part of the painting, its branches extending, with no buildings attached to or screening it | Lower part and right side: blue-green mountains and rocks, waterfalls, and a sea of clouds constitute the natural landscape scenery, with no traces of built elements such as houses or bridges visible
distinction: There are no visible built elements in the painting; only the ancient pine and landscape constitute the scenery, so it is classified as scenic accentuation as the closest category

evidence: Left side and center: houses and pavilions are surrounded and screened by dense trees (a plum grove), with only roofs, eaves, and parts of walls visible, presenting a layering in which buildings are seen within the woods. | Lower left and lower area: built elements are arranged against mountains and rocks and trees, with some structures obscured by foreground trees and rocks, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Overall painting: the inscription "Meilin Wocui" (Lush Green of the Plum Grove) indicates the setting; built elements are scattered among the woodland and screened by natural scenery to form the scene.
distinction: Although the built elements are sited at the foot of the mountain (C1), the more prominent feature of the painting is the screening and revealing of the houses by trees (C2); the concealment-and-revelation relationship dominates the spatial layering.

evidence: Lower left corner: houses are built beside the sloping bank and willow trees, their building sites following the rise and fall of the terrain, presenting a form of houses set on a terrace. | Right side: the building group unfolds facing the water, with some pavilions (waterside pavilions) extending their structures over the water surface and closely connecting with the shoreline of the lotus pond, presenting a layout unfolding along the bank. | Opposite bank in the middle ground: faintly visible houses follow the gentle shoreline and tree clusters at the foot of the distant mountains, sited according to the terrain.
distinction: Although the buildings adorn the waterscape, their main feature is that they are laid out and unfolded according to the sloping bank and waterside terrain (such as waterside pavilions facing the water and houses on the slope), rather than simply serving as visual markers identifying some mountain peak or valley mouth.

evidence: Lower center to right side of the painting: a small path extends from the left, passing through a thatched-roofed fence gate (brushwood gate), and leads to the building group on the right. | Lower center of the painting: a person is sweeping near the small path and the fence gate, reinforcing the sense of travel along the path. | Right side of the painting: the small path finally leads to houses (thatched pavilions) built against the mountain, presenting a spatial process of moving from here to there and approaching the built structures.
distinction: Although the houses built against the mountain have the characteristic of terrain-responsive siting, the clear small path, brushwood gate, and figure activity in the painting constitute more prominent clues for movement through the landscape, dominating the process of spatial entry.

evidence: Right side: a group of houses is built facing the water, with wooden posts visible at the bottom supporting them in the water, arranged along the shoreline and presenting a layout unfolding along the bank. | Center-left: a wooden bridge spans the water connecting to the land, erected according to the water flow and shoreline. | Lower-right foreground: a figure stands by the water beneath a willow, facing the built structures on the opposite bank across the water, highlighting the positional relationship of the built structures sited according to the waterside.
distinction: Although a bridge and figures suggest movement through the space, the bridge does not directly connect to the houses; the form of the houses—piled in the water and unfolding along the bank—is more prominent, dominating as terrain-responsive siting.

evidence: Left-side hillside: a long row of houses is built against the mountain following the slope and direction of the hillside, with the buildings at staggered heights, their building sites closely corresponding to the undulations of the terrain. | Lower-left waterside: a pavilion is built on a stone base at the water's edge, adjacent to the mountains and rocks and the water's edge, presenting an arrangement of houses set on a terrace and unfolding along the bank. | Right-side sloping ground: a small pavilion is built on high ground on the right slope, sited in response to the sloping terrain and harmonizing with the surrounding landscape forms.
distinction: Although trees provide a certain screening of the buildings, what is more prominent in the painting is the overall layout of the building group in response to the mountain forms and slope; terrain-responsive siting plays a stronger role than mere screening and concealment.

evidence: Lower left: houses are arranged beside mountains and rocks and trees, their building sites following the undulations of the terrain. | Right-center: a group of houses sits on terraced sloping platforms, their layout divided according to the slope. | Right edge: houses are built against the slope, forming a corresponding relationship with the surrounding sloping terrain.
distinction: Although the built structures adorn the landscape, their placement according to the ground—sited on slopes and terraces and beside mountains and rocks—is more prominent, dominating the spatial organization of the painting.

evidence: Left-side hillside: a bamboo fence and a roofed fence gate are visible, with a person standing in front of the gate, forming a clear entrance and boundary. | Lower center: thatched cottages are surrounded and half-screened by trees such as banana plants and willows, located deep on the sloping ground behind the fence gate. | Overall composition: from the fence gate on the left to the inner thatched cottages, a spatial journey clue of moving from here to there and turning into the depths is presented.
distinction: Although the thatched cottages have a relationship of concealment and revelation through tree screening, the clear fence gate and figures on the left side of the painting constitute a strong guide for entry, making the spatial process of access to secluded settings dominant.

evidence: Lower right: a house with an enclosing wall and a moon gate, its roof and part of its walls revealed from the dense tree clusters and mountains and rocks behind. | Right center: tall trees and banana leaves cover above and behind the house, forming clear natural screening that leaves the building in a half-hidden, half-revealed state.
distinction: Although the house is located on flat ground, the painting focuses on expressing the relationship of screening and revelation of the building by trees, mountains, and rocks, rather than emphasizing its siting in response to the terrain and sloping bank.

evidence: Middle-ground right: the built structure is sited beside the waterside and mountains and rocks, with platform or pillar structures visible at the bottom, following the waterside terrain and presenting a layout unfolding along the bank | Lower-middle and lower-right parts of the painting: figures stand on the bank, an arched bridge spans the water on the right, and the built structure is located deep in the water inlet, set according to the water flow and the terrain of mountains and rocks
distinction: Although the painting has a bridge and figures forming a clue for movement through the landscape, the figures face toward the trees and no directly visible path connects the bridge and the built structure; the terrain relationship of the built structure sited by the water is more prominent than the process of entry

evidence: Middle ground to distant view: the city wall winds and rises and falls along the ridgeline, its base and course fully following the slope and form of the mountain. | Right middle ground: the city gate and gate tower are built against the mountain cliff, with the base of the buildings closely integrated with the mountain rock. | Lower left corner: several dwellings are sited against the mountain and beside the water, their layout unfolding in response to the sloping ground and waterside.
distinction: Although the city wall and gate tower serve to mark the scenery, their most striking feature is being laid out winding along the mountain contours; the relationship of siting according to the ground is more prominent.

evidence: Center of the painting: a thatched pavilion is built on a protruding mountain-rock platform, its building site closely integrated with the terrain, presenting a posture of houses set on a terrace. | Left side of the painting: a bridge is erected over the water, connecting the mountain cliff with the buildings on the opposite bank, unfolding in response to the waterside terrain. | Right side of the painting: houses are arranged along the sloping bank at the foot of the mountain, forming a layout sited according to the ground together with the surrounding mountains, rocks, and trees.
distinction: Although the painting has bridges and paths, the overall spatial relationship of buildings beside mountains and rocks and the waterside, sited according to the ground, is more prominent and dominant.

evidence: Left side and center of the painting: thatched cottages and pavilions are obscured by the branches and leaves of tall pines and other trees, with only roofs, eaves, and parts of the pillars exposed, presenting layers of concealment and revelation of seeing houses within the woods. | Behind and to the right of the buildings: a bamboo grove and woven fence enclose the buildings, together with the foreground trees forming a screen, leaving the built structures screened by natural scenery. | Lower-left waterside: figures brew tea beside trees and rocks, forming a spatial echo with the screened building courtyard and reinforcing the secluded, quiet effect of the formed setting.
distinction: Although the buildings are located on flat ground by the waterside, the painting mainly organizes spatial layers through the obscuring and revealing of roofs and walls by trees, rather than emphasizing the determining role of terrain in the layout of the buildings.

evidence: Center-left: a group of built structures is surrounded by dense bamboo groves and trees, with only roofs, eaves, and parts of the courtyard exposed, forming a clear layer of screening and revelation. | Right-side water surface: a small bridge connects the waterside with the bamboo grove area, helping to indicate the secluded location of the built structures. | Upper-left distant mountains: a small building is faintly visible halfway up the distant mountains, likewise screened by woodland.
distinction: Although there is a small bridge on the right side of the painting as a clue for entry, the core visual organization and mood creation of the painting mainly rely on the half-screening of the buildings by the bamboo grove, so C2 is more dominant than C4.

evidence: Lower right: a figure can be seen standing on flat ground beneath a pine tree; no houses, pavilions, or other built structures are identifiable. | Lower left and center: mountains and rocks, pine trees, and a stream form the main natural scenery, and the figure is situated within this open natural environment.
distinction: The painting contains no explicit built elements; the figure together with the pine tree and landscape identifies the specific scene of "pine coolness and a healthy person," and it is therefore classified as C3.

evidence: Center-right mountain cliff: a two-story thatched pavilion is built against the cliff, with figures visible inside, and the building site closely integrated with the terrain of mountains and rocks. | Lower right corner: a winding small path and a fence/small bridge are visible, extending upward along the mountain and pointing toward the thatched pavilion, forming an enterable path clue. | Right middle ground: other houses are visible amid the screening woodland, forming spatial layers with the main pavilion, with paths threading between them.
distinction: The thatched pavilion is indeed built in response to the mountain cliff terrain (C1), but the clear path in the lower right corner of the painting guides the eye and the traveler upward to approach the built structure, making the enterable process of journeying the main clue organizing the painting.

evidence: Center-left: houses on the mountainside are half-screened by the vast swirling clouds and mist below and the surrounding trees, with only roofs exposed, forming a spatial layer of seeing houses through a screen. | Lower left corner: houses on the sloping ground are hidden in dense tree clusters, with only parts of the roofs visible, presenting a relationship of houses hidden in the woods and indicating the presence of built structures. | Right side: a pavilion is built on a high rocky platform, and although its form is relatively complete, it is surrounded by trees, forming layers of screening and revelation with the clouds and mist behind.
distinction: Although the pavilion on the right is more eye-catching and marks the scenery at the height, many of the buildings in the painting (especially in the center and lower left) mainly rely on the screening of clouds and mist and trees to construct spatial layers; the overall atmosphere of screening and revelation forming the setting is more dominant.

evidence: Left side: a tall city gate building, with a pavilion on the city wall, the gate open, and figures near the gate. | Lower left: a small bridge connects to the path, with figures on or beside the bridge, their movement directed toward the city gate. | Center and lower right: numerous figures are distributed along the path and open ground, with thatched huts screened in the tree clusters on the right, forming a spatial atmosphere of journeying and gathering.
distinction: Although the city gate is a prominent landmark in the painting, the painting emphasizes more, through the bridge, paths, and the movement of figures, the spatial process of approaching and entering the city gate and the clues for movement through the landscape, so C4 is more apt than C3.

evidence: Lower right corner: part of a house (roof, walls, doors, and windows) is visible, obscured by dense dry tree branches in the foreground, forming a layer of concealment and revelation of seeing houses through a screen. | Center and left side of the painting: a large number of figures gather among trees on sloping ground, distant mountains rendered in pale washes, with built structures existing only as an edge background and not dominating the composition.
distinction: Although the buildings are located on the edge of the sloping ground, the relationship of screening and revelation of parts of the buildings by trees in the painting is more prominent than siting according to the ground.

evidence: Lower right corner: a wooden bridge is visible crossing the waterside or a gully, connecting the two banks and suggesting a traversable clue for movement through the landscape. | Left side and center: willows and figures are active on the sloping bank, while the right side is a large area of unpainted space with an inscription and seal.
distinction: The painting lacks identifiable built elements such as houses, but the bridge in the lower right corner, as a clue for movement through the landscape, suggests spatial connectivity and a process of entry, so C4 is selected.

evidence: Left to center: a building with colonnade and railing is visible, its roof and rear space partly screened by foliage of trees in front of and behind it, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Center to right: the right side of the building connects to a grassy slope along the water, with trees standing between the building and the slope, further enriching the spatial layering between the building and the natural environment.
distinction: Although the building is sited by the waterside slope, the painting emphasizes more the screening and revealing of the building by trees, organizing spatial layers through concealment and revelation, so C2 is more apt than C1.

evidence: Left and center: tall trees stand in front of and around the house, screening part of the building itself and its columns, revealing the roof and the human activity under the eaves, forming a spatial layering of trees in front and house behind. | Center-right: the house roof emerges from dense groves, the lower wall is hidden by trees and grassy slope, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship of seeing the house within the woods. | Right: the side wall of the house is fully visible, but trees extend behind and above it, forming visual screening and connection with the building group on the left through the interpenetration of trees.
distinction: The painting builds its spatial layers mainly through the screening relationship between trees and houses (screening), and although the figure on the right makes a pointing gesture, there is a lack of clearly discernible path or entrance cues to dominate the spatial process of "access to secluded settings."

evidence: Center-right of the painting: a thatched hut is partly screened by surrounding trees and shrubs, with only the roof and part of the wall revealed, presenting a spatial layer hidden within the woods. | Right side of the painting: dense groves screen the building behind, forming an evident concealment-and-revelation relationship.
distinction: Although the house is located on an earthen slope, the painting emphasizes more the relationship of screening and revealing by trees rather than a layout developed in response to terrain.

evidence: Lower left: a bamboo fence and a brushwood gate form an entrance, with a person standing inside the gate, suggesting entry into the interior space from here. | Lower right: a person with a staff crosses a stone bridge; the bridge connects to a path leading into the depth of the painting and upward to the mountain rocks and pavilion. | Upper right: a pavilion is built on the summit, serving as the endpoint of the path's extension or a node for viewing from a height.
distinction: Although there are houses built against the mountain, the painting emphasizes more the guidance of sight and human movement through cues such as the fence gate, small path, and stone bridge, forming an enterable and traversable spatial process.

evidence: Lower right: pavilion and corridor buildings are built against a rocky slope by the bank, presenting a form of setting buildings on a terrace, closely integrated with the terrain. | Center left: houses and densely moored boats are distributed along the waterside slope, presenting a layout unfolding along the bank. | Distant hillside: small buildings are placed high on the slope, following the undulations of the terrain and arranged separately according to the slope.
distinction: The painting mainly shows the placement of buildings in relation to rock, slope, and water; although the ferry boats suggest transportation, the correspondence between built structures and terrain is more dominant.

evidence: Upper center-right: a huge white terrace base is built up in tiers against the cliff, with a double-eaved pavilion above, surrounded by railings, and figures standing on the terrace, presenting a typical layout of setting buildings on a terrace and building in response to the terrain. | Lower right corner: courtyard walls and a gatehouse are arranged along the edge of the mountain foot, the building base unfolding in response to the terrain, forming a vertical spatial echo with the high terrace and pavilion above. | Overall right side: the building complex is distributed vertically along the mountain body, with terrace bases, pavilions, and mountain rocks and clouds tightly interlocking; the height and unfolding of the built structures correspond directly to the natural mountain configuration.
distinction: The core visual focus of the painting is the high terrace and pavilion built up in tiers against the cliff on the right; the correspondence of its base layout with the mountain configuration (C1) is more prominent and dominant than the movement-through-the-landscape path suggested by the gatehouse in the lower right corner (C4).

evidence: Upper left of middle ground: the roof and part of the wall of a house are visible, partly screened by foliage of trees in front and by mountain rocks, presenting a half-hidden, half-revealed state. | Middle ground: the house is hidden behind woods and sloping rocks, and through the screening of natural scenery a spatial layering is formed between the foreground (figures, water buffalo) and the background (built structures).
distinction: Although the house is located on a hillside, the painting emphasizes more its concealment-and-revelation relationship as screened by trees and rocks, rather than a layout placed simply according to terrain.

evidence: Upper center-right: a white-walled building with a circular doorway, its building itself and wall partly screened by pine branches and leaves and mountain rocks in the foreground, with only parts revealed, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Lower center-right: the roof, corridor columns, and interior figures of a waterside open hall (water pavilion) are half-hidden by thick tree trunks and rocks in the foreground, the building faintly appearing among trees and rocks. | Overall right side: the two built structures, upper and lower, present rich foreground-background spatial layers through the layered screening and revealing by trees and rocks; natural scenery deeply participates in creating the architectural mood.
distinction: Although the built structures are placed by water and mountain, the most dominant compositional device in the painting is to show the layering and seclusion of the buildings through screening and revealing by trees and rocks, rather than simply emphasizing their layout in response to terrain.

evidence: Left middle ground: behind the willow trees the columns and roof of a building are revealed, the building partly screened by trees, forming a screening relationship. | Right foreground: willows form a grove, figures gather beneath the trees, boats are moored at the bank, and the trees screen part of the sightline and background.
distinction: The painting mainly presents the layering of buildings screened by trees, rather than emphasizing the path into the buildings.

evidence: Lower left corner: a group of farmhouses is placed close against the left cliff and the base of trees, the house layout unfolding in response to the sloping terrain. | Middle ground to upper right: extensive terraced fields are built in tiers along the hillside terrain, the ridges fully matching the mountain slope, presenting a condition of reclamation following the mountain. | Right side: stone embankments are built at the edges of the terraced fields, meeting the water surface below, the built boundaries following the waterside terrain.
distinction: Although there are field-ridge paths and human activity in the painting, the core of the overall composition lies in how the houses and terraced fields are placed in response to mountain forms and waterside, rather than emphasizing the penetration of a movement path.

evidence: Lower left corner: a pavilion/house is located at the edge of and in gaps within the grove, its roof and part of its columns revealed, partly screened by surrounding foliage, presenting a layering of seeing the house within the woods. | Upper right corner: a pavilion is located behind dense woods, with only the top structure (roof and eaves) revealed, notably screened by trees, forming a spatial relationship of seeing the house across a screen. | Right shoreline: built structures and trees are intermingled along the bank, using the screening and revealing by woodland to indicate the presence of buildings and their level, with concealment and revelation participating in the composition.
distinction: Although the buildings are distributed along the bank, the screening and concealment-and-revelation relationship of trees over buildings (e.g., the upper right pavilion showing only its top) is more prominent and constitutes the main spatial layering, rather than simply emphasizing terrain placement.

evidence: Upper left: a pavilion is built on a flat rock platform jutting from a steep cliff, presenting a form of setting a building on a terrace. | Middle ground: a group of thatched huts is arranged in staggered fashion following the gentle slope of the hillside, in response to the terrain's undulations. | Lower left: thatched huts are arranged by the waterside, adjacent to trees, presenting a layout unfolding along the bank.
distinction: Although the pavilion and pagoda on high ground serve to accentuate the scenery, the multiple built structures in the painting (dwellings, pavilion, pagoda) are all clearly placed according to terrain conditions such as cliff platforms, hillsides, and waterside; C1 better summarizes the overall correspondence between layout and natural configuration.

evidence: Right side: a courtyard wall with a door is visible, and a figure is walking from outside the door into the courtyard, forming a clear entrance cue. | Center to left: inside the courtyard figures water flowers and fetch water, and the ground forms a continuous activity path connecting the courtyard gate on the right with the house on the left. | Left side: the house has open windows and a corridor, with figures active within, showing an enterable interior space.
distinction: Although the built structures are arranged according to terrain, the painting more prominently highlights the spatial process of guiding human activity and sightlines into the courtyard through the gate and paths.

evidence: Center-right of the painting: the roof and eaves of a building emerge from dense pine woods, presenting a state of being half-screened by trees. | Lower center of the painting: a white-walled building is hidden behind the pine woods, with only part of the wall and roof revealed, forming a spatial layer of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although there are paths and figures in the painting, the built structures mainly construct spatial layers through screening and revealing by woodland, rather than emphasizing the route of entry.

evidence: Lower right and middle ground: in the lower right of the painting there is a wooden bridge connecting to a mountain path, and a traveling party is moving through the bridge and plank road toward the deep mountains. | Middle ground to distant view: winding plank roads and mountain paths extend along steep snowy cliffs, linking travelers at different heights and forming a clear travel thread deep into the mountains. | Left middle-distant view: a pagoda is visible in a mountain hollow, and a few buildings appear among the cliffs in the upper right corner, but they are in the distant view or background of the travel route, and the main space is organized by paths.
distinction: Although the buildings (pagoda, houses) in the painting are placed according to the mountain configuration, what dominates the spatial expression of the painting is the travel route formed by the bridge, path, and plank road, guiding the viewer's gaze deep into the secluded valley, rather than simply emphasizing the correspondence between buildings and terrain.

evidence: Center-left of the painting: two thatched huts are hidden in a mountain hollow, with two people standing in front of them; the buildings are half-screened by surrounding mountain rocks and trees. | Right side of the painting and around the buildings: dense pines and bamboo groves screen part of the buildings, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship that gives the buildings a spatial layer of being within the woods and behind the rocks.
distinction: Although the buildings are constructed against the mountain, the painting highlights more their concealment-and-revelation relationship as screened by mountain woods, rather than simply being placed according to terrain.

evidence: Lower right: waterside houses are largely screened by dense weeping willow foliage, with only the roof, part of the wall, and figures under the corridor revealed, forming an evident layer of concealment and revelation. | Lower center: another group of houses is half-hidden behind foreground sloping rocks and groves, the building outlines interwoven with the woodland, increasing the painting's spatial depth.
distinction: Although the buildings are arranged along the waterside, the painting emphasizes more the screening and revealing of the buildings by tree foliage; the feature of forming a realm through screening is more prominent than building in response to terrain.

evidence: Left mountainside: two houses are partly screened by dense trees and mountain rocks, with only the roofs and part of the walls revealed, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Lower right water surface: a bridge spans the water connecting the two banks, suggesting a passage clue across the water body.
distinction: Although a bridge in the painting suggests passage, there is a lack of a clear path connecting the bridge with the screened houses; the feature of houses forming a scene through concealment and revelation by woods and rocks is more prominent.

evidence: Lower right: between withered trees and pine woods, the roofs of two buildings are visible, partly screened by foreground branches and the woodland behind. | Lower right: the buildings are hidden behind trees and rocks, forming a spatial layering of alternating concealment and revelation, presenting the visual effect of seeing houses within the woods.
distinction: Although the buildings are located at the waterside, their concealment-and-revelation relationship as screened and revealed by tree branches and trunks is more prominent in the composition and dominates the spatial expression.

evidence: Right middle ground: a thatched hut built structure is visible, its building itself partly screened by foreground tree branches and trunks and by the rocky slope on the right, with only the roof and part of the wall revealed. | Center-right of the painting: trees and mountain rocks form foreground and middle-ground screens, placing the built structure in a half-hidden, half-revealed state, forming a clear spatial layering and concealment-and-revelation relationship.
