evidence: Center of the painting: a group of pavilion buildings sits on a projecting rocky platform, the building site closely integrated with the form of the mountains and rocks, presenting the form of buildings set on a platform. | Right side of the painting: several houses adjoin the gentle sloping bank and the edge of the woods, distributed in conformity with the terrain.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: a group of buildings (including a two-story pavilion and covered corridors) is partially screened by the large willow trees in the foreground and by the woods and mountains and rocks behind, with only the roofs and part of the walls exposed. | Center-right of the painting: the buildings are situated against mountains and water, screened among dense woodland, forming clear spatial layers and a concealment-and-revelation relationship.
distinction: Although the buildings are situated against mountains and water, the painting places more emphasis on the screening and revealing of the buildings by woodland and mountains and rocks, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship is more prominent.

evidence: Middle ground, left of center: a small building on the cliff face is placed according to the steep mountain terrain. | Right of the middle ground: two pavilions on the mountainside are built against the mountain slope terraces. | Lower middle: a thatched house among the trees sits on the mountain slope, blending with the surrounding terrain.
distinction: Although the stream and stone steps in the lower right of the painting suggest a route of entry, the correspondence between the buildings and the mountain forms and slope terraces is more prominent and widespread, so C1 is closer to the dominant compositional role than C4.

evidence: Lower right: a pavilion building built on a rocky platform is visible, with several figures active inside and on the platform. | Lower right to lower middle: below the built elements are stone steps with railings and a bridge path winding among the mountains and rocks, clearly pointing toward and connecting to the built platform. | Left and distance: pines and distant mountains on the left, together with the built elements and path on the right, form spatial depth and guide the eye to extend toward the built elements.
distinction: Although the built elements are constructed against the mountain rocks, the painting places more emphasis on the spatial process of guiding the viewer into the built elements through path cues such as stone steps and bridges.

evidence: Lower right: a simple plank bridge is visible spanning the waterside, with one person crossing it and another leading an ox under a tree on the bank, constituting a clear cue of a land travel path. | Water surface in the center: a small boat is depicted, suggesting waterborne transport and a relationship of spatial extension. | Overall composition: through the waterside, the plank bridge, the figures' activity, and the boat, the painting organizes a spatial process of travel from one place to another.
distinction: Although the plank bridge is placed at the waterside, the core of the painting lies in the travel route and dynamic spatial process jointly constructed by the figures crossing the bridge, leading the ox, and boating, rather than merely emphasizing the correspondence between buildings and terrain.

evidence: Center and left: a large building complex is built in tiered layers following the mountain terrain, including multi-story pavilions, high platforms, and covered bridges, closely fitting the undulations of the mountains and rocks and the terraces. | Right cliff: buildings cling to the steep cliff, with building sites closely integrated with the form of the mountain mass, presenting the characteristic of buildings set against the cliff. | Overall composition: the layout and staggered heights of the built elements correspond to the natural forms of the surrounding peaks and slope terraces, displaying terrain-responsive spatial relationships.
distinction: Although a screening relationship between trees and buildings exists in the painting, the terrain-responsive relationship in which the building complex follows the mountain and is stacked in tiers is more prominent and dominant.

evidence: Whole painting: the painting depicts a water surface, clumps of reeds, and flocks of water birds swimming and flying; no built elements such as buildings, bridges, or paths are visible.
distinction: No built elements are visible at all in the painting, so its spatial presentation cannot be judged according to the definition; it can only be assigned to the closest category based on the overall visible organization of landscape and water.

evidence: Center to lower right of the painting: a long-bearded figure wearing a bamboo hat and holding a long staff is walking forward along the waterside, presenting the dynamics of travel. | Lower left and background of the painting: water, waterside rocks, and bamboo clumps are in the foreground, with rolling mountain slopes in the background, constituting the natural environment in which the figure walks.
distinction: No explicit built elements are visible in the painting; there is only the travel cue of a figure walking along the waterside, so assigning it to C4 is closer to the visible spatial process than C1, which emphasizes terrain-responsive placement.

evidence: Lower part: a winding dirt road is visible, with figures riding horses and walking on it, forming a clear travel cue that guides the eye to extend deep into the mountains. | Upper middle: at the mountain ridge there is a reddish-brown block-like structure, whose form resembles a pavilion or plank road built against the mountain, but the details are blurred and its coloring is similar to that of the mountains and rocks. | Center: tall pines and clouds and mist screen the direct visual connection between the path below and the suspected built elements above, but spatially a tendency of entering the deep mountains from the foreground is presented.
distinction: The clear travel path and figures' activity in the lower part of the painting constitute the main sense of spatial entry (access to secluded settings), which is more narratively dominant than the placement of the suspected buildings on the mountainside in the upper middle (terrain-responsive).

evidence: Left middle: a pavilion is placed directly on a projecting rocky platform on the cliff, with its building site closely fitting the edge of the terrain. | Lower left corner: a small boat is on the water, echoing spatially with the mountains and rocks and trees on the bank.
distinction: Although the pavilion accentuates the scenery of a corner of the cliff, its placement built against the cliff more directly embodies the built elements' conformity to and use of the terrain conditions.

evidence: Right-center mountainside: the roof and walls of houses are visible, partially screened by the mountains and rocks and trees in front, presenting a layering of seeing houses behind rocks. | Left waterside and below: scattered houses, mostly hidden behind dense trees with white branches, creating the effect of houses concealed in the woods. | Whole painting: buildings and mountains and rocks and trees form clear front-to-back screening relationships; partially exposed eaves and roofs indicate the presence of built elements, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship participates in forming the scenery.
distinction: Although the buildings are situated against mountains and water, the visual dominance of the painting lies in the screening and revealing of buildings by dense trees and mountains and rocks, forming a richly layered screening effect, rather than merely emphasizing the correspondence between building sites and terrain.

evidence: Right-center mountainside: the roof and part of the walls of a building are visible, half screened by the surrounding trees and mountains and rocks, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship. | Overall painting: woodland and mountains and rocks are layered one upon another, wrapping the building within them and forming a deep spatial layering.
distinction: Although the building is set against the mountain, its most striking compositional role is to create spatial layering through screening and revelation by woodland and mountains and rocks, rather than emphasizing terrain-responsive form.

evidence: Lower right corner: several trees and weeds on the bank are visible; no fixed built elements such as houses or pavilions are visible. | Center of the painting: a small boat with two people on the water is a scenic accent, not a built structure. | Upper part: reeds, waterside, and an inscription are visible; no other traces of built elements.
distinction: There are no explicit built elements in the painting; the lone boat serves only as a scenic accent, so the closest category, scenic accentuation, is chosen, but architectural evidence is lacking.

evidence: Background: the background is a landscape painting depicting mountains and rocks, trees, and a waterfall; no explicit built elements are visible. | Foreground: the foreground is a portrait of a figure; the figure sits upright on a chair with a table beside them, which is indoor furnishing, not built elements within a landscape.
distinction: The main subject of the painting is a figure portrait, and no explicit built elements are visible in the background landscape, so its spatial presentation cannot be judged; it is therefore assigned to this category and marked as low confidence.

evidence: Center and lower part of the painting: ancient pines, withered trees, mountains and rocks, a stream, and a tiger are visible; no houses, bridges, or other man-made built elements can be seen. | Upper right: there are an inscription and seals, but these are not treated as evidence of the pictorial space.
distinction: There are no clear man-made built elements in the painting; the tiger and pine trees together form a natural scene, which is only marginally assigned to scenic accentuation.

evidence: Whole painting: the painting is dominated by human activity; figures, trees, mountains and rocks, and tables and furniture are visible, but no clear outlines of houses, pavilions, or other architectural main forms can be seen. | Center and lower part: figures and furniture are scattered according to the gaps and terrain among the mountains, rocks, and trees, presenting a scene of activity that relies on the natural terrain.
distinction: The painting lacks clear architectural entities; only figures and objects distributed among mountains, rocks, and trees are seen, which only marginally corresponds to a terrain-responsive spatial relationship, with no other evident competing interpretation.

evidence: Lower left: the building complex is arranged on the slope at the foot of the mountain, with courtyard walls and a gate tower, unfolding in accordance with the terrain. | Right center: thatched houses are built on a gently sloping platform, and the building base forms a three-dimensional correspondence with the slope. | Upper center, mountainside: pavilions or small buildings cling to the rocks and steep slopes of the mountainside, showing the feature of buildings placed according to the rocks.
distinction: Although the painting contains paths and clues of figures moving through the landscape, the high-and-low staggered arrangement of buildings, sited according to slopes and rocks, is more prominent, and the determining role of terrain in the built layout is dominant.

evidence: Center to upper left of the painting: a winding wooden plank road (path/bridge) is built along the steep cliff face, with a clear structure, clinging to the precipice. | On the plank road and in the lower part of the painting: many figures (riding horses, walking) are advancing on the plank road, and there is also a group in the valley below, showing an evident process of travel and crossing. | Upper left, mountainside: the plank road leads toward a high place, where the outlines of a pass or buildings are faintly visible; the path connects with the built elements, guiding the eye to extend into the depth.
distinction: Although the plank road built along the mountain conforms to terrain-responsive siting, the core of the painting lies in the dynamic process of figures advancing along the plank road and the spatial relationship in which the path guides viewers into the depths, so C4 is more accurate.

evidence: Left and center: towering ink-toned cliffs and gnarled tall trees; the brushwork is coarse and concise, with typical features of finger painting (obvious changes in ink tone; the lines are not drawn with a brush). | Lower left: two figures are depicted, one tall and one short; the tall one holds a staff and appears to be a lofty scholar with an attendant boy, belonging to the scenic figures of landscape painting, with no houses or buildings around them. | Upper right corner: the inscription reads 'Autumn, ninth month of the wuyin year, finger painting by Qieyuan Gao Qipei', indicating that the author is Gao Qipei, confirming it as a finger-painting work in an ink freehand style.
distinction: The main body of the painting is ink freehand landscape (C2), with coarse brushwork, distinct from fine-line or blue-and-green landscape; there are no man-made buildings in the painting, so built_visibility is not_visible.

evidence: Lower right: the building leans against the mountains and rocks on the right, with a base and platform, sited in accordance with the waterside terrain, presenting the form of a building placed on a platform. | Lower right: the building is situated where mountains, rocks, and trees encircle it, with pine branches and leaves covering it above, facing the large waves to the left and above. | Left center: large waves occupy the main body of the painting; the building unfolds along the waterside position, forming an adjacent relationship with the water surface.
distinction: The building leans against mountains and rocks and has a base, conforming to the waterside terrain (C1); although facing the water and the open waves gives it a scenic-accent quality, the relationship between terrain siting and building base is more concretely visible.

evidence: Lower left foreground: a huge pine with luxuriant branches and leaves largely screens the houses below, revealing only part of the eaves, walls, and window lattices, forming a strong relationship of concealment and revelation. | Left middle ground, sloping bank: a group of houses is screened among snow-covered trees and sloping ground; the roofs and structures are faintly visible, in a state of partial screening by woodland. | Overall painting: the built elements (houses) in the painting are mostly behind the screening of trees or mountains and rocks, their existence indicated through partial revelation, emphasizing the spatial layering of 'concealment'.
distinction: Although the houses lean against the waterside slope (C1), what is more visually prominent is the relationship of screening and revelation of the built elements by trees, mountains, and rocks (C2); concealment and revelation forming a setting is the dominant expression.

evidence: Center and lower part of the painting: among screening woodland, a house with a roof, pillars, and railings is visible; the building is partially screened by the tree trunks and branches and leaves in front. | Inside the house: figures inside can be seen through the open doors and windows, further strengthening the spatial layering of the building being half hidden and half revealed among the trees.
distinction: Although the building identifies the woodland scene, the painting places more emphasis on the relationship of screening and revelation of the building by the trees, and the role of concealment and revelation forming a setting is more prominent.

evidence: Center-lower to center: a figure riding a donkey can be seen winding along a mountain path, the path guiding the eye to extend into the depth of the painting. | Upper right: pavilion buildings are faintly visible among the mountain rocks, echoing spatially with the mountain path. | Whole painting: mountains and rocks, trees, and paths interweave, presenting spatial layers that can be traversed and entered deeply.
distinction: The painting mainly guides the eye into depth through figures traveling and mountain paths, emphasizing the spatial process of moving from here to there, rather than merely using a building to identify a certain scene.

evidence: Left center-lower: a bridge or plank road spanning a gorge is visible, connecting the mountain rocks on both sides and forming a clear passage clue. | Overall painting: towering peaks and deep gorges are spatially connected through the bridge, suggesting a path leading from here into the depths.
distinction: The bridge mainly serves as a passage clue guiding spatial entry, rather than as an architectural main body simply sited according to terrain.

evidence: Lower right: two houses are located beside dense trees; the canopy and branches and leaves screen part of the roofs and walls, forming a relationship of seeing houses in the woods through concealment and revelation. | Middle ground: a building is faintly visible in the mist, half screened by the surrounding trees and cloud vapor, presenting a layering of seeing a house through an intervening screen.
distinction: The painting mainly expresses the layers of concealment and revelation formed by buildings borrowing trees and cloud vapor, rather than emphasizing the siting relationship of buildings according to terrain slopes and banks.

evidence: Lower foreground: A thatched pavilion (or thatched cottage) is depicted at the bottom of the painting, with a clear structure, surrounded by pine trees and withered trees; there appear to be figures inside the pavilion, embodying the integration of humans and nature. | Middle ground: The water surface is broad and calm, with a sandbar extending into it; the trees on the sandbar are sparse, creating a sense of deep space. | Upper distance: The main peak rises high, the mountain rocks are rendered with fine texture strokes (cunfa), there are moss dots on the summit, and the mountain forms are steep, occupying the upper half of the painting and establishing the dominant position of the landscape.
distinction: The painting takes a grand landscape scene as its main subject; the architecture (the thatched pavilion) serves only as a scenic accent element in service of a theme of reclusion. It is not a ruled-line painting (j iehua) centered on finely depicting architectural structure, nor is it a figure painting centered on human activity.

evidence: Whole painting: the painting depicts willow trees, watersides, reeds, and multiple flocks of flying birds (geese, ducks, herons); no houses, bridges, or other man-made built elements can be seen. | Center and lower part: birds gather on the sandbar by the water, together with the trees forming a natural scene, lacking built elements as scenic markers.
distinction: There are no built elements in the painting; the birds and trees are naturally distributed and do not form a relationship in which a building identifies the scene; because there are no buildings, assignment to C3 is only the closest description of a natural scene.

evidence: Lower right water surface: a small boat and people on the boat are visible, but this is a means of transport, not a fixed built element. | Lower left and middle ground: mainly trees, sloping banks, and a broad water surface; no traces of houses, bridges, or other buildings can be seen. | Background: towering mountains and vegetation, with no signs of built elements constructed against the mountains.
distinction: There are no clear built elements in the painting; only a small boat dots the water surface, and based on the overall landscape composition it is marginally assigned to scenic accentuation, but it lacks architectural entities.

evidence: Whole painting: the painting presents only calligraphic text; no landscape scenery or built elements can be seen.
distinction: There is no visible relationship between built elements and landscape; this is only a forced classification.

evidence: Right middle ground: at the foot of the distant mountains and on the shoreline there is a row of abbreviated vertical strokes, suspected to be extremely small fences, a bridge, or a shed; the forms are blurry, and their role is to mark the middle-ground position. | Left page and lower right: mainly sloping banks, withered trees, miscellaneous trees, and a figure sitting alone by the water; no other clear built elements can be seen.
distinction: The suspected structures are arranged along the waterside, but because they are extremely abbreviated, they serve more as a visual marker point in the middle ground than as a display of layout relationships sited according to terrain.

evidence: Center-left: a white enclosing wall has an arched doorway (moon gate); steps can be seen inside the gate, connecting the exterior with the inner courtyard, and figures gather beside the gate, presenting a spatial clue for entering the courtyard. | Lower foreground: an open waterside pavilion/terrace with red railings, where figures are active, serves as a near-ground foothold for the visiting space. | Distant waterside: pavilions and buildings are distributed on the mountain slopes and by the water, forming a spatial extension with the middle-ground courtyard through the water surface and shoreline, suggesting deeper travel through the landscape.
distinction: Although trees screen the buildings, the core of the painting lies in the transformation between inner and outer space constructed by the walled arched gate and the entry path, rather than a simple relationship of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Center and lower part of the painting: a thatched pavilion is partially screened by withered trees and bamboo in the foreground and by trees on the right; only the roof and part of the pillars are revealed, forming a spatial layering of alternating concealment and revelation. | Center of the painting: trees are interspersed between the pavilion and the mountains and rocks behind, further enhancing the screening effect of the built element hidden among the woodland.
distinction: Although the pavilion is built on flat ground, the painting places more emphasis on the relationship of screening and revelation of the pavilion by trees, rather than the corresponding siting of the building with the terrain.

evidence: Overall painting: only pale mountain peaks, a dark rock cliff on the right, and a slanting pine tree can be seen; no traces of buildings, bridges, paths, or other built elements are visible. | Right rock cliff and central pine tree: the pine grows from the rock cliff, its trunk and branches extending toward the lower left, forming a front-to-back layering with the mountain peaks behind, but there are no signs of houses concealed or revealed.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built elements and is only marginally assigned based on the overall organization of natural landscape, with no direct competing interpretation.

evidence: Right and center of the painting: mountains and rocks, trees, and cloud vapor are seen encircling; three figures are located within the cloud vapor, and above them are images of a divine beast and a lotus pedestal; no clear traces of houses, bridges, roads, or other built elements can be seen.
distinction: The painting is mainly a combination of religious figures with landscape and cloud vapor, with no clear built elements; based on the position of the visual focus and the surrounding landscape relationships, it is marginally assigned to C3.

evidence: Center: a white gibbon clings to a horizontally extending tree branch, occupying the visual center of the painting. | Below: ink-toned mountains, rocks, and sloping ground are painted, forming a base support. | Above and left: branches and leaves hang down, forming a spatial echo with the central white gibbon.
distinction: No clear built elements can be seen in the painting; based on the role of the white gibbon as a visual focus that concentrates the scene, it is assigned to scenic accentuation.

evidence: Center of the painting: the main subject of the painting is a wild beast, with a blank background; no mountains and rocks, water bodies, trees, or other natural scenery can be seen, nor any traces of buildings, bridges, roads, or other built elements.
distinction: The painting completely lacks a spatial relationship between landscape and built elements; according to the rules, the closest category is forcibly selected.

evidence: Center and left of the painting: multiple pine trees are densely arranged, their roots growing among slope rocks and weeds; no buildings or man-made structures can be seen. | Right and upper part of the painting: the unpainted area contains an inscription and seals, with no spatial depth or clues of built elements.
distinction: No built elements are visible in the painting, and it cannot be clearly matched to any category; it is only marginally assigned based on the overall natural scenery.

evidence: Middle-distant view: a slender pagoda-like building is faintly visible, standing amid hazy trees and mist. | Overall painting: large areas of unpainted space and light color washes render a sense of openness of the waterside or river surface, and the distant pagoda becomes a visual foothold.
distinction: In the distant view the pagoda mainly serves to identify the scene, rather than emphasizing the nearby layers of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Center and lower part of the painting: a long corridor and pavilion houses are partially screened by the trees and bamboo grove in the foreground; the roofs and corridor pillars are faintly visible among the branches and leaves. | Left and center of the painting: tall trees and bamboo groves surround the buildings, forming a spatial layering of alternating concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the buildings lean against mountains and face water, the painting more prominently highlights the screening and revelation of the buildings by woodland, and the feature of concealment and revelation forming a setting is more prominent.

evidence: Left side and central mountain body of the painting: multiple groups of buildings are distributed in staggered heights according to the mountain body; on the left cliff there are pavilions that project outward or are built against the cliff, and on the central mountainside there are groups of halls, sited in accordance with the rise and fall of the mountain forms. | Upper center, mountain summit: a pagoda-like building is constructed at the high point of the summit, occupying the commanding height of the peak and closely integrated with the mountain form. | Lower right corner, waterside: houses are built by the waterside, unfolding according to the waterside terrain, and together with the buildings on the mountainside and summit above they form a layout advancing layer by layer with the mountain forms.
distinction: Although there is local screening of the buildings by woodland in the painting, the terrain-responsive relationship in which buildings are arranged in staggered heights according to the mountain body, slopes, and platforms is more prominent and is the main way of organizing the overall space.

evidence: Whole painting: the painting mainly consists of lotus leaves, lotus flowers, water birds, and an inscription; no traces of buildings, bridges, roads, or other built elements can be seen.
distinction: There are no built elements in the painting, and it cannot be judged how they participate in composing the scene; according to the rules it is assigned to scenic accentuation as the closest category, but it lacks clear evidence.

evidence: Whole painting: the main subject of the painting is a large area of weeping willows, whose branches hang down and cover the waterside; several water birds swim on the water surface or rest on the sloping bank. | Right side: withered trees or wooden stakes can be seen standing among slope rocks, flowers, and grasses; no clear houses, bridges, or other man-made built elements are visible.
distinction: The painting is mainly a natural scene formed by willow trees and water birds, with no clear built elements; the willow trees identify the waterside environment, so it is assigned to C3; if the screening layers of the weeping willows were emphasized it would approach C2, but because of the lack of evidence of built elements neither is exact.

evidence: Center-left of the painting: a figure stands on a slightly raised platform or stone surface; behind and to the side of the figure there are red railings, placed along the edge of the terrain, forming the form of railings set on a platform. | Left and right of the painting: a large tree on the left and a lake rock on the right flank and set off the placement position of the central built element (the railings and the platform where the figure stands), showing that it unfolds relying on the base of natural scenery.
distinction: Although the trees and rocks have a flanking effect on the central space, the red railings are clearly set along the edge of the slope/platform on which the figure stands; the feature of terrain-responsive placement is more direct and dominant than a simple relationship of concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower right: a group of pavilion buildings is visible, partly screened by the foreground pine branches and mountains and rocks, presenting a state of being half hidden and half revealed. | Left center, mountainside: building outlines are faintly visible among the mountains and rocks and trees, screened among the rock gullies and trees. | Overall: the built elements, through the screening and revelation of mountains and rocks and woodland, form evident spatial layers and a relationship of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the built elements in the painting are sited according to the mountain forms, their role in forming spatial layers by being screened by woodland, mountains, and rocks is more prominent.

evidence: Middle right of the painting: the roof and eaves of a two-story pavilion (or pagoda) emerge from dense pine woodland and mountains and rocks, with most of the building's main mass screened by trees. | Slightly right of center of the painting: the built structure is placed deep within the woodland; through the screening of foreground trees and background mountain rocks, a clear spatial layering and a relationship of concealment and revelation are formed.
distinction: Although two figures at the bottom of the painting appear to be walking, suggesting a path, they do not form a clear travel thread leading to the built structure; the most prominent compositional role of the built structure in the painting is its concealment-and-revelation relationship as screened by trees, mountains, and rocks.

evidence: Lower left: among the waterside trees there are extremely faint brushstrokes, suspected to be tiny built structures or a fence, but the details are blurred and cannot be clearly identified. | Whole painting: the painting is dominated by mountains, trees, and waterside, with no obvious clear buildings, paths, or bridges.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built structures; there is only an extremely faint suspected trace in the lower-left corner, so it is assigned to scenic accentuation as the closest weakly related category.

evidence: Whole painting: only a single standing figure is painted at the center of the painting, surrounded by inscriptions and seals; no mountains and rocks, water bodies, trees, or any traces of built structures are seen.
distinction: There are no built structures or landscape elements in the painting, so no actual spatial relationship can be distinguished; it is forcibly classified according to the rules.

evidence: Lower right side: the roofs and walls of several houses are revealed through the dense tree trunks and branches and leaves on the right, forming a layering of houses hidden within the woodland. | Right side: tall trees serve as foreground, screening part of the built structures and placing the buildings in spatial depth behind the trees.
distinction: Although a bridge and figures in the lower-left corner of the painting suggest a path, the screening and revealing relationship of the right-side trees to the houses is more prominent and dominates the spatial presentation of the built structures.

evidence: Left-middle slope: several houses are arranged in a staggered manner according to the mountain slope and terraces, and the building sites are closely integrated with the mountain terrain. | Lower right pine roots: the houses are placed close to the mountain rocks and slope, unfolding in response to the local terrain.
distinction: Although trees screen the buildings at the lower right to some extent, forming a degree of concealment and revelation, the most prominent feature of the built structures in the whole painting is their siting in response to the mountains and terrain, rather than primarily forming a scene through concealment and revelation.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: a figure can be seen sitting before a small table beside rocks under a pine; the small table is simple furniture, and no houses, pavilions, or other built structures are seen. | Overall composition: the painting is dominated by pine trees, mountains and rocks, a stream, and figures, and lacks clear architectural entities participating in the spatial organization.
distinction: There are no clear built structures in the painting; the figure and the small table serve as the visual focus that points out the scene of resting under the pines, and can barely be regarded as a scenic accent, but there is no architectural evidence.

evidence: Right-middle of the painting: a group of buildings is hidden behind trees and slope rocks, with only the roof and part of the walls exposed, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation. | From the lower middle to the right side of the painting: a path winds among the mountains and rocks, and a person is walking along the path toward the buildings on the right.
distinction: Although a path in the painting leads a viewer toward the buildings, the main way the buildings are presented in the composition is half-screened by trees, mountains, and rocks, and the feature of forming a scene through concealment and revelation is more prominent.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: a house building can be seen, with two people sitting facing each other inside; the roof and part of the wall body are exposed. | Around the built structure: the house is surrounded by dense withered trees and bamboo groves, and the trees form an obvious screening and revealing relationship with the building, presenting layering.
distinction: Although the built structure is near the waterside, the painting emphasizes more the screening and revealing of the building by trees, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship is the dominant spatial presentation.

evidence: Left mountainside and valley: multiple groups of houses are placed in a staggered manner according to the mountain slopes and terraces, unfolding in response to the height of the terrain. | Center and right mountain foothills of the painting: the building complex is arranged along the valley slope foot and shoreline, interlocking with the mountain contours and trees. | Lower-middle waterside: some built structures are adjacent to the waterside and stream, presenting an arrangement that unfolds along the bank.
distinction: Although there is screening by trees, the painting emphasizes more the systematic staggered placement of the building complex according to terrain, terraces, and the waterside, and concealment and revelation are not the dominant compositional mode.

evidence: Lower center-left of the painting: there is a small house/pavilion, surrounded by trees and rocks. | Upper middle of the painting: there are towering mountain peaks; the mountains are steep and wreathed in clouds and mist. | Right side of the painting: there are tall trees with luxuriant branches and leaves.
distinction: The main category C1 (landscape) accurately describes the painting's content, and there is no obvious competing interpretation.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: water surface, mountains and rocks, trees, and several figures can be seen; no houses, bridges, pavilions, or other built structures are seen | Upper right corner: there are inscriptions and seals, but they do not constitute evidence of built space within the painting
distinction: Although the figures in the painting are active at the waterside and convey a certain sense of travel, because clear built structures are lacking, the whole leans more toward a resonance between figure accents and the landscape scenery.

evidence: Center of the painting: two towering cliffs face each other, forming a narrow valley mouth or waterway between them, constituting a spatial opening extending into the depths. | In the waterway between the two cliffs: a small canopied boat carrying people passes through, presenting a travel thread of entering from outside to inside and crossing the gorge. | Bottom of the painting: water grass or reeds are painted, suggesting the presence of a waterside and helping to explain the waterway's extension beyond the painting or into the depths.
distinction: Although the small boat identifies the location of the valley mouth (C3), its core role is to guide the gaze to follow the boat into the secluded depths between the two mountains, emphasizing an enterable and traversable spatial process (C4).

evidence: Right middle ground: a red-roofed building emerges from the pine woodland, with the building itself and its columns partially screened by trees, forming an obvious layering of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the building points out the scenery within the woodland, its concealment-and-revelation relationship of being half-screened by the pine woodland is the most striking spatial feature of the painting.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: the roofs, walls, doors, and windows of several houses are revealed from dense tree clusters (including red-leaf trees, bamboo groves, etc.), forming an obvious relationship of concealment and revelation. | Slightly right of center of the painting: a two-story building is half-hidden behind tall trees and bamboo groves, with only part of the roof and upper structure exposed, embodying the screening and revealing effect of trees on the built structures.
distinction: Although the houses are placed in reliance on the terrain, the most prominent spatial organization in the painting is the layer-upon-layer screening of the houses by trees, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship is more significant than siting according to terrain.

evidence: Right side: a steep cliff wall occupies the right half of the painting, with clear brushwork and no buildings attached. | Left side and center: distant mountains, waterside, and unpainted space rendered in pale ink constitute an open water surface space, with no traces of built structures seen.
distinction: No built elements are seen in the painting, and the specific relationship between built structures and landscape cannot be determined; it is only barely assigned based on the overall landscape composition.

evidence: Upper right: a small sailboat can be seen traveling on the water surface, and is the only man-made object in the painting. | Lower middle and lower right: distant mountains, sloping banks, and trees can be seen; no clear houses, bridges, or other built structures are seen.
distinction: There are no clear built structures in the painting; the sailboat, as a scenic accent element, condenses the scenery of the open water surface, so C3 is chosen.

evidence: Upper right: a black squirrel crouches atop a towering red rock | Lower right: the base of the rock outlined in ink supports the red rock above | Left side: a long passage of calligraphic inscription; there are no traces of built structures such as buildings, bridges, or paths in the painting
distinction: There are no built structures in the painting; the squirrel is located at the top of the rock as the visual focus, and its compositional position is closest to scenic accentuation.

evidence: Upper middle of the painting: a white-walled, blue-roofed house sits on a flat terrace at the top of a steep cliff, surrounded by trees. | From the center to the right side of the painting: mountain rocks and slopes form a high platform, and the house's building site is placed in response to the height of the mountain terrain, presenting the form of setting a house on a platform.
distinction: The house clearly relies on the cliff terrace for its placement, and the supporting and responsive relationship of the terrain to the building site (setting a house on a platform) is more significant than its mere role as a visual marker.

evidence: Right middle ground: an arched bridge can be seen spanning between mountains and rocks, accompanied by withered trees beside the bridge, forming a spatial thread connecting the two banks. | Left side and center: large areas of unpainted space and mountain and rock outlines sketched in pale ink; no clear houses or pavilion buildings are seen.
distinction: No clear architectural accents are seen in the painting, but the bridge, as a travel thread, connects the space and better fits the feature of access to secluded settings.

evidence: Right middle: an arched bridge can be seen spanning the terrain, with a figure on the bridge, forming a clear passage thread. | Left middle and lower left: several houses are screened among trees and slope rocks, with paths or waterside extending. | Foreground: horizontal sloping banks or water surface textures guide the gaze to extend into the depths of the painting.
distinction: Although there is a layering of houses screened by trees, the passage thread formed by the bridge and figures more clearly organizes an enterable spatial process.

evidence: Center to right side of the painting: huge mountain rocks occupy the main body of the painting, with prominent forms, condensing the visual center of the painting. | Left side: pine trees grow attached to the mountain rocks, together with the rocks forming the main scenery of the foreground. | Lower left corner: there are extremely tiny traces, suspected to be figures or tiny built structures, but they cannot be reliably identified.
distinction: No clearly identifiable built structures are seen in the painting, so based on the overall landscape composition, the main mountain rocks are taken as the core condensing the scenery and it is assigned to C3.

evidence: Left mountainside: a figure's outline can be seen among the mountains and rocks, suggesting travel activity. | Center to right side: towering mountains and rocks and trees constitute the main space, and the mountain forms extend upward, forming a visual guide. | Overall composition: the forms of the mountains and rocks and the figure's position suggest a spatial process from bottom to top and from outside to inside.
distinction: No clear built structures are seen in the painting, but the direction of the mountain forms and the figure's position suggest a spatial process of travel and going deeper, so it is assigned to C4.

evidence: From slightly right of center to the upper right of the painting: a winding path or ramp connects the built areas at the lower right and upper right, forming an obvious travel thread. | Lower right of the painting: houses are arranged in a staggered manner according to the mountain terrain and trees, and the path passes beside the houses, suggesting an enterable spatial relationship. | Lower left of the painting: figures are active on the path, further strengthening the path's function of passage and travel.
distinction: Although the upper-right houses have the feature of being screened within the woodland, the path connecting the two built areas and its role in guiding travel are more prominent in the painting, so C4 is more apt than C2.

evidence: Left side: towering mountain peaks occupy the left half of the painting; the mountain body is steep, dotted with vegetation. | Lower right and bottom: a gorge is formed between the right sloping bank and the left mountain peak, and a winding water flow passes through the bottom, guiding the gaze to extend into the depths of the painting.
distinction: No built structures are visible in the painting; only the gorge space formed by the water flow and mountains and rocks has a tendency to extend into the depths, so it is barely assigned to C4.

evidence: Lower right corner: among the trees below the cliff, the roofs of two buildings can be seen, partially screened by branches and mountain rocks, presenting a state of being half-hidden and half-revealed. | Middle ground: the water surface is open, with two sailboats, forming a near-far layering with the screened buildings in the lower right corner.
distinction: Although the buildings are located at the mountain foot, the painting mainly presents their layering of concealment and revelation through the screening of trees and mountain rocks, rather than emphasizing their layout unfolding according to terrain.

evidence: Lower foreground waterside of the painting: multiple groups of buildings are placed beside the waterside and slopes, and the house sites unfold in response to the undulations of the terrain. | Lower-middle woodland terraces of the painting: buildings are scattered among the trees and terraces, with the layout staggered according to the height of the terrain, presenting a posture of setting houses on platforms and arranging them along the bank.
distinction: Although the buildings are screened by trees, their layout feature of relying on slopes and adjoining water and being placed in response to the terrain is more prominent, dominating the spatial relationship between built structures and nature.

evidence: Whole image: the image shows a book cover, whose main body is a brocade geometric pattern, with a title slip on the left; no landscape terrain or built elements are seen.
distinction: The image is not landscape painting content and has no spatial relationship between built structures and landscape; it is forcibly classified.

evidence: Left side and lower left: thatched huts or pavilion structures can be seen screened by dense trees, with relatively freehand brushwork | Center and center-right: beside tall trees (resembling pines and cypresses) there are house structures, with darker ink, integrated with the surrounding mountains, rocks, and trees | Lower right and right background: distant mountain outlines sketched in pale ink; in the near lower right there are thatched hut structures and an inscription and seals
distinction: The main subject of the painting is landscape scenery, including trees, thatched huts, and distant mountains, constituting a typical landscape fan painting, distinct from bird-and-flower or figure themes.

evidence: Left middle: between the woodland and mountains and rocks, the roof and structure of a building are faintly revealed, presenting a half-screened, half-revealed state. | Center-left of the painting: dense trees and slope rocks screen the building, constructing the painting's spatial layering through a relationship of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the building is within the mountain woodland, the painting emphasizes more the screening and revealing of the building by trees to form layering, rather than highlighting its layout relationship of being placed according to terrain.

evidence: Slightly left of center: a thatched-roof building is half-screened between the bamboo grove behind and the plum trees in front, with only the roof, eaves, and part of the wooden framework exposed, presenting a layering of a house hidden within the woodland. | Right side: a tiled-roof building is hidden behind huge mountain rocks and plum trees, with part of the walls and roof screened by the rocks, forming a spatial relationship of viewing a house through an intervening layer.
distinction: Although a bridge and path in the painting suggest a travel thread, the half-hidden, half-revealed relationship between the built structures and the surrounding mountains, rocks, and trees is more prominent in the composition and dominates the expression of spatial layering.

evidence: Lower left of the painting, on the bank at the foot of the mountain: a group of buildings is arranged against the mountain foot and among trees; parts of the building bodies are screened by foreground trees, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation. | Right side of the painting, in the pine grove: houses are screened among dense pines, with only parts of the roofs and walls exposed, forming a spatial layering in which houses are seen within the grove.
distinction: Although the buildings are also sited in reliance on the terrain, the pronounced screening-and-exposure relationship between woodland and buildings in the painting (concealment and revelation forming scenery) is more prominent in the composition and dominates the spatial expression.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting, on both banks of the river and the mountain hollow on the right: tiny houses can be seen sited against the waterside and the mountain foot, conforming to the undulations of the terrain and presenting a layout that unfolds along the bank and is distributed separately according to slope. | Middle of the painting, in the valley: built elements are scattered among mountains, rocks, and trees, and the choice of building sites corresponds to the opening and closing of the natural terrain and to its slopes and terraces.
distinction: Although a river in the painting forms a depth-leading guide, there is a lack of clearly discernible entering clues such as bridges or paths; the built elements mainly manifest as a dwelling relationship sited according to terrain, rather than emphasizing a process of travel from one place to another.

evidence: Middle of the painting: a group of thatch-roofed buildings is built facing the water; dense vertical-line structures (appearing to be wooden pile supports or column bases) are visible at the bottom, showing that they are sited against the waterside slope and presenting a layout that unfolds along the bank. | Around the buildings: rocks and trees are beside the buildings, and the building sites correspond closely to the waterside terrain; they are not placed in isolation.
distinction: Although the buildings serve a scenic-accent role in the painting, their form—piles set by the water and construction against the slope—more concretely embodies the constraint and accommodation of the natural terrain (the waterside) on the placement of built elements, so C1 is more apt than C3.

evidence: Whole painting: the painting depicts several mountain peaks with ink washes, with lines of cloud and mist interwoven among them; no traces of built elements such as houses, bridges, or paths are seen. | Lower left: a long inscription and seals are visible, but they do not belong to the built elements in the painting.
distinction: There are no visible built elements in the painting; based on the overall concealment-and-revelation relationship of the mountains, water, and clouds, it is assigned only with difficulty to C2, and there is no other competing interpretation.

evidence: Right side, mountainside: the building group is arranged in staggered fashion according to the mountain's configuration; some buildings are screened by rocks and trees, presenting a half-hidden, half-exposed layering. | Lower left corner: houses are screened behind dense trees, with only parts of the roofs and walls exposed, creating a sense of seeing houses deep within the grove. | Lower middle, waterside: pavilions and water-side structures are surrounded by trees, and buildings and natural scenery interpenetrate; the relationship of concealment and revelation is clear.
distinction: Although the built elements are also sited against mountains and beside water, the painting more strongly emphasizes constructing spatial layers through the screening and exposure of rocks and trees, and the role of concealment and revelation in forming scenery is more dominant.

evidence: Left-center of the painted panel: Behind the trees on the sloping bank, the outline and roof structure of a built structure (a house or pavilion) are visible, presenting a spatial layering screened by trees and alternating between concealment and revelation. | Lower-right part of the painted panel: A figure walks along the waterside, facing toward the built structure on the left, but the main built structure is mostly hidden behind the trees and is not fully open.
distinction: Although a walking figure suggests a hint of movement through the landscape, the built structure in the painting is mainly presented as a layered screening by trees (concealment and revelation), rather than as a sense of entry directly connected by a clear path.

evidence: Whole painting: the main subject of the painting is layered, rounded mountain ridges covered with moss dots, with sloping banks and trees below; no clear traces of built elements such as houses, paths, or bridges are seen. | Upper part: there is a long inscription, but it does not serve as spatial evidence within the painting.
distinction: The painting consists purely of mountains, water, trees, and rocks, with no visible built elements; it is assigned to the closest category based on the overall mountain configuration and terrain.

evidence: Lower left: within the screening of trees, the roofs and walls of several houses are exposed, presenting spatial layering that alternates concealment and exposure. | Middle of the painting, mountain hollow: building outlines are faintly visible in the gaps between rocks and trees, using natural scenery as screening to create pictorial depth.
distinction: The painting is dominated by the screening and exposure of buildings by woodland, mountains, and rocks, and does not present clear movement-through-the-landscape clues such as bridges or paths that guide entry.

evidence: Right middle: houses are hidden behind trees, with roofs and eaves exposed, forming layers of concealment and exposure.
distinction: The buildings mainly rely on woodland screening to present layers of concealment and exposure, and the sense of entry via paths is relatively weak.

evidence: Lower right: a simple small bridge can be seen spanning the water flow at the edge of the sloping bank, connecting the foreground sloping bank with the grove on the right and forming a crossable, enterable spatial clue. | Center to background: behind the nearby sloping bank and trees, clouds and mist swirl and distant mountains faintly appear; the small bridge suggests a visual extension of traveling from here into the depths.
distinction: The small bridge mainly serves as a clue connecting and guiding movement through the landscape, rather than merely pointing out some fixed scenery at a place, so C4 is more apt than C3.

evidence: Beside the rocks on the right: several horizontal and vertical ink lines can be seen, whose forms resemble roof and wall structures; they are screened by foreground rocks, presenting a layering of seeing houses behind the rocks | Water surface at the bottom of the painting: a small boat and figures are depicted, with reeds in the foreground; the water surface is open, and no clear path or ferry-crossing structure connecting to the built elements on shore is seen
distinction: The painting mainly presents a concealment-and-revelation relationship in which suspected built elements are screened by rocks, rather than emphasizing a layout correspondence of adapting to the mountain and following its configuration.

evidence: Right middle: a pavilion building is erected against the mountain, partly screened by pines and rocks, presenting a half-exposed state. | Lower right corner: several groups of houses are surrounded and partly screened by foreground trees and rocks, forming spatial layers of concealment and exposure. | Lower left corner: houses are screened behind withered trees and rocks, with only roofs and parts of walls exposed.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited according to the mountain's configuration, the painting more strongly emphasizes the screening and exposure of buildings by woodland and rocks, and the concealment-and-revelation relationship is the dominant mode of composing the scene.

evidence: Right side: on the right side of the painting a large plant (such as a cabbage) and weeds at the bottom are depicted, with no traces of buildings or man-made built elements | Left side: the left side of the painting consists of calligraphic inscription and seals, with no depiction of landscape or built space
distinction: No built elements are seen in the painting; it is assigned to the closest category according to the rules in the absence of obvious spatial organization.

evidence: Lower right and foreground: sloping banks, withered trees, bamboo clumps, and rocks can be seen; there are no traces of built elements such as houses, bridges, or paths | Middle and distant views: clouds and water are diffuse, distant mountains faintly visible, presenting an open natural landscape space
distinction: The painting consists purely of natural landscape organization, with no man-made built elements seen; therefore assignment to scenic accentuation is only a formal closest-category classification, and in reality there is no object of scenic accentuation.

evidence: Right side: a thatched hut is built on a terrace formed by a cliff, with its roof and structure clearly visible, presenting a layout of establishing a house on a terrace. | Right side and center: the thatched hut is surrounded by bamboo and rocks, and the building site conforms to the platform terrain of the mountain body on the right.
distinction: Although the thatched hut serves to point out a mountain dwelling, its terrain-responsive placement on an obvious terrace is more concrete and dominant.

evidence: Right side, cliff: a group of buildings is arranged level by level according to the contours and platforms of the mountain rock; the roofs are staggered in height and distributed in conformity with the mountain's configuration. | Lower left corner, sloping bank: roofs are visible among trees and sloping rocks, arranged against the terrain of the sloping bank.
distinction: The buildings mainly present a layout relationship of being arranged level by level according to the terrain of the cliff, and screening, concealment, and exposure are secondary effects.

evidence: Lower half: the lower half of the painting consists of continuous mountains and rocks covered with moss dots; no traces of built elements such as houses, pavilions, bridges, or paths are seen. | Upper half: the upper half of the painting consists of calligraphic inscription and seals, with no landscape or built content.
distinction: No clear built elements are seen in the painting; only the forms of mountains and rocks are presented, and it is assigned to the closest category based on the overall visible space.

evidence: Lower left: a small bridge can be seen at the waterside, connecting the land with the water's edge and forming a movement-through-the-landscape clue that crosses the waterside. | Right side: sloping rocks and trees grow densely, contrasting with the open water surface on the left; the small bridge is located at the land-water junction, suggesting an enterable spatial relationship.
distinction: Although the small bridge is tiny and serves a scenic-accent role, its core function lies in connecting the waterside and providing a crossable and enterable path clue, so C4 is more apt than C3.

evidence: Left side: beside the cliff there is a row of clear stone steps (or a plank road) winding upward, guiding the gaze to extend into the depth of the painting. | Lower left to upper left: the stone steps advance level by level along the mountain's configuration, forming a spatial clue that is enterable and travelable.
distinction: The stone steps mainly serve as a movement-through-the-landscape clue guiding the gaze into the depths, emphasizing a spatial process rather than a building subject merely sited according to the terrain.

evidence: Lower left to lower middle of the painting: the building group is located on flat ground at the foot of a high mountain waterfall; the building sites conform to the mountain terrain, and platforms, enclosing walls, and courtyards are visible, presenting a layout of establishing houses on terraces. | Upper right, mountainside: building roofs can be seen hidden among rocks and trees, sited according to the undulations of the mountain's configuration and corresponding to the terrain.
distinction: Although the buildings are surrounded by trees forming screening (C2), the main body of the buildings below is clear and mainly presents a layout sited according to the terrain at the mountain foot (C1); the terrain's participation in the building sites is more dominant.

evidence: Lower right: partly screened by clouds and mist and by clusters of trees, the outline of a building roof with flying eaves and ridge ornaments is faintly visible. | Overall painting: the two main peaks are surrounded by vast clouds and mist, and the buildings are deeply hidden among the mountain forests and cloud vapor, presenting a relationship of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the buildings are located in an open area at the foot of the mountain, their scale is extremely small and they are largely obscured by clouds, mist, and trees; the layered effect of concealment and revelation is more pronounced than their role in identifying the scenery.

evidence: On the water surface at the bottom of the painting: a small boat can be seen floating on the water, surrounded by mountains, rocks, and trees; no fixed houses, pavilions, or other built elements are seen. | Lower right of the painting: trees and sloping rocks are on the bank, forming an open space with the water surface, with no traces of buildings.
distinction: There are no clear built elements in the painting, only a small boat as a scenic accent; therefore, based on the overall landscape composition, the closest category of scenic accentuation is selected.

evidence: Center-left of the painting: a group of houses is surrounded and screened by dense trees (red leaves and green trees) and rocks, with only roofs and parts of walls exposed, presenting spatial layering of houses hidden within the grove. | Left side of the painting: a thatched hut is sited against sloping rocks, screened by trees beside it, forming a concealment-and-revelation relationship with the surrounding natural scenery.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited according to the sloping terrain, the painting more strongly emphasizes the concealment-and-revelation relationship in which buildings are screened and exposed by rocks and trees (as indicated by the inscription "tree pavilion"), and the role of concealment and revelation in forming scenery is more dominant.

evidence: Lower right, water surface: a small boat and the silhouettes of people on it can be seen floating on the water, suggesting a clue of movement on the water. | Left side: rocks and reed clusters form the waterside boundary, contrasting with the open water surface and providing a spatial background for boating.
distinction: The only visible man-made object in the painting is the small boat on the water, which presents a sense of entry through movement on the water, rather than a combination of buildings and terrain or a screening relationship.

evidence: Right side, water surface: a small boat and an angler on the boat can be seen, existing on the water surface as a scenic-accent element. | Center and lower right of the painting: mainly depicts bank trees, reeds, and sloping banks; no clear buildings, bridges, or other architectural built elements are seen.
distinction: The painting lacks clear man-made architectural built elements and uses only a small boat as a scenic accent, so it is assigned to C3 and marked as not_visible.

evidence: Left side of the painting: foreground sloping banks and trees can be seen, with water surface and distant mountains in the middle ground and swirling clouds and mist; no clear houses, bridges, or other built elements are seen. | Right side of the painting: calligraphic inscription and seals, not serving as spatial evidence within the painting.
distinction: No clear built elements are seen in the painting; it is assigned to C1 based on the overall landscape configuration, but lacks evidence of built elements.

evidence: Right side of the painting: a blooming pink peony is depicted, serving as the visual subject of the painting | Left side and lower part of the painting: blue-green branches and leaves extend toward the upper left, and the left side is covered with calligraphic inscription and seals
distinction: The painting is a flower subject, with no clear built elements seen; based on the layout feature of the flower as the visual focus, it is assigned only with difficulty to the scenic-accent category, and no other spatial relationship of built elements can be discerned.

evidence: Whole painting: the painting mainly consists of lotus leaves, orchid grass, bamboo branches, and other plants; no built elements such as buildings, bridges, or paths are seen. | Right side and center: large lotus leaves and interwoven branches and leaves form layers of foreground-background screening, occupying the main body of the painting.
distinction: There are no built elements in the painting; it is assigned to the closest category based on the overall spatial organization of plant screening.

evidence: Left side: large rocks, sloping banks, and water ripples can be seen, with no traces of buildings | Right side: sloping rocks, withered trees, and bamboo clumps can be seen, with no traces of buildings | Center: calligraphic inscription, with no clues of built elements seen
distinction: There are completely no visible built elements in the painting, only natural landscape elements are presented; it is assigned only with difficulty to C1 based on the overall spatial organization.

evidence: Lower right and left-middle water surface: painted boats/vessels are depicted on the water surface at the lower right corner of the foreground and on the left side of the middle ground, suggesting boating activity on the water. | Middle-upper distant view: a small bridge is faintly visible spanning among the distant trees, which together with the boats on the water suggests the connectivity and extension of paths. | Overall composition: the unpainted water surface serves as the main spatial clue, linking the nearby boats, the middle-ground trees, and the distant bridge to form a spatial process from near to deep that is travelable and enterable.
distinction: Although the boats and bridge serve to embellish the scenery (C3), they are distributed along the water surface from near to far in the painting and more strongly organize a travel route that extends the gaze into the depths, conforming to the spatial-process characteristics of access to secluded settings.

evidence: Middle ground left: a group of houses is arranged along a curved shoreline, presenting a layout that unfolds following the bank, with the building base corresponding closely to the water's edge. | Lower left corner: a figure is visible standing on the bank or a bridge, with a few building components beside them, suggesting the integration of human dwelling activity with the terrain.
distinction: Although figures and a path in the lower left corner hint at movement through the landscape, the most prominent feature of the main building group in the painting (the houses in the middle ground) is their arrangement conforming to the waterside terrain, so C1 describes the dominant spatial relationship between buildings and landscape more accurately than C4.

evidence: Right side of the painting: sloping rocks, trees, bamboo clumps, and a small winding path extending forward are visible, but no clear built elements such as houses or bridges are seen.
distinction: The painting contains only natural scenery and a path, lacking built elements; it is assigned to C4 based on the sense of the path's extension, but there is no clear connection to entering built structures.

evidence: Right side: multiple columns of running-script calligraphic inscription are visible | Lower left and lower center: several red seals are visible
distinction: The painting has no landscape or built elements, only calligraphy and seals; no actual spatial relationship can be discerned.

evidence: Top: a pagoda or pavilion is built on the highest peak, occupying the highest point of the mountain mass, placed at the summit following the mountain's form. | Middle: a group of houses is built on cliffs and platforms at the mountainside, distributed in staggered fashion following the slopes and terraces. | Lower part: houses also stand among the woods and slopes below, arranged following the undulations of the terrain.
distinction: Although some buildings are screened by trees, the overall layout in which buildings are staggered according to the mountain's heights and placed on terraces following the slopes is more prominent, dominantly manifesting terrain-responsive siting.

evidence: Middle left: several houses stand at the foot of snow-covered slopes, arranged near the shoreline, with the layout unfolding in conformity with the slope and waterside conditions. | Lower right: a waterside pavilion is built on a rocky high platform at the water's edge, its base facing the water, presenting a placement relationship of setting a house on a terrace and dwelling by the water.
distinction: Although the buildings are clearly visible in the painting, their layout is evidently placed according to the slopes, terraces, and shoreline, embodying the dominant relationship of siting according to the ground rather than serving merely as visual focal points marking the landscape.

evidence: Middle left: a thatched hut is visible deep in a bamboo grove, with one person sitting upright inside. | Lower right: a stone arch bridge spans the water, with one person walking on it carrying something. | Foreground: a winding path extends from beside the bridge, passes through the bamboo grove, and leads to the thatched hut deep within.
distinction: Although the thatched hut is concealed within the bamboo grove in a partly screened state, the painting constructs clear cues of entry and movement through the bridge, the figure, and the winding path, making the spatial process of access to a secluded setting dominant.

evidence: Lower left: a stone arch bridge spans a stream, connecting the left side with the interior of the painting, constituting a clear entry cue and spatial transition. | Lower center: houses are partly screened among trees, located in the spatial extension behind the bridge, suggesting a dwelling space reachable via the path. | Lower right: a pavilion is built facing the shoreline, with a seated figure inside and an extending shoreline beside it, forming a stopping point in the journey and, together with the bridge, constructing a touring sequence from here to there.
distinction: Although the buildings by the water and against the trees show terrain-responsive placement (C1), the painting constructs a more evident touring path and spatial entry process through the bridge, shoreline, and building sequence (bridge–houses–pavilion), so C4 is more dominant.

evidence: Central mountain ridge of the painting: a group of buildings is distributed in stepped, staggered fashion following the mountain's form, their roof outlines conforming to the undulations of the mountain mass. | Left side of the painting: a waterfall descends from above, and the buildings are placed on mountainside terraces beside the waterfall, closely integrated with the terrain. | Lower part of the painting: trees and a shoreline stand at the mountain foot, with buildings located above them at a turning point of the mountain form, presenting a posture of setting houses according to the slope.
distinction: Although the buildings accentuate the mountainside scenery, their layout unfolding with the undulations of the terrain more prominently embodies the characteristics of terrain-responsive siting.

evidence: Lower center: a winding wooden bridge/plank walkway is visible spanning the water, connecting the two banks and providing a clear entry path. | Middle ground and right side of the painting: several small boats are scattered on the water, suggesting that one may reach or travel among the waterways by boat. | Middle-ground water inlet and right bank: houses are built against the water and beside trees, together with the bridge and boats forming a spatial network that can be toured and dwelt in.
distinction: Although trees partly screen the houses, the touring cues formed by the bridge and boats in the painting are more prominent, dominating the sense of spatial entry and movement through the landscape.

evidence: Lower left to center: a clear mountain path winds upward from the lower left corner following the mountain's form, with travelers on the path, leading directly to the gate building in the middle of the painting. | Center: on the water between two mountains stands a pass building with an archway, serving as an extension of the path and a passage into the depths of the water inlet. | Middle right bank: behind the pass, village houses and moored boats are distributed along the shoreline following the mountain's form, presenting a settlement space entered after passing through the pass.
distinction: Although the buildings follow the mountains and face the water, the painting strongly guides the viewer's gaze and touring route into the depths of the painting through the winding mountain path at the lower left and the opening of the pass; the organizing role of the movement cues is more prominent.

evidence: Lower middle of the painting: building roofs and eaves emerge from dense woods, presenting a layering of houses hidden in the forest. | Left side of the painting and among the rocks: the main bodies of the buildings are obscured by rocks and trees, only partially visible, creating an effect of seeing houses through a screening layer. | Overall composition: the buildings are deeply hidden behind natural scenery, and the relationship of concealment and revelation constitutes the main spatial layering.
distinction: Although the buildings are placed on rocky high platforms following the mountains, visually they are mainly obscured by trees; concealment and revelation forming a setting is more prominent than siting according to the ground.

evidence: Upper middle of the right bank: roofs and walls of buildings are visible among trees and rocks, presenting a partly screened relationship of concealment and revelation. | Lower center of the painting: a sailboat is on the river, its bow facing the right bank, forming a clear direction of travel. | Right bank shoreline: the shoreline and ripples guide the gaze from the boat on the river toward the buildings on the bank, constituting an enterable spatial connection.
distinction: Although the buildings on the right bank have a relationship of concealment and revelation screened by trees, the touring cues formed jointly by the boat and the shoreline more prominently express the spatial process of approaching the buildings.

evidence: Middle of the painting, slightly right: house roofs and a pagoda emerge from dense woods, with the main bodies of the buildings obscured by trees, presenting a spatial layering of seeing houses in the forest. | Middle waterside of the painting: the building group is located behind the shoreline, partly obscured by foreground trees and mist, forming a relationship of concealment and revelation by seeing houses through a screening layer.
distinction: Although the buildings are distributed along the shoreline, the visual organization of the painting relies mainly on the screening and revealing of the buildings by trees (partly screened), rather than emphasizing terrain-guided siting of the building layout.

evidence: Lower right of the painting: a thatched hut stands behind woods, its roof and walls emerging through gaps between tree trunks, partly obscured by trees. | Lower half of the painting: many trees stand in the foreground, partly screening the buildings behind them, forming a layering of concealment and revelation in which houses are seen within the forest.
distinction: The buildings exist mainly through being screened and revealed by trees, emphasizing a relationship of concealment and revelation rather than being markedly placed following the undulations of the terrain.
