evidence: Lower left: a wooden bridge crosses the water, and a person on the bridge is walking toward the opposite bank. | Middle left: a thatched pavilion sits among the sloping rocks and trees, forming a spatial echo with the bridge. | Left side: the bridge, the walking figure, and the thatched pavilion together form an excursion route leading from the water toward the built structures in the depth.
distinction: Although the thatched pavilion is partly screened, the painting clearly constructs an excursion process toward the built structures through the bridge and the walking figure, and C4 better summarizes this spatial organization.

evidence: Whole painting: the image presents distant mountains, near banks, water surface, and various trees (such as willows and miscellaneous trees), with no clear traces of built structures such as houses, pavilions, bridges, or paths visible.
distinction: No clear built structures are visible in the painting, so its specific mode of spatial expression cannot be judged; it is assigned only on the basis of the overall landscape composition.

evidence: Lower left: at the edge of the waterside a bridge (or plank walkway) is visible crossing over, connecting the water surface with the land on the bank, forming a clear line of passage. | Middle left: behind the bridge there are pavilion buildings on the bank, which together with the bridge form an accessible and stoppable spatial node. | Middle and right of the painting: houses screened by trees are visible on the mountainside and deep in the woods, suggesting layered space that can be traversed in depth along the waterside or mountain paths.
distinction: The connection of the bridge and buildings forms a clear line of excursion and entry, which better embodies the processual nature of space than mere siting following the mountains and water.

evidence: Middle-right of the painting: a house is half-hidden behind a grove, with only the roof, eaves, and part of the wall exposed, forming a clear relationship of screening and revealing. | Middle-left of the painting: another building appears faintly among the trees, partly obscured by trunks and branches.
distinction: Although the buildings are sited following the mountains and trees, the painting places greater emphasis on the half-screening of the buildings by trees; the effect of concealment and revelation in forming scenery is greater than mere siting according to the land.

evidence: Middle-lower right side: house buildings are visible, with roofs, walls, and fences, located between the foot of the mountain and the woods. | In front of the buildings: trees (including one with red leaves) obscure part of the buildings, forming foreground-background spatial depth. | Around the buildings: the buildings are surrounded and screened by the trees in front and the mountains, rocks, and woods behind, presenting a concealment-and-revelation relationship of seeing houses through a screen.
distinction: Although the buildings serve to accent the mountain dwelling, the concealment-and-revelation relationship in which they are half-screened by trees and rocks is more prominent, constituting the main spatial depth.

evidence: Lower right: several houses are partly screened among trees, with only roofs and part of the wall structure exposed. | Lower center: tree trunks and branches interlace to form the foreground, obscuring some built elements and the mountains and rocks behind, creating a relation of concealment and revelation.
distinction: Although the built elements nestle against the mountains and beside the water, the painting places greater emphasis on the sense of spatial layering produced by trees screening and revealing the houses.

evidence: Right-center of the painting: a two-storey built structure is partly obscured by foreground tree trunks and branches and by the mountains and rocks behind, with only the roof, the upper-storey wall body and the lower-storey supports exposed, forming a clear layering of concealment and revelation. | Lower center of the painting: the foliage and trunks of foreground trees interweave in front of the built structure, placing the building amid screening woodland and indicating its spatial depth.
distinction: Although the building nestles against the mountains and beside the water, the painting places greater emphasis on its layered relation of being screened and revealed by trees and rocks, rather than on mere placement within the terrain.

evidence: Left middle ground: a group of houses and built structures is distributed on the flat waterside ground, surrounded by trees. | Lower left to center left: an arched bridge on the water connects the foreground with the built area on the opposite bank, forming a clear route across the water. | Left side overall: the bridge and the winding shoreline together guide the eye toward the village, presenting a spatial process of passing from here to there and approaching the built elements.
distinction: Although the built elements are arranged along the waterside, the clearly depicted bridge connection in the painting places greater emphasis on the spatial guiding process of crossing the water to enter the built area.

evidence: Left side: a large rock stands at the waterside, striking in form, with a long passage of inscription beside it | Right side: withered trees and bamboo clumps grow beside the rocks, their branches and leaves interlacing to form the main subject of the painting
distinction: The painting is primarily a subject of trees and rocks; no explicit man-made built elements are visible, and trees and rocks form the main subject and visual focus, so it is assigned to C3 as the closest category

evidence: Lower left corner: a thatched pavilion/grass hut is visible, its site placed in accordance with the slope and rocks, presenting the form of a dwelling set on a slope. | Lower center of the painting: the texture of the slope and rocks meets the base of the thatched pavilion, showing that the built structure adheres to the natural terrain.
distinction: Although the thatched pavilion has some vegetation adjacent to it, its main compositional role is shown in its placement in accordance with the slope and rock terrain; its layers of screening are less pronounced than the feature of terrain-responsive placement.

evidence: Lower center of the painting: one person rides a small boat, the boat slender, its bow facing right, presenting the dynamics of movement through the landscape. | Right side of the painting: pale ink outlines mountains and rocks, sloping banks and trees, suggesting the direction or destination of the boat's travel.
distinction: The painting has no fixed built elements; the boat, as a clue to movement through the landscape, suggests the process of entering and journeying through space, which is closer to the painting's dynamics than scenic accentuation.

evidence: Lower center of the painting: two people are visible standing on a sloping bank, facing the open water and distant mountains; no houses, bridges or other built elements are visible. | Right side: trees stand on the nearby sloping bank; distant mountains are on the left, and the center is left as unpainted space representing open water or flat ground.
distinction: There are no explicit built elements in the painting; the figures standing on the bank mark the scene of gazing into the distance, and it is tentatively assigned to scenic accentuation.

evidence: Lower left: a staircase with railings is visible, with two figures walking up along it toward the entrance of the pavilion. | Center and left: the pavilion platform is supported by wooden posts standing on the lotus leaves on the water, with figures seated around on the platform, presenting a spatial process from below to above and from outside to inside.
distinction: The staircase and the figures' lines of movement in the painting clearly construct the spatial connection of entering and reaching the built structure, and the dominant expression is access to secluded settings.

evidence: Whole painting: only pines, miscellaneous trees, mountains and rocks, apes and flying birds are visible; no traces of man-made built elements such as pavilions, houses, bridges or paths can be seen.
distinction: Because the painting entirely lacks man-made built elements, an accurate classification cannot be made on the basis of the actual relationship between architecture and landscape; the closest placeholder category is assigned solely on the basis of the overall natural scenery.

evidence: Lower right: a red bridge or plank-walkway railing is visible extending along the foot of the waterside slope, forming a clear clue to movement through the landscape and a suggestion of an entrance. | Lower left: roofs and structures of houses are visible between the trees and slope rocks, on the same near-ground spatial level as the path/bridge on the right, suggesting reachable built structures.
distinction: Although the houses on the left are screened by trees (consistent with the C2 feature), the red bridge/plank walkway at the lower right forms a strong guiding clue for movement through the landscape, giving the space a momentum of passing from here to there, so C4 better explains its role in spatial organization.

evidence: Lower center of the painting: a simple wooden bridge is visible spanning a stream, connecting the foreground with the mountains, rocks and trees behind, forming a clear clue to crossing and entering. | Lower left side of the painting: built elements (houses) are hidden behind pines and rocks, and through the guidance of the bridge and path, a spatial process of passing from here to there and going deep into a secluded place is presented.
distinction: Although the built elements have a relation of concealment and revelation screened by trees and rocks (C2), the accessible line of movement formed by the bridge and stream path in the painting is more prominent and dominates the spatial organization of journeying and entering.

evidence: Left side: behind trees and mist, the roof and eaves of a pavilion-style building are revealed, presenting a state of being screened by woodland and appearing indistinctly. | Left edge: small houses stand at the waterside, likewise surrounded and screened by the trees around them and the pervading mist. | Center-left: the land on the water is covered with trees, and a small bridge connects the two banks, but the ends of the bridge are mainly vegetation, with no built elements directly adjoining.
distinction: Although there is a small bridge in the painting as a clue to movement through the landscape, the bridge mainly connects vegetation-covered land and does not directly link to the main group of built structures on the left; the built elements are expressed more as forming scenery screened by woodland and mist.

evidence: Center of the painting: a river runs through the painting, with boats carrying people, forming a clue to movement through the landscape on the water. | Both banks: sloping banks, mountains and rocks and bamboo groves surround the water, forming an accessible natural space.
distinction: No explicit buildings are visible in the painting; the spatial process of traveling and entering is presented mainly through the boats on the water and the shoreline, so C4 is chosen; if regarded as a potential dwelling situation arranged by the water, it would approach C1.

evidence: Upper right and central distant view: the roofs and eave corners of multiple pavilions are revealed from golden clouds, their building bodies obscured by cloud and mist, forming a clear layering of concealment and revelation. | Both sides and foreground of the painting: luxuriant tree foliage and branches screen the nearby courtyard railings and the distant edges of buildings, reinforcing pictorial depth and the relation of screening.
distinction: Although the distant buildings are visually striking, their main compositional mode is to create a layering of an immortal realm through screening and revelation by cloud and mist and trees, rather than simply serving as a landmark marking a certain landscape.

evidence: Left center: a thatched hut/pavilion is visible, its building body and roof partly obscured by the slope rocks and trees in front, presenting a half-hidden, half-revealed state. | Lower center of the painting: several withered trees grow on the slope rocks, forming a front-back layering with the building on the left and reinforcing the spatial relation of screening.

evidence: Lower left-center: multiple groups of courtyards and pavilions are arranged in staggered tiers along the mountain slopes and terraces, their sites closely conforming to the undulations of the terrain. | Right lower-center waterside: water pavilions and platforms are built directly facing the water, unfolding along the shoreline. | Mid-slope in the upper center of the painting: small pavilions are placed against the mountains and rocks and woodland, presenting a layout suited to the terrain.
distinction: Although some buildings serve a scenic accentuation role, overall the terrain conditions such as mountains, rocks and waterside more pervasively and dominantly govern the placement of building sites and layouts.

evidence: Central mountain summit: a small pagoda (or pavilion) stands on the highest peak of the snowy mountains, becoming the visual focus and landmark of the whole painting. | Lower left and mid-slope on the right: groups of houses are distributed, interspersed with withered trees and rocks, setting off the main peak.
distinction: The role of the summit building as a visual focus and landmark can better summarize the painting's core compositional intent than the screening or mountain-dependent arrangement of local buildings.

evidence: Center of the painting: two figures wearing bamboo hats are visible standing and talking, one holding a staff and one carrying a basket | Right side and lower left: the outlines of mountains and rocks and sloping banks and several clumps of vegetation are visible, with the figures in a sloping-ground setting
distinction: The painting has no explicit built elements; it is assigned to C1 on the basis of the relation between the figures and the sloping terrain

evidence: Lower center: a wooden bridge spans a stream, and carts, horses and a traveling party are crossing the bridge, forming a clear clue to crossing and entering. | Lower center to right side: the path extends along the waterside toward the gaps between the woodland and rocks on the right, presenting a spatial process in which one may continue to journey and turn into the depths. | Left cliff: pavilions are built halfway up the mountain, with plank walkways connected to the travel route below, further indicating the accessibility of the space.
distinction: Although there are pavilions built against the mountain on the left, the core spatial organization of the painting is the process of entering and journeying formed by the bridge, path and traveling party, so C4 is more dominant than C1.

evidence: Near-ground center: a water pavilion is built directly on a waterside platform base, its site closely conforming to the water surface and rocks, presenting a layout unfolding along the bank. | Right middle ground: a group of buildings is arranged along the mountain foot and trees, the walls meeting the rocks and conforming to the undulations of the terrain. | Left middle-distant view: faintly visible houses and pavilions are scattered among the woodland and sloping banks, presenting a situation of buildings set on terraces and distributed according to slopes.

evidence: Upper left mid-slope: a group of buildings is built in tiered layers against the cliff, roofs staggered and conforming to the height of the mountain. | Lower center of the painting: multiple pavilions and towers are distributed along the mountain foot and rocks, their sites corresponding to the terrain, presenting a layout distributed according to slopes. | Beside the waterside rocks on the right: buildings are erected against the rocks, combining with the forms of the surrounding mountains and rocks and showing a relation of placement according to the ground.

evidence: Center-left: a group of buildings is surrounded by several trees; roofs and walls are partly exposed and partly obscured by trunks and foliage, forming a spatial layering of alternating concealment and revelation. | Lower right: a wooden bridge spans the water, connecting the paths on both banks, with figures active on or near the bridge, suggesting a clue to movement through the landscape.

evidence: Left side: pavilions and towers are built facing the water, with clear platform bases and corridors, their layout unfolding in accordance with the waterside and terrain. | Center: a two-storey pavilion with a courtyard wall is built on the hillside, placed according to the undulations of the mountain, surrounded by trees, showing the feature of buildings set on slopes. | Right side: a small bridge at the waterside connects the two banks, with figures walking, further indicating the continuity of the terrain and the connectivity of space, with built elements closely integrated with the terrain.
distinction: Although there are paths and bridges in the painting guiding the eye and the movement of figures, the main compositional role of the built elements lies in how they are placed and laid out according to site conditions such as mountain forms, slope terraces and the waterside, forming an overall settlement and landscape, rather than simply emphasizing the process of entering.

evidence: Lower right: a small bridge spans a stream connecting the slope rocks on both banks, providing a clear clue to land-based movement through the landscape. | Right-center water surface: boats are moored on the water, suggesting that the water route and ford are accessible, further indicating the paths for entering the painting. | Lower left: buildings are erected against the waterside and willow trees, together with the bridge, boats and shoreline in the foreground forming an approachable, explorable spatial relation.
distinction: Although the buildings being placed by the water is consistent with C1, the combined water-and-land clues to movement through the landscape formed by the bridge, boats and shoreline in the painting are more prominent, emphasizing the spatial process of passing from here to there and approaching the built elements, so C4 is more apt.

evidence: Center-left: a group of buildings is placed in tiers according to the mountain slopes and terraces, supported below by stone-built foundations and extending out into a bridge spanning the water, presenting a layout of buildings set on terraces and unfolding along the bank. | Right side: water-pavilion-type buildings are built facing the water along the bank, their sites closely conforming to the foot of the mountain slope on the right and the shoreline. | Center-rear: high pavilions are hidden deep in the mountain valley, placed according to the heights of the mountain, forming a corresponding relation with the surrounding mountain forms.
distinction: Although trees and mountain masses provide some screening of the buildings, the painting more prominently highlights the close correspondence and terrain-responsive placement of building sites and layouts with site conditions such as mountain forms and the waterside.

evidence: Right middle ground: a section of red railing (bridge or covered corridor) is visible, spanning between plants and rocks, suggesting a path of journeying and spatial connection.
distinction: Although the railing is set according to the terrain, its role as a path clue guiding entry into the space is more prominent, so it is assigned to C4.

evidence: Lower center: a figure riding a donkey is visible traveling along the mountain slope and rocky bank, presenting a state of movement through the landscape | Left side and background: the painting consists of towering snowy mountains, twisted pines and undulating sloping banks; no houses, bridges or other explicit built elements are visible
distinction: The painting has no explicit built elements; there is only a figure journeying among the mountains and waters, so on the basis of the overall spatial organization it is assigned to access to secluded settings as the closest category.

evidence: Upper right: a pavilion is built at the mountainside, placed in reliance on the mountain's configuration and the trees. | Middle left: a small structure is built on a protruding cliff platform, showing the characteristic of setting a building on a platform. | Lower left: a group of houses at the waterside is arranged in reliance on the woodland and the sloping bank, extending along the shore.
distinction: Although the pavilion at the upper right has the effect of being screened by trees, the multiple built elements in the painting (the cliff platform, the waterside village houses) more prominently embody terrain-responsive siting in relation to the topographic conditions.

evidence: Left mountainside: a group of buildings can be seen stacked layer upon layer in reliance on the mountain's configuration, their sites and layout conforming to the slope and undulation of the mountain body. | Lower part and lower left of the painting: buildings are scattered at the waterside and the mountain foot, forming a relationship of placement according to the terrain with the surrounding mountains and rocks, trees, and water surface.
distinction: Although the buildings are partly screened by trees, their overall placement in reliance on the mountain and following its configuration, rising layer upon layer, is the most prominent spatial organization feature in the painting, rather than relying solely on screening to form a scene.

evidence: Upper-right mountainside: the pavilion is placed in reliance on the terrain of the mountain rocks, its site corresponding to the form of the mountains and rocks. | Middle-ground waterside: houses are built facing the water, extending in conformity with the shoreline. | Lower-left corner: houses are placed in reliance on sloping rocks and tree sites, following the undulation of the terrain.
distinction: The built elements in the painting are mainly placed according to site conditions such as mountain forms and the waterside, presenting a relationship of terrain-based placement; although a screening relationship exists, it is not dominant.

evidence: Lower-right water surface: a small boat carrying people can be seen, suggesting a clue of movement by water, but there are no fixed built elements. | Whole painting: the painting consists mainly of mountain peaks, withered trees, rocks, and water surface; no clear built elements such as houses or bridges are seen.
distinction: The painting lacks clear built elements; on the strength of the movement clue of the small boat alone it is assigned to the closest category, access to secluded settings.

evidence: Middle- and distant-view mountainside: a group of buildings and a pagoda can be seen, situated where the mountain configuration turns and clouds and mist swirl, becoming a visual focus and identifying the scenery of the mountainside. | Lower-right corner waterside: at the waterside there are trees, a platform, and a boat, with figures active among them, suggesting the space and accessibility of the waterside. | Overall composition: the towering mountain body and the clouds and mist form opening and closing; the pagoda and temple at the mountainside are located on the open face, condensing the form of the mountain configuration.
